headline: Dubai Parks and Resorts reopens with new attractions and live shows
summary: Dubai Parks and Resorts has reopened after more than six months of closure, with new attractions at Riverland, live shows at Motiongate Dubai and the return of dinosaur-themed glamping.The destination welcomed visitors back on October 7 to Motiongate Dubai, Real Madrid World, Legoland Dubai Resort and The World of Riverland.Fernando Eiroa, chief executive of operator Dubai Holding Entertainment, said preparations for each season begin with visitors.“Every year at the end of the season, we sit and we talk to our customers. We ask them how can we improve,” he told The National.Their feedback helps shape decisions about attractions, live entertainment and dining, he said.New attractions at RiverlandRiverland, the destination’s dining and entertainment district, now offers 14 attractions. New additions include bowling and Lamborghini racing simulators, where visitors can test their driving skills on virtual tracks.These joint activities include go-karting, archery, axe-throwing and mini golf. Motiongate Dubai is also introducing new shows alongside its Hollywood-inspired rides and attractions.At Real Madrid World, visitors can test their football skills, take penalties, play basketball and compete against friends and other guests.“You have to be part of the experience. You have to sweat a little bit to enjoy the experience,” Eiroa said.Dinosaur-themed stays returnT-Rex Glamping, which opened last year, is also returning for the new season.The campsite combines themed tents with animatronic dinosaurs, whose moving tails, lifelike eyes and calls form part of the prehistoric setting.Eiroa said its appeal lay in making the stay itself part of the entertainment, with activities extending beyond a day at the parks.The company is also updating concerts, restaurants and cultural offerings at Global Village ahead of its new season.Dubai's growing appeal as an entertainment destinationEiroa said Dubai’s reputation for theme parks and entertainment had grown over the past five or six years, adding to its established appeal through hotels, restaurants and hospitality.He compared its development with Orlando and Los Angeles, where several theme parks and attractions operate alongside one another. The expansion of attractions in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, he said, was giving international visitors more reasons to travel to the UAE.“We are competitors in a way, but at the same time this is helping the country,” he said.UAE residents also remain an important part of the business, although the balance between domestic and international visitors varies across the group’s destinations.“People don’t come to Dubai to go to a cinema,” Eiroa said, explaining why Roxy Cinemas primarily attracts residents.The View at The Palm draws more international tourists and residents who bring visiting friends and relatives.Through its Truly Amazing campaign, Dubai Holding Entertainment is bringing together attractions including Global Village, Dubai Parks and Resorts, The Green Planet, Roxy Cinemas and The View at The Palm. Eiroa said the company was looking to bundle different experiences, allowing visitors to combine more of its destinations in one trip.

headline: Senne Lammens: Manchester United must learn quickly and cut out defensive errors
summary: Manchester United’s failure to beat bottom-of-the-table Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford on Saturday means the club have made their worst league start since 1986. United have only six points from their first six games and face a daunting run of fixtures, starting with Tuesday’s Champions League tie at Atletico Madrid.Goalkeeper Senne Lammens spoke to media, including The National, after Saturday’s 1-1 draw, which saw United lead through Bryan Mbeumo's 73rd minute strike only to see Dominic Solanke equalise in stoppage time.Q: Can you put your finger on what went wrong? Going ahead was encouraging, but to concede at the end was disappointing.A: It's very disappointing because you find a way to get the game, to get the advantage, to score a goal, to get 1-0 up against 10 men. That's the position you want to be in. So, it's very disappointing to concede the last goal at the end. We need to learn a lot from it, because these are the games you have to try to pull towards yourself. Winning these games is very important if you want to have a good season, so it's very important for us to learn from this and move on, to get these games behind us.What have you made of the team's start this season, with six points from six games? Obviously, it's not the start you would have wanted, especially after the success of last season.I think points say one thing, which is very important, because we are a team who wants to play at the top of the league. But it's not the only thing. In terms of our play, we do some things well, but I think defensively, we can be a bit better, a bit more solid. Today was better because, in the first half, it was a bit more difficult, but you survive, you keep it at zero, and then you are able to pull those games towards yourself.So, yeah, it's like you said. It's a bit like that feeling last season, where maybe we didn't have our A-game, but we were still able to pull those games out and win them. This time, the feeling is that you play better, but you don't really get the wins you deserve. So, it's a bit of a mix of both. You want to play well and also be able to win the games where maybe you don't have your A-game.3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? pic.twitter.com/DuSpvymZfu— OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) October 10, 2026Can I just bring it back to the equaliser? From your perspective, what happened there? It seemed to be another sort of miscommunication between you and Lisandro Martinez.I haven't watched it back yet, but I don't think there was really a miscommunication. First of all, I think the cross needs to be stopped. We need to put more pressure on the guy with the ball because his cross is too easy. Then I think it's a bit of a struggle, a bit of push and pull between the attacker and Licha (Martinez). And, yeah, I think he got away with it. But I don't think there was a miscommunication, no.What did you make of the overall performance today? Tottenham were very dominant in the first 25 or 30 minutes.I think in the first half, everyone could see that we needed to be better with the ball and without it. They had a very good, technically sound plan to try to press us, which was difficult to play out of. Then, at half-time, you could see we made some tactical changes, and a couple of players came on who helped us out as well. Then you could see that we pulled the game towards us, and you had the feeling you were in control of it.Next time, we need to try to start the game like that straight away. Especially here, we need to be able to press their team and control the game.Carlos Baleba impressed on his @manutd debut 🇨🇲 pic.twitter.com/rv7RMAqutd— Premier League (@premierleague) October 10, 2026Can you speak a bit about those players coming in, like Carlos Baleba?It's very important. One of the good things about today was that they came on and helped us out a lot - everyone could see it. We needed that extra spark towards the end, those fresh legs. I'm very happy for them as well that they could show themselves, but that's what we've been seeing in training every day, so for us, it's nothing new. We know we have a very deep squad. Those players are going to have to step up this season as well, and I'm happy they were able to do that today.Can I ask about your reflections on the defence so far this season? It feels like there have been a few occasions when there have been errors or miscommunications. I'm wondering how you see it from your position and what conversations you've had.I agree. I think sometimes, in the end, it comes down to a mistake here or there from someone, but it doesn't really start with that. I think it's a team thing. The manager has been hammering home the message about defending as a team and being able to put pressure on the opposition, especially when it comes to crosses.I think today was better, but then you see that, in the end, one good cross and one good header can cost you the game, or the win can slip away like that. So I understand what you're saying, but I think we've been trying to make a difference there, and I think it's already been better. It's a pity that today, especially at the end, the win slipped away from us.United have to settle for a point.— Manchester United (@ManUtd) October 10, 2026Looking at the schedule, it's not great. You've got three really tough away games coming up. You said it felt like a loss in a way. How do you stay positive?I mean, you can look at it both ways. We know there are a lot of games coming up very quickly. After a disappointment, you can carry that disappointment with you, or you can move on quickly and focus on the fact that there's another game coming up soon.For me personally, if I haven't had the best game, I'm looking forward to the next one to get that sour feeling out of my mouth. So I think that's the mindset we need to have. We know we showed a lot of good things today as well, so we need to take those positives and learn from the bad things.As you say, there are a lot of very important games coming up, but we also love playing those games. We fought last year to be in the Champions League, so we're very happy to be there. And if you want to go far in that competition, you have to win those games as well.

body_text:
Eight Arab regions have selected the films that will represent them in the Best International Feature Film category at the 2027 Academy Awards.

Iraq, Morocco, Palestine, Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan and Saudi Arabia have selected the films that will represent them. Their subjects range from the legacy of Algeria’s civil conflict and Lebanon’s financial crisis to the battle against ISIS in Iraq, the treatment of Moroccan seasonal workers in Spain and daily life during the war in Gaza.

The Academy’s September 30 submission deadline has now passed, with the films entering the next stage of consideration.

Khalid Abdalla: ‘I have gained far more than I have lost’ by backing Palestine

The 15-film shortlist will be announced on December 15, followed by the five final nominees on January 21. The 99th Academy Awards will take place in Los Angeles on March 14, 2027.

This year, Tunisia reached the final five with Kaouther Ben Hania’s The Voice of Hind Rajab, after a record four Arab films made the 15-film shortlist. Alongside The Voice of Hind Rajab, the shortlisted films for 2026 were Iraq’s The President’s Cake, Palestine’s Palestine 36 and Jordan’s All That’s Left of You. Ben Hania’s film ultimately became the only one of the four to reach the final nominations.

Here are the Arab films to know for 2027.

Lebanon has selected Rami Kodeih’s Furies, a heist thriller inspired by the country’s banking crisis.

The film follows sisters Maro and Dalia, who plan to break into a bank to recover their savings because they are unable to access the money, partly to pay for Dalia’s life-saving surgery.

Kodeih and his wife and co-writer, Nora Mariana, told The National that the premise grew out of their own experience after Mariana needed surgery but was unable to access savings held in a Lebanese bank.

Furies, Kodeih’s first feature, has its premiere in the Venezia Spotlight section of this year’s Venice Film Festival, and is backed by George Clooney and Grant Heslov’s Smokehouse Pictures.

Lebanon’s selection committee chose the film unanimously.

Saudi Arabia has selected Anas Ba Tahaf’s A Matter of Life and Death as its submission for Best International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards.

Set in Jeddah, the film stars Sarah Taibah as Hayat, a woman convinced she will die on her 30th birthday. She meets Youssef, played by Yaqoub Al-Farhan, a heart surgeon with an unusually slow heartbeat. Taibah also wrote the screenplay.

The film mixes romance, dark comedy and fantasy, using its central relationship to explore mortality and the fear of what comes next.

Algeria has selected Yanis Koussim’s Roqia, a horror film rooted in the country’s violence during the 1990s.

The film centres on an ageing raqi – a spiritual healer – who is living with Alzheimer's disease, alongside an amnesiac man who returns to his village. Moving between the 1990s and the present, it connects supernatural horror with memories of Algeria’s civil conflict.

Koussim told The National that the story was informed by his own memories of growing up during the period and by research into roqia.

His first feature, Roqia, had its premiere in the Critics’ Week section of the Venice Film Festival in 2025.

Algeria previously received five nominations in the category, winning for Z in 1970.

Iraq has selected No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman, an action drama by Kurdish-Norwegian filmmaker Halkawt Mustafa.

The Kurdish-language film follows Vyan, a sniper who has learnt to suppress her emotions after years of war. When she discovers that her younger sister, believed to have disappeared during a 2014 ISIS assault, may still be alive, she returns to Mosul to find her.

Mustafa has said the film was inspired by Kurdish women who fought ISIS and by his encounters with women Peshmerga fighters on the front line in 2014.

Starring Kurdish actress Avan Jamal and Norwegian actor Thorbjorn Harr, the film is scheduled to have its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival this week, where it is screening in the Venice Open section, out of competition.

The film is a Norway-Iraq-UAE-Sweden co-production, giving this year's Iraqi submission a UAE connection.

It is Mustafa's second film to represent Iraq at the Oscars, following El Clasico in 2016.

Morocco will be represented by Laila Marrakchi's La Mas Dulce, also known internationally as Strawberries.

The film follows Hasna and Meriem, two young Moroccan women who travel to Andalusia to work as seasonal strawberry pickers in the hope of improving the lives of their families.

They instead encounter exploitation, harassment and poor working conditions, eventually facing the decision of whether to speak out against those employing them.

The film had its premiere in the Un Certain Regard section of the Cannes Film Festival in May. Marrakchi has said the project developed after she learnt about Moroccan women working in Spain's strawberry industry and travelled there to understand their experiences.

Morocco's selection committee chose La Mas Dulce unanimously on September 2, citing its subject, technical and artistic qualities as well as its distribution prospects. It was selected from four films under consideration.

The film marked Marrakchi's return to Cannes two decades after Marock, her 2005 debut about young people in Casablanca, and followed her 2013 feature Rock the Casbah.

Palestine has chosen Ahmed Hassouna's documentary Citizen Osama, filmed in northern Gaza during the war.

The 69-minute film follows Osama Al-Ashi, a former artistic photographer who becomes a war documentarian, recording the devastation around him while trying to protect his wife and newborn child.

The film has already emerged as one of the Palestinian highlights of this year's Venice Film Festival line-up. When the programme was announced in July, Citizen Osama was one of two Palestinian features selected, alongside Muayad Alayan's Conversation With the Sea.

It had its world premiere at Venice earlier this month, screening out of competition.

Moving between Al-Ashi's work and his family life, the documentary offers an intimate account of survival in northern Gaza amid hunger, loss and displacement.

Palestinian Minister of Culture Imad Hamdan announced the Oscar selection on August 31 following a recommendation by an independent committee of film professionals.

The selection makes Citizen Osama Palestine's 19th submission in the category since 2003.

Egypt has selected The Stories, a 2025 semi-autobiographical anthology drama written and directed by Abu Bakr Shawky.

It follows the cross-cultural romance between an aspiring Egyptian pianist and an Austrian woman, tracing their lives against the backdrop of Egypt from the late 1960s to the 1980s.

The cast includes Nelly Karim, Ahmed Kamal, Amir El Masry, Sabry Fawaz, Amr Abed, Sherif El Desouky and Ahmed El Azaar.

The film was selected after two rounds of voting by Egypt's selection committee, which considered 36 films produced between September 2025 and September 2026.

It is the second time Egypt has selected a film by Shawky in the category, after Yomeddine in 2018.

Jordan has chosen Zain Duraie’s Sink as its submission.

The drama stars Clara Khoury as Nadia, a mother struggling to respond as her teenage son, Basil (Mohammed Nizar), experiences a worsening mental health crisis.

Duraie described the film as deeply personal and said she wanted to explore mental health through a Jordanian family rather than the kinds of stories Arab filmmakers are often expected to tell internationally.

Sink, Duraie’s first feature, had its premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025 and was later screened at the BFI London and Red Sea film festivals.

The Royal Film Commission said Jordan's selection committee made the choice independently.

analysis.framing: A comprehensive, matter-of-fact roundup of Arab national Oscar submissions for 2027, organized by country with synopses, production details, and selection-process notes.

headline: Middle East latest: UAE among countries to strongly condemn Riyadh airport attack
Fujairah shows why resilience is the Gulf’s greatest energy asset
summary: For a city sometimes unfairly described as “sleepy”, Fujairah is keeping the global energy industry awake these days. The Indian Ocean port has emerged as a crucial hub for the world economy, sustaining the UAE’s energy exports despite the Hormuz crisis.Last week, Fujairah’s importance was highlighted when Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, and chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc), attended the UAE Energy Markets Forum in the city. This continued a hectic run of conferences as the global energy industry emerges from a sticky summer and tries to find a way through conflict and disruption.The biennial WPC Energy Congress takes place in Riyadh this week, its first time in the kingdom and only the second time it has taken place in the Middle East, after Doha in 2011. The event has gone ahead despite the fatal attacks on the Saudi capital’s airport.Then, at the start of next month, executives take on the final boss, at Adipec, the world’s biggest energy event.Probably the most popular word in Fujairah last week was “resilience”. The UAE has managed to sustain, and possibly even increase, its oil exports through the conflict, as well as maintaining its essential imports. The Indian Ocean ports of Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and the others have been crucial.Rather than hasty workarounds, this rapid shift builds on years of preparation. The Habshan-Fujairah oil pipeline, with capacity up to 1.8 million barrels per day, was opened in 2012. Preparation for a second line had begun before the war, with the announcement in May and planned completion next year.Massive oil storage in caverns hewn out of Fujairah’s rugged brown mountains began construction in 2018. Adnoc Logistics and Services has amassed a large fleet of tankers and other ships, which has proved essential for moving oil. Supertankers are now in desperately short supply – it costs more to hire one, $80 million, than to launch SpaceX, a bargain at $74 million.Work on the impressive, modern new railway to Fujairah started in early 2020. The Barakah Nuclear Power Plant, an important part of assuring electricity even when gas facilities came under attack, began splitting atoms in August of that year.Regional preparednessBeyond the UAE, we could highlight similar regional examples of preparedness, such as the Gulf Co-operation Council electricity grid, Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, and the new port, refinery and oil storage facility at Duqm on Oman’s south-east coast. Like Adnoc, Saudi Arabia – with Bahri – Kuwait and Qatar have their own sizeable tanker fleets.Physical assets are only one part of resilience. Adnoc has over several years built a strong trading capability. That was profitable in the years of peace. In months of war, it has been even more important by salvaging supply to customers, and seizing attractive commercial opportunities.These assets were not accumulated with precise foreknowledge of the current conflict. Of course, blockade of Hormuz, or general trouble in the Gulf, has been a known risk since the Tanker War of the 1980s, if not before. In general, though, having a broad set of deployable national assets, whether in one company or several, whether in state or private hands, enables a country to cope with crises of all kinds.That could be regional political unrest as in 2011, a price crash such as that of 2014, a pandemic such as 2020, or a far-off war as in 2022. We do not know what the next challenge may be: a natural disaster, a big climatic upset, an energy technology breakthrough, an international market meltdown over AI or government debt. But combining physical, institutional and human capabilities with a flexible and proactive mindset is the best way to come through such storms.Resilience alone, though, is not enough. When the bombers thundered through the sky on February 28, politicians and observers alike thought it would be a short war. It has now ground on for more than seven months, though most direct strikes on Gulf and Iranian territory have stopped.Other theatres – Yemen, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq – have become entwined. Every regional country, even the non-involved such as Turkey, Egypt and Cyprus, have seen some unwelcome visitor land on their soil, and have suffered disruption to their airspace and trade routes. On Friday, US President Donald Trump announced proudly that Russia’s Vladimir Putin had promised to provide some diesel to ease the growing global fuel crisis, a product of the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine.Handling future crisesThe Gulf energy industry must build on the resilience established so far, establish new options to respond to future crises, and accelerate creating value. Of course, that is not easy to do while the spectre of renewed violence hovers over the region, and while shipping routes are still not functioning freely.The regional countries were, overall, investing heavily and sensibly in their energy industries before this year. They were solidifying their oil upstream, making the downstream more sophisticated, accessing gas for the domestic economy and for export, generating more value from commercial ingenuity, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, electrifying their economies and seizing on transformational new technology in the AI space.Those remain excellent aims, even if specific projects have to be reprioritised for the new regional reality. Regional energy companies can do more. Becoming true international players fills a capital gap, builds their capabilities and somewhat reduces their near-total reliance on the Gulf. They can do more in inventing and deploying truly game-changing hard technologies. These often struggle in the rest of the world because of lack of visionary capital, overregulation and difficulty in co-ordinating diverse interests.Regional energy companies can work together more. Huge gains are possible from networking physical infrastructure – pipelines, ports, electricity grids and data cables. Greater achievements can come from soft integration, such as commercial joint ventures, cross-border investments and technology partnerships.The energy industry, one of the first truly globalised businesses, needs more than most to reimagine or construct institutions that govern its world by laws and not by the missile. The power to convene the world’s leading energy doers and thinkers, as at Adipec in Abu Dhabi, brings positive influence.Finally, at recent events elsewhere, the energy business has sometimes given the impression of being relieved the issue of climate change has been dethroned by that of war. That is a mistake. Conflicts will, by some smart application of strength and diplomacy, be resolved. Climate change, bad or worse, will be with us for the rest of the century and beyond. It will reshape everything we do in energy and itself can inflame war.

headline: Al Nassr Asian Champions League clash in doubt over Riyadh security situation
summary: The AFC Champions League Elite fixture between Al Nassr and Neftchi Fergana is in doubt because of the security situation in Riyadh.At least 12 people died and 309 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Riyadh on Saturday afternoon.The attack was the third on King Khalid International Airport this week by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. Riyadh-based Nassr, who are captained by Cristiano Ronaldo, have a home match against Uzbek side Neftchi scheduled for Monday night.The Asian Football Confederation and the clubs involved have yet to comment on the status of the match.JUST SO YOU KNOW… ABHA VS AL-FAISALY HAS BEEN POSTPONED! 📅TODAY’S ROUND 8 CLASH HAS BEEN MOVED TO OCTOBER 27. pic.twitter.com/MkcuakWskm— All About SPL 🔔 🇸🇦 (@Saudifutbol) October 11, 2026However, one of the Saudi Pro League fixtures scheduled for Sunday evening has been postponed. The game between Abha and Faisaly will be rearranged for later in the month.“The SPL confirmed the decision was made following a review of the circumstances surrounding the match,” the league wrote.“[The decision was taken] in accordance with approved regulatory procedures, ensuring that situations beyond the clubs' control are addressed while maintaining the continuity of the competition.”Abha is around 900 kms to the south-west of Riyadh, and around 200 kms from the Yemen border.Whether the Champions League fixtures will be similarly affected is unclear.There are four matches involving Saudi Arabian clubs in the continental competition scheduled for the next two days.Nassr are the only club playing a home fixture. They are due to host Neftchi at their home ground of Al Awwal Park on Monday.The Uzbek side were already in Riyadh when the attack on the airport happened.Fergana travelled via a direct charter flight, while around 100 fans of the side are also reported to have travelled to Saudi Arabia’s capital for the fixture.The situation is also likely to affect Al Hilal. The four-time Asian champions went ahead with the “Saudi Clasico” against Jeddah’s Al Ittihad on Saturday night.They won 3-2 at the Kingdom Arena in Riyadh, to strengthen their position at the top of the SPL.Simone Inzaghi’s side are due to fly to Doha to face Qatar side Al Sadd, for their fixture scheduled for Tuesday.Qadsiah flew from Dammam to Tashkent on Sunday. The Brendan Rodgers-coached side will face Pakhtakor on Monday.Al Ahli Saudi, the two-time defending champions of Asia, will face Al Wasl on Monday evening. They travelled from Jeddah to Dubai on Saturday.

headline: UAE student inventors and people with disabilities to be offered free IP registration under new rules
summary: The UAE is waiving intellectual property registration fees for student inventors and people with disabilities, removing a key barrier to innovation protection.The Ministry of Economy and Tourism began implementing Cabinet Resolution No 136 of 2026 on September 14, providing full exemptions across 29 services related to patents, industrial designs, utility certificates and integrated circuit layouts.Student inventors and people of determination both benefit from exemptions on 11 shared services, including patent and industrial design registration applications, utility certificate examinations and annual protection fees covering years two through five. Those fees previously ranged from Dh100 to Dh1,000. People of determination receive additional exemptions on nine further services, with original fees of up to Dh9,000, while student inventors are exempt from nine separate services previously costing up to Dh4,500.Fostering creativity and innovationAbdulrahman Al Muaini, Assistant Undersecretary for the Intellectual Property Sector at the Ministry, said the resolution reflected the UAE's commitment to building a comprehensive legislative environment aligned with international standards. "The Cabinet resolution affirms the UAE's vision of fostering creativity and innovation by supporting student inventors and People of Determination, enabling them to register their innovations with ease and protect their rights," Mr Al Muaini said.The move comes against a backdrop of rising demand for intellectual property protection in the UAE. The ministry recorded a 9 per cent increase in patent applications during the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, while utility certificate applications grew by 21 per cent over the same period. Total patent applications in 2025 reached approximately 4,300. The cumulative number of patents, utility certificates and industrial design applications registered in the country has reached 22,184, reflecting growing interest among innovators and businesses in securing industrial property rights. The ministry said it continues to develop its digital infrastructure for IP services in line with the objectives of the We the UAE 2031 vision.

headline: Sudan's Al Burhan accused of political scheming as war puts children at risk
summary: Political figures and analysts have accused the head of the Sudanese Armed Forces, Gen Abdel Fattah Al Burhan, of political manoeuvring and remaining under the influence of the Islamist movement. They have also warned the prolonged civil war is depriving Sudan's children of education and exposing them to forced recruitment.In an interview with Sky News Arabia, Mohamed Abdel Hakam, a leader of the Sumoud alliance, Sudan’s largest civilian coalition, said Gen Al Burhan had full control over the army and the levers of power, but faced constraints on decision-making because of the influence of allied groups, including those within his own office.Mr Abdel Hakam alleged Gen Al Burhan had made significant concessions during his meeting with Massad Boulos, US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs, in Egypt on October 5.Those talks took place on the sidelines of the African Union’s co-ordination meeting, less than two weeks after Washington withheld a visa for Gen Al Burhan ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York. The move was reportedly linked to the army-led administration’s resistance to a US proposal for a 90-day humanitarian ceasefire, followed by political negotiations aimed at ending the war and restoring a transition to civilian rule. Sudan has said it did not reject the proposal but instead submitted comments on it.Political analyst and military expert Hashem Abu Rannat also accused Gen Al Burhan of political scheming, saying the army chief had accepted certain conditions but was reluctant to disclose them to his allies.Mr Abu Rannat said Gen Al Burhan had returned to his allies to inform them that he was prepared to make concessions, while continuing to pursue his objectives in Darfur, including driving out the Janjaweed militia.He claimed the Islamic Movement has a decisive role in shaping political and military decisions, alongside affiliated army officers. “Al Burhan is a tool in the hands of the Islamic Movement,” Mr Abu Rannat said.Meanwhile, Sudanese activist Nagisa Hagar has warned the conflict is depriving an entire generation of Sudanese children of education.She said many children who should have been attending kindergarten or primary school have lost these critical years, leaving them outside of the education system.Ms Hagar also warned that children faced the risk of recruitment by the warring parties, particularly the Sudanese army and groups affiliated with it.She said videos published by these groups showed children being recruited, warning of the serious threat posed by forced recruitment and the imposition of responsibilities on children that should instead be borne by adults and state institutions.The war broke out in April 2023 after a power struggle between the army and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary over the transition to civilian rule and the planned integration of the rival bodies. Repeated diplomatic initiatives have failed to secure a lasting ceasefire.The conflict has created one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. More than 14 million people have been displaced and nearly 20 million face hunger, according to the UN World Food Programme.

headline: Palestinian factions to meet in Egypt for reconciliation talks after election postponed
summary: Egypt has invited leaders of Palestinian factions to meet in Cairo in a renewed bid for reconciliation, after legislative elections scheduled for next month were postponed by President Mahmoud Abbas, sources told The National on Sunday.The meeting proposed for next week will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine.The sources said Khalil Al Haya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads a pro-reform faction within Fatah, the main group in the Palestinian Authority, were among those invited by the Egyptians.As is customary, there has been no official announcement by the Egyptian government on the proposed meeting.Mr Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority, announced on Saturday that the vote would be postponed until September next year, when the presidential election is also due to take place.Sources from various factions have told The National the delay was primarily intended to address what has been described as “Palestinian divisions” before the elections take place. The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation has approved the postponement. It said the delay was due to the lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the PA. Mr Abbas, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term. The deeply unpopular Mr Abbas, who is 90, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption.An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down.Egypt has been trying to reconcile Palestinian factions for years, without success. Its efforts have been led by officials from its spy agency who have taken responsibility for key foreign policy files over the years, traditionally handled by the Foreign Ministry.Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”. However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives.“The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it said in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.” The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.
body_text:
Egypt has invited leaders of Palestinian factions to meet in Cairo in a renewed bid for reconciliation, after legislative elections scheduled for next month were postponed by President Mahmoud Abbas, sources told The National on Sunday.

The meeting proposed for next week will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine.

The sources said Khalil Al Haya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads a pro-reform faction within Fatah, the main group in the Palestinian Authority, were among those invited by the Egyptians.

Special reportThe Gaza ceasefire was meant to end the war. For a mother, paramedic and child, little has changed

As is customary, there has been no official announcement by the Egyptian government on the proposed meeting.

Mr Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority, announced on Saturday that the vote would be postponed until September next year, when the presidential election is also due to take place.

Sources from various factions have told The National the delay was primarily intended to address what has been described as “Palestinian divisions” before the elections take place.

The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation has approved the postponement. It said the delay was due to the lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the PA. Mr Abbas, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term.

The deeply unpopular Mr Abbas, who is 90, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption.

An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down.

Egypt has been trying to reconcile Palestinian factions for years, without success. Its efforts have been led by officials from its spy agency who have taken responsibility for key foreign policy files over the years, traditionally handled by the Foreign Ministry.

Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”.

However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives.

“The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it said in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.”

The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.

analysis.framing: The article frames the postponed Palestinian elections and Egypt's reconciliation invitation around internal Palestinian factional dynamics and President Abbas's domestic political weakness, giving roughly balanced space to Hamas and the Dahlan faction's opposing reactions.

loaded_language.explanation: An editorializing characterization of Abbas's public standing rather than a neutral descriptor; it asserts a political judgment in the reporter's own voice.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Mr Abbas, whose approval ratings are low according to polls

loaded_language.explanation: A loaded phrase that evokes authoritarian governance; while factually rooted in the use of presidential decrees, it carries a negative connotation.
Vague attribution ('reports of') that lends weight to an unverified allegation without naming sources or specifying the reports.
Causal language that frames Hamas's 2006 victory as the direct cause of the Fatah-Hamas rift, simplifying a complex political rupture.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: after which the Fatah-Hamas split occurred

loaded_language.explanation: Editorializing comparison that signals the reporter's assessment of the contrast between faction responses rather than simply presenting them.

omissions: No mention of the specific new date announced for the postponed elections beyond 'September next year'.
No detail on the stated reasons for the delay beyond 'lack of security' and 'Palestinian divisions'.
No reaction from the Israeli government or international actors such as the US or EU.
No mention of the 2007 Gaza takeover by Hamas or the subsequent blockade.
No mention of the number of legislative seats or the electoral system.
No mention of the role of other Palestinian factions such as Islamic Jihad or the PFLP.

headline: US warplane knocks out ship breaching Iran blockade as tankers burn in Hormuz
summary: A US fighter jet knocked out a cargo ship trying to breach Washington’s blockade of Iran, as a tanker caught fire in a Strait of Hormuz lane that has come under attack from Tehran’s forces.US Central Command (Centcom) said the jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged Ocean Molika, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday after its crew had ignored repeated warnings.The ship had left an Iranian port and was trying to transit regional waters in defiance of the blockade. No crew members were harmed, Centcom said in a statement on Sunday.Video footage released by Centom showed an explosion erupting from the ship, sending a plume of smoke into the air, obscuring the vessel.It is the latest escalation in a campaign that began with ships being turned away and is now being enforced with live fire. Since resuming the blockade on July 14, US forces say they have disabled four commercial vessels and turned around 135 more. The restrictions cover ships entering or leaving Iranian ports.The strike on the Ocean Molika comes as commercial vessels in the same waters are being hit by projectiles, fires and, by Iran's account, mines. The cause of the incidents remains unconfirmed but they underline the increasing danger in the vital waterway.Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported an outbound tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz at 11.20pm UAE time on Saturday, causing a fire on board. All crew were reported safe.U.S. Forces Disable Cargo Vessel Attempting to Violate Blockade TAMPA, Fla. — U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) forces disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman, Oct. 10, after the ship’s crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade… pic.twitter.com/qBKcU6gWqR— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) October 11, 2026UKMTO also reported an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman. The advisory, issued on Sunday, gave no further details, with the time of the incident still to be confirmed.Authorities were aware of the incident and investigations were ongoing, it said.Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Navy claimed a supertanker carrying crude oil caught fire after striking a naval mine while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz.The vessel had entered a designated high-risk area before a powerful explosion, the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Iran’s Fars news agency. The account could not be independently verified.Separately, the UAE National Guard Command said 22 people had been rescued from an oil tanker in the Arabian Gulf after a fire broke out on board.A specialised coastguard team responded to a report from the crew, located the vessel and rescued those on board. The 22 people, all Asian citizens, received first aid before being transferred to the relevant authorities. All were in stable medical condition, the command said.
body_text:
A US fighter jet knocked out a cargo ship trying to breach Washington’s blockade of Iran, as a tanker caught fire in a Strait of Hormuz lane that has come under attack from Tehran’s forces.

US Central Command (Centcom) said the jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged Ocean Molika, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday after its crew had ignored repeated warnings.

The ship had left an Iranian port and was trying to transit regional waters in defiance of the blockade. No crew members were harmed, Centcom said in a statement on Sunday.

Video footage released by Centom showed an explosion erupting from the ship, sending a plume of smoke into the air, obscuring the vessel.

It is the latest escalation in a campaign that began with ships being turned away and is now being enforced with live fire. Since resuming the blockade on July 14, US forces say they have disabled four commercial vessels and turned around 135 more. The restrictions cover ships entering or leaving Iranian ports.

The strike on the Ocean Molika comes as commercial vessels in the same waters are being hit by projectiles, fires and, by Iran's account, mines. The cause of the incidents remains unconfirmed but they underline the increasing danger in the vital waterway.

Separately, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported an outbound tanker was struck by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz at 11.20pm UAE time on Saturday, causing a fire on board. All crew were reported safe.

UKMTO also reported an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman. The advisory, issued on Sunday, gave no further details, with the time of the incident still to be confirmed.

Authorities were aware of the incident and investigations were ongoing, it said.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Navy claimed a supertanker carrying crude oil caught fire after striking a naval mine while attempting to leave the Strait of Hormuz.

The vessel had entered a designated high-risk area before a powerful explosion, the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Iran’s Fars news agency. The account could not be independently verified.

Separately, the UAE National Guard Command said 22 people had been rescued from an oil tanker in the Arabian Gulf after a fire broke out on board.

A specialised coastguard team responded to a report from the crew, located the vessel and rescued those on board. The 22 people, all Asian citizens, received first aid before being transferred to the relevant authorities. All were in stable medical condition, the command said.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a US enforcement action against an Iranian blockade breach amid escalating maritime danger in the Strait of Hormuz, attributing the broader threat to Tehran's forces while noting unconfirmed causes of other incidents.

loaded_language.explanation: Colloquial and forceful, implying a decisive blow rather than a precise military action.
Carries a connotation of violation or wrongdoing, framing the ship's action as illegitimate.
Emotionally charged, suggesting deliberate and provocative resistance.
Dramatic phrasing that emphasizes lethality and escalation.
Editorializing adjective that underscores strategic importance without neutral qualification.

omissions: Iran's official response or denial regarding the blockade and the strike on the Ocean Molika
Details on the nationalities or identities of the crew of the Ocean Molika
Independent verification or conflicting accounts of the cause of the tanker fire in the Strait of Hormuz
Context on the legal status of the US blockade under international law
Reactions from other countries or international bodies to the US strike

headline: Diplomats or Quds Force? Zarif's blunt question rattles Iran's old guard
summary: A growing rift over Iran's security strategy has emerged after footage showed former foreign minister Mohammad Javad Zarif questioning Tehran's reliance on military threats and arguing that diplomacy and economic opportunity should take priority over confrontation.The video, which appeared online on Saturday, has triggered a wave of criticism from hardline media as Iran faces mounting economic pressure from a US blockade and renewed uncertainty over the prospect of another conflict.“The balance of power has changed – nuclear weapons do not create deterrence, just as they did not protect Israel or the Soviet Union,” Mr Zarif said in remarks delivered in May last year, shortly before the 12-day war with Israel.Mr Zarif said Iran lacked sufficient uranium to build a nuclear weapon at the time. He argued that Tehran's security-first outlook had distorted its nuclear strategy and regional diplomacy, limiting opportunities to pursue economic and diplomatic interests.The former minister drew a direct contrast between treating neighbouring countries as threats and viewing them as potential partners.“If we see the region as a threat, our ambassadors must be representatives of the Quds Force [but] if we see it as an opportunity, our ambassadors must be businesspeople and diplomats,” he said, referring to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps unit responsible for overseas operations.He also criticised the tendency to frame domestic social issues in security terms. “We even see hijab as a trench line,” Mr Zarif said, calling for a shift away from a threat-based approach.Hardliners hit backThe remarks have drawn a sharp response from Iran’s hardline establishment. The ultraconservative Kayhan newspaper accused Mr Zarif of undermining national security and helping Washington.“Why, precisely at moments when the US finds itself deadlocked and helpless in the face of Iran’s power, do you give the enemy breathing room by launching a suicidal attack on the arms of national security?” a line read.The hardline Tasnim news agency published an editorial attacking Mr Zarif’s comments and demanding an apology, while Raja News questioned whether the judiciary would act against him. No formal judicial action has been established.The backlash comes as Iran’s leadership confronts difficult choices over how long the country can sustain its confrontation with Washington while absorbing the effects of economic restrictions and the US blockade on Strait of Hormuz shipping.Pressure on trade and revenue has intensified concerns about Iran’s economic resilience, adding urgency to arguments that Tehran should seek a diplomatic settlement rather than risk further damage through renewed hostilities.Reformist politician Hossein Marashi, secretary general of the Executives of Construction Party, warned that Iran must avoid decisions that could trigger another war.“Whatever political or military measures are necessary, including any tactical retreat, must be taken to protect Iran and prevent its people from facing even greater and mounting pressure,” Mr Marashi said.He argued that Tehran could not simultaneously preserve all its nuclear ambitions, maintain its military posture, resolve its economic crisis and force the US out of the region. Iran’s leaders, he said, must prioritise national survival and economic recovery.Omid Memarian, senior Iran analyst at the democracy and human rights organisation Dawn, sees the debate as reflecting a broader division over whether continued resistance will strengthen Tehran’s negotiating position or leave the country increasingly vulnerable.“There is a profound and growing divide within Iran, from the highest levels of political decision-making to different segments of society, over how to prevent another war with the United States,” he told The National.Iran’s leverage over shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could become a liability if prolonged disruption prompts Washington to intensify military and economic pressure, Mr Memarian said. “A tactical advantage can become a strategic liability when leaders fail to recognise the moment to cash it in,” he said.The economic consequences could extend beyond immediate trade disruption, with prolonged uncertainty complicating the management of food supplies, fuel reserves and recovery efforts.Foreign attacks, meanwhile, may foster national solidarity without erasing public grievances over domestic conditions.Decision on diplomacyThe approaching US midterm elections on November 3 add another consideration. Some Iranian pragmatists say Tehran should make meaningful concessions and pursue a settlement before the vote, rather than assume mounting economic costs will eventually force US President Donald Trump to retreat.Mr Trump has said the US will not resume military strikes before the elections, citing productive discussions with Iran. Washington has nevertheless continued preparations for possible military operations, leaving fundamental disagreements unresolved.Mr Zarif’s remarks have exposed the political sensitivity of questioning Iran’s deterrence strategy at a moment when its leadership faces pressure on several fronts.The central dispute is whether Tehran should use its remaining leverage to negotiate a sustainable settlement or continue a confrontational approach that could deepen economic hardship and increase the risk of another war.

headline: Al Ain Airport renamed as Tahnoun International Airport
summary: President Sheikh Mohamed has ordered the renaming of Al Ain International Airport to Tahnoun International Airport.The name change, which takes effect immediately, honours the late Sheikh Tahnoun bin Mohammed Al Nahyan's decades of service to the country.Sheikh Tahnoun was the Ruler's Representative of the Eastern Region of the Emirate of Abu Dhabi from the country's founding until his death in 2024.Tahnoun International Airport is the second international airport in the emirate of Abu Dhabi, situated about 18km from the oasis city of Al Ain.The airport currently has scheduled flights for two airlines and serves more than 100,000 passengers annually, according to Abu Dhabi Airports.Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 shows two scheduled flights today: Pakistan International Airlines flight PK144 from Islamabad and Air India Express flight IX336 from Kozhikode.The name change comes two years after Abu Dhabi's main international airport was renamed to Zayed International Airport, in honour of UAE Founding Father, the late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan.

headline: Saudi Arabia presses on with global energy summit after deadly Riyadh airport attack
summary: Saudi Arabia pressed ahead with a major gathering of global energy ministers and industry executives on Sunday, hours after an attack by Yemen's Houthis on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and injured 309.The International Energy Forum's 17th ministerial meeting, hosted by Saudi Arabia and co-hosted by Italy and Nigeria, is being held alongside the WPC Energy Congress, bringing together policymakers and industry leaders.Media access to the ministerial meeting will be restricted, with only journalists invited directly by the IEF permitted to cover the opening remarks, according to a Saudi Energy Ministry spokeswoman.“As you are aware, the ministerial plenary will be held behind closed doors,” she said. No live broadcast pool arrangements were in place, she added.The event is proceeding despite mounting security concerns after repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which have forced airlines to cancel flights and complicated travel arrangements for delegates.Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said on Friday that he would participate in the IEF meeting by video link rather than travel to Riyadh.The WPC Energy Congress, which runs from Sunday until Thursday, is also proceeding as scheduled. Organisers have directed delegates to alternative routes into the Saudi capital, including by road from Dammam on the kingdom's east coast. A projectile landed near King Fahd Airport in Dammam on Saturday, a representative for the Saudi coalition said.Saturday's strike was the third on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in a week and the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, which killed four Saudis and eight foreign citizens, including one from the US.Two attacks on the airport this week killed four people and caused extensive damage to a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac.The latest strike caused widespread disruption to aviation, with about 260 flights cancelled and another 219 delayed on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24.The attacks have heightened security concerns, as Saudi Arabia seeks to maintain its calendar of high-profile international gatherings despite the war's growing regional spillover.Riyadh is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative from October 26 to 29, with organisers saying the event will proceed as planned, with additional security arrangements put in place.

headline: Saudi-led coalition vows to ‘respond decisively’ to deadly Riyadh airport attack
summary: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has vowed to “respond decisively” to a Houthi attack on Riyadh that killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malik condemned Saturday’s strike on King Khalid International Airport as “a full-fledged war crime according to the customary international humanitarian law”.“It is a heinous act that contradicts all principles, values, and ethics,” he said on Sunday morning, adding that the coalition would respond in accordance with international humanitarian law.The airport was closed as a precaution on Saturday. Authorities on Sunday extended the shutdown by 24 hours, until 1am local time on Monday, flight-tracking platform Flightradar24 said. Passengers were advised to check with their airlines for updates.US President Donald Trump said Washington could join Saudi Arabia in strikes against the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, following the attack, which killed an American citizen.Asked whether the US would participate in any Saudi action, Mr Trump said: “We may. We're going to look at it.”“We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he added.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio condemned the strike, saying it had taken “numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen”.“These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Mr Rubio wrote on X. “We stand with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and its people and extend our condolences to the victims and their families.”pic.twitter.com/q5otUrilQm— المتحدث الرسمي باسم قوات التحالف (@CJFCSpox) October 10, 2026UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by the attack and called for an immediate halt to strikes on civilians and civilian infrastructure, warning that such attacks violate international law.UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg described the latest series of attacks as a “grave escalation”, saying it threatened regional security, perpetuated violence and further complicated efforts to secure peace in Yemen. He urged the Houthis to cease the attacks and respect international humanitarian law.Governments in the region and beyond rallied behind Riyadh. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “completely unacceptable”, reaffirming Islamabad’s “unwavering solidarity” with the kingdom and its commitment to Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.Qatar described the strike as a “grave violation” of Saudi sovereignty, stressing that the kingdom’s security was integral to its own and to that of Gulf Co-operation Council states. Jordan also condemned the attack, reporting that one Jordanian was was killed and four wounded.This is now a full regional war. Started by Donald Trump. For no good reason.Chris Murphy, US SenatorKuwait condemned what it described as a “blatant assault” by the Houthis, according to the state-run Kuwait News Agency. It renewed its “absolute solidarity” with Saudi Arabia and called on the international community to take a firm position to protect civilian sites and hold those responsible to account.The Netherlands also condemned the attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on multiple airports that caused casualties. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen expressed condolences to victims’ families, saying the Netherlands stood in “full solidarity with the people of Saudi Arabia and our Gulf partners”.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney called the attacks “abhorrent”, saying there could be no justification for attacking civilian infrastructure.US Democratic Senator Chris Murphy was among those to criticise Mr Trump, writing that the situation now represented “a full regional war” and the US President had started the conflict."This is now a full regional war. Started by Donald Trump. For no good reason," he wrote on X. "It’s a civilian airport that should never, ever be a target. This campaign of terror by the Houthis must stop immediately," he added.

headline: Riyadh airport closure: Emirates, Etihad and other UAE airlines cancel flights
summary: UAE airlines cancelled flights to and from Riyadh on Sunday, with the disruption extending into Monday after the closure of King Khalid International Airport because of a deadly Houthi rebel attack.Etihad Airways confirmed six cancellations between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh on Sunday and two more on Monday. Emirates, flydubai and Air Arabia services connecting Dubai and Sharjah with the Saudi capital were also listed as cancelled on flight-tracking website Flightradar24.An aviation notice said Riyadh airport was closed until midnight on Sunday (1am Monday in UAE). The notice cited precautionary measures and did not specify when passenger operations would resume.Flightradar24 figures as of 9.15am UAE time showed 606 flights to and from Riyadh listed had been cancelled on Sunday, comprising 293 departures and 313 arrivals.Several UAE–Riyadh services remain listed as scheduled for Monday, although their operation will depend on conditions at the airport.The cancellations follow Saturday’s attack, which killed 12 people and injured 309. Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation suspended operations while assessing damage and carrying out safety checks.Flights had already faced days of disruption following earlier attacks.
