body_text:
UAE airlines cancelled flights to and from Riyadh on Sunday, with the disruption extending into Monday after the closure of King Khalid International Airport because of a deadly Houthi rebel attack.

Etihad Airways confirmed six cancellations between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh on Sunday and two more on Monday. Emirates, flydubai and Air Arabia services connecting Dubai and Sharjah with the Saudi capital were also listed as cancelled on flight-tracking website Flightradar24.

An aviation notice said Riyadh airport was closed until midnight on Sunday (1am Monday in UAE). The notice cited precautionary measures and did not specify when passenger operations would resume.

Twelve killed and 309 wounded in attack on Riyadh airport

Flightradar24 figures as of 9.15am UAE time showed 606 flights to and from Riyadh listed had been cancelled on Sunday, comprising 293 departures and 313 arrivals.

Several UAE–Riyadh services remain listed as scheduled for Monday, although their operation will depend on conditions at the airport.

The cancellations follow Saturday’s attack, which killed 12 people and injured 309. Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation suspended operations while assessing damage and carrying out safety checks.

Flights had already faced days of disruption following earlier attacks. Sunday’s cancellations affect services beyond the suspension periods previously announced by some UAE airlines.

Etihad has cancelled flights EY551, EY555 and EY559 from Abu Dhabi’s Zayed International Airport to Riyadh on Sunday, along with returning services EY552, EY556 and EY560.

On Monday, October 12, EY551 from Abu Dhabi to Riyadh and EY552 in the opposite direction are also cancelled.

The airline said further changes were possible and advised passengers to check their flight status before travelling to the airport. Its teams are assisting affected travellers with their arrangements.

Flightradar24 listed Emirates flights EK819 and EK817 from Dubai to Riyadh as cancelled on Sunday, along with EK820 from Riyadh to Dubai.

Emirates flights EK815 and EK819 from Dubai to Riyadh early on Monday were also listed as cancelled, along with returning service EK820.

Flydubai flights FZ847, FZ841 and FZ855 from Dubai to Riyadh were listed as cancelled on Sunday, as was FZ848 from Riyadh to Dubai, according to Flightradar24.

The airline’s earlier advisory covered cancellations to Riyadh and Yanbu through October 10 and Abha through October 11. Sunday’s Riyadh cancellations extend beyond that advisory.

Air Arabia flights G9151 and G9154 from Sharjah to Riyadh were listed as cancelled on Sunday, according to Flightradar24.

Passengers should confirm their flight status directly with their airline before leaving for the airport and check notifications about changes to their booking.

Those whose flights have been cancelled should contact their airline or travel agent about rebooking and refund options. Travellers with onward connections should also confirm whether changes are needed to the rest of their journey.

Several UAE–Riyadh services remain listed as scheduled for Monday, although their operation will depend on conditions at the airport. Passengers should confirm directly with their airline before travelling.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a practical travel disruption for UAE airlines and passengers, with the Houthi attack mentioned as background context rather than the central focus.

loaded_language.explanation: The word 'deadly' is emotionally charged and 'rebel' carries a political label that some outlets avoid in favor of 'Houthi' or 'Houthi fighters'.
Vague bureaucratic phrasing that does not specify what measures were taken or why.

omissions: No mention of who was responsible for the attack beyond 'Houthi rebel attack'.
No details on the nature of the attack (e.g., missile, drone).
No mention of international reactions or condemnation.
No context on the broader conflict in Yemen or Saudi-led coalition operations.
No mention of whether the airport itself was damaged or only nearby areas.

headline: Saudi Clasico: Watkins, Martinelli and Summerville all fire as Al Hilal go top
summary: Al Hilal's three-man former Premier League strikeforce all scored as they beat Al Ittihad 3-2 on Saturday to reclaim top spot in the table. The Riyadh giants spent big to reshape their forward line over the summer, bringing in Ollie Watkins ($60m from Aston Villa), Gabriel Martinelli ($70m from Arsenal) and Crysencio Summerville ($80 million from West Ham) from the English top-flight. All three came good at Kingdom Arena as Al Ittihad were well beaten despite a strong effort and the close scoreline. Former Gunners winger Martinelli opened the scoring on 11 minutes before Al Ittihad striker Youssef En-Nesyri pulled his side level. But parity didn't last long as England striker Watkins struck on 30 minutes to make it 2-1. Summerville then stretched the lead to 3-1 just after the hour mark. Steven Bergwijn scored a penalty in the dying stages to reduce the arrears and complete the scoring. Watkins was pleased with the three points, but felt he should have had another goal, with him having one chalked off for a questionable handball. He said: “It was a high-level match, especially as we had just returned from the international break. We trained for many days, but nothing compares to playing a match at full strength.“It was a top-of-the-table clash, and you can see how important it was to everyone. There is a lot of noise and celebrations, but the most important thing is that we took the three points, and I am very happy.“Honestly, I scored another goal, but unfortunately it was disallowed,” he added. “I know it was a difficult decision, and I will not comment on it, but I felt it was a valid goal.”Al Hilal are now two points clear at the top of the table ahead of Al Qadsiah and Cristiano Ronaldo's Al Nassr, who beat Diriyah 3-0 on Friday night.

headline: UAE IPOs and credit markets primed for growth once war ends, Morgan Stanley executive says
summary: The UAE is expected to see a rebound in initial public offerings once the US-Iran conflict ends, and the country’s credit market is also set to boom, according to a senior Morgan Stanley executive. While there have been no listings in the UAE so far this year, the investment bank is bullish about the capital market prospects despite the uncertainty caused by the war. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows.“I think long term, as the conflicts get resolved or hits some level of stabilisation, you will definitely see a rebound in the IPO marketplace in the UAE,” Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley told The National. “So, we are investing in and have high confidence in that. And we've been so impressed with the leadership on the sort of financial infrastructure in the country all the way around,” he said. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased uncertainty across the Middle East. After the US-Israeli bombing of Iran and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on its Arab neighbours halted in early April, peace in the region has teetered on a fragile ceasefire.A report from the World Bank released last week said Gulf economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. While the International Monetary Fund also anticipates that the Gulf economy will contract this year, the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping, the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said. "I think it [the war] clearly creates a slightly higher and hopefully temporary risk premium in the region, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest," Mr Simkowitz said. The investment bank's commitment to the region is "as strong as it's ever been". "We continue to be thinking about how to invest in growth. Our corporate clients, FDI clients, are still very focused on the demographics in the region, the potential for GDP growth, the diversification that is coming in the marketplace,” he added. There is extreme resilience that has been built in the region, the Morgan Stanley executive said. “There is also real capital strength in the region, and so as they need to either rebuild or redirect energy infrastructure, for example, there is the capability to do so. And … there is international capital ready to help do that,” he explained.Morgan Stanley, which is headquartered in the US and has more than $10 trillion in assets, has been present in the region for the past 20 years. It also opened a new office in Abu Dhabi in 2024. [The war] creates a higher and temporary risk premium, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interestDan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan StanleyThe bank currently has well over 100 employees in the region and it plans to expand its operations further. "We're going to stay very committed to growing that. I think wealth and asset management will be a part of that,” Mr Simkowitz said.The company's current pipeline of deals in the region is still active, he said. "Some element is on pause, and I think it would change a little bit in that people will have to re-underwrite maybe some of their resiliency supply chain and diversification. But I would argue most of it that was on is underway."Credit market boom The Morgan Stanley executive is also bullish about growth in credit markets in the UAE and across the region, with global trends also positive. Credit markets cover bonds, government debt, private credit and bank loans.Globally, asset managers and owners, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, are playing a key role in the credit market, he said. “The credit market has become more important because we're entering into a period where high capex manufacturing is back ... and in that context, you need to spend money, and you need to bridge this ‘build to revenue, build to profitability’ gap … and it is not just banks or governments.”Economic tailwinds from the AI buildout and "surprisingly enduring demand" have bolstered credit conditions in many major economies this year, S&P Global Ratings said in a report this month. But the positive momentum of overall credit stability seen over the past few years will become more difficult to sustain, it said. Heading into the fourth quarter, "risks are building amid the sharp rise in benchmark borrowing costs, including yields on government debt, as investors bet that major central banks have a complex challenge in their fight against inflation", the ratings agency said. In the UAE and the Gulf, the credit market “is coming, and I think that's encouraging”, Mr Simkowitz said. Gulf debt capital markets reached $1.2 trillion outstanding at the end of the first half of this year, according to Fitch Ratings. Even in mature markets like the US, the credit market is evolving and building, Mr Simkowitz said, adding that the growth of a fixed income market or a bond market is "incredibly important”. “Over the last several years, the conversations we've had throughout the Gulf with finance ministries, stock exchanges, and other leadership … has been skewing more and more towards bond markets and credit markets, as we've had some great success with ADX [Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange] and with other exchanges in the Gulf around equities, it's a natural progression,” he said. More than $100 billion has been raised in debt markets in the region this year, he said. "That is really important to continue to satisfy the growth, diversification and resiliency ambitions, it can't all be done with equity, and so you need some element of credit and bond markets.”AI, midterms and outlook The big economic theme is AI, which is "incredibly transformational", Mr Simkowitz said. "It's going to require a lot of capital today to drive an immense amount of productivity in the future."Certainly, the UAE has been at the centre of that. As relative to GDP or even wealth or market cap, the UAE is one of the most important AI players in the world."A recent report by Bain found that the AI industry needs to earn $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to justify the capital being deployed for data centres.Revenue from new product development is projected to become the biggest contributor to the industry, and is estimated to generate about $4.2 trillion to fund the technology's global market within the next half-decade."We're reasonably bullish on AI-related revenue," Mr Simkowitz said. "There's a timing mismatch in that you need to build compute a little ahead, but that timeframe is shrinking ahead of the productivity and the revenue impact."Ultimately, the technology will prove beneficial. "Anything this transformative and large is .. not going to always be linear, and not everyone's going to win. But I would say the users will win, and then I would say there's going to be a group of winners who deliver it, who will win big from an investment perspective."From the political standpoint, investors are keenly watching the US midterm elections early next month. However, Mr Simkowitz stressed that while everybody in the markets will be focused on the midterms, "it's not nearly as consequential" as presidential elections, such as upcoming ones in Brazil or France.Looking ahead, there remains uncertainty in the markets over the US-Iran war, the Ukraine-Russia conflict and economic indicators such as inflation.Mr Simkowitz's outlook for next year? "I think intense and don't be complacent. No one can be complacent. It may not be as dramatic [as this year], but it's going to be intense."

headline: Lionel Messi scores twice for Inter Miami in first game since Argentina farewell
summary: Luis Suarez and Lionel Messi each recorded a brace to help Inter Miami emphatically snap ​a ​five-match winless streak ​with a 4-0 shutout of DC United ⁠on Saturday night in Miami.Messi was playing his first club game since his emotional final match for Argentina in midweek.Suarez also had an ⁠assist for one of Messi's goals ​as Inter Miami (13-5-10, 49 points) moved up to second place in Major League Soccer's ⁠Eastern Conference and one point ahead of the Chicago Fire.German Berterame also recorded two assists while Sergio Reguilon and Rodrigo De Paul each had one."We had to win again, and we did it convincingly ," said Inter Miami coach Kily Gonzalez, satisfied with his team's collective performance.DC United (6-9-12, 30 points) fell further ⁠out of the playoff picture and are now six points behind FC Cincinnati ​for ⁠the conference's final post-season play-in berth.Suarez ‌scored his 14th and 15th goals before he was substituted off in ​the 61st minute. Inter Miami brought their MLS-leading team goals total to 68, and recorded a fifth clean sheet overall and first in 10 matches.Four goals. Three points. 💗🔥 pic.twitter.com/zQ64ocT38f— Inter Miami CF (@InterMiamiCF) October 11, 2026DC United mustered 14 shots overall, but only two on target including a close shot by Matti Peltola that sailed just high and over the crossbar in the second half.Suarez found the mark in the third minute when he converted a long cross from Berterame past DC United goalkeeper Sean Johnson. Reguilon recorded the second assist as he fired the ball ahead to Berterame, allowing him to send a high-arching ball that appeared to be ​redirected right to Suarez.Suarez scored his second in the ‌39th minute after Berterame controlled ⁠a rebound and headed it to him ​right in front of the goal. The goal followed a great chance ​by Messi, ‌who fired a close-range shot that Johnson blocked high into the air, allowing Berterame ⁠to track it down.Messi found his way on to the scoresheet in the ⁠47th minute for his MLS-leading 22nd goal to give Inter Miami a 3-0 edge. The Argentine first fired a shot at the top of the box that was deflected. Suarez controlled the deflection and lobbed a cross to Messi, who ​tapped it past Johnson.Messi recorded his second in the 60th minute when he controlled a back heel from Rodrigo De Paul, jinked past DC United's Lucas Bartlett, and fired the ball just inside the far post.

headline: Manchester United ratings vs Tottenham: Mbeumo strikes but late Solanke goal frustrates Carrick
summary: Manchester United looked set for a much-needed victory but Dominic Solanke scored in stoppage time to salvage a point for 10-man Tottenham at Old Trafford on Saturday. Both teams were in dire need of a win, and when Bryan Mbeumo broke the deadlock in the 73rd minute it seemed as though the pressure would ease on United boss Michael Carrick. Things got worse for Spurs when Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off for a headbutt on Luke Shaw, but Solanke headed home Sandro Tonali's cross deep into stoppage time to earn the visitors a point.“I'm not happy with the amount of points we've got so far, for sure, you know,” said Carrick. “I'm not hiding, there's no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we've got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that's pretty plain.”Man United ratingsSenne Lammens – 5: Mistake gave away possession after two minutes. Solanke spared his blushes. Tottenham had so many chances, yet United again conceded to 10 men. The Belgian fronted up to talk to the media again, but it’s one win from six for United so far, something he didn’t see coming this season. Leny Yoro – 7: In for Dalot who dropped to the bench. Made two last-ditch tackles in the first half, the best of them stopped Van Hecke. Encouraging at right back. As was his performance for France midweek. Lisandro Martinez – 5: Stopped yet another early Spurs attack, but couldn’t get near Solanke, who really should have scored on 51 minutes. A couple of poor passes. Booked for a rash tackle near halfway line. Then poor defending as he looked at his man and not the ball – which went in for Spurs’ equaliser. 3 - Manchester United have failed to win any of their last three Premier League games against sides that have received a red card (D1 L2). Disadvantage? pic.twitter.com/DuSpvymZfu— OptaJoe (@OptaJoe) October 10, 2026Harry Maguire – 6: Heavily involved as United struggled to clear their lines in a frantic, dreadful start. A pirouette on 29 minutes lifted the crowd and proved to be a turning point as the team moved higher.Luke Shaw – 6: It all kicked off on 78 minutes. Outraged by a tackle, he pushed Bentancur to the ground. He was then headed by the Argentine, who got a red. Shaw got a yellow. Before that? United were too slow in the first half and struggled to get the ball from Spurs. But he started the second half brighter and crossed on 47 minutes. Shaw was involved in the build-up for the goal. Smart interception on 84 minutes.Kobbie Mainoo – 6: Lammens left him stranded and Solanke should have scored at the start. Pushed up in second half. Strong block to stop Savio hitting the target on 68 minutes.Youri Tielemans – 5: Slow with the ball and that meant United struggled to connect higher up the pitch. Did put the ball in the net but was offside. Amad Diallo – 6: First start of the season and he was pushed back in front of Yoro as Spurs attacked and attacked. Managed first shot on target on 33 minutes. Ran into a few dead ends. Wild shot over on 48 minutes and came off, as expected, shortly after.Bruno Fernandes – 5: Quiet first half. Worryingly so. Better in second – he moved towards the Stretford End goal after nutmegging Senesi. Shot wide on 63 minutes as he got a lot more of the ball. Booked for a challenge on Van Hecke.Bryan Mbeumo – 7: Got the key goal which put United ahead. Super finish. Before that, a good ball in for Amad after 19 minutes as United managed an attack. Ran and set up Amad on 33 minutes. Showed his pace to get ahead of Senesi on 85 minutes and shoot on target.Matheus Cunha – 7: Striker was more on the left and won possession back in a rare United attack. Urged the fans on in the first half as he asked for more support. Brilliant move after 56 minutes but it was offside. Attacked down the left to set up Mbeumo. Smart use of the ball as United tried to hold on. Swept a shot on target on 89 minutes.Carlos Baleba impressed on his @manutd debut 🇨🇲 pic.twitter.com/rv7RMAqutd— Premier League (@premierleague) October 10, 2026United SubsDiogo Dalot (for Yoro, 58') – 6: First thing he did was get a cross in. Booked in stoppage time.Carlos Baleba (for Tielemans, 58'): Debut for the 22-year-old. Lovely first pass, tackled strongly and incredible pass towards Mbeumo. Impressive technique and running. Joshua Zirkzee (for Amad, 58') – 7: Got a chance from the bench after scoring for the Netherlands in midweek. Effort blocked on 61 minutes. Made a difference with good touches. Defended well at the end. Marcus Rashford (for Cunha, 90') – N/A: Late sub.Ayden Heaven (for Shaw, 90') – N/A: Late sub.

headline: Why international publishers are overlooking Arabic books
summary: For Arabic publishers trying to sell translation rights abroad, the first challenge is getting foreign buyers to consider their books.Many international publishers have little idea of the range available, says Sherif Bakr, general manager of Cairo's Al Arabi Publishing and Distributing.“They don't know what to expect. They don't know what we have. This is why we as an industry needed to extend the variety,” he tells The National from the Frankfurt International Book Fair.Bakr hopes to narrow this gap through the newly launched Arab Voices website, which showcases contemporary literature from across the Arab world. The initiative began in 2020 with a printed catalogue of 32 Egyptian books before expanding online this year.Funded by the EU and launched in July, the platform introduces foreign publishers to books including Palestinian author Bassem Khandaqji's A Mask, the Colour of the Sky – winner of the 2024 International Prize for Arabic Fiction, Egyptian novelist Adel Esmat's At the End of Time and Nora Nagi's The Fuel House.“We now have fantasy, crime, women writing crime novels, women's literature, chick lit, literary fiction and award-winning books. We've also expanded across the Arab world, with 200 titles from 22 countries. We need to give more exposure to writers from across the region, not just the known ones or the famous ones,” Bakr says.Arab Voices joins initiatives such as Leila, an EU-funded European project launched in 2021 to promote contemporary Arabic literature. Based in France, it offers a curated catalogue and resources for publishers and translators, with a focus on Arabic-to-French translation.Meanwhile, the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre is marking the first anniversary of its From Kalima to the World initiative at the book fair on Thursday, announcing 14 new translation and international co-publishing partnerships.For Bakr, the range of books is important, but the selection must also reflect what international publishers are looking for. An open directory would give buyers more titles to sift through without helping them to identify books suited to their markets.“Publishers need a selected, curated list. Something that they know is going to work with them. You can't just put anything,” he says.Literary prize shortlists and winners offer a starting point, although he also considers books that have not received such recognition. A book's success at home is no guarantee of international appeal.“Maybe it's very good locally, but it doesn't travel, or maybe it travels,” he says.Bakr also believes Arab publishers need to be more active at international book fairs, where the emphasis is on networking, rights negotiations and showcasing titles rather than the consumer sales that dominate many regional fairs. He acknowledges the additional costs but believes the investment can pay off.“You have to talk to the publishers and convince them that this book stands up with the others,” he says.International publishers, however, are not always receptive. At a separate Frankfurt discussion on publishing industry challenges, Bakr described how publishers from the Middle East can be overlooked by their foreign counterparts.“We would feel publishers don't reply to us, don't think of us as important,” he said.Foreign publishers and agents can also underestimate the logistical challenges facing regional publishers, including contractual obligations that are far more expensive to fulfil in some markets.Requirements to send free copies to authors, agents and rights holders in several countries can leave Egyptian publishers facing shipping bills greater than the cost of producing the books. Bakr recalls attending fairs with suitcases packed with copies, relying on travelling colleagues to help to deliver them.He also recalls agreeing a $100 advance with a Nordic literary agency, only to struggle to transfer the money because Egyptian bank officials at the time did not understand the purchase of publishing rights. He eventually paid in cash at a book fair. Although restrictions have eased, he says a $100 transfer can still incur about $40 in fees.“We don't have the same banking system,” he says. “We have to be flexible and understanding.”Bakr plans to increase Arab Voices' international outreach after Frankfurt and to expand the platform into a hub carrying publishing news and links to other initiatives.He is reluctant, however, to judge its progress solely by the number of translation deals.“It's not that we have to have a KPI of how many translated books,” he says. “You're building something. It's like soft power. It's about expanding the visibility of what's out there in Arabic literature. There are so many great stories out there, and we just want to help in that effort.”Frankfurt International Book Fair ends on October 11

headline: The Inside Brief: Menzies chief on aviation’s recovery and a lifetime of navigating crises
summary: When you look out of the aircraft window on the apron, the people turning your flight around probably work for Menzies. Its chief executive, Hassan El Houry, manages 65,000 of them across 65 countries and joined me for the launch edition of season two of The Inside Brief.This was days after the security incident on flydubai flight FZ1073, which diverted to Tabuk in Saudi Arabia on September 30 and is now under investigation by UAE authorities. He said the industry's next task is clear.“Airlines need to reinstall confidence in the general public,” he said. What most people do not know, he explained, is how thoroughly staff are screened.“After September 11, airports and airlines introduced an array of security measures for passengers,” Mr El Houry said. “While there are security measures for people that work at airports and airlines, they’re not so much in the spotlight like taking off your shoes and your belt.”That is about to change. “I think what we’ll end up seeing is that a lot of the security measures that are applied to pilots, to cabin crew, to our staff, to airport staff ... will come to the spotlight because it is quite thorough actually.”Every Menzies employee is background-checked and passes through “the same security measures that a passenger does”.And no new bill is coming. “All those security measures are already there,” he said. The bigger pressure is cost.Impact of a deal on the Strait of HormuzJet fuel has risen by 50 per cent or more since the war began, and ticket prices are “two, three, four times more expensive than they were pre-crisis”, Mr El Houry said.Asked whether fuel prices would fall straight away if a lasting peace reopens the Strait of Hormuz, he replied: “Every time there’s been an aviation crisis, we’ve recovered fairly quickly”.After September 11, “it was just a year and a half or two years, and aviation recovered”. Covid-19, the longest crisis, took “about three and a half years”, he said.“When there is some sort of peace and more clarity, I think we’ll recover fairly quickly.”The reason is demand. “Every airline that I’ve been talking to has been telling us that there isn’t a demand problem," he said. “Passengers are still flying. There’s a cost problem.”About five billion passengers will fly this year. “Five billion, that’s a record,” Mr El Houry said. Yet airline profits are expected to halve, from $50 billion last year “to about 25 billion this year”.‘Quitting is permanent’Mr El Houry learnt about risk early. His privileged childhood in Kuwait ended with the Iraqi invasion in 1990. “We were made refugees literally overnight,” he said.The family drove to Baghdad, then Amman, and spent two years in Cyprus. “At any moment you can have a black swan event. You can have a binary event from one to zero literally overnight, and you just have to be resilient enough to overcome it.”Compulsory military service in Lebanon followed. “I would spend 10, 12, 14 hours a day on my feet, and the one idea that kept going through my mind was the pain, the discomfort is temporary, but quitting is permanent.”His tolerance for complaining today? “It’s very low. It’s very low.”The fork in the roadWharton had been his dream since he was 19. It taught him to ask when he does not know. “You have to be humble. You’re not expected to know everything about everything.”Then came the choice: a New York investment bank, with the draw of “walking down Wall Street every day, going up to the 50th floor”, or Agility in Kuwait. “It wasn’t a cash decision,” he said.He chose Agility. “It was probably one of the best decisions I’ve made in my life.”At 28, he was running National Aviation Services, with 200 employees in one country. “Leadership is not a right that you have. You have to earn it.”Today, the combined business is the largest of its kind in the world, and Mr El Houry has the Gulf in his sights. “We don’t need to IPO,” he said. “The barriers to entry in the region are pretty high, but our resolve is much higher.”The Inside Brief with Manus Cranny is available on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and other major platforms.

headline: Arsenal vs Leeds player ratings: Odegaard 8, Guimaraes 7; Calvert-Lewin 7, Trafford 4
summary: Goals from Riccardo Calafiori and substitute Bruno Guimaraes saw Arsenal come from behind to beat Leeds United 2-1 on Saturday.Leeds, who were on top for an hour, had led through James Justin's 55th-minute opener, and it looked like being another difficult afternoon for the champions after their 3-0 defeat to Brighton immediately before the international break. However, Calafiori's equaliser proved the turning point, and was quickly followed by a triple substitution by home boss Mikel Arteta to cement the shift in momentum in favour of his side. One of those subs was Guimaraes, and the Brazil midfielder started and finished a flowing team move to complete the turnaround and secure all three points. “It feels unbelievable. I felt in the last game against Brighton we were not at the level. Today the mentality was bouncing back,” said Guimaraes.“This is my first official game at home. It feels unbelievable to score and it's an important goal, three important points. Great finish and I am very happy.”Arsenal ratingsDavid Raya – 7: Great save to thwart Gudmundsson at end of first half. Kept busy by Leeds, and generally up to challenge. Ben White – 6: Nodded back into a good area for equaliser that Arsenal scarcely deserved at the time. Ezri Konsa – 7: Had his hands full with Calvert-Lewin but had a strong game and distribution improved as match went on. Gabriel – 6: Few sloppy moments from Brazil defender and trademark set-piece threat was absent. Riccardo Calafiori – 7: Gambled and made great run into box to score equaliser and get his team back in the game. Myles Lewis-Skelly – 5: Difficult day after positive start to the season and impressive performances for England. Slow on the ball and ineffective passing. BACK WITH A BANG 💥 pic.twitter.com/uXHc3m0DtX— Arsenal (@Arsenal) October 10, 2026Declan Rice – 7: Enjoyed a rare rest over the international break but struggled as Leeds pressed and disrupted.
