headline: Max Verstappen criticises Singapore track after claiming sprint and pole double
summary: Red Bull's Max Verstappen claimed a double in Singapore on Saturday as he won a chaotic sprint race before clinching pole position for Sunday's Grand Prix. The Dutchman has largely endured a frustrating campaign but will now be fancied to make it back-to-back race victories after his triumph at the Bahrain Grand Prix, hosted in Malaysia last weekend. That breakthrough followed a run of three successive podiums for the four-time world champion.Verstappen will have Ferrari's Charles Leclerc alongside ​him ‌on the ⁠front ​row while ​Lewis ‌Hamilton was ⁠third-fastest. Championship leader ⁠Kimi Antonelli was only fourth-fastest for Mercedes.The result means Verstappen will be on pole for his 250th F1 race and for the first time at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Earlier in the day, Verstappen, 29, had showcased his pace by winning an eventful sprint race staged in tricky conditions.Russell was leading, with the track still wet from an earlier downpour, when he drifted a little wide at the final corner of the first lap and lost control. His Mercedes flew across the track and into the wall.QUALIFYING TOP 10 ✨VerstappenLeclerc Hamilton AntonelliNorrisRussellPiastriGasly Lawson Lindblad#F1 #SingaporeGP pic.twitter.com/bESpfx8Efw— Formula 1 (@F1) October 10, 2026Ferrari's Hamilton took second place, having made a flying start from sixth on the grid with teammate Leclerc taking third.A late collision between the McLarens as Lando Norris tried to pass Oscar Piastri lifted Antonelli into fourth place. The result, combined with Russell's retirement, stretched the Italian's overall lead in the championship to 89 points.Rain had delayed the start of the inaugural sprint at Marina Bay, and with overtaking nearly impossible, the only drama came in the form of collisions and a record nine retirements.“I think ⁠we shouldn't host a sprint where you can't pass,” Verstappen told ​reporters after ⁠notching his first victory at ‌the circuit.“I'm fine, I just do my thing … but it's not what I like. The overtake ​mode, it barely does anything here. You don't really gain a lot on the straights … we need to have a longer straight or like more of a proper hairpin to overtake.”

headline: The imagined Palestinian landscapes of Jordan Nassar's tatreez panels
summary: The Palestinian poet Mahmoud Darwish once dedicated a poem to the frustration he felt at his inability to describe a cloud. Staring up at the sky while walking alone on an unnamed mountain, he wrote that the clouds were “like a cottoned ginned by wind, like a white idea about the meaning of existence”.That poem – and presumably Darwish’ failing words – guides a new series of contemporary artworks by the New York artist Jordan Nassar, on display at No 9 Cork Street in London. The presentation by the Dubai gallery The Third Line is the artist’s first in the UK in a decade.The Manhattan-born Nassar often works with tatreez, a Palestinian cross-stitch embroidery to create fictive landscapes combined with the tradition’s abstract patterning.The piece They Build Homes with Clouds (2026) places green, red and purple-hued mountains against an ochre sky, and beyond them, the sea, embroidered on canvas. The panel is surrounded by four smaller ones depicting a pattern of colourful embroidered squares. The contrast between the repetitive square motifs of tatreez and the organic shapes of the mountain landscapes is startling.Nassar describes these landscapes as “versions of Palestine as they exist in the minds of the diaspora”. “They are the Palestine I heard stories about growing up, half made of imagination. They are dreamlands and utopias that are colourful and fantastical – beautiful and romantic, but bittersweet,” he says.But the sunny, warm-coloured and arid scenes could equally be from an American road movie at the point of driving through the Mojave or Sonoran deserts.The panels are moveable, and appear in distinct geometrical shapes which the artist said were inspired by the Iranian-American artist Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian, who used a similar modular method in her series Convertibles. Farmanfarmaian had pioneered a unique style blending mirror-mosaic technique with influences from postwar abstract expressionism she was exposed to as a student in New York.Nassar says his exploration of Palestinian identity is driven by his own upbringing as a New Yorker. His father is of Palestinian heritage and his mother is Polish. He recalled his childhood in a city that embraced its status as the gateway into the land of immigrants that is the US.“I grew up in the '90s in New York, where multiculturalism was cool. These days people get mad if you're asking about someone's background. But when I was little, that was fine to ask, because everyone was from somewhere,” he told The National. “It was just sharing information because you're curious about people, and you want to tell them about where your family's from,” he said.His paternal grandfather migrated to the US in the 1910s before the Nakba and was a central figure in establishing the Arab American community in the inner suburb of Yonkers. He later sponsored the arrival of hundreds of families displaced by the Nakba.But being American then was a priority for the family as it was for all of the city's fresh wave of immigrants. Nassar’s grandfather opened a cafe that sold hamburgers and milkshakes, and did not teach his children Arabic. “They were never taught Arabic because in the 1940s, '50s and '60s, the mindset was: we're American now, so we speak English,” he said.Questions about belonging and the diaspora experience are therefore central to the work. “That really taps into feelings of not feeling Palestinian enough because I'm ‘only half’, and I grew up in New York. There's this sense (that) I don't do it right,” he said.“I don't speak Arabic fluently and natively. We cook some of the dishes that I grew up with differently than they do in Palestine because it trickled down through generations,” he said. “My work is very American. It's like: I'm gonna do it, do something that's my culture, but also do it my way and that's individual.”Nassar has travelled often to Palestine, and the process behind his work engages with the challenges linked to Israel’s occupation – even if he does not make this explicit. He designs the panels and then commissions the embroideries from craftswomen living in the West Bank.But it can take weeks to have the works taken out of the West Bank and posted to the US. “There’s definitely a consideration of doing things early and assuming that everything is going to have a delay. It can't be tight deadlines,” he said.“First I buy the fabric and ship it to the workshop in Ramallah, because I want this specific fabric,” he said. A friend picks up the finished embroideries and has them driven from the West Bank to Tel Aviv, then Jaffa. Then, a friend in Jaffa posts the fabrics by regular mail to the US – which Nassar says is the simplest step in the process. “She just breaks it up into boxes and sends it in Israel Post, and it honestly comes so fast,” he said. “That’s way faster than trying to ship it from Palestine."The second part of the exhibition reflects on archaeology and the politics of cultural heritage in conflict. A series of hand-cut glass mosaics, inspired by those of the Byzantine church in Jabalia, Gaza, depict an orange tree, a lion, a man and patterning from the original church. Local archaeologists in Gaza say the church was damaged by Israeli shelling. “It has been damaged for sure in the bombing, but we don't know the extent, so it may not be there at all any more,” said Nassar. Nassar’s interest in Byzantine mosaics came from seeing two panels at Ben Gurion International Airport that had been extracted from a church in what is now northern Israel. “That led into this investigation into the use of archaeology and antiquities, not only for propaganda, but for land grabbing,” he said. He also refers to the Roman and Byzantine ruins of Sabastia near Nablus, which Israel recently announced it would expropriate and develop into a tourism hub. “Israel is claiming that they're preserving a historical site. Concurrently, that means that they would have to block off Palestinian access, take more land, and build roads to these sites that then are bifurcating Palestinian land,” he said. Nassar therefore hopes these recreations of the works can be enjoyed outside of these hotly politicised contexts. “They exist outside of being used as propaganda. They can just exist as something for themselves for their own sake,” he said.“I'm not trying to mimic something that looks 2,000 years old. I'm also not trying to match every single colour and try to be perfect. I'm definitely taking liberties,' he said.Nassar wants his work to be “universal” and an expression of daily life, rather than didactic. “Art is about sharing this human experience with other people,” he said. “I'm not trying to make informational work about Palestine because that's not what art is for me,” he said.“I am very opinionated about activism and art. I don't really know if art is the best venue for these things. For me, it's more about human connection,” he said. “It doesn't matter where your family is from. If you have this diaspora experience, hopefully you feel a connection."

headline: Hawkish sentiment returns to IMF and World Bank meetings
summary: The world’s finance ministers and central bankers are set to gather for this year’s IMF and World Bank annual meetings as a new set of inflationary drivers descends on the global economy.This year, representatives from the IMF and World Bank member countries will meet in Bangkok, Thailand, from Monday. The meetings are typically held in Washington for two consecutive years and in another member country every third year. The 2029 annual meetings will be held in Abu Dhabi.During the meetings, the Bretton Woods institutions’ board of governors hold discussions on how international monetary issues should be addressed, while other talks are held on emerging economic trends and regional programmes.This year's meetings come amid a renewed threat of inflation. Supply disruptions from the Iran war are pushing up energy prices, with the Strait of Hormuz’s prolonged partial closure driving the price for Brent crude roughly 30 per cent higher than prewar levels.The expansion of artificial intelligence is placing additional pressure on electricity demand, and the massive debt issuance it requires partially accounts for the recent rise in bond yields, also driven by the US national debt reaching $40 trillion.The global economy is still grappling with the inflationary after-effects of the Covid-19 pandemic and Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Inflation has remained above 2 per cent in the US for more than five years.“While this rise in inflation pales in comparison with what we saw in the immediate wake of the pandemic, it is large enough to be of real concern to central banks, many of whom hadn't wrestled inflation back to its target before this episode had begun,” Karen Dynan, non-resident senior fellow at the Peterson Institute, said during a round-table discussion on Tuesday in Washington.Speaking in Singapore on Tuesday, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said the environment was right for most countries to adopt a “prudently hawkish” posture.The US Federal Reserve, the world’s most influential central bank, entered a new tightening cycle in September after it raised interest rates by a quarter point. The European Central Bank and Bank of Japan have also recently raised rates due to rising inflation. The Bank of England is expected to hike rates next month.Meanwhile, US government borrowing costs have reached multi-decade highs. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, recorded a 24-year high this week. Bond yields in Germany, the UK and Japan are also on the rise.Against this backdrop, Ms Georgieva suggested austerity was back on the menu for advanced economies. “After a succession of shocks where, each time, fiscal policy has had to step in to cushion the impact, populations have grown accustomed to state support. Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” she said.Meeting the moment?The question persists whether the IMF and World Bank have done enough to support low-income and conflict-afflicted countries facing higher funding costs, slower growth and shrinking aid flows.“We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countries,” said Marina Zucker-Marques, a senior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance Initiative.We are living a perfect storm at this moment, especially for low-income countriesSenior academic researcher at Boston University's Global Economic Governance InitiativeSince the Iran war broke out at the end of February, the World Bank has pledged up to $60 billion in financing to help countries absorb the impact of the conflict's energy shock. The African Development Bank Group has launched a $5.1 billion framework to offset the impact of the war's energy and fertiliser crisis on the continent. The Asian Development Bank said it is mobilising $4 billion in financing to help countries withstand the war's impact.The IMF last week said it would provide non-financial support to war-torn Yemen, and reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that would unlock $1.21 billion for the country that is dependent on Gulf energy imports. Bangladesh has also requested a programme due to the war's impact.“The international financial institutions are weathering these crises remarkably well compared to other multilaterals,” Rachel Glennerster, president of the Centre for Global Development, said during a webinar.However, Ms Zucker-Marques questioned how eager low-income countries might be for more funding from the IMF, citing the fund's conditionality for programmes. Ms Georgieva said in April that the fund expected at least a dozen countries, including several in sub-Saharan Africa, to seek new loan programmes to respond to the war's impact on energy prices and supply chain disruptions.The US central bank's new tightening cycle is also expected to lead to higher borrowing costs for low-income countries seeking loans. The Federal Reserve's rate-setting activity directly influences borrowing costs from the IMF, World Bank and other multi-development banks.Traders anticipate the Fed will raise interest rates three more times by July 2027, according to CME Group data.“A lot of people are talking about the bond yields, which is quite important for countries that have access to markets, but also we need to pay attention that the interest rate hike in the US is actually increasing the tide to all types of lending,” Ms Zucker-Marques said.

headline: Menzies Aviation’s Hassan El-Houry on navigating war, airline pressures and global expansion
summary: The war in the Middle East is putting the global aviation industry under unprecedented pressure. Flight schedules have become unpredictable, fuel costs have soared and ticket prices have risen sharply. Yet demand for air travel remains strong, with a record five billion passengers expected to fly this year.For Hassan El-Houry, chief executive officer of Menzies Aviation, one of the world's largest aviation services companies, the challenge is keeping operations running across 365 airports in 65 countries while airlines face a sharp squeeze on profitability.In this episode of The Inside Brief, Manus Cranny speaks to Mr El-Houry about the impact of the conflict on global aviation and why he expects the industry to recover quickly once stability returns.Mr El-Houry also discusses the company's ambitious expansion plans in the Middle East, particularly the UAE, following its acquisition of American aviation services company G2 Secure Staff. He explains why Menzies is determined to compete in the region, whether an IPO is on the table, and why delays to Heathrow's third runway risk weakening Britain's position as a global aviation hub.The conversation also turns to Mr El-Houry's remarkable journey from becoming a refugee during Iraq's invasion of Kuwait to leading a global business. He reflects on the lessons he learnt from military service, becoming a chief executive at just 28, and why human connection and critical thinking remain indispensable in the age of AI.The Inside Brief with Manus Cranny is available on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Spotify and other major platforms.

headline: WhatsApp launches new safety controls: What UAE parents need to know
summary: As the UAE prepares to restrict social media for children under 15, WhatsApp has introduced new features that give parents firmer control over their teenagers' online footprints. Parents will not be able to read the messages their teenagers send or receive. The new features are meant to help parents and teenagers build safer online habits together, offering oversight of potential risks without constant monitoring.WhatsApp says the tools are flexible and can be adjusted or disabled as family needs evolve. Parents can use a six-digit Parent PIN to lock specific privacy settings on a teenager's account. If a teenager tries to change certain restrictions, such as who can view their profile picture, Last Seen status, or add them to groups, they need parental approval.The controls also provide notifications to keep parents informed of changes in their teenager's online activity. Parents receive alerts when their teenager joins or leaves a group, when a group grows significantly, or when a new contact is added.Parents can set who can view their teenager's status updates, whose status updates the teen can access, and how the teen discovers or follows public WhatsApp channels.The update also includes artificial intelligence features. Parents can select either the default 13+ Meta AI experience or a stricter Limited Content option that restricts sensitive topics and adds safeguards. The stricter mode disables private or incognito AI interactions.These controls do not grant parents access to personal messages or calls. End-to-end encryption ensures these remain protected.Balancing oversight with privacyThese controls prompt important questions. How can technology companies protect young users without limiting their independence? Parents need tools to identify risks, while teenagers require opportunities to develop judgment, build trust and learn digital responsibility.Andreas Hassellof, founder and chief executive of technology company Ombori, believes WhatsApp is moving towards a useful balance between parental visibility and personal privacy.“Good digital safety should create visibility without turning childhood into surveillance,” he said.Mr Hassellof said parents should have access to indicators of potentially concerning activity without monitoring every aspect of their teenager's digital life. For example, changes in group membership can prompt parents to check in with their child without needing access to group messages.He added that effective digital safety required both protection and the gradual development of judgment. Platforms face the challenge of giving parents meaningful ways to intervene while letting teenagers build confidence and responsibility in managing their online interactions.Mili Mehta, a Dubai resident and parent of a 15-year-old, welcomed the initiative.“As a parent, I think the parental code is a great initiative. It gives parents greater control over their teen's privacy settings and offers an added layer of safety,” she said.However, Ms Mehta noted that her teenager used WhatsApp less frequently than other platforms. She believes parental controls should extend to the services young people use most, such as Snapchat and Instagram, while respecting their need for independence and privacy.Her concern highlights a limitation of platform-specific safety measures: effective controls on one service cannot address all risks teenagers may face on other platforms.Jenita Clara, a UAE resident and mother of a 13-year-old, also supports the new controls, particularly the Parent PIN and notifications that can help parents identify potential risks early.Ms Clara described an incident where her child was added to a group by someone he barely knew, exposing him to inappropriate videos and language before she became aware. She said this experience showed how easily children can encounter unsuitable content and how hard it can be to leave a group or speak up when pressured.For Ms Clara, parental controls are not about distrust; they are an added safeguard. She believes restrictions on who can add children to groups helps parents to intervene earlier and create opportunities to discuss appropriate online behaviour.Her experience shows why privacy settings and group-related alerts matter, even when parents cannot access the conversations themselves.Should parental controls be on by default?WhatsApp's controls are optional and disabled by default, allowing families to choose whether to activate them. This raises a broader debate about whether platforms should automatically enable age-appropriate safety features for users under 18 or allow families to opt in.Mr Hassellof said platforms should make their strongest age-appropriate protections easy to activate, while allowing families flexibility in choosing the level of oversight they find appropriate.“Safety by design should become the default thinking, even when every control does not need to be switched on by default,” he said.He noted that teenagers vary in maturity and independence. A 13-year-old may require more support than a 17-year-old, so a single set of controls may not suit every family or stage of development.Platforms can make protective settings prominent, clearly explain their benefits, and offer simple ways to configure them, without assuming every teenager requires the same level of supervision.An opt-in approach allows families to discuss expectations and set boundaries together, but it also places greater responsibility on parents to understand available controls and decide when to use them.The broader challenge for technology companies is to make safer choices accessible without making digital independence an all-or-nothing decision.Age-based AI filters are only first stepAs artificial intelligence becomes part of everyday digital services, ensuring young people's safety remains a challenge for parents.Mr Hasselof said age-based filters offer an important first layer of protection, but they cannot address all risks associated with AI interactions.“The next generation of AI safety will be measured by how well systems understand context, not simply how well they recognise age,” he said.A teenager asking an ordinary question and one seeking help with a sensitive or distressing issue may be the same age, but the appropriate AI response could differ greatly. Mr Hassellof also noted that young users might struggle to distinguish factual information from inference or confidently delivered but inaccurate AI-generated answers.He believes age-appropriate behaviour should be integrated into AI products from the outset.Mr Hassellof expects WhatsApp's announcement to raise standards across messaging and social media, as parents increasingly seek consistent protection across the services their children use.“Once safety becomes part of the user experience, it becomes part of the platform's baseline,” he said.

headline: My Own Home: Meet the family who bought their Sharjah home while living in Turkey
summary: My Own Home takes you inside a reader-owned property to ask how much they paid, why they decided to buy and what they have done with it since moving inLaila Ahmed and her family decided they wanted to buy a home in the UAE before completing their relocation from Turkey.She and her husband began exploring the option of moving in 2023 with a specific idea of what they wanted from a property, including privacy and the feeling that it was a place where they could put down roots.They learned about Sharjah Sustainable City later that year and within a week had bought a four-bedroom villa off-plan.Both Canadians with Egyptian heritage, Ms Ahmed, 37, and her husband, Karim, 42, who works in the digital technology sector, paid Dh2.19 million and moved into their home in December 2024.Ms Ahmed, a freelance editor, showed The National around the home she also shared with her daughter Jannah, aged seven; her sons Adam, aged six, and Ibrahim, aged five; and their maid.Please tell us about your homeWe bought a four-bedroom townhouse villa with five bathrooms in phase three of Sustainable City. It has formal and informal living areas. We also have the maid’s room.We have a backyard and two parking spots where we installed an EV charger because we own a Tesla. I have not seen anything remotely close to the layout here. The first things we looked at were the square footage and the floor plan. The use of space is ingenious.And the size of the bedrooms is great. The kids don’t feel like they’re in little caves or anything. It’s a mid-unit. We didn’t want a standalone villa because we felt we would be deprived of that sense of community; we wouldn't really get to know the neighbours.Why did you decide to buy your home?Initially we were going to rent, and then we realised that renting didn't make sense financially. We decided to explore some options, so my husband came on an exploratory trip to look at different projects.He heard about Sustainable City from someone, but because it was the last day, he wasn't able to check it out. We looked it up and it really caught our eye, so we decided to ask one of our friends who lived there to check out the show villa. Our friend went on a Wednesday, and by that Saturday we had made the decision to buy. It was a bit of a gamble, but my husband is a very quick decision-maker.What drew you to this development?We liked the concept and the vision. The developers were delivering, and it felt like a very strong and solid option, a realistic project that would meet our needs in terms of belonging, children's safety and the amenities provided.When we moved to Sharjah, we initially rented a place five minutes away because we wanted the kids to start school in the same district. Later, we were able to move in.Its location is very convenient. We can take the E611 and the E311. We are really close to Sharjah Airport.What made you choose Sharjah?Before moving here, we lived in Turkey for three years, and before that we lived in Canada. We never expected to be in this part of the world.We decided to move to Sharjah because we were looking for a slightly different lifestyle — one that was more community-orientated — and safety was a major factor.We specifically wanted Sharjah because we felt like it had more of the family aspect we were looking for. The children’s school is right by the community, so it’s wonderful for us.What upgrades have you made?The first thing we did was redo the backyard because we knew the kids needed to use it. We’ve completely redone it in a way more conducive to this stage of life, especially with three kids. They want to be able to run around a bit, and we’ve been getting into gardening.We have a deck area where the adults can relax, and we’ve laid some grass. We also have a mini barbecue area and some seating. Because we’re a very active family, we have scooters and bikes. There’s a utility area where we store all of those items.Inside, I really love design. It's kind of a side hobby, and coming from a very DIY country, I did all the painting myself. I've done whatever modifications we've made to the house, except where we've installed glass doors to separate the formal and informal living spaces. That has added a really nice touch to the place.Then it was just picking out art and furniture, and I switched out the kitchen sink because I wanted a granite sink. I changed the faucets to match the aesthetic.I'm leaving the boys' room as it is for now because they are boys who destroy everything, so it will happen eventually.What amenities do you have?There is a gym, a pool and parks. We also have basketball courts, multi-purpose courts that can be used for different sports, and soccer fields. A mosque is being built.We have a book club, a walking group and many other activities being set up by the neighbours. The community spirit is strong.There is a cycling and running track that goes around the city. You don’t feel like you’re walking in the desert because of the greenery and the way they’ve thought about the landscaping.A mall is being built. Some coffee shops and a courtyard with restaurants have opened nearby. The area has developed so much in just the two years we’ve been here. I feel like I’m in a resort.Do you plan to sell or rent it if you move?Who knows if it will be our forever home or if it’s just a home for this phase of our lives. For right now, it’s great, and it’s an investment, so in future we know we will get our money back and more.We’re very content where we are right now, but we are also excited about what’s to come. It’s been great living here and the kids are so happy; they have their friends from school.For now, we’re treating it as our forever home. That’s why we made the modifications because we want it to feel like ours. In terms of renting or selling, we would probably sell it because we've had bad experiences with renters.Do you plan to buy more property?If we had the extra money, we probably would buy here. But right now, we’re happy with just owning the one home. We’re happy with putting our time and effort and investment into it.

headline: Twelve killed and 309 wounded in attack on Riyadh airport
summary: At least 12 people died and 309 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday afternoon.Those killed included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals – two Bangladeshis and one each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan – the General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Sunday.The attack was the third on King Khalid International Airport this week by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. It was the deadliest strike on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade and no threat alert was sounded by the kingdom's warning system.The injured, including some in critical condition, were receiving treatment at several hospitals, the aviation authority said. The UK described the incident as “serious” and airlines including Kuwait’s national carrier cancelled flights.US President Donald Trump said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. “What happened in Saudi Arabia is not acceptable,” he told reporters on Saturday evening on his return to Washington from a political rally. Earlier in the day, Mr Trump said the US may consider whether to join the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthi rebels.“We may. We’re going to look at it," he said.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed an American had been killed in the "reprehensible" attacks.The United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today’s strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen.These reprehensible attacks…— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 10, 2026Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.This week's ⁠two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. The Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond to the attacks.About 260 flights to and from Riyadh were cancelled on Saturday and another 219 were delayed, according to data from air traffic monitor Flightradar24.The Houthis are facing a ground offensive from the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. Soldiers from the internationally recognised Yemeni government and the Saudi air force have been working to take back territory seized by the rebels over the past month near the strategic Bab Al Mandeb Strait.The coalition says it has gained ground, including by retaking the Red Sea port city of Mokha. The Saudi-led group says it aims to “eliminate” the Houthis, who control territory that is home to about 70 per cent of Yemen’s population, including the capital, Sanaa.Saudi ​Arabia and the Yemeni government have carried out hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis claimed some of the raids have killed civilians including women and children.
body_text:
At least 12 people died and 309 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh on Saturday afternoon.

Those killed included four Saudi citizens and eight foreign nationals – two Bangladeshis and one each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan – the General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Sunday.

The attack was the third on King Khalid International Airport this week by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. It was the deadliest strike on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade and no threat alert was sounded by the kingdom's warning system.

EditorialThe Houthis have no answer for Yemen's problems

The injured, including some in critical condition, were receiving treatment at several hospitals, the aviation authority said.

The UK described the incident as “serious” and airlines including Kuwait’s national carrier cancelled flights.

US President Donald Trump said he planned to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

“What happened in Saudi Arabia is not acceptable,” he told reporters on Saturday evening on his return to Washington from a political rally. Earlier in the day, Mr Trump said the US may consider whether to join the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthi rebels.

“We may. We’re going to look at it," he said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed an American had been killed in the "reprehensible" attacks.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.

This week's ⁠two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. The Saudi-led military coalition vowed to respond to the attacks.

About 260 flights to and from Riyadh were cancelled on Saturday and another 219 were delayed, according to data from air traffic monitor Flightradar24.

The Houthis are facing a ground offensive from the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. Soldiers from the internationally recognised Yemeni government and the Saudi air force have been working to take back territory seized by the rebels over the past month near the strategic Bab Al Mandeb Strait.

The coalition says it has gained ground, including by retaking the Red Sea port city of Mokha. The Saudi-led group says it aims to “eliminate” the Houthis, who control territory that is home to about 70 per cent of Yemen’s population, including the capital, Sanaa.

Saudi ​Arabia and the Yemeni government have carried out hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis claimed some of the raids have killed civilians including women and children.

analysis.framing: The article reports the deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport through casualty figures, official statements, and contextual background on the Yemen conflict, maintaining a largely factual and attribution-based tone.

loaded_language.explanation: The label 'Iran-backed' attributes geopolitical sponsorship and carries an implicit adversarial framing, while 'rebels' is a contested term that some outlets replace with 'fighters' or 'militants'.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Houthi forces, who receive support from Iran

loaded_language.explanation: The verb 'flooded' is an emotive metaphor that conveys overwhelming strain and heightens the sense of crisis beyond a neutral description of patient volume.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Hospitals received a large number of wounded patients

loaded_language.explanation: This is a quoted characterization from Secretary Rubio, but its inclusion without distancing language adopts an emotionally charged, condemnatory term into the article's own reporting.

loaded_language.quote: deadliest strike on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade
loaded_language.explanation: The superlative 'deadliest' is dramatic and emphasizes the severity of the attack, though it is a factual comparison that may be verifiable.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: the highest death toll from an attack on Saudi Arabia in over ten years

omissions: No mention of the Houthi claim of responsibility or their stated rationale for the attack.
No details on the type of weapon used (e.g., missile, drone) or the specific target within the airport.
No reporting on civilian casualties from Saudi-led coalition strikes in Yemen beyond a brief mention of Houthi claims.
No independent verification of the casualty figures or the identity of the attackers beyond Saudi and US statements.
No mention of the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Yemen or the broader context of the war.

headline: UAE National Guard rescues 22 people after oil tanker catches fire
summary: The UAE National Guard's Coast Guard division rescued 22 people after a fire broke out on an oil tanker in the Arabian Gulf.A specialised coast guard team responded to the ship's report of a fire and located the tanker. The crew members were rescued and underwent first aid procedures before being transferred to relevant authorities. The rescued individuals were all Asian nationals. The Coast Guard's swift response demonstrated the operational readiness of the country's maritime personnel, who are trained for emergencies in international waters, the National Guard said. All the individuals rescued were in stable medical condition. This incident highlights the vital role of the UAE's maritime security forces in protecting lives in the Arabian Gulf, a key global shipping lane.The National Guard's Coast Guard division collaborates with federal and emirate-level agencies to ensure comprehensive coverage of the UAE's coastline and the broader Arabian Gulf, where maritime incidents are common due to heavy vessel traffic.

headline: Dubai Police says deepfakes getting harder to detect
summary: Dubai Police has warned of the increasing dangers as artificial intelligence makes fake videos and voices harder to detect.A study by the force's Future Foresight Centre has found that rapidly advancing deepfake technologies pose multiple threats that impact public safety, information credibility, the reliability of digital evidence and related decision-making.The research warns that AI-generated content is increasingly difficult to distinguish from authentic material, making manipulated videos, images and audio more convincing. This could enable criminals to better impersonate people, steal identities, deceive the public and spread misinformation.The study coincides with Cybersecurity Awareness Month, observed every October, and forms part of the Ministry of Interior’s Safe UAE Through Your Digital Awareness campaign.When seeing is no longer believingA key finding is that the deepfake challenge extends beyond detecting fabricated content. As manipulation techniques advance, people may increasingly suspect genuine photographs, videos and audio, making it harder to know what to trust.The study highlights the need to verify the origin, authenticity and integrity of digital content to protect individuals and institutions from deception and misinformation.Hamdan Al Ghassiya, director of the Future Foresight Centre at Dubai Police, said generative AI's implications went beyond identifying manipulated material, raising broader concerns about continued trust in genuine digital information.Dr Al Ghassiya warned that those capabilities could enable more sophisticated identity theft, impersonation, fraud, and information manipulation.Proving what is realThis issue presents significant challenges for security authorities, especially when assessing digital evidence in investigations and decision-making. More convincing deepfakes could undermine the reliability of recordings and other digital material, making verification essential for future security operations.Dr Al Ghassiya emphasised that technology alone cannot address the challenges posed by deepfakes. The study calls for a comprehensive approach combining public awareness, digital verification skills and institutional preparedness.The study urges security organisations to be proactive, monitor technological developments, and identify emerging risks before new criminal techniques become widespread, rather than responding after they appear.

headline: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postpones elections to September 2027
summary: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree on Saturday cancelling the legislative elections scheduled for November this year and setting a new date, together with the presidential vote, for September 2027.The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, leading to the rift between the group and the ruling Fatah party. Fatah leader and Palestinian Authority President Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree.The National reported this week that the legislative elections would be postponed, according to sources from the main Palestinian factions.The presidential vote had been due to take place next year, but the decree announced by Mr Abbas on Saturday sets September 11, 2027 as the date for both votes, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation approved the postponement and in a statement said the delay was due to a lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.Election commission head Jamil Al Khalidi told Palestinian media this week that preparations were being made to hold elections in Gaza and the West Bank despite security, logistical and technical hurdles.He said alternatives to traditional ballot boxes and voting ink were being sourced, as Israel continues to block their entry into Gaza.Sources from different factions said the delay was mainly linked to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. Attempts to unite the political factions have often failed due to disagreements about the way forward for Palestine.Systemic problems mean Palestine has lacked a suitable environment for elections for decades. Under an increasingly deadly and aggressive Israeli occupation, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling circle of support.Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.
body_text:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree on Saturday cancelling the legislative elections scheduled for November this year and setting a new date, together with the presidential vote, for September 2027.

The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, leading to the rift between the group and the ruling Fatah party. Fatah leader and Palestinian Authority President Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree.

The National reported this week that the legislative elections would be postponed, according to sources from the main Palestinian factions.

The presidential vote had been due to take place next year, but the decree announced by Mr Abbas on Saturday sets September 11, 2027 as the date for both votes, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.

The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation approved the postponement and in a statement said the delay was due to a lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

Election commission head Jamil Al Khalidi told Palestinian media this week that preparations were being made to hold elections in Gaza and the West Bank despite security, logistical and technical hurdles.

He said alternatives to traditional ballot boxes and voting ink were being sourced, as Israel continues to block their entry into Gaza.

Sources from different factions said the delay was mainly linked to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. Attempts to unite the political factions have often failed due to disagreements about the way forward for Palestine.

Systemic problems mean Palestine has lacked a suitable environment for elections for decades. Under an increasingly deadly and aggressive Israeli occupation, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.

High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling circle of support.

Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.

analysis.framing: The article frames Abbas's election postponement as the act of an unpopular, term-overstaying leader, while situating the delay within Israeli occupation and internal Palestinian division.

loaded_language.quote: has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree
loaded_language.explanation: Combines a precise factual claim with the editorializing verb 'overstayed' and the loaded phrase 'rules by decree', which implies authoritarian governance.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: has remained in office 17 years past the end of his elected term and governs through decrees

loaded_language.quote: increasingly deadly and aggressive Israeli occupation
loaded_language.explanation: The adjectives 'deadly' and 'aggressive' are emotionally charged and editorialize the nature of the occupation rather than describing it neutrally.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Israeli occupation, which has intensified and resulted in rising casualties

loaded_language.quote: state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed
loaded_language.explanation: The hyperbolic verb 'collapsed' paints a dramatic picture of systemic failure without qualification.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: state institutions, finances and the political scene have severely deteriorated

loaded_language.explanation: The adjective 'dwindling' is a subjective characterization suggesting inevitable decline, rather than a neutral description of the size of his support base.
The adverb 'increasingly' implies a trend without providing comparative data, adding an editorial tone to the poll finding.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: unpopular, according to an August poll

omissions: No mention of the specific reasons cited by Abbas or Fatah for the delay beyond the PLO statement, such as the need to prepare election infrastructure or the refusal of Hamas to participate under current conditions.
No reaction or statement from Hamas or other opposition factions regarding the postponement.
No mention of international reactions, such as from the US, EU, or UN, to the cancellation of elections.
No detail on the legal or constitutional basis for extending the presidential term or postponing elections.
No mention of the 2021 election cancellation, which was also postponed indefinitely by Abbas, providing context for repeated delays.

headline: Supporters of jailed former Pakistani leader Imran Khan march towards Islamabad
summary: Thousands of supporters of jailed former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan were marching towards Islamabad on Saturday to demand his release.Khan has been in jail since 2023 and his health is in a critical condition, supporters and family warn. Pakistan's government has said it will not allow the march to enter the capital due to security concerns. “The federal government will take all possible measures to maintain peace and promote public development in the province,” said a government statement.Supporters of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party began their “long march” last Sunday, demanding his release and voicing anti-government sentiment fuelled by harsh economic conditions. Some protesters are carrying red-and-green party flags or holding pictures of Khan.The popular former cricket star has been behind bars since August 2023 and faces scores of charges, ranging from corruption to treason, following anti-establishment riots in the same year.He and his legal team reject the allegations, describing them as politically motivated cases aimed at neutralising his popularity. Khan's sons have been warning about his deteriorating health since last year. His ​lawyers say he has lost significant vision in his right eye while in prison.Last week, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urged the PTI to call off the march and re-enter negotiations with the government. The talks had hit an impasse in the early hours of last Sunday before the march began.The PTI has long accused the government of keeping Mr Khan in prison for convictions secured in politically motivated cases, charges the government rejects.Mr Sharif said the demonstration would have a negative impact on the economy, and warned that undermining the government's efforts would be met with the force of law.“We will not allow this to happen. The law will take its course. Protecting the lives and property of the people is our responsibility, and we will ensure this by all means,” the Prime Minister said.The government has been preparing for weeks for the arrival of demonstrators in Islamabad. The march was first slated for September 27 before being postponed until last Sunday.

headline: Foggy mornings and scattered rain expected across UAE until Tuesday
summary: Drivers travelling between Dubai and Abu Dhabi face more fog in the coming days after poor visibility slowed journeys last week and prompted police to lower speed limits.Abu Dhabi Police urged drivers to exercise caution, reduced speed limits to 80kph on several roads and banned lorries from motorways during poor visibility. Major roads across the Emirates experienced heavy traffic after the fog cleared, causing further traffic delays.Ahmed Habib, from the National Centre of Meteorology, told The National that fog could persist until Tuesday, with varying intensity each day. He said coastal and western areas were particularly susceptible because of the combination of cooling temperatures and high humidity.What is causing the heavy fog?Light winds, high humidity and decreasing temperatures create favourable conditions for low fog. Wind speeds below 10kph allow moisture to accumulate near the ground.Dr Habib explained that as temperatures drop at night, humid air near the surface cools, causing water vapour to condense into droplets and form fog. Fog usually clears as temperatures rise after sunrise or winds increase.The weather department forecast humid conditions overnight and on Monday morning in some coastal and inland areas, which could lead to fog or mist.The UAE will see fair to partly cloudy weather from Sunday to Tuesday. Convective clouds are likely to form in eastern and southern areas on Sunday, possibly extending to inland regions on Monday and bringing a chance of rain. By Tuesday, eastern and western regions could become cloudy, with a chance of scattered showers.When will winter start?The recent foggy conditions coincide with the UAE’s transition to winter. The lowest temperature recorded in the country on Saturday morning was 23.7°C in Raknah, Al Ain, at 5.15am.Dr Habib said the seasonal transition will occur through October and November, with autumn, which began on August 22, giving way to winter around December 22.

headline: S&P lifts UK GDP growth view on resilient consumer spending and services sector
summary: S&P Global Ratings has upgraded its growth outlook for the UK, citing “reasonably resilient” consumer spending and services that have helped shield the economy from the conflict in the Middle East.Real gross domestic product in Europe's second-biggest economy is now expected to climb by 1.3 per cent, from a previous lowered prediction of 1.1 per cent, the New York-based agency said on Friday.S&P analysts noted that hospitality and professional services underpinned economic growth in the second quarter. GDP growth is seen to average 1.4 per cent from 2027 to 2029, expecting the economy to improve if the situation in the Middle East is “contained”.The agency also maintained the UK's long and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at AA, two notches below the top prime grade. An investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises.“The stable outlook reflects our view that the UK economy has remained, and will remain, resilient in the face of the energy shock emanating from the Middle East conflict, with growth remaining reasonably robust,” analysts at S&P wrote.“This is balanced against risks from the UK's constrained fiscal position, elevated public debt levels, and high government spending, including on debt servicing.”S&P also noted the UK's policy direction under Andy Burnham, the UK's sixth prime minister in the past decade. The start of his tenure in July was marked by questions about how he would handle the economy, including how to ensure fiscal discipline.Mr Burnham's government has “focused on devolution, industrial renewal, social care and closer ties with the EU, with simultaneous pledges to respect fiscal prudence”, S&P said.UK inflation was pegged at 3.1 per cent in August, the highest in five months, according to the Office of National Statistics, and well above the Bank of England's 2 per cent threshold. S&P said this has risen on domestic price pressures and energy and transport costs, underpinned by higher hydrocarbon costs.The agency expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 0.25 basis points at its November meeting after maintaining them last month, “then hold that level until the second half of 2027 because the current policy rate level of 3.75 per cent and soft labour market conditions suggest the UK may require less additional policy tightening than the eurozone”.Egypt's growth acceleratesMeanwhile, S&P said Egypt's economy accelerated at its fastest pace in three years, but cautioned the North African nation remains vulnerable to shocks stemming from the conflicts in the Middle East.Real GDP in the Arab world's most populous nation jumped by 5.1 per cent in fiscal 2026, buoyed by non-oil sectors including manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, information and communication technology, and tourism, it said in a separate report. That compares to a 4.7 per cent reading in its previous estimate.Household consumption emerged as a primary factor, boosted by record remittances, easing inflation and stable labour market conditions, it added.S&P, however, projects this growth to ease to 4.5 per cent in the fiscal year 2027, as shipping disruptions related to the war are expected to further pressure trade, logistics and import prices. Consumption and investment activities are also predicted to soften amid persistent uncertainty and rising inflation.Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, according to Capmas data. S&P expects inflation to average 12.9 per cent in fiscal 2027. This might result in a policy reversal from the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates.S&P also kept its B sovereign credit rating on Egypt, which is six levels below investment grade, with a stable outlook.“Nevertheless, we expect the continued implementation of the reform agenda, including the commitment to exchange rate liberalisation, to enhance structural economic competitiveness over the medium term,” the S&P analysts said.

headline: Iraq's Al Sadr seeks statesmanship with push against militias after US withdrawal
summary: Shiite cleric Moqtada Al Sadr is seeking to reinforce a long-standing Iraqi nationalist platform that aims to keep Baghdad out of regional conflicts and curb Iranian influence, experts and officials have told The National. Mr Al Sadr’s push comes as he called for a new chapter between the US and Iraq following the withdrawal of American troops on September 30. The prominent cleric and former battlefield enemy of American troops during the US occupation is at a turning point in his own rebranding. Mr Al Sadr has millions of faithful supporters across Iraq, many of whom were part of his armed militia for years. That has now changed.On the day of the departure of US troops, he dissolved his Promised Day Brigade as well as his armed militia, Saraya al Salam (the Peace Brigades), which will now be under government control. Its members are expected to be incorporated into Iraq’s formal security apparatus under the authority of Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi's government. Mr Al Zaidi has been pushing to disarm all armed groups as Iraq undergoes a political shift following the exit of the US-led coalition forces.Meanwhile, Mr Al Sadr is portraying himself as a statesman seeking to keep Iraq out of regional conflicts while strengthening the state's monopoly on force.The withdrawal of US forces has weakened a key justification used by armed groups to keep their weapons. The question of why armed factions still operate without state control remains. The groups were expected to disarm by the September 30 deadline, but this has since been pushed to June next year.Mr Al Sadr’s recent statement and actions raise some suspicion as to how the process of disarming his militias will play out.Experts and a close aide to Mr Al Sadr told The National that his latest moves should be seen as part of a broader effort to continue his nationalist campaign, which combines religious leadership with political activism.“Mr Al Sadr has long advocated dissolving armed factions, including calling for the disbandment of groups operating outside state control,” Renad Mansour, director of the Iraq Initiative at London's Chatham House, told The National. “But integrating fighters into government institutions does not necessarily resolve questions over their loyalties,” he added.“What we'll have to see is what this actually means in reality. The bigger question is over loyalties: will they then become under a different chain of command, or will they still fall under the informal chain?” Mr Mansour said. Mr Al Sadr's vision for Iraq merges political and religious movements. “He believes that clerics should be active in politics, not isolated to religious affairs only. He is trying to chart his own role in the Iraqi state, one that bridges these different branches,” he said.The cleric's political movement, the Sadrists, have distanced themselves from the mainstream political scene in Iraq during the last few years. In the past decade, Mr Al Sadr has reinvented himself as a nationalist and an anti-corruption campaigner, emerging as a political kingmaker.He has always voiced his concerns over US and Iranian influence on Iraq's internal affairs. The shift in Mr Al Sadr's mindset comes as Iran continues to project influence across the region through allied armed groups, even as some nationalist movements seek to distance themselves from Tehran, said Bente Scheller, head of the Middle East and North Africa division at the Heinrich-Boll-Stiftung Foundation in Berlin.“Proxies are the method of choice in the region, yet because Iran deploys them in its own interest, this often brings them into conflict with their own national interests,” Ms Scheller told The National.By championing the state's monopoly on force, Mr Al Sadr may be seeking both to shield Iraq from becoming entangled in regional conflicts and to strengthen his credentials as a national political leader.“If Sadr now adopts a statesmanlike stance and emphasises the state's monopoly on the use of force, this may serve to take Iraq out of the line of fire,” she said. Setting an example Dhia Al Assadi, a former Iraqi minister and adviser to Mr Al Sadr, told The National that the cleric had long sought to help build a strong and stable Iraq.“Mr Al Sadr has consistently taken the initiative in setting an example. He encourages others to be brave and sensible enough to sacrifice political or material gains for the sake of stabilising and rebuilding Iraq on sound principles,” Mr Al Assadi said.The cleric's vision for the country begins with a “strong and well-founded Iraq, and looks outward to the world on the basis of mutual respect, co-operation, and shared interests”, he added. Based on Mr Al Sadr's recent statements on US-Iraqi ties, the region could benefit if American policymakers adopted a new approach and learnt from past mistakes, he said. Optimism would be limited if Washington continued to pursue narrowly defined interests at the expense of regional stability, Al Assadi added.Marsin Al Shammary, Iraq expert and assistant professor of political science at Boston College, said Mr Al Sadr's most recent policy had been based on playing the “long game in Iraq”.“He foresees a political future for himself and doesn’t want to undermine that by positioning himself as anti-state. We’ve seen in the past that he has a remarkable ability to mobilise and demobilise his followers,” Ms Al Shammary told The National.Another possibility is that he chooses to become closer to the successor to spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Al Sistani, she said, adding that “he has been making overtures towards Najaf recently”. The southern city of Najaf is home to Iraq's senior Shiite clerics and was the site of a 2004 rebellion against US forces by militias loyal to Mr Al Sadr.“Mr Al Sadr and Najaf do agree on one thing and that’s the importance of limiting Iranian influence in succession,” she said. Ms Al Shammary added that the cleric shared a long-term strategy with authorities in Najaf for an Iraq independent of Iran but with friendly ties with the region.

headline: US-Russia energy deal opens up diesel can of worms
summary: US President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia will be supplying diesel to global markets has opened up a can of worms, says analysts.Washington agreed to lift sanctions on the Kremlin in a bid to bring down energy prices, especially for diesel, which is vital to many economic sectors.Analysts, however, have raised alarm bells, saying the numbers Mr Trump has touted will not add up, and highlighting double standards over Russia's conflict with Ukraine and the International Criminal Court.'Happy birthday Putin'The first fallout came from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately after Mr Trump announced the deal.Mr Zelenskyy said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”, and that the Kremlin “will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy”.In a subsequent interview with Axios, Mr Zelenskyy likened the deal to a “birthday present” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on October 7.Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be…— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 9, 2026Mr Zelenskyy apparently also felt betrayed. Last week, the Ukrainian President met Steve Witkoff, the US special envoy to the Middle East, and Jared Kushner, the US envoy for peace (and Mr Trump's son-in-law), to discuss a potential peace breakthrough before the US midterm elections. But nothing was discussed about a potential diesel deal with the Russians.“It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this,” Mr Zelenskyy said in the Axios interview.“If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good … what did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world.”'Fantasy arithmetic'Mr Trump, in a social media post, said that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”.In total, and “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia will deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”, he added.Those numbers “will not work”, according to analysts at Quantum Strategy and Geonomics, which said the figures above are, respectively, 60 per cent, 100 per cent and 200 per cent of Russia's diesel exports.Furthermore, Russia needs to import 80,000 and 140,000 barrels per day of diesel, petrol and other refined products just to run its domestic refineries and make up for the shortages of refined products, Singapore-based Quantum said.Its analysts also pointed out that Ukrainian strikes have taken out more than half of Russia's refining capacity, according to Kyiv's defence ministry. The International Energy Agency estimates that Russia's diesel production capacity has been cut by nearly a third as a result of the attacks.In addition, Russia's exports of diesel and gasoil fell to a decade low of about 144,000 barrels per day in September, down from as high as 270,000 bpd in August and a peak of 820,000 in April, according to Quantum data.“Russia cannot supply the diesel Trump claims it will … technically, the balance [between diesel and other refined product exports and imports] needed to run domestic refineries cannot be switched into supplying Trump without endangering Russian domestic refinery supply in other areas,” the Quantum analysts said.“So Trump's simple fantasy arithmetic is nothing but that … we expect this deal to fail economically.”"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and… pic.twitter.com/tZMCfT95ru— The White House (@WhiteHouse) October 9, 2026Double standardThe US-Russia diesel deal also poses as a double standard. On Friday, Washington imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court, on the same day that former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The move was seen as retaliation for Mr Trump not being awarded the honour, which he claimed he deserved.“The contrast is striking. Sanctions against an institution pursuing accountability for war crimes; sanctions relaxed on energy exports from a country waging a war of aggression against Ukraine,” said Nicolai Kiskalt, a Germany-based partner at global consultancy KPMG.“The US administration has its own arguments: protecting American sovereignty from the ICC’s jurisdiction and bringing down energy prices for American consumers. But from a European perspective, these decisions raise fundamental questions that go far beyond trade, energy or diplomacy.”Riku Huttunen, director general of the energy department at Finland's Economy and Employment Ministry, also called this a “stark contrast” to the US sanctions law aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenue that fuels Russia’s war against Ukraine.“At the same time, there are doubts concerning Russian supplies. Russian oil refining capacities have been destroyed by Ukrainian drone attacks, causing fuel shortages,” he said.“The deal's effects on diesel markets might remain small. The agreed amounts are relatively modest and it is still unclear how the deliveries would be made in practice.”The timing of the US-Russia deal may also be bad, especially for Ukrainians, as winter approaches. Any further attacks on energy infrastructure would prove to be a serious challenge for both the economy and society.“An energy ceasefire was one of the few practical ideas that could have directly protected Ukrainian civilians this winter,” said Robert Potter, founding partner of Washington-based Cyber Activities Group, who is also an expert in geopolitics and security.“The negotiating logic was straightforward: if Moscow wanted sanctions relief or economic concessions, those could potentially be exchanged for something tangible, stopping attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Instead, Trump has handed Putin the economic benefit first,” he said.“That pulls the rug from under one of the few areas where western leverage could have been converted into immediate civilian protection. Worse, the signal to Moscow is really dangerous. Putin can escalate attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, refuse to commit to renewed peace talks, and still receive access to western-linked energy markets because US diesel prices are politically painful ahead of the midterms.”

headline: Dubai introduces digital Nol QR tickets for metro, buses and trams
summary: Public transport passengers in Dubai can now use digital QR codes on their phones to access the metro, trams and buses, eliminating the need for a single-use red paper Nol ticket.Passengers can buy digital Nol QR tickets through the Nol Pay or S'hail apps, the Roads and Transport Authority announced. This option is especially convenient for occasional passengers and visitors who use red Nol tickets for single trips. The fare for a red Nol ticket depends on the number of zones travelled through.To enter the metro, passengers should hold their phone with the QR code facing down over the entry blue gate reader.For bus rides, hold the phone screen facing up with the QR code displayed over the red Nol reader at the entrance until it is accepted. Digital tickets are also valid on the Dubai Tram.Commuters can buy the QR ticket up to 90 days in advance. It becomes valid on first use and expires at midnight that same day. For example, if you activate it at 11pm, it expires at midnight.Regular commuters can keep using their silver, gold and personal Nol cards. The digital QR tickets are an additional option rather than a replacement for existing cards. The silver Nol card holder is permitted in regular-class areas, while the gold Nol card allows passengers access gold class cabins on the Metro and trams at a higher fare. The personal Nol card, also known as the blue Nol card, is issued in the passenger’s name and may offer fare concessions to eligible students, senior Emiratis and residents, and people of determination.

headline: Why Bhuvneshwar Kumar's shock India recall shows that life begins at 30 for fast bowlers
summary: Bhuvneshwar Kumar last played an international match for India in 2022. His international career looked as good as over after England smashed him for 25 runs in two overs in the 2022 T20 World Cup semi-final in Adelaide during a thumping 10-wicket win.His lack of bite with the new ball, in the absence of Jasprit Bumrah, led the team management to quickly move on from him. Mohammad Siraj nestled into the white-ball team and formed a lethal pace trio with Bumrah and Mohammad Shami as India dominated the ensuing ODI World Cup at home, only to lose the final to Australia.India have since won successive T20 World Cups, Asia Cups and Asian Games T20 gold medals, plus the 50-over Champions Trophy. But with the ICC cycle moving out of Asia for the upcoming seasons, India have gone back to the bowler they had decidedly moved on from. In 2023, right-arm seamer Bhuvneshwar had told The National that he just wants to enjoy his remaining years of fast bowling. Now, he is back in the Indian T20 team, at the age of 36, for the forthcoming tour of New Zealand. Actually, he has forced himself back into the Indian set-up. The seamer went back to the drawing board, upped his fitness and recalibrated his game around the shortest format to emerge as the most lethal 20-over pacer in the country.Bhuvneshwar was the driving force behind Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s IPL triumphs, finishing as the second-highest wicket taker last season and delivering match-winning spells in both finals. This season, he took his domestic team Lucknow to the final of the state-level Uttar Pradesh T20 league. Bhuvneshwar’s sustained excellence over two seasons has coincided with the continued struggles of the next crop of Indian fast bowlers.Young quicks like Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar, Mayank Yadav and Anshul Kamboj are among a long list of quicks who have come in and failed to cement their spot in any format.Simple looks easy. It never is. 🙌Bhuvneshwar Kumar on the phase when everyone had a theory about his pace, why he never changed his action, and the years of unseen work behind keeping things simple. ❤️Catch more of Bhuvi candid in the full episode of @bigbasket_com presents… pic.twitter.com/ngdeQUThaj— Royal Challengers Bengaluru (@RCBTweets) October 8, 2026During the recent ODI series against the West Indies, India’s bowling attack conceded 400 runs in the second game and saw the Windies easily chase down a 350-run target in the third ODI.Among the experienced lot, only Siraj and Arshdeep Singh can be viewed as first-choice picks. Everyone else is a work in progress, at best. However, even Arshdeep was pummelled for 45 from his four overs as India were beaten by six wickets by the Windies in the second of five T20s on Friday. It all explains why India’s selectors have gone back to Bhuvneshwar for the T20 series in New Zealand which begins later this month. And which is also why many hope that veteran pacer Shami, 36, finds his way back into the Indian team for next year’s ODI World Cup in southern Africa.Experience mattersBhuvneshwar’s comeback fits perfectly with a peculiar quirk of international cricket – many of the top-ranked fast bowlers across formats are well into their 30s, while most of the best batters are in their mid 20s.sJasprit Bumrah (32), Mitchell Starc (36), Josh Hazlewood (35), Kagiso Rabada (31), Jofra Archer (31), Matt Henry (34), Pat Cummins (33), Ollie Robinson (32), Taskin Ahmed (31), Scott Boland (37) … the list is really long. A few standout exceptions are South Africa’s Marco Jansen (26), Bangladesh tearaway quick Nahid Rana (24) and Pakistan’s Shaheen Afridi (26).Compare that to the best and most promising batters in the world. Harry Brook (27), Shubman Gill (27), Abhishek Sharma (26), Rachin Ravindra (26), Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (15), Dewald Brevis (23), Ishan Kishan (28), Saim Ayub (24), Pathum Nissanka (28) are all young and well on their way to excelling in one or many formats over the coming years. Sure, veterans like Joe Root, Steve Smith, Virat Kohli and others are still piling on the runs. But the next generation is clearly up to the task.That does not seem to be the case with bowling. India’s reliance on Bumrah, decision to go back to Bhuvneshwar and clamour for the return of Shami shows that when it comes to pace bowling, the new crop is not quite matching up to the old stock.One can understand why. Fast bowling requires miles in the legs and bowlers can get that only by playing red ball, multi-day cricket. Only bowlers of a certain vintage have played enough first-class and Test matches and have the experience in their body to last the distance for consecutive seasons or adapt their bowling according to match situations. Those who developed their bowling in the T20 arena don’t seem to have the complete set of tools required to master conditions and formats. Which is why teams are holding on to their older generation of fast bowlers for as long as physically possible, barring Bangladesh who have an exciting and high-class young bowling attack. Now you understand why Australia are squeezing every bit of life out of their awesome quartet of Starc, Hazlewood, Cummins and Boland. That has proven to be the case elsewhere, too. Because, in almost every corner of the world, they just don't make them like they used to.

headline: UAE begins food aid airlift to Gaza under Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge
summary: The UAE began airlifting food aid to Gaza on Friday under the newly launched Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge initiative, aiming to supply more than 10 million meals to Palestinians.Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, along with Operation Knight 3, launched flights from Al Maktoum International Airport carrying food parcels.Sheikh Ahmed, brother of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, died on September 21, and the initiative was launched to recognise his generosity and philanthropic work. It brought together volunteers, community members and admirers of Sheikh Ahmed at Dubai World Trade Centre to prepare food the aid packages for families and children in Gaza.The humanitarian bridge will operate through air and sea transport in seven consignments. Six flights will carry 450 tonnes of food parcels, and one vessel will transport 4,000 tonnes of supplies to meet the basic nutrition needs of people in Gaza.Hammoud Al Afari, director of UAE relief operations under Operation Gallant Knight 3, said the bridge augmented the UAE's humanitarian efforts.“The launch of flights under the Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge reflects the high level of efficiency and expertise of the Emirati teams involved in Operation Gallant Knight 3,” Mr Al Afari said. He added that Operation Gallant Knight 3, launched in November 2023 under the directives of President Sheikh Mohamed, had been a lifeline for Palestinians throughout the conflict. The continuity and geographical reach of its assistance have helped large segments of the population cope with difficult living conditions.The operation has established a model for humanitarian response through its integrated approach combining emergency relief, health care, logistical support, recovery and rehabilitation programmes, he said.Since its launch, the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in humanitarian assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid since 2023. That assistance has included 130,708 tonnes of relief, medical, and food supplies delivered by 796 aircraft, 25 ships and 14,483 lorries.Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, the region's largest humanitarian and community development foundation, recorded expenditure exceeding Dh2.3 billion in 2025, positively impacting approximately 165 million beneficiaries across 122 countries. Its humanitarian aid and relief programmes alone exceeded Dh625 million in expenditure, benefiting more than 53 million people worldwide.Its activities span five main pillars: humanitarian aid and relief, health care and disease control, education and knowledge, innovation and entrepreneurship, and community empowerment.Today, MBRGI encompasses more than 30 initiatives and institutions working across humanitarian, social and development sectors, with particular emphasis on disadvantaged countries and vulnerable communities.
