headline: Israel holding 49 Syrians after 280 armed incursions in September, says UN
summary: Israel is holding 49 Syrians and carried out 280 armed incursions into southern Syria in September, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has said.Released detainees alleged torture and ill-treatment, including beatings, prolonged forced standing and threats against their families, said a statement from Mr Volker's office on Friday.He called on Israeli authorities to halt such actions. The statement said September marked the highest monthly number of armed Israeli incursions since the beginning of the year, according to open-source monitoring.The incursions include “reported raids on homes, restrictions on movement, harassment and intimidation of civilians, arbitrary detention and destruction of livelihoods”, the office said. Forty-nine Syrians remain in Israeli detention, according to information received by the office, although it said it could not independently verify the number. The statement called on Israeli authorities to “cease actions that harass or intimidate civilians in Syrian villages, including raids, restrictions on freedom of movement, detention and destruction of crops”.The remarks by Mr Turk's office come as Syria accuses Israel of building major military fortifications in Syrian territory along the occupied Golan Heights. The Syrian Foreign Ministry said that Israel was working to complete its “Sufa 53 Line”, in violation of previous agreements.Areas near the Golan Heights have experienced an increasing number of Israeli incursions this year. Israeli troops crossed into southern Syria and areas west of Damascus, and occupied parts of those regions, soon after rebel forces led by current President Ahmad Al Shara ousted the regime of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024.The US, which backs Syria's current rulers, has supervised several meetings between Israeli and Syrian officials in an effort to negotiate a peace deal between the two countries. They discussed halting Israeli attacks on Syria and the return of Israeli forces to the 1974 armistice line adjacent to the Golan Heights.

headline: UAE and Saudi Arabia take legal action over online bullying of child with disabilities
summary: The UAE has taken legal action against an individual who posted content on social media that included the bullying of a child with disabilities. The video contained inappropriate innuendo that violates the country’s societal values and morals, the National Media Authority said on Friday.In a statement, the authority said it had co-ordinated with the social media platform to take action against the account and the content's publisher. It also notified authorities to pursue legal measures.The NMA emphasised its rejection of all forms of abuse and bullying, stressing its commitment to protecting children and people with disabilities, preserving their dignity, and safeguarding society.The child’s father had also appealed to authorities in Saudi Arabia to investigate the incident and ensure justice for his son under the Child Protection Law. He condemned the alleged mockery and mistreatment of his son, who is under 15 years old and is a person of determination, and defended the boy's rights.Following the father's appeal, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development said on Friday that the complaint, which circulated on social media, had been referred to authorities and procedures were under way under the kingdom's child protection law.The account has since taken down the post and video.UAE online bullying and abuse lawAlthough the content was reportedly posted by an individual in Saudi Arabia, the UAE maintains a robust legal framework to protect children, combat cyberbullying and address online abuse. This covers content targeting children and people of determination.Federal Law No 3 of 2016 on Child Rights, known as Wadeema’s Law, safeguards children against abuse.The law, which covers UAE nationals and the children of expats, outlines the legal rights of minors and is designed to protect children from physical, verbal and psychological abuse."Although the law does not use the word “bullying” expressly, bullying can fall within its protections and prohibitions," said Nikhat Sardar Khan, a senior lawyerShe explained that Article 32(3) requires the state to ban all forms of violence in educational institutions and to preserve children’s dignity. This can cover physical, verbal, psychological, and other forms of bullying at school."Articles 33 and 34 protect children from physical, psychological or threats to mental integrity. A child-protection specialist may intervene where such harm is threatened. Article 36 prohibits acts of cruelty that affect a child’s emotional, psychological, mental, or moral balance. Serious bullying may meet this description," Ms Khan said.Where conduct amounts to prohibited cruelty under Article 36, Article 69 mandates imprisonment of at least one year and/or a fine of Dh50,000 to Dh100,000. UAE cybercrime law addresses offences committed through digital platforms. To protect public health, peace and order, it targets platforms that spread, publish or circulate fake news, false or misleading reports, or rumours that contradict official information.Violators may face at least one year of imprisonment and a minimum fine of Dh100,000. Penalties increase to two years in jail and a minimum fine of Dh200,000 if the crime occurs during pandemics, emergencies or crises.Federal Decree-Law No 26 of 2025 on Child Digital Safety strengthens protection against online risks and harmful content affecting children. The law applies to internet service providers and digital platforms operating in the UAE or targeting UAE users, regardless of location.

headline: Cristiano Ronaldo hits 980th career goal as he puts Portugal row behind him in Al Nassr win
summary: Cristiano Ronaldo enjoyed a happy return to Riyadh after his troubled international break as he notched his 980th career goal in Al Nassr’s win over Diriyah.The 41-year-old striker could scarcely have asked for an easier night after the controversies of the previous two weeks.The defending Saudi Pro League champions had a routine 3-0 win over Diriyah at Al Awwal Park that was entirely free of aggravation.Ronaldo scored the first himself, pouncing on a loose ball and firing into an empty net after Kingsley Coman had seen his shot saved.The Portugal star looked far sharper than he had in the lead up to the international break, and looked uninhibited by his row with Jorge Jesus, the Portugal coach.Speculation in Europe on the day of the game suggested Ronaldo is going to be suspended by Portugal for his part in the controversy.Ronaldo left the Portugal camp, angered by the decision of Jesus – his former coach at Nassr – not to field him in the second match of the window, as he said had been agreed.In a 1,740-word statement in the days that followed, Ronaldo accused Jesus of lying, and of not treating him as a player “of the stature of Pele and Maradona”.It has been claimed the Portuguese federation could ban Ronaldo for up to six months for his outburst. Despite that, Ronaldo was sharp from the off against Diriyah. He had the ball in the net early on, only for it to be chalked off for offside.That came within a minute of a significant show off support by the Nassr fans. In the eighth minute, a huge banner which covered the entirety of the stand where the home ultras sit was unfurled, saying: “Greatness Is Earned. CR7.”Ronaldo also could have had two assists before he opened the scoring in the 23rd minute, laying on presentable chances for Sadio Mane and Samu Costa.Both saw their shots saved, but it seemed clear that Ronaldo was trying to make a point about being a team player.On that subject, the response to his goal was maybe instructive. When he scored, he raced to the corner flag and did his trademark “Siuu” celebration.He was not exactly engulfed by teammates, though. A few made their way towards him in dribs and drabs, one of whom was Joao Felix, his Portugal teammate.Later in the game, with Nassr 2-0 up after Costa had added the second, Ronaldo might have had a second goal of his own.He and Coman were clean through with just the goalkeeper to beat as the Diriyah defence was AWOL.Coman opted to score himself, though, when he might have squared the ball for Ronaldo. While Ronaldo was the obvious headline act in the game, the win also eased some of the pressure on Ange Postecoglou.Yellow was made for greatness 💛🐐 pic.twitter.com/waRXHef8cR— AlNassr FC (@AlNassrFC_EN) October 9, 2026The Australian coach had made a fine start to his tenure in charge of Nassr at the start of the season, but had grown increasingly irate in the lead in to the international break.That was in response to having his methods questioned after Nassr’s form had stalled, so the 3-0 win immediately on their return was gratefully received.“I thought it was a good performance,” Postecoglou said of a result which takes Nassr up to second in the SPL table. “Obviously, it is always good to win and we scored three good goals, kept a clean sheet.“In general, I thought it was a really good, strong performance and against a difficult opponent, so I'm happy.”

headline: US tech roared back, but is the great investment rotation already over?
summary: Just one month ago, it looked like the glory days might finally be over for US technology stocks, as investors trembled at the prospect of a mighty artificial intelligence bubble.Experts were increasingly urging investors to reduce their exposure by looking beyond the mega-caps towards banks, industrials, smaller companies and emerging markets.Many needed little encouragement. They looked at the trillions being poured into AI infrastructure and wondered whether highly leveraged "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft would ever get a return on that investment.And isn’t investing cyclical anyway? The so-called Magnificent Seven and other tech hopefuls have had it their way for long enough. Surely it must be somebody else’s turn.The great rotation?Experts quickly came up with a name for the shift: the great rotation. But there was one problem: it wasn’t so great.Within weeks, investors were rotating back into technology, with renewed AI enthusiasm sending the Nasdaq careering towards fresh highs. So should we all rotate back again?This isn’t the first time investors have stepped back from big tech. The bull run may have lasted more than a dozen years, but there has been plenty of volatility along the way, notably in 2022 when valuations crashed.Investors started looking beyond tech both at the start of this year and again over the summer, says Jason Hollands, managing director of investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners. “Every time, enthusiasm for the hyperscalers recovered, and it has just taken off again.” The latest rebound is particularly impressive because it has come despite sharply rising bond yields, he says.“Higher yields typically have a negative impact on the discounted cash flow models used to value the forecast earnings of growth stocks several years out.”That should normally hit tech, because it reduces the value of future earnings. There’s another threat too: the prolific amount of debt being issued to finance AI infrastructure.“You might assume that higher financing costs, alongside the debate about whether the speed of AI frontier models should be slowed, would dent enthusiasm but it hasn’t,” Mr Hollands says. “Investor appetite has proven resilient and corporate profit margins continue to impress and surprise.”Dot-com parallelsBut surely this can’t go on?Those worried about the sustainability of AI mania regularly draw parallels with the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, but there’s a huge difference. The hyperscalers have deep pockets and are already making real money.Microsoft’s second-quarter revenue jumped 18 per cent to $90 billion, while Alphabet’s second-quarter revenue rose 24 per cent to $119.8 billion and Amazon’s climbed 20 per cent to $200.6 billion. Cloud services and AI infrastructure were core growth drivers, although Alphabet and Amazon’s net income figures were boosted by non-operating paper gains from start-up investments such as Anthropic and SpaceX.Meta Platforms beat the lot, with revenue jumping 28 per cent to $60.8 billion as AI-optimised recommendation and targeting engines supercharged advertising, boosted by its new Muse AI assistant.“Meta is crushing it, with Mark Zuckerberg’s AI vision finally starting to gain some traction,” Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, says. Despite unprecedented AI capital spending, hyperscaler valuations have actually become more attractive as underlying earnings continue to expand aggressively. Share prices have risen, but earnings have risen even faster. No wonder investors have swung back to the sector.Risks remainYet there are risks. It doesn’t mean investors should stop worrying about valuations. Nobody knows how this technological revolution will play out. Yves Bonzon, group chief investment officer at Julius Baer, describes it as a “binary play”. “Even if everyone agrees on the enormous disruptive potential of AI, nobody really knows what path it will take or where the endgame lies,” he says.Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which floated in June, is the perfect case study. Its established Starlink operation posted a bumper operating profit of $1.66 billion in the second quarter, a 66 per cent jump.By contrast, its cutting-edge AI division swallowed $15.83 billion in capital expenditure and posted a $1.26 billion operating loss, even as revenue surged 247 per cent.Mr Bonzon argues that frontier AI laboratories are the weakest financial link in the AI value chain, yet one of its most important demand drivers. “Their race to develop AI agents with increasing capability is fuelling spending on chips, memory, cloud infrastructure, data centres, and power, even as their own path to profitability remains uncertain, he says.The risk that rapid technological progress will quickly render AI chips obsolete has so far not materialised, he adds. Older generations of processors continue to play an important role, reducing the risk that today’s AI investments become stranded assets, Mr Bonzon says. “While we continue to favour diversification, we no longer see a compelling reason to underweight the large US hyperscalers.”Wider sell-off But now investors have something else to worry about. October opened with a wider stock market sell-off as investors worried about rising oil prices, inflation and government debt, sending bond yields to multi-decade highs. Investors rotated out of equities at speed, and not just technology stocks. Banks, industrials, smaller companies and emerging markets also sold off. What goes around, comes around.Investors had been rotating out of the US dollar, but now they’re rotating back into it too, says Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at trading platform IG. “The dollar just hit its highest level since April 2025, as persistent inflation, resilient US economic activity, and the hawkish Federal Reserve reinforce expectations of further rate hikes,” he says. “Meanwhile, Bitcoin continues to struggle, though at least it has gold and silver for company.”As bond yields rise, investors are rotating into US Treasuries and government bonds, says Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell. “When investors can earn a relatively high return from government debt with limited risk, equities must work harder to justify their additional volatility.”The rotation between equity sectors and asset classes will always ebb and flow, Mr Hollands says. “The more durable trend should be towards greater diversification. That is generally more robust than making large all-or-nothing bets based on the latest spurts of market leadership,” he adds.

headline: As AI reshapes entertainment, can it ever replace human connection?
summary: Artificial intelligence can generate music, create videos and simulate conversations with remarkable sophistication. But as the technology becomes more deeply embedded in entertainment, one question remains: can it replicate the connection audiences feel with another person?The question is particularly relevant to live streaming, where audiences spend hours interacting with creators, often developing relationships that can last for years.Dan Clancy, chief executive of Twitch, believes those relationships are something technology will never be able to reproduce. "People come to live streaming for that human connection," Clancy told The National. "As humans, we yearn for it."Although AI can imitate human behaviour, Clancy argues that audiences recognise the difference between interacting with a person and a digital substitute.Yet AI-generated personalities are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Virtual streamers can now respond to audiences, produce content and maintain an online presence without a human performer directly controlling every interaction.Their growing capabilities raise questions about whether audiences value the personalities they encounter or the knowledge that another person is behind them.A 2026 study published in the International Journal of Information Management found that highly realistic AI streamers could provoke negative emotional responses, potentially discouraging engagement. It also found that a warmer-sounding voice could reduce some of these reactions, suggesting audiences respond to more than a digital personality's appearance.A separate 2025 study in Information & Management, involving 434 respondents, found that a sense of social presence helped foster emotional connections with streamers and a sense of belonging within their communities relationships were also associated with longer viewing times.Neither study establishes whether AI can ultimately replicate human relationships, but both offer insight into what viewers respond to when watching someone live.Clancy says community is central to why live streaming has grown beyond gaming into sports, conversation and other forms of entertainment."Gaming at its foundation is a community experience," he says. "The reason gaming has gotten so big is because it's a social experience."He compares that appeal to watching a television programme such as Game of Thrones, where discussing developments with friends becomes part of the enjoyment.Streaming builds on that experience by allowing viewers to participate as events unfold. Broadcasters can respond to comments, acknowledge regular viewers, or change the direction of a stream based on audience suggestions.It also gives people a place to share interests that might not be represented among their friends or family. Clancy points to gamers finding communities devoted to titles that nobody in their social circle plays.AI, however, still has a place in that experience. Clancy says the technology can help streamers experiment with content and involve their communities.He recalls an American streamer who invited viewers to generate videos featuring him using OpenAI's Sora technology. The streamer then watched the submissions with his audience and selected the funniest.The exercise demonstrated how AI could encourage collaboration without diminishing the creator's role."They could come up with funny ideas of things he was doing, and they could quickly realise them," Clancy says.The distinction between generating content and building relationships also follows Twitch's approach to helping creators grow.While the platform is investing in short-form clips to attract new audiences, Clancy maintains that longer broadcasts are more effective at building lasting connections. "Short-form content is better for discovery; long-form content is better for connection and community."He points to streamers such as Kai Cenat and IShowSpeed, whose popularity has extended beyond gaming into mainstream entertainment.Clancy believes their success comes partly from the time audiences spend with them. Unlike scrolling through brief videos, watching a streamer for hours gives viewers opportunities to become familiar with their personality, interests and interactions with others.That familiarity can develop into an attachment that outlasts its relationship with any individual platform. "The attachment isn't with the platform; it's with the creator."As AI-generated entertainment becomes more widespread, Clancy believes those relationships could become even more valuable."In a world full of swiping and short-form content and AI, people are more than ever looking for that authentic connection with [other] people," he says.

headline: UAE school pupils turn feathers into fertiliser as plans to combat waste take flight
summary: Three enterprising UAE teenagers are turning discarded chicken feathers into biofertiliser in a project they hope could eventually help farmers and reduce agricultural waste.Adit Mital, Anushka Harlalka and Maanit Misra have spent months developing BioFeathers, a process that uses bacteria to break down chicken feathers and convert them into nutrients that can be used by plants.What started as a school science project has now moved into trials at 16 farms and nurseries in the UAE, Oman and India.The Year 13 pupils at Dubai International Academy have also filed a joint provisional patent application and plan to approach Dubai authorities in an effort to expand their plans.Speaking to The National, the teenagers said the idea came from a shared interest in science and the possibility of turning something normally thrown away into something useful.“We saw an opportunity there, or a gap between what is currently being used to get rid of that waste versus what it could actually be used for," Adit said.Several million tons of poultry feathers are discarded around the world every year. They contain a substance that is resistant to natural degradation, which leads to large amounts of waste and environmental concern. The teenagers began by collecting about 2kg of feathers from a poultry farm in Sharjah and spent hours preparing them for lab testing.Their families were initially surprised by the idea, but they later helped the teenagers travel to laboratories and connect with people who could support their work.Turning waste into fertiliserThe pupils wanted to find a way of extracting useful material from feathers without burning or other energy-intensive methods.“The main idea is that chicken feathers basically have keratin in them, and keratin is a very useful protein, but it's also very hard to break down and extract,” Adit said.They began contacting academics and universities through cold emails before working with researchers at the University of Sharjah.“We did a lot of cold emailing to these professors,” Anushka said. “There were limitations to what some people could help us and offer us, so we reached out to more. We did a lot of research.”Through their experiments, the students developed nine nutrient-rich formulations that could be used as fertilisers or plant-growth boosters.Their first laboratory experiments began during the winter break in December 2025. By February, they had completed three rounds of trials before moving on to testing the formulations on plants.Early controlled tests using bok choy and radishes showed some growth measurements about 20 to 30 per cent higher than commercial comparison treatments.However, results are preliminary and further testing is required.Putting plans to the testThe team has since taken the product outside the laboratory and tested it at farms and nurseries in the UAE, Oman and India.The pupils said more than 1,200 farmers have been involved in trials, helping the pupils understand how the product could work in real agricultural settings.“Seeing what is the actual application, what are the requirements to be able to take this further, that is the main thing that we are picking up from farmers," Maanit said.School, exams and 60 plant potsDeveloping the project while attending school has also meant fitting laboratory work around lessons and exams.The pupils spent much of their winter break travelling to Sharjah, at times working in the laboratory almost every day.Regional tensions earlier this year disrupted their access to the university laboratory. Instead of stopping the project, they moved part of the testing home.“I had some 60 plant pots in my backyard, and we would come there every other week, and we would do experiments on them, collecting our data,” Adit said.The group also dealt with delays in obtaining chemicals and problems with laboratory equipment. Adit said the experience forced the group to adapt.“There were nights or evenings where we were there up until almost 7am,” he said. “It became really difficult.”Their teachers, university researchers and families became an important support network.Patent filed as project growsThe pupils filed a joint provisional patent application in April for elements of the process they developed.They said their method builds on existing approaches but includes changes to chemicals, concentrations and other parts of the process.“There were already existing protocols for developing a biofertiliser through the same process, but our method involved a few nuanced and unique takes,” Adit said.The teenagers estimate the raw formula costs less than Dh1 per 100ml to produce. Because the feathers are waste, the main raw material is inexpensive.However, the pupils said packaging, storage and transport would add to the cost if the product were produced on a larger scale.The students now plan to present the project to Dubai Municipality and explore opportunities through the Dubai Farms programme.

headline: Trump lifts US sanctions on Russian diesel amid price surge
summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russia had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.The move comes as Mr Trump faces growing domestic political pressure to bring down rising diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, before November's midterm elections.Mr Trump said in a social media post that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”. The US President said that, “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia would deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”.“Between our total control of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian energy, diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be coming, in record numbers down, and fast!” Mr Trump wrote.The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control released a licence allowing the immediate “sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation” of Russian origin-diesel fuel into the US until April 2027. The department said it did not authorise any debit to an account on the books of a US financial institution of Russia's central bank, its national wealth fund, or its finance ministry.The move drew quick condemnation from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”.“Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” Mr Zelenskyy said.Trump is doing a deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes from the shockingly high diesel prices caused by his own reckless, illegal war in the Middle East. This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target… https://t.co/lEILjnE38R— Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) October 9, 2026US Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer and other members of the Democratic Party expressed dismay at the announcement.“This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target and try to kill American troops in the Middle East and who illegally and viciously invaded our ally Ukraine,” he said on X.Russia was the second-largest diesel exporter in the world after the US before imposing curbs to protect its domestic market. Those supplies have been further hampered by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, including what Kyiv claimed to be an attack on the country's largest oil refinery on Thursday.It is unclear how Russia will supply the diesel amounts announced by Mr Trump.Russia's fossil fuel export revenue fell 8 per cent on a monthly basis in August to €604 million ($676 million) per day, with export volumes falling 7 per cent, according to the Centre for Research on Clean Air, a think tank that has previously condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine.Mr Trump has recently acknowledged the diesel fuel crisis. In September, he publicly called on Mr Zelenskyy to halt its attacks on Russia's oil facilities “because he's causing a shortage of diesel fuel”.G7 member countries last week said they had agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other products through the International Energy Agency to help stabilise markets following pressure from the Trump administration, which had threatened to impose a diesel export ban.IEA members on Wednesday said they had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks and accelerate the release of roughly 100 million barrels of emergency oil reserves. The IEA's members in March agreed to release 425 barrels of reserves to markets as prices surged after the Iran war broke out on February 28, with roughly 325 million barrels having been released so far.Friday's surprise move also appears to defy a Russian sanctions law championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham, which Mr Trump signed into law on September 18. The law codifies the existing US sanctions regime targeting Russia and introduced new tariff authorities with a particular focus on energy exports.Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the House of Representatives Joint Economic Committee who opposed the legislation, called the deal “infuriating”.“Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake,” he wrote on X.The average cost of diesel in the US on Friday was $6.27 per gallon, compared to $3.67 this time last year.

headline: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake hits Panama
summary: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday, sparking warnings about tsunamis off the country's coast.The quake had a depth of 12.6km and its epicentre was in Herrera Province, roughly 200km to the south-west of the Panama Canal, according to the US Geological Survey.Some buildings were reported damaged but the critical Panama Canal was not affected, nor was the passage of ships through the trade waterway.Flights were suspended for several hours at Tocumen International Airport, a major regional hub, but had resumed by Friday evening.The USGS initially registered a magnitude of 8.0 for the earthquake before revising it. Panama’s geological institute reported the quake as a 7.2 magnitude.Local newspaper La Prensa said buildings, businesses, schools and homes in several regions were evacuated following the earthquake.Earthquakes of this magnitude are rare in Panama, and television images ⁠showed elderly residents reduced to tears in the streets as a series of weaker aftershocks ​rattled ⁠the country. “We’re scared. It’s just the ‌two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it ​could fall on us,” Ricardo Brown told Reuters by phone from the Las Minas area of Herrera Province. He said the quake had damaged several other homes.Tremors were felt as far as San Jose, the capital of neighbouring Costa Rica, according to a Reuters witness.Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told local outlet Telemetro Reporta that aftershocks had been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.Videos shared by La Prensa showed that the tower of a cathedral had collapsed, along with several balconies of a residential ​building in Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicentre and ‌Panama City.In the capital, the ⁠service on two lines of the Panama ​City Metro was temporarily suspended for safety reasons, the operator said. Nationwide, the ministry of education ‌ordered schools to close.Panama had been due to hold a national evacuation drill next Monday ​to test the country's emergency response to earthquakes.The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has warned of the potential for tsunami waves off the coast of Panama, as well as the western coasts of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru.The United Arab Emirates expressed its solidarity with the Republic of Panama following the earthquake.In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) affirmed that the UAE stands alongside the Republic of Panama and its people as they address the aftermath of the earthquake.Friday’s quake was the latest to hit Latin America in recent months.Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes in late June that killed nearly 6,500 people, according to the government’s official toll. The quakes caused widespread destruction, particularly along the country’s northern coast. A powerful earthquake hit Colombia on August 10, levelling buildings and causing major damage in cities including Cali and Pereira. The death toll eventually rose above 330, while the government declared an economic emergency as it confronted a rebuilding bill estimated at roughly $10 billion.

headline: Palisades proposes method to retrieve tipped nuclear fuel assembly, but concerns remain
summary: A battle is brewing over how to retrieve a tipped fuel assembly at the soon-to-be-restarted Palisades nuclear reactor in Michigan. The reactor, which closed in 2022 but was purchased by Holtec International, has become a poster child for an AI and data centre-induced nuclear energy renaissance in the US. Efforts to restart the reactor in Covert, Michigan, hit a snag on August 30, when, according to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), one of the fuel assemblies tipped during fuelling, causing resumption to be placed on hold. The NRC said no radiation was released during the incident. But the incident has confirmed concerns about the unorthodox nature of restarting a shuttered nuclear reactor, which are known as “zombie reactors”. According to publicly available documents and correspondence between Palisades workers and the NRC, Holtec International has proposed a method for retrieving the tipped fuel.In the requests Holtec made to the NRC, the company says that the fuel rods have “retained their integrity as primary fission product barrier”. The energy firm also says that the fuel assembly is situated at a 30-degree angle “from the core plate”. Yet an inquiry from the NRC indicates "that fuel assembly exhibits significant bowing".In response to the NRC's question about the bowing, Holtec communicates that the company checked with its fuel vender about the situation. "Based on a review by our fuel vendor, the assembly is expected to straighten out without risk of fuel cladding failure inside the fuel transfer canister," Holtec's response reads in part. In its application, Holtec proposed using a specially designed recovery tool to lift the tilted assembly and a protective canister to support and enclose it during its transfer from the reactor vessel to the spent fuel pool.A news release on Friday from the environmental advocacy group Don't Waste Michigan, however, expressed distrust in Holtec. “This has never been done anywhere, and Holtec has never operated a nuclear power plant,” the non-profit said. The NRC has not yet indicated if it will grant approval to Holtec's proposal. “The peril of Palisades's fuel retrieval is that highly irradiated fuel will be suspended out of water in the plant atmosphere for up to 133 hours,” Don't Waste Michigan alleges. “This will be a highly radioactively contaminated undertaking.” Yet in Holtec's licence amendment request, provided to the NRC on September 30, the company insists that everything will be done according to regulatory limits. “There is no significant increase in the probability of an accident,” the document reads. Shortly after confirming the tipped fuel assembly incident several weeks ago, Holtec said that the reactor's fuel loading had been paused while the company addressed the situation, but that other restart efforts “not dependent on resolution of the fuel-loading matter” were still under way. Despite both the NRC and Holtec confirming that no radiation was released, critics of the Palisades restart often point to the reactor's history of controversy. Before it was bought by Holtec, a 2012 NRC report warned about the work culture at Palisades, where it said safety concerns were often dismissed.In 2016, security staff at the reactor were placed on leave from the plant, which was then owned by Entergy, for failing to properly follow fire-prevention protocol. A little more than a year ago, a worker at Palisades fell off a refuelling bridge into a pool of water, though they were not seriously injured.Arnie Gundersen, a nuclear engineer and expert adviser for Don't Waste Michigan, said that there are plenty of reasons to be concerned about Holtec's efforts to restart the reactor. “It is clear that they want approval to remove the tilted fuel bundle because they want to expedite the refuelling,” he claimed. “They provide no root cause analysis as to how the event happened in order to assure that it cannot happen again. nor have they evaluated any damage within the reactor that the fuel bundle may have caused.”Holtec, however, has previously said that the company is working to figure out why the fuel assembly tipped. “A root cause evaluation has been initiated to determine the cause of the event,” a statement read. It also promised to implement any corrective actions necessary.

headline: Pictures of the week: From French student protests to the reopening of Dubai Miracle Garden
Money & Me: 'I went from The X Factor to having to sell my car to pay staff but now earn Dh130,000 a month’
summary: JJ Thompson has a very varied CV. He came ninth on The X Factor in 2013 as part of a boy band, spent years as a radio presenter before launching a podcast production company during Covid, which ultimately failed.Then, in June 2024, he walked away from a job offer at one of the UAE's biggest radio networks to start from scratch in real estate with no salary. More than two years later, he's earning an average of Dh130,000 a month at Dubai-based property brokerage Strada. How did money feature in your childhood?I think I have some financial trauma. My dad was a business owner and we seemed to have a little bit and then very little. I've always had a bit of an issue with finances. I don't know if it's through ADHD or childhood, but I'm good at spending money.I'm learning to get a hold of money and get rid of it as quickly as possible – forcing myself to buy property, which is weird to say, because either I’ll spend the money or I'll invest in property to make sure it doesn't get spent. What was your first job? What did you earn?A waiter when I was 16 years old, £4.50 an hour. I moved to London from Coventry when I was 19 and had random bar jobs for those three years. I worked for my dad doing roofing but he fired me after a couple of months.When I moved to London, I worked in Harrods, spraying perfume on the ground floor. That's where I met my now-wife. Then I worked in a call centre selling Grazia and Heat magazines for about £6 an hour. Then I got into a boy band, and I did The X Factor. We came ninth in 2013 when I was 22.How did you end up in Dubai?After the band, I did radio in the UK, for Capital Radio, then I moved over to the UAE in 2016 to do it full time for Channel 4. I did the evening show, then the breakfast show. During Covid, there weren't many people advertising, so we didn't get paid. I went down from around Dh18,000 a month to about Dh2,500. I started a podcast company to try to bridge that gap. We got an investor but it failed dramatically – I had to sell my car to pay staff. I gave the business to the investor and said: “I'm going to go into real estate.” It was called a midlife crisis by a few people, which added fuel in the fire. It's gone well. I'm very happy I took the leap and took the risk.What do you earn now?It's month to month, but it's around Dh130,000 a month. My max in radio was Dh19,000. When [the money] came – and it happened so quickly – it was a bit of a Will Smith Pursuit of Happyness moment. I wasn't mentally ready because I was so used to having very little, but always wanting more, always knowing one day I'd get it somehow because I'm very financially ambitious. We had a baby, and I'd turned down a stable job for something where I didn't know if I would earn anything for six months. But I landed my first deal within six days and that got me about Dh150,000. I burst into tears looking at my child. I thought: “We're on to something here and all the risk paid off.” How do you grow your wealth?Mainly real estate. I've invested in two off-plan properties in Abu Dhabi with a client. We've got a property in the UK and we're looking to expand that to three as an Airbnb business in Scotland with my wife. I prefer off-plan investments. I look for higher-risk investments for higher reward rather than safe rental income from a ready property that will net me six per cent.What has been your best investment?They haven't come into fruition yet because they're off-plan, but I would like to think my investment in Hudayriyat Golf Estates in Hudayriyat Island, Abu Dhabi, will probably yield the best return by 2030.Any cherished purchases?I bought a nicer car and then I bought a Rolex, which was always a bit of a goal of mine.What luxuries are important to you?Travel and holidays – that's the most important thing for me, and the most expensive. I've been away once a month this year. My favourite thing is to go away with the family.What financial advice would you give your younger self?I was right in always thinking it's going to be all right. Keep working, keep being ambitious, keep allowing people to laugh at your goals because they're bigger than theirs. Keep going, it will all be all right.

headline: ‘Jareema’: The Arabic word for crime is deployed in courts and cultural debates
summary: Jareema appears in official police reports and courtrooms, as well as in fierce criticism of songs, films and performances.Our Arabic word of the week means crime and describes an act punishable by law, ranging from theft and fraud to murder. The plural is jaraim, meaning “crimes”.Jareema comes from the root letters jim, ra and mim, which also carry meanings associated with wrongdoing and guilt. The verbs ajrama and ajramat mean he or she committed a crime, respectively, while mujrim refers to a criminal. Ijram means criminality and ilm al-ijram is criminology, while masrah al-jareema refers to the crime scene.Modern uses include jaraim elektroniyya, meaning cybercrimes; jareema munazzama, organised crime; and jaraim harb, war crimes. Legal Arabic distinguishes clearly between mujrim, a criminal whose guilt is implied, and muttaham, someone accused of an offence.The accusation can also be figurative. Jareema fi haqq al-fann means a crime against art and may be used to dismiss a song, film or performance as particularly bad.In literature, adab al-jareema refers to crime fiction, while jareema kamila means the perfect crime.The 2022 Egyptian thriller Al Jareema, or El Gareema in Egyptian Arabic, stars Ahmed Ezz, Menna Shalaby and Maged El Kedwany.Set in 1970s Egypt, the film follows an investigation that begins after a man escapes from a psychiatric hospital and new evidence emerges in connection with a series of killings.Another familiar expression is al-jareema la tufid, meaning crime does not pay. It was used as the title of a story in the Egyptian anthology series Helwa El Donia Sokar, involving an online journalist investigating an artist accused of theft.Serious in court and dramatic in conversation, jareema can describe both a criminal act and an offence judged in the court of public opinion.

headline: Self-acceptance was a lifelong struggle, but an autism diagnosis helped make it easier
summary: I wondered for years whether I had ever actually liked myself.It fluctuated, but the fact that it was a question at all told me the answer was negative more often than not.I don’t think I would go so far as to say I hated myself. But at times I wasn't a fan; I allowed myself to be judged by the opinions of others rather than my own. We’re all trying to be the best version of ourselves, for the most part, and not everyone is going to like that.My problem was that for a long time I was changing that version depending on who was looking.I did not understand at the time that I was masking. I learnt to adjust myself to rooms, people and expectations. If enthusiasm for something was poorly received, I would dial it down. If I was too quiet, I would force myself to speak. If an interaction felt awkward, I would replay it afterwards and consider what I should have done differently.It was rarely conscious. I was simply trying to fit in.But constantly considering how you are being perceived has consequences. If your instinct is always to alter yourself in search of acceptance, eventually you start wondering whether the unaltered version is acceptable at all.That contributed heavily to my unease with myself.Autism has become a buzzword in recent years. The word is sometimes thrown around negatively, casually applied to behaviour someone considers strange or used as a catch-all for neurodivergence.That can obscure the fact that autism is a spectrum and presents very differently from one person to another.I am at the high-functioning end of the spectrum. I work, socialise, have relationships, and, from the outside, can probably move through much of everyday life without anyone suspecting I am autistic.That does not mean those things are always easy.Something as ordinary as meeting somebody new can produce disproportionate anxiety. Speaking confidently can require considerable effort, even if the person listening would never know it. A social interaction can bring an internal checklist of when to speak, what to say, whether one is talking too much or too little and how one is coming across.They sound like small difficulties. Repeated every day, they become exhausting.Before my diagnosis, I did not have a framework for understanding why some seemingly simple things required so much effort. The natural response was to assume I was deficient in some way.Why couldn't I just be more confident? Why did certain situations feel harder than they should?A diagnosis did not answer every question, but it gave me context.It also allowed me to look back at myself with considerably more kindness.I could recognise that some of the things I had spent years trying to correct were simply parts of me I had never understood. Being quiet did not always need fixing. Neither did becoming intensely interested in something, needing time alone or finding particular social situations difficult.Perhaps most importantly, I began to understand how much energy I had spent trying to appear comfortable when I wasn't.I still mask. Everybody behaves differently depending on whether they are with family, friends, colleagues or strangers.The difference now is that I feel less compelled to hide myself simply because somebody else might find the real version unusual.More people get to see that person.I am more comfortable being quiet when I have nothing to say. I can be enthusiastic without immediately wondering whether I should tone it down. I can admit that something makes me anxious instead of exhausting myself trying to appear unaffected by it.And the more comfortable I have become allowing other people to see me, the more comfortable I have become with myself.That has been one of the unexpected gifts of diagnosis.It did not change who I was. It changed the way I interpreted who I had always been.Self-acceptance has not arrived all at once. There are still moments when I catch myself viewing my behaviour through somebody else's eyes.But I do it less.And on World Mental Health Day, perhaps it is the one thing I would urge others to consider.If you are old enough to have spent years feeling that there is something different about you or wondering why seemingly ordinary parts of life present challenges others do not, try to find out why.Take reputable screening tests. Read about the experiences of others. And where possible, speak to a qualified professional and seek a proper assessment.Symptoms could be consistent with autism, anxiety or another form of neurodiversity, or they may have a different cause.But there is value in knowing.For years, I could see the difficulties without understanding where they came from. Once I had a clearer picture, the path ahead became easier to see. The challenges did not disappear, but I became better equipped to manage them and less inclined to blame myself for having them.I spent much of my life thinking acceptance had to come from other people first. If they liked the version of me I presented, perhaps I could like myself too.I had the order wrong.Understanding myself made it easier to accept myself. Accepting myself made it easier to show other people who I actually am.And that has made me considerably happier.

headline: Pepe Cucina review: Bring an appetite – and someone willing to share
summary: It’s Friday night and Pepe Cucina has a lively buzz going on. Families on holiday, date-night couples, friends meeting up at the end of a long working week, the vibe is exactly how an Italian restaurant should feel: friendly, welcoming and like you’ve been there before.But just because a restaurant is not stuffy, that doesn’t mean it’s not sophisticated. Pepe Cucina, in JBR, Dubai, is one of those chameleonic places that’s somehow exactly what you want it to be each time you visit.First impressionsThe space is large, meaning no cramped tables and plenty of scope for birthday gatherings and their popular Saturday brunch. Booths, one of which we settled into, line the left side, while banquette tables cut through the middle of the room to create pockets in which to socialise. Through the floor-to-ceiling windows, the vast, revamped terrace awaits diners during the cooler months, with views across Bluewaters Island and Ain Dubai.The menuThe menu is a solid one-pager. No leafing through leather-bound volumes here. We begin with truffle arancini with truffle mayo and chives (Dh35) from the passa il piatto section, which translates as “pass the plate” and is designed for sharing. The arancini balls are excellent: deep-fried and dense, crunchy on the outside and soft and slightly chewy inside, with a delicate truffle sauce for dipping.My dining companion and I decide to share every dish. Luckily, we’re largely on the same page taste-wise. She knows that I get weird about seafood served with its head still on, and I know that she loves Gorgonzola.For our salad, she is very happy with the yellow and red endive with Gorgonzola, pecan nuts and figs (Dh59). The flavours work so easily together that it’s a dish that begs to be eaten with a little of every ingredient on each forkful.One of the things I love about Italian food is that it’s not linear. Dishes arrive at the table with the intention of being left there. There are no “Are you done with that?” questions and plates whisked away before you can decide whether to nab that last arancini. Instead, everything stays to be grazed, mixed and matched and returned to throughout the meal.For our pizza, we go with a margherita (Dh60), a classic among a curated selection of favourites. The base is delightfully thin, the crust slightly burnished and the bubbled cheese turning a caramel colour. Four slices go into our mouths, two into the box to take home.From the pasta and rice selection, we opt for the traditional fusilloni alla Genovese in a pecorino sauce (Dh94). Having never met a ragu I didn’t love, this hearty, rib-sticking pasta smothered in a rich and generous sauce doesn't disappoint. It’s a dish I have sworn to return for later this year as a winter warmer, with big spoonfuls piled on to our plates alongside the salad, pizza and remaining arancini.To offset the delicious carb-heavy density of everything so far, we choose the rock salt-baked sea bass fillet with roasted potatoes (Dh146) from la griglia (the grill). Its delicate flavour and modest portion make it an ideal counterpoint to what has come before. Salt-baking leaves the fillet tender but still meaty, stopping just short of flaking apart on the fork.Gelato, chocolate, cannoli – the dessert list reads like a greatest hits of traditional Italian sweets. Our debate comes down to the fried doughnut with custard cream (Dh59) or the chocolate mousse with hazelnut and balsamic cherry (Dh57). We err on the side of the traditional mousse, which yields thick spoonfuls of gooey, chocolatey deliciousness that stick to the roof of the mouth, leaving a lingering taste of Italy.Standout dishThe sea bass fillet was a standout insomuch as it worked as well on its own as it did within the ensemble of dishes we accumulated. I imagine it paired perfectly with lighter sides such as sauteed greens, lemon and garlic or a tomato and red onion salad, just as it did with the ragu-smothered fusilloni and Gorgonzola-sprinkled endive leaves on our plates.Save or splurgeYou could leave well fed and satisfied from Pepe Cucina having spent around Dh150, assuming a focaccia starter (Dh20), a rigatoni with spicy Gorgonzola sauce and beef ‘nduja (Dh88) and a tomato carpaccio salad (Dh46). There are dishes to suit all budgets, appetites, tastes and preferences for certain regions of Italy. Those looking to splurge should start with the fritto misto (Dh171), al tartufo pizza with truffle sauce, mozzarella and fresh black truffle (Dh143), lobster linguine (Dh355) and grilled lamb chops (Dh215).Contact detailsPepe Cucina is at Address Beach Resort in JBR, Dubai. It's open Monday to Thursday from 4pm to 12am, and from Friday to Sunday from 1pm to 12am. Reservations can be made by calling 04 879 8866.This review was conducted at the invitation of the restaurant

headline: They travelled to the Gulf to build lives back home - a journey to the Indian villages of seven crash victims
summary: A generation ago, the first men from villages in Telangana and Uttar Pradesh left for the Gulf. Most departed because of a letter from someone who had gone before, or a rumour from the tea shop, or just knowing that someone from the next village had gone and had come back with something to show for it. They didn’t really know what to expect. They went anyway.Many of those men later returned. But not all of them, and not always in the ways they hoped. But most came back with real results – enough that everyone around them understood what the journey was worth. A finished house. A child who received more schooling than the village offered. A family who progressed, however slowly, from just getting by to building something.Because of them, the next group went with more confidence. And the group after that did, too. Seven Indian workers died in an Emirates Road crash in Dubai in June 2026, leaving behind families across Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. Burjeel Holdings chairman Dr Shamsheer Vayalil announced a financial support programme for all seven affected families following the accident.The Gulf has been woven into village life across India for four decades, with knowledge of working abroad passed down through generations.The workers were not seeking permanent lives overseas but using earnings abroad to fund homes, education and weddings back in India.“The Gulf was never the destination – it was the path back to where they were always meant to be,” the delegation's head of communications said.I kept thinking about those early journeys during four days in June, when I travelled through villages in Telangana in southern India and Uttar Pradesh in the north to meet the families of workers who died in the Emirates Road accident in Dubai in June 2026. We went to offer support on behalf of Dr Shamsheer Vayalil, chairman and chief executive of Abu Dhabi healthcare company Burjeel Holdings, who had already announced a support programme for all seven families, and to make sure they knew they were not forgotten.I gained something else, too – a close, unhurried look at what the relationship between the Gulf and those villages actually is after four decades. It is not what people assume.In those villages, the Gulf is not an abstraction, nor does it represent a distant aspiration. It is a part of everyday life. Someone is in the region now. Someone returned to their village last year. A young man from the neighbourhood is saving up money to go. Knowledge of how to get there, what working life is like and what the first summer feels like passes from person to person, tested by real experience and refined over years.In the Jagtial district of Telangana, where we met the families of two of those killed in the crash, Saleem Sayyed and Thirupathi Gollapally, almost every conversation turned to the Gulf. Not because we brought it up, but because it was already part of how people thought about their future.That’s what four decades of this relationship have created.Sayyed, from the Telangana village of Namilakonda, had gone to the UAE just months before the accident. One of his children had health problems that needed more money for treatment than he could earn locally. His daughter’s wedding was also being planned. He wanted a better house, better schooling and the means to pay for all of it.Those demands had piled up all at once, as they often do for families with little margin for error. Working in the Gulf was the only option that could enable him to address them all quickly enough.Gollapally was only 22 and was abroad for the first time. He used to call his parents to talk about getting used to the outdoor work, the heat and everything new. His family in Thakkallapalle, in Telangana, remembers those calls well. Now, that’s all they have left.Another of the crash victims, Abdul Rafiq, had returned to the Gulf, having left the region during the pandemic. His daughter is very young, too little to understand what happened. His father, who had already lost two sons in an earlier road accident, sat with us quietly for a while. We didn’t need words.In the Mau district of Uttar Pradesh, the family of another of those killed, Markandey Chauhan, led us along narrow, unpaved lanes to a house that was still unfinished. We saw this in every village – houses built in stages, a new room added whenever someone working abroad sent money, before construction was suspended when the funds ran out and families waited for the next transfer to arrive.Chauhan's daughter, Ankita, had just finished Grade 12 when her father died. She didn’t complete her application for the state entrance exam this year. During our visit, Dr Vayalil, who joined on a video call, asked Ankita what she wanted to study. She said nursing. He told her without hesitation that her education would be fully paid for, and that a job would be waiting for her at his hospital in the UAE once she graduated. Dr Vayalil had moved to the Gulf with big ambitions and built something there. It wasn’t a coincidence that he was the one making this offer to a girl in a village in Mau. It was the promise made a generation ago, still being kept. The atmosphere in the room changed when he spoke because something her father had worked for was going to continue.What struck me most, in every home we visited, was something the families kept saying in different ways. What moved them wasn’t just the financial support. It was that someone from the country where their loved one had worked had come all the way to sit with them, that the place where they had gone had not treated him as replaceable, that it had sent people to his village.That is the part of the India-Gulf relationship that the statistics and the official programmes do not capture. There is an understanding with no official treaty behind it. It is built on something learnt over a generation: that the Gulf offers work and families who send their sons and brothers aren’t simply making a business deal. They are trusting that, in the event that something goes wrong, the place their loved one went to will remember that he was a person with a village, a half-built house, children in school and parents waiting for his call.That trust was honoured after the accident in June. Families in those villages know exactly what that means. They have been watching how the relationship works for four decades.In Kopaganj, Uttar Pradesh, we met the loved ones of Abdul Rasheed, who was also killed in June. A family member told us quietly that before his final trip he thought it would be his last. He planned to save enough money to return home for good.We heard some version of that ambition in almost every home. These weren’t men trying to leave their villages behind. They were using years abroad to build the life they had always wanted at home. The Gulf was never the destination – it was the path back to where they were always meant to be.That’s the thought the trip left us with. Those men weren’t chasing a life overseas. They were building one in India, with whatever work in the UAE could give them, for as long as it took.M Unnikrishnan is head of communications at VPS Health. He was part of the delegation to India that visited the families of those killed in the accident in June 2026

headline: The Diplomat season four: The story so far before Netflix return
summary: Politics, nuclear weapons, diplomatic crises and a high-profile marriage that always seems to be one argument away from divorce, Netflix hit The Diplomat has packed a lot into three seasons.First aired in 2023, the drama follows Kate Wyler (Keri Russell), a career diplomat who is unexpectedly appointed US ambassador to the UK just as an attack on a British warship threatens to spark an international crisis.What has followed – from assassination plots and secret military operations to a dead US president and plenty of political manoeuvring – has turned the show into a must-watch political thriller. Balancing high-stakes international crises with sharp dialogue, humour and the often chaotic relationship between Kate and her husband Hal (Rufus Sewell), the show also boasts a strong cast of complex women in positions of power, including Allison Janney as US President Grace Penn, Nana Mensah as White House chief of staff Billie Appiah and Ali Ahn as Eidra Park, the CIA station chief in London.The show has also been a critical success, with Russell earning three Emmy nominations for her performance as Kate, while Janney won for her role as Grace last month.Season four picks up after a finale that left Kate facing a very different political landscape – with Grace in the White House and her own husband now vice president. Before the series returns on October 15, here is a refresher on what happened in the first three seasons.What is The Diplomat about?When the series begins, Kate is preparing to become US ambassador to Afghanistan – the kind of difficult assignment she relishes – when an attack on the British aircraft carrier HMS Courageous kills 43 sailors and threatens to trigger an international crisis.Instead, President William Rayburn (Michael McKean) sends her to London as US ambassador to the UK. Unknown to Kate, however, the White House has another plan for her. Vice President Grace Penn is expected to leave office because of a scandal involving her husband, and Kate is quietly being assessed as a potential replacement.There is another complication: Hal. A brilliant but notoriously meddlesome diplomat in his own right, Kate's husband struggles to remain in the background while her career takes centre stage. Their marriage, already on the brink of divorce, is further tested when they arrive in London as separating their personal and professional lives becomes nearly impossible.The story so far (spoilers ahead):What happened in The Diplomat season one?Much of the first season revolves around discovering who attacked HMS Courageous. British Prime Minister Nicol Trowbridge (Rory Kinnear) initially suspects Iran, but Kate helps prevent an immediate military response as evidence instead points to unseen Russian mercenary Roman Lenkov.At the same time, Kate grows close to British Foreign Secretary Austin Dennison (David Gyasi), while deputy chief of mission Stuart Hayford (Ato Essandoh) prepares her for the possibility of becoming US vice president – a job she initially has little interest in.The investigation takes Kate and Austin to Paris, where she learns Britain plans to assassinate Lenkov rather than capture him. Realising his death would prevent him from revealing who hired him, Kate begins to suspect Trowbridge himself was behind the attack.Back in London, Hal is due to meet Conservative MP Merritt Grove (Simon Chandler) when a bomb planted in Grove's car explodes. Stuart and his aide Ronnie are caught in the blast, with the season ending before their fates are revealed.What happened in The Diplomat season two?Season two picks up immediately after the explosion. Hal and Stuart survive, although both are injured. Ronnie does not.Kate's investigation eventually leads to Margaret "Meg" Roylin (Celia Imrie), Trowbridge's former political adviser, who was involved in hiring Lenkov's group to attack HMS Courageous. But Trowbridge himself did not order it.Instead, Kate discovers the plan originated with US Vice President Grace Penn, who believed the attack was necessary to protect US national security interests.The revelation leaves Kate believing Grace will have to leave office and, after previously resisting the idea, she finally accepts that she wants to become vice president. Hal decides Washington needs to know and, rather than going through the usual channels, calls President Rayburn directly to tell him what Grace has done.But shortly after learning the truth, Rayburn dies – making Grace Penn president of the US.What happened in The Diplomat season three?Season three begins with Grace sworn in as president, leaving Kate and Hal in the unusual position of knowing she was behind the HMS Courageous plot.But rather than distancing herself from the Wylers, Grace brings them closer – and in a major reversal, it is Hal, not Kate, who becomes vice president.Kate remains in London as their marriage continues to fall apart and begins a relationship with intelligence operative Callum Ellis (Aidan Turner).A new crisis emerges when a Russian submarine carrying a Poseidon torpedo – described as a "doomsday weapon" – is discovered off the English coast. When the weapon later disappears, Kate realises Grace and Hal may have secretly taken it. When Kate confronts Hal, he tells her to tell no one – then immediately informs Grace that Kate knows.Season three ends with Kate and Grace's husband Todd (Bradley Whitford) watching their spouses together, as Kate faces the possibility that the president and her own husband have secretly taken possession of a Russian nuclear weapon – an act that could push the US towards war.What to expect in The Diplomat season four?Netflix says season four begins with a catastrophic event that threatens the fragile peace between the US and UK, while Grace and Hal's attempt to steal Russia's most powerful weapon risks pushing the US towards war.It also creates an unlikely alliance between Kate and Grace's husband Todd, as they join forces to try to stop their spouses.Janney and Whitford have been promoted to series regulars for the new season, alongside Mensah as Billie Appiah.The Diplomat season four premieres on Netflix on October 15

headline: Fight, flight and the courage in between
summary: Somewhere over north-western Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, September 30, flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv suddenly plunged 5,000 metres before eventually landing safely at Tabuk. Although the exact circumstances of the incident are being investigated, a series of actions that averted a major disaster has awed the world.Capt Smit Machchhar was reportedly attacked by his co-pilot. The captain, losing blood fast, fought not only for the controls but also to open the cockpit door. That allowed a handful of passengers to enter and overwhelm the attacker.One of them said he used his knowledge from air-crash documentaries to pull up the plummeting plane, while two reserve pilots rushed to land the stricken plane safely at Tabuk. A dentist-turned-emergency-medic knelt in the aisle to keep the captain alive until the ambulances came.In the two minutes that separated life from death, the 172 people who had done nothing more heroic than buy a ticket or turn up for flight duty were sorted by circumstances into those who acted and the rest. What set them apart?It is not fearlessness. A study of bomb-disposal officers in Northern Ireland found that most experienced acute anxiety like anyone else but performed anyway. Nelson Mandela said it simply: the brave person is not the one who feels no fear, but who conquers it.Such courage is admirable, of course, but it is not an unqualified virtue. Aristotle placed courage somewhere between cowardice and recklessness. Summoning the right amount of courage requires the right fear, in the right measure, being overcome for the right end.Thus, the flydubai responders thought themselves doomed and their courage came from instinctively trying to save themselves. The subtle distinction is with the passengers of United Airlines Flight 93 in 2001, who were certainly doomed but still organised themselves to save people on the ground by forcing the 9/11 hijackers to crash the plane away from built-up Washington.The seeds of courage, if nurtured correctly, lie ready but dormant until an environmental shift obliges them to sproutThese varieties of courage – self-saving or altruistic – take their shape from circumstances. This derives from the biological evolution that drives our perception of threat and how “cornered” we feel after running out of options.Courage also comes in more than one currency. Beyond the physical type, which is costly in the present but gains medals afterwards, there is the moral kind that costs little in the moment but everything afterwards. This is the whistle-blower or dissenter who speaks truth to power, the journalist who exposes wrongdoing, or the official who reveals openly what his institution hides shamefully. Such courage is usually career-ending and rewarded by ostracism or worse. However, societies have often been changed for the better as a consequence.There is no hierarchy of courage as each person is brave in their own way. But courage is most useful when accompanied by competence – possession of the latter may even obligate the former. Thus, the dentist did not suddenly become brave at altitude but felt a responsibility to help because he had the skill to do so. Perhaps courage is inversely proportional to perceived helplessness.What about Saman Kunan, the Thai navy diver who placed his skills at the service of 12 boys he had never met and died ferrying oxygen through a flooded cave in 2018? Or the 10 Beirut firefighters who deliberately drove into danger to contain a port warehouse blaze in 2020 – and perished themselves? They did not just do their jobs but went well beyond. That is the truest form of courage and often extracts a terrible price.But is courage still worthwhile if a person is not usefully skilled? Abdul Aziz grabbed the first thing he could find – a credit card machine – to chase a gunman out of a Christchurch mosque in 2019. His wit to improvise enabled his courage. Then there is the sheer courage of “presence”, a stubborn refusal to leave. This was seen among the doctors who stayed with their patients in an El Fasher Hospital in Darfur, Sudan last year, as murderous militiamen came in. The millions of ordinary Gazans and Ukrainians who stay or the Sudanese returning home despite continuing onslaughts are further examples. We marvel at their resilience, but this is really a kind of grim courage that helps express resistance.It is difficult to construct a comprehensive theory of courage, but some dimensions are identifiable. Most recipients of the Carnegie Medal in the US describe their acts as “intuitive”. Courage on Flight 1073 happened in seconds or it did not happen at all. Therefore, is “deliberation” the enemy of courage?Not necessarily. Take Stanislav Petrov, a Soviet duty officer in 1983 who saw his screens announce an American missile launch, judged it a false alarm and did nothing. His courage of restraint prevented nuclear Armageddon to earn this Encyclopaedia Brittanica tribute on his death: “He is survived by two children, two grandchildren and the entire human race.”Meanwhile, “numbers” can submerge courage. Research on bystanders reveals that more witnesses to an emergency mean less likelihood of anyone acting. This is because when responsibility is diffused, an individual’s share is not large enough to move them. So, the planeload of people on Flight 1073 could have meant collective paralysis but what broke that spell was another aspect of courageous conduct – its infectiousness. When the bloodied captain managed to open the door, his visible courage triggered the first rescuer to act which then sanctioned the next to join, and so on.Militaries know this and that is why they drill soldiers. This trains troops to move their reaction under fire from the part of the mind that debates risk to the part that acts. Repeat risk exposure – as done by firefighters, for example – shrinks fear while improving competence brings the confidence to shrink it further. Meanwhile, the company of colleagues expecting each other to perform so as not to let themselves down shrinks it most of all. In that sense, courage is catching.But is courage acquired or is it inherited? Limited research suggests that genes may play a role but upbringing more so. People low in anxiety and high in empathy are likelier to intervene. And perhaps Aristotle was right in saying that we become braver by doing brave things.That is why awards like the Carnegie Medal exist – to remind ordinary people that extraordinary things may sometimes be expected of them. That builds up a wider culture of courage in society. The traditional Arab code of muruwwa that honours the courageous rescue of distressed strangers does the same. In short, while some people may be born with a higher threshold for acting courageously, everyone’s threshold can be lowered through example and practice.Thus, the seeds of courage, if nurtured correctly, lie ready but dormant until an environmental shift obliges them to sprout. That is how courage sprouted when the climate shifted on Flight 1073. Overwhelmed readers may wonder what they would have done if they had been on that plane. They should take heart. The seeds of courage are not rationed. They are standard issue, planted in all of us by the evolution of our common humanity.

headline: From Italy’s modern defence structure to the ancient Pantheon: A reminder of what survives
summary: I was in Rome for five days last week, spending much of my time looking at Italy through the lens of defence: military operations, naval capabilities, air power, counter-improvised explosive device expertise and the work behind some of the country’s most important security decisions.Then, at the end of the trip, I found myself standing beneath the dome of the Pantheon, looking up at the oculus and wondering how a building almost 2,000 years old had survived for so long.It was an interesting way to end a programme organised by Italy’s Ministry of Defence for foreign media. It had taken me from the country’s joint operations command to its Army Counter-IED Centre of Excellence and Pratica di Mare Air Base. I had also interviewed Defence Minister Guido Crosetto about Italy’s role in a changing security landscape.It had been a glimpse of modern Italy, concerned with military readiness, technology, alliances and the threats of today. The Pantheon offered another perspective.I first visited Rome in 2022, so it was not my first time wandering its streets, stopping to admire its fountains, piazzas and layers of history. The city has a way of making the past feel like part of daily life rather than something preserved behind glass.As my time in Rome drew to a close, visiting the Pantheon made me appreciate it in a different way.The building is extraordinary even before you know its story. The vast concrete dome, the geometric coffers rising towards the 8.9m-wide oculus and the shaft of daylight falling into the circular interior make it easy to understand why the Pantheon continues to astonish visitors. Its dome, with an internal diameter of about 43 metres, remains the largest unreinforced concrete hemispherical dome in the world.I was there with a tour guide and a lieutenant-colonel from the Carabinieri, Italy’s gendarmerie, which carries out policing duties at home and abroad.“Look at the oculus above you,” said the guide. “You might think it’s covered with glass, but it isn’t. It’s completely open to the sky. And I know what you’re going to ask me: What do we do in winter?”She smiled. “Nothing. It rains, of course, but the water falls through the opening. There are drainage holes in the floor to let it run away.”She pointed to several small openings beneath our feet.It was a simple explanation, but it made the building feel all the more remarkable. The Romans had designed it to accommodate the elements, and almost two millennia later, rain still falls through the same opening.However, what fascinated me most was not just how the Romans built the Pantheon. It was how it survived.A second lifeThe present structure dates to the reign of Emperor Hadrian, between AD 118 and 125, although an earlier temple commissioned by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa had stood on the site. Centuries later, after the decline of the Roman Empire, the Pantheon fell into neglect and was looted.“It was damaged and destroyed several times by devastating fires,” said the guide.Then came the decision that would help determine its fate.In AD 609, the Byzantine emperor Phocas gave the Pantheon to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it as a Christian church dedicated to Santa Maria ad Martyres. Its continued religious use helped protect it from the neglect and removal of building materials that affected many other ancient Roman structures during the Middle Ages, the guide explained. There is something striking about that. The Pantheon was not preserved simply because it was too magnificent to destroy. Its conversion gave it a new purpose and helped protect it for centuries to come.Its function changed, but the building endured. That stayed with me as I walked back through Rome.During the previous days there, much of what I had seen was about preparing for the future: military personnel training for emerging threats, aircraft ready for operations and commanders assessing new defence priorities.Mr Crosetto told me that Italy’s defence spending must continue to rise to meet Nato commitments, but that how the money is spent matters just as much.
