He highlighted the need for greater investment in counter-drone measures, artificial intelligence and integrated air defence.The contrast with the Pantheon was hard to miss. Rome makes these differences easy to appreciate. Ancient columns stand beside busy cafes; ruins form part of ordinary streets; monuments that have witnessed emperors, wars and religious change remain woven into the life of the city.When I stepped back into Piazza della Rotonda, the Pantheon stood amid restaurants, tourists and passing crowds, part of the everyday scene.I had come to Rome to learn about Italy’s armed forces and how the country is responding to modern security challenges. Yet it was the visit at the end of the programme that left me thinking about how history survives.The Pantheon’s story is a reminder that preserving the past does not always mean leaving it untouched. Sometimes, giving an old building a new purpose is what allows it to last.

headline: Free of the land: Has leaving the US become the new American dream?
summary: Some blame the cost of health care. Others are worried about gun violence in schools. Many are fed up with the politics, or just want to experience something new. Whatever the reason, increasing numbers of Americans are voting with their feet and choosing to build new lives overseas.According to Census Bureau data, emigration from the US increased significantly last year, a trend that appears set to grow in 2026. While the numbers are small compared to the US's population of about 340 million, the departure of people from America US has contributed to a significant drop in net migration.For Mike Hogan and his wife Mary, the decision to leave the US was helped by a few simple calculations. The former congressional staff member and government relations consultant, 61, has just retired from the Washington area to southern Spain.They had visited France and Portugal, but after several trips to Spain they fell in love with Estepona, a picturesque Costa del Sol town of whitewashed Andalusian houses and flower-filled streets and plazas.Aside from the vibe and the prospect of a calmer pace of life, something else caught Mr Hogan's attention: health care.The Hogans had been paying about $2,500 a month for a US health insurance plan with a $6,000 excess. In Spain, they found private cover costing about $100 a month, with no deductible or co-payment.“I don't know why we can't figure it out here,” Mr Hogan said, shortly before leaving for Spain. He said his decision was “not overtly political”. He and his wife had started thinking of making the move about five years ago, around the time of the Covid-19 pandemic.The number of Americans leaving the US is difficult to measure, but data collected by The Wall Street Journal from 15 countries found that at least 180,000 Americans moved to those nations in 2025. The total figure is probably far higher than that.President Donald Trump's return to the White House did not factor too much into Mr Hogan's plans, although he said it made some aspects of leaving easier to explain. “We're not moving because of politics, but it is embarrassing to try to defend some of the craziness,” he said. There are plenty of anecdotal signs of the trend elsewhere in Europe, where Americans can secure residency through retirement or investment visas, ancestry claims or job offers. Jamal, a taxi driver in Sete in the South of France, told The National that he frequently picks up suitcase-laden Americans at Montpellier Airport who are moving to Europe permanently.A Gallup poll last year found that 21 per cent of Americans said they would like to leave the US and permanently move to another country if they could. That rose to 40 per cent among women aged 15 to 44 – four times the proportion who said the same in a similar poll in 2014.Cynthia Aceituno, 30, a freelance digital marketer from New York, moved to Barcelona last year. She had been considering El Salvador, where her family is from, but after visiting Spain she decided she wanted to stay.Ms Aceituno says the political climate in the US, the cost of living and the pace of life in New York all contributed to the decision. She also feels safer in Spain.“I can walk at night alone and I don't feel like I'm in danger,” she said. She added that she appreciates the way people choose to spend their time in Spain. “They work to live,” Ms Aceituno said – in New York, she feels, they “live to work”.She still works for New York clients remotely, and her hours have shifted because of the six-hour time difference. But the arrangement has allowed her to build a life that she says feels less stressful.Even visiting the doctor was a revelation. When Ms Aceituno went for the first time, she asked how much she owed. “They were like, ‘Oh no, you live here, it's fine, have a nice day,’” she said. “I walked out in shock.”A common perception is that working life can feel a lot less hectic in parts of Europe than in the US. Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development figures back this up, showing that US employees worked an average of 1,800 hours in 2025, compared with 1,633 in Spain.But people who live in Europe often complain about a frustrating job market or being burdened by bureaucracy and taxes.For Ms Aceituno, the trade-off has been worth it. She said she does not contemplate moving back to New York, although she still considers it home and wants to visit her family. “I don't have to stay here if I don't want to,” she said.Meredith Thomas, owner and lead travel writer for the Two Packs And A Pup blog, left the US two years ago with her partner and their dog to travel full-time. She said the US's high cost of living was a major factor in their decision. “Nearly every country we've lived in has been dramatically cheaper than the States,” she said, noting that her family's costs would easily exceed $10,000 a month at home. “Now, even with frequent travel and tourism spending, we average around half that. It's hard to imagine moving back to $50 brunch bills when we can sip a cocktail on the beaches of Vietnam for only $6.”The US-based research firm Dataframe LLC surveyed 1,869 Americans this year to discover why people are leaving the US. For 61 per cent of respondents, the top motivator was looking for a better quality of life, while 58 per cent cited the cost of living in the US as the primary push factor. The survey also found that 38 per cent of American respondents think the country is declining and 50 per cent had been touched by job loss in the last two years, meaning either themselves or someone close to them had lost a job. For Christopher Mannino, concerns over the safety of his children made the decision to leave the US easy. He and his wife had already lived abroad and had been interested in the idea of travelling with their children when the pandemic made them rethink what they wanted from family life.They eventually settled in Malta, where they could work remotely and send their children to school. The decision was not initially political, but the turning point came when their school district introduced active-shooter drills, an almost uniquely American phenomenon in which children as young as four are taught to hide and stay quiet if a gunman bursts into their school.Mr Mannino, a former teacher, remembers seeing the drills when he returned to substitute teaching. He questioned whether that was an environment in which he wanted his children to grow up. His son, who is nine, told him he liked practising the drills because “he knew how to sacrifice himself to save his friends”.“To hear this nine-year-old talking like that … it's just heartbreaking,” Mr Mannino said. “That's not how kids should be growing up. They shouldn't have to worry about any of that.”He said his kids are now thriving at local schools in Malta, and are involved in sports and theatre, learning about another culture and picking up some Maltese.“The kids are doing so much better,” he said. “I feel like they are safer and they are experiencing the world.”

headline: Why banning children from social media may not be enough to keep them safe online
summary: Barring young people from social media platforms may not be enough to keep them safe unless it forms part of a wider online protection plan, experts have told The National.A co-ordinated strategy that takes into account the need for education on best online practices for young people and their parents would be much more effective in addressing issues around digital safety, the experts said.Several countries have imposed bans on people under a certain age using social media. The UAE is among those seeking to enhance online protection, with plans to prevent under-15s from using social media from June 2027."The challenge is different countries have different approaches to this. There needs to be joined-up thinking," said Wayne Denner, co-founder of Beat the Cyber Bully, an initiative that helps educate parents and children on digital safety across the UK, Ireland and UAE."Some approaches may be more effective than others. The challenge is legislation often only covers certain apps, games or platforms and there are others that fall outside of this. It means that bans might not completely close loopholes around inappropriate content, exploitation or abuse. That's why we still want parental involvement and schools guiding young people on appropriate and responsible use of technology."The UAE's ban, announced in June, is to come into force after a one-year grace period, during which social media companies must bring their services in line with the protocols.Australia was the first country to introduce a social media ban. Anyone under the age of 16 is barred from using platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, X and Reddit. But that does not mean that young people are unable to access other forms of social media.Lemon8, which is owned by TikTok's parent company ByteDance, surged in popularity in Australia after it emerged that it was not included in the initial list of banned apps for under-16s. It was later added."There are lesser-known platforms that parents and teachers aren't aware of," Mr Denner said. "There could be bad actors operating on those platforms who know they might not be as moderated as heavily as elsewhere. This presents a safeguarding risk."It can be something of a whack-a-mole scenario. As soon as you bring one of these platforms under the umbrella, another will emerge."Taking hard lineOther countries have also announced social media measures. The UK's ban for under-16s is also to come into effect from June next year. Under-15s will also be stopped from using social media in France from next year.Nations including Spain, Denmark, Greece, Norway, Indonesia and Canada have also announced proposals for similar bans. The EU announced the EU Kids Act last month, which proposes social media bans for under-13s, with limited accounts for those aged between 13 and 15.Educating parents on the dangers around young people having access to the online world is a crucial step in bolstering safety, Mr Denner said. "You should not be handing your child a phone if you haven't received some kind of education on the risks involved," he said."You shouldn't be able to buy a smartphone for your child without some sort of education on it. You wouldn't be allowed to let a young person drive a car without being qualified. It should also be illegal to introduce technology to children without safeguards in place."Last month, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads, agreed on a major settlement over allegations about the addictiveness of its social platforms for children. According to court filings, the social media company could pay up to $17.1 billion, after action from 47 US states and Washington, DC, and other American territories.Bigger pictureThe success of efforts to bar young people from social media platforms will depend on how such restrictions are implemented, said Prof Nathalie Martial-Braz, chancellor of Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi."An age limit works best as one element of a wider approach," she said. "The most promising measures act on the product itself – private accounts by default, no contact from unknown adults, no advertising based on profiling, and limits on features designed to hold attention, such as infinite scroll and autoplay."Education matters as much as regulation, and schools and universities have a part to play. Children who will open an account at 15 need to be prepared for it beforehand."A single global rule is probably out of reach, since countries have chosen 13, 15 or 16 [years of age]. Shared principles and compatible age-verification standards look more achievable."Another important factor is ensuring young people are protected against the risks lurking around the corner, as technology advances amid the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence."AI has changed the nature of the risk," Prof Martial-Braz said. "It drives the recommendation systems that decide what a young person sees. It can also produce harmful content that did not exist before, such as fabricated images of real people, and a child does not need an account to be affected by that. At the same time, AI is part of the solution."I would plead for a sense of proportion. AI offers real benefits for learning, and a university engaged in AI research would be the last to deny it. The question is which uses are appropriate at which age, and with what safeguards. We are better placed to ask it early than we were with social media."New digital frontiersBut not everyone is in agreement about the efficacy of imposing blanket bans on young people using social media. In December last year, Unicef called for "governments, regulators and companies to work with children and families to build digital environments that are safe, inclusive and respect children’s rights".The agency warned that "social media was not a luxury for many children, especially those who are isolated or marginalised – it is a lifeline providing access to learning, connection, play and self-expression".When British authorities announced plans for the ban in June, Kerry Moscogiuri, chief executive of Amnesty International UK, described it as the "right diagnosis but the wrong prescription". She said the onus should fall on social media companies to do more to keep young people safe."Too many social media companies have built products and business models that prioritise keeping children engaged for longer, often at the expense of their well-being, privacy and rights," she said at the time. “But the problem is not that children exist on social media, it’s that social media companies have built platforms that are unsafe by design. Banning under-16s risks treating children as the problem rather than addressing the companies and systems that create the risks in the first place."Dr Katherine Kemp, associate professor at the faculty of law and justice at UNSW Sydney, told The National that broad bans raise issues about data protection and privacy.For some young people, social media could actually provide a lifeline and help them connect with others, she said. "There are some teenagers who successfully use social media to take part in political debate and advocate causes that are important to them," she added."Social media can also provide vital connections for young people who feel isolated because of their gender, sexuality, neurodiversity or ethnic background, especially where they lack connections in their nearby community."

headline: Cartoon for October 10, 2026
£20m penthouse completes makeover of London's South Bank. So, who will Shell out for it?
summary: In the grimy London aftermath of the Second World War, the Festival of Britain was intended as a “tonic for the nation”, turning the rubble of bombed out industrial wasteland into a showcase of British ideas, art and manufacturing.The six-month festival drew 8.5 million visitors to see the temporary Dome of Discovery exhibition and Skylon sculpture that helped popularise the modern architectural style that would sweep Britain and drag it out of the postwar doldrums. It also signalled the regeneration of the area which became the South Bank – complete with riverside walk, Royal Festival Hall concert venue, galleries and Jubilee Gardens.Seventy-five years on, a second regeneration has taken place. Luxury apartments, including a £20 million ($26.4 million) penthouse which has now gone on sale, shops and restaurants have replaced the outdated office buildings that sprang up in the years since the festival. It has been a 10-year project to redevelop the Shell Centre, the global headquarters of the oil company that stare at the Thames. The Shell Tower – designed by Howard Robertson, who also played a part in the design of the UN building in New York – remains as the oil major's HQ, but the three adjoining wings have undergone a 12-year redevelopment odyssey. While the 27-storey main building has stood intact, the former adjoining blocks built on postwar modernist workplace ideas have been demolished. The complex had a full-sized underground swimming pool, four squash courts, sports club, underground cinema/theatre featuring custom artist murals and a famously large staff cafeteria.The £1 billion development known as Southbank Place has been delivered by Braeburn Estates, a joint venture by Qatari Diar and Canary Wharf Group. Its design, by architects Stanton Williams, is described as a “modern response to the brutalist structures of the neighbouring Royal Festival Hall and the Southbank Centre”.This week, The National was given a tour of Seven, the final building in the project, to see the 3,800 sq ft four-bedroom, duplex penthouse that marks the final jigsaw piece in the redevelopment.Each of the 92 apartments in the limestone building is oriented towards the Thames, with large balconies and vast full-height windows.Occupying the 12th and 13th floors, with 900 sq ft of wraparound terrace, from the penthouse you can see trains trundle below into Charing Cross, while the Elizabeth Tower housing Big Ben can be viewed through the spokes of the London Eye only a few hundred yards away.Its riverside location, with protected gardens in front, means it has a panoramic view through its triple-glazed windows of central London and east past St Paul’s and The Shard to Canary Wharf. It’s also low enough to still see people wandering along the pavements or read the numbers on the red buses crossing Waterloo Bridge.Its interiors have been created by award-winning British interior design studio Albion Nord. Much of the furniture is bespoke and was finished in situ, made by UK-based artisans using traditional craftsmanship. It features specially commissioned artworks, cityscape photography, 1940s-style chairs upholstered in soporifically thick wool, a stainless steel kitchen island and a hand-blown hanging glass pendant lighting the living area.The vast majority of buyers of such properties will stick with the decor they see on first viewing, said Ben Johnson, director at Albion Nord. Besides the odd personal item, why would you change what an expert has spent the past 12 months creating? He appears particularly proud of the fluted walls on the spiral staircase and the main bathroom’s oversize shower. For a brutalist-inspired building, it is “not stark or too modern”, he said. “There’s a lot going on. We have been allowed to be bold, with big upholstery for a big space, showing warmth and movement. It’s a comfortable home, not a show apartment.”He also points out the utility room has the best view of any in London, while each room features a “stunning vignette” regardless of which direction the face.So, who would be the likely buyer?“It’s good to have someone in mind, although it often doesn’t end up like that,” said Miles Wood, sales director at Qatari Diar.He is confident the penthouse “will resonate with buyers from the moment they walk in” and envisages the eventual owner being an international buyer with numerous properties around the globe. There is no dominant nationality within the building, with a mix of British, European and Middle Eastern residents.He says the South Bank tends to attract a younger more creative clientele than other areas popular with the world’s super-rich, such as Mayfair, due to its culture and “place of identity”.He cites the main selling points as its “best-in-class” design and furnishing, as well as the building’s amenities including 25 metre pool, yoga studio and gym.Wind sheerBeing on the 12th floor, “it’s not too windy” and as the only apartment on that storey it comes with privacy built in. Plus, “some people just love a penthouse” and there are not that many to choose from with “views of iconic, quintessential London”.Despite the dent that has been done to London’s reputation for safety in recent years, unfairly so, according to Mr Wood, he believes top-end properties will still achieve top prices.The difference is that now buyers are likely to be thinking long term, generational, rather than just a two or three-year investment.“This has been a 10-year journey and the penthouse is the final piece of the jigsaw,” he said. “It’s been an interesting decade, a challenging time for global geopolitics, but people still want to buy best in class. And with its education, culture and law, I believe London is still the best city in the world.”

headline: UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’
summary: The UN special envoy for Yemen warned the Security Council on Friday that the country has returned to all-out conflict, with fighting spreading across several fronts and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to deepen regional instability.“In the past few weeks, Yemen has slid back into full-scale war, with hostilities spreading across multiple front lines,” UN envoy Hans Grundberg told the 15-member council.The Iran-backed Houthis had earlier advanced towards Mokha and the coast along the strategic Bab Al Mandeb strait, while Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had recaptured territory nearby in a counteroffensive launched this week.The conflict has increasingly spilt into Saudi Arabia. Three Saudi citizens, including an airline pilot, were killed in attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a Saudi aircraft on Thursday, Saudi authorities said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks on the airport.Mr Grundberg condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure, including Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport. He also warned that threats against Saudi-linked commercial vessels in the Red Sea risked further destabilising international shipping and energy markets.“These threats are becoming enmeshed with the broader confrontation over control of maritime trade routes and the stresses on the international energy market,” he said.According to the UN, more than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since the beginning of August, the highest level of new displacement since the 2022 truce. In addition, nearly 4,000 people have fled across the Bab Al Mandeb strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia.Despite escalating hostilities, Mr Grundberg urged the warring parties to pursue negotiations. “Unless war is to become Yemen's permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now,” he noted.

headline: Gaza ceasefire: A year of stalled promises
summary: When the Gaza ceasefire came into effect a year ago, Palestinians in the enclave hoped that they could start rebuilding their lives. The truce came in the form of a 20-point plan which specified that aid would enter at scale and the strip would be “redeveloped for the benefit of the people of Gaza”.It also said there would be a demilitarisation process and gradual Israeli withdrawal. While the ceasefire brought much-needed respite after two years of full-scale war, many of the terms of the agreement have stalled, leaving 1.9 million people still displaced. Meanwhile, in the past year, about 1,400 people in Gaza have been killed and Israel has occupied more territory. Humanitarian workers say food, medical supplies, shelters and other lifesaving aid are not being allowed to enter at the capacity needed. In this episode of Beyond the Headlines, host Nada AlTaher looks at what, if anything, has changed for residents in the strip a year since the ceasefire. We hear from Nesma Al-Sallaq. Gaza shelter co-ordinator at the Norwegian Refugee Council, and political analyst Omar Rahman, fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.

headline: The Gaza ceasefire was meant to end the war. For a mother, paramedic and child, little has changed
US failure to prepare for rise of quantum computers could be 'catastrophic' for economy, GAO warns
summary: The development of Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) capable of breaking just about any encryption might be "catastrophic" to the US economy and security, a new federal report says. The recently released analysis from the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) echoes concerns from technology and cyber security experts in recent years about a hypothetical scenario known as “Q-Day", in which quantum computers fall into the wrong hands and are used to crack billions of passwords and break down other encryption methods, resulting in a wave of financial crimes. Conventional computers process data in bits and have a binary value of zero or one, whereas quantum computers can process digits simultaneously using a two-state unit called a qubit. What that means is that data crunching for research can now be done in a fraction of the time, potentially yielding new breakthroughs in science and medical research.Unfortunately, as the report points out, it also could have tremendous ramifications for cyber security. The non-partisan federal watchdog said that it recently made 89 recommendations to more than 20 federal agencies to develop inventories of potentially vulnerable cryptography that would help in identifying funding for "post-quantum cryptography." It published only the broad recommendations that it had conveyed to officials, and details of the others are unknown."We have omitted the original agency comment letters reprinted in the sensitive report due to sensitivity concerns," it said.Though 12 government agencies agreed with the GAO's recommendations, one agency disagreed with several of them, and the US Department of the Interior failed to provide a response. "We continue to believe that all of the recommendations made in the sensitive report are warranted," the GAO's analysis explained. Though the GAO's evaluation about US government preparedness for CRQCs makes for sobering reading, it did point out a silver lining. "Experts say that the probability that a CRQC will be built in the next 10 years is low," the GAO report reads, though it adds that there's a significant risk that bad actors, governments or organisations might be harvesting large amounts of encrypted data right now, and are simply waiting for CRQCs to become available to decrypt it. "The loss of even a small amount of important sensitive information could have a severe effect on federal operations."The World Economic Forum touched on worries related to quantum computers in its Top 10 Emerging Technologies Report for 2026. It listed lattice-based cryptography as being among the more important technologies. Lattice-based cryptography is based on the idea of preserving encrypted data on computers and devices by relying on a series of mathematical problems consisting of complicated grids, also known as lattices, that are impossible for even quantum computers to solve.

headline: US sanctions entire ICC for first time in Trump escalation
summary: The US imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, sanctioning the entire tribunal for the first time as the Trump administration escalated its campaign against the institution in The Hague.Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with “this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us."“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Mr Rubio said in a video posted on social media.The sanctions are expected to restrict the ICC's ability to use the US financial system, with a transition period before most prohibited transactions become unlawful. Previous US sanctions were imposed on individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over investigations involving American and Israeli officials. “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Mr Rubio said. He also warned US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defence” to bring the tribunal under control or face further American efforts to dismantle it “brick by brick”.Today, the Trump Administration is sanctioning the ICC.This action should encourage our Allies within the Court to work for solutions to end this threat to U.S. sovereignty forever. pic.twitter.com/D86dCqLUaZ— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 9, 2026The US action came the same day that ⁠former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The ICC “strongly” rejected the sanctions, calling them an attack on international justice and warning that “history will judge this moment”.“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.ICC President Tomoko Akane urged its member states to defend the institution against mounting US pressure.“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it. The Rome Statute is a collective promise that the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole must not go unpunished. That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it,” she said.The EU called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work”.The latest confrontation follows Mr Trump's call last month for all ICC member states to withdraw from the tribunal, which he called “out of control” and a “rogue institution”.Established in 2002, the ICC has 125 member states, although major powers, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel are not members. Under its founding Rome Statute, the court can prosecute people for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide only when national authorities are unwilling or unable to do so themselves.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also condemned the sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to carry out its work. Human rights groups condemned the US sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to pursue justice for victims of atrocities around the world.“By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, the Trump administration has taken a sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century,” said Omar Shakir, executive director of Dawn, a US-based human rights organisation.“US sanctions threaten to shut the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine, all to shield Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide from justice.”
body_text:
The US imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, sanctioning the entire tribunal for the first time as the Trump administration escalated its campaign against the institution in The Hague.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with “this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us."

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Mr Rubio said in a video posted on social media.

The sanctions are expected to restrict the ICC's ability to use the US financial system, with a transition period before most prohibited transactions become unlawful. Previous US sanctions were imposed on individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over investigations involving American and Israeli officials.

“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Mr Rubio said. He also warned US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defence” to bring the tribunal under control or face further American efforts to dismantle it “brick by brick”.

The US action came the same day that ⁠former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The ICC “strongly” rejected the sanctions, calling them an attack on international justice and warning that “history will judge this moment”.

“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

ICC President Tomoko Akane urged its member states to defend the institution against mounting US pressure.

“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it. The Rome Statute is a collective promise that the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole must not go unpunished. That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it,” she said.

The EU called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work”.

The latest confrontation follows Mr Trump's call last month for all ICC member states to withdraw from the tribunal, which he called “out of control” and a “rogue institution”.

Established in 2002, the ICC has 125 member states, although major powers, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel are not members. Under its founding Rome Statute, the court can prosecute people for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide only when national authorities are unwilling or unable to do so themselves.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also condemned the sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to carry out its work. Human rights groups condemned the US sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to pursue justice for victims of atrocities around the world.

“By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, the Trump administration has taken a sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century,” said Omar Shakir, executive director of Dawn, a US-based human rights organisation.

“US sanctions threaten to shut the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine, all to shield Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide from justice.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the US sanctions as an aggressive escalation by the Trump administration against international justice, emphasizing widespread condemnation from the ICC, EU, UN, and human rights groups while giving limited space to the US rationale.

loaded_language.quote: escalated its campaign against the institution
loaded_language.explanation: The word 'campaign' implies a sustained, coordinated, and possibly hostile effort, adding an editorial tone beyond a neutral description of sanctions.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: imposed additional sanctions on the institution

loaded_language.quote: crippling its ability to operate against us
loaded_language.explanation: This is a direct quote from Marco Rubio, but its inclusion without contextual analysis may amplify the dramatic framing of the sanctions' impact.
The metaphor 'brick by brick' is vivid and suggests a deliberate, destructive process, which can evoke strong negative imagery.

loaded_language.quote: sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century
loaded_language.explanation: This quote from a human rights activist uses a violent metaphor ('sledgehammer') and hyperbolic praise ('most important development in half a century'), which is emotionally charged.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: a severe blow to a significant development in international justice

loaded_language.explanation: This is a direct quote from a human rights activist, but the term 'genocide' is highly charged and legally specific, and its inclusion without attribution to a court finding may be seen as editorializing.

omissions: The US government's stated rationale for the sanctions beyond Rubio's quotes, such as specific concerns about ICC jurisdiction over US personnel.
Reactions from US officials or supporters who defend the sanctions as necessary to protect American sovereignty.
Details about the scope of the sanctions, such as which specific transactions are prohibited and the length of the transition period.
The number of ICC member states that have expressed support for the US position or have remained silent.

headline: El-Sayed and Rogers trade personal attacks in bitter Michigan Senate debate
summary: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, the two candidates vying for a US Senate seat in Michigan, have traded bitter personal attacks during a hostile debate over Iran, Israel and the economy.Their first televised exchange late on Thursday was marked by acrimonious jibes and fundamental disagreements, with tensions spilling over into the commercial break.“I want to take a quick aside and tell you that in 30 years of doing debates, I've never seen it continue during the commercial,” said Rick Albin, the debate's moderator. “But it did.”The heated debate comes during a tight race in the swing state, with less than four weeks until the midterm elections. Michigan is home to about 300,000 Arab Americans, and President Donald Trump has won there twice.The November 3 elections will determine who controls Congress, and Michigan is among the most closely watched Senate races. If Mr El-Sayed, a Democrat, wins, he would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Mr Rogers, a Republican, is an ally of Mr Trump.“Under this guy who's going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp, you're going to continue to pay way more out the nose because he works for corporations and Donald Trump,” Mr El-Sayed said.Recent polling suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming the President for his handling of the issues. His approval rating has sunk to the low 30s. Mr Trump has said the war would end after the midterms and that fuel costs – which rose after Iran put a chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz – would go down shortly after. But the war has been particularly unpopular among voters, and the Trump-endorsed Mr Rogers has run an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.”'Go ahead and say it'Mr Rogers questioned his opponent's credentials, calling Mr El-Sayed a “con man” and accusing him of having ties to armed groups in the Middle East.“He can't condemn Hamas. He can't condemn the Muslim Brotherhood. He says his home is Egypt,” he said.Mr Rogers later suggested that concerns about surveillance could be personal for Mr El Sayed because he or someone in his family might be suspected of terrorism.“Go ahead and say it,” Mr El-Sayed interjected. “You've been tiptoeing around it the whole time.”The candidates also traded accusations over their wealth and property. Mr El-Sayed accused Mr Rogers of owning a home in Florida and two yachts. Mr Rogers countered that Mr El-Sayed's wife owned a home in the UAE and might own one in Egypt. They actually own two rental properties overseas – one in Bangalore and the other in Dubai, but not in Egypt.Abdul El-Sayed asks Mike Rogers how many yachts he owns at the Michigan Senate debate pic.twitter.com/MfzZft2Jcl— Politics Watch (@politics_watch1) October 8, 2026Although the moderator at times struggled to keep the debate focused on policy, the candidates also clashed over their positions on the Middle East.Asked whether any action by Israel would lead him to withdraw support for US military assistance, Mr Rogers said: “I support just as staunchly their right to exist, the right to exist for the Jewish state, and the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood.”Pressed on what might change his position, he said that if Israel were to talk about using nuclear weapons, he would shift stance. Mr El Sayed also faced repeated questions about which country posed a greater threat to the US, Israel or Iran. He called it a “ridiculous hypothetical”.“Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he said. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So, this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part.” When pressed for an answer, he said: “I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One at risk of attacking us. One getting us into wars we have no business fighting.”Highlighting the Islamophobia that Mr El Sayed has been subjected to throughout his campaign, after the debate, Mr Trump attacked Mr El-Sayed in a racist social media post, calling him a “Jihadist lunatic” and referring to him as “Mohammed”.“Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the US fail,” he wrote.The candidates are scheduled to meet for a second and final debate on October 21 in Detroit.

headline: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 9/11-style attack on Tel Aviv and trained for cockpit fight
summary: A flydubai co-pilot attempted to seize control of a passenger jet and crash it into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport in a premeditated suicide attack, UAE prosecutors have said.The UAE's Attorney General, Hamad Al Shamsi, announced on Friday that an investigation into the September 30 incident involving flight FZ1073, bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai, found that the aircraft's Omani co-pilot carried out a terrorist plot to cause mass casualties at the Israeli airport. The suspect, aged 29, was inspired by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and had pursued a career in aviation specifically to carry out a similar operation, according to his confession.Radicalised in AustraliaDr Al Shamsi said investigators traced the suspect's radicalisation to 2017, when he was studying in Melbourne, Australia. During that period, he was exposed to extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. He also attended a mosque affiliated with the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology, where he allegedly came into contact with people connected to a centre managed by a Lebanese man known as Abu Hamza, said to have links to the Muslim Brotherhood.He also said that he had prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing with a private coach.Investigators found that the suspect had used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv to reconnoitre the route and airport ahead of the attack.No indications of extremismThe suspect worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, then briefly for Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. The investigation also examined the procedures under which the suspect had been recruited by flydubai. The findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot’s licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.The attackDuring the incident, he allegedly struck the aircraft's captain, Smit Machchhar, with an emergency axe inside the cockpit. A pilot travelling as a passenger on the return flight noticed the cockpit door behaving unusually, gained entry, and, with the help of crew and passengers, restrained the suspect and rescued the injured captain.The aircraft was diverted and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. The suspect confessed to acting alone, though investigations are continuing to verify that claim. The Public Prosecution also heard statements from the captain, the return flight pilot, his co-pilot and members of the crew. The forensic medical report established that the captain’s injuries were concentrated on the head and consistent with the timing of the incident. The findings were also consistent with the statements made by the suspect and the captain, as well as witness testimony. The Public Prosecution is reviewing recordings, technical reports and possible connections to accomplices.

headline: Dubai Orchestra Foundation established by law to boost emirate's cultural ambitions
summary: Dubai has a new dedicated body to champion orchestral music after Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, signed a law establishing the Dubai Orchestra Foundation.Sheikh Mohammed issued Law No. (20) of 2026, creating the Foundation to advance the arts and orchestral music across the emirate. The body is tasked with strengthening Dubai's regional and international cultural standing, preserving local artistic heritage and showcasing the UAE's musical excellence.Among its core responsibilities, the Foundation will establish a local orchestra, stage performances both within the UAE and abroad, and promote Emirati musical heritage. It will also support emerging talent, including People of Determination, develop an annual calendar of musical events and host international orchestras. The Foundation will build local and global partnerships, support music education and production, and foster collaboration with cultural institutions worldwide.The Law outlines a governance structure headed by a Board of Trustees, comprising a Chairman, Vice Chairman and members with relevant expertise, all appointed by the Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai. The Foundation is expected to contribute to Dubai's broader creative economy, reinforcing the emirate's position as a leading destination for cultural tourism and encouraging investment in the music and performing arts industries.

headline: Dubai Cashless Strategy contributes Dh8bn to economy as it exceeds goals ahead of schedule
summary: The Dubai Cashless Strategy has contributed more than Dh8 billion ($2.18 billion) to the economy, surpassing its goals ahead of its two-year timeframe.The emirate's cashless transactions index hit 90.1 per cent, exceeding the 90 per cent target set for 2026, the Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Friday, quoting figures from Dubai Finance.The Dh8 billion figure was also the target set when the strategy was launched in October 2024. The digital enablement index for the government sector reached 100, reflecting the availability of digital payment methods across institutions and businesses, it said.The initiative achieved strong results across the strategy’s three pillars, with 97 per cent achieved in governance, 95 per cent in society and 93 per cent in innovation, it said. “Operational business continuity was also maintained to ensure the sustainability of these results and maximise their long-term impact,” the report said.Additionally, the community happiness index also hit 90.1 per cent, also surpassing the 90 per cent target.“The strategy reflects the success of Dubai’s model, which is built on a clear vision, integrated roles between the government and private sectors, and the expanding use of technology and innovation to serve people and enhance economic competitiveness,” the DMO said, citing Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence.The Dubai Cashless Strategy was unveiled in October 2024 as the emirate seeks to solidify its standing as one of the world’s top digital cities.The initiative seeks to enable seamless and secure digital payment solutions across both government and private sectors, the media office said. It aligns with the objectives of the Dubai Economic Agenda, the initiative also known as D33.In a separate statement on Friday, top Dubai officials said the achievement marks a new milestone and reinforces Dubai’s position as a leading global hub.“The transition towards a cashless society is not a technological objective in itself. It is part of a broader vision for an interconnected digital city that provides individuals and businesses with easier and more efficient experiences and enables innovation to translate into economic and social value,” said Hamad Al Mansoori, director general of Digital Dubai, which spearheaded the cashless strategy.Helal Almarri, director general of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, noted that the efficiency of transactions is a vital element of the experience of businesses, residents and visitors.“The wider range of payment options enriches the visitor experience, enhances Dubai’s competitiveness and reinforces its position as one of the world’s most accessible and connected cities,” he added.

headline: What's behind the postponement of Palestinian elections and what happens next?
summary: Under intense pressure to reform, President Mahmoud Abbas vowed 2026 would be the year of diplomacy, announcing that Palestine would hold legislative elections in November and Presidential elections next year. Many doubted they would happen, given past experience. Their fears became reality this week, with sources telling The National that the elections are to be delayed again. The last time this happened was in 2021, when Mr Abbas announced that legislative elections were cancelled after hope had been ignited that the Palestinian government might be revived. “This was not a postponement, this was a cancellation,” said Palestinian-Canadian lawyer Dania Buttu, who is the former spokeswoman for the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO). Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree. “This is called authoritarian rule,” she added.This time, the postponement comes at a crucial period, weakening the Palestinian Authority's credibility in the face of a mountain of challenges, including a right-wing Israeli drive to make it impossible to establish statehood, a war that has not stopped in Gaza, and international obligations that have not been fulfilled. Israel has occupied more than half of the Gaza Strip, and its army has killed 70,000 Palestinians there over the course of the three-year war since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks have become more rampant and intense, and conditions inside Israeli prisons are described as torture by Israeli and international rights groups.The conditions for free and fair elections are unlikely to be met in Palestine in the near future, particularly if Benjamin Netanyahu's government survives Israel's own vote set to take place at the end of this month. However, Mr Abbas has also not secured any type of future for Palestine.“When Abu Ammar [Yasser Arafat] was alive, we knew what would happen after he was gone. There would be elections, and Abbas would win. Today, we have no idea,” Ms Buttu said.Palestine's parliament has not met since 2007, the last time since legislative elections, and Mr Abbas has issued at least “three times” more decrees than parliament has passed laws, she added. Despite creating the role of Vice President, Mr Abbas has also bolstered the position of his own son, and a clear plan of action is not in place for when the 90-year-old President dies. Sources from different factions said the roots of the delay are mainly tied to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. But attempts to unite notorious factions within the Palestinian political scene have often failed, stemming from disagreements about the way forward for Palestine. Systemic and endemic problems mean that Palestine has lacked the right environment for elections for decades. Under an occupation that has become more fierce and deadly in recent decades, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.Unpopular leaderHigh-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling support circle.Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.This confirms “the persistence of exceptionally high dissatisfaction with his leadership”, the PSR said in its findings. Driven by what seemed like a crucial moment for change after Mr Abbas's announcement earlier this year that elections would be held, momentum began to build, preparations were set in place and alliances began to form.Inside FatahFirst, municipal elections were held in the West Bank and in one area of Gaza, Deir Al Balah, because the remainder of the strip is simply too destroyed to host an organised vote. The vote went ahead, and despite some criticism, was viewed as a step forward towards larger elections. Then, he held elections in Fatah's Central Committee, where the cracks began to form. Several sources told The National that the vote was clearly “rigged”. People who once seemed to be guaranteed winners were sidelined, while others, like Mr Abbas's son Yasser, gained enough votes to secure a seat on the committee. “In my estimation, this is one of the most significant reasons [for the postponement],” an official with Palestinian Islamic Jihad told The National. “There is internal disarray within the Fatah movement regarding the formation of its electoral list and the distribution of power centres following the movement's Eighth Conference.”Additionally, Fatah is not viewed as a single party. Splits over the years from the group's main members by people who can, in today's political climate, play a significant role, such as Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Kidwa, mean that Fatah no longer represents one single vision. Mr Dahlan, the head of a breakaway faction of Fatah called the Democratic Reform Party, was the Fatah representative in Gaza before being exiled from the group. Similarly, Mr Al Kidwa, who is the nephew of former Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, was expelled from the Fatah party and joined forces with one of Palestine's most prominent political figures, Marwan Al Barghouti, for the elections in 2021 that Mr Abbas also “postponed”. New alliances Mr Dahlan recently met the head of Hamas's politburo, Khalil Al Hayya, in Cairo. Both Mr Dahlan's party and Hamas issued a statement confirming that they had met, cementing further what many had suspected before: that efforts were probably being made to unite against Mr Abbas in upcoming elections.There were also talks that Mr Barghouti himself would join one of the parties running against Mr Abbas – causing the chances of the President's political survival in a poll to shrivel. Only 14 per cent of people would vote for him if Mr Barghouti and Mr Al Hayya ran against him. “New alignments have emerged over the past few months, including a rapprochement between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the faction led by Mohammed Dahlan. This creates the possibility of an electoral map reshaped in a way that makes it difficult for the current leadership to control the outcome,” the PIJ official added. “Thus, postponement becomes a means to realign alliances before heading to the polls.”The future of PalestineA lot of this was expected, and did not come as a surprise for many. In fact, the same public opinion poll showed that 44 per cent of Palestinians did not believe the elections would take place on time. So did many Palestinian experts and watchers. Mr Abbas postponed the 2021 elections under the pretext that Israel would not allow people to cast their vote in occupied East Jerusalem, after it became increasingly apparent that he would lose. Today, the circumstances are significantly more dire.The framework within which the November vote will be postponed is important. In 2021 there was simply an announcement, but if Mr Abbas issues a decree, this should make it legally binding. Additionally, pressure from Europe may also mean that a vote is not “postponed” indefinitely, but takes place later, within a set timeframe. Eyes will now be on France and other European countries that have made reform a condition of their provision of assistance to the Palestinian Authority, now that the decision to postpone has been made but not officially announced.

Under intense pressure to reform, President Mahmoud Abbas vowed 2026 would be the year of diplomacy, announcing that Palestine would hold legislative elections in November and Presidential elections next year.

Many doubted they would happen, given past experience. Their fears became reality this week, with sources telling The National that the elections are to be delayed again. The last time this happened was in 2021, when Mr Abbas announced that legislative elections were cancelled after hope had been ignited that the Palestinian government might be revived.

“This was not a postponement, this was a cancellation,” said Palestinian-Canadian lawyer Dania Buttu, who is the former spokeswoman for the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO). Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree. “This is called authoritarian rule,” she added.

Highly anticipated Palestinian elections likely to be postponed, sources say

This time, the postponement comes at a crucial period, weakening the Palestinian Authority's credibility in the face of a mountain of challenges, including a right-wing Israeli drive to make it impossible to establish statehood, a war that has not stopped in Gaza, and international obligations that have not been fulfilled.

Israel has occupied more than half of the Gaza Strip, and its army has killed 70,000 Palestinians there over the course of the three-year war since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks have become more rampant and intense, and conditions inside Israeli prisons are described as torture by Israeli and international rights groups.

The conditions for free and fair elections are unlikely to be met in Palestine in the near future, particularly if Benjamin Netanyahu's government survives Israel's own vote set to take place at the end of this month. However, Mr Abbas has also not secured any type of future for Palestine.

“When Abu Ammar [Yasser Arafat] was alive, we knew what would happen after he was gone. There would be elections, and Abbas would win. Today, we have no idea,” Ms Buttu said.

Palestine's parliament has not met since 2007, the last time since legislative elections, and Mr Abbas has issued at least “three times” more decrees than parliament has passed laws, she added. Despite creating the role of Vice President, Mr Abbas has also bolstered the position of his own son, and a clear plan of action is not in place for when the 90-year-old President dies.

Sources from different factions said the roots of the delay are mainly tied to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. But attempts to unite notorious factions within the Palestinian political scene have often failed, stemming from disagreements about the way forward for Palestine.

Systemic and endemic problems mean that Palestine has lacked the right environment for elections for decades. Under an occupation that has become more fierce and deadly in recent decades, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.

High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling support circle.

Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.

This confirms “the persistence of exceptionally high dissatisfaction with his leadership”, the PSR said in its findings.

Driven by what seemed like a crucial moment for change after Mr Abbas's announcement earlier this year that elections would be held, momentum began to build, preparations were set in place and alliances began to form.

First, municipal elections were held in the West Bank and in one area of Gaza, Deir Al Balah, because the remainder of the strip is simply too destroyed to host an organised vote.

The vote went ahead, and despite some criticism, was viewed as a step forward towards larger elections. Then, he held elections in Fatah's Central Committee, where the cracks began to form. Several sources told The National that the vote was clearly “rigged”. People who once seemed to be guaranteed winners were sidelined, while others, like Mr Abbas's son Yasser, gained enough votes to secure a seat on the committee.

“In my estimation, this is one of the most significant reasons [for the postponement],” an official with Palestinian Islamic Jihad told The National. “There is internal disarray within the Fatah movement regarding the formation of its electoral list and the distribution of power centres following the movement's Eighth Conference.”

Additionally, Fatah is not viewed as a single party. Splits over the years from the group's main members by people who can, in today's political climate, play a significant role, such as Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Kidwa, mean that Fatah no longer represents one single vision.

Mr Dahlan, the head of a breakaway faction of Fatah called the Democratic Reform Party, was the Fatah representative in Gaza before being exiled from the group. Similarly, Mr Al Kidwa, who is the nephew of former Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, was expelled from the Fatah party and joined forces with one of Palestine's most prominent political figures, Marwan Al Barghouti, for the elections in 2021 that Mr Abbas also “postponed”.

Mr Dahlan recently met the head of Hamas's politburo, Khalil Al Hayya, in Cairo. Both Mr Dahlan's party and Hamas issued a statement confirming that they had met, cementing further what many had suspected before: that efforts were probably being made to unite against Mr Abbas in upcoming elections.

There were also talks that Mr Barghouti himself would join one of the parties running against Mr Abbas – causing the chances of the President's political survival in a poll to shrivel. Only 14 per cent of people would vote for him if Mr Barghouti and Mr Al Hayya ran against him.

“New alignments have emerged over the past few months, including a rapprochement between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the faction led by Mohammed Dahlan. This creates the possibility of an electoral map reshaped in a way that makes it difficult for the current leadership to control the outcome,” the PIJ official added. “Thus, postponement becomes a means to realign alliances before heading to the polls.”

A lot of this was expected, and did not come as a surprise for many. In fact, the same public opinion poll showed that 44 per cent of Palestinians did not believe the elections would take place on time. So did many Palestinian experts and watchers.

Mr Abbas postponed the 2021 elections under the pretext that Israel would not allow people to cast their vote in occupied East Jerusalem, after it became increasingly apparent that he would lose. Today, the circumstances are significantly more dire.

The framework within which the November vote will be postponed is important. In 2021 there was simply an announcement, but if Mr Abbas issues a decree, this should make it legally binding.

Additionally, pressure from Europe may also mean that a vote is not “postponed” indefinitely, but takes place later, within a set timeframe. Eyes will now be on France and other European countries that have made reform a condition of their provision of assistance to the Palestinian Authority, now that the decision to postpone has been made but not officially announced.

analysis.framing: The article frames the postponement of Palestinian elections as a symptom of Mahmoud Abbas's authoritarian rule and internal Fatah dysfunction, while also highlighting Israeli occupation and international pressure as contextual factors.

loaded_language.explanation: A strong, value-laden term that characterizes Abbas's governance as dictatorial, going beyond a neutral description of ruling by decree.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: rule by decree without a legislative mandate

loaded_language.explanation: A colloquial and accusatory term implying deliberate fraud, presented without attribution to a specific source in the text.
A hyperbolic metaphor that exaggerates the scale of difficulties, adding emotional weight.
A negatively charged adjective that casts the factions as infamous, introducing editorial judgment.
An idiomatic phrase that strongly implies near-total failure, heightening the sense of crisis.

omissions: No mention of specific dates or timelines for the postponed elections beyond 'November' and 'next year'.
No direct comment from Mahmoud Abbas or Fatah officials explaining the postponement.
No details on the legal or constitutional process for postponing elections.
No mention of international observers or their assessments.
No coverage of potential reactions from the Biden administration or other key international actors beyond Europe.

headline: President Sheikh Mohamed and Canadian PM Mark Carney discuss UAE-Canada economic ties
summary: President Sheikh Mohamed spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday, with both leaders pledging to deepen bilateral ties across vital sectors, with a particular focus on strengthening economic and investment ties.Advanced technology and AI also featured prominently in the discussions, reflecting both nations' ambitions to position themselves as leaders in emerging industries. The two leaders identified these sectors as central to the development priorities of both countries and pledged their commitment to advancing UAE-Canada relations through long-term, sustainable partnerships. In July, the UAE finalised a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa) with Canada. The trade ​agreement with Ottawa aims to reduce trade barriers to goods, services and ⁠investment, and follows a $50 billion investment commitment from the UAE last November.The Cepa gives Canadian companies better access to the UAE, which remains the largest market for Canada's exports to the Middle East, and could help attract capital into energy, mining, artificial intelligence and ports.Friday's call also touched on a number of regional and international issues of mutual concern. The two leaders exchanged views on developments in the Middle East, with both expressing support for continuing efforts to promote security, stability and peace across the region.The emphasis on AI and advanced technology signals a forward-looking agenda, aligning with the UAE's broader national strategy to diversify its economy and cement its status as a global hub for innovation.

headline: UAE worshippers answer President Sheikh Mohamed's call to pray for rain
summary: Worshippers gathered at mosques across the UAE on Friday to perform Salaat Al Istisqaa, the Islamic prayer for rain.Earlier in the week, President Sheikh Mohamed had called on Emiratis and UAE residents to perform the prayer. The call came as the level of rainfall declines across parts of the Middle East. Through most of 2025, cumulative rainfall in the UAE was significantly below average – about 38 per cent less than the historical baseline and nearly three times lower than in 2024. At Sheikh Hazza bin Sultan Mosque in central Abu Dhabi on Friday, people were hopeful that rain will come soon.Egyptian resident Ibrahim Hamouda, 30, has attended Friday prayers at the mosque for six years. “It is a way for us to call upon our Lord through prayer; specifically, during times of drought,” he said. “It is how we ask God for what we need.”Jordanian Hussam Ali Hamdan was born in Abu Dhabi and has frequented the mosque since 2017. He said that the prayers are not just for humans, but for all living beings.“It is sunna of Prophet Muhammad, where we supplicate and we make duaa to the Almighty Allah to have mercy upon us and to send the rain for us as humans and for the living beings, like the trees and the animals,” Mr Hamdan told The National.Mohammad Arif from India participates in the rain prayers annually, and finds enjoyment in coming together to ask for blessings.“Inshallah Allah will give us rain. It's not only in the UAE, it should be everywhere in the world. We are very lucky to be in this country, but like other places ... I belong to India, this year there are lots of droughts over there in many places. I'll be praying for that also, throughout the world rain should come,” he said.Ahmed Sabir, from Egypt, said that the prayers are a way to ask God for the needs of the people. “It is essential; we must pray and supplicate to God so He may show us mercy, improve our conditions and the weather, ensure our agriculture thrives, and keep everything running smoothly. God’s bounty is vast,” he said.Samir Ashaar, from Egypt, has been coming to the mosque for nine years. He believes this ritual is one that everyone should follow.“May God show us mercy through the rain,” he said. “Everyone ought to attend today, as this prayer – whether considered an obligation or a Sunnah – invites forgiveness and mercy from Allah. God willing, there will be supplication and a favourable response; hopefully, the rain will fall today, by His leave.”

headline: Iraq expects to start transporting crude oil by lorry to Syria from mid-October
summary: Iraq is expecting to begin transporting crude oil via a route to be provided by Syria starting in mid-October, a development that is expected to boost its energy exports that have been hampered by flare-ups in the Strait of Hormuz amid the war in Iran.The crude products will be moved to a port in the Mediterranean Sea using lorries after Iraq requested assistance from Syrian authorities, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing Yousef Qiblawy, chief executive of the state-owned Syrian Petroleum.The agreement between Baghdad and Damascus is “almost done”, and the Iraqi oil exports are expected to “start as soon as possible ... hopefully, by mid-October the first chain of trucks with crude will come to Syria”, he said.The impending move follows a similar energy trade-related co-ordination between the two Middle East nations in late September, in which Iraq began importing petrol through Syria.In April, Syria became the main route for Iraqi fuel oil exports, partially compensating for the disruption to shipments caused by the war in Iran. At least 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi fuel oil have also flowed by lorry to Syria's Baniyas since then.An Iraqi Oil Ministry official had told The National that the first cargo of imported petrol, comprising 32,000 tonnes, was being unloaded at the Baniyas refinery, to be transported to Iraq on lorries.Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations.Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals.The agreements between Iraq and Syria also mark a significant deepening of ties as Baghdad deals with disruption to its trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and as the US pushes for closer relations between the two countries.The strait, through which about a fifth of the world's energy exports passed before the war, remains a flashpoint in the eight-month conflict.The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. The figures include shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and by other methods.Iraq is a major crude oil producer, but faces petrol shortages because of problems with its refineries and the management of its energy infrastructure. Last Sunday, the state-owned Iraqi Oil Tankers Company transported two million barrels of its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades.The move was intended to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, director general Ali Qais said, adding that the company is also in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”.

headline: French lender Natixis CIB expects double-digit growth in Middle East and Asia despite war uncertainty
summary: French lender Natixis Corporate and Investment Banking expects double-digit growth in its Middle East and Asia business this year and next, despite the uncertainty driven by the Iran war and contracting economies.The lender, which has grown in double digits over the past five years in the region, has not been deterred by the geopolitical headwinds. It plans to hire more bankers across the business in markets such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia, said Bruno Le Saint, chief executive of Natixis CIB for Asia Pacific and Middle East. “In the overall region, we want to grow in double digits on average. This is what we've been doing over the past years and going forward we'll keep that pace,” he told The National. “It means that, overall, we hope to be close to 20 per cent in the next two to four years, but it also depends on how quickly we grow the rest of the business.”For the broader Middle East, Natixis CIB expects its business to grow by at least 10 per cent next year, despite the economic challenges caused by the war. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are the two largest regional markets for the French lender.Part of Groupe BPCE, the eurozone's fourth-largest banking group, Natixis CIB is expanding its footprint in the UAE, where it operates from the Dubai International Financial Centre. The Paris-based company has 80 personnel working out of Dubai and it plans to bring more resources, “expanding our workforce and our capabilities on the ground", Mr Le Saint said. “I think it's important because, in the context of the current situation, I don't think there have been many international banks growing staff in this region,” he said.It also plans to further boost its presence in Saudi Arabia, where Natixis CIB operates through its banking subsidiary, Natixis Saudi Arabia Investment Company.“We want to keep growing this,” Mr Le Saint said. “We still think that we are underinvested in Saudi Arabia.” The kingdom's Vision 2030 agenda also aligns well with Natixis CIB’s core financing and investment banking expertise in sectors including telecoms, energy, infrastructure, metals and mining.The bank is also considering expansion into Turkey, "which is also a big economy in the region", Mr Le Saint said of Natixis CIB’s expansion beyond the Arab world. “How do we grow there? It's under exploration for now, but these are the questions we are asking ourselves.”The company currently provides services to clients in markets including Oman and Turkey in the region and covers Central Asia from its Dubai hub.Word of cautionThe Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed.The World Bank said this week that Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects oil-rich economies in the region to contract this year, before enjoying a strong recovery next year – subject to shipping operations returning to normal, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. But Mr Le Saint said he was “quite confident” about Natixis CIB’s growth prospects in the Middle East. “I still think that, even though some economies in the region, from a GDP perspective, are contracting, we have not yet reached our natural market share,” he said. “It's more difficult to reach our natural market share in a market that is contracting, but when we see that our franchise and our expertise fit well with the needs of the client, especially in the current situation, I still think that we can keep growing at this pace.”That projection, however, could change if the Iran war does not end soon, he added. “Of course, if the conflict stays for the next two to three years, what I say might at some point be revisited. But for the foreseeable future, for the next year, I'm very optimistic that we will be growing 10 per cent at least."“We are expanding, we are investing, so we are capturing market share at a time where not everyone has full attention on growing the business here, which I think is quite exciting.”Market impact Although Natixis remains bullish about the long-term economic environment of the Middle East, as well as the bank’s own growth prospects, it has seen a slowdown in the regional debt capital market this year. The volume of deals so far has dropped by about 10 per cent, but the market is “relatively resilient”, Mr Le Saint said.The slowdown is not due to the lack of access to liquidity, but is instead caused by borrowers who "don't want to access it now because they see the yield and the rates are too high”, he said. Borrowers can wait and have several options to raise funds, as well as their own liquidity. “Chinese banks are coming back in the region and are investing massively, especially to support probably, the need to source and help the flow of energy to China,” he said. “I don't think that our clients are in any stress to find liquidity. Many of them are just waiting to see better conditions or to tap a new pool of liquidity."Combined platform Natixis CIB, which is celebrating its 20th anniversary, combined its Asia and Middle East operations at the beginning of last year. The lender offers structured financing solutions, large-scale project funding, leverage and acquisition finance, funding for event-driven transactions as well as trade and structured financing.It primarily focuses on sectors including infrastructure, energy, transport, metals and mining, and technology and aviation.“They are global sectors where you've got investors, capital seekers and capital providers from [all parts] of the world.
