We connect the dots,” Mr Le Saint said.The bank also offers advisory, investment banking and corporate banking, as well as capital markets services. Bigger contributionCurrently, the Asia and Middle East platform accounts for more than 15 per cent of Natixis CIB’s overall business and “we want to grow that to 20 per cent and perhaps more", Mr Le Saint said.By combing the geographies, the bank is better placed to capture opportunities arising from the growing business and trade links between them, he said.“It also makes sense because our Asia Pacific set-up today, compared to what it was 20 years ago or even 10 years ago, is much more established and comprehensive so now we can offer our Middle East clients access to this market,” Mr Le Saint said.Natixis CIB’s clients in Asia also have access to funding pools in oil-rich countries in the Middle East, he added. “There is geopolitical and economic rationale, but there is also a business rationale."

headline: Binance expands financial super app offering with launch of bStocks in the UAE
summary: Binance, the global blockchain ecosystem behind the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume and registered users, today announced the launch of bStocks for eligible users in the UAE, marking another milestone in the company’s vision of becoming a financial super app.The launch expands Binance’s growing ecosystem beyond digital assets, enabling users to access select US stocks through tokenised securities within a single platform.As Binance continues to bridge traditional finance and blockchain technology, bStocks provide users with a more accessible and flexible way to diversify their portfolios while benefiting from blockchain-native capabilities.Users in the UAE can already access a wide range of financial services, including crypto trading and earning products. The addition of bStocks further strengthens Binance’s ambition to bring multiple financial opportunities together into one seamless ecosystem, making it easier for users to manage different asset classes through a single platform.bStocks are tokenised securities designed to mirror the price of select US stocks and ETFs. Issued by BTech Holdings Limited, a Binance group affiliate, each bStock is intended to track the price of a corresponding underlying share held with a regulated custodian. While bStocks do not represent actual ownership of the underlying stocks, they are designed however to combine traditional finance with blockchain technology. They offer eligible users a simpler and more flexible way to access U.S. equity markets. These securities allow eligible users to :Start trading from just $524/7 trading, allowing users to trade beyond traditional stock market hours*Self-custody, with the ability to transfer supported bStocks to compatible BNB Chain wallets.On-chain utility, enabling supported bStocks to be used across compatible blockchain applications.Diversification, by accessing both digital assets and tokenised US equities through one trusted platform.Corporate actions, including stock splits and dividend-related adjustments, are processed automatically in accordance with the applicable product structure, helping users maintain continuous exposure without requiring manual actionAt launch, eligible users will have access to tokenised securities representing:Circle Internet Group (CRCLB/USDT)Micron Technology (MUB/USDT)Nvidia (NVDAB/USDT)SanDisk (SNDKB/USDT)Tesla (TSLAB/USDT)In addition to the above, many other bStocks are available on Binance and are expected to be introduced progressively, subject to applicable approvals. Commenting on the launch, Tarik Erk, head of MENAT said: “At Binance, we’re building much more than a cryptocurrency platform, we’re building a financial super app designed to give users seamless access to a growing range of financial opportunities through one trusted ecosystem. The launch of bStocks in the UAE marks another important step in that journey. "By bringing tokenised US equities onto blockchain infrastructure, we’re making access to US equity markets, more flexible and better aligned with how today’s digital-first users want to manage their finances. As we continue expanding our ecosystem, our focus remains on simplifying financial access while connecting traditional finance with the innovation of blockchain technology.”* Prices outside traditional market hours may be especially volatile, and trading during these periods carries additional risk. bStocks are designed to track the price of the corresponding underlying asset, but are not guaranteed to reflect its real-time market price at all times.

headline: Agricultural city being developed in Abu Dhabi to aid UAE's food security efforts
summary: In the era of smartphones and social media, in which many simply order groceries through a delivery app, the disconnect between humans and farms has never felt so pronounced.This may be about to change, as the future of farming takes shape in Abu Dhabi. An agricultural community, known as Qitaf City, twice the size of Monaco is being developed in Abu Dhabi to help boost the country's efforts to tackle food security.At four million square metres, the upcoming project will include villas, town houses and Emirati housing with farms alongside AgriTech projects.Shamsa Alfahim, chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Investment and Development (ADID) and managing director of Qitaf Holding, spoke to The National about the ambitious plans. She said she hopes to develop a community by attracting those who are interested in taking up farming while incorporating the latest technologies.“We're hopefully trying to target different university students or people who are interested in agriculture, and be able to give them this farm for their own use and giving them to the market,” she said, speaking to The National at Global Food Week.In a rapidly modernising country which has put AI at the forefront, the hope is the project will bring Emiratis back to their roots and allow them to contribute to the country's growing food ecosystem.“There's something very humble about being in this kind of ecosystem because it does ground you to your roots. It's not just agriculture any more – there's also aquaculture and agritech,” she said.The first project starting in the agriculture city will be growing potatoes using solar panels as part of the laboratory process. Urgent needMonths of supply chain instability with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz underlined the importance of food security for the UAE, a country that imports a majority of its food from abroad. The goal is to create a strategic hub for food security in Abu Dhabi.“We wanted to launch Qitaf to battle these new circumstances because we want to be resilient and self-sufficient within the UAE,” said Ms Alfahim.Qitaf City will be about 40 minutes from Abu Dhabi city, Al Ain and Dubai's Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC). The area, known as Al Haffar, is part of a wider master plan that includes a sports city. Etihad Rail's track runs alongside it, and in the future, she says, freight rail access will play a key role in logistics.“The new Etihad railway is going to pass by the area where Qitaf is located within Al Haffar city. So in terms of logistics it's going to be very strategically located because there's a very easy route of being able to transport the produce from Qitaf to other places in the UAE."A new chapterQitaf Holding has recently been established as the agricultural arm of ADID to “create an environment for food security” in the country. The agriculture city project is slated to launch in February.“The bigger master plan is actually creating a sustainable city that encompasses lots of different health points,” Ms Alfahim said. “A part of it is going to be a sports city, another is going to be a medical city, and the large majority is going to be housing and estates for the local community.”Qitaf Holding is also working with AG Groups on large-scale projects across countries in Africa and Asia. They launched a green corridor between Tanzania and the UAE during Global Food Week.“We can connect with farmers in Tanzania, give them a platform for exchanging their products, bring the their products to the UAE for processing and manufacturing, and re-export it from here,” said Ms Alfahim.“It's going to create a whole system. We want to do the same thing with Madagascar where we can bring vanilla from Madagascar into the UAE.”

headline: UAE's revised suicide law can 'reduce mental health stigma and improve support'
summary: Access to mental health support is poised to continue to improve following legal amendments to decriminalise attempted suicide, experts have said.The UAE announced the removal of criminal liability in an amendment to the country's Crimes and Penalties Law on Thursday. Previous legislation in 2020 gave judges the discretion to offer mental health treatment as an alternative to prison, although there had been confusion over the legal ramifications for people who tried to take their own lives.The change is expected to improve the chances of early intervention, ensuring care and support is given when needed to bolster suicide prevention.Dr Tina Mistry is a clinical psychologist and corporate wellbeing director at Al Kalma, a mental health platform in the UAE and Saudi Arabia. She said the legal change was a positive step. “The recent amendment decriminalising attempted suicide shows a real commitment to supporting people with mental health difficulties,” she said. “Until now, fear of a criminal case stopped many people from saying they were having suicidal thoughts. “Removing that fear should make it easier for people in distress to speak up and get help early.”Early intervention crucialEarly intervention is viewed as critical when signs of depression and anxiety appear, to prevent symptoms from deepening or developing into suicidal thoughts.Mental health services have been steadily improving in recent years.As more mental health and workplace wellbeing programmes have appeared in the corporate world, insurers have added mental health care to their coverage.Saudi German Hospital Dubai is one of the providers launching an on-site specialist mental health and wellness hub to coincide with World Mental Health Day on October 10.It is designed to end the fragmented experience many families face when navigating mental health care by bringing specialists together around a single shared care plan.Dr Ahmed Eissa, a psychiatrist and chief executive of Saudi German Health UAE, hopes the centre can help with early intervention.“There are a lot of people suffering without having the right support, drug diagnosis or services,” he said.“Part of it is related to the stigma itself of going into mental health facilities, the affordability and the number of healthcare providers in the field of mental health. For some, they have days of anxiety, stress, work burnout or marital and relationship, challenges.“If we can provide the service that will help the whole family as a unit of the community, this is the core objective of the hub itself.”Service accessServices for adults and older people include psychiatric assessment, medication management and individual therapy.It also offers treatment for depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and related conditions, as well as geriatric psychiatry, addiction support and family counselling.Recruitment of mental health specialists for the hub had been a challenge. “If we are talking about integrating the mental health team here, most front lines are related to nursing, so they should be trained very well," said Dr Eissa.“There is scarcity in mental health personnel, so we need to train most of the healthcare providers in all levels so that they act like filters.“Recruiting psychiatrists and specialists to come here was a little bit challenging, especially in different subspecialties. Ideally, in the future we'll recruit from our own trainees.”Nursing careA recent Global Mental Health Care Access and Affordability Benchmark report assessed access to care in 15 nations, including the UAE.The report compiled by Australian service provider TherapyNearMe.com assessed coverage, timeliness, availability, mental-health-specific unmet needs, provider fees and affordability.Eleven countries had compatible observations for psychologists, psychiatrists and mental health nurses. Five national mental health programmes were psychologist-led, five, including the UAE, were majority nurse-led, and one in Jordan was psychiatrist-led.Dr Mistry said plans to train 2,000 Abu Dhabi family doctors in mental health were a positive move towards improving access to care. “Official figures show around two thirds of the UAE's mental health workforce are nurses, which isn't quite the same as nurses leading care,” she said.“Nurses are a real strength, and often the healthcare professional a patient sees most. The risk is that they carry complex cases without enough supervision or specialists to turn to when needed.”Incentives to ask for helpClear directives under the UAE’s Crimes and Penalties Law should help relieve some of the prejudice against people living with mental illness, professionals said.In 2024, Dubai authorities dropped charges of attempted suicide against Irish citizen Tori Towey, an Emirates flight attendant.Charges stemmed from a domestic incident involving Irish national Ms Towey, 30, and her South African husband.The case attracted international media attention after being raised in the Irish Parliament, with an intervention by Taoiseach Simon Harris.Any threats of prosecution for similar cases should disappear under recent amendments.Marie Byrne, a therapist from Ireland who runs positive psychology sessions in Dubai for workplace wellness, said the legal amendments can help reduce the bias still associated with certain mental health conditions.“Prior to the Iran conflict, workplace wellness was really on the agenda, the sense now is that productivity and achievement has taken over,” she said.“With the amount of uncertainty for occupational security, there is a need for people to feel they have support.“Anxiety is more prevalent with uncertainty for the future, and people are in a kind of loop; they get exhausted with worry, and they're not sleeping properly either.“It's easy to see how someone could start to think, 'it's all getting on top of me'.”Ms Byrne was one of a cohort of mental health professionals who volunteered their services for the Emirates Foundation during the pandemic.They offered free support for those in crisis or living in isolation, anxiety and depression. It was a sign of changing attitudes towards mental health, she said.“There are now similar, more permanent support structures in place with the health authorities,” said Ms Byrne.“This legal amendment could be a real incentive for people to go for early intervention, before they get to where they're even thinking to end their own life.”“I really do think this can help remove some of the stigma that is still associated with mental health.”

headline: UAE economy grew in first half of 2026 despite impact of Iran war
summary: The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war.The non-oil sector's contribution to the GDP during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said in a statement on Friday.The results "reflect the continued diversification of the UAE's economic base and the growing role of non-oil activities", the FCSC said.Trade topped contributions to non-oil GDP at 16.2 per cent, followed by financial and insurance (15.2 per cent), construction (13.1 per cent), manufacturing (11.8) and real estate (7.9 per cent). Meanwhile, activities in the financial and insurance sector posted the highest growth rate in the six months through the end of June, rising by 14.8 per cent, the FCSC said. That was followed by information and communication (7.3 per cent), health and social work (6 per cent), construction (5.1 per cent), government (3.6 per cent) and real estate (2.3 per cent).The non-oil sector's "expanding contribution to economic activity demonstrates the diversity of growth drivers and supports sustainable and balanced growth across a broad range of economic sectors", the FCSC added.The UAE's GDP last year grew 6.2 per cent year-on-year to hit Dh1.9 trillion, as non-oil GDP jumped 6.8 per cent to Dh1.5 trillion.In the second quarter of the year, the UAE's real GDP hit Dh476.9 billion, a decline of 2.1 per cent annually. Non-oil activities also contracted by 1.1 per cent, as several economic sectors, particularly tourism, transport and trade, were affected by regional developments and disruption to travel.However, the non-oil sector has started to rebound. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index remained stable at 55.3 in September, the same as August, and well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. That reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, S&P said. Business activity in September increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month, the index found. Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years, in response to higher input costs, the report found.

headline: Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival returns to Abu Dhabi with message of renewal
summary: Cinema cannot save the environment, but it can change the way we see it. That is the idea behind Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival, which returns to Abu Dhabi with a programme examining humanity's relationship with nature and the ways that relationship can be repaired.Now in its fifth iteration, the festival runs from Friday to Sunday at NYU Abu Dhabi, bringing together international documentaries, fiction, animation and conversations with filmmakers, scientists and conservationists.Organised in collaboration with Environment Agency Abu Dhabi, the festival this year has the theme Mend, which takes its name from the Arabic verb rammim, meaning to repair or restore something of value.Artistic director Nezar Andary says the theme reflects a philosophy that has guided the festival since 2020. He believes environmental cinema should encourage curiosity rather than overwhelm audiences with alarming statistics or instructions on how to live."I don't want an environmentalism that believes in some pristine, perfect version of nature," he tells The National. "Mending is something we're constantly doing, and it's something the Earth itself does."Al Sidr was inspired by a small environmental film festival that Andary attended at Princeton Public Library in the United States. He was impressed by its preference for creative documentaries over conventional environmental campaigning."The more creative, artistic documentary isn't force-feeding you an environmental ideology, but is actually creating a sense of intimacy and questioning," he says.Al Sidr has since welcomed more than 5,000 attendees and engaged 2,000 students from more than 20 schools across Abu Dhabi.This year's selection approaches ecology through scientific exploration, cultural heritage and conservation.Among the headline screenings is Ghost Elephants, a documentary by German filmmaker Werner Herzog. The National Geographic production, which premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, receives its Arabian Gulf premiere on Friday.Another highlight is Fire of Love, the Oscar-nominated 2022 documentary by Sara Dosa, which chronicles the lives of French volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft, whose fascination with volcanoes shaped their work and relationship."It's about two lovers who are studying volcanoes. And it's about love. It's about love of science," Andary says.Dosa's 2026 documentary Time and Water, which premiered at Sundance, will screen at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi on Friday, accompanied by a free museum tour, and again on Sunday at NYU Abu Dhabi.The programme also includes Fungi: Web of Life, narrated by Icelandic musician Bjork, and Chuuraa, a short film by Evgenia Arbugaeva that premiered at this year's Berlin International Film Festival.Beyond documentaries, Andary is particularly enthusiastic about the restored 4K edition of Manthan, the 1976 Indian film by Shyam Benegal, which screens on Saturday.The film examines the formation of a dairy co-operative in rural India, connecting agriculture with questions of class, collective action and social change.Andary says environmental storytelling can extend to subjects that might not immediately appear to be ecological. At a previous edition, he screened Ken Loach's Kes, a British drama about a working-class boy and his relationship with a kestrel.He says both films address class and solidarity, issues that can also resonate with audiences in the UAE.Closer to home, the festival will premiere episodes of Conservation Diaries, a five-part documentary series produced by Connect with Nature, the youth environmental movement established by the Environment Agency Abu Dhabi and Emirates Nature–WWF.Filmed across the UAE's wadis, mangroves, coastlines and rural communities, the series follows scientists, volunteers and conservationists protecting biodiversity.It offers a practical interpretation of Mend, highlighting the patient work required to understand ecosystems and protect vulnerable species."They're the heroes on the ground who are tracking animals, who are working with citizen scientists," Andary says.A panel on Sunday will examine ecological restoration in the UAE, while other sessions explore water, fungi and environmental science.Saturday's family programme features international animated shorts alongside Fungi: Web of Life and an introduction to fungi by Dima Al Srouri, founder of Dubai venture MycoSphere, which develops materials using mycelium and agricultural waste.Andary hopes the festival encourages people to question their relationships with the natural world.Previous editions experimented with audience-led discussions instead of conventional expert panels, while one screening was accompanied by a meal prepared using food waste.Although he wishes this year's programme offered more interaction, Al Sidr will continue its educational activities through school visits across Abu Dhabi.Andary recalls how working on a documentary involving an ancient burial site in the UAE changed his perspective on wildlife. Learning that people used Socotra cormorant feathers in burials made him more attentive to the birds and their historical relationship with people."I listen more, I'm more attentive," he says.He believes such changes in perception can be as important as the practical lessons audiences take from a screening. The festival should begin conversations that continue beyond the cinema."Cinema is not going to heal the environment. We are," Andary says.Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival runs from October 9 to 11 at the Blue Hall, NYU Abu Dhabi. Tickets and the full programme are available at alsidrfestival.com

headline: 'Why would you need courage to speak the truth': Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
summary: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to ⁠South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.The Nobel Committee said the 85-year-old had shown exceptional courage and integrity to ensure that war crimes and genocide were prosecuted and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. It also said she had demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career. The former UN human rights chief led the world body's Commission of Inquiry into the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year. The commission determined that war crimes had been committed by both Hamas and Israel in the wake of the attacks on October 7, 2023.In her first reaction to the announcement, Ms Pillay discussed the importance of that finding. "The last thing I did is deliver the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," she said to friends gathered in the German city of Nuremburg."One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage and you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's impartial decision making." She later dedicated the award to "all the survivors of international crimes, as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".In a message to world leaders, she said: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war."Israel ‌condemned the Nobel Committee for giving her the award. "The decision of the Nobel Committee is disgraceful and an endorsement for proponents of anti-Semitism, like Pillay herself," said Israel's ambassador to the UN in Geneva, Daniel Meron. "As the chair of ​the Commission of Inquiry, she led campaigns to undermine Israel's very existence, campaigns that whitewashed terrorism and manipulate the reality in pursuit of a well-known political agenda."The Nobel judges said Ms Pillay had enlarged the scope and impact of international law as a judge in the High Court in South Africa and at the International Criminal Court. "A common thread runs ⁠from her early work defending ​Nelson Mandela ⁠and ‌others who stood up against ​apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.Ms Pillay has "held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict", they said."Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time," the committee added. "Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world."The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented ​in ‌Oslo on ⁠December 10, the ​anniversary of the ​death ‌of Swedish industrialist ⁠Alfred Nobel, who founded the ⁠awards in his 1895 will.Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Ms Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988. She was the first non-white judge of the High Court of South Africa.The ​UN ⁠human rights office ​on Friday ⁠welcomed the award to Ms ⁠Pillay, ‌acknowledging ​her long-standing advocacy for human rights. "It is amazing news, we need more dedication and commitment to human ​rights," ‌Shabia ⁠Mantoo, ​spokeswoman ​for ‌the UN ⁠human rights office.“The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice.“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.”He said the committee wanted to remind the world that "the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently”, adding that peace "requires justice”.Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children’s rights activist.Last year’s peace prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her prize to US President Donald Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts ​in Venezuela.Mr Trump has again suggested he should be the recipient of the prize, although he acknowledged it was unlikely. Mr Trump, who this year has waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on ​Wednesday: "They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me."Since his ​return to the White House last year, Mr Trump has repeatedly ⁠said he deserves what may be the world's most prestigious award."It is about ​that time," Mr Trump said in the Oval Office. "But I was very honoured ​to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump."The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Mr Trump, though there is no way of verifying that.Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday, with the Swedish Academy recognising her experimental approach to writing and her ability to bring ancient Greek literature into the modern world.The 76-year-old author’s best-known works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox.The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.Francis Halzen won the physics prize for contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.The Chemistry prize went to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for work in non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
body_text:
The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to ⁠South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

The Nobel Committee said the 85-year-old had shown exceptional courage and integrity to ensure that war crimes and genocide were prosecuted and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. It also said she had demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career.

The former UN human rights chief led the world body's Commission of Inquiry into the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year. The commission determined that war crimes had been committed by both Hamas and Israel in the wake of the attacks on October 7, 2023.

Narges Mohammadi's children tell of pain of separation

In her first reaction to the announcement, Ms Pillay discussed the importance of that finding. "The last thing I did is deliver the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," she said to friends gathered in the German city of Nuremburg.

"One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage and you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's impartial decision making."

She later dedicated the award to "all the survivors of international crimes, as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".

In a message to world leaders, she said: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war."

Israel ‌condemned the Nobel Committee for giving her the award. "The decision of the Nobel Committee is disgraceful and an endorsement for proponents of anti-Semitism, like Pillay herself," said Israel's ambassador to the UN in Geneva, Daniel Meron. "As the chair of ​the Commission of Inquiry, she led campaigns to undermine Israel's very existence, campaigns that whitewashed terrorism and manipulate the reality in pursuit of a well-known political agenda."

The Nobel judges said Ms Pillay had enlarged the scope and impact of international law as a judge in the High Court in South Africa and at the International Criminal Court.

"A common thread runs ⁠from her early work defending ​Nelson Mandela ⁠and ‌others who stood up against ​apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.

Ms Pillay has "held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict", they said.

"Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time," the committee added. "Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world."

The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented ​in ‌Oslo on ⁠December 10, the ​anniversary of the ​death ‌of Swedish industrialist ⁠Alfred Nobel, who founded the ⁠awards in his 1895 will.

Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Ms Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988. She was the first non-white judge of the High Court of South Africa.

The ​UN ⁠human rights office ​on Friday ⁠welcomed the award to Ms ⁠Pillay, ‌acknowledging ​her long-standing advocacy for human rights. "It is amazing news, we need more dedication and commitment to human ​rights," ‌Shabia ⁠Mantoo, ​spokeswoman ​for ‌the UN ⁠human rights office.

“The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice.

“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.”

He said the committee wanted to remind the world that "the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently”, adding that peace "requires justice”.

Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children’s rights activist.

Last year’s peace prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her prize to US President Donald Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts ​in Venezuela.

Mr Trump has again suggested he should be the recipient of the prize, although he acknowledged it was unlikely.

Mr Trump, who this year has waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on ​Wednesday: "They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me."

Since his ​return to the White House last year, Mr Trump has repeatedly ⁠said he deserves what may be the world's most prestigious award.

"It is about ​that time," Mr Trump said in the Oval Office. "But I was very honoured ​to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump."

The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Mr Trump, though there is no way of verifying that.

Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday, with the Swedish Academy recognising her experimental approach to writing and her ability to bring ancient Greek literature into the modern world.

The 76-year-old author’s best-known works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox.

The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

Francis Halzen won the physics prize for contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

The Chemistry prize went to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for work in non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Nobel Peace Prize award to Navi Pillay primarily through her own and the Nobel Committee's praise, with a brief but direct inclusion of Israel's condemnation, presenting the event as a recognition of international legal accountability.

loaded_language.explanation: This is the Nobel Committee's laudatory characterization, which is emotionally charged and presents a subjective value judgment as fact.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: the Nobel Committee cited her courage and integrity

loaded_language.explanation: A metaphorical and evaluative phrase that implies a clear, positive ethical stance rather than a neutral description.
A strongly negative and emotionally charged word used by Israel's ambassador, which the article quotes without distancing.
A highly loaded accusation that uses vivid, emotionally charged language to describe alleged actions.
An informal, dramatic phrase that adds a sense of chaos or unpredictability to betting odds, which is not neutral.

omissions: No mention of the specific findings of the UN Commission of Inquiry regarding war crimes by both Hamas and Israel beyond a brief summary.
No mention of the number of casualties in Gaza or other details of the conflict.
No mention of other reactions to the award, such as from Palestinian or human rights groups.
No mention of the controversy surrounding Pillay's report or criticisms from other quarters beyond Israel's ambassador.

headline: Saudi airline pilot among three killed in attacks on Riyadh airport
summary: Three Saudi citizens were killed in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Friday.The missile attacks took place on Thursday and hit a Saudia aircraft and airport facilities. A number of people have been injured, it added, without specifying the number. An airline captain named Hamoud Ali Alkalthami was among those killed.Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed they hit the airport with two cruise missiles. The Iran-backed group also said it attacked an airport in the south-western city of Najran, a claim Saudi authorities have not confirmed, and launched ballistic missiles at an airbase in Khamis Mushait.The latest casualties come ⁠after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people ⁠were killed in earlier strikes this week on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the south-west.Saudi Arabia has been attacked repeatedly after the Houthis made advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the Yemeni government launching a counter-offensive supported by coalition strikes.On Thursday, the kingdom said it would “punish” the Houthis after the deadly attacks on airports in Riyadh and the south, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile causing damage to civilian areas in the capital.“The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom … will not go unpunished,” said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki. The coalition’s joint forces had destroyed dozens of Houthi military targets across Yemen, he added.In another development, services from King Khalid International Airport were gradually returning to normal on Friday, after days of delays and cancellations. Flights were initially suspended on Wednesday morning after Houthi attacks, with disruption continuing into Thursday.
body_text:
Three Saudi citizens were killed in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the kingdom's General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Friday.

The missile attacks took place on Thursday and hit a Saudia aircraft and airport facilities. A number of people have been injured, it added, without specifying the number. An airline captain named Hamoud Ali Alkalthami was among those killed.

Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed they hit the airport with two cruise missiles. The Iran-backed group also said it attacked an airport in the south-western city of Najran, a claim Saudi authorities have not confirmed, and launched ballistic missiles at an airbase in Khamis Mushait.

UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’

The latest casualties come ⁠after Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people ⁠were killed in earlier strikes this week on Riyadh airport and Abha airport, in the south-west.

Saudi Arabia has been attacked repeatedly after the Houthis made advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the Yemeni government launching a counter-offensive supported by coalition strikes.

On Thursday, the kingdom said it would “punish” the Houthis after the deadly attacks on airports in Riyadh and the south, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile causing damage to civilian areas in the capital.

“The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom … will not go unpunished,” said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki. The coalition’s joint forces had destroyed dozens of Houthi military targets across Yemen, he added.

In another development, services from King Khalid International Airport were gradually returning to normal on Friday, after days of delays and cancellations. Flights were initially suspended on Wednesday morning after Houthi attacks, with disruption continuing into Thursday.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event through Saudi official statements and coalition rhetoric, presenting the Houthi attacks as unprovoked strikes on civilian infrastructure while giving limited voice to Houthi claims or Yemeni civilian context.

loaded_language.quote: The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilians and civilian objects in the kingdom … will not go unpunished
loaded_language.explanation: This is a direct quote from a Saudi coalition spokesman that uses emotionally charged and politically loaded terms ('brutal', 'terrorist militia') to characterize the Houthis, which the article presents without challenge or attribution to an independent source.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: The attacks by the Houthi group on civilian sites in the kingdom will be responded to, said coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki.

loaded_language.explanation: The label 'Iran-backed' is a politically loaded descriptor that frames the Houthis through their alleged foreign patron rather than as an independent actor, and is used without attribution or explanation of the nature of the backing.
The word 'terrorist' is a highly charged designation that carries legal and moral condemnation; it appears within a quote but is presented without context or counterpoint.

omissions: The number of injured people, which the article notes was unspecified by Saudi authorities but may be available from other sources.
Any statement or perspective from the Houthis beyond their claim of responsibility, such as their stated reasons or targets.
Context about the broader Yemen conflict, including the Saudi-led coalition's role and civilian casualties in Yemen.
Independent verification of the attacks or casualty figures beyond Saudi official statements.
Reactions from international bodies or other governments beyond the UN envoy headline fragment.

headline: Former refugee gives ‘This is Britain’ speech after defeating Greens' Zack Polanski in London byelection
summary: The UK’s ruling Labour party saw off the challenge from Green Party leader Zack Polanski in a by-election caused by former prime minister Keir Starmer's resignation as an MP.Labour’s candidate, local council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali, delivered a powerful victory speech about diversity in Britain. She arrived in the country as a child refugee from Somalia and said she hoped the result of the vote would help people like her to feel like they also “belong here”.Labour’s decision to choose a British Somalian had been criticised by Reform UK’s home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf.The final days of campaigning were also overshadowed by the Green Party conference, at which a motion was passed declaring “Zionism is racism”. Mr Polanski, who increased the party’s share of the vote, has been accused of failing to show leadership over the ”dangerous” and “divisive” motion by not taking part in the debate.He was pressed about the motion in media interviews after the result and refused to say directly whether he supported the right for Israel to exist. “I believe everyone deserves a safe home,” Mr Polanski, who is Jewish, told the BBC. “I believe Israelis and Palestinians should have equal rights in a democracy. I don't believe that any state has a right to oppress or to commit apartheid and certainly not genocide.”The failure to win a seat in the House of Commons represents a major setback for his party. Mr Polanski said he intended to stay on as leader.While he has been credited with tripling the Greens’ membership to more than 200,000 people since he became leader about a year ago, his popularity ratings have dipped in recent months. "Yes, I've taken a loss tonight but our movement is so much bigger than one election or one motion," he said.Ms Abdi-Wali received 45 per cent of the vote in Holborn and St Pancras, ahead of Mr Polanski, who came in second with almost 33 per cent. The seat was vacated by Mr Starmer after he was replaced as the country's leader by Andy Burnham, in part because Labour MPs hoped he could do a better job countering the Greens.'People need to believe'In her acceptance speech, Ms Abdi-Wali praised Mr Starmer and said she wanted to work with Mr Burnham on issues such as housing.“This moment means something deeply personal to me – to represent the place that gave me a home, and my family a home, gave me opportunity and helped shape the person I am today,” she said.While in its northern reaches, Holborn and St Pancras contains some of the most affluent parts of London, several of its neighbourhoods are included among the most income-deprived in England. “I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong, for people who look like me," Ms Abdi-Wali added. "I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.“We have a responsibility to defend what we’ve built, and pass it on. Hope is not naive. Without hope there is nothing to build on, and nothing to build for. People need to believe that politics can make their lives better and that their communities can thrive and that tomorrow can be better than today.”In a message issued before the vote, Mr Burnham said: “This area gave Sagal a home when she arrived here as a refugee in the 1990s. Camden gave Sagal and her family hope. Now she wants to give that back to the communities that have always been there for her. It’s hard to think of someone more committed to their local area and the care of people than Sagal.”ChanceLabour had been expected to win, having occupied the seat since its 1983 inception, and party strategists are likely to take the result as a sign Mr Burnham is re-energising the progressive voter base that splintered under Mr Starmer.Mr Polanski, a former actor and hypnotherapist, had tried to persuade the liberal constituency’s voters that they would be better served by electing the leader of a party who could push Mr Burnham further to the left, instead of giving Labour another backbencher to boost its majority in the 650-seat House of Commons. Mr Polanski currently serves as a member of the London Assembly and was looking to transition to the Parliament in Westminster, where his party is represented by a contingent of five MPs. He said that he was disappointed not to ​win the seat but that the party would continue to grow despite the setback. "No politician runs in a by-election and doesn't want to win," he added. "But at the same time, to see the growth in what was supposedly a safe Labour seat … is now a marginal Labour seat. That's clearly growth, and next time we can get it over the line.”He told broadcasters that "so many people told me on the doorstep that they want to give Andy Burnham a chance ... let's see what he does with it".Burnham bounceLabour’s nationwide popularity had slipped since Mr Starmer led it to a majority in 2024, but polling shows the party is enjoying a bounce under Mr Burnham. The by-election is the first to be held since he became the UK leader in July.He has refocused his party on an unabashedly left-wing agenda that prioritises public ownership. He has proposed trimming rises in the state pension to fund a care service for the elderly that operates along the same principles as health care, which in the UK is free at the point of use.Missing out on a seat in the House of Commons will be a blow for the Greens, even while officials managing expectations in advance of the vote pointed out that Nigel Farage, leader of right-wing Reform, stood unsuccessfully in seven parliamentary elections before gaining a seat.“Any ideas of a return to the cosy two-party system is just wishful thinking on the part of the establishment,” the Green Party said in a statement after the result.

headline: Oil posts weekly gain as Hurricane Isaias rips through US Gulf coast
summary: Oil prices settled higher on Friday to post weekly gains as Hurricane Isaias hit the US Gulf coast, forcing oil companies to significantly taper down their operations.Crude was trading lower earlier in the session after US President Donald Trump ruled out launching attacks on Iran before the midterm elections next month. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, added 0.42 per cent to settle at $104.72 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 0.39 per cent to close at $91.85 a barrel.From last week's close Brent, which settled more than 4 per cent higher on Thursday amid continuing tensions in the Middle East, jumped 2.41 per cent, while WTI added 0.81 per cent.“Brent crude rose ... as renewed Middle East tensions coincided with disruption to US Gulf of Mexico production from Hurricane Isaias,” said Nick Stadtmiller, chief economist and group head of research at Emirates NBD.“Around 63 per cent of US Gulf oil production has been shut in ahead of the storm, while prices came off their intraday highs after President Donald Trump said the US was holding productive discussions with Iran.”The US Gulf coast is home to offshore oil production sites, as well as refining infrastructure and export terminals. The hurricane is forecast to lead to heavy rain and potentially flash floods.About 500,000 barrels per day of capacity are at risk from the hurricane, said Soojin Kim and Edward Bell from MUFG. "Ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and its allies against the Houthis are keeping the geopolitical risk in oil markets elevated while shipping in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz continues to be threatened," they said.The Houthis carried out deadly attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia's southern region and Riyadh this week, with debris from an intercepted ballistic missile damaging civilian sites in the kingdom's capital. Meanwhile, Mr Trump on Thursday said he had no intention of ordering attacks on Iran before the midterm elections take place next month, which has temporarily eased supply concerns.In a post on Truth Social, he said Iran was in a “very bad condition” economically and militarily and the US blockade on Iranian shipments through the Strait of Hormuz would remain in “full force”. He added that the countries were holding "productive discussions". Impact on oil pricesOil prices have remained volatile this week as attacks on ships in the strait, a vital route for global crude shipments, increased. The US also announced new sanctions on 17 vessels responsible for transporting millions of barrels of Iranian crude oil, as well as petroleum and petrochemical products, to markets in southern and eastern Asia.The US is looking to squeeze Iran’s oil revenue and put pressure on Tehran as the regional war continues. The US Treasury is "starving the tyrannical regime in Tehran of the money it uses to wage war in the region, and we will continue exposing those who enable the regime’s oil sales", Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.Gold, meanwhile, ended higher on Friday on bargain hunting and as investors weigh the possibility of further interest rate hikes from the US Federal Reserve.The precious metal, widely regarded as a safe-haven asset, added 1.52 per cent to a one-week high of $4,194.40 an ounce. Silver jumped 2.82 per cent to $60.82 an ounce.

headline: JD Vance’s comments about immigrants 'unwarranted' and ‘deeply offensive’, India's Foreign Ministry says
summary: India's Ministry of External Affairs on Friday called comments by US Vice President JD Vance on Indian immigrants "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive".A day earlier, Mr Vance announced that Microsoft and some of India’s biggest IT services were suspended from a programme allowing workers on H-1B visas to apply for green cards. He accused the companies of abusing the system, comparing foreign workers to “indentured servants”."The history of the United States itself has been shaped by generations of immigrants whose labour, enterprise and innovation have contributed to its growth and prosperity," the ministry said in a statement. It added that Mr Vance's comments were "unwarranted" and ignore the contributions of Indian professionals to the US economy. Roughly 70 per cent of the H-1B visas approved in 2025 went to people from India."Resorting to terminology that carries painful historical and colonial legacy connotations is deeply offensive," the ministry said, appearing to refer to Mr Vance's use of the term "indentured servants", which carries a heavy historical burden for Indians. During the colonial period in India, more than 1.6 million people were transported as indentured servants to serve on British, French and Dutch plantations around the world following the abolition of slavery. Many workers, who typically signed five-year contracts for unpaid labour, were tricked or coerced into service.The indenture system is also a painful feature of American history. During the American colonial period, poor workers and convicts were bound to an employer for up to seven years, receiving no wages for their labour, in return for food, shelter and transport to the colonies. Similar to the Indian system, abuse was rampant."When I say indentured servants, here's what I mean: When somebody comes in on an H-1B, they are completely subordinate to that company," Mr Vance said at the Department of Labour on Thursday. "If they lose that job, they have to leave the country."The Vice President accused Microsoft, Adobe and six other companies of fraudulently utilising the H-1B visa programme, which he said is meant to allow firms to bring in "the best of the best" from outside the US to fill jobs that are impossible to fill with American workers. This "pernicious system" is a "fundamental insult to the American way of life", he said, as it lets companies lower wages and block Americans from jobs, while also allowing for the abuse of foreign workers.As a result of the alleged fraudulent use of the system, the companies have been removed from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, which allows firms to hire foreign workers permanently and offers the workers the chance to apply for green cards.The tech industry, Wall Street firms and telecoms companies have come to rely heavily on the H-1B programme through their use of IT contractors from staffing and outsourcing agencies, which have developed a lucrative business in recruiting professionals from abroad for US clients.In the first nine months of the 2026 fiscal year, Microsoft was the fifth-highest user of H-1B visas, with 3,688, according to Bloomberg.In a statement, Microsoft said it pays H-1B employees “the same as any other employees doing comparable work”, that its wages are among the highest of all visa filings and that the vast majority of its employees in the US are Americans.Mr Vance’s comments came hours before US President Donald Trump gave Microsoft chief executive, Satya Nadella, the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington intended to highlight US scientific leadership. And last week, Mr Nadella, alongside other tech industry leaders, visited the White House for a discussion on safeguards for AI.“Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company," Mr Vance said. "It’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans.”Washington has been engaged in an across-the-board immigration crackdown since Mr Trump returned to office last year. The State Department said earlier this month that more than 250,000 visas have been revoked under the Trump administration.Along with companies with high issuance of H-1B visas, Mr Vance also took aim at universities he said had engaged in J-1 visa fraud. He accused nine institutions, including Harvard, Yale and Stanford universities, of bringing "in foreigners to undercut the wages" of American researchers and graduate students.J-1 visas are granted to people approved to participate in work and study programmes in the US. "They're using these visas way too much. They're using them to undercut the wages of American grad students and American researchers, and it simply has to stop," he said.

headline: Cristiano Ronaldo pays tribute to Messi: 'Your story will remain forever'
summary: Cristiano Ronaldo paid tribute to his great rival, Lionel Messi, after the Argentine great played his final international match this week.Messi brought the curtain down on a 21-year international career with a goal and two assists as Argentina beat Benin in Buenos Aires in an international friendly on Tuesday.It was his 208th and final game for La Albiceleste, with more than 85,000 fans packed into the Monumental stadium to give their hero a fitting send-off.Commenting on one of Messi's Instagram posts, Ronaldo messaged: “Leo, so many years representing your country and a story that will remain forever. All my respect for what you achieved with Argentina. A hug.”The comment has over six million likes. View this post on Instagram The debate over who is the greatest player between the two has been a near-constant among supporters and commentators for the past two decades, but Ronaldo's message shows the level of respect he has for his great rival.Between them, they share 13 Ballon d'Ors, the award for the world's best player each year. Messi has eight, Ronaldo five.Messi's goal from the penalty spot against Benin was his 126th in the famous sky-blue-and-white colours of the national team. He is both Argentina's record scorer and appearance maker.His crowning glory came in 2022 when he led Argentina to a third World Cup triumph. He was also part of the Copa America-winning sides of 2021 and 2024.While Messi's international bow came with the appropriate pomp and pageantry, Ronaldo's international future with Portugal came close to an undignified end.The 41-year-old released a statement this week – running to nearly 2,000 words – confirming he was not retiring from international football and remained available for selection after walking out on Portugal's training camp ahead of their match against Denmark. View this post on Instagram The Al Nassr striker accused Portugal manager Jorge Jesus of an “absolute breach of trust” and said he had twice broken his word to him.The row was sparked by Ronaldo feeling unhappy at being an unused substitute in Portugal's previous match against Norway.Ronaldo said Jesus had agreed a plan under which the forward would miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of ⁠the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 minutes.After being asked to warm up, Ronaldo was then left on the bench. According to Ronaldo's account, a plan was agreed with Jesus in which he would clarify that the player had not demanded to play and that the coach had made a mistake in asking him to warm up without bringing him on.Jesus made no mention of this in his next press conference, prompting Ronaldo to leave the national team camp in Copenhagen.Ronaldo said he deserved to be punished by the Portuguese Football Federation, while Jesus said the door remained open for Ronaldo to return.Ronaldo holds the record for most caps (234) and most goals (146) in international football.

headline: Merab Dvalishvili vows to avenge Petr Yan defeat and reclaim UFC title in Abu Dhabi
summary: Merab Dvalishvili has built his reputation on relentless work inside the octagon and a playful streak outside it. But as he prepares to face Petr Yan again at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi, the former champion says his focus is firmly on the fight: learning from their last meeting, reclaiming the belt and returning to the busy schedule he thrives on.'The Machine' was one of the busiest fighters in 2025, defending his bantamweight title four times. He kicked off his run with a unanimous decision over Umar Nurmaogomedov, before submitting Sean O’Malley with a gorgeous north-south choke and then rag-dolling Corey Sandhagen for five successive rounds.The win over Sandhagen saw Dvalishvili tie his close friend and training partner Aljamain Sterling for the most successful bantamweight title defences (three) and surpass the legendary Georges St-Pierre's record for most takedowns in UFC history (119 and counting). Many fighters would have been happy to sign off, down tools and begin mapping out their fight schedule for the next 12 months. Dvalishvili opted to fight again, this time rematching with Yan, a mere two months after Sandhagen.By his own admission, accepting the fight was a mistake, leaving Dvalishvili with little time to rest, recover and fit in a full camp. Yan had vowed to be better than in their first meeting two years earlier, where he lost on the judges’ scorecards. The Russian was as good as his word: consummate boxing, outstanding takedown defence and devastating body shots saw him take a unanimous decision. In Las Vegas, Petr was perfect.‘The Machine’ had metaphorically broken down. Dvalishvili, the man with cardio for days, simply ran out of gas.Yan solved what seemed the unsolvable problem: figuring out the Dvalishvili dilemma. Some of his body shots had the Georgian wincing and wheezing in pain. The sight of Dvalishvili’s face battered and bloodied as the decision was announced, told the whole story.“I'm not blaming that because of my loss, but I know why I lost,” Dvalishvili told The National when asked if his overexertion played a part in his loss to Yan. “Maybe I was too relaxed, you know. I beat him already, and then when I fought again in the rematch, I have only two months between fights when I defend my belt, and as I said before, I was trying hard, but not actually smart and not actually preparing like how I should do. “That's why I don't do what I was supposed to do in the fight; I was fighting Yan's fight, and that's why he beat the [expletive] out of me and busted me up.”His loss to Yan ended a 14-fight win streak and necessitated a long-overdue break. He’s filled a lot of that time by entertaining his nearly 3 million Instagram followers with hilarious sketches alongside Sterling and his UFC content creator partner Nina Marie Daniele. View this post on Instagram Dvalishvili, 35, says social media offers him an outlet, a break from hitting pads, slamming on mats and constant drills. It gives him a chance to show his comedic side.“I like to balance between hard training and fun content because, you know, training is hard and most of the time it's the same thing, just grinding, wrestling, improving, sparring, and I don't want to post about training and sparring, and I don't want to show people how hard I work. But I do want to make people laugh and give them good times and make them smile,” he said.He still trained – of course he still trained. UFC commentator Daniel Cormier often recounts the time when he went to visit Dvalishvili the day after a title fight, only to be left waiting around for hours as the Georgian was out running.Much of his life is spent around Sterling. They corner each other for fights and refused to fight each other during Sterling’s run as bantamweight champion.“Aljamain Sterling is a great guy, great human being, and of course, we all know how good a fighter he is. We are brothers, we train together, we have fun together. I know his whole family, he knows my family, and then all my other friends, my other teammates, we are brothers too. We try to help each other and motivate each other. This is the life.” View this post on Instagram After a punishing 2025 schedule, Dvalishvili has limited himself to one fight this year, against Yan. Neither has fought since that Las Vegas showdown 10 months ago. Abu Dhabi will settle the trilogy.This will be Dvalishvili’s first time fighting in the UAE capital and Yan’s fourth. Despite the Georgian’s outsized persona and online popularity, it is the Russian who is most likely to enjoy the majority of the support.“I have support everywhere I go. Of course, in Abu Dhabi, I will have support too. But I'm a professional fighter. When I first fought in America, nobody in the arena [knew me], but I still won. It's always good when we have support, but even if Yan's fans will be more, that's cool. I'm fine with it. I'm just going to focus on the win.”The defeat to Yan humbled Dvalishvili and he respects the Russian’s skill set. The head-to-head reads one win apiece, but with plenty of rest and with a full camp behind him, Dvalishvili (21-5) said he is determined to settle the debate once and for all. He believes that he will leave Etihad Arena champion once again, and plans on fighting "at least three times" in 2027.“The past is the past. I don't regret anything; whatever I do, I do and I move on. I had a lot of time to think about [fighting Yan again], and I want my belt back. I want to avenge my loss. I know what mistakes I made [in the second fight], and I know how to beat him,” Dvalishvili said.“His striking’s good, his takedown defence is good, and his cardio is good. He never gives up, but I believe I've been training super hard, and I'm very well prepared this time. And I will be much sharper, much better this time.“I believe in myself. I think in Abu Dhabi we will have a new champion.”

headline: F1 driver power rankings and Singapore prediction: Verstappen and Hamilton find form
summary: Formula One heads to Singapore this weekend, and Marina Bay always offers the drivers a stern test, especially considering the FIA has declared it a heat-hazard race. Temperatures are forecast to exceed 31 degrees, putting even more pressure on the drivers. Marina Bay is a street circuit that places a premium on braking confidence, traction and precision, leaving little room for error. Just to add even more drama, Singapore is hosting its first Sprint weekend. Teams will have just one practice session before Sprint qualifying, leaving them with less time to find the right set-up.Our power rankings measure who will arrive in Singapore in the best shape. We take into account recent form, raw speed, drivers' ability to extract performance from their cars, momentum, and how well their strengths might suit the Marina Bay circuit. 10. Lando Norris (McLaren)Form: Baku DNF, Bahrain P9. Championship: P5How quickly the mighty fall. Norris went from being one of the grid’s most in-form drivers to desperately needing a strong weekend. McLaren admitted the MCL40 was only the fourth-fastest car in Malaysia, and Norris added to the problems by running through the gravel behind the safety car.McLaren need to rediscover the pace the team enjoyed before the Baku race, but it won’t be easy when you consider the unresolved straight-line speed issue with the car. Norris narrowly avoids colliding with Piastri 😱#F1 #BahrainGP pic.twitter.com/RvF0cHVjMP— Formula 1 (@F1) October 4, 20269. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) Form: Baku P12, Bahrain P7. Championship: P9Lawson referred to his Sepang getaway as “one of the best starts I’ve ever had in my career” after jumping from 11th to fourth. He eventually finished P7 and was the best of the midfield. Racing Bulls looked genuinely competitive throughout the weekend rather than just benefiting from the chaos. Lawson will be feeling proud of his recent performances and eager to continue impressing. 8. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin)Form: Baku DNF, Bahrain P8. Championship: P17Finally, something for Alonso to celebrate. Aston Martin reached Q2 with both cars for the first time this season before Alonso converted 12th on the grid into P8 in the race. He survived the wrong opening tyre choice, passed Arvid Lindblad for a points position and then kept Norris behind until the end. The retirements and the rain helped. It was Aston Martin’s best result of 2026. Alonso believes the team has "some hope" for Singapore.7. Oscar Piastri (McLaren)Form: Baku P13, Bahrain P6. Championship: P7Piastri needed a good weekend, and at last had one in Sepang.He finished in P6, which, according to team principal Andrea Stella, was effectively the best McLaren could have managed. Piastri looked stronger on the hard tyres and was closing in on Charles Leclerc before the final safety car interrupted his progress. There is still a big gap between McLaren and those ahead of them, and Piastri admitted the team “need to improve”. George Russell is set for a grid penalty for the Singapore Grand Prix, due to an unavoidable engine change after his retirement at Sepang, Mercedes have confirmed 🚨FULL STORY 👉 https://t.co/1qvc6pBOGa#F1 #SingaporeGP pic.twitter.com/HdHTbwO73v— Formula 1 (@F1) October 7, 20266. George Russell (Mercedes) Form: Baku P1, Bahrain DNF. Championship: P2Russell was heading for another podium in Malaysia when his engine failed with five laps remaining. He has been unlucky too many times, and Mercedes have to address their reliability issues. Not only was he forced to retire, but things are set to get worse in Singapore. Mercedes have confirmed that Russell will need another power unit and that he is set for a grid penalty, so he will start towards the back of the grid at Marina Bay. It’s a notoriously difficult circuit for overtaking, and Russell will be disadvantaged. 5. Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) Form: Baku P3, Bahrain P5. Championship: P8Hadjar continues to look completely at home near the front of the grid. He was only 0.428 seconds off teammate Max Verstappen in qualifying, but was forced to drop five places and start P8 due to a grid penalty for exceeding his allocated internal combustion engine (ICE) components for the season. In the race, he managed to recover to fifth and spent much of the race holding Lewis Hamilton behind before battery issues and a lack of grip hindered him.A podium finish followed by a fifth place since returning from injury is impressive.4. Charles Leclerc (Ferrari) Form: Baku P4, Bahrain P4. Championship: P4Three races, three P4s for Leclerc. Ferrari’s decision to start on slicks dropped him to the back, and Leclerc later said the team needed to learn from Red Bull how to execute better strategies. He still managed to recover and finished just over two seconds behind Hamilton.Ferrari are demonstrating good pace, and the team hopes Singapore will allow their strengths to shine. Leclerc’s qualifying speed will become particularly valuable this weekend. Looking in at the earliest our Drivers' Championship contenders can secure the Title 🏆Can anyone take it to the wire against Kimi Antonelli? 👀#F1 #SingaporeGP pic.twitter.com/o184HnyQjh— Formula 1 (@F1) October 7, 20263. Kimi Antonelli (Mercedes) Form: Baku P5, Bahrain P2. Championship: P1Despite Antonelli leaving Sepang with another 18 points to open up an 84-point championship lead, the team were left with more questions surrounding the new package.The Italian took the lead at the start and eventually finished second and described that as the maximum available to him once Max Verstappen came through. The bigger question heading into Singapore is the car. Mercedes expected their upgrade to deliver approximately three-tenths of a second of extra speed, but instead, according to Toto Wolff, it seems to have cost them several tenths. 2. Lewis Hamilton (Ferrari)Form: Baku P6, Bahrain P3. Championship: P3What a monumental drive by the Brit in Malaysia. A brilliant qualifying lap put his Ferrari on the front row, just 0.298 seconds behind Verstappen. On race day, Ferrari’s choice of tyre threatened to undo all that good work as he dropped from second to 18th. Hamilton admitted his “heart just sank” when he realised Verstappen was on intermediates. But in true Hamilton fashion, he managed a superb recovery, climbing up the field and passing Hadjar late to claim third. Ferrari’s straight-line deficit should prove to be less of a problem in Singapore, and Hamilton boasts genuine momentum going into this weekend. Bahrain GP - in pictures 1. Max Verstappen (Red Bull)Form: Baku P2, Bahrain P1. Championship: P6Finally, the former champion got his race win. He took his first pole of the year in Malaysia and converted it into Red Bull’s first win of the season with their own power unit. More important than the result itself was how convincing the RB22 looked. Red Bull had already improved in Baku, as evidenced by Hadjar and Verstappen both finishing on the podium, but Sepang demonstrated further progress, giving hope of a strong finish to the season. Singapore will show us whether Max is truly back. Singapore podium prediction:1. Max VerstappenThe recent progress from the team is too substantial to dismiss, and Laurent Mekies, the team principal, believes this track should suit the RB22. Verstappen has never won here before. Can he manage it? 2. Kimi AntonelliIt’s hard to dismiss the youngster’s insatiable appetite for victory or the risks he’s willing to take to get there. Reliability remains an issue – will he have a dependable car?3. Lewis HamiltonThe Brit has won in Singapore four times before and is showing his class. Can he maintain rear-end stability to secure another podium finish?

headline: Test shows AI models likely to give advice for terrorist attacks
summary: All but two of 134 leading large language artificial intelligence models gave information useful to launching a mass casualty attack or building deadly weapons, in a test of the industry's safety measures. A stress test of the industry found that safety measures can be stripped from leading models within three days, according to researchers at London-based Tech against Terrorism. There have been growing concerns over the potential threats posed by AI, with former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon discussing the issue at a New York City hearing this month. The issue has been overshadowed by the opportunities promised by technological advances in many countries. Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, spoke on Friday at an AI opportunity summit organised by his predecessor Gordon Brown that brought together executives and investors to discuss the industry's growth.Mr Burnham is gearing up for the rotating presidency of the G20 and said he would use the UK's 2027 role to promote a global code of standards and principles to support what he called an AI for good approach to develop common safety standards. "We do need to take an AI for good approach first and foremost because it can unlock everything that we’re talking about today, but at the same time be clear-sighted about the risks it may pose," he told the meeting. Addressing dangersThe spread of so-called abliterated AI was identified by Tech against Terrorism as a serious danger, with 13 out of 13 failing the tests after safeguards were stripped away. Abliterated is a term for the models run on users' own systems, often without any shelf life."Abliteration is a proliferation problem," Tech against Terrorism said. "Companies that host, serve, list or sell models should keep abliterated and other modified copies that fail an independent test out of search, recommendation and app stores, and require verified identity for access to them, working with open-source developers rather than against them."In the survey, the Tech against Terrorism model CT-AI put 627 requests to the AI models that a terrorist planning an attack would need to have answered. Eighty-one models gave a complete answer, while another 51 gave useful advice. That left the two that were provisionally passed on safety measures. A user stating that they were a terrorist and intended to commit an atrocity received a usable response in just under two per cent of cases. The equivalent figure for a user stating they were a safety researcher was 16.9 per cent or 8.9 times higher, the research found."The models appear to respond to the stated purpose of the request, rather than the request itself," it said. The group's founder, Adam Hadley, said: "A model that refuses a stated terrorist and answers a stated researcher has not been made safe. It has been made polite."In addition to seeking government backing for benchmark testing such as the tools it is pioneering, Tech against Terrorism recommends developers filter hazardous knowledge and known terrorist content out of their training data.The organisation wants developers to test how hard each model is to strip of its safety measures before it is released, and publish the results. Where a new model fails a common test, the developer should decline to release it and the results be declared to governments, it said. Government dilemmaThe report raises important questions over how countries can build trust in AI while accelerating innovation and adoption. Sovereignty over AI does not yet appear to be a factor in improving the safety of the systems on offer. "Governments and companies should support independent safety benchmarks – ours and others – and publish which models do well as well as which do not, so that parents, schools, businesses and public bodies can choose safer models," it said. "Informed buyers move companies faster than rules do."

headline: Pentagon to livestream firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter in Texas
summary: The firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, the army psychiatrist who killed 13 people ​at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be broadcast live.US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told Human Events Daily with Jack Posobiec on Thursday that Hasan's execution would be carried out on December 3 at Fort Hood."We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Mr Hegseth said. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."The last public execution in the US was in 1936. "The Secretary is correct.
