Fatah leader and Palestinian Authority President Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree.The National reported this week that the legislative elections would be postponed, according to sources from the main Palestinian factions.The presidential vote had been due to take place next year, but the decree announced by Mr Abbas on Saturday sets September 11, 2027 as the date for both votes, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation approved the postponement and in a statement said the delay was due to a lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.Election commission head Jamil Al Khalidi told Palestinian media this week that preparations were being made to hold elections in Gaza and the West Bank despite security, logistical and technical hurdles.He said alternatives to traditional ballot boxes and voting ink were being sourced, as Israel continues to block their entry into Gaza.Sources from different factions said the delay was mainly linked to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. Attempts to unite the political factions have often failed due to disagreements about the way forward for Palestine.Systemic problems mean Palestine has lacked a suitable environment for elections for decades. Under an increasingly deadly and aggressive Israeli occupation, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling circle of support.Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.
body_text:
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas issued a decree on Saturday cancelling the legislative elections scheduled for November this year and setting a new date, together with the presidential vote, for September 2027.

The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, leading to the rift between the group and the ruling Fatah party. Fatah leader and Palestinian Authority President Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree.

The National reported this week that the legislative elections would be postponed, according to sources from the main Palestinian factions.

The presidential vote had been due to take place next year, but the decree announced by Mr Abbas on Saturday sets September 11, 2027 as the date for both votes, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.

The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation approved the postponement and in a statement said the delay was due to a lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the occupied West Bank.

Election commission head Jamil Al Khalidi told Palestinian media this week that preparations were being made to hold elections in Gaza and the West Bank despite security, logistical and technical hurdles.

He said alternatives to traditional ballot boxes and voting ink were being sourced, as Israel continues to block their entry into Gaza.

Sources from different factions said the delay was mainly linked to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. Attempts to unite the political factions have often failed due to disagreements about the way forward for Palestine.

Systemic problems mean Palestine has lacked a suitable environment for elections for decades. Under an increasingly deadly and aggressive Israeli occupation, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.

High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling circle of support.

Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.

analysis.framing: The article frames Abbas's election postponement as a symptom of his authoritarian overreach and declining legitimacy, set against a backdrop of Israeli occupation and internal Palestinian dysfunction.

loaded_language.quote: has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree
loaded_language.explanation: The phrase 'overstayed his term' implies an illegitimate extension of power, and 'rules by decree' evokes authoritarian governance, both carrying negative connotations.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: has remained in office beyond his elected term and governs through decrees

loaded_language.quote: increasingly deadly and aggressive Israeli occupation
loaded_language.explanation: The adjectives 'deadly' and 'aggressive' are emotionally charged and editorialize the nature of the occupation, rather than using neutral descriptors like 'ongoing' or 'long-standing'.

loaded_language.quote: state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed
loaded_language.explanation: The phrase 'all but collapsed' is a dramatic characterization that may overstate the situation, using hyperbolic language to convey dysfunction.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: state institutions, finances and the political scene have severely deteriorated

loaded_language.explanation: The word 'dwindling' suggests a decline that may be editorializing, implying weakening support without providing specific evidence in the immediate context.

omissions: No mention of specific reasons cited by Abbas or Fatah for the delay beyond security concerns, such as the need for reconciliation with Hamas.
No mention of international reactions or statements from other countries regarding the postponement.
No mention of the exact number of years since the last legislative election (2006) or the fact that Abbas was elected in 2005, though the article does state these facts.
No mention of the possibility that the delay could be a tactic to avoid electoral defeat for Fatah.

headline: Supporters of jailed former Pakistani leader Imran Khan march towards Islamabad
summary: Thousands of supporters of jailed former Pakistani prime minister Imran Khan were marching towards Islamabad on Saturday to demand his release.Khan has been in jail since 2023 and his health is in a critical condition, supporters and family warn. Pakistan's government has said it will not allow the march to enter the capital due to security concerns. “The federal government will take all possible measures to maintain peace and promote public development in the province,” said a government statement.Supporters of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party began their “long march” last Sunday, demanding his release and voicing anti-government sentiment fuelled by harsh economic conditions. Some protesters are carrying red-and-green party flags or holding pictures of Khan.The popular former cricket star has been behind bars since August 2023 and faces scores of charges, ranging from corruption to treason, following anti-establishment riots in the same year.He and his legal team reject the allegations, describing them as politically motivated cases aimed at neutralising his popularity. Khan's sons have been warning about his deteriorating health since last year. His ​lawyers say he has lost significant vision in his right eye while in prison.Last week, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urged the PTI to call off the march and re-enter negotiations with the government. The talks had hit an impasse in the early hours of last Sunday before the march began.The PTI has long accused the government of keeping Mr Khan in prison for convictions secured in politically motivated cases, charges the government rejects.Mr Sharif said the demonstration would have a negative impact on the economy, and warned that undermining the government's efforts would be met with the force of law.“We will not allow this to happen. The law will take its course. Protecting the lives and property of the people is our responsibility, and we will ensure this by all means,” the Prime Minister said.The government has been preparing for weeks for the arrival of demonstrators in Islamabad. The march was first slated for September 27 before being postponed until last Sunday.

headline: Foggy mornings and scattered rain expected across UAE until Tuesday
summary: Drivers travelling between Dubai and Abu Dhabi face more fog in the coming days after poor visibility slowed journeys last week and prompted police to lower speed limits.Abu Dhabi Police urged drivers to exercise caution, reduced speed limits to 80kph on several roads and banned lorries from motorways during poor visibility. Major roads across the Emirates experienced heavy traffic after the fog cleared, causing further traffic delays.Ahmed Habib, from the National Centre of Meteorology, told The National that fog could persist until Tuesday, with varying intensity each day. He said coastal and western areas were particularly susceptible because of the combination of cooling temperatures and high humidity.What is causing the heavy fog?Light winds, high humidity and decreasing temperatures create favourable conditions for low fog. Wind speeds below 10kph allow moisture to accumulate near the ground.Dr Habib explained that as temperatures drop at night, humid air near the surface cools, causing water vapour to condense into droplets and form fog. Fog usually clears as temperatures rise after sunrise or winds increase.The weather department forecast humid conditions overnight and on Monday morning in some coastal and inland areas, which could lead to fog or mist.The UAE will see fair to partly cloudy weather from Sunday to Tuesday. Convective clouds are likely to form in eastern and southern areas on Sunday, possibly extending to inland regions on Monday and bringing a chance of rain. By Tuesday, eastern and western regions could become cloudy, with a chance of scattered showers.When will winter start?The recent foggy conditions coincide with the UAE’s transition to winter. The lowest temperature recorded in the country on Saturday morning was 23.7°C in Raknah, Al Ain, at 5.15am.Dr Habib said the seasonal transition will occur through October and November, with autumn, which began on August 22, giving way to winter around December 22.

headline: S&P lifts UK GDP growth view on resilient consumer spending and services sector
summary: S&P Global Ratings has upgraded its growth outlook for the UK, citing “reasonably resilient” consumer spending and services that have helped shield the economy from the conflict in the Middle East.Real gross domestic product in Europe's second-biggest economy is now expected to climb by 1.3 per cent, from a previous lowered prediction of 1.1 per cent, the New York-based agency said on Friday.S&P analysts noted that hospitality and professional services underpinned economic growth in the second quarter. GDP growth is seen to average 1.4 per cent from 2027 to 2029, expecting the economy to improve if the situation in the Middle East is “contained”.The agency also maintained the UK's long and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at AA, two notches below the top prime grade. An investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises.“The stable outlook reflects our view that the UK economy has remained, and will remain, resilient in the face of the energy shock emanating from the Middle East conflict, with growth remaining reasonably robust,” analysts at S&P wrote.“This is balanced against risks from the UK's constrained fiscal position, elevated public debt levels, and high government spending, including on debt servicing.”S&P also noted the UK's policy direction under Andy Burnham, the UK's sixth prime minister in the past decade. The start of his tenure in July was marked by questions about how he would handle the economy, including how to ensure fiscal discipline.Mr Burnham's government has “focused on devolution, industrial renewal, social care and closer ties with the EU, with simultaneous pledges to respect fiscal prudence”, S&P said.UK inflation was pegged at 3.1 per cent in August, the highest in five months, according to the Office of National Statistics, and well above the Bank of England's 2 per cent threshold. S&P said this has risen on domestic price pressures and energy and transport costs, underpinned by higher hydrocarbon costs.The agency expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 0.25 basis points at its November meeting after maintaining them last month, “then hold that level until the second half of 2027 because the current policy rate level of 3.75 per cent and soft labour market conditions suggest the UK may require less additional policy tightening than the eurozone”.Egypt's growth acceleratesMeanwhile, S&P said Egypt's economy accelerated at its fastest pace in three years, but cautioned the North African nation remains vulnerable to shocks stemming from the conflicts in the Middle East.Real GDP in the Arab world's most populous nation jumped by 5.1 per cent in fiscal 2026, buoyed by non-oil sectors including manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, information and communication technology, and tourism, it said in a separate report. That compares to a 4.7 per cent reading in its previous estimate.Household consumption emerged as a primary factor, boosted by record remittances, easing inflation and stable labour market conditions, it added.S&P, however, projects this growth to ease to 4.5 per cent in the fiscal year 2027, as shipping disruptions related to the war are expected to further pressure trade, logistics and import prices. Consumption and investment activities are also predicted to soften amid persistent uncertainty and rising inflation.Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, according to Capmas data. S&P expects inflation to average 12.9 per cent in fiscal 2027. This might result in a policy reversal from the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates.S&P also kept its B sovereign credit rating on Egypt, which is six levels below investment grade, with a stable outlook.“Nevertheless, we expect the continued implementation of the reform agenda, including the commitment to exchange rate liberalisation, to enhance structural economic competitiveness over the medium term,” the S&P analysts said.

headline: Iraq's Al Sadr seeks statesmanship with push against militias after US withdrawal
summary: Shiite cleric Moqtada Al Sadr is seeking to reinforce a long-standing Iraqi nationalist platform that aims to keep Baghdad out of regional conflicts and curb Iranian influence, experts and officials have told The National. Mr Al Sadr’s push comes as he called for a new chapter between the US and Iraq following the withdrawal of American troops on September 30. The prominent cleric and former battlefield enemy of American troops during the US occupation is at a turning point in his own rebranding. Mr Al Sadr has millions of faithful supporters across Iraq, many of whom were part of his armed militia for years. That has now changed.On the day of the departure of US troops, he dissolved his Promised Day Brigade as well as his armed militia, Saraya al Salam (the Peace Brigades), which will now be under government control. Its members are expected to be incorporated into Iraq’s formal security apparatus under the authority of Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi's government. Mr Al Zaidi has been pushing to disarm all armed groups as Iraq undergoes a political shift following the exit of the US-led coalition forces.Meanwhile, Mr Al Sadr is portraying himself as a statesman seeking to keep Iraq out of regional conflicts while strengthening the state's monopoly on force.The withdrawal of US forces has weakened a key justification used by armed groups to keep their weapons. The question of why armed factions still operate without state control remains. The groups were expected to disarm by the September 30 deadline, but this has since been pushed to June next year.Mr Al Sadr’s recent statement and actions raise some suspicion as to how the process of disarming his militias will play out.Experts and a close aide to Mr Al Sadr told The National that his latest moves should be seen as part of a broader effort to continue his nationalist campaign, which combines religious leadership with political activism.“Mr Al Sadr has long advocated dissolving armed factions, including calling for the disbandment of groups operating outside state control,” Renad Mansour, director of the Iraq Initiative at London's Chatham House, told The National. “But integrating fighters into government institutions does not necessarily resolve questions over their loyalties,” he added.“What we'll have to see is what this actually means in reality. The bigger question is over loyalties: will they then become under a different chain of command, or will they still fall under the informal chain?” Mr Mansour said. Mr Al Sadr's vision for Iraq merges political and religious movements. “He believes that clerics should be active in politics, not isolated to religious affairs only. He is trying to chart his own role in the Iraqi state, one that bridges these different branches,” he said.The cleric's political movement, the Sadrists, have distanced themselves from the mainstream political scene in Iraq during the last few years. In the past decade, Mr Al Sadr has reinvented himself as a nationalist and an anti-corruption campaigner, emerging as a political kingmaker.He has always voiced his concerns over US and Iranian influence on Iraq's internal affairs. The shift in Mr Al Sadr's mindset comes as Iran continues to project influence across the region through allied armed groups, even as some nationalist movements seek to distance themselves from Tehran, said Bente Scheller, head of the Middle East and North Africa division at the Heinrich-Boll-Stiftung Foundation in Berlin.“Proxies are the method of choice in the region, yet because Iran deploys them in its own interest, this often brings them into conflict with their own national interests,” Ms Scheller told The National.By championing the state's monopoly on force, Mr Al Sadr may be seeking both to shield Iraq from becoming entangled in regional conflicts and to strengthen his credentials as a national political leader.“If Sadr now adopts a statesmanlike stance and emphasises the state's monopoly on the use of force, this may serve to take Iraq out of the line of fire,” she said. Setting an example Dhia Al Assadi, a former Iraqi minister and adviser to Mr Al Sadr, told The National that the cleric had long sought to help build a strong and stable Iraq.“Mr Al Sadr has consistently taken the initiative in setting an example. He encourages others to be brave and sensible enough to sacrifice political or material gains for the sake of stabilising and rebuilding Iraq on sound principles,” Mr Al Assadi said.The cleric's vision for the country begins with a “strong and well-founded Iraq, and looks outward to the world on the basis of mutual respect, co-operation, and shared interests”, he added. Based on Mr Al Sadr's recent statements on US-Iraqi ties, the region could benefit if American policymakers adopted a new approach and learnt from past mistakes, he said. Optimism would be limited if Washington continued to pursue narrowly defined interests at the expense of regional stability, Al Assadi added.Marsin Al Shammary, Iraq expert and assistant professor of political science at Boston College, said Mr Al Sadr's most recent policy had been based on playing the “long game in Iraq”.“He foresees a political future for himself and doesn’t want to undermine that by positioning himself as anti-state. We’ve seen in the past that he has a remarkable ability to mobilise and demobilise his followers,” Ms Al Shammary told The National.Another possibility is that he chooses to become closer to the successor to spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Al Sistani, she said, adding that “he has been making overtures towards Najaf recently”. The southern city of Najaf is home to Iraq's senior Shiite clerics and was the site of a 2004 rebellion against US forces by militias loyal to Mr Al Sadr.“Mr Al Sadr and Najaf do agree on one thing and that’s the importance of limiting Iranian influence in succession,” she said. Ms Al Shammary added that the cleric shared a long-term strategy with authorities in Najaf for an Iraq independent of Iran but with friendly ties with the region.

headline: US-Russia energy deal opens up diesel can of worms
summary: US President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia will be supplying diesel to global markets has opened up a can of worms, says analysts.Washington agreed to lift sanctions on the Kremlin in a bid to bring down energy prices, especially for diesel, which is vital to many economic sectors.Analysts, however, have raised alarm bells, saying the numbers Mr Trump has touted will not add up, and highlighting double standards over Russia's conflict with Ukraine and the International Criminal Court.'Happy birthday Putin'The first fallout came from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately after Mr Trump announced the deal.Mr Zelenskyy said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”, and that the Kremlin “will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy”.In a subsequent interview with Axios, Mr Zelenskyy likened the deal to a “birthday present” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on October 7.Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be…— Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 9, 2026Mr Zelenskyy apparently also felt betrayed. Last week, the Ukrainian President met Steve Witkoff, the US special envoy to the Middle East, and Jared Kushner, the US envoy for peace (and Mr Trump's son-in-law), to discuss a potential peace breakthrough before the US midterm elections. But nothing was discussed about a potential diesel deal with the Russians.“It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this,” Mr Zelenskyy said in the Axios interview.“If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good … what did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world.”'Fantasy arithmetic'Mr Trump, in a social media post, said that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”.In total, and “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia will deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”, he added.Those numbers “will not work”, according to analysts at Quantum Strategy and Geonomics, which said the figures above are, respectively, 60 per cent, 100 per cent and 200 per cent of Russia's diesel exports.Furthermore, Russia needs to import 80,000 and 140,000 barrels per day of diesel, petrol and other refined products just to run its domestic refineries and make up for the shortages of refined products, Singapore-based Quantum said.Its analysts also pointed out that Ukrainian strikes have taken out more than half of Russia's refining capacity, according to Kyiv's defence ministry. The International Energy Agency estimates that Russia's diesel production capacity has been cut by nearly a third as a result of the attacks.In addition, Russia's exports of diesel and gasoil fell to a decade low of about 144,000 barrels per day in September, down from as high as 270,000 bpd in August and a peak of 820,000 in April, according to Quantum data.“Russia cannot supply the diesel Trump claims it will … technically, the balance [between diesel and other refined product exports and imports] needed to run domestic refineries cannot be switched into supplying Trump without endangering Russian domestic refinery supply in other areas,” the Quantum analysts said.“So Trump's simple fantasy arithmetic is nothing but that … we expect this deal to fail economically.”"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and… pic.twitter.com/tZMCfT95ru— The White House (@WhiteHouse) October 9, 2026Double standardThe US-Russia diesel deal also poses as a double standard. On Friday, Washington imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court, on the same day that former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The move was seen as retaliation for Mr Trump not being awarded the honour, which he claimed he deserved.“The contrast is striking. Sanctions against an institution pursuing accountability for war crimes; sanctions relaxed on energy exports from a country waging a war of aggression against Ukraine,” said Nicolai Kiskalt, a Germany-based partner at global consultancy KPMG.“The US administration has its own arguments: protecting American sovereignty from the ICC’s jurisdiction and bringing down energy prices for American consumers. But from a European perspective, these decisions raise fundamental questions that go far beyond trade, energy or diplomacy.”Riku Huttunen, director general of the energy department at Finland's Economy and Employment Ministry, also called this a “stark contrast” to the US sanctions law aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenue that fuels Russia’s war against Ukraine.“At the same time, there are doubts concerning Russian supplies. Russian oil refining capacities have been destroyed by Ukrainian drone attacks, causing fuel shortages,” he said.“The deal's effects on diesel markets might remain small. The agreed amounts are relatively modest and it is still unclear how the deliveries would be made in practice.”The timing of the US-Russia deal may also be bad, especially for Ukrainians, as winter approaches. Any further attacks on energy infrastructure would prove to be a serious challenge for both the economy and society.“An energy ceasefire was one of the few practical ideas that could have directly protected Ukrainian civilians this winter,” said Robert Potter, founding partner of Washington-based Cyber Activities Group, who is also an expert in geopolitics and security.“The negotiating logic was straightforward: if Moscow wanted sanctions relief or economic concessions, those could potentially be exchanged for something tangible, stopping attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Instead, Trump has handed Putin the economic benefit first,” he said.“That pulls the rug from under one of the few areas where western leverage could have been converted into immediate civilian protection. Worse, the signal to Moscow is really dangerous. Putin can escalate attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, refuse to commit to renewed peace talks, and still receive access to western-linked energy markets because US diesel prices are politically painful ahead of the midterms.”

headline: Dubai introduces digital Nol QR tickets for metro, buses and trams
summary: Public transport passengers in Dubai can now use digital QR codes on their phones to access the metro, trams and buses, eliminating the need for a single-use red paper Nol ticket.Passengers can buy digital Nol QR tickets through the Nol Pay or S'hail apps, the Roads and Transport Authority announced. This option is especially convenient for occasional passengers and visitors who use red Nol tickets for single trips. The fare for a red Nol ticket depends on the number of zones travelled through.To enter the metro, passengers should hold their phone with the QR code facing down over the entry blue gate reader.For bus rides, hold the phone screen facing up with the QR code displayed over the red Nol reader at the entrance until it is accepted. Digital tickets are also valid on the Dubai Tram.Commuters can buy the QR ticket up to 90 days in advance. It becomes valid on first use and expires at midnight that same day. For example, if you activate it at 11pm, it expires at midnight.Regular commuters can keep using their silver, gold and personal Nol cards. The digital QR tickets are an additional option rather than a replacement for existing cards. The silver Nol card holder is permitted in regular-class areas, while the gold Nol card allows passengers access gold class cabins on the Metro and trams at a higher fare. The personal Nol card, also known as the blue Nol card, is issued in the passenger’s name and may offer fare concessions to eligible students, senior Emiratis and residents, and people of determination.

headline: Why Bhuvneshwar Kumar's shock India recall shows that life begins at 30 for fast bowlers
summary: Bhuvneshwar Kumar last played an international match for India in 2022. His international career looked as good as over after England smashed him for 25 runs in two overs in the 2022 T20 World Cup semi-final in Adelaide during a thumping 10-wicket win.His lack of bite with the new ball, in the absence of Jasprit Bumrah, led the team management to quickly move on from him. Mohammad Siraj nestled into the white-ball team and formed a lethal pace trio with Bumrah and Mohammad Shami as India dominated the ensuing ODI World Cup at home, only to lose the final to Australia.India have since won successive T20 World Cups, Asia Cups and Asian Games T20 gold medals, plus the 50-over Champions Trophy. But with the ICC cycle moving out of Asia for the upcoming seasons, India have gone back to the bowler they had decidedly moved on from. In 2023, right-arm seamer Bhuvneshwar had told The National that he just wants to enjoy his remaining years of fast bowling. Now, he is back in the Indian T20 team, at the age of 36, for the forthcoming tour of New Zealand. Actually, he has forced himself back into the Indian set-up. The seamer went back to the drawing board, upped his fitness and recalibrated his game around the shortest format to emerge as the most lethal 20-over pacer in the country.Bhuvneshwar was the driving force behind Royal Challengers Bengaluru’s IPL triumphs, finishing as the second-highest wicket taker last season and delivering match-winning spells in both finals. This season, he took his domestic team Lucknow to the final of the state-level Uttar Pradesh T20 league. Bhuvneshwar’s sustained excellence over two seasons has coincided with the continued struggles of the next crop of Indian fast bowlers.Young quicks like Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar, Mayank Yadav and Anshul Kamboj are among a long list of quicks who have come in and failed to cement their spot in any format.Simple looks easy. It never is. 🙌Bhuvneshwar Kumar on the phase when everyone had a theory about his pace, why he never changed his action, and the years of unseen work behind keeping things simple. ❤️Catch more of Bhuvi candid in the full episode of @bigbasket_com presents… pic.twitter.com/ngdeQUThaj— Royal Challengers Bengaluru (@RCBTweets) October 8, 2026During the recent ODI series against the West Indies, India’s bowling attack conceded 400 runs in the second game and saw the Windies easily chase down a 350-run target in the third ODI.Among the experienced lot, only Siraj and Arshdeep Singh can be viewed as first-choice picks. Everyone else is a work in progress, at best. However, even Arshdeep was pummelled for 45 from his four overs as India were beaten by six wickets by the Windies in the second of five T20s on Friday. It all explains why India’s selectors have gone back to Bhuvneshwar for the T20 series in New Zealand which begins later this month. And which is also why many hope that veteran pacer Shami, 36, finds his way back into the Indian team for next year’s ODI World Cup in southern Africa.Experience mattersBhuvneshwar’s comeback fits perfectly with a peculiar quirk of international cricket – many of the top-ranked fast bowlers across formats are well into their 30s, while most of the best batters are in their mid 20s.sJasprit Bumrah (32), Mitchell Starc (36), Josh Hazlewood (35), Kagiso Rabada (31), Jofra Archer (31), Matt Henry (34), Pat Cummins (33), Ollie Robinson (32), Taskin Ahmed (31), Scott Boland (37) … the list is really long. A few standout exceptions are South Africa’s Marco Jansen (26), Bangladesh tearaway quick Nahid Rana (24) and Pakistan’s Shaheen Afridi (26).Compare that to the best and most promising batters in the world. Harry Brook (27), Shubman Gill (27), Abhishek Sharma (26), Rachin Ravindra (26), Vaibhav Sooryavanshi (15), Dewald Brevis (23), Ishan Kishan (28), Saim Ayub (24), Pathum Nissanka (28) are all young and well on their way to excelling in one or many formats over the coming years. Sure, veterans like Joe Root, Steve Smith, Virat Kohli and others are still piling on the runs. But the next generation is clearly up to the task.That does not seem to be the case with bowling. India’s reliance on Bumrah, decision to go back to Bhuvneshwar and clamour for the return of Shami shows that when it comes to pace bowling, the new crop is not quite matching up to the old stock.One can understand why. Fast bowling requires miles in the legs and bowlers can get that only by playing red ball, multi-day cricket. Only bowlers of a certain vintage have played enough first-class and Test matches and have the experience in their body to last the distance for consecutive seasons or adapt their bowling according to match situations. Those who developed their bowling in the T20 arena don’t seem to have the complete set of tools required to master conditions and formats. Which is why teams are holding on to their older generation of fast bowlers for as long as physically possible, barring Bangladesh who have an exciting and high-class young bowling attack. Now you understand why Australia are squeezing every bit of life out of their awesome quartet of Starc, Hazlewood, Cummins and Boland. That has proven to be the case elsewhere, too. Because, in almost every corner of the world, they just don't make them like they used to.

headline: UAE begins food aid airlift to Gaza under Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge
summary: The UAE began airlifting food aid to Gaza on Friday under the newly launched Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge initiative, aiming to supply more than 10 million meals to Palestinians.Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, along with Operation Knight 3, launched flights from Al Maktoum International Airport carrying food parcels.Sheikh Ahmed, brother of Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, died on September 21, and the initiative was launched to recognise his generosity and philanthropic work. It brought together volunteers, community members and admirers of Sheikh Ahmed at Dubai World Trade Centre to prepare food the aid packages for families and children in Gaza.The humanitarian bridge will operate through air and sea transport in seven consignments. Six flights will carry 450 tonnes of food parcels, and one vessel will transport 4,000 tonnes of supplies to meet the basic nutrition needs of people in Gaza.Hammoud Al Afari, director of UAE relief operations under Operation Gallant Knight 3, said the bridge augmented the UAE's humanitarian efforts.“The launch of flights under the Ahmed bin Rashid Humanitarian Bridge reflects the high level of efficiency and expertise of the Emirati teams involved in Operation Gallant Knight 3,” Mr Al Afari said. He added that Operation Gallant Knight 3, launched in November 2023 under the directives of President Sheikh Mohamed, had been a lifeline for Palestinians throughout the conflict. The continuity and geographical reach of its assistance have helped large segments of the population cope with difficult living conditions.The operation has established a model for humanitarian response through its integrated approach combining emergency relief, health care, logistical support, recovery and rehabilitation programmes, he said.Since its launch, the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in humanitarian assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid since 2023. That assistance has included 130,708 tonnes of relief, medical, and food supplies delivered by 796 aircraft, 25 ships and 14,483 lorries.Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, the region's largest humanitarian and community development foundation, recorded expenditure exceeding Dh2.3 billion in 2025, positively impacting approximately 165 million beneficiaries across 122 countries. Its humanitarian aid and relief programmes alone exceeded Dh625 million in expenditure, benefiting more than 53 million people worldwide.Its activities span five main pillars: humanitarian aid and relief, health care and disease control, education and knowledge, innovation and entrepreneurship, and community empowerment.Today, MBRGI encompasses more than 30 initiatives and institutions working across humanitarian, social and development sectors, with particular emphasis on disadvantaged countries and vulnerable communities.

headline: Israel holding 49 Syrians after 280 armed incursions in September, says UN
summary: Israel is holding 49 Syrians and carried out 280 armed incursions into southern Syria in September, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has said.Released detainees alleged torture and ill-treatment, including beatings, prolonged forced standing and threats against their families, said a statement from Mr Volker's office on Friday.He called on Israeli authorities to halt such actions. The statement said September marked the highest monthly number of armed Israeli incursions since the beginning of the year, according to open-source monitoring.The incursions include “reported raids on homes, restrictions on movement, harassment and intimidation of civilians, arbitrary detention and destruction of livelihoods”, the office said. Forty-nine Syrians remain in Israeli detention, according to information received by the office, although it said it could not independently verify the number. The statement called on Israeli authorities to “cease actions that harass or intimidate civilians in Syrian villages, including raids, restrictions on freedom of movement, detention and destruction of crops”.The remarks by Mr Turk's office come as Syria accuses Israel of building major military fortifications in Syrian territory along the occupied Golan Heights. The Syrian Foreign Ministry said that Israel was working to complete its “Sufa 53 Line”, in violation of previous agreements.Areas near the Golan Heights have experienced an increasing number of Israeli incursions this year. Israeli troops crossed into southern Syria and areas west of Damascus, and occupied parts of those regions, soon after rebel forces led by current President Ahmad Al Shara ousted the regime of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024.The US, which backs Syria's current rulers, has supervised several meetings between Israeli and Syrian officials in an effort to negotiate a peace deal between the two countries. They discussed halting Israeli attacks on Syria and the return of Israeli forces to the 1974 armistice line adjacent to the Golan Heights.

headline: UAE and Saudi Arabia take legal action over online bullying of child with disabilities
summary: The UAE has taken legal action against an individual who posted content on social media that included the bullying of a child with disabilities. The video contained inappropriate innuendo that violates the country’s societal values and morals, the National Media Authority said on Friday.In a statement, the authority said it had co-ordinated with the social media platform to take action against the account and the content's publisher. It also notified authorities to pursue legal measures.The NMA emphasised its rejection of all forms of abuse and bullying, stressing its commitment to protecting children and people with disabilities, preserving their dignity, and safeguarding society.The child’s father had also appealed to authorities in Saudi Arabia to investigate the incident and ensure justice for his son under the Child Protection Law. He condemned the alleged mockery and mistreatment of his son, who is under 15 years old and is a person of determination, and defended the boy's rights.Following the father's appeal, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Human Resources and Social Development said on Friday that the complaint, which circulated on social media, had been referred to authorities and procedures were under way under the kingdom's child protection law.The account has since taken down the post and video.UAE online bullying and abuse lawAlthough the content was reportedly posted by an individual in Saudi Arabia, the UAE maintains a robust legal framework to protect children, combat cyberbullying and address online abuse. This covers content targeting children and people of determination.Federal Law No 3 of 2016 on Child Rights, known as Wadeema’s Law, safeguards children against abuse.The law, which covers UAE nationals and the children of expats, outlines the legal rights of minors and is designed to protect children from physical, verbal and psychological abuse."Although the law does not use the word “bullying” expressly, bullying can fall within its protections and prohibitions," said Nikhat Sardar Khan, a senior lawyerShe explained that Article 32(3) requires the state to ban all forms of violence in educational institutions and to preserve children’s dignity. This can cover physical, verbal, psychological, and other forms of bullying at school."Articles 33 and 34 protect children from physical, psychological or threats to mental integrity. A child-protection specialist may intervene where such harm is threatened. Article 36 prohibits acts of cruelty that affect a child’s emotional, psychological, mental, or moral balance. Serious bullying may meet this description," Ms Khan said.Where conduct amounts to prohibited cruelty under Article 36, Article 69 mandates imprisonment of at least one year and/or a fine of Dh50,000 to Dh100,000. UAE cybercrime law addresses offences committed through digital platforms. To protect public health, peace and order, it targets platforms that spread, publish or circulate fake news, false or misleading reports, or rumours that contradict official information.Violators may face at least one year of imprisonment and a minimum fine of Dh100,000. Penalties increase to two years in jail and a minimum fine of Dh200,000 if the crime occurs during pandemics, emergencies or crises.Federal Decree-Law No 26 of 2025 on Child Digital Safety strengthens protection against online risks and harmful content affecting children. The law applies to internet service providers and digital platforms operating in the UAE or targeting UAE users, regardless of location.

headline: Cristiano Ronaldo hits 980th career goal as he puts Portugal row behind him in Al Nassr win
summary: Cristiano Ronaldo enjoyed a happy return to Riyadh after his troubled international break as he notched his 980th career goal in Al Nassr’s win over Diriyah.The 41-year-old striker could scarcely have asked for an easier night after the controversies of the previous two weeks.The defending Saudi Pro League champions had a routine 3-0 win over Diriyah at Al Awwal Park that was entirely free of aggravation.Ronaldo scored the first himself, pouncing on a loose ball and firing into an empty net after Kingsley Coman had seen his shot saved.The Portugal star looked far sharper than he had in the lead up to the international break, and looked uninhibited by his row with Jorge Jesus, the Portugal coach.Speculation in Europe on the day of the game suggested Ronaldo is going to be suspended by Portugal for his part in the controversy.Ronaldo left the Portugal camp, angered by the decision of Jesus – his former coach at Nassr – not to field him in the second match of the window, as he said had been agreed.In a 1,740-word statement in the days that followed, Ronaldo accused Jesus of lying, and of not treating him as a player “of the stature of Pele and Maradona”.It has been claimed the Portuguese federation could ban Ronaldo for up to six months for his outburst. Despite that, Ronaldo was sharp from the off against Diriyah. He had the ball in the net early on, only for it to be chalked off for offside.That came within a minute of a significant show off support by the Nassr fans. In the eighth minute, a huge banner which covered the entirety of the stand where the home ultras sit was unfurled, saying: “Greatness Is Earned. CR7.”Ronaldo also could have had two assists before he opened the scoring in the 23rd minute, laying on presentable chances for Sadio Mane and Samu Costa.Both saw their shots saved, but it seemed clear that Ronaldo was trying to make a point about being a team player.On that subject, the response to his goal was maybe instructive. When he scored, he raced to the corner flag and did his trademark “Siuu” celebration.He was not exactly engulfed by teammates, though. A few made their way towards him in dribs and drabs, one of whom was Joao Felix, his Portugal teammate.Later in the game, with Nassr 2-0 up after Costa had added the second, Ronaldo might have had a second goal of his own.He and Coman were clean through with just the goalkeeper to beat as the Diriyah defence was AWOL.Coman opted to score himself, though, when he might have squared the ball for Ronaldo. While Ronaldo was the obvious headline act in the game, the win also eased some of the pressure on Ange Postecoglou.Yellow was made for greatness 💛🐐 pic.twitter.com/waRXHef8cR— AlNassr FC (@AlNassrFC_EN) October 9, 2026The Australian coach had made a fine start to his tenure in charge of Nassr at the start of the season, but had grown increasingly irate in the lead in to the international break.That was in response to having his methods questioned after Nassr’s form had stalled, so the 3-0 win immediately on their return was gratefully received.“I thought it was a good performance,” Postecoglou said of a result which takes Nassr up to second in the SPL table. “Obviously, it is always good to win and we scored three good goals, kept a clean sheet.“In general, I thought it was a really good, strong performance and against a difficult opponent, so I'm happy.”

headline: US tech roared back, but is the great investment rotation already over?
summary: Just one month ago, it looked like the glory days might finally be over for US technology stocks, as investors trembled at the prospect of a mighty artificial intelligence bubble.Experts were increasingly urging investors to reduce their exposure by looking beyond the mega-caps towards banks, industrials, smaller companies and emerging markets.Many needed little encouragement. They looked at the trillions being poured into AI infrastructure and wondered whether highly leveraged "hyperscalers" such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft would ever get a return on that investment.And isn’t investing cyclical anyway? The so-called Magnificent Seven and other tech hopefuls have had it their way for long enough. Surely it must be somebody else’s turn.The great rotation?Experts quickly came up with a name for the shift: the great rotation. But there was one problem: it wasn’t so great.Within weeks, investors were rotating back into technology, with renewed AI enthusiasm sending the Nasdaq careering towards fresh highs. So should we all rotate back again?This isn’t the first time investors have stepped back from big tech. The bull run may have lasted more than a dozen years, but there has been plenty of volatility along the way, notably in 2022 when valuations crashed.Investors started looking beyond tech both at the start of this year and again over the summer, says Jason Hollands, managing director of investment platform Bestinvest by Evelyn Partners. “Every time, enthusiasm for the hyperscalers recovered, and it has just taken off again.” The latest rebound is particularly impressive because it has come despite sharply rising bond yields, he says.“Higher yields typically have a negative impact on the discounted cash flow models used to value the forecast earnings of growth stocks several years out.”That should normally hit tech, because it reduces the value of future earnings. There’s another threat too: the prolific amount of debt being issued to finance AI infrastructure.“You might assume that higher financing costs, alongside the debate about whether the speed of AI frontier models should be slowed, would dent enthusiasm but it hasn’t,” Mr Hollands says. “Investor appetite has proven resilient and corporate profit margins continue to impress and surprise.”Dot-com parallelsBut surely this can’t go on?Those worried about the sustainability of AI mania regularly draw parallels with the dot-com boom of the late 1990s, but there’s a huge difference. The hyperscalers have deep pockets and are already making real money.Microsoft’s second-quarter revenue jumped 18 per cent to $90 billion, while Alphabet’s second-quarter revenue rose 24 per cent to $119.8 billion and Amazon’s climbed 20 per cent to $200.6 billion. Cloud services and AI infrastructure were core growth drivers, although Alphabet and Amazon’s net income figures were boosted by non-operating paper gains from start-up investments such as Anthropic and SpaceX.Meta Platforms beat the lot, with revenue jumping 28 per cent to $60.8 billion as AI-optimised recommendation and targeting engines supercharged advertising, boosted by its new Muse AI assistant.“Meta is crushing it, with Mark Zuckerberg’s AI vision finally starting to gain some traction,” Matt Britzman, senior equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, says. Despite unprecedented AI capital spending, hyperscaler valuations have actually become more attractive as underlying earnings continue to expand aggressively. Share prices have risen, but earnings have risen even faster. No wonder investors have swung back to the sector.Risks remainYet there are risks. It doesn’t mean investors should stop worrying about valuations. Nobody knows how this technological revolution will play out. Yves Bonzon, group chief investment officer at Julius Baer, describes it as a “binary play”. “Even if everyone agrees on the enormous disruptive potential of AI, nobody really knows what path it will take or where the endgame lies,” he says.Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which floated in June, is the perfect case study. Its established Starlink operation posted a bumper operating profit of $1.66 billion in the second quarter, a 66 per cent jump.By contrast, its cutting-edge AI division swallowed $15.83 billion in capital expenditure and posted a $1.26 billion operating loss, even as revenue surged 247 per cent.Mr Bonzon argues that frontier AI laboratories are the weakest financial link in the AI value chain, yet one of its most important demand drivers. “Their race to develop AI agents with increasing capability is fuelling spending on chips, memory, cloud infrastructure, data centres, and power, even as their own path to profitability remains uncertain, he says.The risk that rapid technological progress will quickly render AI chips obsolete has so far not materialised, he adds. Older generations of processors continue to play an important role, reducing the risk that today’s AI investments become stranded assets, Mr Bonzon says. “While we continue to favour diversification, we no longer see a compelling reason to underweight the large US hyperscalers.”Wider sell-off But now investors have something else to worry about. October opened with a wider stock market sell-off as investors worried about rising oil prices, inflation and government debt, sending bond yields to multi-decade highs. Investors rotated out of equities at speed, and not just technology stocks. Banks, industrials, smaller companies and emerging markets also sold off. What goes around, comes around.Investors had been rotating out of the US dollar, but now they’re rotating back into it too, says Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at trading platform IG. “The dollar just hit its highest level since April 2025, as persistent inflation, resilient US economic activity, and the hawkish Federal Reserve reinforce expectations of further rate hikes,” he says. “Meanwhile, Bitcoin continues to struggle, though at least it has gold and silver for company.”As bond yields rise, investors are rotating into US Treasuries and government bonds, says Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell. “When investors can earn a relatively high return from government debt with limited risk, equities must work harder to justify their additional volatility.”The rotation between equity sectors and asset classes will always ebb and flow, Mr Hollands says. “The more durable trend should be towards greater diversification. That is generally more robust than making large all-or-nothing bets based on the latest spurts of market leadership,” he adds.

headline: As AI reshapes entertainment, can it ever replace human connection?
summary: Artificial intelligence can generate music, create videos and simulate conversations with remarkable sophistication. But as the technology becomes more deeply embedded in entertainment, one question remains: can it replicate the connection audiences feel with another person?The question is particularly relevant to live streaming, where audiences spend hours interacting with creators, often developing relationships that can last for years.Dan Clancy, chief executive of Twitch, believes those relationships are something technology will never be able to reproduce. "People come to live streaming for that human connection," Clancy told The National. "As humans, we yearn for it."Although AI can imitate human behaviour, Clancy argues that audiences recognise the difference between interacting with a person and a digital substitute.Yet AI-generated personalities are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Virtual streamers can now respond to audiences, produce content and maintain an online presence without a human performer directly controlling every interaction.Their growing capabilities raise questions about whether audiences value the personalities they encounter or the knowledge that another person is behind them.A 2026 study published in the International Journal of Information Management found that highly realistic AI streamers could provoke negative emotional responses, potentially discouraging engagement. It also found that a warmer-sounding voice could reduce some of these reactions, suggesting audiences respond to more than a digital personality's appearance.A separate 2025 study in Information & Management, involving 434 respondents, found that a sense of social presence helped foster emotional connections with streamers and a sense of belonging within their communities relationships were also associated with longer viewing times.Neither study establishes whether AI can ultimately replicate human relationships, but both offer insight into what viewers respond to when watching someone live.Clancy says community is central to why live streaming has grown beyond gaming into sports, conversation and other forms of entertainment."Gaming at its foundation is a community experience," he says. "The reason gaming has gotten so big is because it's a social experience."He compares that appeal to watching a television programme such as Game of Thrones, where discussing developments with friends becomes part of the enjoyment.Streaming builds on that experience by allowing viewers to participate as events unfold. Broadcasters can respond to comments, acknowledge regular viewers, or change the direction of a stream based on audience suggestions.It also gives people a place to share interests that might not be represented among their friends or family. Clancy points to gamers finding communities devoted to titles that nobody in their social circle plays.AI, however, still has a place in that experience. Clancy says the technology can help streamers experiment with content and involve their communities.He recalls an American streamer who invited viewers to generate videos featuring him using OpenAI's Sora technology. The streamer then watched the submissions with his audience and selected the funniest.The exercise demonstrated how AI could encourage collaboration without diminishing the creator's role."They could come up with funny ideas of things he was doing, and they could quickly realise them," Clancy says.The distinction between generating content and building relationships also follows Twitch's approach to helping creators grow.While the platform is investing in short-form clips to attract new audiences, Clancy maintains that longer broadcasts are more effective at building lasting connections. "Short-form content is better for discovery; long-form content is better for connection and community."He points to streamers such as Kai Cenat and IShowSpeed, whose popularity has extended beyond gaming into mainstream entertainment.Clancy believes their success comes partly from the time audiences spend with them. Unlike scrolling through brief videos, watching a streamer for hours gives viewers opportunities to become familiar with their personality, interests and interactions with others.That familiarity can develop into an attachment that outlasts its relationship with any individual platform. "The attachment isn't with the platform; it's with the creator."As AI-generated entertainment becomes more widespread, Clancy believes those relationships could become even more valuable."In a world full of swiping and short-form content and AI, people are more than ever looking for that authentic connection with [other] people," he says.

headline: UAE school pupils turn feathers into fertiliser as plans to combat waste take flight
summary: Three enterprising UAE teenagers are turning discarded chicken feathers into biofertiliser in a project they hope could eventually help farmers and reduce agricultural waste.Adit Mital, Anushka Harlalka and Maanit Misra have spent months developing BioFeathers, a process that uses bacteria to break down chicken feathers and convert them into nutrients that can be used by plants.What started as a school science project has now moved into trials at 16 farms and nurseries in the UAE, Oman and India.The Year 13 pupils at Dubai International Academy have also filed a joint provisional patent application and plan to approach Dubai authorities in an effort to expand their plans.Speaking to The National, the teenagers said the idea came from a shared interest in science and the possibility of turning something normally thrown away into something useful.“We saw an opportunity there, or a gap between what is currently being used to get rid of that waste versus what it could actually be used for," Adit said.Several million tons of poultry feathers are discarded around the world every year. They contain a substance that is resistant to natural degradation, which leads to large amounts of waste and environmental concern. The teenagers began by collecting about 2kg of feathers from a poultry farm in Sharjah and spent hours preparing them for lab testing.Their families were initially surprised by the idea, but they later helped the teenagers travel to laboratories and connect with people who could support their work.Turning waste into fertiliserThe pupils wanted to find a way of extracting useful material from feathers without burning or other energy-intensive methods.“The main idea is that chicken feathers basically have keratin in them, and keratin is a very useful protein, but it's also very hard to break down and extract,” Adit said.They began contacting academics and universities through cold emails before working with researchers at the University of Sharjah.“We did a lot of cold emailing to these professors,” Anushka said. “There were limitations to what some people could help us and offer us, so we reached out to more. We did a lot of research.”Through their experiments, the students developed nine nutrient-rich formulations that could be used as fertilisers or plant-growth boosters.Their first laboratory experiments began during the winter break in December 2025. By February, they had completed three rounds of trials before moving on to testing the formulations on plants.Early controlled tests using bok choy and radishes showed some growth measurements about 20 to 30 per cent higher than commercial comparison treatments.However, results are preliminary and further testing is required.Putting plans to the testThe team has since taken the product outside the laboratory and tested it at farms and nurseries in the UAE, Oman and India.The pupils said more than 1,200 farmers have been involved in trials, helping the pupils understand how the product could work in real agricultural settings.“Seeing what is the actual application, what are the requirements to be able to take this further, that is the main thing that we are picking up from farmers," Maanit said.School, exams and 60 plant potsDeveloping the project while attending school has also meant fitting laboratory work around lessons and exams.The pupils spent much of their winter break travelling to Sharjah, at times working in the laboratory almost every day.Regional tensions earlier this year disrupted their access to the university laboratory. Instead of stopping the project, they moved part of the testing home.“I had some 60 plant pots in my backyard, and we would come there every other week, and we would do experiments on them, collecting our data,” Adit said.The group also dealt with delays in obtaining chemicals and problems with laboratory equipment. Adit said the experience forced the group to adapt.“There were nights or evenings where we were there up until almost 7am,” he said. “It became really difficult.”Their teachers, university researchers and families became an important support network.Patent filed as project growsThe pupils filed a joint provisional patent application in April for elements of the process they developed.They said their method builds on existing approaches but includes changes to chemicals, concentrations and other parts of the process.“There were already existing protocols for developing a biofertiliser through the same process, but our method involved a few nuanced and unique takes,” Adit said.The teenagers estimate the raw formula costs less than Dh1 per 100ml to produce. Because the feathers are waste, the main raw material is inexpensive.However, the pupils said packaging, storage and transport would add to the cost if the product were produced on a larger scale.The students now plan to present the project to Dubai Municipality and explore opportunities through the Dubai Farms programme.

headline: Trump lifts US sanctions on Russian diesel amid price surge
summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday said Russia had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.The move comes as Mr Trump faces growing domestic political pressure to bring down rising diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, before November's midterm elections.Mr Trump said in a social media post that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”. The US President said that, “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia would deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”.“Between our total control of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian energy, diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be coming, in record numbers down, and fast!” Mr Trump wrote.The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control released a licence allowing the immediate “sale, delivery, offloading, or importation, including importation” of Russian origin-diesel fuel into the US until April 2027. The department said it did not authorise any debit to an account on the books of a US financial institution of Russia's central bank, its national wealth fund, or its finance ministry.The move drew quick condemnation from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”.“Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy,” Mr Zelenskyy said.Trump is doing a deal with the devil to try to help his flailing political fortunes from the shockingly high diesel prices caused by his own reckless, illegal war in the Middle East. This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target… https://t.co/lEILjnE38R— Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) October 9, 2026US Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer and other members of the Democratic Party expressed dismay at the announcement.“This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target and try to kill American troops in the Middle East and who illegally and viciously invaded our ally Ukraine,” he said on X.Russia was the second-largest diesel exporter in the world after the US before imposing curbs to protect its domestic market. Those supplies have been further hampered by Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, including what Kyiv claimed to be an attack on the country's largest oil refinery on Thursday.It is unclear how Russia will supply the diesel amounts announced by Mr Trump.Russia's fossil fuel export revenue fell 8 per cent on a monthly basis in August to €604 million ($676 million) per day, with export volumes falling 7 per cent, according to the Centre for Research on Clean Air, a think tank that has previously condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine.Mr Trump has recently acknowledged the diesel fuel crisis. In September, he publicly called on Mr Zelenskyy to halt its attacks on Russia's oil facilities “because he's causing a shortage of diesel fuel”.G7 member countries last week said they had agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and other products through the International Energy Agency to help stabilise markets following pressure from the Trump administration, which had threatened to impose a diesel export ban.IEA members on Wednesday said they had agreed to prioritise the release of diesel stocks and accelerate the release of roughly 100 million barrels of emergency oil reserves. The IEA's members in March agreed to release 425 barrels of reserves to markets as prices surged after the Iran war broke out on February 28, with roughly 325 million barrels having been released so far.Friday's surprise move also appears to defy a Russian sanctions law championed by the late senator Lindsey Graham, which Mr Trump signed into law on September 18. The law codifies the existing US sanctions regime targeting Russia and introduced new tariff authorities with a particular focus on energy exports.Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the House of Representatives Joint Economic Committee who opposed the legislation, called the deal “infuriating”.“Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake,” he wrote on X.The average cost of diesel in the US on Friday was $6.27 per gallon, compared to $3.67 this time last year.

headline: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake hits Panama
summary: A 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Panama on Friday, sparking warnings about tsunamis off the country's coast.The quake had a depth of 12.6km and its epicentre was in Herrera Province, roughly 200km to the south-west of the Panama Canal, according to the US Geological Survey.Some buildings were reported damaged but the critical Panama Canal was not affected, nor was the passage of ships through the trade waterway.Flights were suspended for several hours at Tocumen International Airport, a major regional hub, but had resumed by Friday evening.The USGS initially registered a magnitude of 8.0 for the earthquake before revising it. Panama’s geological institute reported the quake as a 7.2 magnitude.Local newspaper La Prensa said buildings, businesses, schools and homes in several regions were evacuated following the earthquake.Earthquakes of this magnitude are rare in Panama, and television images ⁠showed elderly residents reduced to tears in the streets as a series of weaker aftershocks ​rattled ⁠the country. “We’re scared. It’s just the ‌two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it ​could fall on us,” Ricardo Brown told Reuters by phone from the Las Minas area of Herrera Province. He said the quake had damaged several other homes.Tremors were felt as far as San Jose, the capital of neighbouring Costa Rica, according to a Reuters witness.Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told local outlet Telemetro Reporta that aftershocks had been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.Videos shared by La Prensa showed that the tower of a cathedral had collapsed, along with several balconies of a residential ​building in Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicentre and ‌Panama City.In the capital, the ⁠service on two lines of the Panama ​City Metro was temporarily suspended for safety reasons, the operator said. Nationwide, the ministry of education ‌ordered schools to close.Panama had been due to hold a national evacuation drill next Monday ​to test the country's emergency response to earthquakes.The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has warned of the potential for tsunami waves off the coast of Panama, as well as the western coasts of Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru.The United Arab Emirates expressed its solidarity with the Republic of Panama following the earthquake.In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) affirmed that the UAE stands alongside the Republic of Panama and its people as they address the aftermath of the earthquake.Friday’s quake was the latest to hit Latin America in recent months.Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes in late June that killed nearly 6,500 people, according to the government’s official toll. The quakes caused widespread destruction, particularly along the country’s northern coast. A powerful earthquake hit Colombia on August 10, levelling buildings and causing major damage in cities including Cali and Pereira. The death toll eventually rose above 330, while the government declared an economic emergency as it confronted a rebuilding bill estimated at roughly $10 billion.

headline: Palisades proposes method to retrieve tipped nuclear fuel assembly, but concerns remain
summary: A battle is brewing over how to retrieve a tipped fuel assembly at the soon-to-be-restarted Palisades nuclear reactor in Michigan. The reactor, which closed in 2022 but was purchased by Holtec International, has become a poster child for an AI and data centre-induced nuclear energy renaissance in the US. Efforts to restart the reactor in Covert, Michigan, hit a snag on August 30, when, according to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), one of the fuel assemblies tipped during fuelling, causing resumption to be placed on hold. The NRC said no radiation was released during the incident. But the incident has confirmed concerns about the unorthodox nature of restarting a shuttered nuclear reactor, which are known as “zombie reactors”. According to publicly available documents and correspondence between Palisades workers and the NRC, Holtec International has proposed a method for retrieving the tipped fuel.In the requests Holtec made to the NRC, the company says that the fuel rods have “retained their integrity as primary fission product barrier”. The energy firm also says that the fuel assembly is situated at a 30-degree angle “from the core plate”. Yet an inquiry from the NRC indicates "that fuel assembly exhibits significant bowing".In response to the NRC's question about the bowing, Holtec communicates that the company checked with its fuel vender about the situation. "Based on a review by our fuel vendor, the assembly is expected to straighten out without risk of fuel cladding failure inside the fuel transfer canister," Holtec's response reads in part. In its application, Holtec proposed using a specially designed recovery tool to lift the tilted assembly and a protective canister to support and enclose it during its transfer from the reactor vessel to the spent fuel pool.A news release on Friday from the environmental advocacy group Don't Waste Michigan, however, expressed distrust in Holtec. “This has never been done anywhere, and Holtec has never operated a nuclear power plant,” the non-profit said. The NRC has not yet indicated if it will grant approval to Holtec's proposal. “The peril of Palisades's fuel retrieval is that highly irradiated fuel will be suspended out of water in the plant atmosphere for up to 133 hours,” Don't Waste Michigan alleges. “This will be a highly radioactively contaminated undertaking.” Yet in Holtec's licence amendment request, provided to the NRC on September 30, the company insists that everything will be done according to regulatory limits. “There is no significant increase in the probability of an accident,” the document reads. Shortly after confirming the tipped fuel assembly incident several weeks ago, Holtec said that the reactor's fuel loading had been paused while the company addressed the situation, but that other restart efforts “not dependent on resolution of the fuel-loading matter” were still under way. Despite both the NRC and Holtec confirming that no radiation was released, critics of the Palisades restart often point to the reactor's history of controversy. Before it was bought by Holtec, a 2012 NRC report warned about the work culture at Palisades, where it said safety concerns were often dismissed.In 2016, security staff at the reactor were placed on leave from the plant, which was then owned by Entergy, for failing to properly follow fire-prevention protocol. A little more than a year ago, a worker at Palisades fell off a refuelling bridge into a pool of water, though they were not seriously injured.Arnie Gundersen, a nuclear engineer and expert adviser for Don't Waste Michigan, said that there are plenty of reasons to be concerned about Holtec's efforts to restart the reactor. “It is clear that they want approval to remove the tilted fuel bundle because they want to expedite the refuelling,” he claimed. “They provide no root cause analysis as to how the event happened in order to assure that it cannot happen again. nor have they evaluated any damage within the reactor that the fuel bundle may have caused.”Holtec, however, has previously said that the company is working to figure out why the fuel assembly tipped. “A root cause evaluation has been initiated to determine the cause of the event,” a statement read. It also promised to implement any corrective actions necessary.

headline: Pictures of the week: From French student protests to the reopening of Dubai Miracle Garden
Money & Me: 'I went from The X Factor to having to sell my car to pay staff but now earn Dh130,000 a month’
summary: JJ Thompson has a very varied CV. He came ninth on The X Factor in 2013 as part of a boy band, spent years as a radio presenter before launching a podcast production company during Covid, which ultimately failed.Then, in June 2024, he walked away from a job offer at one of the UAE's biggest radio networks to start from scratch in real estate with no salary. More than two years later, he's earning an average of Dh130,000 a month at Dubai-based property brokerage Strada. How did money feature in your childhood?I think I have some financial trauma. My dad was a business owner and we seemed to have a little bit and then very little. I've always had a bit of an issue with finances. I don't know if it's through ADHD or childhood, but I'm good at spending money.I'm learning to get a hold of money and get rid of it as quickly as possible – forcing myself to buy property, which is weird to say, because either I’ll spend the money or I'll invest in property to make sure it doesn't get spent. What was your first job? What did you earn?A waiter when I was 16 years old, £4.50 an hour. I moved to London from Coventry when I was 19 and had random bar jobs for those three years. I worked for my dad doing roofing but he fired me after a couple of months.When I moved to London, I worked in Harrods, spraying perfume on the ground floor. That's where I met my now-wife. Then I worked in a call centre selling Grazia and Heat magazines for about £6 an hour. Then I got into a boy band, and I did The X Factor. We came ninth in 2013 when I was 22.How did you end up in Dubai?After the band, I did radio in the UK, for Capital Radio, then I moved over to the UAE in 2016 to do it full time for Channel 4. I did the evening show, then the breakfast show. During Covid, there weren't many people advertising, so we didn't get paid. I went down from around Dh18,000 a month to about Dh2,500. I started a podcast company to try to bridge that gap. We got an investor but it failed dramatically – I had to sell my car to pay staff. I gave the business to the investor and said: “I'm going to go into real estate.” It was called a midlife crisis by a few people, which added fuel in the fire. It's gone well. I'm very happy I took the leap and took the risk.What do you earn now?It's month to month, but it's around Dh130,000 a month. My max in radio was Dh19,000. When [the money] came – and it happened so quickly – it was a bit of a Will Smith Pursuit of Happyness moment. I wasn't mentally ready because I was so used to having very little, but always wanting more, always knowing one day I'd get it somehow because I'm very financially ambitious. We had a baby, and I'd turned down a stable job for something where I didn't know if I would earn anything for six months. But I landed my first deal within six days and that got me about Dh150,000. I burst into tears looking at my child. I thought: “We're on to something here and all the risk paid off.” How do you grow your wealth?Mainly real estate. I've invested in two off-plan properties in Abu Dhabi with a client. We've got a property in the UK and we're looking to expand that to three as an Airbnb business in Scotland with my wife. I prefer off-plan investments.
