I look for higher-risk investments for higher reward rather than safe rental income from a ready property that will net me six per cent.What has been your best investment?They haven't come into fruition yet because they're off-plan, but I would like to think my investment in Hudayriyat Golf Estates in Hudayriyat Island, Abu Dhabi, will probably yield the best return by 2030.Any cherished purchases?I bought a nicer car and then I bought a Rolex, which was always a bit of a goal of mine.What luxuries are important to you?Travel and holidays – that's the most important thing for me, and the most expensive. I've been away once a month this year. My favourite thing is to go away with the family.What financial advice would you give your younger self?I was right in always thinking it's going to be all right. Keep working, keep being ambitious, keep allowing people to laugh at your goals because they're bigger than theirs. Keep going, it will all be all right.

headline: ‘Jareema’: The Arabic word for crime is deployed in courts and cultural debates
summary: Jareema appears in official police reports and courtrooms, as well as in fierce criticism of songs, films and performances.Our Arabic word of the week means crime and describes an act punishable by law, ranging from theft and fraud to murder. The plural is jaraim, meaning “crimes”.Jareema comes from the root letters jim, ra and mim, which also carry meanings associated with wrongdoing and guilt. The verbs ajrama and ajramat mean he or she committed a crime, respectively, while mujrim refers to a criminal. Ijram means criminality and ilm al-ijram is criminology, while masrah al-jareema refers to the crime scene.Modern uses include jaraim elektroniyya, meaning cybercrimes; jareema munazzama, organised crime; and jaraim harb, war crimes. Legal Arabic distinguishes clearly between mujrim, a criminal whose guilt is implied, and muttaham, someone accused of an offence.The accusation can also be figurative. Jareema fi haqq al-fann means a crime against art and may be used to dismiss a song, film or performance as particularly bad.In literature, adab al-jareema refers to crime fiction, while jareema kamila means the perfect crime.The 2022 Egyptian thriller Al Jareema, or El Gareema in Egyptian Arabic, stars Ahmed Ezz, Menna Shalaby and Maged El Kedwany.Set in 1970s Egypt, the film follows an investigation that begins after a man escapes from a psychiatric hospital and new evidence emerges in connection with a series of killings.Another familiar expression is al-jareema la tufid, meaning crime does not pay. It was used as the title of a story in the Egyptian anthology series Helwa El Donia Sokar, involving an online journalist investigating an artist accused of theft.Serious in court and dramatic in conversation, jareema can describe both a criminal act and an offence judged in the court of public opinion.

headline: Self-acceptance was a lifelong struggle, but an autism diagnosis helped make it easier
summary: I wondered for years whether I had ever actually liked myself.It fluctuated, but the fact that it was a question at all told me the answer was negative more often than not.I don’t think I would go so far as to say I hated myself. But at times I wasn't a fan; I allowed myself to be judged by the opinions of others rather than my own. We’re all trying to be the best version of ourselves, for the most part, and not everyone is going to like that.My problem was that for a long time I was changing that version depending on who was looking.I did not understand at the time that I was masking. I learnt to adjust myself to rooms, people and expectations. If enthusiasm for something was poorly received, I would dial it down. If I was too quiet, I would force myself to speak. If an interaction felt awkward, I would replay it afterwards and consider what I should have done differently.It was rarely conscious. I was simply trying to fit in.But constantly considering how you are being perceived has consequences. If your instinct is always to alter yourself in search of acceptance, eventually you start wondering whether the unaltered version is acceptable at all.That contributed heavily to my unease with myself.Autism has become a buzzword in recent years. The word is sometimes thrown around negatively, casually applied to behaviour someone considers strange or used as a catch-all for neurodivergence.That can obscure the fact that autism is a spectrum and presents very differently from one person to another.I am at the high-functioning end of the spectrum. I work, socialise, have relationships, and, from the outside, can probably move through much of everyday life without anyone suspecting I am autistic.That does not mean those things are always easy.Something as ordinary as meeting somebody new can produce disproportionate anxiety. Speaking confidently can require considerable effort, even if the person listening would never know it. A social interaction can bring an internal checklist of when to speak, what to say, whether one is talking too much or too little and how one is coming across.They sound like small difficulties. Repeated every day, they become exhausting.Before my diagnosis, I did not have a framework for understanding why some seemingly simple things required so much effort. The natural response was to assume I was deficient in some way.Why couldn't I just be more confident? Why did certain situations feel harder than they should?A diagnosis did not answer every question, but it gave me context.It also allowed me to look back at myself with considerably more kindness.I could recognise that some of the things I had spent years trying to correct were simply parts of me I had never understood. Being quiet did not always need fixing. Neither did becoming intensely interested in something, needing time alone or finding particular social situations difficult.Perhaps most importantly, I began to understand how much energy I had spent trying to appear comfortable when I wasn't.I still mask. Everybody behaves differently depending on whether they are with family, friends, colleagues or strangers.The difference now is that I feel less compelled to hide myself simply because somebody else might find the real version unusual.More people get to see that person.I am more comfortable being quiet when I have nothing to say. I can be enthusiastic without immediately wondering whether I should tone it down. I can admit that something makes me anxious instead of exhausting myself trying to appear unaffected by it.And the more comfortable I have become allowing other people to see me, the more comfortable I have become with myself.That has been one of the unexpected gifts of diagnosis.It did not change who I was. It changed the way I interpreted who I had always been.Self-acceptance has not arrived all at once. There are still moments when I catch myself viewing my behaviour through somebody else's eyes.But I do it less.And on World Mental Health Day, perhaps it is the one thing I would urge others to consider.If you are old enough to have spent years feeling that there is something different about you or wondering why seemingly ordinary parts of life present challenges others do not, try to find out why.Take reputable screening tests. Read about the experiences of others. And where possible, speak to a qualified professional and seek a proper assessment.Symptoms could be consistent with autism, anxiety or another form of neurodiversity, or they may have a different cause.But there is value in knowing.For years, I could see the difficulties without understanding where they came from. Once I had a clearer picture, the path ahead became easier to see. The challenges did not disappear, but I became better equipped to manage them and less inclined to blame myself for having them.I spent much of my life thinking acceptance had to come from other people first. If they liked the version of me I presented, perhaps I could like myself too.I had the order wrong.Understanding myself made it easier to accept myself. Accepting myself made it easier to show other people who I actually am.And that has made me considerably happier.

headline: Pepe Cucina review: Bring an appetite – and someone willing to share
summary: It’s Friday night and Pepe Cucina has a lively buzz going on. Families on holiday, date-night couples, friends meeting up at the end of a long working week, the vibe is exactly how an Italian restaurant should feel: friendly, welcoming and like you’ve been there before.But just because a restaurant is not stuffy, that doesn’t mean it’s not sophisticated. Pepe Cucina, in JBR, Dubai, is one of those chameleonic places that’s somehow exactly what you want it to be each time you visit.First impressionsThe space is large, meaning no cramped tables and plenty of scope for birthday gatherings and their popular Saturday brunch. Booths, one of which we settled into, line the left side, while banquette tables cut through the middle of the room to create pockets in which to socialise. Through the floor-to-ceiling windows, the vast, revamped terrace awaits diners during the cooler months, with views across Bluewaters Island and Ain Dubai.The menuThe menu is a solid one-pager. No leafing through leather-bound volumes here. We begin with truffle arancini with truffle mayo and chives (Dh35) from the passa il piatto section, which translates as “pass the plate” and is designed for sharing. The arancini balls are excellent: deep-fried and dense, crunchy on the outside and soft and slightly chewy inside, with a delicate truffle sauce for dipping.My dining companion and I decide to share every dish. Luckily, we’re largely on the same page taste-wise. She knows that I get weird about seafood served with its head still on, and I know that she loves Gorgonzola.For our salad, she is very happy with the yellow and red endive with Gorgonzola, pecan nuts and figs (Dh59). The flavours work so easily together that it’s a dish that begs to be eaten with a little of every ingredient on each forkful.One of the things I love about Italian food is that it’s not linear. Dishes arrive at the table with the intention of being left there. There are no “Are you done with that?” questions and plates whisked away before you can decide whether to nab that last arancini. Instead, everything stays to be grazed, mixed and matched and returned to throughout the meal.For our pizza, we go with a margherita (Dh60), a classic among a curated selection of favourites. The base is delightfully thin, the crust slightly burnished and the bubbled cheese turning a caramel colour. Four slices go into our mouths, two into the box to take home.From the pasta and rice selection, we opt for the traditional fusilloni alla Genovese in a pecorino sauce (Dh94). Having never met a ragu I didn’t love, this hearty, rib-sticking pasta smothered in a rich and generous sauce doesn't disappoint. It’s a dish I have sworn to return for later this year as a winter warmer, with big spoonfuls piled on to our plates alongside the salad, pizza and remaining arancini.To offset the delicious carb-heavy density of everything so far, we choose the rock salt-baked sea bass fillet with roasted potatoes (Dh146) from la griglia (the grill). Its delicate flavour and modest portion make it an ideal counterpoint to what has come before. Salt-baking leaves the fillet tender but still meaty, stopping just short of flaking apart on the fork.Gelato, chocolate, cannoli – the dessert list reads like a greatest hits of traditional Italian sweets. Our debate comes down to the fried doughnut with custard cream (Dh59) or the chocolate mousse with hazelnut and balsamic cherry (Dh57). We err on the side of the traditional mousse, which yields thick spoonfuls of gooey, chocolatey deliciousness that stick to the roof of the mouth, leaving a lingering taste of Italy.Standout dishThe sea bass fillet was a standout insomuch as it worked as well on its own as it did within the ensemble of dishes we accumulated. I imagine it paired perfectly with lighter sides such as sauteed greens, lemon and garlic or a tomato and red onion salad, just as it did with the ragu-smothered fusilloni and Gorgonzola-sprinkled endive leaves on our plates.Save or splurgeYou could leave well fed and satisfied from Pepe Cucina having spent around Dh150, assuming a focaccia starter (Dh20), a rigatoni with spicy Gorgonzola sauce and beef ‘nduja (Dh88) and a tomato carpaccio salad (Dh46). There are dishes to suit all budgets, appetites, tastes and preferences for certain regions of Italy. Those looking to splurge should start with the fritto misto (Dh171), al tartufo pizza with truffle sauce, mozzarella and fresh black truffle (Dh143), lobster linguine (Dh355) and grilled lamb chops (Dh215).Contact detailsPepe Cucina is at Address Beach Resort in JBR, Dubai. It's open Monday to Thursday from 4pm to 12am, and from Friday to Sunday from 1pm to 12am. Reservations can be made by calling 04 879 8866.This review was conducted at the invitation of the restaurant

headline: They travelled to the Gulf to build lives back home - a journey to the Indian villages of seven crash victims
summary: A generation ago, the first men from villages in Telangana and Uttar Pradesh left for the Gulf. Most departed because of a letter from someone who had gone before, or a rumour from the tea shop, or just knowing that someone from the next village had gone and had come back with something to show for it. They didn’t really know what to expect. They went anyway.Many of those men later returned. But not all of them, and not always in the ways they hoped. But most came back with real results – enough that everyone around them understood what the journey was worth. A finished house. A child who received more schooling than the village offered. A family who progressed, however slowly, from just getting by to building something.Because of them, the next group went with more confidence. And the group after that did, too. Seven Indian workers died in an Emirates Road crash in Dubai in June 2026, leaving behind families across Telangana and Uttar Pradesh. Burjeel Holdings chairman Dr Shamsheer Vayalil announced a financial support programme for all seven affected families following the accident.The Gulf has been woven into village life across India for four decades, with knowledge of working abroad passed down through generations.The workers were not seeking permanent lives overseas but using earnings abroad to fund homes, education and weddings back in India.“The Gulf was never the destination – it was the path back to where they were always meant to be,” the delegation's head of communications said.I kept thinking about those early journeys during four days in June, when I travelled through villages in Telangana in southern India and Uttar Pradesh in the north to meet the families of workers who died in the Emirates Road accident in Dubai in June 2026. We went to offer support on behalf of Dr Shamsheer Vayalil, chairman and chief executive of Abu Dhabi healthcare company Burjeel Holdings, who had already announced a support programme for all seven families, and to make sure they knew they were not forgotten.I gained something else, too – a close, unhurried look at what the relationship between the Gulf and those villages actually is after four decades. It is not what people assume.In those villages, the Gulf is not an abstraction, nor does it represent a distant aspiration. It is a part of everyday life. Someone is in the region now. Someone returned to their village last year. A young man from the neighbourhood is saving up money to go. Knowledge of how to get there, what working life is like and what the first summer feels like passes from person to person, tested by real experience and refined over years.In the Jagtial district of Telangana, where we met the families of two of those killed in the crash, Saleem Sayyed and Thirupathi Gollapally, almost every conversation turned to the Gulf. Not because we brought it up, but because it was already part of how people thought about their future.That’s what four decades of this relationship have created.Sayyed, from the Telangana village of Namilakonda, had gone to the UAE just months before the accident. One of his children had health problems that needed more money for treatment than he could earn locally. His daughter’s wedding was also being planned. He wanted a better house, better schooling and the means to pay for all of it.Those demands had piled up all at once, as they often do for families with little margin for error. Working in the Gulf was the only option that could enable him to address them all quickly enough.Gollapally was only 22 and was abroad for the first time. He used to call his parents to talk about getting used to the outdoor work, the heat and everything new. His family in Thakkallapalle, in Telangana, remembers those calls well. Now, that’s all they have left.Another of the crash victims, Abdul Rafiq, had returned to the Gulf, having left the region during the pandemic. His daughter is very young, too little to understand what happened. His father, who had already lost two sons in an earlier road accident, sat with us quietly for a while. We didn’t need words.In the Mau district of Uttar Pradesh, the family of another of those killed, Markandey Chauhan, led us along narrow, unpaved lanes to a house that was still unfinished. We saw this in every village – houses built in stages, a new room added whenever someone working abroad sent money, before construction was suspended when the funds ran out and families waited for the next transfer to arrive.Chauhan's daughter, Ankita, had just finished Grade 12 when her father died. She didn’t complete her application for the state entrance exam this year. During our visit, Dr Vayalil, who joined on a video call, asked Ankita what she wanted to study. She said nursing. He told her without hesitation that her education would be fully paid for, and that a job would be waiting for her at his hospital in the UAE once she graduated. Dr Vayalil had moved to the Gulf with big ambitions and built something there. It wasn’t a coincidence that he was the one making this offer to a girl in a village in Mau. It was the promise made a generation ago, still being kept. The atmosphere in the room changed when he spoke because something her father had worked for was going to continue.What struck me most, in every home we visited, was something the families kept saying in different ways. What moved them wasn’t just the financial support. It was that someone from the country where their loved one had worked had come all the way to sit with them, that the place where they had gone had not treated him as replaceable, that it had sent people to his village.That is the part of the India-Gulf relationship that the statistics and the official programmes do not capture. There is an understanding with no official treaty behind it. It is built on something learnt over a generation: that the Gulf offers work and families who send their sons and brothers aren’t simply making a business deal. They are trusting that, in the event that something goes wrong, the place their loved one went to will remember that he was a person with a village, a half-built house, children in school and parents waiting for his call.That trust was honoured after the accident in June. Families in those villages know exactly what that means. They have been watching how the relationship works for four decades.In Kopaganj, Uttar Pradesh, we met the loved ones of Abdul Rasheed, who was also killed in June. A family member told us quietly that before his final trip he thought it would be his last. He planned to save enough money to return home for good.We heard some version of that ambition in almost every home. These weren’t men trying to leave their villages behind. They were using years abroad to build the life they had always wanted at home. The Gulf was never the destination – it was the path back to where they were always meant to be.That’s the thought the trip left us with. Those men weren’t chasing a life overseas. They were building one in India, with whatever work in the UAE could give them, for as long as it took.M Unnikrishnan is head of communications at VPS Health. He was part of the delegation to India that visited the families of those killed in the accident in June 2026

headline: The Diplomat season four: The story so far before Netflix return
summary: Politics, nuclear weapons, diplomatic crises and a high-profile marriage that always seems to be one argument away from divorce, Netflix hit The Diplomat has packed a lot into three seasons.First aired in 2023, the drama follows Kate Wyler (Keri Russell), a career diplomat who is unexpectedly appointed US ambassador to the UK just as an attack on a British warship threatens to spark an international crisis.What has followed – from assassination plots and secret military operations to a dead US president and plenty of political manoeuvring – has turned the show into a must-watch political thriller. Balancing high-stakes international crises with sharp dialogue, humour and the often chaotic relationship between Kate and her husband Hal (Rufus Sewell), the show also boasts a strong cast of complex women in positions of power, including Allison Janney as US President Grace Penn, Nana Mensah as White House chief of staff Billie Appiah and Ali Ahn as Eidra Park, the CIA station chief in London.The show has also been a critical success, with Russell earning three Emmy nominations for her performance as Kate, while Janney won for her role as Grace last month.Season four picks up after a finale that left Kate facing a very different political landscape – with Grace in the White House and her own husband now vice president. Before the series returns on October 15, here is a refresher on what happened in the first three seasons.What is The Diplomat about?When the series begins, Kate is preparing to become US ambassador to Afghanistan – the kind of difficult assignment she relishes – when an attack on the British aircraft carrier HMS Courageous kills 43 sailors and threatens to trigger an international crisis.Instead, President William Rayburn (Michael McKean) sends her to London as US ambassador to the UK. Unknown to Kate, however, the White House has another plan for her. Vice President Grace Penn is expected to leave office because of a scandal involving her husband, and Kate is quietly being assessed as a potential replacement.There is another complication: Hal. A brilliant but notoriously meddlesome diplomat in his own right, Kate's husband struggles to remain in the background while her career takes centre stage. Their marriage, already on the brink of divorce, is further tested when they arrive in London as separating their personal and professional lives becomes nearly impossible.The story so far (spoilers ahead):What happened in The Diplomat season one?Much of the first season revolves around discovering who attacked HMS Courageous. British Prime Minister Nicol Trowbridge (Rory Kinnear) initially suspects Iran, but Kate helps prevent an immediate military response as evidence instead points to unseen Russian mercenary Roman Lenkov.At the same time, Kate grows close to British Foreign Secretary Austin Dennison (David Gyasi), while deputy chief of mission Stuart Hayford (Ato Essandoh) prepares her for the possibility of becoming US vice president – a job she initially has little interest in.The investigation takes Kate and Austin to Paris, where she learns Britain plans to assassinate Lenkov rather than capture him. Realising his death would prevent him from revealing who hired him, Kate begins to suspect Trowbridge himself was behind the attack.Back in London, Hal is due to meet Conservative MP Merritt Grove (Simon Chandler) when a bomb planted in Grove's car explodes. Stuart and his aide Ronnie are caught in the blast, with the season ending before their fates are revealed.What happened in The Diplomat season two?Season two picks up immediately after the explosion. Hal and Stuart survive, although both are injured. Ronnie does not.Kate's investigation eventually leads to Margaret "Meg" Roylin (Celia Imrie), Trowbridge's former political adviser, who was involved in hiring Lenkov's group to attack HMS Courageous. But Trowbridge himself did not order it.Instead, Kate discovers the plan originated with US Vice President Grace Penn, who believed the attack was necessary to protect US national security interests.The revelation leaves Kate believing Grace will have to leave office and, after previously resisting the idea, she finally accepts that she wants to become vice president. Hal decides Washington needs to know and, rather than going through the usual channels, calls President Rayburn directly to tell him what Grace has done.But shortly after learning the truth, Rayburn dies – making Grace Penn president of the US.What happened in The Diplomat season three?Season three begins with Grace sworn in as president, leaving Kate and Hal in the unusual position of knowing she was behind the HMS Courageous plot.But rather than distancing herself from the Wylers, Grace brings them closer – and in a major reversal, it is Hal, not Kate, who becomes vice president.Kate remains in London as their marriage continues to fall apart and begins a relationship with intelligence operative Callum Ellis (Aidan Turner).A new crisis emerges when a Russian submarine carrying a Poseidon torpedo – described as a "doomsday weapon" – is discovered off the English coast. When the weapon later disappears, Kate realises Grace and Hal may have secretly taken it. When Kate confronts Hal, he tells her to tell no one – then immediately informs Grace that Kate knows.Season three ends with Kate and Grace's husband Todd (Bradley Whitford) watching their spouses together, as Kate faces the possibility that the president and her own husband have secretly taken possession of a Russian nuclear weapon – an act that could push the US towards war.What to expect in The Diplomat season four?Netflix says season four begins with a catastrophic event that threatens the fragile peace between the US and UK, while Grace and Hal's attempt to steal Russia's most powerful weapon risks pushing the US towards war.It also creates an unlikely alliance between Kate and Grace's husband Todd, as they join forces to try to stop their spouses.Janney and Whitford have been promoted to series regulars for the new season, alongside Mensah as Billie Appiah.The Diplomat season four premieres on Netflix on October 15

headline: Fight, flight and the courage in between
summary: Somewhere over north-western Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, September 30, flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv suddenly plunged 5,000 metres before eventually landing safely at Tabuk. Although the exact circumstances of the incident are being investigated, a series of actions that averted a major disaster has awed the world.Capt Smit Machchhar was reportedly attacked by his co-pilot. The captain, losing blood fast, fought not only for the controls but also to open the cockpit door. That allowed a handful of passengers to enter and overwhelm the attacker.One of them said he used his knowledge from air-crash documentaries to pull up the plummeting plane, while two reserve pilots rushed to land the stricken plane safely at Tabuk. A dentist-turned-emergency-medic knelt in the aisle to keep the captain alive until the ambulances came.In the two minutes that separated life from death, the 172 people who had done nothing more heroic than buy a ticket or turn up for flight duty were sorted by circumstances into those who acted and the rest. What set them apart?It is not fearlessness. A study of bomb-disposal officers in Northern Ireland found that most experienced acute anxiety like anyone else but performed anyway. Nelson Mandela said it simply: the brave person is not the one who feels no fear, but who conquers it.Such courage is admirable, of course, but it is not an unqualified virtue. Aristotle placed courage somewhere between cowardice and recklessness. Summoning the right amount of courage requires the right fear, in the right measure, being overcome for the right end.Thus, the flydubai responders thought themselves doomed and their courage came from instinctively trying to save themselves. The subtle distinction is with the passengers of United Airlines Flight 93 in 2001, who were certainly doomed but still organised themselves to save people on the ground by forcing the 9/11 hijackers to crash the plane away from built-up Washington.The seeds of courage, if nurtured correctly, lie ready but dormant until an environmental shift obliges them to sproutThese varieties of courage – self-saving or altruistic – take their shape from circumstances. This derives from the biological evolution that drives our perception of threat and how “cornered” we feel after running out of options.Courage also comes in more than one currency. Beyond the physical type, which is costly in the present but gains medals afterwards, there is the moral kind that costs little in the moment but everything afterwards. This is the whistle-blower or dissenter who speaks truth to power, the journalist who exposes wrongdoing, or the official who reveals openly what his institution hides shamefully. Such courage is usually career-ending and rewarded by ostracism or worse. However, societies have often been changed for the better as a consequence.There is no hierarchy of courage as each person is brave in their own way. But courage is most useful when accompanied by competence – possession of the latter may even obligate the former. Thus, the dentist did not suddenly become brave at altitude but felt a responsibility to help because he had the skill to do so. Perhaps courage is inversely proportional to perceived helplessness.What about Saman Kunan, the Thai navy diver who placed his skills at the service of 12 boys he had never met and died ferrying oxygen through a flooded cave in 2018? Or the 10 Beirut firefighters who deliberately drove into danger to contain a port warehouse blaze in 2020 – and perished themselves? They did not just do their jobs but went well beyond. That is the truest form of courage and often extracts a terrible price.But is courage still worthwhile if a person is not usefully skilled? Abdul Aziz grabbed the first thing he could find – a credit card machine – to chase a gunman out of a Christchurch mosque in 2019. His wit to improvise enabled his courage. Then there is the sheer courage of “presence”, a stubborn refusal to leave. This was seen among the doctors who stayed with their patients in an El Fasher Hospital in Darfur, Sudan last year, as murderous militiamen came in. The millions of ordinary Gazans and Ukrainians who stay or the Sudanese returning home despite continuing onslaughts are further examples. We marvel at their resilience, but this is really a kind of grim courage that helps express resistance.It is difficult to construct a comprehensive theory of courage, but some dimensions are identifiable. Most recipients of the Carnegie Medal in the US describe their acts as “intuitive”. Courage on Flight 1073 happened in seconds or it did not happen at all. Therefore, is “deliberation” the enemy of courage?Not necessarily. Take Stanislav Petrov, a Soviet duty officer in 1983 who saw his screens announce an American missile launch, judged it a false alarm and did nothing. His courage of restraint prevented nuclear Armageddon to earn this Encyclopaedia Brittanica tribute on his death: “He is survived by two children, two grandchildren and the entire human race.”Meanwhile, “numbers” can submerge courage. Research on bystanders reveals that more witnesses to an emergency mean less likelihood of anyone acting. This is because when responsibility is diffused, an individual’s share is not large enough to move them. So, the planeload of people on Flight 1073 could have meant collective paralysis but what broke that spell was another aspect of courageous conduct – its infectiousness. When the bloodied captain managed to open the door, his visible courage triggered the first rescuer to act which then sanctioned the next to join, and so on.Militaries know this and that is why they drill soldiers. This trains troops to move their reaction under fire from the part of the mind that debates risk to the part that acts. Repeat risk exposure – as done by firefighters, for example – shrinks fear while improving competence brings the confidence to shrink it further. Meanwhile, the company of colleagues expecting each other to perform so as not to let themselves down shrinks it most of all. In that sense, courage is catching.But is courage acquired or is it inherited? Limited research suggests that genes may play a role but upbringing more so. People low in anxiety and high in empathy are likelier to intervene. And perhaps Aristotle was right in saying that we become braver by doing brave things.That is why awards like the Carnegie Medal exist – to remind ordinary people that extraordinary things may sometimes be expected of them. That builds up a wider culture of courage in society. The traditional Arab code of muruwwa that honours the courageous rescue of distressed strangers does the same. In short, while some people may be born with a higher threshold for acting courageously, everyone’s threshold can be lowered through example and practice.Thus, the seeds of courage, if nurtured correctly, lie ready but dormant until an environmental shift obliges them to sprout. That is how courage sprouted when the climate shifted on Flight 1073. Overwhelmed readers may wonder what they would have done if they had been on that plane. They should take heart. The seeds of courage are not rationed. They are standard issue, planted in all of us by the evolution of our common humanity.

headline: From Italy’s modern defence structure to the ancient Pantheon: A reminder of what survives
summary: I was in Rome for five days last week, spending much of my time looking at Italy through the lens of defence: military operations, naval capabilities, air power, counter-improvised explosive device expertise and the work behind some of the country’s most important security decisions.Then, at the end of the trip, I found myself standing beneath the dome of the Pantheon, looking up at the oculus and wondering how a building almost 2,000 years old had survived for so long.It was an interesting way to end a programme organised by Italy’s Ministry of Defence for foreign media. It had taken me from the country’s joint operations command to its Army Counter-IED Centre of Excellence and Pratica di Mare Air Base. I had also interviewed Defence Minister Guido Crosetto about Italy’s role in a changing security landscape.It had been a glimpse of modern Italy, concerned with military readiness, technology, alliances and the threats of today. The Pantheon offered another perspective.I first visited Rome in 2022, so it was not my first time wandering its streets, stopping to admire its fountains, piazzas and layers of history. The city has a way of making the past feel like part of daily life rather than something preserved behind glass.As my time in Rome drew to a close, visiting the Pantheon made me appreciate it in a different way.The building is extraordinary even before you know its story. The vast concrete dome, the geometric coffers rising towards the 8.9m-wide oculus and the shaft of daylight falling into the circular interior make it easy to understand why the Pantheon continues to astonish visitors. Its dome, with an internal diameter of about 43 metres, remains the largest unreinforced concrete hemispherical dome in the world.I was there with a tour guide and a lieutenant-colonel from the Carabinieri, Italy’s gendarmerie, which carries out policing duties at home and abroad.“Look at the oculus above you,” said the guide. “You might think it’s covered with glass, but it isn’t. It’s completely open to the sky. And I know what you’re going to ask me: What do we do in winter?”She smiled. “Nothing. It rains, of course, but the water falls through the opening. There are drainage holes in the floor to let it run away.”She pointed to several small openings beneath our feet.It was a simple explanation, but it made the building feel all the more remarkable. The Romans had designed it to accommodate the elements, and almost two millennia later, rain still falls through the same opening.However, what fascinated me most was not just how the Romans built the Pantheon. It was how it survived.A second lifeThe present structure dates to the reign of Emperor Hadrian, between AD 118 and 125, although an earlier temple commissioned by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa had stood on the site. Centuries later, after the decline of the Roman Empire, the Pantheon fell into neglect and was looted.“It was damaged and destroyed several times by devastating fires,” said the guide.Then came the decision that would help determine its fate.In AD 609, the Byzantine emperor Phocas gave the Pantheon to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it as a Christian church dedicated to Santa Maria ad Martyres. Its continued religious use helped protect it from the neglect and removal of building materials that affected many other ancient Roman structures during the Middle Ages, the guide explained. There is something striking about that. The Pantheon was not preserved simply because it was too magnificent to destroy. Its conversion gave it a new purpose and helped protect it for centuries to come.Its function changed, but the building endured. That stayed with me as I walked back through Rome.During the previous days there, much of what I had seen was about preparing for the future: military personnel training for emerging threats, aircraft ready for operations and commanders assessing new defence priorities.Mr Crosetto told me that Italy’s defence spending must continue to rise to meet Nato commitments, but that how the money is spent matters just as much. He highlighted the need for greater investment in counter-drone measures, artificial intelligence and integrated air defence.The contrast with the Pantheon was hard to miss. Rome makes these differences easy to appreciate. Ancient columns stand beside busy cafes; ruins form part of ordinary streets; monuments that have witnessed emperors, wars and religious change remain woven into the life of the city.When I stepped back into Piazza della Rotonda, the Pantheon stood amid restaurants, tourists and passing crowds, part of the everyday scene.I had come to Rome to learn about Italy’s armed forces and how the country is responding to modern security challenges. Yet it was the visit at the end of the programme that left me thinking about how history survives.The Pantheon’s story is a reminder that preserving the past does not always mean leaving it untouched. Sometimes, giving an old building a new purpose is what allows it to last.

headline: Free of the land: Has leaving the US become the new American dream?
summary: Some blame the cost of health care. Others are worried about gun violence in schools. Many are fed up with the politics, or just want to experience something new. Whatever the reason, increasing numbers of Americans are voting with their feet and choosing to build new lives overseas.According to Census Bureau data, emigration from the US increased significantly last year, a trend that appears set to grow in 2026. While the numbers are small compared to the US's population of about 340 million, the departure of people from America US has contributed to a significant drop in net migration.For Mike Hogan and his wife Mary, the decision to leave the US was helped by a few simple calculations. The former congressional staff member and government relations consultant, 61, has just retired from the Washington area to southern Spain.They had visited France and Portugal, but after several trips to Spain they fell in love with Estepona, a picturesque Costa del Sol town of whitewashed Andalusian houses and flower-filled streets and plazas.Aside from the vibe and the prospect of a calmer pace of life, something else caught Mr Hogan's attention: health care.The Hogans had been paying about $2,500 a month for a US health insurance plan with a $6,000 excess. In Spain, they found private cover costing about $100 a month, with no deductible or co-payment.“I don't know why we can't figure it out here,” Mr Hogan said, shortly before leaving for Spain. He said his decision was “not overtly political”. He and his wife had started thinking of making the move about five years ago, around the time of the Covid-19 pandemic.The number of Americans leaving the US is difficult to measure, but data collected by The Wall Street Journal from 15 countries found that at least 180,000 Americans moved to those nations in 2025. The total figure is probably far higher than that.President Donald Trump's return to the White House did not factor too much into Mr Hogan's plans, although he said it made some aspects of leaving easier to explain. “We're not moving because of politics, but it is embarrassing to try to defend some of the craziness,” he said. There are plenty of anecdotal signs of the trend elsewhere in Europe, where Americans can secure residency through retirement or investment visas, ancestry claims or job offers. Jamal, a taxi driver in Sete in the South of France, told The National that he frequently picks up suitcase-laden Americans at Montpellier Airport who are moving to Europe permanently.A Gallup poll last year found that 21 per cent of Americans said they would like to leave the US and permanently move to another country if they could. That rose to 40 per cent among women aged 15 to 44 – four times the proportion who said the same in a similar poll in 2014.Cynthia Aceituno, 30, a freelance digital marketer from New York, moved to Barcelona last year. She had been considering El Salvador, where her family is from, but after visiting Spain she decided she wanted to stay.Ms Aceituno says the political climate in the US, the cost of living and the pace of life in New York all contributed to the decision. She also feels safer in Spain.“I can walk at night alone and I don't feel like I'm in danger,” she said. She added that she appreciates the way people choose to spend their time in Spain. “They work to live,” Ms Aceituno said – in New York, she feels, they “live to work”.She still works for New York clients remotely, and her hours have shifted because of the six-hour time difference. But the arrangement has allowed her to build a life that she says feels less stressful.Even visiting the doctor was a revelation. When Ms Aceituno went for the first time, she asked how much she owed. “They were like, ‘Oh no, you live here, it's fine, have a nice day,’” she said. “I walked out in shock.”A common perception is that working life can feel a lot less hectic in parts of Europe than in the US. Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development figures back this up, showing that US employees worked an average of 1,800 hours in 2025, compared with 1,633 in Spain.But people who live in Europe often complain about a frustrating job market or being burdened by bureaucracy and taxes.For Ms Aceituno, the trade-off has been worth it. She said she does not contemplate moving back to New York, although she still considers it home and wants to visit her family. “I don't have to stay here if I don't want to,” she said.Meredith Thomas, owner and lead travel writer for the Two Packs And A Pup blog, left the US two years ago with her partner and their dog to travel full-time. She said the US's high cost of living was a major factor in their decision. “Nearly every country we've lived in has been dramatically cheaper than the States,” she said, noting that her family's costs would easily exceed $10,000 a month at home. “Now, even with frequent travel and tourism spending, we average around half that. It's hard to imagine moving back to $50 brunch bills when we can sip a cocktail on the beaches of Vietnam for only $6.”The US-based research firm Dataframe LLC surveyed 1,869 Americans this year to discover why people are leaving the US. For 61 per cent of respondents, the top motivator was looking for a better quality of life, while 58 per cent cited the cost of living in the US as the primary push factor. The survey also found that 38 per cent of American respondents think the country is declining and 50 per cent had been touched by job loss in the last two years, meaning either themselves or someone close to them had lost a job. For Christopher Mannino, concerns over the safety of his children made the decision to leave the US easy. He and his wife had already lived abroad and had been interested in the idea of travelling with their children when the pandemic made them rethink what they wanted from family life.They eventually settled in Malta, where they could work remotely and send their children to school. The decision was not initially political, but the turning point came when their school district introduced active-shooter drills, an almost uniquely American phenomenon in which children as young as four are taught to hide and stay quiet if a gunman bursts into their school.Mr Mannino, a former teacher, remembers seeing the drills when he returned to substitute teaching. He questioned whether that was an environment in which he wanted his children to grow up. His son, who is nine, told him he liked practising the drills because “he knew how to sacrifice himself to save his friends”.“To hear this nine-year-old talking like that … it's just heartbreaking,” Mr Mannino said. “That's not how kids should be growing up. They shouldn't have to worry about any of that.”He said his kids are now thriving at local schools in Malta, and are involved in sports and theatre, learning about another culture and picking up some Maltese.“The kids are doing so much better,” he said. “I feel like they are safer and they are experiencing the world.”

headline: Why banning children from social media may not be enough to keep them safe online
summary: Barring young people from social media platforms may not be enough to keep them safe unless it forms part of a wider online protection plan, experts have told The National.A co-ordinated strategy that takes into account the need for education on best online practices for young people and their parents would be much more effective in addressing issues around digital safety, the experts said.Several countries have imposed bans on people under a certain age using social media. The UAE is among those seeking to enhance online protection, with plans to prevent under-15s from using social media from June 2027."The challenge is different countries have different approaches to this. There needs to be joined-up thinking," said Wayne Denner, co-founder of Beat the Cyber Bully, an initiative that helps educate parents and children on digital safety across the UK, Ireland and UAE."Some approaches may be more effective than others. The challenge is legislation often only covers certain apps, games or platforms and there are others that fall outside of this. It means that bans might not completely close loopholes around inappropriate content, exploitation or abuse. That's why we still want parental involvement and schools guiding young people on appropriate and responsible use of technology."The UAE's ban, announced in June, is to come into force after a one-year grace period, during which social media companies must bring their services in line with the protocols.Australia was the first country to introduce a social media ban. Anyone under the age of 16 is barred from using platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, X and Reddit. But that does not mean that young people are unable to access other forms of social media.Lemon8, which is owned by TikTok's parent company ByteDance, surged in popularity in Australia after it emerged that it was not included in the initial list of banned apps for under-16s. It was later added."There are lesser-known platforms that parents and teachers aren't aware of," Mr Denner said. "There could be bad actors operating on those platforms who know they might not be as moderated as heavily as elsewhere. This presents a safeguarding risk."It can be something of a whack-a-mole scenario. As soon as you bring one of these platforms under the umbrella, another will emerge."Taking hard lineOther countries have also announced social media measures. The UK's ban for under-16s is also to come into effect from June next year. Under-15s will also be stopped from using social media in France from next year.Nations including Spain, Denmark, Greece, Norway, Indonesia and Canada have also announced proposals for similar bans. The EU announced the EU Kids Act last month, which proposes social media bans for under-13s, with limited accounts for those aged between 13 and 15.Educating parents on the dangers around young people having access to the online world is a crucial step in bolstering safety, Mr Denner said. "You should not be handing your child a phone if you haven't received some kind of education on the risks involved," he said."You shouldn't be able to buy a smartphone for your child without some sort of education on it. You wouldn't be allowed to let a young person drive a car without being qualified. It should also be illegal to introduce technology to children without safeguards in place."Last month, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads, agreed on a major settlement over allegations about the addictiveness of its social platforms for children. According to court filings, the social media company could pay up to $17.1 billion, after action from 47 US states and Washington, DC, and other American territories.Bigger pictureThe success of efforts to bar young people from social media platforms will depend on how such restrictions are implemented, said Prof Nathalie Martial-Braz, chancellor of Sorbonne University Abu Dhabi."An age limit works best as one element of a wider approach," she said. "The most promising measures act on the product itself – private accounts by default, no contact from unknown adults, no advertising based on profiling, and limits on features designed to hold attention, such as infinite scroll and autoplay."Education matters as much as regulation, and schools and universities have a part to play. Children who will open an account at 15 need to be prepared for it beforehand."A single global rule is probably out of reach, since countries have chosen 13, 15 or 16 [years of age]. Shared principles and compatible age-verification standards look more achievable."Another important factor is ensuring young people are protected against the risks lurking around the corner, as technology advances amid the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence."AI has changed the nature of the risk," Prof Martial-Braz said. "It drives the recommendation systems that decide what a young person sees. It can also produce harmful content that did not exist before, such as fabricated images of real people, and a child does not need an account to be affected by that. At the same time, AI is part of the solution."I would plead for a sense of proportion. AI offers real benefits for learning, and a university engaged in AI research would be the last to deny it. The question is which uses are appropriate at which age, and with what safeguards. We are better placed to ask it early than we were with social media."New digital frontiersBut not everyone is in agreement about the efficacy of imposing blanket bans on young people using social media. In December last year, Unicef called for "governments, regulators and companies to work with children and families to build digital environments that are safe, inclusive and respect children’s rights".The agency warned that "social media was not a luxury for many children, especially those who are isolated or marginalised – it is a lifeline providing access to learning, connection, play and self-expression".When British authorities announced plans for the ban in June, Kerry Moscogiuri, chief executive of Amnesty International UK, described it as the "right diagnosis but the wrong prescription". She said the onus should fall on social media companies to do more to keep young people safe."Too many social media companies have built products and business models that prioritise keeping children engaged for longer, often at the expense of their well-being, privacy and rights," she said at the time. “But the problem is not that children exist on social media, it’s that social media companies have built platforms that are unsafe by design. Banning under-16s risks treating children as the problem rather than addressing the companies and systems that create the risks in the first place."Dr Katherine Kemp, associate professor at the faculty of law and justice at UNSW Sydney, told The National that broad bans raise issues about data protection and privacy.For some young people, social media could actually provide a lifeline and help them connect with others, she said. "There are some teenagers who successfully use social media to take part in political debate and advocate causes that are important to them," she added."Social media can also provide vital connections for young people who feel isolated because of their gender, sexuality, neurodiversity or ethnic background, especially where they lack connections in their nearby community."

headline: Cartoon for October 10, 2026
£20m penthouse completes makeover of London's South Bank. So, who will Shell out for it?
summary: In the grimy London aftermath of the Second World War, the Festival of Britain was intended as a “tonic for the nation”, turning the rubble of bombed out industrial wasteland into a showcase of British ideas, art and manufacturing.The six-month festival drew 8.5 million visitors to see the temporary Dome of Discovery exhibition and Skylon sculpture that helped popularise the modern architectural style that would sweep Britain and drag it out of the postwar doldrums. It also signalled the regeneration of the area which became the South Bank – complete with riverside walk, Royal Festival Hall concert venue, galleries and Jubilee Gardens.Seventy-five years on, a second regeneration has taken place. Luxury apartments, including a £20 million ($26.4 million) penthouse which has now gone on sale, shops and restaurants have replaced the outdated office buildings that sprang up in the years since the festival. It has been a 10-year project to redevelop the Shell Centre, the global headquarters of the oil company that stare at the Thames. The Shell Tower – designed by Howard Robertson, who also played a part in the design of the UN building in New York – remains as the oil major's HQ, but the three adjoining wings have undergone a 12-year redevelopment odyssey. While the 27-storey main building has stood intact, the former adjoining blocks built on postwar modernist workplace ideas have been demolished. The complex had a full-sized underground swimming pool, four squash courts, sports club, underground cinema/theatre featuring custom artist murals and a famously large staff cafeteria.The £1 billion development known as Southbank Place has been delivered by Braeburn Estates, a joint venture by Qatari Diar and Canary Wharf Group. Its design, by architects Stanton Williams, is described as a “modern response to the brutalist structures of the neighbouring Royal Festival Hall and the Southbank Centre”.This week, The National was given a tour of Seven, the final building in the project, to see the 3,800 sq ft four-bedroom, duplex penthouse that marks the final jigsaw piece in the redevelopment.Each of the 92 apartments in the limestone building is oriented towards the Thames, with large balconies and vast full-height windows.Occupying the 12th and 13th floors, with 900 sq ft of wraparound terrace, from the penthouse you can see trains trundle below into Charing Cross, while the Elizabeth Tower housing Big Ben can be viewed through the spokes of the London Eye only a few hundred yards away.Its riverside location, with protected gardens in front, means it has a panoramic view through its triple-glazed windows of central London and east past St Paul’s and The Shard to Canary Wharf. It’s also low enough to still see people wandering along the pavements or read the numbers on the red buses crossing Waterloo Bridge.Its interiors have been created by award-winning British interior design studio Albion Nord. Much of the furniture is bespoke and was finished in situ, made by UK-based artisans using traditional craftsmanship. It features specially commissioned artworks, cityscape photography, 1940s-style chairs upholstered in soporifically thick wool, a stainless steel kitchen island and a hand-blown hanging glass pendant lighting the living area.The vast majority of buyers of such properties will stick with the decor they see on first viewing, said Ben Johnson, director at Albion Nord. Besides the odd personal item, why would you change what an expert has spent the past 12 months creating? He appears particularly proud of the fluted walls on the spiral staircase and the main bathroom’s oversize shower. For a brutalist-inspired building, it is “not stark or too modern”, he said. “There’s a lot going on. We have been allowed to be bold, with big upholstery for a big space, showing warmth and movement. It’s a comfortable home, not a show apartment.”He also points out the utility room has the best view of any in London, while each room features a “stunning vignette” regardless of which direction the face.So, who would be the likely buyer?“It’s good to have someone in mind, although it often doesn’t end up like that,” said Miles Wood, sales director at Qatari Diar.He is confident the penthouse “will resonate with buyers from the moment they walk in” and envisages the eventual owner being an international buyer with numerous properties around the globe. There is no dominant nationality within the building, with a mix of British, European and Middle Eastern residents.He says the South Bank tends to attract a younger more creative clientele than other areas popular with the world’s super-rich, such as Mayfair, due to its culture and “place of identity”.He cites the main selling points as its “best-in-class” design and furnishing, as well as the building’s amenities including 25 metre pool, yoga studio and gym.Wind sheerBeing on the 12th floor, “it’s not too windy” and as the only apartment on that storey it comes with privacy built in. Plus, “some people just love a penthouse” and there are not that many to choose from with “views of iconic, quintessential London”.Despite the dent that has been done to London’s reputation for safety in recent years, unfairly so, according to Mr Wood, he believes top-end properties will still achieve top prices.The difference is that now buyers are likely to be thinking long term, generational, rather than just a two or three-year investment.“This has been a 10-year journey and the penthouse is the final piece of the jigsaw,” he said. “It’s been an interesting decade, a challenging time for global geopolitics, but people still want to buy best in class. And with its education, culture and law, I believe London is still the best city in the world.”

headline: UN envoy warns Yemen has returned to ‘full-scale war’
summary: The UN special envoy for Yemen warned the Security Council on Friday that the country has returned to all-out conflict, with fighting spreading across several fronts and Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia threatening to deepen regional instability.“In the past few weeks, Yemen has slid back into full-scale war, with hostilities spreading across multiple front lines,” UN envoy Hans Grundberg told the 15-member council.The Iran-backed Houthis had earlier advanced towards Mokha and the coast along the strategic Bab Al Mandeb strait, while Yemen's internationally recognised government said it had recaptured territory nearby in a counteroffensive launched this week.The conflict has increasingly spilt into Saudi Arabia. Three Saudi citizens, including an airline pilot, were killed in attacks on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport and a Saudi aircraft on Thursday, Saudi authorities said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks on the airport.Mr Grundberg condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure, including Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport. He also warned that threats against Saudi-linked commercial vessels in the Red Sea risked further destabilising international shipping and energy markets.“These threats are becoming enmeshed with the broader confrontation over control of maritime trade routes and the stresses on the international energy market,” he said.According to the UN, more than 200,000 people have been displaced across Yemen since the beginning of August, the highest level of new displacement since the 2022 truce. In addition, nearly 4,000 people have fled across the Bab Al Mandeb strait to seek safety in Djibouti and Somalia.Despite escalating hostilities, Mr Grundberg urged the warring parties to pursue negotiations. “Unless war is to become Yemen's permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now,” he noted.

headline: Gaza ceasefire: A year of stalled promises
summary: When the Gaza ceasefire came into effect a year ago, Palestinians in the enclave hoped that they could start rebuilding their lives. The truce came in the form of a 20-point plan which specified that aid would enter at scale and the strip would be “redeveloped for the benefit of the people of Gaza”.It also said there would be a demilitarisation process and gradual Israeli withdrawal. While the ceasefire brought much-needed respite after two years of full-scale war, many of the terms of the agreement have stalled, leaving 1.9 million people still displaced. Meanwhile, in the past year, about 1,400 people in Gaza have been killed and Israel has occupied more territory. Humanitarian workers say food, medical supplies, shelters and other lifesaving aid are not being allowed to enter at the capacity needed. In this episode of Beyond the Headlines, host Nada AlTaher looks at what, if anything, has changed for residents in the strip a year since the ceasefire. We hear from Nesma Al-Sallaq. Gaza shelter co-ordinator at the Norwegian Refugee Council, and political analyst Omar Rahman, fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs.

headline: The Gaza ceasefire was meant to end the war. For a mother, paramedic and child, little has changed
US failure to prepare for rise of quantum computers could be 'catastrophic' for economy, GAO warns
summary: The development of Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) capable of breaking just about any encryption might be "catastrophic" to the US economy and security, a new federal report says. The recently released analysis from the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) echoes concerns from technology and cyber security experts in recent years about a hypothetical scenario known as “Q-Day", in which quantum computers fall into the wrong hands and are used to crack billions of passwords and break down other encryption methods, resulting in a wave of financial crimes. Conventional computers process data in bits and have a binary value of zero or one, whereas quantum computers can process digits simultaneously using a two-state unit called a qubit. What that means is that data crunching for research can now be done in a fraction of the time, potentially yielding new breakthroughs in science and medical research.Unfortunately, as the report points out, it also could have tremendous ramifications for cyber security. The non-partisan federal watchdog said that it recently made 89 recommendations to more than 20 federal agencies to develop inventories of potentially vulnerable cryptography that would help in identifying funding for "post-quantum cryptography." It published only the broad recommendations that it had conveyed to officials, and details of the others are unknown."We have omitted the original agency comment letters reprinted in the sensitive report due to sensitivity concerns," it said.Though 12 government agencies agreed with the GAO's recommendations, one agency disagreed with several of them, and the US Department of the Interior failed to provide a response. "We continue to believe that all of the recommendations made in the sensitive report are warranted," the GAO's analysis explained. Though the GAO's evaluation about US government preparedness for CRQCs makes for sobering reading, it did point out a silver lining. "Experts say that the probability that a CRQC will be built in the next 10 years is low," the GAO report reads, though it adds that there's a significant risk that bad actors, governments or organisations might be harvesting large amounts of encrypted data right now, and are simply waiting for CRQCs to become available to decrypt it. "The loss of even a small amount of important sensitive information could have a severe effect on federal operations."The World Economic Forum touched on worries related to quantum computers in its Top 10 Emerging Technologies Report for 2026. It listed lattice-based cryptography as being among the more important technologies. Lattice-based cryptography is based on the idea of preserving encrypted data on computers and devices by relying on a series of mathematical problems consisting of complicated grids, also known as lattices, that are impossible for even quantum computers to solve.

headline: US sanctions entire ICC for first time in Trump escalation
summary: The US imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, sanctioning the entire tribunal for the first time as the Trump administration escalated its campaign against the institution in The Hague.Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with “this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us."“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Mr Rubio said in a video posted on social media.The sanctions are expected to restrict the ICC's ability to use the US financial system, with a transition period before most prohibited transactions become unlawful. Previous US sanctions were imposed on individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over investigations involving American and Israeli officials. “President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Mr Rubio said. He also warned US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defence” to bring the tribunal under control or face further American efforts to dismantle it “brick by brick”.Today, the Trump Administration is sanctioning the ICC.This action should encourage our Allies within the Court to work for solutions to end this threat to U.S. sovereignty forever. pic.twitter.com/D86dCqLUaZ— Secretary Marco Rubio (@SecRubio) October 9, 2026The US action came the same day that ⁠former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The ICC “strongly” rejected the sanctions, calling them an attack on international justice and warning that “history will judge this moment”.“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.ICC President Tomoko Akane urged its member states to defend the institution against mounting US pressure.“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it. The Rome Statute is a collective promise that the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole must not go unpunished. That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it,” she said.The EU called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work”.The latest confrontation follows Mr Trump's call last month for all ICC member states to withdraw from the tribunal, which he called “out of control” and a “rogue institution”.Established in 2002, the ICC has 125 member states, although major powers, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel are not members. Under its founding Rome Statute, the court can prosecute people for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide only when national authorities are unwilling or unable to do so themselves.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also condemned the sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to carry out its work. Human rights groups condemned the US sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to pursue justice for victims of atrocities around the world.“By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, the Trump administration has taken a sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century,” said Omar Shakir, executive director of Dawn, a US-based human rights organisation.“US sanctions threaten to shut the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine, all to shield Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide from justice.”
body_text:
The US imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, sanctioning the entire tribunal for the first time as the Trump administration escalated its campaign against the institution in The Hague.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with “this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate against us."

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Mr Rubio said in a video posted on social media.

The sanctions are expected to restrict the ICC's ability to use the US financial system, with a transition period before most prohibited transactions become unlawful. Previous US sanctions were imposed on individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over investigations involving American and Israeli officials.

“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Mr Rubio said. He also warned US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defence” to bring the tribunal under control or face further American efforts to dismantle it “brick by brick”.

The US action came the same day that ⁠former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The ICC “strongly” rejected the sanctions, calling them an attack on international justice and warning that “history will judge this moment”.

“It is an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the Court from doing what it was created to do. It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

ICC President Tomoko Akane urged its member states to defend the institution against mounting US pressure.

“The Court cannot stand alone. Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it. The Rome Statute is a collective promise that the most serious crimes of concern to the international community as a whole must not go unpunished. That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it,” she said.

The EU called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work”.

The latest confrontation follows Mr Trump's call last month for all ICC member states to withdraw from the tribunal, which he called “out of control” and a “rogue institution”.

Established in 2002, the ICC has 125 member states, although major powers, including the US, Russia, China, India and Israel are not members. Under its founding Rome Statute, the court can prosecute people for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide only when national authorities are unwilling or unable to do so themselves.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres also condemned the sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to carry out its work. Human rights groups condemned the US sanctions, warning that they could severely undermine the court's ability to pursue justice for victims of atrocities around the world.

“By sanctioning the entire International Criminal Court, the Trump administration has taken a sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century,” said Omar Shakir, executive director of Dawn, a US-based human rights organisation.

“US sanctions threaten to shut the last viable road to justice for millions of victims of serious crimes, from Gaza and Sudan to Afghanistan and Ukraine, all to shield Israeli officials who have perpetrated a genocide from justice.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the US sanctions as an aggressive escalation by the Trump administration against international justice, emphasizing widespread condemnation from the ICC, EU, UN, and human rights groups while giving minimal space to the US rationale.

loaded_language.quote: escalated its campaign against the institution
loaded_language.explanation: The word 'campaign' implies a sustained, coordinated, and possibly hostile effort, adding an editorial tone beyond a neutral description of sanctions.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: imposed additional sanctions on the institution

loaded_language.quote: crippling its ability to operate against us
loaded_language.explanation: The verb 'crippling' is emotionally charged and dramatic, though it appears within a direct quote from Marco Rubio.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: severely restricting its ability to operate against us

loaded_language.quote: sledgehammer to the most important development in international justice in half a century
loaded_language.explanation: This metaphor is highly emotive and hyperbolic, though it is a direct quote from a human rights activist.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: a severe blow to a major development in international justice

loaded_language.explanation: The term 'genocide' is a serious legal and moral accusation with strong emotional weight, though it appears in a direct quote from a human rights activist.
