Any statement from Israeli officials or supporters of the sanctions defending the action.
The specific legal basis or details of the sanctions, such as which entities or individuals are affected and the exact nature of the financial restrictions.
Reactions from US allies who are ICC members that might support the sanctions or express concerns about the ICC's actions.

headline: El-Sayed and Rogers trade personal attacks in bitter Michigan Senate debate
summary: Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers, the two candidates vying for a US Senate seat in Michigan, have traded bitter personal attacks during a hostile debate over Iran, Israel and the economy.Their first televised exchange late on Thursday was marked by acrimonious jibes and fundamental disagreements, with tensions spilling over into the commercial break.“I want to take a quick aside and tell you that in 30 years of doing debates, I've never seen it continue during the commercial,” said Rick Albin, the debate's moderator. “But it did.”The heated debate comes during a tight race in the swing state, with less than four weeks until the midterm elections. Michigan is home to about 300,000 Arab Americans, and President Donald Trump has won there twice.The November 3 elections will determine who controls Congress, and Michigan is among the most closely watched Senate races. If Mr El-Sayed, a Democrat, wins, he would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Mr Rogers, a Republican, is an ally of Mr Trump.“Under this guy who's going to rubber stamp everything Donald Trump tells him to rubber stamp, you're going to continue to pay way more out the nose because he works for corporations and Donald Trump,” Mr El-Sayed said.Recent polling suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming the President for his handling of the issues. His approval rating has sunk to the low 30s. Mr Trump has said the war would end after the midterms and that fuel costs – which rose after Iran put a chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz – would go down shortly after. But the war has been particularly unpopular among voters, and the Trump-endorsed Mr Rogers has run an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.”'Go ahead and say it'Mr Rogers questioned his opponent's credentials, calling Mr El-Sayed a “con man” and accusing him of having ties to armed groups in the Middle East.“He can't condemn Hamas. He can't condemn the Muslim Brotherhood. He says his home is Egypt,” he said.Mr Rogers later suggested that concerns about surveillance could be personal for Mr El Sayed because he or someone in his family might be suspected of terrorism.“Go ahead and say it,” Mr El-Sayed interjected. “You've been tiptoeing around it the whole time.”The candidates also traded accusations over their wealth and property. Mr El-Sayed accused Mr Rogers of owning a home in Florida and two yachts. Mr Rogers countered that Mr El-Sayed's wife owned a home in the UAE and might own one in Egypt. They actually own two rental properties overseas – one in Bangalore and the other in Dubai, but not in Egypt.Abdul El-Sayed asks Mike Rogers how many yachts he owns at the Michigan Senate debate pic.twitter.com/MfzZft2Jcl— Politics Watch (@politics_watch1) October 8, 2026Although the moderator at times struggled to keep the debate focused on policy, the candidates also clashed over their positions on the Middle East.Asked whether any action by Israel would lead him to withdraw support for US military assistance, Mr Rogers said: “I support just as staunchly their right to exist, the right to exist for the Jewish state, and the right to defend itself in a very difficult neighbourhood.”Pressed on what might change his position, he said that if Israel were to talk about using nuclear weapons, he would shift stance. Mr El Sayed also faced repeated questions about which country posed a greater threat to the US, Israel or Iran. He called it a “ridiculous hypothetical”.“Our ostensible ally in Israel has lobbied us to go to war with Iran,” he said. “We have watched as Iran has responded by bombing all kinds of countries in the Middle East and then choking off the world’s energy supply. So, this is a situation in which I don’t think we should be a part.” When pressed for an answer, he said: “I think both of them have proven dangerous in their own way. One at risk of attacking us. One getting us into wars we have no business fighting.”Highlighting the Islamophobia that Mr El Sayed has been subjected to throughout his campaign, after the debate, Mr Trump attacked Mr El-Sayed in a racist social media post, calling him a “Jihadist lunatic” and referring to him as “Mohammed”.“Mohammed is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our country, the Black People of Detroit, and wants to see the US fail,” he wrote.The candidates are scheduled to meet for a second and final debate on October 21 in Detroit.

headline: Flydubai co-pilot attempted 9/11-style attack on Tel Aviv and trained for cockpit fight
summary: A flydubai co-pilot attempted to seize control of a passenger jet and crash it into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport in a premeditated suicide attack, UAE prosecutors have said.The UAE's Attorney General, Hamad Al Shamsi, announced on Friday that an investigation into the September 30 incident involving flight FZ1073, bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai, found that the aircraft's Omani co-pilot carried out a terrorist plot to cause mass casualties at the Israeli airport. The suspect, aged 29, was inspired by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and had pursued a career in aviation specifically to carry out a similar operation, according to his confession.Radicalised in AustraliaDr Al Shamsi said investigators traced the suspect's radicalisation to 2017, when he was studying in Melbourne, Australia. During that period, he was exposed to extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. He also attended a mosque affiliated with the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology, where he allegedly came into contact with people connected to a centre managed by a Lebanese man known as Abu Hamza, said to have links to the Muslim Brotherhood.He also said that he had prepared himself psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing with a private coach.Investigators found that the suspect had used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv to reconnoitre the route and airport ahead of the attack.No indications of extremismThe suspect worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, then briefly for Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. The investigation also examined the procedures under which the suspect had been recruited by flydubai. The findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot’s licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot.The attackDuring the incident, he allegedly struck the aircraft's captain, Smit Machchhar, with an emergency axe inside the cockpit. A pilot travelling as a passenger on the return flight noticed the cockpit door behaving unusually, gained entry, and, with the help of crew and passengers, restrained the suspect and rescued the injured captain.The aircraft was diverted and landed safely at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia. The suspect confessed to acting alone, though investigations are continuing to verify that claim. The Public Prosecution also heard statements from the captain, the return flight pilot, his co-pilot and members of the crew. The forensic medical report established that the captain’s injuries were concentrated on the head and consistent with the timing of the incident. The findings were also consistent with the statements made by the suspect and the captain, as well as witness testimony. The Public Prosecution is reviewing recordings, technical reports and possible connections to accomplices.

headline: Dubai Orchestra Foundation established by law to boost emirate's cultural ambitions
summary: Dubai has a new dedicated body to champion orchestral music after Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, signed a law establishing the Dubai Orchestra Foundation.Sheikh Mohammed issued Law No. (20) of 2026, creating the Foundation to advance the arts and orchestral music across the emirate. The body is tasked with strengthening Dubai's regional and international cultural standing, preserving local artistic heritage and showcasing the UAE's musical excellence.Among its core responsibilities, the Foundation will establish a local orchestra, stage performances both within the UAE and abroad, and promote Emirati musical heritage. It will also support emerging talent, including People of Determination, develop an annual calendar of musical events and host international orchestras. The Foundation will build local and global partnerships, support music education and production, and foster collaboration with cultural institutions worldwide.The Law outlines a governance structure headed by a Board of Trustees, comprising a Chairman, Vice Chairman and members with relevant expertise, all appointed by the Chairman of The Executive Council of Dubai. The Foundation is expected to contribute to Dubai's broader creative economy, reinforcing the emirate's position as a leading destination for cultural tourism and encouraging investment in the music and performing arts industries.

headline: Dubai Cashless Strategy contributes Dh8bn to economy as it exceeds goals ahead of schedule
summary: The Dubai Cashless Strategy has contributed more than Dh8 billion ($2.18 billion) to the economy, surpassing its goals ahead of its two-year timeframe.The emirate's cashless transactions index hit 90.1 per cent, exceeding the 90 per cent target set for 2026, the Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Friday, quoting figures from Dubai Finance.The Dh8 billion figure was also the target set when the strategy was launched in October 2024. The digital enablement index for the government sector reached 100, reflecting the availability of digital payment methods across institutions and businesses, it said.The initiative achieved strong results across the strategy’s three pillars, with 97 per cent achieved in governance, 95 per cent in society and 93 per cent in innovation, it said. “Operational business continuity was also maintained to ensure the sustainability of these results and maximise their long-term impact,” the report said.Additionally, the community happiness index also hit 90.1 per cent, also surpassing the 90 per cent target.“The strategy reflects the success of Dubai’s model, which is built on a clear vision, integrated roles between the government and private sectors, and the expanding use of technology and innovation to serve people and enhance economic competitiveness,” the DMO said, citing Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence.The Dubai Cashless Strategy was unveiled in October 2024 as the emirate seeks to solidify its standing as one of the world’s top digital cities.The initiative seeks to enable seamless and secure digital payment solutions across both government and private sectors, the media office said. It aligns with the objectives of the Dubai Economic Agenda, the initiative also known as D33.In a separate statement on Friday, top Dubai officials said the achievement marks a new milestone and reinforces Dubai’s position as a leading global hub.“The transition towards a cashless society is not a technological objective in itself. It is part of a broader vision for an interconnected digital city that provides individuals and businesses with easier and more efficient experiences and enables innovation to translate into economic and social value,” said Hamad Al Mansoori, director general of Digital Dubai, which spearheaded the cashless strategy.Helal Almarri, director general of the Dubai Department of Economy and Tourism, noted that the efficiency of transactions is a vital element of the experience of businesses, residents and visitors.“The wider range of payment options enriches the visitor experience, enhances Dubai’s competitiveness and reinforces its position as one of the world’s most accessible and connected cities,” he added.

headline: What's behind the postponement of Palestinian elections and what happens next?
summary: Under intense pressure to reform, President Mahmoud Abbas vowed 2026 would be the year of diplomacy, announcing that Palestine would hold legislative elections in November and Presidential elections next year. Many doubted they would happen, given past experience. Their fears became reality this week, with sources telling The National that the elections are to be delayed again. The last time this happened was in 2021, when Mr Abbas announced that legislative elections were cancelled after hope had been ignited that the Palestinian government might be revived. “This was not a postponement, this was a cancellation,” said Palestinian-Canadian lawyer Dania Buttu, who is the former spokeswoman for the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO). Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree. “This is called authoritarian rule,” she added.This time, the postponement comes at a crucial period, weakening the Palestinian Authority's credibility in the face of a mountain of challenges, including a right-wing Israeli drive to make it impossible to establish statehood, a war that has not stopped in Gaza, and international obligations that have not been fulfilled. Israel has occupied more than half of the Gaza Strip, and its army has killed 70,000 Palestinians there over the course of the three-year war since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks have become more rampant and intense, and conditions inside Israeli prisons are described as torture by Israeli and international rights groups.The conditions for free and fair elections are unlikely to be met in Palestine in the near future, particularly if Benjamin Netanyahu's government survives Israel's own vote set to take place at the end of this month. However, Mr Abbas has also not secured any type of future for Palestine.“When Abu Ammar [Yasser Arafat] was alive, we knew what would happen after he was gone. There would be elections, and Abbas would win. Today, we have no idea,” Ms Buttu said.Palestine's parliament has not met since 2007, the last time since legislative elections, and Mr Abbas has issued at least “three times” more decrees than parliament has passed laws, she added. Despite creating the role of Vice President, Mr Abbas has also bolstered the position of his own son, and a clear plan of action is not in place for when the 90-year-old President dies. Sources from different factions said the roots of the delay are mainly tied to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. But attempts to unite notorious factions within the Palestinian political scene have often failed, stemming from disagreements about the way forward for Palestine. Systemic and endemic problems mean that Palestine has lacked the right environment for elections for decades. Under an occupation that has become more fierce and deadly in recent decades, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.Unpopular leaderHigh-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling support circle.Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.This confirms “the persistence of exceptionally high dissatisfaction with his leadership”, the PSR said in its findings. Driven by what seemed like a crucial moment for change after Mr Abbas's announcement earlier this year that elections would be held, momentum began to build, preparations were set in place and alliances began to form.Inside FatahFirst, municipal elections were held in the West Bank and in one area of Gaza, Deir Al Balah, because the remainder of the strip is simply too destroyed to host an organised vote. The vote went ahead, and despite some criticism, was viewed as a step forward towards larger elections. Then, he held elections in Fatah's Central Committee, where the cracks began to form. Several sources told The National that the vote was clearly “rigged”. People who once seemed to be guaranteed winners were sidelined, while others, like Mr Abbas's son Yasser, gained enough votes to secure a seat on the committee. “In my estimation, this is one of the most significant reasons [for the postponement],” an official with Palestinian Islamic Jihad told The National. “There is internal disarray within the Fatah movement regarding the formation of its electoral list and the distribution of power centres following the movement's Eighth Conference.”Additionally, Fatah is not viewed as a single party. Splits over the years from the group's main members by people who can, in today's political climate, play a significant role, such as Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Kidwa, mean that Fatah no longer represents one single vision. Mr Dahlan, the head of a breakaway faction of Fatah called the Democratic Reform Party, was the Fatah representative in Gaza before being exiled from the group. Both Mr Dahlan's party and Hamas issued a statement confirming that they had met, cementing further what many had suspected before: that efforts were probably being made to unite against Mr Abbas in upcoming elections.There were also talks that Mr Barghouti himself would join one of the parties running against Mr Abbas – causing the chances of the President's political survival in a poll to shrivel. Only 14 per cent of people would vote for him if Mr Barghouti and Mr Al Hayya ran against him. “New alignments have emerged over the past few months, including a rapprochement between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the faction led by Mohammed Dahlan. This creates the possibility of an electoral map reshaped in a way that makes it difficult for the current leadership to control the outcome,” the PIJ official added. “Thus, postponement becomes a means to realign alliances before heading to the polls.”The future of PalestineA lot of this was expected, and did not come as a surprise for many. In fact, the same public opinion poll showed that 44 per cent of Palestinians did not believe the elections would take place on time. So did many Palestinian experts and watchers. Mr Abbas postponed the 2021 elections under the pretext that Israel would not allow people to cast their vote in occupied East Jerusalem, after it became increasingly apparent that he would lose. Today, the circumstances are significantly more dire.The framework within which the November vote will be postponed is important. In 2021 there was simply an announcement, but if Mr Abbas issues a decree, this should make it legally binding. Additionally, pressure from Europe may also mean that a vote is not “postponed” indefinitely, but takes place later, within a set timeframe. Eyes will now be on France and other European countries that have made reform a condition of their provision of assistance to the Palestinian Authority, now that the decision to postpone has been made but not officially announced.
body_text:
Under intense pressure to reform, President Mahmoud Abbas vowed 2026 would be the year of diplomacy, announcing that Palestine would hold legislative elections in November and Presidential elections next year.

Many doubted they would happen, given past experience. Their fears became reality this week, with sources telling The National that the elections are to be delayed again. The last time this happened was in 2021, when Mr Abbas announced that legislative elections were cancelled after hope had been ignited that the Palestinian government might be revived.

“This was not a postponement, this was a cancellation,” said Palestinian-Canadian lawyer Dania Buttu, who is the former spokeswoman for the Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO). Mr Abbas, who was elected in 2005, has overstayed his term by 17 years and now rules by decree. “This is called authoritarian rule,” she added.

Highly anticipated Palestinian elections likely to be postponed, sources say

This time, the postponement comes at a crucial period, weakening the Palestinian Authority's credibility in the face of a mountain of challenges, including a right-wing Israeli drive to make it impossible to establish statehood, a war that has not stopped in Gaza, and international obligations that have not been fulfilled.

Israel has occupied more than half of the Gaza Strip, and its army has killed 70,000 Palestinians there over the course of the three-year war since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. In the occupied West Bank, settler attacks have become more rampant and intense, and conditions inside Israeli prisons are described as torture by Israeli and international rights groups.

The conditions for free and fair elections are unlikely to be met in Palestine in the near future, particularly if Benjamin Netanyahu's government survives Israel's own vote set to take place at the end of this month. However, Mr Abbas has also not secured any type of future for Palestine.

“When Abu Ammar [Yasser Arafat] was alive, we knew what would happen after he was gone. There would be elections, and Abbas would win. Today, we have no idea,” Ms Buttu said.

Palestine's parliament has not met since 2007, the last time since legislative elections, and Mr Abbas has issued at least “three times” more decrees than parliament has passed laws, she added. Despite creating the role of Vice President, Mr Abbas has also bolstered the position of his own son, and a clear plan of action is not in place for when the 90-year-old President dies.

Sources from different factions said the roots of the delay are mainly tied to holding a national dialogue in Egypt and ending “Palestinian division” before going to the polls. But attempts to unite notorious factions within the Palestinian political scene have often failed, stemming from disagreements about the way forward for Palestine.

Systemic and endemic problems mean that Palestine has lacked the right environment for elections for decades. Under an occupation that has become more fierce and deadly in recent decades, state institutions, finances and the political scene have all but collapsed.

High-level meetings and tactical alliances between factions looking to unseat Mr Abbas and his ruling Fatah party have been taking place, causing anxiety in the President's dwindling support circle.

Mr Abbas has become increasingly unpopular in Palestine. An August opinion poll by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research (PSR) surveyed 1,270 people and showed that 79 per cent wanted him to resign.

This confirms “the persistence of exceptionally high dissatisfaction with his leadership”, the PSR said in its findings.

Driven by what seemed like a crucial moment for change after Mr Abbas's announcement earlier this year that elections would be held, momentum began to build, preparations were set in place and alliances began to form.

First, municipal elections were held in the West Bank and in one area of Gaza, Deir Al Balah, because the remainder of the strip is simply too destroyed to host an organised vote.

The vote went ahead, and despite some criticism, was viewed as a step forward towards larger elections. Then, he held elections in Fatah's Central Committee, where the cracks began to form. Several sources told The National that the vote was clearly “rigged”. People who once seemed to be guaranteed winners were sidelined, while others, like Mr Abbas's son Yasser, gained enough votes to secure a seat on the committee.

“In my estimation, this is one of the most significant reasons [for the postponement],” an official with Palestinian Islamic Jihad told The National. “There is internal disarray within the Fatah movement regarding the formation of its electoral list and the distribution of power centres following the movement's Eighth Conference.”

Additionally, Fatah is not viewed as a single party. Splits over the years from the group's main members by people who can, in today's political climate, play a significant role, such as Mohammad Dahlan and Nasser Al Kidwa, mean that Fatah no longer represents one single vision.

Mr Dahlan, the head of a breakaway faction of Fatah called the Democratic Reform Party, was the Fatah representative in Gaza before being exiled from the group. Similarly, Mr Al Kidwa, who is the nephew of former Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, was expelled from the Fatah party and joined forces with one of Palestine's most prominent political figures, Marwan Al Barghouti, for the elections in 2021 that Mr Abbas also “postponed”.

Mr Dahlan recently met the head of Hamas's politburo, Khalil Al Hayya, in Cairo. Both Mr Dahlan's party and Hamas issued a statement confirming that they had met, cementing further what many had suspected before: that efforts were probably being made to unite against Mr Abbas in upcoming elections.

There were also talks that Mr Barghouti himself would join one of the parties running against Mr Abbas – causing the chances of the President's political survival in a poll to shrivel. Only 14 per cent of people would vote for him if Mr Barghouti and Mr Al Hayya ran against him.

“New alignments have emerged over the past few months, including a rapprochement between Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the faction led by Mohammed Dahlan. This creates the possibility of an electoral map reshaped in a way that makes it difficult for the current leadership to control the outcome,” the PIJ official added. “Thus, postponement becomes a means to realign alliances before heading to the polls.”

A lot of this was expected, and did not come as a surprise for many. In fact, the same public opinion poll showed that 44 per cent of Palestinians did not believe the elections would take place on time. So did many Palestinian experts and watchers.

Mr Abbas postponed the 2021 elections under the pretext that Israel would not allow people to cast their vote in occupied East Jerusalem, after it became increasingly apparent that he would lose. Today, the circumstances are significantly more dire.

The framework within which the November vote will be postponed is important. In 2021 there was simply an announcement, but if Mr Abbas issues a decree, this should make it legally binding.

Additionally, pressure from Europe may also mean that a vote is not “postponed” indefinitely, but takes place later, within a set timeframe. Eyes will now be on France and other European countries that have made reform a condition of their provision of assistance to the Palestinian Authority, now that the decision to postpone has been made but not officially announced.

analysis.framing: The article frames the postponement of Palestinian elections as a symptom of President Mahmoud Abbas's authoritarian drift and internal Fatah dysfunction, set against a backdrop of Israeli occupation and international pressure.

loaded_language.explanation: A strong, value-laden term that characterizes Abbas's governance as dictatorial, going beyond a neutral description of ruling by decree.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: rule by decree without a legislative mandate

loaded_language.explanation: Colloquial and accusatory, implying deliberate fraud without providing direct evidence in the article.
Emotionally charged adjective that casts Palestinian political groups in a negative light.
Metaphorical and hyperbolic, emphasizing the severity of problems in a dramatic way.
Vivid, emotive verb that suggests a humiliating decline rather than a simple decrease.

omissions: No mention of specific dates or timelines for the postponed elections beyond 'November' and 'next year'.
No direct comment from President Mahmoud Abbas or his office on the postponement.
No details on the exact mechanism or official announcement of the delay (e.g., whether a decree has been issued).
No mention of international reactions beyond Europe, such as from the US or UN.
No coverage of potential protests or public reactions within Palestine to the postponement.

headline: President Sheikh Mohamed and Canadian PM Mark Carney discuss UAE-Canada economic ties
summary: President Sheikh Mohamed spoke with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Friday, with both leaders pledging to deepen bilateral ties across vital sectors, with a particular focus on strengthening economic and investment ties.Advanced technology and AI also featured prominently in the discussions, reflecting both nations' ambitions to position themselves as leaders in emerging industries. The two leaders identified these sectors as central to the development priorities of both countries and pledged their commitment to advancing UAE-Canada relations through long-term, sustainable partnerships. In July, the UAE finalised a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa) with Canada. The trade ​agreement with Ottawa aims to reduce trade barriers to goods, services and ⁠investment, and follows a $50 billion investment commitment from the UAE last November.The Cepa gives Canadian companies better access to the UAE, which remains the largest market for Canada's exports to the Middle East, and could help attract capital into energy, mining, artificial intelligence and ports.Friday's call also touched on a number of regional and international issues of mutual concern. The two leaders exchanged views on developments in the Middle East, with both expressing support for continuing efforts to promote security, stability and peace across the region.The emphasis on AI and advanced technology signals a forward-looking agenda, aligning with the UAE's broader national strategy to diversify its economy and cement its status as a global hub for innovation.

headline: UAE worshippers answer President Sheikh Mohamed's call to pray for rain
summary: Worshippers gathered at mosques across the UAE on Friday to perform Salaat Al Istisqaa, the Islamic prayer for rain.Earlier in the week, President Sheikh Mohamed had called on Emiratis and UAE residents to perform the prayer. The call came as the level of rainfall declines across parts of the Middle East. Through most of 2025, cumulative rainfall in the UAE was significantly below average – about 38 per cent less than the historical baseline and nearly three times lower than in 2024. At Sheikh Hazza bin Sultan Mosque in central Abu Dhabi on Friday, people were hopeful that rain will come soon.Egyptian resident Ibrahim Hamouda, 30, has attended Friday prayers at the mosque for six years. “It is a way for us to call upon our Lord through prayer; specifically, during times of drought,” he said. “It is how we ask God for what we need.”Jordanian Hussam Ali Hamdan was born in Abu Dhabi and has frequented the mosque since 2017. He said that the prayers are not just for humans, but for all living beings.“It is sunna of Prophet Muhammad, where we supplicate and we make duaa to the Almighty Allah to have mercy upon us and to send the rain for us as humans and for the living beings, like the trees and the animals,” Mr Hamdan told The National.Mohammad Arif from India participates in the rain prayers annually, and finds enjoyment in coming together to ask for blessings.“Inshallah Allah will give us rain. It's not only in the UAE, it should be everywhere in the world. We are very lucky to be in this country, but like other places ... I belong to India, this year there are lots of droughts over there in many places. I'll be praying for that also, throughout the world rain should come,” he said.Ahmed Sabir, from Egypt, said that the prayers are a way to ask God for the needs of the people. “It is essential; we must pray and supplicate to God so He may show us mercy, improve our conditions and the weather, ensure our agriculture thrives, and keep everything running smoothly. God’s bounty is vast,” he said.Samir Ashaar, from Egypt, has been coming to the mosque for nine years. He believes this ritual is one that everyone should follow.“May God show us mercy through the rain,” he said. “Everyone ought to attend today, as this prayer – whether considered an obligation or a Sunnah – invites forgiveness and mercy from Allah. God willing, there will be supplication and a favourable response; hopefully, the rain will fall today, by His leave.”

headline: Iraq expects to start transporting crude oil by lorry to Syria from mid-October
summary: Iraq is expecting to begin transporting crude oil via a route to be provided by Syria starting in mid-October, a development that is expected to boost its energy exports that have been hampered by flare-ups in the Strait of Hormuz amid the war in Iran.The crude products will be moved to a port in the Mediterranean Sea using lorries after Iraq requested assistance from Syrian authorities, Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing Yousef Qiblawy, chief executive of the state-owned Syrian Petroleum.The agreement between Baghdad and Damascus is “almost done”, and the Iraqi oil exports are expected to “start as soon as possible ... hopefully, by mid-October the first chain of trucks with crude will come to Syria”, he said.The impending move follows a similar energy trade-related co-ordination between the two Middle East nations in late September, in which Iraq began importing petrol through Syria.In April, Syria became the main route for Iraqi fuel oil exports, partially compensating for the disruption to shipments caused by the war in Iran. At least 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi fuel oil have also flowed by lorry to Syria's Baniyas since then.An Iraqi Oil Ministry official had told The National that the first cargo of imported petrol, comprising 32,000 tonnes, was being unloaded at the Baniyas refinery, to be transported to Iraq on lorries.Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations.Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals.The agreements between Iraq and Syria also mark a significant deepening of ties as Baghdad deals with disruption to its trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and as the US pushes for closer relations between the two countries.The strait, through which about a fifth of the world's energy exports passed before the war, remains a flashpoint in the eight-month conflict.The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. The figures include shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and by other methods.Iraq is a major crude oil producer, but faces petrol shortages because of problems with its refineries and the management of its energy infrastructure. Last Sunday, the state-owned Iraqi Oil Tankers Company transported two million barrels of its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades.The move was intended to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, director general Ali Qais said, adding that the company is also in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”.

headline: French lender Natixis CIB expects double-digit growth in Middle East and Asia despite war uncertainty
summary: French lender Natixis Corporate and Investment Banking expects double-digit growth in its Middle East and Asia business this year and next, despite the uncertainty driven by the Iran war and contracting economies.The lender, which has grown in double digits over the past five years in the region, has not been deterred by the geopolitical headwinds. It plans to hire more bankers across the business in markets such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia, said Bruno Le Saint, chief executive of Natixis CIB for Asia Pacific and Middle East. “In the overall region, we want to grow in double digits on average. This is what we've been doing over the past years and going forward we'll keep that pace,” he told The National. “It means that, overall, we hope to be close to 20 per cent in the next two to four years, but it also depends on how quickly we grow the rest of the business.”For the broader Middle East, Natixis CIB expects its business to grow by at least 10 per cent next year, despite the economic challenges caused by the war. The UAE and Saudi Arabia are the two largest regional markets for the French lender.Part of Groupe BPCE, the eurozone's fourth-largest banking group, Natixis CIB is expanding its footprint in the UAE, where it operates from the Dubai International Financial Centre. The Paris-based company has 80 personnel working out of Dubai and it plans to bring more resources, “expanding our workforce and our capabilities on the ground", Mr Le Saint said. “I think it's important because, in the context of the current situation, I don't think there have been many international banks growing staff in this region,” he said.It also plans to further boost its presence in Saudi Arabia, where Natixis CIB operates through its banking subsidiary, Natixis Saudi Arabia Investment Company.“We want to keep growing this,” Mr Le Saint said. “We still think that we are underinvested in Saudi Arabia.” The kingdom's Vision 2030 agenda also aligns well with Natixis CIB’s core financing and investment banking expertise in sectors including telecoms, energy, infrastructure, metals and mining.The bank is also considering expansion into Turkey, "which is also a big economy in the region", Mr Le Saint said of Natixis CIB’s expansion beyond the Arab world. “How do we grow there? It's under exploration for now, but these are the questions we are asking ourselves.”The company currently provides services to clients in markets including Oman and Turkey in the region and covers Central Asia from its Dubai hub.Word of cautionThe Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed.The World Bank said this week that Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects oil-rich economies in the region to contract this year, before enjoying a strong recovery next year – subject to shipping operations returning to normal, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said. But Mr Le Saint said he was “quite confident” about Natixis CIB’s growth prospects in the Middle East. “I still think that, even though some economies in the region, from a GDP perspective, are contracting, we have not yet reached our natural market share,” he said. “It's more difficult to reach our natural market share in a market that is contracting, but when we see that our franchise and our expertise fit well with the needs of the client, especially in the current situation, I still think that we can keep growing at this pace.”That projection, however, could change if the Iran war does not end soon, he added. “Of course, if the conflict stays for the next two to three years, what I say might at some point be revisited. But for the foreseeable future, for the next year, I'm very optimistic that we will be growing 10 per cent at least."“We are expanding, we are investing, so we are capturing market share at a time where not everyone has full attention on growing the business here, which I think is quite exciting.”Market impact Although Natixis remains bullish about the long-term economic environment of the Middle East, as well as the bank’s own growth prospects, it has seen a slowdown in the regional debt capital market this year. The volume of deals so far has dropped by about 10 per cent, but the market is “relatively resilient”, Mr Le Saint said.The slowdown is not due to the lack of access to liquidity, but is instead caused by borrowers who "don't want to access it now because they see the yield and the rates are too high”, he said. Borrowers can wait and have several options to raise funds, as well as their own liquidity. “Chinese banks are coming back in the region and are investing massively, especially to support probably, the need to source and help the flow of energy to China,” he said. “I don't think that our clients are in any stress to find liquidity. Many of them are just waiting to see better conditions or to tap a new pool of liquidity."Combined platform Natixis CIB, which is celebrating its 20th anniversary, combined its Asia and Middle East operations at the beginning of last year. The lender offers structured financing solutions, large-scale project funding, leverage and acquisition finance, funding for event-driven transactions as well as trade and structured financing.It primarily focuses on sectors including infrastructure, energy, transport, metals and mining, and technology and aviation.“They are global sectors where you've got investors, capital seekers and capital providers from [all parts] of the world. We connect the dots,” Mr Le Saint said.The bank also offers advisory, investment banking and corporate banking, as well as capital markets services. Bigger contributionCurrently, the Asia and Middle East platform accounts for more than 15 per cent of Natixis CIB’s overall business and “we want to grow that to 20 per cent and perhaps more", Mr Le Saint said.By combing the geographies, the bank is better placed to capture opportunities arising from the growing business and trade links between them, he said.“It also makes sense because our Asia Pacific set-up today, compared to what it was 20 years ago or even 10 years ago, is much more established and comprehensive so now we can offer our Middle East clients access to this market,” Mr Le Saint said.Natixis CIB’s clients in Asia also have access to funding pools in oil-rich countries in the Middle East, he added. “There is geopolitical and economic rationale, but there is also a business rationale."

headline: Binance expands financial super app offering with launch of bStocks in the UAE
summary: Binance, the global blockchain ecosystem behind the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange by trading volume and registered users, today announced the launch of bStocks for eligible users in the UAE, marking another milestone in the company’s vision of becoming a financial super app.The launch expands Binance’s growing ecosystem beyond digital assets, enabling users to access select US stocks through tokenised securities within a single platform.As Binance continues to bridge traditional finance and blockchain technology, bStocks provide users with a more accessible and flexible way to diversify their portfolios while benefiting from blockchain-native capabilities.Users in the UAE can already access a wide range of financial services, including crypto trading and earning products. The addition of bStocks further strengthens Binance’s ambition to bring multiple financial opportunities together into one seamless ecosystem, making it easier for users to manage different asset classes through a single platform.bStocks are tokenised securities designed to mirror the price of select US stocks and ETFs. Issued by BTech Holdings Limited, a Binance group affiliate, each bStock is intended to track the price of a corresponding underlying share held with a regulated custodian. While bStocks do not represent actual ownership of the underlying stocks, they are designed however to combine traditional finance with blockchain technology. They offer eligible users a simpler and more flexible way to access U.S. equity markets. These securities allow eligible users to :Start trading from just $524/7 trading, allowing users to trade beyond traditional stock market hours*Self-custody, with the ability to transfer supported bStocks to compatible BNB Chain wallets.On-chain utility, enabling supported bStocks to be used across compatible blockchain applications.Diversification, by accessing both digital assets and tokenised US equities through one trusted platform.Corporate actions, including stock splits and dividend-related adjustments, are processed automatically in accordance with the applicable product structure, helping users maintain continuous exposure without requiring manual actionAt launch, eligible users will have access to tokenised securities representing:Circle Internet Group (CRCLB/USDT)Micron Technology (MUB/USDT)Nvidia (NVDAB/USDT)SanDisk (SNDKB/USDT)Tesla (TSLAB/USDT)In addition to the above, many other bStocks are available on Binance and are expected to be introduced progressively, subject to applicable approvals. Commenting on the launch, Tarik Erk, head of MENAT said: “At Binance, we’re building much more than a cryptocurrency platform, we’re building a financial super app designed to give users seamless access to a growing range of financial opportunities through one trusted ecosystem. The launch of bStocks in the UAE marks another important step in that journey. "By bringing tokenised US equities onto blockchain infrastructure, we’re making access to US equity markets, more flexible and better aligned with how today’s digital-first users want to manage their finances. As we continue expanding our ecosystem, our focus remains on simplifying financial access while connecting traditional finance with the innovation of blockchain technology.”* Prices outside traditional market hours may be especially volatile, and trading during these periods carries additional risk. bStocks are designed to track the price of the corresponding underlying asset, but are not guaranteed to reflect its real-time market price at all times.

headline: Agricultural city being developed in Abu Dhabi to aid UAE's food security efforts
summary: In the era of smartphones and social media, in which many simply order groceries through a delivery app, the disconnect between humans and farms has never felt so pronounced.This may be about to change, as the future of farming takes shape in Abu Dhabi. An agricultural community, known as Qitaf City, twice the size of Monaco is being developed in Abu Dhabi to help boost the country's efforts to tackle food security.At four million square metres, the upcoming project will include villas, town houses and Emirati housing with farms alongside AgriTech projects.Shamsa Alfahim, chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Investment and Development (ADID) and managing director of Qitaf Holding, spoke to The National about the ambitious plans. She said she hopes to develop a community by attracting those who are interested in taking up farming while incorporating the latest technologies.“We're hopefully trying to target different university students or people who are interested in agriculture, and be able to give them this farm for their own use and giving them to the market,” she said, speaking to The National at Global Food Week.In a rapidly modernising country which has put AI at the forefront, the hope is the project will bring Emiratis back to their roots and allow them to contribute to the country's growing food ecosystem.“There's something very humble about being in this kind of ecosystem because it does ground you to your roots. It's not just agriculture any more – there's also aquaculture and agritech,” she said.The first project starting in the agriculture city will be growing potatoes using solar panels as part of the laboratory process. Urgent needMonths of supply chain instability with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz underlined the importance of food security for the UAE, a country that imports a majority of its food from abroad. The goal is to create a strategic hub for food security in Abu Dhabi.“We wanted to launch Qitaf to battle these new circumstances because we want to be resilient and self-sufficient within the UAE,” said Ms Alfahim.Qitaf City will be about 40 minutes from Abu Dhabi city, Al Ain and Dubai's Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC). The area, known as Al Haffar, is part of a wider master plan that includes a sports city. Etihad Rail's track runs alongside it, and in the future, she says, freight rail access will play a key role in logistics.“The new Etihad railway is going to pass by the area where Qitaf is located within Al Haffar city. So in terms of logistics it's going to be very strategically located because there's a very easy route of being able to transport the produce from Qitaf to other places in the UAE."A new chapterQitaf Holding has recently been established as the agricultural arm of ADID to “create an environment for food security” in the country. The agriculture city project is slated to launch in February.“The bigger master plan is actually creating a sustainable city that encompasses lots of different health points,” Ms Alfahim said. “A part of it is going to be a sports city, another is going to be a medical city, and the large majority is going to be housing and estates for the local community.”Qitaf Holding is also working with AG Groups on large-scale projects across countries in Africa and Asia. They launched a green corridor between Tanzania and the UAE during Global Food Week.“We can connect with farmers in Tanzania, give them a platform for exchanging their products, bring the their products to the UAE for processing and manufacturing, and re-export it from here,” said Ms Alfahim.“It's going to create a whole system. We want to do the same thing with Madagascar where we can bring vanilla from Madagascar into the UAE.”

headline: UAE's revised suicide law can 'reduce mental health stigma and improve support'
summary: Access to mental health support is poised to continue to improve following legal amendments to decriminalise attempted suicide, experts have said.The UAE announced the removal of criminal liability in an amendment to the country's Crimes and Penalties Law on Thursday. Previous legislation in 2020 gave judges the discretion to offer mental health treatment as an alternative to prison, although there had been confusion over the legal ramifications for people who tried to take their own lives.The change is expected to improve the chances of early intervention, ensuring care and support is given when needed to bolster suicide prevention.Dr Tina Mistry is a clinical psychologist and corporate wellbeing director at Al Kalma, a mental health platform in the UAE and Saudi Arabia. She said the legal change was a positive step. “The recent amendment decriminalising attempted suicide shows a real commitment to supporting people with mental health difficulties,” she said. “Until now, fear of a criminal case stopped many people from saying they were having suicidal thoughts. “Removing that fear should make it easier for people in distress to speak up and get help early.”Early intervention crucialEarly intervention is viewed as critical when signs of depression and anxiety appear, to prevent symptoms from deepening or developing into suicidal thoughts.Mental health services have been steadily improving in recent years.As more mental health and workplace wellbeing programmes have appeared in the corporate world, insurers have added mental health care to their coverage.Saudi German Hospital Dubai is one of the providers launching an on-site specialist mental health and wellness hub to coincide with World Mental Health Day on October 10.It is designed to end the fragmented experience many families face when navigating mental health care by bringing specialists together around a single shared care plan.Dr Ahmed Eissa, a psychiatrist and chief executive of Saudi German Health UAE, hopes the centre can help with early intervention.“There are a lot of people suffering without having the right support, drug diagnosis or services,” he said.“Part of it is related to the stigma itself of going into mental health facilities, the affordability and the number of healthcare providers in the field of mental health. For some, they have days of anxiety, stress, work burnout or marital and relationship, challenges.“If we can provide the service that will help the whole family as a unit of the community, this is the core objective of the hub itself.”Service accessServices for adults and older people include psychiatric assessment, medication management and individual therapy.It also offers treatment for depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and related conditions, as well as geriatric psychiatry, addiction support and family counselling.Recruitment of mental health specialists for the hub had been a challenge. “If we are talking about integrating the mental health team here, most front lines are related to nursing, so they should be trained very well," said Dr Eissa.“There is scarcity in mental health personnel, so we need to train most of the healthcare providers in all levels so that they act like filters.“Recruiting psychiatrists and specialists to come here was a little bit challenging, especially in different subspecialties. Ideally, in the future we'll recruit from our own trainees.”Nursing careA recent Global Mental Health Care Access and Affordability Benchmark report assessed access to care in 15 nations, including the UAE.The report compiled by Australian service provider TherapyNearMe.com assessed coverage, timeliness, availability, mental-health-specific unmet needs, provider fees and affordability.Eleven countries had compatible observations for psychologists, psychiatrists and mental health nurses. Five national mental health programmes were psychologist-led, five, including the UAE, were majority nurse-led, and one in Jordan was psychiatrist-led.Dr Mistry said plans to train 2,000 Abu Dhabi family doctors in mental health were a positive move towards improving access to care. “Official figures show around two thirds of the UAE's mental health workforce are nurses, which isn't quite the same as nurses leading care,” she said.“Nurses are a real strength, and often the healthcare professional a patient sees most. The risk is that they carry complex cases without enough supervision or specialists to turn to when needed.”Incentives to ask for helpClear directives under the UAE’s Crimes and Penalties Law should help relieve some of the prejudice against people living with mental illness, professionals said.In 2024, Dubai authorities dropped charges of attempted suicide against Irish citizen Tori Towey, an Emirates flight attendant.Charges stemmed from a domestic incident involving Irish national Ms Towey, 30, and her South African husband.The case attracted international media attention after being raised in the Irish Parliament, with an intervention by Taoiseach Simon Harris.Any threats of prosecution for similar cases should disappear under recent amendments.Marie Byrne, a therapist from Ireland who runs positive psychology sessions in Dubai for workplace wellness, said the legal amendments can help reduce the bias still associated with certain mental health conditions.“Prior to the Iran conflict, workplace wellness was really on the agenda, the sense now is that productivity and achievement has taken over,” she said.“With the amount of uncertainty for occupational security, there is a need for people to feel they have support.“Anxiety is more prevalent with uncertainty for the future, and people are in a kind of loop; they get exhausted with worry, and they're not sleeping properly either.“It's easy to see how someone could start to think, 'it's all getting on top of me'.”Ms Byrne was one of a cohort of mental health professionals who volunteered their services for the Emirates Foundation during the pandemic.They offered free support for those in crisis or living in isolation, anxiety and depression. It was a sign of changing attitudes towards mental health, she said.“There are now similar, more permanent support structures in place with the health authorities,” said Ms Byrne.“This legal amendment could be a real incentive for people to go for early intervention, before they get to where they're even thinking to end their own life.”“I really do think this can help remove some of the stigma that is still associated with mental health.”

headline: UAE economy grew in first half of 2026 despite impact of Iran war
summary: The UAE's real gross domestic product grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war.The non-oil sector's contribution to the GDP during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said in a statement on Friday.The results "reflect the continued diversification of the UAE's economic base and the growing role of non-oil activities", the FCSC said.Trade topped contributions to non-oil GDP at 16.2 per cent, followed by financial and insurance (15.2 per cent), construction (13.1 per cent), manufacturing (11.8) and real estate (7.9 per cent). Meanwhile, activities in the financial and insurance sector posted the highest growth rate in the six months through the end of June, rising by 14.8 per cent, the FCSC said. That was followed by information and communication (7.3 per cent), health and social work (6 per cent), construction (5.1 per cent), government (3.6 per cent) and real estate (2.3 per cent).The non-oil sector's "expanding contribution to economic activity demonstrates the diversity of growth drivers and supports sustainable and balanced growth across a broad range of economic sectors", the FCSC added.The UAE's GDP last year grew 6.2 per cent year-on-year to hit Dh1.9 trillion, as non-oil GDP jumped 6.8 per cent to Dh1.5 trillion.In the second quarter of the year, the UAE's real GDP hit Dh476.9 billion, a decline of 2.1 per cent annually. Non-oil activities also contracted by 1.1 per cent, as several economic sectors, particularly tourism, transport and trade, were affected by regional developments and disruption to travel.However, the non-oil sector has started to rebound. The seasonally adjusted S&P Global UAE Purchasing Managers' Index remained stable at 55.3 in September, the same as August, and well above the 50 mark that indicates growth in economic activity. That reading is “another indication that the non-oil economy has moved past the midyear slowdown linked to the Middle East conflict”, S&P said. Business activity in September increased rapidly and higher output requirements encouraged companies to expand purchasing activity and employment, with staffing numbers rising modestly last month, the index found. Demand conditions in the UAE non-oil private sector also continued to improve markedly in September, boosting pricing power and enabling companies to raise their selling prices at the fastest pace in more than 15 years, in response to higher input costs, the report found.

headline: Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival returns to Abu Dhabi with message of renewal
summary: Cinema cannot save the environment, but it can change the way we see it. That is the idea behind Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival, which returns to Abu Dhabi with a programme examining humanity's relationship with nature and the ways that relationship can be repaired.Now in its fifth iteration, the festival runs from Friday to Sunday at NYU Abu Dhabi, bringing together international documentaries, fiction, animation and conversations with filmmakers, scientists and conservationists.Organised in collaboration with Environment Agency Abu Dhabi, the festival this year has the theme Mend, which takes its name from the Arabic verb rammim, meaning to repair or restore something of value.Artistic director Nezar Andary says the theme reflects a philosophy that has guided the festival since 2020. He believes environmental cinema should encourage curiosity rather than overwhelm audiences with alarming statistics or instructions on how to live."I don't want an environmentalism that believes in some pristine, perfect version of nature," he tells The National. "Mending is something we're constantly doing, and it's something the Earth itself does."Al Sidr was inspired by a small environmental film festival that Andary attended at Princeton Public Library in the United States. He was impressed by its preference for creative documentaries over conventional environmental campaigning."The more creative, artistic documentary isn't force-feeding you an environmental ideology, but is actually creating a sense of intimacy and questioning," he says.Al Sidr has since welcomed more than 5,000 attendees and engaged 2,000 students from more than 20 schools across Abu Dhabi.This year's selection approaches ecology through scientific exploration, cultural heritage and conservation.Among the headline screenings is Ghost Elephants, a documentary by German filmmaker Werner Herzog. The National Geographic production, which premiered at the Venice International Film Festival, receives its Arabian Gulf premiere on Friday.Another highlight is Fire of Love, the Oscar-nominated 2022 documentary by Sara Dosa, which chronicles the lives of French volcanologists Katia and Maurice Krafft, whose fascination with volcanoes shaped their work and relationship."It's about two lovers who are studying volcanoes. And it's about love. It's about love of science," Andary says.Dosa's 2026 documentary Time and Water, which premiered at Sundance, will screen at the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi on Friday, accompanied by a free museum tour, and again on Sunday at NYU Abu Dhabi.The programme also includes Fungi: Web of Life, narrated by Icelandic musician Bjork, and Chuuraa, a short film by Evgenia Arbugaeva that premiered at this year's Berlin International Film Festival.Beyond documentaries, Andary is particularly enthusiastic about the restored 4K edition of Manthan, the 1976 Indian film by Shyam Benegal, which screens on Saturday.The film examines the formation of a dairy co-operative in rural India, connecting agriculture with questions of class, collective action and social change.Andary says environmental storytelling can extend to subjects that might not immediately appear to be ecological. At a previous edition, he screened Ken Loach's Kes, a British drama about a working-class boy and his relationship with a kestrel.He says both films address class and solidarity, issues that can also resonate with audiences in the UAE.Closer to home, the festival will premiere episodes of Conservation Diaries, a five-part documentary series produced by Connect with Nature, the youth environmental movement established by the Environment Agency Abu Dhabi and Emirates Nature–WWF.Filmed across the UAE's wadis, mangroves, coastlines and rural communities, the series follows scientists, volunteers and conservationists protecting biodiversity.It offers a practical interpretation of Mend, highlighting the patient work required to understand ecosystems and protect vulnerable species."They're the heroes on the ground who are tracking animals, who are working with citizen scientists," Andary says.A panel on Sunday will examine ecological restoration in the UAE, while other sessions explore water, fungi and environmental science.Saturday's family programme features international animated shorts alongside Fungi: Web of Life and an introduction to fungi by Dima Al Srouri, founder of Dubai venture MycoSphere, which develops materials using mycelium and agricultural waste.Andary hopes the festival encourages people to question their relationships with the natural world.Previous editions experimented with audience-led discussions instead of conventional expert panels, while one screening was accompanied by a meal prepared using food waste.Although he wishes this year's programme offered more interaction, Al Sidr will continue its educational activities through school visits across Abu Dhabi.Andary recalls how working on a documentary involving an ancient burial site in the UAE changed his perspective on wildlife. Learning that people used Socotra cormorant feathers in burials made him more attentive to the birds and their historical relationship with people."I listen more, I'm more attentive," he says.He believes such changes in perception can be as important as the practical lessons audiences take from a screening. The festival should begin conversations that continue beyond the cinema."Cinema is not going to heal the environment. We are," Andary says.Al Sidr Environmental Film Festival runs from October 9 to 11 at the Blue Hall, NYU Abu Dhabi. Tickets and the full programme are available at alsidrfestival.com

headline: 'Why would you need courage to speak the truth': Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
summary: The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to ⁠South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.The Nobel Committee said the 85-year-old had shown exceptional courage and integrity to ensure that war crimes and genocide were prosecuted and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. It also said she had demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career. The former UN human rights chief led the world body's Commission of Inquiry into the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year. The commission determined that war crimes had been committed by both Hamas and Israel in the wake of the attacks on October 7, 2023.In her first reaction to the announcement, Ms Pillay discussed the importance of that finding. "The last thing I did is deliver the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," she said to friends gathered in the German city of Nuremburg."One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage and you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's impartial decision making." She later dedicated the award to "all the survivors of international crimes, as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".In a message to world leaders, she said: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war."Israel ‌condemned the Nobel Committee for giving her the award. "The decision of the Nobel Committee is disgraceful and an endorsement for proponents of anti-Semitism, like Pillay herself," said Israel's ambassador to the UN in Geneva, Daniel Meron. "As the chair of ​the Commission of Inquiry, she led campaigns to undermine Israel's very existence, campaigns that whitewashed terrorism and manipulate the reality in pursuit of a well-known political agenda."The Nobel judges said Ms Pillay had enlarged the scope and impact of international law as a judge in the High Court in South Africa and at the International Criminal Court. "A common thread runs ⁠from her early work defending ​Nelson Mandela ⁠and ‌others who stood up against ​apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.Ms Pillay has "held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict", they said."Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time," the committee added. "Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world."The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented ​in ‌Oslo on ⁠December 10, the ​anniversary of the ​death ‌of Swedish industrialist ⁠Alfred Nobel, who founded the ⁠awards in his 1895 will.Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Ms Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988. She was the first non-white judge of the High Court of South Africa.The ​UN ⁠human rights office ​on Friday ⁠welcomed the award to Ms ⁠Pillay, ‌acknowledging ​her long-standing advocacy for human rights. "It is amazing news, we need more dedication and commitment to human ​rights," ‌Shabia ⁠Mantoo, ​spokeswoman ​for ‌the UN ⁠human rights office.“The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice.“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.”He said the committee wanted to remind the world that "the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently”, adding that peace "requires justice”.Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children’s rights activist.Last year’s peace prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her prize to US President Donald Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts ​in Venezuela.Mr Trump has again suggested he should be the recipient of the prize, although he acknowledged it was unlikely. Mr Trump, who this year has waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on ​Wednesday: "They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me."Since his ​return to the White House last year, Mr Trump has repeatedly ⁠said he deserves what may be the world's most prestigious award."It is about ​that time," Mr Trump said in the Oval Office. "But I was very honoured ​to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump."The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Mr Trump, though there is no way of verifying that.Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday, with the Swedish Academy recognising her experimental approach to writing and her ability to bring ancient Greek literature into the modern world.The 76-year-old author’s best-known works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox.The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.Francis Halzen won the physics prize for contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.The Chemistry prize went to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for work in non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.
body_text:
The 2026 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to ⁠South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

The Nobel Committee said the 85-year-old had shown exceptional courage and integrity to ensure that war crimes and genocide were prosecuted and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict. It also said she had demonstrated a firm moral compass in her long career.

The former UN human rights chief led the world body's Commission of Inquiry into the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year. The commission determined that war crimes had been committed by both Hamas and Israel in the wake of the attacks on October 7, 2023.

Narges Mohammadi's children tell of pain of separation

In her first reaction to the announcement, Ms Pillay discussed the importance of that finding. "The last thing I did is deliver the report on Gaza, naming what's happening there as genocide," she said to friends gathered in the German city of Nuremburg.

"One of the main reactions to that report was paying tribute to me for my courage and you can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth? You interpret the law, you look at all the facts, so it's impartial decision making."

She later dedicated the award to "all the survivors of international crimes, as well as to practitioners and defenders of international justice whose compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign".

In a message to world leaders, she said: "You are under legal obligation ... to protect human rights and refrain from war."

Israel ‌condemned the Nobel Committee for giving her the award. "The decision of the Nobel Committee is disgraceful and an endorsement for proponents of anti-Semitism, like Pillay herself," said Israel's ambassador to the UN in Geneva, Daniel Meron. "As the chair of ​the Commission of Inquiry, she led campaigns to undermine Israel's very existence, campaigns that whitewashed terrorism and manipulate the reality in pursuit of a well-known political agenda."

The Nobel judges said Ms Pillay had enlarged the scope and impact of international law as a judge in the High Court in South Africa and at the International Criminal Court.

"A common thread runs ⁠from her early work defending ​Nelson Mandela ⁠and ‌others who stood up against ​apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time," the committee said.

Ms Pillay has "held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict", they said.

"Navi Pillay is one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time," the committee added. "Her distinguished career reminds us of the need to support, fortify and expand the global rule of law. Navi Pillay’s commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world."

The prize, worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or about $1.2 million, is due to be presented ​in ‌Oslo on ⁠December 10, the ​anniversary of the ​death ‌of Swedish industrialist ⁠Alfred Nobel, who founded the ⁠awards in his 1895 will.

Born into an Indian Tamil family in Durban, South Africa, Ms Pillay founded her own law firm in 1967 and earned a doctorate from Harvard University in 1988. She was the first non-white judge of the High Court of South Africa.

The ​UN ⁠human rights office ​on Friday ⁠welcomed the award to Ms ⁠Pillay, ‌acknowledging ​her long-standing advocacy for human rights. "It is amazing news, we need more dedication and commitment to human ​rights," ‌Shabia ⁠Mantoo, ​spokeswoman ​for ‌the UN ⁠human rights office.

“The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack,” said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chairman of the Norwegian Nobel Committee. “We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice.

“Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.”

He said the committee wanted to remind the world that "the rule of law, national and international, underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently”, adding that peace "requires justice”.

Ahead of the award, there were wild swings in betting on the Polymarket platform, with Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of late Russian opposition leader Alexey Navalny emerging as the frontrunner overnight. An hour before the announcement, she was neck-and-neck with Mykola Kuleba, Ukrainian children’s rights activist.

Last year’s peace prize winner, Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her prize to US President Donald Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts ​in Venezuela.

Mr Trump has again suggested he should be the recipient of the prize, although he acknowledged it was unlikely.

Mr Trump, who this year has waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on ​Wednesday: "They have a ​reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me."

Since his ​return to the White House last year, Mr Trump has repeatedly ⁠said he deserves what may be the world's most prestigious award.

"It is about ​that time," Mr Trump said in the Oval Office. "But I was very honoured ​to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump."

The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Mr Trump, though there is no way of verifying that.

Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday, with the Swedish Academy recognising her experimental approach to writing and her ability to bring ancient Greek literature into the modern world.

The 76-year-old author’s best-known works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband and Nox.

The prize for physiology or medicine was awarded to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

Francis Halzen won the physics prize for contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.

The Chemistry prize went to Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai for work in non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Nobel Peace Prize award to Navi Pillay primarily through her own defense of her Gaza genocide finding and Israel's condemnation, with extensive verbatim quotes from both sides and minimal editorializing.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged term used by Israel's ambassador to condemn the Nobel Committee's decision; it is a direct quote but carries strong moral condemnation.
Highly charged accusation that frames the award as legitimizing anti-Semitism; direct quote from Israeli ambassador.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: support for those accused of anti-Semitism

loaded_language.explanation: Metaphorical and emotionally loaded phrase alleging deliberate cover-up of terrorism; direct quote from Israeli ambassador.
Accusatory language implying deliberate distortion; direct quote from Israeli ambassador.
Colloquial and slightly sensational term describing betting odds fluctuations; adds color but is not neutral.

omissions: No mention of the specific findings or details of the UN Commission of Inquiry report on Gaza beyond the genocide characterization.
No mention of Palestinian casualties or humanitarian situation in Gaza.
No mention of other international reactions beyond Israel and the UN human rights office.
No mention of the Nobel Committee's full citation or the exact wording of the award.
No mention of Pillay's role as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights beyond a brief reference.

headline: Saudi airline pilot among three killed in attacks on Riyadh airport
