headline: Riyadh airport attacked again after Houthi missile strike that killed 13 and injured hundreds
summary: Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was attacked again on Sunday after a missile strike by Yemen's Houthi rebels killed 13 people and injured more than 300, sparking global condemnation, including from the UN, the EU and the UAE.The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government said a projectile struck the airport's Terminal 4, causing a fire, while a missile was intercepted in the vicinity. Operations at the airport were suspended after Saturday's deadly attack. Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree earlier on Sunday issued a warning to "all air shipping companies, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace – as they are subject to targeting". India's ​embassy ​in Riyadh said on Sunday ⁠that an Indian citizen injured in Saturday's attack had died. "We ⁠are in touch with ​the ⁠family ‌and will provide ​all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains," the embassy said in a post on X.The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said Sunday's attack "resulted in injuries, and that an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities is under way".In a statement on Sunday, the Houthis said Riyadh airport was one of four Saudi targets struck in the previous 24 hours. They also claimed to have carried out attacks on Saudi oil company Aramco's Shugadam gas site and Tanajib oil refinery in the Eastern Province, as well as King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, none of which were confirmed by Saudi Arabia.UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by Saturday's attack.“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately,” Mr Guterres said in a statement.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the attack as an “appalling act of terror”, saying there could be no justification for indiscriminate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.Ms Kallas expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a quick recovery. She said she remained in close contact with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan.EU foreign ministers will discuss increasing tension in the region on Monday, Ms Kallas said, adding that improved co-ordination between the bloc’s Red Sea naval Operation Aspides and the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition was crucial.The UAE condemned the Houthi attacks in the strongest terms, saying they were a “flagrant violation” of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and threatened its security and stability.The UAE Foreign Ministry reaffirmed the country’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and support for all measures aimed at protecting the kingdom’s security and stability. It also extended condolences to the victims’ families and wished the injured a quick recovery.Pakistan and Turkey, which signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia in August, also condemned the attack.Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “completely unacceptable”, saying strikes on civilians and critical infrastructure must cease immediately. He reaffirmed Islamabad’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.Turkey's Foreign Ministry said in a statement: "Actions that threaten regional security and stability and undermine the international community’s joint efforts to establish peace must be ended immediately.""Turkey also reiterated its support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity." UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg described the attacks on Saudi Arabia as a “grave escalation” that threatened regional security, perpetuated violence and further complicated peace efforts in Yemen.“I repeat my call on [the Houthis] to cease these attacks,” Mr Grundberg said, repeating the need to respect international humanitarian law, including bans on directing attacks against civilians and civilian objects.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned what he called a “horrific terrorist attack” on the airport.“Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve,” Mr Netanyahu said in a statement.“Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East – one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, co-operation and prosperity for all the peoples of our region,” he said, extending condolences to the victims’ families and wishing the injured a full recovery.Russia also condemned the attack, with its Foreign Ministry saying the situation in the Middle East could be resolved only through diplomatic means that take into account the interests of all countries in the region, Russian news agency Interfax reported.Egypt condemned continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, describing them as a flagrant violation of international law. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Egypt was working to bring home the body of a citizen killed in the attack, who was identified as Azza Ramzy Mohamed Hassan, 28, a flight attendant who worked for Saudi airline flynas.British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled" by the attack on the airport. "My thoughts are with those families who have lost loved ones, and those injured in this horrific attack,” he said on X, urging British nationals to avoid the airport, follow advice from Saudi authorities and consult the UK government’s travel guidance for the kingdom.Kuwait condemned the attack as a violation of international law and international humanitarian law, warning that it posed a serious threat to civil aviation and civilians. It reaffirmed its solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said the kingdom’s security was integral to that of Kuwait and other Gulf states.Iraq also condemned the attack, calling for a comprehensive halt to military operations and urging all parties to spare civilians and civilian infrastructure. Baghdad repeated its support for dialogue and diplomacy as alternatives to military action.Syria described the attack as a violation of Saudi sovereignty and a threat to regional security and civil aviation. Its Foreign Ministry expressed condolences to Saudi Arabia and the families of the victims, including a Syrian national killed in the strike, and backed measures to protect the kingdom’s security.Qatar reaffirmed its solidarity with Saudi Arabia, describing the attacks as a “grave violation” of the kingdom’s sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security, civilian safety and air navigation.Jordan condemned the attack after a Jordanian citizen was reported among the dead and four were wounded. body_text:
Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was attacked again on Sunday after a missile strike by Yemen's Houthi rebels killed 13 people and injured more than 300, sparking global condemnation, including from the UN, the EU and the UAE.

The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's government said a projectile struck the airport's Terminal 4, causing a fire, while a missile was intercepted in the vicinity. Operations at the airport were suspended after Saturday's deadly attack.

Houthi military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree earlier on Sunday issued a warning to "all air shipping companies, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using Saudi airports and airspace – as they are subject to targeting".

EditorialIran cannot distance itself from outsourced violence

India's ​embassy ​in Riyadh said on Sunday ⁠that an Indian citizen injured in Saturday's attack had died. "We ⁠are in touch with ​the ⁠family ‌and will provide ​all support for ensuring the early repatriation of mortal remains," the embassy said in a post on X.

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said Sunday's attack "resulted in injuries, and that an assessment of the damage and verification of the safety of the facilities is under way".

In a statement on Sunday, the Houthis said Riyadh airport was one of four Saudi targets struck in the previous 24 hours. They also claimed to have carried out attacks on Saudi oil company Aramco's Shugadam gas site and Tanajib oil refinery in the Eastern Province, as well as King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, none of which were confirmed by Saudi Arabia.

UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres said he was “deeply shocked” by Saturday's attack.

“Attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a violation of international law. These attacks must cease immediately,” Mr Guterres said in a statement.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the attack as an “appalling act of terror”, saying there could be no justification for indiscriminate attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure.

Ms Kallas expressed solidarity with Saudi Arabia, offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a quick recovery. She said she remained in close contact with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan.

EU foreign ministers will discuss increasing tension in the region on Monday, Ms Kallas said, adding that improved co-ordination between the bloc’s Red Sea naval Operation Aspides and the Saudi-led Multinational Maritime Defence Coalition was crucial.

The UAE condemned the Houthi attacks in the strongest terms, saying they were a “flagrant violation” of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and threatened its security and stability.

The UAE Foreign Ministry reaffirmed the country’s full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and support for all measures aimed at protecting the kingdom’s security and stability. It also extended condolences to the victims’ families and wished the injured a quick recovery.

Pakistan and Turkey, which signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia in August, also condemned the attack.

Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called the attack “completely unacceptable”, saying strikes on civilians and critical infrastructure must cease immediately. He reaffirmed Islamabad’s solidarity with Saudi Arabia and its commitment to the kingdom’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security under the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement.

Turkey's Foreign Ministry said in a statement: "Actions that threaten regional security and stability and undermine the international community’s joint efforts to establish peace must be ended immediately."

"Turkey also reiterated its support for Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity."

UN special envoy for Yemen Hans Grundberg described the attacks on Saudi Arabia as a “grave escalation” that threatened regional security, perpetuated violence and further complicated peace efforts in Yemen.

“I repeat my call on [the Houthis] to cease these attacks,” Mr Grundberg said, repeating the need to respect international humanitarian law, including bans on directing attacks against civilians and civilian objects.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned what he called a “horrific terrorist attack” on the airport.

“Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve,” Mr Netanyahu said in a statement.

“Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East – one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, co-operation and prosperity for all the peoples of our region,” he said, extending condolences to the victims’ families and wishing the injured a full recovery.

Russia also condemned the attack, with its Foreign Ministry saying the situation in the Middle East could be resolved only through diplomatic means that take into account the interests of all countries in the region, Russian news agency Interfax reported.

Egypt condemned continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, describing them as a flagrant violation of international law. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Egypt was working to bring home the body of a citizen killed in the attack, who was identified as Azza Ramzy Mohamed Hassan, 28, a flight attendant who worked for Saudi airline flynas.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said he was "appalled" by the attack on the airport.

"My thoughts are with those families who have lost loved ones, and those injured in this horrific attack,” he said on X, urging British nationals to avoid the airport, follow advice from Saudi authorities and consult the UK government’s travel guidance for the kingdom.

Kuwait condemned the attack as a violation of international law and international humanitarian law, warning that it posed a serious threat to civil aviation and civilians. It reaffirmed its solidarity with Saudi Arabia and said the kingdom’s security was integral to that of Kuwait and other Gulf states.

Iraq also condemned the attack, calling for a comprehensive halt to military operations and urging all parties to spare civilians and civilian infrastructure. Baghdad repeated its support for dialogue and diplomacy as alternatives to military action.

Syria described the attack as a violation of Saudi sovereignty and a threat to regional security and civil aviation. Its Foreign Ministry expressed condolences to Saudi Arabia and the families of the victims, including a Syrian national killed in the strike, and backed measures to protect the kingdom’s security.

Qatar reaffirmed its solidarity with Saudi Arabia, describing the attacks as a “grave violation” of the kingdom’s sovereignty and a direct threat to regional security, civilian safety and air navigation.

Jordan condemned the attack after a Jordanian citizen was reported among the dead and four were wounded. Its Foreign Ministry said the Jordanian ambassador in Riyadh was co-ordinating with Saudi authorities to provide assistance and medical care.

Conveys serious alarm and urgency through a quoted official's characterization.
Employs strong, condemnatory language from a quoted official.

Context about the ongoing Saudi-led intervention in Yemen
Casualty figures from the Saudi-led coalition's operations in Yemen

headline: Trump revokes decades-old restrictions on US-Lebanon flights
summary: US President Donald Trump has lifted decades-old restrictions on flights between the US and Lebanon, removing a major obstacle to restoring direct air links.Mr Trump said restrictions imposed under four presidential determinations issued in 1985, 1992, 1998 and 2007 were “no longer necessary” to ensure the security of aircraft.He signed the decision on September 30 and it was published in the Federal Register.It follows a meeting between Mr Trump and Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House in July, during which Mr Aoun requested that the restrictions be lifted.Mr Aoun welcomed the move, describing it as “a sign of confidence in the measures taken by the Lebanese state to guarantee the security of civil aviation”.He thanked Mr Trump for responding favourably to his request, as well as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio for following up on the matter. Mr Aoun also reaffirmed Lebanon’s commitment to international civil aviation security standards and expressed hope that the decision would strengthen co-operation between Beirut and Washington.Lebanese ambassador to Washington, Nada Mouawad, also welcomed the decision, saying it “opens the door to the resumption of direct flights between Lebanon and the United States”.The restrictions were introduced in 1985 by the administration of president Ronald Reagan after the hijacking of TWA Flight 847 by alleged Hezbollah militants.The flight, travelling from Athens to Rome, was forced to land in Beirut. The hijackers killed a US Navy diver aboard the plane during the subsequent 17-day hostage crisis.Subsequent US administrations gradually eased the restrictions. In 1992, foreign carriers were permitted to transport cargo to Lebanon. In 1998, ticket sales to Lebanon and flights with stopovers were authorised, while a 2007 decision granted exemptions to certain American carriers operating under contracts with the US government.The measures continued to prevent the restoration of direct commercial air links between the two countries.Mr Trump's decision revokes all four presidential determinations and directs the US Secretary of Transportation to implement the change immediately, including by removing any conflicting regulations, rules or orders.However, the lifting of the restrictions does not mean direct commercial flights between the US and Lebanon will resume immediately.

headline: Manchester City block out the noise to defeat Liverpool at Anfield
summary: Manchester City completed a thumping win over Liverpool in an emotionally charged match at Anfield on Sunday. headline: Iran says US response to its proposal to reopen Hormuz was 'insufficient'
summary: DUBAI, Oct 11 (Reuters) - The United States' response to Iran's seven conditions in a proposal to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was "insufficient", Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, was quoted by state media on Sunday as saying. Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, to which the US later replied via Qatari intermediaries.
body_text:
DUBAI, Oct 11 (Reuters) - The United States' response to Iran's seven conditions in a proposal to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz was "insufficient", Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, was quoted by state media on Sunday as saying.

Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, to which the US later replied via Qatari intermediaries.

Washington needs to clarify the issues that remain unclear to Tehran, Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said, adding "we presented seven conditions to the Americans and clearly stated that the Strait of Hormuz would not be opened to them, and no negotiations would take place, until these conditions are met."

The White House did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Rezaei said Iran is "no longer in the process of responding to the Americans".

"In their response, they have accepted some of our conditions, while others remain unclear," he added.

Tehran said late in September that it had received a US response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed ceasefire in the Gulf, days after US President Donald Trump said he had rejected it.

Qatar and other mediators have transmitted messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

(Reporting by Elwely Elwelly, Yasmine Ghania, Menna Ala El Din and Steve Holland; Editing by Susan Fenton)

The adjective 'strategic' is an editorial descriptor emphasizing geopolitical importance rather than a neutral geographic label.
The word 'collapsed' implies failure and carries a negative connotation about the state of the truce.

loaded_language.explanation: This quoted phrase is vague and indirect, leaving unclear whether Iran has halted diplomacy entirely or merely stopped a specific response.

headline: Manchester City block out the noise to defeat Liverpool at Anfield
summary: Manchester City completed a thumping win over Liverpool in an emotionally charged match at Anfield on Sunday. In their first game since the Premier League's findings, City secured a 3-0 win over a 10-man Liverpool.The match was evenly balanced in the first half but took a decisive turn in the second after Ryan Gravenberch was shown a red card in the 62nd minute. Erling Haaland gave City the lead three minutes later before Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki completed a statement win.An independent commission found Manchester City guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period.The club have lodged an appeal against the verdict and continue to maintain their innocence, arguing that the commission's decision contains “clear material errors” and that City have evidence supporting their position.Liverpool fans, however, created a hostile atmosphere on Sunday with 60,000 in attendance. Home supporters drowned out the announcement of City's team ⁠with boos and chants."It looked like the fans had the time of their lives... I think my Dad enjoyed himself!"Erling Haaland on celebrating with the fans and his father after scoring at Anfield. pic.twitter.com/ODEi78AWPF— Sky Sports Premier League (@SkySportsPL) October 11, 2026Victory gave City six wins from six and moved them three points clear of Arsenal on 18 points, providing an impressive response ​on the pitch after a turbulent period away from it. Liverpool are ninth after their first league loss of the season.Enzo Maresca's side stood ​firm against Liverpool's early pressure and a fevered atmosphere before taking control after Gravenberch was sent off in the 62nd minute for a second booking following a foul on Doku.Haaland then struck three minutes later, smashing a left-footed shot past Alisson after Doku worked the ball into the box and his attempted shot was deflected into the path of the Norwegian.Doku doubled the lead in the 68th minute with ​a long-range shot that curled ‌into the far ⁠top corner. Cherki completed the ​rout in the 78th minute when he ​let ‌the ball roll through to Josko Gvardiol before turning into ⁠the box to meet his teammate's pass and ⁠slot the ball home.After the match, Haaland said the team showed amazing character.“Every single person [who is] part of Man City, and every fan, this is a lovely moment that will stay with us for a long time,” Haaland told sky Sports.“It was tough, it was hard but we showed amazing character from back to front. So proud of everyone.“It's always tough to come here, if you look at the record, it's tough. “Important to stay strong mentally, stick together and do what you can do. And the thing we can do something about is to play good football and fight together. That's the only thing we can do.”City midfielder Elliot Anderson echoed Haaland's sentiments.“A tough place to come and we stuck together and fought for each other. We've showed courage,” Anderson told Sky Sports.“It was more than normal, arriving into Anfield and the first 10 minutes of the game. We did well to quieten the crowd. Struggled first half but second we were better and then the goals came.“I enjoy the crowd, the noise, I thrive on it and that's when I come alive. It gives me confidence.”

headline: Madinet Masr’s SAFE offers fractional real estate investment from EGP 5,000
summary: Egyptian real estate developer Madinet Masr has launched a new phase of SAFE Investments, its fractional real estate investment platform, offering investors access to selected property opportunities with investments starting at EGP 5,000 per share. The offering recorded strong initial demand, with more than 3,100 investment shares sold on the first day, reflecting investor interest in more accessible and flexible ways to participate in Egypt’s real estate market. Through its digital platform, SAFE enables investors to gain fractional exposure to selected real estate assets without purchasing an entire property. Investors make a one-time payment for their investment shares, with no subsequent instalments or payment schedules, providing a simpler approach to real estate investment. The platform offers access to selected real estate opportunities from leading developers across Egypt, including Madinet Masr and other developers. Since its launch, SAFE has expanded its investor base and investment activity. To date, the platform has sold more than 23,000 investment shares to over 5,200 investors, while more than 40% of its investors have returned to invest in additional opportunities, indicating repeat-investment activity and continued engagement with the platform. SAFE currently manages more than EGP 1bn in assets under management and has distributed over EGP 50m in rental income to investors. Its digital reach has also grown, with the SAFE application recording more than 175,000 installs. A key component of SAFE’s offering is its investor-to-investor resale marketplace, which allows investors to offer some or all of their investment shares for resale before the targeted exit of the underlying asset, providing an additional option for liquidity. To date, the marketplace has facilitated the resale of more than 1,900 investment shares, with selected transactions recording annualised returns exceeding 40%. By combining fractional ownership, access to income-generating real estate opportunities, digital accessibility and a dedicated resale marketplace, SAFE offers an alternative model for participating in property investment. The platform provides investors with exposure to features traditionally associated with real estate investment, including asset ownership, rental income, potential capital appreciation and greater flexibility in reselling their shares. With investment opportunities starting at EGP 5,000, SAFE aims to broaden access to selected real estate assets and enable a wider segment of individuals to participate in fractional property ownership.

headline: Aqar Exit records EGP 8.8bn in deals as property listings reach EGP 124bn
summary: Aqar Exit, a platform specialising in Egypt’s real estate contract assignment market, recorded 35,184 purchase requests in September, while 3,618 new units were listed on the platform, according to its second monthly Real Estate Assignment Market Index report. Average daily purchase requests rose 58% to 1,060, up from 671 in the previous period, while the average number of deals closed per week increased 148% to 85, compared with 34 previously. Daily new listings remained broadly stable, averaging 109 units against 112 in the previous period. Mahmoud Ammar, founder and chairman of Aqar Exit, said demand was accelerating faster than the growth in new listings, providing further insight into purchasing power, buyer behaviour and transaction activity in the assignment market. Aqar Exit listings reach EGP 124bn As of October 8, 2026, the platform had 8,534 units listed or under review, with an estimated market value of EGP 124bn. Of these, 7,801 were active listings, with original contract values totalling around EGP 89.2bn. Since its launch, Aqar Exit has registered 14,845 assignment records involving 11,833 sellers, alongside 67,013 purchase requests from 32,870 buyers. Listings received 925,982 views over the past 30 days and were added to users’ favourites 61,666 times. Meanwhile, 32.3% of buyers inquired about more than one unit. The platform recorded 638 closed deals since launch, with an estimated market value of EGP 8.8bn. Of these, 404 were closed during the past month, compared with 233 in the previous period. Units spent an average of 18 days on the market before deals were closed, while 25% of transactions were completed within nine days or less. Demand was strongest for units priced below EGP 3m, which averaged 11.1 purchase requests each, compared with 2.2 requests for properties priced above EGP 20m. Average available cash liquidity among buyers stood at around EGP 1m, while their average affordable monthly instalment was EGP 50,000. These figures raise questions about whether prices of newly launched properties align with the purchasing power and financing capacity of some buyers. Average payments reach 26.6% before assignment On the supply side, the average amount paid against the original contract value when units were listed for assignment stood at 26.6%. Meanwhile, 90.1% of cases with available contract-age data involved units listed within the first two years after the original contracts were signed. A total of 2,695 sellers, representing 34.6% of listed units, were willing to forgo part of their financial entitlements to exit their contracts faster. In addition, 19.8% of sellers in the sample with available payment-status data had already fallen behind on instalments. Willingness to accept reduced entitlements declined as the proportion of the unit’s value already paid increased. The share stood at 39.2% among sellers who had paid less than 20% of the unit’s value, 34.5% among those who had paid 20–40%, and 26.8% among those who had paid more than 40%. The report also estimated paper gains of around EGP 26bn, reflecting the difference between original contract prices and the estimated market values of listed units. Their continued availability for assignment highlights the role of liquidity needs and the timing of cash requirements in sellers’ decisions to exit contracts. Buyers using Gulf-based phone numbers accounted for 13.3% of total buyers on the platform, rising to 14.8% among new buyers during the latest month. Ammar said regular monitoring of the assignment market provides a clearer picture of supply and demand, deal closure rates and buyer interest across price segments, helping market participants better understand buyer and seller behaviour.

headline: Developers call for hybrid real estate regulatory model drawing on UAE, Saudi and UK experiences
summary: Developers operating in the Egyptian market are calling for a comprehensive real estate regulatory framework combining the UAE’s project oversight and escrow accounts, Saudi Arabia’s pre-licensing requirements for off-plan sales, and the UK’s emphasis on transparency and consumer protection. The call comes amid renewed government efforts to tighten oversight of the real estate market following recent directives from President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi to regulate the sector and take firm action against developers that fail to deliver projects on schedule. With developers selling units before construction is completed and offering instalment plans extending over several years, the sector increasingly depends on regulators’ ability to ensure timely delivery, protect buyers’ savings and maintain confidence in the market. As investment volumes grow and residential developments become increasingly complex, industry experts argue that effective regulation must extend beyond sales and licensing to cover project execution, financial oversight, disclosure requirements and dispute-resolution mechanisms. International experience offers several approaches to addressing these challenges, although experts caution that Egypt should develop a framework suited to its own market rather than replicate another country’s system wholesale. UAE model: Centralised oversight and escrow accounts Alaa Fekry, chairperson of Beta Egypt and vice chairperson of the Real Estate Development Committee at the Egyptian Businessmen’s Association, said Dubai offers one of the region’s most established models for real estate regulation. The UAE model combines project registration and licensing, developer oversight, regulation of off-plan sales and safeguards for buyers’ funds, with the Dubai Land Department and other relevant authorities playing key supervisory roles. Escrow accounts are among the system’s main pillars. Developers selling properties off-plan are required to establish separate escrow accounts for individual projects, with withdrawals subject to regulatory controls designed to ensure that buyers’ payments are directed towards the developments for which they were collected. This approach helps reduce the risk of developers diverting funds from one project to finance another, while strengthening the link between customer payments and construction progress. The model also relies on digital services and greater access to information, allowing buyers to verify project licensing, check development status and obtain relevant details before committing their money. Fekry said Egypt could benefit from adopting similar safeguards, particularly as off-plan sales remain an important source of financing for residential developments. However, implementing such measures would require clear rules governing the release of funds, effective monitoring and sufficient institutional capacity to supervise projects throughout their development. Saudi Arabia: Licensing before off-plan sales Saudi Arabia offers another approach through the General Real Estate Authority and the Wafi programme, which regulates off-plan sales and leasing. Under this framework, developers and projects must meet regulatory requirements before properties can be marketed for off-plan sale. The system also incorporates project-specific escrow accounts and controls on the use of buyers’ payments. This means that off-plan sales are treated as a regulated activity requiring prior approval, rather than simply a marketing and contractual process between developers and customers. The framework also provides mechanisms for addressing troubled projects, offering a more structured approach to managing delays and protecting buyers when developments encounter difficulties. Fekry said the Saudi experience provides useful lessons for Egypt, particularly in strengthening pre-sale requirements and ensuring that developers demonstrate their readiness to execute projects before collecting payments from customers. For Egypt, such an approach could help address concerns over projects being marketed before developers have met essential requirements relating to land ownership, permits, designs and implementation capacity. UK model: Transparency and accountability While the UAE and Saudi models place considerable emphasis on project oversight and financial safeguards, the UK experience offers lessons in transparency, consumer rights and accountability after a sale. Tarek Eid, board member of the Arab Kuwaiti Group and executive director of its real estate arm, Beit Al-Istithmar Al-Arabi, said the British approach places importance on clear standards governing property sales, contractual obligations, delivery and after-sales services. The system also provides channels for buyers to raise complaints with specialised bodies over issues such as construction quality and developer performance, alongside continuing developer responsibilities for after-sales services. Eid said these principles are relevant to Egypt, where buyers need reliable information about project specifications, delivery schedules and contractual commitments. Greater transparency could also help reduce disputes arising from discrepancies between advertised properties and delivered units, as well as delays and unclear contractual terms. What regulatory model is best suited to Egypt? Fekry argued that Egypt should develop a hybrid regulatory model combining key elements of the UAE and Saudi experiences while incorporating international best practices in transparency and consumer protection. The proposed framework would centre on a strong, independent regulatory authority responsible for licensing, inspections, developer supervision and monitoring project implementation. It would also introduce escrow accounts gradually, particularly for off-plan developments, with withdrawals linked to actual construction progress. Such an approach would seek to ensure that customer payments are used for their intended purpose while allowing developers to access funds in line with clearly defined implementation milestones. Gradual implementation to avoid disrupting investment Industry executives warned that regulatory reform should be introduced gradually to avoid placing excessive burdens on developers or disrupting investment and construction activity. Fekry recommended beginning with large developments and off-plan projects while granting companies a transition period to comply with the new requirements. A phased approach could allow regulators to test oversight mechanisms, strengthen enforcement capacity and address implementation challenges before extending the framework across the wider market. Eid said reform should begin with mandatory project licensing before sales, supported by a comprehensive file covering land ownership, permits, project costs, financing arrangements, construction schedules and the developer’s capacity to complete the development. He also called for an early-warning system and a digital platform to monitor construction progress, financial liquidity and expected delivery dates, while classifying projects according to their risk levels. Such tools could help authorities identify potential delays and financial difficulties before they develop into major problems for buyers. Regulation should also extend to advertising and brokerage activities, including measures to prevent the promotion of unlicensed projects and misleading property advertisements. Eid proposed establishing a specialised body to protect real estate consumers and respond quickly to complaints involving delayed delivery, discrepancies in property specifications and misleading marketing. He also stressed that regulators should have mechanisms to rescue distressed projects before resorting to punitive measures, where feasible. These could include restructuring, replacing contractors or management teams, or transferring projects to qualified developers capable of completing construction. Balancing buyer protection with market stability Egypt’s regulatory challenge is to strengthen buyer protection without undermining the financing mechanisms on which much of the property development sector relies. Off-plan sales and instalment-based payment plans help developers finance construction and enable buyers to spread payments over several years. However, without effective oversight, these arrangements can expose customers to delays, incomplete projects and uncertainty over how their payments are used. A stronger framework would therefore need to balance financial safeguards with practical financing requirements while ensuring consistent enforcement across developers and projects. The experiences of the UAE, Saudi Arabia and the UK suggest that no single measure can address every risk. Licensing, escrow accounts, transparent disclosure, construction monitoring and accessible dispute-resolution mechanisms are most effective when they operate as parts of an integrated system. For Egypt, the priority is to establish a regulatory structure that combines preventive oversight with effective enforcement and clear accountability, while introducing changes at a pace that allows the market to adapt.

headline: Al Ahly celebrates October War victory with cultural, educational programme
summary: Al Ahly Sporting Club marked Egypt’s October 1973 War victory with a programme of cultural, educational and community activities across its branches, bringing members together through concerts, children’s workshops, young talent showcases and historical visits. Organised by the club’s auxiliary committees, the celebrations highlighted Al Ahly’s role beyond the sporting arena, using music, education and community engagement to commemorate a defining chapter in Egypt’s national history. Al Ahly’s Sheikh Zayed branch hosted on October 8 the “Egyptian Melodies” concert, as familiar patriotic songs, including “Ya Habibti Ya Masr” and “Fiha Haga Helwa”, brought music and national memory together, as part of the club’s commemorations of Egypt’s October War victory. Organised by the Cultural Committee, headed by Khaled Galal, under the supervision of the Supreme Committee for Auxiliary Committees, led by engineer Walid Mabrouk, and in cooperation with the Executive Administration, headed by Executive Director Khaled Morsi, the concert formed part of a broader programme of cultural, artistic and educational activities across Al Ahly’s branches. The programme included children’s workshops, young talent showcases and historical visits, highlighting the club’s role in connecting its members with national occasions and offering experiences beyond sports. The celebrations also underscored Al Ahly’s broader social and cultural role, creating opportunities for members of different ages and interests to engage with culture, history and community activities. When culture becomes a way to remember Mariam Samih, rapporteur of the Cultural Committee at Al Ahly’s Sheikh Zayed branch, said the October Victory concert attracted a large number of club members, reflecting their interest in the activities organised across the club’s branches. She stressed that committee rapporteurs and members had an important responsibility to serve the club’s members, adding that Al Ahly’s role extended beyond sports to encompass social and cultural responsibilities. The Cultural Committee contributes to this broader mission by organising activities that respond to members’ interests. Samih emphasised that the October War victory were too important a national occasion to pass without celebration, particularly at the beginning of a new committee year. She noted that organising events to mark the anniversary had long been an established tradition at Al Ahly. She added that the committee carefully selects musical ensembles and singers whose performances suit the significance of the occasion and the club’s standing. It often chooses groups associated with the Cairo Opera House and Arabic music, whose performances have received positive feedback from members. The committee also seeks to link its activities to national occasions and significant events throughout the year. Samih concluded by expressing her pride in belonging to Al Ahly, describing it as a major institution whose role extends well beyond sports. Mahmoud El Khatib A first appearance at Al Ahly For the “Egyptian Melodies” ensemble, the concert marked a new experience: its first performance at an Al Ahly branch. Led by maestro Mazen Daraz, the ensemble presented a programme of patriotic songs and familiar Egyptian melodies. The performers included Mariam Essmat, Malak Hany, Sherouk Wael, Jenna El-Gendy, El-Sayed Rizk, Ziad Wael, Hazem Emad and Mohamed Nabil. The ensemble regularly performs at El Sawy Culturewheel and the Cairo Opera House, and its members include graduates of music institutes and conservatories. Daraz said preparations began with selecting the programme and rehearsing the songs ahead of the performance. He expressed his pleasure at the ensemble’s first appearance at the Sheikh Zayed branch and welcomed the positive reception and feedback from attendees. The choice of music was central to the evening. Patriotic songs carry associations that extend beyond their melodies, evoking shared memories and moments in Egypt’s national history. Performed before an audience gathered to commemorate the October War victory, they offered a cultural way of engaging with the anniversary. Rather than treating the occasion solely as a historical date, the concert brought its significance into the present through a live performance that club members could experience together. Activities across Al Ahly’s branches Walid Mabrouk, head of Al Ahly Club’s Supreme Committee for Auxiliary Committees, said the celebrations marking the October War victory reflected the club’s commitment to expanding its cultural, educational and community role, in line with the vision and directives of club president Mahmoud El Khatib and the objectives of the “Ahly Family” programme. Mabrouk added that the programme extended beyond musical performances to include educational workshops, historical visits and opportunities for young members to showcase their talents. He noted that the auxiliary committees, under the supervision of the Supreme Committee for Auxiliary Committees and in cooperation with the club’s Executive Administration, sought to organise a comprehensive range of activities that brought members together, strengthened their connection with Al Ahly and highlighted the club’s role beyond sporting competitions. Walid Mabrouk At the Sheikh Zayed branch, the Children’s Committee, headed by Dina Amer, organised a workshop in which children made and painted model aeroplanes. The programme also included an educational video about the October War and a quiz for children aged nine to 14. The activities aimed to introduce children to the events of the war through interactive experiences suited to their age group. The Pioneers Committee, headed by Fouad Ismail, also organised a visit to the October War Panorama in New Cairo, giving participants an opportunity to learn about the history of the war and revisit its events through a direct educational experience. As part of efforts to discover and nurture young talent, the Children’s Committee gave gifted young club members the opportunity to participate in concerts celebrating the October War victory, performing alongside the Basma band at the Nasr City and Gezira branches. These events provided children with a platform to showcase their artistic abilities and encouraged their participation in the club’s cultural activities. Khaled Galal Meanwhile, the Cultural Committee, headed by Khaled Galal, organised a series of musical performances across the club’s branches. These included the “Egyptian Melodies” concert at the Sheikh Zayed branch on October 8; performances by the Ashaq El-Nagham ensemble, led by Dr Mohamed Abdel Sattar, at the Gezira branch on October 8 and the New Cairo branch on October 9; and a performance by the Sohbet El-Simsimia ensemble at the Nasr City branch on October 9. Mabrouk emphasised that delivering a programme of this diversity required close coordination among the club’s various departments, including Public Relations, Security and Services, under the leadership of Executive Director Khaled Morsi. He said this cooperation helped ensure the smooth organisation of the events and provided suitable conditions for members to participate in cultural and community activities. He added that these efforts reflected the Al Ahly Board of Directors’ commitment to implementing the objectives of the “Ahly Family” programme. Mabrouk concluded that the auxiliary committees sought to make national occasions meaningful experiences for members of different ages and interests, while reinforcing the club’s role as an institution that brings its community together through sports, culture, education and community engagement. Mariam Samih A role beyond the sporting arena The October commemorations brought together music, education, talent development and historical remembrance, offering members different ways to engage with the anniversary. While the Cultural Committee used live performances to connect audiences with Egypt’s musical heritage and national memory, the Children’s and Pioneers Committees approached the occasion through educational, artistic and historical activities. At Sheikh Zayed, the “Egyptian Melodies” concert illustrated how music could bring members together. On stage, performers delivered familiar patriotic songs, while members of the audience gathered to share the experience. Elsewhere across the club, committees translated the same commemoration into opportunities for learning, artistic expression and historical engagement. Through this combination of cultural performances, children’s activities and historical visits, Al Ahly’s October programme demonstrated how a sporting institution can also provide space for cultural participation, talent development and shared experiences among its members.

headline: 2nd super tanker hits naval mine in Strait of Hormuz: IRGC
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 11 (MNA) – The IRGC Navy’s public relations office announced that a super tanker exploded and caught fire in its engine room after striking a sea mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz earlier on Sunday.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 11 (MNA) – The IRGC Navy’s public relations office announced that a super tanker exploded and caught fire in its engine room after striking a sea mine in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz earlier on Sunday.

The IRGC Navy said the super tanker, which was carrying crude oil and attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz, had switched off all of its navigation systems and violated the rules governing passage through the strait. It said the incident occurred after the vessel traveled through an unauthorized route.

According to the IRGC Navy, this was the third tanker identified as violating the rules that had struck sea mines along an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire since the previous day.

The IRGC Navy warned that all vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that switch off their navigation and identification systems would be identified as hostile and would face a forceful and decisive response.

analysis.framing: The article presents the tanker incident entirely through the IRGC Navy's public relations office, framing the vessel as a rule-violating intruder that was legitimately struck by a sea mine.

loaded_language.quote: violated the rules governing passage through the strait
loaded_language.explanation: States a contested legal characterization as established fact, adopting the IRGC's framing without attribution to an independent source.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: which the IRGC said had violated the rules governing passage through the strait

loaded_language.explanation: Presents the IRGC's designation of the route as settled fact rather than an assertion by one party to the incident.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: a route the IRGC described as unauthorized

loaded_language.explanation: Escalatory security terminology that frames civilian vessels as military threats.
Vague, militaristic phrasing that signals threat without specifying what action would be taken.

omissions: Identity, nationality, or flag state of the tanker or its crew
Any statement from the vessel's owner, operator, or flag state
Independent or third-party confirmation of a mine strike
Details on casualties, injuries, or environmental damage
Any denial or alternative account of the incident

headline: Iran says US response to proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz is insufficient

They have given their reply, and we consider it insufficient. They must clarify the issues that remain ambiguous to us.” Tehran effectively blocked the strait by attacking ships and laying mines after being attacked by Israel and the US in February at the start of the Iran war. The US has retaliated by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports. Iran and the US exchanged proposals to end the conflict through mediators during the UN General Assembly at the end of September. body_text:
Iran sent seven conditions to the US for reopening the Strait of Hormuz but the American response has been "insufficient", the head of the Supreme ⁠National ​Security Council told state media.

Mohsen Rezaei said Washington had approached Tehran through three channels over the past two months – Pakistan, Qatar and Iraq – asking Iran to present its proposals for reopening the strategic waterway.

“About two weeks ago, we communicated seven conditions to the Americans, stating explicitly that until these conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened to them and no negotiations will take place,” Mr Rezaei said.

“The Americans have now responded. While they have accepted some of our conditions, others remain unresolved.

“We are no longer in the process of responding to the Americans. They have given their reply, and we consider it insufficient. They must clarify the issues that remain ambiguous to us.”

Tehran effectively blocked the strait by attacking ships and laying mines after being attacked by Israel and the US in February at the start of the Iran war. The US has retaliated by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports.

Iran and the US exchanged proposals to end the conflict through mediators during the UN General Assembly at the end of September. Sources close to the Iranian delegation and western diplomats told The National at the time that Tehran offered no concessions from its publicly stated position and was waiting for Washington to respond to demands presented at the talks.

Mr Rezaei said Iran could derive economic benefits from controlling the strait, describing it as a major national asset.

“The Gulf cannot be secure without Iran’s management of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. “We do not merely mean closing the passage or collecting transit tolls; our interests extend far beyond that. Of course, we can certainly generate economic benefits from the Strait of Hormuz."

The US has rejected Tehran's proposal that Iran and Oman, which sits on the southern side of the strait, should jointly manage the waterway, saying ships should have free passage under international law.

analysis.framing: The article frames the story around Iran's rejection of the US response to its seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, presenting Iranian official statements alongside US and international-law positions.

loaded_language.quote: Tehran effectively blocked the strait by attacking ships and laying mines
loaded_language.explanation: The adverb 'effectively' and the active-voice verbs 'attacking' and 'laying mines' present Iran's actions as deliberate and aggressive, while the surrounding clause 'after being attacked by Israel and the US' is passive and does not name an agent.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Iran blocked the strait after Israel and the US attacked it; ships were attacked and mines were laid.

loaded_language.quote: The US has retaliated by imposing a blockade of Iranian ports.
loaded_language.explanation: 'Retaliated' frames the US blockade as a response to Iranian action, implying a cycle of escalation in which the US move is reactive rather than initiating.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: The US imposed a blockade of Iranian ports.

loaded_language.quote: Tehran offered no concessions from its publicly stated position
loaded_language.explanation: The phrase 'no concessions' is a characterization of Iran's negotiating stance that is attributed to unnamed sources, and it carries a negative connotation of inflexibility.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Tehran maintained its publicly stated position.

omissions: The specific content of the seven conditions Iran sent to the US.
The specific US conditions or response that Iran deemed insufficient.
The number or identity of the conditions the US accepted versus those left unresolved.
Any US official statement or reaction to Rezaei's remarks.
The impact of the strait closure on global oil prices or shipping.
The number of ships attacked or mines laid, or any casualties.
The legal basis or international reaction to the US blockade of Iranian ports.

headline: Madinet Masr’s SAFE offers fractional real estate investment from EGP 5,000
summary: Egyptian real estate developer Madinet Masr has launched a new phase of SAFE Investments, its fractional real estate investment platform, offering investors access to selected property opportunities with investments starting at EGP 5,000 per share. The offering recorded strong initial demand, with more than 3,100 investment shares sold on the first day, reflecting investor interest in more accessible and flexible ways to participate in Egypt’s real estate market. Through its digital platform, SAFE enables investors to gain fractional exposure to selected real estate assets without purchasing an entire property. Investors make a one-time payment for their investment shares, with no subsequent instalments or payment schedules, providing a simpler approach to real estate investment. The platform offers access to selected real estate opportunities from leading developers across Egypt, including Madinet Masr and other developers. Since its launch, SAFE has expanded its investor base and investment activity. To date, the platform has sold more than 23,000 investment shares to over 5,200 investors, while more than 40% of its investors have returned to invest in additional opportunities, indicating repeat-investment activity and continued engagement with the platform. SAFE currently manages more than EGP 1bn in assets under management and has distributed over EGP 50m in rental income to investors. Its digital reach has also grown, with the SAFE application recording more than 175,000 installs. A key component of SAFE’s offering is its investor-to-investor resale marketplace, which allows investors to offer some or all of their investment shares for resale before the targeted exit of the underlying asset, providing an additional option for liquidity. To date, the marketplace has facilitated the resale of more than 1,900 investment shares, with selected transactions recording annualised returns exceeding 40%. By combining fractional ownership, access to income-generating real estate opportunities, digital accessibility and a dedicated resale marketplace, SAFE offers an alternative model for participating in property investment. The platform provides investors with exposure to features traditionally associated with real estate investment, including asset ownership, rental income, potential capital appreciation and greater flexibility in reselling their shares. With investment opportunities starting at EGP 5,000, SAFE aims to broaden access to selected real estate assets and enable a wider segment of individuals to participate in fractional property ownership.

headline: Aqar Exit records EGP 8.8bn in deals as property listings reach EGP 124bn
summary: Aqar Exit, a platform specialising in Egypt’s real estate contract assignment market, recorded 35,184 purchase requests in September, while 3,618 new units were listed on the platform, according to its second monthly Real Estate Assignment Market Index report. Average daily purchase requests rose 58% to 1,060, up from 671 in the previous period, while the average number of deals closed per week increased 148% to 85, compared with 34 previously. Daily new listings remained broadly stable, averaging 109 units against 112 in the previous period. Mahmoud Ammar, founder and chairman of Aqar Exit, said demand was accelerating faster than the growth in new listings, providing further insight into purchasing power, buyer behaviour and transaction activity in the assignment market. Aqar Exit listings reach EGP 124bn As of October 8, 2026, the platform had 8,534 units listed or under review, with an estimated market value of EGP 124bn. Of these, 7,801 were active listings, with original contract values totalling around EGP 89.2bn. Since its launch, Aqar Exit has registered 14,845 assignment records involving 11,833 sellers, alongside 67,013 purchase requests from 32,870 buyers. Listings received 925,982 views over the past 30 days and were added to users’ favourites 61,666 times. Meanwhile, 32.3% of buyers inquired about more than one unit. The platform recorded 638 closed deals since launch, with an estimated market value of EGP 8.8bn. Of these, 404 were closed during the past month, compared with 233 in the previous period. Units spent an average of 18 days on the market before deals were closed, while 25% of transactions were completed within nine days or less. Demand was strongest for units priced below EGP 3m, which averaged 11.1 purchase requests each, compared with 2.2 requests for properties priced above EGP 20m. Average available cash liquidity among buyers stood at around EGP 1m, while their average affordable monthly instalment was EGP 50,000. These figures raise questions about whether prices of newly launched properties align with the purchasing power and financing capacity of some buyers. Average payments reach 26.6% before assignment On the supply side, the average amount paid against the original contract value when units were listed for assignment stood at 26.6%. Meanwhile, 90.1% of cases with available contract-age data involved units listed within the first two years after the original contracts were signed. A total of 2,695 sellers, representing 34.6% of listed units, were willing to forgo part of their financial entitlements to exit their contracts faster. In addition, 19.8% of sellers in the sample with available payment-status data had already fallen behind on instalments. Willingness to accept reduced entitlements declined as the proportion of the unit’s value already paid increased. The share stood at 39.2% among sellers who had paid less than 20% of the unit’s value, 34.5% among those who had paid 20–40%, and 26.8% among those who had paid more than 40%. The report also estimated paper gains of around EGP 26bn, reflecting the difference between original contract prices and the estimated market values of listed units. Their continued availability for assignment highlights the role of liquidity needs and the timing of cash requirements in sellers’ decisions to exit contracts. Buyers using Gulf-based phone numbers accounted for 13.3% of total buyers on the platform, rising to 14.8% among new buyers during the latest month. Ammar said regular monitoring of the assignment market provides a clearer picture of supply and demand, deal closure rates and buyer interest across price segments, helping market participants better understand buyer and seller behaviour.

headline: Developers call for hybrid real estate regulatory model drawing on UAE, Saudi and UK experiences
summary: Developers operating in the Egyptian market are calling for a comprehensive real estate regulatory framework combining the UAE’s project oversight and escrow accounts, Saudi Arabia’s pre-licensing requirements for off-plan sales, and the UK’s emphasis on transparency and consumer protection. The call comes amid renewed government efforts to tighten oversight of the real estate market following recent directives from President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi to regulate the sector and take firm action against developers that fail to deliver projects on schedule. With developers selling units before construction is completed and offering instalment plans extending over several years, the sector increasingly depends on regulators’ ability to ensure timely delivery, protect buyers’ savings and maintain confidence in the market. As investment volumes grow and residential developments become increasingly complex, industry experts argue that effective regulation must extend beyond sales and licensing to cover project execution, financial oversight, disclosure requirements and dispute-resolution mechanisms. International experience offers several approaches to addressing these challenges, although experts caution that Egypt should develop a framework suited to its own market rather than replicate another country’s system wholesale. UAE model: Centralised oversight and escrow accounts Alaa Fekry, chairperson of Beta Egypt and vice chairperson of the Real Estate Development Committee at the Egyptian Businessmen’s Association, said Dubai offers one of the region’s most established models for real estate regulation. The UAE model combines project registration and licensing, developer oversight, regulation of off-plan sales and safeguards for buyers’ funds, with the Dubai Land Department and other relevant authorities playing key supervisory roles. Escrow accounts are among the system’s main pillars. Developers selling properties off-plan are required to establish separate escrow accounts for individual projects, with withdrawals subject to regulatory controls designed to ensure that buyers’ payments are directed towards the developments for which they were collected. This approach helps reduce the risk of developers diverting funds from one project to finance another, while strengthening the link between customer payments and construction progress. The model also relies on digital services and greater access to information, allowing buyers to verify project licensing, check development status and obtain relevant details before committing their money. Fekry said Egypt could benefit from adopting similar safeguards, particularly as off-plan sales remain an important source of financing for residential developments. However, implementing such measures would require clear rules governing the release of funds, effective monitoring and sufficient institutional capacity to supervise projects throughout their development. Saudi Arabia: Licensing before off-plan sales Saudi Arabia offers another approach through the General Real Estate Authority and the Wafi programme, which regulates off-plan sales and leasing. Under this framework, developers and projects must meet regulatory requirements before properties can be marketed for off-plan sale. The system also incorporates project-specific escrow accounts and controls on the use of buyers’ payments. This means that off-plan sales are treated as a regulated activity requiring prior approval, rather than simply a marketing and contractual process between developers and customers. The framework also provides mechanisms for addressing troubled projects, offering a more structured approach to managing delays and protecting buyers when developments encounter difficulties. Fekry said the Saudi experience provides useful lessons for Egypt, particularly in strengthening pre-sale requirements and ensuring that developers demonstrate their readiness to execute projects before collecting payments from customers. For Egypt, such an approach could help address concerns over projects being marketed before developers have met essential requirements relating to land ownership, permits, designs and implementation capacity. UK model: Transparency and accountability While the UAE and Saudi models place considerable emphasis on project oversight and financial safeguards, the UK experience offers lessons in transparency, consumer rights and accountability after a sale. Tarek Eid, board member of the Arab Kuwaiti Group and executive director of its real estate arm, Beit Al-Istithmar Al-Arabi, said the British approach places importance on clear standards governing property sales, contractual obligations, delivery and after-sales services. The system also provides channels for buyers to raise complaints with specialised bodies over issues such as construction quality and developer performance, alongside continuing developer responsibilities for after-sales services. Eid said these principles are relevant to Egypt, where buyers need reliable information about project specifications, delivery schedules and contractual commitments. Greater transparency could also help reduce disputes arising from discrepancies between advertised properties and delivered units, as well as delays and unclear contractual terms. What regulatory model is best suited to Egypt? Fekry argued that Egypt should develop a hybrid regulatory model combining key elements of the UAE and Saudi experiences while incorporating international best practices in transparency and consumer protection. The proposed framework would centre on a strong, independent regulatory authority responsible for licensing, inspections, developer supervision and monitoring project implementation. It would also introduce escrow accounts gradually, particularly for off-plan developments, with withdrawals linked to actual construction progress. Such an approach would seek to ensure that customer payments are used for their intended purpose while allowing developers to access funds in line with clearly defined implementation milestones. Gradual implementation to avoid disrupting investment Industry executives warned that regulatory reform should be introduced gradually to avoid placing excessive burdens on developers or disrupting investment and construction activity. Fekry recommended beginning with large developments and off-plan projects while granting companies a transition period to comply with the new requirements. A phased approach could allow regulators to test oversight mechanisms, strengthen enforcement capacity and address implementation challenges before extending the framework across the wider market. Eid said reform should begin with mandatory project licensing before sales, supported by a comprehensive file covering land ownership, permits, project costs, financing arrangements, construction schedules and the developer’s capacity to complete the development. He also called for an early-warning system and a digital platform to monitor construction progress, financial liquidity and expected delivery dates, while classifying projects according to their risk levels. Such tools could help authorities identify potential delays and financial difficulties before they develop into major problems for buyers. Regulation should also extend to advertising and brokerage activities, including measures to prevent the promotion of unlicensed projects and misleading property advertisements. Eid proposed establishing a specialised body to protect real estate consumers and respond quickly to complaints involving delayed delivery, discrepancies in property specifications and misleading marketing. He also stressed that regulators should have mechanisms to rescue distressed projects before resorting to punitive measures, where feasible. These could include restructuring, replacing contractors or management teams, or transferring projects to qualified developers capable of completing construction. Balancing buyer protection with market stability Egypt’s regulatory challenge is to strengthen buyer protection without undermining the financing mechanisms on which much of the property development sector relies. Off-plan sales and instalment-based payment plans help developers finance construction and enable buyers to spread payments over several years. However, without effective oversight, these arrangements can expose customers to delays, incomplete projects and uncertainty over how their payments are used. A stronger framework would therefore need to balance financial safeguards with practical financing requirements while ensuring consistent enforcement across developers and projects. The experiences of the UAE, Saudi Arabia and the UK suggest that no single measure can address every risk. Licensing, escrow accounts, transparent disclosure, construction monitoring and accessible dispute-resolution mechanisms are most effective when they operate as parts of an integrated system. For Egypt, the priority is to establish a regulatory structure that combines preventive oversight with effective enforcement and clear accountability, while introducing changes at a pace that allows the market to adapt.

headline: Al Ahly celebrates October War victory with cultural, educational programme
summary: Al Ahly Sporting Club marked Egypt’s October 1973 War victory with a programme of cultural, educational and community activities across its branches, bringing members together through concerts, children’s workshops, young talent showcases and historical visits. Organised by the club’s auxiliary committees, the celebrations highlighted Al Ahly’s role beyond the sporting arena, using music, education and community engagement to commemorate a defining chapter in Egypt’s national history. Al Ahly’s Sheikh Zayed branch hosted on October 8 the “Egyptian Melodies” concert, as familiar patriotic songs, including “Ya Habibti Ya Masr” and “Fiha Haga Helwa”, brought music and national memory together, as part of the club’s commemorations of Egypt’s October War victory. Organised by the Cultural Committee, headed by Khaled Galal, under the supervision of the Supreme Committee for Auxiliary Committees, led by engineer Walid Mabrouk, and in cooperation with the Executive Administration, headed by Executive Director Khaled Morsi, the concert formed part of a broader programme of cultural, artistic and educational activities across Al Ahly’s branches. The programme included children’s workshops, young talent showcases and historical visits, highlighting the club’s role in connecting its members with national occasions and offering experiences beyond sports. The celebrations also underscored Al Ahly’s broader social and cultural role, creating opportunities for members of different ages and interests to engage with culture, history and community activities. When culture becomes a way to remember Mariam Samih, rapporteur of the Cultural Committee at Al Ahly’s Sheikh Zayed branch, said the October Victory concert attracted a large number of club members, reflecting their interest in the activities organised across the club’s branches. She stressed that committee rapporteurs and members had an important responsibility to serve the club’s members, adding that Al Ahly’s role extended beyond sports to encompass social and cultural responsibilities. The Cultural Committee contributes to this broader mission by organising activities that respond to members’ interests. Samih emphasised that the October War victory were too important a national occasion to pass without celebration, particularly at the beginning of a new committee year. She noted that organising events to mark the anniversary had long been an established tradition at Al Ahly. She added that the committee carefully selects musical ensembles and singers whose performances suit the significance of the occasion and the club’s standing. It often chooses groups associated with the Cairo Opera House and Arabic music, whose performances have received positive feedback from members. The committee also seeks to link its activities to national occasions and significant events throughout the year. Samih concluded by expressing her pride in belonging to Al Ahly, describing it as a major institution whose role extends well beyond sports. Mahmoud El Khatib A first appearance at Al Ahly For the “Egyptian Melodies” ensemble, the concert marked a new experience: its first performance at an Al Ahly branch. Led by maestro Mazen Daraz, the ensemble presented a programme of patriotic songs and familiar Egyptian melodies. The performers included Mariam Essmat, Malak Hany, Sherouk Wael, Jenna El-Gendy, El-Sayed Rizk, Ziad Wael, Hazem Emad and Mohamed Nabil. The ensemble regularly performs at El Sawy Culturewheel and the Cairo Opera House, and its members include graduates of music institutes and conservatories. Daraz said preparations began with selecting the programme and rehearsing the songs ahead of the performance. He expressed his pleasure at the ensemble’s first appearance at the Sheikh Zayed branch and welcomed the positive reception and feedback from attendees. The choice of music was central to the evening. Patriotic songs carry associations that extend beyond their melodies, evoking shared memories and moments in Egypt’s national history. Performed before an audience gathered to commemorate the October War victory, they offered a cultural way of engaging with the anniversary. Rather than treating the occasion solely as a historical date, the concert brought its significance into the present through a live performance that club members could experience together. Activities across Al Ahly’s branches Walid Mabrouk, head of Al Ahly Club’s Supreme Committee for Auxiliary Committees, said the celebrations marking the October War victory reflected the club’s commitment to expanding its cultural, educational and community role, in line with the vision and directives of club president Mahmoud El Khatib and the objectives of the “Ahly Family” programme. Mabrouk added that the programme extended beyond musical performances to include educational workshops, historical visits and opportunities for young members to showcase their talents. He noted that the auxiliary committees, under the supervision of the Supreme Committee for Auxiliary Committees and in cooperation with the club’s Executive Administration, sought to organise a comprehensive range of activities that brought members together, strengthened their connection with Al Ahly and highlighted the club’s role beyond sporting competitions. Walid Mabrouk At the Sheikh Zayed branch, the Children’s Committee, headed by Dina Amer, organised a workshop in which children made and painted model aeroplanes. The programme also included an educational video about the October War and a quiz for children aged nine to 14. The activities aimed to introduce children to the events of the war through interactive experiences suited to their age group. The Pioneers Committee, headed by Fouad Ismail, also organised a visit to the October War Panorama in New Cairo, giving participants an opportunity to learn about the history of the war and revisit its events through a direct educational experience. As part of efforts to discover and nurture young talent, the Children’s Committee gave gifted young club members the opportunity to participate in concerts celebrating the October War victory, performing alongside the Basma band at the Nasr City and Gezira branches. These events provided children with a platform to showcase their artistic abilities and encouraged their participation in the club’s cultural activities. Khaled Galal Meanwhile, the Cultural Committee, headed by Khaled Galal, organised a series of musical performances across the club’s branches. These included the “Egyptian Melodies” concert at the Sheikh Zayed branch on October 8; performances by the Ashaq El-Nagham ensemble, led by Dr Mohamed Abdel Sattar, at the Gezira branch on October 8 and the New Cairo branch on October 9; and a performance by the Sohbet El-Simsimia ensemble at the Nasr City branch on October 9. Mabrouk emphasised that delivering a programme of this diversity required close coordination among the club’s various departments, including Public Relations, Security and Services, under the leadership of Executive Director Khaled Morsi. He said this cooperation helped ensure the smooth organisation of the events and provided suitable conditions for members to participate in cultural and community activities. He added that these efforts reflected the Al Ahly Board of Directors’ commitment to implementing the objectives of the “Ahly Family” programme. Mabrouk concluded that the auxiliary committees sought to make national occasions meaningful experiences for members of different ages and interests, while reinforcing the club’s role as an institution that brings its community together through sports, culture, education and community engagement. Mariam Samih A role beyond the sporting arena The October commemorations brought together music, education, talent development and historical remembrance, offering members different ways to engage with the anniversary. While the Cultural Committee used live performances to connect audiences with Egypt’s musical heritage and national memory, the Children’s and Pioneers Committees approached the occasion through educational, artistic and historical activities. At Sheikh Zayed, the “Egyptian Melodies” concert illustrated how music could bring members together. On stage, performers delivered familiar patriotic songs, while members of the audience gathered to share the experience. Elsewhere across the club, committees translated the same commemoration into opportunities for learning, artistic expression and historical engagement. Through this combination of cultural performances, children’s activities and historical visits, Al Ahly’s October programme demonstrated how a sporting institution can also provide space for cultural participation, talent development and shared experiences among its members.
