headline: One dead in new attack on Saudi airport, a day after Houthi strike kills 13
summary: By Jana Choukeir, Maha El Dahan, Timour Azhari and Yasmine GhaniaDUBAI/RIYADH, Oct 11 (Reuters) - One person was killed and nearly a dozenhurt in a new attack Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
body_text:
By Jana Choukeir, Maha El Dahan, Timour Azhari and Yasmine Ghania

DUBAI/RIYADH, Oct 11 (Reuters) - One person was killed and nearly a dozenhurt in a new attack Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said an unidentified projectile had targeted Riyadh's international airport Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire. Eleven people were woundedin addition to the fatality, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

Coalition forces also said Saudi air defences had intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of King Khalid International Airport. They later added that a drone had been intercepted and destroyed in the country's Eastern Province, and a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait had been intercepted.Emergency alerts were also issued in Abha, in the south, early on Monday but the danger had since passed, the Saudi Civil Defense said.

The strikes have exposed vulnerabilities in Saudi defence capabilities as the kingdom wages an air campaign against the ​Houthis, who are fighting a ground war in Yemen against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

Footage released by Saudi state television of the Saturday attack on the Riyadh airport showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, while parts of the roof appeared to cave in.

The airport was closed after the attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.

HOUTHIS CLAIM RESPONSIBILITY FOR OTHER ATTACKS

In a televised speech on Sunday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree claimed responsibility for Saturday's attack and said the group had also struck the airport inDammam in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province and two facilities of Saudi oil giant Saudi Aramco.

The Saudi government's media office and Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

The Saudi civil aviation authority confirmed the strike onDammam's King Fahd International Airport late on Sunday, adding that "damage assessments and safety inspections of airport facilities are under way."

An eyewitness aboard a taxiing aircraft at Dammamtold Reuters that around 8:30 p.m. (1730 GMT) on Sunday, they saw a projectile strike the tarmac beside several parked aircraft, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate. Passengers disembarked and were told to leave.

Flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed several delays and cancellations on Sunday for arrivals and departures atDammam airport, the kingdom's third-largest.

The Houthis earlier on Sunday had ‌renewed their warning against ​using Saudi ​airports. "We urge everyone to take our warnings seriously, and Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions," the group said.

Britain's embassy in Saudi Arabia in a post on X advised British citizens against all but essential travel to Jeddah, Dammam and all airports in the kingdom except the airport in Medina.

US aviation authorities issued a notice to US airlines to use caution while flying to or over the kingdom.

'WORSE IS YET TO COME,' HOUTHIS WARN

Saudi Arabia has recently stepped up its military involvement in Yemen, launching strikes against theHouthis and backing a government counteroffensive after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month.

The Houthis said on Sunday that Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in Yemen in the past 24 hours. "Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," Yemen's Houthi-run foreign ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah television.

headline: (LEAD) N. Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles toward East Sea: JCS
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward ...
body_text:
(ATTN: RECASTS headline, lead; UPDATES throughout with details; ADDS byline) By Kim Hyun-soo

SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Monday, South Korea's military said, less than two weeks after it launched a suspected hypersonic ballistic missile.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said it detected the launch at about 9:20 a.m. from the Pyongyang area and the missile flew more than 900 kilometers.

"The South Korean military has stepped up its surveillance to prepare for additional launches and is maintaining an all-out readiness posture, while closely sharing relevant information with the United States and Japan," the JCS said in a notice.

The latest launch came after the North fired one ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea on Oct. 3.

North Korean state media reported the following day that Pyongyang launched an intermediate-range strategic missile as part of efforts to train missile troops operating the "hypersonic strategic weapon system."

Monday's launch also came just days after South Korea conducted its first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) on Thursday in an apparent show of force against North Korea following last month's land mine blast south of the border.

Tensions between the two Koreas have heightened since the Sept. 21 explosion on the South's side of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them critically.

The JCS concluded its recent joint investigation with the U.N. Command that found land mines deliberately planted by North Korean troops were behind the cause of the blast.

Pyongyang has flatly denied responsibility for the incident, accusing Seoul of fabricating the findings, and warning of "immediate and merciless" retaliation if Seoul takes counteraction.

headline: Airstrikes kill dozens of gold miners on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
summary: At least 72 workers were killed in airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border on Saturday, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday. The Emergency Lawyers organisation accused Egypt’s air force of the attack. AFP could not independently verify the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.
body_text:
At least 72 workers were killed in airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border on Saturday, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday. The Emergency Lawyers organisation accused Egypt’s air force of the attack. AFP could not independently verify the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.

Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 03:28Modified: 12/10/2026 - 03:29

At least 72 workers were killed by airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region.

The Emergency Lawyers rights organisation accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the attack. AFP could not independently confirm the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.

The attack on Saturday was the second this year on Jabal al-Uqaydat, after airstrikes, reportedly by Egypt, killed 23 workers in the informal gold mining site in June.

The Egyptian army did not claim the strikes but said at the time that it had conducted a "large-scale operation" against illegal gold mining within its borders.

The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halayeb triangle. Cairo is however a key ally of Sudan's army, at war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

Read moreAt least 82 killed in gold mine collapse in remote area of Sudan, paramilitary RSF say

The attack on Saturday "resulted in the deaths of 72 civilian miners, according to preliminary information, while efforts to document and verify the casualty toll are ongoing," said the Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan's war.

Two survivors described to AFP their harrowing escape from the mine.

Miner Abdelaziz Youssef said a jet appeared overhead at around 8:00 am (0600 GMT) on Saturday and "struck five times, many people were killed".

"We ran up the mountain terrified of another strike," he told AFP.

Another survivor, Sharaf Ali, said there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.

"After the airstrike people scattered, some people came to Al-Ansary market, others went in the other direction, that's why no one knows how many exactly were killed," he said from the gold market, just south of the Halayeb triangle.

Both survivors said they saw bodies on the ground as they fled, with many more feared trapped under the rubble, hours away from any urban centre.

Read moreCentral African Republic gold mine collapse kills more than 100

Since April 2023, the conflict has killed more than 200,000 people and created a deep humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides' war efforts.

The rugged mountainous area, home to bountiful mineral deposits, stretches for hundreds of kilometres and includes the disputed Halayeb triangle.

The Emergency Lawyers said the attack occurred within Sudanese territory.

"The repeated attacks on the gold- and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan's natural resources," it said.

The Egyptian army in June said it carried out its operation "within Egyptian territory".

It said 223 people were detained, including 136 foreign nationals, and announced a campaign to counter "illegal gold mining and arms smuggling" in the area.

Despite backing Sudan's army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border -- which stretches 1,200 kilometres from the Red Sea to Libya -- a major threat to its security.

East of the Nile River, the porous border has for years been a thriving conduit for gold, illicit trade and human trafficking, which Egypt has tried to stem including by using mass deportations.

headline: NATO top commander to warn Russia over alliance’s ability to counter attack
summary: NATO’s top military commander is expected to warn Russia on Monday that the alliance can counter any attack, officials said. US General Alexus Grynkewich will outline his “theory of victory” at a Warsaw security conference amid Western concerns over Moscow’s alleged campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s wartime backers.
body_text:
NATO’s top military commander is expected to warn Russia on Monday that the alliance can counter any attack, officials said. US General Alexus Grynkewich will outline his “theory of victory” at a Warsaw security conference amid Western concerns over Moscow’s alleged campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s wartime backers.

Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 03:41Modified: 12/10/2026 - 03:45

NATO's top military commander is expected to deliver a warning to Russia on Monday over the alliance's ability to counter any attack, as worries grow over the threat from Moscow.

NATO officials have said US General Alexus Grynkewich -- the alliance's Supreme Allied Commander Europe -- will elaborate his "theory of victory" over any potential attack at a security conference in Warsaw.

The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a "hybrid" campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's backers in the war against Russia.

Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.

"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe's theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO's advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance's deterrence and defence plans," Colonel Martin O'Donnell, a spokesman for the US general, said last week.

"But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked," O'Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

NATO -- which was founded in the wake of World War II to counter the Soviet Union -- traditionally closely guards its defence plans to counter any attack by Russia.

Grynkewich's intervention looks unlikely to divulge many new details on NATO's strategy and is intended to both send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance's eastern flank.

NATO insists it remains a defensive alliance and has no intention of attacking Russia.

Western officials say that Moscow's "hybrid attacks" have become more reckless as the Kremlin's forces are stalled in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life.

The alliance -- whose primary purpose is deterring an armed Russian invasion -- has struggled to work out how to cope with incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict.

NATO civilian head Mark Rutte has urged countries to keep "calm, carry on and support Ukraine".

"We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger," Rutte said last month.

But the uptick in Russian activity comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are currently bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the Pentagon conducts a review of its deployments on the continent.

The results of the process are expected to be announced towards the end of the year.

European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump.

North Korea on Monday fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, Seoul's military said, after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the countries' heavily fortified border.

"Our military detected around 09:20 (00:20 GMT) several ballistic missiles launched from the Pyongyang area towards the East Sea," the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a statement, referring to the Sea of Japan.

"Our military has stepped up surveillance and vigilance against possible additional launches," it added.

Japan's defence ministry separately confirmed the launch of at least one suspected ballistic missile.

Tensions between the two Koreas have soared since three South Korean soldiers were injured last month when two landmines detonated in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that divides the two countries.

A joint Seoul-UN investigation concluded that North Korea had planted the landmines over a year ago, something Pyongyang has angrily denied.

Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts

Pyongyang has since launched a ballistic missile it says incorporated artificial intelligence, while Seoul last week announced the successful test of its first homegrown hypersonic weapon.

Kim Yo Jong, powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the North's October 3 launch featured a missile "capable of changing its flight orbit at a low altitude and AI was introduced into it".

Seoul said days later that it had tested a domestically produced hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV), a weapon carried into the upper atmosphere by rocket boosters or ballistic missiles before gliding towards its targets.

South Korea's presidential office said the HGV offered "a new deterrence capability capable of striking key targets within the Korean Peninsula's operational environment".

Since the September 21 landmine incident, Seoul has demanded an apology, something Kim Yo Jong has blasted as "despicable, while rejecting a planned transfer of medical equipment from Seoul.

"If they (South Korea) truly wish to restore relations between the DPRK and South Korea, they should be mindful of the other side's feelings in every word and deed, and first demonstrate the utmost respect, consideration and sincerity," she said Thursday, using her country's official acronym.

The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two Koreas.

Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war since the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce, not a peace treaty.

headline: Airstrikes kill dozens of gold miners on Egypt-Sudan border, rights group says
summary: At least 72 workers were killed in airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border on Saturday, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday. The Emergency Lawyers organisation accused Egypt’s air force of the attack. AFP could not independently verify the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.
body_text:
At least 72 workers were killed in airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border on Saturday, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday. The Emergency Lawyers organisation accused Egypt’s air force of the attack. AFP could not independently verify the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.

Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 03:28Modified: 12/10/2026 - 03:29

At least 72 workers were killed by airstrikes on a gold mine on the Sudan-Egypt border, a Sudanese rights group said on Sunday, after survivors described scenes of chaos in the mountainous region.

The Emergency Lawyers rights organisation accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the attack. AFP could not independently confirm the account and Egypt has issued no official comment.

The attack on Saturday was the second this year on Jabal al-Uqaydat, after airstrikes, reportedly by Egypt, killed 23 workers in the informal gold mining site in June.

The Egyptian army did not claim the strikes but said at the time that it had conducted a "large-scale operation" against illegal gold mining within its borders.

The border between Sudan and Egypt is disputed, with both countries claiming the resource-rich Halayeb triangle. Cairo is however a key ally of Sudan's army, at war with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

Read moreAt least 82 killed in gold mine collapse in remote area of Sudan, paramilitary RSF say

The attack on Saturday "resulted in the deaths of 72 civilian miners, according to preliminary information, while efforts to document and verify the casualty toll are ongoing," said the Emergency Lawyers, which documents atrocities in Sudan's war.

Two survivors described to AFP their harrowing escape from the mine.

Miner Abdelaziz Youssef said a jet appeared overhead at around 8:00 am (0600 GMT) on Saturday and "struck five times, many people were killed".

"We ran up the mountain terrified of another strike," he told AFP.

Another survivor, Sharaf Ali, said there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.

"After the airstrike people scattered, some people came to Al-Ansary market, others went in the other direction, that's why no one knows how many exactly were killed," he said from the gold market, just south of the Halayeb triangle.

Both survivors said they saw bodies on the ground as they fled, with many more feared trapped under the rubble, hours away from any urban centre.

Read moreCentral African Republic gold mine collapse kills more than 100

Since April 2023, the conflict has killed more than 200,000 people and created a deep humanitarian crisis that has pushed many into the dangerous gold mining industry, which fuels both sides' war efforts.

The rugged mountainous area, home to bountiful mineral deposits, stretches for hundreds of kilometres and includes the disputed Halayeb triangle.

The Emergency Lawyers said the attack occurred within Sudanese territory.

"The repeated attacks on the gold- and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan's natural resources," it said.

The Egyptian army in June said it carried out its operation "within Egyptian territory".

It said 223 people were detained, including 136 foreign nationals, and announced a campaign to counter "illegal gold mining and arms smuggling" in the area.

Despite backing Sudan's army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border -- which stretches 1,200 kilometres from the Red Sea to Libya -- a major threat to its security.

East of the Nile River, the porous border has for years been a thriving conduit for gold, illicit trade and human trafficking, which Egypt has tried to stem including by using mass deportations.

headline: From Brazil to North Macedonia, Arabic literature finds new routes to readers through Frankfurt Book Fair
summary: Arabic books are finding new readers in Brazil, India and North Macedonia through a series of translation and co-publishing agreements signed at the Frankfurt Book Fair.The Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre announced 14 projects in seven languages, teaming up with 10 publishing and cultural partners, to mark the first anniversary of Kalima to the World. The programme was launched at last year's fair to support the translation and publication of Emirati and Arab books internationally.The new projects cover fiction, children's literature, history, heritage and social subjects, with editions planned in Portuguese, Macedonian, Hindi, Urdu, Greek, Spanish and English. Titles and publication dates are expected soon.North Macedonian publishing house Bata Press, which has released works by Egyptian Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz and contemporary Arab authors, is preparing to publish an Emirati novel about life in the UAE before its oil-driven development.Its publisher, Filip Batkoski, sees cultural connections between North Macedonia and the Arab world, particularly through their shared Ottoman history.“Actually, we have a lot of shared cultural heritage between the Arab world and North Macedonia. For example, we have been 500 years in the Ottoman Empire. And the Ottoman Empire has, of course, a huge impact from the Arabic world,” he said.“You cannot believe how many things we have in common between Arab people and us. I would say we are closer to Arab people than to western Europe or the United States.”The Frankfurt projects also include Hindi and Urdu translations through partnerships with India's National Book Trust and Pakistan's Book Corner and National Book Foundation. Greek publishers Kaktos and Vakxikon are also participating.The effort to reach more international readers has been extended through a separate agreement signed at the fair between the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre and the Arab Publishers Association, an industry body representing publishers across the Middle East and North Africa.The partnership aims to expand the catalogue of Arabic titles available for translation and introduce them to international publishers.Speaking to The National, Mohamed Rashad, president of the association, said the aim was to reverse the "longstanding emphasis on translating foreign literature into Arabic", rather than taking Arabic writing to readers abroad.“For many years, what we have seen at Arab book fairs is that translation has always been from foreign languages into Arabic,” he said. “Yet we have enormous treasures in our heritage, history and civilisation.”Arab publishers were invited to nominate two or three books each, after which a specialist committee of writers, critics, translators and other experts examined more than 100 titles for inclusion in the catalogue.“Every publisher believes their book is the most important and deserves to be translated,” Rashad says. “Of course, that is not necessarily true. There must be certain criteria, and specialists who can make these decisions.”The catalogue is intended to introduce international publishers to a wider selection of Arab authors, with the centre's support helping to facilitate translation and provide funding.For Brazilian publisher Leonardo Garzaro, whose company Editora Rua do Sabao is among the partners, the opportunity is as much about challenging perceptions as it is about introducing new authors.“Many people in Brazil think about the Arab world as just one big thing. Literature can help them to understand, oh, this is the Emirates, this is Egyptian, this is Palestine. So they understand better the region and the different people who build the region,” he said.His company has already published almost 15 Arabic titles outside the initiative, including Iman Mersal's In the Footsteps of Enayat Al-Zayyat, which won the 2021 Sheikh Zayed Book Award for Literature.While its treatment of women's rights appealed to him, Garzaro said literary merit did not always translate into commercial appeal.“Sometimes a book is an award winner but doesn't work in Brazil because it's very specific,” he said. “But sometimes, as a publisher, you just like a book because you think it's important. You need to be brave and take a chance in order to help push your respective market and expand your readership.”Having worked with Abu Dhabi's publishing representatives for five years, Garzaro says that consistency can determine whether a publisher builds a collection of translated works or abandons plans to enter a new market.“That reliability is so important. While the budget is great, publishing is ultimately a business based on relationships. It's about building trust and ensuring the person you're dealing with is reliable. That's one of the first things we look for when meeting potential partners, apart from the budget,” he said.Saeed Al Tunaiji, executive director of the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre, said the growing interest from international publishers was opening new markets for Emirati authors and Arabic literature.“Usually, Arabic books are translated into one or two languages, but now we are seeing interest in Arabic books and culture from speakers of these other languages,” he said. “Today, different cultures and language communities around the world have a real desire to discover Arabic literature and culture, as well as young, creative Emirati writers.”
body_text:
Arabic books are finding new readers in Brazil, India and North Macedonia through a series of translation and co-publishing agreements signed at the Frankfurt Book Fair.

The Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre announced 14 projects in seven languages, teaming up with 10 publishing and cultural partners, to mark the first anniversary of Kalima to the World. The programme was launched at last year's fair to support the translation and publication of Emirati and Arab books internationally.

The new projects cover fiction, children's literature, history, heritage and social subjects, with editions planned in Portuguese, Macedonian, Hindi, Urdu, Greek, Spanish and English. Titles and publication dates are expected soon.

Emirati stories are finding global readers at the Frankfurt Book Fair

North Macedonian publishing house Bata Press, which has released works by Egyptian Nobel laureate Naguib Mahfouz and contemporary Arab authors, is preparing to publish an Emirati novel about life in the UAE before its oil-driven development.

Its publisher, Filip Batkoski, sees cultural connections between North Macedonia and the Arab world, particularly through their shared Ottoman history.

“Actually, we have a lot of shared cultural heritage between the Arab world and North Macedonia. For example, we have been 500 years in the Ottoman Empire. And the Ottoman Empire has, of course, a huge impact from the Arabic world,” he said.

“You cannot believe how many things we have in common between Arab people and us. I would say we are closer to Arab people than to western Europe or the United States.”

The Frankfurt projects also include Hindi and Urdu translations through partnerships with India's National Book Trust and Pakistan's Book Corner and National Book Foundation. Greek publishers Kaktos and Vakxikon are also participating.

The effort to reach more international readers has been extended through a separate agreement signed at the fair between the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre and the Arab Publishers Association, an industry body representing publishers across the Middle East and North Africa.

The partnership aims to expand the catalogue of Arabic titles available for translation and introduce them to international publishers.

Speaking to The National, Mohamed Rashad, president of the association, said the aim was to reverse the "longstanding emphasis on translating foreign literature into Arabic", rather than taking Arabic writing to readers abroad.

“For many years, what we have seen at Arab book fairs is that translation has always been from foreign languages into Arabic,” he said. “Yet we have enormous treasures in our heritage, history and civilisation.”

Arab publishers were invited to nominate two or three books each, after which a specialist committee of writers, critics, translators and other experts examined more than 100 titles for inclusion in the catalogue.

“Every publisher believes their book is the most important and deserves to be translated,” Rashad says. “Of course, that is not necessarily true. There must be certain criteria, and specialists who can make these decisions.”

The catalogue is intended to introduce international publishers to a wider selection of Arab authors, with the centre's support helping to facilitate translation and provide funding.

For Brazilian publisher Leonardo Garzaro, whose company Editora Rua do Sabao is among the partners, the opportunity is as much about challenging perceptions as it is about introducing new authors.

“Many people in Brazil think about the Arab world as just one big thing. Literature can help them to understand, oh, this is the Emirates, this is Egyptian, this is Palestine. So they understand better the region and the different people who build the region,” he said.

His company has already published almost 15 Arabic titles outside the initiative, including Iman Mersal's In the Footsteps of Enayat Al-Zayyat, which won the 2021 Sheikh Zayed Book Award for Literature.

While its treatment of women's rights appealed to him, Garzaro said literary merit did not always translate into commercial appeal.

“Sometimes a book is an award winner but doesn't work in Brazil because it's very specific,” he said. “But sometimes, as a publisher, you just like a book because you think it's important. You need to be brave and take a chance in order to help push your respective market and expand your readership.”

Having worked with Abu Dhabi's publishing representatives for five years, Garzaro says that consistency can determine whether a publisher builds a collection of translated works or abandons plans to enter a new market.

“That reliability is so important. While the budget is great, publishing is ultimately a business based on relationships. It's about building trust and ensuring the person you're dealing with is reliable. That's one of the first things we look for when meeting potential partners, apart from the budget,” he said.

Saeed Al Tunaiji, executive director of the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre, said the growing interest from international publishers was opening new markets for Emirati authors and Arabic literature.

“Usually, Arabic books are translated into one or two languages, but now we are seeing interest in Arabic books and culture from speakers of these other languages,” he said. “Today, different cultures and language communities around the world have a real desire to discover Arabic literature and culture, as well as young, creative Emirati writers.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the Frankfurt Book Fair agreements as a positive milestone for Arabic literature reaching new global readers, emphasizing cultural connections and publisher enthusiasm.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged and vague, elevating cultural heritage to a grandiose status without specific detail.
Emphasizes authenticity and intensity of interest, which is subjective and not quantifiable.

loaded_language.quote: You cannot believe how many things we have in common
loaded_language.explanation: Hyperbolic and conversational, designed to evoke surprise and warmth rather than provide factual information.

omissions: No mention of the political or human rights context in the UAE or the broader Arab world that might affect publishing.
No critical perspective on the funding or influence of the Abu Dhabi Arabic Language Centre.
No details on the financial terms or scale of the translation projects beyond the number of projects and languages.

headline: NATO top commander to warn Russia over alliance’s ability to counter-attack
summary: NATO’s top military commander is expected to warn Russia on Monday that the alliance can counter any attack, officials said. US General Alexus Grynkewich will outline his “theory of victory” at a Warsaw security conference amid Western concerns over Moscow’s alleged campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s wartime backers.
body_text:
NATO’s top military commander is expected to warn Russia on Monday that the alliance can counter any attack, officials said. US General Alexus Grynkewich will outline his “theory of victory” at a Warsaw security conference amid Western concerns over Moscow’s alleged campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine’s wartime backers.

Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 03:41Modified: 12/10/2026 - 04:00

NATO's top military commander is expected to deliver a warning to Russia on Monday over the alliance's ability to counter any attack, as worries grow over the threat from Moscow.

NATO officials have said US General Alexus Grynkewich -- the alliance's Supreme Allied Commander Europe -- will elaborate his "theory of victory" over any potential attack at a security conference in Warsaw.

The move from the top military commander comes as NATO seeks to send a message to Moscow to halt what Western officials say is a "hybrid" campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's backers in the war against Russia.

Fears have grown in recent months that the Kremlin is stepping up its actions after high-profile incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport.

"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe's theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO's advantage, which is consistent with and grounded upon the alliance's deterrence and defence plans," Colonel Martin O'Donnell, a spokesman for the US general, said last week.

"But given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked," O'Donnell said, noting the theory sets out a framework to do just that.

NATO -- which was founded in the wake of World War II to counter the Soviet Union -- traditionally closely guards its defence plans to counter any attack by Russia.

Grynkewich's intervention looks unlikely to divulge many new details on NATO's strategy and is intended to both send a signal to Moscow and reassure members on the alliance's eastern flank.

NATO insists it remains a defensive alliance and has no intention of attacking Russia.

Western officials say that Moscow's "hybrid attacks" have become more reckless as the Kremlin's forces are stalled in Ukraine, and that they risk causing significant loss of life.

The alliance -- whose primary purpose is deterring an armed Russian invasion -- has struggled to work out how to cope with incidents in the grey zone beneath open conflict.

NATO civilian head Mark Rutte has urged countries to keep "calm, carry on and support Ukraine".

"We should not be naive... about Russia, but they know we are stronger," Rutte said last month.

But the uptick in Russian activity comes at a time of potential vulnerability for Europe. Allies are currently bracing for possible cuts to US forces in Europe as the Pentagon conducts a review of its deployments on the continent.

The results of the process are expected to be announced towards the end of the year.

European countries are already rushing to bolster their militaries as doubts have soared over the reliability of the United States under President Donald Trump.

body_text:
(ATTN: RECASTS headline, lead; UPDATES with more details throughout; TRIMS; ADDS photo)By Kim Hyun-soo

SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Monday, South Korea's military said, in an apparent show of force against the South's recent successful test-fire of a hypersonic missile.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said it detected the launch at about 9:20 a.m. from the Pyongyang area and that at least one of the missiles flew more than 900 kilometers.

"Initial analysis suggests (Monday's launch) was seen as a protest against the successful launch of our hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) and a display of the North's achievements under its five-year plan to bolster defense capabilities and a deliberate show of its missile capabilities," JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young told a press briefing.

When asked if the missiles launched were hypersonic or intermediate-range missiles, Jang declined to comment, saying the military needs to further analyze the specifications of the launch.

South Korea conducted its first test launch of a HGV on Thursday in an apparent show of force against North Korea following the Sept. 21 mine blast on the South's side of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

A joint investigation with the U.N. Command earlier determined that the explosions were caused by antipersonnel land mines planted deliberately by North Korea. Pyongyang has denied any responsibility, accusing Seoul of fabricating its findings.

A hypersonic missile is usually hard to intercept with existing missile defense shields. It travels at a speed of at least Mach 5 -- five times the speed of sound -- and is designed to be maneuverable on unpredictable flight paths and fly at low altitudes.

The North's latest missile launch came after it fired one ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea on Oct. 3.

headline: IRGC Navy warns ships against turning off navigation systems
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Iran’s IRGC Navy chief Ali Azmaei has warned that ships in the Strait of Hormuz that switch off their navigation and identification systems will be classified as hostile and face decisive action.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Iran’s IRGC Navy chief Ali Azmaei has warned that ships in the Strait of Hormuz that switch off their navigation and identification systems will be classified as hostile and face decisive action.

Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has warned vessels operating in the Strait of Hormuz against switching off their navigation and identification systems, saying violators will be treated as hostile.

Navy Commander Ali Azmaei issued the warning in a post on social media, stating that any vessel in the strait that disables these systems would be identified as hostile and face a firm response.

headline: Third oil tanker catches fire in Hormuz after hitting mine
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – A third oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine, according to Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps, which said the vessel had attempted to cross an unauthorized route despite warnings.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – A third oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine, according to Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps, which said the vessel had attempted to cross an unauthorized route despite warnings.

A third oil tanker caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after striking a naval mine, according to a statement from the naval forces of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC).

The tanker, a shuttle tanker carrying 750,000 barrels of crude oil, attempted to pass through an unauthorized route on Sunday afternoon despite warnings from the IRGC Navy, the force’s public relations office said.

According to the statement, the vessel struck a naval mine, triggering an explosion and a severe fire.

The incident is the third such case involving an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.

headline: North Korea fires several missiles, Seoul says

body_text:
SEOUL, October 12. /TASS/. The military of the Republic of Korea (ROK) claimed that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) fired several ballistic missiles toward the Sea of Japan on Monday, News1 reported, citing South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS).

According to it, the missiles were fired at about 9:20 a.m. local time (0:20 a.m. GMT) from an area near Pyongyang and flew approximately 900 km. The South Korean military maintains readiness for any additional launches and exchanges information with the United States and Japan.

The DPRK last test-launched a ballistic missile on October 3. The projectile was fired toward the Sea of Japan from the Wonsan area.

headline: The best EVs to buy in the UAE for every budget
summary: As recently as five years ago, it seemed unimaginable that electric vehicles would find any traction in the UAE. Given that fuel was relatively cheap in our region and the EV recharging infrastructure was still in its infancy, the business case for battery-powered vehicles seemed tenuous, at best.However, times change and so do buyer demands. Petrol prices are now edging towards Dh4.50 a litre; filling up even a compact Toyota Corolla can cost more than Dh200. For drivers of larger SUVs, the expense is considerably higher – a full tank in the latest Nissan Patrol costs more than Dh400, while older models can guzzle Dh600.In this context, an EV makes financial sense, particularly for people with access to a wall-mounted home charger. Even without one, the savings can be considerable. Depending on the vehicle's battery size, a full charge at a Dewa or Adnoc charging station typically costs little more than Dh80 ($22).Alongside rising petrol prices, the UAE's public EV charging network has continued to expand, with about 2,800 charging points across the country and more expected in the coming years. As electric vehicles become an increasingly practical option for motorists, here are some of the best models currently available in the UAE.Under Dh100,000JAC E30X (From Dh69,995) Behind the JAC E30X’s slightly cartoonish appearance lurks a capable and well-built car for its modest asking price. Although tiny in overall dimensions, the E30X's wheel-at-each-corner stance endows it with a 2,620 mm wheelbase, making it surprisingly spacious inside. With a single electric motor sending 95hp or 136hp (depending on trim level) to the front wheels, the JAC is no rocket ship, but it nevertheless feels decently zippy around town. Even the base model gets automatic LED headlights, retracting flush door handles, Apple CarPlay/Android Auto, faux-leather trim, cruise control and a 12.8-inch infotainment screen.Polestar 2 (from Dh89,900)With a starting price under Dh90,000, the Polestar 2 seems an unbelievable value for money. There is a catch, though, as the cars on offer for this price are part of the dealership’s 2024 inventory. However, they still have zero kilometres on the odometer and are still considered new. With the Polestar’s 272hp electric motor delivering a brisk 0-100kph split of 6.4 seconds and a touring range of 546km, there isn't anything equivalent at this price. Top it off with Swedish (such as Volvo) levels of build quality and safety, and the Polestar 2 seems a compelling buy – even if you’re getting a 2024 model-year car.Dh100,000 to 125,000Smart #3 (From Dh110,900)The perky-looking Smart #3 is a fusion of East and West, as the brand is German but the car itself is built in China. In its base form, the five-door compact SUV is equipped with a 66kWh battery and a single electric motor that sends a beefy 268hp and 384Nm to the front wheels. It’s a sprightly performer, sprinting from standstill to 100kph in 5.8 seconds, while touring range is also respectable at 430km (claimed). Standard features include a panoramic sunroof, a 12.8-inch central display and a 10-inch head-up display. The safety kit includes adaptive cruise control, automatic parking assist, lane-keeping assist, automatic emergency braking and a 360-degree camera.GAC Aion V (From Dh124,900)Billed as a Tesla Model Y rival, the GAC Aion V offers ample interior space and a generous feature list at a budget price. Propulsion for the Aion V is provided by a single e-motor that produces 204hp and 240Nm, channelled through the front wheels. GAC claims the Aion V, equipped with a 75.26kWh battery, can cover up to 510km on a full charge, based on the European WLTP test cycle. There’s also a lengthy list of standard features, such as a 14.6-inch touchscreen with Apple CarPlay/Android Auto, a nine-speaker sound system, navigation, a 9.8-inch digital instrument cluster, dual-zone climate control, a hands-free tailgate and 19-inch alloy wheels.Dh125,000 to 150,000Volvo EX30 (From Dh129,000)The Volvo EX30 is another value-packed offering as it provides the Swedish marque’s customary levels of build quality and safety at a wallet-friendly price. The stubby SUV has a distinctive profile, and that’s not a bad thing in a sea of vehicles that seem virtual clones of each other. In base trim, a single electric motor sends 272hp and 343Nm to the rear wheels, delivering 0-100kph split in 5.7 seconds and a maximum touring range of 337km (claimed). Included at no extra cost are Harman Kardon premium audio, dual-zone climate-control air-conditioning, 19-inch alloys, reversing camera, front and rear parking sensors, and front, side andcurtain airbags. Kia EV3 (From Dh141,645)The ultra-futuristic-looking EV3 embodies Kia’s latest design language, and everything under the skin is similarly cutting-edge. The EV3’s minimalistic interior is dominated by a pair of 12.3-inch screens – one for the instrument cluster and the other for the infotainment system. Conveniences include a powered tailgate, sliding-table centre console, bottle holders in all four doors and a 25-litre "frunk" (front trunk) that supplements the 460-litre rear load bay. Safety is enhanced via a surround-view monitor, Smart Cruise Control (SCC), Reverse Parking Collision-avoidance Assist (PCA-R), Forward Collision-avoidance Assist 2 (FCA 2) and Remote Smart Parking Assist (RSPA). Dh150,000 to 175,000Hyundai Ioniq 5 (From Dh153,000)Hyundai’s stylish Ioniq 5 was launched five years ago, but it still looks just as good as it did back in 2021. With an expansive three-metre wheelbase, the Ioniq 5 offers acres of sprawling space inside, while the relatively high roofline makes for generous headroom and good visibility in all directions. Power output ranges from 170hp in single-motor entry variants to 305hp in the dual-motor flagship, with the latter accelerating from 0-100kph in only 5.2 seconds. Hyundai says the Ioniq 5, underpinned by an 800-volt architecture, can charge from 10 to 80 per cent in just 18 minutes with a 350kW fast charger.BYD Sealion 7 (From Dh158,900)Quality cars at an affordable price are the key to BYD’s meteoric success (it now sells more EVs globally than Tesla), and the Sealion 7 is a case in point. The largeish coupe-mimicking SUV has great fit and finish inside and out and the extensive standard kit list includes a panoramic sunroof, 19-inch alloys, 15.6-inch infotainment screen, 12-speaker audio, LED headlights with cornering function and plenty more. The base model is propelled by a single electric motor that drives the rear wheels, and outputs of 308hp and 380Nm are sufficient to deliver sprightly performance – as evidenced by a 0-100kph dash in 6.7 seconds. Dh175,000 to 200,000Tesla Model Y (From Dh178,670)Tesla has become ubiquitous in the electric vehicle market over the past decade as the Model 3 and Model Y are popular models in the UAE. The swoopy Model Y SUV offers greater space and utility than its Model 3 sibling, and a midlife refresh last year resolved the slightly awkward styling of the 2020 original. The Model Y’s cabin is ultra-minimalist, and the instrument cluster has been removed, as all information is now displayed on the central infotainment screen. Even the single-motor entry model is rapid (0-100kph in 5.6 seconds) and it has an impressive range (661km claimed).Xpeng G9 (From Dh192,500)Xpeng debuted in the UAE only two years ago, but the Chinese brand has already carved a foothold, with stylish offerings at keen prices serving as its foundation. With a clean, elegantly sculpted profile, the medium-large G9 SUV manages to avoid the frumpiness that distinguishes many vehicles of this ilk. Inside, there's a 10.25-inch digital instrument panel, plus dual 15-inch high-definition displays – one for infotainment and one for the passenger – while soft-touch materials throughout the cabin make for a premium ambience. Xpeng quotes a 502km range for the base model, while its 800-volt architecture enables super-fast charging (10 to 80 per cent in just 15 minutes).Dh200,000-plusAudi Q6 Sportback e-tron (From Dh247,900)Audi was one of the EV pioneers in the UAE, as the original e-tron SUV was launched locally at the end of 2018. The four-ringed brand has since fleshed out its battery-electric range, with the Q6 Sportback e-tron standing out as one of the marque’s best-value EVs. The entry version kicks off just under Dh250,000, and the price includes a five-year service package, roadside assistance and registration. This price gets you a stylish coupe-like SUV with Audi’s customary quality feel. Powered by a single 252hp electric motor, the Q6 Sportback e-tron offers a claimed 656km touring range and fast-charge capability (10 to 80 per cent in 22 minutes).BMW iX3 (From Dh360,000)The latest BMW iX3 is the first embodiment of the Bavarian marque’s "Neue Klasse" design language, and it therefore stands clearly apart from any models that preceded it. While the Neue Klasse platform is optimised for electric powertrains, it can also accommodate petrol engines. The initial iX3 model offered in the UAE is the high-spec dual-motor iX3 50 xDrive that is priced from Dh360,000 ($98,022), including a service package and insurance. One of its trump cards is a new "Heart of Joy" control unit that’s said to deliver class-leading dynamics and handling precision. BMW quotes a maximum touring range of 805km (claimed) and 0-100kph in 4.9 seconds, so the debutant’s stats bode well.

headline: BOK chief to attend G20, IMF-WBG meetings in Bangkok
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top central banker will attend a meetin...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top central banker will attend a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) finance ministers and central bank chiefs to be held in Thailand this week, the Bank of Korea (BOK) said Monday.

BOK Gov. Shin Hyun-song will join the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting, set to take place in Bangkok, where participants will discuss global economic conditions, growth and global imbalances, according to the central bank.

He will also attend the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Group (IMF-WBG) meetings, where discussions will focus on the global economic outlook and financial stability.

While in Bangkok, the BOK governor is scheduled to hold separate talks with high-ranking officials from the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and other major central banks to exchange views on recent international developments.

He will also participate in CNN's Global Perspectives, a live event series convening leaders, CEOs and innovators for conversations on issues covering culture, technology and business, along with Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala of Nigeria, director-general of the World Trade Organization (WTO), and Bernard Mensah, president of International at Bank of America, according to the BOK.

(ATTN: RECASTS headline, lead; UPDATES with more details throughout; TRIMS; ADDS photo)By Kim Hyun-soo

SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- North Korea launched multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Monday, South Korea's military said, in an apparent show of force against the South's recent successful test-fire of a hypersonic missile.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said it detected the launch at about 9:20 a.m. from the Pyongyang area and that at least one of the missiles flew more than 900 kilometers.

"Initial analysis suggests (Monday's launch) was seen as a protest against the successful launch of our hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) and a display of the North's achievements under its five-year plan to bolster defense capabilities and a deliberate show of its missile capabilities," JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young told a press briefing.

When asked if the missiles launched were hypersonic or intermediate-range missiles, Jang declined to comment, saying the military needs to further analyze the specifications of the launch.

South Korea conducted its first test launch of a HGV on Thursday in an apparent show of force against North Korea following the Sept. 21 mine blast on the South's side of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ).

A joint investigation with the U.N. Command earlier determined that the explosions were caused by antipersonnel land mines planted deliberately by North Korea. Pyongyang has denied any responsibility, accusing Seoul of fabricating its findings.

A hypersonic missile is usually hard to intercept with existing missile defense shields. It travels at a speed of at least Mach 5 -- five times the speed of sound -- and is designed to be maneuverable on unpredictable flight paths and fly at low altitudes.

The North's latest missile launch came after it fired one ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the East Sea on Oct. 3.

North Korean state media reported the following day that Pyongyang launched an intermediate-range strategic missile as part of efforts to train missile troops operating the "hypersonic strategic weapon system."

The North last fired ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area on Aug. 20.

headline: Africa: AU Commission Chairperson Congratulates Navi Pillay On Nobel Peace Prize
summary: [SAnews.gov.za] The Chairperson of the African Union (AU) Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has congratulated South African jurist Navanethem "Navi" Pillay on being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, recognising her contributions to international justice, human rights and peace.
body_text:
The Chairperson of the African Union (AU) Commission, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, has congratulated South African jurist Navanethem "Navi" Pillay on being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, recognising her contributions to international justice, human rights and peace.

In a statement, Youssouf described the award as a well-deserved recognition of Pillay's lifelong dedication to justice, human dignity and peace, saying her contributions to international law and accountability had left an enduring legacy for Africa and the world.

He highlighted her distinguished career, from her struggle against apartheid in South Africa to her service at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the International Criminal Court and the United Nations.

"Her work advancing accountability for genocide, crimes against humanity and conflict-related sexual violence has helped strengthen the foundations of international justice," he said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Youssouf also underscored the significance of Pillay's achievement for African women and girls, describing her as a source of pride for the continent and an inspiration to future generations.

He noted that her career exemplified the vital contribution of African women to global leadership, international institutions and the advancement of universal principles.

At a time when international law and multilateral institutions face mounting challenges, Youssouf said the award served as a reminder that lasting peace must be grounded in justice, accountability and respect for the rule of law.

He reaffirmed that these principles remained central to the AU's commitment to the peaceful resolution of conflicts, the protection of civilians and the realisation of Agenda 2063's aspirations for a peaceful, secure and prosperous Africa.

The AU Commission Chairperson reiterated the continental body's determination to uphold international law, strengthen multilateral cooperation and advance its commitment to Silencing the Guns across the continent.

He joined the Government and people of South Africa, Africans across the continent and the diaspora in celebrating the recognition of Pillay's lifelong commitment to justice, human dignity and peace. - SAnews.gov.za

body_text:
A Dubai resident detained for five years over a contract dispute has left Iraq to be reunited with his family.

Australian engineer Robert Pether, 50, was released from prison in Baghdad in June last year but had remained in Iraq due to a ban on him leaving the country over financial claims linked to the case.

Mr Pether's wife, Desree, confirmed to The National on Monday morning that her husband was due to arrive in Ireland, where the family live, around 9.25am local time.

UN fears for Dubai resident held in Iraq for five years

"The Australian Government welcomes the Iraqi Government's decision to allow Mr Robert Pether to leave Iraq today," said Penny Wong, Australian Minister of Foreign Affairs.

"I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family. Mr Pether had been imprisoned in Iraq for more than four years and was later subject to travel restrictions that prevented him from leaving the country.

"I thank the Australian officials whose tireless work helped achieve this outcome, as well as the Irish authorities for their close cooperation throughout this process. I wish Mr Pether and his family all the very best as they reunite."

Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, who both lived in Dubai at the time, were jailed in August 2021 and fined $12 million after a contract dispute between his employer and authorities in Baghdad. Mr Radwan has also left Iraq.

They were released from prison last year. In 2025, the Office of the US Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs pushed for his release. This followed a call from Australia's Foreign Minister Penny Wong for Mr Pether to be allowed to return home to his family.

Since being released from prison, Mr Pether had been staying either with friends or in hotels, with the cost of food and accommodation falling on him and his family.

UN experts expressed “grave concern” earlier this year over the health of Mr Pether. The office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issued a statement in June, highlighting a “particularly alarming” situation given Mr Pether's declining health, which was compounded by a lack of access to specialist medical care and the psychological toll of his “prolonged detention and uncertainty”.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention issued a report in 2022 describing Mr Pether’s imprisonment as “arbitrary and in contravention of international law”.

A ruling in 2023 by the International Chamber of Commerce's International Court of Arbitration said that the central bank in Iraq was to blame for the contractual dispute.

Mr Pether and Mr Radwan were arrested when they travelled to Iraq for what they thought was a routine business meeting. Employed as an engineer in Dubai for CME, Mr Pether was contracted to work on the central bank's headquarters near the Tigris.

The men were detained during the meeting. They each received a five-year jail sentence and were ordered by an Iraqi court to pay $12 million. The dispute was over a $33 million contract awarded to CME in 2015.

The project was put on hold a year later, with plummeting oil prices and Iraq’s war against ISIS put forward as the main reasons. Work resumed in 2018, with CME working for 39 of the 48 months as set out in the contract.

Payment was received for 32 of those months before it was withheld. CME was asked by the central bank to extend the contract by three months to make up for work suspended because of the coronavirus pandemic.

The Australian government said it recognised the significant impact of Mr Pether's detention on him and his family and pledged to continue to offer consular support in an effort to allow him to finally leave Iraq.

headline: The best EVs to buy in the UAE for every budget
summary: As recently as five years ago, it seemed unimaginable that electric vehicles would find any traction in the UAE. Given that fuel was relatively cheap in our region and the EV recharging infrastructure was still in its infancy, the business case for battery-powered vehicles seemed tenuous, at best.However, times change and so do buyer demands. Petrol prices are now edging towards Dh4.50 a litre; filling up even a compact Toyota Corolla can cost more than Dh200. For drivers of larger SUVs, the expense is considerably higher – a full tank in the latest Nissan Patrol costs more than Dh400, while older models can guzzle Dh600.In this context, an EV makes financial sense, particularly for people with access to a wall-mounted home charger. Even without one, the savings can be considerable. Depending on the vehicle's battery size, a full charge at a Dewa or Adnoc charging station typically costs little more than Dh80 ($22).Alongside rising petrol prices, the UAE's public EV charging network has continued to expand, with about 2,800 charging points across the country and more expected in the coming years. As electric vehicles become an increasingly practical option for motorists, here are some of the best models currently available in the UAE.Under Dh100,000JAC E30X (From Dh69,995) Behind the JAC E30X’s slightly cartoonish appearance lurks a capable and well-built car for its modest asking price. Although tiny in overall dimensions, the E30X's wheel-at-each-corner stance endows it with a 2,620 mm wheelbase, making it surprisingly spacious inside. With a single electric motor sending 95hp or 136hp (depending on trim level) to the front wheels, the JAC is no rocket ship, but it nevertheless feels decently zippy around town. Even the base model gets automatic LED headlights, retracting flush door handles, Apple CarPlay/Android Auto, faux-leather trim, cruise control and a 12.8-inch infotainment screen.Polestar 2 (from Dh89,900)With a starting price under Dh90,000, the Polestar 2 seems an unbelievable value for money. There is a catch, though, as the cars on offer for this price are part of the dealership’s 2024 inventory. However, they still have zero kilometres on the odometer and are still considered new. With the Polestar’s 272hp electric motor delivering a brisk 0-100kph split of 6.4 seconds and a touring range of 546km, there isn't anything equivalent at this price. Top it off with Swedish (such as Volvo) levels of build quality and safety, and the Polestar 2 seems a compelling buy – even if you’re getting a 2024 model-year car.Dh100,000 to 125,000Smart #3 (From Dh110,900)The perky-looking Smart #3 is a fusion of East and West, as the brand is German but the car itself is built in China. In its base form, the five-door compact SUV is equipped with a 66kWh battery and a single electric motor that sends a beefy 268hp and 384Nm to the front wheels. It’s a sprightly performer, sprinting from standstill to 100kph in 5.8 seconds, while touring range is also respectable at 430km (claimed). Standard features include a panoramic sunroof, a 12.8-inch central display and a 10-inch head-up display. The safety kit includes adaptive cruise control, automatic parking assist, lane-keeping assist, automatic emergency braking and a 360-degree camera.GAC Aion V (From Dh124,900)Billed as a Tesla Model Y rival, the GAC Aion V offers ample interior space and a generous feature list at a budget price. Propulsion for the Aion V is provided by a single e-motor that produces 204hp and 240Nm, channelled through the front wheels. GAC claims the Aion V, equipped with a 75.26kWh battery, can cover up to 510km on a full charge, based on the European WLTP test cycle. There’s also a lengthy list of standard features, such as a 14.6-inch touchscreen with Apple CarPlay/Android Auto, a nine-speaker sound system, navigation, a 9.8-inch digital instrument cluster, dual-zone climate control, a hands-free tailgate and 19-inch alloy wheels.Dh125,000 to 150,000Volvo EX30 (From Dh129,000)The Volvo EX30 is another value-packed offering as it provides the Swedish marque’s customary levels of build quality and safety at a wallet-friendly price. The stubby SUV has a distinctive profile, and that’s not a bad thing in a sea of vehicles that seem virtual clones of each other. In base trim, a single electric motor sends 272hp and 343Nm to the rear wheels, delivering 0-100kph split in 5.7 seconds and a maximum touring range of 337km (claimed). Included at no extra cost are Harman Kardon premium audio, dual-zone climate-control air-conditioning, 19-inch alloys, reversing camera, front and rear parking sensors, and front, side andcurtain airbags. Kia EV3 (From Dh141,645)The ultra-futuristic-looking EV3 embodies Kia’s latest design language, and everything under the skin is similarly cutting-edge. The EV3’s minimalistic interior is dominated by a pair of 12.3-inch screens – one for the instrument cluster and the other for the infotainment system. Conveniences include a powered tailgate, sliding-table centre console, bottle holders in all four doors and a 25-litre "frunk" (front trunk) that supplements the 460-litre rear load bay. headline: BOK chief to attend G20, IMF-WBG meetings in Bangkok
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top central banker will attend a meetin...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top central banker will attend a meeting of the Group of 20 (G20) finance ministers and central bank chiefs to be held in Thailand this week, the Bank of Korea (BOK) said Monday.

BOK Gov. Shin Hyun-song will join the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting, set to take place in Bangkok, where participants will discuss global economic conditions, growth and global imbalances, according to the central bank.

He will also attend the International Monetary Fund-World Bank Group (IMF-WBG) meetings, where discussions will focus on the global economic outlook and financial stability.

While in Bangkok, the BOK governor is scheduled to hold separate talks with high-ranking officials from the Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank and other major central banks to exchange views on recent international developments.

He will also participate in CNN's Global Perspectives, a live event series convening leaders, CEOs and innovators for conversations on issues covering culture, technology and business, along with Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala of Nigeria, director-general of the World Trade Organization (WTO), and Bernard Mensah, president of International at Bank of America, according to the BOK.

headline: EU promises Ukraine more funds for drones
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has promised that the European Union will next week allocate more funds to buy missiles and drones for Ukraine.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has promised that the European Union will next week allocate more funds to buy missiles and drones for Ukraine.

"I conveyed our solidarity with the Ukrainian people. And my full support for <…> Zelensky <…>. Ukraine will be front and center at this week’s European Council. We will discuss its funding needs for the year ahead and how to mobilize fresh global support. This week, the EU will also provide further funding for drones and missiles. To strengthen Ukraine’s defenses and protect its skies," she wrote on X after a phone call with Vladimir Zelensky.

She reassured Zelensky of full support following US President Donald Trump’s remarks that Ukraine needs a new president.

She also pledged that the European Union will soon "open two further clusters of chapters in the negotiations." "The momentum is real," she added.

omissions: No mention of the scale or specific amount of EU funds previously allocated to Ukraine
No mention of EU member state disagreements or procedural hurdles in approving new funds
No mention of Russia's response or the military situation on the ground

headline: Flash floods in Nepal again: Warning bells for Himalaya, lessons for India
body_text:
A sudden surge of water, mud, boulders and debris swept through settlements along Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki river in Gorkha district early on October 11, causing damage to infrastructure.

Early reports pointed to a landslide above Siuribas that blocked the Chumke Khola stream. Officials also suspected that a temporary blockage near Chekampar may have broken, releasing a sudden surge downstream.

The fresh Nepal incident has renewed concerns about sudden floods across the Himalaya, where retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and large quantities of loose sediment can combine to produce destructive flows.

The Indian Express spoke to experts to understand what caused the Fresh floods in Nepal

The immediate trigger appears to have involved a sudden release of water and debris, but the precise mechanism has not been conclusively established.

Speaking to The Indian Express, Manish Mehta, a glaciologist at the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology in Uttarakhand’s Dehradun, said his initial assessment was based on the available visuals and reports. He said the event appeared consistent with a possible glacial lake outburst flood or an avalanche involving ice and rock, but this was not a confirmed finding about the flood’s origin.

Why do these floods carry so much mud and rock?

Mehta explained that high-altitude Himalayan terrain contains large quantities of loose material shaped by erosion and past glacial activity. Glaciers transport and deposit sediment, while weathering and erosion continue to break down mountain slopes.

“Warming is happening, snow is melting. When snow melts, the cohesion between rock and ice ends,” he said.

He explained that loose material in upper mountain valleys can be mobilised by rainfall or a sudden release of water.

As the surge moves down the valley, it picks up additional sediment, boulders and vegetation, turning into a dense slurry.

P D Pant, director of the School of Earth and Environmental Science at Uttarakhand Open University, also highlighted the sediment content visible in footage of the flood going around on social media.

Speaking to The Indian Express, Pant said “The amount of gravel and sediment coming in is very high. That is causing more damage,”

In simple terms, the danger is not determined by water volume alone. A flood carrying heavy rocks and dense sediment can exert enormous force on houses, bridges and roads.

Mehta said that, based on the initial videos, the current event did not appear as catastrophic as the earlier one. He suggested that the width of the valley and the location of settlements could help explain the apparent difference.

“The valley the last time was very narrow and concise, you were sitting on the river bed,” he said. He contrasted this with the current location, saying that the wider valley could have influenced how the flood spread.

The same broad categories of hazards exist across the Indian Himalaya, including Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Ladakh, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. However, the precise mechanisms differ from one disaster to another.

The 2013 Kedarnath disaster involved exceptionally heavy rainfall, flooding and the mobilisation of sediment and debris. It is commonly discussed in the context of extreme rainfall and cloudburst-related flooding. A cloudburst is an intense, localised rainfall event; it is not the same as a GLOF or a landslide-dam breach.

The 2021 Chamoli disaster involved a massive rock-and-ice mass movement in the Rishiganga valley that generated a destructive downstream surge. It demonstrated how a high-altitude slope failure can rapidly transform into a major disaster, affecting river infrastructure and hydropower projects.

Pant said “similar hazards could occur across the Himalayan arc, from Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh, including Uttarakhand. The broad risk associated with glaciers, unstable slopes and sudden floods was not confined to one part of the Himalaya.”

Why are such floods occurring repeatedly? How much is climate change responsible?

Climate change is altering the conditions in which Himalayan hazards develop, but it does not establish the cause of any individual flood.

As temperatures rise, glaciers lose mass and retreat. The space left behind can form depressions where water accumulates. Some of these lakes are held back by moraines — deposits of sand, silt, gravel and boulders left by glaciers.

Pant explained that when a glacier retreats, a lake can form in the space left behind. He also explained that a moraine is not solid bedrock but a barrier composed of loose material.

Because such barriers can be vulnerable to erosion and failure, a sudden influx of water, overtopping or a breach can release a large volume of water downstream.

Pant also pointed to the role of prolonged or intense rainfall. If water accumulates in a lake or behind a landslide obstruction, it can contribute to a sudden release.

In areas where ice helps bind material together, changes in temperature and melting can make slopes more susceptible to failure.

Pant said climate change was the biggest factor behind retreating glaciers.

Scientific research, including assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, has documented glacier loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya and other mountain regions. This supports the conclusion that warming is changing the physical environment in which mountain hazards occur.

What is the way forward?

For Uttarakhand and the other Himalayan states in India, the challenge is to identify vulnerable lakes and unstable slopes, monitor changes and ensure that information reaches downstream settlements quickly enough for people to act.

Satellite observations can help map lakes, track glacier retreat and identify changes in the landscape. But satellite monitoring alone may not provide the real-time information needed to detect a rapidly rising lake or an impending failure of a natural dam.

This is where ground-based sensors can help. Mehta emphasised the need for early-warning systems across the Himalayan terrain.

“Basically, it is essential to install or establish an early warning system in the Himalayan terrain,” he said adding that the need was especially pressing because of the difficulty of protecting settlements once a destructive surge had begun.

Pant similarly said sensors could, where conditions allow, provide warnings hours in advance, giving authorities time to evacuate vulnerable settlements. “At least we can inform downstream settlements several hours in advance. We can evacuate them,” he said.

An Award-winning journalist covering the state of Uttarakhand, Vidheesha Kuntamalla has reported on education, policy and social justice. She has broken news and written investigative stories on education, some of which have prompted responses from central universities and government authorities. She uses the Right to Information Act as a reporting tool and enjoys telling people-driven stories through long-form journalism. Vidheesha joined The Indian Express’s Delhi City team in 2023, where she has been part of the education coverage in the newsroom, reporting on policy, institutions, and issues affecting students and communities. Her journalism career began in 2020 as a freelance journalist after she left a career in civil engineering. She covered her home states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, focusing on gender, social justice, and politics. body_text:
UAE clubs might have been battling to bridge the gap to their star-studded Saudi Arabian rivals in recent seasons.

But there are signs that sides from the Emirates could challenge for honours in the AFC Champions League again this term.

Al Ain made a major statement when they thrashed Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr 4-0 on the opening day of the AFC Champions League Elite season last month.

Arabian Gulf Cup: UAE have plenty to work with despite final defeat

Now Al Wasl have their chance to make a mark against celebrated Saudi Arabian opposition, too, when Asian competition returns this week.

Over the past two seasons in continental competition, Wasl have twice been beaten 4-0 by Nassr – with Ronaldo scoring in each fixture.

And yet they will have reason for optimism when they host another expensively assembled Saudi club, Al Ahli, in Zabeel on Monday night.

On the surface, it seems like a daunting task for the Dubai side. Ahli have been champions of Asia in each of the past two seasons.

Ivan Toney, their English striker, has scored 11 goals in eight games at the start of the Saudi Pro League season. That is quite the haul, given Ahli have not exactly dominated: they have lost three of those eight matches.

Plus, many of Ahli’s players are returning to club commitments buoyed by success with the Saudi Arabia national team in the Arabian Gulf Cup.

That includes Feras Al Buraikan, the Ahli striker who scored in the final win against the UAE.

But Wasl have made a bright start to the season themselves. They have lost just once in the UAE Pro League and are the division’s leading scorers.

They also had an uplifting three matches in the Adib Cup while many stars were away on international duty, winning all three.

Wasl can pick at the fragile confidence of their guests, who are in the early stages of a rebuild following the departure of some influential figures this summer.
