headline: North Korea's missile launches appear to be response to South Korea’s hypersonic weapon test: Military
summary: South Korean military says launches may also be aimed at demonstrating progress under Pyongyang's five-year defense development plan
body_text:
Anadolu Ajansı © 2026

North Korea's ballistic missile launches Monday appeared to be a response to South Korea's successful test of a hypersonic glide vehicle last week, said the South Korean military.

The assessment came after North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea, with at least one traveling more than 900 kilometers (559 miles), according to Yonhap News Agency.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches around 9.20 am local time (0020GMT) from the Pyongyang area.

JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the launches could also be intended to demonstrate progress under North Korea's five-year defense development plan, Yonhap reported.

Jang declined to confirm whether the missiles were hypersonic or intermediate-range weapons, saying further technical analysis was required.

South Korea conducted its first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle Thursday, in an apparent demonstration of its advanced missile capabilities.

Japan also detected two suspected ballistic missiles, which reportedly fell outside its exclusive economic zone.

The latest launches come amid tensions following a Sept. 21 land mine explosion in the Demilitarized Zone that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.

Seoul accused North Korean troops of deliberately planting the mines following a joint investigation with the UN Command.

Pyongyang denied responsibility, accused Seoul of fabricating the findings and warned of retaliation against any military counteraction.

North Korea has so far not issued a public statement on Monday's launches.

headline: Flash floods in Nepal again: Warning bells for Himalaya, lessons for India
body_text:
A sudden surge of water, mud, boulders and debris swept through settlements along Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki river in Gorkha district early on October 11, causing damage to infrastructure.

Early reports pointed to a landslide above Siuribas that blocked the Chumke Khola stream. Officials also suspected that a temporary blockage near Chekampar may have broken, releasing a sudden surge downstream.

The fresh Nepal incident has renewed concerns about sudden floods across the Himalaya, where retreating glaciers, unstable mountain slopes and large quantities of loose sediment can combine to produce destructive flows.

The Indian Express spoke to experts to understand what caused the Fresh floods in Nepal

The immediate trigger appears to have involved a sudden release of water and debris, but the precise mechanism has not been conclusively established.

Speaking to The Indian Express, Manish Mehta, a glaciologist at the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology in Uttarakhand’s Dehradun, said his initial assessment was based on the available visuals and reports. He said the event appeared consistent with a possible glacial lake outburst flood or an avalanche involving ice and rock, but this was not a confirmed finding about the flood’s origin.

Why do these floods carry so much mud and rock?

Mehta explained that high-altitude Himalayan terrain contains large quantities of loose material shaped by erosion and past glacial activity. Glaciers transport and deposit sediment, while weathering and erosion continue to break down mountain slopes.

“Warming is happening, snow is melting. When snow melts, the cohesion between rock and ice ends,” he said.

He explained that loose material in upper mountain valleys can be mobilised by rainfall or a sudden release of water.

As the surge moves down the valley, it picks up additional sediment, boulders and vegetation, turning into a dense slurry.

P D Pant, director of the School of Earth and Environmental Science at Uttarakhand Open University, also highlighted the sediment content visible in footage of the flood going around on social media.

Speaking to The Indian Express, Pant said “The amount of gravel and sediment coming in is very high. That is causing more damage,”

In simple terms, the danger is not determined by water volume alone. A flood carrying heavy rocks and dense sediment can exert enormous force on houses, bridges and roads.

Mehta said that, based on the initial videos, the current event did not appear as catastrophic as the earlier one. He suggested that the width of the valley and the location of settlements could help explain the apparent difference.

“The valley the last time was very narrow and concise, you were sitting on the river bed,” he said. He contrasted this with the current location, saying that the wider valley could have influenced how the flood spread.

The same broad categories of hazards exist across the Indian Himalaya, including Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Ladakh, Sikkim and Arunachal Pradesh. However, the precise mechanisms differ from one disaster to another.

The 2013 Kedarnath disaster involved exceptionally heavy rainfall, flooding and the mobilisation of sediment and debris. It is commonly discussed in the context of extreme rainfall and cloudburst-related flooding. A cloudburst is an intense, localised rainfall event; it is not the same as a GLOF or a landslide-dam breach.

The 2021 Chamoli disaster involved a massive rock-and-ice mass movement in the Rishiganga valley that generated a destructive downstream surge. It demonstrated how a high-altitude slope failure can rapidly transform into a major disaster, affecting river infrastructure and hydropower projects.

Pant said “similar hazards could occur across the Himalayan arc, from Kashmir to Arunachal Pradesh, including Uttarakhand. The broad risk associated with glaciers, unstable slopes and sudden floods was not confined to one part of the Himalaya.”

Why are such floods occurring repeatedly? How much is climate change responsible?

Climate change is altering the conditions in which Himalayan hazards develop, but it does not establish the cause of any individual flood.

As temperatures rise, glaciers lose mass and retreat. The space left behind can form depressions where water accumulates. Some of these lakes are held back by moraines — deposits of sand, silt, gravel and boulders left by glaciers.

Pant explained that when a glacier retreats, a lake can form in the space left behind. He also explained that a moraine is not solid bedrock but a barrier composed of loose material.

Because such barriers can be vulnerable to erosion and failure, a sudden influx of water, overtopping or a breach can release a large volume of water downstream.

Pant also pointed to the role of prolonged or intense rainfall. If water accumulates in a lake or behind a landslide obstruction, it can contribute to a sudden release.

In areas where ice helps bind material together, changes in temperature and melting can make slopes more susceptible to failure.

Pant said climate change was the biggest factor behind retreating glaciers.

Scientific research, including assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, has documented glacier loss across the Hindu Kush Himalaya and other mountain regions. This supports the conclusion that warming is changing the physical environment in which mountain hazards occur.

What is the way forward?

For Uttarakhand and the other Himalayan states in India, the challenge is to identify vulnerable lakes and unstable slopes, monitor changes and ensure that information reaches downstream settlements quickly enough for people to act.

Satellite observations can help map lakes, track glacier retreat and identify changes in the landscape. But satellite monitoring alone may not provide the real-time information needed to detect a rapidly rising lake or an impending failure of a natural dam.

This is where ground-based sensors can help. Mehta emphasised the need for early-warning systems across the Himalayan terrain.

“Basically, it is essential to install or establish an early warning system in the Himalayan terrain,” he said adding that the need was especially pressing because of the difficulty of protecting settlements once a destructive surge had begun.

Pant similarly said sensors could, where conditions allow, provide warnings hours in advance, giving authorities time to evacuate vulnerable settlements. “At least we can inform downstream settlements several hours in advance. We can evacuate them,” he said.

An Award-winning journalist covering the state of Uttarakhand, Vidheesha Kuntamalla has reported on education, policy and social justice. She has broken news and written investigative stories on education, some of which have prompted responses from central universities and government authorities. She uses the Right to Information Act as a reporting tool and enjoys telling people-driven stories through long-form journalism. Vidheesha joined The Indian Express’s Delhi City team in 2023, where she has been part of the education coverage in the newsroom, reporting on policy, institutions, and issues affecting students and communities. Her journalism career began in 2020 as a freelance journalist after she left a career in civil engineering. She covered her home states of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, focusing on gender, social justice, and politics. headline: Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia condemn Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
summary: ANKARA, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia condemned attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Riyadh's international airport, saying they were a "dangerous escalation that cannot be justified or accepted under any pretext".One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by theHouthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
body_text:
ANKARA, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia condemned attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Riyadh's international airport, saying they were a "dangerous escalation that cannot be justified or accepted under any pretext".

One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by theHouthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The group of regional powers - dubbed the R4 - reaffirmed their solidarity and support for Saudi Arabia, including full support for all "legitimate measures and steps" it takes to counter the attacks, deter threats and prevent them from happening again.

"The Group holds the Houthi militia fully accountable for the results of these attacks and any repercussions that come with it that threaten regional and international peace and security, and demands the immediate and unconditional halt of these attacks," they said in a joint statement on Sunday.

NATO member Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan signed a joint defence pact with Saudi Arabia in August, under which an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all. Last week, the countries said they had agreed to implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks.

On Thursday, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Turkey was assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia, butruled out troop deployment and Turkish participation in offensive operations. A day earlier, officials had told Reuters that Ankara was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Riyadh.

Turkish support for Saudi Arabia has largely been in a bilateral capacity so far, as Turkey's parliament has not yet officially ratified the joint defence pact. The agreement is expected to be submitted to parliament in the coming days.

Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has provided Saudi Arabia withdefence equipment and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels have intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports in the past week, hitting sites in Riyadh, Abha, Jazan and Najran, with a projectile also damaging Dammam's airport.

The strikes have disrupted air travel and caused civilian casualties, with Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport bearing the brunt of the aggression. The escalation included a missile attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured hundreds, Saudi authorities said. A further attack on Riyadh airport on Sunday killed one more person.

October 6: Saudi authorities reported attacks on King Abdullah bin Abdulaziz International Airport in Jazan and Najran International Airport, in the south. Three people were injured. Saudi air defences also intercepted a ballistic missile fired at Khamis Mushait.

October 7: Strikes on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport killed three foreign citizens and injured 36, Saudi authorities said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attacks.

October 8: At least one attack hit King Khalid International Airport. Three Saudi citizens were killed, including an airline pilot, and several people were injured. An aircraft belonging to state carrier Saudia was damaged and smoke was seen rising from the airport.

October 10: A Houthi missile struck King Khalid International Airport, initially killing 12 people and injuring 309, Saudi authorities said. The dead included Saudis and citizens of Bangladesh, the US, Egypt, Jordan, Palestine, Syria and Sudan. The toll rose to 13 on Sunday after an injured Indian citizen died. Airport operations were suspended and flights were cancelled or diverted.

October 11: A projectile struck Terminals 3 and 4 at Riyadh airport, killing a Pakistani citizen and injuring 11. The Saudi-led coalition also said a projectile fell near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and that the damage was being assessed. The Houthis claimed responsibility.

Riyadh's airport has been struck four times in five days, and at least 20 people have been killed. The Houthis have said Saudi airspace is a military zone. The coalition has vowed to “respond decisively” and says it is continuing strikes on Houthi launch sites.

Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.

Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, has called for stronger Gulf security and collective defence, warning that threats against one Gulf state put the entire region at risk.

In a statement posted on X, Dr Gargash said the security of Gulf states as a whole was "indivisible".

“Since the start of the aggression against the Gulf Arab states, based on the aggressor's mistaken assessment that they were the weakest link in a war we sought to avoid, it has become clear that we are all targeted and that our security is indivisible,” he said.

He stressed that attacks against Saudi Arabia also threatened the wider Gulf. “Targeting our sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” he added.

Dr Gargash called for renewed regional co-ordination, particularly in security and defence, and stronger collective security arrangements. “There is a need to revitalise joint Gulf action, particularly in its security and defence dimensions, and to strengthen the collective security system,” he said.

He warned that shortcomings in regional co-operation had contributed to the current challenges. “This is the dimension in which there has been a serious shortcoming, which encouraged others to overstep against us,” Dr Gargash said. “Gulf security is a shared responsibility that cannot tolerate neglect or delay."

body_text:
The UAE’s leading cricketers started their tour of Dallas for their latest Cricket World Cup League Two tri-series conflicted by feelings of a potential loss of earnings.

Now they face the prospect of having to play for survival as one-day international cricketers altogether after a dismal sequence of performances.

The national team suffered a third loss in a row on Sunday as they were soundly beaten by the United States by five wickets.

They lost with over 11 overs to spare. So consigned to their fate were they, they did not even bother bringing up the field to prevent the single that was needed to win the game.

It leaves them last placed in CWCL2, and in a fight to retain their status in ODI cricket.

It is a sorry state for a side who have underachieved for years, and now face the threat of relegation to the third tier of 50-over international cricket.

Even with one more tri-series still to play, involving the Netherlands and Oman in the UAE later this month, they are now guaranteed to be playing in the World Cup Qualifier Play-off in December.

They had started the trip to Dallas with fanciful ambitions of playing their way into the top four of CWCL2.

That would have avoided the need to participate in the play-off, and advancing straight to the global qualifier in February.

More pressingly, it would have made the players available for the ILT20 in December. Six of the 15-player squad had earned contracts to play in that competition, on deals ranging from $10,000 to $95,000.

To avoid the scheduling clash, they would have had to have won all eight of their remaining matches, and hoped results elsewhere went their way. Instead, they saw one match washed out, and lost the other three.

Finishing in the top six of CWCL2 now looks beyond the UAE, too. To do that, they would have to win all four matches against the Netherlands and Oman, and hope sixth-placed Nepal lost all their remaining three matches.

So now ODI status – and the vast tranche of ICC funding that it unlocks – is in jeopardy.

The rules governing ODI status are complex, and have yet to be publicly confirmed by the ICC.

The play-off is an eight-team tournament involving the bottom four sides from CWCL2, plus two sides each from the two feeder Challenger Leagues that make up the third tier of ODI cricket’s competition structure.

It is likely the UAE will likely have to finish above both sides who won those feeder leagues for them to retain their ODI privileges.

Italy – who have former UAE coach Dougie Brown on their coaching staff - finished top of Challenge League B, and came up to the play-off with Uganda.

Challenge League A will conclude in Kenya this month. Jersey are top of the table, with Kuwait in second.

If the UAE are to continue in ODI cricket via the play-off, they will have to find a remedy to their chronic batting failings.

After making 330 in their first match in Dallas, they crumbled to 134 against Namibia, then 213 in the last game against the United States.

“It was tough luck for us on this tour,” Harpreet Bhatia, the UAE captain, said after defeat on Sunday.

“I hope the boys will learn from this series. We were always short of runs in the last couple of games. We will work things out and see what we can do from here.

“The way we played the first game, it was close. We scored 330, then after that there was a problem with scoring runs in the last two games.

“We were always short. I feel we were 40 or 50 runs short today and if we could have got 280 I think it could have been a good game for us.”

headline: Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia condemn Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport
summary: ANKARA, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia condemned attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Riyadh's international airport, saying they were a "dangerous escalation that cannot be justified or accepted under any pretext".One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by theHouthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
body_text:
ANKARA, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt and Saudi Arabia condemned attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants on Riyadh's international airport, saying they were a "dangerous escalation that cannot be justified or accepted under any pretext".

One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack on Riyadh's international airport on Sunday, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by theHouthis that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The group of regional powers - dubbed the R4 - reaffirmed their solidarity and support for Saudi Arabia, including full support for all "legitimate measures and steps" it takes to counter the attacks, deter threats and prevent them from happening again.

"The Group holds the Houthi militia fully accountable for the results of these attacks and any repercussions that come with it that threaten regional and international peace and security, and demands the immediate and unconditional halt of these attacks," they said in a joint statement on Sunday.

NATO member Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan signed a joint defence pact with Saudi Arabia in August, under which an attack on one party constitutes an attack on all. Last week, the countries said they had agreed to implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks.

On Thursday, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Turkey was assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia, butruled out troop deployment and Turkish participation in offensive operations. A day earlier, officials had told Reuters that Ankara was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Riyadh.

Turkish support for Saudi Arabia has largely been in a bilateral capacity so far, as Turkey's parliament has not yet officially ratified the joint defence pact. The agreement is expected to be submitted to parliament in the coming days.

Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has provided Saudi Arabia withdefence equipment and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu; editing by Lincoln Feast.)

Both main crude contracts sank more than one percent following Trump's declaration, even as it sparked astonishment in Kyiv, which also said Moscow had struck multiple power plants in the country.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he was seeking further details of the announcement, but added that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well".

Russia has yet to confirm its agreement.

body_text:
UAE airlines have continued to cancel flights to and from Riyadh, with travel disruption extending into Tuesday after King Khalid International Airport was closed following a deadly Houthi attack.

Etihad Airways has announced cancellations for Monday and Tuesday, with services to Dammam and Jeddah also affected. Emirates, flydubai and Air Arabia have also cancelled flights connecting Dubai and Sharjah with the Saudi capital.

The disruption comes as the closure of the Riyadh airport is extended until midnight on Tuesday (1am on Wednesday, UAE time), Flightradar24 said. An earlier aviation notice had indicated the airport would remain closed until midnight on Sunday. The latest notice referred to precautionary measures, but did not specify when passenger operations would resume.

Twelve killed and 309 wounded in attack on Riyadh airport

Flightradar24 listed more than 500 flights to and from Riyadh as being cancelled on Monday.

The airport was attacked on Sunday, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Houthis killed 13 people and injured more than 300. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation suspended operations and began assessing the damage.

Flights had already faced days of disruption owing to earlier attacks. The latest cancellations extend beyond the suspension periods previously announced by some UAE airlines.

Etihad has cancelled several flights between Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia on Monday and Tuesday, affecting services to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah.

According to the airline's latest travel advisory, Monday's cancellations include flights EY559 and EY560 between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. But Etihad's flight listings also show outbound Riyadh services EY551 and EY555 as being cancelled.

Four flights between Abu Dhabi and Dammam – EY573, EY574, EY575 and EY576 – have also been cancelled on Monday, along with Jeddah services EY601, EY602, EY603 and EY604.

Further cancellations are scheduled for Tuesday, including Dammam services EY575 and EY576, Jeddah flights EY602, EY603 and EY604, and Riyadh services EY551 and EY552.

Passengers are advised to check their flight status directly with Etihad before travelling, as further changes are possible.

Emirates' flight status website shows all six services between Dubai and Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday. These include outbound flights EK815, EK817 and EK819, along with returning services EK816, EK818 and EK820.

Four flights remain cancelled on Tuesday, including EK815, EK817 and EK819 from Dubai to Riyadh and the return service EK816. Flights EK818 and EK820 from Riyadh to Dubai have not yet been cancelled, but are subject to further changes.

Flydubai has cancelled flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh up to and including Wednesday, amid the disruption to services to Saudi Arabia.

“Flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh have been cancelled up to and including October 14,” a flydubai representative told The National. “We continue to monitor the situation closely and we will update our customers through our official channels regarding any amendments to our flight schedules.”

The latest cancellations extend the airline's earlier advisory, which covered flights to Riyadh and Yanbu through October 10, and Abha through October 11.

According to Air Arabia's official flight status website, flights G9151 and G9154 from Sharjah to Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday and Tuesday. Flight G9195 from Sharjah to Abha is also listed as cancelled on both days.

Those with plans to travel should confirm their flight status directly with their airline before leaving for the airport and check notifications about changes to their booking.

Passengers whose flights have been cancelled should contact their airline or travel agent about rebooking and refund options. Travellers with onward connections should also confirm whether changes are needed to the rest of their journey.

Several services between the UAE and Riyadh remain as scheduled for Monday, although those operations depend on conditions at the airport. Passengers should confirm the status of their flight directly with their airline before travelling.

analysis.framing: The article focuses on the practical impact of the Riyadh airport closure on UAE airline passengers, providing detailed flight cancellations and travel advice while briefly noting the deadly Houthi attack that triggered the closure.

loaded_language.explanation: The adjective 'deadly' is emotionally charged and emphasizes the lethal outcome, which could evoke fear or sympathy.
This phrase is vague and does not specify what actions are being taken, potentially obscuring the severity of the situation.

omissions: Details about the Houthi attack itself, such as the number of casualties or the extent of damage, are only briefly mentioned and not elaborated.
No context on the broader conflict in Yemen or the Houthi movement's motivations.
Lack of information on how the airport closure affects non-UAE airlines or international travel beyond the region.

headline: Africa: AU to Push for Financial Reforms, Debt Relief At IMF-World Bank Meetings
summary: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- The African Union (AU) will push for reforms to the global financial system, improved debt resolution mechanisms and stronger financial independence for the continent during the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF)-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
body_text:
Nairobi — The African Union (AU) will push for reforms to the global financial system, improved debt resolution mechanisms and stronger financial independence for the continent during the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF)-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

The meetings, scheduled for October 12-18, will provide a platform for the AU to advance Africa's priorities on international tax cooperation, financial integration and access to resources for development.

The continental body said it would host four side events from October 13 to 16, focusing on international tax cooperation, operationalising African Union financial institutions, enabling instant cross-border payments and advancing effective debt resolution mechanisms.

"These discussions build on the AU's ongoing work to reform the global financial architecture, strengthen Africa's financial independence and unlock more resources for the continent's development," the organisation said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The focus on debt resolution comes as African countries seek sustainable ways to manage debt obligations while financing infrastructure, public services and economic development.

More effective debt-resolution mechanisms could be part of broader efforts to address financing constraints facing developing economies.

The AU will also use the meetings to advance discussions on international tax cooperation, an area central to efforts to strengthen domestic resource mobilisation and ensure African countries participate in shaping global tax rules.

Operationalising African Union financial institutions is another priority, reflecting the bloc's ambition to strengthen Africa's financial capacity and expand its ability to mobilise resources for continental development.

The proposed discussions on instant cross-border payments will focus on improving financial connectivity across African markets. More efficient payment systems can reduce transaction barriers, support regional trade, and facilitate cross-border payments.

The four engagements form part of the AU's broader efforts to influence reforms to the international financial architecture and increase the resources available to support Africa's development priorities.

The outcomes of the discussions could help shape the continent's engagement with international financial institutions on debt sustainability, taxation, regional financial integration and development financing.

headline: Gargash calls for stronger Gulf security and collective defence
summary: Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, has called for stronger Gulf security and collective defence, warning that threats against one Gulf state put the entire region at risk.In a statement posted on X, Dr Gargash said the security of Gulf states as a whole was "indivisible".“Since the start of the aggression against the Gulf Arab states, based on the aggressor's mistaken assessment that they were the weakest link in a war we sought to avoid, it has become clear that we are all targeted and that our security is indivisible,” he said.He stressed that attacks against Saudi Arabia also threatened the wider Gulf. “Targeting our sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” he added.Dr Gargash called for renewed regional co-ordination, particularly in security and defence, and stronger collective security arrangements. “There is a need to revitalise joint Gulf action, particularly in its security and defence dimensions, and to strengthen the collective security system,” he said.He warned that shortcomings in regional co-operation had contributed to the current challenges. “This is the dimension in which there has been a serious shortcoming, which encouraged others to overstep against us,” Dr Gargash said. “Gulf security is a shared responsibility that cannot tolerate neglect or delay."
body_text:
Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, has called for stronger Gulf security and collective defence, warning that threats against one Gulf state put the entire region at risk.

In a statement posted on X, Dr Gargash said the security of Gulf states as a whole was "indivisible".

“Since the start of the aggression against the Gulf Arab states, based on the aggressor's mistaken assessment that they were the weakest link in a war we sought to avoid, it has become clear that we are all targeted and that our security is indivisible,” he said.

He stressed that attacks against Saudi Arabia also threatened the wider Gulf. “Targeting our sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” he added.

Dr Gargash called for renewed regional co-ordination, particularly in security and defence, and stronger collective security arrangements. “There is a need to revitalise joint Gulf action, particularly in its security and defence dimensions, and to strengthen the collective security system,” he said.

He warned that shortcomings in regional co-operation had contributed to the current challenges. “This is the dimension in which there has been a serious shortcoming, which encouraged others to overstep against us,” Dr Gargash said. “Gulf security is a shared responsibility that cannot tolerate neglect or delay."

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a straightforward report of a UAE official's call for Gulf collective security, presenting his statements through direct quotation without independent verification or contextualization.

loaded_language.quote: aggression against the Gulf Arab states
loaded_language.explanation: The term 'aggression' is a loaded, legally charged word that presupposes an unprovoked attack and assigns blame, rather than using neutral language like 'military action' or 'strikes'.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: military action against the Gulf Arab states

loaded_language.explanation: Labeling a party as 'the aggressor' and calling their assessment 'mistaken' adopts the speaker's characterization as fact, rather than attributing it as an opinion.

loaded_language.quote: encouraged others to overstep against us
loaded_language.explanation: The phrase 'overstep against us' is vague and emotionally charged, implying unjustified encroachment without specifying the nature of the actions.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: encouraged others to take action against us

loaded_language.explanation: The adjective 'sisterly' is an emotive, familial term that conveys closeness and solidarity, rather than a neutral descriptor like 'neighboring' or 'Saudi'.

There is no mention of any response or reaction from other Gulf states or international actors.
The article does not include any independent verification or alternative perspectives on the situation.

body_text:
The UAE’s leading cricketers started their tour of Dallas for their latest Cricket World Cup League Two tri-series conflicted by feelings of a potential loss of earnings.

Now they face the prospect of having to play for survival as one-day international cricketers altogether after a dismal sequence of performances.

The national team suffered a third loss in a row on Sunday as they were soundly beaten by the United States by five wickets.

They lost with over 11 overs to spare. So consigned to their fate were they, they did not even bother bringing up the field to prevent the single that was needed to win the game.

It leaves them last placed in CWCL2, and in a fight to retain their status in ODI cricket.

It is a sorry state for a side who have underachieved for years, and now face the threat of relegation to the third tier of 50-over international cricket.

Even with one more tri-series still to play, involving the Netherlands and Oman in the UAE later this month, they are now guaranteed to be playing in the World Cup Qualifier Play-off in December.

They had started the trip to Dallas with fanciful ambitions of playing their way into the top four of CWCL2.

That would have avoided the need to participate in the play-off, and advancing straight to the global qualifier in February.

More pressingly, it would have made the players available for the ILT20 in December. Six of the 15-player squad had earned contracts to play in that competition, on deals ranging from $10,000 to $95,000.

To avoid the scheduling clash, they would have had to have won all eight of their remaining matches, and hoped results elsewhere went their way. Instead, they saw one match washed out, and lost the other three.

Finishing in the top six of CWCL2 now looks beyond the UAE, too. To do that, they would have to win all four matches against the Netherlands and Oman, and hope sixth-placed Nepal lost all their remaining three matches.

So now ODI status – and the vast tranche of ICC funding that it unlocks – is in jeopardy.

The rules governing ODI status are complex, and have yet to be publicly confirmed by the ICC.

The play-off is an eight-team tournament involving the bottom four sides from CWCL2, plus two sides each from the two feeder Challenger Leagues that make up the third tier of ODI cricket’s competition structure.

It is likely the UAE will likely have to finish above both sides who won those feeder leagues for them to retain their ODI privileges.

Italy – who have former UAE coach Dougie Brown on their coaching staff - finished top of Challenge League B, and came up to the play-off with Uganda.

Challenge League A will conclude in Kenya this month. Jersey are top of the table, with Kuwait in second.

If the UAE are to continue in ODI cricket via the play-off, they will have to find a remedy to their chronic batting failings.

After making 330 in their first match in Dallas, they crumbled to 134 against Namibia, then 213 in the last game against the United States.

“It was tough luck for us on this tour,” Harpreet Bhatia, the UAE captain, said after defeat on Sunday.

“I hope the boys will learn from this series. We were always short of runs in the last couple of games. We will work things out and see what we can do from here.

“The way we played the first game, it was close. We scored 330, then after that there was a problem with scoring runs in the last two games.

“We were always short. I feel we were 40 or 50 runs short today and if we could have got 280 I think it could have been a good game for us.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the UAE cricket team's losses as a self-inflicted collapse that jeopardizes their ODI status and players' financial opportunities, emphasizing underachievement and chronic batting failures.

Emphasizes the severity of defeat in a dramatic way.

Editorializes about long-term performance without providing specific evidence.
Uses 'chronic' to imply a persistent, almost diseased problem, which is emotionally loaded.

headline: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an 'energy ceasefire'
summary: President Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.(Image credit: Andrii Marienko)
body_text:
A rescue worker puts out a fire at residential houses destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Andrii Marienko/AP hide caption

WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.

Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"

Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.

"Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening."

The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia."

Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter."

Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin "had one answer to all of them — 'nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world."

He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.

"We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ."

On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.

Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.

Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

"Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.

"With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.

Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy's term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.

Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.

Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.

He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.

The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

"Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.

Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.

"I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."

Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.

Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience." He said they affected "healthcare, and everything else."

body_text:
Mohamed Salah set a new Turkish Super Lig record over the weekend, becoming the fastest player to register 10 goal contributions.

The Egyptian laid on an assist for teammate Francolino in Trabzonspor's 3-0 win over Samsunspor on Saturday; it was his third assist of the campaign.

Added to his seven goals since his summer move from Liverpool, Salah has reached double figures in goal contributions in only seven games for his new club.

Egypt lose South Africa friendly as Salah's absence continues

Salah leads the Super Lig scoring charts alongside Gift Orban of Umit Sortif. Victor Osimhen (Galatasaray), Vedat Muriqi (Fenerbahce) and Eldor Shomurodov (Istanbul Basaksehir) have all scored six goals.

His assist against Samsunspor also took him level at the top of the assists chart.

Trabzonspor are fifth in the Turkish Super Lig, three points behind league leaders Galatasaray, whom Trabzon beat 4-0 before the recent international break.

A return to domestic action comes after Salah endured a turbulent time with his national team during the international break.

Salah left Egypt's camp ahead of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan after a reported falling out with coach Hossam Hassan.

Salah was substituted in Egypt's previous match against Angola after only 60 minutes, with Pharaohs coach Hassan saying Salah was taken off for "technical reasons".

News then broke that Salah had left the national team camp, with the Egypt captain also said to have taken exception to Hassan's comments about injured goalkeeper Mohamed El Shenawy.

The Egyptian Football Association released a statement saying that the plan, made before the Angola game, was always for Salah to sit out the match against South Sudan in Juba as the game would be played on an artificial pitch, before rejoining the rest of the squad for the friendly against South Africa in Cairo on October 4.

Salah did not return, and Egypt lost the match 1-0. Several news outlets reported that he travelled to England before returning to Turkey to begin training with Trabzonspor ahead of the league's resumption on October 10.

Boxing legend Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez is set to defy security concerns and go ahead with his bout against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh, according to organiser Turki Alalshikh.

Alvarez is slated to face Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title in the Saudi capital on October 31, but the event has been thrown into doubt after several days of deadly strikes on the city.

One person was killed and 11 injured in an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, according to Saudi authorities. That came a day after a Houthi-claimed strike killed 13 people and injured more than 300.

Al Nassr ACL clash in doubt over Riyadh security situation

Alalshikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority and a global boxing power broker, said in a social media post that the event would go ahead as planned, and that Alvarez had confirmed he was happy to proceed.

“Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Alalshikh posted on X on Sunday night. “He fears nothing.

“My country is home to the two Holy Mosques, land of peace, safety, rich civilisation, deep history, and kind-hearted people. Thank you to everyone who checked in and showed support. Hard times reveal true friends.”

The Saudi Pro League postponed Sunday's match between Abha and Al Faisaly, while it remains unclear whether Monday's Asian Champions League match between Al Nassr and Neftchi Fergana will go ahead.

“The SPL confirmed the decision was made following a review of the circumstances surrounding the match,” the league said. "[The decision was taken] in accordance with approved regulatory procedures, ensuring that situations beyond the clubs' control are addressed while maintaining the continuity of the competition.”

Abha is around 900km south-west of Riyadh and approximately 200km from the Yemen border.

Saudi sport has seen several major events cancelled this year, including April's Formula One Grand Prix and next month's World Rally Championship.

The October 31 boxing card at Kingdom Arena is dubbed “Mexico vs the Rest of the World” and is headlined by Alvarez's attempt to recapture a version of the 168lb world title.

The 36-year-old (63-3-2) has not fought since losing to Terence Crawford last September.

It was reported by The Athletic on Sunday night that Alvarez remained eager to press ahead with the Riyadh bout, and that broadcaster DAZN was advancing in its plans to cover the event on the ground in Saudi Arabia.

headline: Haikou launches two direct air routes to Malaysia
summary: Haikou Meilan International Airport in south China's Hainan Province launched two direct routes to Malaysia on Sunday, connecting Haikou with Penang and Kota Kinabalu.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- Haikou Meilan International Airport in south China's Hainan Province launched two direct routes to Malaysia on Sunday, connecting Haikou with Penang and Kota Kinabalu.

The new routes are expected to boost tourism spending as travelers take advantage of the mutual visa exemption policy between China and Malaysia. They will also support economic and trade cooperation, cultural and tourism exchanges, and business travel between the Hainan Free Trade Port and ASEAN countries.

The Haikou-Penang route is operated by Hainan Airlines using Boeing 737-series aircraft, with flights every Wednesday and Sunday.

The Haikou-Kota Kinabalu route is operated by 9 Air, also using Boeing 737-series aircraft, with three flights every two weeks: on Friday and Sunday in one week and Wednesday in the next.

The airport said it has operated 45 international passenger routes serving 28 overseas cities so far in 2026. Its international network spans Southeast Asia, Northeast Asia, the Middle East, Australia and New Zealand, Europe, and North America.

The airport said it would continue to launch new international routes and increase flight frequencies while improving services for international passengers throughout their journeys.

headline: Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an 'energy ceasefire'
summary: President Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire," but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.(Image credit: Andrii Marienko)
body_text:
A rescue worker puts out a fire at residential houses destroyed in a Russian strike on Kharkiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Andrii Marienko/AP hide caption

WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement.

Trump's brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: "Do not break it!"

Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country "welcomed" the announcement by Trump as "good news for everyone," Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv.

"Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian 'shaheds' all day today," he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . "There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening."

The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was "ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure — and we count on the same readiness from Russia."

Russia has sought to deny Ukrainian civilians power, heat and running water during the war, hoping to wear down public resistance to Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukrainian officials describe the strategy as "weaponizing winter."

Zelenskyy said Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps but Russian President Vladimir Putin "had one answer to all of them — 'nyet.' We do hope that he will finally say something different to America, Ukraine, and the entire world."

He said Kyiv is maintaining contact with the U.S., and he thanked Americans for their support. He said on X that he had spoken about the development with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

In an interview broadcast earlier Sunday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to stop striking Russian refineries if Moscow halted attacks on Ukraine's energy system, and he asked Trump to press the Kremlin to agree.

"We are asking President Trump, (to) give them (a) signal, not (to) attack energy infrastructure of Ukraine," he told ABC's "This Week ."

On Sept. 14, Trump claimed on social media that both countries had agreed "not to hit" each other's energy infrastructure but offered no details on that proposal either. While Zelenskyy had said Ukraine was ready to comply if Russia did, nothing came of the proposal.

Trump said Saturday it was time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war and blaming him for high diesel prices in the U.S.

Zelenskyy said in response to Trump's comments that Ukraine could hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

"Give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections," he said, adding that Ukraine would be ready to accept whatever choice its people made.

"With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," he said. Holding an election during the war would be unlawful and that Ukraine would need security guarantees to allow for safe voting, Zelenskyy added.

Ukraine has been under martial law since Putin launched the full-scale invasion in February 2022, and the Ukrainian Constitution bars elections while it remains in force. Beyond the legal barrier, a nationwide vote would be vulnerable to Russian attacks, and organizing one is widely seen as logistically impossible, with roughly a fifth of the country held by Russia, millions of Ukrainians displaced abroad and soldiers on the front line. Zelenskyy's term formally expired in May 2024, but the constitution allows him to remain in office until a new president is sworn in.

The exchange came as Kyiv pressed its campaign against Russian infrastructure, with a drone attack on Sunday shutting down a data center in the city of Vladimir, east of Moscow, run by technology giant Yandex. It was the third strike on the company's facilities in four days.

Russia and Ukraine have been waging a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line.

Trump, who on Friday struck a deal with Putin to buy diesel from Moscow in an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of U.S. midterm elections, has been urging Zelenskyy for weeks to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure.

He has sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran, which has driven up world energy prices. Ukrainian and European officials reacted to the diesel deal with dismay, saying it will help pay for Russia's war effort.

The Ukrainian drone attack on the Yandex data center in Vladimir caused outages across the company's services, leaving users in dozens of Russian cities and in Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia unable to order taxis or access banking services, according to Russian independent news outlet Astra.

"Operations at the data center have been completely halted. There were no injuries," said the Yandex Cloud Telegram channel, which updates service availability.

Moscow residents described disruption to everyday tasks. Pavel Belyavskiy, a driver for Yandex Taxi, said it was unclear whether orders were coming through at all, and that he had to cancel several rides after waiting a long time because he could not reach the passenger.

"I'd press the 'call' button to contact them, but nothing happens," he said. "There's nothing I can do, so I'm just forced to cancel."

Igor Mann said he tried to check on an order on the Yandex Market shopping platform but the page was unavailable, and connecting through a virtual private network did not help. "Nothing worked," he said.

Another Muscovite, Eduard Malyavko, said the outages had a "direct impact" and weren't just about "convenience." He said they affected "healthcare, and everything else."

On Thursday, a drone attack took a Yandex data center offline in the Ryazan region, southeast of Moscow. The next day, Ukrainian drones hit the company's major data center in the Kaluga region, southwest of Moscow, disabling part of the facility, Yandex said.

Yandex, often described as Russia's Google, runs the country's most popular search engine and a wide range of digital services, and is heavily involved in Russia's artificial intelligence development.

Elsewhere, search and rescue operations ended in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia after a Russian bombing on Saturday, according to Ivan Fedorov, former regional head and co-chair of the regional defense council.

Zelenskyy said 23 people were killed in the attack, including four children. More than 30 people were wounded, Fedorov said, with eight still hospitalized.

A man was killed and two women wounded in a Ukrainian drone strike on Russia's Bryansk border region, local officials said Sunday.

headline: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 12, 2026
summary: [allAfrica]
body_text:
139 Dead, 84 Missing After Migrant Boat Capsizes off Djibouti

At least 139 migrants have died, and 84 remain missing after a boat carrying 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen capsized near Obock. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said about 82 people survived. Search and rescue operations continue. The agency described the incident as one of the deadliest shipwrecks along the Eastern Route, which connects the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula. The tragedy comes at a time when migration flows through Djibouti are increasing, with thousands of migrants stranded without access to basic services. The IOM is providing food, shelter, healthcare, and psychological support to survivors. It is calling on governments to increase safe and legal migration pathways to avert further loss of life. The UN Resident Coordinator in Djibouti, Jose Barahona, also extended condolences to the families of victims and stressed the critical need for international cooperation to protect persons on the move.

72 Civilians Killed in Air Strikes on Sudanese Gold Mines

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

At least 72 civilians have reportedly been killed in air strikes targeting artisanal gold miners in Sudan's River Nile state. The attack allegedly struck mining camps and excavation sites near the Egyptian border. Reports suggest the death toll could rise. Neither Egypt nor Sudan's de facto authorities had commented on the incident. Emergency Lawyers condemned the strikes, warning that deliberately targeting unarmed civilians could constitute war crimes. The attack comes amid mounting tensions along the border where Egypt has in the past been accused of targeting informal mining sites as part of efforts to combat smuggling and illegal activities. Sudan's civil war has fuelled the growth of artisanal mining, raising concerns about civilian safety, illicit gold trafficking and the possible financing of armed groups.

Ruto Accuses Uhuru Kenyatta of Funding Political Rivals Ahead of 2027 Election

Kenyan President William Ruto has intensified his criticism of retired President Uhuru Kenyatta, accusing political opponents of sponsoring rivals to undermine his administration ahead of the 2027 General Election. Speaking in Likuyani, Ruto said his government was committed to fighting tribalism, discrimination and inequality by ensuring development projects reach all regions. He has previously accused Kenyatta of financing opposition figures, including Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, although these remain political allegations. Ruto defended his development agenda, highlighting affordable housing, road construction and funding for a County Aggregation Centre in Likuyani to support farmers. He urged Kenyans to unite ahead of the election, presenting equitable development and national cohesion as key priorities of his administration.

South Africa Seeks Court Guidance on New Border Asylum Registration System

South Africa's government plans to seek court guidance on implementing a Constitutional Court judgment on asylum applications. The Department of Home Affairs is set to introduce a new registration and appointment system by 10 November 2026. The judgment declared unconstitutional provisions allowing asylum seekers to be deported for entering the country without a transit visa. Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi said the government wants a supervisory order to clarify implementation requirements while ensuring compliance with the law. Under the proposed system, applicants will register their intention to seek asylum and receive a receipt confirming their details and appointment. The receipt will provide protection against removal to countries where applicants could face persecution, but will not grant refugee status. The government is also pursuing legislative reforms and plans to relocate refugee reception centres to ports of entry, beginning with Beitbridge in December.

Kenya's Eliud Kipchoge Wins Melbourne Marathon in Record Time

Kenyan running legend Eliud Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon in a course-record time of 2:09:10 at the age of 41. The two-time Olympic gold medalist claimed his first marathon victory since the 2023 Berlin Marathon, ahead of Australia's Thomas do Canto and Reece Edwards. Kipchoge said that he can still compete with the younger athletes. He hopes to inspire the next generation of runners. The race is part of his global quest to run a marathon on all seven continents, with proceeds supporting his foundation's work in education, environmental sustainability and health. Kipchoge is widely regarded as one of the greatest distance runners of all time and famously recorded an unofficial sub-two-hour marathon in Vienna in 2019.

headline: Melbourne man linked to suspected flydubai hijacker condemns 'false accusations'
summary: A Melbourne man whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has hit out at "false accusations". The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda's September 11, 2001 suicide attacks, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media last week.
body_text:
A Melbourne man whose Islamic community centre has been linked by prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates to the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain of a flydubai jet has hit out at "false accusations".

The Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from Al-Qaeda's September 11, 2001 suicide attacks, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media last week.

The prosecutor said the co-pilot first became radicalised while studying in Australia "through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks".

The prosecutor alleged he was acquainted there with an organization known as "My Centre" managed by a Lebanese man called Abu Hamza.

Neither "My Centre" nor Abu Hamza are accused of any criminal wrongdoing.

In a video posted on social media, Abu Hamza -- also named by local media as Samir Mohtadi -- struck back at what he called "false accusations".

"Right through the ages... those who're righteous, they've always been attacked, abused, accused, killed, imprisoned -- and this is the way it is," he said.

"The best thing sometimes is not to say anything," he added.

"They're going to continue accusing you... making false accusations."

He did not comment directly on the UAE prosecutor's claims.

During the September 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane's Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.

Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board "noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner", according to the findings.

After gaining entry, he "intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect".

The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.

Police and intelligence services in Australia have said they are investigating the man's links to the country.

Police in New Zealand said last week he had spent time in the country on a six-month student visa, where he completed a portion of his flight training, national broadcaster RNZ said.

Mohamed Salah set a new Turkish Super Lig record over the weekend, becoming the fastest player to register 10 goal contributions.

The Egyptian laid on an assist for teammate Francolino in Trabzonspor's 3-0 win over Samsunspor on Saturday; it was his third assist of the campaign.

Added to his seven goals since his summer move from Liverpool, Salah has reached double figures in goal contributions in only seven games for his new club.

Egypt lose South Africa friendly as Salah's absence continues

Salah leads the Super Lig scoring charts alongside Gift Orban of Umit Sortif. Victor Osimhen (Galatasaray), Vedat Muriqi (Fenerbahce) and Eldor Shomurodov (Istanbul Basaksehir) have all scored six goals.

His assist against Samsunspor also took him level at the top of the assists chart.

Trabzonspor are fifth in the Turkish Super Lig, three points behind league leaders Galatasaray, whom Trabzon beat 4-0 before the recent international break.

A return to domestic action comes after Salah endured a turbulent time with his national team during the international break.

Salah left Egypt's camp ahead of their Africa Cup of Nations qualifier against South Sudan after a reported falling out with coach Hossam Hassan.

Salah was substituted in Egypt's previous match against Angola after only 60 minutes, with Pharaohs coach Hassan saying Salah was taken off for "technical reasons".

News then broke that Salah had left the national team camp, with the Egypt captain also said to have taken exception to Hassan's comments about injured goalkeeper Mohamed El Shenawy.

The Egyptian Football Association released a statement saying that the plan, made before the Angola game, was always for Salah to sit out the match against South Sudan in Juba as the game would be played on an artificial pitch, before rejoining the rest of the squad for the friendly against South Africa in Cairo on October 4.

Salah did not return, and Egypt lost the match 1-0. Several news outlets reported that he travelled to England before returning to Turkey to begin training with Trabzonspor ahead of the league's resumption on October 10.

Boxing legend Saul 'Canelo' Alvarez is set to defy security concerns and go ahead with his bout against Christian Mbilli in Riyadh, according to organiser Turki Alalshikh.

Alvarez is slated to face Mbilli for the WBC super middleweight title in the Saudi capital on October 31, but the event has been thrown into doubt after several days of deadly strikes on the city.

One person was killed and 11 injured in an attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, according to Saudi authorities. That came a day after a Houthi-claimed strike killed 13 people and injured more than 300.

Al Nassr ACL clash in doubt over Riyadh security situation

Alalshikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia's General Entertainment Authority and a global boxing power broker, said in a social media post that the event would go ahead as planned, and that Alvarez had confirmed he was happy to proceed.

“Canelo reached out and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Alalshikh posted on X on Sunday night. “He fears nothing.

“My country is home to the two Holy Mosques, land of peace, safety, rich civilisation, deep history, and kind-hearted people. Thank you to everyone who checked in and showed support. Hard times reveal true friends.”

The Saudi Pro League postponed Sunday's match between Abha and Al Faisaly, while it remains unclear whether Monday's Asian Champions League match between Al Nassr and Neftchi Fergana will go ahead.

“The SPL confirmed the decision was made following a review of the circumstances surrounding the match,” the league said. "[The decision was taken] in accordance with approved regulatory procedures, ensuring that situations beyond the clubs' control are addressed while maintaining the continuity of the competition.”

Abha is around 900km south-west of Riyadh and approximately 200km from the Yemen border.

Saudi sport has seen several major events cancelled this year, including April's Formula One Grand Prix and next month's World Rally Championship.

The October 31 boxing card at Kingdom Arena is dubbed “Mexico vs the Rest of the World” and is headlined by Alvarez's attempt to recapture a version of the 168lb world title.

The 36-year-old (63-3-2) has not fought since losing to Terence Crawford last September.

It was reported by The Athletic on Sunday night that Alvarez remained eager to press ahead with the Riyadh bout, and that broadcaster DAZN was advancing in its plans to cover the event on the ground in Saudi Arabia.

headline: Haikou launches two direct air routes to Malaysia
summary: Haikou Meilan International Airport in south China's Hainan Province launched two direct routes to Malaysia on Sunday, connecting Haikou with Penang and Kota Kinabalu.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- Haikou Meilan International Airport in south China's Hainan Province launched two direct routes to Malaysia on Sunday, connecting Haikou with Penang and Kota Kinabalu.

The new routes are expected to boost tourism spending as travelers take advantage of the mutual visa exemption policy between China and Malaysia. They will also support economic and trade cooperation, cultural and tourism exchanges, and business travel between the Hainan Free Trade Port and ASEAN countries.

The Haikou-Penang route is operated by Hainan Airlines using Boeing 737-series aircraft, with flights every Wednesday and Sunday.

The Haikou-Kota Kinabalu route is operated by 9 Air, also using Boeing 737-series aircraft, with three flights every two weeks: on Friday and Sunday in one week and Wednesday in the next.

The airport said it has operated 45 international passenger routes serving 28 overseas cities so far in 2026. Its international network spans Southeast Asia, Northeast Asia, the Middle East, Australia and New Zealand, Europe, and North America.

The airport said it would continue to launch new international routes and increase flight frequencies while improving services for international passengers throughout their journeys.

headline: ‘Don’t drag Supreme Court into politics’: CJI Surya Kant amid Delhi protests
body_text:
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said Monday the Supreme Court “should not be dragged into” the politics of the ongoing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and that nothing should impede its functioning or the movement of lawyers and litigants.

Presiding over a three-judge bench, CJI Kant made the remarks when Senior Advocate Atmaram Nadkarni and Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) President Pradeep Rai mentioned petitions regarding the detention of lawyers during the protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) against Gyanesh Kumar.

Agreeing to take them up on Tuesday, the CJI said, “All these democratic activities should take place, but at least in Supreme Court functioning…”.

Nadkarni said his petition is by an independent lawyer expressing genuine difficulties.

“I have appealed to protesters also… But the Supreme Court should not be dragged into any kind of this. (Protest) peacefully. There should not be any impediment or obstruction in the functioning, in the movement of the lawyers, movement of the court staff, movement of the litigants,” the CJI said.

Rai said, “I have made a statement in this regard that they should not bring the court into all this and they should also be responsible political parties”.

The CJI’s remarks assume significance as they come on a day the Congress party has called for an Opposition march to the Supreme Court after Justice Kant turned down its request for a meeting, citing the pendency of cases and the court’s inability to address such grievances through administrative channels.

Led by Rahul Gandhi, the delegation will seek a halt to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demand the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)’s resignation.

‘Send a strong message to the police’

Meanwhile, hearing a request to take up a fresh petition against the detention of lawyers in Saturday’s protests, the CJI said: “Every lawyer, every member of the bar has the right to be a part of the peaceful protests, wherever the identified locations are there…”.

Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, who mentioned the plea, said lawyers were “dragged through streets”. Sankaranarayanan said prohibitory orders passed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita were not available in the public domain. BNSS Section 16 deals with the local jurisdiction of executive magistrates.

“We have also challenged the vires of one section. Our Senior Advocates are being dragged through streets. Mr Shadan Farasat was dragged through streets. It was most unseemly. It shouldn’t have happened,” Sankaranarayanan said.

“Your lordships have said we must try to exercise restraint. Once I would hope your lordships to say the same to the police; that has not come from this bench so far. I hope that happens. The excesses the police are allowing… Hooligans are running around attacking children”.

The CJI said he doesn’t want to say anything as of now.

Sankaranarayanan said children were hit on their heads with lathis and the police are “proudly saying we have done this”. “I am shocked. I have never seen a senior advocate being dragged through the streets. Two more, Mr Dinesh Dwivedi and Ms Uttara Babbar, were detained in buses. It is very sad,” he said.

“At some point, the bench will come to the rescue of the Bar and the citizens of the country and send a strong message to the police. The cops think they can get away with anything.”

The CJI said he will list the matter to be heard Tuesday along with other similar petitions challenging the detentions and restrictions on public utilities.

The CJI’s remarks also come a day after the Supreme Court directed authorities to prevent illegal detentions, ensure free movement, and allow Metro and train services to operate normally amid protests in the Capital, while permitting restrictions necessary to maintain law and order. It also said internet services should not be disrupted, subject to lawful restrictions.

A special bench of Justices Bagchi and Mohana took up petitions challenging restrictions imposed on Saturday, which the petitioners alleged violated the court’s Friday order directing that Metro and train movement should not be completely halted. The pleas also raised concerns over the detention of protesters, including political leaders.

Finding a prima facie case of contempt, the court issued notices to the Centre, Delhi Police, and the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), directing them to file counter-affidavits and compliance reports by Tuesday.

Pending further proceedings, the bench ordered that Metro and rail services should function normally unless restrictions are required to address threats to public order under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Ananthakrishnan G. is a Senior Assistant Editor with The Indian Express. He has been in the field for over 26 years, kicking off his journalism career as a freelancer in the late nineties with bylines in The Hindu. A graduate in law, he practised in the District judiciary in Kerala for about two years before switching to journalism. His first permanent assignment was with The Press Trust of India in Delhi where he was assigned to cover the lower courts and various commissions of inquiry. He reported from the Delhi High Court and the Supreme Court of India during his first stint with The Indian Express in 2005-2006. Currently, in his second stint with the daily newspaper, he reports from the Supreme Court and writes on topics related to law and the administration of justice. Legal reporting is his forte though he has extensive experience in political and community reporting too, having spent a decade as Kerala state correspondent, The Times of India and The Telegraph. He is a stickler for facts and has several impactful stories to his credit. ... Read More
