headline: Israeli strike kills two people in Gaza, medics say
summary: CAIRO, Oct 12 (Reuters) - An Israeli strike killed at least two Palestinians in the southern Gaza Strip on Monday, health officials said.The Israeli military said it targeted a militant in the area, without giving further information.Late on Sunday, an Israeli airstrike hit a tent in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, killing three people, medics said. The Israeli military told Reuters on Monday they struck militants in the area.
body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 12 (Reuters) - An Israeli strike killed at least two Palestinians in the southern Gaza Strip on Monday, health officials said.

The Israeli military said it targeted a militant in the area, without giving further information.

Late on Sunday, an Israeli airstrike hit a tent in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, killing three people, medics said. The Israeli military told Reuters on Monday they struck militants in the area.

Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of a ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks.

Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal.

Last year's US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

Gaza health officials have said at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period.

(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Ros Russell)

No Israeli casualty figures for the Monday strike or the Sunday tent strike.
No context on the total death toll since the start of the conflict, only since the October 2025 ceasefire.

headline: 4 Palestinians martyred in Gaza Strip in Israeli aggression
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – At least four Palestinians have been killed and several others wounded in an Israeli regime's air strike on the southern Gaza Strip, regional media reported Sunday.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – At least four Palestinians have been killed and several others wounded in an Israeli regime's air strike on the southern Gaza Strip, regional media reported Sunday.

The strike targeted a fuel depot this evening in the Al-Buraq Al-Janoubi area, west of Khan Younis, the Palestinian Wafa news agency reported, according to Al Jazeera.

Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed at least 74,377 people and wounded 175,398 others since October 2023, according to the latest Health Ministry figures.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as an Israeli act of aggression causing Palestinian martyrs, emphasizing Palestinian suffering and using politically charged terminology.

loaded_language.explanation: The term 'martyred' carries religious and emotional connotations, implying a noble sacrifice rather than a neutral death, and is often used to evoke sympathy and moral condemnation of the perpetrator.
The phrase 'Israeli regime' is a politically loaded term that delegitimizes Israel, rather than using a neutral descriptor like 'Israeli military' or 'Israeli forces'.
The word 'genocidal' is a highly charged legal and moral accusation that characterizes the conflict as an intentional mass extermination, rather than a neutral term like 'war' or 'military campaign'.
The term 'aggression' is a loaded term that implies unprovoked attack and carries a strong negative judgment, whereas a neutral term would be 'military action' or 'strike'.

omissions: Israeli military statement or context about the strike (e.g., targeting militants or weapons depot)
Identification of the victims (e.g., civilians, combatants, ages)
Mention of any Israeli casualties or ongoing conflict context
Verification or independent confirmation of the death toll from non-Palestinian sources

headline: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
summary: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday.The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said.“AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said.“That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital.The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday.About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said.Profound consequencesMs Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital.The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres.“It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day.The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings.Impact on entry-level jobsWorld Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets.Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates.“There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said.Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies.“AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”
body_text:
Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday.

The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said.

“AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said.

“That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital.

The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday.

About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said.

Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital.

The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres.

“It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day.

The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets.

Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates.

“There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said.

Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies.

“AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

headline: Military superiority cannot guarantee peace in the Middle East
summary: The deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday was another reminder of how vulnerable civilian life and economic activity have become to the region’s wars. At least 13 people were killed, hundreds were injured and air traffic was disrupted. The consequences extended well beyond the airport itself. The attack also illustrated a larger strategic problem – an armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone else.This has become one of the defining features of conflict in the Middle East. Military power remains decisive in determining what happens on the battlefield, but it has proved far less effective in deciding what happens afterwards. The ability to inflict damage is increasingly detached from the ability to impose a political settlement. In some cases, preventing an adversary from achieving its objectives has become a strategy in its own right.The war involving Iran, the US and Israel has brought this problem into sharp focus. Washington and Israel enjoy military and technological advantages that Tehran cannot match. Iran has suffered extensive military and economic damage. Yet it retains the means to prolong the confrontation and threaten interests far beyond its borders, particularly through its ability to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.This is not a balance of military power. Iran cannot impose losses on the US comparable to those it has sustained. However, it can complicate Washington’s calculations, raise the economic cost of continuing the war and make a satisfactory political conclusion harder to achieve. American military superiority, meanwhile, has not been sufficient to compel Tehran to accept Washington’s terms.The result is a confrontation in which military pressure continues without producing the political outcome either side seeks.What we are witnessing might be described as the emergence of a “veto over peace”. Certain states and armed groups have acquired the means to obstruct settlements even when they lack the power to impose their own. Their influence comes from the damage they can threaten, the agreements they can undermine and the violence they can resume.Such a veto requires no formal recognition. A group capable of attacking an airport, disrupting a shipping lane or reopening a military front can make its effective consent necessary for a settlement to endure.There is, of course, an important distinction between opposing an unjust agreement and deliberately sabotaging peace. A settlement that ignores legitimate rights or leaves the causes of conflict unresolved may create the conditions for another war. The problem arises when actors use the threat of renewed violence to preserve political influence or economic privileges that might be diminished by a return to stability.This points to a distinction often overlooked in discussions about ending wars. Some conflicts continue because the parties cannot bring them to a conclusion. Others persist because influential actors have little interest in doing so.In the first case, the obstacle lies in the balance of power and the difficulty of agreeing on enforceable terms. In the second, the obstacle is political. War may protect established interests, strengthen military institutions, postpone domestic decisions or provide leverage that would be lost in peacetime. Both conditions can exist within the same conflict.Iran illustrates the complexity. The national interest in ending isolation and restoring economic activity does not necessarily coincide with the interests of every institution that has gained influence during decades of sanctions and confrontation. Greater openness could benefit Iranian society while unsettling entrenched centres of power.That does not mean these actors necessarily oppose every settlement. But any agreement that alters the internal distribution of power may encounter resistance. This raises a question that goes beyond the terms negotiated with Tehran: can Iran’s political leadership ensure that all those who possess the means of escalation will comply?An understanding over the Strait of Hormuz, for example, could be negotiated through diplomatic channels and then undermined by a single maritime incident. The problem is especially difficult when those capable of wrecking an agreement do not bear the full political or economic consequences of doing so.An armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone elseSimilar difficulties are apparent elsewhere. Israel’s military superiority has not resolved the political future of Gaza or the Palestinian question. In Lebanon, durable stability remains tied to the state’s authority over decisions of war and peace, the future of Hezbollah’s weapons and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory. In Yemen, weakening the Houthis militarily would not, by itself, resolve the divisions that have undermined the state.These conflicts are different in their causes and responsibilities. What they share is a widening gap between the ability to stop fighting temporarily and the ability to prevent its return.Who, then, can actually end these wars?In many cases, the necessary authority is divided among several actors. One has the military power to halt hostilities. Another has the political authority to negotiate and make concessions. Others may hold the means to enforce an agreement or undermine it.A government can sign a peace deal without being able to bind the armed groups operating within its territory. An external power can enforce a ceasefire without resolving the political grievances that threaten it. Even the most capable guarantor will struggle if those able to restart the fighting believe the benefits outweigh the costs.This is also where the limits of American power become apparent. The US remains the most consequential external security actor in the Middle East. No other country can match its regional military capabilities and intelligence resources. Yet Washington's ability to change the military balance does not give it equivalent control over the political decisions of every actor involved.Additional mediation by China, Russia or European powers may help create opportunities for compromise. It cannot substitute for political authority capable of delivering on an agreement.For the Gulf states, these questions are particularly consequential. Their economies depend on reliable maritime access, functioning airports, secure energy infrastructure and the confidence of international investors. Even limited military disruptions can have effects that extend far beyond the immediate target.The challenge is therefore not confined to preventing another major war. It also involves reducing the ability of hostile actors to keep Gulf economies under the persistent threat of disruption.The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem. Any agreement that restores navigation would be welcome, but its terms matter as much as its immediate results. Reopening the waterway in exchange for recognising an Iranian right to determine which vessels may pass would merely institutionalise a new source of insecurity.Co-operation among the states bordering the strait on navigation and maritime safety is both legitimate and necessary. Granting any one state discretionary political control over an international shipping route is a different proposition.Gulf states must therefore have a substantive role in shaping the regional security arrangements that follow the war. Their security cannot be dependent on understandings negotiated by others, particularly when those understandings could leave the sources of future threats intact.Military deterrence remains essential, but it must be accompanied by stronger economic resilience, diversified trade and energy routes, and diplomatic arrangements that make renewed aggression costly. Above all, the interests of states exposed to the consequences of war must be represented in the negotiations intended to end it.The Middle East’s wars are not necessarily impossible to resolve. History offers many examples of conflicts that resisted military victory but eventually ended through political compromise. What changed was not always the balance of military power. Often, it was the calculation of those who had previously found reason to continue fighting.That is the political challenge facing the region today. Ending wars requires more than persuading adversaries to accept a ceasefire. It requires changing the interests that make renewed conflict attractive.As long as societies bear the greatest costs of war while some of those with the power to reignite it continue to benefit from its continuation, peace will remain fragile. The real measure of a settlement is not whether it stops the fighting today, but whether it deprives those who would resume it tomorrow of the incentive and the means to do so.
body_text:
The deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday was another reminder of how vulnerable civilian life and economic activity have become to the region’s wars. At least 13 people were killed, hundreds were injured and air traffic was disrupted. The consequences extended well beyond the airport itself. The attack also illustrated a larger strategic problem – an armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone else.

This has become one of the defining features of conflict in the Middle East. Military power remains decisive in determining what happens on the battlefield, but it has proved far less effective in deciding what happens afterwards. The ability to inflict damage is increasingly detached from the ability to impose a political settlement. In some cases, preventing an adversary from achieving its objectives has become a strategy in its own right.

The war involving Iran, the US and Israel has brought this problem into sharp focus. Washington and Israel enjoy military and technological advantages that Tehran cannot match. Iran has suffered extensive military and economic damage. Yet it retains the means to prolong the confrontation and threaten interests far beyond its borders, particularly through its ability to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

This is not a balance of military power. Iran cannot impose losses on the US comparable to those it has sustained. However, it can complicate Washington’s calculations, raise the economic cost of continuing the war and make a satisfactory political conclusion harder to achieve. American military superiority, meanwhile, has not been sufficient to compel Tehran to accept Washington’s terms.

The result is a confrontation in which military pressure continues without producing the political outcome either side seeks.

What we are witnessing might be described as the emergence of a “veto over peace”. Certain states and armed groups have acquired the means to obstruct settlements even when they lack the power to impose their own. Their influence comes from the damage they can threaten, the agreements they can undermine and the violence they can resume.

Such a veto requires no formal recognition. A group capable of attacking an airport, disrupting a shipping lane or reopening a military front can make its effective consent necessary for a settlement to endure.

There is, of course, an important distinction between opposing an unjust agreement and deliberately sabotaging peace. A settlement that ignores legitimate rights or leaves the causes of conflict unresolved may create the conditions for another war. The problem arises when actors use the threat of renewed violence to preserve political influence or economic privileges that might be diminished by a return to stability.

This points to a distinction often overlooked in discussions about ending wars. Some conflicts continue because the parties cannot bring them to a conclusion. Others persist because influential actors have little interest in doing so.

In the first case, the obstacle lies in the balance of power and the difficulty of agreeing on enforceable terms. In the second, the obstacle is political. War may protect established interests, strengthen military institutions, postpone domestic decisions or provide leverage that would be lost in peacetime. Both conditions can exist within the same conflict.

Iran illustrates the complexity. The national interest in ending isolation and restoring economic activity does not necessarily coincide with the interests of every institution that has gained influence during decades of sanctions and confrontation. Greater openness could benefit Iranian society while unsettling entrenched centres of power.

That does not mean these actors necessarily oppose every settlement. But any agreement that alters the internal distribution of power may encounter resistance. This raises a question that goes beyond the terms negotiated with Tehran: can Iran’s political leadership ensure that all those who possess the means of escalation will comply?

An understanding over the Strait of Hormuz, for example, could be negotiated through diplomatic channels and then undermined by a single maritime incident. The problem is especially difficult when those capable of wrecking an agreement do not bear the full political or economic consequences of doing so.

Similar difficulties are apparent elsewhere. Israel’s military superiority has not resolved the political future of Gaza or the Palestinian question. In Lebanon, durable stability remains tied to the state’s authority over decisions of war and peace, the future of Hezbollah’s weapons and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory. In Yemen, weakening the Houthis militarily would not, by itself, resolve the divisions that have undermined the state.

These conflicts are different in their causes and responsibilities. What they share is a widening gap between the ability to stop fighting temporarily and the ability to prevent its return.

Who, then, can actually end these wars?

In many cases, the necessary authority is divided among several actors. One has the military power to halt hostilities. Another has the political authority to negotiate and make concessions. Others may hold the means to enforce an agreement or undermine it.

A government can sign a peace deal without being able to bind the armed groups operating within its territory. An external power can enforce a ceasefire without resolving the political grievances that threaten it. Even the most capable guarantor will struggle if those able to restart the fighting believe the benefits outweigh the costs.

This is also where the limits of American power become apparent. The US remains the most consequential external security actor in the Middle East. No other country can match its regional military capabilities and intelligence resources. Yet Washington's ability to change the military balance does not give it equivalent control over the political decisions of every actor involved.

Additional mediation by China, Russia or European powers may help create opportunities for compromise. It cannot substitute for political authority capable of delivering on an agreement.

For the Gulf states, these questions are particularly consequential. Their economies depend on reliable maritime access, functioning airports, secure energy infrastructure and the confidence of international investors. Even limited military disruptions can have effects that extend far beyond the immediate target.

The challenge is therefore not confined to preventing another major war. It also involves reducing the ability of hostile actors to keep Gulf economies under the persistent threat of disruption.

The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem. Any agreement that restores navigation would be welcome, but its terms matter as much as its immediate results. Reopening the waterway in exchange for recognising an Iranian right to determine which vessels may pass would merely institutionalise a new source of insecurity.

Co-operation among the states bordering the strait on navigation and maritime safety is both legitimate and necessary. Granting any one state discretionary political control over an international shipping route is a different proposition.

Gulf states must therefore have a substantive role in shaping the regional security arrangements that follow the war. Their security cannot be dependent on understandings negotiated by others, particularly when those understandings could leave the sources of future threats intact.

Military deterrence remains essential, but it must be accompanied by stronger economic resilience, diversified trade and energy routes, and diplomatic arrangements that make renewed aggression costly. Above all, the interests of states exposed to the consequences of war must be represented in the negotiations intended to end it.

The Middle East’s wars are not necessarily impossible to resolve. History offers many examples of conflicts that resisted military victory but eventually ended through political compromise. What changed was not always the balance of military power. Often, it was the calculation of those who had previously found reason to continue fighting.

That is the political challenge facing the region today. Ending wars requires more than persuading adversaries to accept a ceasefire. It requires changing the interests that make renewed conflict attractive.

As long as societies bear the greatest costs of war while some of those with the power to reignite it continue to benefit from its continuation, peace will remain fragile. The real measure of a settlement is not whether it stops the fighting today, but whether it deprives those who would resume it tomorrow of the incentive and the means to do so.

headline: Russia’s tennis star Mirra Andreeva climbs to third in WTA rankings
summary: Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina remains at the top of the rankings, followed by Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus
body_text:
LONDON, October 12. /TASS/. Russia’s Mirra Andreeva has climbed two places to third in the updated Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) rankings published on the organization’s website.

Last week, Andreeva made it to the final of a tournament in Beijing, where she was defeated by China’s Qinwen Zheng. This is the first time in her career that Andreeva has reached the world’s top 3.

Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina remains at the top of the rankings, followed by Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus.

Other Russians in the top 100 are Diana Shnaider (13th), Anna Kalinskaya (21st), Ekaterina Alexandrova (24th), Liudmila Samsonova (43rd), and Alina Korneeva (74th).

headline: ‘Don’t drag Supreme Court into politics’: CJI Surya Kant amid Delhi protests
body_text:
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said Monday the Supreme Court “should not be dragged into” the politics of the ongoing protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and that nothing should impede its functioning or the movement of lawyers and litigants.

Presiding over a three-judge bench, CJI Kant made the remarks when Senior Advocate Atmaram Nadkarni and Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA) President Pradeep Rai mentioned petitions regarding the detention of lawyers during the protests called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) against Gyanesh Kumar.

Agreeing to take them up on Tuesday, the CJI said, “All these democratic activities should take place, but at least in Supreme Court functioning…”.

Nadkarni said his petition is by an independent lawyer expressing genuine difficulties.

“I have appealed to protesters also… But the Supreme Court should not be dragged into any kind of this. (Protest) peacefully. There should not be any impediment or obstruction in the functioning, in the movement of the lawyers, movement of the court staff, movement of the litigants,” the CJI said.

Rai said, “I have made a statement in this regard that they should not bring the court into all this and they should also be responsible political parties”.

The CJI’s remarks assume significance as they come on a day the Congress party has called for an Opposition march to the Supreme Court after Justice Kant turned down its request for a meeting, citing the pendency of cases and the court’s inability to address such grievances through administrative channels.

Led by Rahul Gandhi, the delegation will seek a halt to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demand the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC)’s resignation.

‘Send a strong message to the police’

Meanwhile, hearing a request to take up a fresh petition against the detention of lawyers in Saturday’s protests, the CJI said: “Every lawyer, every member of the bar has the right to be a part of the peaceful protests, wherever the identified locations are there…”.

Senior Advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, who mentioned the plea, said lawyers were “dragged through streets”. Sankaranarayanan said prohibitory orders passed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita were not available in the public domain. BNSS Section 16 deals with the local jurisdiction of executive magistrates.

“We have also challenged the vires of one section. Our Senior Advocates are being dragged through streets. Mr Shadan Farasat was dragged through streets. It was most unseemly. It shouldn’t have happened,” Sankaranarayanan said.

“Your lordships have said we must try to exercise restraint. Once I would hope your lordships to say the same to the police; that has not come from this bench so far. I hope that happens. The excesses the police are allowing… Hooligans are running around attacking children”.

The CJI said he doesn’t want to say anything as of now.

Sankaranarayanan said children were hit on their heads with lathis and the police are “proudly saying we have done this”. “I am shocked. I have never seen a senior advocate being dragged through the streets. Two more, Mr Dinesh Dwivedi and Ms Uttara Babbar, were detained in buses. It is very sad,” he said.

“At some point, the bench will come to the rescue of the Bar and the citizens of the country and send a strong message to the police. The cops think they can get away with anything.”

The CJI said he will list the matter to be heard Tuesday along with other similar petitions challenging the detentions and restrictions on public utilities.

The CJI’s remarks also come a day after the Supreme Court directed authorities to prevent illegal detentions, ensure free movement, and allow Metro and train services to operate normally amid protests in the Capital, while permitting restrictions necessary to maintain law and order. It also said internet services should not be disrupted, subject to lawful restrictions.

A special bench of Justices Bagchi and Mohana took up petitions challenging restrictions imposed on Saturday, which the petitioners alleged violated the court’s Friday order directing that Metro and train movement should not be completely halted. The pleas also raised concerns over the detention of protesters, including political leaders.

Finding a prima facie case of contempt, the court issued notices to the Centre, Delhi Police, and the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), directing them to file counter-affidavits and compliance reports by Tuesday.

Pending further proceedings, the bench ordered that Metro and rail services should function normally unless restrictions are required to address threats to public order under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Ananthakrishnan G. is a Senior Assistant Editor with The Indian Express. He has been in the field for over 26 years, kicking off his journalism career as a freelancer in the late nineties with bylines in The Hindu. A graduate in law, he practised in the District judiciary in Kerala for about two years before switching to journalism. His first permanent assignment was with The Press Trust of India in Delhi where he was assigned to cover the lower courts and various commissions of inquiry. He reported from the Delhi High Court and the Supreme Court of India during his first stint with The Indian Express in 2005-2006. Currently, in his second stint with the daily newspaper, he reports from the Supreme Court and writes on topics related to law and the administration of justice. Legal reporting is his forte though he has extensive experience in political and community reporting too, having spent a decade as Kerala state correspondent, The Times of India and The Telegraph. He is a stickler for facts and has several impactful stories to his credit. ... Read More

headline: S. Korea to provide US$500,000 in aid to drought-hit Honduras
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to provide $500,000 in humani...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to provide $500,000 in humanitarian assistance to Honduras to help the country cope with a persistent drought, the foreign ministry said Monday.

A severe drought has affected the Central American country since May, leaving some 620,000 people facing severe food insecurity and suffering from malnutrition, according to the ministry, citing an appeal by the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

"We hope the assistance would help affected communities return to normal life as soon as possible," the ministry said in a release.

headline: China bars Belize, Paraguay ministers from entry over Taiwan ties
summary: Belize's Foreign Minister Fonseca, Paraguay's Information and Communication Technologies Minister Villate sanctioned over their countries' diplomatic ties with Taiwan
body_text:
China on Monday said it had imposed sanctions on ministers from Belize and Paraguay, including visa and entry bans, over their countries' diplomatic ties with Taiwan.

Belize's Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca and Paraguay's Information and Communication Technologies Minister Gustavo Villate were sanctioned as "certain anti-China politicians" have in recent years supported diplomatic relations with Taiwan in their respective countries through their actions and statements on China-related issues that "damaged China's core interests," according to two separate statements by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

The sanctions include asset freezes in China and a ban on Chinese organizations and individuals engaging in transactions or cooperation with the two ministers.

The measures aim to safeguard China's "sovereignty, security and development interests" and oppose "separatist activities" aimed at "Taiwan independence," the ministry said.

headline: Israel not expected to attack Iran before elections, opposition leader says
summary: Yair Lapid accuses Netanyahu of using prospect of war with Iran or potential attack on Israel for election campaigning
body_text:
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid said Monday that intelligence available to him does not indicate that Israel is expected to go to war with Iran before the country’s parliamentary elections on Oct. 27.

Lapid accused Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of using warnings about a possible war with Iran or an attack on Israel as part of his election campaign.

As opposition leader, Lapid receives security and military briefings from Netanyahu, particularly concerning major military operations or the possibility of war.

Speaking to local radio station 103 FM, Lapid criticized Netanyahu’s handling of security threats ahead of the elections.

“The prime minister can dominate the agenda by warning of an imminent terrorist attack or a war with Iran. Whether that is good for Israel is a question voters should ask themselves,” he said.

Israeli media reported that Netanyahu chaired a security meeting Sunday evening to discuss developments concerning Iran.

“Based on the intelligence available to me, no war with Iran is expected before the elections,” Lapid added.

The Oct. 27 elections are widely viewed as a major political test for Netanyahu and opposition parties seeking to form an alternative government.

Recent opinion polls have shown opposition parties ahead of Netanyahu’s bloc, but without a clear parliamentary majority to form a government.

On Sept. 29, Netanyahu warned that Israel’s enemies might attempt attacks ahead of the elections, prompting Lapid to accuse him of spreading fear for political purposes.

​​​​​​​Following a security briefing with Netanyahu, Lapid said there was no reason to alarm the public and insisted that the elections should proceed as scheduled.

body_text:
Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday.

The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said.

“AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said.

“That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital.

The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday.

About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said.

Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital.

The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres.

“It is a transformative technology. It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day.

The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia, Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings.

World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets.

Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates.

“There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said.

Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies.

“AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

headline: Military superiority cannot guarantee peace in the Middle East
summary: The deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday was another reminder of how vulnerable civilian life and economic activity have become to the region’s wars. At least 13 people were killed, hundreds were injured and air traffic was disrupted. The consequences extended well beyond the airport itself. The attack also illustrated a larger strategic problem – an armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone else.This has become one of the defining features of conflict in the Middle East. Military power remains decisive in determining what happens on the battlefield, but it has proved far less effective in deciding what happens afterwards. The ability to inflict damage is increasingly detached from the ability to impose a political settlement. In some cases, preventing an adversary from achieving its objectives has become a strategy in its own right.The war involving Iran, the US and Israel has brought this problem into sharp focus. Washington and Israel enjoy military and technological advantages that Tehran cannot match. Iran has suffered extensive military and economic damage. Yet it retains the means to prolong the confrontation and threaten interests far beyond its borders, particularly through its ability to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.This is not a balance of military power. Iran cannot impose losses on the US comparable to those it has sustained. However, it can complicate Washington’s calculations, raise the economic cost of continuing the war and make a satisfactory political conclusion harder to achieve. American military superiority, meanwhile, has not been sufficient to compel Tehran to accept Washington’s terms.The result is a confrontation in which military pressure continues without producing the political outcome either side seeks.What we are witnessing might be described as the emergence of a “veto over peace”. Certain states and armed groups have acquired the means to obstruct settlements even when they lack the power to impose their own. Their influence comes from the damage they can threaten, the agreements they can undermine and the violence they can resume.Such a veto requires no formal recognition. A group capable of attacking an airport, disrupting a shipping lane or reopening a military front can make its effective consent necessary for a settlement to endure.There is, of course, an important distinction between opposing an unjust agreement and deliberately sabotaging peace. A settlement that ignores legitimate rights or leaves the causes of conflict unresolved may create the conditions for another war. The problem arises when actors use the threat of renewed violence to preserve political influence or economic privileges that might be diminished by a return to stability.This points to a distinction often overlooked in discussions about ending wars. Some conflicts continue because the parties cannot bring them to a conclusion. Others persist because influential actors have little interest in doing so.In the first case, the obstacle lies in the balance of power and the difficulty of agreeing on enforceable terms. In the second, the obstacle is political. War may protect established interests, strengthen military institutions, postpone domestic decisions or provide leverage that would be lost in peacetime. Both conditions can exist within the same conflict.Iran illustrates the complexity. The national interest in ending isolation and restoring economic activity does not necessarily coincide with the interests of every institution that has gained influence during decades of sanctions and confrontation. Greater openness could benefit Iranian society while unsettling entrenched centres of power.That does not mean these actors necessarily oppose every settlement. But any agreement that alters the internal distribution of power may encounter resistance. This raises a question that goes beyond the terms negotiated with Tehran: can Iran’s political leadership ensure that all those who possess the means of escalation will comply?An understanding over the Strait of Hormuz, for example, could be negotiated through diplomatic channels and then undermined by a single maritime incident. The problem is especially difficult when those capable of wrecking an agreement do not bear the full political or economic consequences of doing so.An armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone elseSimilar difficulties are apparent elsewhere. Israel’s military superiority has not resolved the political future of Gaza or the Palestinian question. In Lebanon, durable stability remains tied to the state’s authority over decisions of war and peace, the future of Hezbollah’s weapons and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory. In Yemen, weakening the Houthis militarily would not, by itself, resolve the divisions that have undermined the state.These conflicts are different in their causes and responsibilities. What they share is a widening gap between the ability to stop fighting temporarily and the ability to prevent its return.Who, then, can actually end these wars?In many cases, the necessary authority is divided among several actors. One has the military power to halt hostilities. Another has the political authority to negotiate and make concessions. Others may hold the means to enforce an agreement or undermine it.A government can sign a peace deal without being able to bind the armed groups operating within its territory. An external power can enforce a ceasefire without resolving the political grievances that threaten it. Even the most capable guarantor will struggle if those able to restart the fighting believe the benefits outweigh the costs.This is also where the limits of American power become apparent. The US remains the most consequential external security actor in the Middle East. No other country can match its regional military capabilities and intelligence resources. Yet Washington's ability to change the military balance does not give it equivalent control over the political decisions of every actor involved.Additional mediation by China, Russia or European powers may help create opportunities for compromise. It cannot substitute for political authority capable of delivering on an agreement.For the Gulf states, these questions are particularly consequential. Their economies depend on reliable maritime access, functioning airports, secure energy infrastructure and the confidence of international investors. Even limited military disruptions can have effects that extend far beyond the immediate target.The challenge is therefore not confined to preventing another major war. It also involves reducing the ability of hostile actors to keep Gulf economies under the persistent threat of disruption.The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem. Any agreement that restores navigation would be welcome, but its terms matter as much as its immediate results. Reopening the waterway in exchange for recognising an Iranian right to determine which vessels may pass would merely institutionalise a new source of insecurity.Co-operation among the states bordering the strait on navigation and maritime safety is both legitimate and necessary. Granting any one state discretionary political control over an international shipping route is a different proposition.Gulf states must therefore have a substantive role in shaping the regional security arrangements that follow the war. Their security cannot be dependent on understandings negotiated by others, particularly when those understandings could leave the sources of future threats intact.Military deterrence remains essential, but it must be accompanied by stronger economic resilience, diversified trade and energy routes, and diplomatic arrangements that make renewed aggression costly. Above all, the interests of states exposed to the consequences of war must be represented in the negotiations intended to end it.The Middle East’s wars are not necessarily impossible to resolve. History offers many examples of conflicts that resisted military victory but eventually ended through political compromise. What changed was not always the balance of military power. Often, it was the calculation of those who had previously found reason to continue fighting.That is the political challenge facing the region today. Ending wars requires more than persuading adversaries to accept a ceasefire. It requires changing the interests that make renewed conflict attractive.As long as societies bear the greatest costs of war while some of those with the power to reignite it continue to benefit from its continuation, peace will remain fragile. The real measure of a settlement is not whether it stops the fighting today, but whether it deprives those who would resume it tomorrow of the incentive and the means to do so.
body_text:
The deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday was another reminder of how vulnerable civilian life and economic activity have become to the region’s wars. At least 13 people were killed, hundreds were injured and air traffic was disrupted. The consequences extended well beyond the airport itself. The attack also illustrated a larger strategic problem – an armed group does not need to win a war to make its continuation costly for everyone else.

This has become one of the defining features of conflict in the Middle East. Military power remains decisive in determining what happens on the battlefield, but it has proved far less effective in deciding what happens afterwards. The ability to inflict damage is increasingly detached from the ability to impose a political settlement. In some cases, preventing an adversary from achieving its objectives has become a strategy in its own right.

The war involving Iran, the US and Israel has brought this problem into sharp focus. Washington and Israel enjoy military and technological advantages that Tehran cannot match. Iran has suffered extensive military and economic damage. Yet it retains the means to prolong the confrontation and threaten interests far beyond its borders, particularly through its ability to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

This is not a balance of military power. Iran cannot impose losses on the US comparable to those it has sustained. However, it can complicate Washington’s calculations, raise the economic cost of continuing the war and make a satisfactory political conclusion harder to achieve. American military superiority, meanwhile, has not been sufficient to compel Tehran to accept Washington’s terms.

The result is a confrontation in which military pressure continues without producing the political outcome either side seeks.

What we are witnessing might be described as the emergence of a “veto over peace”. Certain states and armed groups have acquired the means to obstruct settlements even when they lack the power to impose their own. Their influence comes from the damage they can threaten, the agreements they can undermine and the violence they can resume.

Such a veto requires no formal recognition. A group capable of attacking an airport, disrupting a shipping lane or reopening a military front can make its effective consent necessary for a settlement to endure.

There is, of course, an important distinction between opposing an unjust agreement and deliberately sabotaging peace. A settlement that ignores legitimate rights or leaves the causes of conflict unresolved may create the conditions for another war. The problem arises when actors use the threat of renewed violence to preserve political influence or economic privileges that might be diminished by a return to stability.

This points to a distinction often overlooked in discussions about ending wars. Some conflicts continue because the parties cannot bring them to a conclusion. Others persist because influential actors have little interest in doing so.

In the first case, the obstacle lies in the balance of power and the difficulty of agreeing on enforceable terms. In the second, the obstacle is political. War may protect established interests, strengthen military institutions, postpone domestic decisions or provide leverage that would be lost in peacetime. Both conditions can exist within the same conflict.

Iran illustrates the complexity. The national interest in ending isolation and restoring economic activity does not necessarily coincide with the interests of every institution that has gained influence during decades of sanctions and confrontation. Greater openness could benefit Iranian society while unsettling entrenched centres of power.

That does not mean these actors necessarily oppose every settlement. But any agreement that alters the internal distribution of power may encounter resistance. This raises a question that goes beyond the terms negotiated with Tehran: can Iran’s political leadership ensure that all those who possess the means of escalation will comply?

An understanding over the Strait of Hormuz, for example, could be negotiated through diplomatic channels and then undermined by a single maritime incident. The problem is especially difficult when those capable of wrecking an agreement do not bear the full political or economic consequences of doing so.

Similar difficulties are apparent elsewhere. Israel’s military superiority has not resolved the political future of Gaza or the Palestinian question. In Lebanon, durable stability remains tied to the state’s authority over decisions of war and peace, the future of Hezbollah’s weapons and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Lebanese territory. In Yemen, weakening the Houthis militarily would not, by itself, resolve the divisions that have undermined the state.

These conflicts are different in their causes and responsibilities. What they share is a widening gap between the ability to stop fighting temporarily and the ability to prevent its return.

Who, then, can actually end these wars?

In many cases, the necessary authority is divided among several actors. One has the military power to halt hostilities. Another has the political authority to negotiate and make concessions. Others may hold the means to enforce an agreement or undermine it.

A government can sign a peace deal without being able to bind the armed groups operating within its territory. An external power can enforce a ceasefire without resolving the political grievances that threaten it. Even the most capable guarantor will struggle if those able to restart the fighting believe the benefits outweigh the costs.

This is also where the limits of American power become apparent. The US remains the most consequential external security actor in the Middle East. No other country can match its regional military capabilities and intelligence resources. Yet Washington's ability to change the military balance does not give it equivalent control over the political decisions of every actor involved.

Additional mediation by China, Russia or European powers may help create opportunities for compromise. It cannot substitute for political authority capable of delivering on an agreement.

For the Gulf states, these questions are particularly consequential. Their economies depend on reliable maritime access, functioning airports, secure energy infrastructure and the confidence of international investors. Even limited military disruptions can have effects that extend far beyond the immediate target.

The challenge is therefore not confined to preventing another major war. It also involves reducing the ability of hostile actors to keep Gulf economies under the persistent threat of disruption.

The Strait of Hormuz is central to this problem. Any agreement that restores navigation would be welcome, but its terms matter as much as its immediate results. Reopening the waterway in exchange for recognising an Iranian right to determine which vessels may pass would merely institutionalise a new source of insecurity.

Co-operation among the states bordering the strait on navigation and maritime safety is both legitimate and necessary. Granting any one state discretionary political control over an international shipping route is a different proposition.

Gulf states must therefore have a substantive role in shaping the regional security arrangements that follow the war. Their security cannot be dependent on understandings negotiated by others, particularly when those understandings could leave the sources of future threats intact.

Military deterrence remains essential, but it must be accompanied by stronger economic resilience, diversified trade and energy routes, and diplomatic arrangements that make renewed aggression costly. Above all, the interests of states exposed to the consequences of war must be represented in the negotiations intended to end it.

The Middle East’s wars are not necessarily impossible to resolve. History offers many examples of conflicts that resisted military victory but eventually ended through political compromise. What changed was not always the balance of military power. Often, it was the calculation of those who had previously found reason to continue fighting.

That is the political challenge facing the region today. Ending wars requires more than persuading adversaries to accept a ceasefire. It requires changing the interests that make renewed conflict attractive.

As long as societies bear the greatest costs of war while some of those with the power to reignite it continue to benefit from its continuation, peace will remain fragile. The real measure of a settlement is not whether it stops the fighting today, but whether it deprives those who would resume it tomorrow of the incentive and the means to do so.

headline: Russia’s tennis star Mirra Andreeva climbs to third in WTA rankings
summary: Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina remains at the top of the rankings, followed by Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus
body_text:
LONDON, October 12. /TASS/. Russia’s Mirra Andreeva has climbed two places to third in the updated Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) rankings published on the organization’s website.

Last week, Andreeva made it to the final of a tournament in Beijing, where she was defeated by China’s Qinwen Zheng. This is the first time in her career that Andreeva has reached the world’s top 3.

Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina remains at the top of the rankings, followed by Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus.

Other Russians in the top 100 are Diana Shnaider (13th), Anna Kalinskaya (21st), Ekaterina Alexandrova (24th), Liudmila Samsonova (43rd), and Alina Korneeva (74th).

The statement announcing the decision did not specify when operations would resume. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
body_text:
Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 10:41

Saudi Arabia's civil aviation body extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's international airport Monday following a series of deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels over the weekend. The statement announcing the decision did not specify when operations would resume. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.

The European Union on Monday formally added almost 1,600 new individuals and entities to its sanctions blacklist over Russia's war on Ukraine.

"This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war. Europe is again showing a united front. More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said that his country would retaliate if Moscow did not agree to the "energy ceasefire" that US President Donald Trump unilaterally announced on Sunday.

"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond," Zelensky said in a video address to a security forum in Warsaw. "If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people."

Iran ​is still ​reviewing a US response to its ​proposal ‌regarding ⁠the reopening ‌of the Strait of ⁠Hormuz and will reply ​to Washington ‌via intermediaries when the review ‌is over, ​foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.

Baghaei also ​told a ​press conference ​that Iran continues to exchange messages via ⁠the intermediaries.

Saudi Arabia's civil aviation body extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's international airport Monday following a series of deadly Houthi attacks.

"The General Authority of Civil Aviation has announced the extension of the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in order to complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of the facilities and their operational readiness," the authority said in a statement.

It did not specify when operations would resume.

China condemned recent attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, expressing "serious concern" about the intensifying conflict between Riyadh and the Yemeni group.

"China condemns the attacks that caused heavy casualties and expresses serious concern over the intensification of the conflict," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing.

Saudi ​Energy ​Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said ​the ‌events ⁠of ‌recent weeks were serious ⁠and the kingdom's ​response must ‌be "equally serious".

Yemen's ‌Houthis have stepped ​up their attacks on the kingdom, killing ​more than ​15 ​people in ​two weeks.

Emirati ​presidential adviser ​Anwar Gargash called on Gulf countries to strengthen their security cooperation, saying that targeting Saudi ‌Arabia undermined ​the security of all Gulf states.

"It is necessary to revive joint action by the Gulf countries, particularly in security and defence, and to strengthen the collective security system," Gargash wrote on X.

Neglect of ​collective ​Gulf security ​had "emboldened others" to ​overreach against regional states, he added.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said ​⁠that it reclassified an ‌incident in the vicinity of ⁠Sohar anchorage in Oman as ​an attack after confirmation ‌that the tanker was struck by ‌a drone.

Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it had extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh following a series of attacks on the facility.

In a statement, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said the suspension was extended to complete necessary procedures to verify the safety of airport facilities and their operational readiness.

The authority did not specify when operations would resume.

The decision followed attacks on the airport over the weekend.

On Sunday afternoon, an unidentified projectile struck the airport’s Terminal 4, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, according to Saudi authorities. The Saudi-led coalition also said it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.

A day earlier, on Saturday, a Houthi attack struck a passenger terminal at the airport, killing 13 people and injuring 309 others, according to Saudi authorities.

The Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of carrying out Saturday’s attack and described the strike as a “full-fledged war crime.”

​​​​​​​The attacks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with airports and other civilian and energy facilities targeted in recent days.

Twelve killed and 309 wounded in attack on Riyadh airport

Etihad has cancelled several flights between Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia on Monday and Tuesday, affecting services to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah.

According to the airline's latest travel advisory, Monday's cancellations include flights EY559 and EY560 between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. But Etihad's flight listings also show outbound Riyadh services EY551 and EY555 as being cancelled.

Four flights between Abu Dhabi and Dammam – EY573, EY574, EY575 and EY576 – have also been cancelled on Monday, along with Jeddah services EY601, EY602, EY603 and EY604.

Further cancellations are scheduled for Tuesday, including Dammam services EY575 and EY576, Jeddah flights EY602, EY603 and EY604, and Riyadh services EY551 and EY552.

Passengers are advised to check their flight status directly with Etihad before travelling, as further changes are possible.

Emirates' flight status website shows all six services between Dubai and Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday. These include outbound flights EK815, EK817 and EK819, along with returning services EK816, EK818 and EK820.

Four flights remain cancelled on Tuesday, including EK815, EK817 and EK819 from Dubai to Riyadh and the return service EK816. Return services EK818 and EK820 have not yet been listed as cancelled, although this does not confirm they will operate.

Flydubai has cancelled flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh up to and including Wednesday, amid the disruption to services to Saudi Arabia.

“Flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh have been cancelled up to and including October 14,” a flydubai representative told The National. “We continue to monitor the situation closely and we will update our customers through our official channels regarding any amendments to our flight schedules.”

The latest cancellations extend the airline's earlier advisory, which covered flights to Riyadh and Yanbu through October 10, and Abha through October 11.

According to Air Arabia's official flight status website, flights G9151 and G9154 from Sharjah to Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday and Tuesday. Flight G9195 from Sharjah to Abha is also listed as cancelled on both days.

Those with plans to travel should confirm their flight status directly with their airline before leaving for the airport and check notifications about changes to their booking.

Passengers whose flights have been cancelled should contact their airline or travel agent about rebooking and refund options. Travellers with onward connections should also confirm whether changes are needed to the rest of their journey.

body_text:
At least 72 gold miners have been killed in an air strike in northern Sudan that three Sudanese groups blamed on neighbouring Egypt.

Emergency Lawyers, a coalition of pro-democracy groups known by its acronym Somood and Sudan Doctors' Network each condemned the air strike and accused the military-aligned government in Sudan of not doing enough to protect its people and the country's territorial integrity.

All three said the air strike took place inside Sudan.

“We reject the targeting of civilians and putting their lives at risk, which cannot be justified on security grounds,” Somood said in a statement. “The leadership of the relevant authorities appointed by the armed forces bear the responsibility for what happens in areas under its control.”

Emergency Doctors put the death toll at 72, while Sudan Doctors' Network gave an initial tally of 13 dead and 28 wounded, warning the death toll was likely to rise.

Somood, Sudan's main opposition group, did not give a figure.

There has been no official word from the Sudanese or Egyptian governments on the incident. However, sources in Cairo confirmed the air strike took place, saying it was carried out at first light on Saturday targeting illegal gold prospectors operating on Egyptian territory near the Sudanese border.

“They had repeatedly been warned to leave the area but they never did,” said one source.

An image widely shared online appeared to show a leaflet dropped by Egyptian aircraft over the area before the strike.

Titled “final security warning”, the leaflets threatened the illegal miners with “immediate targeting” unless they left the area. They also called on them to surrender with their equipment. “Your lives are more valuable,” the leaflets told the miners.

The authenticity of the image could not immediately be verified by The National. The leaflet claimed the miners were operating inside Egyptian territory and said any action against them would be necessary to protect Egypt's resources.

Images ​and videos shared online, which The National was unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn in rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s.

One video showed a military helicopter flying over the site but it was unclear whether it was before or after the air strike.

There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative income.

Egypt's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drug and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. It said 87 Egyptians and 136 foreigners had been arrested.

Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign interests seeking quick profit. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011.

The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold, with many venturing independently and randomly into mining. Some estimates put the number of men involved at around two million.

Official figures place government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion, but experts say smuggling and local use of gold outside official channels account for far more. In 2025, for example, Sudan’s gold production was around 70 tonnes, but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated locally in primitive refineries.

Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda

headline: Skies over Saudi capital Riyadh largely empty after deadly Houthi strikes on airport
summary: Oct 12 (Reuters) - The skies above the Saudi capital Riyadh were largely empty on Mondayafter deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on the city's airport, with about 60% of scheduled flights expected to be cancelled, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
body_text:
Oct 12 (Reuters) - The skies above the Saudi capital Riyadh were largely empty on Mondayafter deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on the city's airport, with about 60% of scheduled flights expected to be cancelled, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah,cancelled 99.7% of all scheduled flights on Sunday, Cirium data showed. More than a third of flights scheduled across the kingdom were not expected to operate on Monday, while flight tracking website FlightRadar24 estimated cancellations at Riyadh airport of about 78%.

The Saudi capital's airport remained closed on Sunday after an attack that killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. The strike followed another attack claimed by the Houthis a day earlier that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. The Federal Aviation Administration told US airlines on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.

(Reporting by Joanna Plucinska in London and Gianluca Lo Nostro in Gdansk; Editing by Matt Scuffham)

headline: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
summary: By Sarah El Safty and Jana ChoukeirDUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-alignedHouthis.The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organisers released early Monday.
body_text:
By Sarah El Safty and Jana Choukeir

DUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-alignedHouthis.

The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organisers released early Monday.

“To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you,” said Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who opened Monday’s session of the gathering for energy policy and industry.

“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart…Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”

Prince Abdulaziz said the events of recent weeks were serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious".

The strikes are a blow to Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's multi-billion-dollar programme to diversify the economy away from oil, modernise society and position the kingdom as an investment and tourism hub.

Hosting international events is a priority of the programme, which was already facing delays and recalibrations. Prince Abdulaziz said the kingdom must remain focused on the decades ahead and Vision 2030 must continue.

The WPC Energy Congress was originally scheduled for April of this year, but was postponed after the US and Israeli war on Iran began in late February. Saudi Arabia was named host in October 2022, the first time the event, first held in Britain in 1933, has been held in the kingdom.

Chief executives of major energy companies are a regular fixture at WPC Energy events and had been scheduled to speak on stage this week about global oil and gas markets, energy security and the energy transition.

A BP spokesperson said the company had "made every effort to participate" in the conference. "Unfortunately, due to travel disruption we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our long-standing partnerships across the region."

Shell declined to comment and TotalEnergies,ExxonMobil and Chevron did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

The WPC Energy Congress is taking place this week at a conference centre some 10 kilometres (6 miles) from Riyadh’s international airport, which has been attacked four times in the last week.

One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack ​on the airport on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.

(Reporting by Jana Choukeir and Sarah El Safty in Dubai; Additional reporting by Stephanie Kelly and Shadia NasrallaWriting by Andrew MillsEditing by Andrew Heavens, Peter Graff)
