headline: China, EU reach consensus on hybrid and electric vehicle trade: spokesperson
summary: China and the European Union have reached a series of understandings on hybrid and electric vehicle trade through continued dialogue under their trade and investment consultation mechanism, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said Monday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- China and the European Union have reached a series of understandings on hybrid and electric vehicle trade through continued dialogue under their trade and investment consultation mechanism, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said Monday.

The spokesperson was responding to a question about recent talks between China and the EU on hybrid and electric vehicle trade, which helped avert an escalation of tensions, and about media speculation over the details of the hybrid vehicle arrangements, including quotas.

China and the EU held intensive consultations on trade in hybrid and electric vehicles on the basis of mutual respect and equality, seeking to balance trade and economic differences with each other's concerns, the spokesperson said.

On hybrid vehicles, the two sides confirmed three basic principles, the spokesperson said.

First, respect for facts. According to Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024 and 302,000 in 2025. The two sides agreed on an upward adjustment based on the 2025 figure to ensure export opportunities and stable growth for Chinese enterprises, while taking into account the reasonable concerns of both industries in light of actual circumstances, the spokesperson said.

Second, non-discrimination. No measures will specifically target Chinese products, let alone discriminate against Chinese enterprises. The quota allocated to China will be no lower than that allocated to any other source of imports into the EU, the spokesperson said.

Third, compliance. The two sides confirmed that the trade arrangements should comply with World Trade Organization rules. China reserves all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to seek dispute settlement and request trade compensation, the spokesperson said. These three principles have been upheld throughout the process and provide a solid foundation for safeguarding the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises, the spokesperson added.

Regarding electric vehicles, China and the EU achieved a "soft landing" in the anti-subsidy case in January, and the EU issued general guidance on price undertaking offers. The EU will actively advance procedures related to company-specific price undertakings in the electric vehicle case, as well as other review procedures, the spokesperson said.

The understandings, reached on the basis of reciprocity and mutual benefit, effectively safeguard the interests of Chinese enterprises and help prevent an escalation of China-EU trade frictions. They also provide a stable, predictable and sustainable trade and investment environment for both sides, helping promote the stable, balanced and healthy development of bilateral economic and trade relations, the spokesperson said.

headline: UAE teenager Mariam Kareem’s stunning rise from school runner to Asian Games champion
summary: After a dream summer that saw her place fourth in the 400m hurdles at the World Athletics U20 Championships and clinch gold at the Asian Games, Emirati teenager Mariam Kareem is still trying to wrap her head around everything she has accomplished over the past couple of months. The 18-year-old hurdler started her season running 57.39 seconds at a Grand Prix in Addis Ababa in April and finished it with a stunning 54.31s to top the podium at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, two weeks ago. The time Kareem clocked in Japan didn’t just earn her the gold medal; it also saw her set an Asian Games record in the 400m hurdles, as well as a new Asian U20 record. In August, Kareem, who is based in Sharjah, clocked a time of 56.27s to place fourth at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, finishing just 0.28s shy of the podium. She felt confident she would be fast at the Asian Games the following month, but never expected she would be able to shave nearly two seconds off her time to secure the gold. “I would say it was an unexpected thing for me,” a smiling Kareem told The National. “After the Eugene World Juniors, I had a lot of training, a lot of sessions, a lot of correction. So I was expecting a very fast time, but not that fast or a gold medal. In Japan, I had a lot of ups and downs there. I really struggled with the time zone change.“I was tense, I was scared. I was a bit sick, but thank Allah for everything. I just had to put everything behind me and focus on my personal events.” View this post on Instagram Kareem’s success in Nagoya made headlines, not just in the UAE, but across the region, and she was given quite the reception when she returned to the Emirates, both at the airport and at a special event held by her sponsors 'On' to celebrate her historic gold medal. “I'm still taking everything slowly. There's a lot of people around, a lot of messages, a lot of congratulations, a lot of places I've been to. It's my first time being in this situation, so I'm taking it easy,” said Kareem. “It really took me by surprise. I’m just trying to wrap my head around all the news, the messages, and to keep on doing the good work. I really hope I can keep up with the work and continue.”Things have been happening fast for Kareem. It was just three years ago that she was scouted by the UAE Athletics Federation, which saw potential in her when she was competing at her high school in Dubai and at her local club. Kareem, who liked running but wasn’t really into competing, was encouraged by a coach from the federation to take athletics seriously. She was barely 16 at the time. “He was really a great mentor for me,” Kareem recalls. “He advised me; he talked to me like a father. He told me, ‘Continue training; I believe you have a potential in you. You can go far. There's a bright future ahead’. “I was not really into athletics. I just loved running, but not really that passionate to compete at the high level. So he talked me into it.” View this post on Instagram Kareem initially ran 200m and 400m flat, but urged by her coach, who saw she had the height and flexibility, switched to the 400m hurdles, which has become her signature event. “Representing my country with pride, it was something that I really wanted to do. So I was happy to. I'm going out there, coming back with medals, representing my country, raising the country flag,” she said. “So I was really happy and excited and I love doing it. So I'm going to continue doing it and keep on the good work.”Kareem is achieving what no Emirati woman has achieved before, and she is well aware that there is the potential to make history every time she steps on the track. “For now, there is no pressure, but it's still giving me motivation to go forward, to do more and so that at least our country can be up in the world,” she explained. “My aim is to continue raising the national flag up and keep making names for the country before anybody can come and take the place from me. Because I cannot be here forever. So, there's still going to be young athletes that can still come from here.”Kareem is the fifth of six siblings, none of whom are athletes. She jokes that they all want to start running now that they’re witnessing her success. Her mother has been her biggest supporter from day one, and she remembers her father being sceptical of her running career at first. That scepticism has since dissipated, and her father was the first to call to congratulate her when she took gold in Nagoya. I'd like to go the Olympics, the World Championship, the Asian Championship. So, just hope to compete and to work hardMariam Kareem“After I collected the medal, my dad called and he was so proud of me, was so excited,” she revealed. “Coming from a family like that, and I'm making names, going far, he’s like, ‘Ah, I should have supported her when I had the chance’. I was like, ‘It's OK, you still have the chance, I'm very young, you can still support me’,” she added with a laugh.Kareem is now enjoying some well-deserved downtime during this offseason before she starts training again for her upcoming goals. “Getting the gold medal in the Asian Games and the Games record has given me the confidence that I can still achieve a lot in the future. So I want to improve my performances and go to compete at the higher level,” she said. “I'd like to go the Olympics, the World Championship, the Asian Championship. So, just hope to compete and to work hard. Not just to compete, I want to go there and have fun, be the best, and be at the podium. So, that's just my aims for the future.”Before the LA 2028 Olympics, Kareem is hoping she can compete in the Diamond League in 2027 to line up against the world’s best for an entire season. She immediately lights up when asked which athlete she'd most like to meet if she makes the Olympics.“Sydney [McLaughlin-Levrone]. I'd love to meet her. She's a role model to me,” she says with a grin. “The fact that she can do anything. She can play in 400 flat, 400 hurdles; she can do multiple events. And she doesn't look like she's doing more, but she's giving all her best. It feels like she's not doing anything. View this post on Instagram “I want to be like her, at least make names, have a lot, the world records, six-time world record. I really hope to be at the LA Olympics, so that at least I can see her and compete with her at the lanes. So that's my biggest dream right now, to compete with her, yes.”In the span of three years, Kareem went from being a kid who loved running but was not too keen on competing to being an Asian Games champion and Asian U20 record holder. What were her biggest lessons during this transformation?“Athletics taught me a lot. Taught me discipline, taught me patience, taught me consistency. I think I've learnt a lot,” she says.“I've learnt how to stay consistent in what I'm doing and keep doing what I love and keep making names, keep going forward. From one minute to another, now I'm [running] 54, so that is consistency. “I keep on training, I keep on believing in myself, my coach, my teammates, our training. I know I can go further, I can run very fast. So I just have learnt that consistency is the key.”

The time Kareem clocked in Japan didn’t just earn her the gold medal; it also saw her set an Asian Games record in the 400m hurdles, as well as a new Asian U20 record.

‘My country deserves this’: UAE Asian Games champions on gold and World Pro aims

In August, Kareem, who is based in Sharjah, clocked a time of 56.27s to place fourth at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, finishing just 0.28s shy of the podium.

She felt confident she would be fast at the Asian Games the following month, but never expected she would be able to shave nearly two seconds off her time to secure the gold.

“I would say it was an unexpected thing for me,” a smiling Kareem told The National.

“After the Eugene World Juniors, I had a lot of training, a lot of sessions, a lot of correction. So I was expecting a very fast time, but not that fast or a gold medal. In Japan, I had a lot of ups and downs there. I really struggled with the time zone change.

“I was tense, I was scared. I was a bit sick, but thank Allah for everything. I just had to put everything behind me and focus on my personal events.”

Kareem’s success in Nagoya made headlines, not just in the UAE, but across the region, and she was given quite the reception when she returned to the Emirates, both at the airport and at a special event held by her sponsors 'On' to celebrate her historic gold medal.

“I'm still taking everything slowly. There's a lot of people around, a lot of messages, a lot of congratulations, a lot of places I've been to. It's my first time being in this situation, so I'm taking it easy,” said Kareem.

“It really took me by surprise. I’m just trying to wrap my head around all the news, the messages, and to keep on doing the good work. I really hope I can keep up with the work and continue.”

Things have been happening fast for Kareem. It was just three years ago that she was scouted by the UAE Athletics Federation, which saw potential in her when she was competing at her high school in Dubai and at her local club.

Kareem, who liked running but wasn’t really into competing, was encouraged by a coach from the federation to take athletics seriously. She was barely 16 at the time.

“He was really a great mentor for me,” Kareem recalls. “He advised me; he talked to me like a father. He told me, ‘Continue training; I believe you have a potential in you. You can go far. There's a bright future ahead’.

“I was not really into athletics. I just loved running, but not really that passionate to compete at the high level. So he talked me into it.”

Kareem initially ran 200m and 400m flat, but urged by her coach, who saw she had the height and flexibility, switched to the 400m hurdles, which has become her signature event.

“Representing my country with pride, it was something that I really wanted to do. So I was happy to. I'm going out there, coming back with medals, representing my country, raising the country flag,” she said.

“So I was really happy and excited and I love doing it. So I'm going to continue doing it and keep on the good work.”

Kareem is achieving what no Emirati woman has achieved before, and she is well aware that there is the potential to make history every time she steps on the track.

“For now, there is no pressure, but it's still giving me motivation to go forward, to do more and so that at least our country can be up in the world,” she explained.

“My aim is to continue raising the national flag up and keep making names for the country before anybody can come and take the place from me. Because I cannot be here forever. So, there's still going to be young athletes that can still come from here.”

Kareem is the fifth of six siblings, none of whom are athletes. She jokes that they all want to start running now that they’re witnessing her success. Her mother has been her biggest supporter from day one, and she remembers her father being sceptical of her running career at first.

That scepticism has since dissipated, and her father was the first to call to congratulate her when she took gold in Nagoya.

“After I collected the medal, my dad called and he was so proud of me, was so excited,” she revealed. “Coming from a family like that, and I'm making names, going far, he’s like, ‘Ah, I should have supported her when I had the chance’. I was like, ‘It's OK, you still have the chance, I'm very young, you can still support me’,” she added with a laugh.

Kareem is now enjoying some well-deserved downtime during this offseason before she starts training again for her upcoming goals.

“Getting the gold medal in the Asian Games and the Games record has given me the confidence that I can still achieve a lot in the future. So I want to improve my performances and go to compete at the higher level,” she said.

“I'd like to go the Olympics, the World Championship, the Asian Championship. So, just hope to compete and to work hard. Not just to compete, I want to go there and have fun, be the best, and be at the podium. So, that's just my aims for the future.”

Before the LA 2028 Olympics, Kareem is hoping she can compete in the Diamond League in 2027 to line up against the world’s best for an entire season. She immediately lights up when asked which athlete she'd most like to meet if she makes the Olympics.

“Sydney [McLaughlin-Levrone]. I'd love to meet her. She's a role model to me,” she says with a grin.

“The fact that she can do anything. She can play in 400 flat, 400 hurdles; she can do multiple events. And she doesn't look like she's doing more, but she's giving all her best. It feels like she's not doing anything.

“I want to be like her, at least make names, have a lot, the world records, six-time world record. I really hope to be at the LA Olympics, so that at least I can see her and compete with her at the lanes. So that's my biggest dream right now, to compete with her, yes.”

In the span of three years, Kareem went from being a kid who loved running but was not too keen on competing to being an Asian Games champion and Asian U20 record holder.

What were her biggest lessons during this transformation?

“Athletics taught me a lot. Taught me discipline, taught me patience, taught me consistency. I think I've learnt a lot,” she says.

“I've learnt how to stay consistent in what I'm doing and keep doing what I love and keep making names, keep going forward. From one minute to another, now I'm [running] 54, so that is consistency.

“I keep on training, I keep on believing in myself, my coach, my teammates, our training. I know I can go further, I can run very fast. So I just have learnt that consistency is the key.”

body_text:
Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year.

IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday.

A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules.

Oman's economy to grow 3.5% in 2026 on favourable trade logistics, S&P says

A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added.

“IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business."

IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre.

The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said.

Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil, with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base.

Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040.

The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country.

It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy.

Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.

headline: Live: Saudi Arabia extends suspension of operations at Riyadh airport after deadly Houthi attacks
summary: Saudi Arabia's civil aviation body extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's international airport Monday following a series of deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels over the weekend. The statement announcing the decision did not specify when operations would resume. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.
body_text:
Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 10:41

Saudi Arabia's civil aviation body extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's international airport Monday following a series of deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels over the weekend. The statement announcing the decision did not specify when operations would resume. Follow our liveblog for the latest developments.

The European Union on Monday formally added almost 1,600 new individuals and entities to its sanctions blacklist over Russia's war on Ukraine.

"This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war. Europe is again showing a united front. More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said that his country would retaliate if Moscow did not agree to the "energy ceasefire" that US President Donald Trump unilaterally announced on Sunday.

"If Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond," Zelensky said in a video address to a security forum in Warsaw. "If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure and stop killing our people."

Iran ​is still ​reviewing a US response to its ​proposal ‌regarding ⁠the reopening ‌of the Strait of ⁠Hormuz and will reply ​to Washington ‌via intermediaries when the review ‌is over, ​foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.

Baghaei also ​told a ​press conference ​that Iran continues to exchange messages via ⁠the intermediaries.

Saudi Arabia's civil aviation body extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh's international airport Monday following a series of deadly Houthi attacks.

"The General Authority of Civil Aviation has announced the extension of the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in order to complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of the facilities and their operational readiness," the authority said in a statement.

It did not specify when operations would resume.

China condemned recent attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia, expressing "serious concern" about the intensifying conflict between Riyadh and the Yemeni group.

"China condemns the attacks that caused heavy casualties and expresses serious concern over the intensification of the conflict," foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told a regular briefing.

Saudi ​Energy ​Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said ​the ‌events ⁠of ‌recent weeks were serious ⁠and the kingdom's ​response must ‌be "equally serious".

Yemen's ‌Houthis have stepped ​up their attacks on the kingdom, killing ​more than ​15 ​people in ​two weeks.

Emirati ​presidential adviser ​Anwar Gargash called on Gulf countries to strengthen their security cooperation, saying that targeting Saudi ‌Arabia undermined ​the security of all Gulf states.

"It is necessary to revive joint action by the Gulf countries, particularly in security and defence, and to strengthen the collective security system," Gargash wrote on X.

Neglect of ​collective ​Gulf security ​had "emboldened others" to ​overreach against regional states, he added.

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said ​⁠that it reclassified an ‌incident in the vicinity of ⁠Sohar anchorage in Oman as ​an attack after confirmation ‌that the tanker was struck by ‌a drone.

Saudi Arabia's foreign ​minister spoke with his Iranian counterpart about the recent escalation of the regional ​conflict ‌and efforts to ⁠lower tensions, the Saudi state news agency ‌reported.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AP and AFP)

headline: Saudi Arabia extends suspension of operations at Riyadh airport following Houthi attacks
summary: Civil aviation authority says suspension extended to complete safety inspections, ensure operational readiness of King Khalid International Airport
body_text:
Saudi Arabia announced Monday that it had extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh following a series of attacks on the facility.

In a statement, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said the suspension was extended to complete necessary procedures to verify the safety of airport facilities and their operational readiness.

The authority did not specify when operations would resume.

The decision followed attacks on the airport over the weekend.

On Sunday afternoon, an unidentified projectile struck the airport’s Terminal 4, killing a Pakistani resident and injuring 11 others, according to Saudi authorities. The Saudi-led coalition also said it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile near the airport.

A day earlier, on Saturday, a Houthi attack struck a passenger terminal at the airport, killing 13 people and injuring 309 others, according to Saudi authorities.

The Saudi-led coalition accused the Houthis of carrying out Saturday’s attack and described the strike as a “full-fledged war crime.”

​​​​​​​The attacks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with airports and other civilian and energy facilities targeted in recent days.

body_text:
Saudi Arabia has extended the suspension of operations at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport following deadly attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels at the weekend.

The General Authority of Civil Aviation said on Monday that the suspension would continue while checks on the safety and operational readiness of airport facilities were completed. It did not give a reopening date or time.

UAE airlines have continued to cancel services to and from Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Wednesday. Flights to other Saudi destinations, including Dammam, Jeddah and Abha, have also been affected.

Twelve killed and 309 wounded in attack on Riyadh airport

Etihad has cancelled several flights between Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia on Monday and Tuesday, affecting services to Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah.

According to the airline's latest travel advisory, Monday's cancellations include flights EY559 and EY560 between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh. But Etihad's flight listings also show outbound Riyadh services EY551 and EY555 as being cancelled.

Four flights between Abu Dhabi and Dammam – EY573, EY574, EY575 and EY576 – have also been cancelled on Monday, along with Jeddah services EY601, EY602, EY603 and EY604.

Further cancellations are scheduled for Tuesday, including Dammam services EY575 and EY576, Jeddah flights EY602, EY603 and EY604, and Riyadh services EY551 and EY552.

Passengers are advised to check their flight status directly with Etihad before travelling, as further changes are possible.

Emirates' flight status website shows all six services between Dubai and Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday. These include outbound flights EK815, EK817 and EK819, along with returning services EK816, EK818 and EK820.

Four flights remain cancelled on Tuesday, including EK815, EK817 and EK819 from Dubai to Riyadh and the return service EK816. Return services EK818 and EK820 have not yet been listed as cancelled, although this does not confirm they will operate.

Flydubai has cancelled flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh up to and including Wednesday, amid the disruption to services to Saudi Arabia.

“Flights to Abha, Dammam and Riyadh have been cancelled up to and including October 14,” a flydubai representative told The National. “We continue to monitor the situation closely and we will update our customers through our official channels regarding any amendments to our flight schedules.”

The latest cancellations extend the airline's earlier advisory, which covered flights to Riyadh and Yanbu through October 10, and Abha through October 11.

According to Air Arabia's official flight status website, flights G9151 and G9154 from Sharjah to Riyadh have been cancelled on Monday and Tuesday. Flight G9195 from Sharjah to Abha is also listed as cancelled on both days.

Those with plans to travel should confirm their flight status directly with their airline before leaving for the airport and check notifications about changes to their booking.

Passengers whose flights have been cancelled should contact their airline or travel agent about rebooking and refund options. Travellers with onward connections should also confirm whether changes are needed to the rest of their journey.

However, sources in Cairo confirmed the air strike took place, saying it was carried out at first light on Saturday targeting illegal gold prospectors operating on Egyptian territory near the Sudanese border.“They had repeatedly been warned to leave the area but they never did,” said one source.An image widely shared online appeared to show a leaflet dropped by Egyptian aircraft over the area before the strike.Titled “final security warning”, the leaflets threatened the illegal miners with “immediate targeting” unless they left the area. They also called on them to surrender with their equipment. “Your lives are more valuable,” the leaflets told the miners.The authenticity of the image could not immediately be verified by The National. The leaflet claimed the miners were operating inside Egyptian territory and said any action against them would be necessary to protect Egypt's resources.Images ​and videos shared online, which The National was unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn in rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s.One video showed a military helicopter flying over the site but it was unclear whether it was before or after the air strike.There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative income.Egypt's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drug and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011.The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold, with many venturing independently and randomly into mining. Some estimates put the number of men involved at around two million.Official figures place government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion, but experts say smuggling and local use of gold outside official channels account for far more. body_text:
At least 72 gold miners have been killed in an air strike in northern Sudan that three Sudanese groups blamed on neighbouring Egypt.

Emergency Lawyers, a coalition of pro-democracy groups known by its acronym Somood and Sudan Doctors' Network each condemned the air strike and accused the military-aligned government in Sudan of not doing enough to protect its people and the country's territorial integrity.

All three said the air strike took place inside Sudan.

“We reject the targeting of civilians and putting their lives at risk, which cannot be justified on security grounds,” Somood said in a statement. “The leadership of the relevant authorities appointed by the armed forces bear the responsibility for what happens in areas under its control.”

Emergency Doctors put the death toll at 72, while Sudan Doctors' Network gave an initial tally of 13 dead and 28 wounded, warning the death toll was likely to rise.

Somood, Sudan's main opposition group, did not give a figure.

There has been no official word from the Sudanese or Egyptian governments on the incident. However, sources in Cairo confirmed the air strike took place, saying it was carried out at first light on Saturday targeting illegal gold prospectors operating on Egyptian territory near the Sudanese border.

“They had repeatedly been warned to leave the area but they never did,” said one source.

An image widely shared online appeared to show a leaflet dropped by Egyptian aircraft over the area before the strike.

Titled “final security warning”, the leaflets threatened the illegal miners with “immediate targeting” unless they left the area. They also called on them to surrender with their equipment. “Your lives are more valuable,” the leaflets told the miners.

The authenticity of the image could not immediately be verified by The National. The leaflet claimed the miners were operating inside Egyptian territory and said any action against them would be necessary to protect Egypt's resources.

Images ​and videos shared online, which The National was unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn in rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s.

One video showed a military helicopter flying over the site but it was unclear whether it was before or after the air strike.

There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative income.

Egypt's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drug and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. It said 87 Egyptians and 136 foreigners had been arrested.

Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign interests seeking quick profit. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011.

The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold, with many venturing independently and randomly into mining. Some estimates put the number of men involved at around two million.

Official figures place government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion, but experts say smuggling and local use of gold outside official channels account for far more. In 2025, for example, Sudan’s gold production was around 70 tonnes, but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated locally in primitive refineries.

Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda

headline: Iranian nation to never surrender: AEOI chief says
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Denouncing the US threats to attack Iran’s nuclear sites, Head of the Atomic energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) Mohammad Eslami has said that the noble nation of the Islamic Iran will never surrender under any circumstances.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Denouncing the US threats to attack Iran’s nuclear sites, Head of the Atomic energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) Mohammad Eslami has said that the noble nation of the Islamic Iran will never surrender under any circumstances.

Speaking at the conference “Ecocide: The Silent War Crime” on Sunday, Eslami stated that Iranian combatants and powerful Armed Forces of the country have delivered firm and harsh responses to the enemy.

However, he emphasized that a fundamental difference between Iran and its adversaries is that Iran’s Armed Forces, guided by the teachings of Islam, target only military objectives and refrain from retaliating against civilians.

He further stated that recent attacks had targeted not only Iran’s nuclear facilities, whose destruction could have serious environmental consequences, but also non-nuclear sites, including refineries, petrochemical complexes and irradiation centers affiliated with the AEOI. These facilities, he noted, provide valuable services in healthcare, food safety and protecting public security.

According to Eslami, attacking centers where radioactive sources are used to conduct measurements, control safety processes and monitor production demonstrated the attackers’ disregard for human life, the environment and the rights of future generations.

headline: Pezeshkian attends university Academic Year opening ceremony
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended Shahid Beheshti University of Tehran on Monday for the opening ceremony of the universities and academic centers of the country in the New Academic Year.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended Shahid Beheshti University of Tehran on Monday for the opening ceremony of the universities and academic centers of the country in the New Academic Year.

Prior to attending the ceremony, President Pezeshkian inaugurated an exhibition showcasing selected works from the seventh edition of the "Incidents and Disasters" Photography Contest entitled "Standing Firm for Iran", special of the Third Imposed War [Ramadan War].

The ceremony was also attended by Minister of Science, Research and Technology Hossein Simaei Sarraf, Health Minister Mohammad-Reza Zafarghandi, the head of the Leader’s Office, a number of university chancellors as well as the university students.

During the ceremony, Pezeshkian first commemorated the name and memory of schoolchildren martyred in Minab Elementary School following the US and Israeli attack on February 28, noted, “I believe that finding a way out of the current situation is possible through the efforts of academics and university students.”

Scientists and scholars are striving to acquire knowledge and capability to overcome these challenges, he said, adding, “We believe in this issue that if cooperation and interaction is established among all pillars of the government and elites of the country, many of problems will be resolved in the best possible way.”

headline: Skies over Saudi capital Riyadh largely empty after deadly Houthi strikes on airport
summary: Oct 12 (Reuters) - The skies above the Saudi capital Riyadh were largely empty on Mondayafter deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on the city's airport, with about 60% of scheduled flights expected to be cancelled, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
body_text:
Oct 12 (Reuters) - The skies above the Saudi capital Riyadh were largely empty on Mondayafter deadly attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis on the city's airport, with about 60% of scheduled flights expected to be cancelled, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah,cancelled 99.7% of all scheduled flights on Sunday, Cirium data showed. More than a third of flights scheduled across the kingdom were not expected to operate on Monday, while flight tracking website FlightRadar24 estimated cancellations at Riyadh airport of about 78%.

The Saudi capital's airport remained closed on Sunday after an attack that killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. The strike followed another attack claimed by the Houthis a day earlier that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi civil aviation in years, forcing airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services. The Federal Aviation Administration told US airlines on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.

(Reporting by Joanna Plucinska in London and Gianluca Lo Nostro in Gdansk; Editing by Matt Scuffham)

headline: Top oil executives dropped from event schedule after Riyadh attacks
summary: By Sarah El Safty and Jana ChoukeirDUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-alignedHouthis.The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organisers released early Monday.
body_text:
By Sarah El Safty and Jana Choukeir

DUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Several top energy executives were dropped from the schedule of the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, as Saudi authorities pressed ahead with the event despite deadly attacks on the capital claimed by Yemen's Iran-alignedHouthis.

The chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell, Chevron and BP had all been expected at the event, which began on Sunday, but were no longer on the agenda that conference organisers released early Monday.

“To everyone who travelled to Riyadh, thank you,” said Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, who opened Monday’s session of the gathering for energy policy and industry.

“You know this country is safe and that we hold your protection at whole heart…Our gathering here does not mean the risk is gone.”

Prince Abdulaziz said the events of recent weeks were serious and that the kingdom’s response must be “equally serious".

The strikes are a blow to Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia's multi-billion-dollar programme to diversify the economy away from oil, modernise society and position the kingdom as an investment and tourism hub.

Hosting international events is a priority of the programme, which was already facing delays and recalibrations. Prince Abdulaziz said the kingdom must remain focused on the decades ahead and Vision 2030 must continue.

The WPC Energy Congress was originally scheduled for April of this year, but was postponed after the US and Israeli war on Iran began in late February. Saudi Arabia was named host in October 2022, the first time the event, first held in Britain in 1933, has been held in the kingdom.

Chief executives of major energy companies are a regular fixture at WPC Energy events and had been scheduled to speak on stage this week about global oil and gas markets, energy security and the energy transition.

A BP spokesperson said the company had "made every effort to participate" in the conference. "Unfortunately, due to travel disruption we are unable to be there in person. We greatly value our long-standing partnerships across the region."

Shell declined to comment and TotalEnergies,ExxonMobil and Chevron did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

The WPC Energy Congress is taking place this week at a conference centre some 10 kilometres (6 miles) from Riyadh’s international airport, which has been attacked four times in the last week.

One person was killed and nearly a dozen hurt in a new attack ​on the airport on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities reported, a day after a strike claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.

(Reporting by Jana Choukeir and Sarah El Safty in Dubai; Additional reporting by Stephanie Kelly and Shadia NasrallaWriting by Andrew MillsEditing by Andrew Heavens, Peter Graff)

headline: Saudi Arabia says oil supply to continue to flow despite Riyadh attacks
summary: Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier.“The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress. “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.”The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11.The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack.But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time.“Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.”The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints.Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added.He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd.The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added.“Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said.At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”.The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks.“The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”
body_text:
Saudi Arabia sought to reassure the world’s energy industry that escalating attacks on the kingdom would not disrupt its role as a major oil supplier.

“The word ‘fear’ in the Saudi dictionary does not exist,” Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said on Monday at the opening of the WPC Energy Congress. “We, as Saudis, are fearless, combatant and determined people.”

The remarks came after King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was struck four times in five days, emphasising the growing security risks facing the world’s biggest crude exporter amid the Iran war. A missile attack on the airport on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309, Saudi authorities said. Another projectile struck the airport on Sunday evening, killing one person and injuring 11.

LatestSaudi Arabia extends suspension of operations at Riyadh airport

The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen blamed the Iran-backed Houthi rebels for Saturday’s attack.

But Riyadh is to press ahead with a week of high-level energy meetings, including Sunday’s International Energy Forum ministerial talks and the WPC congress, which the kingdom is hosting for the first time.

“Riyadh is the capital of energy security and your presence here today proves that,” Prince Abdulaziz told delegates. “Our gathering today does not mean that risks have disappeared.”

The attacks have sharpened focus on Saudi Arabia’s ability to keep oil flowing during periods of conflict, particularly as threats mount around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab Al Mandeb strait, two of the world’s most important energy chokepoints.

Prince Abdulaziz said Saudi Arabia’s ability to withstand disruption was the result of decades of investment in storage, redundancy and alternative export routes. “Resilience is built before a crisis begins,” he added.

He referred to the kingdom’s East-West pipeline, which carries crude from eastern oilfields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, allowing exports to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. The flow was halted after Houthi attacks in September, before recovering to about 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, compared with capacity of about seven million bpd.

The disruption showed the importance of restoring operations quickly, Prince Abdulaziz said. Resilience depends not only on infrastructure but also on domestic expertise, he added.

“Pipelines do not repair themselves. Our systems do not restore themselves. Facilities do not restart themselves. People do,” he said.

At Sunday’s IEF meeting, he pledged that Saudi Arabia would continue to supply domestic and international customers “regardless of circumstances”.

The gathering took place against an increasingly volatile market backdrop. Brent crude hovered at about $104 a barrel on Monday as the Riyadh attacks and strikes on two tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and Oman added to geopolitical risks.

“The events of recent weeks are serious,” Prince Abdulaziz said. “Our response must be equally serious.”

headline: China, EU reach consensus on hybrid and electric vehicle trade: spokesperson
summary: China and the European Union have reached a series of understandings on hybrid and electric vehicle trade through continued dialogue under their trade and investment consultation mechanism, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said Monday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- China and the European Union have reached a series of understandings on hybrid and electric vehicle trade through continued dialogue under their trade and investment consultation mechanism, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce said Monday.

The spokesperson was responding to a question about recent talks between China and the EU on hybrid and electric vehicle trade, which helped avert an escalation of tensions, and about media speculation over the details of the hybrid vehicle arrangements, including quotas.

China and the EU held intensive consultations on trade in hybrid and electric vehicles on the basis of mutual respect and equality, seeking to balance trade and economic differences with each other's concerns, the spokesperson said.

On hybrid vehicles, the two sides confirmed three basic principles, the spokesperson said.

First, respect for facts. According to Eurostat, the EU's statistics office, the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024 and 302,000 in 2025. The two sides agreed on an upward adjustment based on the 2025 figure to ensure export opportunities and stable growth for Chinese enterprises, while taking into account the reasonable concerns of both industries in light of actual circumstances, the spokesperson said.

Second, non-discrimination. No measures will specifically target Chinese products, let alone discriminate against Chinese enterprises. The quota allocated to China will be no lower than that allocated to any other source of imports into the EU, the spokesperson said.

Third, compliance. The two sides confirmed that the trade arrangements should comply with World Trade Organization rules. China reserves all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to seek dispute settlement and request trade compensation, the spokesperson said. These three principles have been upheld throughout the process and provide a solid foundation for safeguarding the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises, the spokesperson added.

Regarding electric vehicles, China and the EU achieved a "soft landing" in the anti-subsidy case in January, and the EU issued general guidance on price undertaking offers. The EU will actively advance procedures related to company-specific price undertakings in the electric vehicle case, as well as other review procedures, the spokesperson said.

The understandings, reached on the basis of reciprocity and mutual benefit, effectively safeguard the interests of Chinese enterprises and help prevent an escalation of China-EU trade frictions. They also provide a stable, predictable and sustainable trade and investment environment for both sides, helping promote the stable, balanced and healthy development of bilateral economic and trade relations, the spokesperson said.

headline: UAE teenager Mariam Kareem’s stunning rise from school runner to Asian Games champion
summary: After a dream summer that saw her place fourth in the 400m hurdles at the World Athletics U20 Championships and clinch gold at the Asian Games, Emirati teenager Mariam Kareem is still trying to wrap her head around everything she has accomplished over the past couple of months. The 18-year-old hurdler started her season running 57.39 seconds at a Grand Prix in Addis Ababa in April and finished it with a stunning 54.31s to top the podium at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, two weeks ago. The time Kareem clocked in Japan didn’t just earn her the gold medal; it also saw her set an Asian Games record in the 400m hurdles, as well as a new Asian U20 record. In August, Kareem, who is based in Sharjah, clocked a time of 56.27s to place fourth at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, finishing just 0.28s shy of the podium. She felt confident she would be fast at the Asian Games the following month, but never expected she would be able to shave nearly two seconds off her time to secure the gold. “I would say it was an unexpected thing for me,” a smiling Kareem told The National. “After the Eugene World Juniors, I had a lot of training, a lot of sessions, a lot of correction. So I was expecting a very fast time, but not that fast or a gold medal. In Japan, I had a lot of ups and downs there. I really struggled with the time zone change.“I was tense, I was scared. I was a bit sick, but thank Allah for everything. I just had to put everything behind me and focus on my personal events.” View this post on Instagram Kareem’s success in Nagoya made headlines, not just in the UAE, but across the region, and she was given quite the reception when she returned to the Emirates, both at the airport and at a special event held by her sponsors 'On' to celebrate her historic gold medal. “I'm still taking everything slowly. There's a lot of people around, a lot of messages, a lot of congratulations, a lot of places I've been to. It's my first time being in this situation, so I'm taking it easy,” said Kareem. “It really took me by surprise. I’m just trying to wrap my head around all the news, the messages, and to keep on doing the good work. I really hope I can keep up with the work and continue.”Things have been happening fast for Kareem. It was just three years ago that she was scouted by the UAE Athletics Federation, which saw potential in her when she was competing at her high school in Dubai and at her local club. Kareem, who liked running but wasn’t really into competing, was encouraged by a coach from the federation to take athletics seriously. She was barely 16 at the time. “He was really a great mentor for me,” Kareem recalls. “He advised me; he talked to me like a father. He told me, ‘Continue training; I believe you have a potential in you. You can go far. There's a bright future ahead’. “I was not really into athletics. I just loved running, but not really that passionate to compete at the high level. So he talked me into it.” View this post on Instagram Kareem initially ran 200m and 400m flat, but urged by her coach, who saw she had the height and flexibility, switched to the 400m hurdles, which has become her signature event. “Representing my country with pride, it was something that I really wanted to do. So I was happy to. I'm going out there, coming back with medals, representing my country, raising the country flag,” she said. “So I was really happy and excited and I love doing it. So I'm going to continue doing it and keep on the good work.”Kareem is achieving what no Emirati woman has achieved before, and she is well aware that there is the potential to make history every time she steps on the track. “For now, there is no pressure, but it's still giving me motivation to go forward, to do more and so that at least our country can be up in the world,” she explained. “My aim is to continue raising the national flag up and keep making names for the country before anybody can come and take the place from me. Because I cannot be here forever. So, there's still going to be young athletes that can still come from here.”Kareem is the fifth of six siblings, none of whom are athletes. She jokes that they all want to start running now that they’re witnessing her success. Her mother has been her biggest supporter from day one, and she remembers her father being sceptical of her running career at first. That scepticism has since dissipated, and her father was the first to call to congratulate her when she took gold in Nagoya. So, just hope to compete and to work hardMariam Kareem“After I collected the medal, my dad called and he was so proud of me, was so excited,” she revealed. “Coming from a family like that, and I'm making names, going far, he’s like, ‘Ah, I should have supported her when I had the chance’. I was like, ‘It's OK, you still have the chance, I'm very young, you can still support me’,” she added with a laugh.Kareem is now enjoying some well-deserved downtime during this offseason before she starts training again for her upcoming goals. “Getting the gold medal in the Asian Games and the Games record has given me the confidence that I can still achieve a lot in the future. So I want to improve my performances and go to compete at the higher level,” she said. “I'd like to go the Olympics, the World Championship, the Asian Championship. So, just hope to compete and to work hard. Not just to compete, I want to go there and have fun, be the best, and be at the podium. So, that's just my aims for the future.”Before the LA 2028 Olympics, Kareem is hoping she can compete in the Diamond League in 2027 to line up against the world’s best for an entire season. She's a role model to me,” she says with a grin. “The fact that she can do anything. She can play in 400 flat, 400 hurdles; she can do multiple events. body_text:
After a dream summer that saw her place fourth in the 400m hurdles at the World Athletics U20 Championships and clinch gold at the Asian Games, Emirati teenager Mariam Kareem is still trying to wrap her head around everything she has accomplished over the past couple of months.

The 18-year-old hurdler started her season running 57.39 seconds at a Grand Prix in Addis Ababa in April and finished it with a stunning 54.31s to top the podium at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, two weeks ago.

The time Kareem clocked in Japan didn’t just earn her the gold medal; it also saw her set an Asian Games record in the 400m hurdles, as well as a new Asian U20 record.

‘My country deserves this’: UAE Asian Games champions on gold and World Pro aims

In August, Kareem, who is based in Sharjah, clocked a time of 56.27s to place fourth at the World Athletics U20 Championships in Eugene, Oregon, finishing just 0.28s shy of the podium.

She felt confident she would be fast at the Asian Games the following month, but never expected she would be able to shave nearly two seconds off her time to secure the gold.

“I would say it was an unexpected thing for me,” a smiling Kareem told The National.

“After the Eugene World Juniors, I had a lot of training, a lot of sessions, a lot of correction. So I was expecting a very fast time, but not that fast or a gold medal. In Japan, I had a lot of ups and downs there. I really struggled with the time zone change.

“I was tense, I was scared. I was a bit sick, but thank Allah for everything. I just had to put everything behind me and focus on my personal events.”

Kareem’s success in Nagoya made headlines, not just in the UAE, but across the region, and she was given quite the reception when she returned to the Emirates, both at the airport and at a special event held by her sponsors 'On' to celebrate her historic gold medal.

“I'm still taking everything slowly. There's a lot of people around, a lot of messages, a lot of congratulations, a lot of places I've been to. It's my first time being in this situation, so I'm taking it easy,” said Kareem.

“It really took me by surprise. I’m just trying to wrap my head around all the news, the messages, and to keep on doing the good work. I really hope I can keep up with the work and continue.”

Things have been happening fast for Kareem. It was just three years ago that she was scouted by the UAE Athletics Federation, which saw potential in her when she was competing at her high school in Dubai and at her local club.

Kareem, who liked running but wasn’t really into competing, was encouraged by a coach from the federation to take athletics seriously. She was barely 16 at the time.

“He was really a great mentor for me,” Kareem recalls. “He advised me; he talked to me like a father. He told me, ‘Continue training; I believe you have a potential in you. You can go far. There's a bright future ahead’.

“I was not really into athletics. I just loved running, but not really that passionate to compete at the high level. So he talked me into it.”

Kareem initially ran 200m and 400m flat, but urged by her coach, who saw she had the height and flexibility, switched to the 400m hurdles, which has become her signature event.

“Representing my country with pride, it was something that I really wanted to do. So I was happy to. I'm going out there, coming back with medals, representing my country, raising the country flag,” she said.

“So I was really happy and excited and I love doing it. So I'm going to continue doing it and keep on the good work.”

Kareem is achieving what no Emirati woman has achieved before, and she is well aware that there is the potential to make history every time she steps on the track.

“For now, there is no pressure, but it's still giving me motivation to go forward, to do more and so that at least our country can be up in the world,” she explained.

“My aim is to continue raising the national flag up and keep making names for the country before anybody can come and take the place from me. Because I cannot be here forever. So, there's still going to be young athletes that can still come from here.”

Kareem is the fifth of six siblings, none of whom are athletes. She jokes that they all want to start running now that they’re witnessing her success. Her mother has been her biggest supporter from day one, and she remembers her father being sceptical of her running career at first.

That scepticism has since dissipated, and her father was the first to call to congratulate her when she took gold in Nagoya.

“After I collected the medal, my dad called and he was so proud of me, was so excited,” she revealed. “Coming from a family like that, and I'm making names, going far, he’s like, ‘Ah, I should have supported her when I had the chance’. I was like, ‘It's OK, you still have the chance, I'm very young, you can still support me’,” she added with a laugh.

Kareem is now enjoying some well-deserved downtime during this offseason before she starts training again for her upcoming goals.

“Getting the gold medal in the Asian Games and the Games record has given me the confidence that I can still achieve a lot in the future. So I want to improve my performances and go to compete at the higher level,” she said.

“I'd like to go the Olympics, the World Championship, the Asian Championship. So, just hope to compete and to work hard. Not just to compete, I want to go there and have fun, be the best, and be at the podium. So, that's just my aims for the future.”

Before the LA 2028 Olympics, Kareem is hoping she can compete in the Diamond League in 2027 to line up against the world’s best for an entire season. She immediately lights up when asked which athlete she'd most like to meet if she makes the Olympics.

“Sydney [McLaughlin-Levrone]. I'd love to meet her. She's a role model to me,” she says with a grin.

“The fact that she can do anything. She can play in 400 flat, 400 hurdles; she can do multiple events. And she doesn't look like she's doing more, but she's giving all her best. It feels like she's not doing anything.

“I want to be like her, at least make names, have a lot, the world records, six-time world record. I really hope to be at the LA Olympics, so that at least I can see her and compete with her at the lanes. So that's my biggest dream right now, to compete with her, yes.”

In the span of three years, Kareem went from being a kid who loved running but was not too keen on competing to being an Asian Games champion and Asian U20 record holder.

What were her biggest lessons during this transformation?

“Athletics taught me a lot. Taught me discipline, taught me patience, taught me consistency. I think I've learnt a lot,” she says.

“I've learnt how to stay consistent in what I'm doing and keep doing what I love and keep making names, keep going forward. From one minute to another, now I'm [running] 54, so that is consistency.

“I keep on training, I keep on believing in myself, my coach, my teammates, our training. I know I can go further, I can run very fast. So I just have learnt that consistency is the key.”

headline: Oman aims to launch new international financial centre by 2027

Oman plans to launch full licensing at its new international financial centre by 2027 and is to begin registering companies later this year.

IFC Oman, the plans for which were first revealed in January, is currently working on its legal framework, rule book and registry system, it said in a statement on Monday.

A package of laws for business registration and licensing, financial services regulation and an independent dispute resolution framework are to be issued shortly, the financial centre said. They will provide the legal basis for IFC Oman’s authorities to adopt an initial package of regulations and rules.

Oman's economy to grow 3.5% in 2026 on favourable trade logistics, S&P says

A registry system, which will enable businesses to submit their applications online, is to move into the testing phase soon, the statement added.

“IFC Oman is accelerating towards opening its doors, with its legal, regulatory and digital infrastructure moving into place," said Mahmood Al Aweini, chairman of the IFC Oman Authority Board. "The centre will offer global businesses and investors a stable and competitive place to do business."

IFC Oman will join other existing financial centres in the Gulf, including Abu Dhabi's international financial centre ADGM, the Dubai International Financial Centre and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh, as well as the Qatar Financial Centre.

The financial centre has started boosting its international outreach to engage prospective businesses, investors and professional services firms around the world, the statement said.

Oman has been taking steps to diversify its economy away from oil, with investments in sectors such as logistics, manufacturing and property helping to expand its non-oil economic base.

Under its economic and social reforms programme, Oman aims to reduce its dependence on oil income from about 30 per cent to 16 per cent by 2030 and 8.4 per cent by 2040.

The sultanate has also announced the introduction of personal income tax starting in 2028, with a 5 per cent rate of tax on annual income exceeding 42,000 Omani rials ($109,134). Muscat also unveiled a golden visa programme in August to attract more foreign investment into the country.

It also has plans to build a new economic area centred on developing its artificial intelligence capabilities, as it aims to accelerate its technology sector to strengthen its economy.

Last month, S&P Global Ratings boosted the economic growth forecast for Oman to 3.5 per cent on the back of favourable trade logistics amid the Iran war. The outlook is more than double the previous 1.6 per cent real GDP growth estimate for the sultanate. It is also higher than the 2.3 per cent growth posted by Oman last year.

headline: MEP Raphael Glucksmann wins centre-left primary to run for French presidency
summary: Raphael Glucksmann, a pro-Ukraine defender of liberal democracy, has won a centre-left presidential primary, paving the way for him to run next year in the race to succeed President French Emmanuel Macron.Mr Glucksmann won with 66 per cent of the vote. He will now seek to unify the left in the hope of winning next year's election in which far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite.“We are going to put an end to the psychological, cultural, political and ideological hegemony of brutes over the French left,” Mr Glucksmann, 46, told radio France Inter on Monday. “Finally, we have a democratic left that is regaining momentum and can win the presidential election.”Mr Glucksmann is co-president of centre-left political party Place Publique. He has been a member of the European Parliament since 2019 and is a prominent supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and of the Uighur minority in China.His campaign has highlighted the role of his partner, Lebanese-French journalist Lea Salame, who has had to step back from presenting the evening news on national broadcaster France 2 to avoid accusations of any conflict of interest. Ms Salame, the daughter of prominent Lebanese diplomat Ghassan Salame, will continue to anchor a weekly non-political talk show.“Thinking of Lea Salame,” Valerie Trierweiler, a journalist and former partner of former socialist president Francois Hollande, wrote on X immediately after the announcement of Mr Glucksmann's victory late on Sunday. Uphill battleMr Glucksmann faces an uphill battle to be elected, with recent polls projecting Ms Le Pen to win more than 30 per cent of the vote, and hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon and centre-right former prime minister Edouard Philippe trailing at around 15 per cent. Mr Glucksmann is sitting at about 9 per cent.The first round of the election takes place in April 2027.Divisions on the left are viewed as the main obstacle to defeating Ms Le Pen's far-right political party, the National Rally, which has never governed in France. Founded by her father Jean-Marie Le Pen and Nazi sympathisers in the 1970s, its popularity has skyrocketed in recent years as the party has campaigned to demonstrate more moderate views.The centre has so far struggled to make its voice heard in the presidential campaign. Mr Glucksmann has rejected the possibility of an alliance with Mr Melenchon. A controversial topic of the left's campaign has been the Gaza war. Mr Melenchon describes Israel's military campaign as genocide, while Mr Glucksmann uses expressions such as “war crimes” and “crimes against humanity”. His critics have attempted to portray him as holding similar views to the sitting president, Mr Macron, who has used comparable rhetoric on the Israel-Palestine conflict, while also remaining staunchly pro-Ukraine. However, Mr Glucksmann has distanced himself from Mr Macron's pro-business policies by championing measures such as increasing taxation on inheritance. In power since 2017, Mr Macron cannot run again next year. Since losing a majority in parliament last year after a snap election, Mr Macron's government has struggled to implement new policies and has had to freeze what many regard as much-needed pension reforms.Many residential candidates, such as Mr Philippe, have distanced themselves from Mr Macron's legacy as France struggles with a debt crisis, social unrest and nationwide school protests.
body_text:
Raphael Glucksmann, a pro-Ukraine defender of liberal democracy, has won a centre-left presidential primary, paving the way for him to run next year in the race to succeed President French Emmanuel Macron.

Mr Glucksmann won with 66 per cent of the vote. He will now seek to unify the left in the hope of winning next year's election in which far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favourite.

“We are going to put an end to the psychological, cultural, political and ideological hegemony of brutes over the French left,” Mr Glucksmann, 46, told radio France Inter on Monday. “Finally, we have a democratic left that is regaining momentum and can win the presidential election.”

French government offers olive branch to student protest movement

Mr Glucksmann is co-president of centre-left political party Place Publique. He has been a member of the European Parliament since 2019 and is a prominent supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and of the Uighur minority in China.

His campaign has highlighted the role of his partner, Lebanese-French journalist Lea Salame, who has had to step back from presenting the evening news on national broadcaster France 2 to avoid accusations of any conflict of interest.

Ms Salame, the daughter of prominent Lebanese diplomat Ghassan Salame, will continue to anchor a weekly non-political talk show.

“Thinking of Lea Salame,” Valerie Trierweiler, a journalist and former partner of former socialist president Francois Hollande, wrote on X immediately after the announcement of Mr Glucksmann's victory late on Sunday.

Mr Glucksmann faces an uphill battle to be elected, with recent polls projecting Ms Le Pen to win more than 30 per cent of the vote, and hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon and centre-right former prime minister Edouard Philippe trailing at around 15 per cent. Mr Glucksmann is sitting at about 9 per cent.

The first round of the election takes place in April 2027.

Divisions on the left are viewed as the main obstacle to defeating Ms Le Pen's far-right political party, the National Rally, which has never governed in France.

Founded by her father Jean-Marie Le Pen and Nazi sympathisers in the 1970s, its popularity has skyrocketed in recent years as the party has campaigned to demonstrate more moderate views.

The centre has so far struggled to make its voice heard in the presidential campaign. Mr Glucksmann has rejected the possibility of an alliance with Mr Melenchon.

A controversial topic of the left's campaign has been the Gaza war. Mr Melenchon describes Israel's military campaign as genocide, while Mr Glucksmann uses expressions such as “war crimes” and “crimes against humanity”.

His critics have attempted to portray him as holding similar views to the sitting president, Mr Macron, who has used comparable rhetoric on the Israel-Palestine conflict, while also remaining staunchly pro-Ukraine.

However, Mr Glucksmann has distanced himself from Mr Macron's pro-business policies by championing measures such as increasing taxation on inheritance.

In power since 2017, Mr Macron cannot run again next year. Since losing a majority in parliament last year after a snap election, Mr Macron's government has struggled to implement new policies and has had to freeze what many regard as much-needed pension reforms.

Many residential candidates, such as Mr Philippe, have distanced themselves from Mr Macron's legacy as France struggles with a debt crisis, social unrest and nationwide school protests.

headline: Iran says it will reply to US response on Hormuz proposal once review over
summary: DUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
body_text:
DUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.

Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

After a June interim ceasefire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a US response. But the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying on Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations.

A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.

Regarding the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, an Iranian ally, Baghaei reiterated Tehran's openness to help resolve the crisis through dialogue.

"The issue of Yemen should have been resolved a long time ago with the (UN) roadmap and we had said we would support any agreement reached by Yemenis and Saudis [...] Our request is that this situation be resolved through dialogue."

(Reporting by Dubai NewsroomEditing by Gareth Jones, Aidan Lewis)
