headline: EU sanctions against Russia show their limitations — newspaper
summary: According to the report, TAV Airports continues to handle Ural Airlines flights at Antalya Airport in Turkey through a joint venture with the German company Fraport, despite sanctions imposed by Brussels in June 2024
body_text:
LONDON, October 12. /TASS/. EU sanctions against Russia have shown limited effectiveness, the Financial Times reported, citing the continued handling of Ural Airlines flights by Aeroports de Paris (ADP) as an example.

According to the newspaper, TAV Airports, a subsidiary of the French government-controlled operator ADP, continues to handle Ural Airlines flights at Antalya Airport in Turkey through a joint venture with the German company Fraport, despite sanctions imposed by Brussels in June 2024.

The Financial Times noted that as of September 21, the airport’s online departure board listed at least 54 Ural Airlines flights to Moscow and Volgograd.

ADP stated that it has no influence over airlines’ decisions in Antalya, as these decisions are made exclusively by the Turkish authorities. The company added that, when a sanctioned carrier operates flights to Antalya, TAV provides "only the minimum level of services as required by local regulations and governmental contractual obligations."

headline: EU adopts nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military industry
summary: Foreign policy chief describes decision as 'single largest expansion' of bloc's sanctions list since Ukraine war began in 2022
body_text:
EU foreign ministers have adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, the bloc's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced Monday.

In a statement through US social media company X, Kallas described the move as the "single largest expansion" of the EU's sanctions list since the war in Ukraine began in February 2022.

"More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles. We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she said.

Separately, the EU Council announced that it had decided to extend its sanctions framework targeting the proliferation and use of chemical weapons for five years, until Oct. 30, 2031.

The council also extended the validity of individual sanctions listings under the framework for one year, until Oct. 30, 2027.

According to the statement, the restrictive measures currently apply to 31 individuals and six entities.

Those listed are subject to asset freezes, while EU citizens and companies are prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to them, directly or indirectly.

The individuals listed are also subject to travel bans to the EU.

headline: NATO 'intentionally ambiguous' on what could trigger Article 5 — commander
summary: According to Alexus Grynkewich, the alliance could also invoke "other articles" if needed
body_text:
BRUSSELS, October 12. /TASS/. NATO deliberately preserves uncertainty about what could lead to invoking Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for collective defense in case of an attack on a member state, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich said.

"We are intentionally ambiguous about what would cause Article 5 to be triggered," he told Poland’s TVP World in an interview.

According to Grynkewich, the alliance could also invoke "other articles" if needed, including Article 4, which calls for consultations within the NATO Council if a member state believes its security is under threat.

The general pointed out that Article 4 had been invoked "zero times" even during the Cold War. "Allies consulted and dealt with the issue without any formal mechanism. And I think that that’s a model of just staying calm, carrying on and working our way through this," he added.

Earlier, Bloomberg reported that "NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defense technologies like drones and AI into traditional power." The document, called "Theory of Victory," will be presented by Grynkewich on October 12. Sources told Bloomberg that the goal is to clarify how the alliance would handle a possible incursion into NATO territory. Grynkewich’s spokesman declined to discuss details of the plan, emphasizing that the alliance was "purely defensive."

According to the Bloomberg report, if NATO was attacked, "it would block an incursion with a mix of land forces and other assets from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a concept relying on low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting." "After gaining freedom of maneuver, it would seek to destroy enemy command and control" with the goal of defeating enemy forces "quickly and overwhelmingly," the news agency added.

headline: 24 S. Koreans on tourist visas nabbed in Nepal over religious program
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- Twenty-four South Koreans have been arrested in Nepal...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- Twenty-four South Koreans have been arrested in Nepal for participating in a religious program while visiting the country on tourist visas, local media reported Monday.

According to Nepalese online news outlet Ratopati, the arrests were recently made after they took part in the religious training program at New Covenant College, a Christian educational institution in the Morang district of Koshi province in eastern Nepal.

New Covenant College operates with support from a South Korea-based Christian missionary organization and provides religious studies and education, according to local reports.

Nepalese police reportedly arrested the South Koreans after determining that some of their activities may have violated the terms of their tourist visas.

Foreign nationals entering Nepal on tourist visas are not permitted to engage in religious education or missionary activities.

Seoul's foreign ministry said it was aware of the arrests and had been in close contact with Nepalese authorities through the South Korean Embassy in Nepal since learning of the incident.

The ministry said it could not disclose further details to protect the individuals' privacy and because the Nepalese authorities' investigation was ongoing.

headline: 🔴 Americans Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel Prize in Economics
body_text:
The 2026 Nobel economics prize has been awarded to US economists ⁠Robert Hall ​and Michael Woodford, the Royal Swedish Academy of ‌Sciences said on Monday.

Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 11:54Modified: 12/10/2026 - 12:03

⁠Robert Hall ​and Michael Woodford on Monday won ​the 2026 Nobel economics prize for their work into how monetary and fiscal policy can help stabilise fluctuations in the economy.

The pair were recognised "for microeconomic foundations of ​macroeconomic ‌stabilisation", ⁠the Royal Swedish Academy of ‌Sciences said on Monday.

The ⁠prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank ​Prize in ‌Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is ‌the final prize to ​be given out this year and is worth ​12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 ​million).

The economics ⁠prize, first awarded in 1969, is not one of the original five awards created in the ​1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred ‌Nobel, but was established by Sweden's central bank.

The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three ‌women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on ​how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

headline: Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford win Nobel Prize for Economics 2026
body_text:
The Nobel Prize in Economics has been awarded to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm announced the names of the two American economists.

According to John Hassler, chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, “The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world.”

BREAKING NEWS The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has decided to award the 2026 Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford “for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.”

#NobelPrize https://t.co/2i7ktB1Q2b

— The Nobel Prize (@NobelPrize) October 12, 2026

Hassler added, “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”

The Nobel Prize in Economics was earlier known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. Last week, the Nobel honour was announced in physics, chemistry, peace, medicine, and literature.

headline: Israeli strike kills two people in Gaza, medics say
summary: CAIRO, Oct 12 (Reuters) - An Israeli strike killed at least two Palestinians in the southern Gaza Strip on Monday, health officials said.The Israeli military said it targeted a militant in the area, without giving further information.Late on Sunday, an Israeli airstrike hit a tent in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, killing three people, medics said. The Israeli military told Reuters on Monday they struck militants in the area.
body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 12 (Reuters) - An Israeli strike killed at least two Palestinians in the southern Gaza Strip on Monday, health officials said.

The Israeli military said it targeted a militant in the area, without giving further information.

Late on Sunday, an Israeli airstrike hit a tent in the Mawasi area of Khan Younis in southern Gaza, killing three people, medics said. The Israeli military told Reuters on Monday they struck militants in the area.

Israel, which says Hamas has been rearming and launching attacks in violation of a ceasefire, has stepped up strikes on the group in recent weeks.

Hamas has denied trying to carry out attacks or rebuild its arsenal and accuses Israel of undermining the Gaza peace deal.

Last year's US-brokered Gaza ceasefire calls for the eventual reconstruction of the territory. But little progress has been made towards implementing a deal to end the conflict that includes terms for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw its troops.

Gaza health officials have said at least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the October 2025 ceasefire. Israel says four of its soldiers have been killed by militants in Gaza over the same period.

(Reporting by Nidal al-Mughrabi; Editing by Andrew Heavens and Ros Russell)

headline: Press review: Russia-US diesel deal changes Ukraine game and Riyadh airport attack fallout
summary: Top stories from the Russian press on Monday, October 12th
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. The Russia-US diesel deal changes the landscape of the Ukraine conflict; Saudi Arabia weighs a response after Houthis attack airport in Riyadh; and Slovakia will ask the European Commission to allow it to import fuel from Russia regardless of the planned ban. These stories topped Monday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.

The latest telephone conversation between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump has significantly altered the situation around Ukraine, with a deal reportedly struck between the two leaders on supplies of Russian diesel to the US. What's more, Washington has temporarily eased restrictions on Russian fuel and increased pressure on Kiev to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries. However, some believe European countries may try to use Ukraine to prevent the new Russian-US agreements from being implemented. Meanwhile, experts believe the deal itself is primarily a political play because the stated volumes of fuel are not large enough to have a noticeable impact on the American market.

The agreement on diesel fuel is the first tangible result of renewed direct contact between Moscow and Washington, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik told Izvestia. According to him, Russia would like to develop economic ties with the US independent of the Ukrainian conflict. "This is a significant step toward each other, which suggests that this area of cooperation can expand to other issues without the Ukrainian conflict serving as this giant obstacle to the development of Russia-US relations," the diplomat noted.

This deal also served as a signal to Kiev after Trump had repeatedly urged Ukraine not to attack Russian fuel infrastructure, Konstantin Sukhoverkhov, a program manager at the Russian International Affairs Council, pointed out. According to him, Washington might have viewed Kiev's refusal to heed these requests as a disregard for a country that continues to support Ukraine. Trump, for his part, demonstrated that he is capable of negotiating directly with Moscow, if necessary, without waiting for a change in Kiev’s position.

"We are witnessing a fundamentally new situation: this is the most significant positive development in US-Russia relations since the Anchorage summit and, at the same time, the deepest crisis in US-Ukraine relations since February 2025," Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti. Until now, the US had stated that any practical cooperation with Russia would be possible only after at least a ceasefire in Ukraine. Now, however, the position has changed: the diesel deal is not contingent on a truce in any way, the analyst emphasized.

Experts believe that Russian diesel fuel will not be sufficient to make up for the global shortfall of petroleum products. According to the most conservative estimates, global demand for diesel fuel exceeds 58 million metric tons per month, excluding maritime shipments, Open Oil Market CEO Sergey Tereshkin noted. However, the expert pointed out that the impact of the deal should not be underestimated. Analysts believe that Russian diesel shipments will help stabilize global prices in the short term, particularly in the US and the EU.

On October 11, the Saudi authorities suspended operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh indefinitely, immediately following the deadliest airstrike on the facility since the start of the Middle East crisis earlier this year. According to media reports, missiles struck Terminals 3 and 4, causing serious damage to the airport and prompting the collapse of part of the roof onto people inside. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation reported that 12 people were killed and 309 civilians were injured. While it's widely believed that the Houthis of Yemen’s Ansar Allah rebel group were behind the attack, they have not yet officially claimed responsibility.

Ivan Bocharov, program manager at the Russian International Affairs Council, told Vedomosti that it won't be easy for the Saudis to claim any kind of military victory over the Houthis. According to him, this would require establishing Saudi control over enemy territory, which would precipitate a costly guerrilla war. Moreover, today’s methods of warfare, the international situation, and the threats differ from those of the previous stage of the crisis. "It is easier to negotiate with Ansar Allah than to defeat them. Yemen is an extremely fragmented country, and unifying it by military means is difficult," the Middle East expert emphasized.

Saudi Arabia will most likely intensify its bombing campaign in Yemen and attempt to directly involve the US in the military operation against the Houthis, Yury Lyamin, a senior researcher at the Center for Analysis of Strategies and Technologies, noted. However, the Americans are doing everything they can to avoid that prospect, especially in the run-up to the midterm elections. "The signatories to the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will likely limit themselves to sending an insignificant number of specialists to the country to bolster its air defense. However, Pakistan and Turkey do not have sufficient resources of their own for this," the expert stressed.

Bocharov did not rule out the possibility of the Saudis carrying out a ground invasion in Yemen. Should they do that, though, the Saudi army risks getting bogged down there for an indefinite period, the analyst warned. "Riyadh is theoretically ready for talks, but the current escalation is a consequence of accumulated regional problems. The conditions for dialogue are not yet ripe," he pointed out.

The attack on the Riyadh airport damages Saudi Arabia’s image as a safe place to live and conduct international business, expert Nikolay Sukhov emphasized, and it is especially damaging for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud, the de facto head of Saudi Arabia. "The Houthis are well aware of this vulnerability. All they need to do is periodically demonstrate their ability to disrupt airport, energy facility, and transport network operations, thereby raising the economic and political cost of continuing the war," the expert stressed.

Despite a general ban on importing gas from Russia, Slovakia plans to begin talks with the European Commission to continue doing just that. Earlier, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen confirmed that EU countries will be expected to halt Russian gas purchases by the end of 2027. However, reports indicate the EU is facing a record fuel shortage which could hit as early as this winter. Experts note that landlocked countries like Hungary and Slovakia may suffer more than others.

Slovakia will request a transition period from the European Commission while it continues receiving fuel supplies from Russia, National Council Deputy Speaker Tibor Gaspar told Izvestia. According to him, "the decision to completely halt imports of Russian gas is not in the interests of either Slovakia or the EU as a whole." "We have filed a lawsuit with the EU Court of Justice and intend to use all available legal means to protect Slovakia’s energy security. At the same time, we will negotiate with the European Commission on the possibility of securing a sufficient transition period to continue Russian gas supplies, if necessary," the politician noted.

In light of potential force majeure situations, Brussels will likely extend Slovakia’s authorization to purchase Russian gas, Mikhail Vedernikov, a leading researcher at the Institute of Europe under the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized. With parliamentary elections scheduled for next year, it is crucial for the country’s authorities to ensure uninterrupted gas supplies. The country has already secured the necessary reserves for the coming winter thanks to its contract with Russia's Gazprom, Slovak Economy Minister Denisa Sakova pointed out.

Moreover, the country has no access to the sea, which means it will have to bring LNG in from Croatia, which will cost more, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund, stressed. According to the expert, a 20-30% increase in gas prices could create significant economic problems for Bratislava. The Slovak authorities are already spending large sums to compensate for rising gas and electricity rates for the population. More than 400 million euros have been allocated for this purpose alone this year.

The energy crisis in Europe will only get worse if the continent moves to completely reject Russian resources, Yushkov emphasized. Brussels' concern, however, is not to protect European businesses and citizens, but to hurt Russia economically. Nevertheless, growing resistance to such a policy indicates that Europe will not be able to completely abandon Russian energy resources.

The South Korean authorities hope to launch regular commercial voyages along the Northern Sea Route. A final decision will be made after reviewing the results of a soon-to-be-completed maiden voyage by a South Korean container ship that delivered goods to Europe in August. The Northern Sea Route is 35% shorter than the traditional route through the Suez Canal, reducing travel time and fuel costs. Diversifying shipping routes is also important given the escalating conflict in the Middle East. However, if Seoul decides to actively use the Northern Sea Route, it risks facing pressure and sanctions from the US, and it will also need to invest heavily in the construction of high-level ice-class vessels.

Seoul has organized a pilot commercial voyage to Europe via the Northern Sea Route and is currently awaiting its completion. The vessel set sail on August 22 and will return to the port of Busan on October 12, after which a decision may be made to launch regular voyages, South Korean Ambassador to Moscow Lee Sok-bae told Izvestia. "This project is extremely important. Most likely, our relevant ministries and agencies will conduct a comprehensive study based on the results of this maiden voyage, and then we will consider the possibility of organizing regular service in the medium and long term," he said.

Seoul’s interest in the Northern Sea Route has intensified following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East, Alexander Zhebin, a leading researcher at the Center for Korean Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences, pointed out. In particular, regular Houthi attacks in the Red Sea have made the Suez Canal route high-risk and sharply increased ship insurance costs. Enter Europe, one of Seoul’s main trading partners. According to the European Commission, trade between the EU and South Korea totaled 124 billion euros in 2025.

However, to establish regular voyages along the Northern Sea Route, South Korea must address several challenges. The US may apply various forms of pressure to Seoul, Zhebin noted. At the same time, the South Korean authorities will argue that their actions are driven by vital economic necessity in their dialogue with the Americans. Therefore, it remains unclear whether this voyage will mark the beginning of a long-term project or remain a one-time endeavor, Konstantin Asmolov, a leading researcher at the Center for Korean Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.

According to Zhebin, Seoul’s intentions can only be judged once South Korea begins investing heavily in the Northern Sea Route's infrastructure rather than merely using it. He predicts that in the future, this country could indeed become a regular user of the Northern Sea Route. If current climate trends continue, year-round shipping on the Northern Sea Route could become a reality, Asmolov noted. Such a scenario would radically transform the global freight transport system.

On October 10, India's opposition parties held multi-day protests that resulted in the detention of over 5,000 people. The rallies and marches were organized by the recently formed Cockroach Janta Party youth movement and the Indian National Developmental Inclusive Alliance (INDIA), a coalition of opposition parties including the country’s oldest party, the Indian National Congress, led by Rahul Gandhi. The metro in New Delhi was shut down amid the protests, and opposition demonstrations also took place in India’s largest city, Mumbai.

Street protests are quite common in India, Yevgenia Zeegofer, a junior research fellow at the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Vedomosti. For now, the Indian authorities are trying to contain the scale and intensity of the protests by using force. However, it is likely that people will take to the streets again. The protests are currently directed against India’s Election Commission reforms. The opposition and protesters claim that many have been deprived of their right to vote, while the government maintains that it has mainly removed deceased individuals from the voter rolls. Overall, however, according to Zeegofer, the protests draw attention to the problems facing Indian youth and the issues that concern this generation. They are unlikely to topple the Narendra Modi government, but they could cause it trouble, as tensions will persist, the expert emphasized.

Ilya Spektor, a senior research fellow at the Institute of Asian and African Studies, believes that the activities of the young protesters and the opposition are unlikely to pose any real serious problems for the Modi government, which has already weathered many serious protests.

In turn, Tatyana Shaumyan, head of the Center for Indian Studies under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta that these protests are organic, not the result of external influence. "Of course, India has an adversary on the international stage. That is Pakistan. There are terrorist groups that have committed crimes in India. But I don’t think any external force is provoking the current protests. As for the Cockroach Janta Party, it is more of a short-lived phenomenon. This party has no serious program for reforming the country. Demonstrations take place in all democratic countries and do not always lead to the fall of governments. The government in India is strong. It will undoubtedly cope with the current problems," she stressed.

headline: Iran says it will reply to US response on Hormuz proposal once review over
summary: DUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
body_text:
DUBAI, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Iran is still reviewing a US response to its proposal regarding the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and will reply to Washington via intermediaries when the review is over, foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.

Baghaei also told a press conference that Iran continues to exchange messages via intermediaries, without elaborating. Qatar and Pakistan, among others, have acted as mediators in efforts to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

After a June interim ceasefire crumbled and on-off strikes resumed, Iran presented its proposal in mid-September and later confirmed receipt of a US response. But the process has since stalled, with Iran’s security chief saying on Sunday that Washington’s response did not sufficiently address Tehran’s seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to negotiations.

A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.

Regarding the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis, an Iranian ally, Baghaei reiterated Tehran's openness to help resolve the crisis through dialogue.

"The issue of Yemen should have been resolved a long time ago with the (UN) roadmap and we had said we would support any agreement reached by Yemenis and Saudis [...] Our request is that this situation be resolved through dialogue."

(Reporting by Dubai NewsroomEditing by Gareth Jones, Aidan Lewis)

headline: EU sanctions against Russia show their limitations — newspaper
summary: According to the report, TAV Airports continues to handle Ural Airlines flights at Antalya Airport in Turkey through a joint venture with the German company Fraport, despite sanctions imposed by Brussels in June 2024
body_text:
LONDON, October 12. /TASS/. EU sanctions against Russia have shown limited effectiveness, the Financial Times reported, citing the continued handling of Ural Airlines flights by Aeroports de Paris (ADP) as an example.

According to the newspaper, TAV Airports, a subsidiary of the French government-controlled operator ADP, continues to handle Ural Airlines flights at Antalya Airport in Turkey through a joint venture with the German company Fraport, despite sanctions imposed by Brussels in June 2024.

The Financial Times noted that as of September 21, the airport’s online departure board listed at least 54 Ural Airlines flights to Moscow and Volgograd.

ADP stated that it has no influence over airlines’ decisions in Antalya, as these decisions are made exclusively by the Turkish authorities. The company added that, when a sanctioned carrier operates flights to Antalya, TAV provides "only the minimum level of services as required by local regulations and governmental contractual obligations."

headline: EU adopts nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military industry
summary: Foreign policy chief describes decision as 'single largest expansion' of bloc's sanctions list since Ukraine war began in 2022
body_text:
EU foreign ministers have adopted nearly 1,600 new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex, the bloc's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced Monday.

In a statement through US social media company X, Kallas described the move as the "single largest expansion" of the EU's sanctions list since the war in Ukraine began in February 2022.

"More than half are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles. We are making it significantly harder, slower and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians," she said.

Separately, the EU Council announced that it had decided to extend its sanctions framework targeting the proliferation and use of chemical weapons for five years, until Oct. 30, 2031.

The council also extended the validity of individual sanctions listings under the framework for one year, until Oct. 30, 2027.

According to the statement, the restrictive measures currently apply to 31 individuals and six entities.

Those listed are subject to asset freezes, while EU citizens and companies are prohibited from making funds or economic resources available to them, directly or indirectly.

The individuals listed are also subject to travel bans to the EU.

headline: NATO 'intentionally ambiguous' on what could trigger Article 5 — commander
summary: According to Alexus Grynkewich, the alliance could also invoke "other articles" if needed
body_text:
BRUSSELS, October 12. /TASS/. NATO deliberately preserves uncertainty about what could lead to invoking Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, which provides for collective defense in case of an attack on a member state, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich said.

"We are intentionally ambiguous about what would cause Article 5 to be triggered," he told Poland’s TVP World in an interview.

According to Grynkewich, the alliance could also invoke "other articles" if needed, including Article 4, which calls for consultations within the NATO Council if a member state believes its security is under threat.

The general pointed out that Article 4 had been invoked "zero times" even during the Cold War. "Allies consulted and dealt with the issue without any formal mechanism. And I think that that’s a model of just staying calm, carrying on and working our way through this," he added.

Earlier, Bloomberg reported that "NATO’s top military commander is working on a strategy for achieving a quick victory against a Russian attack on its eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defense technologies like drones and AI into traditional power." The document, called "Theory of Victory," will be presented by Grynkewich on October 12. Sources told Bloomberg that the goal is to clarify how the alliance would handle a possible incursion into NATO territory. Grynkewich’s spokesman declined to discuss details of the plan, emphasizing that the alliance was "purely defensive."

According to the Bloomberg report, if NATO was attacked, "it would block an incursion with a mix of land forces and other assets from NATO’s Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, a concept relying on low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting." "After gaining freedom of maneuver, it would seek to destroy enemy command and control" with the goal of defeating enemy forces "quickly and overwhelmingly," the news agency added.

headline: 24 S. Koreans on tourist visas nabbed in Nepal over religious program
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- Twenty-four South Koreans have been arrested in Nepal...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- Twenty-four South Koreans have been arrested in Nepal for participating in a religious program while visiting the country on tourist visas, local media reported Monday.

According to Nepalese online news outlet Ratopati, the arrests were recently made after they took part in the religious training program at New Covenant College, a Christian educational institution in the Morang district of Koshi province in eastern Nepal.

New Covenant College operates with support from a South Korea-based Christian missionary organization and provides religious studies and education, according to local reports.

Nepalese police reportedly arrested the South Koreans after determining that some of their activities may have violated the terms of their tourist visas.

Foreign nationals entering Nepal on tourist visas are not permitted to engage in religious education or missionary activities.

Seoul's foreign ministry said it was aware of the arrests and had been in close contact with Nepalese authorities through the South Korean Embassy in Nepal since learning of the incident.

The ministry said it could not disclose further details to protect the individuals' privacy and because the Nepalese authorities' investigation was ongoing.

headline: Americans Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize for work on stabilisation
summary: STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.The prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final prize to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).
body_text:
STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.

The prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final prize to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

The two laureates developed new macroeconomic models that improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy, enabling well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures that can reduce the intensity of damaging swings in the economy.

"The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume."

The economics prize, first awarded in 1969, is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden's central bank.

The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.

Analysis by the Institute for Scientific Information, part of Clarivate, had picked researchers working on monetary policy, the economics of information technology and evolutionary economic theory as possible recipients.

Last year's winners, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on "creative destruction" and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.

The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last week.

($1 = 10.0028 Swedish crowns)

(Reporting by Simon Johnson, Niklas Pollard, Johan Ahlander and Marie Mannes in Stockholm, Terje Solsvik in Oslo, Mark John in London; Editing by Alex Richardson and Toby Chopra)

headline: US economists Hall, Woodford win 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics
summary: Hall and Woodford's approach focuses on building models on microeconomic foundations rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables
body_text:
Anadolu Ajansı © 2026

US economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics during a news conference.

Hall and Woodford demonstrated how to reconstruct economic models to revitalize stabilization policies.

Their approach focuses on building models on microeconomic foundations rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables like inflation, production and consumption.

This method provides a deeper understanding of how the combined actions of individual households and businesses affect the overall economy.

Born in the US state of California in 1943, Hall continues his work as an economics professor at Stanford University.

Woodford, born in the US state of Massachusetts in 1955, serves as an economics professor at Columbia University.

headline: Africa: UN Human Rights Chief Hails Award of Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay
summary: [allAfrica] Geneva -- United Nations Human Rights Chief Volker Türk spoke with pride on Friday for global human rights when he ''warmly'' congratulated South African Navi Pillay for winning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for those who fight for the rights of others.
body_text:
Geneva — United Nations Human Rights Chief Volker Türk spoke with pride on Friday for global human rights when he “warmly” congratulated South African Navi Pillay for winning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for those who fight for the rights of others.

“This is a proud moment for the global human rights movement. I warmly congratulate Navi. To say it is well-deserved is an understatement,” Türk, the high commissioner for Human Rights, told journalists at the UN in Geneva.

“At a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power, this award is particularly poignant,” said the UN Human Rights chief.

He noted that the award goes to people around the world who dedicate their lives to defending human rights, “often at great risk to their security.”

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Pillay is a South African jurist who served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014.

She is a South African of Tamil origin and was the first black woman judge of the High Court of South Africa.

Pillay has also served as a judge of the International Criminal Court and president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

She was born and raised in Durban, South Africa’s third-largest city, where she later attended the University of Natal, receiving her Bachelor of Arts in 1963 and her Bachelor of Law in 1965.

“This award to Navi Pillay is a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything - to peace, security and prosperity,” said Türk.

“She embodies international law – having served in many functions, both in South Africa and internationally as a judge of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the International Criminal Court, and the now International Court of Justice.”

During her 28 years as a lawyer in South Africa, including the apartheid era, she defended anti-apartheid activists from the African National Congress, the Unity Movement, the Black Consciousness Movement, and the Azapo.

“On behalf of all her colleagues at the UN Human Rights Office, thank yo,u Navi. You continue to inspire us and millions of others. We will prevail,” said Türk.

The Nobel Peace Prize is worth 12 million Swedish crowns, around $1.2 million.

The Nobel Committee will present it in Oslo on December 10, 2026, the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who established the awards.

headline: Qatar’s energy minister: ‘Keep energy above politics’, as Doha and Riyadh sign cooperation MoU
summary: Qatar and Saudi Arabia sign an energy MoU, as Al-Kaabi urges the world to keep energy “above politics”. Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy President and CEO…
body_text:
Qatar and Saudi Arabia sign an energy MoU, as Al-Kaabi urges the world to keep energy “above politics”.

Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi called for a new world energy order in which energy is kept above politics and never made a victim or target of conflict, in remarks at the 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial Meeting in Riyadh on Sunday.

“Energy security must unite us, not divide us; it must be protected, not weaponised,” he said, according to a QatarEnergy statement.

On the sidelines of the meeting, Qatar and Saudi Arabia signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) laying the framework for joint cooperation across the energy industry. Al-Kaabi signed for Qatar, and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud signed for the kingdom.

The MoU covers oil and gas and their derivatives, refining, petrochemicals, electricity, clean hydrogen, renewable energy, and energy efficiency and storage. It also addresses emission reduction and climate change mitigation technologies, including carbon capture, transport, reuse and storage, and coordination on energy, sustainability and climate change in international initiatives and frameworks. It will take effect once legal procedures are completed in both countries.

In his address, Al-Kaabi said the conflict in the region has caused “by far, the world’s worst energy crisis,” affecting the flow of around 20% of the world’s hydrocarbon supplies. He said many energy assets across the region had been targeted, causing tens of billions of dollars in damage and severe volatility in global markets.

“If there is one lesson we have learned from the past few months, it is that energy security, as critical as it is to the global economy, remains highly vulnerable and inseparable from geopolitical security,” he said.

Al-Kaabi also pointed to the human cost, noting that a billion people still lack access to electricity and that about four billion depend on food produced using manufactured fertilisers. “The impact on all those lives should remind us of our shared responsibility to safeguard energy security, protect the free flow of energy, and keep energy above politics and conflicts,” he said.

He urged the forum to explore every avenue to protect energy infrastructure during conflict. “It is a real problem that energy infrastructure has become both an economic asset and a strategic military target,” he said.

He opened his remarks by expressing Qatar’s “unwavering solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its leadership and people during these times”.

“I offer my sincere condolences to the families of those killed in these horrible attacks and wish a speedy recovery to the injured,” he added.

The ministerial meeting was held under the theme “Energy Security – A Shared Responsibility: Market Fundamentals, Supply Chain Resilience, and the New Dynamics of Demand and Supply.”

It was opened by Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and attended by energy ministers, government representatives, industry leaders and international organisations. It forms part of Riyadh Energy Week, alongside the 25th WPC Energy Congress.

headline: 'Being allowed to leave does not erase injustice': Former Dubai resident leaves Iraq after years of detention

Mr Radwan has now also left Iraq.“I was an engineer,” said Mr Pether, speaking at a press conference on Monday. “I was an employee doing my job. I had a wife and children waiting for me at home. I was there because I made a choice to help a war-torn country rebuild. That followed a call from Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, calling for Mr Pether to be allowed to return home to his family.Since his release, Mr Pether had stayed either with friends or in hotels, with the cost of food and accommodation falling on him and his family.Health issuesDuring his detention, Mr Pether's health deteriorated, which led to the office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issuing a statement in June, highlighting the “particularly alarming” situation, which was compounded by a lack of access to specialist medical care and the psychological toll of his “prolonged detention and uncertainty”.Mr Pether said that “coming home today should never be mistaken for that injustice somehow having been corrected. It wasn't. Not even close. Coming home is not exoneration and being allowed to leave is not justice.“Our convictions have not been overturned. Neither of us has been exonerated. We were innocent when we were taken on April 7, 2021 and we remain innocent today.”Mr Pether said that when he was released from prison he was only hours from death, with his body shutting down, after months of critical illness and excruciating pain, only to find that he remained trapped in Iraq. “I didn't have my passport, visa or identity documents and I had no ability to move around freely or safely, leave the country or even go to a hospital,” said Mr Pether.“Travel bans prevented me from returning to my family and from accessing the medical treatment I desperately needed outside Iraq.”Mr Pether said he was forced to sign a waiver before being allowed to leave Iraq and return to his family.“I signed it because I wanted to go home. There was no choice. After more than five years, with my health deteriorating and my family waiting for me, there was no meaningful choice between signing a document and remaining trapped in Iraq,” he said.“So, I want to be very clear about something. I am incredibly grateful to be standing here. I am overwhelmed to finally be home. But gratitude for being home does not erase what happened to me for even one second. Freedom should never have been something that had to be bargained for.”He also spoke of the emotional impact felt by his family and praised his wife for her campaigning on his behalf.“My wife and my children have lived this every single day with me. Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try to bring me home,” said Mr Pether.“They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances no child should ever have to carry. A former Dubai resident detained in Iraq for more than five years said being allowed to return to his family shouldn't mask the injustice he was forced to endure.

Australian engineer Robert Pether, 50, was reunited with his family in Ireland on Monday after being allowed to leave Iraq having been sent to jail over a contract dispute involving his employer.

Mr Pether was released from prison last year but had to remain in Iraq because he was barred from leaving due to financial claims linked to the case.

Dubai resident leaves Iraq after being detained for five years

Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, both of whom lived in Dubai at the time, had travelled to Iraq for what they expected to be a routine business meeting but ended up being jailed in August 2021 and fined $12 million over a contract dispute between their employers and authorities in Baghdad. Mr Radwan has now also left Iraq.

“I was an engineer,” said Mr Pether, speaking at a press conference on Monday. “I was an employee doing my job. I had a wife and children waiting for me at home. I was there because I made a choice to help a war-torn country rebuild. I never came home.”

The travel ban Baghdad had imposed on Mr Pether and Mr Radwan led to the office of the US Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs to push for their release. That followed a call from Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, calling for Mr Pether to be allowed to return home to his family.

Since his release, Mr Pether had stayed either with friends or in hotels, with the cost of food and accommodation falling on him and his family.

During his detention, Mr Pether's health deteriorated, which led to the office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issuing a statement in June, highlighting the “particularly alarming” situation, which was compounded by a lack of access to specialist medical care and the psychological toll of his “prolonged detention and uncertainty”.

Mr Pether said that “coming home today should never be mistaken for that injustice somehow having been corrected. It wasn't. Not even close. Coming home is not exoneration and being allowed to leave is not justice.

“Our convictions have not been overturned. Neither of us has been exonerated. We were innocent when we were taken on April 7, 2021 and we remain innocent today.”

Mr Pether said that when he was released from prison he was only hours from death, with his body shutting down, after months of critical illness and excruciating pain, only to find that he remained trapped in Iraq.

“I didn't have my passport, visa or identity documents and I had no ability to move around freely or safely, leave the country or even go to a hospital,” said Mr Pether.

“Travel bans prevented me from returning to my family and from accessing the medical treatment I desperately needed outside Iraq.”

Mr Pether said he was forced to sign a waiver before being allowed to leave Iraq and return to his family.

“I signed it because I wanted to go home. There was no choice. After more than five years, with my health deteriorating and my family waiting for me, there was no meaningful choice between signing a document and remaining trapped in Iraq,” he said.

“So, I want to be very clear about something. I am incredibly grateful to be standing here. I am overwhelmed to finally be home. But gratitude for being home does not erase what happened to me for even one second. Freedom should never have been something that had to be bargained for.”

He also spoke of the emotional impact felt by his family and praised his wife for her campaigning on his behalf.

“My wife and my children have lived this every single day with me. Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try to bring me home,” said Mr Pether.

“They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances no child should ever have to carry. I am so thankful for my wife Desree, always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together, all while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her, too.”

Ms Wong released a statement on Monday morning. “The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government's decision to allow Robert Pether to leave Iraq today,” she said. “I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family.

“Mr Pether had been imprisoned in Iraq for more than four years and was later subject to travel restrictions that prevented him from leaving the country.

“I thank the Australian officials whose tireless work helped achieve this outcome, as well as the Irish authorities for their close co-operation throughout this process. I wish Mr Pether and his family all the very best as they reunite,” Ms Wong said.

body_text:
US President Donald Trump's declaration of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine has raised questions over its validity, after Moscow offered no confirmation about the truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement.

The move sent oil and diesel prices into decline early on Monday, but analysts cautioned that even a sustained halt to attacks on energy infrastructure would offer limited relief to global fuel markets, with much of Russia's refining capacity offline after months of Ukrainian drone strikes.

Brent fell 1.3 per cent to $103.35 a barrel in early trading, while West Texas Intermediate declined 1.4 per cent to $90.55 a barrel. ICE gas oil futures, a benchmark for diesel, dropped about 3 per cent.

Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'

The oil benchmarks pared losses by midday, with Brent trading 1.10 per cent higher at $105.87 a barrel by 1.55pm UAE time, while WTI was up 1.13 per cent at $92.89 a barrel.

“Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported a ceasefire but was awaiting details from Washington. A similar announcement by Mr Trump in September failed to produce a lasting halt to strikes.

“Only time will tell how durable it proves to be,” said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at Swiss bank UBS. “We have seen similar commitments in the past that ultimately failed to hold.”

The announcement follows a US Treasury decision on October 9 to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027, after Mr Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release additional fuel into global markets.

But the volumes are modest relative to the scale of the disruption. The proposed 300,000 tonnes for the rest of this month equates to about 100,000 barrels a day, Mr Staunovo said.

That “would only partially offset the decline in seaborne diesel exports, which in September were around 1.3 million barrels per day below the levels seen at the start of the year”, he said.

Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of energy geopolitics at the University of Oslo, said Washington's decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel for six months marked a significant shift in energy geopolitics that threatened to undermine western unity against Moscow.

He described the move as the clearest failure yet of efforts to isolate Russia through energy sanctions. “What remains unsaid regarding the guarantees that Russia had from the US for supplying diesel is far more important than the few details we know so far about the energy ceasefire,” Mr Sassi said.

Ukraine's response would also be a test of its relationship with Washington, potentially increasing pressure on the European Union to sustain support for Kyiv without US backing, he added.

Russia's capacity to deliver the additional fuel is also in doubt.

Its diesel exports fell from about 706,000 bpd in January to 47,000 bpd in August and almost nothing last month, according to Kpler data, as Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and curtailed fuel production.

Total Russian oil exports declined to about 6.8 million bpd in September from 8 million bpd in May. Shipments to India, Russia's biggest buyer, have more than halved since June to 1.2 million bpd, the data showed.

The drop highlights the difficulty of restoring Russian fuel supplies without first repairing damaged infrastructure, a process that could take months even if attacks cease.

S&P Global Commodity Insights said the announcement could weigh on diesel refining margins but only if Russian exports increase. “We see the immediate market impact as limited,” analysts James Bambino and Richard Joswick said.

Additional Russian shipments would cover only about 10 per cent of the global shortfall in diesel exports, assuming they represent new supply rather than cargoes diverted from existing buyers, S&P Global said.

About half of Russia's refining capacity is offline and repairs could take months, limiting the scope for a rapid recovery.

Any additional cargoes are likely to remain in the Atlantic Basin, potentially reaching the US East Coast or Brazil and freeing up US Gulf Coast supplies for Europe.

That could put downwards pressure on diesel margins in north-west Europe and the US but only “as long as a ceasefire holds”, the analysts said.

Even if Russian fuel exports recover, the broader oil market remains exposed to disruption in the Middle East, where the Iran war has restricted supplies and forced major changes to established shipping routes.

Crude has largely remained above $100 a barrel in recent weeks as attacks on infrastructure and shipping continue to threaten supplies from the Gulf.

Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85, saying Gulf supply disruption was likely to ease more slowly than previously expected. The bank estimates geopolitical tension is adding slightly more than $20 a barrel to prices and does not assume a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict.

“Potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the bank's analysts said.

headline: From confusion to conviction: A British official's visit to Luoyang
summary: How can an ancient city protect its historic sites while breathing new life into urban development? headline: Zelenskyy urges US to act to ensure Russia abides by 'energy ceasefire'
summary: Ukraine is ready to agree to a deal with Russia to halt attacks on each other’s energy supplies, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.Mr Zelenskyy was responding to US President Donald Trump’s announcement that there would be an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Speaking by video at the Warsaw Security Conference, the Ukrainian leader said he learnt about the proposed truce from the media, after Mr Trump made the announcement on his Truth Social platform on Sunday.“If the Americans need it, we are ready to sign these guarantees to make sure they can be trusted. It’s important that we all see this situation in the same way,” Mr Zelenskyy said.But he said Russian President Vladimir Putin “doesn’t read Truth Social” and that Ukraine continued to come under attack. Mr Zelenskyy added that “if Russia doesn’t agree to energy ceasefire, we will respond”.He urged ⁠Washington to step in to ensure that Moscow abided by the ⁠terms of the putative agreement."There were ​Russian ⁠violations ‌of the energy ceasefire announced ​by President Trump," he said. "We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take."This energy ceasefire, it ⁠can work, and it can ⁠become a major step towards ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and ​make sure Russians respect it."As Mr Trump made his announcement, large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water as repair crews struggled to restore power after Russian strikes. A power plant in Kharkiv, in the north-east, also came under attack.“All morning today, more and more Russian jet-powered Shaheds have continued to enter our skies over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities,” said Mr Zelenskyy, referring to Iranian-supplied drones used by Russia in the war. “We shoot down many of them and, if we didn’t, there would clearly be even more damage to our energy infrastructure.”Mr Zelenskyy ended his address by urging Ukraine's allies to dedicate their time to making sure the US gets "one clear message". "An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social,” he said. “We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together, Europe and the United States."At the weekend, Mr Zelenskyy held talks with key allies, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte.French President ​Emmanuel Macron ​said ​on Monday that ⁠he had not ⁠seen any ​signs in the past ⁠48 hours of Russia respecting an energy ceasefire."We can only reopen the debate on ​the energy ‌situation if there ⁠is real ​ceasefire which is ​respected ‌by both sides," Mr Macron said at the Paris ⁠Autoshow. "I have not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from ​the Russian side."Mr Burnham told Mr Zelenskyy that he recognised “the past 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine" and stressed his "complete solidarity” with Kyiv, according to a Downing Street readout of the call between the two leaders.The pair discussed the "importance of maintaining pressure on Russia” and Mr Burnham made it clear that the UK “would continue to strengthen its sanctions on Russia and take further action to constrain the Russian war machine”. Mr Carney’s office said he had spoken with Mr Zelenskyy about Mr Trump’s “diesel deal” with Russia, which aims to immediately release 300,000 tonnes of the fuel to global markets in an effort to curb rising costs. The Canadian leader said the agreement was in "direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe".Mr Zelenskyy has proposed a 60-day ceasefire to allow his country to hold ⁠presidential elections, but that was immediately rejected by Russia. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said his country wanted a long-term peace deal rather than a temporary ceasefire.

But he said Russian President Vladimir Putin “doesn’t read Truth Social” and that Ukraine continued to come under attack. Mr Zelenskyy added that “if Russia doesn’t agree to energy ceasefire, we will respond”.

He urged ⁠Washington to step in to ensure that Moscow abided by the ⁠terms of the putative agreement.

"There were ​Russian ⁠violations ‌of the energy ceasefire announced ​by President Trump," he said. "We are waiting for the details of the conditions between the Americans and Russians, and we are waiting to see one specific step the Americans are ready to take.

"This energy ceasefire, it ⁠can work, and it can ⁠become a major step towards ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and ​make sure Russians respect it."

As Mr Trump made his announcement, large parts of Kyiv were without electricity and water as repair crews struggled to restore power after Russian strikes. A power plant in Kharkiv, in the north-east, also came under attack.

“All morning today, more and more Russian jet-powered Shaheds have continued to enter our skies over Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities,” said Mr Zelenskyy, referring to Iranian-supplied drones used by Russia in the war. “We shoot down many of them and, if we didn’t, there would clearly be even more damage to our energy infrastructure.”

Mr Zelenskyy ended his address by urging Ukraine's allies to dedicate their time to making sure the US gets "one clear message". "An energy ceasefire and other steps to reduce escalation and guarantee security are truly needed here – in reality, not just on Truth Social,” he said.

“We need to end Russia's war. We need to guarantee security. We need to stand together, Europe and the United States."

At the weekend, Mr Zelenskyy held talks with key allies, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte.

French President ​Emmanuel Macron ​said ​on Monday that ⁠he had not ⁠seen any ​signs in the past ⁠48 hours of Russia respecting an energy ceasefire.

"We can only reopen the debate on ​the energy ‌situation if there ⁠is real ​ceasefire which is ​respected ‌by both sides," Mr Macron said at the Paris ⁠Autoshow. "I have not noted, over the last 48 hours, any energy ceasefire coming from ​the Russian side."

headline: Americans Hall and Woodford win Nobel economics prize for work on stabilisation
summary: STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.The prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final prize to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).
body_text:
STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize for "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences said on Monday.

The prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final prize to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

The two laureates developed new macroeconomic models that improved our ability to implement effective stabilisation policy, enabling well-timed fiscal and monetary policy measures that can reduce the intensity of damaging swings in the economy.

"The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume."

The economics prize, first awarded in 1969, is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden's central bank.

The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.

Analysis by the Institute for Scientific Information, part of Clarivate, had picked researchers working on monetary policy, the economics of information technology and evolutionary economic theory as possible recipients.

Last year's winners, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on "creative destruction" and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.

The Nobel prizes for medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace were announced last week.

($1 = 10.0028 Swedish crowns)

(Reporting by Simon Johnson, Niklas Pollard, Johan Ahlander and Marie Mannes in Stockholm, Terje Solsvik in Oslo, Mark John in London; Editing by Alex Richardson and Toby Chopra)

headline: US economists Hall, Woodford win 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics
summary: Hall and Woodford's approach focuses on building models on microeconomic foundations rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables
body_text:
Anadolu Ajansı © 2026

US economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics during a news conference.

Hall and Woodford demonstrated how to reconstruct economic models to revitalize stabilization policies.

Their approach focuses on building models on microeconomic foundations rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables like inflation, production and consumption.

This method provides a deeper understanding of how the combined actions of individual households and businesses affect the overall economy.

Born in the US state of California in 1943, Hall continues his work as an economics professor at Stanford University.

Woodford, born in the US state of Massachusetts in 1955, serves as an economics professor at Columbia University.

headline: Africa: UN Human Rights Chief Hails Award of Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay
summary: [allAfrica] Geneva -- United Nations Human Rights Chief Volker Türk spoke with pride on Friday for global human rights when he ''warmly'' congratulated South African Navi Pillay for winning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for those who fight for the rights of others.
body_text:
Geneva — United Nations Human Rights Chief Volker Türk spoke with pride on Friday for global human rights when he “warmly” congratulated South African Navi Pillay for winning the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for those who fight for the rights of others.

“This is a proud moment for the global human rights movement. I warmly congratulate Navi. To say it is well-deserved is an understatement,” Türk, the high commissioner for Human Rights, told journalists at the UN in Geneva.

“At a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power, this award is particularly poignant,” said the UN Human Rights chief.

He noted that the award goes to people around the world who dedicate their lives to defending human rights, “often at great risk to their security.”

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Pillay is a South African jurist who served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014.

She is a South African of Tamil origin and was the first black woman judge of the High Court of South Africa.

Pillay has also served as a judge of the International Criminal Court and president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda.

She was born and raised in Durban, South Africa’s third-largest city, where she later attended the University of Natal, receiving her Bachelor of Arts in 1963 and her Bachelor of Law in 1965.

“This award to Navi Pillay is a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything - to peace, security and prosperity,” said Türk.

“She embodies international law – having served in many functions, both in South Africa and internationally as a judge of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, the International Criminal Court, and the now International Court of Justice.”

During her 28 years as a lawyer in South Africa, including the apartheid era, she defended anti-apartheid activists from the African National Congress, the Unity Movement, the Black Consciousness Movement, and the Azapo.

“On behalf of all her colleagues at the UN Human Rights Office, thank yo,u Navi. You continue to inspire us and millions of others. We will prevail,” said Türk.

The Nobel Peace Prize is worth 12 million Swedish crowns, around $1.2 million.

The Nobel Committee will present it in Oslo on December 10, 2026, the anniversary of the death of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel, who established the awards.

headline: Establishing US military base in Poland to take years, NATO supreme allied commander says
summary: According to Alexus Grynkewich, the timeline will depend on how long it takes to build the necessary infrastructure
body_text:
BRUSSELS, October 12. /TASS/. NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich said establishing a permanent US military base in Poland would take years because the necessary infrastructure must be built first.

In an interview with Polish TV channel TVP World, Grynkewich said the timeline would depend on how long it took to build the necessary infrastructure.

Grynkewich noted that a permanent US military presence would also involve relocating service members’ families, requiring the construction of schools, hospitals, and other essential facilities.

In late September, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said Warsaw wanted to host up to 10,000 US troops at the proposed permanent military base. He noted that Poland already has a permanent US missile defense facility on its territory and confirmed that a second base is under discussion. Sikorski added that approximately 7,000 US service members are currently stationed in Poland on a rotational basis.

On June 3, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz submitted a formal proposal to establish a permanent US military base in Poland to Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. In early September, a US delegation visited Poland and inspected potential sites for the facility. On September 17, US President Donald Trump said there had been "great progress" in talks on the issue.

headline: US, Israel seeking to devour Eastern wealth: IRGC advisor
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – A senior commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) says the United States and occupying regime of Israel lack a civilization of their own and seek to plunder wealth and resources of the East.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 12 (MNA) – A senior commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) says the United States and occupying regime of Israel lack a civilization of their own and seek to plunder wealth and resources of the East.

Brigadier General Ali Balali an advisor to the commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force made the remarks in an interview on Monday.

“Civilization belongs to the East, and they have no civilization of their own,” he said.

He added that the United States and Israel were seeking to prevent the emergence of “a new Islamic civilization.”

Balali urged neighboring Muslim countries to recognize that Washington and its allies do not want the peoples of the East and the Muslim world to become more capable or prosperous, but instead seek only to "fill their own pockets."

He further said Western powers had built their strength through the mass killings of Indigenous peoples in the Americas and populations in Africa.

He cited European countries, including France and Belgium, as examples of this historical record, criticizing Western powers for committing crimes while claiming to advocate peace and justice.

“Yet they have no history or civilization to be proud of, because civilization belongs to the East and the Muslim world,” the IRGC advisor said.

He added that Western powers were resisting the establishment of a global order based on Islamic civilization but would ultimately fail to prevent it.

Balali’s comments came amid repeated threats by US President Donald Trump since the US-Israeli war against Iran began on February 28, according to Press TV.

On April 1, Trump threatened to bombard Iran and said US forces would “bring them back to the stone ages.” He also threatened to destroy Iranian power plants and other infrastructure.

Days later, on April 7, Trump issued an even broader warning, declaring that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again” if Iran failed to meet his demands. The statement drew international attention amid fears of further escalation and threats against critical infrastructure.

headline: Russia not seeking split between US, Europe over Ukraine conflict — Kremlin spokesman
summary: Dmitry Peskov said Moscow is looking for effective measures and responsible solutions that will provide for a peaceful settlement
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Russia is not seeking a split between the United States and Europe over the Ukraine conflict but a solution that could pave the way for a peaceful settlement, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

"We aren’t seeking a split here but we are looking for really effective measures and responsible solutions that will enable us to reach a peaceful settlement," he said when asked whether Moscow believed US President Donald Trump’s position on a peaceful solution to the Ukraine issue would lead to a split between the US and Europe.

US President Donald Trump said earlier that it was time for Ukraine "to get a new president." "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," because Zelensky "could have made many deals that, for some reason, he never does," the US president noted.

Meanwhile, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen assured Zelensky of the European Union’s support following Trump’s statements and added that the EU would allocate funds to purchase more projectiles and drones for Kiev.

headline: US says Hormuz oil flows recover to 14 million bpd despite Saudi attacks

"We are here as your partners," he said, reiterating the US's "unwavering support for Saudi Arabia".Mr Wright warned the recovery in crude supplies had yet to ease pressure on fuel markets, with diesel prices remaining "very high", and jet fuel and petrol prices also elevated.
