body_text:
Up to 14 million barrels of oil a day are moving through the Strait of Hormuz, with Gulf crude flows recovering to between 80 and 90 per cent of prewar levels, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said.

Additional supplies from the Gulf are also being transported through pipelines bypassing Hormuz, Mr Wright said on Monday, addressing the 25th WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh remotely.

"The crude problem we talked a lot about – it's still there but it's mostly handled," he said, offering a more optimistic assessment than ship-tracking data suggests.

Figures from analytics firm Kpler show oil exports through Hormuz averaged slightly under nine million bpd in September, the highest monthly level since the war began, but only about 44 per cent of the 20.6 million bpd recorded in February.

About 22 vessels crossed the strait daily in the 30 days to October 12, about two thirds of them tankers, according to Kpler. The data is provisional and subject to revision as tracking information is updated, reflecting movements registered by 2pm UAE time on October 12.

Laden crude tankers leaving the Gulf carried about 8.9 million bpd over the past month, mostly from Saudi Arabia and Iraq.

The figures are not directly comparable with Mr Wright's broader recovery estimate, which includes supplies transported through bypass pipelines. Kpler's September data nevertheless suggests lower volumes through Hormuz than those cited by the US official.

Mr Wright's comments came after an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured about 300, underscoring the security risks facing the world's biggest oil-exporting region.

"I want to start out by strongly condemning the cowardly attacks by the Houthis on the people of Saudi Arabia, on civilian infrastructure," Mr Wright said in addressing the energy congress on Monday.

He reaffirmed Washington's commitment to the kingdom as energy ministers and industry executives gathered in Riyadh despite heightened security concerns. "We are here as your partners," he said, reiterating the US's "unwavering support for Saudi Arabia".

Mr Wright warned the recovery in crude supplies had yet to ease pressure on fuel markets, with diesel prices remaining "very high", and jet fuel and petrol prices also elevated. "The challenge is still here and the challenge is still ahead of us," he said.

headline: Russia, Lebanon to resume meetings of intergovernmental commission on trade — Lavrov
summary: The Russian and Lebanese sides reaffirmed their "mutual commitment to further expanding political dialogue and strengthening partnership ties in various areas" during the negotiations
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Russia and Lebanon have agreed to resume the work of the intergovernmental commission on trade, economic, scientific, and technical cooperation as soon as possible, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.

The Russian and Lebanese sides reaffirmed their "mutual commitment to further expanding political dialogue and strengthening partnership ties in various areas" during the negotiations, he told a press conference following talks with Lebanon’s Foreign Minister Youssef Raji.

"It is necessary to pay particular attention to the trade and economic area," Lavrov said. "To this end, we agreed to resume the work of the intergovernmental commission on trade, economic, scientific, and technical cooperation, which has not met since 2018, as soon as possible," he added.

headline: UAE wealth set to hit $6 trillion in 2030 despite short-term war volatility

In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group said. Real, or physical, assets with intrinsic value such as property portfolios reached $2.4 trillion in 2025, jumping from $2.2 trillion at the end of the previous year. Financial wealth grew to $1.4 trillion in 2025, rising from $1.2 trillion a year earlier, while liabilities for the same period rose from $210 billion to $220 billion. The report estimates liabilities to rise to $340 billion by 2030. The Iran war has introduced “short-term volatility across Middle Eastern markets, with investor sentiment shaped by geopolitical uncertainty and oil-price movements”, said Lukasz Rey, managing director and partner at BCG.“While we anticipate slightly lower growth over the next one to two years, a rebound is expected towards the latter part of the decade.”Sovereign wealth strength, economic diversification agendas, family-business liquidity events and private capital activity will all help drive wealth creation in the country, Mr Rey said.Caution to prevailBCG, he said, expects wealth managers to remain cautious in the near term. However, “the region's wealth development story remains structurally resilient over the five-year projection horizon”, Mr Rey added.The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed.The World Bank last week said Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April. The International Monetary Fund also expects economies in the region to contract this year but anticipates a sharp expansion next year once the conflict settles, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said.Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country remains a magnet for the ultra-wealthy, as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers. A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices and institutional partners.Concentration of wealthThe UAE’s financial wealth remains concentrated among high-net-worth individuals, with “the composition of wealth expected to evolve by 2030 as more wealth accumulates within the lower high-net-worth segment”, the BCG report said. The country had about 500 ultra-high-net-worth individuals – those with assets in excess of $100 million – in 2025. That number is expected to jump to about 800 by the end of the decade, while their share of total financial wealth will rise marginally from 26.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent. The upper high-net-worth segment, featuring people with assets of $20 million to $100 million, is forecast to grow from about 2,700 to 4,200 individuals, with their share of wealth broadly stable, rising from 7.4 per cent in 2025 to 7.6 per cent in 2030.Meanwhile, the group of 200,000 lower high-net-worth individuals, with an asset range of $1 million to $20 million, are estimated to increase their share of financial wealth from 29.3 per cent in 2025 to 31.5 per cent in 2030. The affluent segment with assets worth $1 million is expected to expand from about 500,000 to 600,000 individuals in 2030. However, its share of wealth will decline from 15.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent, BCG data found. Centre of choiceThe UAE also continues to strengthen its position as a global wealth booking centre, with cross-border wealth belonging to international clients and booked in the country jumping more than 11 per cent to $721 billion last year. Currency and deposits, valued at $471.8 billion in 2025, are projected to rise more than 10 per cent annually to $778.9 billion by 2030. Bonds are estimated to grow almost 12 per cent on an annual basis to $27.8 billion, while equities are expected to reach jump to $591.9 billion by 2030, from $419.4 billion last year, BCG found.
body_text:
Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East, a new report has found.

In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group said.

The sharp projected increase, driven by a rise in real assets and financial wealth, “points to the UAE's long-term wealth creation potential”, BCG said in its Global Wealth Report 2026: The Great Reordering report on Monday.

UAE remains magnet for ultra-wealthy undeterred by war disruption

Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion.

Real, or physical, assets with intrinsic value such as property portfolios reached $2.4 trillion in 2025, jumping from $2.2 trillion at the end of the previous year. Financial wealth grew to $1.4 trillion in 2025, rising from $1.2 trillion a year earlier, while liabilities for the same period rose from $210 billion to $220 billion. The report estimates liabilities to rise to $340 billion by 2030.

The Iran war has introduced “short-term volatility across Middle Eastern markets, with investor sentiment shaped by geopolitical uncertainty and oil-price movements”, said Lukasz Rey, managing director and partner at BCG.

“While we anticipate slightly lower growth over the next one to two years, a rebound is expected towards the latter part of the decade.”

Sovereign wealth strength, economic diversification agendas, family-business liquidity events and private capital activity will all help drive wealth creation in the country, Mr Rey said.

BCG, he said, expects wealth managers to remain cautious in the near term. However, “the region's wealth development story remains structurally resilient over the five-year projection horizon”, Mr Rey added.

The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased economic uncertainty across the Middle East. Despite a halt in all-out hostilities since early April, several attempts to reach a permanent deal to end the conflict have failed.

The World Bank last week said Gulf economies would contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downwards revision of 5.7 percentage points from its forecast in April.

The International Monetary Fund also expects economies in the region to contract this year but anticipates a sharp expansion next year once the conflict settles, managing director Kristalina Georgieva said.

Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country remains a magnet for the ultra-wealthy, as well as global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers.

A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the world's largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices and institutional partners.

The UAE’s financial wealth remains concentrated among high-net-worth individuals, with “the composition of wealth expected to evolve by 2030 as more wealth accumulates within the lower high-net-worth segment”, the BCG report said.

The country had about 500 ultra-high-net-worth individuals – those with assets in excess of $100 million – in 2025. That number is expected to jump to about 800 by the end of the decade, while their share of total financial wealth will rise marginally from 26.3 per cent to 26.5 per cent.

The upper high-net-worth segment, featuring people with assets of $20 million to $100 million, is forecast to grow from about 2,700 to 4,200 individuals, with their share of wealth broadly stable, rising from 7.4 per cent in 2025 to 7.6 per cent in 2030.

Meanwhile, the group of 200,000 lower high-net-worth individuals, with an asset range of $1 million to $20 million, are estimated to increase their share of financial wealth from 29.3 per cent in 2025 to 31.5 per cent in 2030.

The affluent segment with assets worth $1 million is expected to expand from about 500,000 to 600,000 individuals in 2030. However, its share of wealth will decline from 15.5 per cent to 14.6 per cent, BCG data found.

The UAE also continues to strengthen its position as a global wealth booking centre, with cross-border wealth belonging to international clients and booked in the country jumping more than 11 per cent to $721 billion last year.

Currency and deposits, valued at $471.8 billion in 2025, are projected to rise more than 10 per cent annually to $778.9 billion by 2030.

Bonds are estimated to grow almost 12 per cent on an annual basis to $27.8 billion, while equities are expected to reach jump to $591.9 billion by 2030, from $419.4 billion last year, BCG found.

headline: Qatar’s energy minister: ‘Keep energy above politics’, as Doha and Riyadh sign cooperation MoU
summary: Qatar and Saudi Arabia sign an energy MoU, as Al-Kaabi urges the world to keep energy “above politics”. Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy President and CEO…
body_text:
Qatar and Saudi Arabia sign an energy MoU, as Al-Kaabi urges the world to keep energy “above politics”.

Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al-Kaabi called for a new world energy order in which energy is kept above politics and never made a victim or target of conflict, in remarks at the 17th International Energy Forum (IEF) Ministerial Meeting in Riyadh on Sunday.

“Energy security must unite us, not divide us; it must be protected, not weaponised,” he said, according to a QatarEnergy statement.

On the sidelines of the meeting, Qatar and Saudi Arabia signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) laying the framework for joint cooperation across the energy industry. Al-Kaabi signed for Qatar, and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman Al Saud signed for the kingdom.

The MoU covers oil and gas and their derivatives, refining, petrochemicals, electricity, clean hydrogen, renewable energy, and energy efficiency and storage. It also addresses emission reduction and climate change mitigation technologies, including carbon capture, transport, reuse and storage, and coordination on energy, sustainability and climate change in international initiatives and frameworks. It will take effect once legal procedures are completed in both countries.

In his address, Al-Kaabi said the conflict in the region has caused “by far, the world’s worst energy crisis,” affecting the flow of around 20% of the world’s hydrocarbon supplies. He said many energy assets across the region had been targeted, causing tens of billions of dollars in damage and severe volatility in global markets.

“If there is one lesson we have learned from the past few months, it is that energy security, as critical as it is to the global economy, remains highly vulnerable and inseparable from geopolitical security,” he said.

Al-Kaabi also pointed to the human cost, noting that a billion people still lack access to electricity and that about four billion depend on food produced using manufactured fertilisers. “The impact on all those lives should remind us of our shared responsibility to safeguard energy security, protect the free flow of energy, and keep energy above politics and conflicts,” he said.

He urged the forum to explore every avenue to protect energy infrastructure during conflict. “It is a real problem that energy infrastructure has become both an economic asset and a strategic military target,” he said.

He opened his remarks by expressing Qatar’s “unwavering solidarity with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, its leadership and people during these times”.

“I offer my sincere condolences to the families of those killed in these horrible attacks and wish a speedy recovery to the injured,” he added.

The ministerial meeting was held under the theme “Energy Security – A Shared Responsibility: Market Fundamentals, Supply Chain Resilience, and the New Dynamics of Demand and Supply.”

It was opened by Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman and attended by energy ministers, government representatives, industry leaders and international organisations. It forms part of Riyadh Energy Week, alongside the 25th WPC Energy Congress.

headline: 'Being allowed to leave does not erase injustice': Former Dubai resident leaves Iraq after years of detention

A former Dubai resident detained in Iraq for more than five years said being allowed to return to his family shouldn't mask the injustice he was forced to endure.

Australian engineer Robert Pether, 50, was reunited with his family in Ireland on Monday after being allowed to leave Iraq having been sent to jail over a contract dispute involving his employer.

Mr Pether was released from prison last year but had to remain in Iraq because he was barred from leaving due to financial claims linked to the case.

Dubai resident leaves Iraq after being detained for five years

Mr Pether and his Egyptian co-worker Khaled Radwan, both of whom lived in Dubai at the time, had travelled to Iraq for what they expected to be a routine business meeting but ended up being jailed in August 2021 and fined $12 million over a contract dispute between their employers and authorities in Baghdad. Mr Radwan has now also left Iraq.

“I was an engineer,” said Mr Pether, speaking at a press conference on Monday. “I was an employee doing my job. I had a wife and children waiting for me at home. I was there because I made a choice to help a war-torn country rebuild. I never came home.”

The travel ban Baghdad had imposed on Mr Pether and Mr Radwan led to the office of the US Special Presidential Envoy for Hostage Affairs to push for their release. That followed a call from Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong, calling for Mr Pether to be allowed to return home to his family.

Since his release, Mr Pether had stayed either with friends or in hotels, with the cost of food and accommodation falling on him and his family.

During his detention, Mr Pether's health deteriorated, which led to the office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights issuing a statement in June, highlighting the “particularly alarming” situation, which was compounded by a lack of access to specialist medical care and the psychological toll of his “prolonged detention and uncertainty”.

Mr Pether said that “coming home today should never be mistaken for that injustice somehow having been corrected. It wasn't. Not even close. Coming home is not exoneration and being allowed to leave is not justice.

“Our convictions have not been overturned. Neither of us has been exonerated. We were innocent when we were taken on April 7, 2021 and we remain innocent today.”

Mr Pether said that when he was released from prison he was only hours from death, with his body shutting down, after months of critical illness and excruciating pain, only to find that he remained trapped in Iraq.

“I didn't have my passport, visa or identity documents and I had no ability to move around freely or safely, leave the country or even go to a hospital,” said Mr Pether.

“Travel bans prevented me from returning to my family and from accessing the medical treatment I desperately needed outside Iraq.”

Mr Pether said he was forced to sign a waiver before being allowed to leave Iraq and return to his family.

“I signed it because I wanted to go home. There was no choice. After more than five years, with my health deteriorating and my family waiting for me, there was no meaningful choice between signing a document and remaining trapped in Iraq,” he said.

“So, I want to be very clear about something. I am incredibly grateful to be standing here. I am overwhelmed to finally be home. But gratitude for being home does not erase what happened to me for even one second. Freedom should never have been something that had to be bargained for.”

He also spoke of the emotional impact felt by his family and praised his wife for her campaigning on his behalf.

“My wife and my children have lived this every single day with me. Our children lost years with their dad. They watched their mum fight every day to try to bring me home,” said Mr Pether.

“They grew up with uncertainty, fear and circumstances no child should ever have to carry. I am so thankful for my wife Desree, always fighting for me, while at the same time holding our family together, all while dealing with a situation that took an enormous toll on her, too.”

Ms Wong released a statement on Monday morning. “The Australian government welcomes the Iraqi government's decision to allow Robert Pether to leave Iraq today,” she said. “I spoke to Mr Pether shortly before his departure from Baghdad and am pleased he is now free to move forward with his life and be reunited with his family.

“Mr Pether had been imprisoned in Iraq for more than four years and was later subject to travel restrictions that prevented him from leaving the country.

“I thank the Australian officials whose tireless work helped achieve this outcome, as well as the Irish authorities for their close co-operation throughout this process. I wish Mr Pether and his family all the very best as they reunite,” Ms Wong said.

body_text:
US President Donald Trump's declaration of an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine has raised questions over its validity, after Moscow offered no confirmation about the truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement.

The move sent oil and diesel prices into decline early on Monday, but analysts cautioned that even a sustained halt to attacks on energy infrastructure would offer limited relief to global fuel markets, with much of Russia's refining capacity offline after months of Ukrainian drone strikes.

Brent fell 1.3 per cent to $103.35 a barrel in early trading, while West Texas Intermediate declined 1.4 per cent to $90.55 a barrel. ICE gas oil futures, a benchmark for diesel, dropped about 3 per cent.

Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'

The oil benchmarks pared losses by midday, with Brent trading 1.10 per cent higher at $105.87 a barrel by 1.55pm UAE time, while WTI was up 1.13 per cent at $92.89 a barrel.

“Effective immediately, there is an energy ceasefire in the war between Russia and Ukraine,” Mr Trump wrote on Truth Social on Sunday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv supported a ceasefire but was awaiting details from Washington. A similar announcement by Mr Trump in September failed to produce a lasting halt to strikes.

“Only time will tell how durable it proves to be,” said Giovanni Staunovo, commodity analyst at Swiss bank UBS. “We have seen similar commitments in the past that ultimately failed to hold.”

The announcement follows a US Treasury decision on October 9 to temporarily ease sanctions on Russian diesel transactions until April 7, 2027, after Mr Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release additional fuel into global markets.

But the volumes are modest relative to the scale of the disruption. The proposed 300,000 tonnes for the rest of this month equates to about 100,000 barrels a day, Mr Staunovo said.

That “would only partially offset the decline in seaborne diesel exports, which in September were around 1.3 million barrels per day below the levels seen at the start of the year”, he said.

Francesco Sassi, assistant professor of energy geopolitics at the University of Oslo, said Washington's decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel for six months marked a significant shift in energy geopolitics that threatened to undermine western unity against Moscow.

He described the move as the clearest failure yet of efforts to isolate Russia through energy sanctions. “What remains unsaid regarding the guarantees that Russia had from the US for supplying diesel is far more important than the few details we know so far about the energy ceasefire,” Mr Sassi said.

Ukraine's response would also be a test of its relationship with Washington, potentially increasing pressure on the European Union to sustain support for Kyiv without US backing, he added.

Russia's capacity to deliver the additional fuel is also in doubt.

Its diesel exports fell from about 706,000 bpd in January to 47,000 bpd in August and almost nothing last month, according to Kpler data, as Ukrainian drone attacks damaged refineries and curtailed fuel production.

Total Russian oil exports declined to about 6.8 million bpd in September from 8 million bpd in May. Shipments to India, Russia's biggest buyer, have more than halved since June to 1.2 million bpd, the data showed.

The drop highlights the difficulty of restoring Russian fuel supplies without first repairing damaged infrastructure, a process that could take months even if attacks cease.

S&P Global Commodity Insights said the announcement could weigh on diesel refining margins but only if Russian exports increase. “We see the immediate market impact as limited,” analysts James Bambino and Richard Joswick said.

Additional Russian shipments would cover only about 10 per cent of the global shortfall in diesel exports, assuming they represent new supply rather than cargoes diverted from existing buyers, S&P Global said.

About half of Russia's refining capacity is offline and repairs could take months, limiting the scope for a rapid recovery.

Any additional cargoes are likely to remain in the Atlantic Basin, potentially reaching the US East Coast or Brazil and freeing up US Gulf Coast supplies for Europe.

That could put downwards pressure on diesel margins in north-west Europe and the US but only “as long as a ceasefire holds”, the analysts said.

Even if Russian fuel exports recover, the broader oil market remains exposed to disruption in the Middle East, where the Iran war has restricted supplies and forced major changes to established shipping routes.

Crude has largely remained above $100 a barrel in recent weeks as attacks on infrastructure and shipping continue to threaten supplies from the Gulf.

Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 a barrel from $85, saying Gulf supply disruption was likely to ease more slowly than previously expected. The bank estimates geopolitical tension is adding slightly more than $20 a barrel to prices and does not assume a quick resolution to the US-Iran conflict.

“Potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the bank's analysts said.

headline: Russia to continue providing humanitarian assistance to Lebanon — Lavrov
summary: According to the Russian top diplomat, Moscow and Beirut have traditionally maintained friendly relations
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Moscow is always ready to support its Lebanese friends and will continue to provide humanitarian assistance to Beirut, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said as he opened talks with Lebanese Minister of Foreign Affairs and Emigrants Youssef Rajji.

"I would like to express my sincere gratitude to you for finding the opportunity to visit Russia at a time when Lebanon and the Lebanese people are facing a very severe crisis resulting from the military operations and military escalation that Israel is conducting against your country. In this regard, I would like to unequivocally reiterate Russia’s fundamental position in favor of ensuring Lebanon’s sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity," Lavrov emphasized.

According to the top Russian diplomat, Moscow and Beirut have traditionally maintained friendly relations. "We have always been ready to support our Lebanese friends, including in the current situation, where almost one million Lebanese citizens have been seriously affected, with their rights violated, and the humanitarian situation in Lebanon remaining tense," Lavrov said.

"In April, we sent humanitarian aid to your country for those in need, and we will continue to provide further assistance through humanitarian supplies," he added.

headline: From confusion to conviction: A British official's visit to Luoyang
summary: How can an ancient city protect its historic sites while breathing new life into urban development? He praised Luoyang for doing an excellent job of balancing urban renewal with cultural heritage protection, offering valuable insights for other cities facing the same challenge.

headline: Pilot, flight attendant and widowed mother among victims of Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia

At least 20 people were killed in a series of attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid and Abha international airports in Saudi Arabia’s Asir province last week, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi rebels stepped up attacks on the kingdom.

The victims include a Saudi airline pilot, an Egyptian flight attendant and a Syrian widowed mother of four. Saudi and foreign citizens were among the dead, while hundreds of people have been injured, Saudi authorities say.

Among those killed in Saturday’s attack in Riyadh were four Saudis and eight foreign citizens. The death toll from that strike rose to 13 after an injured Indian citizen was confirmed dead. A Pakistani citizen was killed in a separate attack on Sunday, Saudi authorities said, while 11 were injured. The foreign victims included two Bangladeshis and citizens of the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan.

LatestSaudi Arabia extends suspension of operations at Riyadh airport

More than 300 people were wounded in Saturday's attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade. This marks a sharp escalation in the war in Yemen, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government in its battle against the Houthis, raising fears the fighting could widen and draw in American forces.

US President Donald Trump ​said on Saturday his country was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February.

Details about some of those killed have emerged through official statements, diplomatic missions and reports from their families.

Capt Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, a pilot with Saudi Arabia’s national carrier Saudia, was among three Saudi citizens killed in attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport last Thursday. The airline confirmed his death in a statement. Saudi authorities said airport facilities and a Saudia aircraft had been struck.

Azza Ramzy, 28, worked as a flight attendant for Saudi airline flynas. She died from injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, Egypt’s Foreign Ministry said. Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty directed the Egyptian embassy and the general consulate in Riyadh to expedite the transfer of her body to Egypt. Egyptian media reported that she was from Beheira governorate, in the north of the country.

Buthaina Ahmad Oweida, a widowed mother of four, had lived in Saudi Arabia for five years and was based in Makkah. She lost contact with her family on Saturday while returning from Riyadh, where she had been visiting her sister. Her brother told Syria’s state-run news agency Sana that the Syrian consul later informed him of her death, citing official confirmation from the Saudi government. The Syrian embassy in Riyadh said she was killed in an attack on King Khalid International Airport.

Talal Al Dani was among those killed in Saturday’s attack, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry. The Palestinian embassy in Saudi Arabia said it was handling arrangements concerning his body and providing support to his family.

Ali, from Hyderabad, was travelling with his family on an Umrah pilgrimage when he was injured in Saturday’s attack. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed his death on Sunday and said it was in contact with his family to help arrange the repatriation of his remains.

Footage released by Saudi state television of the attack on ‌the Riyadh airport on Saturday showed scores of religious pilgrims lined up at a gate as they prepared to travel to Islam's two holiest sites, Makkah and Madinah. A bright orange flash sent people running in panic, ​while parts of the roof appeared to cave in.

The airport was closed after the attack. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation has since extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh until midnight on Tuesday.

headline: Fire burns down Paris's oldest covered food market
summary: A fire "completely destroyed" Paris's historic Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges overnight Monday, authorities said. The cause of the fire that swept through the capital's oldest covered food market remains unknown.
body_text:
A fire "completely destroyed" Paris's historic Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges overnight Monday, authorities said. The cause of the fire that swept through the capital's oldest covered food market remains unknown.

Issued on: 12/10/2026 - 10:02

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

A fire has destroyed the French capital's oldest covered food market, a popular street food venue named after red-clad orphans, authorities said on Monday.

The Marché Couvert des Enfants Rouges in the Marais district has existed since 1615, and draws its name from the red outfits that orphans wore at a hospital near the market until 1772.

Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, the French city of Lyon and Mexico City.

"The market was completely destroyed" overnight from Sunday to Monday, Lieutenant Colonel Pierre de Bouvier told reporters on site in the early hours of the morning.

"Nothing remains of the covered market," he said, adding that it's metal structure had "partially collapsed" inside.

Read moreSounding the fire alarm: Why French firefighters are on strike

One firefighter was lightly injured in the blaze, De Bouvier said.

The mayor of the central Paris district, Ariel Weil, said he was relieved the fire was under control and would not spread further.

"The worst has been avoided," he said. "No neighbouring buildings have been affected."

The deal was mediated by Washington and Paris and endorsed by Ankara. It sought to end hostilities between Kurdish forces and the new Syrian authorities, while establishing a road map for incorporating the north-east into state institutions, while offering specific linguistic and cultural rights as well as political representation.In January, Mr Al Shara issued a decree, after weeks of violence, offering concessions designed to foster goodwill with Syria's Kurdish population. But she said the measures remained incomplete, particularly regarding the right to education in the Kurdish language.Kurdish existence had been acknowledged for the first time in Syrian history, she said, but mechanisms were still needed to fulfil the decree on the ground. She said the government was responsible for establishing those mechanisms and ensuring stability.Tension has risen in north-east Syria over the future of Kurdish-language education, with students protesting against restrictions imposed by the new authorities in Damascus. body_text:
Syria's constitution must guarantee the rights of the Kurdish community, the country's largest ethnic minority group, a veteran politician has said, warning that the move towards a more centralised state risks fuelling tension.

Damascus has worked to integrate Kurdish-led troops into the military.

Ilham Ahmed, a Syrian Kurdish leader, told the Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil, Iraq, that the integration process had made significant headway, but remained a work in progress as the Kurds stake out a claim in the new Syrian political dispensation under President Ahmad Al Shara.

Ms Ahmed, a senior figure in the former Kurdish-led autonomous administration in north-east Syria, is now a member of the foreign relations committee in the Syrian parliament.

She said the process of merging the Syrian Democratic Forces with the military had helped to relink cities, reopen border crossings and create conditions for greater stability following the fall of Bashar Al Assad’s regime.

The experience of self-administration had demonstrated the importance of women’s participation in public life, Ms Ahmed added.

But she warned that their role in institutions and decision-making was now diminishing despite the integration process.

“Today, we are seeing that despite the merging process, there is a regression in the role of women and in their roles and participation in institutions and in decision making process,” she said.

Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi announced in August from the city of Qamishli that the integration of the Kurdish administration into Syria’s state institutions was complete.

The move built on an agreement struck between Damascus and the SDF in January. The deal was mediated by Washington and Paris and endorsed by Ankara. It sought to end hostilities between Kurdish forces and the new Syrian authorities, while establishing a road map for incorporating the north-east into state institutions, while offering specific linguistic and cultural rights as well as political representation.

In January, Mr Al Shara issued a decree, after weeks of violence, offering concessions designed to foster goodwill with Syria's Kurdish population. They included recognising Nowruz as a national holiday and recognising Kurdish as a national language that may be taught in public and private schools in Kurdish-populated areas.

He also granted Syrian nationality to previously stateless Kurds.

Ms Ahmed described the presidential decree recognising Kurdish identity, language and the community’s place in Syria as a historic achievement. But she said the measures remained incomplete, particularly regarding the right to education in the Kurdish language.

Kurdish existence had been acknowledged for the first time in Syrian history, she said, but mechanisms were still needed to fulfil the decree on the ground. She said the government was responsible for establishing those mechanisms and ensuring stability.

Tension has risen in north-east Syria over the future of Kurdish-language education, with students protesting against restrictions imposed by the new authorities in Damascus.

The Education Ministry's decision to limit instruction in Kurdish has prompted demonstrations in areas including Hasakah, Qamishli and Kobani, where pupils and teachers are demanding the right to study in their mother tongue.

Ms Ahmed said recurring hostilities were linked to discrimination, adding that the integration process remained at a stage of testing and observation.

She also challenged the negative perception of decentralisation in Syria, arguing that it was too often portrayed as a threat to the country’s territorial unity.

“In general, when we talk about decentralisation in Syria, it’s like we’re talking about the devil,” she said. Last year when The National sat down to speak to Ms Ahmed in the run up to the integration, she spoke of the importance of federalism as the main priority for Kurdish leaders.

"It appears as if decentralisation would divide Syria but it’s not like that. We are moving into a more centralised state which will cause more tension,” she said.

“Speaking and learning more languages does not lead to dividing the country or segmenting it. It strengthens the Syrian culture."

analysis.framing: The article frames the story around Kurdish leader Ilham Ahmed's call for constitutional protections for Kurdish rights, presenting her warnings about centralization and women's participation alongside factual context about the integration process.

loaded_language.explanation: Uses the metaphor 'fuelling' to suggest an active, escalating danger, which is more vivid and alarmist than a neutral description.
An evaluative phrase that endorses the significance of the decree rather than simply reporting it.

loaded_language.explanation: A colorful, emotionally charged simile that dramatizes the negative perception of decentralization.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: it is often portrayed very negatively

loaded_language.explanation: The word 'regression' implies a backward step and carries a negative value judgment.

Jon Rahm will continue his reintegration into golf’s established tours when he tees it up at the Abu Dhabi Aldar Championship for the first time next month.

The Spanish Ryder Cup star has been confirmed for the penultimate competition of the DP World Tour season, taking place at Yas Links from November 5 to 8.

As a previous Race to Dubai winner, Rahm has enjoyed some of his finest successes in the UAE.

He has won the season’s finale, the DP World Tour Championship at Jumeirah Golf Estates, three times – in 2017, 2019 and 2022.

And yet this will be his first time in the capital.

“I’ve had some of the best weeks of my career in the UAE, so I’m really looking forward to playing in Abu Dhabi for the first time,” Rahm said.

“I’ve heard great things about Yas Links, and I’m looking forward to playing there. It’ll be great to get started in Abu Dhabi before heading to Dubai the following week.”

He will join a field that will include fellow stars like Rory McIlroy and Patrick Reed, who are vying with each other to win the Race to Dubai.

Reed signalled at the start of this season he was ending his association with the breakaway LIV Golf tour.

After winning the Dubai Desert Classic and heading to Bahrain, he said he hoped to play his way back on to the PGA Tour in the United States via Europe’s tour. The top 10 players in the Race to Dubai rankings are eligible for PGA Tour cards.

Rahm is now also in the throes of exiting LIV. The rebel tour is set to be restructured after losing funding from Saudi Arabia.

Players who sign up to LIV Golf next season will not be allowed to be members of the European Tour in 2027.

Players have been told they have to make a choice regarding where they play. Many of LIV’s leading stars, like Reed and Brooks Koepka, have already made for the exit.

Rahm has also signalled he will not be part of the new-look series. In May, he reached an agreement with the DP World Tour to maintain his membership, and ensure his availability for the Ryder Cup.

Participation in certain DP World Tour events was part of that, leading to him playing in the two-legged play-off finals in Abu Dhabi and then Dubai.

While his schedule for next season is unclear, he might pursue a similar route back to the PGA Tour in the US which Reed has taken this season.

Rahm could yet finish in the top 10 of the Race to Dubai standings this season. He is currently 46th in the standings, but could leap up with strong performances in Dubai and Abu Dhabi.

However, he would not yet be eligible for a return to the PGA Tour. Rahm won the individual LIV title for the third time in August.

There is an automatic year ban for LIV players, so he would not be able to play there until August 28, 2027.

analysis.framing: The article frames Jon Rahm's Abu Dhabi debut primarily as part of his reintegration into established tours and his exit from LIV Golf, with a neutral, matter-of-fact tone.

An informal, slightly dramatic phrase suggesting a rush or eagerness to leave, which may exaggerate the situation.
The phrase 'in the throes of' is dramatic and suggests struggle or difficulty, adding emotional weight.

No mention of other players' reactions or the broader context of the PGA Tour-LIV merger talks.

body_text:
The UAE Cabinet has approved its federal budget for 2027 to 2029 with spending of Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion).

The allocation marks an increase of 28.3 per cent compared to the previous three years, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai said on Monday.

The Cabinet also approved the 2027 budget with expenditure of Dh90.1 billion.

Main sectors covered by the new federal budget include community protection and safety, the economy of the future, future-orientated education, employment and empowerment, health and quality of life, leadership, government affairs and international relations, the UAE Government Media Office said in a statement. The budget will also focus on industry, technology, energy, infrastructure, culture, media and sports.

“Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged … Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen,” Sheikh Mohammed said in a post on X.

The UAE last year launched its 2027-2029 budget cycle, focusing on sustainability, artificial intelligence and efficiency.

It followed four consecutive cycles during which the total federal budget reached about Dh900 billion ($245 billion), officials said in July last year, adding that the cycle focuses on sectors such as education, health care, social welfare and core government services.

The UAE's economy grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war.

The non-oil sector's contribution to the country's gross domestic product during the six-month period increased by 1.8 per cent to 79.2 per cent, the Federal Competitiveness and Statistics Centre said last week.

The Iran war has tipped the Middle East into one of its worst geopolitical crises in decades. The conflict, which began on February 28, led to Iranian strikes on its Arab neighbours and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

The UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, continues to grow despite the conflict.

Ratings agency Fitch said on Monday that the UAE non-oil growth model is broadly resilient to the war baseline. The non-oil growth model of the UAE has leveraged a role as a hub between Asia and Europe “backed by a favourable operating environment, supportive government policy, and the ability to attract and retain foreign labour and visitors”, it said in a report.

It added that it expects further measures to “improve the operating environment along with a smoothing of administrative procedures” for corporates and residents, backed by higher spending and other sources of financial support at the sovereign and government-related entity level.

“Fitch sees structural strengths that will support the resilience of the non-oil economy. However, a persistent period of regional insecurity will call into question logistical advantages and perceptions of the country as a commercial and financial centre and tourism destination,” said Paul Gamble, senior director at Fitch Ratings.

The approval of the budget confirms the UAE government’s “keenness to achieve a balance between current development requirements and investment in future opportunities, and to establish a government financial system characterised by flexibility, efficiency and sustainability”, the media office said on Monday.

It enhances the UAE’s position among the most advanced and prosperous countries in the world, it added.

The breakdown for the year is as follows:

Dh34.6 billion (38.4 per cent) – Social development and social benefits

Dh29.1 billion (32.3 per cent) – Government affairs

Dh17.8 billion (19.7 per cent) – Federal expenses

Dh5.6 billion (6.2 per cent) – Financial assets and investments

Dh3 billion (3.4 per cent) – Infrastructure and economic resources

headline: Closure of Riyadh airport extended after deadly Houthi strikes
summary: By Gianluca Lo NostroOct 12 (Reuters) - Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
body_text:
By Gianluca Lo Nostro

Oct 12 (Reuters) - Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East.

The airport cancelled 99.7% of all scheduled flights on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. An air traffic tracker from Flightradar24 showed no planes over the city.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.

Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways was among the airlines that further extended Saudi flight cancellations, affecting around 20 flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Monday and Tuesday.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.

(Reporting by Joanna Plucinska in London, Gianluca Lo Nostro in Gdansk, Federico Maccioni in Dubai and Menna Alaa El Din in Cairo; Editing by Matt Scuffham, Aidan Lewis)

headline: Americans Hall, Woodford win Nobel prize for work on stabilising economies
summary: By Simon Johnson and Johan AhlanderSTOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies."With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.
body_text:
By Simon Johnson and Johan Ahlander

STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.

"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

The prestigious award, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final prize to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

One of the laureates' key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.

headline: Closure of Riyadh airport extended after deadly Houthi strikes
summary: By Gianluca Lo NostroOct 12 (Reuters) - Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.
body_text:
By Gianluca Lo Nostro

Oct 12 (Reuters) - Saudi authorities said on Monday they were extending the suspension of operations at the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, after deadly weekend attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.

Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement.

The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East.

The airport cancelled 99.7% of all scheduled flights on Sunday, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. An air traffic tracker from Flightradar24 showed no planes over the city.

The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia.

Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until October 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a previous suspension of services to and from the Saudi capital until the end of the month.

Abu Dhabi’s Etihad Airways was among the airlines that further extended Saudi flight cancellations, affecting around 20 flights to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Monday and Tuesday.

The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6% this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity.

The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.

STOCKHOLM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - US academics Robert Hall and Michael Woodford won the 2026 Nobel economics prize on Monday for decades of work developing ground-up models currently used by central banks and finance ministries across the world to stabilise economies.

"With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume," John Hassler, Chair of the Committee for the Prize in Economic Sciences, said in a statement.

Woodford and Hall are frequently name-checked by the world's top central banks which, after a 2022 inflation surge in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, are currently grappling with the energy shock triggered by the Iran war.

One of the laureates' key insights is that economies could only be kept on an even keel by taking into account the millions of decisions made at a micro-level by households and businesses, rather than by using top-down theories of how economies work.

"...Authorities shouldn't view stabilization of the economy as an exercise that is simply conducted by people pulling levers to control the economy independently of what people in the economy understand about this," Columbia University's Woodford, 70, told a news conference.

Another is the "output gap", a measure of demand pressure building up in an economy and how efficiently resources are being used - the goal of stabilisation policy being to steer that gap towards zero.

CORE CENTRAL BANK CONCEPTS

Hall has served as adviser to the US Treasury Department, the Justice Department and the Federal Reserve Board.

His insight in a 1978 paper that household decisions on consumption are a perfect indicator of their expectations was used by Woodford in a model on how consumption is determined.

Woodford also showed that central banks can stimulate or suppress economic activity by adjusting interest rates, rather than just by the amount of money in circulation.

Such concepts remain core to central banking today. Forward guidance became especially important after the 2008 financial crisis, when rates were near zero or even negative and standard monetary policy seemed to be out of ammunition.

Now, however, some are questioning how relevant it is given the amount of uncertainty in the global economy - with new US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh a notable sceptic.

The economics prize, formally known as the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, is the final award to be given out this year and is worth 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

First awarded in 1969, it is not one of the original five awards created in the 1895 will of industrialist and dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, but was established by Sweden's central bank.

The majority of previous laureates have been from the United States. Only three women have ever won, most recently Claudia Goldin in 2023 for work on how gender has affected pay and employment over time in the United States.

Last year's winners, Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt, won for work on "creative destruction" and how new technology and production methods can boost growth and living standards.

headline: Russian troops liberate two communities in Ukraine operation over past day — top brass
summary: Russia's Battlegroup Center units took control over the settlement of Lidino in the DPR and Battlegroup East units - over the settlement of Nikolskoye in the Zaporozhye Region
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated two communities in the Donetsk People’s Republic and the Zaporozhye Region over the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

"Battlegroup Center units liberated the settlement of Lidino in the Donetsk People’s Republic through active operations. <…> Battlegroup East units kept advancing deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlement of Nikolskoye in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said in a statement.

The Ukrainian army lost roughly 1,355 troops in battles with Russian forces in all the frontline areas over the past 24 hours, according to the latest data on the special military operation in Ukraine released by Russia’s Defense Ministry.

The latest figures show that the Ukrainian army lost over 295 troops, an armored personnel carrier and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup North, roughly 220 troops and two armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup West and about 195 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup South.

During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army also lost roughly 330 troops and four armored combat vehicles in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center, over 275 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup East and more than 40 troops and an armored combat vehicle in the responsibility area of the Battlegroup Dnepr, the latest figures show.

Russia’s Battlegroup North forces are fighting for the liberation of four communities in the Kharkov Region and tightening the ring of encirclement of Ukrainian troops in that area, the ministry reported.

"Battlegroup North units are tightening the ring of encirclement in the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. In the pocket of encirclement, they are fighting for the liberation of the communities of Nikolayevka, Varvarovka, Nefyodovka and Chyornoye in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.

During the last 24-hour period, the Ukrainian army lost over 55 troops, a motor vehicle and five ground robotic platforms in the pocket of encirclement, it specified.

Battlegroup North forces are expanding the outer area of control and continue battles for taking control of the settlements of Prikolotnoye, Kotovka and Gogino in the Kharkov Region, the ministry said.

Russia’s Battlegroup North forces inflicted more than 295 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored personnel carrier and two armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.

In the Kharkov direction, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Svetlichnoye, Slatino, Martovoye, Shirokoye, Bugayevka and Veliky Burluk in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.

In the Sumy direction, Battlegroup North units struck formations of two mechanized brigades of the Ukrainian army and three territorial defense brigades in areas near the settlements of Yuryevo, Barilovka, Radkovka, Velikaya Rybitsa and Olshanka in the Sumy Region, it said.

Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 295 personnel, an armored personnel carrier, two armored combat vehicles, eight motor vehicles and a field artillery gun in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the past 24 hours, it specified.

Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted roughly 220 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed two enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.

"Battlegroup West units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of two mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Volchy Yar, Berezovka, Blagodatovka, Tamarganovka, Osinovo, Maleyevka and Grushevka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said.

The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 220 personnel, two armored combat vehicles, nine motor vehicles and two electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it said.

Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted roughly 195 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.

"Battlegroup South units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade, an unmanned systems brigade of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Yasnogorka, Belenkoye, Nikolayevka, Vasilevskaya Pustosh, Druzhkovka, Semyonovka, Kramatorsk and Slavyansk in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.

The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 195 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 23 motor vehicles, two artillery guns and an electronic warfare station in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.

Russia’s Battlegroup Center forces continue advancing in their battles for the liberation of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, the ministry reported.

"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, assault groups of the 51st Army advanced in the town’s central and northwestern parts. Marine infantry formations continued mopping up western quarters of the town and the territory of the Dobropolskaya coalmine," the ministry said.

During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup Center forces thwarted the Ukrainian army’s attempt using up to a platoon of personnel without armor to relieve the surrounded enemy troops, it said.

In the past 24 hours, Battlegroup Center units liberated 216 buildings, including four production structures and eliminated roughly 35 Ukrainian troops in Dobropolye, the ministry said.

Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted roughly 330 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed four enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.

During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup Center units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an airborne brigade of the Ukrainian army and three National Guard brigades in areas near the settlements of Staroraiskoye, Novoandreyevka, Maryevka, Novoyavlenka, Svyatogorovka, Belozerskoye and Vesyolaya Gora in the Donetsk People’s Republic, Andronovka and Tarasovka in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.

The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 330 personnel, four armored combat vehicles, eight motor vehicles, a field artillery gun, two electronic warfare stations and an electronic surveillance system in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.

Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 275 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.

During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, two air assault brigades, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade in areas near the settlements of Ivanovka, Podgavrilovka, Kolomiytsy, Orestopol and Skotovatoye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Vasinovka, Ternovka and Volnyanka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.

The Ukrainian army lost more than 275 personnel, an armored combat vehicle and 12 motor vehicles in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.

Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated more than 40 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past day, the ministry reported.

"Battlegroup Dnepr units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of a mechanized brigade, a mountain assault brigade and an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Orekhov, Kushugum, Zapasnoye and Preobrazhenka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.

"Over 40 Ukrainian military personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 19 motor vehicles and two electronic warfare stations were destroyed," it said.

Russian troops struck transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian army and enemy deployment areas over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.

"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, workshops producing unmanned aerial vehicles and their launch sites, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 149 locations," the ministry said.

Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 646 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and five smart bombs over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.

"Air defense capabilities shot down five guided aerial bombs and 646 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.

Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 259,820 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,202 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,786 multiple rocket launchers, 36,701 field artillery guns and mortars and 74,309 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

headline: IN BRIEF: Kremlin remarks on 'energy truce,' US negotiators’ efforts
summary: Russia wants lasting peace in Ukraine and is ready to do everything necessary to achieve it, Dmitry Peskov pointed out
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. The possibility of an "energy truce," US negotiators’ efforts on Ukraine, and the Nord Stream sabotage investigation were the main topics of Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov’s briefing.

TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.

- The Kremlin cannot comment on the "energy truce" issue at this point: "Communication is ongoing. As soon as we have something to say on the issue, we will certainly inform you."

- Russia wants lasting peace in Ukraine and is ready to do everything necessary to achieve it: "The Kremlin has said repeatedly, and President [of Russia Vladimir] Putin has said so as well, along with officials at other levels: we want lasting peace, not a ceasefire, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it."

- Europe clearly does not belong to the "peace camp" seeking a settlement to the Ukrainian conflict; instead, it is part of the "war camp" that is doing everything it can to prolong the crisis: "The Europeans clearly do not belong to the ‘peace camp,’ which seeks a path to a peaceful settlement [of the conflict in Ukraine]. The Europeans are, rather, the ‘war camp,’ which continues to do everything it can to prevent this conflict from ending."

- Moscow welcomes the work of American negotiators on a peaceful settlement in Ukraine: "We are much more impressed by the efforts of American negotiators. We are grateful to them for pursuing those efforts."

- Russia is not seeking a split between the United States and Europe over the Ukraine conflict but a solution that could help pave the way toward a peaceful settlement: "We aren’t seeking a split here but we are looking for really effective measures and responsible solutions that will enable us to reach a peaceful settlement."

- The Kremlin expects the perpetrators and those behind the Nord Stream pipeline sabotage to be identified during the trial, which is set to begin on October 14: "We expect objectivity. We expect a verdict to be announced. We expect the perpetrators to be named, as well as those who ordered the attack. That would be very important."

- "I think no one has any doubt about who was actually behind it."

- Russian President Vladimir Putin and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev did not discuss the case of 11 Russians detained by Azerbaijan last year during the CIS summit. The 11 Russians remain in detention in Azerbaijan, and Moscow continues to stay in touch with Baku on the issue: "This issue was not discussed at the highest level. However, we are in contact with our Azerbaijani friends on this matter as well."

- Russia genuinely hopes the issue will be resolved soon: "We sincerely hope that this problem, too, will be resolved soon."

analysis.framing: The article presents a curated, verbatim compilation of Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov's briefing statements, foregrounding Russian government positions on peace talks, US negotiators, and the Nord Stream investigation without external context or challenge.

loaded_language.quote: The Europeans are, rather, the ‘war camp,’ which continues to do everything it can to prevent this conflict from ending.
loaded_language.explanation: The phrase 'war camp' is a charged, binary label that frames European actors as deliberately obstructionist rather than as parties with their own security concerns; it is presented as a direct quote without contextualization.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: European countries have continued to support Ukraine militarily, which Russia says prolongs the conflict.

loaded_language.quote: We are much more impressed by the efforts of American negotiators.
loaded_language.explanation: 'Much more impressed' is a subjective, evaluative phrase that signals approval of one set of negotiators over others, introducing a comparative judgment into a summary of diplomatic positions.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: We view the efforts of American negotiators more favorably.

loaded_language.quote: I think no one has any doubt about who was actually behind it.
loaded_language.explanation: This is an insinuating statement that implies a known culprit without naming one, relying on shared assumption rather than evidence; it is left unelaborated in the article.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Russia has previously suggested it knows who was responsible.

loaded_language.quote: we want lasting peace, not a ceasefire, and we are ready to do everything possible to achieve it.
loaded_language.explanation: 'Lasting peace' and 'everything possible' are broad, aspirational phrases that frame Russia's position as maximally constructive without specifying conditions or actions.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: Russia says it seeks a long-term settlement rather than a temporary ceasefire.

omissions: No mention of Ukraine's or European officials' responses to Peskov's 'war camp' characterization.
No context on the status of the 'energy truce' talks or what they would entail.
No reference to international reactions to the Nord Stream investigation or prior findings by other governments.
No mention of ongoing battlefield conditions or recent developments in the war.
No independent verification or challenge to Peskov's claim that Russia is 'ready to do everything possible' for peace.
