headline: Watching Virat Kohli, Steve Smith tackle spin: Australia A star’s secret to dominating India A
body_text:
Nathan McSweeney was the highest scorer for Australia A as they ended their tour of India with a 2-1 win in a 50-over series against India A in Puducherry. McSweeney finished with 194 runs in three innings at an average of 64.66. The 27-year-old spoke about how he prepared for the conditions and it included studying how some of the greats of the game have gone about their business in India.

“I think obviously coming to India as, an Australian, it’s a heavy spin focus and you try and work hard and watch the great Indian players on how they play spin,” McSweeney told the host broadcaster after the white-ball series ended on Sunday.

“[Watching] Virat Kohli on YouTube trying to study how he goes about it, Steve Smith, other Australians that have come over and done really well. So, there’s plenty of analysts and data that we are given as well. So, it’s nice to action that out in the middle and execute it fairly well.”

Widely rated as one of the greatest ODI batsmen of all-time, Kohli is currently enjoying late resurgence in his career. He has played 133 ODIs in India in which he has scored 7035 runs at an average of 62.81 with 28 centuries and 36 half-centuries.

Smith’s ODI record in India may not be consistent with his high standards – 838 runs in 29 matches at an average of 38.09 with one century and six half-centuries – but it’s a different story in Test cricket. In the 10 Tests that Smith has played in India thus far, the 37-year-old has scored 805 runs at an average of 50.31 with three centuries and a half-century. He is set to add to that number later this year when Australia tour India for a five-match Test series.

McSweeney managed to throw India A’s spinners off their lines with his adept footwork. “I’m very pleased to come over here in good conditions and spend some time in the middle, which is always nice and a series win in India is no easy feat by any international team coming over,” McSweeney said. “It’s a very tough place to come and play cricket against tough competition always. So, yeah, well done to our boys and it’s nice to get a series win.”

headline: Saudi Arabia faces new missile and drone fire after major attacks on airports
summary: By Timour AzhariRIYADH, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted.
body_text:
RIYADH, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia said it was facing a new barrage of incoming fire on Monday and that Riyadh airport would remain shut for now, days after Saturday's deadly missile strike on a departure terminal that was claimed by Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis.

Incoming drones and missiles were reported by the Saudi-led coalition backing government forces in Yemen, though there was no immediate news of whether they were intercepted.

The Houthis have been attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities since last week as part of a rapidly escalating conflict that has spilled over from the wider regional conflagration between the United States and Iran.

Those attacks have shut down parts of Saudi airspace,suspending operations at Riyadh airport, and largely emptying the skies over the capital even as the city hosts a major energy conference.

Saudi Arabia now faces a nightmare predicament, havingre-entered Yemen's civil war to push the Houthis from the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait oil route and stop the group making further gains after its sudden advances in September.

With the Yemeni forces Riyadh supports having made some gains against the Houthis around Bab el-Mandeb but still on the back foot on other fronts, Yemeni military sources said, any pressure on the Houthis could take time to pay off.

Saudi Arabia's long-time regional rival Iran offered to mediate between its Houthi allies and the kingdom. "We have repeatedly expressed our readiness to help facilitate dialogue between the parties," foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday.

Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure.

The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans.

UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION

Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals.

"The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said.

Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh; additional reporting by Jana Choukeir and Parisa Hafezi in Dubai; Writing by Angus McDowall; Editing by Toby Chopra)

headline: Lebanon's dark history of assassinations raised after half tonne of explosives seized
summary: The seizure of half a tonne of explosives by Lebanese security forces – the second such incident in a matter of weeks – has sparked uproar in Lebanon, where the country's grim history of political assassinations has risen to the fore again.Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said on Monday that there would be “no leniency” in the investigation and that the government “will not tolerate anyone who dares to toy with the country's security, safety and stability”.About 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4 were discovered in a lorry bound for Beirut when it was stopped at an Internal Security Forces checkpoint at Dahr Al Baidar in the Bekaa Valley, officials said. Two men travelling in the vehicle were detained and the explosives handed over to the army, with the investigation now in the hands of a military court. A senior security source told The National. said the explosive package contained nails and ball bearings. The source said such seizures “were not common” and that there was added concern after the army intercepted a similarly sized package of TNT near the border with Syria two weeks ago.“I understand the anxiety gripping the Lebanese people upon the news of this truck's interception and the materials it was transporting, especially since C4 has been used in several of the infamous political assassinations in modern Lebanese history,” Mr Salam said in a post on X on Monday. In the 2000s and early 2010s, several high-profile opponents of the Assad regime in Syria and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah were killed or had attempts made on their lives using explosives. Former prime minister Rafic Hariri was killed along with 20 others when a one-tonne lorry bomb was detonated as his convoy was driving in Beirut on February 14, 2005. The UN's Special Tribunal for Lebanon has convicted Hezbollah members of that attack.Some in Lebanon are already linking the explosives seizures to Hezbollah, even though officials stress that the investigation is continuing. An official of the Iran-backed political party and armed group did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Mr Salam said Lebanese could “rest assured that we will not relent in pursuing the investigation and expanding it, to identify every individual involved in this criminal operation, those behind them, uncover their plans and objectives, and bring them all to justice to receive the punishment they deserve”.Hezbollah is under intense pressure both internationally and domestically amid a push to disarm. The government banned its military wing earlier this year after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel as part of the wider regional Iran war. Mr Salam's government has also declared its intent – under pressure from the US and Israel – to bring all weapons under state control. The explosives seizures have stirred memories of Lebanon's past political violence. May Chidiac, a journalist and former government minister who survived an assassination attempt in 2005, said her attackers had tried to kill her with a combination of C4 and TNT. “I survived by a miracle, but many of my friends who deserved to live were killed,” she said.

Meanwhile, despite intensified Saudi airstrikes against the group, including what Yemeni television said were hits on al-Jawf province on Monday, the Houthis show no sign of letting up their own barrage of attacks on Saudi infrastructure.

The group has repeatedly threatened to target airports and airspace, as well as Saudi oil installations that provide the engine for the kingdom's economy and its ambitious development plans.

UAE CALLS FOR JOINT GULF ACTION

Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at Monday's conference that the kingdom would stay focused on bringing in investment as part of its wider economic development goals.

"The development of our energy system and industrial capability continues," he said.

Saudi Arabia's neighbour the United Arab Emirates on Monday called for a revival of joint Gulf action on security and defence in response to the attacks. UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the targeting of Saudi Arabia undermined the security of all Gulf states and added that the neglect of collective Gulf security had "emboldened others" to overreach against regional states.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE had been partners in the Yemen conflict for years, but they backed different forces within the Yemeni military coalition supporting the government and fell out last winter.

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Washington was considering joining Saudi Arabia in strikes on the Houthis, but there has been no sign yet of any US action.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh; additional reporting by Jana Choukeir and Parisa Hafezi in Dubai; Writing by Angus McDowall; Editing by Toby Chopra)

The seizure of half a tonne of explosives by Lebanese security forces – the second such incident in a matter of weeks – has sparked uproar in Lebanon, where the country's grim history of political assassinations has risen to the fore again.

Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said on Monday that there would be “no leniency” in the investigation and that the government “will not tolerate anyone who dares to toy with the country's security, safety and stability”.

About 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4 were discovered in a lorry bound for Beirut when it was stopped at an Internal Security Forces checkpoint at Dahr Al Baidar in the Bekaa Valley, officials said. Two men travelling in the vehicle were detained and the explosives handed over to the army, with the investigation now in the hands of a military court.

A senior security source told The National. said the explosive package contained nails and ball bearings. The source said such seizures “were not common” and that there was added concern after the army intercepted a similarly sized package of TNT near the border with Syria two weeks ago.

“I understand the anxiety gripping the Lebanese people upon the news of this truck's interception and the materials it was transporting, especially since C4 has been used in several of the infamous political assassinations in modern Lebanese history,” Mr Salam said in a post on X on Monday.

In the 2000s and early 2010s, several high-profile opponents of the Assad regime in Syria and its Lebanese ally Hezbollah were killed or had attempts made on their lives using explosives. Former prime minister Rafic Hariri was killed along with 20 others when a one-tonne lorry bomb was detonated as his convoy was driving in Beirut on February 14, 2005. The UN's Special Tribunal for Lebanon has convicted Hezbollah members of that attack.

Some in Lebanon are already linking the explosives seizures to Hezbollah, even though officials stress that the investigation is continuing. An official of the Iran-backed political party and armed group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr Salam said Lebanese could “rest assured that we will not relent in pursuing the investigation and expanding it, to identify every individual involved in this criminal operation, those behind them, uncover their plans and objectives, and bring them all to justice to receive the punishment they deserve”.

Hezbollah is under intense pressure both internationally and domestically amid a push to disarm. The government banned its military wing earlier this year after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel as part of the wider regional Iran war. Mr Salam's government has also declared its intent – under pressure from the US and Israel – to bring all weapons under state control.

The explosives seizures have stirred memories of Lebanon's past political violence. May Chidiac, a journalist and former government minister who survived an assassination attempt in 2005, said her attackers had tried to kill her with a combination of C4 and TNT.

“I survived by a miracle, but many of my friends who deserved to live were killed,” she said.

headline: Saudi says resilience tested, vows response after deadly airport attacks
summary: Saudi Arabia's energy minister on Monday said the country had been tested but would mount a "serious" response after a string of attacks on Riyadh's international airport by Yemen's Houthis that left 18 people dead. Lethal airport strikes since last week have rocked the world's top oil exporter, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.
body_text:
Saudi Arabia's energy minister on Monday said the country had been tested but would mount a "serious" response after a string of attacks on Riyadh's international airport by Yemen's Houthis that left 18 people dead.

Lethal airport strikes since last week have rocked the world's top oil exporter, which is pursuing an expensive economic reform drive aimed at attracting foreign investment.

Yemen's civil war, where a Saudi-led military coalition supports the government against the Iran-backed Houthis, has reignited months into the US-Iran conflict that has roiled energy markets and plunged the Middle East into crisis.

"Energy security can't be taken for granted," Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told an energy conference in Riyadh, as oil prices topped $105 a barrel.

"The events of recent weeks are serious, our response must be equally serious."

"For Saudi Arabia, these circumstances have tested our infrastructure, our institutions, our people, and our resilience," he added.

On Saturday, Houthi strikes killed 13 people and wounded hundreds at King Khalid International Airport -- the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in more than a decade.

Four people died in earlier attacks on Wednesday and Thursday, and another was killed on Sunday. Operations remained suspended at the sprawling airport on Riyadh's outskirts on Monday.

CCTV footage of Saturday's attack released by Saudi authorities showed Muslim pilgrims in religious attire waiting in departure lounges before a sudden flash tore through the building and brought down flaming debris.

The atmosphere in Riyadh remained tense on Monday, as state broadcaster Al Ekhbariya said the military coalition was responding to drone and missile threats, and Australia's embassy warned its citizens in the city to shelter in place.

The Houthis on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the previous 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting Saudi transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".

Hours later, the coalition said yet another projectile had struck Riyadh airport, sparking a fire, while air defences intercepted a missile nearby.

AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the capital on Sunday.

"The whole house shook," said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the city's north.

Riyadh's airport was not the only one to suffer a deadly attack: early on Monday, officials said one person had been killed and 11 wounded in a strike on Dammam airport.

The Saudi-led coalition said Monday that it had also "intercepted and destroyed" a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.

Riyadh hosts a packed calendar of events at this time of year, including its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference, which draws foreign leaders and business titans.

Despite vast spending on military hardware, the Houthi attacks on oil, military and transport facilities across the large, mostly desert country are stretching Saudi defences.

"Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it's simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves," said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.

The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday's attack a "full-fledged war crime" and vowed to "respond decisively".

The attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

Iran, which backs the Houthis, said Monday it was "deeply concerned" over the recent escalation.

Witnesses to Saturday's strike described chaos in the aftermath.

"Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood," a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.

Ottawa University's Juneau said the Houthis now "want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them".

headline: Newsweek magazine puts out shortlist of candidates who could unseat Zelensky

body_text:
NEW YORK, October 12. /TASS/. Newsweek has put out a shortlist of candidates who could replace Vladimir Zelensky amid US President Donald Trump's calls for a change of power in Kiev.

According to Newsweek, the main contenders are former Ukraine’s Commander-in-Chief, now ambassador to the United Kingdom Valery Zaluzhny, former head of the General Staff Kirill Budanov, former Defense Minister Mikhail Fyodorov and former Ukrainian President Pyotr Poroshenko with Zaluzhny named as the most likely to unseat Zelensky if an election were to take place. According to a Rating Group survey, 64% of respondents trust Zaluzhny compared to 53% trusting Zelensky. Almost 23% of respondents would vote for Zelensky, while more than 20% for Zaluzhny.

Budanov's trust rating stands at about 53%, and Fyodorov's at 38%. 7.6% of respondents are ready to vote for Fyodorov in the first round, while 6.7% are ready to vote for Budanov.

Poroshenko, who served as the country's president in 2014-2019, remains an active opposition MP, according to the magazine. In 2025, Zelensky imposed sanctions against him, including asset freezes, on grounds related to national security.

Last week Trump said Ukraine has to hold elections, with The Wall Street Journal suggesting this showed how deep the schism in relations with Zelensky had gotten, almost as bad as last winter, when the two very publicly quarrelled in the Oval Office. The Financial Times quoted unnamed European officials as saying that the US presidential administration is threatening to stop the arms procurement program and the provision of intelligence information to Ukraine.

Axios quoted White House sources as saying that Trump is angry with Zelensky and expects Kiev to stop attacks on Russian refineries. Trump believes that the cost of fuel in the United States is rising because of these strikes, and is angry that Zelensky takes Washington's support for Kiev for granted.

body_text:
European foreign ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Monday agreed to establish a support mission to the Lebanese army with an initial mandate of three years.

The mission will work to strengthen the capacity of the Lebanese army and the Internal Security Forces, as well as to support maritime security, the European Council said in a statement.

The training mission is part of a European effort to retain an international presence in Lebanon after the UN Interim Force withdraws on December 31. Unifil has been deployed on the southern border with Israel since 1978, at the start of a 22-year Israeli occupation of south Lebanon.

South Lebanon faces security gap as Unifil withdrawal nears

“Europe is invested in Lebanon's future,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. “With this new mission – a major update of our security ties – we continue to support the country’s institutions in restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people.”

The European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, will co-ordinate closely with the UN and other international partners supporting Lebanon's security sector, the European Council said.

Support for the army will include land border surveillance and control, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-smuggling and operational co-ordination. The ISF will be trained in areas such as combating cybercrime and smuggling.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the EU mission would replace the army to support the Lebanese police in their day-to-day duties, so that it could focus on its core work.

Dylan Macchiarini Crosson, EU researcher at think tank International Crisis Group, said that while EUSM Lebanon would not replace Unifil, it would be a centrepiece of the bloc's engagement in the country.

He called on the EU to deploy quickly, building on the €160 million in military assistance it has provided over the past three years.

“Yet the mission does not directly address the core security concern for Lebanon and its international partners: maintaining an international presence in the south to support the Lebanese state, prevent Hezbollah’s military resurgence and deter further Israeli intervention,” Mr Crosson said.

“The initiative nevertheless gives the EU more entry points. It should use its channels and leverage to press Israel and Hezbollah to abide by the ceasefire, advocate for a reconstituted international force in the south – perhaps one led by some EU member states – and expand humanitarian and development assistance.”

France and Italy are looking into establishing a separate mission to help the Lebanese army disarm Hezbollah, but this has yet to take shape. European states have no intention of directly being in charge of disarming the pro-Iran militia, which kept its weapons after the end of the civil war in 1990 to fight the Israeli occupation.

The hope is that disarming Hezbollah would encourage the withdrawal of Israel, which currently occupies roughly 7 per cent of southern Lebanese territory and has destroyed a number of villages to establish a so-called buffer zone. US-brokered peace talks have stalled as Israel says it will withdraw only if Hezbollah disarms but Lebanon wants Israel to withdraw first.

Western states have long pressured the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah, which they consider a terrorist organisation. But Lebanese politicians have lacked the political will – Hezbollah being represented in arliament – to pit the historically weak Lebanese army against the regional militia's powerful military arsenal.

analysis.framing: The article frames the EU's new support mission for the Lebanese army as a timely response to the looming Unifil withdrawal, while noting expert skepticism about whether it addresses core security concerns.

NEW YORK, October 12. /TASS/. Newsweek has put out a shortlist of candidates who could replace Vladimir Zelensky amid US President Donald Trump's calls for a change of power in Kiev.

Budanov's trust rating stands at about 53%, and Fyodorov's at 38%. 7.6% of respondents are ready to vote for Fyodorov in the first round, while 6.7% are ready to vote for Budanov.

Poroshenko, who served as the country's president in 2014-2019, remains an active opposition MP, according to the magazine. In 2025, Zelensky imposed sanctions against him, including asset freezes, on grounds related to national security.

Last week Trump said Ukraine has to hold elections, with The Wall Street Journal suggesting this showed how deep the schism in relations with Zelensky had gotten, almost as bad as last winter, when the two very publicly quarrelled in the Oval Office. The Financial Times quoted unnamed European officials as saying that the US presidential administration is threatening to stop the arms procurement program and the provision of intelligence information to Ukraine.

Axios quoted White House sources as saying that Trump is angry with Zelensky and expects Kiev to stop attacks on Russian refineries. Trump believes that the cost of fuel in the United States is rising because of these strikes, and is angry that Zelensky takes Washington's support for Kiev for granted.

body_text:
European foreign ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Monday agreed to establish a support mission to the Lebanese army with an initial mandate of three years.

The mission will work to strengthen the capacity of the Lebanese army and the Internal Security Forces, as well as to support maritime security, the European Council said in a statement.

The training mission is part of a European effort to retain an international presence in Lebanon after the UN Interim Force withdraws on December 31. Unifil has been deployed on the southern border with Israel since 1978, at the start of a 22-year Israeli occupation of south Lebanon.

South Lebanon faces security gap as Unifil withdrawal nears

“Europe is invested in Lebanon's future,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said. “With this new mission – a major update of our security ties – we continue to support the country’s institutions in restoring full sovereignty and building lasting stability for the Lebanese people.”

The European Union Support Mission in Lebanon, or EUSM Lebanon, will co-ordinate closely with the UN and other international partners supporting Lebanon's security sector, the European Council said.

Support for the army will include land border surveillance and control, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, counter-smuggling and operational co-ordination. The ISF will be trained in areas such as combating cybercrime and smuggling.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the EU mission would replace the army to support the Lebanese police in their day-to-day duties, so that it could focus on its core work.

Dylan Macchiarini Crosson, EU researcher at think tank International Crisis Group, said that while EUSM Lebanon would not replace Unifil, it would be a centrepiece of the bloc's engagement in the country.

He called on the EU to deploy quickly, building on the €160 million in military assistance it has provided over the past three years.

“Yet the mission does not directly address the core security concern for Lebanon and its international partners: maintaining an international presence in the south to support the Lebanese state, prevent Hezbollah’s military resurgence and deter further Israeli intervention,” Mr Crosson said.

“The initiative nevertheless gives the EU more entry points. It should use its channels and leverage to press Israel and Hezbollah to abide by the ceasefire, advocate for a reconstituted international force in the south – perhaps one led by some EU member states – and expand humanitarian and development assistance.”

France and Italy are looking into establishing a separate mission to help the Lebanese army disarm Hezbollah, but this has yet to take shape. European states have no intention of directly being in charge of disarming the pro-Iran militia, which kept its weapons after the end of the civil war in 1990 to fight the Israeli occupation.

The hope is that disarming Hezbollah would encourage the withdrawal of Israel, which currently occupies roughly 7 per cent of southern Lebanese territory and has destroyed a number of villages to establish a so-called buffer zone. US-brokered peace talks have stalled as Israel says it will withdraw only if Hezbollah disarms but Lebanon wants Israel to withdraw first.

Western states have long pressured the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah, which they consider a terrorist organisation. But Lebanese politicians have lacked the political will – Hezbollah being represented in arliament – to pit the historically weak Lebanese army against the regional militia's powerful military arsenal.

headline: Saudi crown prince moves between bunker-equipped palaces amid Houthi attacks — media
summary: Amid intensifying Houthi attacks, Saudi Arabia is searching worldwide for air defense systems and has asked its military ally Pakistan for help, The Wall Street Journal reported
body_text:
NEW YORK, October 12. /TASS/. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud is moving between heavily guarded palaces equipped with bunkers amid attacks by Yemen’s Houthi movement, Ansar Allah, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.

According to the newspaper, the crown prince last appeared in public on Tuesday, when he donated blood as part of a national donation drive. Since then, he has been shuttling between bunker-equipped palaces under heightened security. A handpicked security team personally selected by the crown prince is providing his protection, the newspaper reported, citing officials familiar with his movements.

Amid intensifying Houthi attacks, Saudi Arabia is searching worldwide for air defense systems and has asked its military ally Pakistan for help, the newspaper reported, citing people familiar with the kingdom’s deliberations. Riyadh is also seeking to recruit foreign fighters to support its Yemeni allies. At the same time, the kingdom is increasingly pursuing a diplomatic solution to the conflict, which otherwise appears difficult to contain, according to the report.

On October 10, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation reported that at least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Riyadh Airport. On October 11, the authority reported another attack that left several people injured. On the same day, Ansar Allah acknowledged that it had carried out "four large-scale operations using ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones" over a 24-hour period.

Armed conflict between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has continued in Yemen since August 2014. In July, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, putting Red Sea shipping at risk, and subsequently attacked several Saudi-owned oil tankers. In early August, Ansar Allah launched an offensive in southwestern Yemen. On September 10-11, the movement took control of the port city of Mocha and other key positions along the coast, heightening the threat to Saudi oil shipments through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. On October 4, Yemeni government forces announced the launch of a major military operation to retake territories held by the rebels.

headline: Netherlands uses Kiev battlefield data to train own troops — Defense Ministry
summary: According to Dilan Yesilgoz-Zegerius, while initially partner countries were "trying to help" Ukraine, now they themselves are learning from Kiev and using its experience to develop their own armies
body_text:
THE HAGUE, October 12. /TASS/. The Dutch armed forces is using Ukraine's experience in the conflict with Russia to train its own military personnel, said Defense Minister Dilan Yesilgoz-Zegerius.

"Our armed forces are really training as we speak every day with the knowledge the Ukrainians have," she told the Warsaw Security Forum. According to Yesilgoz-Zegerius, while initially partner countries were "trying to help" Ukraine, now they themselves are learning from Kiev and using its experience to develop their own armies.

Earlier in October, the Dutch Defense Ministry said that the country receives data from Ukraine on the operational use of military systems, which can be used to develop, train and improve artificial intelligence (AI) models. It was noted that agreements on intellectual property rights to AI models, algorithms and other technologies created or improved using Ukrainian operational data remain a subject of discussion. Kiev offers to transfer part of the data to Dutch companies and research organizations.

The comments from Yesilgoz-Zegerius come as the kingdom builds up a large·scale military potential. According to the draft budget presented by the government on September 15, 28.9 billion euros are to be allocated to defense needs in 2027. By 2030, the Defense Ministry expects to increase the number of its personnel -- including military personnel, reservists and civilian staff -- to more than 100,000. The agency attributes the need to build up military potential, in particular, by claiming "threats" from Russia.

Moscow has repeatedly denied claims about its desire to attack NATO countries. Russian President Vladimir Putin described such statements by Western politicians as an attempt to intimidate their population and justify an increase in military spending. Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that the alliance is following the path of "reckless militarization," and the image of Russia as a threat is being used to justify the decision to increase the defense spending of the bloc’s member states to 5% of GDP.

headline: Adieu aux ‘Enfants Rouges’: Tears and shock as fire destroys Paris’s oldest covered food market
summary: A devastating blaze destroyed the French capital’s oldest covered food market in the early hours of Monday, stripping Paris of a cherished venue popular with locals and tourists alike. Traders and residents said the destruction of the Enfants Rouges market, named after a 16th-century orphanage, had left them feeling “orphaned” themselves.
body_text:
A devastating blaze destroyed the French capital’s oldest covered food market in the early hours of Monday, stripping Paris of a cherished venue popular with locals and tourists alike. Traders and residents said the destruction of the Enfants Rouges market, named after a 16th-century orphanage, had left them feeling “orphaned” themselves.

New Yorkers Lorrie and Ricky so enjoyed discovering the Marché des Enfants Rouges (Red children’s market) a few days ago, that they decided to pay another visit to its celebrated food stalls before leaving the French capital.

But when they approached the centuries-old venue on Monday morning, they were greeted by police cordons, fire trucks and a foul, acrid smell hanging over this picturesque neighbourhood in central Paris.

“It was such a lovely place, so charming – and now it’s gone,” said Ricky, gazing at the blackened entrance to the Enfants Rouges. “It’s tragic.”

Read moreFire destroys Paris's oldest covered food market

A spectacular blaze tore through the iconic covered market overnight, gutting its iron and glass roof and torching all 17 food stalls. Video footage on social media showed huge flames and billowing smoke rising above the venue, hemmed in between buildings on the northern edge of the Marais district popular with tourists.

After touring the site, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the market had been “completely destroyed”. He thanked firefighters who battled the blaze for over two hours – for ensuring that it did not spread to surrounding buildings in the densely populated area known for its cozy cafes and stylish boutiques.

There were no casualties aside from a firefighter who suffered “minor injuries”, Grégoire told reporters. It was the only consolation for shopkeepers huddled together on a sidewalk – many in tears as they listened to accounts of the devastation wrought by the flames.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

“We’re all a big family, and now we’ve been orphaned,” said Ahmed Ouaddi, whose Moroccan couscous stall had been a fixture of the market for decades. “Our livelihoods have gone up in smoke.”

Founded in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII, the Enfants Rouges was the oldest covered market still in operation in Paris. It owed its name to a nearby 16th-century orphanage whose young residents wore red clothing, a symbol of Christian charity at the time.

A buzzing hub for locals and tourists alike, the market offered fresh produce and specialties from around the world. The industry magazine Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, Mexico City and France’s culinary capital – Lyon.

To those nostalgic for the Paris of old, it provided a small taste of what the historic Les Halles, the city’s sprawling central market, was like before it was gutted and turned into a giant mall in the 1970s.

In recent years, the Enfants Rouges had become too touristy – and pricey – for many Parisians, in step with the area’s rapid gentrification. But it remained “the heart and soul” of the neighbourhood, said Ouaddi.

“It was the oldest and prettiest market in Paris. We all loved it and we’re all in shock today,” said local pharmacist Virginie Prulhière, still shaken from the blaze, her voice breaking as she gazed at the fire truck parked where her partner’s stall would normally be standing.

“It was also a symbol of resistance, because people here fought to preserve it,” she added, referring to a grassroots campaign in the 1990s against plans to tear down the market and replace it with an underground carpark and housing units.

Residents looked on in disbelief Monday morning as firefighters accompanied the Paris mayor and other officials to inspect the smouldering ruins. Some asked why it had not been possible to save at least part of the structure, noting that the nearest fire station is located just minutes away.

Local authorities said the fire broke out at 3am (01:00 GMT) but the fire brigade did not receive a call until over an hour later. More than 150 firefighters and dozens of vehicles were mobilised to battle the blaze. Their efforts were hampered by the layout of the market, surrounded by buildings on all sides and accessible only through alleyways too narrow for most vehicles.

The cause of the blaze is not yet known.

Read moreSounding the fire alarm: Why French firefighters are on strike

“Luckily, no one was hurt, and that’s the most important thing,” said Alexis Abbou, the market’s manager, striving to remain upbeat as he sought to console its shopkeepers and caterers. “We’ll start all over again and rebuild this wonderful place,” he added.

Paris Mayor Grégoire promised to find a temporary relocation for the traders “so they can resume their business as soon as possible”. In a post on X, Serge Papin, the minister for small businesses and tourism, said the French state would “stand alongside Paris City Hall to help with reconstruction”.

Ariel Weil, mayor of the third arrondissement (district) that housed the market, also recalled the fight to save the market in the 1990s, as he vowed to restore it to its former glory.

“The Enfants Rouges survived a threat to replace it with a carpark,” he said. “It will survive this fire, too.”

headline: UK PM Burnham says Iran's IRGC likely behind RAF Fairford incident
summary: LONDON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.The RAF Fairford base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran but last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of the planes.U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.
body_text:
LONDON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The RAF Fairford base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran but last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of the planes.

U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," Burnham told parliament.

The alleged plot came to light when five British men were arrested in the early hours of September 27 by three vans near the base on ​suspected terrorism and explosive offences.

They were later released without charge on ‌police ⁠bail "under stringent conditions". Police said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in the vans, and detectives said they were considering ​whether a foreign ​state had ⁠been involved.

Two other men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been arrested and released.

"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."

Iran has rejected any suggestion it was involved in the incident at Fairford, saying it amounted to "unfounded and malicious ​speculations".

The British authorities have accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots in Britain.

In July, Britain used new powers designed to stop the use of state-sponsored proxies to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group accused of being behind attacks at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media.

(Reporting by Sam Tobin; writing by Michael Holden; editing by Kate Holton)

headline: AI could boost Asian growth but widen regional divide: IMF
summary: Advanced economies expected to adopt AI earlier, while emerging markets could face delays of 1 to 2 decades
body_text:
Anadolu Ajansı © 2026

Artificial intelligence could add as much as 1 percentage point to annual growth in advanced Asian economies over the long term but risks widening regional disparities, according to an International Monetary Fund study.

The IMF working paper, AI and Economic Divergence in Asia, examines how differences in capital, skills, productivity and digital infrastructure could affect countries’ ability to adopt the technology.

The study estimates that AI could raise average annual growth by 0.5 to 1 percentage point in advanced Asian economies and by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point in emerging-market and developing economies, depending on the pace of technological progress.

Advanced economies such as Singapore and South Korea are positioned to adopt AI faster because of their strong digital infrastructure, skilled workforces and access to capital.

Many emerging Asian economies, however, could begin widespread adoption one or two decades later, with substantially longer delays possible in low-income countries.

Before adoption accelerates, emerging and developing economies could record annual growth about 0.5 to 0.6 percentage point lower than under a scenario without the global AI transition.

The divergence could become self-reinforcing as early adopters attract investment and accumulate capital faster. Stronger global demand for capital could also raise interest rates, making it more difficult for late adopters to finance the infrastructure needed to catch up.

The findings are based on model simulations rather than economic forecasts and depend heavily on the assumed speed of technological development.

The paper also found that AI could reshape employment because the technology is capital-intensive and favors skilled labor, potentially reducing labor’s overall share of income.

The study was highlighted as the IMF and World Bank opened their annual meetings in Bangkok, where AI’s effects on productivity, employment and inequality are among the main topics.

Its current capacity is equal to about seven days of average winter demand. Centrica, the owner of British Gas, has warned that its Rough storage facility could close when its operating consent expires in April, unless the government backs its plans for the site. The company has proposed investing £2 billion ($2.64 billion) to redevelop the site, which accounts for about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity.Britain is unlikely to run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House.“The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said.Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”.European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf.The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group.“It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters.Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels.EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves.Britain’s electricity system is also under pressure. The National Energy System Operator issued a precautionary margin notice on October 6 as weak wind generation tightened available supplies, highlighting continued reliance on gas-fired power.A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further.Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high.The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.
body_text:
Britain faces a prolonged energy squeeze as European gas prices surge more than 150 per cent this year and dwindling reserves threaten to keep costs high through winter.

The price rise brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on its fragile economy before the October 28 Budget.

Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas.

Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to just 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity is equal to about seven days of average winter demand.

Centrica, the owner of British Gas, has warned that its Rough storage facility could close when its operating consent expires in April, unless the government backs its plans for the site. The company has proposed investing £2 billion ($2.64 billion) to redevelop the site, which accounts for about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity.

Britain is unlikely to run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House.

“The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said.

Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”.

European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf.

The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group.

“It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters.

Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels.

EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March.

In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves.

Britain’s electricity system is also under pressure. The National Energy System Operator issued a precautionary margin notice on October 6 as weak wind generation tightened available supplies, highlighting continued reliance on gas-fired power.

A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further.

Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high.

The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

headline: Saudi Arabia faces challenge of repeated and simultaneous attacks
summary: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have demonstrated that its build-up of batteries of air defence must stretch to all corners of the country. Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest Patriot operator, said Nawaf Obaid of King’s College London’s Department of War Studies.“Saudi Arabia does not lack air defences,” he told The National. “It possesses one of the world’s most sophisticated integrated air and missile defence architectures, protecting a country larger than Western Europe.“The fundamental challenge is that no existing system, including those protecting the United States, can guarantee the interception of repeated, simultaneous attacks involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.”The kingdom is buying seven batteries of Thaad (Terminal High Altitude Area Defence), the largest programme outside the US, he added. The extensive use of missile interceptors during the Iran war has meant there is a need for renewed stocks, experts have told The National.Despite having the world’s second-largest air defence system, 13 people were killed when King Khalid International Airport was struck by what are thought to have been ballistic missiles, causing widespread damage and leaving 308 wounded.Countries around the world will now be looking at how to defend airports, but experts suggest close-in defence will be nearly impossible, given the number and size of civilian and military sites that could be attacked.“An attack like the one we saw on Saturday on Riyadh Airport would in normal circumstances have been met with lavish application of Thaad at high altitude and Patriot on incoming,” said Dr Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer.“But what is clear is that Thaad and Patriot are not available in quantity and we’re seeing leakage.”Interceptor expenditureMilitary analyst Francis Tusa said the scale of interceptor expenditure during the war had put significant pressure on American stocks, with consequences for allies globally.During one attack on a US airbase in Jordan, it is estimated up to 80 Patriots were fired in one night, leading to a rapid dwindling of the stockpile, he said. “The generals have told Trump that ‘we haven’t got the rounds left’.”There is also the issue of the rebel Houthis' improving arsenal that includes manoeuvring ballistic missiles. The Iranian-derived Palestine-2 has a range of about 2,000km and hypersonic capabilities, including manoeuvrability, making interception more difficult during its terminal phase.The US has expended an estimated 1,500 Patriots and has about 800 left. Saudi Arabia had more than 1,800 Patriot interceptors and has used a large number defending itself from Iran and the Houthis.Saudi arsenalOther defences include the South Korean KM-SAM, a medium-range system also owned by the UAE that is designed to intercept aircraft and incoming missiles.British frustration Saudi Arabia requested further defensive support from Britain's ministry of defence in the weeks leading up to the current attacks but the requests failed to secure ministerial approval. Saudi Arabian counterparts were left frustrated at the UK inaction. body_text:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have demonstrated that its build-up of batteries of air defence must stretch to all corners of the country.

Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest Patriot operator, said Nawaf Obaid of King’s College London’s Department of War Studies.

“Saudi Arabia does not lack air defences,” he told The National. “It possesses one of the world’s most sophisticated integrated air and missile defence architectures, protecting a country larger than Western Europe.

Pilot, flight attendant and widow among victims of Houthi attacks

“The fundamental challenge is that no existing system, including those protecting the United States, can guarantee the interception of repeated, simultaneous attacks involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.”

The kingdom is buying seven batteries of Thaad (Terminal High Altitude Area Defence), the largest programme outside the US, he added. The extensive use of missile interceptors during the Iran war has meant there is a need for renewed stocks, experts have told The National.

Despite having the world’s second-largest air defence system, 13 people were killed when King Khalid International Airport was struck by what are thought to have been ballistic missiles, causing widespread damage and leaving 308 wounded.

Countries around the world will now be looking at how to defend airports, but experts suggest close-in defence will be nearly impossible, given the number and size of civilian and military sites that could be attacked.

“An attack like the one we saw on Saturday on Riyadh Airport would in normal circumstances have been met with lavish application of Thaad at high altitude and Patriot on incoming,” said Dr Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer.

“But what is clear is that Thaad and Patriot are not available in quantity and we’re seeing leakage.”

Military analyst Francis Tusa said the scale of interceptor expenditure during the war had put significant pressure on American stocks, with consequences for allies globally.

During one attack on a US airbase in Jordan, it is estimated up to 80 Patriots were fired in one night, leading to a rapid dwindling of the stockpile, he said. “The generals have told Trump that ‘we haven’t got the rounds left’.”

There is also the issue of the rebel Houthis' improving arsenal that includes manoeuvring ballistic missiles. The Iranian-derived Palestine-2 has a range of about 2,000km and hypersonic capabilities, including manoeuvrability, making interception more difficult during its terminal phase.

The US has expended an estimated 1,500 Patriots and has about 800 left. Saudi Arabia had more than 1,800 Patriot interceptors and has used a large number defending itself from Iran and the Houthis.

Other defences include the South Korean KM-SAM, a medium-range system also owned by the UAE that is designed to intercept aircraft and incoming missiles.

Saudi Arabia requested further defensive support from Britain's ministry of defence in the weeks leading up to the current attacks but the requests failed to secure ministerial approval. Saudi Arabian counterparts were left frustrated at the UK inaction.

The UK has contributed, with its Sky Sabre system providing a medium-range defensive layer using Common Anti-Air Modular Missiles, surveillance radar and integrated command-and-control systems, Mr Obaid said.

British industry can offer other options, which can be used for “point defence”, to stop close-in threats.

“The UK has got the Starstreak high-velocity missile, with 8km to 9km range, and is unjammable,” said Mr Tusa, editor of Defence Eye. “It’s also probably £100,000 [$132,300] a shot.”

The £40,000 Martlet missile, which uses a high-explosive warhead rather than Starstreak’s three tungsten darts, is another comparatively inexpensive option, he said.

As a vast country with considerable infrastructure, Saudi Arabia’s commanders have to decide where best to position radars and interceptors without being able to protect everywhere.

The resources for a single site are significant. “For Patriot, you’d normally get one, maybe two radars, two command systems, and four to six missile launchers,” Mr Tusa said.

Dr Nusbacher also questioned why commercial airports in the Middle East should be expected to have dedicated close-in air defence when comparable facilities in the West do not.

“Heathrow doesn’t have close-in air defence, and why would you expect King Khalid Airport to have close-in air defence?” she said.

Until recently, there was little expectation that Gulf states would face sustained attacks, she added. But the changing picture is now forcing a “major reassessment” of how civilian infrastructure should be protected.

Robert Tollast, a military analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said defending one site could also leave others exposed.

There is a risk of “putting so much resource into interceptors around that facility that you leave other critical areas uncovered”, he said. Destroying energy infrastructure outside the summer months “could also be disastrous”.

One response would be to improve intelligence and attack missile launchers before they fire, as Saudi Arabia depends heavily on US satellite intelligence.

Given the scale of the emergency, US manufacturers are attempting to increase interceptor production – an estimated 2,000 Thaad and Patriots have been fired this year – but replenishing stocks could take up to 30 months.

Dr Nusbacher said defence planners had not anticipated the “profligate use of high-value, exquisite air defence systems” during a war “lasting more than a few weeks”.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as exposing fundamental limitations in even the world's most sophisticated air defense systems, emphasizing the strategic dilemma of defending vast territory against evolving missile threats.

Vague term that implies failure or breach without specifying the nature or extent of the problem, potentially sensationalizing the situation.

headline: PKK pulls out of Metina in northern Iraq amid Turkey peace process
summary: The withdrawal comes as the peace process between Turkey and the militant group gains momentum alongside increasing security cooperation between Ankara and Baghdad.
body_text:
ANKARA — The Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) has withdrawn from four areas in northern Iraq as part of an ongoing peace process aimed at ending more than four decades of conflict between Turkey and the militant group, according to Turkish security sources.

The PKK, which is headquartered in the northern Iraqi mountains, has waged an armed insurgency against Turkey since 1984 for Kurdish self-rule inside the country. It announced in May 2025 that it would disband and dissolve itself as part of ongoing peace talks the Turkish government launched in 2024. The militant group is considered a terror outfit by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

What happened: The PKK completed its evacuation of four positions in the Metina region near the Turkish border last Thursday, Turkey’s public broadcaster TRT and state-run Anadolu Agency said, citing security sources on Monday. Metina has frequently been the scene of clashes between Turkish forces and the PKK.

The move came as part of ongoing efforts to evacuate areas “considered to pose a risk of conflict for Turkey’s security,” Turkish security sources said, in a statement carried by Anadolu and the TRT.

New Yorkers Lorrie and Ricky so enjoyed discovering the Marché des Enfants Rouges (Red children’s market) a few days ago, that they decided to pay another visit to its celebrated food stalls before leaving the French capital.

But when they approached the centuries-old venue on Monday morning, they were greeted by police cordons, fire trucks and a foul, acrid smell hanging over this picturesque neighbourhood in central Paris.

“It was such a lovely place, so charming – and now it’s gone,” said Ricky, gazing at the blackened entrance to the Enfants Rouges. “It’s tragic.”

Read moreFire destroys Paris's oldest covered food market

A spectacular blaze tore through the iconic covered market overnight, gutting its iron and glass roof and torching all 17 food stalls. Video footage on social media showed huge flames and billowing smoke rising above the venue, hemmed in between buildings on the northern edge of the Marais district popular with tourists.

After touring the site, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the market had been “completely destroyed”. He thanked firefighters who battled the blaze for over two hours – for ensuring that it did not spread to surrounding buildings in the densely populated area known for its cozy cafes and stylish boutiques.

There were no casualties aside from a firefighter who suffered “minor injuries”, Grégoire told reporters. It was the only consolation for shopkeepers huddled together on a sidewalk – many in tears as they listened to accounts of the devastation wrought by the flames.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

“We’re all a big family, and now we’ve been orphaned,” said Ahmed Ouaddi, whose Moroccan couscous stall had been a fixture of the market for decades. “Our livelihoods have gone up in smoke.”

Founded in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII, the Enfants Rouges was the oldest covered market still in operation in Paris. It owed its name to a nearby 16th-century orphanage whose young residents wore red clothing, a symbol of Christian charity at the time.

A buzzing hub for locals and tourists alike, the market offered fresh produce and specialties from around the world. The industry magazine Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, Mexico City and France’s culinary capital – Lyon.

To those nostalgic for the Paris of old, it provided a small taste of what the historic Les Halles, the city’s sprawling central market, was like before it was gutted and turned into a giant mall in the 1970s.

In recent years, the Enfants Rouges had become too touristy – and pricey – for many Parisians, in step with the area’s rapid gentrification. But it remained “the heart and soul” of the neighbourhood, said Ouaddi.

“It was the oldest and prettiest market in Paris. We all loved it and we’re all in shock today,” said local pharmacist Virginie Prulhière, still shaken from the blaze, her voice breaking as she gazed at the fire truck parked where her partner’s stall would normally be standing.

“It was also a symbol of resistance, because people here fought to preserve it,” she added, referring to a grassroots campaign in the 1990s against plans to tear down the market and replace it with an underground carpark and housing units.

Residents looked on in disbelief Monday morning as firefighters accompanied the Paris mayor and other officials to inspect the smouldering ruins. Some asked why it had not been possible to save at least part of the structure, noting that the nearest fire station is located just minutes away.

Local authorities said the fire broke out at 3am (01:00 GMT) but the fire brigade did not receive a call until over an hour later. More than 150 firefighters and dozens of vehicles were mobilised to battle the blaze. Their efforts were hampered by the layout of the market, surrounded by buildings on all sides and accessible only through alleyways too narrow for most vehicles.

The cause of the blaze is not yet known.

Read moreSounding the fire alarm: Why French firefighters are on strike

“Luckily, no one was hurt, and that’s the most important thing,” said Alexis Abbou, the market’s manager, striving to remain upbeat as he sought to console its shopkeepers and caterers. “We’ll start all over again and rebuild this wonderful place,” he added.

Paris Mayor Grégoire promised to find a temporary relocation for the traders “so they can resume their business as soon as possible”. In a post on X, Serge Papin, the minister for small businesses and tourism, said the French state would “stand alongside Paris City Hall to help with reconstruction”.

Ariel Weil, mayor of the third arrondissement (district) that housed the market, also recalled the fight to save the market in the 1990s, as he vowed to restore it to its former glory.

“The Enfants Rouges survived a threat to replace it with a carpark,” he said. “It will survive this fire, too.”

headline: UK PM Burnham says Iran's IRGC likely behind RAF Fairford incident
summary: LONDON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.The RAF Fairford base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran but last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of the planes.U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.
body_text:
LONDON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford air base in Britain was "highly likely" to have been coordinated in Iran, and almost certainly directed by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The RAF Fairford base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran but last week, US President Donald Trump said a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of the planes.

U.S. officials have told Reuters that there had been a suspected plot involving Iran to launch a drone attack.

"I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard (IRGC)," Burnham told parliament.

The alleged plot came to light when five British men were arrested in the early hours of September 27 by three vans near the base on ​suspected terrorism and explosive offences.

They were later released without charge on ‌police ⁠bail "under stringent conditions". Police said petrol but no viable explosive had been found in the vans, and detectives said they were considering ​whether a foreign ​state had ⁠been involved.

Two other men, including a British-Iranian national, have also been arrested and released.

"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil," Burnham said. "We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams, and we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity of Iran and the IRGC to do us harm."

Iran has rejected any suggestion it was involved in the incident at Fairford, saying it amounted to "unfounded and malicious ​speculations".

The British authorities have accused Iran of being involved in numerous plots in Britain.

In July, Britain used new powers designed to stop the use of state-sponsored proxies to ban support for the IRGC and a linked group accused of being behind attacks at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media.

(Reporting by Sam Tobin; writing by Michael Holden; editing by Kate Holton)

headline: AI could boost Asian growth but widen regional divide: IMF
summary: Advanced economies expected to adopt AI earlier, while emerging markets could face delays of 1 to 2 decades
body_text:
Artificial intelligence could add as much as 1 percentage point to annual growth in advanced Asian economies over the long term but risks widening regional disparities, according to an International Monetary Fund study.

The IMF working paper, AI and Economic Divergence in Asia, examines how differences in capital, skills, productivity and digital infrastructure could affect countries’ ability to adopt the technology.

The study estimates that AI could raise average annual growth by 0.5 to 1 percentage point in advanced Asian economies and by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point in emerging-market and developing economies, depending on the pace of technological progress.

Advanced economies such as Singapore and South Korea are positioned to adopt AI faster because of their strong digital infrastructure, skilled workforces and access to capital.

Many emerging Asian economies, however, could begin widespread adoption one or two decades later, with substantially longer delays possible in low-income countries.

Before adoption accelerates, emerging and developing economies could record annual growth about 0.5 to 0.6 percentage point lower than under a scenario without the global AI transition.

The divergence could become self-reinforcing as early adopters attract investment and accumulate capital faster. Stronger global demand for capital could also raise interest rates, making it more difficult for late adopters to finance the infrastructure needed to catch up.

The findings are based on model simulations rather than economic forecasts and depend heavily on the assumed speed of technological development.

The paper also found that AI could reshape employment because the technology is capital-intensive and favors skilled labor, potentially reducing labor’s overall share of income.

The study was highlighted as the IMF and World Bank opened their annual meetings in Bangkok, where AI’s effects on productivity, employment and inequality are among the main topics.

headline: Britain faces energy crisis as European gas prices jump 150% this year
summary: Britain faces a prolonged energy squeeze as European gas prices surge more than 150 per cent this year and dwindling reserves threaten to keep costs high through winter.The price rise brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on its fragile economy before the October 28 Budget.Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas.Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to just 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity is equal to about seven days of average winter demand. Centrica, the owner of British Gas, has warned that its Rough storage facility could close when its operating consent expires in April, unless the government backs its plans for the site. The company has proposed investing £2 billion ($2.64 billion) to redevelop the site, which accounts for about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity.Britain is unlikely to run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House.“The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said.Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”.European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf.The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group.“It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters.Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels.EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March. In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves.Britain’s electricity system is also under pressure. The National Energy System Operator issued a precautionary margin notice on October 6 as weak wind generation tightened available supplies, highlighting continued reliance on gas-fired power.A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire.
