body_text:
Britain faces a prolonged energy squeeze as European gas prices surge more than 150 per cent this year and dwindling reserves threaten to keep costs high through winter.

The price rise brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on its fragile economy before the October 28 Budget.

Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas.

Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage. In 2024, its storage capacity amounted to just 5 per cent of annual gas demand, compared with an EU average of 29 per cent, according to government figures. Its current capacity is equal to about seven days of average winter demand.

Centrica, the owner of British Gas, has warned that its Rough storage facility could close when its operating consent expires in April, unless the government backs its plans for the site. The company has proposed investing £2 billion ($2.64 billion) to redevelop the site, which accounts for about half of Britain’s gas storage capacity.

Britain is unlikely to run short of gas this winter, but its limited reserves leave it increasingly exposed to global supply disruptions and competition for liquefied natural gas, according to Neil Quilliam, associate fellow for the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House.

“The greater risk is not a physical shortage of gas, but a period of tight supply, higher prices and increased competition for LNG cargoes if winter is unusually cold or if there are disruptions to Norwegian supplies or global gas markets,” he said.

Britain still benefits from North Sea production, Norwegian imports, LNG terminals and interconnectors with Europe, which should provide sufficient supplies under normal conditions, he said. However, “the margin for error is becoming uncomfortably small”.

European gas storage is expected to be just 75 to 78 per cent full by November 1, about 10 percentage points below the five-year average, as the Iran war continues to disrupt liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf.

The supply constraints could persist into next year even if the Iran war ends, with analysts warning that competition for alternative LNG cargoes and the need to replenish depleted reserves could keep prices high. Even with average winter weather, north-west European reserves could fall to about 20 per cent by early April, according to the London Stock Exchange Group.

“It’s not just this coming winter that we are tight, but we risk being tight the next summer,” Yuriy Onyshkiv, an analyst at LSEG, told Reuters.

Entsog warned last week that strong LNG deliveries would be needed throughout the winter to maintain European storage levels.

EU gas storage was 72 per cent full at the start of October, compared with about 83 per cent a year earlier. Entsog’s central scenario has EU inventories falling to about 30 per cent by the end of March.

In its worst case – a severe winter combined with tight LNG supply and a halt to Russian pipeline flows – stocks would drop to 11 per cent, the level of the bloc’s remaining strategic reserves.

Britain’s electricity system is also under pressure. The National Energy System Operator issued a precautionary margin notice on October 6 as weak wind generation tightened available supplies, highlighting continued reliance on gas-fired power.

A further challenge comes on January 1, when an exemption allowing imports of diesel and jet fuel refined from Russian crude in third countries is due to expire. In the same month, the EU’s full ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect, which is expected to tighten European gas supply further.

Consultancy Cornwall Insight forecasts a 16 per cent increase in Britain’s annual household energy price cap to £1,999 in January, after a 4 per cent rise this month that took bills to a three-year high.

The outlook adds to pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government before the budget, with limited fiscal room expected to constrain further support for consumers.

analysis.framing: The article frames the story around Britain's vulnerability to a European gas price surge and low storage levels, emphasizing economic and household risks while noting that a physical shortage is unlikely.

body_text:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have demonstrated that its build-up of batteries of air defence must stretch to all corners of the country.

Saudi Arabia is the world’s second-largest Patriot operator, said Nawaf Obaid of King’s College London’s Department of War Studies.

“Saudi Arabia does not lack air defences,” he told The National. “It possesses one of the world’s most sophisticated integrated air and missile defence architectures, protecting a country larger than Western Europe.

Pilot, flight attendant and widow among victims of Houthi attacks

“The fundamental challenge is that no existing system, including those protecting the United States, can guarantee the interception of repeated, simultaneous attacks involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones.”

The kingdom is buying seven batteries of Thaad (Terminal High Altitude Area Defence), the largest programme outside the US, he added. The extensive use of missile interceptors during the Iran war has meant there is a need for renewed stocks, experts have told The National.

Despite having the world’s second-largest air defence system, 13 people were killed when King Khalid International Airport was struck by what are thought to have been ballistic missiles, causing widespread damage and leaving 308 wounded.

Countries around the world will now be looking at how to defend airports, but experts suggest close-in defence will be nearly impossible, given the number and size of civilian and military sites that could be attacked.

“An attack like the one we saw on Saturday on Riyadh Airport would in normal circumstances have been met with lavish application of Thaad at high altitude and Patriot on incoming,” said Dr Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer.

“But what is clear is that Thaad and Patriot are not available in quantity and we’re seeing leakage.”

Military analyst Francis Tusa said the scale of interceptor expenditure during the war had put significant pressure on American stocks, with consequences for allies globally.

During one attack on a US airbase in Jordan, it is estimated up to 80 Patriots were fired in one night, leading to a rapid dwindling of the stockpile, he said. “The generals have told Trump that ‘we haven’t got the rounds left’.”

There is also the issue of the rebel Houthis' improving arsenal that includes manoeuvring ballistic missiles. The Iranian-derived Palestine-2 has a range of about 2,000km and hypersonic capabilities, including manoeuvrability, making interception more difficult during its terminal phase.

The US has expended an estimated 1,500 Patriots and has about 800 left. Saudi Arabia had more than 1,800 Patriot interceptors and has used a large number defending itself from Iran and the Houthis.

Other defences include the South Korean KM-SAM, a medium-range system also owned by the UAE that is designed to intercept aircraft and incoming missiles.

Saudi Arabia requested further defensive support from Britain's ministry of defence in the weeks leading up to the current attacks but the requests failed to secure ministerial approval. Saudi Arabian counterparts were left frustrated at the UK inaction.

The UK has contributed, with its Sky Sabre system providing a medium-range defensive layer using Common Anti-Air Modular Missiles, surveillance radar and integrated command-and-control systems, Mr Obaid said.

British industry can offer other options, which can be used for “point defence”, to stop close-in threats.

“The UK has got the Starstreak high-velocity missile, with 8km to 9km range, and is unjammable,” said Mr Tusa, editor of Defence Eye. “It’s also probably £100,000 [$132,300] a shot.”

The £40,000 Martlet missile, which uses a high-explosive warhead rather than Starstreak’s three tungsten darts, is another comparatively inexpensive option, he said.

As a vast country with considerable infrastructure, Saudi Arabia’s commanders have to decide where best to position radars and interceptors without being able to protect everywhere.

The resources for a single site are significant. “For Patriot, you’d normally get one, maybe two radars, two command systems, and four to six missile launchers,” Mr Tusa said.

Dr Nusbacher also questioned why commercial airports in the Middle East should be expected to have dedicated close-in air defence when comparable facilities in the West do not.

“Heathrow doesn’t have close-in air defence, and why would you expect King Khalid Airport to have close-in air defence?” she said.

Until recently, there was little expectation that Gulf states would face sustained attacks, she added. But the changing picture is now forcing a “major reassessment” of how civilian infrastructure should be protected.

Robert Tollast, a military analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said defending one site could also leave others exposed.

There is a risk of “putting so much resource into interceptors around that facility that you leave other critical areas uncovered”, he said. Destroying energy infrastructure outside the summer months “could also be disastrous”.

One response would be to improve intelligence and attack missile launchers before they fire, as Saudi Arabia depends heavily on US satellite intelligence.

Given the scale of the emergency, US manufacturers are attempting to increase interceptor production – an estimated 2,000 Thaad and Patriots have been fired this year – but replenishing stocks could take up to 30 months.

Dr Nusbacher said defence planners had not anticipated the “profligate use of high-value, exquisite air defence systems” during a war “lasting more than a few weeks”.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as exposing fundamental limitations in even the world's most sophisticated air defense systems, with emphasis on interceptor shortages and the impossibility of comprehensive protection.

Vague and emotionally charged term implying failure or breach, rather than a neutral description of interceptors missing targets.
Emotionally loaded and judgmental, implying wasteful or reckless expenditure rather than simply high consumption.
Vague and editorializing, using an aesthetic term to describe military technology, which adds subjective value judgment.

In the Middle East, Saudi Arabia reported new drone and cruise missile attacks on Monday, following strikes on Riyadh's airport over the weekend. Attacks on tankers in the critical Strait of Hormuz have also intensified, even as more crude oil flows from the Persian Gulf.

headline: PKK pulls out of Metina in northern Iraq amid Turkey peace process
summary: The withdrawal comes as the peace process between Turkey and the militant group gains momentum alongside increasing security cooperation between Ankara and Baghdad.
body_text:
ANKARA — The Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) has withdrawn from four areas in northern Iraq as part of an ongoing peace process aimed at ending more than four decades of conflict between Turkey and the militant group, according to Turkish security sources.

The PKK, which is headquartered in the northern Iraqi mountains, has waged an armed insurgency against Turkey since 1984 for Kurdish self-rule inside the country. It announced in May 2025 that it would disband and dissolve itself as part of ongoing peace talks the Turkish government launched in 2024. The militant group is considered a terror outfit by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

What happened: The PKK completed its evacuation of four positions in the Metina region near the Turkish border last Thursday, Turkey’s public broadcaster TRT and state-run Anadolu Agency said, citing security sources on Monday. Metina has frequently been the scene of clashes between Turkish forces and the PKK.

The move came as part of ongoing efforts to evacuate areas “considered to pose a risk of conflict for Turkey’s security,” Turkish security sources said, in a statement carried by Anadolu and the TRT.

analysis.framing: The article frames the PKK's withdrawal from Metina as a concrete step in an ongoing Turkey-PKK peace process, attributing the information to Turkish state and security sources.

US federal agents conducted a predawn raid on the home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday, US media reported.

The search followed a criminal fraud investigation into Ms Omar's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by the Somali-born politician's late father when she was a child, Fox News reported, quoting unidentified sources.

She has repeatedly denied allegations of wrongdoing, calling them false and politically motivated.

“Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations ​executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of a continuing federal investigation,” a department representative told AP.

Neither the Justice Department nor a representative for Ms Omar immediately returned The National's request for comment.

Ms Omar was taken to the US as a child, fleeing the civil war in Somalia. She became a US citizen at the age of 17 in 2000 and, in 2018, was elected to Congress to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis. Ms Omar is seeking another term for the seat on November 3.

An outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, Ms Omar has been a frequent target of his attacks. He has previously suggested she should leave the country.

In February, he said Ms Omar and fellow Democrat Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be “institutionalised” after they criticised his remarks during the State of Union address.

Mr Trump has also recently attacked Abdul El Sayed, who is aiming to win a US Senate seat in Michigan. Should he win, Mr El Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

Mr Trump has used anti-Muslim language in online attacks against the Democrat, calling him a “jihadist lunatic”.

US federal agents searched the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar on Monday as part of a criminal investigation, officials said, marking a dramatic escalation in US President Donald Trump's confrontation with the outspoken lawmaker.

The search – three weeks before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress – was conducted by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, according to Fox News, citing sources familiar with the matter.

The cable network reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation concerning immigration paperwork submitted on behalf of the Somali-born congresswoman by her late father when she was a child.

Trump's border enforcement chief Tom Homan told Fox News he was unwilling to give details ahead of any official announcement but confirmed that an "investigation was ongoing for a while" and that "there was a warrant executed this morning."

Read moreMan arrested after attacking Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar at town hall in Minneapolis

US media quoted the Department of Justice (DOJ) confirming that agents had carried out a court-authorised search in the Washington area, but officials did not identify Omar or disclose the nature of the investigation.

"Today in the Washington DC, area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the DOJ. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

The search reportedly began around 6:00am, with several agents wearing HSI jackets seen outside Omar's Washington residence, according to Fox News.

Omar, 44, is a leftist Democrat and fierce critic of Trump – particularly of his administration's sweeping crackdown on immigration.

The Republican president has repeatedly clashed with Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child and has frequently been the target of his political attacks.

She is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents in Congress.

Trump and his Republican allies have for years argued that non-citizens vote in significant numbers in US elections, which is a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment and deportation.

"What we are seeing is illegal aliens voting, non-citizens who are not eligible to vote voting, or those fraudulently registering to voters who are not eligible to vote," Attorney General Todd Blanche said last month.

"So, just to put a finer point on this, in under two years, this administration has charged nearly four times as many non-citizen voting cases as the last administration brought in four years, and we're currently investigating hundreds of cases across the country," he said.

But studies consistently find non-citizen voting to be too rare an offence to have affected the outcome of any federal election.

An election fraud database kept by the conservative Heritage Foundation – dating back decades – contains just 1,619 cases of election-related offences, of which non-citizen voting makes up a tiny 5.5 percent.

headline: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate
summary: Opposition parties say revisions to the list of eligible voters favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party. Authorities have removed more than 130 million names from the voter roll.(Image credit: Manish Swarup)
body_text:
Security personnel in riot gear arrive to escort workers of India's opposition Congress party as they gather for a march toward the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, on Monday. Manish Swarup/AP hide caption

NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.

Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.

Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.

Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution.

"We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi.

Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi.

Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists."

Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.

The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

body_text:
BENGHAZI, Libya, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Libya's eastern-based authorities have seized about 400 kg of hashish worth around 6 million dinars ($934,000) and arrested some suspects near the coastal city of Tobruk, officials said.

Libya has become a major drug transit route as gangs exploit the turmoil and conflict since 2011 when former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a NATO-backed uprising.

The anti-drugs agency's information and documentation officer, Ahmed al-Mismari, told Reuters that Saturday's operation took place at a house in an agricultural area southeast of the city.

"The preliminary investigations revealed the shipment had been smuggled across the border with Egypt and was intended for local marketing and distribution within the Libyan market," Mismari said.

The detainees, whose number was not confirmed, were from Libya and Egypt.

Pictures posted by the agency showed a large quantity of hashish wrapped in gold and black patterned packages marked with symbols including a horse and the year 2026.

Also on Saturday, a Libyan National Army brigade seized more than 1.3 million narcotic pills after a firefight with smugglers in the southeastern town of Kufra. Three soldiers were injured, according to an army statement.

(Reporting by Ayman Werfalli; Writing by Ahmed Elumami; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

PRETORIA, October 12. /TASS/. African Energy Week (AEW), the largest event of its kind on the continent, has kicked off in Cape Town in the southwestern part of South Africa, eNCA TV channel reported.

Some 10,000 representatives from all segments of the energy sector, including personnel from 1,500 companies across more than 100 countries, have arrived in Cape Town to participate, the report said. The mission comprises 13 companies interested in developing partnerships with businesses in South Africa and other African nations. The Russian Export Center is organizing the mission. The forum’s primary goal is to transform partnerships into commercially viable projects.

The program of African Energy Week features around 100 key events, including investment forums and business workshops. The primary objective of the event is to attract capital to Africa’s energy sector for the exploration and development of new fields, the expansion of energy infrastructure, in the gas industry in the first place, and the implementation of advanced production methods, including in the green energy sector. Ensuring Africa’s energy security is a key item on the agenda. The AEW will run until October 16.

headline: European sanctions hampering Italian entrepreneurs’ work in Russia — envoy to Italy
summary: Alexey Paramonov noted that an increasing share of the Italian public questioned whether their government’s current anti-Russian course served the interests of the population
body_text:
ROME, October 12. /TASS/. European sanctions, which Italy has signed up to, are hindering Italian entrepreneurs who continue to do business in Russia, while the overall competitiveness of the Italian economy is deteriorating, Russian Ambassador to Italy Alexey Paramonov told TASS.

"Italy’s joining the European Union’s illegal sanctions has turned Italian entrepreneurs in Russia into sort of outcasts in their own country. Nothing of the sort has ever happened in history. They complained at a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Infrastructure and Transport Matteo Salvini in Milano on September 14 that conditions in Italy were far worse for them than in Russia, their bank accounts were being closed, various artificial obstacles were being created for their business operations, and they were almost being branded ‘enemies of the state’. Yet, many in Italy are convinced that the Russian and Italian economies are perfectly complementary," the diplomat said.

An increasing share of the Italian public, including the business community, is questioning whether their government’s current anti-Russian course serves the interests of the population, he noted. "Italy is gradually coming to its senses and realizing that an excessively high price has been paid for participating in Brussels’ sanctions policy against our country," Paramonov stressed.

Italy itself is the main loser in this regard, with its economy becoming less competitive compared with other major European and global producers, he said. Meanwhile, "the Russian economy does not depend solely on Italy: the majority of goods previously imported from the Apennine Peninsula have been successfully replaced by either domestic producers or suppliers from friendly third countries," Paramonov added.

According to figures provided by the Italian side, up to 300 Italian companies continue to operate in Russia. Compared with 2013, total trade turnover has fallen from 30 billion to 7 billion euros, while Italian exports have dropped from 10 billion to 3.5 billion euros.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States acknowledged Monday that there have been limitations in communication with the White House, amid concerns over apparent friction in bilateral intelligence cooperation.

Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the South Korean Embassy in Washington, responding to questions about communication between Seoul and Washington.

"I acknowledge that there are limitations in our communication with the White House," Kang said.

The remarks follow growing speculation over bilateral friction after South Korea's National Intelligence Service acknowledged it was excluded from a June trilateral meeting, also involving Japan, on North Korean cyber threats. Local media reports indicated the agency was left out at Washington's request.

South Korea and the U.S. have faced signs of friction in the intelligence field after Seoul Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's public disclosure of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility in Kusong, North Korea, in March.

headline: Tourist flow from Vietnam to Russia to rise by at least 30% following visa waiver
summary: The tourism industry views granting visa-free entry to Russia for Vietnamese citizens as a crucial step for the development of inbound tourism to Russia
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Demand from Vietnamese tourists for trips to Russia could rise by at least 30% due to the visa waiver, the Association of Tour Operators of Russia (ATOR) told TASS.

"ATOR expects the introduction of visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens (who currently use the e-visa system) to boost interest in tourism to Russia and lead to an increase in tourist flow from the country of at least 25-30%," the association said.

The tourism industry views granting visa-free entry to Russia for Vietnamese citizens as a crucial step for the development of inbound tourism to Russia. Tour operators consider the Vietnamese market promising in terms of both the potential number of visits and the quality of the tourist flow, ATOR explained.

"Vietnamese clients book comprehensive sightseeing programs across Russia and are willing to spend significant sums within the country on memorable experience and impressions. Beyond the major tourist hubs of Moscow and St. Petersburg, Vietnamese tourists show great interest in the Russian North," experts said.

Tourist traffic from Vietnam to Russia climbed by 69% in the first half of 2026 year-on-year, while total inbound traffic (for all purposes of visit) increased by 10.7%, the association noted.

On October 12, Russian President Vladimir Putin introduced a visa-free regime for Vietnamese citizens for one year, until October 15, 2027. Under this regime, they may visit Russia for up to 30 days for tourism, business, or other purposes, according to the presidential decree.

headline: PKK withdraws from Turkish border area in Iraqi Kurdistan
summary: Militants from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) have withdrawn from four camps in northern Iraq, Turkish security sources said on Monday, as part of a drawn-out disarmament process that could eventually include the return of former militants to Turkey. Fighters from the PKK withdrew from “four shelters” in the Metina area near the border with Turkey in Iraq’s Kurdistan region, security sources told state news agency Anadolu. The PKK last week said it had evacuated four “war tunnels” in the Metina area and withdrawn fighters from Turkey in the days before that. The moves showed it had “fulfilled” its strategy “to end the armed struggle against Turkey”, the group said. The Turkish sources did not mention withdrawals from Turkey but said the PKK's departure from the locations in Iraq’s Kurdistan region was part of efforts to evacuate locations that “pose a risk of conflict to Turkey’s security”. Neither Turkey nor the PKK said where the militants went next. The group is known to have locations in both federally-controlled Iraq and the Kurdistan region, including its headquarters in the Qandil Mountains. The PKK said last year it had withdrawn from other areas near the border with Turkey.The moves are part of a process of dissolution of the PKK, whose insurgents fought a 40-year conflict with the Turkish state until the group’s jailed leader, Abdullah Ocalan, last year called for it to dissolve and disarm. The conflict killed at least 40,000 people on both sides, spilt across Turkey’s borders with Syria and Iraq, and left an indelible mark on Turkish society, where up to one-fifth of the 86 million population is ethnically Kurdish. Turkey has long regarded the PKK as its main national security threat, and, alongside the EU and US, has designated the group as a terrorist organisation.Turkey’s parliament in August passed legislation that provides a legal framework and procedures for the PKK’s dissolution. It allows for the suspension of some prison sentences and the postponement of other trials and investigations, depending on the severity of the alleged offences. PKK members who live abroad, many in the group’s base in the Qandil Mountains, could be allowed to return home and reintegrate into society, although Turkish veterans’ groups have vehemently opposed such measures. The aim is to eventually ensure “social reconciliation” to end more than four decades of internal strife, Anadolu reported on Monday. But measures under the legislation can only take effect once Turkey's National Security Council is convinced that the PKK has completely dissolved and surrendered all its weapons – something that has not yet happened. Mehmet Ucum, a senior adviser to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said last month that the NSC would confirm the PKK’s dissolution and disarmament complete “by the end of this year at the latest”. Tuncer Bakirhan, co-chair of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), said last week that some former militants could return as soon as this month, but a lot depended on the confirmation of their legal status. “People return not to a place where they don't know what will happen to them tomorrow, but to a place where their law, status, and security are defined,” he told the independent leftist Evrensel media outlet in an interview. Kurdish politicians, who do not belong to the PKK but have liaised between the group and the Turkish government, have criticised the peace process for moving too slowly and failing to provide Turkey’s Kurdish minority with greater access to cultural, political and social rights. Elected Kurdish mayors in the country’s south-east, whom the Turkish government replaced with political appointees, have not been reinstated, and people dismissed from their jobs over alleged PKK links have not been allowed to return to work. “Even the simplest steps are not being taken,” Mr Bakirhan said in separate remarks to MPs last week. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz told state media on Wednesday that the PKK’s dissolution process requires “patience”. The PKK has demanded that Turkey release Ocalan, who has been in prison for more than two decades, as part of the dissolution process, but Turkey has made no such pledges: the move would be highly unpopular among much of Turkish society after the decades of unrest and loss of life caused by the conflict between the PKK and the state. Ocalan could have a role on a disarmament committee as part of the dissolution process but would not be released from prison, presidential adviser Mr Ucum said last month.

The Turkish sources did not mention withdrawals from Turkey but said the PKK's departure from the locations in Iraq’s Kurdistan region was part of efforts to evacuate locations that “pose a risk of conflict to Turkey’s security”.

Neither Turkey nor the PKK said where the militants went next. The group is known to have locations in both federally-controlled Iraq and the Kurdistan region, including its headquarters in the Qandil Mountains. The PKK said last year it had withdrawn from other areas near the border with Turkey.

The moves are part of a process of dissolution of the PKK, whose insurgents fought a 40-year conflict with the Turkish state until the group’s jailed leader, Abdullah Ocalan, last year called for it to dissolve and disarm.

The conflict killed at least 40,000 people on both sides, spilt across Turkey’s borders with Syria and Iraq, and left an indelible mark on Turkish society, where up to one-fifth of the 86 million population is ethnically Kurdish. Turkey has long regarded the PKK as its main national security threat, and, alongside the EU and US, has designated the group as a terrorist organisation.

Turkey’s parliament in August passed legislation that provides a legal framework and procedures for the PKK’s dissolution. It allows for the suspension of some prison sentences and the postponement of other trials and investigations, depending on the severity of the alleged offences.

PKK members who live abroad, many in the group’s base in the Qandil Mountains, could be allowed to return home and reintegrate into society, although Turkish veterans’ groups have vehemently opposed such measures.

The aim is to eventually ensure “social reconciliation” to end more than four decades of internal strife, Anadolu reported on Monday.

But measures under the legislation can only take effect once Turkey's National Security Council is convinced that the PKK has completely dissolved and surrendered all its weapons – something that has not yet happened. Mehmet Ucum, a senior adviser to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said last month that the NSC would confirm the PKK’s dissolution and disarmament complete “by the end of this year at the latest”.

Tuncer Bakirhan, co-chair of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), said last week that some former militants could return as soon as this month, but a lot depended on the confirmation of their legal status.

“People return not to a place where they don't know what will happen to them tomorrow, but to a place where their law, status, and security are defined,” he told the independent leftist Evrensel media outlet in an interview.

Kurdish politicians, who do not belong to the PKK but have liaised between the group and the Turkish government, have criticised the peace process for moving too slowly and failing to provide Turkey’s Kurdish minority with greater access to cultural, political and social rights. Elected Kurdish mayors in the country’s south-east, whom the Turkish government replaced with political appointees, have not been reinstated, and people dismissed from their jobs over alleged PKK links have not been allowed to return to work.

“Even the simplest steps are not being taken,” Mr Bakirhan said in separate remarks to MPs last week.

Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz told state media on Wednesday that the PKK’s dissolution process requires “patience”.

The PKK has demanded that Turkey release Ocalan, who has been in prison for more than two decades, as part of the dissolution process, but Turkey has made no such pledges: the move would be highly unpopular among much of Turkish society after the decades of unrest and loss of life caused by the conflict between the PKK and the state.

Ocalan could have a role on a disarmament committee as part of the dissolution process but would not be released from prison, presidential adviser Mr Ucum said last month.

body_text:
The UAE is recruiting 50 content creators to produce digital material on water sustainability before a major UN conference in Abu Dhabi this December.

The National Media Authority, in partnership with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Federal Youth Authority, has launched the Blue Content Creators Programme, with applications open from October 12 to 30.

The initiative will train 50 Emiratis and UAE residents to produce digital content raising awareness of water issues and highlighting the country's sustainability and innovation efforts.

UN conference will shine spotlight on world's water crisis, says UAE minister

The programme comes as the UAE prepares to co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from December 8-10. It aims to equip young people with skills to communicate the links between water, human health, food, energy and development to audiences at home and abroad.

Abdulla Balalaa, Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said the programme would bring new perspectives to water issues.

"The decisions we make today about water will shape the world inherited by future generations," Mr Balalaa said. "It is essential that young people's voices and ideas help guide these decisions.

"As the UAE prepares to welcome the world to Abu Dhabi for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, I look forward to the fresh perspectives and innovative ideas young content creators will bring to water issues, the questions they will raise, and the stories and experiences they will highlight.

"Their participation will enrich the conference with new ideas and ambitious creative contributions, encourage us to examine challenges from different perspectives, and reinforce our shared responsibility to translate the discussions in Abu Dhabi into practical action that delivers tangible benefits to individuals and communities."

Mohammed Al Shehhi, secretary general of the National Media Authority, said the UAE places water at the heart of its sustainable development efforts.

"Raising awareness of these issues strengthens public understanding of the challenges and encourages community participation in addressing them," he said.

The programme includes three weeks of training in November, covering water issues, storytelling, video production, digital publishing strategies and the use of artificial intelligence tools in content creation.

Participants will then apply these skills to produce content related to the UN conference in December. Applications are open to UAE citizens and residents aged 18 to 35 with an interest in content creation, media, water, the environment or sustainability, with selections made to reflect the diversity of UAE society.

US federal agents conducted a predawn raid on the home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar on Monday, US media reported.

The search followed a criminal fraud investigation into Ms Omar's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by the Somali-born politician's late father when she was a child, Fox News reported, quoting unidentified sources.

She has repeatedly denied allegations of wrongdoing, calling them false and politically motivated.

“Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations ​executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of a continuing federal investigation,” a department representative told AP.

Neither the Justice Department nor a representative for Ms Omar immediately returned The National's request for comment.

Ms Omar was taken to the US as a child, fleeing the civil war in Somalia. She became a US citizen at the age of 17 in 2000 and, in 2018, was elected to Congress to represent Minnesota's 5th District, which includes all of Minneapolis. Ms Omar is seeking another term for the seat on November 3.

An outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, Ms Omar has been a frequent target of his attacks. He has previously suggested she should leave the country.

In February, he said Ms Omar and fellow Democrat Rashida Tlaib of Michigan, who is also Muslim, should be “institutionalised” after they criticised his remarks during the State of Union address.

Mr Trump has also recently attacked Abdul El Sayed, who is aiming to win a US Senate seat in Michigan. Should he win, Mr El Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the upper chamber of Congress.

Mr Trump has used anti-Muslim language in online attacks against the Democrat, calling him a “jihadist lunatic”.

US federal agents searched the Washington home of Democratic congresswoman Ilhan Omar on Monday as part of a criminal investigation, officials said, marking a dramatic escalation in US President Donald Trump's confrontation with the outspoken lawmaker.

The search – three weeks before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress – was conducted by agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of US immigration enforcement, according to Fox News, citing sources familiar with the matter.

The cable network reported that the operation was linked to a criminal fraud investigation concerning immigration paperwork submitted on behalf of the Somali-born congresswoman by her late father when she was a child.

Trump's border enforcement chief Tom Homan told Fox News he was unwilling to give details ahead of any official announcement but confirmed that an "investigation was ongoing for a while" and that "there was a warrant executed this morning."

Read moreMan arrested after attacking Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar at town hall in Minneapolis

US media quoted the Department of Justice (DOJ) confirming that agents had carried out a court-authorised search in the Washington area, but officials did not identify Omar or disclose the nature of the investigation.

"Today in the Washington DC, area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the DOJ. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

The search reportedly began around 6:00am, with several agents wearing HSI jackets seen outside Omar's Washington residence, according to Fox News.

Omar, 44, is a leftist Democrat and fierce critic of Trump – particularly of his administration's sweeping crackdown on immigration.

The Republican president has repeatedly clashed with Omar, who came to the United States from Somalia as a child and has frequently been the target of his political attacks.

In September, Homan said that Omar was the subject of an ongoing criminal investigation, but again declined to provide details.

Omar said at the time that Homeland Security officials had not contacted her about any investigation, dismissing the allegations against her as politically motivated attacks.

There was no immediate public response from Omar to Monday's search. AFP sought comment from her office and the Trump administration.

Omar was first elected to Congress in 2018 and represents a district including Minneapolis, which is home to one of the largest Somali communities in the United States.

She is a member of the group of left-wing Democratic lawmakers known as "The Squad," who have been among Trump's most vocal opponents in Congress.

No charges against Omar were announced in connection with Monday's search.

Trump and his Republican allies have for years argued that non-citizens vote in significant numbers in US elections, which is a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment and deportation.

Read moreUS Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial voter 'verification' system

"What we are seeing is illegal aliens voting, non-citizens who are not eligible to vote voting, or those fraudulently registering to voters who are not eligible to vote," Attorney General Todd Blanche said last month.

"So, just to put a finer point on this, in under two years, this administration has charged nearly four times as many non-citizen voting cases as the last administration brought in four years, and we're currently investigating hundreds of cases across the country," he said.

But studies consistently find non-citizen voting to be too rare an offence to have affected the outcome of any federal election.

An election fraud database kept by the conservative Heritage Foundation – dating back decades – contains just 1,619 cases of election-related offences, of which non-citizen voting makes up a tiny 5.5 percent.

headline: India's opposition parties march to top court as protests over voter lists escalate
summary: Opposition parties say revisions to the list of eligible voters favor Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party. Authorities have removed more than 130 million names from the voter roll.(Image credit: Manish Swarup)
body_text:
Security personnel in riot gear arrive to escort workers of India's opposition Congress party as they gather for a march toward the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, on Monday. Manish Swarup/AP hide caption

NEW DELHI — India's opposition parties marched to the Supreme Court on Monday to protest a purge of voter lists they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi's party, after police detained thousands of activists over the weekend in a sweeping crackdown in New Delhi.

Several opposition lawmakers and thousands of supporters marched through the capital and submitted a petition to the chief justice alleging irregularities in the nationwide revision of voter lists.

Protests led by the "Cockroach" youth movement have intensified since election authorities began the revision last year, removing more than 130 million voters from the lists. The protesters, including opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

Critics say the process is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters. Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party and the Election Commission deny allegations of manipulation, saying the move is needed to remove duplicate and ineligible names.

Ahead of the march, authorities closed six metro stations in the capital on Monday and warned of traffic disruptions.

Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi of the Congress party described the growing protests as a fight to defend the constitution.

"We will not back down," he told reporters in New Delhi.

Gandhi, scion of India's most influential political dynasty, is seeking to turn the protests into a broader challenge to Modi.

Gandhi briefly rode through the crowd in an open bus, waving a copy of India's Constitution. Thousands of his party supporters, student activists and other protesters followed in tow. The turnout marked a sharp contrast with the weekend, when authorities briefly detained thousands, including leaders of the "Cockroach" movement and journalists, and effectively locked down much of the capital to prevent large-scale protests.

Modi has not publicly commented on the protests, but leaders of his party have dismissed them, with some calling the activists "anarchists."

Meanwhile, New Delhi police announced Monday that Jantar Mantar, a longtime site of mass protests in the capital, would no longer be a designated venue for rallies. Police said three replacement sites had been chosen.

The "Cockroach" movement earlier this year staged a sit-in at Jantar Mantar that lasted for weeks, forcing the resignation of Modi's education minister in July.

summary: BENGHAZI, Libya, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Libya's eastern-based authorities have seized about 400 kg of hashish worth around 6 million dinars ($934,000) and arrested some suspects near the coastal city of Tobruk, officials said.Libya has become a major drug transit route as gangs exploit the turmoil and conflict since 2011 when former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a NATO-backed uprising.The anti-drugs agency's information and documentation officer, Ahmed al-Mismari, told Reuters that Saturday's operation took place at a house in an agricultural area southeast of the city.
body_text:
BENGHAZI, Libya, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Libya's eastern-based authorities have seized about 400 kg of hashish worth around 6 million dinars ($934,000) and arrested some suspects near the coastal city of Tobruk, officials said.

Libya has become a major drug transit route as gangs exploit the turmoil and conflict since 2011 when former ruler Muammar Gaddafi was toppled in a NATO-backed uprising.

The anti-drugs agency's information and documentation officer, Ahmed al-Mismari, told Reuters that Saturday's operation took place at a house in an agricultural area southeast of the city.

"The preliminary investigations revealed the shipment had been smuggled across the border with Egypt and was intended for local marketing and distribution within the Libyan market," Mismari said.

The detainees, whose number was not confirmed, were from Libya and Egypt.

Pictures posted by the agency showed a large quantity of hashish wrapped in gold and black patterned packages marked with symbols including a horse and the year 2026.

Also on Saturday, a Libyan National Army brigade seized more than 1.3 million narcotic pills after a firefight with smugglers in the southeastern town of Kufra. Three soldiers were injured, according to an army statement.

(Reporting by Ayman Werfalli; Writing by Ahmed Elumami; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

headline: African Energy Week kicks off in Cape Town, South Africa
summary: Russia is represented at the AEW by almost twenty companies
body_text:
PRETORIA, October 12. /TASS/. African Energy Week (AEW), the largest event of its kind on the continent, has kicked off in Cape Town in the southwestern part of South Africa, eNCA TV channel reported.

Some 10,000 representatives from all segments of the energy sector, including personnel from 1,500 companies across more than 100 countries, have arrived in Cape Town to participate, the report said. The main theme of this year’s event is "Invest in African Energies: Affordable and Abundant Energy Additions."

Russia is represented at the AEW by almost twenty companies. On October 13, a Russian business mission under the Made in Russia national brand will take place as part of the event. The mission comprises 13 companies interested in developing partnerships with businesses in South Africa and other African nations. The Russian Export Center is organizing the mission. The Russia-Africa Energy Investment Forum will take place on October 15, showcasing the most promising projects in the energy sector. The forum’s primary goal is to transform partnerships into commercially viable projects.

The program of African Energy Week features around 100 key events, including investment forums and business workshops. The primary objective of the event is to attract capital to Africa’s energy sector for the exploration and development of new fields, the expansion of energy infrastructure, in the gas industry in the first place, and the implementation of advanced production methods, including in the green energy sector. Ensuring Africa’s energy security is a key item on the agenda. The AEW will run until October 16.

headline: European sanctions hampering Italian entrepreneurs’ work in Russia — envoy to Italy
summary: Alexey Paramonov noted that an increasing share of the Italian public questioned whether their government’s current anti-Russian course served the interests of the population
body_text:
ROME, October 12. /TASS/. European sanctions, which Italy has signed up to, are hindering Italian entrepreneurs who continue to do business in Russia, while the overall competitiveness of the Italian economy is deteriorating, Russian Ambassador to Italy Alexey Paramonov told TASS.

"Italy’s joining the European Union’s illegal sanctions has turned Italian entrepreneurs in Russia into sort of outcasts in their own country. Nothing of the sort has ever happened in history. They complained at a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Infrastructure and Transport Matteo Salvini in Milano on September 14 that conditions in Italy were far worse for them than in Russia, their bank accounts were being closed, various artificial obstacles were being created for their business operations, and they were almost being branded ‘enemies of the state’. Yet, many in Italy are convinced that the Russian and Italian economies are perfectly complementary," the diplomat said.

An increasing share of the Italian public, including the business community, is questioning whether their government’s current anti-Russian course serves the interests of the population, he noted. "Italy is gradually coming to its senses and realizing that an excessively high price has been paid for participating in Brussels’ sanctions policy against our country," Paramonov stressed.

Italy itself is the main loser in this regard, with its economy becoming less competitive compared with other major European and global producers, he said. Meanwhile, "the Russian economy does not depend solely on Italy: the majority of goods previously imported from the Apennine Peninsula have been successfully replaced by either domestic producers or suppliers from friendly third countries," Paramonov added.

According to figures provided by the Italian side, up to 300 Italian companies continue to operate in Russia. Compared with 2013, total trade turnover has fallen from 30 billion to 7 billion euros, while Italian exports have dropped from 10 billion to 3.5 billion euros.

headline: Trump has all necessary tools to replace Zelensky — former Ukrainian Prime Minister
summary: According to Nikolay Azarov, the United States have all the means to establish a regime in Ukraine that could hold elections, pursue a peace process and reach a normal agreement
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has all the means at his disposal to replace Vladimir Zelensky, former Ukrainian Prime Minister Nikolay Azarov (2010-2014) said.

"Trump, that is, the US administration, has absolutely all the means not only to replace Zelensky, but also to establish a more or less normal regime in Ukraine that could hold elections, pursue a peace process and reach a normal agreement," Azarov said on the Rossiya-24 television channel.

Earlier, US President Donald Trump said elections needed to be held in Ukraine. The Wall Street Journal noted that the US leader’s remarks indicated that relations with Zelensky had deteriorated to their lowest point since the winter of last year. Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported, citing unnamed European officials, that the US administration was threatening to halt its weapons procurement program and the provision of intelligence to Ukraine.

loaded_language.explanation: Dramatic phrasing that heightens the sense of crisis, though it is attributed to The Wall Street Journal.

headline: S. Korea's top envoy to U.S. acknowledges limitations in high-level communication with White House
summary: WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States ack...
body_text:
WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States acknowledged Monday that there have been limitations in communication with the White House, amid concerns over apparent friction in bilateral intelligence cooperation.

Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the South Korean Embassy in Washington, responding to questions about communication between Seoul and Washington.

"I acknowledge that there are limitations in our communication with the White House," Kang said.

The remarks follow growing speculation over bilateral friction after South Korea's National Intelligence Service acknowledged it was excluded from a June trilateral meeting, also involving Japan, on North Korean cyber threats. Local media reports indicated the agency was left out at Washington's request.

South Korea and the U.S. have faced signs of friction in the intelligence field after Seoul Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's public disclosure of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility in Kusong, North Korea, in March.

headline: Tourist flow from Vietnam to Russia to rise by at least 30% following visa waiver
summary: The tourism industry views granting visa-free entry to Russia for Vietnamese citizens as a crucial step for the development of inbound tourism to Russia
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 12. /TASS/. Demand from Vietnamese tourists for trips to Russia could rise by at least 30% due to the visa waiver, the Association of Tour Operators of Russia (ATOR) told TASS.

"ATOR expects the introduction of visa-free entry for Vietnamese citizens (who currently use the e-visa system) to boost interest in tourism to Russia and lead to an increase in tourist flow from the country of at least 25-30%," the association said.

The tourism industry views granting visa-free entry to Russia for Vietnamese citizens as a crucial step for the development of inbound tourism to Russia. Tour operators consider the Vietnamese market promising in terms of both the potential number of visits and the quality of the tourist flow, ATOR explained.

"Vietnamese clients book comprehensive sightseeing programs across Russia and are willing to spend significant sums within the country on memorable experience and impressions. Beyond the major tourist hubs of Moscow and St. Petersburg, Vietnamese tourists show great interest in the Russian North," experts said.

Tourist traffic from Vietnam to Russia climbed by 69% in the first half of 2026 year-on-year, while total inbound traffic (for all purposes of visit) increased by 10.7%, the association noted.

On October 12, Russian President Vladimir Putin introduced a visa-free regime for Vietnamese citizens for one year, until October 15, 2027. Under this regime, they may visit Russia for up to 30 days for tourism, business, or other purposes, according to the presidential decree.

headline: China, Russia hold similar views on Northern Sea Route — Chinese foreign minister
summary: The Chinese top diplomat described the ocean as the "blue connecting thread," upon which the security and long-term development of all countries depend
body_text:
BEIJING, October 12. /TASS/. China and Russia share similar views on the development of the Northern Sea Route, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.

"China’s efforts to build the Ice Silk Road and Russia’s efforts to develop the Northern Sea Route are fully aligned. The importance of cooperation on maritime issues within the framework of the comprehensive strategic partnership between the People’s Republic of China and the Russian Federation continues to grow," the website of the Chinese Foreign Ministry quotes Wang Yi as saying.

He met in Beijing with Nikolay Patrushev, an aide to the Russian president and chairman of the Maritime Collegium.

According to the top Chinese diplomat, profound changes are unfolding in the modern world. He described the ocean as the "blue connecting thread," upon which the security and long-term development of all countries depend.

"China and Russia, as permanent members of the UN Security Council and maritime powers, bear significant responsibility for international maritime affairs and have extensive opportunities for cooperation," Wang Yi added.

headline: PKK withdraws from Turkish border area in Iraqi Kurdistan
summary: Militants from the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) have withdrawn from four camps in northern Iraq, Turkish security sources said on Monday, as part of a drawn-out disarmament process that could eventually include the return of former militants to Turkey. Fighters from the PKK withdrew from “four shelters” in the Metina area near the border with Turkey in Iraq’s Kurdistan region, security sources told state news agency Anadolu. The PKK last week said it had evacuated four “war tunnels” in the Metina area and withdrawn fighters from Turkey in the days before that. The moves showed it had “fulfilled” its strategy “to end the armed struggle against Turkey”, the group said. The Turkish sources did not mention withdrawals from Turkey but said the PKK's departure from the locations in Iraq’s Kurdistan region was part of efforts to evacuate locations that “pose a risk of conflict to Turkey’s security”. Neither Turkey nor the PKK said where the militants went next. The group is known to have locations in both federally-controlled Iraq and the Kurdistan region, including its headquarters in the Qandil Mountains. The PKK said last year it had withdrawn from other areas near the border with Turkey.The moves are part of a process of dissolution of the PKK, whose insurgents fought a 40-year conflict with the Turkish state until the group’s jailed leader, Abdullah Ocalan, last year called for it to dissolve and disarm. The conflict killed at least 40,000 people on both sides, spilt across Turkey’s borders with Syria and Iraq, and left an indelible mark on Turkish society, where up to one-fifth of the 86 million population is ethnically Kurdish. Turkey has long regarded the PKK as its main national security threat, and, alongside the EU and US, has designated the group as a terrorist organisation.Turkey’s parliament in August passed legislation that provides a legal framework and procedures for the PKK’s dissolution. It allows for the suspension of some prison sentences and the postponement of other trials and investigations, depending on the severity of the alleged offences. PKK members who live abroad, many in the group’s base in the Qandil Mountains, could be allowed to return home and reintegrate into society, although Turkish veterans’ groups have vehemently opposed such measures. The aim is to eventually ensure “social reconciliation” to end more than four decades of internal strife, Anadolu reported on Monday. But measures under the legislation can only take effect once Turkey's National Security Council is convinced that the PKK has completely dissolved and surrendered all its weapons – something that has not yet happened. Mehmet Ucum, a senior adviser to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said last month that the NSC would confirm the PKK’s dissolution and disarmament complete “by the end of this year at the latest”. Tuncer Bakirhan, co-chair of the pro-Kurdish Peoples' Equality and Democracy Party (DEM), said last week that some former militants could return as soon as this month, but a lot depended on the confirmation of their legal status. “People return not to a place where they don't know what will happen to them tomorrow, but to a place where their law, status, and security are defined,” he told the independent leftist Evrensel media outlet in an interview. Kurdish politicians, who do not belong to the PKK but have liaised between the group and the Turkish government, have criticised the peace process for moving too slowly and failing to provide Turkey’s Kurdish minority with greater access to cultural, political and social rights. Elected Kurdish mayors in the country’s south-east, whom the Turkish government replaced with political appointees, have not been reinstated, and people dismissed from their jobs over alleged PKK links have not been allowed to return to work. “Even the simplest steps are not being taken,” Mr Bakirhan said in separate remarks to MPs last week. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz told state media on Wednesday that the PKK’s dissolution process requires “patience”. The PKK has demanded that Turkey release Ocalan, who has been in prison for more than two decades, as part of the dissolution process, but Turkey has made no such pledges: the move would be highly unpopular among much of Turkish society after the decades of unrest and loss of life caused by the conflict between the PKK and the state. Ocalan could have a role on a disarmament committee as part of the dissolution process but would not be released from prison, presidential adviser Mr Ucum said last month.

headline: Young content creators to be trained in water awareness before UN conference in Abu Dhabi
summary: The UAE is recruiting 50 content creators to produce digital material on water sustainability before a major UN conference in Abu Dhabi this December.The National Media Authority, in partnership with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Federal Youth Authority, has launched the Blue Content Creators Programme, with applications open from October 12 to 30.The initiative will train 50 Emiratis and UAE residents to produce digital content raising awareness of water issues and highlighting the country's sustainability and innovation efforts. The programme comes as the UAE prepares to co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from December 8-10. It aims to equip young people with skills to communicate the links between water, human health, food, energy and development to audiences at home and abroad.Abdulla Balalaa, Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said the programme would bring new perspectives to water issues. "The decisions we make today about water will shape the world inherited by future generations," Mr Balalaa said. "It is essential that young people's voices and ideas help guide these decisions.Fresh ideas and vision"As the UAE prepares to welcome the world to Abu Dhabi for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, I look forward to the fresh perspectives and innovative ideas young content creators will bring to water issues, the questions they will raise, and the stories and experiences they will highlight. "Their participation will enrich the conference with new ideas and ambitious creative contributions, encourage us to examine challenges from different perspectives, and reinforce our shared responsibility to translate the discussions in Abu Dhabi into practical action that delivers tangible benefits to individuals and communities."Mohammed Al Shehhi, secretary general of the National Media Authority, said the UAE places water at the heart of its sustainable development efforts. "Raising awareness of these issues strengthens public understanding of the challenges and encourages community participation in addressing them," he said.The programme includes three weeks of training in November, covering water issues, storytelling, video production, digital publishing strategies and the use of artificial intelligence tools in content creation. Participants will then apply these skills to produce content related to the UN conference in December. Applications are open to UAE citizens and residents aged 18 to 35 with an interest in content creation, media, water, the environment or sustainability, with selections made to reflect the diversity of UAE society.
body_text:
The UAE is recruiting 50 content creators to produce digital material on water sustainability before a major UN conference in Abu Dhabi this December.

The National Media Authority, in partnership with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Federal Youth Authority, has launched the Blue Content Creators Programme, with applications open from October 12 to 30.

The initiative will train 50 Emiratis and UAE residents to produce digital content raising awareness of water issues and highlighting the country's sustainability and innovation efforts.

UN conference will shine spotlight on world's water crisis, says UAE minister

The programme comes as the UAE prepares to co-host the 2026 UN Water Conference with Senegal in Abu Dhabi from December 8-10. It aims to equip young people with skills to communicate the links between water, human health, food, energy and development to audiences at home and abroad.

Abdulla Balalaa, Assistant Minister of Foreign Affairs for Energy and Sustainability, said the programme would bring new perspectives to water issues.

"The decisions we make today about water will shape the world inherited by future generations," Mr Balalaa said. "It is essential that young people's voices and ideas help guide these decisions.

"As the UAE prepares to welcome the world to Abu Dhabi for the 2026 United Nations Water Conference, I look forward to the fresh perspectives and innovative ideas young content creators will bring to water issues, the questions they will raise, and the stories and experiences they will highlight.

"Their participation will enrich the conference with new ideas and ambitious creative contributions, encourage us to examine challenges from different perspectives, and reinforce our shared responsibility to translate the discussions in Abu Dhabi into practical action that delivers tangible benefits to individuals and communities."

Mohammed Al Shehhi, secretary general of the National Media Authority, said the UAE places water at the heart of its sustainable development efforts.

"Raising awareness of these issues strengthens public understanding of the challenges and encourages community participation in addressing them," he said.

The programme includes three weeks of training in November, covering water issues, storytelling, video production, digital publishing strategies and the use of artificial intelligence tools in content creation.

Participants will then apply these skills to produce content related to the UN conference in December. Applications are open to UAE citizens and residents aged 18 to 35 with an interest in content creation, media, water, the environment or sustainability, with selections made to reflect the diversity of UAE society.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Blue Content Creators Programme as a forward-looking, youth-empowering initiative that showcases the UAE's sustainability leadership ahead of the 2026 UN Water Conference.

headline: British airbase plot 'almost certainly directed' by Iran Guards: UK PM
summary: Britain's government Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind a major scare at a UK airbase used by the United States, as allies including Washington warned Tehran against hostile acts. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the British parliament that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) "almost certainly directed" an incident at Royal Air Force Fairford in southwest England last month.
body_text:
Britain's government Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind a major scare at a UK airbase used by the United States, as allies including Washington warned Tehran against hostile acts.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the British parliament that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) "almost certainly directed" an incident at Royal Air Force Fairford in southwest England last month.

The US, which had been using the base for its war in Iran, abruptly withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the site last week after the mysterious episode on September 27.

Burnham said Britain's assessment of the incident was that it "is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".

"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams," he told MPs.

Shortly afterwards, 29 countries, including the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France and Germany, released a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks".

The statement said such attacks included "acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners".

"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," it read.

The Foreign Office confirmed in its own statement Monday that Iran's ambassador to the UK had been summoned for talks.

"We are also announcing the designation of two Iranian nationals for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," foreign minister Ed Miliband said.

The foreign ministry said the individuals included Ruhollah Bazghandi, the IRGC's head of counterespionage operations, who is "now subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification".

Speculation has swirled about the incident since police were called to the base after a local farmer reported a group of men with several white vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.

Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, seven suspects arrested in the days following, including a British-Iranian national, have all since been released on bail. None has been charged.

The incident was declared "major" by British authorities and triggered the evacuation of a nearby village.

But the source and nature of the threat have remained shrouded in mystery.

Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but did recover some petrol, according to officials.

Burnham has previously said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, which Tehran has rejected.

Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes had been seen taking off and landing at the base.

US President Donald Trump has said Washington withdrew its bombers because of "threats" he believed were linked to Tehran.

In the foreign ministry statement, Miliband noted that the UK had already "designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) under our new state threats powers, and imposed major sanctions on those responsible for Iran's malign activity".

headline: PROFILE - Who are Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, recipients of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics?
summary: Robert E. Hall, professor of economics at Stanford University, focuses extensively on economic fluctuations and business cycles
body_text:
US economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics on Monday "for microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilization."

Hall and Woodford demonstrated how to reconstruct economic models to revitalize stabilization policies.

Their approach focuses on building models on microeconomic foundations rather than relying on statistical links between macroeconomic variables like inflation, production and consumption.

This method provides a deeper understanding of how the combined actions of individual households and businesses affect the overall economy.

Robert E. Hall, born in 1943, is an economist at Stanford University, where he is a professor of economics and a senior fellow at the Hoover Institution. He is generally regarded as a macroeconomist but describes himself as an applied economist.

Hall earned his bachelor’s degree in economics from the University of California, Berkeley, and his doctorate from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology under economist Robert Solow.

His work has focused extensively on economic fluctuations and business cycles. Since 1978, Hall has chaired the Business Cycle Dating Committee of the National Bureau of Economic Research, the body responsible for determining the beginning and end of US recessions.

He served as president of the American Economic Association in 2010 and is a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and the Econometric Society.

Michael Woodford, born in 1955, is an American macroeconomist and monetary theorist at Columbia University. His research has focused particularly on monetary policy and how expectations about future economic conditions influence economic decisions.

Woodford earned a bachelor’s degree from the University of Chicago, a law degree from Yale University and a doctorate in economics from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

He began his academic career at Columbia and later taught at the University of Chicago and Princeton University before returning to Columbia in 2004, where he holds the John Bates Clark Chair.

Woodford has received several major honors, including the Deutsche Bank Prize, the Erwin Plein Nemmers Prize in Economics and the BBVA Foundation Frontiers of Knowledge Award.

Hall and Woodford were recognized for helping rebuild macroeconomic theory on microeconomic foundations.

Earlier macroeconomic models often relied on statistical relationships between broad indicators such as inflation, production and consumption. Hall and Woodford instead emphasized the decisions of individual households and businesses and how those decisions collectively shape the economy.

A key insight in their work is that households and companies are forward-looking. Their decisions on issues such as saving, spending and pricing depend not only on current conditions but also on what they expect to happen in the future.

This means that governments and central banks can influence economic activity not only through immediate measures such as interest-rate changes and government spending, but also by communicating credible plans about future economic policy.

The approach helped revitalize stabilization policy after the economic turmoil of the 1970s, when high inflation, unemployment and weak growth raised doubts about the effectiveness of traditional Keynesian models.

According to the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, their work provided a stable theoretical foundation for models now used by central banks and governments to respond to economic shocks, including energy crises and sudden changes in household consumption.

In practical terms, their research has improved policymakers’ ability to smooth economic booms and recessions by understanding how policy decisions affect the expectations and behavior of households and businesses.
