headline: Likely unexploded ordnance kills teenager in northern Israel
summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - A 14-year-old Israeli boy was killed and 24people were injured when what was most likely an unexplodedordnance went off during a school hiking trip near the border with Lebanon, Israel's ambulance service said on Monday.The area is littered with explosive devices from Israel's conflict with the Lebanese militia group Hezbollah.Rockets and missiles aimed at Israel from southern Lebanon sometimes fail to explode on impact, which can create risks for civilians years in the future.
body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - A 14-year-old Israeli boy was killed and 24people were injured when what was most likely an unexplodedordnance went off during a school hiking trip near the border with Lebanon, Israel's ambulance service said on Monday.

The area is littered with explosive devices from Israel's conflict with the Lebanese militia group Hezbollah.

Rockets and missiles aimed at Israel from southern Lebanon sometimes fail to explode on impact, which can create risks for civilians years in the future.

Deputy Commissioner Meir Eliyahu, speaking at the scene, said that an unexploded device had most likely gone off after being picked up by one of the students.

"There were penetrating injuries, most likely the result of shrapnel impact from which fragments injured the patients," said Efrat Ohana, a paramedic at the site.

Some 22 boys, 2 seriously, and 2 adults were injured in the incident, the ambulance service said.

The Israeli military said that the device was likely an unexploded cluster munition from Hezbollah.

Daniel Levy, Israel's chief of police, said they would be reviewing whether to halt school trips in the area.

(Reporting by Pesha Magid; Editing by Toby Chopra)

headline: (LEAD) S. Korea's top envoy to U.S. acknowledges limitations in high-level communication with White House

By Chang Dong-woo(ATTN: UPDATES with more details from para 6)

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States acknowledged Monday that there have been limitations in communication with the White House, amid concerns over apparent friction in bilateral intelligence cooperation.

Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the South Korean Embassy in Washington, responding to questions about communication between Seoul and Washington.

"I acknowledge that there are limitations in our communication with the White House," Kang said.

The remarks follow growing speculation over bilateral friction after South Korea's National Intelligence Service acknowledged it was excluded from a June trilateral meeting, also involving Japan, on North Korean cyber threats. Local media reports indicated the agency was left out at Washington's request.

South Korea and the U.S. have faced signs of friction in the intelligence field after Seoul Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's public disclosure of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility in Kusong, North Korea, in March.

Regarding the controversy, the ambassador said she is aware that "intelligence agencies of the two countries have communicated with each other" and that "progress has been made" in terms of improving cooperation.

Kang also said she is unaware of any complaints raised by the U.S. side against the unification minister or South Korea's National Intelligence Service Director Lee Jong-seok.

"There have been various consultations regarding problems in connection with intelligence cooperation, but there have not been any complaints raised against any individual," Kang said.

Regarding the possibility of another North Korea-U.S. summit, the ambassador said she is aware that there has not been any concrete progress. "There is always the possibility, but it is hard to speak (of) in terms of numbers (likelihood)."

According to Kang, the subject of a possible North Korea-U.S. summit has become a topic of daily consultation between Seoul and Washington in terms of intelligence sharing.

headline: Iraq should not pose threat to Gulf states, President of Kurdistan region says
summary: President Nechirvan Barzani of Iraq's Kurdistan region has said weapons must be held by the Iraqi government and warned that the country must not threaten Gulf states, as Baghdad enters a new phase following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces.“Iraq should not be a threat to Gulf countries. Iraq should never do that, that is not sovereignty,” Mr Barzani said at the annual Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil on Monday. “Weapons should be in the hands of the government,” he added, arguing that Iraq needed to strengthen its ability to exercise sovereignty and take responsibility for its own security.The remarks come as Iraq faces pressure to bring armed factions under state control following attacks by Iran-aligned groups on targets in Iraq and across the region. The US-led coalition against ISIS completed its military withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, with security co-operation between Baghdad and Washington now moving towards a bilateral framework.In a statement marking October 1 as the day of full Iraqi sovereignty following the withdrawal, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said the serious work of dealing with weapons outside state control began now.Mr Barzani said Iraq no longer needed such a large international coalition after 12 years of its presence, adding that the country should develop bilateral security relationships with partner states. “We thank them, but we are happy today that Iraq stands on its feet,” he said. However, he stressed that the Kurdistan region still needed air defence systems to protect itself, following repeated drone and missile attacks.On the wider regional situation amid the Iran war, Mr Barzani said the changes unfolding across the Middle East presented both opportunities and threats for the Kurds, but he believed the opportunities could outweigh the risks. The greatest threat to Iraq, he said, was economic uncertainty, particularly the country's dependence on oil exports.“If the Strait of Hormuz is not resolved, it will be a long-term challenge,” he said, referring to the vital waterway through which a significant share of the world's oil supply passes and which has been effectively blockaded by Iran since the war began. He also warned that Iraq and the Kurdistan region faced challenges in maintaining stable relations with neighbouring countries while navigating the shifting regional landscape. Mr Barzani was more critical of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, saying their actions during the war had placed the Kurdistan region in a difficult position.“The opposition Iranian forces unfortunately behaved irresponsibly and put the Kurdistan region in an embarrassing position,” he said. He said the Kurdistan region's position had been clear from the beginning and that it would not become involved in the war.Reports that Iranian Kurdish opposition fighters were preparing to cross into Iran emerged in early March, after the Iran war broke out. Several media outlets reported that Washington had contacted Iranian Kurdish groups based in Iraq about a possible ground operation, with some fighters said to be on standby near the border. However, the groups denied that their forces had crossed into Iran. Iraqi Kurdish officials also rejected reports of an incursion, amid fears that any involvement could draw the Kurdistan region into the conflict and provoke further Iranian attacks. “It was not our war,” Mr Barzani said.The Kurdistan region shares a border of more than 600km with Iran. Mr Barzani said it was impossible for Erbil to allow its territory to become a staging ground for an attack on its neighbour.He said the regional government had closed the border during the early days of the conflict and deployed forces along it, making clear that it would not allow anyone to use the Kurdistan region to attack Iran.
body_text:
President Nechirvan Barzani of Iraq's Kurdistan region has said weapons must be held by the Iraqi government and warned that the country must not threaten Gulf states, as Baghdad enters a new phase following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces.

“Iraq should not be a threat to Gulf countries. Iraq should never do that, that is not sovereignty,” Mr Barzani said at the annual Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil on Monday. “Weapons should be in the hands of the government,” he added, arguing that Iraq needed to strengthen its ability to exercise sovereignty and take responsibility for its own security.

The remarks come as Iraq faces pressure to bring armed factions under state control following attacks by Iran-aligned groups on targets in Iraq and across the region. The US-led coalition against ISIS completed its military withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, with security co-operation between Baghdad and Washington now moving towards a bilateral framework.

In a statement marking October 1 as the day of full Iraqi sovereignty following the withdrawal, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said the serious work of dealing with weapons outside state control began now.

Mr Barzani said Iraq no longer needed such a large international coalition after 12 years of its presence, adding that the country should develop bilateral security relationships with partner states. “We thank them, but we are happy today that Iraq stands on its feet,” he said. However, he stressed that the Kurdistan region still needed air defence systems to protect itself, following repeated drone and missile attacks.

On the wider regional situation amid the Iran war, Mr Barzani said the changes unfolding across the Middle East presented both opportunities and threats for the Kurds, but he believed the opportunities could outweigh the risks. The greatest threat to Iraq, he said, was economic uncertainty, particularly the country's dependence on oil exports.

“If the Strait of Hormuz is not resolved, it will be a long-term challenge,” he said, referring to the vital waterway through which a significant share of the world's oil supply passes and which has been effectively blockaded by Iran since the war began.

He also warned that Iraq and the Kurdistan region faced challenges in maintaining stable relations with neighbouring countries while navigating the shifting regional landscape. Mr Barzani was more critical of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, saying their actions during the war had placed the Kurdistan region in a difficult position.

“The opposition Iranian forces unfortunately behaved irresponsibly and put the Kurdistan region in an embarrassing position,” he said. He said the Kurdistan region's position had been clear from the beginning and that it would not become involved in the war.

Reports that Iranian Kurdish opposition fighters were preparing to cross into Iran emerged in early March, after the Iran war broke out. Several media outlets reported that Washington had contacted Iranian Kurdish groups based in Iraq about a possible ground operation, with some fighters said to be on standby near the border.

However, the groups denied that their forces had crossed into Iran. Iraqi Kurdish officials also rejected reports of an incursion, amid fears that any involvement could draw the Kurdistan region into the conflict and provoke further Iranian attacks. “It was not our war,” Mr Barzani said.

The Kurdistan region shares a border of more than 600km with Iran. Mr Barzani said it was impossible for Erbil to allow its territory to become a staging ground for an attack on its neighbour.

He said the regional government had closed the border during the early days of the conflict and deployed forces along it, making clear that it would not allow anyone to use the Kurdistan region to attack Iran.

headline: Top Chinese diplomat praises close cooperation and growing trust with Russia
summary: Wang Yi stressed that under the leadership of the two countries’ leaders China and Russia remained steadfastly committed to the long-term cause of national revitalization
body_text:
BEIJING, October 12. /TASS/. Trust and cooperation between Russia and China have grown significantly stronger, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.

"The Chinese and Russian presidents, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, maintain close contacts, steering relations between the two countries toward a higher quality and level. <…> Strategic trust between our countries has become even more solid, cooperation in all spheres has become more sustainable, and all-round coordination has grown closer," he said at a meeting with visiting Russian presidential aide and chairman of the Maritime Board Nikolay Patrushev, as quoted by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

The top Chinese diplomat also conveyed Xi’s greetings to Putin, saying that under the leadership of the two countries’ leaders China and Russia "remain steadfastly committed to the long-term cause of national revitalization, uphold a historic stance on defending international justice, and steadily develop bilateral relations."

He also recalled that Russia had held parliamentary elections in September and welcomed their results as "reflecting the Russian people’s will."

headline: Europe must wake up, join efforts to settle Ukraine conflict — Czech prime minister
summary: Commenting on the Russia-US agreement on diesel supplies, Andrej Babis called it a complete shock
body_text:
PRAGUE, October 12. /TASS/. Europe must wake up and join efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine, Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis said.

"Europe must wake up and start addressing this situation as a whole, as well as take part in settling the conflict in Ukraine," the CTK news agency quoted him as saying. Commenting on the Russia-US agreement on diesel supplies, Babis called it a complete shock.

The Czech prime minister, who will represent his country at the upcoming EU summit, said Vladimir Zelensky is expected to attend the meeting in Brussels. European leaders will discuss the situation in Ukraine, but it remains to be seen whether the Russia-US agreements will lead to a change in their rhetoric, he added.

On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call during which they discussed, among other issues, petroleum product supplies. Putin said Russia had reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russia is beginning to lift its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule and is prepared to supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel in October, 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million metric tons in December, with supplies potentially reaching 3 million metric tons per month in the future. The US administration is exempting Russian diesel supplies to global markets from US sanctions through April 7, 2027.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event through Czech Prime Minister Babis's call for Europe to engage in Ukraine conflict settlement, while prominently detailing Russia-US diesel supply agreements and sanctions exemptions.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged phrase attributed to Babis, conveying strong surprise without neutral qualification.

omissions: No mention of Ukraine's official response to the Russia-US diesel agreement or the EU summit agenda.
No context on European Union sanctions policy regarding Russian diesel or potential divisions among EU member states.
No details on the duration or terms of the Russia-US agreement beyond the sanctions exemption date.

headline: China ready to safeguard maritime interests, navigation with Russia — foreign minister
summary: According to Wang Yi, China and Russia should harness the ocean to develop Sino-Russian relations, "contribute to improving global maritime affairs management and promote the formation of a maritime community with a common destiny"
body_text:
BEIJING, October 12. /TASS/. China is ready to cooperate with Russia to protect their shared maritime interests and ensure normal navigation in the Asia-Pacific region, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.

"China is ready to work together with Russia, enhance coordination between the two countries' maritime strategies, capitalize on their complementary advantages, protect each other's legitimate maritime rights and interests, maintain maritime security in the Asia-Pacific region, and ensure normal navigation along key sea routes worldwide," the Chinese Foreign Ministry quoted Wang Yi as saying.

Wang Yi met with Nikolay Patrushev, Russian presidential aide and Chairman of the Maritime Board, in Beijing.

The top Chinese diplomat said it was necessary to respect the sovereignty and security of states adjacent to the sea, ensure stable energy supplies, and maintain the safe operation of production and supply chains. He also highlighted the importance of broader exchanges of views on maritime and Arctic issues.

According to Wang Yi, China and Russia should harness the ocean to develop Sino-Russian relations, "contribute to improving global maritime affairs management, and promote the formation of a maritime community with a common destiny."

loaded_language.explanation: A vague, ideologically loaded phrase echoing Chinese state diplomatic rhetoric that implies a shared geopolitical project without specifying its terms.

headline: Opinion | On the Same Page: A Reading of Egypt’s National Identity Charter
summary: Writing in December 1934, Egyptian intellectual Ahmed Hassan al-Zayyat grappled with anxieties of modernisation. “The radio has defeated the poet in every coffeehouse, just as the machine has defeated man in every field of work! In every one of these coffeehouses stands a machine of this marvellous invention, enticing popular tastes with art, training ears resistant to music, awakening unheeding minds to knowledge, and endearing literature to souls unconcerned with it… Yet despite all this, I am deeply saddened by the death of the storyteller, and profoundly grieved by the loss of the poet.” Across the ages, Egyptians have repeatedly set the rhythm and tone of human expression, adapting new technologies to share knowledge, tell stories and shape culture. The National Identity Conference tuned that conversation to its latest frequency with “Identity in the Digital Age” as a central theme encompassing artificial intelligence, misinformation, social media and the pressures of rapid technological change. From 21 to 23 September 2026, officials, academics, artists and around 450 young Egyptians from all 27 governorates came together at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, culminating in the presentation of the National Identity Charter, “Deep Roots and Renewed Vision.” The Charter describes Egyptian identity as “enduring in its foundations while evolving in the ways it is expressed,” presenting continuity and change not as opposing forces but complementary dimensions of Egypt’s identity. The Charter returns repeatedly to consensus and mutual trust, presenting them as foundations of social cohesion and national identity. There is much to be said for this conception of cohesion, particularly in its emphasis on a shared sense of belonging. Yet the language of consensus raises an important question for a document that places such emphasis on diversity. Consensus need not mean agreement on every question, and a plural society may be held together less by uniformity of belief than by agreement on the principles that allow differences to coexist. The Charter itself acknowledges that Egyptians have diverse individual identities and that national identity must embrace this diversity. Its challenge, then, is to distinguish between a shared national framework and a requirement of shared conclusions: between agreeing on the rules of belonging and agreeing on what belonging must look like. Mutual trust can strengthen that framework while allowing citizens to hold different cultural and social understandings within it. Read alongside Article 50 of the 2014 Constitution, which describes Egypt’s cultural heritage as a national and human wealth encompassing its diversities and calls for the protection of cultural pluralism, the Charter invites a useful question: can consensus be understood not as the absence of disagreement, but as a shared commitment to living with it? Nadine Loza The document’s recognition of Egypt’s rural, urban, coastal, Bedouin and desert communities as integral components of Egyptian cultural diversity reflects a commitment to inclusion and to ensuring that all Egyptians are visible within the national narrative. The Charter’s specific reference to Bedouin communities is particularly noteworthy because they are the only distinct cultural community explicitly named within its discussion of Egyptian cultural diversity. This raises a broader principle of identity-making: recognition can sometimes have the effect of emphasising the very distinctions it seeks to transcend. The designation of particular communities as distinct categories can, even when intended to affirm their place within the nation, create tension within the broader national “we”. The Charter’s emphasis on equal and inclusive citizenship provides an important common framework, while its recognition of Bedouin cultural heritage and way of life illustrates the importance of giving cultural particularity its proper place within a common national identity. The opposite problem is also worth keeping in view: the absence of categories can make communities invisible for purposes of measurement and public policy. The current debate in the United States over whether and how race and ethnicity should be collected in the census illustrates this distinction. The US Census Bureau has argued that such data are important for understanding disparities, civil-rights enforcement and representation but a current federal proposal would remove race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census altogether. If adopted, that would raise a different form of recognition problem—not the symbolic othering that can accompany classification, but the loss of statistical visibility needed to identify particular communities and their circumstances. Recognition need not mean either emphasising difference or making it invisible; the more useful distinction is between recognising cultural difference as part of an inclusive national identity and measuring difference where doing so is necessary to understand and address inequalities. The Bibliotheca Alexandrina Charter’s recognition of the role of mothers in transmitting stories, proverbs, songs and practices reflects a key social reality: in many households, mothers have carried a substantial share of the work of intergenerational transmission. Yet describing an existing division of labour can also risk making it seem natural or expected. The Charter rightly calls for greater support for families, but the preservation of cultural identity should not become a responsibility attached disproportionately to mothers simply because they have historically carried much of it. Fathers, grandparents, schools, teachers, cultural institutions, media organisations and public bodies can all help shape how children encounter Egypt. The more we appreciate the contribution of mothers, the more important it becomes to understand cultural transmission as a shared responsibility. The Charter notes that “the contemporary digital age is fraught with risks” and calls for “critical awareness and digital literacy, particularly among younger generations.” Education, entertainment, promotional content and personal expression appear on the same screen, while the usual signifiers that help us distinguish between them are becoming blurred. Although young people often have greater practical fluency with the internet, knowing how to use a platform is not the same as being a conscious user of it. Digital literacy, therefore, increasingly requires an element of epistemic literacy: the ability to evaluate the information encountered online, including its source, context, credibility and why it was produced. As AI makes fabricated content more convincing, these judgements become more important. This is an intergenerational challenge, requiring adults as well as young people to navigate an information environment shaped by AI-generated content, deepfakes and other forms of synthetic media. Building on this, Egypt should also adopt and enforce transparent practices across the wider information environment, including traditional media, requiring disclosure of the use of AI in news, advertising, music, images, videos, text and other published content. The Charter’s call to involve youth in designing and implementing cultural programmes is significant, but that participation should be fair and inclusive, ensuring that all young people have meaningful access to digital and cultural spaces and opportunities to discover and develop their creative abilities. We must additionally ensure that children have safe spaces offline where they can engage their imagination and express themselves without judgement, receive sound advice, reliable support and clear knowledge. Egypt’s constitutional framework provides a strong foundation for integrating national identity within education. Article 19 states that education aims to build character, nurture talents, promote innovation and cultivate values of citizenship, tolerance and non-discrimination, while Article 24 positions Arabic, religious education and national history as core subjects for all pre-university students. The National Identity Charter similarly identifies collective memory, language and cultural heritage as fundamental pillars of identity, while calling for greater awareness of Egypt’s long history and diverse civilisational influences. In alignment with this vision, the Ministry of Education’s August 2024 policy integrated Arabic and history into the graduation requirements for international curricula students, with each subject accounting for 10 percent of the overall grade. When the requirements were introduced, their impact varied depending on where students were in their education. Students in the earlier years of their schooling could incorporate the new subjects from the outset, whereas those already approaching graduation had less time to adjust to subjects that had not previously been part of their curriculum. More fundamentally, formal assessment is only one part of education. A standardised examination can establish whether a student has retained enough information to pass, but it cannot measure what they genuinely understand, their curiosity, or their ability to interpret and make meaningful use of what they have learned. A locally grounded curriculum allows students to engage with the culture, history, language and heritage they physically inhabit. There is little reason to assume that the love life of Henry VIII, or the intricacies of the Battle of Hastings—whose account has itself recently been subject to scholarly reconsideration—should be more relevant to the education of a young Egyptian than their own extraordinary, tangible historical inheritance. All students should learn about other societies and cultures while gaining a fuller understanding of the nation to which they themselves belong. Egypt is the country most immediately associated with history itself, and its civilisation remains a source of fascination and study throughout the world—its achievements, language and culture have shaped all that followed. Wherever their education or future takes them, a strong knowledge of Egypt gives them a deeper sense of the identity they carry with them and of the country they represent. Language may be one of the clearest expressions of the Charter’s understanding of identity. It describes Arabic as “the official language, the principal pillar of Egypt’s shared culture, and the means of communication and expression among Egyptians,” while recognising that its colloquial dialects “form part of the richness of Egyptian culture.” The Charter is right to insist on “mastering foreign languages without allowing them to replace the mother tongue, diminish the status of Arabic, or stigmatize those who are educated in Arabic”. An education in Arabic is a point of pride; the concern should be whether the schools, facilities and teaching standards that deliver it are adequately funded and properly supported. An accent, dialect or varying fluency should never detract from the effort and courage involved in communicating and learning in any language, or distract from the substance of what is being said. The relationship between language and identity takes on new significance as AI reconfigures the infosphere. Egypt’s national Arabic language model, Karnak, and Karnak Chat, launched in August 2026, represent an effort to ensure that these technologies can understand Modern Standard Arabic, Egyptian colloquial Arabic and cultural context. Alongside this, digitising archives, literature, oral histories and artistic works ensures that more of Egypt’s cultural memory remains available to the systems through which future generations will encounter knowledge. There is also a less obvious possibility: AI can strengthen national identity by giving countries new ways to preserve, access and share their own cultural and linguistic resources. Egypt’s National AI Strategy 2025–2030 reflects an effort to develop these capabilities within Egypt and apply them to areas of national and cultural importance. In this sense, technological change need not only test cultural continuity; it can also give that continuity new means of transmission. The radio once seemed to make the storyteller unnecessary. Instead, the story found another way to travel. Nearly a century later, machines have become far more capable of carrying, producing and transforming language, even as the distinctions between the person who creates, the machine that produces and the audience that receives grow quieter. The Charter asks what must endure as the forms around it change. Identity, after all, does not belong to the past; each generation inherits the conversation, finds a new medium for it, and leaves something of its own for the next to answer. Nadine Loza is a development strategist, opinion columnist, and Founding Director of the Egypt Diaspora Initiative.

headline: British airbase plot 'almost certainly directed' by Iran Guards: UK PM
summary: Britain's government Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind a major scare at a UK airbase used by the United States, as allies including Washington warned Tehran against hostile acts. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the British parliament that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) "almost certainly directed" an incident at Royal Air Force Fairford in southwest England last month.
body_text:
Britain's government Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of being behind a major scare at a UK airbase used by the United States, as allies including Washington warned Tehran against hostile acts.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham told the British parliament that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) "almost certainly directed" an incident at Royal Air Force Fairford in southwest England last month.

The US, which had been using the base for its war in Iran, abruptly withdrew all its B-1 bombers from the site last week after the mysterious episode on September 27.

Burnham said Britain's assessment of the incident was that it "is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".

"We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran's use of criminal networks, using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams," he told MPs.

Shortly afterwards, 29 countries, including the US, Britain, Australia, Canada, France and Germany, released a joint statement denouncing "in the strongest terms Iran’s use of violent attacks".

The statement said such attacks included "acts of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities against us and our partners".

"Any attempt by Iran to threaten, silence, intimidate, harass, harm, or coerce people on our territories through proxies or any other means is unacceptable," it read.

The Foreign Office confirmed in its own statement Monday that Iran's ambassador to the UK had been summoned for talks.

"We are also announcing the designation of two Iranian nationals for their role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime, with the clear intent of threatening, planning or conducting attacks overseas," foreign minister Ed Miliband said.

The foreign ministry said the individuals included Ruhollah Bazghandi, the IRGC's head of counterespionage operations, who is "now subject to an immediate asset freeze, travel ban and director disqualification".

Speculation has swirled about the incident since police were called to the base after a local farmer reported a group of men with several white vans engaged in "suspicious" activity.

Despite a major counter-terrorism probe, seven suspects arrested in the days following, including a British-Iranian national, have all since been released on bail. None has been charged.

The incident was declared "major" by British authorities and triggered the evacuation of a nearby village.

But the source and nature of the threat have remained shrouded in mystery.

Investigators did not find any explosives in the vans, but did recover some petrol, according to officials.

Burnham has previously said there were "strong indications that Iran played a part" in the incident, which Tehran has rejected.

Britain gave Washington permission in March to use Fairford for "specific defensive operations into Iran," and US bombers and other planes had been seen taking off and landing at the base.

US President Donald Trump has said Washington withdrew its bombers because of "threats" he believed were linked to Tehran.

In the foreign ministry statement, Miliband noted that the UK had already "designated the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) under our new state threats powers, and imposed major sanctions on those responsible for Iran's malign activity".

headline: Likely unexploded ordnance kills teenager in northern Israel
summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - A 14-year-old Israeli boy was killed and 24people were injured when what was most likely an unexplodedordnance went off during a school hiking trip near the border with Lebanon, Israel's ambulance service said on Monday.The area is littered with explosive devices from Israel's conflict with the Lebanese militia group Hezbollah.Rockets and missiles aimed at Israel from southern Lebanon sometimes fail to explode on impact, which can create risks for civilians years in the future.
body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 12 (Reuters) - A 14-year-old Israeli boy was killed and 24people were injured when what was most likely an unexplodedordnance went off during a school hiking trip near the border with Lebanon, Israel's ambulance service said on Monday.

The area is littered with explosive devices from Israel's conflict with the Lebanese militia group Hezbollah.

Rockets and missiles aimed at Israel from southern Lebanon sometimes fail to explode on impact, which can create risks for civilians years in the future.

Deputy Commissioner Meir Eliyahu, speaking at the scene, said that an unexploded device had most likely gone off after being picked up by one of the students.

"There were penetrating injuries, most likely the result of shrapnel impact from which fragments injured the patients," said Efrat Ohana, a paramedic at the site.

Some 22 boys, 2 seriously, and 2 adults were injured in the incident, the ambulance service said.

The Israeli military said that the device was likely an unexploded cluster munition from Hezbollah.

Daniel Levy, Israel's chief of police, said they would be reviewing whether to halt school trips in the area.

(Reporting by Pesha Magid; Editing by Toby Chopra)

headline: (LEAD) S. Korea's top envoy to U.S. acknowledges limitations in high-level communication with White House
summary: WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States ack...
body_text:
By Chang Dong-woo(ATTN: UPDATES with more details from para 6)

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States acknowledged Monday that there have been limitations in communication with the White House, amid concerns over apparent friction in bilateral intelligence cooperation.

Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the South Korean Embassy in Washington, responding to questions about communication between Seoul and Washington.

"I acknowledge that there are limitations in our communication with the White House," Kang said.

The remarks follow growing speculation over bilateral friction after South Korea's National Intelligence Service acknowledged it was excluded from a June trilateral meeting, also involving Japan, on North Korean cyber threats. Local media reports indicated the agency was left out at Washington's request.

South Korea and the U.S. have faced signs of friction in the intelligence field after Seoul Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's public disclosure of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility in Kusong, North Korea, in March.

Regarding the controversy, the ambassador said she is aware that "intelligence agencies of the two countries have communicated with each other" and that "progress has been made" in terms of improving cooperation.

Kang also said she is unaware of any complaints raised by the U.S. side against the unification minister or South Korea's National Intelligence Service Director Lee Jong-seok.

"There have been various consultations regarding problems in connection with intelligence cooperation, but there have not been any complaints raised against any individual," Kang said.

Regarding the possibility of another North Korea-U.S. summit, the ambassador said she is aware that there has not been any concrete progress. "There is always the possibility, but it is hard to speak (of) in terms of numbers (likelihood)."

According to Kang, the subject of a possible North Korea-U.S. summit has become a topic of daily consultation between Seoul and Washington in terms of intelligence sharing.

President Nechirvan Barzani of Iraq's Kurdistan region has said weapons must be held by the Iraqi government and warned that the country must not threaten Gulf states, as Baghdad enters a new phase following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces.

“Iraq should not be a threat to Gulf countries. Iraq should never do that, that is not sovereignty,” Mr Barzani said at the annual Middle East Research Institute Forum in Erbil on Monday. “Weapons should be in the hands of the government,” he added, arguing that Iraq needed to strengthen its ability to exercise sovereignty and take responsibility for its own security.

The remarks come as Iraq faces pressure to bring armed factions under state control following attacks by Iran-aligned groups on targets in Iraq and across the region. The US-led coalition against ISIS completed its military withdrawal from Iraq on September 30, with security co-operation between Baghdad and Washington now moving towards a bilateral framework.

In a statement marking October 1 as the day of full Iraqi sovereignty following the withdrawal, Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi said the serious work of dealing with weapons outside state control began now.

Mr Barzani said Iraq no longer needed such a large international coalition after 12 years of its presence, adding that the country should develop bilateral security relationships with partner states. “We thank them, but we are happy today that Iraq stands on its feet,” he said. However, he stressed that the Kurdistan region still needed air defence systems to protect itself, following repeated drone and missile attacks.

On the wider regional situation amid the Iran war, Mr Barzani said the changes unfolding across the Middle East presented both opportunities and threats for the Kurds, but he believed the opportunities could outweigh the risks. The greatest threat to Iraq, he said, was economic uncertainty, particularly the country's dependence on oil exports.

“If the Strait of Hormuz is not resolved, it will be a long-term challenge,” he said, referring to the vital waterway through which a significant share of the world's oil supply passes and which has been effectively blockaded by Iran since the war began.

He also warned that Iraq and the Kurdistan region faced challenges in maintaining stable relations with neighbouring countries while navigating the shifting regional landscape. Mr Barzani was more critical of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups, saying their actions during the war had placed the Kurdistan region in a difficult position.

“The opposition Iranian forces unfortunately behaved irresponsibly and put the Kurdistan region in an embarrassing position,” he said. He said the Kurdistan region's position had been clear from the beginning and that it would not become involved in the war.

Reports that Iranian Kurdish opposition fighters were preparing to cross into Iran emerged in early March, after the Iran war broke out. Several media outlets reported that Washington had contacted Iranian Kurdish groups based in Iraq about a possible ground operation, with some fighters said to be on standby near the border.

However, the groups denied that their forces had crossed into Iran. Iraqi Kurdish officials also rejected reports of an incursion, amid fears that any involvement could draw the Kurdistan region into the conflict and provoke further Iranian attacks. “It was not our war,” Mr Barzani said.

The Kurdistan region shares a border of more than 600km with Iran. Mr Barzani said it was impossible for Erbil to allow its territory to become a staging ground for an attack on its neighbour.

He said the regional government had closed the border during the early days of the conflict and deployed forces along it, making clear that it would not allow anyone to use the Kurdistan region to attack Iran.

headline: Top Chinese diplomat praises close cooperation and growing trust with Russia
summary: Wang Yi stressed that under the leadership of the two countries’ leaders China and Russia remained steadfastly committed to the long-term cause of national revitalization
body_text:
BEIJING, October 12. /TASS/. Trust and cooperation between Russia and China have grown significantly stronger, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.

"The Chinese and Russian presidents, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, maintain close contacts, steering relations between the two countries toward a higher quality and level. <…> Strategic trust between our countries has become even more solid, cooperation in all spheres has become more sustainable, and all-round coordination has grown closer," he said at a meeting with visiting Russian presidential aide and chairman of the Maritime Board Nikolay Patrushev, as quoted by the Chinese Foreign Ministry.

The top Chinese diplomat also conveyed Xi’s greetings to Putin, saying that under the leadership of the two countries’ leaders China and Russia "remain steadfastly committed to the long-term cause of national revitalization, uphold a historic stance on defending international justice, and steadily develop bilateral relations."

He also recalled that Russia had held parliamentary elections in September and welcomed their results as "reflecting the Russian people’s will."

headline: Europe must wake up, join efforts to settle Ukraine conflict — Czech prime minister
summary: Commenting on the Russia-US agreement on diesel supplies, Andrej Babis called it a complete shock
body_text:
PRAGUE, October 12. /TASS/. Europe must wake up and join efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine, Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis said.

"Europe must wake up and start addressing this situation as a whole, as well as take part in settling the conflict in Ukraine," the CTK news agency quoted him as saying. Commenting on the Russia-US agreement on diesel supplies, Babis called it a complete shock.

The Czech prime minister, who will represent his country at the upcoming EU summit, said Vladimir Zelensky is expected to attend the meeting in Brussels. European leaders will discuss the situation in Ukraine, but it remains to be seen whether the Russia-US agreements will lead to a change in their rhetoric, he added.

On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a phone call during which they discussed, among other issues, petroleum product supplies. Putin said Russia had reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russia is beginning to lift its ban on diesel exports ahead of schedule and is prepared to supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel in October, 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million metric tons in December, with supplies potentially reaching 3 million metric tons per month in the future. The US administration is exempting Russian diesel supplies to global markets from US sanctions through April 7, 2027.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event through Czech Prime Minister Babis's call for Europe to engage in resolving the Ukraine conflict, while prominently detailing Russia-US diesel supply agreements and US sanctions exemptions, presenting these developments in a matter-of-fact manner.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged phrase attributed to Babis, conveying strong surprise without neutral qualification.

omissions: No mention of the ongoing conflict's impact on Ukraine or civilian casualties.
No details on European Union's existing sanctions policy on Russia or reactions from other EU leaders.
No context on why the diesel agreement might be controversial or its implications for Ukraine.

headline: China ready to safeguard maritime interests, navigation with Russia — foreign minister
summary: According to Wang Yi, China and Russia should harness the ocean to develop Sino-Russian relations, "contribute to improving global maritime affairs management and promote the formation of a maritime community with a common destiny"
body_text:
BEIJING, October 12. /TASS/. China is ready to cooperate with Russia to protect their shared maritime interests and ensure normal navigation in the Asia-Pacific region, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said.

"China is ready to work together with Russia, enhance coordination between the two countries' maritime strategies, capitalize on their complementary advantages, protect each other's legitimate maritime rights and interests, maintain maritime security in the Asia-Pacific region, and ensure normal navigation along key sea routes worldwide," the Chinese Foreign Ministry quoted Wang Yi as saying.

Wang Yi met with Nikolay Patrushev, Russian presidential aide and Chairman of the Maritime Board, in Beijing.

The top Chinese diplomat said it was necessary to respect the sovereignty and security of states adjacent to the sea, ensure stable energy supplies, and maintain the safe operation of production and supply chains. He also highlighted the importance of broader exchanges of views on maritime and Arctic issues.

According to Wang Yi, China and Russia should harness the ocean to develop Sino-Russian relations, "contribute to improving global maritime affairs management, and promote the formation of a maritime community with a common destiny."

headline: Opinion | On the Same Page: A Reading of Egypt’s National Identity Charter
summary: Writing in December 1934, Egyptian intellectual Ahmed Hassan al-Zayyat grappled with anxieties of modernisation. “The radio has defeated the poet in every coffeehouse, just as the machine has defeated man in every field of work! In every one of these coffeehouses stands a machine of this marvellous invention, enticing popular tastes with art, training ears resistant to music, awakening unheeding minds to knowledge, and endearing literature to souls unconcerned with it… Yet despite all this, I am deeply saddened by the death of the storyteller, and profoundly grieved by the loss of the poet.” Across the ages, Egyptians have repeatedly set the rhythm and tone of human expression, adapting new technologies to share knowledge, tell stories and shape culture. The National Identity Conference tuned that conversation to its latest frequency with “Identity in the Digital Age” as a central theme encompassing artificial intelligence, misinformation, social media and the pressures of rapid technological change. From 21 to 23 September 2026, officials, academics, artists and around 450 young Egyptians from all 27 governorates came together at the Bibliotheca Alexandrina, culminating in the presentation of the National Identity Charter, “Deep Roots and Renewed Vision.” The Charter describes Egyptian identity as “enduring in its foundations while evolving in the ways it is expressed,” presenting continuity and change not as opposing forces but complementary dimensions of Egypt’s identity. The Charter returns repeatedly to consensus and mutual trust, presenting them as foundations of social cohesion and national identity. There is much to be said for this conception of cohesion, particularly in its emphasis on a shared sense of belonging. Yet the language of consensus raises an important question for a document that places such emphasis on diversity. Consensus need not mean agreement on every question, and a plural society may be held together less by uniformity of belief than by agreement on the principles that allow differences to coexist. The Charter itself acknowledges that Egyptians have diverse individual identities and that national identity must embrace this diversity. Its challenge, then, is to distinguish between a shared national framework and a requirement of shared conclusions: between agreeing on the rules of belonging and agreeing on what belonging must look like. Mutual trust can strengthen that framework while allowing citizens to hold different cultural and social understandings within it. Read alongside Article 50 of the 2014 Constitution, which describes Egypt’s cultural heritage as a national and human wealth encompassing its diversities and calls for the protection of cultural pluralism, the Charter invites a useful question: can consensus be understood not as the absence of disagreement, but as a shared commitment to living with it? Nadine Loza The document’s recognition of Egypt’s rural, urban, coastal, Bedouin and desert communities as integral components of Egyptian cultural diversity reflects a commitment to inclusion and to ensuring that all Egyptians are visible within the national narrative. The Charter’s specific reference to Bedouin communities is particularly noteworthy because they are the only distinct cultural community explicitly named within its discussion of Egyptian cultural diversity. This raises a broader principle of identity-making: recognition can sometimes have the effect of emphasising the very distinctions it seeks to transcend. The designation of particular communities as distinct categories can, even when intended to affirm their place within the nation, create tension within the broader national “we”. The Charter’s emphasis on equal and inclusive citizenship provides an important common framework, while its recognition of Bedouin cultural heritage and way of life illustrates the importance of giving cultural particularity its proper place within a common national identity. The opposite problem is also worth keeping in view: the absence of categories can make communities invisible for purposes of measurement and public policy. The current debate in the United States over whether and how race and ethnicity should be collected in the census illustrates this distinction. The US Census Bureau has argued that such data are important for understanding disparities, civil-rights enforcement and representation but a current federal proposal would remove race and ethnicity questions from the decennial census altogether. If adopted, that would raise a different form of recognition problem—not the symbolic othering that can accompany classification, but the loss of statistical visibility needed to identify particular communities and their circumstances. Recognition need not mean either emphasising difference or making it invisible; the more useful distinction is between recognising cultural difference as part of an inclusive national identity and measuring difference where doing so is necessary to understand and address inequalities. The Bibliotheca Alexandrina Charter’s recognition of the role of mothers in transmitting stories, proverbs, songs and practices reflects a key social reality: in many households, mothers have carried a substantial share of the work of intergenerational transmission. Yet describing an existing division of labour can also risk making it seem natural or expected. The Charter rightly calls for greater support for families, but the preservation of cultural identity should not become a responsibility attached disproportionately to mothers simply because they have historically carried much of it. Fathers, grandparents, schools, teachers, cultural institutions, media organisations and public bodies can all help shape how children encounter Egypt. The more we appreciate the contribution of mothers, the more important it becomes to understand cultural transmission as a shared responsibility. The Charter notes that “the contemporary digital age is fraught with risks” and calls for “critical awareness and digital literacy, particularly among younger generations.” Education, entertainment, promotional content and personal expression appear on the same screen, while the usual signifiers that help us distinguish between them are becoming blurred. Although young people often have greater practical fluency with the internet, knowing how to use a platform is not the same as being a conscious user of it. Digital literacy, therefore, increasingly requires an element of epistemic literacy: the ability to evaluate the information encountered online, including its source, context, credibility and why it was produced. As AI makes fabricated content more convincing, these judgements become more important. This is an intergenerational challenge, requiring adults as well as young people to navigate an information environment shaped by AI-generated content, deepfakes and other forms of synthetic media. Building on this, Egypt should also adopt and enforce transparent practices across the wider information environment, including traditional media, requiring disclosure of the use of AI in news, advertising, music, images, videos, text and other published content. The Charter’s call to involve youth in designing and implementing cultural programmes is significant, but that participation should be fair and inclusive, ensuring that all young people have meaningful access to digital and cultural spaces and opportunities to discover and develop their creative abilities. We must additionally ensure that children have safe spaces offline where they can engage their imagination and express themselves without judgement, receive sound advice, reliable support and clear knowledge. Egypt’s constitutional framework provides a strong foundation for integrating national identity within education. Article 19 states that education aims to build character, nurture talents, promote innovation and cultivate values of citizenship, tolerance and non-discrimination, while Article 24 positions Arabic, religious education and national history as core subjects for all pre-university students. The National Identity Charter similarly identifies collective memory, language and cultural heritage as fundamental pillars of identity, while calling for greater awareness of Egypt’s long history and diverse civilisational influences. In alignment with this vision, the Ministry of Education’s August 2024 policy integrated Arabic and history into the graduation requirements for international curricula students, with each subject accounting for 10 percent of the overall grade. When the requirements were introduced, their impact varied depending on where students were in their education. Students in the earlier years of their schooling could incorporate the new subjects from the outset, whereas those already approaching graduation had less time to adjust to subjects that had not previously been part of their curriculum. More fundamentally, formal assessment is only one part of education. A standardised examination can establish whether a student has retained enough information to pass, but it cannot measure what they genuinely understand, their curiosity, or their ability to interpret and make meaningful use of what they have learned. A locally grounded curriculum allows students to engage with the culture, history, language and heritage they physically inhabit. There is little reason to assume that the love life of Henry VIII, or the intricacies of the Battle of Hastings—whose account has itself recently been subject to scholarly reconsideration—should be more relevant to the education of a young Egyptian than their own extraordinary, tangible historical inheritance. All students should learn about other societies and cultures while gaining a fuller understanding of the nation to which they themselves belong. Egypt is the country most immediately associated with history itself, and its civilisation remains a source of fascination and study throughout the world—its achievements, language and culture have shaped all that followed. Wherever their education or future takes them, a strong knowledge of Egypt gives them a deeper sense of the identity they carry with them and of the country they represent. Language may be one of the clearest expressions of the Charter’s understanding of identity. It describes Arabic as “the official language, the principal pillar of Egypt’s shared culture, and the means of communication and expression among Egyptians,” while recognising that its colloquial dialects “form part of the richness of Egyptian culture.” The Charter is right to insist on “mastering foreign languages without allowing them to replace the mother tongue, diminish the status of Arabic, or stigmatize those who are educated in Arabic”. An education in Arabic is a point of pride; the concern should be whether the schools, facilities and teaching standards that deliver it are adequately funded and properly supported. An accent, dialect or varying fluency should never detract from the effort and courage involved in communicating and learning in any language, or distract from the substance of what is being said. The relationship between language and identity takes on new significance as AI reconfigures the infosphere. Egypt’s national Arabic language model, Karnak, and Karnak Chat, launched in August 2026, represent an effort to ensure that these technologies can understand Modern Standard Arabic, Egyptian colloquial Arabic and cultural context. Alongside this, digitising archives, literature, oral histories and artistic works ensures that more of Egypt’s cultural memory remains available to the systems through which future generations will encounter knowledge. There is also a less obvious possibility: AI can strengthen national identity by giving countries new ways to preserve, access and share their own cultural and linguistic resources. Egypt’s National AI Strategy 2025–2030 reflects an effort to develop these capabilities within Egypt and apply them to areas of national and cultural importance. In this sense, technological change need not only test cultural continuity; it can also give that continuity new means of transmission. The radio once seemed to make the storyteller unnecessary. Instead, the story found another way to travel. Nearly a century later, machines have become far more capable of carrying, producing and transforming language, even as the distinctions between the person who creates, the machine that produces and the audience that receives grow quieter. The Charter asks what must endure as the forms around it change. Identity, after all, does not belong to the past; each generation inherits the conversation, finds a new medium for it, and leaves something of its own for the next to answer. Nadine Loza is a development strategist, opinion columnist, and Founding Director of the Egypt Diaspora Initiative.

headline: Iran offers Saudi-Yemen dialogue as fighting, Houthi attacks escalate
summary: The Saudi-backed government in Yemen passed a draft law designating the Iran-backed Houthis as a terror group, as the US considers further action against the group over its attacks against Saudi Arabia.
body_text:
Iran offered to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensified and Yemen’s Saudi-backed government advanced legislation targeting the group’s activities and financing.

The diplomatic exchange came after a weekend of deadly strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport and amid a Saudi-backed offensive against the Houthis along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

What happened: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke Sunday with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, about the regional escalation and efforts to reduce tensions, according to the Saudi account of the call.

Iran’s Foreign Ministry said Araghchi offered assistance to initiate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and facilitate a political solution. He warned that reliance on military action would further complicate the situation.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event around Iran's diplomatic offer to mediate between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, set against escalating Houthi attacks and a Saudi-backed government's terror designation.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged term emphasizing lethality and violence.
Suggests increasing severity, adding dramatic tone.

Yemen's Houthi rebels launched fresh attacks against Saudi Arabia on Monday, following deadly missile strikes on Riyadh's international airport that killed passengers, some of whom were preparing to board flights to perform Umrah.

Saudi authorities extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport until midnight on October 17 following an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured more than 300, and another on Sunday in which one person was killed.

The King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was also hit on Sunday evening, Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Civil Aviation said, with the damage being assessed.

Pilot, flight attendant and widow among victims of Houthi attacks

The strikes came as Yemeni government forces, backed by the Saudi-led coalition, clashed with Houthi rebels on the outskirts of the strategic south-western city of Taiz, repelling fresh attacks amid warnings that a tightening rebel siege is worsening conditions inside the Yemeni city. A military spokesman said on Monday that air strikes prevented the Houthis from sending reinforcements to Taiz.

At least 20 people have been killed in a series of attacks since last week on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the Abha international airport in Saudi Arabia’s Asir province. Saudi state TV broadcast footage of the moment a missile struck the passenger terminal in Riyadh on Saturday, with flashes of light filling the screen as travellers, including pilgrims in white robes, scrambled for cover.

Ali, from Hyderabad, was travelling with his family on an Umrah pilgrimage when he was injured in Saturday’s attack. The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed his death on Sunday and said it was in contact with his family to help arrange the repatriation of his remains.

Etihad Airways cancelled all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until Monday, October 19, extending disruption to services between the UAE and the Saudi capital into next week. Flydubai has also cancelled Riyadh flights until Wednesday, October 14, while Emirates and Air Arabia services have been affected.

The Saudi-led coalition said it responded to drone and cruise missile threats against the kingdom on Monday, as hostilities with the Iran-backed Houthis continued despite diplomatic efforts, including a phone call between the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Iran, which supports the Houthis.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told his Saudi counterpart Prince Faisal bin Farhan that Tehran was ready to "provide assistance" to start talks between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis to reach a "political solution", Iranian state media reported.

"The Foreign Minister of our country, expressing concern over the escalation of tensions, emphasised that insisting on a military approach and ignoring political solutions would complicate the existing situation," Mr Araghchi was quoted as saying.

Amid the continued attacks on Saudi Arabia, Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, called for stronger Gulf security and collective defence.

In his statement posted on X, Dr Gargash said the security of Gulf states as a whole was "indivisible". He stressed that attacks against Saudi Arabia also threatened the wider Gulf. “Targeting our sisterly kingdom of Saudi Arabia undermines the security of the UAE and all Gulf states,” he added. He warned that shortcomings in regional co-operation had contributed to the current challenges.

US Central Command chief Adm Brad Cooper said the US and its regional allies were deploying the “largest air-defence umbrella in the world” to deter Iranian attacks, describing the effort as part of an “enduring security architecture” in the Middle East.

“It was a vision we discussed with our regional allies and partners,” he told the audience in a recorded message at Trends Global's sixth annual conference in Abu Dhabi on Monday. “Earlier this year, during Operation Epic Fury, we validated at full scale and in actual combat the Middle East Air Defence network known as Mead.

“Through our combined efforts, we transformed a concept into the most sophisticated and largest air-defence umbrella in the world,” he added.

“For the first time in history, US air defenders stood shoulder-to-shoulder with allies and partners across the Middle East, linking national systems in real time. And so together we intercepted thousands of Iranian attack drones and missiles with an integrated shield built on mutual trust. This is partnership in action.”

This vivid verb phrase is dramatic and sensory, heightening the sense of panic and danger.

loaded_language.explanation: The adjective 'sisterly' is an emotive, diplomatic term that conveys closeness and solidarity, reflecting a particular political perspective.

headline: (2nd LD) S. Korean envoy says progress made in intelligence cooperation with U.S. amid friction concerns
summary: WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States sai...
body_text:
By Chang Dong-woo(ATTN: REWRITES headline, lead; ADDS more details in paras 8-9; RECASTS throughout)

WASHINGTON, Oct. 12 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's top envoy to the United States said Monday that progress has been made in improving intelligence cooperation between Seoul and Washington, amid concerns over apparent friction between the two allies.

Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the South Korean Embassy in Washington, responding to questions about bilateral intelligence cooperation.

Regarding the controversy, the ambassador said she is aware that "intelligence agencies of the two countries have communicated with each other" and that "progress has been made" in terms of improving cooperation.

The remarks follow growing speculation over bilateral friction after South Korea's National Intelligence Service acknowledged it was excluded from a June trilateral meeting, also involving Japan, on North Korean cyber threats. Local media reports indicated the agency was left out at Washington's request.

South Korea and the U.S. have experienced friction in the intelligence field after Seoul Unification Minister Chung Dong-young's public disclosure of a North Korean uranium enrichment facility in Kusong, North Korea, in March.

Kang also said she is unaware of any complaints raised by the U.S. side against the unification minister or South Korea's National Intelligence Service Director Lee Jong-seok.

"There have been various consultations regarding problems in connection with intelligence cooperation, but there have not been any complaints raised against any individual," Kang said.

Kang said she had received a phone call from Chung following his remarks about North Korea's nuclear facility in Kusong and had conveyed his explanation to U.S. officials through diplomatic channels.

She did not elaborate on how U.S. officials responded to Chung's explanation.

The ambassador also acknowledged limitations in high-level communication with the White House.

"I acknowledge that there are limitations in our communication with the White House," Kang said.

Regarding the possibility of another North Korea-U.S. summit, the ambassador said she is aware that there has not been any concrete progress. "There is always the possibility, but it is hard to speak (of) in terms of numbers (likelihood)."

According to Kang, the subject of a possible North Korea-U.S. summit has become a topic of daily consultation between Seoul and Washington in terms of intelligence sharing.

odissy@yna.co.kr(END)

loaded_language.neutral_alternative: stated that high-level communication has been restricted

omissions: Details on the specific nature of the intelligence cooperation progress
U.S. officials' responses to Chung's explanation
Context on why South Korea was excluded from the June trilateral meeting

body_text:
Al Ahli Saudi left Dubai with three points towards their bid for a hat-trick of Asian Champions League titles after a fiery meeting with Al Wasl.

Roger Ibanez and Francisco Trincao, two big-money imports to Saudi Arabian football, scored, before Feras Albrikan clinched a 3-1 win in stoppage time.

The margin of defeat was harsh on a spirited Wasl side, who deserved more than the lone strike by Pedro Malheiro in first-half stoppage time.

Given the gap they were bridging to the high-spending Saudi Pro League side, the home players fully merited the backing they got from their fans on a hostile night in Zabeel.

Before kick-off, Ahli’s players stood on the 18-yard line and were serenaded with their club anthem by the travelling supporters.

Around 200 had made the trip from Jeddah, but they were drowned out by the noise of the home faithful. The Ultras Junoon are always loud, but they were particularly rowdy when the Ahli anthem was being sung.

The home players responded. Wasl’s start was bright, and they fashioned the first opening, only for Siaka Sidibe to blaze over from the edge of the box.

Home optimism was dissipated in the 20th minute, though, when Ibanez headed in the opener for Ahli.

The Brazil centre-back, who was called into the Selecao squad by Carlo Ancelotti for the World Cup this summer, is renowned for his leap.

Despite common knowledge of his aerial prowess, he was unchallenged at the back post to make it 1-0.

The visitors nearly doubled their lead 10 minutes later, but were saved by the post as Eduard Spertsyan’s shot bounced away to safety.

Wasl’s defence was being cut open with greater regularity, and they were lucky not to be a long way behind by the break.

Their fortune continued when Adryelson, the Wasl defender evaded a red card.

After a confrontation in the box, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, went down. Replays showed Adryelson had squared up to him, and lightly pushed his forehead towards his opponent.

Shamat tumbled to the floor and rolled around as if he was mortally wounded. It was enough of a show to persuade VAR to recommend the referee take a second look at the monitor.

Usually, that is ominous for the perceived offender. Justice was served, though, as Abdulrahman Al Jassim, the Qatari official, decided he was right the first time, and stayed with a yellow card.

Adryelson nearly provided the perfect riposte; from the ensuing free-kick for Wasl, he bundled the ball into the net, only for it to be ruled out for offside.

The hosts were level by the break, though. In stoppage time at the end of the half, a long range effort from Malheiro, Wasl’s right back, found its way into the net after some limp goalkeeping.

Shamat had fully established himself as public enemy No 1. At the start of the second half, he was playing on the wing in front of the hardcore or Wasl’s supporters.

They frequently lobbed plastic water bottles in his direction. Rather than fuss, he waved a hand at them, encouraging the fans to bring it on.

Just before the hour mark, Trincao ruined the home fans’ fun. The Portuguese forward finished clinically to restore the away side’s lead.

Wasl should have levelled shortly after following a rapid counter-attack, but Serginho hit the post with the goal at his mercy.

Even when he went off, Shamat caused rancour. After an innocuous incident, he went down clutching his shoulder.

He looked in genuine pain, and had to be stretchered off on the back of the medical golf buggy.

It turned out that his injury was not so severe that he could wave with both arms as he was taken past the Ahli supporters.

That added to the fury of the home fans, and even the players were so incensed they threw bottles in his direction as the buggy went past the home dugout.

Ahli’s bench sprung to his defence, and the two sets of replacements and substituted players had to be separated.

Wasl had their chances as they chased the game, but their hopes were finally dashed when Albrikan scored Ahli’s third in stoppage time.

analysis.framing: The article frames the match as a fiery, controversy-filled contest in which a spirited but outgunned Al Wasl side were harshly beaten by big-spending Al Ahli, with the narrative centering on Al Ahli forward Saleh Abu Al Shamat's theatrics and the resulting hostility from Wasl fans and players.

headline: Egypt’s FM discusses expanding economic, parliamentary ties with Thai officials
summary: Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a series of meetings with government and parliamentary officials in Thailand on Monday at the start of a visit to Bangkok aimed at strengthening political, economic, investment and educational cooperation between the two countries. Abdelatty met Thai Industry Minister Varawut Silpa-archa to discuss ways to expand trade and investment and strengthen industrial cooperation, including potential joint manufacturing projects in rubber, petrochemicals and tyres. He said Egypt sought to benefit from Thailand’s experience in industrial localisation, innovation, digital transformation and sustainability while boosting domestic production and industrial exports. Abdelatty also highlighted investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE), citing HI TECH as the first Thai industrial project in the zone. He called for leveraging the project’s presence to attract further Thai investment to Egypt. Thailand’s industry minister expressed interest in expanding cooperation within the economic zone and exploring new manufacturing and investment opportunities in Egypt. In a separate meeting, Abdelatty met Sophon Saram, President of Thailand’s House of Representatives and National Assembly, to discuss bilateral relations, parliamentary cooperation and ways to expand economic and investment ties. Abdelatty said bilateral relations had gained momentum in 2026, citing the eighth round of political consultations held in Cairo and reciprocal parliamentary visits. He called for developing a practical roadmap to advance political, economic and development cooperation between the two countries. He invited the Thai parliamentary speaker to visit Egypt and discussed strengthening educational and cultural ties, including partnerships between Egyptian and Thai universities, scholarship programmes and Al-Azhar’s role in educating Thai students. Abdelatty also called for increased Thai investment in Egypt and improved access for Egyptian agricultural products to the Thai market. He later met Yoonadi Waba, chairman of the Thai-Egyptian Parliamentary Friendship Group, and other group members to discuss expanding parliamentary exchanges, establishing direct contacts between specialised committees and maintaining regular dialogue with Egypt’s House of Representatives and Senate. The talks also covered vocational training, expanding scholarship exchanges and ways for parliamentarians to encourage closer ties between the two countries’ business communities. In another meeting, Abdelatty held talks with Nirat Yoopakdee, chairman of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee, on parliamentary and economic cooperation, as well as regional and international developments. Abdelatty called for activating the joint trade committee agreed upon in December 2024, stressing that Egypt could serve as a gateway for Thai companies seeking access to African and European markets, while Thailand could offer Egyptian products and investors greater access to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) markets. He also welcomed Thailand’s efforts to deepen its engagement with Africa and affirmed Egypt’s readiness to support stronger Thai-African economic and development cooperation. The two sides exchanged views on developments in the Asia-Pacific region and the Middle East and agreed to continue consultations on issues of mutual interest.

He said Egypt sought to benefit from Thailand’s experience in industrial localisation, innovation, digital transformation and sustainability while boosting domestic production and industrial exports.

Abdelatty also highlighted investment opportunities in the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE), citing HI TECH as the first Thai industrial project in the zone. He called for leveraging the project’s presence to attract further Thai investment to Egypt.

Abdelatty also called for increased Thai investment in Egypt and improved access for Egyptian agricultural products to the Thai market.
