Hall and Michael Woodford winning the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics, UNICEF India naming Smriti Mandhana as its celebrity advocate, Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project achieving a major milestone, and IIT Bombay inviting applications for 30 ad hoc counsellor positions and more.

In a recent turn of events, Delhi Police has removed Jantar Mantar from the list of designated protest sites and named Ramlila Ground, Burari Ground and CBD Ground in East Delhi as alternative venues for demonstrations amid the ongoing CJP protest. The decision follows recommendations by a committee constituted by the Union Home Ministry.

The Kerala Assembly has passed a resolution seeking the removal of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The assembly also demanded that the panel selecting the election commissioners include the Prime Minister, the Lok Sabha Leader of Opposition and the Chief Justice of India.

Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford have been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”.

Around 60% of scheduled flights at Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia are likely to be cancelled following attacks by Houthi forces that killed more than a dozen people over the weekend.

The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) India has named India batter Smriti Mandhana as its celebrity advocate. Mandhana has also been handed over the India captaincy after Harmanpreet Kaur stepped down as the captain of the Indian Women’s Cricket Team.

The Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train project has completed the installation of all 14 portal beams over the Delhi-Mumbai Rajdhani railway line in Vadodara, Gujarat, clearing a major obstruction in constructing the elevated track.

SpaceX owner Elon Musk has promised affordable Starlink satellite internet services across India to compete with Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio. His commitment comes ahead of Jio’s planned IPO, targeting a valuation of $106 billion. Both companies’ satellite internet services are awaiting their final security clearances to launch in India.

The Student Wellness Centre (SWC) at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Bombay has invited applications for 30 ad hoc counsellor positions, including 26 student counsellors and four senior counsellors following the alleged death by suicide of second-year BTech student Sahil Wakode.

headline: Türkiye urges Israel to stop ‘reckless’ attacks in Syria
summary: 'The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria,' Permanent Representative to UN Ahmet Yildiz says, adding Israel's actions 'are getting out of control'
body_text:
Türkiye’s UN envoy called on Israel to end its “reckless acts” in Syria and fully comply with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement.

“Lasting stability is essential for Syria to rebuild its economy, attract investment, and participate in regional energy and connectivity projects,” Türkiye's Permanent Representative to the United Nations Ahmet Yildiz told a session of the UN Security Council on Monday.

“Israel’s continued violations of Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity undermine these prospects and show disregard for international law,” Yildiz said.

“The situation is particularly alarming in southern Syria, where continued military incursions and expansionist actions and words are getting out of control,” he added.

Yildiz said Israel’s recent resumption of activities along the so-called “Sufa 53 line” in Quneitra was a further attempt to undermine the 1974 agreement and impose a fait accompli on the ground.

“These reckless acts must stop,” he said.

He urged Israel to comply with the 1974 agreement and relevant Security Council resolutions, particularly Resolution 497, and to withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan.

“A stable, sovereign and unified Syria capable of securing its borders, defeating terrorist organizations and contributing to regional peace and economic cooperation serves the interests of all, including Israel,” he added.

“The dissolution of the so-called SDF has opened a new chapter in the integration process,” Yildiz said.

“Remaining arrangements should be finalized and fully implemented without delay, in a manner that reinforces Syria’s sovereignty, unity and social cohesion,” he added.

Yildiz described the fight against terrorism as “a critical priority” and welcomed Damascus’ cooperation with the global coalition for the enduring defeat of ISIS (Daesh).

“Security and economic recovery must advance hand in hand,” he said.

On refugees, Yildiz said the number of Syrians under temporary protection in Türkiye once exceeded 4 million and now stands at around 2.2 million.

He said returns have been gradual because of economic conditions, security concerns and Israeli incursions.

Since Bashar al-Assad’s fall on Dec. 8, 2024, Israel has expanded its military operations in Syria, moving troops into the Golan buffer zone and nearby positions.

​​​​​​​Syria demands the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the areas they occupied and maintains its commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement. Israel claims its movements are driven by security considerations.

Addressing the same session, Syria’s UN representative Ibrahim Olabi said those claiming to seek security “should not be killing Syrian citizens within Syrian territory.”

“They should know very well that there is only one path towards security, which is international legitimacy and the resolutions of the (UN Security) Council,” the envoy said.

“Every time they open fire on Syria, they are, as the world has witnessed, at the same time opening fire on itself locally and internationally,” he added.

Olabi also urged support for economic recovery, investment, job creation and reconstruction.

He called for help rehabilitating schools, hospitals and water and electricity networks and for resources and expertise to clear mines and other remnants of war.

headline: 'Breaking Bad' actor RJ Mitte dies at 34
summary: Actor known for playing Walter 'Flynn' White Jr. also advocated for disability rights; cause of death not disclosed
body_text:

US actor RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr. in the television series "Breaking Bad," has died at the age of 34, according to media reports Monday.

Representatives for Mitte confirmed his death to US-based entertainment news outlets Variety and TMZ. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed.

Mitte portrayed the son of Walter White, played by Bryan Cranston, and Skyler White, played by Anna Gunn, in the AMC crime drama created by Vince Gilligan, which aired 2008-2013.

“It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his representative said in a statement to Variety.

“Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.”

Beyond acting, Mitte advocated for people with disabilities, serving as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He also headed the Mitte Foundation, a charitable organization supporting philanthropic initiatives and challenging stereotypes about people with disabilities.

Following "Breaking Bad," Mitte appeared in several television series and films, including "Switched at Birth," Netflix's superhero series "The Guardians of Justice," the 2017 science fiction film "The Recall" and the 2020 thriller "The Oak Room."

According to Variety, Mitte had been promoting his latest film, "Talking to Strangers," and appearing on podcasts in the days before his death.

Several projects involving the actor were also in various stages of production and pre-production.

headline: 'Breaking Bad' actor and disability activist RJ Mitte dies aged 34
summary: "Breaking Bad" actor RJ Mitte, who played Walter White Jr. in the hit US television series, has died aged 34, his representatives said Monday. The actor, who lived with cerebral palsy, also became a prominent disability rights advocate, championing inclusion and representation in film and television.
body_text:
"Breaking Bad" actor RJ Mitte, who played Walter White Jr. in the hit US television series, has died aged 34, his representatives said Monday. The actor, who lived with cerebral palsy, also became a prominent disability rights advocate, championing inclusion and representation in film and television.

Issued on: 13/10/2026 - 03:43

RJ Mitte, the actor best known for playing Walter White Jr. in the award-winning TV series "Breaking Bad", has died, his representatives told AFP on Monday. He was 34.

The cause of death for the actor, who lived with cerebral palsy, was not immediately revealed.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," said a statement issued by Sean Reilly.

A teenage Mitte first appeared in "Breaking Bad" in 2008 as the son of chemistry-teacher-turned-drug-kingpin Walter White, a role that won Bryan Cranston global acclaim.

"Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," Reilly said.

That campaigning evolved into working as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and for Shriners Children's, a non-profit hospital network.

"He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities," Reilly added.

"Breaking Bad", which ran for five seasons between 2008 and 2013, is routinely acclaimed as groundbreaking television, and was recently named by The New York Times as the best TV show of the 21st century.

Co-stars rushed to pay tribute to the performer, with Aaron Paul – who played Jesse Pinkman, White's young partner in crime – saying he was "at a loss" over the news.

"RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said, according to The Hollywood Reporter.

"And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that."

Dean Norris, who starred in the series as Mitte's on-screen uncle, a special agent with the Drug Enforcement Agency, said he was "heartbroken" by the news of the young man's death.

"Though RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set," Norris wrote on social media.

"He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed. This is so heartbreaking, I can't believe it. Thinking of him and his family."

Fellow actor and disability campaigner Marlee Matlin, who appeared with Mitte in "Cinemability: The Art of Inclusion", a documentary that examined the history of disability portrayals in US film and television, said her heart was "shattered."

"There will never be another like RJ Mitte. You will always have a place in my heart. RIP," wrote Matlin, who became the first deaf actress to win an Oscar when she scooped the top honour for "Children of a Lesser God."

headline: IMF says AI investment propping up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook
summary: By David LawderBANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The global economy will still manage to top 3% real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1%, a slight uptick from the 3.0% it predicted in July.
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The global economy will still manage to top 3% real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.

Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1%, a slight uptick from the 3.0% it predicted in July.

The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5%.

For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4% global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage point from April.

The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week.

"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks to growth tilted to the downside," the IMF's new chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told reporters.

"A prolonged conflict in the Middle East could put additional pressures on inflation and slow down growth. A worsening of fiscal prospects, a reassessment of AI profitability, and extreme weather events could further weaken the outlook," she added.

Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF's deputy research director, told Reuters in an interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5% this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on.

The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April.

Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47% of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains.

Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3% this year compared with the 1.7% growth predicted in July.

Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6%, 16%, 16.7%, 15.6% and 3.9%, respectively.

UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE

Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3% for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content.

Euro zone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1% from 0.9% in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defense spending in EU countries. Britain's 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage point from July to 1.3% due to larger AI investment.

The IMF forecast China's growth at 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports.

India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy at 7.0% for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment.

The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% for 2027.

ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS

Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of $96 per barrel for 2026 and $87 in 2027.

But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to $130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2%.

AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6% by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China.

But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialize, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8% directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4% by 2028.

This shift would also trigger a sharp reduction in asset prices and tighter financial conditions that cause a major drop in consumption, particularly in the US, the IMF said. Higher global bond yields would further reduce activity, with a combined global output reduction of 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output.

The IMF also warned that elevated public debt levels, particularly in advanced economies, increase the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs that can weigh on growth prospects. It urged governments to stop delaying action to rebuild fiscal buffers and articulate credible medium-term plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels — advice that IMF officials plan to push at the Bangkok meetings.

(Reporting by David Lawder; Editing by Paul Simao)

analysis.framing: The article frames the IMF's World Economic Outlook as a data-driven forecast in which AI investment props up global growth while war, debt, and AI uncertainty pose mounting downside risks.

Emotionally evocative phrase that frames economic divergence as abandonment rather than neutral 'not benefiting' or 'excluded'.
Charged adjective that conveys instability and danger beyond the neutral 'uncertain' or 'risky'.
Intensifying adjective that emphasizes severity; neutral reporting could simply state the contraction figures.
Dramatic phrasing that frames the downgrades as a blow rather than neutral 'largest downward revisions'.

omissions: No mention of the IMF's specific policy recommendations beyond fiscal buffers, such as monetary policy guidance or structural reforms.
No reaction or commentary from officials of the most-affected Gulf countries or Iran.
No discussion of how the war's origins or the US-Israeli role might affect the IMF's assumptions.
No comparison to other forecasters' estimates (e.g., World Bank, OECD) for context.

body_text:
The Middle East continues to reveal traces of its ancient past, with discoveries offering new insight into how early civilisations lived, worshipped and organised society.

Since January, archaeologists have uncovered ancient burial chambers, royal monuments and prehistoric artworks. Some finds may answer long-standing historical questions, while others are challenging what we know about the region's earliest communities.

Here are six of the most significant discoveries announced over the year so far.

New species of ancient Egyptian crocodile discovered from Sphinx rocks

A burial chamber uncovered at the Qattarah Necropolis in Al Ain has revealed evidence of funerary traditions that endured for at least 1,000 years.

Announced by the Department of Culture and Tourism – Abu Dhabi in July, the chamber was 11 metres long and 2.5 metres wide. Dating back to the Wadi Suq period, it remained in use into the Iron Age, suggesting successive generations continued to bury their dead at the same site.

Archaeologists recovered weapons, vessels and personal ornaments, providing clues about the customs of the communities that inhabited the region.

The chamber's entrance faces the East, potentially allowing the rising Sun to illuminate its interior, although whether this carries symbolic significance remains uncertain.

The discovery adds to Al Ain's archaeological importance, with its Unesco-listed sites already documenting thousands of years of settlement, burial practices and technological development.

An inscription bearing the name of a long-lost Egyptian city may finally help settle an archaeological mystery dating back almost 140 years.

Discovered at Tell Abu Seify, near the Suez Canal, the sandstone lintel bears the royal titles of Ramses II, who ruled Egypt during the 13th century BC. It also records the restoration of a statue of Horus, described as Lord of the City of Masn.

Announced in August, the find strengthens the possibility that Tell Abu Seify was the ancient settlement, although further investigation is required to confirm its identity.

Excavations have also revealed a temple complex, defensive walls, roads and evidence of Roman military occupation.

Establishing the city's whereabouts could help researchers reconstruct Egypt's eastern frontier, particularly the Horus Military Road, which connected the Nile Delta with Sinai and territories farther east.

More than 2,600 years since the reign of King Ashurbanipal, archaeologists have uncovered a monument documenting the ambitions of one of Assyria's most powerful rulers.

The two-metre stone stele was discovered in June at Shamash Gate in Nineveh, once the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. It features cuneiform inscriptions and relief carvings associated with Ashurbanipal's reign from 668BC to 627BC.

The inscriptions offer further evidence of how the king developed Nineveh and commemorated his achievements through public monuments.

The discovery also carries significance for the city's modern history. Nineveh's archaeological remains suffered extensive destruction during ISIS's occupation of the Mosul area between 2014 and 2017.

Recovered by a joint Iraqi-American archaeological mission, the stele contributes to efforts to document and preserve one of the ancient Middle East's most important cities.

An ancient bronze ring recovered from the Mediterranean Sea bears a rare depiction of one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

It was announced last week that the signet ring had been discovered during underwater excavations at Antirhodos, a submerged island that once housed a royal palace in Alexandria's Great Harbour.

Its engraving depicts the Lighthouse of Alexandria and resembles representations found on Roman-era coins. Archaeologists have yet to establish the ring's precise date or identify its owner, but it is believed to be the first known depiction of the monument on a signet ring.

Constructed during the third century BC, the lighthouse guided ships into Alexandria's harbour for centuries before successive earthquakes brought about its destruction.

The discovery adds to the limited surviving visual record of the structure, whose appearance is known largely through ancient descriptions and representations.

A human face carved into a limestone pillar is providing new evidence of artistic expression among some of the world's earliest settled communities.

Unveiled in November 2025, the discovery was made at Karahantepe in south-eastern Turkey, a Neolithic site dating back about 11,000 years.

The 1.4-metre T-shaped pillar features deep-set eyes and a prominent nose. It is the first known example of a human face represented directly on this type of pillar at the region's prehistoric sites.

Similar structures have been found at nearby Gobeklitepe, with archaeologists suggesting their forms may represent stylised human figures. The discovery at Karahantepe lends weight to that interpretation.

Alongside other sculptures and monumental structures uncovered at the site, the pillar reveals the sophistication of prehistoric artistic and ceremonial traditions thousands of years before the emergence of writing or cities.

Paintings, engravings and inscriptions spanning thousands of years have been documented at a previously unknown archaeological site in South Sinai.

Announced by Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities in February, the discovery was made on the Umm Iraq Plateau, where researchers identified a natural sandstone rock shelter extending more than 100 metres.

Its walls contain prehistoric paintings depicting animals and other figures, alongside later engravings and inscriptions. Archaeologists have also documented pottery fragments and material associated with different periods of human activity.

Some of the earliest artwork is believed to predate the emergence of the ancient Egyptian state, although further research is needed to refine its chronology.

The site is particularly valuable for its unusually long archaeological record. Its changing imagery and inscriptions suggest communities returned to the same location across vastly different historical periods, leaving evidence of their environments, beliefs and artistic traditions.

headline: IMF raises S. Korea's growth forecast to 3.3 pct amid chip supercycle
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday rais...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday raised its growth forecast for South Korea in 2026 to 3.3 percent, citing strong semiconductor exports that more than offset the fallout from the Middle East war.

The Washington-based organization released the assessment in the World Economic Outlook report, raising its forecast by 0.7 percentage point from its July projection. The revised figure exceeded its global growth forecast of 3.1 percent.

The report was released to coincide with the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, which began Monday in Bangkok and will run through Sunday.

The IMF projected South Korea's economy will grow 2.8 percent in 2027, up 0.3 percentage point from its previous forecast.

The organization identified South Korea and Taiwan as key trading partners in the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware industry, noting developments in the two economies could have spillover effects on raw material exporters and manufacturing hubs.

On the global economy, the IMF said downside risks, including tensions in the Middle East and trade fragmentation, persist but have eased since July.

It cited commodity price volatility, inflationary pressures, a reassessment of expected productivity gains from AI and a possible resurgence in trade tensions as downside risks.

A prolonged AI technology upcycle and a restructuring of energy supply chains, however, could provide upward momentum, the IMF added.

The Ministry of Finance and Economy said the latest forecast reflects South Korea's robust exports of AI hardware and chips, noting the upward revision of 0.7 percentage point exceeded the 0.4 percentage-point increase for the group of 41 advanced economies, whose growth forecast stood at 2.1 percent for 2026.

The ministry, however, noted uncertainties persist, including the prolonged Middle East war and higher consumer prices weighing on households.

The government will work to address economic disparities and improve people's livelihoods to bolster the economy's growth potential, the ministry added.

Earlier this month, the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) projected South Korea's economy will expand 3.3 percent this year, raising its previous forecast from 3.1 percent.

Last month, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) also marked up its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea to 3.7 percent from 2.6 percent, also citing the country's robust exports.

In September, South Korea's exports soared 83.5 percent from a year earlier to a record US$120.9 billion, driven by a surge in chip shipments.

Semiconductor exports exceeded $60 billion for the first time last month, boosting overall outbound shipments.

analysis.framing: The article frames the IMF's upward revision of South Korea's 2026 growth forecast as a direct result of a semiconductor export boom, presenting the news through a largely positive economic lens while noting government-acknowledged uncertainties.

loaded_language.explanation: The headline uses 'supercycle' to describe the semiconductor boom, an intensified term that suggests an unusually strong and sustained upswing, adding dramatic emphasis beyond a neutral description.

Airports are being forced to rethink how they protect passengers and keep flights running as missile and drone attacks pose an increasingly serious threat to civilian aviation, industry experts have warned.

Repeated attacks by Houthi rebels in Saudi Arabia, alongside months of disruption caused by the war in Iran, have exposed the vulnerability of airports to modern warfare and the difficulty of maintaining operations during prolonged security crises.

Industry leaders gathered at the Dubai Airport Show on Monday said airports were investing in new technology and contingency planning to withstand threats from military strikes to cyber attacks, while acknowledging that no facility could ever be completely secure.

Riyadh airport closure: Etihad cancels flights until October 19

Tim Walder, chairman of the British Aviation Group, said the changing nature of global conflicts had created unprecedented challenges for airport operators.

“What we’re seeing today is a completely different set of challenges being faced geopolitically,” he said. “Resilience isn’t something that’s 100 per cent, it’s always going to fail on occasions, but we learn faster.

“The key thing is the airport can be a leader in terms of understanding where the threats can come from, such as cybersecurity and climate change.”

Mr Walder, whose company offers expertise on meeting the challenges of the global aviation industry, said supporting passengers during a crisis was critical to retaining confidence.

“If something goes down, you lose passenger confidence and you can lose that for a long time,” he said. “Cyber-attacks are obviously high up there when talking about risk and we are seeing different levels of that.

“A few months ago in the UK and Europe, hackers attacked the software that supports the check-in process and that impacted a number of airports in Europe, including London and Brussels.

“These attacks aren't going to be just necessarily hitting an individual airport or airline, they're going to hit a network. The question is how do we make the network more resilient as well.”

Critical Gulf transit hubs and other major infrastructure are increasingly connecting site security with dedicated anti-drone and air defence measures to improve protection at airports.

International gateways to the region have increased perimeter screening and police patrols near airports, while others have implemented terminal entry checkpoints in response to raised threat levels in the Middle East.

Exhibitors at Dubai World Trade Centre displayed the latest countermeasures and showed how drone technology was rapidly advancing to help secure airspace.

Udi Lowy, sales director for the Gulf Co-operation Council and India at D-Fend Solutions, said his company’s EnforceAir Plus system was capable of hijacking unidentified drones and bringing them under control.

“Drones are quite a new threat in the world, so most of the technologies just adopt [existing] air-defence mechanisms for drones,” he said. “We are using cyber systems that detect the communication of the drone and we have the ability to retract the relevant information from the drone itself.”

Rather than jamming a drone’s signal to bring it down, potentially causing damage or injuries on the ground, the EnforceAir Plus system takes over its controls and lands it safely nearby. It can then verify from where the drone was deployed and by whom.

The system can even be programmed to deal with a swarm attacking airspace simultaneously, Mr Lowy said.

“Sometimes, a kid can fly a drone and create mayhem. Rather than jamming all signals, we cherry-pick the signal we want to interfere with and actually take the drone itself. “We don't interfere with any other signal, so there is no interference with airplanes.”

The Ministry of Defence has reported a total of 2,265 drone attacks on the country since February 28, when the Iran war broke out, with Dubai International Airport handling 111 aerial threat alerts.

Future airport developments, including the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport, will feature blast-proof designs and hardened concrete shells to bolster defences against aerial attacks.

Speaking on a panel at Dubai Airport Show on operational resilience under pressure, Binu Gopal, chief operating officer at Ras Al Khaimah International Airport, said the priority in a crisis was to maintain operations as safely and efficiently as possible.

“We prepare for multiple kinds of disruption which may occur at the airport,” he said. “Resilience is the ability to continue our operations even when we face some kind of disruption, maintain critical activities and respond to the disturbance, and get back to normal safely and efficiently.

“This cuts across the entire ecosystem, be it set operations, terminal operations, airlines, ground-handling operations, customs and immigration. However, during a crisis, it becomes more and more interdependent. For us it is not about having a contingency plan, it's about how well we are able to respond as a team.”

body_text:
The International Monetary Fund has significantly lowered its 2026 projections for economies across the Gulf due to the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and pushed back its forecast on the waterway's reopening.

In its latest World Economic Outlook, released on Tuesday, the IMF also slashed its forecasts for the broader region. The Middle East and North Africa economy is estimated to contract by 2 per cent this year, a downward revision of 3.1 percentage points from its April projections. It is the only region expected to record an economic contraction this year.

The IMF maintained its 2026 forecast for global growth at 3.1 per cent and lifted its projection for 2027 from to 3.4 per cent.

Hawkish sentiment returns to IMF and World Bank meetings

“This is the net result of two main forces that are shaping the outlook,” IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told reporters, referring to the negative supply shock from the Iran war and the positive demand shock from the AI infrastructure boom.

The fund said the global economy had so far been able to withstand the impact from the Iran war energy shock due to a combination of factors including supply adjustment, a drawdown of inventories, lower energy intensity, and households and companies adapting to higher prices.

The latest forecasts come as Saudi Arabia vowed to press on with bringing its oil supplies to market despite escalating attacks on the kingdom in recent days by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The number of vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz have declined in recent days after tanker attacks reached their highest weekly count this year on October 9. One tanker crossed the waterway on Saturday, down from eight the day before, data from analytics firm Kpler showed.

Confirmed total Hormuz clearance stands at roughly 11.9 million barrels per day, or about 30 per cent below its pre-war baseline, Kpler data showed, although daily readings have swung wildly.

Energy supply disruptions from the Iran war are the latest in a round of shocks the global economy has weathered in recent years. These have included the 2025 tariffs row, Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Covid-19 pandemic and the global tightening cycle that followed.

“The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits,” Ms Tenreyro said. “The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space and rebuilding supply-side resilience.”

The fund said the economic outlook is highly uneven across countries, reflecting differences in their exposure to commodities, AI-related activity and borrowing costs.

Overall GDP growth in the US is forecast to be 2.3 per cent, compared to 1.1 per cent for the euro area, 1.3 per cent for the UK, 0.7 per cent in Japan and 1.1 per cent in Canada.

Growth in China, which is classified as an emerging economy, is forecast to slow to 4.5 per cent growth in 2026, compared to 7 per cent for India and 3.6 per cent for Pakistan.

The IMF projects the UAE's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, conditional on the normalisation of shipping routes and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

The new projections for the Middle East's second-largest economy reflect a downgrade of 7 percentage points for 2026 and an upgrade of 2.4 percentage points for 2027 compared to the fund's April forecast.

Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3, 16.7 and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026.

The fund also lowered its forecasts for Saudi Arabia, but expects the decline to be less sharp compared to Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar because of its diversified export routes. The fund expects Saudi Arabia to slow from a positive growth rate of 4.6 per cent last year to a 3.3 per cent contraction this year.

Oman is the only GCC member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent.

The latest forecast assumes the gradual reopening of the Strait of Hormuz will resume in March 2027, with a return to prewar conditions by October. It also notes that uncertainty is assumed to remain elevated throughout next year.

Under these conditions, oil exporters are expected to see economic activity rebound next year, similar to the UAE. Overall GDP growth in Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar would expand by 13.9, 17.1 and 18.8, respectively, the fund said. Saudi Arabia's economic activity would accelerate at a 7.9 per cent pace. The kingdom's ministry of finance last week said its economy was forecast to grow by 12.8 per cent next year.

Other oil exporters also faced downgrades for 2026 including Iraq at minus 16 per cent and Iran at minus 7.6 per cent, with the latter also impacted by enhanced sanctions and a US naval blockade.

Meanwhile, the fund said importers in the region were expected to remain relatively resilient. Egypt's economy is forecast to expand by a 5.1 per cent pace in 2026, more than 8 percentage points lower than the IMF's April forecast. Morocco's economy is set grow by 4.5 per cent and Jordan's by 2.7 per cent. The fund did not submit projections for Lebanon.

The fund said that while the Iran war and AI buildout were driving growth in opposite directions, both were adding to inflationary pressures.

Global headline inflation is set to increase to 4.7 per cent in 2026 before easing to 4.1 per cent in 2027, a cumulative upwards projection of 0.7 percentage points.

Ms Tenreyro said this was driving up borrowing costs in advanced economies at a time when public debt was already high. The US Federal Reserve and other central banks in advanced economies have already begun raising interest rates or are expected to this quarter.

“This interaction of high debt and high financing costs, in turn, has heightened fiscal concerns and risks,” Ms Tenreyro said.

Global bonds have been under significant pressure in recent weeks over fears of higher energy prices, higher-for-longer interest rates and concerns over unchecked government spending.

The yield on the 10-year US Treasury, a benchmark for global borrowing costs, has recently traded at its highest level since 2002. Bonds in Japan, France, Germany and the UK have also recently hit multi-decade highs.

Pimco, a global investment management firm, warned last week the yield on the 10-Year Treasury could hit 6 per cent for the first time since 2000.

headline: Russian emergencies minister conveys greetings from president, PM to North Korean premier

PYONGYANG, October 13. /TASS/. Russian Emergencies Minister Alexander Kurenkov met with North Korean Premier Pak Thae Song in Pyongyang and conveyed greetings from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin.

"First of all, I congratulate you on the 81st anniversary of the founding of the Korean Workers’ Party and convey greetings from Russian President Vladimir Putin and Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin," he said.

Kurenkov noted that Russia seeks to strengthen cooperation with its North Korean counterparts under the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership between the two countries. "We also seek to develop cooperation between our emergency response agencies in a spirit of friendship and good neighborliness," he said.

The previous day, Kurenkov met with North Korean Minister of Disaster Management Kim Chol Nam. The two sides discussed priority areas for joint work in detail.

headline: Israel brands Netherlands 'antisemitism hotspot' over ban on Israeli football fans
summary: Israeli Foreign Ministry lashes out after Dutch city upholds ban on Hapoel Be'er Sheva supporters attending Europa League match over security concerns
body_text:
Israel accused the Netherlands of becoming an "antisemitism hotspot" Monday after authorities in the Dutch city of Alkmaar upheld a ban on Israeli football fans attending a Europa League match despite diplomatic pressure from Tel Aviv.

Supporters of the Israeli club Hapoel Be'er Sheva have been barred from attending the Oct. 15 match against AZ Alkmaar after local authorities classified the fixture as "very high risk" over concerns about protests and possible clashes.

In a statement on the US social media platform X, the Israeli Foreign Ministry claimed the decision "rewards those who threaten and incite violence" and "runs counter to the very spirit of sport."

The ministry accused Dutch authorities of banning "the victims, not the attackers," referring to clashes involving Israeli football fans in Amsterdam in November 2024.

It also claimed that antisemitic attacks in the Netherlands were being fueled by anti-Israel rhetoric from Dutch politicians and public figures.

The ministry described the ban, along with a boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest due to the inclusion of Israel amid the war in Gaza, as "yet another stain" on the Netherlands, accusing the country of increasingly becoming one of the world's leading "hotspots for antisemitism."

There was no immediate response from Dutch authorities to the Israeli accusations.

Earlier Monday, The Times of Israel reported that Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar had raised the issue with his Dutch counterpart, Tom Berendsen, as Israel sought to overturn the ban.

Israeli officials also contacted the Dutch Foreign Ministry and Alkmaar municipality, pressing for Israeli supporters to be allowed into the stadium and for their safety to be guaranteed, according to the report.

The dispute comes nearly two years after unrest surrounding a match between Maccabi Tel Aviv and Ajax in Amsterdam in November 2024.

The clashes were preceded by racist and anti-Palestinian chants from Israeli supporters as well as incidents of vandalism and the tearing down of a Palestinian flag.

In August, the Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS announced it would boycott the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest over Israel's participation, marking the second consecutive year of its boycott.

headline: S. Korea, U.S., Japan hold consultations over N. Korea's latest missile launches
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- Senior diplomats from South Korea, the United States ...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- Senior diplomats from South Korea, the United States and Japan held telephone consultations Tuesday to share information and discuss responses to North Korea's latest ballistic missile launches, Seoul's foreign ministry said.

On Monday, North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles toward the East Sea, according to South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS). The North said Tuesday it test-fired a "tactical" ballistic missile the previous day to verify technological improvements to a key component of its weapons systems.

Baek Yong-jin, director general for Korean Peninsula policy at Seoul's foreign ministry, spoke with David Wilezol, deputy assistant secretary for Northeast Asia at the U.S. State Department, and Takashi Ariyoshi, a senior official at Japan's foreign ministry, the ministry said.

"The three officials shared relevant information and discussed future responses," the ministry said in a press release.

"The foreign affairs authorities of the three countries operate a channel for promptly sharing information and assessments whenever North Korea launches ballistic missiles," it added.

headline: N. Korea, Russia agree to expand cooperation in disaster response
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea and Russia have signed an agreement to ex...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea and Russia have signed an agreement to expand bilateral cooperation on disaster management for the next three years, the North's state media reported Tuesday.

Kim Chol-nam, the North's minister of disaster management, and Aleksandr Kurenkov, the Russian minister of extraordinary situations, signed the agreement in Pyongyang the previous day to boost cooperation on the matter from 2027-2029, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).

The "successes and experience gained by the two countries in the work to prevent disaster were exchanged and the issues of boosting bilateral exchange and cooperation were discussed," according to the report.

A delegation from Russia's emergency ministry arrived in Pyongyang on Sunday for talks with its North Korean counterpart on ways to deepen cooperation in disaster management.

The visit came as the Russian ministry and the North's corresponding ministry signed an agreement on specialist training and scientific and technical cooperation in December.

headline: SK earthon begins oil production at offshore field in Vietnam
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- SK earthon Co., a South Korean oil exploration and pr...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- SK earthon Co., a South Korean oil exploration and production (E&P) company, said Tuesday oil production has recently begun at an offshore field in Vietnam where it holds a stake.

U.S.-based Murphy Oil Corp., the operator of Block 15-1/05, began production at the Lac Da Vang field in the Cuu Long Basin late last month, SK earthon said in a press release.

SK earthon holds a 25 percent stake in the block, having invested in the project in 2007. Murphy Oil and Vietnam's state-run PetroVietnam Exploration Production Corp. (PVEP) hold 40 percent and 35 percent stakes, respectively.

The block is estimated to contain total oil reserves of 60 million barrels, with production expected to reach up to 25,000 barrels per day when the project is fully developed, the company said.

"We will continue to expand its oil exploration and development activities in Vietnam to secure a stable energy supply amid rising geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions," a company official said.

SK earthon has been expanding its E&P operations in China and Southeast Asia to help improve the profitability of its parent company, SK Innovation, a major South Korean refiner. Since 2022, SK earthon has generated more than 1 trillion won (US$748 million) in annual revenue from its overseas E&P projects.

SK earthon is a wholly owned subsidiary of SK Innovation, the refining arm of SK Group, a conglomerate with interests spanning semiconductors to construction.

headline: Yonhap News to hold forum on economic cooperation between S. Korea, Japan
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- Yonhap News Agency, South Korea's leading newswire, s...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- Yonhap News Agency, South Korea's leading newswire, said Tuesday it will host a forum next month to explore ways to boost economic ties between South Korea and Japan amid growing global uncertainties.

Under the theme of "A fragmenting global economy, connecting Korean and Japanese markets," the 2026 Future Economy Forum will take place in Seoul on Nov. 3, bringing together business leaders, policymakers and academics from both countries to discuss avenues for closer cooperation and shared prosperity, according to Yonhap.

Yonhap President and CEO Hwang Dae-il will deliver opening remarks, while Chey Tae-won, chairman of SK Group and the Korea Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI), will give congratulatory remarks. Chey has long advocated the creation of a Korea-Japan economic community.

Speakers will also include Hiroaki Ishiguro, head of the global strategy division at Lotte Holdings Co.; Lee Sang-yup, chief technology officer of LG Uplus Corp.; and former South Korean Foreign Minister Yoon Young-kwan, who heads the Asan Institute for Policy Studies.

The forum will feature three sessions examining how Seoul and Tokyo can move beyond competition to become strategic partners, the potential for a bilateral economic community and ways to jointly address challenges posed by rapidly aging populations.

The event comes as geopolitical tensions, including an intensifying U.S.-China rivalry and ongoing conflicts in the Middle East and elsewhere, contribute to the fragmentation of global trade and supply chains.

The event is supported by Japan's Kyodo News, South Korea's industry ministry and the KCCI.

Preregistration for the forum is open from Oct. 13-28, Yonhap said.

Yonhap launched the Future Economy Forum in 2024, focusing on the state and challenges of South Korea's advanced industries, particularly semiconductors. Last year's forum examined economic cooperation between South Korea and Africa, highlighting opportunities for partnerships with the continent.

graceoh@yna.co.kr(END)

RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," said a representative for Mitte.

The American actor died on Monday in Brownsville, Texas.

Mitte appeared across all five seasons of the AMC hit drama, which ran from 2008 to 2013, playing the teenage son of Bryan Cranston’s chemistry teacher turned drug dealer. Like his character, also known as Flynn, Mitte had cerebral palsy.

The role brought him international recognition and provided a platform for his work advocating for people with disabilities, including greater representation in the entertainment industry.

Cranston was among those who paid tribute, remembering Mitte’s enthusiasm for acting and the years they spent working together.

“I’ll miss you, son,” he wrote on Instagram.

Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman in the series, also expressed his sadness.

“RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed,” he said.

Dean Norris, who played Hank Schrader, recalled looking out for Mitte as a young actor on set and said he would be greatly missed.

Tributes also came from his co-stars on Switched at Birth, including actress and disability rights advocate Marlee Matlin.

“My heart is shattered. There will never be another like RJ Mitte,” she wrote on Instagram.

Lea Thompson, who also worked with Mitte on the series, remembered him as “joyous, professional, and kind”, and said his work had inspired many.

Born and raised in Jackson, Mississippi, Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at the age of three. He moved to Los Angeles in 2006 and took small television roles before joining Breaking Bad as a teenager.

He appeared in 56 episodes and was part of the cast that won the Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding ensemble in a drama series in 2014.

His subsequent television credits included Switched at Birth, Now Apocalypse and The Guardians of Justice. On film, he appeared in The Recall and The Oak Room, among other projects.

In the 2021 drama Triumph, he played a high school student with cerebral palsy determined to become a wrestler, continuing his work portraying characters whose experiences reflected aspects of his own.

Away from acting, Mitte served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, and as president of the Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic and community initiatives. His representatives highlighted his efforts to challenge stereotypes and improve opportunities for people with disabilities.

headline: IMF upgrades 2026 growth forecast but warns of 'split' outlook
summary: The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday forecast that global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected due to advanced economies' "resilience" in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned that low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock. In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organization's Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the Fund raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent, compared to 3.5 percent growth in 2025.
body_text:
The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday forecast that global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected due to advanced economies' "resilience" in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned that low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock.

In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organization's Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the Fund raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent, compared to 3.5 percent growth in 2025.

The IMF warned that while many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in artificial intelligence (AI) technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices due to the US war on Iran.

"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks to growth tilted to the downside," said Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's chief economist.

The United States' war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran's retaliatory actions.

Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95 percent above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.

The war is in its eighth month, and Tenreyro warned that "a prolonged conflict in the Middle East could put additional pressures on inflation and slow down growth."

Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a "bifurcated outlook" in its WEO report.

The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a "fragmented" world economy.

"Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest," it said.

"At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions."

The IMF's split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.

The Middle East and Central Asia region, exposed directly to the Iran war as Tehran has targeted Washington's Gulf allies, saw the IMF forecast economic contraction of 0.3 percent in 2026.

Saudi Arabia saw one of the sharpest falls in projected growth, with the IMF forecasting a contraction of 3.3 percent -- a cut in the forecast of 5.0 percentage points.

The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.

In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.

The world's advanced economies were forecast to grow by 2.1 percent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.

Growth in China, the world's second-largest economy, was expected to slow by 0.5 percentage points to 4.5 percent this year, the IMF said, mainly due to weak domestic demand.

Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7 percent in 2026, fuelled by the Iran war and the AI boom, with effects spread across both advanced and developing economies.

IMF Chief Economist Tenreyro warned that "urgent action" was required by all countries in the face of downside risks.

On the fiscal side, she called on governments to only use temporary and targeted measures to help ease the burden on the public of high energy and other costs.

In lockstep, "monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability," she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.

"The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits," she said. "The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space, and rebuilding supply-side resilience."

Our correspondents are already on the next chapter. Read everything they file, from $2/week.

analysis.framing: The article frames the IMF's upgraded 2026 growth forecast around a 'split' or 'bifurcated' global outlook, emphasizing the divergence between AI-booming advanced economies and war-exposed, energy-importing low-income countries.

loaded_language.explanation: The compound modifier 'war-fuelled' is emotionally charged and attributes causality in a compressed, dramatic way rather than stating the mechanism neutrally.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: energy prices elevated by the war

loaded_language.quote: plunged the Middle East into violence
loaded_language.explanation: 'Plunged' is a vivid, dramatic verb that heightens the sense of sudden crisis compared to more neutral verbs like 'led to' or 'contributed to'.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: led to violence in the Middle East

'Stark' is an emotive intensifier that dramatizes the situation of poorer countries beyond what the data alone conveys.
'Buoyed' is a metaphorical, somewhat positive-charged verb that softens the description of advanced-economy growth compared to a neutral 'supported by'.

omissions: No mention of the IMF's specific growth forecasts for other major economies such as the euro area, Japan, or India, which are typically included in World Economic Outlook coverage.
No mention of the IMF's forecast for the United States itself, despite the US being central to the war and AI boom described.
No mention of the human cost or casualty figures from the US war on Iran, which other coverage of the conflict may include.
No mention of the IMF's specific inflation forecasts for individual regions or countries, only the global figure.
No mention of the IMF's policy recommendations beyond fiscal and monetary measures, such as structural reforms or international cooperation.

body_text:
Cristiano Ronaldo was on the scoresheet as Al Nassr got their AFC Champions League Elite campaign back on track with a comfortable win over Neftchi Fergana.

Ronaldo scored the second of Nassr's goals just before the break after Angelo Gabriel had given the hosts a 33rd-minute lead.

Alishev Odilov had reduced the deficit in the 51st minute before an Anvarjon Gofurov own goal sealed a 3-1 victory for Nassr.

Al Ahli overcome Al Wasl in fiery AFC Champions League clash

Kick-off was delayed at Al Awwal Park due to a security alert issued by Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence. Riyadh has suffered a series of ​deadly ​attacks ‌by the ⁠Iran-aligned Houthis over the past week.

Supporters were allowed to remain in their seats as authorities carried out safety protocols before the match kicked off 20 minutes after it was scheduled.

Ronaldo, 41, was spotted kissing the badge on his shirt during the warm-up. He was also pictured holding the shirt up to his face to cover his eyes in an emotional moment.

The Portuguese superstar scored the 981st goal of his career in the 42nd minute, latching on to a knockdown from Ayman Yahya in the area before firing past Neftchi goalkeeper Botirali Ergashev.

"Important win tonight. We keep building," Ronaldo posted in a message on his social media channels after the match.

Angelo broke the deadlock in the 33rd minute, meeting a cross inside the box and turning the ball into the net to give Al Nassr the lead.

Odilov capitalised on a Nawaf Boushal blunder to spark life back into the Uzbek champions in the 51st minute, but a red card shown to Ali Bayev for violent conduct after he caught Nassr defender Mohamed Simakan swung momentum back in Nassr's favour.

Nassr made the extra man count on 78 minutes. Bojan Cecer turned the ball into his own net, handing the Saudi champions all three points and their first win in this season's competition after they were routed 4-0 in their first match at Al Ain.

Ange Postecoglou revealed after the match that he had been worried about his players' mental state before the match following the deadly attacks on Riyadh.

“I was worried about the players during the match because I care about them, but I was very happy with the professionalism they showed,” the Australian told reporters.

Postecoglou said the club will monitor injuries to Kingsley Coman and Mohamed Simakan.

French forward Coman was forced off injured after only 13 minutes, while Simakan was withdrawn following the red-card challenge by Bayev.

Al Ain maintained their 100 per cent start to the league phase with a thumping win over Iraq's Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basrah.

Houssine Rahimi struck twice as Al Ain raced to a 4-0 lead at the break, as the former champions cruised to a second successive win in emphatic fashion.

Alejandro Romero had opened the scoring in the 13th minute before Saed Al Rodsan turned into his own net to double Al Ain's advantage.

Rahimi, who struck twice for Al Ain in their victory over Nassr in September, grabbed another brace against Al Quwa before half-time to kill the contest.

Mohammed Jawad grabbed a consolation goal in the 89th minute.

“We know what we can do, and the players did their job excellently until the end. They deserve this victory," Al Ain coach Vladimir Ivic told reporters.

“We sent a message to ourselves about what we can do, and that is the most important thing for me.”

Victory took Al Ain top of Group B ahead of Esteghlal on goal difference.

Tijjani Reijnders was on target as Al Qadsiah were held to a 1-1 draw at Pakhtakor.

headline: Russia says Europe bought $320 billion in hydrocarbons since 2022
summary: Russia said on Monday that European Union countries had bought $320.7 billion worth of its energy resources since 2022, despite sanctions over the war in Ukraine. The figure fuelled tensions as European officials criticised a US deal to import Russian diesel, while Stockholm called for the bloc to use frozen Russian assets to boost support for Kyiv.
body_text:
Russia said on Monday that European Union countries had bought $320.7 billion worth of its energy resources since 2022, despite sanctions over the war in Ukraine. The figure fuelled tensions as European officials criticised a US deal to import Russian diesel, while Stockholm called for the bloc to use frozen Russian assets to boost support for Kyiv.

Issued on: 13/10/2026 - 05:10

Russia said on Monday that it had sold European countries more than $320 billion worth of hydrocarbons since 2022, despite sanctions imposed over the war in Ukraine.

"For the period from 2022 to today, this figure amounts to $320.7 billion. This is the volume of energy resource deliveries to European Union countries," Russian Deputy Prime Minister in charge of energy Alexander Novak said on television.

He said European countries purchased $21.3 billion worth of Russian hydrocarbons in the first nine months of 2026 alone.

"In other words, despite sanctions-related restrictions, we continue to supply energy resources in certain areas for which exemptions have been granted," he added.

Novak said Russian oil exports may reach their pre-war levels by the end of the year.

Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard pointed to the Russian figure as she arrived in Luxembourg on Monday for a meeting with her European Union counterparts.

She contrasted it with the 218.7 billion euros ($244 billion) in support that the EU had sent to Ukraine since the start of the war.

Yesterday’s call for stronger collective defence in the Gulf by Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to President Sheikh Mohamed, comes at a moment when a beleaguered Iran and its remaining armed proxies have decided to escalate and target the Arab world's largest economy.

As the Iran-backed Houthis’ repeated strikes on travellers at Riyadh’s King Khalid airport show, the human cost of failing to deter attacks or intercept missiles is steep. Such attacks also strike at the region's prosperity, something that depends on transport networks, energy infrastructure, the environment and the confidence that connect active economies and those who benefit from them.

A threat to an airport or a shipping route has consequences well beyond the country directly targeted. Airlines reassess risks to flights and businesses are forced to reconsider other supply chains. Investors also have to debate the costs of operating in a volatile region. Even the mere threat of disruption can come with a heavy price tag.

As we have seen since the Iran conflict began in February, aviation is particularly vulnerable. The Gulf’s position as a global hub depends on reliable connections between Europe, Asia and Africa. Attacks, such as those seen in Riyadh, can force airlines to reroute flights, increasing costs and disrupting travel. From this tourism, trade and international connections are imperilled.

Environmental security presents another shared challenge. Attacks on oil centres, tankers and other energy infrastructure risk causing pollution that crosses international borders and presents a generational problem. The region's marine environment is already under pressure, while the concentration of energy infrastructure and shipping in a relatively confined Strait of Hormuz makes the consequences of a major spill particularly serious.

Economic security is equally inseparable from the wider crisis. Arab states may be competitors in some markets, but their economies are also linked. Disruption in one country can ripple through its neighbours.

Joint environmental response arrangements and plans to protect critical infrastructure could also improve the region’s joint ability to withstand the kind of shocking events witnessed in recent days in Saudi Arabia.

This does not mean individual Gulf countries suddenly dropping their individual national priorities or resolving every difference of opinion. It is more a question of building on the long-standing ties that unite Gulf societies and recognising the that although economic interdependence can create shared prosperity it can also come with common responses to threats. At a time when ideological actors are lashing out at those around them, the eventual outcome may just be a more aligned approach by Arab neighbours to the challenges that face them.

headline: AI investment props up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook, IMF says
summary: By David LawderBANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The global economy will still manage to top 3% real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1%, a slight uptick from the 3.0% it predicted in July.
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The global economy will still manage to top 3% real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday.

Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1%, a slight uptick from the 3.0% it predicted in July.

The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5%.

For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4% global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage point from April.

The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week.

"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding," the IMF's chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told a news conference. "We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience."

She said major downside risks to growth include a prolonged, intensified war in the Middle East that spikes inflation pressures, rising bond yields that raise government borrowing costs, El Nino-driven extreme weather events and a reassessment of AI profitability that craters investment and asset prices.

Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF's deputy research director, told Reuters in a separate interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5% this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on.

The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95% of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April.

Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47% of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains.

Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran, with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3% this year compared with the 1.7% growth predicted in July.

Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6%, 16%, 16.7%, 15.6% and 3.9%, respectively.

UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE

Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3% for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content.

Euro zone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1% from 0.9% in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defense spending in EU countries. Britain's 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage point from July to 1.3% due to larger AI investment.

The IMF forecast China's growth at 4.5% for 2026 and 4.0% for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports.

India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy at 7.0% for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment.

The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7% in 2026 and 4.1% for 2027.

ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS

Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of $96 per barrel for 2026 and $87 in 2027.

But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to $130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2%.

AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6% by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China.

But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialize, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8% directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4% by 2028.

This shift would also trigger a sharp reduction in asset prices and tighter financial conditions that cause a major drop in consumption, particularly in the US, the IMF said. Higher global bond yields would further reduce activity, with a combined global output reduction of 1.1% by 2028, including a 1.8% drop in US output.

The IMF also warned that elevated public debt levels, particularly in advanced economies, increase the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs that can weigh on growth prospects. It urged governments to stop delaying action to rebuild fiscal buffers and articulate credible medium-term plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels — advice that IMF officials plan to push at the Bangkok meetings.

(Reporting by David Lawder; Editing by Paul Simao and John Mair)

headline: Qatar Airways suspends flights to Riyadh, Dammam
summary: The carrier said it is closely monitoring developments in Saudi Arabia in coordination with the relevant authorities
body_text:
DOHA, October 13. /TASS/. Qatar Airways has temporarily suspended flights to and from the Saudi cities of Riyadh and Dammam for safety reasons, the airline said in a notice.

The carrier said it is closely monitoring developments in Saudi Arabia in coordination with the relevant authorities. "Due to the current situation, flights to and from Riyadh (RUH) and Dammam (DMM) are temporarily suspended," the notice said. The airline stressed that passenger and crew safety remains its highest priority.

Earlier, Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation announced an extension of the closure of Riyadh’s airport following recent attacks, citing the need to "complete the necessary procedures to verify the safety of airport facilities and their operational readiness in coordination with the competent authorities."

Yemen’s rebel Ansar Allah movement - the Houthis - attacked the airport in the Saudi capital on October 10 and 11. According to Saudi authorities, the first strike killed at least 12 people and injured more than 300. The second attack killed one person, injured 11 others and caused damage to the airport.

body_text:
RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr in Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," said a representative for Mitte.

The American actor died on Monday in Brownsville, Texas.

Mitte appeared across all five seasons of the AMC hit drama, which ran from 2008 to 2013, playing the teenage son of Bryan Cranston’s chemistry teacher turned drug dealer. Like his character, also known as Flynn, Mitte had cerebral palsy.

The role brought him international recognition and provided a platform for his work advocating for people with disabilities, including greater representation in the entertainment industry.

Cranston was among those who paid tribute, remembering Mitte’s enthusiasm for acting and the years they spent working together.

“I’ll miss you, son,” he wrote on Instagram.

Aaron Paul, who played Jesse Pinkman in the series, also expressed his sadness.

“RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed,” he said.

Dean Norris, who played Hank Schrader, recalled looking out for Mitte as a young actor on set and said he would be greatly missed.

Tributes also came from his co-stars on Switched at Birth, including actress and disability rights advocate Marlee Matlin.

“My heart is shattered. There will never be another like RJ Mitte,” she wrote on Instagram.

Lea Thompson, who also worked with Mitte on the series, remembered him as “joyous, professional, and kind”, and said his work had inspired many.

Born and raised in Jackson, Mississippi, Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at the age of three. He moved to Los Angeles in 2006 and took small television roles before joining Breaking Bad as a teenager.

He appeared in 56 episodes and was part of the cast that won the Screen Actors Guild award for outstanding ensemble in a drama series in 2014.

His subsequent television credits included Switched at Birth, Now Apocalypse and The Guardians of Justice. On film, he appeared in The Recall and The Oak Room, among other projects.

In the 2021 drama Triumph, he played a high school student with cerebral palsy determined to become a wrestler, continuing his work portraying characters whose experiences reflected aspects of his own.

Away from acting, Mitte served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s, and as president of the Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic and community initiatives. His representatives highlighted his efforts to challenge stereotypes and improve opportunities for people with disabilities.
