headline: China invites Russian Knights to Airshow China in Zhuhai
summary: Mayor Wu Zetong stressed that expanding international participation is "the main direction for Airshow China’s development"
body_text:
BEIJING, October 13. /TASS/. China has invited the Russian Knights aerobatic team to the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, known as Airshow China, in Zhuhai in the southern province of Guangdong this December, the city’s mayor Wu Zetong said.

"The Russian Knights aerobatic team will perform at the upcoming airshow again. The team is well known to audiences, having participated in Airshow China seven times since 1998. Its virtuoso performances have left a deep impression on the public and won widespread affection," he said at a news conference in response to a TASS question.

Wu stressed that expanding international participation is "the main direction for Airshow China’s development." He said the flying displays will be "even more spectacular," with pilots from the United Arab Emirates joining the Russian Knights. "For the first time since 2016, two foreign military aerobatic teams will participate in Airshow China together," he added.

The Bayi Aerobatic Team of China’s People’s Liberation Army Air Force will also "perform an aerial ballet" alongside them, the mayor said.

China’s largest aviation and aerospace exhibition takes place in the coastal city of Zhuhai, attracting hundreds of companies from several countries. Russian defense companies regularly participate. The exhibition focuses on military and civilian aircraft, space, navigation and radar equipment, aircraft weapons, rocket engines, fire control systems and air defenses. Its 16th edition will run from December 7 to 13.

body_text:
Saudi Arabia has vowed to remain strong as the coalition it leads against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced the interception of missiles fired at Riyadh and the south of the kingdom on Monday.

“We strongly condemn the Houthi terrorist attacks targeting civilians and civilian facilities in the kingdom," Minister of Media Salman Al Dosary said.

At a government media conference in Riyadh, he praised security forces and the military, saying the kingdom would "remain strong and united" behind its leadership and continue its development efforts despite the attacks.

Timeline: Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi airports

Early on Tuesday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait in the south-west of the kingdom. Coalition spokesman Col Turki Al Malki announced the interception in a post on X.

The statement did not say where the missiles were launched from or whether the incident caused any casualties or damage. The Houthis had claimed a "direct hit" in a ballistic missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Monday night.

The Iran-backed group's military spokesman, Yahya Saree, repeated its warning "to all international airlines, experts, employees, workers and passengers from all countries of the world against flights to Saudi airports, as they are unsafe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah".

He also claimed a drone launched at the Khamis Mushait airbase resulted in a "direct hit".

Saudi authorities extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport until midnight on October 17 after an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured more than 300. An attack on Sunday killed one person.

Meanwhile, pro-government forces and the Houthis are battling for control of the key city of Taiz. Rights groups have raised the alarm on the humanitarian situation inside the city, where people are cut off from food, water, medical and energy supplies amid what some organisations described as a "siege".

"Within five days, the city lost its main supply route for goods and commodities: Taiz–Al-Turbah–Lahj–Aden, following the Houthi group’s takeover of areas west and south of Taiz," the Studies and Economic Media Centre in Yemen said in a report this week. The government also closed the eastern route used by civilians for security reasons, it added.

The International Organisation for Migration estimates that more than 216,000 people have been displaced since the escalations in Yemen began in August. At least 172,000 of them are from Taiz.

The UN said it was providing assistance to those in need but that reaching them was proving difficult, especially with key roads closed. That has disrupted "civilian movement, commercial supplies and humanitarian access", the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in a briefing on Monday.

At least 54 civilians have been killed, half of them children, the agency said. "A further 171 civilians have been injured, including 107 women and children," it added.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event through Saudi official statements and coalition announcements, presenting the kingdom as a victim of Houthi attacks while also noting the humanitarian toll in Yemen.

The word 'siege' is emotionally charged and suggests a deliberate and harsh encirclement, though it is attributed to some organizations.

body_text:
At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, maritime agency reports show, as Iran increases its campaign to halt US-backed efforts to move oil through the vital waterway.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency issued delayed reports yesterday covering six vessels struck on Sunday – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage.

The UKMTO reclassified the Sohar incident from suspicious activity to an attack after confirming a tanker had been struck by a drone. Local authorities assisted in evacuating the crew. In a separate incident, an outbound tanker was damaged when it was hit on its port side, although all crew members were reported safe.

Hormuz traffic hits lowest level in two months as tanker attacks surge

The incidents follow a sustained increase in attacks, attempted attacks and the harassment of commercial vessels. The US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Centre said that showed Iran’s “intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels”.

The centre's assessment followed reports of at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, quoting maritime security sources.

The International Maritime Organisation recorded nine vessel-related incidents in the same period, reflecting differences in verification and reporting.

Iran has accompanied the pressure on shipping with increasingly explicit warnings to vessels attempting to transit the strait. On Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a crude oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route with its navigation systems switched off.

Shipping analyst Sal Mercogliano said video circulating with the claim did not appear to show a mine strike, as the vessel was stationary and there was no underwater explosion. The IRGC claimed any tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait would face a similar fate.

Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint co-ordinator of Iran’s army, issued a further warning on Sunday. “We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” he said.

On Monday, the IRGC said it had struck a supertanker attempting to transit the strait with its transponders switched off. Seatrade reported a separate Iranian claim that a supertanker had been hit. The incident not been confirmed.

Earlier this month, a crude tanker was struck while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, but the threat to commercial shipping has also extended beyond the waterway. A vessel reported being hit by projectiles about 95km north of Madinat Ash Shamal in Qatar, with casualties reported.

The Panama-flagged crude carrier Gem No 2 was struck by a drone, with reports placing the vessel about 25km west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. The resulting fire was extinguished and Indian officials said the vessel’s 22 crew members were safe.

The attacks and warnings have sharpened the divide between Tehran’s claims of control over the waterway and Washington’s assessment of shipping conditions.

Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the IRGC's commander, said Iran would close routes it considered to be illegal, including passages along Oman’s coast.

“The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mr Naqdi was quoted as saying by the Fars news agency.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected that assessment last week, saying commercial oil flows had largely recovered despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt shipping. “The Strait of Hormuz is open. There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he said. “So they’ve lost complete control of the strait.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the surge in Strait of Hormuz attacks as an escalating Iranian campaign against US-backed oil shipping, while presenting both Iranian claims of control and US counter-claims as a sharpening divide.

body_text:
In today’s episode of Trending Middle East, Yemen’s Houthi rebels launch further attacks against Saudi Arabia as authorities extend the closure of Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport until October 17. The attacks have disrupted flights across the region, with Etihad Airways cancelling services between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until October 19.

The UK imposes sanctions on two Iranian citizens accused of involvement in plots to carry out attacks in the country, while Tehran denies involvement.

Meanwhile, Pakistan detains allies of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan after imposing emergency rule and suspending the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

The International Monetary Fund sharply downgrades its Gulf economic forecasts because of the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, projecting a 3.9 per cent contraction in the UAE economy this year.

In the UAE, the Cabinet approves a Dh292.5 billion ($$79.64 billion) federal budget for 2027 to 2029, an increase of 28.3 per cent compared with the previous three-year period.

'Further' implies an ongoing, escalating pattern and carries a subtle editorial weight by framing the action as part of a continuing hostile campaign.
'Prolonged' is a subjective characterization of duration that suggests excessive or problematic length, rather than simply stating the closure has continued.

body_text:
Marino Pusic said something needs to be done to stop fans throwing bottles at players, terming it “dangerous”.

The Al Ahli Saudi coach was speaking after his side’s 3-1 win over Al Wasl in Dubai on Monday night.

The AFC Champions League Elite group match was played in an electric atmosphere created by 4,500 supporters at the Zabeel Stadium.

Al Ahli overcome Al Wasl in fiery AFC Champions League clash

Emotions boiled over at points, though, with many plastic bottles and cups being thrown onto the pitch.

In particular, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, became a target after irritating supporters with his antics.

First, he invoked ire after being perceived to feign injury in an altercation with Adryelson, the Wasl defender.

When he was playing on the wing near Wasl’s diehard supporters in the second half, he was pelted with bottles. He responded by gesturing to them to throw more.

Later in the game he was stretchered off on a medical buggy with a shoulder injury.

The injury did not stop him from goading the home supporters, and celebrating when he went past the away section.

That led to more aggravation, with even a couple of bottles being lobbed his way from the Wasl bench – leading to a confrontation between the opposing sets of substitutes.

The issue of bottle throwing is not unique to Wasl. Most high profile fixtures in the region see instances of projectiles being thrown at moments of tension in the game.

With matches played in high temperatures, clubs make water readily available to supporters.

At Al Ain, for example, that now takes the form of paper cups alongside large water coolers at the back of stands.

Other clubs provide small bottles or plastic cups of water. Sometimes these are thrown by irate fans, targeting players, coaching staff, or match officials.

It happened at the AFC Champions League Elite final last season, which Ahli themselves ended up winning.

High profile international fixtures between Qatar and the UAE have also been notable for it happening.

Pusic joined Ahli, the two-time Asian champions, ahead of this season after leaving Abu Dhabi club Al Jazira.

He said he does not want the passion of supporters to be diluted, and pointed out that the fixture against Wasl ended with cordial relations between the two sides.

But the Croatian-Dutch coach said players and officials should not have projectiles thrown at them.

“It could be a problem with people throwing very dangerous things on the pitch, because players and staff members [could] be hurt by these kind of things,” Pusic said.

“I feel always pity about things when that happens. The passion and the support must be always there, and that's good. I like that part as well.

“But as you can see, after the game, it was everything was nice, fine, like it should be.

“In the heat of the moment, things can happen. But it's dangerous when you throw too much. It shouldn't happen, of course. But we are professionals; we are used to a lot of things.”

The result leaves Wasl without a point after two matches in the Champions League, with many supporters voicing their frustration with coach Rui Vitoria.

Roger Ibanez, who scored the first goal for Ahli, said his side were glad to get out of Dubai with the three points.

“We knew it would be a tough game,” said the Brazil centre back, who was the player of the match.

“We played here two years ago when we also got the result, and today was again a really tough match but we got the result.

“We did a good job. Inside of the pitch, the players who started and the players who came in helped a lot.

“Now let's go home and recover because we have a tough match [in the Saudi Pro League against Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr on Thursday].”

Al Ain maintained their sparkling start to the Champions League and they sit at the top of the 16-team table.

The UAE double winners followed up their opening day thrashing of Al Nassr with a 4-1 win over Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basra.

headline: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 13, 2026
summary: [allAfrica]
body_text:
WHO Launches Five-Year Strategy to Detect Health Threats Faster

The World Health Organization (WHO) has launched a new five-year strategy to help every country detect and understand emerging health threats within 24 hours of their appearance by 2030. The strategy builds on the work of the WHO Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, established in 2021 after the COVID-19 pandemic exposed gaps. Since its creation, the Hub has worked with 160 WHO member states, 190 partner organisations and thousands of scientists and policymakers to strengthen global disease surveillance. The plan focuses on five key initiatives, including using artificial intelligence to identify potential health threats, strengthening genomic sequencing to track emerging pathogens and connecting experts in data science and disease modelling. It will also support countries in sharing health data securely and improving cooperation between human, animal and environmental health systems. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the strategy provides a clear path towards a world where countries can respond to health threats before they develop into major crises. The organisation says sustained investment and international partnerships will be essential to achieving this goal.

South Africa's Deputy Police Chief Resigns Amid Criminal Charges

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

South Africa's Deputy National Police Commissioner, Lieutenant General Shadrack Sibiya, has resigned from the police service three weeks after being charged with sexual offences. His lawyer submitted the resignation letter during a disciplinary hearing. Police spokesperson Athlenda Mathe said his departure would be treated as a dishonourable discharge because he was still facing disciplinary proceedings at the time of his resignation. Sibiya has been in custody since his arrest in September. Sibiya faces several serious allegations, including the sexual grooming of a 16-year-old girl, rape, human trafficking and links to organised crime figures. He denies the allegations of criminal links and sexual grooming. He admits having sex with an 18-year-old woman but maintains that it was consensual. Allegations against him also emerged during the Madlanga Commission, a public inquiry investigating claims of police corruption and collusion with criminal networks. He has been accused of interfering with investigations into political killings in KwaZulu-Natal and receiving cash and 20 impalas from an alleged criminal kingpin in exchange for a police contract. Sibiya has denied the allegations.

Renewed Fighting in Tigray Raises Fears of Wider Regional War

Renewed fighting in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region is raising fears of a wider conflict involving Eritrea and other neighbouring countries. Tensions escalated after reports that Eritrean forces crossed into Ethiopia, prompting Ethiopian forces to launch drone strikes against troops and equipment. Eritrea has denied reports of the incursion, while accusing Ethiopia of using the allegations as a pretext to pursue its ambitions for access to the Red Sea port of Assab. Local sources, however, reported clashes involving Eritrean forces at several locations in Tigray. The renewed violence follows the collapse of a fragile peace agreement that ended the 2020–2022 war. The conflict is unfolding amid shifting alliances between rival armed groups and growing tensions between Ethiopia and its neighbours. Tigray's ruling Tigray People's Liberation Front has vowed to continue fighting after federal forces and a pro-government militia captured the regional capital, Mekelle, on 3 October. The TPLF has also aligned with other opposition groups seeking to challenge Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Analysts warn that the conflict could develop into three possible scenarios: the proliferation of armed groups, a prolonged military stalemate, or a full-scale war between Ethiopia and Eritrea. The humanitarian consequences could be severe, particularly in Tigray, where about one million people remain displaced, and nearly four million need urgent assistance. Drought, food shortages, and difficulties delivering aid are adding to the crisis.

Drought and Conflict Push Sudan Closer to Famine

The risk of famine is growing in parts of Sudan as severe drought worsens the humanitarian crisis caused by ongoing conflict, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a global food security monitoring partnership supported by United Nations agencies. A new alert warns that malnutrition is worsening in several areas, particularly in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Aid organisations are struggling to reach affected communities because of insecurity, restricted access and a severe shortage of funding. In Eastern Jebel Marra, South Darfur, surveys in two displacement camps found acute malnutrition among children at 38% and 30.8%, both above the threshold associated with famine. More than half of Sudan has been affected by the drought, destroying crops and leaving families without enough food or income. In North Darfur, 64% of cropland is showing poor plant growth and late rains have not managed to save most cereal crops. Food prices are expected to continue to rise. There has also been mass displacement in Greater Kordofan, where since October 2025 more than 300,000 people have been forced to flee their homes. Attacks and insecurity are putting aid workers at risk, while many children are going without life-saving treatment for severe malnutrition. By 8 October, less than half of Sudan's humanitarian appeal had been funded. The IPC has called for an end to the fighting, safe access for aid agencies and a major increase in funding to prevent further loss of life.

Lagos Court Clears Way for Inquest into Chimamanda Adichie's Son's Death

The Lagos State High Court has cleared the way for a coroner's inquest into the death of Nkanu Esege, the son of renowned Nigerian author Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie. Justice Aishat Opesanwo dismissed an application by Eurapharma Care Services Nigeria Limited, which operates Euracare Multi-Specialist Hospital, seeking to stop the inquiry. The hospital argued that the cremation of Nkanu's body made a post-mortem examination impossible and deprived the coroner of the authority to proceed. Nkanu died on 7 January 2026 following medical procedures, prompting an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death. In her ruling, Justice Opesanwo said the law requires an inquest when the circumstances of a death meet the conditions set out in the Coroners System Law of Lagos State 2007. She said that the absence of the body did not automatically prevent the inquiry from taking place or make it speculative. The judge also rejected the hospital's arguments concerning the handling of statements and evidence from medical personnel, saying the coroner has discretion over how the proceedings are conducted. She stressed that a coroner's inquest is a fact-finding exercise intended to establish who died, and how, when and where the death occurred. It is not a criminal trial to determine guilt or assign blame. The ruling allows the inquest to proceed.

headline: Morning Briefing: Oct. 13, 2026
summary: Anadolu’s recap of top stories from around the globe
body_text:
Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Tuesday, including Saudi Arabia extending the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh following a series of attacks by Yemen’s Houthi group, UK blaming Iran for air base plot and announcing sanctions, and federal law enforcement authorities conducting a raid on US Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, DC residence.

Saudi Arabia announced that it had extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh following a series of attacks on the facility.

In a statement, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said the suspension was extended to complete necessary procedures to verify the safety of airport facilities and their operational readiness.

The authority did not specify when operations would resume.

The decision followed attacks on the airport over the weekend.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Monday that last month’s alleged terror plot targeting a British air base was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), as he announced fresh sanctions against two Iranian men.

Addressing Parliament, Burnham said the UK assessment was that the alleged plot, which led to five arrests on suspicion of terror offenses, was highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran.

“I can confirm our assessment that it is highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard,” he told MPs.

In late September, a major security incident occurred at RAF Fairford, a Gloucestershire airbase used by the US Air Force. The incident triggered a large-scale counter-terrorism investigation.

Iran on Monday again rejected British allegations that Tehran was involved in the incident, while reiterating its willingness to cooperate in examining the case, state news agency IRNA reported.

Federal law enforcement authorities raided the Washington, DC residence of Democratic US Rep. Ilhan Omar amid an investigation into her immigration records.

Federal personnel executed the court-approved operation around 6 am local time (1000GMT), centering on a criminal fraud inquiry concerning immigration documents completed during the childhood of the Democratic lawmaker, who was born in the Horn of Africa nation of Somalia.

"Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a department spokesperson told Fox News, underlining that the raid is part of an ongoing federal investigation.

Omar criticized the search at her home, describing the operation as an effort by the Trump administration to intimidate political opponents.

Microsoft on Monday unveiled its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, with plans to expand deployment of its own chips starting in 2027 and make them the primary inference system for its products and services.

Microsoft expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading graphics processing unit-based systems. A configuration containing 96 accelerators can deliver up to seven times the rack-level token throughput of Maia 200, according to the company.

South Korea’s Defense Ministry on Monday opened the military’s first artificial intelligence (AI) transformation base to develop robotic systems capable of performing dangerous military operations.

The facility, located in Pangyo, south of Seoul, will train humanoid and multi-legged robots using physical AI data and advanced AI models, Yonhap News Agency reported, citing the ministry.

Around 150 officials, including representatives from the science and industry ministries, attended the opening ceremony.

US actor RJ Mitte, best known for playing Walter White Jr. in the television series "Breaking Bad," has died at the age of 34, according to media reports.

Representatives for Mitte confirmed his death to US-based entertainment news outlets Variety and TMZ. The cause of death was not immediately disclosed.

Mitte portrayed the son of Walter White, played by Bryan Cranston, and Skyler White, played by Anna Gunn, in the AMC crime drama created by Vince Gilligan which aired 2008-2013.

A jersey worn by sports legend Michael Jordan during the 1998 NBA Finals has sold for $14 million, setting what auction house Hunt Auctions said is a record for basketball memorabilia.

Jordan wore the Chicago Bulls’ red jersey during Game 2 of the finals against the Utah Jazz, helping his team secure a victory that tied the series at 1-1. The Bulls went on to win the series in six games, securing Jordan’s sixth and final NBA championship.

Hunt Auctions said the jersey was purchased in a private sale by Miami real estate investor Ron Firman, according to The Guardian.

The exhibition focuses on military and civilian aircraft, space, navigation and radar equipment, aircraft weapons, rocket engines, fire control systems and air defenses. Its 16th edition will run from December 7 to 13.

body_text:
Saudi Arabia has vowed to remain strong as the coalition it leads against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced the interception of missiles fired at Riyadh and the south of the kingdom on Monday.

“We strongly condemn the Houthi terrorist attacks targeting civilians and civilian facilities in the kingdom," Minister of Media Salman Al Dosary said.

At a government media conference in Riyadh, he praised security forces and the military, saying the kingdom would "remain strong and united" behind its leadership and continue its development efforts despite the attacks.

Timeline: Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi airports

Early on Tuesday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait in the south-west of the kingdom. Coalition spokesman Col Turki Al Malki announced the interception in a post on X.

The statement did not say where the missiles were launched from or whether the incident caused any casualties or damage. The Houthis had claimed a "direct hit" in a ballistic missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Monday night.

The Iran-backed group's military spokesman, Yahya Saree, repeated its warning "to all international airlines, experts, employees, workers and passengers from all countries of the world against flights to Saudi airports, as they are unsafe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah".

He also claimed a drone launched at the Khamis Mushait airbase resulted in a "direct hit".

Saudi authorities extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport until midnight on October 17 after an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured more than 300. An attack on Sunday killed one person.

Meanwhile, pro-government forces and the Houthis are battling for control of the key city of Taiz. Rights groups have raised the alarm on the humanitarian situation inside the city, where people are cut off from food, water, medical and energy supplies amid what some organisations described as a "siege".

"Within five days, the city lost its main supply route for goods and commodities: Taiz–Al-Turbah–Lahj–Aden, following the Houthi group’s takeover of areas west and south of Taiz," the Studies and Economic Media Centre in Yemen said in a report this week. The government also closed the eastern route used by civilians for security reasons, it added.

The International Organisation for Migration estimates that more than 216,000 people have been displaced since the escalations in Yemen began in August. At least 172,000 of them are from Taiz.

The UN said it was providing assistance to those in need but that reaching them was proving difficult, especially with key roads closed. That has disrupted "civilian movement, commercial supplies and humanitarian access", the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in a briefing on Monday.

At least 54 civilians have been killed, half of them children, the agency said. "A further 171 civilians have been injured, including 107 women and children," it added.

headline: Strait of Hormuz attacks surge as Iran steps up campaign against US-backed oil shipping
summary: At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, maritime agency reports show, as Iran increases its campaign to halt US-backed efforts to move oil through the vital waterway.The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency issued delayed reports yesterday covering six vessels struck on Sunday – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage.The UKMTO reclassified the Sohar incident from suspicious activity to an attack after confirming a tanker had been struck by a drone. Local authorities assisted in evacuating the crew. In a separate incident, an outbound tanker was damaged when it was hit on its port side, although all crew members were reported safe.The incidents follow a sustained increase in attacks, attempted attacks and the harassment of commercial vessels. The US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Centre said that showed Iran’s “intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels”.The centre's assessment followed reports of at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, quoting maritime security sources.The International Maritime Organisation recorded nine vessel-related incidents in the same period, reflecting differences in verification and reporting.UKMTO WARNING 169-26Click here to view the full warning⤵️https://t.co/RPA5f2EHIf#MaritimeSecurity #MarSec pic.twitter.com/D28qf30tRn— UKMTO Operations Centre (@UK_MTO) October 12, 2026Iran has accompanied the pressure on shipping with increasingly explicit warnings to vessels attempting to transit the strait. On Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a crude oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route with its navigation systems switched off. Shipping analyst Sal Mercogliano said video circulating with the claim did not appear to show a mine strike, as the vessel was stationary and there was no underwater explosion. The IRGC claimed any tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait would face a similar fate.Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint co-ordinator of Iran’s army, issued a further warning on Sunday. “We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” he said.On Monday, the IRGC said it had struck a supertanker attempting to transit the strait with its transponders switched off. Seatrade reported a separate Iranian claim that a supertanker had been hit. body_text:
At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, maritime agency reports show, as Iran increases its campaign to halt US-backed efforts to move oil through the vital waterway.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency issued delayed reports yesterday covering six vessels struck on Sunday – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage.

The UKMTO reclassified the Sohar incident from suspicious activity to an attack after confirming a tanker had been struck by a drone. Local authorities assisted in evacuating the crew. In a separate incident, an outbound tanker was damaged when it was hit on its port side, although all crew members were reported safe.

Hormuz traffic hits lowest level in two months as tanker attacks surge

The incidents follow a sustained increase in attacks, attempted attacks and the harassment of commercial vessels. The US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Centre said that showed Iran’s “intent to assert [its] presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels”.

The centre's assessment followed reports of at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the strait between September 28 and October 5, Reuters reported, quoting maritime security sources.

The International Maritime Organisation recorded nine vessel-related incidents in the same period, reflecting differences in verification and reporting.

Iran has accompanied the pressure on shipping with increasingly explicit warnings to vessels attempting to transit the strait. On Saturday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a crude oil supertanker had struck a naval mine and suffered a major fire while using an unauthorised route with its navigation systems switched off.

Shipping analyst Sal Mercogliano said video circulating with the claim did not appear to show a mine strike, as the vessel was stationary and there was no underwater explosion. The IRGC claimed any tanker that “wishes to ignore the security and rules” of the strait would face a similar fate.

Habibollah Sayyari, chief of staff and joint co-ordinator of Iran’s army, issued a further warning on Sunday. “We have struck blows against enemy vessels. If anything else happens against Iran, we will strike them again,” he said.

On Monday, the IRGC said it had struck a supertanker attempting to transit the strait with its transponders switched off. Seatrade reported a separate Iranian claim that a supertanker had been hit. The incident not been confirmed.

Earlier this month, a crude tanker was struck while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, but the threat to commercial shipping has also extended beyond the waterway. A vessel reported being hit by projectiles about 95km north of Madinat Ash Shamal in Qatar, with casualties reported.

The Panama-flagged crude carrier Gem No 2 was struck by a drone, with reports placing the vessel about 25km west of Al Jazeera in the UAE. The resulting fire was extinguished and Indian officials said the vessel’s 22 crew members were safe.

The attacks and warnings have sharpened the divide between Tehran’s claims of control over the waterway and Washington’s assessment of shipping conditions.

Mohammadreza Naqdi, an adviser to the IRGC's commander, said Iran would close routes it considered to be illegal, including passages along Oman’s coast.

“The Strait of Hormuz is closed and the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran have full control over it,” Mr Naqdi was quoted as saying by the Fars news agency.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio rejected that assessment last week, saying commercial oil flows had largely recovered despite Iran’s efforts to disrupt shipping. “The Strait of Hormuz is open. There’s almost as much oil flowing out now as there was before this conflict began,” he said. “So they’ve lost complete control of the strait.”

The attacks have disrupted flights across the region, with Etihad Airways cancelling services between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh until October 19.

The UK imposes sanctions on two Iranian citizens accused of involvement in plots to carry out attacks in the country, while Tehran denies involvement.

Meanwhile, Pakistan detains allies of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan after imposing emergency rule and suspending the provincial government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

The International Monetary Fund sharply downgrades its Gulf economic forecasts because of the prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, projecting a 3.9 per cent contraction in the UAE economy this year.

In the UAE, the Cabinet approves a Dh292.5 billion ($$79.64 billion) federal budget for 2027 to 2029, an increase of 28.3 per cent compared with the previous three-year period.

body_text:
Marino Pusic said something needs to be done to stop fans throwing bottles at players, terming it “dangerous”.

The Al Ahli Saudi coach was speaking after his side’s 3-1 win over Al Wasl in Dubai on Monday night.

The AFC Champions League Elite group match was played in an electric atmosphere created by 4,500 supporters at the Zabeel Stadium.

Al Ahli overcome Al Wasl in fiery AFC Champions League clash

Emotions boiled over at points, though, with many plastic bottles and cups being thrown onto the pitch.

In particular, Saleh Abu Al Shamat, the Ahli forward, became a target after irritating supporters with his antics.

First, he invoked ire after being perceived to feign injury in an altercation with Adryelson, the Wasl defender.

When he was playing on the wing near Wasl’s diehard supporters in the second half, he was pelted with bottles. He responded by gesturing to them to throw more.

Later in the game he was stretchered off on a medical buggy with a shoulder injury.

The injury did not stop him from goading the home supporters, and celebrating when he went past the away section.

That led to more aggravation, with even a couple of bottles being lobbed his way from the Wasl bench – leading to a confrontation between the opposing sets of substitutes.

The issue of bottle throwing is not unique to Wasl. Most high profile fixtures in the region see instances of projectiles being thrown at moments of tension in the game.

With matches played in high temperatures, clubs make water readily available to supporters.

At Al Ain, for example, that now takes the form of paper cups alongside large water coolers at the back of stands.

Other clubs provide small bottles or plastic cups of water. Sometimes these are thrown by irate fans, targeting players, coaching staff, or match officials.

It happened at the AFC Champions League Elite final last season, which Ahli themselves ended up winning.

High profile international fixtures between Qatar and the UAE have also been notable for it happening.

Pusic joined Ahli, the two-time Asian champions, ahead of this season after leaving Abu Dhabi club Al Jazira.

He said he does not want the passion of supporters to be diluted, and pointed out that the fixture against Wasl ended with cordial relations between the two sides.

But the Croatian-Dutch coach said players and officials should not have projectiles thrown at them.

“It could be a problem with people throwing very dangerous things on the pitch, because players and staff members [could] be hurt by these kind of things,” Pusic said.

“I feel always pity about things when that happens. The passion and the support must be always there, and that's good. I like that part as well.

“But as you can see, after the game, it was everything was nice, fine, like it should be.

“In the heat of the moment, things can happen. But it's dangerous when you throw too much. It shouldn't happen, of course. But we are professionals; we are used to a lot of things.”

The result leaves Wasl without a point after two matches in the Champions League, with many supporters voicing their frustration with coach Rui Vitoria.

Roger Ibanez, who scored the first goal for Ahli, said his side were glad to get out of Dubai with the three points.

“We knew it would be a tough game,” said the Brazil centre back, who was the player of the match.

“We played here two years ago when we also got the result, and today was again a really tough match but we got the result.

“We did a good job. Inside of the pitch, the players who started and the players who came in helped a lot.

“Now let's go home and recover because we have a tough match [in the Saudi Pro League against Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr on Thursday].”

Al Ain maintained their sparkling start to the Champions League and they sit at the top of the 16-team table.

The UAE double winners followed up their opening day thrashing of Al Nassr with a 4-1 win over Al Quwa Al Jawiya in Basra.

headline: Africa: UN Adopts Pandemic Declaration As U.S., Israel and Argentina Vote Against
summary: [Capital FM] Nairobi -- The United Nations General Assembly has adopted a political declaration calling for stronger global cooperation to prevent and respond to future pandemics, with the United States, Israel and Argentina voting against the text.
body_text:
Nairobi — The United Nations General Assembly has adopted a political declaration calling for stronger global cooperation to prevent and respond to future pandemics, with the United States, Israel and Argentina voting against the text.

The declaration received 153 votes in favour, while New Zealand and Paraguay abstained, according to the reported voting record.

Rwanda, which co-facilitated the intergovernmental negotiations alongside Armenia, welcomed the adoption, describing it as an important step towards building a more resilient global health system capable of protecting lives from future pandemics.

In a statement, Rwanda's Permanent Mission to the United Nations said the country was proud to have worked with Armenia to facilitate the negotiations.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Rwanda is proud to have co-facilitated the intergovernmental negotiations alongside Armenia and welcomes today's adoption as an important step towards building a more resilient global health architecture, better equipped to protect lives from the threat of pandemics," the Mission said.

The declaration seeks to strengthen disease surveillance, improve emergency preparedness, expand access to vaccines and treatments, and mobilize sustainable financing to help countries respond to future health emergencies.

Its adoption followed disagreements that prevented the text from being approved by consensus at a high-level meeting on September 25, pushing the matter back to the General Assembly for consideration.

The declaration acknowledges that the world remains insufficiently prepared for future pandemics despite lessons learned from COVID-19 and other health emergencies.

It calls for coordinated action guided by scientific evidence, equity, respect for human rights and international solidarity.

It recognises that countries retain primary responsibility for the health and well-being of their populations but emphasises the need for regional and international cooperation to address infectious diseases that cross national borders.

A key issue is the outstanding negotiation of the Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing Annex to the World Health Organization Pandemic Agreement, adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2025.

The proposed system is intended to facilitate the sharing of pathogen materials and genetic sequence information while ensuring that countries receive a fair share of the benefits arising from their use, including vaccines, treatments and diagnostic tools.

The Pandemic Agreement cannot be opened for signature until member states conclude negotiations on the annex, which has remained a point of disagreement among countries.

World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus welcomed the declaration, urging governments to translate their commitments into action, particularly by finalizing negotiations on the benefit-sharing framework.

"This important milestone reflects a shared commitment to equity, global solidarity and collective action to make the world safer from future pandemics," Ghebreyesus said.

"We also welcome the ambition to successfully conclude negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex."

The declaration also highlights inequalities exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic, when access to vaccines, diagnostics and treatments varied significantly between countries.

It calls for increased investment in local and regional research, manufacturing and regulatory capacity, particularly in developing countries, to improve access to affordable medical products and reduce dependence on external suppliers during health emergencies.

Member states are further urged to strengthen early-warning systems, laboratory capacity, vaccination programmes and surveillance while improving coordination between human, animal and environmental health under the One Health approach.

Financing remains another major challenge. The declaration notes that international funding arrangements are fragmented and insufficiently coordinated, highlighting an estimated annual pandemic preparedness financing gap of $15 billion.

It calls for stronger domestic investment, international assistance and better coordination among existing global health financing mechanisms.

The text also emphasizes the need to maintain essential health services during emergencies, including routine immunization, maternal and child healthcare and mental health support.

It calls for measures to address misinformation and disinformation that can undermine public confidence in health authorities.

Although the declaration establishes a political commitment to stronger pandemic preparedness, it is not legally binding.

Its implementation will depend on action by individual governments and continued international cooperation.

The General Assembly has requested a report from the UN Secretary-General, prepared in consultation with WHO and other relevant agencies, during its 83rd session to review implementation and recommend further action.

The adoption marks another step in international efforts to prepare for future health emergencies, although negotiations on pathogen access and benefit-sharing remain central to determining how global cooperation will translate into equitable access to medical countermeasures.

headline: France’s angry youth are demanding a future – not just better schools
summary: Last week, on my way through the Latin Quarter, a neighbourhood in Paris, I passed the gates of Lycee Henri-IV. It is one of the most elite schools in France, the kind of place that produces philosophers, scientists and presidents – the equivalent of getting into Harvard or Yale universities, but for high-school students. A cluster of teenagers in hoodies stood outside holding signs. They were very young and very annoyed.Today, near Boulevard Raspail, I came across more students. “If we are old enough for you to use violence against us, we’re old enough for you to listen to us,” said a 17-year-old marching through the leafy district of the French capital.Violence has not reached this wealthy neighbourhood bordering the Jardin du Luxembourg. But students at the Institut Catholique, which Pope Leo XIV visited two weeks ago, are joining in solidarity and resistance against President Emmanuel Macron’s government, calling for change.The protests began on September 21 at Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, a suburb in the Val-de-Marne, south-east of Paris. Many other schools in the Ile-de-France region quickly joined, followed by Marseille, Lille, Rennes and Strasbourg. As the days pass, the students’ demands have grown. At first, the protests were about the lack of resources in public schools: teacher shortages, classes of 35 or more, leaking buildings and long days that start at 8am and run into the evening.Now the rallying cry is about a generation that feels unheard and is inheriting a dysfunctional world it did not create.I have spent three decades watching young people take to the streets: in Cairo, in Aleppo, in Belgrade, in Ramallah, in Kyiv. Some, like in Belgrade, were successful – the students overthrew Slobodan Milosevic. My first year as a new mother in France, 2005, brought the riots triggered by the electrocution of two teenagers. They later spread across the country’s suburbs, with burning cars and real violence. LFI’s Manuel Bompard replied that the government was sliding into conspiracy theory. He is credited with being strong on foreign policy, less so on domestic issues. Meanwhile, the National Rally, the far-right party founded by the late Jean-Marie Le Pen in 1972, is on the rise. With Mr Macron close to the end of his term next year, the RN believes the Elysee is finally within reach. Jordan Bardella, its 31-year-old president, has spent years cultivating young voters even as he faces allegations, which he strongly denies, of anti-Semitic messages from the 2010s.LFI is finding a niche, particularly among the young. The teenagers did not miss the timing, and neither should we.“Most of all, we’re fed up with the high cost of living,” an 18-year-old political science student told me. body_text:
Last week, on my way through the Latin Quarter, a neighbourhood in Paris, I passed the gates of Lycee Henri-IV. It is one of the most elite schools in France, the kind of place that produces philosophers, scientists and presidents – the equivalent of getting into Harvard or Yale universities, but for high-school students. A cluster of teenagers in hoodies stood outside holding signs. They were very young and very annoyed.

Today, near Boulevard Raspail, I came across more students. “If we are old enough for you to use violence against us, we’re old enough for you to listen to us,” said a 17-year-old marching through the leafy district of the French capital.

Violence has not reached this wealthy neighbourhood bordering the Jardin du Luxembourg. But students at the Institut Catholique, which Pope Leo XIV visited two weeks ago, are joining in solidarity and resistance against President Emmanuel Macron’s government, calling for change.

French youths move to street protests after weeks of school clashes

The protests began on September 21 at Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil, a suburb in the Val-de-Marne, south-east of Paris. Many other schools in the Ile-de-France region quickly joined, followed by Marseille, Lille, Rennes and Strasbourg. As the days pass, the students’ demands have grown. At first, the protests were about the lack of resources in public schools: teacher shortages, classes of 35 or more, leaking buildings and long days that start at 8am and run into the evening.

Now the rallying cry is about a generation that feels unheard and is inheriting a dysfunctional world it did not create.

I have spent three decades watching young people take to the streets: in Cairo, in Aleppo, in Belgrade, in Ramallah, in Kyiv. Some, like in Belgrade, were successful – the students overthrew Slobodan Milosevic. My first year as a new mother in France, 2005, brought the riots triggered by the electrocution of two teenagers. They later spread across the country’s suburbs, with burning cars and real violence. The deaths of the teenagers were the trigger, but the real causes were unemployment, discrimination and broken relations with the police.

The first thing I learnt about the protests in France is that the stated grievance is rarely the whole story. What is happening now is no exception. The French are exceptional at protesting. Their protests are effective, and the protesters know they work. The country has a culture of dissent that goes back to the French Revolution, and taking to the streets is seen as a civic duty rather than a disruption. That legacy runs through May 1968, when a general strike drew in between seven and 10 million workers. It all began with a handful of students at Nanterre, whose early grievances included dormitory rules.

The grievances behind this latest movement should embarrass the government. On October 1, according to the Interior Ministry, 1,027 of France’s roughly 3,700 lycees were affected, 222 of them blockaded. Bins burned in Toulouse and Rennes. There was tear gas in Strasbourg and Lille, and a school in Nantes was firebombed. The Justice Minister, Gerald Darmanin, says about 2,000 people have been arrested since the movement began, the majority of them minors. More than 400 schools were closed the following day. The student who lives with me and studies at Institut Catholique just came home disgruntled because protesters were blocking the streets.

The government’s response is predictable: condemnation, a crisis meeting, protest bans outside closed schools. Next come the endless TV and radio shows looking for a scapegoat. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office called it a manoeuvre organised by La France Insoumise, the hard-left party. LFI’s Manuel Bompard replied that the government was sliding into conspiracy theory. Bally Bagayoko, the LFI mayor of Saint-Denis and France’s answer to New York City’s Zohran Mamdani, put himself between riot police and students and was tear-gassed for it, an amazing moment caught on camera and widely shared this week.

Remember that all this is happening in the run-up to a presidential election that fills most of us with dread. Mr Macron, whom I voted for, is on his way out. He is barred from running again next May, because Article 6 of the Constitution limits a president to two consecutive terms.

Personally, I like Mr Macron, but I’m in a minority. He is credited with being strong on foreign policy, less so on domestic issues. Meanwhile, the National Rally, the far-right party founded by the late Jean-Marie Le Pen in 1972, is on the rise. With Mr Macron close to the end of his term next year, the RN believes the Elysee is finally within reach. Jordan Bardella, its 31-year-old president, has spent years cultivating young voters even as he faces allegations, which he strongly denies, of anti-Semitic messages from the 2010s.

LFI is finding a niche, particularly among the young. It’s no coincidence that the protests came to a head in the same week the government unveiled a budget built on spending cuts and tax rises to bring down France’s deficit. The teenagers did not miss the timing, and neither should we.

“Most of all, we’re fed up with the high cost of living,” an 18-year-old political science student told me. She ran through the cost of food, cell phones, metro transport and drinks in a cafe. It’s not Manhattan or London, but salaries in France are lower.

I expect the protests to be put down fairly soon, but it will be telling to see who benefits most. Marine Le Pen, daughter of Jean-Marie, blamed LFI for stoking the unrest, and her officials have demanded damage reports and crisis meetings. RN supporters aren’t on the streets, and they don’t need to be. They are content to watch France lose control of its schools and its young. This plays nicely into the party’s education platform, which promises a “big bang of authority”: phone bans, uniforms and sanctions that reach families’ benefits.

They are standing back, watching the left fall on its face.

It remains to be seen whether the RN will win young supporters once the protests actually end. But the real story here is generational, and it began long before the protests.

In 2023, Mr Macron forced through pension reform raising the retirement age from 62 to 64. Millions marched against it, many of them young people who saw that the changes meant they would have to work longer. I remember watching French TV and being amazed how many young people were protesting against pensions. But they saw it as their future being crushed. France’s wealth sits disproportionately with older owners of property and savings. Its debt, and now its austerity, will fall on the young.

Whether French teenagers are reading budget tables and spread sheets, or not, they do understand that their classrooms are cold because a radiator has not been fixed for a year. They do understand that their teachers are exhausted and cannot give them the time or attention they need. They do understand that they are being handed a world threatened by war in Eastern Europe, with Russia’s latest hybrid war, a mounting national debt and high unemployment for recent graduates.

Mr Macron came to power in 2017 as the young man who would modernise France. It was his youth that attracted so many of us: youth and energy which the older politicians lack. But he is leaving office a middle-aged weary man with teenagers in the streets demanding a better world.

At the very least, he has to listen to them before deciding who to blame.

headline: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies at 34: Neurologist explains cerebral palsy, the condition he lived with
body_text:
Actor RJ Mitte died Monday at age 34 in Brownsville, Texas. The talent management agency that represented the actor said in a statement, “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte.” As per a report by People, his representative said that the actor who had cerebral palsy died by suicide.

Mitte played Walter White Jr. in the acclaimed American crime drama Breaking Bad, drawing on his own experience of living with cerebral palsy to bring authenticity to the character.

DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.

To learn more about neurological disorders, we spoke with an expert.

Dr Prashant Makhija, consultant neurologist at Wockhardt Hospitals, Mumbai Central, said cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of neurological conditions that affect movement, muscle control, posture, and balance. “It results from damage to, or abnormal development of, the developing brain, usually before birth, during delivery or in early infancy. The condition is non-progressive, meaning the original brain injury does not worsen over time, although its physical effects can change as a person grows older,” Dr Makhija told indianexpress.com.

The impact varies considerably from one individual to another. “Some people may have mild muscle stiffness or difficulty with coordination, while others may experience significant challenges with walking, maintaining balance, controlling their movements or performing everyday tasks. The disorders can also affect speech, swallowing, and fine motor skills, such as writing or handling small objects. In some cases, cerebral palsy may coexist with epilepsy, vision or hearing difficulties, or intellectual disabilities, but these are not present in everyone,” Dr Makhija mentioned.

The brain coordinates signals that tell our muscles when and how to move. “When the areas responsible for movement are affected early in life, these signals may not function as expected. This can lead to spasticity, where muscles become unusually stiff, or involuntary movements that make precise actions difficult.”

Over time, persistent muscle stiffness can restrict joint movement and contribute to contractures, where muscles and tendons shorten. “Some individuals may develop difficulties with posture, walking or balance. The severity depends on which parts of the brain are affected and how extensively movement control is impaired,” shared Dr Makhija.

Absolutely, affirmed Dr Makhija. “A diagnosis of cerebral palsy does not automatically mean a person will be dependent on others. Many people study, work, pursue relationships and participate actively in society. The level of independence depends on the individual’s needs, mobility and associated difficulties,” said Dr Makhija.

Physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy and appropriate medical treatment can help improve mobility, build functional skills and support daily activities. “Assistive devices, including braces, walkers and wheelchairs, may also help people move around more comfortably and independently,” Dr Makhija shared.

Early intervention is particularly valuable because it helps children develop skills and manage complications as they grow. “For adults, regular assessment can identify emerging concerns, including pain, joint stiffness and fatigue,” said Dr Makhija.

The underlying brain injury does not progressively worsen, but physical challenges can change over time. Some adults experience increased pain, fatigue, joint problems or reduced mobility because of long-standing muscle stiffness and the extra effort required for movement. Regular follow-up, exercise suited to individual abilities and timely rehabilitation can help manage these challenges and maintain quality of life.

headline: Iran accused of waging 'systematic campaign' against UK
summary: Iran is conducting a “systematic campaign” against UK interests that should be met with offensive action by security services, a politician and former British Army officer has said.Mike Martin, who served on several tours with the Intelligence Corps in Afghanistan, urged Britain's Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to take much tougher action against the regime, which has been blamed for several attacks and plots, including the recent incident at RAF Fairford, a base that had been used by US aircraft. Seven men have been arrested and released on bail while inquiries into a potential bomb plot continue, with the US withdrawing its B-1 bomber aircraft in the meantime.Two Iranians have been arrested for allegedly planning a lethal attack on Manchester’s Jewish community.Ms Mahmood announced on Monday that the government has created a specialist counter-terrorism section to tackle state threats from countries such as Iran. However, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he suspected the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the Fairford incident, Mr Martin told parliament during an urgent debate on UK national security: “I think it’s safe to say that there’s a systematic Iranian campaign on British soil.”The Liberal Democrat MP, who sits on the defence committee, said the government’s measures against Iran, which included imposing sanctions on the head of counter-espionage operations in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and summoning the Iranian ambassador in London, were “largely defensive in nature”.“Sometimes offence is the best form of defence, and I wonder whether the Home Secretary has considered that perhaps we need to increase the costs on the Iranians for their actions and considered signalling that fact to the Iranians to deter them from future activity?” Mr Martin said.Former deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden told parliament on Monday that Iran considered the UK its enemy and “smells weakness”. He said Iran had attempted attacks at bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, Akrotiri in Cyprus and Fairford in Gloucestershire.The UK introduced sanctions on the IRGC in July, after the first two incidents and a series of attacks against dissidents in previous years.Ms Mahmood said the threats from Iran have been discussed with Britain’s allies. “We will always make sure we take both collective action to deal with the threats we all face, but also make sure we are always protecting the British national interests,” she said.She said she would not provide “a running commentary on wider discussions”, but added the government “will always take every appropriate step to keep our people safe”.In her statement, Ms Mahmood outlined how the new National Security Act gives the government “powerful new tools to tackle state threats”. She announced her department was “building a specialist mission in counterterror policing to disrupt state threats and tightening security around military bases”. Britain will also establish a National Centre for Information Defence to tackle disinformation from states and will give “intelligence agencies and police stronger powers to bear down on cybercriminals”.In addressing the threat posed by states such as Iran, she said: “Make no mistake: our police and security services are on permanent watch.”Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France ​and Germany, issued a statement on Monday condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts ‌of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber attacks, and other ⁠hybrid activities against us and our partners”.“The UK has also ​concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks ​and proxy actors,” ‌the statement added.Mr Burnham said: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity if Iran and the IRGC do us harm.”
body_text:
Iran is conducting a “systematic campaign” against UK interests that should be met with offensive action by security services, a politician and former British Army officer has said.

Mike Martin, who served on several tours with the Intelligence Corps in Afghanistan, urged Britain's Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to take much tougher action against the regime, which has been blamed for several attacks and plots, including the recent incident at RAF Fairford, a base that had been used by US aircraft. Seven men have been arrested and released on bail while inquiries into a potential bomb plot continue, with the US withdrawing its B-1 bomber aircraft in the meantime.

Two Iranians have been arrested for allegedly planning a lethal attack on Manchester’s Jewish community.

Diplomacy or war? US-Iran deadlock reaches fork in the road

Ms Mahmood announced on Monday that the government has created a specialist counter-terrorism section to tackle state threats from countries such as Iran.

However, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he suspected the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps was behind the Fairford incident, Mr Martin told parliament during an urgent debate on UK national security: “I think it’s safe to say that there’s a systematic Iranian campaign on British soil.”

The Liberal Democrat MP, who sits on the defence committee, said the government’s measures against Iran, which included imposing sanctions on the head of counter-espionage operations in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and summoning the Iranian ambassador in London, were “largely defensive in nature”.

“Sometimes offence is the best form of defence, and I wonder whether the Home Secretary has considered that perhaps we need to increase the costs on the Iranians for their actions and considered signalling that fact to the Iranians to deter them from future activity?” Mr Martin said.

Former deputy prime minister Oliver Dowden told parliament on Monday that Iran considered the UK its enemy and “smells weakness”. He said Iran had attempted attacks at bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean, Akrotiri in Cyprus and Fairford in Gloucestershire.

The UK introduced sanctions on the IRGC in July, after the first two incidents and a series of attacks against dissidents in previous years.

Ms Mahmood said the threats from Iran have been discussed with Britain’s allies. “We will always make sure we take both collective action to deal with the threats we all face, but also make sure we are always protecting the British national interests,” she said.

She said she would not provide “a running commentary on wider discussions”, but added the government “will always take every appropriate step to keep our people safe”.

In her statement, Ms Mahmood outlined how the new National Security Act gives the government “powerful new tools to tackle state threats”. She announced her department was “building a specialist mission in counterterror policing to disrupt state threats and tightening security around military bases”.

Britain will also establish a National Centre for Information Defence to tackle disinformation from states and will give “intelligence agencies and police stronger powers to bear down on cybercriminals”.

In addressing the threat posed by states such as Iran, she said: “Make no mistake: our police and security services are on permanent watch.”

Foreign ministries from almost 30 countries including the US, Canada, France ​and Germany, issued a statement on Monday condemning “Iran’s use of violent attacks, including the acts ‌of lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber attacks, and other ⁠hybrid activities against us and our partners”.

“The UK has also ​concluded this event demonstrates the IRGC’s continued willingness to project hostile activity beyond its borders through covert networks ​and proxy actors,” ‌the statement added.

Mr Burnham said: “We will not tolerate these threats on our soil. We will crack down on Iran’s use of criminal networks using our full range of powers to target them and their funding streams. And we will bring further sanctions to restrict the capacity if Iran and the IRGC do us harm.”

headline: North Korea tests technically upgraded ballistic missile component — news agency
summary: According to KCNA, the modernization is expected to lead to significant improvements in the power and accuracy of North Korea’s offensive weapons systems
body_text:
PYONGYANG, October 13. /TASS/. North Korea’s Missile Administration conducted a test launch of a tactical ballistic missile to verify a technically upgraded key component, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) reported.

"The technical upgrade of the key component, confirmed today, is a major success," the DPRK Missile Administration stated.

According to KCNA, the modernization is expected to lead to significant improvements in the power and accuracy of North Korea’s offensive weapons systems. The agency did not specify which component of the missile was upgraded.

The test took place on October 12 as part of regular work by the DPRK Missile Administration and its subordinate research institutes aimed at improving weapons systems.

US President Donald Trump could cut off Ukraine’s access to US intelligence or pressure Elon Musk to disable SpaceX’s Starlink internet service for Kiev, Politico Europe reported.

body_text:
Towards the end of summer in the emerald-green tea estate of Margaret's Hope, the weather cannot make up its mind. One moment, drizzle comes soft and steady through the tall pine trees. Next, mist rolls in and swallows everything as the hills play hide-and-seek with the sky.

A steep tarmac road drops from the main hill cart path through rows of tea bushes. At the bottom, about 11 kilometres north of Kurseong town, a pond sits hidden in the mist. Sedge, a dense waterside plant common to Himalayan wetlands, stands along its edges like a barricade.

In the hill villages of Darjeeling, India, these ponds have long been more than bodies of water.

Finest Darjeeling tea is losing its steam due to climate change

“Local communities have been protecting this species long before any funding or international recognition,” says Barkha Subba, a Darjeeling conservation biologist. “These wetlands are deeply intertwined with local culture and religious beliefs.”

What they have been protecting is one of India's last remaining breeding grounds for the Himalayan salamander, known locally as gora or pani chepara in Nepali. They are sometimes described as a tiny dragon that swims quietly in mountain ponds. Growing up to 20 centimetres long, they are also called crocodile newts, for the ridges along their dark bodies.

Scientifically known as Tylototriton verrucosus, it is listed as near threatened on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List of Threatened Species, with a declining population trend.

Ramesh Rai, 55, moves around the pond in a white cotton T-shirt and rubber gumboots, parting the sedge and scanning the water. He is searching for eggs tucked into submerged vegetation.

Ramesh is the munshi of Margaret's Hope tea estate, head of the workforce that keeps the 160-year-old site running. His grandfather and father worked this land. He was born and grew up here and has known the gora since childhood.

“There is a place called Gorabari not far from here,” he says, pointing at the tea bushes above the pond. “In the past the gora used to be found throughout the garden fields up there. The place was named after them. That is how many there once were.” Gorabari translates as the garden of the salamander.

In 1993, Ramesh noticed the gora losing ground. While planting tea, he saw ponds shrinking, eggs dying and habitat being consumed by human activity and a shifting climate. He began protecting the salamanders without formal conservation training. In 2005, he wrote about the vanishing creature in the first issue of Sahityashri, a Nepali literary journal printed within the estate.

MK Rai, 42, farms land around the estate. “In June, July, August, you would see them on the road,” he says. “We called them baby dragons then. We did not know their value.”

Now tourists arrive with cameras and picnics, often leaving plastic on the bank. The two men have helped build the nursery pond with estate management and join clean-up campaigns run with Subba's organisation, the Federation of Societies for Environmental Protection, or Fosep.

“Saving the salamander,” MK says, “means saving our culture, too.”

Subba grew up in these hills, hearing stories of tigers, forests and mountain spirits from her grandmother. She studied biological sciences, completed a doctorate on high-elevation amphibians and returned to Darjeeling to work on conservation.

In 2014, researcher Kartik Vasudevan of CCMB Hyderabad mapped 38 salamander habitats across Darjeeling. When Subba returned to check them, most were gone or severely degraded. Wetlands had dried up and invasive species had moved in.

“Climate change is no longer a myth or a mystery,” she tells The National. “It is a fact we are seeing in everyday life. And the salamander is one of the clearest signs of what is being lost.”

A peer-reviewed study published in Atmosphere in December 2024, analysing Darjeeling's temperature and rainfall records between 1991 and 2023, found that total rainfall has increased while maximum temperatures have also risen significantly. The rains are coming harder and shorter, not steadier.

The salamander's entire life cycle is tied to the monsoon. With the first rain, it emerges from hibernation and returns to the same pond in which it was born; behaviour scientists call this site fidelity. Destroy that wetland and the species has nowhere else to go.

At Margaret's Hope, 1,500 metres above sea level, salamanders mate and lay 60 to 90 eggs in submerged vegetation. But if the rain stops after two days, the shallow pool dries quickly and the clutch desiccates before hatching.

“They lay eggs thinking there will be rain for another month,” Subba says. “Then suddenly the rain stops, the sun comes out, the pool dries up. The whole generation dies off.”

The threat to the species doesn't stop there.

Carp and guppies, which have been released into the main pond by local religious communities, eat eggs and larvae. Invasive phragmites grass has choked the banks. But, above all, it is climate change.

In a bid to help the species, Ramesh, with members of the community and estate management, built a 1.8m-by-3m nursery pond with a vegetated island close to the main pond. Every March and April, he searches for clutches and moves them away from fish, herons and snakes, monitoring them for 12 to 15 days until they hatch. He is not paid for this work.

Subba grew up in these hills and has been coming to Margaret's Hope since childhood. However, 2020 was the first time she came as a scientist, specifically to map the district's salamander habitats. What she found when she arrived surprised her. The community had already been doing the work without her. Around 2015, when the pond had nearly dried up and invasive grass had taken over, residents and estate management cleared it by hand. The salamanders returned.

When Subba met Ramesh, she found something harder to teach than biology: decades of watching. “For him,” she says, “the salamanders are like his children.”

Their collaboration now has formal backing. This year Subba received the 2026 Whitley Award, a prestigious British conservation prize, presented by Princess Anne at London's Royal Geographical Society. She was recognised for protecting seven critical breeding sites across Darjeeling. Margaret's Hope is one of them.

Subba plans to extend the work to Nepal and Bhutan, creating a transboundary framework for a species that knows no borders. An estimated 5,000 individuals survive in the wild, with about 80 per cent living outside protected areas on tea garden land and private holdings.

As the mist thickens again, Ramesh moves on, steady and unhurried. What began in 1993 as one man's effort to protect a disappearing species has grown into a wider conservation movement, bringing together local knowledge, community action and scientific expertise. But at the water's edge, his work remains much the same: watching, waiting and protecting what is left.
