headline: IMF projects average oil price at $95.74 per barrel in 2026 and $87.39 in 2027
summary: The average price of oil in US dollars a barrel was $67.74 in 2025
body_text:
BANGKOK, October 13. /TASS/. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts that the average price of a barrel of oil will be $95.74 this year and $87.39 in 2027. This forecast is included in the organization's latest World Economic Outlook report, released in Bangkok, where the governing bodies of the IMF and the World Bank are holding their off-site meetings.

"The average price of oil in US dollars a barrel was $67.74 in 2025; the assumed price, based on futures markets, is $95.74 in 2026 and $87.39 in 2027," the report says.

According to the authors, oil prices are projected to rise by 41.6% this year and fall by 8.7% next year. These figures represent upward revisions of 9.5 and 3.1 percentage points, respectively, compared to the Fund's previous World Economic Outlook report released in July.

Fund experts emphasize that the forecast factors in an expected recovery of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to pre-war levels between March and October 2027. However, they note that if the war between the US and Iran is not resolved by June 2027, shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait would be effectively paralyzed and damage to oil infrastructure would escalate. Consequently, a resumption of oil supplies should not be expected before the end of 2027. In such a scenario, the experts forecast that oil prices could climb to $130 per barrel between the fourth quarter of this year and the first quarter of 2027, returning to baseline scenario levels only by the fourth quarter of next year.

Natural gas prices are estimated by Fund experts to rise by 48% this year compared to 2025 levels. Fertilizer prices are projected to increase by an average of 10% in 2026 compared to the previous year.

body_text:
Egypt and Sudan say they are investigating the deadly shooting of two Egyptians in Khartoum, an attack that followed the weekend death of scores of Sudanese goldminers in an air strike near the Egyptian border.

Police in Sudan said they have apprehended the gunman whom they identified as Ibrahim Abdullah Adam, 23. They say he has admitted carrying out the attack, in which a third Egyptian was wounded, to avenge the death of his brother in Saturday's air strike.

They said all three Egyptians were lorry drivers. A Sudanese police officer was also wounded in an exchange of fire before the gunman's arrest.

UN Security Council extends arms embargo in Sudan's Darfur as US pushes for nationwide ban

“The investigation is continuing to establish the circumstances of the incident and its motives,” police said late on Monday night. “We will firmly deal with the matter under the law.”

Neither Egypt nor Sudan publicly have said who was behind the air strike. The Egyptian military issued a statement saying troops and police were continuing to counter “illegal” gold prospecting in the country's Eastern Desert.

It said it had dropped flyers on what it called criminal elements, warning them they must stop illegal mining “so that full sovereignty is safeguarded inside the Egyptian state's borders”.

Egypt's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, said it was closely following the “regrettable” shooting in Khartoum. It said Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Sudanese counterpart in the military-backed government, Mohieldin Salem, spoke on the phone on Monday evening.

It added that the ministers “emphasised the mutual respect that binds the two nations, including respect for each other's sovereignty, and the safety and integrity of their territories and borders”.

The air strike near the border was initially reported by human rights and watchdog groups in Sudan, including the Emergency Lawyers, the civilian-led Somoud alliance and the Sudan Doctors' Network.

They gave widely varying death toll figures, from 13 to 72. Some media reports in Sudan put the figure as high as 200.

“We reject the targeting of civilians and putting their lives at risk, which cannot be justified on security grounds,” Somoud said. “The leadership of the relevant authorities appointed by the armed forces bears the responsibility for what happens in areas under their control.”

Sudan's military-led Sovereign Council said the air strike took place in the border region with Egypt. “The leadership in the two brotherly nations have been in contact since immediately after the incident took place to guarantee the protection of lives and safeguarding relations between the two peoples, find out the circumstances of the incident and give public opinion ownership of the facts,” it said.

Images ​and video shared online, which The National has been unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn across rubble, others wrapped in green sheets and angry survivors, mostly men in their 20s or 30s.

There has been an influx of gold prospectors in northern Sudan in recent years as the civil war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has hit the economy hard, driving hundreds of thousands to seek alternative sources of income.

Egypt's military said in June it was engaged in a large-scale operation in the south of the country to tackle gangs involved in drugs and arms trafficking, as well as illegal gold prospecting. It said 87 Egyptians and 136 foreigners had been arrested.

Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign parties seeking quick profit. In several ways, the current gold rush is a by-product of most of the country’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011.

The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold in Sudan. Some estimates put the number of artisanal miners involved at about two million.

Official figures place Sudanese government revenue from gold exports at about $2 billion but experts say smuggling and the use of gold outside official channels account for far more.

Last year, Sudan’s gold production was about 70 tonnes but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated primitive localised refineries.

Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda

headline: China has exclusive economic zone and continental shelf in waters east of the Taiwan island: FM
summary: China has exclusive economic zone and continental shelf in waters east of the Taiwan island, and it is fully within China's sovereign rights and jurisdiction, therefore legitimate, lawful and beyond reproach, for China to carry out activities in these waters, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning said on Monday.
body_text:
(ECNA) -- China has exclusive economic zone and continental shelf in waters east of the Taiwan island, and it is fully within China's sovereign rights and jurisdiction, therefore legitimate, lawful and beyond reproach, for China to carry out activities in these waters, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning said on Monday.

Mao made the remarks when asked about the U.S. State Department's description of China's maritime activities off Taiwan's east coast as "deeply destabilizing."

Mao said that the party that instigates troubles and disrupts stability in this part of waters has never been the Chinese side.

Mao said that the Taiwan question is China's internal affair that brooks no external interference. "The U.S. needs to abide by the one-China principle and the three China-U.S. joint communiqués, handle the Taiwan question prudently, and take concrete actions to uphold the overall China-U.S. relations and peace and stability in the region," he said.

body_text:
Saudi Arabia has vowed to remain strong as the coalition it leads against Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels announced the interception of missiles fired at Riyadh and the south of the kingdom on Monday.

“We strongly condemn the Houthi terrorist attacks targeting civilians and civilian facilities in the kingdom," Minister of Media Salman Al Dosary said.

At a government media conference in Riyadh, he praised security forces and the military, saying the kingdom would "remain strong and united" behind its leadership and continue its development efforts despite the attacks.

Timeline: Houthis escalate attacks on Saudi airports

Early on Tuesday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Khamis Mushait in the south-west of the kingdom. Coalition spokesman Col Turki Al Malki announced the interception in a post on X.

The statement did not say where the missiles were launched from or whether the incident caused any casualties or damage. The Houthis had claimed a "direct hit" in a ballistic missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Monday night.

The Iran-backed group's military spokesman, Yahya Saree, repeated its warning "to all international airlines, experts, employees, workers and passengers from all countries of the world against flights to Saudi airports, as they are unsafe, with the exception of the airports and airspace of the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah".

He also claimed a drone launched at the Khamis Mushait airbase resulted in a "direct hit".

Saudi authorities extended the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport until midnight on October 17 after an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and injured more than 300. An attack on Sunday killed one person.

Meanwhile, pro-government forces and the Houthis are battling for control of the key city of Taiz. Rights groups have raised the alarm on the humanitarian situation inside the city, where people are cut off from food, water, medical and energy supplies amid what some organisations described as a "siege".

"Within five days, the city lost its main supply route for goods and commodities: Taiz–Al-Turbah–Lahj–Aden, following the Houthi group’s takeover of areas west and south of Taiz," the Studies and Economic Media Centre in Yemen said in a report this week. The government also closed the eastern route used by civilians for security reasons, it added.

The International Organisation for Migration estimates that more than 216,000 people have been displaced since the escalations in Yemen began in August. At least 172,000 of them are from Taiz.

The UN said it was providing assistance to those in need but that reaching them was proving difficult, especially with key roads closed. That has disrupted "civilian movement, commercial supplies and humanitarian access", the UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said in a briefing on Monday.

At least 54 civilians have been killed, half of them children, the agency said. "A further 171 civilians have been injured, including 107 women and children," it added.

headline: IMF upgrades 2026 global growth forecast but war and debt threaten outlook
summary: The IMF has raised its 2026 global growth forecast slightly to 3.1%, citing the resilience of advanced economies despite rising energy prices caused by the Iran war. But it warned that poorer countries that are not benefiting from the AI boom remain particularly vulnerable to energy shocks, economic uncertainty and mounting debt.
body_text:
The IMF has raised its 2026 global growth forecast slightly to 3.1%, citing the resilience of advanced economies despite rising energy prices caused by the Iran war. But it warned that poorer countries that are not benefiting from the AI boom remain particularly vulnerable to energy shocks, economic uncertainty and mounting debt.

Issued on: 13/10/2026 - 05:57Modified: 13/10/2026 - 11:43

The International Monetary Fund on Tuesday forecast global growth in 2026 would slow less than previously expected because of advanced economies' "resilience" in the face of war-fuelled energy prices, but warned low-income countries remained vulnerable to the supply shock.

In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organisation's Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent, compared with 3.5 percent growth in 2025.

It warned that while many advanced economies have been buoyed by rising investment in artificial intelligence (AI) technology, poorer countries that are not benefiting from that boom face stark choices as they deal with high energy prices caused by the Iran war.

"The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is under strain, with risks tilted to the downside," Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF's chief economist, told journalists in Bangkok.

Watch moreCan AI play a role in reducing inequality?

With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing – a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock.

"What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of inflation, and that involves food security, that involves energy security ... while also keeping in mind the medium-term stability," said Deniz Igan, chief of the IMF's World Economic Studies division.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel discussion: "We have to recognise that the world that used to value only one thing, economic efficiency ... now is a world in which security considerations have to be factored in."

The United States' war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran's retaliation.

Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95 percent above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.

On Monday night, blasts resounded across Saudi Arabia's capital as the war's impact widens into that country, with Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi forces hitting oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs.

Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a "bifurcated outlook" in its WEO report.

The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a "fragmented" world economy.

"Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest," it said.

"At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions."

Responding to AFP, Tenreyro said AI had been a major factor driving the world economy, accounting for almost half of the increase in global trade from 2023 to 2025.

The IMF's split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.

The Middle East and Central Asia region – exposed directly to the Iran war – is expected to suffer a 0.3 percent contraction in 2026.

Saudi Arabia's is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3 percent – representing a 5.0 percentage point cut in the Fund's forecast.

The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.

Read moreHow is the EU responding to record fuel prices?

In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.

The world's advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1 percent in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain such as Taiwan and South Korea posting significantly higher figures.

Growth in China, the world's second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, mainly because of weak domestic demand.

Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7 percent in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies.

Tenreyro warned that urgent action was required by all countries in the face of downside risks, and called on governments to only use temporary, targeted measures to help ease the burden on the public of high energy and other costs.

In lockstep, "monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability", she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.

Georgieva told audience members: "Macroeconomic and financial stability is your first line of defence. It is a source of security."

body_text:
WARSAW, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Police have detained two more people in connection with a fire at a Starlink station in Poland last month, private broadcaster RMF FM reported on Tuesday, citing anonymous sources, bringing the total to four.

Earlier on Tuesday RMF said that German police had detained a woman in Berlin in the case. It then reported the detention of a fourth person, without providing any further details.

Poland said on Monday that two Turkish men had been detained in Germany on suspicion of being responsible for the blaze.

The blaze at the Starlink station in central Poland in September engulfed its power system and backup generator. Poland said at the time it believed the fire was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military, and blamed Russia.

RMF reported that the detained woman in Germany may have acted as a driver and that Polish prosecutors would now assess the extent of her involvement and decide whether there were grounds to seek her extradition.

It did not give the woman's nationality or any other details.

The German Interior Ministry was not immediately available for comment. Poland's National Prosecutor's Office also had no immediate comment.

A spokesperson for Germany's Federal Criminal Police said the agency coordinated the exchange of information between Polish and German authorities in connection with the detention of three individuals.

Officials from several European Union countries have warned for months that Russia has been mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine.

Moscow says such accusations are baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.

(Reporting by Alan Charlish, Marek Strzelecki and Pawel Florkiewicz in Warsaw, Kirsti Knolle in BerlinEditing by Gareth Jones)

The fourth and final piece of the deal would be a ceasefire along the existing front line.

According to The Washington Post, "the diplomatic push" for the plan came at a recent meeting in Florida involving US, European and Ukrainian negotiators.

headline: Saudi Arabia faces economic contraction as war woes mount
summary: Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, faces a major economic contraction this year, the IMF said Tuesday, as deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis squeeze a country already suffering from the Middle East war. Saudi Arabia's GDP is expected to shrink by 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said in its latest World Economic Outlook report, predicting a regional drop over Iran's blockading of the Strait of Hormuz.
body_text:
Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, faces a major economic contraction this year, the IMF said Tuesday, as deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis squeeze a country already suffering from the Middle East war.

Saudi Arabia's GDP is expected to shrink by 3.3 percent, the International Monetary Fund said in its latest World Economic Outlook report, predicting a regional drop over Iran's blockading of the Strait of Hormuz.

The report was compiled before 13 people were killed on Saturday -- the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade -- during a series of lethal Houthi strikes on Riyadh's international airport.

The kingdom was already facing headwinds from Iran's chokehold on Hormuz, a vital shipping route for oil and gas, since the start of the Middle East war in February, when the US and Israel attacked Iran.

But the restart in July of Yemen's frozen civil war, pitting a Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally-recognised government against the rival Houthis, has further roiled the kingdom and brought the fight to its own soil.

Houthi attacks have targeted Saudi oil facilities, oil tankers in the Red Sea -- Saudi Arabia's alternative export route -- and transport hubs including airports.

Blasts resounded over the Saudi capital again late on Monday, with the Saudi coalition saying it had intercepted a Houthi missile and the group announcing it had once again targeted the airport, whose operations remain suspended.

In the evening, mobile phones received a government alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat", before the announcement of the interception.

Saturday's airport attack prompted US President Donald Trump to say he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis, after having reportedly rebuffed previous requests for help from the kingdom.

The Houthis warned the US against intervention, with political bureau member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti telling AFP they would target American interests in the region.

Bukhaiti said the purpose of the campaign against Saudi targets was to send a message to the crown prince "that he can no longer wage aggression against Yemen from a safe position".

Riyadh's coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, in a long-running civil war that has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.

In its latest global report, the IMF said the regional economy was projected to contract by 0.3 percent this year, compared to its projected 1.9 percent growth six months ago.

It cited "a longer closure of the Strait of Hormuz, compared with the baseline assumptions in the April" report, predicting a major rebound in 2027 based on the expected reopening of the waterway.

Since the Middle East war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, Tehran has sought to impose its control over the Strait of Hormuz, repeatedly attacking ships that transit without its authorisation.

The US has imposed its own counter-blockade on Iranian ports, and has escorted friendly ships through the waterway in increasing numbers.

The fund noted that Saudi Arabia is among the least affected exporters in the region, pointing to "an economy with more diversified export routes".

Saudi Arabia has made use of its East-West oil pipeline to bypass the Hormuz strait and send crude to its Red Sea coast.

However, the pipeline was temporarily shut in September after it was hit by strikes blamed on Iran-backed groups in Iraq.

body_text:
Qatar's revenue fell 42 per cent in the first half of this year, as exports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) dropped due to the impact of the Iran war, Emir Sheikh Tamim said during a Shura Council meeting.

LNG exports from Qatar, the world’s second-largest supplier before the conflict, has fallen sharply due to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz as well attacks on its Ras Laffan complex.

“The crisis naturally had an adverse impact on public finances, with total revenues falling by 42 per cent during the first half of the year, while public expenditures decreased by 14 per cent – all without compromising essential services or development priorities,” Sheikh Tamim said.

Dubai inflation climbs as Iran war pushes up fuel cost

“We decided against curtailing essential services and chose not to alter development priorities, aiming to sustain the economic momentum Qatar is experiencing.”

Measures taken before the crisis, such as strengthening reserves, reducing public debt, adopting conservative oil-price assumptions in the budget and developing non-oil revenue, helped Qatar absorb the economic fallout, he said.

About 17 per cent of Qatar’s LNG capacity is offline after Iranian strikes damaged two of its 14 export trains, removing 12.8 million tonnes a year from the market.

QatarEnergy has said repairs will take three to five years, meaning even a safe reopening of Hormuz would restore access to only part of Qatar’s prewar supply. Gas prices have soared globally due to the disruption.

Disruption to Qatar's energy sector affects markets and consumers worldwide, the Emir said on Tuesday.

“The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, along with direct damage to some energy facilities in Ras Laffan Industrial City, has disrupted a significant portion of the country's exports,” he said.

However, the economic fallout is concentrated mainly in the energy sector, while non-hydrocarbon industries continue to grow, accounting for about 80 per cent of real gross domestic product, he added.

“This reflects the national economy's ability to withstand and continue growing under exceptional and complex circumstances,” Sheikh Tamim said.

Economies across the Gulf are projected to contract by an average of 4.3 per cent for 2026, down 5.7 percentage points from April, driven by lower export volumes due to the Strait of Hormuz's closure, leading to significant losses in output and government revenue, the World Bank said last week.

Qatar's economy is estimated to be hit the hardest among all countries in the region, facing a 20.9 per cent contraction this year, compared to 1.8 per cent growth in 2025, the World Bank said.

The estimate would represent the country's weakest economic performance in five decades, after its average monthly gas production fell by about 67 per cent between March and July due to damage sustained at its sites.

Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund in its update this week said it expects Qatar's economy to contract by 15.6 per cent this year, before rebounding to growth of 18.8 per cent in 2027.

However, Qatar will emerge from the regional crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes, Sheikh Tamim said.

“We have a portfolio of projects and investment opportunities valued at approximately 221 billion riyals [$60.7 billion] over the next five years,” he said.

Planned investments will cover infrastructure, public-private partnerships and private-sector projects in real estate and hospitality, he added.

Sheikh Tamim said Qatar had faced three simultaneous responsibilities during the crisis: protecting its sovereignty, fulfilling its role in global energy and economic security, and keeping diplomatic channels open.

“Our strategy for shouldering these responsibilities consisted of four main elements: first, firmly defending the homeland without being drawn into war; second, maintaining services, supply chains and economic activity; third, contributing to efforts to secure a ceasefire and open waterways; and fourth, encouraging negotiations and seeking opportunities to return to talks to reach peaceful solutions to the conflict,” he said.

Sheikh Tamim said the goal is “not merely to return to the pre-crisis status quo, but to use recovery as a springboard to accelerate economic diversification and strengthen national capabilities”.

“God willing, Qatar will emerge from this crisis more resilient and better adapted to global changes,” he added.

headline: Russia’s Diana Shnaider advances to second round of Wuhan tennis tournament
summary: In the next round, she will face the winner of the match between Yulia Putintseva of Kazakhstan and Zeynep Sonmez of Turkey
body_text:
BEIJING, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Diana Shnaider has defeated Britain’s Katie Boulter in the first round of a Women's Tennis Association (WTA) tournament in Wuhan, China.

The 11th-seeded Shnaider won 6-3, 6-1. In the next round, she will face the winner of the match between Yulia Putintseva of Kazakhstan and Zeynep Sonmez of Turkey, both of whom made the main draw through qualification.

Shnaider, 22, is currently 13th in the WTA rankings. She has won five WTA singles titles, with her semifinal appearance at the 2026 French Open being her best result to date at majors.

The Wuhan Open, part of the WTA 1000 series of tournaments, is played on hard courts and offers a total purse of $4 mln. Coco Gauff of the United States won the tournament last year.

body_text:
Dubai's inflation rate eased slightly in September, even as rising fuel costs pushed petrol pump prices up.

Inflation stood at 5.03 per cent, down from the 5.54 per cent annualised rise recorded in August and the 5.7 per cent peak for this year reached in June.

The figures were released by the Dubai Data and Statistics Establishment on Tuesday.

UAE and Saudi non-oil sectors maintain growth trajectory despite war

Meanwhile, Dubai’s General Monthly Consumer Price Index decreased by 0.05 per cent month-on-month in September on falling airfares and cheaper holiday packages.

Airfares on a monthly basis fell by 23.44 per cent and holiday packages dropped 12.47 per cent from the August level.

However, on an annual basis, the transport division was the biggest contributor to the rise in consumer prices in September, climbing 14.7 per cent.

The increase in transport charges was driven by a 37.52 per cent rise in the cost of fuels and lubricants for personal transport, as well as a 13.48 per cent rise in passenger transport by air, according to the latest government data.

The transport segment, which accounts for 9 per cent of Dubai’s Consumer Price Index basket, has been the main driver of inflation in the emirate over the past several months amid a rise in prices petrol prices.

The UAE lifted fuel subsidies in 2015 and prices are evaluated on a monthly basis, based on movements in global markets. Petrol prices in the Emirates rose for a third consecutive month for October as prices in global oil markets remain elevated amid escalating geopolitical concerns in the Middle East.

Global crude prices, which surged by nearly 109 per cent during the peak of the war, now in its eighth month, are still more than 70 per cent higher on concerns of a possible resumption in fighting between the US and Iran.

Brent crude, which hovered around the $110 per barrel mark in September, has largely remained above $100 over the past few weeks.

The West Texas Intermediate benchmark passed $105 a barrel in September as the Strait of Hormuz remained a flashpoint. Increasing attacks on Saudi infrastructure in the Red Sea by the Houthi rebels in Yemen have added another layer of risk to energy supplies from the region.

Despite economic headwinds, Dubai's economy has largely skirted the deeper slump experienced by some neighbours.

Non-oil private sector business activity in the emirate, which is one of the largest business and tourism centres in the Middle East, also maintained a sharp growth trajectory.

The Purchasing Managers' Index stood at 54.5 in September, up from 54.1 in August, indicating a “solid improvement” in Dubai, as the pace of growth was fastest in 2026, S&P Global Markets Intelligence said earlier this month.

The boost to the emirate’s non-oil economic activity was largely driven by a “sharp and accelerated increase in output” as new orders also rose markedly and employment in the emirate rose, according to the PMI survey data.

The tourism and retail sectors in the emirate have also bounced back from the initial shock of the war. Property, among the top contributors to the emirate’s economy, has also held up relatively well.

The food and drinks category increased by an annualised 8.05 per cent last month, while housing, water, electricity, gas and domestic fuel rose by almost 6.23 per cent, “as a result of the growth of the average residential rental prices in most areas of the emirate during September”, the latest government data shows.

headline: FSB detains Russian woman over Ukraine-backed plot to attack military airfield
summary: According to Russia’s Federal Security Service, the woman retrieved nine drones equipped with explosive devices, along with drone control equipment, from previously established caches and took them to a rented garage
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained a Russian woman suspected of preparing a drone attack on a military airfield on orders from the Security Service of Ukraine, the FSB said in a statement.

"The Federal Security Service in the Voronezh Region has foiled a large-scale act of sabotage and terrorism orchestrated by the Security Service of Ukraine, which planned to attack the Russian Defense Ministry’s Baltimor military airfield with short-range drones," the statement reads.

Law enforcement operations made it possible to expose and disrupt the illegal activities of a Russian woman who had been recruited by a Ukrainian intelligence officer during a trip to Ukraine in 2022. "Acting on instructions from her handler, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage, where she planned to assemble and launch drones meant to be used to destroy infrastructure and aircraft, as well as kill military airfield staff," the FSB said. The drones were supposed to be operated remotely by personnel based in Ukraine.

According to the FSB, the woman retrieved nine drones equipped with explosive devices, along with drone control equipment, from previously established caches and took them to the garage. Each drone carried 500 grams of foreign-made explosives.

"FSB officers responded immediately after receiving intel, promptly detaining the accomplice of Ukrainian intelligence agencies and preventing the act of sabotage before it was carried out, thus containing the potential consequences of the Kiev regime’s actions against the military facility," the agency stressed.

The suspect has been taken into custody. "Efforts are ongoing to establish all circumstances of the crime and identify all those involved," the FSB added.

headline: Africa: Economics Nobel - How This Year's Winners Helped to Smooth the Cycle of Economic Peaks and Troughs
summary: [The Conversation Africa] The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to the American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. The prize was awarded in recognition of their development of macroeconomic models that helped to reduce the length and depth of economic downturns.
body_text:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to the American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. The prize was awarded in recognition of their development of macroeconomic models that helped to reduce the length and depth of economic downturns.

According to the Academy, the economists' work in macroeconomic modelling has given policymakers additional tools to smooth out the economic cycle. As well as reducing the severity of downturns, their work also helped to cool the potentially negative impacts of economic booms.

Economies are known to follow cycles of downturns and upturns - and economists have long sought to find ways to tame these. More than a century ago, British economist John Maynard Keynes developed an approach to managing the economy that came to be known as Keynesianism.

Before this, the classical "laissez-faire" approach dominated. According to this doctrine, in an economic downturn, markets would eventually clear and the economy would rebound. Any attempt by government to directly influence the economy would not work and could even make things worse.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Keynes disagreed with the classical view. He believed that economies could get locked into a downward spiral that would deepen recessions and lead to economic depression. Instead, he argued that governments could actively use the levers of monetary policy (adjusting interest rates) and fiscal policy (lowering taxes and government spending) to improve the health of the economy.

In the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash, the US was in a deep economic depression. Franklin D. Roosevelt won a landslide presidential victory in 1932 and his "New Deal" approach to economic policy was similar to what Keynes advocated. The US economy recovered, and the Keynesian school would dominate policymaking in many advanced economies after the second world war.

But the oil crisis of the 1970s changed everything. The Keynesian approach was ineffective in dealing with low growth, spiralling inflation and high unemployment. Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher won elections in the US and UK with promises of "smaller government" economic policy, including lower taxes, privatisation and deregulation. Keynesianism needed a rebuild.

Decisions of consumers and businesses

Hall and Woodford became part of the "New Keynesian" school that emerged in the 1980s. Their approach was to build models that looked at decisions made by millions of individuals and businesses rather than just considering macroeconomic variables like production, inflation, consumption and unemployment.

Hall, of Stanford University in California, is an expert in consumption theory. According to his "random walk hypothesis", decisions made by households on whether to spend or save were directly influenced by their expectations about future income and economic conditions. In other words, they were not just based on their current financial conditions. As consumption makes up around 70% of GDP in advanced economies, these insights were important.

Woodford, of Columbia University in New York, is an expert in supply-side macroeconomics, specifically the role that expectations play in price-setting and inflation. In his 2003 book, Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, he proved that a central bank could influence economic activity by managing the public's expectations about what might happen to interest rates in future.

Up until the 1990s, central bank policymaking was secretive and could sometimes take markets by surprise. Hall and Woodford's insights changed this. In the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, the central banks of most major advanced economies adopted an approach known as "forward guidance".

This policy saw central bank governors provide greater transparency about their monetary policy intentions. Forward guidance policy announcements provide a clear assessment of both the economic outlook and how this might affect inflation. They also set out how central bank policy could react to these assessments.

As with most policy approaches, forward guidance has both advocates and critics. Research from the European Central Bank shows that clear communication from central banks reduces short-term interest rate volatility. There is also some evidence that after the 2008 financial crisis, expectations that inflation would remain low helped to keep interest rates down. This probably encouraged spending and investment, which aided economic recovery.

But critics believe that forward guidance has no impact on long-term interest rates and say it is debatable if it has any impact on short-term rates. They also argue that setting expectations about interest rates can strip credibility from central banks. This could happen if economic policy needs to be altered to deal with sudden shocks, for example.

The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine are driving up energy prices and inflation expectations. The forward guidance from many central bankers is pointing to higher inflation and perhaps the need for higher interest rates.

Anyone coming off a fixed-rate mortgage might be sceptical of the idea that policy tools can lower short-term interest rate expectations. This is not to say that Hall and Woodford's work has not been transformative. But economies are difficult beasts - and debates around central bank policymaking are sure to continue.

headline: US economists win Nobel for research helping policymakers navigate crises
summary: Two American economists, Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University, have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on economic stabilisation. Their research helps policymakers and central banks better understand economic fluctuations, manage recessions and inflation, and account for public expectations when shaping economic policy. The prize money, worth around $1.2 million, will be shared equally between the two laureates.

headline: 6 Iranians from Royan Inst. earn places in world top 2% list
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Six Iranian scientists affiliated with the Royan Institute made it into the latest world’s top 2% scientists list, which evaluates researchers worldwide based on citation data and indicators of scientific impact.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Six Iranian scientists affiliated with the Royan Institute made it into the latest world’s top 2% scientists list, which evaluates researchers worldwide based on citation data and indicators of scientific impact.

The researchers are affiliated with the Academic Center for Education, Culture and Research Activities (ACECR), and their inclusion marks an increase from five Royan Institute researchers recognized in the previous edition, according to the Institute’s Public Relations and International Affairs Office.

The six researchers are Dr. Hossein Baharvand, Dr. Mohammad Hossein Nasr-Esfahani, Dr. Mohammad Reza Baghban Islami, Dr. Reza Omrani-Samani, Dr. Masoud Vosough, and Dr. Ashraf Moini.

The World’s Top 2% Scientists list assesses researchers across scientific disciplines and subfields using citation-based indicators and other measures of research performance, including citation counts, the Hirsch index (h-index), and the composite C-score.

Compiled using data from the Scopus citation database in collaboration with Stanford University and published by Elsevier, the assessment is widely used to evaluate the scientific impact of researchers and their contributions to their respective fields.

Royan Institute’s representation on the list has remained consistent in recent years, with five researchers recognized in 2023, four in 2024, and five in 2025. The latest assessment raises that number to six, highlighting the Institute’s continued presence in international scientific rankings.

headline: Hezbollah outlines financial aid plan for Lebanese with destroyed homes
summary: By Maya Gebeily and Laila BassamOct 13 (Reuters) - Lebanon's Hezbollah will provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes have been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable during this year's war with Israel, the chairman of the group's Executive Council said on Tuesday.Reuters reported last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million from Iran to help displaced Lebanese families, citing two people with direct knowledge of the transfer, though the US disputed Tehran's ability to provide such financial assistance.
body_text:
By Maya Gebeily and Laila Bassam

Oct 13 (Reuters) - Lebanon's Hezbollah will provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes have been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable during this year's war with Israel, the chairman of the group's Executive Council said on Tuesday.

Reuters reported last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million from Iran to help displaced Lebanese families, citing two people with direct knowledge of the transfer, though the US disputed Tehran's ability to provide such financial assistance.

Under the plan presented by Executive Council chairman Ali Damoush, eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs will receive $14,000, including $8,000 for furniture and $6,000 for rent. Families elsewhere in Lebanon will receive $12,000, comprising $8,000 for furniture and $4,000 for rent, maintaining the same rates as in 2024.

Damoush said the assistance would cover families whose homes were destroyed, deemed uninhabitable following technical assessments or severely damaged, as well as those displaced from Israeli-occupied areas or nearby locations.

The aid will be restricted to families who used the affected properties as their primary residences and do not own a second home, excluding summer homes and abandoned properties.

Payments will be made in four instalments over one year, starting with $3,500 for families in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $3,000 elsewhere.

Damoush said eligibility and the type of assistance would be determined according to a set of criteria assessing the extent of damage to each property.

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE UPROOTED BY THE WAR

Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the ​group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2, days after the US and Israel began attacks on Iran.

Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people, according to Lebanon's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Hezbollah received the cash last month despite tightening US economic pressure on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, according to the two people who spoke to Reuters.

At the time, a Hezbollah official ​said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the ⁠funds.

The United States disputed the Reuters report, saying the money was "not there". Iran has not commented.

Damoush on Tuesday declined to comment on either the Reuters report or the US reaction, and declined to provide a figure for the total amount Hezbollah would dedicate to shelter support.

(Reporting by Maya Gebeily and Laila Bassam; Writing by Tala RamadanEditing by Gareth Jones)

headline: IMF warns UK of risk of inflation ahead of government’s first budget
summary: The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday.The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget. It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies, said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023.“The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported.Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported.The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported. The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. body_text:
The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday.

The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget.

It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies, said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023.

Prime Minister Burnham signals higher defence spending

“The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported.

Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported.

The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. Previous governments have failed to achieve the same goal.

Britain is facing a prolonged energy squeeze after the price of European gas surged more than 150 per cent this year. Dwindling gas reserves threaten to keep British consumers' costs high through winter.

The price increase brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on the UK's fragile economy.

Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas.

Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage, which leave it vulnerable supply disruptions and global market price volatility.

In its latest World Economic Outlook published on Tuesday, the Washington-based IMF said debt-burdened economies such as the UK should restrict any public relief to “targeted and temporary” measures so they can still be able to pull inflation back.

The multilateral lender expects UK inflation to climb to 3.3 per cent this year and ease to 2.8 per cent next year. The UK aims to bring inflation back to its 2 per cent target and the market expects the Bank of England to start raising rates from next month.

Rebuilding the fiscal space is “urgent”, given elevated debt as well as higher borrowing costs and increasing demands on public budgets, against an ever-worsening global geopolitical backdrop, the latest IMF report warned.

“Support measures should be used sparingly, designed in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy, and unwound rapidly as the shock dissipates,” the report advised economies supporting elevated debt levels.

The fund expects the UK economy to grow 1.3 per cent this year, an upward revision of 0.5 percentage points from the fund’s projections in April. Growth, however, is estimated to edge lower to 1.2 per cent next year as “higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”, the IMF added.

“The IMF projections draw attention to both the resilience and the fragility of Britain’s economic prospects,” said Valentin Boboc, chief economist at Institute of Economic Affairs.

“Despite stronger-than-expected growth this year, the longer-term outlook remains disappointing due to high taxes, expensive energy and other impediments to investment.”

Before the budget, the Chancellor needs to focus on “removing obstacles to growth” and should restrain spending, Mr Boboc said.

The country must restore business confidence and “recognise that Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity”, he added.

headline: Trump says does not believe China, Russia helping Iran
summary: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he does not believe that China and Russia are helping Iran, adding that they have "too much to lose." Trump has faced pressure over reports that Chinese and Russian entities have supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops. Responding to comments that China and Russia are helping Iran, Trump said in a post on Truth Social: "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all."
body_text:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he does not believe that China and Russia are helping Iran, adding that they have "too much to lose."

Trump has faced pressure over reports that Chinese and Russian entities have supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.

Responding to comments that China and Russia are helping Iran, Trump said in a post on Truth Social: "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all."

"They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!" he added.

Trump said in July that he did not believe China and Russia were selling weapons to Iran, warning that "it would be very bad for them" if they did.

China and Russia both maintain strong ties with Iran but have refrained from getting directly involved in the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

Since the outbreak of the war, Russia has sent humanitarian aid to Iran, but has otherwise not officially announced any concrete assistance.

The Kremlin has denied US media reports claiming that Moscow passed sensitive intelligence to Iran, including the locations of US warships and aircraft in the region.

China has sharply condemned US and Israeli strikes while also criticizing Iranian attacks on Gulf states and the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.

China has previously supplied Iran with drones as well as equipment that can be used for both civilian and military purposes.

Beijing has denied reports that the country's top semiconductor firm, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, has sent chipmaking tools to Iran.

China and Russia have also been accused of helping Iran circumvent international sanctions targeting its oil sales.

Trump has frequently taken a more deferential tone toward Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin than he has toward some of Washington's own allies, saying that they must be respected as the leaders of major world powers.

Our correspondents are already on the next chapter. Read everything they file, from $2/week.

analysis.framing: The article reports Trump's denial of Chinese and Russian assistance to Iran while cataloging the specific allegations and denials from all parties involved.

loaded_language.explanation: The adverb 'sharply' adds emotional intensity to the description of China's diplomatic response, implying harshness beyond a neutral statement of fact.
The phrase characterizes Trump's posture toward Xi and Putin as submissive, which carries a negative editorial judgment about his approach.

omissions: Specific details of the intelligence allegedly shared by Russia, such as the locations of US warships and aircraft, are mentioned only as a denial by the Kremlin rather than as a reported fact.
The nature of the 'pressure' Trump faced over the reports is not elaborated with specific sources or congressional reactions.
No mention of the US or Israeli perspective on the accuracy of the intelligence-sharing reports beyond Trump's denial.

headline: Press review: Russia-US gas deal riles Europe as Putin says no bombs on Ukraine vote day
summary: Top stories from the Russian press on Tuesday, October 10th
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Europe seeks to derail the Russia-US diesel deal; Moscow is ready to halt strikes on Ukraine on its election day; and the US and Iran can't seem to agree on de-escalation at sea. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.

The European Union will try to disrupt Russian fuel supplies to the United States and step up pressure on Moscow, experts interviewed by Izvestia said. Foreign ministers of EU member states have approved the bloc’s 22nd package of sanctions on Russia. However, the EU remains divided, with some countries planning to promote a pragmatic approach to relations with Russia.

The EU isn't happy about the Russia-US fuel agreement and will try to disrupt supplies, political scientist Denis Denisov said. One thing it could do is send its leaders on a series of visits to US President Donald Trump in a bid to persuade him to abandon the deal, the way they did following the Russia-US talks in Alaska. Besides, Europe has high hopes for the Democratic Party’s potential victory in the upcoming US midterm congressional elections.

Still, the EU is divided over how to approach Russia as some member states call for dialogue with Moscow. Bulgaria and Slovakia seek to maintain Russian energy supplies, which the EU intends to stop as early as next year, St. Petersburg State University professor Natalya Yeryomina stressed. However, as Brussels will work to derail the Russia-US deal, it won’t allow EU members to reach similar agreements with Moscow, the political scientist pointed out.

Meanwhile, the Russia-US diesel deal has caused a stir not only in Europe and Ukraine but also in the US Congress, Vedomosti notes. A bipartisan group of seven senators has called on Trump to drop Russian diesel imports.

If Democrats win the midterm elections, the deal could be scrapped through a bill fully banning the import of Russian petroleum products, provided it is backed by some Republicans, said Vadim Kozlov, head of the Internal Policy Department at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for US and Canadian Studies. "A move to reverse course on the deal is unlikely to gain support from enough lawmakers at this point because Trump is sure to portray it as Congress obstructing efforts to lower US diesel prices," the expert concluded.

Russia is not prepared to accept the 60-day ceasefire proposed by Vladimir Zelensky, who has claimed that this would allow presidential elections to be held in Ukraine. However, Russian President Vladimir Putin has indicated that what he is willing to do is halt strikes on Ukraine on the day of the vote, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. In the meantime, Moscow remains open to talks, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told Izvestia.

Some are clamoring for elections to be held in Ukraine, said Igor Markov, a former member of the country’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada. And the reasons go beyond simply changing the government. According to Markov, some of the country’s elite already expect the domestic political struggle to intensify once hostilities are over. That's when people will be blamed for decisions made over the past several years, including major corruption crimes, he explained.

Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary State Development, believes that elections in Ukraine could facilitate negotiations on resolving the crisis.

Still, settlement efforts are being hampered by the position taken by the majority of European Union countries, which continue to supply Kiev with weapons and actually encourage it to prolong the conflict. By contrast, the United States under Donald Trump is seeking to find a diplomatic way out of the crisis, even though Washington has not completely halted its support for Kiev.

A change of president in Kiev would not guarantee a shift in Ukraine’s approach to the conflict. Whoever succeeds Zelensky would have to take Brussels’ position into account, while the European Union appears to believe that continued confrontation serves its interests. Notably, European leaders choose to ignore Moscow’s direct statements that Russia has neither plans nor reasons to engage in an armed conflict with the EU. Within this framework, Ukraine’s leader remains merely a variable in someone else’s strategic equation.

A brief lull in strikes in the Persian Gulf was once again disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. With talks stalled, the United States and Iran could engage in another round of active hostilities after the US midterm elections, Vedomosti writes.

Alexey Yurk, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, doubts that the election outcome will significantly affect the US president’s position. "Congressional resolutions calling for an end to military operations are advisory in nature and can in no way stop the White House," the expert said.

After the elections, Trump will no longer be so worried about how the American public views his foreign policy actions in the Middle East, Ilya Vaskin, junior researcher at the Higher School of Economics’ Center for the Study of the Middle East, Caucasus and Central Asia, pointed out. On the other hand, the expert did not rule out the possibility that the Democrats could take control of Congress following the vote, making it much harder for the White House to conduct combat operations.

In terms of prospects for an agreement, Washington and Tehran and pretty far apart in their positions on most issues, including the status of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions on Iran, Yurk noted. The sides have also lost all trust in each other, making it all but impossible for either party to concede anything, as the United States has repeatedly launched military operations against Iran in the midst of negotiations, the political scientist added.

In the event of an escalation, hostilities are likely to enter a more destructive phase, Yury Lyamin, senior researcher at the Center for Strategies and Technologies, warned. The US military could launch massive strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure, while Tehran could retaliate by targeting oil and gas facilities and other critical economic sectors of US regional allies, the analyst said.

Saudi Arabia has found itself in a difficult position amid its conflict with the Houthis. A coalition led by Riyadh previously announced a large-scale military operation against the movement, but Saudi Arabia has so far limited its involvement to targeted airstrikes, while it is Yemeni government forces that have engaged in combat, Izvestia notes.

Middle East expert Kirill Semyonov believes that Saudi Arabia has no other option but to launch a ground operation because the Houthis are pursuing a policy of maximum pressure on Riyadh.

The Ansar Allah Houthi movement openly describes itself as Tehran’s main ally in the fight against the United States and Israel. In order to end the conflict, Riyadh will have to enter direct talks with Iran on dividing spheres of influence in the region, Danila Krylov, a researcher with the Department of the Middle and Post-Soviet East at the Institute of Scientific Information on Social Sciences of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.

Successful Houthi attacks on airports have prompted media reports highlighting the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s air defenses. In 2017, Riyadh signed a memorandum on purchasing Russia’s S-400 air defense systems but later abandoned the plan under pressure from the United States. Saudi Arabia eventually yielded to Washington’s demands and signed a separate contract to buy US-made THAAD missile defense systems.

Now, the US has in fact left its once-strategic ally to its own devices, as Americans are unable to supply Riyadh with enough interceptors, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes. That said, Saudi Arabia has turned to France, Britain, Egypt and Pakistan for additional weapons. With the Strait of Hormuz remaining a dangerous route and US President Donald Trump with his hands full on the eve of the November midterm elections, Saudi Arabia is hastily seeking to form a regional coalition willing to fight the Houthis in Yemen without Washington’s support. However, Riyadh will be the one to bear the costs of the war, which could turn out to be the fatal straw breaking the back of the Saudi economy, which is already hemorrhaging money amid the US-Iran conflict.

Russian and foreign analysts have lowered their forecasts for Russian grain exports. Disruptions to shipments through Black Sea ports, the main channel for agricultural exports, is being cited as the main reason, Nezavisimaya Gazeta reports.

Exporters are exploring alternative shipping options though ports in the Far East. Chinese ports could become transit hubs for supplies to various countries, said Ksenia Bolomatova, executive director of the Russian Grain Association. The Baltic Sea route serves traditional destinations of Russian grain exports such as the Middle East, Turkey and North Africa. However, shipping grain to Southeast Asian countries via this route is more difficult, so developing Far Eastern terminals is necessary, the expert stressed.

The Russian Grain Association believes that other exporters will not be able to fully compensate for the shortfall in Russian grain supplies. "Moreover, customers will have to pay more for what they receive, as we have already seen a price rise of 30%," Bolomatova warned.

Amid the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, Russian grain exports along traditional routes remain largely constrained, Finam analyst Alexander Potavin agrees. "The main grain export route used to run through Russia’s southern ports on the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Now, it has been disrupted. There are some alternatives but those routes are longer and more expensive, nor can they ensure the same volumes of supplies at this point. Agricultural products can be shipped via Baltic ports, including Ust Luga, which is well suited for exports to Turkey, North Africa and the Middle East, but it now takes much longer to deliver grain from southern Russia to these ports, and it also costs more," the expert added.

"Grain exports through the Far East are more convenient for Asian customers, but they require additional rail and port infrastructure. As a result, it turns out that disruptions affecting Azov and Black Sea ports, as well as risks associated with shipments across the Black Sea, are complicating Russian grain exports this year," Potavin concluded.

TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

body_text:
Formula One has announced a 10-year agreement to bring the sport back to Africa, with Rwanda set to host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s.

The agreement sees the sport head back to the continent for the first time since 1993, when the South African Grand Prix left the calendar.

Racing will take place at a new circuit in Bugesera, which is expected to be completed early in the next decade. The circuit will be located approximately 40 kilometres south of the capital, Kigali.

The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board.

“Today is a landmark moment for Formula One,” said Stefano Domenicali, president and chief executive of F1. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

“Africa has always been part of Formula One’s future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.”

The announcement is expected to be well received by Ferrari star Lewis Hamilton, who has long been an advocate of the sport returning to Africa. Hamilton reaffirmed his stance on the need for an African F1 race in Singapore at the weekend.

“I’ve always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa. It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, and the most beautiful continent,” said Hamilton.

Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: “Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement. Rwanda is proud to host the Formula One African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa.”

Mohammed ben Sulayem, FIA president, said: “The return of the FIA Formula One World Championship to Africa is a historic moment for our sport and an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport.”

headline: Africa: Economics Nobel - How This Year's Winners Helped to Smooth the Cycle of Economic Peaks and Troughs
summary: [The Conversation Africa] The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to the American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. The prize was awarded in recognition of their development of macroeconomic models that helped to reduce the length and depth of economic downturns.
body_text:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to the American economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford. The prize was awarded in recognition of their development of macroeconomic models that helped to reduce the length and depth of economic downturns.

According to the Academy, the economists' work in macroeconomic modelling has given policymakers additional tools to smooth out the economic cycle. As well as reducing the severity of downturns, their work also helped to cool the potentially negative impacts of economic booms.

Economies are known to follow cycles of downturns and upturns - and economists have long sought to find ways to tame these. More than a century ago, British economist John Maynard Keynes developed an approach to managing the economy that came to be known as Keynesianism.

Before this, the classical "laissez-faire" approach dominated. According to this doctrine, in an economic downturn, markets would eventually clear and the economy would rebound. Any attempt by government to directly influence the economy would not work and could even make things worse.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Keynes disagreed with the classical view. He believed that economies could get locked into a downward spiral that would deepen recessions and lead to economic depression. Instead, he argued that governments could actively use the levers of monetary policy (adjusting interest rates) and fiscal policy (lowering taxes and government spending) to improve the health of the economy.

In the aftermath of the 1929 Wall Street crash, the US was in a deep economic depression. Franklin D. Roosevelt won a landslide presidential victory in 1932 and his "New Deal" approach to economic policy was similar to what Keynes advocated. The US economy recovered, and the Keynesian school would dominate policymaking in many advanced economies after the second world war.

But the oil crisis of the 1970s changed everything. The Keynesian approach was ineffective in dealing with low growth, spiralling inflation and high unemployment. Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher won elections in the US and UK with promises of "smaller government" economic policy, including lower taxes, privatisation and deregulation. Keynesianism needed a rebuild.

Decisions of consumers and businesses

Hall and Woodford became part of the "New Keynesian" school that emerged in the 1980s. Their approach was to build models that looked at decisions made by millions of individuals and businesses rather than just considering macroeconomic variables like production, inflation, consumption and unemployment.

Hall, of Stanford University in California, is an expert in consumption theory. According to his "random walk hypothesis", decisions made by households on whether to spend or save were directly influenced by their expectations about future income and economic conditions. In other words, they were not just based on their current financial conditions. As consumption makes up around 70% of GDP in advanced economies, these insights were important.

Woodford, of Columbia University in New York, is an expert in supply-side macroeconomics, specifically the role that expectations play in price-setting and inflation. In his 2003 book, Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, he proved that a central bank could influence economic activity by managing the public's expectations about what might happen to interest rates in future.

Up until the 1990s, central bank policymaking was secretive and could sometimes take markets by surprise. Hall and Woodford's insights changed this. In the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crisis, the central banks of most major advanced economies adopted an approach known as "forward guidance".

This policy saw central bank governors provide greater transparency about their monetary policy intentions. Forward guidance policy announcements provide a clear assessment of both the economic outlook and how this might affect inflation. They also set out how central bank policy could react to these assessments.

As with most policy approaches, forward guidance has both advocates and critics. Research from the European Central Bank shows that clear communication from central banks reduces short-term interest rate volatility. There is also some evidence that after the 2008 financial crisis, expectations that inflation would remain low helped to keep interest rates down. This probably encouraged spending and investment, which aided economic recovery.

But critics believe that forward guidance has no impact on long-term interest rates and say it is debatable if it has any impact on short-term rates. They also argue that setting expectations about interest rates can strip credibility from central banks. This could happen if economic policy needs to be altered to deal with sudden shocks, for example.

The conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine are driving up energy prices and inflation expectations. The forward guidance from many central bankers is pointing to higher inflation and perhaps the need for higher interest rates.

Anyone coming off a fixed-rate mortgage might be sceptical of the idea that policy tools can lower short-term interest rate expectations. This is not to say that Hall and Woodford's work has not been transformative. But economies are difficult beasts - and debates around central bank policymaking are sure to continue.

headline: 6 Iranians from Royan Inst. earn places in world top 2% list
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Six Iranian scientists affiliated with the Royan Institute made it into the latest world’s top 2% scientists list, which evaluates researchers worldwide based on citation data and indicators of scientific impact.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Six Iranian scientists affiliated with the Royan Institute made it into the latest world’s top 2% scientists list, which evaluates researchers worldwide based on citation data and indicators of scientific impact.

The researchers are affiliated with the Academic Center for Education, Culture and Research Activities (ACECR), and their inclusion marks an increase from five Royan Institute researchers recognized in the previous edition, according to the Institute’s Public Relations and International Affairs Office.

The six researchers are Dr. Hossein Baharvand, Dr. Mohammad Hossein Nasr-Esfahani, Dr. Mohammad Reza Baghban Islami, Dr. Reza Omrani-Samani, Dr. Masoud Vosough, and Dr. Ashraf Moini.

The World’s Top 2% Scientists list assesses researchers across scientific disciplines and subfields using citation-based indicators and other measures of research performance, including citation counts, the Hirsch index (h-index), and the composite C-score.

Compiled using data from the Scopus citation database in collaboration with Stanford University and published by Elsevier, the assessment is widely used to evaluate the scientific impact of researchers and their contributions to their respective fields.

Royan Institute’s representation on the list has remained consistent in recent years, with five researchers recognized in 2023, four in 2024, and five in 2025. The latest assessment raises that number to six, highlighting the Institute’s continued presence in international scientific rankings.

TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Iran’s ambassador to has strongly condemned US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s remarks in Athens about Iranian civilization, terming the remarks raised by Rubio as deep rooted in ignorance and prejudice.

Mohammad Hossein Mokhtari called Rubio’s recent comments at the Acropolis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an “unethical and provocative act,” saying the US official had used the occasion to justify hawkish positions and threats against Iran out of desperation.

Human civilization’s history is not a field for political fantasies or judgments born of ignorance and prejudice, Mokhtari said. Civilizations were built over thousands of years through human thought, culture, knowledge and effort, and their legacy could not be dismissed through superficial claims or distorted accounts, he added.

Mokhtari highlighted Iran’s historical and spiritual standing, citing references to the country in religious texts. In the Old Testament, he said, Cyrus the Great is presented as the Lord’s anointed and chosen instrument for fulfilling divine will. The books of Ezra, Daniel, and Esther also refer to Persian kings, the grandeur of the Persian Empire, and their role in the fate of nations.
