headline: Hezbollah outlines financial aid plan for Lebanese with destroyed homes
summary: By Maya Gebeily and Laila BassamOct 13 (Reuters) - Lebanon's Hezbollah will provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes have been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable during this year's war with Israel, the chairman of the group's Executive Council said on Tuesday.Reuters reported last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million from Iran to help displaced Lebanese families, citing two people with direct knowledge of the transfer, though the US disputed Tehran's ability to provide such financial assistance.
body_text:
By Maya Gebeily and Laila Bassam

Oct 13 (Reuters) - Lebanon's Hezbollah will provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes have been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable during this year's war with Israel, the chairman of the group's Executive Council said on Tuesday.

Reuters reported last week that Hezbollah had received $200 million from Iran to help displaced Lebanese families, citing two people with direct knowledge of the transfer, though the US disputed Tehran's ability to provide such financial assistance.

Under the plan presented by Executive Council chairman Ali Damoush, eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs will receive $14,000, including $8,000 for furniture and $6,000 for rent. Families elsewhere in Lebanon will receive $12,000, comprising $8,000 for furniture and $4,000 for rent, maintaining the same rates as in 2024.

Damoush said the assistance would cover families whose homes were destroyed, deemed uninhabitable following technical assessments or severely damaged, as well as those displaced from Israeli-occupied areas or nearby locations.

The aid will be restricted to families who used the affected properties as their primary residences and do not own a second home, excluding summer homes and abandoned properties.

Payments will be made in four instalments over one year, starting with $3,500 for families in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $3,000 elsewhere.

Damoush said eligibility and the type of assistance would be determined according to a set of criteria assessing the extent of damage to each property.

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE UPROOTED BY THE WAR

Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the ​group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2, days after the US and Israel began attacks on Iran.

Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people, according to Lebanon's health ministry, which does not distinguish between civilians and combatants.

Hezbollah received the cash last month despite tightening US economic pressure on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, according to the two people who spoke to Reuters.

At the time, a Hezbollah official ​said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the ⁠funds.

The United States disputed the Reuters report, saying the money was "not there". Iran has not commented.

Damoush on Tuesday declined to comment on either the Reuters report or the US reaction, and declined to provide a figure for the total amount Hezbollah would dedicate to shelter support.

(Reporting by Maya Gebeily and Laila Bassam; Writing by Tala RamadanEditing by Gareth Jones)

body_text:
The debt-laden UK economy needs to stay the course on deficit reduction and use cost-of-living relief sparingly or risk reigniting inflation, the International Monetary Fund warned on Tuesday.

The warning comes just over two weeks before UK Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, presents his first annual budget.

It is important there is no slippage in the face of higher debt interest costs and pressure to spend more on ⁠defence and energy subsidies, said the new IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro, who served as a Bank of England policymaker from ⁠2017 to 2023.

Prime Minister Burnham signals higher defence spending

“The UK has already started the [fiscal] consolidation path … It is on that trajectory, and the message for the UK is simply stay the course and continue on that trajectory,” Ms Tenreyro said at press conference in Bangkok, Reuters reported.

Mr Healey is preparing to announce a series of time-limited giveaways to help voters with the cost of living in the budget on October 28, Bloomberg reported.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies on Monday also urged the Chancellor to address a £35 billion ($46 billion) hole in the spending plans or risk delivering a “work of fiction”, the Financial Times reported.

The UK government ran a budget deficit of 4.4 per cent of gross domestic product last year and aims to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029-30 fiscal year. Previous governments have failed to achieve the same goal.

Britain is facing a prolonged energy squeeze after the price of European gas surged more than 150 per cent this year. Dwindling gas reserves threaten to keep British consumers' costs high through winter.

The price increase brings the prospect of higher household bills, renewed inflation and further pressure on the UK's fragile economy.

Underground gas storage in Britain was just 48 per cent full at the start of October, compared with 94 per cent in Portugal and 99 per cent in Poland, according to figures reported alongside the latest winter outlook from the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas.

Britain has historically relied on imported gas rather than extensive domestic storage, which leave it vulnerable supply disruptions and global market price volatility.

In its latest World Economic Outlook published on Tuesday, the Washington-based IMF said debt-burdened economies such as the UK should restrict any public relief to “targeted and temporary” measures so they can still be able to pull inflation back.

The multilateral lender expects UK inflation to climb to 3.3 per cent this year and ease to 2.8 per cent next year. The UK aims to bring inflation back to its 2 per cent target and the market expects the Bank of England to start raising rates from next month.

Rebuilding the fiscal space is “urgent”, given elevated debt as well as higher borrowing costs and increasing demands on public budgets, against an ever-worsening global geopolitical backdrop, the latest IMF report warned.

“Support measures should be used sparingly, designed in a way not to complicate the task of monetary policy, and unwound rapidly as the shock dissipates,” the report advised economies supporting elevated debt levels.

The fund expects the UK economy to grow 1.3 per cent this year, an upward revision of 0.5 percentage points from the fund’s projections in April. Growth, however, is estimated to edge lower to 1.2 per cent next year as “higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”, the IMF added.

“The IMF projections draw attention to both the resilience and the fragility of Britain’s economic prospects,” said Valentin Boboc, chief economist at Institute of Economic Affairs.

“Despite stronger-than-expected growth this year, the longer-term outlook remains disappointing due to high taxes, expensive energy and other impediments to investment.”

Before the budget, the Chancellor needs to focus on “removing obstacles to growth” and should restrain spending, Mr Boboc said.

The country must restore business confidence and “recognise that Britain cannot tax its way to prosperity”, he added.

analysis.framing: The article frames the IMF's warning as a caution against fiscal expansion and cost-of-living relief, emphasizing deficit reduction, inflation risk, and business-friendly commentary over potential benefits of public spending.

Vague and emotive descriptor that suggests vulnerability without specifying concrete weaknesses.

Dramatic and vague phrasing that heightens a sense of crisis without providing specifics.

loaded_language.explanation: Quoted opinion from IEA that is a loaded political slogan, presenting a contested economic view as a truism.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: tax increases alone are unlikely to achieve prosperity

omissions: Perspectives from economists or officials who argue that targeted cost-of-living relief is necessary to support vulnerable households during the energy crisis.
Details on how the UK's energy price surge compares to other European countries or the role of Brexit in energy trade.
The potential positive effects of government spending on growth or public welfare, as mentioned in other coverage.
Context on the Bank of England's previous interest rate decisions and their impact on inflation.

headline: Trump says does not believe China, Russia helping Iran
summary: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he does not believe that China and Russia are helping Iran, adding that they have "too much to lose." Trump has faced pressure over reports that Chinese and Russian entities have supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops. Responding to comments that China and Russia are helping Iran, Trump said in a post on Truth Social: "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all."
body_text:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he does not believe that China and Russia are helping Iran, adding that they have "too much to lose."

Trump has faced pressure over reports that Chinese and Russian entities have supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.

Responding to comments that China and Russia are helping Iran, Trump said in a post on Truth Social: "If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all."

"They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!" he added.

Trump said in July that he did not believe China and Russia were selling weapons to Iran, warning that "it would be very bad for them" if they did.

China and Russia both maintain strong ties with Iran but have refrained from getting directly involved in the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.

Since the outbreak of the war, Russia has sent humanitarian aid to Iran, but has otherwise not officially announced any concrete assistance.

The Kremlin has denied US media reports claiming that Moscow passed sensitive intelligence to Iran, including the locations of US warships and aircraft in the region.

China has sharply condemned US and Israeli strikes while also criticizing Iranian attacks on Gulf states and the blocking of the Strait of Hormuz.

China has previously supplied Iran with drones as well as equipment that can be used for both civilian and military purposes.

Beijing has denied reports that the country's top semiconductor firm, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation, has sent chipmaking tools to Iran.

China and Russia have also been accused of helping Iran circumvent international sanctions targeting its oil sales.

Trump has frequently taken a more deferential tone toward Chinese President Xi Jinping and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin than he has toward some of Washington's own allies, saying that they must be respected as the leaders of major world powers.

headline: Press review: Russia-US gas deal riles Europe as Putin says no bombs on Ukraine vote day
summary: Top stories from the Russian press on Tuesday, October 10th
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Europe seeks to derail the Russia-US diesel deal; Moscow is ready to halt strikes on Ukraine on its election day; and the US and Iran can't seem to agree on de-escalation at sea. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.

The European Union will try to disrupt Russian fuel supplies to the United States and step up pressure on Moscow, experts interviewed by Izvestia said. Foreign ministers of EU member states have approved the bloc’s 22nd package of sanctions on Russia. However, the EU remains divided, with some countries planning to promote a pragmatic approach to relations with Russia.

The EU isn't happy about the Russia-US fuel agreement and will try to disrupt supplies, political scientist Denis Denisov said. One thing it could do is send its leaders on a series of visits to US President Donald Trump in a bid to persuade him to abandon the deal, the way they did following the Russia-US talks in Alaska. Besides, Europe has high hopes for the Democratic Party’s potential victory in the upcoming US midterm congressional elections.

Still, the EU is divided over how to approach Russia as some member states call for dialogue with Moscow. Bulgaria and Slovakia seek to maintain Russian energy supplies, which the EU intends to stop as early as next year, St. Petersburg State University professor Natalya Yeryomina stressed. However, as Brussels will work to derail the Russia-US deal, it won’t allow EU members to reach similar agreements with Moscow, the political scientist pointed out.

Meanwhile, the Russia-US diesel deal has caused a stir not only in Europe and Ukraine but also in the US Congress, Vedomosti notes. A bipartisan group of seven senators has called on Trump to drop Russian diesel imports.

If Democrats win the midterm elections, the deal could be scrapped through a bill fully banning the import of Russian petroleum products, provided it is backed by some Republicans, said Vadim Kozlov, head of the Internal Policy Department at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for US and Canadian Studies. "A move to reverse course on the deal is unlikely to gain support from enough lawmakers at this point because Trump is sure to portray it as Congress obstructing efforts to lower US diesel prices," the expert concluded.

Russia is not prepared to accept the 60-day ceasefire proposed by Vladimir Zelensky, who has claimed that this would allow presidential elections to be held in Ukraine. However, Russian President Vladimir Putin has indicated that what he is willing to do is halt strikes on Ukraine on the day of the vote, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. In the meantime, Moscow remains open to talks, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told Izvestia.

Some are clamoring for elections to be held in Ukraine, said Igor Markov, a former member of the country’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada. And the reasons go beyond simply changing the government. According to Markov, some of the country’s elite already expect the domestic political struggle to intensify once hostilities are over. That's when people will be blamed for decisions made over the past several years, including major corruption crimes, he explained.

Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary State Development, believes that elections in Ukraine could facilitate negotiations on resolving the crisis.

Still, settlement efforts are being hampered by the position taken by the majority of European Union countries, which continue to supply Kiev with weapons and actually encourage it to prolong the conflict. By contrast, the United States under Donald Trump is seeking to find a diplomatic way out of the crisis, even though Washington has not completely halted its support for Kiev.

A change of president in Kiev would not guarantee a shift in Ukraine’s approach to the conflict. Whoever succeeds Zelensky would have to take Brussels’ position into account, while the European Union appears to believe that continued confrontation serves its interests. Notably, European leaders choose to ignore Moscow’s direct statements that Russia has neither plans nor reasons to engage in an armed conflict with the EU. Within this framework, Ukraine’s leader remains merely a variable in someone else’s strategic equation.

A brief lull in strikes in the Persian Gulf was once again disrupted by attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. With talks stalled, the United States and Iran could engage in another round of active hostilities after the US midterm elections, Vedomosti writes.

Alexey Yurk, a researcher at the Center for Middle East Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, doubts that the election outcome will significantly affect the US president’s position. "Congressional resolutions calling for an end to military operations are advisory in nature and can in no way stop the White House," the expert said.

After the elections, Trump will no longer be so worried about how the American public views his foreign policy actions in the Middle East, Ilya Vaskin, junior researcher at the Higher School of Economics’ Center for the Study of the Middle East, Caucasus and Central Asia, pointed out. On the other hand, the expert did not rule out the possibility that the Democrats could take control of Congress following the vote, making it much harder for the White House to conduct combat operations.

In terms of prospects for an agreement, Washington and Tehran and pretty far apart in their positions on most issues, including the status of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear program and sanctions on Iran, Yurk noted. The sides have also lost all trust in each other, making it all but impossible for either party to concede anything, as the United States has repeatedly launched military operations against Iran in the midst of negotiations, the political scientist added.

In the event of an escalation, hostilities are likely to enter a more destructive phase, Yury Lyamin, senior researcher at the Center for Strategies and Technologies, warned. The US military could launch massive strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure, while Tehran could retaliate by targeting oil and gas facilities and other critical economic sectors of US regional allies, the analyst said.

Saudi Arabia has found itself in a difficult position amid its conflict with the Houthis. A coalition led by Riyadh previously announced a large-scale military operation against the movement, but Saudi Arabia has so far limited its involvement to targeted airstrikes, while it is Yemeni government forces that have engaged in combat, Izvestia notes.

Middle East expert Kirill Semyonov believes that Saudi Arabia has no other option but to launch a ground operation because the Houthis are pursuing a policy of maximum pressure on Riyadh.

The Ansar Allah Houthi movement openly describes itself as Tehran’s main ally in the fight against the United States and Israel. In order to end the conflict, Riyadh will have to enter direct talks with Iran on dividing spheres of influence in the region, Danila Krylov, a researcher with the Department of the Middle and Post-Soviet East at the Institute of Scientific Information on Social Sciences of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.

Successful Houthi attacks on airports have prompted media reports highlighting the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia’s air defenses. In 2017, Riyadh signed a memorandum on purchasing Russia’s S-400 air defense systems but later abandoned the plan under pressure from the United States. Saudi Arabia eventually yielded to Washington’s demands and signed a separate contract to buy US-made THAAD missile defense systems.

Now, the US has in fact left its once-strategic ally to its own devices, as Americans are unable to supply Riyadh with enough interceptors, Rossiyskaya Gazeta writes. That said, Saudi Arabia has turned to France, Britain, Egypt and Pakistan for additional weapons. With the Strait of Hormuz remaining a dangerous route and US President Donald Trump with his hands full on the eve of the November midterm elections, Saudi Arabia is hastily seeking to form a regional coalition willing to fight the Houthis in Yemen without Washington’s support. However, Riyadh will be the one to bear the costs of the war, which could turn out to be the fatal straw breaking the back of the Saudi economy, which is already hemorrhaging money amid the US-Iran conflict.

Russian and foreign analysts have lowered their forecasts for Russian grain exports. Disruptions to shipments through Black Sea ports, the main channel for agricultural exports, is being cited as the main reason, Nezavisimaya Gazeta reports.

Exporters are exploring alternative shipping options though ports in the Far East. Chinese ports could become transit hubs for supplies to various countries, said Ksenia Bolomatova, executive director of the Russian Grain Association. The Baltic Sea route serves traditional destinations of Russian grain exports such as the Middle East, Turkey and North Africa. However, shipping grain to Southeast Asian countries via this route is more difficult, so developing Far Eastern terminals is necessary, the expert stressed.

The Russian Grain Association believes that other exporters will not be able to fully compensate for the shortfall in Russian grain supplies. "Moreover, customers will have to pay more for what they receive, as we have already seen a price rise of 30%," Bolomatova warned.

Amid the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, Russian grain exports along traditional routes remain largely constrained, Finam analyst Alexander Potavin agrees. "The main grain export route used to run through Russia’s southern ports on the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Now, it has been disrupted. There are some alternatives but those routes are longer and more expensive, nor can they ensure the same volumes of supplies at this point. Agricultural products can be shipped via Baltic ports, including Ust Luga, which is well suited for exports to Turkey, North Africa and the Middle East, but it now takes much longer to deliver grain from southern Russia to these ports, and it also costs more," the expert added.

"Grain exports through the Far East are more convenient for Asian customers, but they require additional rail and port infrastructure. As a result, it turns out that disruptions affecting Azov and Black Sea ports, as well as risks associated with shipments across the Black Sea, are complicating Russian grain exports this year," Potavin concluded.

TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

body_text:
Formula One has announced a 10-year agreement to bring the sport back to Africa, with Rwanda set to host the African Grand Prix from the early 2030s.

The agreement sees the sport head back to the continent for the first time since 1993, when the South African Grand Prix left the calendar.

Racing will take place at a new circuit in Bugesera, which is expected to be completed early in the next decade. The circuit will be located approximately 40 kilometres south of the capital, Kigali.

The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board.

“Today is a landmark moment for Formula One,” said Stefano Domenicali, president and chief executive of F1. “With Rwanda joining the calendar from the next decade, our sport will race in every inhabited continent, bringing the World Championship closer than ever to fans around the globe.

“Africa has always been part of Formula One’s future, and from the beginning we were determined to return in the right way, with the right partner, a long-term commitment and a clear vision for creating meaningful impact.”

The announcement is expected to be well received by Ferrari star Lewis Hamilton, who has long been an advocate of the sport returning to Africa. Hamilton reaffirmed his stance on the need for an African F1 race in Singapore at the weekend.

“I’ve always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa. It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, and the most beautiful continent,” said Hamilton.

Rwanda President Paul Kagame said: “Today belongs to Africa. For more than three decades, the world’s premier motorsport championship has raced without this continent, and that changes with this agreement. Rwanda is proud to host the Formula One African Grand Prix, and to share this moment with more than 100 million fans across Africa.”

Mohammed ben Sulayem, FIA president, said: “The return of the FIA Formula One World Championship to Africa is a historic moment for our sport and an important step in the continued global growth of motorsport.”

headline: Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home
summary: The government is using millions of taxpayers' dollars on pro-Trump ads, even after the president said this would not happen. And, federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home.(Image credit: Alex Wong)
body_text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.

President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption

Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.

The safest way to protect yourself from measles when traveling is to be vaccinated. Malte Mueller/Getty Images hide caption

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.

When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981. Ernst Haas/Getty Images hide caption

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.

U.S. economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are announced as the winners of the 2026 Nobel prize in economics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on Monday. Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

headline: Meta launches new AI models to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic
summary: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are designed for coding, can remember information across conversations
body_text:
Meta has launched two new artificial intelligence models as the technology company seeks to compete more directly with leading systems developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are Meta’s most capable models to date and are designed for personal and professional AI agents, the company said in an announcement on Monday.

The models can perform long-running tasks, use computers, and work in specialized areas including law, finance, and health. Meta said they can also handle complex coding projects, delegate work to smaller AI agents and recover from errors without abandoning the original goal.

One of their main features, Active Memory, allows the AI to retain important information about a user across multiple conversations and retrieve it when relevant.

Another feature, Active Focus, is intended to keep an AI agent working when it encounters difficulties by trying alternative approaches, adapting to new information, and seeking clarification when necessary.

Meta said the models could help users perform tasks ranging from understanding a lease or navigating an insurance claim to analyzing finances and building an application.

Muse Wonder is now available to developers through the Meta Model API and the company’s Muse Code programming tool. The more capable Muse Wonder Full is available through paid Muse Code subscriptions, with plans starting at $50 per month for access to Meta’s most advanced models.

Muse Wonder will later be incorporated into Meta’s Muse personal assistant, initially for subscribers.

Meta published benchmark results that it said showed the models matching or outperforming some systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on selected coding, memory, and professional tasks. The broader performance of the models will still need to be assessed through independent testing.

The company said it trained the Wonder family to protect private information, refuse assistance with harmful activity, and strengthen defenses against cyberattacks. A more detailed safety report is expected to be released later.

The launch forms part of Meta’s broader push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described as “personal superintelligence,” AI systems capable of understanding users’ goals, preferences and long-term needs.

Unlike some earlier Meta models released with downloadable weights, the company did not announce plans to make the Wonder models open source.

"Act 5" of the French high schoolers' protest movement takes place this Tuesday, with other students and teachers also set to join the demonstrations. Le Figaro announces that politicians from the left and far left will partake, as well as groups against police brutality, the Yellow Vests and a group of farmers. This "convergence of fights" comes against "a backdrop of violence," according to the right-wing daily. It doubles down on its criticism that the student movement's demands are "absurd and confusing." The right-wing paper L'Opinion looks at how this generation of student protests has put itself at the heart of the French presidential campaign. In May 2027, one in every nine voters will be between the ages of 18 and 24. The challenge for parties now is to seduce a "protest-oriented, pluralistic generation with a propensity for abstention."

In the left-wing papers, Libération headlines with a quote from Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, one of France's major unions. She said: "For the last decade, young people have been treated like dogs", hailing the "lucidity" of the high school protesters. It comes as the French budget will be debated in parliament this Tuesday. L'Humanité, the Communist paper, warns of a "state of emergency" concerning French schools. It accuses the government and local authorities of passing the buck on how to finance much-needed renovations of certain French school establishments.

Staying in France, MPs will hold a solemn vote in parliament this Tuesday on a bill to fight sexual violence against women and children. The divisive bill was brought forward by 140 associations representing women and child victims and ­debated vigorously late last month. L'Humanité looks at two key articles that didn't make the cut. The first article aimed to protect female victims without French papers from being deported from France. NGOs have asked the government to review this article again and are promising to debate it in the Senate, when the bill heads there after the MPs' vote. The second article proposed the creation of special paid leave for victims of violence. The rejection of this measure was all the more “strange” because it had the support of NGOs and the government too. Amnesty International has criticised the bill for excluding the "most vulnerable and susceptible women" – trans women, foreigners and sex workers. If adopted, this law would be a failure because it would not protect those who need protecting, the NGO says on its website.

We head next to India, where the front pages headline on a "March for Democracy" led by opposition supporters in New Delhi on Monday. Thousands marched through the capital to the Indian Supreme Court. They called on the election chief to resign, accusing him of electoral roll fraud. According to them, tens of millions of voters' names have been struck off the electoral lists. The government says they were duplicates or deceased voters, but the opposition says Modi's government is deliberately excluding Muslim voters. Pictures of that march are splashed across the front pages of the Hindu and the Free Press Journal. The Indian Express notes the government's reaction. It accused opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and his party of "pure theatrics."

Elsewhere, The Times of London publishes an investigation accusing FIFA of not declaring a second salary paid to its president, Gianni Infantino. In addition to his salary and bonus, the investigation reveals that FIFA did not publicly disclose an extra $1.76 million paid to Infantino in 2024, plus similar sums in 2025 and 2026. Critics say this is a clear violation of FIFA rules. Sources say that some of the undisclosed money paid to Infantino was used to fund a luxury lifestyle in Miami in the lead-up to the World Cup, including a waterfront mansion rental. The Times investigation reveals that Infantino received two separate salaries – one from FIFA, declared; the other from a World Cup organising company, undeclared. The allegations will add pressure on the FIFA boss to resign. He became highly unpopular after his short-lived plan in July to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Finally, a little cat in China has become a viral star! The China Daily reports on a furry feline in Guangzhou called MeiMei, who was named after a cat on a popular TV series. Her story began in 2022 when her owner Chen found her near a railway station. He left his job to rescue stray animals and decided to keep MeiMei instead of rehousing her. He started sharing videos of her and people expressed concern for her well-being – not just from China but from around the world. Then he spent six months explaining that she was a stray cat and concern turned to love for her. Some devoted MeiMei fans travel from as far as Chile, Romania and Morocco. But like a real diva, she is aloof and indifferent – only cooperating with fan interactions when food is involved!

headline: S. Korea maintains demand for Ukraine's apology over N.K. POW disclosure
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- South Korea is continuing efforts to resolve its rece...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- South Korea is continuing efforts to resolve its recent diplomatic dispute with Ukraine while maintaining its demand for an apology from Kyiv over its disclosure of the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.

"The government hopes that all pending issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably," ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon told a press briefing. "To that end, we will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side and are currently maintaining communication."

The statement came after Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the matter had been "resolved" in an interview with RBC-Ukraine on Monday (local time).

"Everything stemmed from different interpretations of the confidentiality requirements at various stages of the transfer of the prisoners of war. Ukraine fulfilled all its obligations," Sybiha was quoted as saying by RBC-Ukraine.

The report said Seoul was continuing to escalate the situation by recalling its ambassador, despite Kyiv's view that the dispute had been resolved.

Asked whether Seoul's demand for an apology remained in place, a separate foreign ministry official said, "Yes," adding that the two countries were still in talks to find an amicable solution.

The two countries have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two North Korean soldiers in an address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month.

The soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia and arrived in South Korea in mid-September.

Seoul has said a nondisclosure agreement was reached with Kyiv at Ukraine's request to protect the soldiers and their families, who remain in North Korea. It has accused Zelenskyy of breaching the agreement, while Kyiv has denied that any such agreement existed.

The South Korean government has demanded an official explanation and apology. In protest, Seoul recalled its ambassador to Ukraine.

While maintaining its demand for an apology, Seoul is seeking a diplomatic resolution to the dispute.

"Both sides are communicating to manage and resolve pending issues, and we are consulting closely with our ambassador, who has been recalled, throughout this process," the spokesperson said. "We hope the Ukrainian side will respond positively to these diplomatic efforts."

headline: Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home
summary: The government is using millions of taxpayers' dollars on pro-Trump ads, even after the president said this would not happen. And, federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's D.C. home.(Image credit: Alex Wong)
body_text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.

President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption

Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.

Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.

The safest way to protect yourself from measles when traveling is to be vaccinated. Malte Mueller/Getty Images hide caption

Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.

The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.

When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981. Ernst Haas/Getty Images hide caption

The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.

U.S. economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are announced as the winners of the 2026 Nobel prize in economics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on Monday. Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

body_text:
Building on the momentum of its recently launched Muse AI personal agent, Meta on Monday, October 12, unveiled its most capable frontier AI models yet, designed to power personal and professional AI agents.

Initially code-named ‘Watermelon’, the Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full models deliver state-of-the-art performance on certain tasks related to coding as well as delegating AI agents to work through complex legal or financial questions, according to Meta.

It claimed that the new models mark a big leap over its predecessors, such as Muse Spark and Muse Glimmer, developed by the Meta Superintelligence Team, the social media giant’s specialised AI unit led by Scale AI co-founder Alexandr Wang.

What makes Muse Wonder stand out from the crowded AI frontier, according to Meta, is its ‘Active Memory’ feature that allows the model to retain user context for weeks or months to better fulfill tasks, and its ‘Active Focus’ capability, which enables AI agents to stay focused on tasks and persist until they are completed.

With Muse Wonder, Meta is looking to consolidate its position in the AI race after gaining ground on rivals such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic following the triumphant rollout of its Muse agent, which is designed to help with every-day tasks and errands.

It marks a significant turnaround for Meta, whose AI efforts previously went through a slump, prompting CEO Mark Zuckerberg to go on an aggressive hiring spree over the past 14 months.

Besides putting talent at the helm, the Zuckerberg-led overhaul of Meta’s AI operations has involved pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into building out the infrastructure needed to support AI models. Meta’s AI strategy heavily relies on consumers as the target audience. Most agentic AI use cases so far have not been aimed at normal users, but it appears that Meta’s Muse and similar offerings are seeing more broad-based adoption.

Meta’s competitive advantage is also about where its AI offerings could be deployed. The Instagram and WhatsApp parent has the distribution network to make Muse more useful and deeply embedded in people’s digital lives

But the company’s current position in the AI race depends on how Meta’s claims about its latest AI models hold up to outside testing and usage by researchers and developers. Another potential hurdle could be Meta’s track record on privacy and data use, which might make some users reluctant to trust it with more of their personal information than ever before.

our research process starts with evals. we developed the Personal Superintelligence Index (PSI) internally to help us measure the important dimensions of what actually makes a model useful for personal agents, vs just focusing on external benchmarks.

the end result is that our model is incredible for personal agents in many subtle and important ways, including Active Memory and Active Focus.

i’m especially proud of our research team for taking a particular focus on developing useful models. the whole point of building advanced frontier models is to make them useful to real people, and we have thought about that every step of the way in our research process.

muse wonder is quite advanced across the board, and certainly has big model smell (which we quantified!), but is truly state of the art for personal agents.

— Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) October 12, 2026

“These are true frontier models. We really think they are competitive with the best models out there, and particularly state of the art on personal and professional agentic work,” Meta AI Chief Alexandr Wang was quoted as saying in an interview.

“I would tell folks they should try it out and judge for themselves. I think the rest of the ecosystem has been really focused on coding agents. We do genuinely think that we’ve taken a differentiated focus to make the personal-agent use case really sing,” Wang added.

Currently, Muse Wonder is accessible to developers via the Meta Model API and Muse Code. The API pricing for enterprise developers is $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

Muse Wonder Full is only available for Muse Code subscribers. Additionally, the new models will soon power the widely downloaded Muse AI app, though access will initially be limited to app subscribers.

The development process of Muse Wonder reflects Zuckerberg’s vision of personal superintelligence, which is rooted in the idea that people should use AI to achieve their personal goals.

Meta said that it has trained the model at its gigawatt-scale Prometheus data centre on complex tasks pertaining to work and everyday life. Meta also said it used multilingual training datasets for Muse Wonder, comprising data across worldwide languages. Earlier this year, the company’s controversial efforts to gather employees’ computer movements to train its AI systems, was put on hold following backlash and an internal security lapse.

Muse Wonder can process text, image, video, and voice inputs but can only output text. It has a context window of one million tokens at inference. The two main characteristics of both models are:

-Active Memory: It allows the model to remember what matters and recognise when earlier information becomes relevant. It can also carry over user context across conversations and retrieve details from them in order to complete the task at hand.

-Active Focus: This capability ensures that the AI agents continue working toward a challenging task by trying alternative approaches, working through blockers, and adapting to new information. It asks for clarification when needed and checks in before taking important actions, according to Meta.

The persistence of advanced AI systems in running long-horizon tasks has been cited by AI researchers as a contributing factor of misalignment or unwanted behaviour among AI agents.

The combination of Active Memory and Active Focus lets Muse Wonder excel at frontier coding, according to Meta. This includes building software that requires tracking, making changes across a codebase, and working through repeated cycles of testing and revision.

Beyond software development, Meta also showcased scripted demos of Muse Wonder-powered AI agents organising complex personal plans and working across web applications to help users with house hunting and moving across the country. The company also highlighted professional uses including financial analysis, legal document preparation, and automating insurance-related workflows.

Intelligence Index, an independent benchmark assessing models on reasoning, knowledge, coding and professional tasks, gave Wonder Full a score of 56, which means that it ties with Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 and surpasses OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, Google’s Gemini 4 Argon, and Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1. The standard Muse Wonder model scored 52, coming in one point behind GPT-6 Astra.

Meta also published benchmark results which suggest that Wonder Full is particularly competitive on sustained software engineering. For instance, on SWE-Marathon, Wonder Full scores 57.5 against 46.3 for Opus 5.5 and 42.5 for GPT-6 Astra. On the legal benchmark, its 13.1 score substantially outperforms the compared models.

However, both Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra outperformed Wonder Full on Terminal-Bench 4.0. Opus also beat Wonder Full on health-related questions.

Meta said that Muse Wonder comes with its strongest safeguards to date against CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear) and cyber misuse. It also ensures access to frontier cyber capabilities for defensive use, in accordance with the Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework.

The company claimed Muse Wonder is its most aligned model to date and said that a more detailed report on safety evaluations would be published soon. To be sure, Meta joined companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic to disclose security incidents driven by its misaligned AI agents.

In August 2026, the company said that one of its AI agents hacked a third-party service when it was undergoing safety testing. Meta pointed to a misconfiguration by sandbox provider Irregular, which was running a cybersecurity valuation for the tech giant’s agents that were not supposed to have had internet access.

headline: Meta launches new AI models to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic
summary: Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are designed for coding, can remember information across conversations
body_text:
Meta has launched two new artificial intelligence models as the technology company seeks to compete more directly with leading systems developed by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full are Meta’s most capable models to date and are designed for personal and professional AI agents, the company said in an announcement on Monday.

The models can perform long-running tasks, use computers, and work in specialized areas including law, finance, and health. Meta said they can also handle complex coding projects, delegate work to smaller AI agents and recover from errors without abandoning the original goal.

One of their main features, Active Memory, allows the AI to retain important information about a user across multiple conversations and retrieve it when relevant.

Another feature, Active Focus, is intended to keep an AI agent working when it encounters difficulties by trying alternative approaches, adapting to new information, and seeking clarification when necessary.

Meta said the models could help users perform tasks ranging from understanding a lease or navigating an insurance claim to analyzing finances and building an application.

Muse Wonder is now available to developers through the Meta Model API and the company’s Muse Code programming tool. The more capable Muse Wonder Full is available through paid Muse Code subscriptions, with plans starting at $50 per month for access to Meta’s most advanced models.

Muse Wonder will later be incorporated into Meta’s Muse personal assistant, initially for subscribers.

Meta published benchmark results that it said showed the models matching or outperforming some systems from OpenAI and Anthropic on selected coding, memory, and professional tasks. The broader performance of the models will still need to be assessed through independent testing.

The company said it trained the Wonder family to protect private information, refuse assistance with harmful activity, and strengthen defenses against cyberattacks. A more detailed safety report is expected to be released later.

The launch forms part of Meta’s broader push toward what CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described as “personal superintelligence,” AI systems capable of understanding users’ goals, preferences and long-term needs.

Unlike some earlier Meta models released with downloadable weights, the company did not announce plans to make the Wonder models open source.

headline: Russia invites China to invest in its hospitality sector — envoy
summary: Boris Titov adde that a branch of Russia's National Center could also open at the Beijing Exhibition Center in the future
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia has invited China to invest in its domestic hospitality infrastructure, jointly manage existing hotel chains, and expand bilateral organized tourism, Boris Titov, Russia’s presidential envoy for sustainable development goals, told TASS on Tuesday.

The statement followed a meeting between the Russian delegation from the Russia-China Committee for Friendship, Peace and Development and the leadership of the state-owned Beijing Tourism Group in Beijing.

"Our colleagues from Tourism.RF corporate group proposed that their Chinese counterparts invest in Russian hospitality facilities and jointly manage existing hotel networks," Titov said.

He noted that the initiative aims to double the number of organized Chinese tourists within a year through more extensive outreach. Titov acknowledged that China remains less familiar to Russian travelers than Turkey, while Chinese tourists are similarly unfamiliar with Russian destinations outside Moscow and St. Petersburg.

Beijing Tourism Group is a major state-owned conglomerate with operations in the lodging, retail, and entertainment sectors, Titov explained. "This includes the historic 'Moscow' restaurant in Beijing. We have proposed closer cooperation at this venue with prominent Russian restaurateurs, specifically the Arkady Novikov Group," he added, noting that a branch of Russia's National Center could also open at the Beijing Exhibition Center in the future.

headline: Kremlin spokesman addresses US-Europe ‘peace plan’ for Ukraine, diesel deal
summary: According to Dmitry Peskov, diesel fuel supply agreements serve the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Media reports about the alleged preparation of a US-European "peace plan" for Ukraine, the diesel agreement between Moscow and Washington, and the situation surrounding the provision of intelligence to Kiev were among the main topics discussed during Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov’s briefing on October 13.

TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.

- Russian President Vladimir Putin will meet with Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin at the Kremlin today.

- The Russian leader will also have an international telephone conversation.

- The Kremlin has seen a report in The Washington Post about the United States and Europe moving toward a joint peace proposal on Ukraine but has received no information about it: "We have seen media reports but we have heard nothing about it."

- Moscow continues contacts on a possible "energy ceasefire," but there have been no new developments since yesterday: "We discussed this issue yesterday, and for now I have nothing to add to what we said then. Contacts on this matter are continuing."

- There is no connection between the diesel agreement with the United States and Russia’s position on Ukraine; rather, it is a mutually beneficial example of Russian-US cooperation: "I don’t see any connection here. In fact, it is an example of Russia-US cooperation that benefits both parties a lot."

- European Union sanctions and other unilateral actions could hamper the implementation of the fuel deal between Russia and the United States: "That it could interfere is beyond doubt."

- European cynicism is a subject of widespread discussion in international media: "The issue of European cynicism, as [US Treasury Secretary Scott] Bessent put it, is being widely discussed in global media."

- European countries themselves remain major purchasers of Russian crude oil and petroleum products: "The fact is that European countries, just like all other nations, are heavy buyers of Russian oil and Russian petroleum products."

- Diesel fuel supply agreements serve the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets: "This corresponds to interests of the United States, this corresponds to interests of international energy markets, and is in line with interests of the Russian Federation, and so it takes place."

- Russia is selling and will continue to sell energy resources, its competitive commodity, on international markets: "Russia in this aspect is a country presenting its competitive commodity to global markets. We will continue doing that."

- The Kremlin is not aware of US President Donald Trump’s alleged plans to suspend intelligence sharing with Kiev or disable the Starlink internet service in Ukraine if Kiev continues strikes on Russian refineries: "We know nothing about it."

- Moscow’s position regarding a potential meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky or the need for Ukraine to hold an election is well known and unchanged: "Yesterday, we repeatedly talked about it and I have nothing to add. No changes here. Our position on all these issues is very well known."

- It is too early to discuss a compensation mechanism for financial losses that users of Yandex services may have incurred following Ukrainian attacks on the company: "It is premature to talk about financial losses at this point. You know that the company is strong and powerful. Yes, it is facing difficulties now. Of course, this issue is currently being discussed in the government, but the company is taking emergency measures to deal with the aftermath of this attack."

headline: India reiterates Ladakh ‘integral, inalienable’ part of country amid China’s remarks
body_text:
The Ministry of External Affairs on Tuesday rejected China’s objection to India announcing standard names of places in Ladakh. In an official statement, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said, “Union Territory of Ladakh is integral part of India, no amount of denial by Chinese side can change this established fact.”

The Ministry reiterated that standard names of places in Ladakh have been given to facilitate their accurate recognition and better awareness.

MEA’s remarks come shortly after China strongly opposed India’s decision to assign standardised names to 28 strategic locations and geographical features in Ladakh, claiming that the areas belonged to it.

“China has never recognised the so-called ‘Union Territory of Ladakh’ unilaterally and illegally established by India,” Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told a media briefing.

“The move is illegal and invalid and cannot change the fact that the relevant areas in the western sector of the China-India boundary have always belonged to China,” she said.

Divya A reports on travel, tourism, culture and social issues - not necessarily in that order - for The Indian Express. MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. A US-registered NATO reconnaissance aircraft has been spotted again over the neutral waters of the Black Sea, a source in air traffic control services told TASS, noting that this is the aircraft’s first flight in the area since the beginning of the week.

"The Bombardier ARTEMIS II reconnaissance aircraft has been spotted again over the neutral waters of the Black Sea, where it is flying from west to east and back in the southern part of the water area," the source said. He noted that the aircraft is flying at an altitude of about 10 km, without using the civil aviation flight routes and without entering the airspace of any country.

The source recalled that this aircraft is permanently based at the airfield in Constanta, Romania, from where it typically takes off on weekdays for operating in the areas over the Black Sea, the Baltic states, or near the Kaliningrad Region. He also emphasized that the aircraft had already flown over the Black Sea last week. On Wednesday, October 7, it was accompanied by a Swedish Air Force Gulfstream S102B Korpen radar intelligence aircraft, which was flying a similar route.

The source noted in this regard that in late July, the Bombardier ARTEMIS II set a sort of record by remaining over the Black Sea for nine hours.

headline: The Times: How Infantino's 'second salary' paid for luxury life in Miami
summary: PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 13: "Act 5" of the French high school protest movement begins as teachers and farmers could join in too. The Times of London publishes an investigation that shows FIFA boss Gianni Infantino received a second, undeclared salary. Finally, a cat in China goes viral with people flocking from around the world to meet her.
body_text:

Issued on: 13/10/2026 - 12:59

PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 13: "Act 5" of the French high school protest movement begins as teachers and farmers could join in too. In India, thousands of opposition supporters have marched to the Supreme Court demanding the resignation of the electoral board chief over fraud allegations. The Times of London publishes an investigation that shows FIFA boss Gianni Infantino received a second, undeclared salary. Finally, a cat in China goes viral with people flocking from around the world to meet her.

"Act 5" of the French high schoolers' protest movement takes place this Tuesday, with other students and teachers also set to join the demonstrations. Le Figaro announces that politicians from the left and far left will partake, as well as groups against police brutality, the Yellow Vests and a group of farmers. This "convergence of fights" comes against "a backdrop of violence," according to the right-wing daily. It doubles down on its criticism that the student movement's demands are "absurd and confusing." The right-wing paper L'Opinion looks at how this generation of student protests has put itself at the heart of the French presidential campaign. In May 2027, one in every nine voters will be between the ages of 18 and 24. The challenge for parties now is to seduce a "protest-oriented, pluralistic generation with a propensity for abstention."

In the left-wing papers, Libération headlines with a quote from Sophie Binet, the head of the CGT union, one of France's major unions. She said: "For the last decade, young people have been treated like dogs", hailing the "lucidity" of the high school protesters. It comes as the French budget will be debated in parliament this Tuesday. L'Humanité, the Communist paper, warns of a "state of emergency" concerning French schools. It accuses the government and local authorities of passing the buck on how to finance much-needed renovations of certain French school establishments.

Staying in France, MPs will hold a solemn vote in parliament this Tuesday on a bill to fight sexual violence against women and children. The divisive bill was brought forward by 140 associations representing women and child victims and ­debated vigorously late last month. L'Humanité looks at two key articles that didn't make the cut. The first article aimed to protect female victims without French papers from being deported from France. NGOs have asked the government to review this article again and are promising to debate it in the Senate, when the bill heads there after the MPs' vote. The second article proposed the creation of special paid leave for victims of violence. The rejection of this measure was all the more “strange” because it had the support of NGOs and the government too. Amnesty International has criticised the bill for excluding the "most vulnerable and susceptible women" – trans women, foreigners and sex workers. If adopted, this law would be a failure because it would not protect those who need protecting, the NGO says on its website.

We head next to India, where the front pages headline on a "March for Democracy" led by opposition supporters in New Delhi on Monday. Thousands marched through the capital to the Indian Supreme Court. They called on the election chief to resign, accusing him of electoral roll fraud. According to them, tens of millions of voters' names have been struck off the electoral lists. The government says they were duplicates or deceased voters, but the opposition says Modi's government is deliberately excluding Muslim voters. Pictures of that march are splashed across the front pages of the Hindu and the Free Press Journal. The Indian Express notes the government's reaction. It accused opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and his party of "pure theatrics."

Elsewhere, The Times of London publishes an investigation accusing FIFA of not declaring a second salary paid to its president, Gianni Infantino. In addition to his salary and bonus, the investigation reveals that FIFA did not publicly disclose an extra $1.76 million paid to Infantino in 2024, plus similar sums in 2025 and 2026. Critics say this is a clear violation of FIFA rules. Sources say that some of the undisclosed money paid to Infantino was used to fund a luxury lifestyle in Miami in the lead-up to the World Cup, including a waterfront mansion rental. The Times investigation reveals that Infantino received two separate salaries – one from FIFA, declared; the other from a World Cup organising company, undeclared. The allegations will add pressure on the FIFA boss to resign. He became highly unpopular after his short-lived plan in July to sell off stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

Finally, a little cat in China has become a viral star! The China Daily reports on a furry feline in Guangzhou called MeiMei, who was named after a cat on a popular TV series. Her story began in 2022 when her owner Chen found her near a railway station. He left his job to rescue stray animals and decided to keep MeiMei instead of rehousing her. He started sharing videos of her and people expressed concern for her well-being – not just from China but from around the world. headline: S. Korea maintains demand for Ukraine's apology over N.K. POW disclosure
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- South Korea is continuing efforts to resolve its rece...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- South Korea is continuing efforts to resolve its recent diplomatic dispute with Ukraine while maintaining its demand for an apology from Kyiv over its disclosure of the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.

"The government hopes that all pending issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably," ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon told a press briefing. "To that end, we will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side and are currently maintaining communication."

The statement came after Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the matter had been "resolved" in an interview with RBC-Ukraine on Monday (local time).

"Everything stemmed from different interpretations of the confidentiality requirements at various stages of the transfer of the prisoners of war. Ukraine fulfilled all its obligations," Sybiha was quoted as saying by RBC-Ukraine.

The report said Seoul was continuing to escalate the situation by recalling its ambassador, despite Kyiv's view that the dispute had been resolved.

Asked whether Seoul's demand for an apology remained in place, a separate foreign ministry official said, "Yes," adding that the two countries were still in talks to find an amicable solution.

The two countries have been embroiled in a diplomatic dispute since Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two North Korean soldiers in an address to the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month.

The soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia and arrived in South Korea in mid-September.

Seoul has said a nondisclosure agreement was reached with Kyiv at Ukraine's request to protect the soldiers and their families, who remain in North Korea. It has accused Zelenskyy of breaching the agreement, while Kyiv has denied that any such agreement existed.

The South Korean government has demanded an official explanation and apology. In protest, Seoul recalled its ambassador to Ukraine.

While maintaining its demand for an apology, Seoul is seeking a diplomatic resolution to the dispute.

"Both sides are communicating to manage and resolve pending issues, and we are consulting closely with our ambassador, who has been recalled, throughout this process," the spokesperson said. "We hope the Ukrainian side will respond positively to these diplomatic efforts."

headline: 10 best countries in the world 2026: Greece leads, India ranks among the top 20
body_text:
Condé Nast Traveller recently released the list for The Best Countries in the World 2026, as part of its Readers’ Choice Awards, which marked its 29th edition in 2026.

Thousands of respondents around the world submitted ratings on a secure voting website between April 1 and June 30, 2026. The survey’s questionnaire contained candidates across various categories, including hotels, resorts, airlines, cities, islands, cruise lines, etc.

The candidates needed a minimum number of responses to be considered. They were judged using a standard five-point scale (excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor), which was then converted into a percentage. The final score was determined by averaging these ratings.

Greece earned the title of the best country in the world for 2026 with a score of 98.14. Condé Nast Traveller said some of the country’s top-rated spots are attracting record-breaking tourist numbers. These include Santorini, Mykonos, Crete, Paros, Hydra, Ios, and Tinos.

Athens has emerged from being just a historic marvel and now boasts booming creative energy, including avant-garde galleries and amazing hotels. It ranks among Europe’s unexpectedly coolest capitals.

Japan, Italy, and Turkey ranked second, third, and fourth, respectively, followed by Portugal, Costa Rica, and Croatia in fifth, sixth, and seventh places. Indonesia and Kenya ranked eighth and ninth, while Thailand rounded out the top 10.

Costa Rica and Kenya made the top 10 list for the first time. India ranked 17th with a score of 92.11, placing it in the top 20 best countries in the world.

Source: Condé Nast Traveller

headline: Saudi Arabia strikes Yemen capital as Houthis vow to retaliate
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.

The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten the kingdom, Yemen and international waterways.

It said the Iran-aligned group was using the sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar to "supply its arsenal of missiles and drones" to attack Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

YPC said the facility did not currently hold any stocks of petroleum products and that targeting it did not affect oil reserves or supply chains.

However, the Houthis had earlier threatened a "harsh and painful" response to any strikes on Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.

The group renewed earlier warnings it had issued to oil workers in Saudi Arabia, telling them to stay away from sites that could be potential targets.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia for a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Hormuz Strait leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.

While a government offensive aimed at driving back the Houthis beginning a week ago pushed them off the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains of its own around the city of Taiz this month.

Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, the Turkish presidency said.

Turkey and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, though Turkey still needs to ratify the treaty in parliament.

US President Donald Trump also spoke to Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, he told reporters, adding that the Houthis were "behaving very badly".

He said he may ask Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.

Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic starting on February 28.

Iran, Riyadh's longtime arch regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan and Yomna Ehab; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne and Cynthia Osterman)

body_text:
The war between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalated further on Tuesday, as both sides traded threats against oil installations.

The coalition announced that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including Al Sabahah station in the capital Sanaa and piers used for loading fuel at the port of Hodeidah.

Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said the Houthis had been using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals.

Airports forced to review security as missile and drone threats rise

He added that the operation had been focused on neutralising the Houthis’ ability to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the Red Sea and international shipping lanes.

Earlier in the day, the coalition had urged civilians to leave Al Sabahah, owned by the Yemen Petroleum Company, before what it described as a “special operation”. The order was published on social media by Maj Gen Al Malki, alongside a map of the area.

In response to the strikes, the Houthis announced that oil installations in Saudi Arabia would be considered legitimate targets and that any civilians working at those sites should stay away.

The coalition also said it had intercepted three missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia on Monday evening and yesterday. One of the projectiles was aimed at Riyadh, while the others were heading towards the city of Khamis Mushait, Maj Gen Al Malki said.

In the past weeks, Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure, including a strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday that left 13 people dead and 308 injured.

However, although the attacks have disrupted travel and forced schools in Riyadh to switch to remote learning, the city’s roads remained crowded yesterday, offices were open and sporting events took place as planned, residents told The National.

“The usual traffic is there. The streets are full of cars,” said Christina, a Lebanese citizen who lives in the Saudi capital.

“I’m working from the office and the roads look completely normal on my way to work.”

Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi yesterday, during which he pushed for an immediate halt to all attacks on Saudi Arabia, his ministry said in a statement.

Mr Abdelatty was quoted as saying that there could be no justification for the attacks.
