headline: Saudi Arabia strikes Yemen capital as Houthis vow to retaliate
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Tuesday after a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts, part of a rapidly escalating war between the sides.

The Houthis have for a week been targeting Saudi airports, including a strike on Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people, in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten the kingdom, Yemen and international waterways.

It said the Iran-aligned group was using the sites in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar to "supply its arsenal of missiles and drones" to attack Saudi Arabia and commercial vessels in the Red Sea.

YPC said the facility did not currently hold any stocks of petroleum products and that targeting it did not affect oil reserves or supply chains.

However, the Houthis had earlier threatened a "harsh and painful" response to any strikes on Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.

The group renewed earlier warnings it had issued to oil workers in Saudi Arabia, telling them to stay away from sites that could be potential targets.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia for a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Hormuz Strait leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.

While a government offensive aimed at driving back the Houthis beginning a week ago pushed them off the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains of its own around the city of Taiz this month.

Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan told Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday that Ankara would stand by the kingdom, the Turkish presidency said.

Turkey and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia this summer, though Turkey still needs to ratify the treaty in parliament.

US President Donald Trump also spoke to Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, he told reporters, adding that the Houthis were "behaving very badly".

He said he may ask Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.

Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic starting on February 28.

Iran, Riyadh's longtime arch regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan and Yomna Ehab; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne and Cynthia Osterman)

body_text:
The war between the Saudi-led coalition and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels escalated further on Tuesday, as both sides traded threats against oil installations.

The coalition announced that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including Al Sabahah station in the capital Sanaa and piers used for loading fuel at the port of Hodeidah.

Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki said the Houthis had been using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals.

Airports forced to review security as missile and drone threats rise

He added that the operation had been focused on neutralising the Houthis’ ability to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen, the Red Sea and international shipping lanes.

Earlier in the day, the coalition had urged civilians to leave Al Sabahah, owned by the Yemen Petroleum Company, before what it described as a “special operation”. The order was published on social media by Maj Gen Al Malki, alongside a map of the area.

In response to the strikes, the Houthis announced that oil installations in Saudi Arabia would be considered legitimate targets and that any civilians working at those sites should stay away.

The coalition also said it had intercepted three missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia on Monday evening and yesterday. One of the projectiles was aimed at Riyadh, while the others were heading towards the city of Khamis Mushait, Maj Gen Al Malki said.

In the past weeks, Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi attacks on civilian infrastructure, including a strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Saturday that left 13 people dead and 308 injured.

However, although the attacks have disrupted travel and forced schools in Riyadh to switch to remote learning, the city’s roads remained crowded yesterday, offices were open and sporting events took place as planned, residents told The National.

“The usual traffic is there. The streets are full of cars,” said Christina, a Lebanese citizen who lives in the Saudi capital.

“I’m working from the office and the roads look completely normal on my way to work.”

Meanwhile, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi yesterday, during which he pushed for an immediate halt to all attacks on Saudi Arabia, his ministry said in a statement.

Mr Abdelatty was quoted as saying that there could be no justification for the attacks.

summary: Houthi media reported an ​attack ‌by Saudi Arabia on ⁠the ‌Yemen Oil Company ⁠in Sanaa on Tuesday, which came ‌shortly after the ‌Saudi-led coalition ​ordered the evacuation of the ​facility ​ahead of ​a military ​operation. Issued on: 13/10/2026 - 16:53Modified: 13/10/2026 - 18:18

Houthi media reported that Saudi Arabia struck an oil facility near Sanaa on Tuesday, after the Saudi-led coalition ordered civilians to evacuate the site.

An AFP correspondent in Sanaa reported hearing an explosion, while a breaking news alert on the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV said "Saudi aggression targets the oil company in Al-Sabaha, west of Sanaa".

The Saudi-led coalition had previously signalled an imminent attack, warning civilians in the surrounding area to get out.

Yemen's Houthi-run health ministry also said two people were killed in a separate event, when an oil company in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah was attacked, and blamed Saudi Arabia for the strike.

There was no ​immediate ​Saudi ​confirmation.

Read moreFrench embassy in Riyadh tells citizens to avoid Saudi airports targeted by Houthis

After a series of attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports and oil facilities, it was the first time the coalition battling the Houthis has issued an evacuation order for Yemen's Sanaa since their war flared up again in July.

The coalition demanded "that civilians evacuate the site of the Yemen Petroleum Company, the al-Sabaha Central Station in Sanaa... for their own safety", said spokesman Turki al-Maliki on X, referring to a site on the western outskirts of the capital.

The Houthis issued a swift warning that a strike would be met with a "tough and painful response", telling employees to evacuate Saudi oil giant Aramco facilities and threatening to hit Riyadh's international airport, which they struck several times in the past week.

An attack there on Saturday left 13 people dead, rocking the world's top crude oil exporter and deepening the war in Yemen, where it backs the internationally recognised government.

Read moreSaudi Arabia threatens 'decisive' response after Riyadh airport strike kills at least 12

The kingdom was still weathering fresh attacks on Tuesday, with the coalition saying its forces intercepted three drones north of Riyadh.

Many countries have since issued travel warnings to their citizens in Saudi Arabia, most recently France, which told its citizens to avoid the airports in Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam on Tuesday.

US President Donald Trump also spoke to Mohammed bin Salman on Tuesday, he told reporters, adding that the Houthis were "behaving very badly". He said he may ask Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests.

The Saudi coalition has supported Yemen's government militarily since 2015, in a long-running civil war against the Houthis that has created a deeply entrenched humanitarian crisis in the impoverished country.

headline: Africa: Rwanda Set to Welcome Formula One Back to Africa, 30 Years Later
summary: [New Times] Frenchman Alain Prost claimed the last of his four Formula One world championships at the Kyalami Circuit near Johannesburg, South Africa, in 1993, the last time the continent hosted a Grand Prix. The event's subsequent collapse brought Formula One's presence in Africa to an abrupt end.
body_text:
Frenchman Alain Prost claimed the last of his four Formula One world championships at the Kyalami Circuit near Johannesburg, South Africa, in 1993, the last time the continent hosted a Grand Prix. The event's subsequent collapse brought Formula One's presence in Africa to an abrupt end.

More than three decades later, Africa is preparing for a likely return to the sport's calendar, with Rwanda securing a 10-year partnership to host a Grand Prix, with the inaugural race projected for the early 2030s.

South Africa and Morocco have also been linked to efforts to bring Formula One back to the continent, but Rwanda's agreement marks a significant step towards making that ambition a reality.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

For Rwanda, however, the proposed Grand Prix is beyond motor racing. The government sees it as an opportunity to attract investment, boost tourism, create jobs and develop technical skills, while positioning the country as a regional hub for business and international sporting events.

During an exclusive interview with The New Times, Sports Minister Nelly Mukazayire said Rwanda viewed the agreement as a responsibility to the wider continent, with the potential to open new opportunities for African talent and businesses.

"The excitement of F1 had been for so long left out of Africa, and Africans are known to be good fans," she said, describing the partnership as a long-term commitment whose benefits should be felt beyond Rwanda.

With Africa's population estimated at around 1.3 billion, much of it young, Mukazayire said bringing Formula One back would offer opportunities to expand participation in a sport that has largely been absent from the continent for decades.

The announcement follows President Paul Kagame's declaration at the FIA Awards in Kigali in 2024 that Rwanda was bidding to host a Formula One Grand Prix.

ALSO READ: Kagame says Rwanda's bid to host Formula 1 Grand Prix 'progressing well'

Why Rwanda secured the deal

According to Rwanda Development Board (RDB) Chief Executive Officer Jean-Guy Afrika, the country's experience in hosting major international sporting events was among the factors that strengthened its bid.

Rwanda has hosted several high-profile competitions and gatherings, including the Basketball Africa League (BAL), the 2025 UCI Road World Championships, the FIFA Congress and the FIA Awards.

Afrika said the country had demonstrated its ability to organise large-scale events while presenting a broader vision that links the proposed Grand Prix to tourism, infrastructure and economic development.

"I think there are several reasons why F1 ended up choosing Rwanda. It's not the first time that we organise a large-scale sporting event. We've already shown an ability to execute and deliver large-scale events here in Rwanda," he said.

"The second one was probably vision, and it was very clear when we started bidding for the event to happen here that it was bigger than just F1 itself and was part of a larger project that ties with the airport and driving tourism," he added.

The government is pursuing the project through a consortium involving public institutions, private-sector partners and technical specialists, working alongside Formula One and the Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA).

Afrika also emphasised that Rwanda's selection should not prevent other African countries from pursuing opportunities to host the sport in the future.

"We very much welcome other countries joining and placing bids and competing for Formula One," he said.

A huge boost for tourism

The planned Grand Prix will be presented by Visit Rwanda, extending the country's strategy of using international sports partnerships to raise its profile and attract visitors.

The tourism brand has partnered with prominent sporting organisations, including English football clubs Arsenal and Bayern Munich, French side Paris Saint-Germain, Spanish club Atlético de Madrid, the NBA's Los Angeles Clippers and the NFL's Los Angeles Rams. Rwanda has also been involved in the Basketball Africa League.

ALSO READ: Hamilton, Verstappen welcome Africa's potential return to F1 calendar

Afrika described Formula One as a natural extension of the strategy, offering access to a global audience while creating opportunities to attract more international and African tourists.

"It's a continuation of the strategy to use sports to increase the country's visibility and drive inbound tourism. The strategy has been very successful," he said.

According to Afrika, Rwanda recorded $685 million in tourism receipts in 2025 and is targeting $1.9 billion in 2026.

He said the Grand Prix would support efforts to grow tourism by attracting visitors beyond the race itself, with opportunities to promote Rwanda as a destination for leisure, business and other sporting activities.

More than 100 million Africans follow Formula One, according to figures cited by Afrika, with approximately 60 per cent of the audience aged below 35.

"The idea is to continue to use Visit Rwanda, which is presenting the F1 race, to drive tourism to the country and, in this particular case, not only global tourism but also African tourism," he said.

The size and age profile of the audience, he added, make the continent an important market for Formula One as it seeks to expand its reach.

Bugesera airport city at the centre of investment plans

Rwanda expects the Grand Prix to stimulate economic activity across hospitality, construction, transport, logistics, retail, financial services and real estate.

Afrika said the event should be viewed as a long-term investment rather than expenditure on a single race, with potential returns extending across the wider economy.

"It's an investment. It's not an expenditure for a single event. And it's a long-term investment with several ways in which we expect returns to come back to the economy," he said.

A key part of the plan is the development of Bugesera International Airport and an airport city around the facility. The proposed commercial hub is expected to accommodate logistics operations, hotels, apartments, restaurants and other businesses serving travellers and investors.

According to Afrika, the new airport is expected to increase passenger-handling capacity from about one million to more than five million, creating additional opportunities for businesses serving international arrivals.

He said the Grand Prix could amplify the economic potential of these developments by generating demand for accommodation, transport, food services, retail and other activities.

"Hotels, restaurants, retail outlets, but also logistics, because when tourists visit, they have to be able to move. Financial services, because there will be a lot of transactions happening," he said.

Construction is also expected to benefit as Rwanda develops the infrastructure needed for the race, including access roads and facilities for teams, officials, spectators and other visitors.

Beyond existing businesses, the government hopes the event will encourage new investors to establish operations around the airport city.

"We also expect it to drive new investments, not just for existing investments and hotels and hospitality to benefit, but for new investments to come in," Afrika said.

He added that new businesses could create jobs, expand the tax base and increase government revenue available for infrastructure and social and economic development.

However, the scale of those benefits will depend on how effectively Rwanda attracts investors and converts the expected increase in demand into sustainable business activity.

Preparing for a decade of racing

Under the agreement, Rwanda expects to host a Grand Prix annually for 10 years, with the first race projected for the early 2030s.

Mukazayire said preparations would extend well beyond the construction of a racing circuit, requiring investment in transport, accommodation, restaurants, entertainment, operational systems and the workforce needed to deliver the event.

She acknowledged that hosting Formula One would be a major undertaking but said Rwanda would draw on its experience in organising international competitions and seek expertise from across Africa and beyond.

"Our target is to make sure that we run an African Grand Prix that represents long-term value for Rwandans and for Africa," she said.

The government's ambition is to integrate the race into a wider ecosystem of infrastructure and services, ensuring that investments made ahead of the inaugural event continue to support economic activity throughout the partnership.

Afrika said the new infrastructures in Bugesera including the airport and other amenities that are part of the Airport City supporting will be important elements of that broader vision, with Formula One expected to help increase demand for the facilities and services being developed.

Creating opportunities for young Rwandans

Beyond tourism and investment, the government wants the Grand Prix to support local talent development and create career opportunities in motorsport.

Mukazayire said the initiative aligns with Rwanda's sports strategy, which prioritises talent development, increased participation and employment.

She noted that motorsport encompasses much more than professional driving, offering opportunities in engineering, mechanics, vehicle technology, technical support and event management.

ALSO READ: F1 in Rwanda: A gateway to opportunities for African youth

The government also envisages establishing a motorsport academy to help young Rwandans develop the skills needed to participate in the industry.

"We're being intentional in giving an opportunity to an African or a young Rwandan to also enter into that sport," she said.

"There is a place for a young Rwandan in this motorsport, whether it's behind the wheel, whether it's crafting the wheel or even running the event," she added.

The expected economic activity could also create employment in hospitality, construction, transport, retail and financial services, opening opportunities for people whose skills are not directly related to racing.

For Africa more broadly, the return of Formula One could provide a platform to develop technical expertise, strengthen participation in motorsport and connect local talent with the global industry.

Rwanda's challenge will be to translate the agreement into tangible benefits through infrastructure development, investment, training and job creation.

As preparations move forward, the government is betting that the Grand Prix can become more than a sporting spectacle, serving as a catalyst for tourism, business expansion and the development of motorsport in Rwanda and across Africa.

headline: New White House spokesperson says US$54 bln tied to Alaska gas project in S. Korean investment package
summary: WASHINGTON, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- New White House Press Secretary Katie Zachariah ...
body_text:
WASHINGTON, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- New White House Press Secretary Katie Zachariah said Tuesday that US$54 billion was tied to an Alaska liquefied natural gas (LNG) project as part of a South Korean energy investment package, despite uncertainty over Seoul's participation in the project.

Zachariah made the remarks during her first official press briefing at the White House while highlighting the South Korean energy investment package worth up to $200 billion that U.S. President Donald Trump announced earlier this month.

"President Trump also unveiled a South Korea energy investment package of up to $200 billion in the United States. This is an amazing deal. This includes as much as $120 billion to build eight large-scale nuclear power plants," Zachariah said.

"In addition to that, there is $54 billion tied to the Alaska LNG pipeline and terminal to service the Pacific Rim and sell fuel to our allies as well as $22.3 billion for a 6-gigawatt natural gas power facility in Texas."

Following Trump's announcement, South Korea's industry ministry, however, said the Alaska project had not yet been finalized, stressing that its commercial viability and other factors would need to be reviewed before any investment decision is made.

headline: ‘My president… sorry, my husband’: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia’s awkward debut
body_text:
Katie Zacharia, US President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary, made an awkward beginning to her first press briefing on Tuesday, briefly confusing her boss with her husband while answering a question about balancing the demanding job with raising four children.

Zacharia, who succeeded Karoline Leavitt after she left the role in August, appeared before reporters for just 14 minutes, taking questions from three news outlets before abruptly ending the briefing.

The Independent reported that the mix-up happened when a reporter asked Zacharia how she would manage family life along with the responsibilities of being White House press secretary. Leavitt had cited the demands of the job and her desire to spend more time with her children when she announced her departure.

“The idea of not spending evenings with my kids is completely unacceptable, so my president… excuse me, my husband, is out here,” Zacharia said, which prompted laughter in the briefing room.

Katie Zacharia slips up: My president– Excuse me, my husband. That’s a good one. Ha ha ha https://t.co/RTacfHXDVL

She then attempted to recover with a joke, saying, “That’s a good one,” before returning to praise for Trump and his decision to appoint her for the role.

Zacharia said her family would move to Washington, DC, from California. She also argued that Trump’s willingness to appoint a mother of four demonstrated his support for working women with families.

News agency Associated Press reported that Zacharia began the briefing with a prepared statement highlighting Trump’s policies on energy, tariffs and immigration, as well as his campaign appearances ahead of the November midterm elections.

She described her role as an opportunity to amplify the president’s agenda.

I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she told reporters.

She said Trump was “his own best spokesperson”. She took her first question from right-wing outlet Breitbart News, and committed to retaining the expanded media rotation introduced by Leavitt to bring more outlets into White House briefings and the press pool.

But her debut was brief. She ended the session by telling reporters they could ask Trump their questions as he prepared to leave the White House aboard Marine One.

In fact, I am going to end it because President Trump is heading out to Marine One for our historic trip to Alaska, and we can ask him all the questions out there,” she said.

The Independent reported that Trump was not scheduled to depart for Alaska for several hours.

headline: Palestinian officials say Israeli army wounds two in Ramallah raid
summary: Israeli army fire wounded two Palestinians on Tuesday during a raid in the city of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian health ministry. A hospital in the city received "a young man with a serious gunshot wound to the lower back and a 14-year-old with a live bullet wound to the upper thigh, in addition to numerous cases of suffocation, as a result of the (Israeli army) assault on Ramallah", the ministry said.
body_text:
Israeli army fire wounded two Palestinians on Tuesday during a raid in the city of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, according to the Palestinian health ministry.

A hospital in the city received "a young man with a serious gunshot wound to the lower back and a 14-year-old with a live bullet wound to the upper thigh, in addition to numerous cases of suffocation, as a result of the (Israeli army) assault on Ramallah", the ministry said.

The army raided the former headquarters of the Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, seizing documents and furniture, according to AFP journalists who witnessed and filmed the scene.

Israel had closed the organisation's office in August 2022 along with six other Palestinian NGOs and civil society groups after designating them "terrorist organisations".

Photos and video footage taken by AFP on Tuesday showed Israeli soldiers moving furniture, office equipment, and folders out of the office and onto a trailer attached to a military vehicle.

The army also reaffixed its order for the organisation's closure on the front door of the premises.

Israeli forces were deployed in the neighbourhood for nearly four hours, fired tear gas and stun grenades toward a group of reporters, and wounded four of them, according to AFP journalists and eyewitnesses.

The Israeli army did not immediately respond to AFP's request for comment on the operation.

In a separate incident on Tuesday, four Palestinians from the same family were injured after settlers stormed their home in the village of Talfit, south of Nablus in the northern West Bank, according to a medical source and a family member.

Youssef Abu Aisheh, 43, told AFP that settlers knocked on his door presenting themselves as soldiers, then entered his home and assaulted him, his wife, and their seven children.

"They banged on the door violently and said they were soldiers, and when I opened the door I was shocked to find they were settlers wearing jeans, vests, and black masks, and carrying clubs," he said.

As a result of the assault, his daughter suffered a broken leg, his wife a deep head wound, while he and another daughter were bruised, Abu Aisheh said, adding that the Israeli police did not respond to his request for help.

The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said that it transported the wounded to a clinic in the nearby town of Qabalan.

Violence in the West Bank, which has been occupied by Israel since 1967, has escalated in parallel with the war in the Gaza Strip, sparked by Hamas's attack on October 7, 2023.

Attacks by settlers against West Bank Palestinians have become a daily occurrence in recent months, including physical assaults, crop theft and the vandalisation of houses, places of worship, and vehicles.

Attacks against Israelis have also been recorded, including a Palestinian gunning down an Israeli settler near Ramallah last month.

In a statement on Tuesday, the Israeli army announced that it had foiled an attack in the northern West Bank.

"Four Islamic Jihad terrorists who were planning to carry out a terror attack... were apprehended," the army said.

The army added that it had arrested a wanted man in the town of Beit Rima near Ramallah on suspicion of arms trafficking.

Excluding east Jerusalem, about three million Palestinians live in the West Bank along with more than 500,000 Israelis residing in settlements, considered illegal under international law.

headline: Israeli army arrests 30 Palestinians as occupiers assault family in occupied West Bank
summary: Israeli occupiers wearing army uniforms assault Palestinian family in Talfit, leaving several injured
body_text:
The Israeli army rounded up 30 Palestinians in military raids across the occupied West Bank on Tuesday, while occupiers assaulted a Palestinian family near Nablus, leaving several people injured.

The Prisoners’ Media Office said Israeli forces carried out widespread raids involving searches of homes and the conversion of one house into an interrogation center.

The arrests were concentrated in the northern Nablus province, where 15 Palestinians were detained in the village of Tell, 12 in Asira al-Shamaliya and another in Talfit, the office said.

Israeli forces also raided several homes in Asira al-Shamaliya and turned one into an interrogation center.

Another Palestinian was arrested in Tubas in the northeastern West Bank and one more in Hebron in the south after Israeli forces raided and searched their homes, the same source said.

Separately, several Palestinians were injured early Tuesday when Israeli occupiers wearing military uniforms attacked a family in Talfit, south of Nablus, according to local sources.

The sources told Anadolu that the occupiers, disguised as Israeli soldiers, knocked on the door of the home of Yusuf Munawwar Abu Aisha before severely beating him and members of his family.

Several family members sustained injuries and bruises and were taken to a hospital.

The Israeli army simultaneously raided several Palestinian homes in the village, according to the same sources.

Two more Palestinians were also injured when Israeli occupiers assaulted them while they were harvesting olives in the town of Beit Lid near Tulkarem in the northern West Bank.

The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said its teams treated two Palestinians injured after being beaten by Israeli occupiers on agricultural land in Beit Lid during the olive harvest.

Israeli army raids and attacks by occupiers against Palestinians and their property have intensified across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.

body_text:
Apple has introduced HomeView, a device that the company says incorporates artificial intelligence-driven Siri and an easy-to-use interface to help people at home.

A video posted to Apple's website and social media accounts shows a busy family in the kitchen one morning using the device to answer questions, communicate with others and set reminders.

“Siri, ping me my keys,” a woman asks HomeView as she tries to leave her home. The HomePod speaker causes her keys to give off a beeping noise, presumably with the help of Apple's AirTag.

In the video and on the HomeView webpage, Apple says the product is only “available in English to start”.

The company says HomeView will be available on November 13 with prices starting at $299. Two options will be available: a device that rests on surfaces and a version that mounts on a wall.

Before Apple's HomeView announcement, Anshika Jain, principal analyst for the technology market analysis firm Counterpoint, said that such a device would help the US technology giant strengthen its consumer product offerings.

“The upcoming display-based device could become a central interface for controlling smart home products, accessing content and services, and interacting with Apple’s AI capabilities, potentially giving Apple a stronger foothold in the smart home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said.

Apple also seems prepared to allow devices made by other companies to work with HomeView.

“Designed in collaboration with Apple and select brands, Apple Home Collection accessories – including smart cameras, thermostats and a door lock – are simple to set up, easy to use, and private with data that’s encrypted end-to-end in Apple Home,” the company posted to its site. It added that the collection of devices would arrive at a later date.

Mohit Agrawal, research director with Counterpoint, said that this aspect was intriguing.

“Rather than buying its way in, as Amazon did with Ring and Google with Nest, Apple is partnering with LG and Schneider Electric,” he explained.

“This lets it fill out the home quickly, from the front door to the thermostat, while keeping control of the experience through Siri and the Home app.”

Apple seems to be positioning the forthcoming HomeView product as a device that is used passively in day-to-day life.

“HomeView does the heavy lifting when you’re busy around the house,” a description reads. “And with a vibrant display and powerful acoustics, your music, videos and calls look and sound amazing … meet the new heart of your home.”

According to technology news outlet, The Verge, HomeView will be initially available in the US, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, South Africa and India.

Also on Tuesday, Apple announced its HomePod mini speaker devices would be getting an upgrade.

“Siri on HomePod mini 2 puts a powerful, AI assistant right at the centre of your home,” the company said. “Once set up with your iPhone or iPad, Siri draws on broad world knowledge and your personal context to help you find what you need and get more done every day.”

The HomePod 2 will be available on October 30, with prices starting at $149.

Apple touts improved sound, touch controls, a mesh design and a woven power cord among the HomePod's improvements.

“With Apple Intelligence and a more capable Siri, the company is positioning HomePod as an entry point into an AI-powered home ecosystem,” Ms Jain said.

“Still, shipment growth is likely to remain modest in low single digits YoY [year over year] as the market continues to face saturation and longer replacement cycles.”

Apple's TV console has gone several years without an update, but that changed on Tuesday with the unveiling of Apple TV 4K.

The company says the updated console has an A19 processor that assists in delivering 4K video quality, and it will also have a Siri remote.

Apple TV 4K will be available on November 13, with prices starting at $299.

“Apple TV 4K delivers the ultimate cinematic experience, from shows and movies to games and workouts,” the company said. “With the new, more powerful Siri AI and built-in microphones, enjoying what you love is as easy as using your voice.”

headline: Apple debuts HomeView, a smart display powered by Siri AI; new HomePod Mini 2 and Apple TV 4k
body_text:
After much anticipation, Apple has unveiled its latest lineup of devices for the home. On Tuesday, October 13, the iPhone maker introduced HomeView, a seven-inch smart display powered by Siri AI. Designed to serve as a shared household screen, it becomes personalised the moment someone steps in front of it. Apple also announced the HomePod Mini 2, Apple TV 4K, and a range of smart home accessories called the Apple Home Collection.

Apple said the new products are built around three core principles: they must be intelligent, personal, and private.

HomeView is Apple’s latest home-focused device that has been built for entertainment, staying in touch with loved ones, and managing the smart home. It features a seven-inch Liquid Retina Display meant to be glanced at from anywhere in a room. It comes in silver, starlight, rose pink, and space grey colours. Further, users can customise the display with favourite photos, weather updates, and animations of their choice. The key feature here is how HomeView adapts to whoever is using it. The device recognises people by face and switches from a shared household view to a personalised one, showing calendars, messages, and reminders. Apple said that the data is not stored on HomeView; rather, it is pulled from the user’s iPhone and vanishes from the screen the moment the person walks away, ensuring that the next user sees their own information.

Siri AI is central to HomeView. It sits at the core of HomeView and draws on personal context from the user’s iPhone. A demo video showed a family using it to find a recipe a parent had texted, check the calendar, and manage a chaotic morning. The examples of everyday use included asking when to leave for a meeting or whether there is a Starbucks at the user’s airport terminal, with the device already aware of the flight details on the user’s phone. Apart from an array of intelligent features, the HomeView also plays music, podcasts and TV. It supports FaceTime calls, shows recipes while users cook, and controls smart home accessories. Apple has also introduced a wall-mounted version with the same display and features, along with an audio experience that is tuned for wall placement.

Apple said that FaceTime is a standout feature on HomeView. The device uses Centre Stage, which pairs an ultra-wide camera with on-device algorithms to track where a person’s torso is. This means if a user is cooking in the kitchen and moving around, the camera pans to keep them in frame. When more people join the call, it widens the shot to fit them. Apple said it put considerable thought into the FaceTime experience so it would work well on a device that stays in one place.

Apple emphasised that privacy is at the core of all its products, and HomeView was designed with privacy in mind. For HomeView specifically, the camera and microphone feeds are secured and processed within exclaves, which are compartmentalised, protected runtimes separate from the operating system. They can’t be accessed by anyone, including Apple. Consequently, to access personal content, a user needs to have been recognised by HomeView, have their iPhone on the same Wi-Fi network, and have recently unlocked it. In case HomeView determines that it cannot recognise a user for any reason, the user will get a confirmation on their phone.

HomeView is compatible with iPhones running on the latest iOS. Both the tabletop and wall-mounted models will be priced at Rs 39,900. Pre-orders will begin on October 13 with availability from November 1 in eight countries: Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, and the US. The device will ship with English as the primary language for now, but more languages will be added soon.

Apple has introduced the new HomePod Mini 2 in blue, green, and pink alongside the existing white and midnight options. A notable addition to the new generation of HomePod Mini is a feature called Sound Glow that makes the light on the top of the speaker glow in colours similar to those of the album art of the song being played. The colours are soft and not meant to pop out, and users also have the option to disable it. Besides, the HomePod Mini 2 can also be connected to a Mac and serve as its audio output for everything from video calls to games. During the demo, Apple showed a HomePod Mini colour-matched to an iMac.

Now, with Siri AI, the speaker can handle broader knowledge questions, offer greater music discovery, and use a paired iPhone for personal context, such as updating events to a shared family calendar for everyone to stay in sync. The new HomePod Mini 2 is priced at Rs 18,900, with pre-orders beginning on October 13 and sales starting on October 30 across regions where HomePod is currently sold. Meanwhile, Siri AI will come to the speaker in a future software update in the same eight countries in English.

After nearly four years, Apple has finally introduced its latest generation of the Apple TV 4K. The new Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room. Now, users can ask for recommendations of shows and movies. Besides, the device also features far-field microphones that allow hands-free voice control. With personal context from the iPhone, users can simply play a song their friend texted them or ask for a show a friend recommended, and it starts playing. Another interesting feature is that users can now ask Siri where the remote is, and Siri Remote will play a sound. It also supports Find My with Precision Finding. Apple said that users can connect up to four compatible HomePod speakers to the new Apple TV 4K to experience surround sound that automatically calibrates to the room. According to Apple, this is one of the easiest ways to set up a home theatre.

Apple TV 4K’s far-field microphones allow users to sit comfortably and talk directly to Siri without the need to get up and fetch the remote. Users can ask queries about the shows, movies, and sports playing on the screen, and Siri AI responds with a non-obstructive text bubble in real time. Exclusive to this device, the Apple TV 4K comes with the ability to have a home theatre surround sound experience. During the demo, Apple TV 4K was paired with four HomePod speakers – two in front and two at the back – and the device delivered high-quality sound. The device automatically calibrated the audio levels to perfectly tune according to the ambience.

The new Apple TV 4K is priced at Rs 39,900, with pre-orders starting from October 13 and availability from November 13 in regions where Apple TV is sold. Siri AI will arrive on Apple TV in beta in the same countries – Australia, Canada, India, New Zealand, the UK, and the US, in English to start.

Apple has also introduced the Apple Home Collection, a range of accessories built by LG Electronics and Schneider Electric and designed in collaboration with Apple. The lineup includes an indoor camera, an outdoor camera, video doorbell, door lock, thermostat and sensors. The indoor camera tilts down automatically when the user arrives home, for added privacy, while the outdoor camera offers an optional floodlight that brightens gradually when motion is detected. While the video doorbell recognises who is at the door, the door lock unlocks automatically as the user approaches by sensing an iPhone or Apple Watch. Meanwhile, the thermostats and sensors adjust through the day to balance comfort and energy savings.

The cameras are HomeKit video cameras that spot familiar faces, packages and pets, with video history stored in iCloud. Setup for these devices happens through the iPhone, with no extra apps or new accounts, and all communication is end-to-end encrypted.

The cameras will be available in the US, Canada and the UK. The thermostats and door lock, designed to North American standards, will launch in the US and Canada. Availability begins in December. Apple said this collection will not launch in the regions where Home View is available, so it is likely irrelevant to buyers there.

The author is in New York at the invitation of Apple.

Bijin Jose serves as an Assistant Editor at Indian Express Online in New Delhi. A seasoned technology journalist with a diverse portfolio, he brings over a decade of experience in the media industry to his coverage of the evolving digital landscape and emerging technologies. Experience & Career Bijin commenced his journalistic journey in 2013 as a citizen journalist with The Times of India. His career trajectory includes significant tenures at prestigious media organizations including India Today Digital and The Economic Times. This diverse professional background, ranging from legacy print institutions to dynamic digital platforms, culminated in his current leadership role at The Indian Express, where he helps shape the publication's technology narrative. Expertise & Focus Areas Bijin has transitioned from general reporting to a specialized focus on the intersection of technology and humanity. His key areas of expertise include: Artificial Intelligence: deeply tracking developments in AI, providing nuanced perspectives on its ethical,industrial, and societal implications. Tech Commentary: moving beyond product specifications to analyze how technology reshapes daily life. Diverse Reporting Foundation: draws upon a robust background in crime reporting and cultural features to bring a human-centric approach to technical storytelling. Authoritativeness & Trust Bijin’s editorial voice is informed by a strong academic foundation, holding a Bachelor of Arts in English from Maharaja Sayajirao University, Vadodara, and a Master of Arts in English Literature. This literary background enables him to deconstruct complex technical jargon into accessible, compelling narratives. The Iranian deputy foreign minister said that Tehran has always maintained a constructive approach toward diplomacy and negotiations, while remaining prepared for any possible scenario.

headline: (2nd LD) 8 injured in knife attack in Incheon; Lee calls for thorough probe
summary: INCHEON, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- Eight people were injured after a man went on a sta...
body_text:
(ATTN: UPDATES throughout with details; RECASTS headline, lead; ADDS photo)

INCHEON, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- Eight people were injured after a man went on a stabbing spree in a commercial complex in Incheon, west of Seoul, on Tuesday, police said.

The 59-year-old man attacked people with knives fastened to both his hands at 1:40 p.m. while moving on an escalator between the second basement floor -- where a Homeplus supermarket is located -- and the second floor above ground, according to Namdong Police Station.

The man was subdued by shoppers and later apprehended by police officers, who were questioning him in custody.

All eight victims were rushed to hospitals, including a woman in her 20s in cardiac arrest. The woman recovered from cardiac arrest after undergoing emergency surgery but has not regained consciousness.

Police plan to seek a warrant for the suspect's formal arrest Wednesday after questioning him about his motive.

The suspect was found to be carrying a large quantity of drugs and wearing an electronic ankle monitor for a previous conviction, police said.

He reportedly told police that he had taken drugs at the time of the attack.

The suspect had been ordered to wear an ankle monitor for 10 years, until February 2029, after serving a four-year prison term in 2019 for attempting to murder his former wife.

Later in the day, President Lee Jae Myung visited the Incheon Metropolitan Police Agency to receive a briefing on the incident and called for a thorough investigation, the presidential office said in a written briefing.

Lee ordered officials to come up with "special" measures against violent crimes that threaten the people's daily lives, according to Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations and communication.

Lee also called on officials to mobilize all resources to prevent violent crimes and swiftly respond to them, while ordering a thorough examination of the management system for those wearing ankle monitors.

The justice ministry apologized over the incident, saying that it will investigate the management of its electronic ankle monitor system.

"(We) deeply apologize for causing great concern to the public," the justice ministry said. "(We) will comprehensively reexamine the electronic monitoring and supervision system and swiftly come up with necessary improvements and supplementary measures."

Kim Jong-chul, acting chief of the National Police Agency, instructed police to conduct a swift and thorough investigation into the attack in a virtual meeting with police agency chiefs across the country.

He also ordered strengthened preventive measures against violent crimes by deploying sufficient police personnel in crowded public places.

headline: US envoy says next UN Secretary General should be chosen on merit, not rotation or gender

body_text:
US President Donald Trump’s special envoy for global partnerships said on Tuesday that the next UN Secretary General should be chosen on merit rather than regional rotation or gender, as these are “political traditions” rather than “legal rules” under the UN Charter.

“The world should choose the best person for the job – based on merit, reform and results,” Paolo Zampolli said on social media. “After 18 years at the United Nations, I believe this is a moment to think bigger about the future of the institution.”

The Security Council is to select a successor to Secretary General Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31.

The Trump administration has so far kept its preferences private, leaving uncertainty over who it might support in a contest that has drawn seven candidates, including Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina’s Rafael Grossi.

Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan has emerged as the front-runner, but her support has shown signs of weakening.

In the fifth round of informal straw voting on October 7, Ms Grynspan received nine “encourage” votes and six “discourage” votes, with no council members expressing “no opinion”. That was a setback from the previous round, on September 29, when she won 10 votes in favour, three against and two with no opinion.

To secure the post, a candidate must win at least nine votes in the Security Council without a veto from any of its five permanent members – the US, Britain, France, Russia and China.

The selection process has long been shaped by unwritten diplomatic conventions, including the expectation that the post should rotate among the world’s regions.

Since 1946, the position has been held by leaders from Europe, Asia, Africa and Latin America, although no formal rotation system exists.

The organisation has also never been led by a woman in its 81-year history, despite repeated calls from member states for more women's representation.

The final decision rests largely with the Security Council’s five permanent members, each of which can block a candidate regardless of how much support that person has.

“The UN Charter only offers limited guidance about the process for selecting a new UN Secretary General. It requires the Security Council to recommend an individual for the General Assembly to appoint to the role,” said Daniel Forti, head of UN affairs at the International Crisis Group.

Much of the process, he said, had evolved through changes to council procedures and agreements with the General Assembly.

The expectation of regional representation developed through decades of diplomatic practice and non-binding General Assembly resolutions.

A 1997 General Assembly resolution called for regional rotation and gender to be taken into account when selecting a secretary general, while a 2015 resolution encouraged member states to nominate women. Neither resolution is legally binding.

Another long-standing convention has excluded citizens of the five permanent Security Council member states from the post, reflecting concerns that a major power could exert undue influence over the institution.

“Many other factors, whether the demand for regional rotation, the push for the UN to select its first woman secretary general, or commitments about the SG not being a P5 national, are all informal conventions,” Mr Forti said. "They are not binding on the Security Council even if they weigh heavily in the court of public opinion."

The veto is a different matter.

“The UN Charter is indirect, but unequivocal, about the permanent members’ veto privileges in the Secretary General selection process,” Mr Forti said. “No one questions that the recommendation of a new UN leader is a substantive decision, so the permanent members’ veto authorities are inconvenient but undisputed.”

headline: UK ambassador summoned to Iran’s foreign ministry
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – The British ambassador to Tehran, Hugo Shorter, was summoned to Iran’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday over baseless allegations by senior British officials linking Tehran to an alleged incident at RAF Fairford military base.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – The British ambassador to Tehran, Hugo Shorter, was summoned to Iran’s Foreign Ministry on Tuesday over baseless allegations by senior British officials linking Tehran to an alleged incident at RAF Fairford military base.

Alireza Yousefi, assistant foreign minister and director general for Western Europe at Iran’s Foreign Ministry, conveyed the Islamic Republic’s strong protest against what he described as Britain’s irresponsible and destructive approach toward Iran.

Yousefi categorically rejected the British government’s allegations against Iran, stressing that British officials could not evade accountability and their international responsibilities by deflecting blame and making unfounded accusations against Tehran.

He said Britain remained responsible for its participation in the US and Israeli military aggression against Iran, as well as for its long-standing hosting of anti-Iranian terrorist groups and elements.

Condemning Britain’s irresponsible actions as part of what he described as an anti-Iran campaign, Yousefi said such conduct was entirely inconsistent with the British government’s international legal obligations.

He stressed that the British government must provide, without delay, documents and evidence supporting its allegations against Iran concerning the alleged incident at RAF Fairford. Otherwise, the Islamic Republic would seriously reconsider bilateral relations, he warned, adding that the British government would bear responsibility for the consequences.

The British ambassador said he would convey Iran’s position to the officials in his country.

headline: US to have so many POWs in Iran in case of ground invasion
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the commander-in-chief of IRGC, said the United States would have so many troops captured if it launched a ground invasion of Iran, which would force it to surrender.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the commander-in-chief of IRGC, said the United States would have so many troops captured if it launched a ground invasion of Iran, which would force it to surrender.

In comments published on Tuesday, Naqdi said that Iran’s armed forces have the capabilities needed to respond to threats and that their decisions and calculations should be trusted, as military operations and their timing are determined by strategic considerations and national interests.

Naqdi dismissed the prospect of a US ground invasion, saying that even in highly private American meetings, the subject might not have been discussed at all.

He said the United States talked about a ground invasion in its media messaging but had not even discussed it privately or whispered about it among themselves because, in his view, American officials understood the consequences.

Naqdi questioned why any rational decision-maker would contemplate a ground invasion of Iran after those experiences. “If they spent $3 trillion or $4 trillion there and their wars lasted 20 years, what would happen here, where the war would not even last 20 days?” he said.

He added that US forces would be captured in such large numbers that Washington would be forced to surrender and raise the flag of surrender.

Naqdi reiterated that he did not believe US officials had even held preliminary discussions about a ground invasion, arguing that they knew they could not carry it out.

body_text:
A bipartisan group of US senators on Tuesday called on President Donald Trump to rescind his deal allow Russian diesel exports, saying it will prolong the Ukraine war and put at risk the lives of American troops in the Middle East.

Mr Trump last week said that during a call, Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets.

The deal comes amid growing domestic political pressure on Mr Trump to lower diesel prices, caused by supply constraints during the Iran war and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, before the November 3 midterm elections.

US-Russia energy deal opens up diesel can of worms

A letter signed by 12 senators, including former Republican senate leader Mitch McConnell, said granting Moscow the ability to freely sell diesel damages American security interests.

It "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war. This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies. It should be rescinded", the letter reads.

They also claim that Mr Putin will use the money to help Iran's war effort against the US.

US intelligence sources, senior European officials, the UK government and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have accused Russia of helping Iran. US media reports, quoting officials, have said Moscow provided Tehran with information on American military assets in the region.

The deal "will have a negligible impact on fuel prices, but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance its security co-operation with China, Iran and North Korea. It will also endanger service members operating overseas in support of Operation Epic Fury".

Mr Trump on Monday acknowledged that Russia and China may be helping Iran "at a very low level" but said he does not "believe" they are.

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said Mr Putin has failed to respect a purported truce on energy infrastructure attacks.

"Zelenskyy has agreed. Putin continues bombing. Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool and hoping to weaponise a freezing, starving, bloody winter against Ukraine," Mr Blumenthal said on X.

The Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Last month, Congress passed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which allows Mr Trump and future American presidents to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major importers of Russian energy meeting specified criteria.

The US Treasury Department has issued a special exemption as part of Mr Trump's deal with Mr Putin, but some elected officials have questioned the legality of that special licence.

And a 2022 law prevents the US importing Russian energy unless a president consults with Congress and observes a 90-day waiting period.

“Congress was clear: the US should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our Nato allies," a different group of senators wrote in a statement at the weekend.

headline: Zelenskyy tells NPR Ukraine wants peace but will hit Russia until it follows ceasefire
summary: In an interview with NPR, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he was informed the U.S. warned it could cut off access to U.S. weapons and intelligence, but that it hasn't happened yet.(Image credit: Svet Jacqueline for NPR)
body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy speaks with NPR in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Tuesday. Svet Jacqueline for NPR hide caption

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukraine remains focused on ending the war with Russia that has lasted nearly five years and continues to view the United States as a reliable partner, despite rocky relations with the Trump administration, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told NPR Tuesday.

Zelenskyy said his military generals told him they'd received the message that they could lose access to U.S. weapons and intelligence, but that it hasn't happened yet.

Asked whether the U.S. had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, Trump told reporters Tuesday: "We are helping them and we are sharing intel, we want the war to end."

Zelenskyy said he wants the war to end too but Ukraine will keep striking Russia's war machine unless there is a ceasefire respected by both sides. Russian President Vladimir Putin doesn't respond to diplomacy, the Ukrainian leader said, "he understands force."

Zelenskyy also said he found out about President Trump's claim that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire "through social like you" — meaning, from Trump's post on his Truth Social account on Sunday.

Zelenskyy's sit-down with NPR comes at a time of renewed tensions with the White House. On Friday, Trump moved to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, blindsiding Kyiv. Zelenskyy called it a "a weak decision by strong partners." Trump lashed back over the weekend saying, "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," a leader who would reach a peace deal with Putin.

Then on Sunday, Trump announced on social media a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure — catching Kyiv by surprise again — even as Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure continued.

All this comes as Trump continues to tout his relationship with Putin, raising fresh questions about the future of U.S. support for Ukraine — and the direction of Washington's approach to ending the war.

Asked what he thinks about Trump blaming Ukraine for the high cost of diesel, Zelenskyy said most people "know why their prices on any kind of energy, including diesel, raised up, why they increased. Because of Hormuz. Yes. Because of blocking the Strait of Hormuz."

He said Trump's decisions to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel would not influence "the price in the United States. I'm sure … because the volume is not enough."

But he said the move would provide the Kremlin with more money to spend on its war.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

summary: WASHINGTON, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea is gaining experience in deploying t...

WASHINGTON, Oct. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea is gaining experience in deploying troops and sustaining military operations over long distances through its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, the commander of U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) said Tuesday.

U.S. Gen. Xavier Brunson made the remarks during a dialogue hosted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, highlighting the military benefits Pyongyang has gained from deploying troops and supplying weapons to support Moscow in the war.

"They've learned how to go from North Korea to find themselves in Russia to move men, weapons and equipment there, as well to build supply lines that would allow them to support the Russian war effort," Brunson said when asked about the experiences Pyongyang gained through its participation in the conflict.

Brunson stressed that North Korea's military has gained experience in strategic movement, mobilization and logistics, allowing it to develop capabilities that extend beyond tactical lessons learned on the battlefield.

The commander warned that North Korea's military is becoming increasingly capable of incorporating battlefield experience into its forces, posing new challenges for South Korea and the United States in maintaining deterrence on the Korean Peninsula.

He also highlighted the military equipment North Korea has received from Russia in return for supporting its war effort, including electronic warfare jammers.

In June 2024, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a comprehensive strategic partnership treaty, under which North Korea has deployed troops and provided conventional weapons to support Russia's war with Ukraine.

On the envisioned transfer of wartime operational control (OPCON) from Washington to Seoul, Brunson reiterated his support for a conditions-based transition, stressing the importance of meeting agreed military requirements before proceeding with the handover.

"I am in full support of OPCON transfer that is conditions based, full stop," he said.

"At the end of the day, if my president, if my secretary of war tell me, 'Execute right now,' I go, 'Yes, but here are the risks inherent in doing this without having fully met the conditions, securing the critical capabilities that are necessary.'"

On South Korea's defense industry, Brunson praised its advanced manufacturing capabilities and highlighted the potential for greater cooperation in maintaining and repairing U.S. military equipment in the region, rather than sending it back to the U.S. for maintenance.

"We could develop things in Korea that we would then apply across the region," he said, envisioning a regional maintenance, repair and overhaul hub that could leverage South Korean industrial capabilities to support U.S. military operations across the Indo-Pacific.

headline: Iran mum as Azerbaijan’s school hijab ban, Israel ties test alliance with Turkey
summary: Azerbaijan’s restrictions on Islamic dress in schools have sparked an unusual public spat with Turkey, exposing tensions beneath the allies’ close political and security ties.

Tensions between the ruling parties of Turkey and one of its closest regional allies, Azerbaijan, continued to escalate on Tuesday over Baku’s effective ban on Islamic-style outfits for pupils and teachers in state-run schools, amid ongoing protests against the rules across the energy-rich former Soviet Turkic state.

The New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), led by the country’s strongman President Ilham Aliyev, took sharp aim at Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s top adviser, Oktay Saral, on Tuesday over comments he made on social media describing the hijab as a “requirement of faith” and calling on Baku to “reverse this mistake as soon as possible.”

Saral’s remarks followed an outcry among Islamic activists in Turkey in response to viral footage of tearful Azerbaijani female students and their parents slamming the changes, which were introduced through a government decree issued in mid-September. Similar restrictions for teachers followed on Oct. 6. “The right to education should not be sacrificed to any ideological impositions,” Saral said in his Oct. 12 post on X, calling the measures “unacceptable.” It was a tipping point.

Aliyev’s party said it had exercised restraint thus far so as not to jeopardize the “historic bonds of friendship that unite the peoples of Azerbaijan and Turkey.” “However,” the party's statement continued, “the recent escalation of this information campaign targeting Azerbaijan, which has become more aggressive, systematic and openly defamatory, and in particular the involvement in it of a person holding the position of Chief Adviser to the President of Turkey and members of parliament from [Turkey’s] ruling Justice and Development Party, makes it necessary for us to state our position publicly.” Should the rebukes not stop, bilateral ties would suffer, it warned.

body_text:
Whoop's decision to provide an Arabic option on its platform is part of a broader commitment to the Middle East, its Egyptian-American chief executive Will Ahmed has said.

Arabic has joined English, French, German, Latin American Spanish, European Portuguese and Italian as languages available on the wearable fitness tracker company's app.

Mr Ahmed said the addition of Arabic was meaningful for him.

“My father is Egyptian and immigrated to the United States, and when I was younger I had the fortune of being able to travel with him throughout the Middle East,” he told The National.

“I think the first time I visited the UAE was when I was 14 or 15, and I’ve been coming back to the region ever since.”

He added that the Gulf was “our fastest-growing market globally” and said the company viewed the expansion of wearable use in the region as “a critical footprint for growth”.

“Launching the Whoop experience in Arabic is part of our wider commitment to residents of the GCC, giving native speakers access to personal health insights in the language they use every day,” Mr Ahmed said.

Though some technology companies have struggled to implement the nuances and diversity of Arabic, Mr Ahmed said that Whoop spent a lot of time working closely with Arabic-speaking members to ensure that the launch would be seamless.

“Their feedback helped us identify where we could improve and get the details right,” he said.

The Arabic language option will be rolled out gradually and will be available in the most recent version of the company's app.

Whoop's co-founder also said he viewed the region as quick to embrace the idea that technology can empower people to take care of their health. His Boston-based company shares that vision, he added.

“Our continued commitment to the GCC comes from a deep respect for the leadership in the region and what they’re trying to accomplish,” he said.

On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the Arabic option with a video posted to its social media accounts showing users throughout the Middle East working out while wearing Whoop devices.

“Yallah!” posted Mr Ahmed as he shared the video.

He launched Whoop in 2012 into a crowded wearable technology market. The company has grown steadily, amassing a loyal following, particularly among professional athletes.

In a recent interview with The National, Dr Ami Bhatt, who joined Whoop as its first chief medical officer in July, said she was encouraged to see that more women across the Middle East were turning to the company's devices as a way to better understand their health.

“Across the GCC, female member growth has increased more than 90 per cent year-over-year, with strong growth across every market we track,” she said.

Her comments about the Middle East echoed the sentiments of Mr Ahmed, who in August said the fitness-tracker company would open a second office in the UAE, calling the move “critical for growth”.

In March, Whoop announced $575 million in funding from a group of international investors led by Abu Dhabi and Qatari sovereign wealth funds.

The Series G round was led by three Gulf investors: Mubadala Investment Company, 2PointZero Group and the Qatar Investment Authority.

Whoop partners with fitness initiatives such as the Dubai Fitness Challenge and Doha Marathon. It also “serves as the official health and performance wearable” of UAE Team Emirates-XRG and Al Nassr Football Club.

The company was at the centre of controversy during this year's Australian Open when officials made tennis players, including Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner, remove their Whoop devices.

“Data is not steroids,” Mr Ahmed posted on his X account in protest.

In April, Mr Ahmed hailed announcements that Whoops can be worn in the French Open, Wimbledon and US Open.

headline: Trump says Houthis trying to drive up oil prices ahead of US midterm elections
summary: By Jacob Bogage and Nandita BoseWASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi militants of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and warned that he would "never forget" their attacks on Saudi Arabia, amid a widening regional conflict fueled by the US war with Iran."The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, accusing the group of resuming attacks at Iran's behest after a period of relative quiet following US strikes in Yemen last year.
body_text:
By Jacob Bogage and Nandita Bose

WASHINGTON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Tuesday accused Yemen's Houthi militants of deliberately trying to drive up oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections and warned that he would "never forget" their attacks on Saudi Arabia, amid a widening regional conflict fueled by the US war with Iran.

"The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post, accusing the group of resuming attacks at Iran's behest after a period of relative quiet following US strikes in Yemen last year.

Trump also made clear that his warning would extend beyond the November 3 midterm elections, saying, "I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!"

The warning followed a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport that have killed at least 13 people, wounded more than 300 and forced the closure of the airport.

Earlier on Tuesday, Trump told reporters he "might" ask Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan to intervene in support of Saudi interests. "President Erdogan, I think, would do as I ask," Trump said.

The Houthis, who control large parts of Yemen, have been fighting the Saudi-backed Yemeni government in a civil war since 2014. The conflict has intensified amid the eight-month US-Iran war, with the group escalating attacks on commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait.

The renewed attacks have raised concerns about disruptions to global oil supplies and shipping routes, threatening to push energy prices higher.

(Reporting by Jacob Bogage and Nandita Bose; editing by Michelle Nichols)

headline: In Yemen's Taiz, shelling worsens and prices spiral
summary: Oct 13 (Reuters) - With their city encircled by Houthi fighters, residents of Taiz say they face intensifying bombardment and dwindling supplies as the Iran-aligned group tightens its grip on surrounding areas.Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has emerged as a major theatre of the conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, after their war was reignited last month by the U.S.-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.The Houthis cut off a main road from Taiz to Aden last week, leaving government forces encircled.
body_text:
Oct 13 (Reuters) - With their city encircled by Houthi fighters, residents of Taiz say they face intensifying bombardment and dwindling supplies as the Iran-aligned group tightens its grip on surrounding areas.

Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has emerged as a major theatre of the conflict between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government, after their war was reignited last month by the U.S.-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.

The Houthis cut off a main road from Taiz to Aden last week, leaving government forces encircled.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said the situation in Taiz had significantly deteriorated in recent days, and that people, basic supplies and humanitarian goods could not enter the city, driving up prices.

Yemen's internationally recognised government launched a campaign last week to recapture areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a global shipping artery.

But the Houthis have kept up the pressure near Taiz, seizing the town of Mudiriyat al-Misrakh some 25 km (15 miles) south of the city on Monday, military sources said.

Residents reported heavy shelling of Taiz city on Monday night.

Government sources said the Houthis were to blame.

A spokesperson for the Houthis did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"We lived a night of terror because of the continuous bombardment," said Ahmed Mahmoud, a resident reached by phone. "This morning there is calm and worry. The streets are empty."

Yassine Muqbil, another Taiz resident contacted by phone, said there had been widespread shelling and his child was too afraid to go outside.

Taiz city had an estimated population of almost 600,000, Katja Juric, IOM's Aden-based Head of Programmes, told Reuters. Government sources said 80,000 had fled in the latest fighting.

Military sources reported fighting in al-Dabab, 10 km (6 miles) from Taiz, and on Sabar Mountain, which overlooks the city to the south, saying government forces who had withdrawn from surrounding areas had regrouped in the city.

Yemeni government warplanes targeted Houthi fighters and equipment in Dabab and Misrakh, government forces said in a statement on Tuesday.

For the Houthis, seizing Taiz city would be a big boost 12 years since the war first erupted. It would leave oil-rich Marib as the last city under government control in northern Yemen.

Mohammed Al-Qadhi, a political and conflict analyst, said Monday evening's heavy shelling and the “tight siege” imposed by Houthi fighters indicated increasing pressure on the city.

"The Houthis know the value of Taiz governorate," he said, noting that its countryside overlooks the coastline and Bab el-Mandeb and that it had served as a bastion of "resistance against the Houthis and their ideology".

The Yemen war erupted in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south.

Fearful of growing Iranian influence and ​chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis in early 2015 to restore the government.

The resulting civil war triggered one of the world's biggest humanitarian crises and led to years of fighting and devastating airstrikes by the Saudi-led coalition.

The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that maintained peace until this year.

In Taiz city, prices of basic goods have shot up.

"By God, we know families who cannot find their daily food," resident Nashwan Saad said on Sunday, adding that a sack of wheat had gone up by as much as some 40%.

IOM's Juric said access to Taiz city had been "significantly constrained", noting that a small bottle of water now cost up to $4. "The prices of basic commodities that are still available in the city have gone up significantly," she said.

"People are rushing to purchase and to stockpile basic commodities as they're anticipating a prolonged conflict and also further supply disruptions in the city."

Abdulrahman al-Qulaia, director general of the Ministry of Industry and Trade Office in Taiz, cautioned against panic.

"We appeal to the entire international community concerned with this matter, to humanitarian organisations and civil society organisations, to work seriously to provide these needs ... and lift the siege on the province."

(Additional reporting by Zainab Elhaj in London and Tom Perry in Beirut; Writing by Tom Perry; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)
