body_text:
UAE universities must overhaul their courses and teaching methods to keep pace with artificial intelligence and the rapidly changing demands of the jobs market, the acting Minister of Higher Education and Scientific Research has said.

Dr Abdulrahman Al Awar called for closer collaboration between universities and industry. He warned that emerging technologies were transforming the skills employers require and creating an urgent need to rethink how students are taught.

He was speaking at the Zayed Education Foundation’s Partnerships for the Future event, in Abu Dhabi, where 12 institutions came together to strengthen collaboration and expand opportunities for home-grown scholars.

UAE minister: teachers vital to learning in the age of AI

“Economies and job markets are undergoing a radical and rapid change, and it is happening at a very rapid pace,” Dr Al Awar said. “New technologies, including artificial intelligence, are creating new opportunities and changing the skills that the market needs.

“Fundamental changes must happen in engaging higher education institutions and economic sectors and redesigning the curricula and the skills of both faculty and students.”

He said the ministry’s Outcome-Based Evaluation Framework was challenging universities to meet those demands and become more competitive in shaping the future of higher education in the UAE.

“The UAE vision for higher education is centred on creating a vibrant higher education ecosystem that is future-ready, globally competitive and connected to the needs of our students, our economy, and our society,” he said.

An updated guidebook for the framework was released earlier this year following consultations involving 735 representatives from higher education institutions across the country.

Change has not just been called for from the top, but also by students. The National spoke to two Ruwwad Zayed Scholars about their hopes for the future of higher education.

Noor Odeh, a UAE resident from Jordan, is a member of the first cohort of the masters scholars and is studying computational data science at Khalifa University. She scrapped her plans to study at an Australian university to stay in the UAE.

“I want to be a changemaker. So it's not just the degree that I got excited about when I was accepted [for the scholarship]. It was more that will get to do something for my community because I will receive guidance,” she said.

She believes the future of higher education will rely on hands-on experiences and skills rather than grades and metrics.

“We need to put less focus on numbers like GPA [grade point average], and more about the skills that you're learning. What has helped me the most was not just the knowledge that I got from my degree, but the skills that I gained,” Ms Odeh said.

Fellow Ruwwad Zayed Scholar Jassem Alkhoori is studying digital transformation at Zayed University. He agrees that higher education needs to be agile and keep pace with technological development.

“I think currently the education system follows guidelines that are very outdated. Now that AI is actually overtaking most simple tasks such as screening papers, I think there should be more education on how to use these tools to help with research,” he told The National.

The push for a competitive higher education sector has accelerated in recent years and has taken major steps since the founding of the country's first university, the United Arab Emirates University, 50 years ago.

Zayed Education Foundation hopes to create opportunities for 100,000 students by 2035 and recently announced the first cohort of 50 Ruwwad Zayed Scholars – exceptional Emirati and Arab students who will pursue master’s degrees at universities in the UAE.

Saeed Al Nazari, secretary general of the Great Arab Minds initiative – which recognises and empowers exceptional Arab scholars, scientists and innovators – told The National that the talented minds from the region must be nurtured.

“With whatever happening around us – conflicts, news, social media, AI – sometimes we even forget to look up to our people in this region who are doing brilliant stuff,” he said.

“This region has always been part of the momentum to move educational research forward globally. The good thing is that we have so many people who are willing to invest in knowledge economy. We just sometimes need to connect the dots.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the story around a top-down call for UAE higher education reform to meet AI-era job market demands, balanced with supportive student and official voices, and presented in a promotional, progress-oriented tone.

loaded_language.explanation: The adjective 'exceptional' is a subjective, praise-laden descriptor that editorializes the quality of the scholarship recipients rather than stating a neutral fact.
This colloquial, emotionally positive phrase is vague and evaluative, used by a quoted source to praise regional achievements without specific detail.
The intensifier 'very' combined with 'outdated' is a strong, subjective characterization of the education system, presented as a student's opinion but framed as a clear deficiency.
The word 'radical' is emotionally charged and suggests dramatic, possibly disruptive transformation, amplifying the sense of urgency beyond a neutral description.
These are aspirational, buzzword-style terms that promote a positive vision without concrete metrics, functioning as promotional language.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: prepared for future needs and internationally competitive

omissions: No mention of potential challenges, criticisms, or downsides of the proposed overhaul, such as implementation costs, faculty resistance, or risks of over-focusing on AI at the expense of other disciplines.
No alternative viewpoints from education experts or stakeholders who might question the pace or direction of reform.
No specific details on how the Outcome-Based Evaluation Framework will be enforced or what consequences universities might face for non-compliance.
No mention of the broader geopolitical or economic context that might be driving the urgency, such as global AI competition or regional instability.

corrections.reason: The 70/30 split is an arbitrary numeric estimate not directly derivable from the article text; no objective method is provided to ground this ratio.

headline: Housekeeper cleared of stealing Jordanian princess’s jewels
summary: A long-serving housekeeper has been found not guilty of stealing expensive jewellery from her employer, a Jordanian princess.A jury in London took less than two hours to clear Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, of theft.She had been accused of stealing several items from the home in Belgravia when Princess Firyal, 81, flew to Jordan at the outbreak of Covid in 2020.Princess Firyal was married to Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, from 1964 to 1978.She had told Southwark Crown Court that she had been alerted that items from her jewellery collection were missing when a jeweller friend called to tell her they had appeared for auction in Canterbury. The items included a custom-made sapphire and diamond ring.The court heard police found Princess Firyal’s wedding ring, a pair of earrings and a necklace during a search of Ms Taborda Henao’s home in Fulham. The princess thought the wedding ring had been lost years earlier.Ms Taborda Henao, who is from Colombia and had worked for Princess Firyal for 11 years, told the court, through a Spanish interpreter, that the princess had called her a thief and made similar accusations against other people. Ms Taborda Henao’s nephew, Julian Ramirez, was said to have acted as a conduit for the sale of the items. He was also arrested but fled to Colombia in October 2023 while on police bail.
body_text:
A long-serving housekeeper has been found not guilty of stealing expensive jewellery from her employer, a Jordanian princess.

A jury in London took less than two hours to clear Maria Virgelina Taborda Henao, 71, of theft.

She had been accused of stealing several items from the home in Belgravia when Princess Firyal, 81, flew to Jordan at the outbreak of Covid in 2020.

Princess Firyal was married to Prince Muhammad bin Talal, the younger brother of King Hussein of Jordan, from 1964 to 1978.

She had told Southwark Crown Court that she had been alerted that items from her jewellery collection were missing when a jeweller friend called to tell her they had appeared for auction in Canterbury. The items included a custom-made sapphire and diamond ring.

The court heard police found Princess Firyal’s wedding ring, a pair of earrings and a necklace during a search of Ms Taborda Henao’s home in Fulham. The princess thought the wedding ring had been lost years earlier.

Ms Taborda Henao, who is from Colombia and had worked for Princess Firyal for 11 years, told the court, through a Spanish interpreter, that the princess had called her a thief and made similar accusations against other people.

Ms Taborda Henao’s nephew, Julian Ramirez, was said to have acted as a conduit for the sale of the items. He was also arrested but fled to Colombia in October 2023 while on police bail.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a straightforward acquittal report, presenting the verdict, the accusation, and key court evidence in a matter-of-fact sequence without advocating for either side.
omissions: The housekeeper's defense arguments or explanation for why the jewelry was found in her home
Any statement from Princess Firyal or her representatives after the verdict
The specific charges or counts the jury deliberated on
The judge's instructions or any comments made by the judge during the trial
The exact date of the verdict or the trial's duration
Any information about whether the nephew, Julian Ramirez, is still at large or facing extradition

corrections.reason: The listed omissions include items that are not clearly absent from the article or are not standard omissions for a short acquittal report. For example, the article does mention the defense's explanation (the princess called her a thief and made similar accusations against others), and the nephew's flight to Colombia is stated. Other items like judge's instructions or post-verdict statements are not necessarily expected in a brief news report and their absence does not constitute a meaningful omission.

headline: IMF projects Gulf rebound in 2027. Can energy production keep pace?
summary: Restoring shipping access in the Strait of Hormuz is only part of the recovery, as Gulf producers also need to repair damaged infrastructure to avoid further disruption to production and exports.
body_text:
The International Monetary Fund forecast a downturn in Middle Eastern economies this year as the war that began in February continues to disrupt activity, according to its report released Tuesday. However, it expected the region to rebound next year, provided the Strait of Hormuz reopens by March 2027.

Details: The economies of the Middle East and Central Asia, which the Washington-based institution groups as one region, are forecast to contract by 0.3% in 2026, a sharp downgrade from the 1.9% expansion the IMF projected in April. The IMF cited the prolonged disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for one-fifth of global oil supplies in peacetime, for the downgraded outlook.

Kuwait, Iraq and Qatar face the most severe contractions in gross domestic product, at 16.7%, 16% and 15.6%, respectively. Bahrain is forecast to shrink by 11.3%.The United Arab Emirates' economy is expected to contract by 3.9% this year before rebounding at a 7.7% growth rate in 2027.

Saudi Arabia is projected to contract by 3.3%, having partly offset the hit to its energy sector by boosting oil exports through the East-West Pipeline. In 2027, the kingdom's GDP is expected to rebound by 7.9%.

analysis.framing: The article frames the IMF's regional economic forecast around the Strait of Hormuz disruption and energy production recovery, emphasizing GDP contractions and rebound projections.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally emphasizes the magnitude of the revision beyond a neutral descriptor.
Intensifies the description of GDP declines with a dramatic adjective.
Colloquial and slightly dramatic phrasing for an economic impact.

omissions: No mention of the war's humanitarian toll or civilian casualties.
No discussion of global oil price effects or consumer impacts outside the Gulf.
No alternative economic forecasts from other institutions for comparison.

corrections.reason: The article is a factual report of IMF forecasts with no discernible political framing or ideological slant; a 'center' rating is plausible but not directly verifiable from the text alone.
The listed tone keywords are subjective interpretations not directly attributable to specific wording in the article.

headline: Germany scrambles jets after airline radio glitch sends false hijack alert
summary: FRANKFURT, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A flight from Greece to Germany landed safely in Nuremberg on Tuesday after a cockpit hijack alert that the airline attributed to a malfunction prompted the German air force to scramble two fighter jets.Corendon Airlines blamed a malfunction in the radio communication system and said that "no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger".
body_text:
FRANKFURT, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A flight from Greece to Germany landed safely in Nuremberg on Tuesday after a cockpit hijack alert that the airline attributed to a malfunction prompted the German air force to scramble two fighter jets.

Corendon Airlines blamed a malfunction in the radio communication system and said that "no emergency situation occurred and that at no point were the passengers, flight crew or aircraft in any danger".

The incident on the Boeing 737-800, which had departed from the Greek island of Corfu, forced a brief suspension of operations at Nuremberg Airport, the plane's scheduled destination, the airport said. Flight operations later returned to normal.

"From the cockpit, the code '7500' (hijacking case) was transmitted, and furthermore, the pilot could no longer be reached by radio. For safety reasons, various alarm scrambles were then triggered," German police said on X.

A German air force spokesperson said that two Eurofighter jets scrambled from Neuburg Air Base in southern Germany and accompanied the passenger jet until it landed.

Germany has two of those alarm squads, each with two fighter jets, to assess the situation when communication with civilian air crews is lost, which happens about once or twice a month, according to the air force's website.

The alert comes less than a month after the co-pilot of a jet bound for Israel from Dubai attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, with the United Arab Emirates' prosecutor general calling the incident a "terrorist attack".

Corendon, a Turkey-based leisure airline, said the emergency code had been transmitted while the jet was in Croatian airspace "due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system".

"The situation was immediately monitored, investigations were promptly initiated and all necessary preparations were made. The aircraft landed safely at Nuremberg Airport," it said.

A possible drone sighting had already disrupted air traffic at the airport overnight into Tuesday.

German authorities have been on heightened alert since a failed attack involving an explosives-laden drone at a German airport in August, which authorities blamed on Russia.

Russia has denied any involvement.

(Reporting by Ludwig Burger, Kirsti Knolle and Emanuele Berro; additional reporting by Gianluca Lo Nostro, Klaus Lauer and Thomas Seythal; Editing by Matthias Williams, Linda Pasquini and Alison Williams)

analysis.framing: The article frames the incident as a false alarm caused by a technical malfunction, while contextualizing it within a broader pattern of recent security scares in Germany.

loaded_language.explanation: The verb 'scrambles' is dramatic and typically used for urgent military responses, heightening the sense of emergency.
The word 'false' is a conclusion that may not have been fully established at the time of the alert, though the airline later attributed it to a malfunction.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: hijack alert later attributed to a malfunction

loaded_language.explanation: This phrase conveys a vague sense of ongoing threat without specifying concrete measures.
Quoting the UAE prosecutor general's characterization of a separate incident introduces emotionally charged language that may amplify the perceived threat level.

omissions: The number of passengers and crew on board the Corendon flight.
The duration of the flight operations suspension at Nuremberg Airport.
Any statement from German aviation authorities beyond the police tweet.
Whether the malfunction was specific to the aircraft or a broader system issue.

corrections.reason: The quoted phrase 'false hijack alert' does not appear verbatim in the article text. The article uses 'hijack alert' and 'false' separately (e.g., 'hijack alert' in the first paragraph, 'false' not directly modifying it). The analysis claims this as a quote, but it is not present as a contiguous phrase.

headline: Factbox-MI5 chief lists Iran, Russia, AI and terrorists among threats to UK
summary: LONDON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - MI5 spy chief Ken McCallum delivered his annual speech on Tuesday outlining his view of the threats to Britain, from hostile states such as Iran and Russia to the development of artificial intelligence.Here is a summary of the main threats and issues he detailed in his speech and subsequent questions from media:RUSSIA
body_text:
LONDON, Oct 13 (Reuters) - MI5 spy chief Ken McCallum delivered his annual speech on Tuesday outlining his view of the threats to Britain, from hostile states such as Iran and Russia to the development of artificial intelligence.

Here is a summary of the main threats and issues he detailed in his speech and subsequent questions from media:

McCallum called Russia, which denies involvement in hostile acts in Britain and other Western countries, "aggressor number one". He said it was escalating "hybrid" warfare, staying below the threshold that would trigger a direct NATO response.

He said Russia's capabilities had been reduced by the expulsion of 1,000 officials from embassies since the invasion of Ukraine, which meant it had to rely on native volunteers and criminal proxies.

Tehran is also using criminal proxies - to target opponents, Iranian media organisations and Israeli interests in Britain - and has expanded its hybrid campaign in the last year, McCallum said.

He said operations connected to Iran had yielded more than 50 arrests in the UK, and that many had been aimed at Jewish communities.

The other shift had been "Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites", he said.

Tehran also rejects accusations of malign activity in Britain.

ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

McCallum said AI was "supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders", producing tailored propaganda and material for individuals.

MI5 has caught potential attackers using it to try to improve reconnaissance and attack methodologies. AI-enabled drones added a new challenge, he said.

McCallum said the greatest concern about the misuse of AI was terrorists developing bioweapons or even creating new pathogens.

AI also presented a risk in itself.

"Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are, is capable of out-thinking us. This is genuinely novel and deserves the serious attention it is getting."

Britain in April raised its national terrorism ​threat level to "severe", meaning an attack within the next six months is highly likely.

McCallum said Al Qaeda and Islamic State continued to inspire plots, and MI5 was still having to respond to attempts to carry out mass-casualty attacks.

He said the most marked trend of the last year had been the increase in cases where extreme anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievances were tipping over into terrorist intent.

An investigation into one 13-year-old who had been radicalised by extreme right-wing ideology had led to an unnamed foreign partner thwarting a lethal attack on its soil, he said.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Russia had interfered in Britain's 2016 referendum vote to leave the European Union, something Moscow has denied.

Asked about such interference, McCallum said it was public knowledge that Russian media such as Russia Today "came in pretty strongly around the time of the referendum", and there had been a certain amount of activity from trolls and bots.

But he said Russian online trolling had been comparatively unimpressive.

(Reporting by Michael Holden; Editing by Kevin Liffey)

headline: Saudi Arabia's strategic deadlock against Ansarullah
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – The recent attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the expansion of clashes on Yemen's fronts show that the security costs of Riyadh's regional policy continue to rise.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 13 (MNA) – The recent attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the expansion of clashes on Yemen's fronts show that the security costs of Riyadh's regional policy continue to rise.

After more than a decade of military intervention in Yemen, Saudi Arabia now faces a crisis whose consequences have gone beyond the battlefields and affected the security of vital infrastructure, international credibility, and Mohammed bin Salman's economic programs. The recent attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and the expansion of clashes on Yemen's fronts show that the security costs of Riyadh's regional policy continue to rise. These developments once again highlight a strategic reality: purchasing advanced weapons and relying on the support of foreign powers alone cannot create lasting security.

According to published reports, the attack on Saturday, October 10 on Riyadh International Airport left at least 12 dead and more than 300 wounded. Another attack on Sunday also left one dead and 11 wounded. Following these incidents, the airport's operations were disrupted and airlines canceled their flights. These Ansarullah attacks have raised questions about Saudi Arabia's defensive capability against missile and drone attacks.

The importance of these developments is not limited to the number of casualties or material damage. Riyadh Airport is one of Saudi Arabia's important communication hubs and the gateway for investors, international company executives, and foreign tourists into the country. Disruption in the operations of such a center can have consequences beyond the security domain and affect economic actors' confidence in the stability of the investment environment. This issue is doubly important for a country that, through the implementation of Vision 2030, seeks to reduce its dependence on oil revenues and become a regional hub for tourism, technology, and investment.

In recent years, Mohammed bin Salman has pursued major projects, including NEOM, with the aim of transforming Saudi Arabia's economic structure. However, the realization of such programs requires a stable environment, secure infrastructure, and investor confidence. When the capital's airport is targeted by attacks and airlines are forced to cancel their flights, the issue is not just the ability to counter a military attack; rather, the international credibility of a country that wants to present itself as a safe destination for business and tourism is also put to the test.

Foreign Support; Security Guarantee or Strategic Dependence?

One of the most important dimensions of Saudi Arabia's current crisis is the limitation of this country's reliance on foreign allies. Over the past decades, Riyadh has spent enormous sums on purchasing advanced weapons, air defense systems, and Western fighter jets. Despite this, recent attacks have shown that possessing advanced military equipment does not necessarily mean immunity against attacks. Defending a country's extensive infrastructure against combined missile and drone attacks requires operational readiness, sufficient stocks of interceptor missiles, an early warning network, and sustained counter-capability.

Under such circumstances, requesting help from allies to strengthen air defense can cover part of Saudi Arabia's immediate needs, but it will not be a substitute for a sustainable security strategy. There is a fundamental difference between selling weapons, exchanging intelligence, providing technical support, and direct entry into a military conflict. Western governments may support Saudi Arabia within the framework of their own interests, but this support does not necessarily mean accepting the costs of a long and high-risk confrontation with Ansarullah.

Washington's behavior also demonstrates the importance of this limitation. In 2025, after about 52 days of airstrikes against Ansarullah, the United States halted its operations with an agreement mediated by Oman. This agreement did not mean the destruction of Ansarullah's military capability, and the group's threats against shipping were not completely eliminated. Nevertheless, this experience showed that air superiority and firepower, without achieving specific political objectives, do not necessarily lead to a desirable strategic result.

Now, too, America's direct entry into the Saudi-Ansarullah conflicts can create new costs. The expansion of military operations, the consumption of interceptor missile stockpiles, and the possibility of intensified threats against shipping routes complicate Washington's calculations. Especially since regional developments and the continuation of the crisis between Iran and America have imposed additional pressure on Washington's military resources and strategic decision-making. Therefore, Riyadh cannot consider foreign support as a definitive guarantee for preventing attacks or winning a long confrontation.

The Return of the Costs of Intervention in Yemen

The root of Saudi Arabia's current deadlock must be sought in a policy that was pursued from 2015 with the aim of changing the balance of power in Yemen. The military intervention of the Saudi-led coalition and the participation of the UAE not only did not lead to the removal of Ansarullah from Yemen's political and military equations, but over the years created extensive human, economic, and security costs. Airstrikes, restrictions on the entry of goods, and the difficulty of people's access to food, medicine, and medical services have imposed heavy pressure on Yemeni society.

Now, with the renewed intensification of clashes, part of the consequences of this policy has returned inside Saudi Arabia. Developments on various Yemeni fronts, including around Taiz and the Red Sea coasts, have gained greater strategic importance. At the same time, the situation in the coastal areas and the vicinity of Bab al-Mandab can complicate Riyadh's security calculations. Of course, the control status of these areas on the battlefield is variable, and an accurate assessment requires reliable and up-to-date information.

Bab al-Mandab is one of the important passages of global trade and energy transfer. Any intensification of conflict in this region can increase maritime transportation costs and affect the security of trade routes. From this perspective, the Yemen crisis is no longer merely an internal matter or a dispute between Riyadh and Ansarullah, but has become linked to the security of the Red Sea, international trade, and the interests of regional and transregional powers.

From a political perspective as well, current developments show that military pressure alone cannot eliminate the will of an actor with deep roots in Yemen's internal equations. Over the past years, Ansarullah has been able to maintain its political and military structure despite extensive attacks and economic and military pressures, and to impose costs on its regional rivals. This reality does not necessarily mean the absolute superiority of this group or the end of Saudi Arabia's military capability; rather, it shows that achieving political objectives through the military path faces serious limitations.

The Way Out of the Deadlock

Saudi Arabia now faces two simultaneous pressures: on the one hand, the necessity of defending vital infrastructure and reducing vulnerability to attacks; on the other hand, the increasing costs of continuing intervention in Yemen and the difficulty of achieving a sustainable political result. The continuation of the cycle of attack and response may expand the scope of damages, threaten the security of maritime routes, and spend more resources on military costs instead of economic development.

The way out of this situation is not merely increasing weapons purchases or pinning hopes on the direct entry of foreign powers. Riyadh must accept that sustainable security on its southern borders will not be achievable without taking into account Yemen's political and social realities. Stopping attacks, reducing humanitarian restrictions, moving toward an inclusive political agreement, and accepting the determining role of Yemenis in determining their country's future can provide the ground for reducing tension.

The experience of more than a decade of intervention in Yemen has a strategic lesson for Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region: military power and foreign support cannot substitute for understanding the realities on the ground and a political settlement of differences. If Riyadh continues to tie its security to weapons purchases and the promises of foreign allies and refrains from reviewing its regional policy, the possibility of repeating costly crises will remain. Ultimately, relying on foreign powers without creating sustainable mechanisms for resolving regional disputes is, more than a guarantee of security, a kind of leaning on the wind.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Riyadh airport attacks as evidence that Saudi Arabia's reliance on military power and foreign allies has produced a strategic deadlock, arguing that only a political settlement accounting for Yemeni realities can bring sustainable security.

A poetic, editorializing metaphor that dismisses reliance on foreign powers as futile and unstable.

loaded_language.explanation: Elevates Ansarullah's local standing with sympathetic phrasing, implying legitimacy and resilience.

headline: King Felipe VI says Ceuta is ‘inalienable’ part of Spain in landmark visit
summary: King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta on Tuesday for the first time in 14 years, with the monarch reaffirming Spain’s sovereignty over the North African enclaves claimed by Morocco. The landmark visit comes amid strained relations with Rabat and the aftermath of a mass migrant influx that saw makeshift camps cleared ahead of the royals’ arrival.
body_text:
King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia visited Ceuta on Tuesday for the first time in 14 years, with the monarch reaffirming Spain’s sovereignty over the North African enclaves claimed by Morocco. The landmark visit comes amid strained relations with Rabat and the aftermath of a mass migrant influx that saw makeshift camps cleared ahead of the royals’ arrival.

Issued on: 13/10/2026 - 17:17Modified: 13/10/2026 - 21:13

Cheering crowds waving Spanish flags filled Ceuta on Tuesday as King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia made a diplomatically sensitive visit to the city following July's migrant influx from Morocco.

Their trip is the first royal visit since 2007, when a diplomatic crisis erupted with neighbouring Morocco, which claims sovereignty over Ceuta and Spain's other North African territory of Melilla.

Addressing civilians in Ceuta, the king said Morocco's relationship to Spain and the ‌EU must be grounded in respect, "while always adhering to the principle that Ceuta is Spain; Ceuta is Europe."

"Ceuta and Melilla are an inalienable part of the political and national reality that is Spain. The sovereignty and territorial integrity of our country are not negotiable," Felipe said.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

More than 70,000 migrants streamed into the small city of around 80,000 inhabitants in an unprecedented surge on July 30-31. Scores died.

Most returned to Morocco in the following hours, but thousands have remained for weeks in often dire conditions, sleeping rough in the streets or on the beach.

The crisis has angered locals and damaged Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez before a November 29 general election in which migration will feature prominently.

Felipe and Letizia greeted the well-wishers who thronged the streets, stopping to shake hands and exchange words with them en route to the city hall to meet local authorities.

Read more‘We won’t go back’: Young Moroccan migrants in Ceuta refuse to abandon their European dream

People raised their phones to take pictures of the royal couple, while some wore T-shirts bearing the slogan "Ceuta is not for sale. Ceuta must be defended".

Cristina Carrasco, a 50-year-old civil servant who waited all morning to see the royals, told AFP "it was a pleasure and a source of pride" to have shaken hands with Felipe.

"We all told him, 'don't forget us,' and he said, 'no, we won't forget you,'" recounted Carrasco, who felt "grateful and proud" about a visit that "we deserved".

Retiree Silvia Salmeron, 71, said the visit "was a breath of fresh air. I got goosebumps".

At the city hall, Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas thanked Felipe and Letizia for coming in "the most difficult moment of our recent history".

Ceuta is "a pressure cooker that could explode at any time", he said.

The authorities have set up thousands of places in temporary shelters and cleared the main camps on the beaches, but some migrants continue to live on the surrounding hills and the streets.

Read moreLast Ceuta migrant camp removed ahead of Spanish king's visit

Ana Maria Diaz, a 69-year-old pensioner, said the king should have come earlier to see the makeshift migrant encampments and visit the outlying areas of Ceuta where they concentrate.

"You don't see it here but if you go to the outlying neighbourhoods... it's terrible," Diaz, who was holding a Spanish flag, told AFP.

The government insists it must respect international law by assessing whether the migrants are entitled to asylum, while hundreds of unaccompanied children cannot be summarily deported.

The royals will visit a cemetery where they will pay tribute to the migrants who died – most by drowning as they tried to swim around a border barrier.

Felipe is also due to make a speech during a meeting with members of Ceuta's civil society before the monarchs travel to Melilla on Wednesday.

The visit comes at a particularly sensitive time for Spain's historically delicate relations with Morocco, as rumours swirl over the potential role Rabat may have played in the July rush.

Read more'No facts': Morocco denies involvement in deadly Ceuta migrant rush

The Spanish right has accused Morocco of orchestrating it for political motives, which Rabat and Sanchez have denied.

Moroccan King Mohammed VI broke his silence on Friday, condemning "the irresponsible statements made by certain political and media circles and their blatant instrumentalisation of the situation", in apparent reference to Spanish criticism.

On Monday, newspaper El Pais reported that Moroccan warships repeatedly entered Ceuta's waters during and after the rush in a rare violation of Spanish sovereignty.

Spanish government spokeswoman Elma Saiz confirmed but played down the report on Tuesday, speaking of "a one-off incident that was resolved in a completely normal manner".

(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

headline: Russia expects UN High Commissioner to be impartial on situation in Ukraine — diplomat
summary: According to Gennady Gatilov, in just one week, from September 28 to October 4, as many as 235 civilians were affected in shelling attacks by the Kiev regime
body_text:
GENEVA, October 13. /TASS/. It is becoming increasingly evident that UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk is unable to perform his job impartially and in good faith, Russian Permanent Representative to the UN Geneva office and other Geneva-based international organizations Gennady Gatilov said.

In a statement posted on the Russian mission’s Telegram channel, Gatilov highlighted Turk’s October 8 commentary on the situation in Ukraine, in which he groundlessly accused Russia. "I regret to state that, once again, we are witnessing your lightning-fast reaction’ once Ukrainian issues are involved and there is an opportunity to make baseless accusations against our country. At the same time, in your typical hypocritical manner, you mention crimes committed by the Ukrainian military against the Russian civilian population only in passing, in a single line," he noted, adding that Turk has once again failed to find the strength to "condemn the Ukrainian army’s terrorist attacks that are taking place practically every day."

According to the Russian diplomat, in just one week, from September 28 to October 4, as many as "235 civilians were affected in shelling attacks by the Ukrainian Nazis: 206 civilians were wounded, including 19 minors; 29 people were killed, including 2 children." Ukrainian militants deliberately hit trucks and a storage facility holding humanitarian cargoes from the International Committee of the Red Cross in Donetsk. Ukraine’s blockade of Aleshki continues, triggering a humanitarian crisis. "Time and again, we keep on pointing out to you that such a politically biased stance on the Ukrainian crisis on the part of a high-ranking UN official is unacceptable," Gatilov stressed.

"Your inability to fulfil your mandate objectively, impartially, and conscientiously is becoming increasingly evident to the international community. And this has confirmed that your appointment to this position by the UN General Assembly was flawed," he emphasized and called on the UN High Commissioner and his office "to finally stop indiscriminately whitewashing the bloody Kiev regime, to demonstrate genuine impartiality and independence, and to begin assessing the situation surrounding Ukraine objectively."

body_text:
Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, resigned on Tuesday amid accusations she had asked for favours from donors and others in exchange for influence.

The ​White ⁠House first announced President Donald Trump had asked her to step down, with new press secretary Katie Zacharia describing Ms Guilfoyle as “a ⁠wonderful ​asset to ​the ‌team”.

“From my first day as ambassador, I have worked tirelessly to advance President Trump’s America First agenda, strengthen our strategic alliance with Greece, and deliver meaningful victories for the American people,” Ms Guilfoyle said in a post on X following the announcement. She thanked Mr Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for their support.

It came a day after Mr Trump said his administration was scrutinising Ms Guilfoyle following allegations of unethical conduct, and reports he was considering removing her from the diplomatic post.

A Wall Street Journal report alleged that Ms Guilfoyle had solicited or accepted money or other benefits from private individuals while offering to use her influence and connections with administration officials to help further their interests.

Mr Trump's son, Donald Jr, had been engaged to Ms Guilfoyle before they broke up in 2024.

“Kimberly Guilfoyle was not a member of my family. I guess she dated my son a long time ago. I didn't like what I read,” Mr Trump told reporters outside the White House.

The newspaper reported that in one instance Ms Guilfoyle had asked a long-time Trump donor for $100,000 to help pay off an American Express credit card bill before her 2025 confirmation hearing in exchange for access to officials.

Ms Guilfoyle said that the allegations against her were false. Her lawyers have disputed key parts of The Wall Street Journal’s reporting. The US embassy in Athens told the newspaper she had followed State Department ethics and all gift-reporting requirements.

“I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional,” she said. “I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service.”

headline: The only path to lasting peace is a single, secular, democratic state of Israel-Palestine
body_text:
Earlier this month, the Green Party of England and Wales voted to declare Zionism a form of racism. The reaction was immediate and ferocious, well out of proportion for a party with only five MPs. Jewish groups condemned the motion as antisemitic. The Israeli government branded the Greens a body legitimising terrorism and banned its leader, who is himself Jewish, from entering Israel. Lost in the uproar was the truly significant wording hidden inside the resolution’s text. For the first time, a mainstream Western political party was calling ‘’for the establishment of a single democratic state throughout historic Palestine.” In short, a ‘’one state solution’’.

The conventional wisdom that has dictated international diplomacy, including India’s, for three decades — the two-state solution — is well and truly dead. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s repeated insistence that Israeli security leaves no room for Palestinian sovereignty merely stated aloud what 30 years of policy had achieved. With elections imminent, Israel’s political opposition has failed to present a clear or convincing mandate for Palestinian statehood. Public support for two states, low to start with, has collapsed — dropping to 17 per cent in recent Pew polling as security concerns continue to escalate three years after the October 7 Hamas attack and the devastating Israeli retaliation on Gaza.

The unworkability of a two-state solution goes beyond Israeli domestic politics. A separate Palestinian state, along the borders prior to the 1967 Six-Day War, is no longer viable. Anyone who has travelled through the West Bank knows that 30 years of expanding hilltop settlements, military outposts, restricted bypass roads, and dividing fences have fractured the territory into an absurd patchwork quilt of jurisdictions. You cannot build a coherent, sovereign state with a sustainable economy on a land so fragmented. Getting the 750,000-odd Israeli settlers in the occupied territories to relocate to Israel’s legal borders is well nigh impossible.

Israel cannot occupy Gaza indefinitely. It may have degraded Hamas militarily, but it cannot crush the humiliation and despair that feed Palestinian militancy. Continuing down this path will only cement Israel’s status as a global pariah.

As the Greens’ resolution proposes, the only available path to lasting peace is a single, secular, democratic state of Israel-Palestine with equal rights for all residents, Jewish and Arab alike. Persisting with the ideal of the two-state solution only prolongs an oppressive status quo.

Sceptics will point out that a one-state solution is highly unrealistic: Israelis and Palestinians are too deeply divided by decades of trauma to ever share a single country. But every other option is even more delusional. Ask Israelis: Would you prefer an armed, hostile neighbor on your doorstep, or full integration with 5.5 million Palestinians alongside the 2 million Arab citizens already living more or less peacefully in Israel (albeit as second-class citizens)? Ask Palestinians: Would you prefer to cling to the illusion of having your own country, or gain equal democratic rights in a prosperous power?

These are very difficult questions and it will take time to change hearts and minds on both sides. But history demonstrates that entrenched ethnic and sectarian conflicts can transition into shared democratic governance. Multiethnic democracies like Belgium have managed complex linguistic and cultural divisions within a constitutional framework that guarantees protections for different ethnic groups. Israeli Jews would need these safeguards, ideally underwritten by acceptable foreign powers, to overcome their fears over being outnumbered by Palestinian Arabs. Northern Ireland showed that after decades of sectarian violence, former enemies can share power under a single democratic system overseen by Britain and the Republic of Ireland. Other precedents — South Africa, Bosnia, even fragile Lebanon — are far from perfect, but they prove that shared governance is possible, and vastly superior to endless war and misery.

A shared state is not an anti-Zionist anomaly; it echoes Zionism’s founders, many of whom were democratic socialists rooted in liberal, humanistic values. In his 1902 utopian novel Altneuland (“Old New Land”), Theodor Herzl, the founder of modern political Zionism, envisioned a secular state where Arab citizens held equal voting rights, sat in parliament, and benefited from economic advancement. Herzl would be appalled to see his vision hijacked by ethnonationalists like Netanyahu.

Persisting with the myth of two states only guarantees endless bloodletting. The Green Party’s resolution should be seized as a catalyst to kick-start the process of building consensus around a single democratic state where Israelis and Palestinians share peace, dignity, and equal rights. India can play a critical role in this. Despite its recent tilt towards Israel, India’s historically staunch support for Palestinian rights gives it sufficient credibility to take the lead in evolving a one-state solution. This might just be the bold leap of political imagination required to return India to the top table of multilateral diplomacy.

The writer is an investor

analysis.framing: The article argues that the two-state solution is dead and advocates for a single secular democratic Israel-Palestine, framing this as the only path to lasting peace and urging India to lead the effort.

headline: Russian diplomat delivers remarks on West’s piracy, Russia’s audience growth in Germany
summary: Maria Zakharova highlighted that the audience in Germany that sympathizes with Russia had become more active after the closure of the Russian House in Berlin
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The number of people who sympathize with Russia in Germany has not decreased following the closure of the Russian House in Berlin; on the contrary, these people have become more active, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said at the 3rd International Catherine Forum.

She also noted that by seizing tankers, the West is trying to revive maritime piracy, but the world apparently sees how destructive such actions are.

TASS has compiled the spokeswoman’s key statements.

Russia continues its humanitarian work in Germany after the closure of the Russian House in Berlin, now in an online format: "The Russian House in Friedrichstrasse, which had been operating since 1984, has been closed. Germany has denounced the intergovernment agreement. Another consulate general, in Bonn, has been closed. But our work has not stopped. It has simply shifted to the online format. At this point. As for the future, we will be looking for other formats. Not because that is how the task has been framed within our country, but because we see a positive response, and even urgent calls, for Russia not to withdraw from there and continue maintaining its humanitarian and cultural presence."

The audience in Germany that sympathizes with Russia has not shrunk but has become more active after the closure of the Russian House in Berlin: After all, despite the reduction in these venues, which was carried out by the German authorities, the audience is not shrinking; on the contrary, it is only growing. And this is despite the direct pressure, blackmail, and threats from the German authorities."

German residents who have no Russian roots but who "want to develop themselves and their children, to give them the opportunity to learn foreign languages, marched with picket signs around the building of the Russian House in Berlin, demanding that their own government not do this": "They are not foreign agents or influence agents. They are people who understand the contribution of Russia and Russian culture to the world’s heritage, who understand that the world would never have been as it is today, in the very best sense of the word, without Russian scientists, people of education, culture, and arts, and who simply want to develop on their own. They don’t demand any money from their country’s government, they simply want it to make a decision in their favor, in favor of German citizens."

The West is seeking to revive maritime piracy by seizing tankers in international waters: "Maritime piracy the West is seeking to revive adds to the destabilization of the situation around the world."

Western countries have "broken free from the constraints of international law and immediately tried to destroy it and do away with the law of the sea as well."

There is no doubt that the world sees how destructive such actions are: "The West was constrained by [legal frameworks], and this prevented them from carrying out their expansionist policies. I think that, in time, everyone will come to understand just how utterly destructive their actions are."

Russia is open to absolutely all mass media outlets: "We never shut out any correspondents, nor do we close our country off to them."

"We are open to all media outlets because that is how people receive information. We understand that if we are not represented there, that place will be taken by those who disseminate Russophobic and anti-Russian information."

The number of repatriates in Russia is expected to increase by the end of 2026: "As of today, 14,967 people have registered with Russia’s Migration Service under the state program during the first nine months of 2026. Of these, 6,025 are repatriates. By the end of the year, their number is expected to rise further compared to 2025."

Consulates have issued nearly 2,000 visas to foreign nationals seeking temporary residence permits in Russia who share traditional values: "According to the consular department, as of October 4, 2026, Russian consular offices have issued 1,989 visas under Decree No. 702 [‘On Providing Humanitarian Support to Persons Who Share Traditional Russian Spiritual and Moral Values’]."

Russia will never abandon its stance that Kosovo is part of Serbia and will continue to support the UN Security Council’s relevant Resolution 1244: "We often hear people say: "Nowadays, we often hear: how long are you going to keep fighting for this UN Security Council Resolution 1244, which states that Kosovo is part of Serbia?" We will stand firm for it and there is no other choice for us."

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a platform for Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova's assertions, presenting her claims about Western 'piracy,' German pressure, and Russia's growing sympathetic audience as newsworthy statements without independent verification or opposing viewpoints.

loaded_language.explanation: Uses the highly charged term 'piracy' to describe tanker seizures, evoking criminality and lawlessness rather than a neutral legal or political dispute.

headline: OPEC+ countries increase oil production by 956,000 bpd in September — report
summary: Saudi Arabia recorded the largest increase in oil production, while Kuwait saw the largest output decline in the reporting period
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. OPEC+ nations participating in the oil output cut agreement increased their crude production by 956,000 barrels per day (bpd) month-on-month in September, according to data from the latest OPEC monthly report.

Excluding Iran, Libya, and Venezuela - which are exempt from the deal - as well as the UAE, which withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+ effective May 1, the alliance's output stood at 30.753 million bpd.

OPEC+ previously extended the deadline for members to compensate for earlier overproduction through the end of 2026, though an updated schedule has not yet been released. The previous timeline envisaged the compensation period ending in June 2026. Consequently, the alliance's baseline September quota stood at 36.206 million bpd, meaning actual production fell short of the target allocation by 5.453 million bpd.

Among the OPEC+ nations, Saudi Arabia recorded the largest increase in oil production in September, scaling up output by 744,000 bpd to 8.001 million bpd. Other producers also boosted output: Iraq ramped up production by 386,000 bpd to 3.920 million bpd, Kazakhstan by 22,000 bpd to 1.851 million bpd, and Algeria by 3,000 bpd to 1.003 million bpd. Meanwhile, Kuwait’s oil production dropped by 140,000 bpd to 1.766 million bpd, and Russia pared output by 38,000 bpd to 8.643 million bpd, while Oman’s production remained virtually flat month-on-month at 939,000 bpd.

Among OPEC members exempt from the alliance's production curbs, Libya saw its output drop by 59,000 bpd to 1.291 million bpd in September, while Iran’s production fell by 99,000 bpd to 1.957 million bpd. Venezuela, however, marginally increased production by 18,000 bpd to 1.150 million bpd. Meanwhile, the UAE, which recently withdrew from OPEC and OPEC+, boosted its oil output by 86,000 bpd to 3.917 million bpd.

headline: OPEC again revises downward global oil demand growth outlook in 2026
summary: The figure is expected to grow by 0.2 mln barrels per day and the demand will stand at 105.72 mln bpd, OPEC said in its October report
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. The Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) has revised downward its international oil demand growth forecast for 2026.

The figure is expected to grow by 0.2 mln barrels per day (bpd) and the demand will stand at 105.72 mln bpd, OPEC said in its October report. The organization expected one month earlier that the global demand will grow by 0.4 mln bpd in 2026.

The decline by about 0.2 mln bpd is expected in OECD countries, while non-OECD nations are expected to show growth by 0.4 mln bpd.

OPEC at the same time increased its outlook for 2027. The organization now expects the global oil demand to grow by 2.6 mln bpd annually. The increase by 0.5 mln bpd is projected in OECD countries, and by about 2 mln bpd in non-OECD countries.

headline: Is China seeking to restrict Taiwan’s cultural presence?
body_text:
Written by Chi-Hui Lin

When Taiwanese author Yang Shuang-zi’s “Taiwan Travelogue” won the 2026 International Booker Prize, it marked a historic breakthrough on the global stage. But behind the triumph lay a sharp geopolitical reality.

On stage, Lin King, who translated the book into English, gave voice to the anxiety looming over Taiwan, where she spent a large part of her childhood.

“In 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, I made the explicit decision that rather than translating Sinophone works indiscriminately, I would only translate writing from Taiwan for the foreseeable future,” she said in her acceptance speech. “I will continue to do so until the day comes that my homeland’s sovereignty is no longer a provocation or a punchline — until no English speaker feels comfortable saying to me, ‘I really should come visit you in Taiwan while it still exists.'”

“Taiwan Travelogue” follows a young Japanese writer visiting Japanese-colonized Taiwan in May 1938 on an official government-sponsored lecture tour. As she and her Taiwanese interpreter explore local street food together, a subtle intimacy unfolds between them. The narrative centers Taiwan’s history rather than Beijing’s preferred “Greater China” framework.

“Literature and politics are directly connected,” Yang told DW. “Politics determines the allocation of resources, and the allocation of resources determines which works get pulled out, held up high and defined as ‘good literature.’ The idea that politics can just be kept out of it doesn’t exist.”

A few days after the 2026 International Booker Prize was announced, China’s Taiwan Affairs Office reacted by saying: “Writers from both sides of the Taiwan Strait should firmly uphold a national standpoint, respect historical facts, and squarely face the immense suffering inflicted upon the Chinese people … by Japan’s war of aggression and fascism.”

“From China’s perspective, they do not want to see Taiwan’s voice gain prominence.” Yang said.

Her book demonstrates that Taiwanese culture is shaped by multiple historical strands — including indigenous, Japanese colonial and local Han influences, rather than being merely a “branch of Chinese culture.”

During Yang’s German book tour this October, an event at the Literaturhaus in Munich sparked controversy when the writer’s interpreter significantly shortened certain statements concerning Taiwan, China, history, and politics. The interpreter later admitted that there had been oversights and shortcomings in the translation but denied deliberately deleting content due to their political stance or the situation in Taiwan.

Beijing claims Taiwan as a Chinese province and has long threatened to use force to bring the island under its control. Taiwan’s democratically elected president has rejected Beijing’s assertion that its laws apply to Taiwan.

Since 1949, Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence, maintaining its own government, military, and legal systems while facing ongoing military pressure from Beijing.

China’s monitoring of Taiwanese international engagement reaches far further than words over a literature prize.

“The target of suppression and harassment primarily include outspoken individuals, exiled activists, diaspora community organizers, alongside their family members and close affiliates back home,” said Dr. Yan-ho Lai, senior fellow of Georgetown Center for Asian Law. “From the PRC’s (People’s Republic of China) eyes, these groups are a threat to regime security, as they are able to amplify the dissenting voices and alternative stories of China to the West.”

In April this year, Taiwanese barista Lin Shao-hsing, also known as Bala, won the 2026 World Latte Art Championship in the United States. Soon after, all mention of Taiwan as it related to Bala’s win was removed from the official World Coffee Championships website.

It now says that Bala was representing “the competition body of Chinese Taipei,” a term often used in international contests, such as the Olympics, to refer to Taiwan, but almost never used in Taiwan itself.

According to a 2026 poll by National Chengchi University’s Election Study Center, the vast majority of people in Taiwan identify as “Taiwanese,” while only 2.5% identify as Chinese.

In 2024, China allegedly planned to stage a “car collision” during Taiwanese Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim’s visit to the Czech capital Prague.

Czech intelligence officials told local media that the incident had been part of a much larger and escalatory plan by Chinese diplomats and intelligence officers working out of the Chinese embassy in Prague.

In early October this year, the FBI said authorities arrested a woman in California for allegedly spying on the son of Taiwan’s president.

According to the US Department of Justice, the woman had traveled to Seattle in 2025 under instructions from Beijing to monitor the Taiwanese president’s son and his family, capturing photos, video footage, and license plate information.

During a press conference on October 6, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it “consistently opposes the hype surrounding so-called ‘Chinese spies’ and the smearing and vilification of China.”

“It reflects the ambiguity and limitation of international law, that the PRC using soft power to restrict the visibility of Taiwan may not directly fall into international law arena, as Taiwan is not recognized by international bodies as a sovereign state party.” said Dr. Lai.

headline: The US targeting the International Criminal Court is a slippery slope to nowhere good

And we don’t want it.”Washington is undoubtedly entitled to resist the wildest demands of the court, but it is in principle setting a precedent that the US and the rest of the world could come to regret.Overarching global bodies perform a necessary function in a world where scores of nations are growing and interacting in pursuit of common development. In any event, the need for this architecture is the most important element to remained focused on.It is not just courts and the highest echelons of international law that come under a shadow when the US takes this sort of action. There is also the UN, which has a number of agencies under its umbrella, such as the World Bank Group. There are also a number of private and public institutions that are dedicated to a “force for good” impact. There are even areas of scientific and research co-operation to tackle issues such as health, metrological developments and geographic changes.To some critics, this is an archipelago of the legal industry that has become a historical aberration. Calling out poor performances or abuses of powers is, therefore, a natural effort that restores balance in the international system.As an unchallenged superpower, the US had an outsized role in judging how the far the balance had tilted one way or another – even in situations where it had not subscribed to the international body, such as the ICC. They were of no help to me,” he said. Leaving aside the record of settling or initiating wars, you have in Mr Trump’s statement the fundamental starting point of the US administration.The problem is, when the fabric of global co-operation starts to get worn down by sanctions, it has to rely on the willingness of people to volunteer to undertake any given mission. That is a wider point than suggesting that people will no longer work for free or give their backing to appeals that are led by international institutions.The campaign amounts to an attack on those who offer their professional skills, talent and dedication to the inner workings of the world. For many, the difference between signing up for good works and suffering the penalties of a powerful system that turns against international work is a dividing line they would not cross.Just for personal reasons, including to insulate themselves and their families, they will find that the appeal of making a contribution has diminished or been extinguished. A bad idea begets worse ones, so don’t be surprised if the world ends up in the worst possible situation.
body_text:
The US government’s moves to sanction the International Criminal Court represent an unwelcome distraction that sets a dangerous precedent for the rest of the world.

The ICC is certainly an elitist organisation, and it is intrusive in certain areas to the point of justifying reforms and new safeguards. But that should not disguise the wider harms that come from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s latest pushback against the court.

Mr Rubio has warned that Washington will demolish the ICC “brick by brick” unless it ends the overreach of prosecuting US citizens for alleged battlefield crimes. “Republicans and Democrats alike rejected the idea that the International Criminal Court had the power to prosecute American citizens, military service members or political leaders,” he said earlier this month. “America never joined the court. We don’t need it. And we don’t want it.”

Washington is undoubtedly entitled to resist the wildest demands of the court, but it is in principle setting a precedent that the US and the rest of the world could come to regret.

Overarching global bodies perform a necessary function in a world where scores of nations are growing and interacting in pursuit of common development. There is a well-established set of benefits that stems from having a common point at which countries establish rules and guidelines on how to co-operate better together.

The people who work in these international systems are more often motivated to carry forward the principles and ideals of global co-operation than the pursuit of a narrow agenda or ideology. In any event, the need for this architecture is the most important element to remained focused on.

It is not just courts and the highest echelons of international law that come under a shadow when the US takes this sort of action. There is also the UN, which has a number of agencies under its umbrella, such as the World Bank Group. There are also a number of private and public institutions that are dedicated to a “force for good” impact. There are even areas of scientific and research co-operation to tackle issues such as health, metrological developments and geographic changes.

To some critics, this is an archipelago of the legal industry that has become a historical aberration. Calling out poor performances or abuses of powers is, therefore, a natural effort that restores balance in the international system.

As an unchallenged superpower, the US had an outsized role in judging how the far the balance had tilted one way or another – even in situations where it had not subscribed to the international body, such as the ICC. But President Donald Trump has gone even further across his two terms.

For a sample of his view on global institutions, his reaction to the Nobel Peace Prize given last week to Navi Pillay – the jurist who has carried out inquiries for the UN – was tellingly dismissive. “In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations. They were of no help to me,” he said. Leaving aside the record of settling or initiating wars, you have in Mr Trump’s statement the fundamental starting point of the US administration.

The problem is, when the fabric of global co-operation starts to get worn down by sanctions, it has to rely on the willingness of people to volunteer to undertake any given mission. That is a wider point than suggesting that people will no longer work for free or give their backing to appeals that are led by international institutions.

The campaign amounts to an attack on those who offer their professional skills, talent and dedication to the inner workings of the world. For many, the difference between signing up for good works and suffering the penalties of a powerful system that turns against international work is a dividing line they would not cross.

Just for personal reasons, including to insulate themselves and their families, they will find that the appeal of making a contribution has diminished or been extinguished. The ethos that dies, then, becomes impossible to replace. What come next are the cynical and the exploitative instincts of those with an agenda.

That sets the international system on a collision course within itself and among the nation-states that have a clear need for good rules of the road.

Also, as frustrating as it might be for the US to suffer constant challenges, there is a reflection of its own strength across the international system. Undermining that extension of its own powerful role in the world is, ultimately, not in its interest.

It is the quiet death of the best people not turning up that will be the consequence of applying system-wide sanctions. Mission creep will follow, too, as sanctions tend to be addictive for policymakers with few tools as easy to embrace in a world of grey choices and negative developments.

Other countries might even emulate the US government’s actions, which would lead to the worst sort of competitive dynamic. Within the global system, the leadership is bound to go into defensive mode. Co-operation could succumb to confrontation. Reform could become an illusory platitude.

There is little positive to say about what might follow. A bad idea begets worse ones, so don’t be surprised if the world ends up in the worst possible situation.

headline: UK intelligence chief warns of 'major shift' after Iran attacks military bases
summary: Iran has raised the stakes in its sabotage efforts against military bases in the UK with Tehran behind multiple plots, the head of the UK's domestic intelligence service warned. Authorities have arrested scores of people suspected of working for Iran, as the level of state-backed threats against the UK exceeds terrorism and extremist activity, Ken McCallum, the director general of MI5, revealed on Tuesday.“Over the last 12 months, our Iran-linked operations have led to more than 50 arrests in the UK,” he said. “The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tehran was "highly likely" behind a suspected plot against RAF Fairford on Monday. The base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran since the war was launched in February. The plot prompted a security alert and led to US President Donald Trump withdrawing planes from the air base. Seven people have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in the incident.Two more suspects were arrested last week at the RAF Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire, which is known to be used by US intelligence agencies. Mr McCallum warned an even greater threat existed elsewhere, raising the prospect of more "aggressive and sophisticated" tactics spreading to the UK."Clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary ​Guard Corps] has quite ‌deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology," he said.Iran has previously attempted attacks at UK bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and Akrotiri in Cyprus.The UK has prosecuted dozens of people for carrying out attacks on Jewish sites and on dissidents active in London and other parts of the UK. Mr McCallum's last national security update a year ago revealed that there were 15 active plots disrupted within the UK. In his latest his annual report he added that all state threats, including from Russia and China, had quadrupled. He referred to interconnected financial systems, energy grids, supply chains and manufacturing bases – designed during simpler times for maximum efficiency – as key vulnerabilities to disruption and coercion by foreign actors.EU supportKaja Kallas, the EU's foreign affairs minister, expressed solidarity with the British government on Tuesday, following Mr Burnham's statement. "UK has now concluded that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard was almost certainly behind the threat to Fairford airbase," she said. "Iran’s campaign of intimidation and chaos extends well beyond the Middle East. "The EU has already designated the Revolutionary Guard as a terrorist organisation. We have sanctioned Iranian officials for undermining freedom of navigation and serious human rights violations. The UK is a close partner, and we stand firmly with them."
body_text:
Iran has raised the stakes in its sabotage efforts against military bases in the UK with Tehran behind multiple plots, the head of the UK's domestic intelligence service warned.

Authorities have arrested scores of people suspected of working for Iran, as the level of state-backed threats against the UK exceeds terrorism and extremist activity, Ken McCallum, the director general of MI5, revealed on Tuesday.

“Over the last 12 months, our Iran-linked operations have led to more than 50 arrests in the UK,” he said. “The other major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites.”

Withdrawal of US bombers from UK base signals 'success' for Iran

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Tehran was "highly likely" behind a suspected plot against RAF Fairford on Monday.

The base had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran since the war was launched in February. The plot prompted a security alert and led to US President Donald Trump withdrawing planes from the air base. Seven people have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in the incident.

Two more suspects were arrested last week at the RAF Molesworth base in Cambridgeshire, which is known to be used by US intelligence agencies.

Mr McCallum warned an even greater threat existed elsewhere, raising the prospect of more "aggressive and sophisticated" tactics spreading to the UK.

"Clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary ​Guard Corps] has quite ‌deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology," he said.

Iran has previously attempted attacks at UK bases in Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean and Akrotiri in Cyprus.

The Steadfast Noon exercise is held annually as "part of NATO’s efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the Alliance’s deterrence and defense." It involves dual-capable aircraft designed to carry both conventional and nuclear munitions.

headline: Can South Korea and Ukraine resolve their diplomatic spat?
body_text:
Written By Julian Ryall

South Korea’s ambassador to Kyiv returned to Seoul on Saturday, his recall the latest in a series of tit-for-tat actions that have severely strained bilateral ties.

The sudden deterioration in their relationship can be traced back to September 23, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the United Nations General Assembly in New York that Ukraine had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea.

The soldiers had been captured by Ukrainian forces in the Russian Kursk region in January 2025 as they fought alongside Russian troops.

The South Korean government immediately expressed its anger at Zelenskyy’s revelation, insisting that the two governments had reached an agreement to keep the transfer of the two men in mid-September a secret.

Kyiv hit back, by saying that no confidentiality agreement had been in place, to which South Korea accused Ukraine of effectively lying and demanded an official explanation and an apology.

Ukraine has attempted to smooth over what it has called a “diplomatic understanding,” but stopped short of the public apology that was expected in Seoul.

Then, reports emerged last week that a close adviser to Zelenskyy had said that more than 176,000 tons of diesel and other energy products were shipped to Russia from South Korean ports in July and August of this year, which would be a breach of international sanctions.

The office of president Lee Jae Myung in Seoul denied the accusation, and two days later recalled its ambassador to Kyiv.

There are several reasons why South Korea wanted to keep the POW transfer secret, Erwin Tan, a professor of international politics at Hankuk University, told DW.

“The first was that revealing that the POWs had been repatriated to South Korea would result in Pyongyang retaliating against the families of the men for surrendering,” Tan said.

“Seoul also wanted to maintain a channel for communication with Pyongyang,” Tan said. “This is a major consideration for the left-leaning wing of Korean politics, which includes President Lee and has historically favored seeking rapprochement with the North.”

Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation, agrees that the South Korean government wanted to avoid “friction” with the North.

But Kim pointed out that it was always very likely that both Moscow and Pyongyang would find out about the transfer sooner or later and that Lee was being criticized in some quarters at home for appearing weak.

“There is criticism that Lee’s administration is effectively appeasing the North, that it has become too soft, and that is a very worrisome situation,” Kim said. Yet he admits to being surprised at how quickly the issue escalated.

“I think Lee was very angry that he was publicly being accused of lying about the agreement and it rapidly grew into a very messy confrontation,” he said.

While it is unclear why Zelenskyy used his high-profile UN speech to announce the repatriation of the two POWs, Kim believes it may have been a calculated move to win more support from Seoul.

Kyiv could have carried out a prisoner swap with the Russians and won the freedom of some of its own men in return.

But, Kim pointed out, Ukraine instead chose to accede to Seoul’s request in the hope that South Korea would respond with additional financial and possibly even military support. That move appears to have backfired.

Professor Tan anticipates that the two governments will continue to “vent steam” over the issue.

“Given the high profile nature of the mutual accusations, both sides will probably engage in a mutual blame game for the immediate future, but I doubt that it will turn into a long-term case of mutual acrimony,” he said.

“I anticipate that after the furor has died down and the press is looking for the next new story, both sides will quietly resume contact on the basis of mutual pragmatism.”

headline: Russia remains key supplier of oil to China, India in August — OPEC
summary: Russia provided 45% of India's oil imports in August, while another 12% came from the UAE, and 9% from Venezuela, the OPEC reported
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia was again the largest supplier of oil to India (accounting for 45% of the country's oil imports) and to China (30% of the country's oil imports) in August 2026, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) said in its report.

In particular, Russia provided 45% of India's oil imports in August, while another 12% came from the UAE, and 9% from Venezuela, the OPEC reported, citing data from Kpler analytical firm.

India's total oil imports in August 2026 decreased relative to July, averaging 4.5 million barrels per day (bpd) compared to 5.05 million bpd the month before.

In the meantime, China's oil imports continued to recover in August, increasing from 8.38 million bpd to 8.89 million bpd, which is 6% more than the previous month. Russia remained the largest supplier of oil to China, with its share of supplies during the reporting period standing at 30%, while Brazil provided another 10% of supplies, and Saudi Arabia accounted for 8% of supplies.
