headline: Bipartisan group of senators call on Trump to rescind Russian diesel deal
summary: Six Democratic and six Republican senators wrote a letter calling on President Trump to withdraw from his recent deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin. (Image credit: Win McNamee)
body_text:
President Trump stops to speak to members of the media as he departs the White House on Oct. 13, 2026. Win McNamee/Getty Images hide caption

A bipartisan group of senators is calling on President Trump to rescind his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, calling it a "betrayal of the people of Ukraine."

Last week, Trump announced via social media he had struck a deal with Putin, whereby Russia will supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and one million tons "immediately thereafter."

"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump wrote.

His announcement stunned lawmakers, who passed legislation this summer directing the president to impose significant tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil.

Those sanctions are aimed at targeting Russian officials, companies and financial institutions helping fuel Russia's war in Ukraine. The legislation was named in memory of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham, who helped negotiate Trump's support for the package.

"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our allies; it should be rescinded," wrote six Republican and six Democratic senators in a letter Tuesday to the president.

"The deal you struck with President Vladimir Putin on October 9th will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," it read.

Senators said they recognized the need to lower energy costs for Americans — but maintained that allowing Russian diesel into global markets will offer "limited to no relief to Americans."

They added the deal "only provides Putin with more fuel to finance his war machine and enables Russia to continue its brutal attacks on Ukrainian civilians."

When asked about the letter, the White House referred back to comments President Trump made to reporters on Tuesday about concerns that Russia will use proceeds from the diesel agreement to purchase weapons.

"Nobody's telling me anything," Trump said. "That's a diesel deal. Not for us. That's being released into the world. That's not being released to us. That's a diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market, because the world market suffered with high prices."

The letter was signed by Democrats Richard Blumenthal, Chris Coons, Dick Durbin, Jack Reed, Jeanne Shaheen and Sheldon Whitehouse. They were joined by Republicans Alan Armstrong, Susan Collins, John Cornyn, Mitch McConnell, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis.

headline: Wheat prices post sharpest drop in over 2 years amid easing geopolitical risks
summary: Russia-Ukraine peace prospects, weaker-than-expected El Nino, and stronger US dollar rendering American wheat more expensive drive down wheat futures to $6.75 per bushel in September
body_text:
Anadolu Ajansı © 2026

Wheat prices plummeted by 12.7% in September to $6.75 per bushel, the sharpest monthly decline since June 2024, after reaching an intramonth peak of $7.95, as a potential peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, favorable weather conditions, and declining demand came to the fore.

Climate and geopolitical developments influenced wheat's supply and demand, but the commodity still ended the month around 35% above its initial value at the start of the year, having concluded January at the $5-a-bushel level.

Zafer Ergezen, a futures and commodity markets expert, told Anadolu that earlier price rallies were supported by supply risks affecting Black Sea grain exports, but recent market dynamics shifted downward as US-Russia relations developed positively.

“Along with the El Nino effect being weaker than expected, a short-term weakening of US wheat exports and concerns over a global economic growth slowdown are among the main drivers pulling wheat prices down,” he said.

With the prices of Russian and Ukrainian wheat falling, US wheat remained expensive relative to European wheat, decreasing demand for wheat produced in the US.

“American wheat was expensive due to the stronger dollar, driving up the dollar cost of wheat, which is among the factors that made European wheat more attractive,” he added.

WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. The US and Israel are readying to resume a large-scale military operation against Iran before the parliamentary elections in Israel on October 27 and the midterm elections to the US Congress on November 3, Axios quoted US administration sources as saying.

According to it, US President Donald Trump and Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last week discussed "the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and US elections." At the same time, most of Trump’s advisers advocate maintaining economic and other forms of pressure on Tehran. On October 13, Trump said the US would soon decide on further actions against Iran.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the United States resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the agreements on the Strait of Hormuz. About 25% of the world’s oil and about 20% of liquefied natural gas are transported through it. Later the American administration effectively signaled its intention to cease the use of large-scale military force against Iran and to shift to an attempt to choke it through sanctions.

headline: Booms heard near Saudi Aramco headquarters as Houthi conflict escalates
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Loud booms were heard on Tuesday night near the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, the world's largest and the backbone of the kingdom's economy, in Dhahran, six sources told Reuters, amid an escalating war between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - Loud booms were heard on Tuesday night near the headquarters of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, the world's largest and the backbone of the kingdom's economy, in Dhahran, six sources told Reuters, amid an escalating war between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition.

There was no official comment from the company, Saudi Aramco. A source with direct knowledge of the matter told Reuters the Aramco headquarters had been struck, though it was unclear if the building had been hit directly or by falling debris.

One source said the Aramco headquarters was on fire in Dhahran, the center of the Saudi oil industry in Eastern Province. An evacuation order for the building had been issued, four sources said.

The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area without providing further details.

Authorities also reported drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country's southern region.

The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes including one on Saturday that killed 13 people.

The Houthis earlier said Saudi Arabia was attacking the Yemeni capital Sanaa and a Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan and Yomna Ehab; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne, Cynthia Osterman and Sanjeev Miglani)

WASHINGTON, October 13. /TASS/. The US and Israel are readying to resume a large-scale military operation against Iran before the parliamentary elections in Israel on October 27 and the midterm elections to the US Congress on November 3, Axios quoted US administration sources as saying.

At the same time, most of Trump’s advisers advocate maintaining economic and other forms of pressure on Tehran. On October 13, Trump said the US would soon decide on further actions against Iran.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, on the night of July 8, the United States resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the agreements on the Strait of Hormuz. About 25% of the world’s oil and about 20% of liquefied natural gas are transported through it. Later the American administration effectively signaled its intention to cease the use of large-scale military force against Iran and to shift to an attempt to choke it through sanctions.

body_text:
Bank of America was ordered to pay more than $1.2 billion in fines after the Treasury Department said the company breached anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, the agency said on Tuesday.

The Treasury Department said the fine is the third-largest in its history. Bank of America was also ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comprotroller of the Currency, the largest ever issued by the OCC.

The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over 475 “apparent violations” of sanctions against “Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism”.

Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US, with more than 70 million clients, and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for customers every year. It enables more than $450 trillion of payments in employee payrolls, supplier payments and corporate credit cards. It also processes an average of $1.9 trillion in wire transfers a day globally for clients.

“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire us financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."

The Treasury Department said Bank of America admitted it wilfully breached the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to assist the Treasury in detecting and preventing money laundering.

The department said the US bank failed to report to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with more than $1 billion implicating national security and other risks pointing to Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and other activity “with a substantial nexus to the south-west border”.

The OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against the bank in 2024 over deficiencies related to its Bank Secrecy Act and compliance programmes.

“The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable,” said Jonathan Gould, Comproller of the Currency.

Tuesday's fine followed an action from the OCC last week, in which American Express was fined $350 million after its compliance programme allowed about $13 billion in suspected money laundering activity to go undetected for more than a decade.

Bank of America is due to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday.

headline: Missile hits headquarters of Saudi Aramco, source says, as Houthi conflict escalates
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A ballistic missile hit the headquarters complex of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, the world's largest and the backbone of the kingdom's economy, a company source told Reuters, amid an escalating war between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A ballistic missile hit the headquarters complex of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, the world's largest and the backbone of the kingdom's economy, a company source told Reuters, amid an escalating war between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition.

An office tower in the Saudi Aramco complex in the eastern city of Dhahran was struck on Tuesday night and the top three floors were damaged, the source said. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire.

The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.

Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the complex. There was no official comment from Saudi Aramco.

The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.

Authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country's southern region.

The Houthis had earlier threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.

The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets.

The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Saturday that killed 13 people.

The Houthis earlier on Tuesday said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Tuesday before the strike on Saudi Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.

While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz this month.

Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.

Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28.

Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional archrival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan and Yomna Ehab; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne, Cynthia Osterman, Sanjeev Miglani and Edmund Klamann)

headline: Planning Minister outlines 67% private sector investment target and African integration vision at World Bank-IMF meetings
summary: Egypt aims to increase the private sector’s share of total national investments to 67% by 2030, up from 57.7% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year and 43.1% in 2023/2024, Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom announced. Speaking at a panel discussion titled “Africa’s Promising Future: Structural Reforms, Trade Integration, and Private Sector-Led Growth” during the 81st Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, Rostom said the government plans to achieve this target by implementing its State Ownership Policy, ensuring competitive neutrality, streamlining administrative procedures, and expanding single-window services for investors. Rostom stated that the Egyptian economy registered a real GDP growth rate of 5.1% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year. He added that total foreign exchange assets reached $73.1bn, while the overall balance of payments recorded a surplus of $6.4bn over the same period. In the energy sector, the minister noted that the full settlement of arrears owed to international oil companies in June 2026 helped restore confidence in Egypt’s energy market. He said Egypt is expanding renewable energy projects in partnership with the private sector, targeting a 42% share of clean energy in its energy mix by 2030. Addressing broader regional issues, Rostom argued that Africa has historically been treated primarily as a source of raw agricultural goods and minerals without sufficient local industrial processing. He stressed the importance of industrial deepening across the continent to capture higher value-add, strengthen supply chains, and generate local energy and employment. “For decades, Africa remained treated as a food basket, without achieving sufficient industrial deepening,” Rostom said. “The real challenge for Africa lies in the speed of converting structural reforms into sustainable job opportunities for youth.” Rostom also highlighted the Infrastructure Financing Guarantee Mechanism as a practical framework for regional cooperation to attract investment into major development projects. He cited the full implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the simplification of customs procedures, cross-border electrical interconnections, and green hydrogen initiatives as critical elements for regional value chain integration and energy security.

headline: Egypt’s FM discusses food security, financing and regional cooperation in Bangkok
summary: Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a series of meetings and participated in ministerial sessions in Bangkok on Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), focusing on food security, maritime routes, development financing, economic reform and cooperation with international and Gulf institutions. Abdelatty, who serves as Egypt’s governor at the World Bank, participated in a ministerial meeting on food security and critical maritime corridors attended by World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed and Egyptian Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom. He said food security was closely linked to the stability of global supply chains and strategic shipping routes, warning that ongoing disruptions were driving up freight, food and fertiliser costs and placing additional pressure on developing economies. Abdelatty said Egypt was strengthening its strategic reserves, diversifying import sources, increasing domestic production and expanding storage capacity. He also affirmed Cairo’s readiness to work with development partners to host a global hub for grain storage, supply and trade. He proposed four priorities for strengthening global resilience to food crises: maintaining the flow of food, fertiliser and energy trade; providing insurance and financial guarantees for essential shipments; offering rapid and flexible financing to countries affected by higher import costs; and strengthening preparedness through strategic reserves, early-warning systems and closer coordination among exporters, importers and transit countries. In a separate meeting with World Bank Vice President for the Middle East and North Africa Ousmane Dione, Abdelatty discussed completing the third and final phase of Egypt’s Development Policy Financing framework following the conclusion of the second phase. He also invited the World Bank to participate in the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development, scheduled for November. The talks also covered reforming the international financial architecture, strengthening the lending capacity of multilateral development banks and developing innovative financing instruments to address rising sovereign debt burdens in low- and middle-income countries. Abdelatty also discussed water cooperation with Dione, reiterating Egypt’s support for Nile Basin countries’ right to development and dam construction, provided that projects comply with international law and its relevant principles, including avoiding harm, prior notification, consultation and consensus. He referred to a newly established Egyptian mechanism to finance projects in Nile Basin countries, including dams in countries in the southern part of the basin. Abdelatty also met with Saudi Fund for Development Chief Executive Sultan bin Abdulrahman Al-Marshad to discuss expanding development cooperation in Egypt, particularly in infrastructure and support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. He called for a greater role for Arab development institutions in providing flexible financing to economies affected by regional escalation, higher financing costs and supply-chain disruptions. Al-Marshad said the fund was keen to continue supporting development in Egypt and explore broader trilateral cooperation in Africa. In talks with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Abdelatty stressed that the security of Gulf states was an integral part of Egyptian national security. The two sides condemned recent attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their support for the kingdom’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity. They also discussed holding the second Egypt–GCC Investment and Trade Forum in New Alamein to promote investment, trade, energy cooperation and supply-chain integration. They further emphasised the importance of continuing political consultations under the Egypt–GCC Joint Action Plan for 2024–2028. Abdelatty separately met with World Bank Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics Michael Kremer to present key elements of Egypt’s planned national economic transformation programme. The discussions covered the government’s privatisation programme, the management of state-owned companies and efforts to expand the private sector’s contribution to economic growth, exports and job creation. The two sides also discussed food security, agricultural technology and measures to improve soil productivity. In another meeting, Abdelatty held talks with Kuwaiti Finance Minister Yaqoub Al-Rifai on increasing Kuwaiti investment in Egypt and identifying sectors and projects offering opportunities for private-sector participation. They also discussed strengthening Arab coordination within the World Bank on development financing, fiscal reform and regional priorities. Abdelatty expressed Egypt’s interest in expanding cooperation with the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development. Abdelatty later addressed a meeting of ministers and governors of the Group of 24 (G24), calling for reform of international financing mechanisms and more responsive global financial institutions capable of addressing the needs of developing economies. He said Egypt was expanding investment in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, ports, renewable energy and green hydrogen, while promoting manufacturing, local value chains and job creation. Abdelatty also called for stronger regional economic integration and the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area to support growth and development across the continent.

body_text:
Pope Leo XIV has had lung cancer diagnosed after surgeons ⁠removed a part of his right lung on Tuesday, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, has adenocarcinoma, ​a common form of lung cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the Vatican said.

He was admitted to Rome's ⁠Gemelli Hospital for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent health check-up.

The Vatican said earlier on Tuesday that the operation had been successful, before providing a more detailed update from the Pope's lead surgeon and personal physician.

"In order to make the procedure ⁠curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," the medical update said, making it clear that the aim was to eliminate ​all cancerous ⁠tissue.

Medical experts said that in order to assess the Pope's case they would need to know the size of the tumour ​removed from him and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes.

Pope Leo is due to make an 11-day tour of ⁠Uruguay, Argentina and Peru starting from November 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead. The Vatican has cancelled all of his audiences until October 21 to give him time to recuperate.

The American-born pontiff revealed during his regular Sunday blessing on October 11 that doctors had discovered the nodule.

The late Pope Francis, Pope Leo's predecessor, was admitted to hospital several times as he grew frail in his later years. He ​died aged 88 in April ‌2025.

Pope Leo was elected leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Roman Catholics in May 2025.

He has left his mark on the papacy by addressing the social and ethical implications of artificial intelligence and has grown increasingly critical of US military actions, challenging the administration of President Donald Trump's argument that God was on the side of the US in its conflict with Iran.

Bank of America was ordered to pay more than $1.2 billion in fines after the Treasury Department said the company breached anti-money laundering and sanctions laws, the agency said on Tuesday.

The Treasury Department said the fine is the third-largest in its history. Bank of America was also ordered to pay $750 million to the Office of the Comprotroller of the Currency, the largest ever issued by the OCC.

The department's Office of Foreign Assets Control also announced an $11.6 million settlement with Bank of America over 475 “apparent violations” of sanctions against “Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics and global terrorism”.

Bank of America is the second-largest bank in the US, with more than 70 million clients, and processes about $4.5 trillion in payments for customers every year. It enables more than $450 trillion of payments in employee payrolls, supplier payments and corporate credit cards. It also processes an average of $1.9 trillion in wire transfers a day globally for clients.

“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money-laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire us financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement.

“Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law."

The Treasury Department said Bank of America admitted it wilfully breached the Bank Secrecy Act, which requires banks to assist the Treasury in detecting and preventing money laundering.

The department said the US bank failed to report to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, with more than $1 billion implicating national security and other risks pointing to Chinese money laundering networks, fraud and other activity “with a substantial nexus to the south-west border”.

The OCC issued a cease-and-desist order against the bank in 2024 over deficiencies related to its Bank Secrecy Act and compliance programmes.

“The bank’s poor response to its BSA deficiencies is unacceptable,” said Jonathan Gould, Comproller of the Currency.

Tuesday's fine followed an action from the OCC last week, in which American Express was fined $350 million after its compliance programme allowed about $13 billion in suspected money laundering activity to go undetected for more than a decade.

Bank of America is due to report its third-quarter earnings on Wednesday.

headline: Missile hits headquarters of Saudi Aramco, source says, as Houthi conflict escalates
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A ballistic missile hit the headquarters complex of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, the world's largest and the backbone of the kingdom's economy, a company source told Reuters, amid an escalating war between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - A ballistic missile hit the headquarters complex of Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company, the world's largest and the backbone of the kingdom's economy, a company source told Reuters, amid an escalating war between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and a Saudi-led coalition.

An office tower in the Saudi Aramco complex in the eastern city of Dhahran was struck on Tuesday night and the top three floors were damaged, the source said. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire.

The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.

Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the complex. There was no official comment from Saudi Aramco.

The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.

Authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country's southern region.

The Houthis had earlier threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.

The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets.

The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces against the Houthis in Yemen's reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Saturday that killed 13 people.

The Houthis earlier on Tuesday said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Tuesday before the strike on Saudi Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country even as it hosts a major energy conference.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.

While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz this month.

Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.

Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28.

Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional archrival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan and Yomna Ehab; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne, Cynthia Osterman, Sanjeev Miglani and Edmund Klamann)

headline: Planning Minister outlines 67% private sector investment target and African integration vision at World Bank-IMF meetings
summary: Egypt aims to increase the private sector’s share of total national investments to 67% by 2030, up from 57.7% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year and 43.1% in 2023/2024, Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom announced. Speaking at a panel discussion titled “Africa’s Promising Future: Structural Reforms, Trade Integration, and Private Sector-Led Growth” during the 81st Annual Meetings of the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund in Bangkok, Rostom said the government plans to achieve this target by implementing its State Ownership Policy, ensuring competitive neutrality, streamlining administrative procedures, and expanding single-window services for investors. Rostom stated that the Egyptian economy registered a real GDP growth rate of 5.1% in the 2025/2026 fiscal year. He added that total foreign exchange assets reached $73.1bn, while the overall balance of payments recorded a surplus of $6.4bn over the same period. In the energy sector, the minister noted that the full settlement of arrears owed to international oil companies in June 2026 helped restore confidence in Egypt’s energy market. He said Egypt is expanding renewable energy projects in partnership with the private sector, targeting a 42% share of clean energy in its energy mix by 2030. Addressing broader regional issues, Rostom argued that Africa has historically been treated primarily as a source of raw agricultural goods and minerals without sufficient local industrial processing. He stressed the importance of industrial deepening across the continent to capture higher value-add, strengthen supply chains, and generate local energy and employment. “For decades, Africa remained treated as a food basket, without achieving sufficient industrial deepening,” Rostom said. “The real challenge for Africa lies in the speed of converting structural reforms into sustainable job opportunities for youth.” Rostom also highlighted the Infrastructure Financing Guarantee Mechanism as a practical framework for regional cooperation to attract investment into major development projects. He cited the full implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), the simplification of customs procedures, cross-border electrical interconnections, and green hydrogen initiatives as critical elements for regional value chain integration and energy security.

headline: Egypt’s FM discusses food security, financing and regional cooperation in Bangkok
summary: Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a series of meetings and participated in ministerial sessions in Bangkok on Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), focusing on food security, maritime routes, development financing, economic reform and cooperation with international and Gulf institutions. Abdelatty, who serves as Egypt’s governor at the World Bank, participated in a ministerial meeting on food security and critical maritime corridors attended by World Bank Group President Ajay Banga, UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed and Egyptian Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom. He said food security was closely linked to the stability of global supply chains and strategic shipping routes, warning that ongoing disruptions were driving up freight, food and fertiliser costs and placing additional pressure on developing economies. Abdelatty said Egypt was strengthening its strategic reserves, diversifying import sources, increasing domestic production and expanding storage capacity. He also affirmed Cairo’s readiness to work with development partners to host a global hub for grain storage, supply and trade. He proposed four priorities for strengthening global resilience to food crises: maintaining the flow of food, fertiliser and energy trade; providing insurance and financial guarantees for essential shipments; offering rapid and flexible financing to countries affected by higher import costs; and strengthening preparedness through strategic reserves, early-warning systems and closer coordination among exporters, importers and transit countries. In a separate meeting with World Bank Vice President for the Middle East and North Africa Ousmane Dione, Abdelatty discussed completing the third and final phase of Egypt’s Development Policy Financing framework following the conclusion of the second phase. He also invited the World Bank to participate in the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development, scheduled for November. The talks also covered reforming the international financial architecture, strengthening the lending capacity of multilateral development banks and developing innovative financing instruments to address rising sovereign debt burdens in low- and middle-income countries. Abdelatty also discussed water cooperation with Dione, reiterating Egypt’s support for Nile Basin countries’ right to development and dam construction, provided that projects comply with international law and its relevant principles, including avoiding harm, prior notification, consultation and consensus. He referred to a newly established Egyptian mechanism to finance projects in Nile Basin countries, including dams in countries in the southern part of the basin. Abdelatty also met with Saudi Fund for Development Chief Executive Sultan bin Abdulrahman Al-Marshad to discuss expanding development cooperation in Egypt, particularly in infrastructure and support for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. He called for a greater role for Arab development institutions in providing flexible financing to economies affected by regional escalation, higher financing costs and supply-chain disruptions. Al-Marshad said the fund was keen to continue supporting development in Egypt and explore broader trilateral cooperation in Africa. In talks with Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Abdelatty stressed that the security of Gulf states was an integral part of Egyptian national security. The two sides condemned recent attacks targeting Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed their support for the kingdom’s security, sovereignty and territorial integrity. They also discussed holding the second Egypt–GCC Investment and Trade Forum in New Alamein to promote investment, trade, energy cooperation and supply-chain integration. They further emphasised the importance of continuing political consultations under the Egypt–GCC Joint Action Plan for 2024–2028. Abdelatty separately met with World Bank Chief Economist and Senior Vice President for Development Economics Michael Kremer to present key elements of Egypt’s planned national economic transformation programme. The discussions covered the government’s privatisation programme, the management of state-owned companies and efforts to expand the private sector’s contribution to economic growth, exports and job creation. The two sides also discussed food security, agricultural technology and measures to improve soil productivity. In another meeting, Abdelatty held talks with Kuwaiti Finance Minister Yaqoub Al-Rifai on increasing Kuwaiti investment in Egypt and identifying sectors and projects offering opportunities for private-sector participation. They also discussed strengthening Arab coordination within the World Bank on development financing, fiscal reform and regional priorities. Abdelatty expressed Egypt’s interest in expanding cooperation with the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development. Abdelatty later addressed a meeting of ministers and governors of the Group of 24 (G24), calling for reform of international financing mechanisms and more responsive global financial institutions capable of addressing the needs of developing economies. He said Egypt was expanding investment in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, ports, renewable energy and green hydrogen, while promoting manufacturing, local value chains and job creation. Abdelatty also called for stronger regional economic integration and the implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area to support growth and development across the continent.

headline: Pakistan urges US, Iran to honor peace agreement amid rising Gulf tensions
summary: President Zardari calls for restraint, safe passage through Strait of Hormuz during meeting with visiting Russian interior minister
body_text:
Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on Tuesday urged the US and Iran to exercise restraint and honor their commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, a framework agreement reached in June to resolve the Middle East conflict.

Zardari called for differences to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, emphasizing the importance of safe maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

His remarks came during a meeting with Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev in Islamabad, according to a statement from the president's office.

Zardari expressed deep concern over escalating tensions in the Gulf, particularly attacks on maritime traffic, energy installations and critical infrastructure.

He warned that the conflict posed serious challenges to regional stability, global energy security, trade and supply chains, stressing the need to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states.

Kolokoltsev is on a four-day official visit to Pakistan, the first by a Russian interior minister to the South Asian country.

He said bilateral trade, which stood at $243.4 million in the 2025 financial year, remained below its potential and urged both countries to translate their leaders' goodwill into tangible results.

Kolokoltsev agreed that trade volumes did not reflect the strength of bilateral relations, saying there was considerable room for expansion.

He also invited Zardari to visit Russia.

Separately, Kolokoltsev held talks with Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on combating organized crime, terrorism, extremism, illicit arms and drug trafficking, and cybercrime, including telephone scams, phishing and cryptocurrency pyramid schemes.

The Russian minister said law enforcement cooperation was rooted in friendly and mutually beneficial bilateral relations, according to a statement from the Russian Embassy in Islamabad.

headline: Egypt re-elected to chair Arab Electricity Council’s Executive Bureau for second consecutive term
summary: Egypt has been unanimously re-elected to chair the Executive Bureau of the Arab Ministerial Council for Electricity for a second consecutive term, with Algeria elected vice-chair, the Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said. The decision was taken during the 16th session of the Arab Ministerial Council for Electricity, hosted by Saudi Arabia in Riyadh over two days, with the participation of Arab electricity ministers, official delegations, experts, representatives of the Arab League’s energy department and international financing institutions. The re-election reflects Egypt’s role in supporting joint Arab cooperation within the framework of the League of Arab States, the ministry said. Mahmoud Esmat, Minister of Electricity and Renewable Energy, said Egypt would continue working with Arab partners to implement the Arab Common Electricity Market Agreement and advance comprehensive electricity interconnection across the region. The agreement was signed during the council’s 15th session, hosted by Egypt in the New Administrative Capital. Establishing a common Arab electricity market would mark the culmination of nearly two decades of efforts to achieve comprehensive electricity interconnection among Arab countries and establish an integrated regional market, Esmat said. He highlighted the importance of completing joint Arab electricity interconnection projects to establish an integrated market operating according to economic principles. Esmat cited the Egypt–Saudi Arabia electricity interconnection project, which has entered trial operation, as a model and a foundation for expanding electricity interconnection across the Arab region. He added that the next phase would require stronger cooperation, coordinated efforts and faster completion of the necessary procedures, alongside the development of an institutional framework to manage the common market. The minister also stressed the importance of exchanging expertise, building capacity and training personnel to address challenges, capitalise on available opportunities and apply modern technologies to the operation and management of the Arab Common Electricity Market.

headline: Egypt signs MoU with China’s C&D to develop dry bulk terminal at Al Max Port
summary: Egypt’s Ministry of Transport has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Chinese company Xiamen C&D to develop a specialised dry bulk terminal at Al Max Port in Alexandria, as part of efforts to develop Greater Alexandria Port and the Sokhna–Alexandria logistics corridor. The MoU was signed by the Alexandria Port Authority, represented by its Chairperson Ehab Salah, and C&D, represented by its Managing Director and CEO Lü Rongdian. The signing ceremony was attended by Minister of Transport Kamel Al-Wazir, Deputy Minister of Transport for Maritime Affairs Nehad Shaheen, Maritime Transport Sector Head Hussein El-Geziry, and officials from both sides. According to the ministry, the terminal is the first of four planned at Al Max Port. The project aims to strengthen Egypt’s position as a regional hub for transport, logistics and transit trade, while expanding the role of Egyptian ports in international trade and integrating them more closely into global supply chains. The proposed development plan includes upgrading marine berths to accommodate large vessels, expanding storage yards, modernising cargo-handling facilities and establishing a logistics centre to streamline truck movements. It also includes improving connections with the national railway network to strengthen integration between maritime, rail and road transport. Al-Wazir said the project would involve developing a specialised terminal for non-clean dry bulk cargo, supported by storage yards, silos and advanced cargo-handling facilities. The design includes two main berths capable of accommodating large cargo vessels. Upon completion, Alexandria Port is expected to be able to accommodate three large vessels simultaneously, the minister said. The project is also expected to create thousands of direct and indirect jobs during construction and operation, particularly in transport, logistics, storage and supporting industrial services. Al-Wazir added that the terminal would help reduce supply chain costs, improve the movement of raw materials and finished products, and enhance the competitiveness of Egyptian exports, particularly in the cement, steel and heavy industries. The technical plan also incorporates an environmental management system designed to comply with international standards, the ministry said. The project forms part of the government’s broader strategy to modernise Egyptian seaports, attract foreign investment and expand private-sector participation in transport infrastructure, in line with Egypt Vision 2030. For his part, Lü Rongdian said Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt and his meeting with President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi had helped attract Chinese companies to the Egyptian market and opened up investment opportunities across several sectors, including transport, logistics and related industries. Lü thanked the Ministry of Transport for its confidence in C&D and its support for cooperation with the company. He added that C&D aimed to make the project one of the most significant maritime transport and port developments in the Mediterranean. The company would work with its Egyptian partners to accelerate implementation and ensure efficient delivery, he said, describing the terminal as a potential starting point for further cooperation in developing other port terminals and manufacturing commercial vessels. Such cooperation would help strengthen bilateral ties and expand collaboration across supply chains, Lü added.

headline: H&L Egypt raises investment to $30m for South Korean sportswear factory in West Qantara
summary: The Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) has laid the foundation stone for a South Korean sportswear manufacturing plant in the West Qantara Industrial Zone, with planned investments doubling to $30m from an initial $15m, as Egypt seeks to attract further South Korean investment following President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi’s visit to South Korea. Mostafa Shikhon, chairperson of SCZONE, attended Tuesday’s groundbreaking ceremony alongside Kim Wan-jong, South Korea’s ambassador to Egypt; Mohamed Ibrahim, SCZONE vice-chairperson for the Northern Zone; Ahmed Essam El-Din, deputy governor of Ismailia; and representatives of the company and local authorities. The H&L Egypt Apparel project will cover 42,000 square metres and involve the establishment of a smart, environmentally friendly factory equipped with advanced manufacturing technologies. The facility is expected to create approximately 2,000 direct jobs and expand Egypt’s sportswear manufacturing capacity. Shikhon said the project marked an important step towards attracting South Korean investment to SCZONE, particularly as relations between Egypt and South Korea have advanced to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership. He added that the authority hoped the project would pave the way for a broader wave of South Korean investment across its industrial zones, citing the competitive advantages available to investors. The West Qantara Industrial Zone currently hosts 54 projects representing nine nationalities, with total investments of approximately $1.54bn, according to Shikhon. Textiles and ready-made garments account for the largest share of industrial activity in the zone, with 43 projects. He said SCZONE continued to support investors by providing an attractive investment environment and integrated infrastructure, with the aim of enhancing the competitiveness of Egyptian products, boosting exports and creating jobs. Kim Wan-jong said the H&L Egypt project would strengthen industrial and investment cooperation between Egypt and South Korea. He highlighted SCZONE’s strategic location and Egypt’s free trade agreements as advantages for manufacturing and exporting to international markets. The ambassador expressed hope that the project would serve as a successful model of cooperation between South Korean industrial expertise and Egyptian workers, encouraging further investment from South Korean companies in the economic zone. Lee Seung-jun, CEO of H&L Egypt Apparel, said the project marked an important beginning for the company’s operations in Egypt. He added that the company aimed to establish an advanced industrial base capable of competing in global markets by adopting modern technologies and applying quality and sustainability standards in sportswear manufacturing. The project is the first investment by a South Korean company to be contracted within SCZONE, with the agreement signed in November 2025. The increase in planned investment from $15m to $30m reflects the company’s confidence in the zone’s investment potential and its prospects as a base for expansion into international markets, according to SCZONE.

headline: Opinion | The El Alamein Declaration: New Red Lines in the Horn of Africa
summary: The El Alamein Declaration, issued following the October 4 meeting between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, represents an attempt to redraw some of the rules of the strategic balance in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa—not by creating a new military alliance, but by bringing together a set of issues that have until now largely been treated as separate crises. The significance of the declaration lies precisely in this linkage. Maritime security in the Red Sea, Ethiopia’s quest for access to the sea, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam dispute, Sudan’s territorial integrity and Somalia’s position on the Somaliland question are now being placed within a single regional framework. This reflects a growing recognition that the crises of the Horn of Africa have become so interconnected that managing them in isolation is increasingly difficult, if not impossible. Ethiopia’s absence from both the meeting and the resulting document carries an unmistakable political message. Yet it does not necessarily mean that the four countries are seeking to construct an explicitly anti-Ethiopian bloc. What they share is a particular conception of regional sovereignty: the rejection of attempts to create new realities through unilateral action, whether concerning ports and maritime corridors, transboundary resources or the territorial integrity of states. This distinction is important. The emerging alignment is less about containing Ethiopia as a country than about establishing limits on how regional power can be exercised. Ethiopia remains too large, too strategically located and too deeply embedded in the political and economic architecture of the Horn of Africa to be excluded from any sustainable regional order. The issue, therefore, is not whether Ethiopia should have access to the sea, but under what political and legal conditions that access should be secured. Marwa El-Shinawy This becomes particularly significant in the Red Sea. The declaration’s emphasis on the principle that the management and security of the Red Sea should primarily be the responsibility of its littoral states reflects a political position, not a rewriting of international law. But it also reflects the determination of coastal states to retain a central role in shaping the security and strategic arrangements of a waterway that has become the focus of intensifying regional and international competition. The Red Sea is no longer merely a maritime corridor linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean. It has become an increasingly contested strategic space where shipping routes, ports, military deployments, energy security and regional rivalries intersect. Any attempt to alter the balance along its shores therefore carries consequences well beyond the immediate countries involved. At the centre of this equation is Ethiopia. Since losing its direct access to the sea following Eritrea’s independence in 1993, maritime access has become a strategic and economic imperative for Addis Ababa. That imperative intensified after Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland in January 2024, an agreement Mogadishu rejected as an infringement on Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Yet Ethiopia’s need for reliable access to the sea does not give it a right to exercise sovereignty over another state’s territory. Conversely, protecting the sovereignty of coastal states does not necessarily require denying Ethiopia stable, long-term commercial access to ports. This is where the real space for a future settlement lies: in separating access from sovereignty, commerce from military presence, and economic necessity from territorial control. Ethiopia can have predictable access to international maritime trade without that access becoming a vehicle for establishing sovereign or military footholds inside another country. That distinction could prove decisive. If Ethiopia’s legitimate economic requirements are treated as inherently illegitimate, the result will be greater securitisation of the dispute and deeper regional polarisation. But if maritime access is negotiated through transparent, internationally recognised and commercially grounded arrangements, the issue could become a point of managed interdependence rather than a trigger for confrontation. A similar logic applies to the Nile dispute. Reaffirming the principles of avoiding significant harm, consultation and prior notification does not create new rules of international law. It does, however, place the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam issue within a broader conversation about regional security and stability rather than leaving it confined to the traditional trilateral framework involving Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia. This broader framing matters because the GERD dispute is no longer simply a technical disagreement over water management. It has become intertwined with questions of trust, sovereignty, development, strategic influence and the distribution of power in the Horn of Africa. Any durable arrangement will therefore have to address not only water flows and operating rules, but also the wider security environment in which the dam dispute has evolved. The Sudan and Somaliland questions are linked in the declaration through an even broader principle: resistance to altering the region’s political geography through unilateral faits accomplis. In both cases, sovereignty and territorial integrity are placed at the centre of the four countries’ understanding of regional order. But this is also where the limits of the emerging alignment become apparent. The four states do not share identical political interests, security priorities or foreign-policy calculations. Their cooperation is therefore better understood as an alignment of interests than as a coherent regional alliance. Nor does the declaration establish mutual-defence obligations, create joint forces or announce the establishment of military bases. Its immediate significance consequently lies less in military power than in political coordination, diplomatic signalling and the collective ability to raise the costs of unilateral action. For Egypt, however, the real test will be how this diplomatic leverage is used. A strategy aimed at permanently containing Ethiopia would neither be realistic nor sustainable. Addis Ababa will remain a central actor in any long-term political, economic or security arrangement in the Horn of Africa. Its geography and demographic and economic weight ensure that it will continue to seek secure and dependable access to maritime trade. Egypt’s strategic objective, therefore, should not be to exclude Ethiopia from the emerging regional order, but to shape the rules under which Ethiopia participates in it. This requires a delicate balance. Cairo needs to strengthen coordination with the Red Sea and Horn of Africa states while keeping open channels for negotiation with Addis Ababa. It must make unilateral moves costlier without making negotiated compromise politically impossible. That is ultimately the strategic value of the El Alamein Declaration. Its importance will not be measured by the sharpness of its language or by the number of issues it brings together. It will be measured by whether the four countries can transform their overlapping interests into a durable negotiating framework—one capable of deterring unilateral action while leaving sufficient political space for diplomacy. The Horn of Africa does not necessarily need more red lines. It needs clearer rules for managing competing interests before those interests harden into permanent confrontation. If the El Alamein Declaration is an attempt to alter the negotiating balance before the balance of power shifts again, its success will depend on whether it can move beyond the declaration of positions towards the construction of workable regional arrangements. The real challenge, therefore, is not to create another bloc in an already fragmented region. It is to establish a regional order in which sovereignty is protected, maritime access remains open, transboundary resources are governed through negotiated rules, and no single actor can alter the strategic map simply by creating facts on the ground. That would make the El Alamein Declaration more than a diplomatic statement. It would make it an early blueprint for a new regional balance. Marwa El-Shinawy, Academic and Writer

It is to establish a regional order in which sovereignty is protected, maritime access remains open, transboundary resources are governed through negotiated rules, and no single actor can alter the strategic map simply by creating facts on the ground.

That would make the El Alamein Declaration more than a diplomatic statement. It would make it an early blueprint for a new regional balance.

Marwa El-Shinawy, Academic and Writer

headline: Opinion | Trump and Xi: Who Holds the Keys to Power in the New World Order?
summary: The warmth of the reception extended by US President Donald Trump to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping—including meeting him at the foot of the aircraft steps—markedly exceeded customary White House protocols and ceremonial norms. This stands in sharp contrast, at the very least, to Trump’s most recent visit to Beijing, where he was greeted at the airport by Yang Jiechi, then serving as State Councilor for Foreign Affairs. This scene may not signal a broader realignment in the balance of power between the two nations. On the ground, however, Beijing has, over recent years, successfully constructed instruments of influence that extend far beyond trade into technology, supply chains, and critical minerals—securing spheres of influence that were previously subordinate to Washington, not merely abroad but even within US territory itself. The summit has concluded, yet the core issues continue to cloud relations between the two powers. As is customary, Xi laid out his red lines concerning Taiwan and urged Trump to handle the matter with the utmost caution, reaffirming that China’s position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity is unambiguous and non-negotiable. Both sides are navigating a fraught phase of commercial and political negotiations, waging wars by other means across multiple hot and cold fronts—from Taiwan to Venezuela, via the Middle East and Europe. At the heart of this contest lies the issue of rare earth elements and the technology used to separate them, one of the most consequential strategic questions that may well determine the future of the global order. Washington regards this struggle as an effort to preserve its eroding influence worldwide; Beijing views it as part of the transition of the international system toward a more multipolar world in which the United States is no longer the sole hegemonic power. Prof. Hatem Sadek Beijing grounds its vision in the instruments it already possesses. Rare earth elements—seventeen in number—are now used in a vast array of advanced technologies, from electronics and electric vehicles to defense systems and artificial intelligence data centers. Separating these rare earths from one another, however, proves far more difficult than extracting them. Herein lies China’s true strength: it resides not merely in the volume of what it mines but in its command of the more complex stages of the value chain—above all, separation, refining, and the manufacture of permanent magnets. These magnets are essential components across a wide spectrum of advanced American industries, including defense and aerospace, rendering control over their production a matter that transcends economics and touches national security itself. China demonstrated the scale of its leverage over the rare-earth market through a series of export controls imposed in 2025, which disrupted global supply chains. Following subsequent understandings reached between the two sides, Beijing suspended the implementation of certain expanded restrictions while retaining a system of permits and controls that continues to cause concern for American industry. Although the United States possesses rare-earth deposits, it operates only a handful of mines. China, by contrast, enjoys a broad industrial base and cumulative expertise in processing and separation; the United States faces a far steeper challenge in rapidly reconstituting these capabilities. According to the International Energy Agency, in 2024 China accounted for approximately 60 percent of global mined production of the rare earth elements used in magnet manufacturing and roughly 91 percent of global refined production of those elements. For the United States, leaving processing in Chinese hands remains the swiftest and least costly solution—yet it leaves America exposed to Beijing’s restrictions. Even if Washington elects to invest in domestic separation and refining capacity, the endeavor would require years and startup costs measured in the billions of dollars, with no guarantee of final product quality. The result is a clear asymmetry of instruments. Washington wields tariffs, advanced semiconductors, investment restrictions, financial power, sanctions, and access to cutting-edge technologies, including sophisticated artificial intelligence chips. Beijing, for its part, commands a different arsenal: manufacturing scale, supply-chain dominance, rare and critical minerals, processing capacity, and access to one of the world’s largest markets. Beneath these economic negotiations, however, lies a deeper security dilemma. Taiwan remains one of the most sensitive and dangerous issues in the Washington–Beijing relationship. During their May meeting in Beijing, Xi warned Trump that mismanagement of the crisis could drive bilateral relations into “a very dangerous place.” On this occasion, he again urged the American president to handle the matter with caution. Added to the foregoing is artificial intelligence, which has become the most complex issue of all. The two powers compete for mastery of it, yet neither can manage it alone. Measures intended to enhance security by one side—export controls, technology restrictions, military deployments, and supply-chain diversification—can be interpreted by the other as preparations for containment. With the summit concluded, levels of trust between Washington and Beijing remain exceedingly low. The world has come to view US–China relations primarily through the lexicon of economic disputes and tariffs. Those terms, however, have become markedly inadequate. The relationship has recently transformed into a competition over new, sophisticated chokepoints. Perhaps both sides will ultimately have to accept the most difficult reality of all: that the other will not disappear anytime soon. America will remain a formidable technological, financial, and military power. China will remain a formidable industrial, commercial, and geopolitical force. This is the truth. It is what Xi Jinping articulated at the summit when he observed that “cooperation between China and the United States may not solve all the world’s problems, but without our cooperation, it will be difficult to solve many of them.” In the end, the picture appears far more intricate than a mere contest over spheres of influence or control of mines. Strategic wealth resides not solely in the ownership of rare earths but in the capacity to separate, refine, and transform them into materials used in the industries of the future. And it is precisely here that one of the keys to the balance of power in the emerging world order may be found: not merely who possesses the mineral, but who possesses the technology that renders it usable. Prof. Hatem Sadek, Helwan University

headline: Egypt targets new investor segments across diverse financing markets: Kouchouk
summary: Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk said Egypt aims to reach new investor segments across diverse financing markets and secure more competitive terms to reduce financing costs. Kouchouk said Egypt was looking to embark on a new phase of bilateral cooperation to advance the financing of Egyptian projects in partnership with the private sector and develop a joint list of priority economic activities to support sustainable growth.

headline: Southern Yemeni leader calls for 'mobilization’ against Houthis as war escalates
summary: Aidarous al-Zubaidi, who leads the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council separatist group, called on southern Yemenis to fight for regional autonomy and against the Houthis, while condemning attacks on Saudi Arabia.
body_text:
Southern Yemen separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi called for a “popular mobilization” against the Houthis and in defense of autonomy for the south on Tuesday, making his first television appearance since his Southern Transitional Council (STC) lost its territory to the government in January.

Zubaidi’s address comes as the Saudi-backed government forces, supported by former STC affiliates and other groups in the south, work to reverse gains made by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels along Yemen’s Red Sea coast.

What happened: Zubaidi pleaded with southern Yemenis to “mobilize” against the Houthis and in defense of the “political entity” in the south.

“We declare the general popular mobilization to defend the south and its national liberation project, and to continue the national defense battle against the Houthi militias and their Iranian expansionist project, and all extremist groups, targeting our people, its political entity and its armed forces throughout the Arab territories of the Arab Republic on the borders before May 22, 1990,” he said, referring to South Yemen, which was independent from 1967 to 1990.

headline: Saudi Aramco administrative building attacked, limited fire reported
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen'sIran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified.Authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen'sIran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified.

Authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths.

A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran. The source said an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire.

The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.

The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Saturday that killed 13 people.

Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country.

Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the Aramco complex.

The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.

Authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country's southern region.

Four people were injured in Riyadh after fragments from two Houthi missiles fell following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defense said on Wednesday. The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defense spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, a man and a child.

The Houthis had threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.

The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets.

TheHouthis earlier on Tuesday said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Tuesday before the strike on Saudi Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.

While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz this month.

Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.

Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28.

Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan, Yomna Ehab and Enas Alashray; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne, Cynthia Osterman, Sanjeev Miglani and Edmund Klamann)

headline: Pakistan urges US, Iran to honor peace agreement amid rising Gulf tensions
summary: President Zardari calls for restraint, safe passage through Strait of Hormuz during meeting with visiting Russian interior minister
body_text:
Pakistani President Asif Ali Zardari on Tuesday urged the US and Iran to exercise restraint and honor their commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, a framework agreement reached in June to resolve the Middle East conflict.

Zardari called for differences to be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy, emphasizing the importance of safe maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

His remarks came during a meeting with Russian Interior Minister Vladimir Kolokoltsev in Islamabad, according to a statement from the president's office.

Zardari expressed deep concern over escalating tensions in the Gulf, particularly attacks on maritime traffic, energy installations and critical infrastructure.

He warned that the conflict posed serious challenges to regional stability, global energy security, trade and supply chains, stressing the need to respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of all states.

Kolokoltsev is on a four-day official visit to Pakistan, the first by a Russian interior minister to the South Asian country.

He said bilateral trade, which stood at $243.4 million in the 2025 financial year, remained below its potential and urged both countries to translate their leaders' goodwill into tangible results.

Kolokoltsev agreed that trade volumes did not reflect the strength of bilateral relations, saying there was considerable room for expansion.

He also invited Zardari to visit Russia.

Separately, Kolokoltsev held talks with Pakistani Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi on combating organized crime, terrorism, extremism, illicit arms and drug trafficking, and cybercrime, including telephone scams, phishing and cryptocurrency pyramid schemes.

The Russian minister said law enforcement cooperation was rooted in friendly and mutually beneficial bilateral relations, according to a statement from the Russian Embassy in Islamabad.
