headline: Egypt re-elected to chair Arab Electricity Council’s Executive Bureau for second consecutive term
summary: Egypt has been unanimously re-elected to chair the Executive Bureau of the Arab Ministerial Council for Electricity for a second consecutive term, with Algeria elected vice-chair, the Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said. The decision was taken during the 16th session of the Arab Ministerial Council for Electricity, hosted by Saudi Arabia in Riyadh over two days, with the participation of Arab electricity ministers, official delegations, experts, representatives of the Arab League’s energy department and international financing institutions. The re-election reflects Egypt’s role in supporting joint Arab cooperation within the framework of the League of Arab States, the ministry said. Mahmoud Esmat, Minister of Electricity and Renewable Energy, said Egypt would continue working with Arab partners to implement the Arab Common Electricity Market Agreement and advance comprehensive electricity interconnection across the region. The agreement was signed during the council’s 15th session, hosted by Egypt in the New Administrative Capital. Establishing a common Arab electricity market would mark the culmination of nearly two decades of efforts to achieve comprehensive electricity interconnection among Arab countries and establish an integrated regional market, Esmat said. He highlighted the importance of completing joint Arab electricity interconnection projects to establish an integrated market operating according to economic principles. Esmat cited the Egypt–Saudi Arabia electricity interconnection project, which has entered trial operation, as a model and a foundation for expanding electricity interconnection across the Arab region. He added that the next phase would require stronger cooperation, coordinated efforts and faster completion of the necessary procedures, alongside the development of an institutional framework to manage the common market. The minister also stressed the importance of exchanging expertise, building capacity and training personnel to address challenges, capitalise on available opportunities and apply modern technologies to the operation and management of the Arab Common Electricity Market.

headline: Egypt signs MoU with China’s C&D to develop dry bulk terminal at Al Max Port
summary: Egypt’s Ministry of Transport has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Chinese company Xiamen C&D to develop a specialised dry bulk terminal at Al Max Port in Alexandria, as part of efforts to develop Greater Alexandria Port and the Sokhna–Alexandria logistics corridor. The MoU was signed by the Alexandria Port Authority, represented by its Chairperson Ehab Salah, and C&D, represented by its Managing Director and CEO Lü Rongdian. The signing ceremony was attended by Minister of Transport Kamel Al-Wazir, Deputy Minister of Transport for Maritime Affairs Nehad Shaheen, Maritime Transport Sector Head Hussein El-Geziry, and officials from both sides. According to the ministry, the terminal is the first of four planned at Al Max Port. The project aims to strengthen Egypt’s position as a regional hub for transport, logistics and transit trade, while expanding the role of Egyptian ports in international trade and integrating them more closely into global supply chains. The proposed development plan includes upgrading marine berths to accommodate large vessels, expanding storage yards, modernising cargo-handling facilities and establishing a logistics centre to streamline truck movements. It also includes improving connections with the national railway network to strengthen integration between maritime, rail and road transport. Al-Wazir said the project would involve developing a specialised terminal for non-clean dry bulk cargo, supported by storage yards, silos and advanced cargo-handling facilities. The design includes two main berths capable of accommodating large cargo vessels. Upon completion, Alexandria Port is expected to be able to accommodate three large vessels simultaneously, the minister said. The project is also expected to create thousands of direct and indirect jobs during construction and operation, particularly in transport, logistics, storage and supporting industrial services. Al-Wazir added that the terminal would help reduce supply chain costs, improve the movement of raw materials and finished products, and enhance the competitiveness of Egyptian exports, particularly in the cement, steel and heavy industries. The technical plan also incorporates an environmental management system designed to comply with international standards, the ministry said. The project forms part of the government’s broader strategy to modernise Egyptian seaports, attract foreign investment and expand private-sector participation in transport infrastructure, in line with Egypt Vision 2030. For his part, Lü Rongdian said Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt and his meeting with President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi had helped attract Chinese companies to the Egyptian market and opened up investment opportunities across several sectors, including transport, logistics and related industries. Lü thanked the Ministry of Transport for its confidence in C&D and its support for cooperation with the company. He added that C&D aimed to make the project one of the most significant maritime transport and port developments in the Mediterranean. The company would work with its Egyptian partners to accelerate implementation and ensure efficient delivery, he said, describing the terminal as a potential starting point for further cooperation in developing other port terminals and manufacturing commercial vessels. Such cooperation would help strengthen bilateral ties and expand collaboration across supply chains, Lü added.

headline: H&L Egypt raises investment to $30m for South Korean sportswear factory in West Qantara
summary: The Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) has laid the foundation stone for a South Korean sportswear manufacturing plant in the West Qantara Industrial Zone, with planned investments doubling to $30m from an initial $15m, as Egypt seeks to attract further South Korean investment following President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi’s visit to South Korea. Mostafa Shikhon, chairperson of SCZONE, attended Tuesday’s groundbreaking ceremony alongside Kim Wan-jong, South Korea’s ambassador to Egypt; Mohamed Ibrahim, SCZONE vice-chairperson for the Northern Zone; Ahmed Essam El-Din, deputy governor of Ismailia; and representatives of the company and local authorities. The H&L Egypt Apparel project will cover 42,000 square metres and involve the establishment of a smart, environmentally friendly factory equipped with advanced manufacturing technologies. The facility is expected to create approximately 2,000 direct jobs and expand Egypt’s sportswear manufacturing capacity. Shikhon said the project marked an important step towards attracting South Korean investment to SCZONE, particularly as relations between Egypt and South Korea have advanced to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership. He added that the authority hoped the project would pave the way for a broader wave of South Korean investment across its industrial zones, citing the competitive advantages available to investors. The West Qantara Industrial Zone currently hosts 54 projects representing nine nationalities, with total investments of approximately $1.54bn, according to Shikhon. Textiles and ready-made garments account for the largest share of industrial activity in the zone, with 43 projects. He said SCZONE continued to support investors by providing an attractive investment environment and integrated infrastructure, with the aim of enhancing the competitiveness of Egyptian products, boosting exports and creating jobs. Kim Wan-jong said the H&L Egypt project would strengthen industrial and investment cooperation between Egypt and South Korea. He highlighted SCZONE’s strategic location and Egypt’s free trade agreements as advantages for manufacturing and exporting to international markets. The ambassador expressed hope that the project would serve as a successful model of cooperation between South Korean industrial expertise and Egyptian workers, encouraging further investment from South Korean companies in the economic zone. Lee Seung-jun, CEO of H&L Egypt Apparel, said the project marked an important beginning for the company’s operations in Egypt. He added that the company aimed to establish an advanced industrial base capable of competing in global markets by adopting modern technologies and applying quality and sustainability standards in sportswear manufacturing. The project is the first investment by a South Korean company to be contracted within SCZONE, with the agreement signed in November 2025. The increase in planned investment from $15m to $30m reflects the company’s confidence in the zone’s investment potential and its prospects as a base for expansion into international markets, according to SCZONE.

headline: Opinion | The El Alamein Declaration: New Red Lines in the Horn of Africa
summary: The El Alamein Declaration, issued following the October 4 meeting between Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud and Sudanese Sovereignty Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, represents an attempt to redraw some of the rules of the strategic balance in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa—not by creating a new military alliance, but by bringing together a set of issues that have until now largely been treated as separate crises. The significance of the declaration lies precisely in this linkage. Maritime security in the Red Sea, Ethiopia’s quest for access to the sea, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam dispute, Sudan’s territorial integrity and Somalia’s position on the Somaliland question are now being placed within a single regional framework. This reflects a growing recognition that the crises of the Horn of Africa have become so interconnected that managing them in isolation is increasingly difficult, if not impossible. Ethiopia’s absence from both the meeting and the resulting document carries an unmistakable political message. Yet it does not necessarily mean that the four countries are seeking to construct an explicitly anti-Ethiopian bloc. What they share is a particular conception of regional sovereignty: the rejection of attempts to create new realities through unilateral action, whether concerning ports and maritime corridors, transboundary resources or the territorial integrity of states. This distinction is important. The emerging alignment is less about containing Ethiopia as a country than about establishing limits on how regional power can be exercised. Ethiopia remains too large, too strategically located and too deeply embedded in the political and economic architecture of the Horn of Africa to be excluded from any sustainable regional order. The issue, therefore, is not whether Ethiopia should have access to the sea, but under what political and legal conditions that access should be secured. Marwa El-Shinawy This becomes particularly significant in the Red Sea. The declaration’s emphasis on the principle that the management and security of the Red Sea should primarily be the responsibility of its littoral states reflects a political position, not a rewriting of international law. But it also reflects the determination of coastal states to retain a central role in shaping the security and strategic arrangements of a waterway that has become the focus of intensifying regional and international competition. The Red Sea is no longer merely a maritime corridor linking the Indian Ocean to the Mediterranean. It has become an increasingly contested strategic space where shipping routes, ports, military deployments, energy security and regional rivalries intersect. Any attempt to alter the balance along its shores therefore carries consequences well beyond the immediate countries involved. At the centre of this equation is Ethiopia. Since losing its direct access to the sea following Eritrea’s independence in 1993, maritime access has become a strategic and economic imperative for Addis Ababa. That imperative intensified after Ethiopia signed a memorandum of understanding with Somaliland in January 2024, an agreement Mogadishu rejected as an infringement on Somalia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Yet Ethiopia’s need for reliable access to the sea does not give it a right to exercise sovereignty over another state’s territory. Conversely, protecting the sovereignty of coastal states does not necessarily require denying Ethiopia stable, long-term commercial access to ports. This is where the real space for a future settlement lies: in separating access from sovereignty, commerce from military presence, and economic necessity from territorial control. Ethiopia can have predictable access to international maritime trade without that access becoming a vehicle for establishing sovereign or military footholds inside another country. That distinction could prove decisive. If Ethiopia’s legitimate economic requirements are treated as inherently illegitimate, the result will be greater securitisation of the dispute and deeper regional polarisation. But if maritime access is negotiated through transparent, internationally recognised and commercially grounded arrangements, the issue could become a point of managed interdependence rather than a trigger for confrontation. A similar logic applies to the Nile dispute. Reaffirming the principles of avoiding significant harm, consultation and prior notification does not create new rules of international law. It does, however, place the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam issue within a broader conversation about regional security and stability rather than leaving it confined to the traditional trilateral framework involving Egypt, Sudan and Ethiopia. This broader framing matters because the GERD dispute is no longer simply a technical disagreement over water management. It has become intertwined with questions of trust, sovereignty, development, strategic influence and the distribution of power in the Horn of Africa. Any durable arrangement will therefore have to address not only water flows and operating rules, but also the wider security environment in which the dam dispute has evolved. The Sudan and Somaliland questions are linked in the declaration through an even broader principle: resistance to altering the region’s political geography through unilateral faits accomplis. In both cases, sovereignty and territorial integrity are placed at the centre of the four countries’ understanding of regional order. But this is also where the limits of the emerging alignment become apparent. The four states do not share identical political interests, security priorities or foreign-policy calculations. Their cooperation is therefore better understood as an alignment of interests than as a coherent regional alliance. Nor does the declaration establish mutual-defence obligations, create joint forces or announce the establishment of military bases. Its immediate significance consequently lies less in military power than in political coordination, diplomatic signalling and the collective ability to raise the costs of unilateral action. For Egypt, however, the real test will be how this diplomatic leverage is used. A strategy aimed at permanently containing Ethiopia would neither be realistic nor sustainable. Addis Ababa will remain a central actor in any long-term political, economic or security arrangement in the Horn of Africa. Its geography and demographic and economic weight ensure that it will continue to seek secure and dependable access to maritime trade. Egypt’s strategic objective, therefore, should not be to exclude Ethiopia from the emerging regional order, but to shape the rules under which Ethiopia participates in it. This requires a delicate balance. Cairo needs to strengthen coordination with the Red Sea and Horn of Africa states while keeping open channels for negotiation with Addis Ababa. It must make unilateral moves costlier without making negotiated compromise politically impossible. That is ultimately the strategic value of the El Alamein Declaration. Its importance will not be measured by the sharpness of its language or by the number of issues it brings together. It will be measured by whether the four countries can transform their overlapping interests into a durable negotiating framework—one capable of deterring unilateral action while leaving sufficient political space for diplomacy. The Horn of Africa does not necessarily need more red lines. It needs clearer rules for managing competing interests before those interests harden into permanent confrontation. If the El Alamein Declaration is an attempt to alter the negotiating balance before the balance of power shifts again, its success will depend on whether it can move beyond the declaration of positions towards the construction of workable regional arrangements. The real challenge, therefore, is not to create another bloc in an already fragmented region. It is to establish a regional order in which sovereignty is protected, maritime access remains open, transboundary resources are governed through negotiated rules, and no single actor can alter the strategic map simply by creating facts on the ground. That would make the El Alamein Declaration more than a diplomatic statement. It would make it an early blueprint for a new regional balance. Marwa El-Shinawy, Academic and Writer

headline: Opinion | Trump and Xi: Who Holds the Keys to Power in the New World Order?
summary: The warmth of the reception extended by US President Donald Trump to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping—including meeting him at the foot of the aircraft steps—markedly exceeded customary White House protocols and ceremonial norms. This stands in sharp contrast, at the very least, to Trump’s most recent visit to Beijing, where he was greeted at the airport by Yang Jiechi, then serving as State Councilor for Foreign Affairs. This scene may not signal a broader realignment in the balance of power between the two nations. On the ground, however, Beijing has, over recent years, successfully constructed instruments of influence that extend far beyond trade into technology, supply chains, and critical minerals—securing spheres of influence that were previously subordinate to Washington, not merely abroad but even within US territory itself. The summit has concluded, yet the core issues continue to cloud relations between the two powers. As is customary, Xi laid out his red lines concerning Taiwan and urged Trump to handle the matter with the utmost caution, reaffirming that China’s position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity is unambiguous and non-negotiable. Both sides are navigating a fraught phase of commercial and political negotiations, waging wars by other means across multiple hot and cold fronts—from Taiwan to Venezuela, via the Middle East and Europe. At the heart of this contest lies the issue of rare earth elements and the technology used to separate them, one of the most consequential strategic questions that may well determine the future of the global order. Washington regards this struggle as an effort to preserve its eroding influence worldwide; Beijing views it as part of the transition of the international system toward a more multipolar world in which the United States is no longer the sole hegemonic power. Prof. Hatem Sadek Beijing grounds its vision in the instruments it already possesses. Rare earth elements—seventeen in number—are now used in a vast array of advanced technologies, from electronics and electric vehicles to defense systems and artificial intelligence data centers. Separating these rare earths from one another, however, proves far more difficult than extracting them. Herein lies China’s true strength: it resides not merely in the volume of what it mines but in its command of the more complex stages of the value chain—above all, separation, refining, and the manufacture of permanent magnets. These magnets are essential components across a wide spectrum of advanced American industries, including defense and aerospace, rendering control over their production a matter that transcends economics and touches national security itself. The warmth of the reception extended by US President Donald Trump to his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping—including meeting him at the foot of the aircraft steps—markedly exceeded customary White House protocols and ceremonial norms. This stands in sharp contrast, at the very least, to Trump’s most recent visit to Beijing, where he was greeted at the airport by Yang Jiechi, then serving as State Councilor for Foreign Affairs.

This scene may not signal a broader realignment in the balance of power between the two nations. On the ground, however, Beijing has, over recent years, successfully constructed instruments of influence that extend far beyond trade into technology, supply chains, and critical minerals—securing spheres of influence that were previously subordinate to Washington, not merely abroad but even within US territory itself.

The summit has concluded, yet the core issues continue to cloud relations between the two powers. As is customary, Xi laid out his red lines concerning Taiwan and urged Trump to handle the matter with the utmost caution, reaffirming that China’s position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity is unambiguous and non-negotiable.

Both sides are navigating a fraught phase of commercial and political negotiations, waging wars by other means across multiple hot and cold fronts—from Taiwan to Venezuela, via the Middle East and Europe. At the heart of this contest lies the issue of rare earth elements and the technology used to separate them, one of the most consequential strategic questions that may well determine the future of the global order.

Washington regards this struggle as an effort to preserve its eroding influence worldwide; Beijing views it as part of the transition of the international system toward a more multipolar world in which the United States is no longer the sole hegemonic power.

Beijing grounds its vision in the instruments it already possesses. Rare earth elements—seventeen in number—are now used in a vast array of advanced technologies, from electronics and electric vehicles to defense systems and artificial intelligence data centers. Separating these rare earths from one another, however, proves far more difficult than extracting them. Herein lies China’s true strength: it resides not merely in the volume of what it mines but in its command of the more complex stages of the value chain—above all, separation, refining, and the manufacture of permanent magnets. Following subsequent understandings reached between the two sides, Beijing suspended the implementation of certain expanded restrictions while retaining a system of permits and controls that continues to cause concern for American industry.

Although the United States possesses rare-earth deposits, it operates only a handful of mines. China, by contrast, enjoys a broad industrial base and cumulative expertise in processing and separation; the United States faces a far steeper challenge in rapidly reconstituting these capabilities.

According to the International Energy Agency, in 2024 China accounted for approximately 60 percent of global mined production of the rare earth elements used in magnet manufacturing and roughly 91 percent of global refined production of those elements.

During their May meeting in Beijing, Xi warned Trump that mismanagement of the crisis could drive bilateral relations into “a very dangerous place.” On this occasion, he again urged the American president to handle the matter with caution.

Added to the foregoing is artificial intelligence, which has become the most complex issue of all. The two powers compete for mastery of it, yet neither can manage it alone. Measures intended to enhance security by one side—export controls, technology restrictions, military deployments, and supply-chain diversification—can be interpreted by the other as preparations for containment.

With the summit concluded, levels of trust between Washington and Beijing remain exceedingly low. The relationship has recently transformed into a competition over new, sophisticated chokepoints.

Perhaps both sides will ultimately have to accept the most difficult reality of all: that the other will not disappear anytime soon. America will remain a formidable technological, financial, and military power. China will remain a formidable industrial, commercial, and geopolitical force. This is the truth. headline: Saudi Aramco administrative building attacked, limited fire reported
summary: By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDinRIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen'sIran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified.Authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari and Menna AlaaElDin

RIYADH, Oct 13 (Reuters) - An administrative building belonging to Saudi Arabia's state-owned oil company Saudi Aramco in the eastern city of Dhahran was attacked, causing a limited fire, the Energy Ministry said in a statement on Wednesday as fighting between Yemen'sIran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified.

Authorities responded to the incident late on Tuesday and took necessary measures, the ministry said, adding that there were no injuries or deaths.

A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex in Dhahran. The source said an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged. The source and two other people with knowledge of the matter said the building was on fire.

The complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.

The Houthis have for a week been firing ballistic missiles and drones at key Saudi sites in retaliation for the kingdom's backing of government forces in Yemen's reignited civil war. Riyadh’s international airport has received four strikes, including one on Saturday that killed 13 people.

Saturday's ballistic missile strike on Riyadh airport was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade, with further attacks grounding flights across the country.

Earlier, six sources told Reuters they heard loud booms near the Aramco complex.

The Saudi-led coalition said fragments of a missile that it had intercepted and destroyed in Dhahran had fallen on a residential area, without providing further details.

Authorities also reported that drones and missiles were intercepted and destroyed in the capital, Riyadh, and the country's southern region.

Four people were injured in Riyadh after fragments from two Houthi missiles fell following their interception and destruction, Saudi Civil Defense said on Wednesday. The debris caused limited damage to 15 homes in the capital, the Civil Defense spokesperson said, adding that the injured were two women, a man and a child.

The Houthis had threatened a "harsh and painful" response to Saudi-led strikes on the Yemeni capital Sanaa, with spokesperson Yahya Saree saying targets could include the Saudi Aramco headquarters in Dhahran and an oil refinery in Riyadh.

The group has warned oil workers in Saudi Arabia to stay away from sites that could be targets.

TheHouthis earlier on Tuesday said Saudi Arabia was attacking Sanaa, and the Saudi-led coalition warned civilians to stay away from an oil depot on the city's outskirts.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah television reported that the Saudi-led coalition had targeted the Yemen Petroleum Company's Sabah central station, a fuel depot on the outskirts of Sanaa.

The coalition said in a statement on Tuesday evening that it attacked the station and other sites in an operation aimed at "neutralizing the capabilities of Houthis" to threaten Saudi Arabia, Yemen and international waterways.

The Saudi cabinet, chaired by de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, issued a statement on Tuesday before the strike on Saudi Aramco saying the Houthis would face consequences for their repeated attacks on the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, has become a more vital route for Saudi and other global energy supplies since the start of the Iran war in February, when Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz leading from the Gulf to the Indian Ocean.

While a government offensive that began a week ago pushed the Houthis from the area closest to the strait, the group remains embedded nearby and has made gains around the city of Taiz this month.

Saudi Arabia has been seeking wider support from allies for its campaign against the Houthis and to help it ward off their missile and drone attacks.

Washington, Saudi Arabia's strongest ally and longtime security guarantor, has so far rebuffed Saudi efforts to bring it directly into the war against the Houthis.

The Yemen conflict has resumed as a spillover from the wider US-Iran war that began with the US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic on February 28.

Iran, Saudi Arabia's longtime regional rival, has offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, its foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday in statements reiterated by the ministry on Monday.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari, Menna Alaa El Din, Yasmine Ghania, Tala Ramadan, Yomna Ehab and Enas Alashray; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Andrew Cawthorne, Cynthia Osterman, Sanjeev Miglani and Edmund Klamann)

headline: Russia to convene Arria-formula meeting on human rights violations in Ukraine on Oct. 14
summary: The format suggests the participation of all members of the UN Security Council
body_text:
UN, October 14. /TASS/. The UN Security Council will hold an informal Arria-formula meeting at Russia’s initiative on October 14, focused on human rights violations in Ukraine, according to the Security Council’s work program.

The meeting is titled "Piercing the Blind Spots of Violations of International Humanitarian Law and International Human Rights Law in the Context of the Ukrainian Crisis."

The Arria-formula meetings provide interested council members an opportunity to engage in a direct dialogue with high representatives of governments and international organizations, as well as non-state parties, on matters with which they are concerned and which fall within the purview of responsibility of the Security Council. The process is named after Ambassador Diego Arria of Venezuela, who initiated the practice in 1992. The format suggests the participation of all members of the Security Council.

headline: Egypt explores Indonesian experience in health financing, pooled procurement
summary: Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar discussed with his Indonesian counterpart, Budi Sadikin, ways to draw on Indonesia’s experience in health project financing and the pooled procurement of medical equipment, as the two countries explored broader cooperation in hospital infrastructure, medical technology, oncology and workforce training. The talks were held at the headquarters of Egypt’s Ministry of Health and Population in the New Administrative Capital, where the two sides discussed expanding cooperation to develop their health systems and exchange technical expertise. According to the ministry, the meeting covered the modernisation of medical equipment and the use of pooled procurement mechanisms to reduce costs, improve resource efficiency and expand access to diagnostic and treatment services. The Indonesian minister outlined his country’s experience in mobilising financing, grants and concessional loans to accelerate health-sector development projects. Both sides discussed how similar approaches could inform health financing in Egypt. The meeting also addressed the importance of training medical personnel alongside the introduction of advanced equipment and technologies, ensuring that specialised staff are available to operate and maintain them effectively. The two ministers discussed cooperation in cancer care, with the Indonesian side expressing interest in Egypt’s experience in developing oncology services and exchanging expertise in the field. Talks also covered potential joint efforts to support health systems in African countries through technical cooperation and international financing mechanisms designed to accelerate health infrastructure projects and expand access to essential and specialised medical services. Indonesia expressed readiness to share its experience in health project financing and explore cooperation with international financial institutions on projects in Egypt and Africa. The discussions also addressed what the ministry described as strengthening health sovereignty through research and development, expanding domestic production of medical products and improving access to vaccines, medicines and health technologies, particularly during health emergencies and pandemics. The two sides agreed to maintain coordination between their health ministries and expand cooperation. However, the statement did not announce specific projects, financing commitments or implementation timelines.

headline: Egypt backs financing for 36 projects in southern Nile Basin states: Sewilam
summary: Egypt has backed efforts to mobilise financing for a package of 36 projects in southern Nile Basin countries, covering hydropower, electricity interconnections, transmission lines, water supply and multipurpose infrastructure, Minister of Water Resources and Irrigation Hani Sewilam said. Sewilam made the remarks during a meeting in Berlin with Wolf-Jürgen, head of Germany’s Federal Academy for Security Policy, and an accompanying delegation to discuss Egyptian-German cooperation in water resources and support for water and climate adaptation projects in Africa. He said the 36 projects fall under the Nile Basin Initiative’s investment programme, which aims to identify priority projects and strengthen their technical, environmental and social readiness ahead of financing and implementation. Sewilam also highlighted a newly launched Egyptian financing mechanism, initially funded with $100m, to study and implement development projects in Nile Basin countries based on their priorities. These include infrastructure and dam projects in the southern basin states. Egypt has already implemented more than $120m worth of cooperation projects in Nile Basin countries and elsewhere in Africa, he said. The projects have included drilling approximately 365 wells, installing solar-powered groundwater stations, constructing rainwater-harvesting reservoirs and river ports, and establishing rainfall and flood forecasting centres and water-quality laboratories. Egyptian programmes have also covered flood protection, aquatic weed control and training for around 1,650 participants from Nile Basin and other African countries, according to the ministry. During the meeting, Sewilam and the German delegation discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in water research and practical applications, as well as the water-energy-food-ecosystems nexus and support for the Pan African Centre for Water and Climate Adaptation. The minister also outlined Egypt’s “Water System 2.0” approach, which focuses on maximising the return from each unit of water, expanding the use of digital technologies, improving water-system operations and governance, and making greater use of research and innovation. The talks also addressed Egypt’s role as chair of the African Water Facility and ongoing cooperation with Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development to help African countries prepare water and climate projects that are ready for financing. Sewilam said international river management should be based on cooperation, consultation and mutual benefit among riparian states, while adhering to international law.

headline: CMA CGM continues return to Suez Canal as authority reports surge in large vessel transits

headline: Hyundai Motor Group to invest US$15.5 bln in India through 2032
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's Hyundai Motor Group said Wednesday it w...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's Hyundai Motor Group said Wednesday it will invest US$15.5 billion in India through 2032, underscoring the country's importance to its global growth strategy.

The group's Executive Chair Euisun Chung announced the investment during a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi on Tuesday, the group said in a press release.

"India is a key strategic market for Hyundai Motor Group's future growth, expansion into emerging markets and next-generation automotive innovation. The investment will be made over seven years starting this year," Chung said.

The investment will go toward expanding manufacturing capacity, developing research and development (R&D) infrastructure, fostering local suppliers to increase parts localization, and advancing future technologies, the release said.

To implement the investment plan, the group plans to establish a dedicated investment entity in India.

With a population of 1.47 billion, India is the world's third-largest automobile market after China and the United States.

Automakers seeking to compete in India need local production facilities, as import tariffs can reach 70 percent to 110 percent.

Hyundai Motor Co. operates two plants in Chennai and another in Pune, while its smaller affiliate Kia Corp. operates a plant in Anantapur. The facilities have a combined annual production capacity of 1.4 million vehicles, which is expected to increase with further investment.

Hyundai and Kia sold a combined 852,164 vehicles in India last year, accounting for 18.7 percent of the country's passenger vehicle market and ranking second behind Maruti Suzuki India Ltd.

headline: Saudi employee arrested for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
summary: A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company's San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday. "We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement. body_text:
A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company's San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

"We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.

OpenAI's security team found the device late last month and the employee, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on October 9, the US Justice Department said.

Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room," according to a Justice Department statement.

He was allegedly caught on camera "near" the conference room multiple times but was not authorized to participate in meetings located there.

He used a "productivity tool" to search for more information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the statement.

A chatbot account connected to Alfozan's spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting memory cards.

"This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.

"The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America's cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats," Clayton added.

The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate in artificial intelligence, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence."

Saudi Arabia's state-backed AI firm Humain invested $3 billion in Elon Musk's xAI shortly before the American billionaire's space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.

Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data center in Saudi Arabia.

It was not immediately clear what, if any information the recording device was able to collect.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.

A second device was found by OpenAI's security team when they searched an unattended bag that belonged to Alfozan, according to the Justice Department.

Alfozan was caught on security footage from inside the restricted conference room where he appeared to look behind the television where the recording device had been placed, the Department said.

A LinkedIn account matching Alfozan's name and resume show that he previously worked at Facebook-owner Meta, as well as an AI startup and a venture capital firm.

He was also a student at University of California at Berkeley and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The Justice Department said Alfozen had been charged with "using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications," for which he could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

It did not accuse Alfozan nor Saudi Arabia, which is a close US ally, of spying activity in its statement on Tuesday.

Alfozan is expected to appear at a federal court hearing on October 19.

In 2022, a former Twitter worker, Ahmad Abouammo, was found guilty of spying for Saudi officials keen to unmask critics on the platform.

headline: How will a diesel deal with Russia impact the U.S. market?
summary: The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the U.S. in September. Can President Trump's deal for Russia to release more diesel onto the market bring the price down?
body_text:
The price of diesel hit an all-time high in the U.S. in September. Can President Trump's deal for Russia to release more diesel onto the market bring the price down?

OK, there are plenty of legal and political questions surrounding President Trump's deal to get Russia to release more oil to the U.S. and global markets. And, of course, a lot of Americans are wondering how that deal could affect the price of diesel. NPR energy reporter Willa Rubin joins us now to talk about all of this. Hi, Willa.

WILLA RUBIN, BYLINE: Hi, Ailsa.

CHANG: Hi. OK, so give us the lay of the land here. What is happening with the price of diesel in the U.S. right now?

RUBIN: Well, it hit an all-time high a few weeks ago, which is important for the U.S. economy. You know, our industrial supply chain relies on diesel, tractors that farmers use, trucks that bring your food from farms eventually to the grocery store. If diesel is expensive, that contributes to the price of everything that you buy. Now, the price of a gallon has come down a little bit since that September high. On average, it's now $6.27, according to AAA, but that is still really high. Diesel is about $2.60 more than this time last year.

CHANG: OK, and explain this to me. What did President Trump say about how he expects this deal would work exactly?

RUBIN: Yeah, so in a post on Truth Social on Friday, President Trump said that Russia had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and to global markets immediately. But, like, is that a little or a lot in terms of how much the U.S. actually uses?

CHANG: Yeah, which is it?

RUBIN: Yeah. So to put this in context for the rest of October, Will O'Neil is an analyst at S&P Global Energy. He's a follower of all things diesel.

WILL O'NEIL: Because I could even do some quick Excel math. So 300,000 tons over the course of 20 days is...

RUBIN: I love that you broke out an Excel spreadsheet mid conversation (laughter).

O'NEIL: That's what I do. That's my job.

RUBIN: So he figured out that if you convert tons to barrels and the U.S. uses up to 4 million barrels a day, the entire amount expected to be released in October adds up to about half the diesel the U.S. uses in just one day.

O'NEIL: It's drops in the bucket.

RUBIN: Drops in the bucket. And if you do some more math using the entire amount expected to be released over the coming months, O'Neil said it adds up to about nine days' worth.

CHANG: Let me ask you this. Is Russia really in any position to export all of this diesel?

RUBIN: Analysts in the U.S. don't know, but what...

RUBIN: ...They do know is that Russia's refinery capacity has been significantly reduced by Ukraine's strikes. O'Neil says it's probably reduced 40- to 45% of their capacity.

O'NEIL: Ukrainian drone strikes have taken so much of its refining capacity offline that it just simply doesn't have the diesel production to send to global markets.

RUBIN: He says this deal does not change that reality. Russia has had an export ban since July, though they partially lifted it on Saturday. Also worth noting, the U.S. has had wide ranging sanctions on Russian energy since its full scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. On Friday, the Treasury Department announced it was temporarily waiving sanctions on diesel for about six months. And this has gotten some pushback from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle. This is a really complicated situation, Ailsa, with a lot of moving parts.

CHANG: Clearly. OK, if Russia really can bring this diesel to market, could that help lower prices in the U.S., you think, eventually?

RUBIN: Big picture, what drives diesel prices is global demand. And there's a global diesel deficit right now. A good chunk of that is due to the war in Iran. Claudio Galimberti is a partner and chief economist at Rystad Energy. He says the world is missing up to 1.5 million barrels per day that normally come from the Middle East and another million barrels that would come from Russia.

CLAUDIO GALIMBERTI: So it's a huge gap, and this deal only address (ph) a very small portion of that.

CHANG: OK, Willa, I'm no economist, but it sounds like he doesn't think this will really lower prices all that much. Am I getting that right?

RUBIN: Yeah. Analysts told me we will only start to see big meaningful drops in prices by solving these bottlenecks by ending the wars.

CHANG: That is NPR's Willa Rubin. Thank you so much, Willa.

RUBIN: Thank you so much, Ailsa.

VerdictThe numbers suggest that both Haaland and Mbappe stand a reasonable chance of surpassing Ronaldo’s mark if they can stay fit and play in the majority of matches for their respective clubs.Both will be helped by the extra games offered by the competition’s new format, with teams now guaranteed eight league phase games as opposed to the six group games Ronaldo used to get before the knockouts. If anything, this exercise really underlines Ronaldo’s incredible longevity and potency in front of goal. Interestingly, he scored goal number 140 on his 183rd and final Champions League appearance in a 2-0 win for Manchester United over Villarreal on November 23, 2021. He was 36 years, nine months and 18 days old at the time.Should Mbappe manage to stay at Madrid into the twilight of his career, then you would have to give him a shot, given the number of goals he has scored since his move to Los Blancos, and their consistency in reaching the latter stages of the competition year after year. Ronaldo was 33 when he left Madrid, while Mbappe's compatriot, Karim Benzema, stayed there until he was 35. That said, averaging 11 per season to get there by the time he is 35 is a big ask, and he may need to keep playing into the second half of his 30s to eventually top the list. Haaland, 19 months younger than Mbappe, will feel that 141 is an achievable target if he can regularly play 10 or more games per season in the competition. As the younger man, and with the better goals-per-game ratio, you'd have to make the Manchester City striker a firm favourite. The X-factor is, of course, Mbappe's Real Madrid form. His 15 last season was the third most ever behind Ronaldo in 2015/16 (16) and 2013/14 (17). body_text:
Erling Haaland’s two goals against Porto on the opening matchday of the 2026/27 Champions League maintained the Manchester City striker’s incredible scoring rate in the competition.

Haaland has scored 59 goals from 59 games at the elite level of European club football, giving him the best goals-per-game ratio of any notable player in its history.

In fact, he is the only player to have scored a significant number of goals at a rate of at least one per game. It’s also the best scoring rate of the three active players among the Champions League's all-time top scorers: Haaland, Harry Kane and Kylian Mbappe.

The benchmark, however, is still some way off for all three. Cristiano Ronaldo is out in front with a staggering 140 goals from 183 appearances in the competition.

So, this raises the question: Can one of this generation’s elite goalscorers actually beat Ronaldo’s record?

Kane has an impressive haul of 54 goals in 70 games, but at 33, the England captain can almost certainly be ruled out of the race. Sadly for him, he stayed at Tottenham Hotspur for too long.

That leaves us with Haaland and Mbappe. Both are in action on Tuesday night, with Manchester City hosting PSG and Real Madrid visiting Roma.

Below is an appraisal of each man’s chances of going down as European club football’s greatest-ever goalscorer.

Haaland, 26, made his Champions League debut for RB Salzburg against Genk on September 17, 2019, and scored a hat-trick. Of course he did.

Since then, as stated above, he has scored at a rate of a goal per game in the competition. His best return came in 2022/23, when he scored 12 times in 11 games and ended up with a winner’s medal. He currently sits seventh on the all-time list.

This season will be his eighth in the Champions League. Among those, there is an outlier – 2021/22 – when he played just three games, scoring as many goals, as his then club, Borussia Dortmund, made an early exit.

Every other season, he has played at least eight games. If we remove that campaign and the current one, then he has a tally of 54 goals in 55 games across six seasons, at an average of nine goals per season.

By that calculation, he will need another 9.1 seasons (including the current one) to get the 82 goals he requires to break Ronaldo’s record – form, fitness and participation willing, of course.

That means Haaland needs to continue scoring at the same rate until the 2035/36 season. The Norwegian star, born in July 2000, will be 35 by then.

It’s a big ask to be so consistent for so long, but in this era of supreme athleticism, it’s far from inconceivable. There’s also the frightening prospect that he could still get better and increase his goal output.

Mbappe, 27, has 71 goals in 99 Champions League games following his strike in Real Madrid’s 2-1 victory over Inter Milan in their opening game of the 2026/27 competition. That took him to joint-fifth with Raul in the all-time list.

He made his UCL debut on September 27, 2016, with a 13-minute cameo off the bench in Monaco’s 1-1 draw with Bayer Leverkusen.

He is now into his 11th season of Champions League football. Mbappe has managed at least eight games in each of his first 10 seasons, making his average a pleasingly concise seven goals per season, with 70 goals across the 10 completed campaigns.

At that rate, he will need exactly 10 more to chalk up the 70 goals he requires to surpass Ronaldo. Mbappe will be 38 heading into the back end of the 2036/37 season.

It's clear he needs to speed up, and there's ample evidence to suggest that he has. His goals-per-game rate has spiked sharply since he moved to Real Madrid in 2024.

The France striker managed an incredible 15 goals in 11 games last term – his best return – while he has a total of 22 in 25 games in his two completed seasons at the club.

At an average of 11 per campaign, he would need another six-and-a-half seasons to potentially put him within striking distance of the record by the 2032/33 season, when he will be 34, turning 35 in December.

The numbers suggest that both Haaland and Mbappe stand a reasonable chance of surpassing Ronaldo’s mark if they can stay fit and play in the majority of matches for their respective clubs.

Both will be helped by the extra games offered by the competition’s new format, with teams now guaranteed eight league phase games as opposed to the six group games Ronaldo used to get before the knockouts.

If anything, this exercise really underlines Ronaldo’s incredible longevity and potency in front of goal. Interestingly, he scored goal number 140 on his 183rd and final Champions League appearance in a 2-0 win for Manchester United over Villarreal on November 23, 2021. He was 36 years, nine months and 18 days old at the time.

Should Mbappe manage to stay at Madrid into the twilight of his career, then you would have to give him a shot, given the number of goals he has scored since his move to Los Blancos, and their consistency in reaching the latter stages of the competition year after year. Ronaldo was 33 when he left Madrid, while Mbappe's compatriot, Karim Benzema, stayed there until he was 35.

That said, averaging 11 per season to get there by the time he is 35 is a big ask, and he may need to keep playing into the second half of his 30s to eventually top the list.

Haaland, 19 months younger than Mbappe, will feel that 141 is an achievable target if he can regularly play 10 or more games per season in the competition.

As the younger man, and with the better goals-per-game ratio, you'd have to make the Manchester City striker a firm favourite. The X-factor is, of course, Mbappe's Real Madrid form. His 15 last season was the third most ever behind Ronaldo in 2015/16 (16) and 2013/14 (17).

Either way, it seems certain that both men will finish their careers considered among the finest goalscorers in modern football history. If either eventually stands alone as the best, remains to be seen.

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- A bridge between North Korea and China will officially open to traffic this week after sitting idle for more than a decade following its construction, according to a Chinese news report on Wednesday.

The New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the North Korean city of Sinuiju and Dandong in China, will open Thursday, according to China's Xinhua News Agency.

The construction of the four-lane motor bridge began in October 2011 and wrapped up in October 2014, but it stood unused for years because North Korea did not finish the buildings and infrastructure on its side.

Vehicles have recently been spotted crossing the 3,024-meter bridge, raising the possibility of a test run.

The bridge, which is expected to boost trade and personnel exchanges between the two countries, opens after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged at their June summit in Pyongyang to raise their ties to a strategic level and enhance exchanges.

headline: IMF lowers S. Korea's gov't debt forecasts on improved tax revenue prospects
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its f...
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- The International Monetary Fund (IMF) lowered its forecasts for South Korea's government debt to gross domestic product (GDP) ratio through 2031, citing its strong economic growth and prospects for improved revenue conditions, the budget ministry said Wednesday.

The Washington-based organization said in the IMF Fiscal Monitor report that Seoul's government gross debt-to-GDP ratio would reach 46.1 percent this year, projecting it will remain in the mid-40 percent to low-50 percent range through 2031.

The 2026 projection marks a decrease of 8.3 percentage points from the April edition.

The IMF also expected the ratio will reach 51.3 percent in 2031, down 11.8 percentage points from its April forecast.

The projected ratio for this year represents around 37 percent of the Group of Seven average of 123.6 percent and 43 percent of the average of 107.6 percent for 38 advanced economies.

The Ministry of Planning and Budget said the IMF's latest assessment reflects South Korea's efforts to create a virtuous cycle in which expansionary fiscal policy supports economic growth, which in turn generates stronger tax revenue.

The IMF highlighted South Korea's strong GDP growth, coupled with prospects for improved revenue conditions through 2030, the ministry added.

South Korea will continue efforts to invest proactively to bolster the country's growth potential and ensure fiscal sustainability, creating a virtuous cycle between fiscal policy and economic growth, the ministry said.

Earlier this week, the IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea to 3.3 percent, up 0.7 percentage point from its July projection, citing strong semiconductor exports that more than offset the fallout from the Middle East war.

The 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, meanwhile, kicked off in Bangkok on Monday and will run through Sunday.

headline: 'There are no dreams left': Families of two sailors missing after drone attack off Oman speak of their grief
summary: Two families are “sick with grief” waiting for news of two young sailors missing days after an empty tanker was struck by a drone off Oman. The oil tanker, MT Petro Dolphin, was hit near the Sohar anchorage on Sunday. Relatives in two northern Indian villages are waiting for information on Amit Singh, 20, and Bir Bahadur Yadav, 25, who were on the main deck when the drone struck and fire spread. Of the 12 crew on the Nicaraguan-flagged tanker, nine Indians and one Bangladeshi national were rescued and two seafarers are missing, India’s External Affairs Ministry has said. It was the first sailing job for both men, and their relatives have described the incomprehensible loss they felt on learning of the attack. “Amit’s parents are in and out of consciousness, they cannot cope. It’s all finished, there are no dreams left, it’s all broken,” Amit Singh’s uncle, Ravindar Singh, told The National from Gopala village in Uttar Pradesh.“It’s as if they are dead. As long as they live, they will be in this condition, like death. We are trying to support them but what can we say to comfort them?”Maritime agency reports show that at least 12 tankers have been attacked in the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz in the past week as Iran steps up its campaign to stop US-backed efforts to move oil. There have been 24 seafarer deaths and 104 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the Middle East since the Iran war began on February 28, according to the International Maritime Organisation. Shattered dreams An experienced seafarer, Ravindar Singh, 40, spoke to rescued crew members to find out his nephew’s location when the drone struck. He says there is no hope of survival. “The men told me Amit was working on the main deck in the exact same place of the drone attack. We know he is no more,” Mr Singh said. “The crew were evacuated by fishermen. They went around the vessel to search in case the sailors had jumped into the sea, but found nothing.”Video shot by the crew captures the fire and smoke engulfing sections of the tanker, and a sailor can be heard crying out: “My two crew have gone, Allah, my two men have died.” Amit Singh was from a poor farming community and his family were happy when he followed his uncle into the merchant navy. He signed on with the tanker in January as an able seaman, and his work covered navigation, mooring, handling cargo and maintenance of the ship’s deck equipment.His uncle, a sailor for 20 years, spoke of the rising danger as merchant ships are targeted in the Iran-US and Russia-Ukraine wars. Ravindar Singh returned home in May after a projectile landed near his ship in the Black Sea. His nephew was due to complete his contract on October 20, and the men had planned to find a safe voyage together. “Amit was excited about coming home,” Mr Singh said. “After the Iran war, it is the worst condition for sailors. But Amit’s vessel was not in the Strait of Hormuz, it was in anchorage. How can it be that sailors are not safe near the port?”Mr Singh spoke of his nephew’s plans to build a better life for his family. “Amit was starting out in life. He wanted to save money to get his older sister married. His parents live on a small farm and he wanted a better life for them.“This is so wrong. Why should Amit be gone? We are just seamen. We are like drivers, we load and unload cargo, we do as we are told. But they are targeting us. If the ship is the target, at least give sailors a warning. Property damage can be fixed but a sailor’s life is gone.”Someone’s son, someone’s brother The family of the second sailor, Bir Bahadur Yadav, also from Uttar Pradesh in northern India, tried to shield his mother from news that he was missing, but she learnt from villagers who heard it on television.“I didn’t want to tell my mother until we were sure but now she knows, her spirit is broken/. She is constantly crying,” Mantoo Yadav, Bir’s elder brother, told The National from India. He works in Abu Dhabi and was visiting home when the attack occurred. “In this war, why are sailors being killed? It is someone’s son, someone’s husband, someone’s brother who is dying. What will you get from killing our brothers?”The night before the drone attack, Bir Bahadur spoke to his family about wanting to return home. The youngest of four, he worked as a wiper, cleaning the engine room and machinery. He had four months remaining on a nine-month contract. “We had a long talk. He told us he had seen attacks and saw one ship hit nearby,” Mr Yadav said. “Bir was worried his ship would become a target. But he thought he should stay and finish the contract. We told him to come home but it was too late.”Mr Yadav, 36, said his younger brother was focused on completing seafarer certifications to earn a higher rank.“Bir wanted to work hard, finish exams to get a good position. He was serious when he spoke but could also make people laugh. He was very loving,” said Mr Yadav.The family continues to hold on to hope. “We have been told that we will know about Bir only when the ship is brought to shore and checked,” Mr Yadav said. “The crew saw the attack and know the other sailor is no more. But the crew did not see Bir. “What if he managed to jump off? There is 10 per cent hope that he is still alive. Maybe in the rescue, they will find him unconscious.”Waiting for news Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, spoke of the trauma families suffer as they wait for news from search operations. “It's tough. When a vessel is hit by drone or rocket, there is fire and waterlogging,” said Mr Yadav, who is not related to the missing sailor. “It takes time to search the area for missing sailors, and families may not get an answer for days.”Neither Iran nor the US has taken responsibility for the drone strike. Maritime associations have called for more protection for sailors as the war continues. “This tanker was anchored off Sohar, so what was the need to hit this vessel? The only danger is for sailors,” Mr Yadav said. “It’s a very alarming situation and the threat to sailors is growing. Families are suffering. We need strong measures to protect seafarers.”India’s External Affairs Ministry has condemned the attacks. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation,” the Indian government said. “Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease.”

headline: Libya moves past war stage, threat of new crisis remains — envoy
summary: Ambassador to Iran Ali Juma Hassan Fadil says that a final political and institutional settlement has not yet been reached
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Libya has moved past the stage of large-scale war, Ali Juma Hassan Fadil, Libya's Ambassador to Iran, said in an interview with TASS, adding though that the threat of a crisis in a new form exists.

"Libya’s current state can be characterized as a state of ‘relative yet incomplete stability’. The country has moved past the stage of large-scale war of previous years. However, a final political and institutional settlement has not yet been reached. The absence of a major war itself does not imply the onset of a full-fledged peace," he said.

"Today, the Libyan issue goes beyond a single dispute that can be resolved through an agreement between two individuals or institutions. It comprises several interconnected levels: the legitimacy of institutions, the constitutional and legal framework for elections, the distribution of powers and resources, the unification of sovereign and security institutions, relations between the center and regions, and national reconciliation. Therefore, a solution limited merely to the formation of a new government, without those issues being solved, risks replicating the crisis in a different form," the diplomat explained.

headline: Trump asks US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign over allegations
summary: President Donald Trump asked US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign on Tuesday after reports alleged she sought $100,000 from a Trump supporter to pay personal credit card debt and accepted luxury trips and hotel stays from wealthy Greek businessmen. Guilfoyle denied wrongdoing and vowed to defend her reputation.
body_text:
President Donald Trump asked US ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign on Tuesday after reports alleged she sought $100,000 from a Trump supporter to pay personal credit card debt and accepted luxury trips and hotel stays from wealthy Greek businessmen. Guilfoyle denied wrongdoing and vowed to defend her reputation.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 05:23

US President Donald Trump forced his ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle out of the administration on Tuesday, amid allegations that she sought money from one of his supporters and accepted lavish hospitality from wealthy Greek businessmen.

"We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign," Trump's new press secretary Katie Zacharia told reporters at her first White House briefing.

The announcement came a day after Trump acknowledged that he was considering dismissing Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and ex-fiancée of his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr.

"She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump told reporters after the announcement, adding that he had not spoken to her, but that "she will not be there."

In a statement on X, Guilfoyle rejected the allegations against her and defended her record as ambassador, highlighting efforts to boost US energy exports and strengthen security ties with Greece.

"These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote.

Guilfoyle thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, pledging her continued loyalty to the president while acknowledging that her time as ambassador "may be coming to an end."

Guilfoyle has faced mounting scrutiny following a series of reports by The Wall Street Journal about her financial dealings and relationships with wealthy businessmen.

The newspaper reported that she asked Eric Deters, an influential Trump supporter, to pay off $100,000 in personal credit card debt shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025.

She requested he complete the transaction through a wire transfer so as not to leave a paper trail, the paper said.

"Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," she wrote to Deters in a message accompanied by instructions for paying her credit card company, according to the Journal, which published screenshots of the exchanges.

Deters refused to make the payment, telling the newspaper that doing so would have cost him his marriage.

Guilfoyle's lawyer has disputed the authenticity of the messages and denied wrongdoing.

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle boasted of luxury trips and hotel stays funded by wealthy Greek businessmen, citing hundreds of messages, emails and other records, including recorded conversations.

She travelled to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, aboard a private jet with Alexandros Exarchou, chief executive of Greek construction company Aktor Group, according to the newspaper.

Guilfoyle also spent Christmas at the exclusive Swiss ski resort of Gstaad with Greek shipping magnate Nikolas Tsakos, and stayed at a luxury Paris hotel on a trip with him, with Tsakos footing the bill, the Journal reported.

The State Department's inspector general is investigating whether Guilfoyle received improper gifts, according to US media reports.

The revelations emerged as Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Europe last week, including a stop in Athens, where he declined to comment on the allegations.

Guilfoyle, a prominent figure in Trump's Make America Great Again movement, was appointed ambassador after her engagement to Donald Trump Jr. ended.

A former prosecutor and television commentator, she was previously married to California's Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom.

headline: Live: Saudi Arabia reports Aramco building hit and four wounded in Houthi missile attacks
summary: Saudi Arabia reported damage to an Aramco building in Dhahran and four people wounded in Riyadh on Wednesday, after the kingdom intercepted Houthi missiles targeting the capital. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
body_text:
Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 05:39Modified: 14/10/2026 - 05:42

Saudi Arabia reported damage to an Aramco building in Dhahran and four people wounded in Riyadh on Wednesday, after the kingdom intercepted Houthi missiles targeting the capital. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.

Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.

Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.

Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.

The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.

Saudi Arabia said on Wednesday that an attack on an Aramco building in the kingdom's east sparked a "limited fire" and that debris from intercepted Houthi missiles wounded four people in the capital Riyadh.

It came hours after the Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen's Houthis said it had intercepted several missiles on Tuesday evening, including over Riyadh.

A Saudi energy ministry official said an administrative building belonging to oil giant Aramco in Dhahran was struck on Tuesday evening, resulting in a "limited fire" but "no casualties or fatalities".

Saudi Arabia's civil defence agency said on Wednesday that four people – two women, a man and a child – were wounded by debris from two intercepted Houthi cruise missiles in the capital and that 15 homes were damaged.

Welcome to the France 24 liveblog covering events in the Middle East. You can catch up on yesterday's developments here.

body_text:
Chinese robotics companies are looking to the Gulf as a possible manufacturing centre for the next generation of AI-powered machines, as the region's capital, energy resources and industrial ambitions create opportunities for partnerships.

Beijing-based robotics company LinkerBot is among those exploring opportunities in the UAE, where it is in talks with major institutions on potential partnerships, Weber Su, the company's vice president and head of global markets, said during the AIM Summit in Dubai on Tuesday.

One model being considered would involve Chinese companies supplying advanced robotics parts, while the UAE provides capital-intensive assembly and automated production.

Such an arrangement could allow Gulf countries to take part directly in making advanced robots, rather than mainly buying the technology.

“That could be the business model that we are exploring with Middle Eastern countries, particularly in UAE,” Mr Su said.

LinkerBot specialises in dexterous robotic hands, enabling machines to grasp and manipulate objects. It has expanded into components including reducers and micromotors that control robotic movement.

The potential collaboration reflects a broader trend in which Asian companies seek international manufacturing partners, while Gulf economies use their capital, energy and infrastructure to build higher-value industries. In September, Chinese electric and extended-range vehicle maker ROX Motor began producing vehicles in Abu Dhabi.

The UAE, meanwhile, is also boosting manufacturing and under its Operation 300bn strategy aims to increase the industrial sector's contribution to gross domestic product to Dh300 billion by 2031.

The country's industrial exports rose 25 per cent last year to a record Dh262 billion, with medium and high-technology exports increasing 42 per cent to Dh92 billion, according to the Ministry of Industry and Advanced Technology.

The UAE is also investing in automation to improve manufacturing competitiveness.

Mr Su said Chinese companies could increasingly focus on specialised robotics parts, while Gulf partners develop the capital-intensive assembly operations needed to bring those technologies to market.

Turning that potential into commercially successful partnerships will require investment agreements, viable production models and sustained demand for AI-powered machines.

The potential partnerships come as the technology industry moves towards what investors and developers describe as the next stage of artificial intelligence: physical AI.

Chinese AI developers including DeepSeek, Zhipu AI and Moonshot AI are becoming increasingly competitive with their US rivals, offering advanced models at lower costs, according to Joseph Zeng, founder and chief investment officer of Hong Kong-based Arcadia Fund Management Group.

While generative AI has focused on chatbots, content creation and software applications, the next phase is expected to bring intelligent systems into the physical world.

Physical AI combines advanced AI models with robotics, allowing machines to interpret their surroundings, make decisions and perform tasks traditionally requiring human intervention.

Unlike conventional industrial robots, which are generally programmed for repetitive movements, the ambition is to develop machines capable of adapting to different situations.

Applications could include robotic hands manipulating unfamiliar objects, autonomous machines working across production lines and robots assisting hospital patients.

Mr Su said advances in computing power and AI models were making these capabilities increasingly possible.

LinkerBot is developing robotic hands with built-in movement ability that could eventually be combined with sophisticated AI systems to perform a wider range of tasks.

“We're going to have skill stores similar to the app stores,” Mr Su said.

China's manufacturing scale could give its companies an advantage as the technology shifts towards commercial production.

The country installed about 295,000 industrial robots in 2024, accounting for 54 per cent of global installations, according to the International Federation of Robotics.

The figures refer to factory robots rather than humanoids, but demonstrate the scale of China's industrial automation industry and supporting supply chains.

SK hynix held 50 per cent of the global high-bandwidth memory market by revenue in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung accounted for 33 per cent, according to Counterpoint Research data reported by the Yonhap news agency.

"Physical AI provides a lot of opportunities for investors,” said Mr Zeng, whose investments include ByteDance and Zhipu AI in China, as well as South Korea's SK hynix and Samsung.

The next stage of AI would require advances in computing hardware and infrastructure, he added.

He identified high-bandwidth memory, optical transceivers and robotics components among the technologies benefitting from rising investment. Health care could also become an important market.

During a recent visit to Suzhou, near Shanghai, Mr Zeng said he encountered a company developing a voice-controlled robot designed to assist bedridden patients with repositioning and personal care.

Mr Su said humanoid robots could eventually help to care for elderly people and children in smaller communities, where shrinking populations make it difficult to attract doctors and maintain healthcare services.

While fully autonomous, general-purpose robots are still being developed, their potential to ease labour shortages, reduce care costs and extend essential services to underserved communities illustrates the social and economic impact physical AI could have beyond factories.

For the Gulf, opportunities could include using autonomous systems in established industries.

Mr Zeng highlighted electric and autonomous heavy-duty trucks for mining and industrial operations, alongside energy storage and cleaner power technologies.

Energy is also becoming increasingly important to AI investment.

Global data-centre electricity use is expected to more than double to about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.

The forecast highlights the importance of electricity generation, storage and cooling infrastructure as AI adoption accelerates.

For Gulf countries with substantial energy resources and growing renewable power capacity, this creates another potential area of collaboration with Asian technology developers.
