I fought for them, I gave everything,” he said last week in an interview with Corriere dello Sport.“What do I expect from the Olimpico? I do not expect banners. I do not expect anything. I expect respect.”
body_text:
The idea that Jose Mourinho was the man to restore order to the mayhem that is Real Madrid and prevent a third successive campaign without a major trophy appears to be unravelling fast.

Last season was a turbulent one for Los Blancos that saw managers sacked, players jeered by their own fans, teammates fighting each other, all topped off by bitter rivals Barcelona securing a second successive La Liga title.

To control a dressing room of rampant egos, Madrid president Florentino Perez turned to the biggest coaching ego of them all, brining Mourinho back for his second stint at a club who sacked him back in 2013. But just nine matches into the new season, all is not well in the Spanish capital.

On Saturday at the Bernabeu, Madrid were labouring towards a 1-0 win over Villarreal – courtesy of teenager Yan Diomande's first goal for the club – when Vinicius Junior scored with a clinical first-time finish.

It sparked ferocious celebrations from the attacker, with Mourinho sprinting across the pitch to join in. But the joyous scenes were cut short when referee Isidro Diaz de Mera Escuderos was asked to view the pitchside monitor by VAR, where he saw Vinicius clearly pulling the hair of Nathan Saliba in the build-up to the goal.

Just 20 minutes after coming off the bench to replace Trent Alexander-Arnold, Vinicius was shown a red card and the scene quickly descended into chaos as furious Madrid players surrounded the referee, while the Brazilian had to be dragged away by teammates.

An incandescent Mourinho, who had already spent the entire game berating officials, earned himself a yellow card, then refused to appear for the post-match press conference.

The player himself has since issued a brief apology on social media – saying “sorry to the team and the fans” – but could now receive a three-match ban that would see him miss the Clasico on October 25 against a table-topping Barca team that has won eight from eight in La Liga so far.

While Mourinho continues to rant and rave about perceived refereeing agendas against his team, the fact remains they are not playing well. They find themselves in fourth place, six points shy of Barca, having lost to Real Betis and the derby against Atletico Madrid, where Mourinho was again left bemoaning refereeing decisions.

And the biggest puzzle facing the veteran Portuguese is coaxing Vinicius – who signed a bumper new six-year contract extension over the summer – back into top form.

The 26-year-old has managed just one goal in 672 minutes of action this season prompting questions as to why Mourinho has not turned to other attacking options in his squad.

“Some players need time to get back to their usual level … and I’m not going to hide from that,” he insisted ahead of the Villarreal game.

“I never criticise the Madrid fan base; I only respect it. It breaks my heart to see a boy like him suffer. He wants to become that Vinicius again who wins matches and makes the difference … Vini deserves support.”

Mourinho has also found himself defending top-scorer Kylian Mbappe – who has eight goals in nine games, taking his Madrid career tally to 94 in 112 matches – after the French attacker was criticised for making trips to Paris and Switzerland while still recovering from a minor knee injury picked up on international duty.

“What I can promise is when a Real Madrid player doesn't behave the way a Real Madrid player is supposed to … They won't have the chance to whistle, because they'll be at home,” said the 63-year-old, who dismissed the criticism as “ridiculous” while also accusing the media of trying to turn Madrid fans against Mbappe.

After starting their Uefa Champions League campaign with a 2-1 win over Inter Milan – with Mbappe and Federico Valverde on target – they now face another of Mourinho's former clubs in Roma at the Stadio Olympico on Wednesday.

The Italian side are currently third in Serie A after drawing 0-0 at Como on Sunday, when they had top-scorer Donyell Malen shown a straight red card for a reckless tackle on home defender Kaiki. The Giallorossi's opening European game saw them draw with Fenerbahce in Turkey.

Mourinho's three-year spell in the Italian capital was a trademark mix of success and controversy that ended in the sack.

He guided Roma to their first major European crown when they defeated Feyenoord 1-0 in 2022's inaugural Europa Conference League final, which also meant Mourinho became the first manager to win all four major European trophies, having previously lifted the Uefa Cup, Champions League and Europa League.

“I knew the moment I arrived what it meant to the people,” said Mourinho after the match in Tirana. “They had been waiting for something like this. This was not work tonight, this was history. We had to write history. We wrote it.”

But 12 months later, Mourinho was once again left ranting at officials after Roma were beaten by Sevilla on penalties in a Europa League final that witnessed a tournament record 13 yellow cards. His infamous foul-mouthed tirade at referee Anthony Taylor in the car park after the game earned him a four-match ban.

The following season, Mourinho was sacked after a poor run of results, but the Portuguese insists his love for the club remains intact. “I think the bond between me and the Roma fans was created by the fact … they understood that for me there was only Roma and the Roma fans. I fought for them, I gave everything,” he said last week in an interview with Corriere dello Sport.

“What do I expect from the Olimpico? I do not expect banners. I do not expect anything. I expect respect.”

headline: S. Korea, U.S. agree to hold key defense talks after midterm elections: sources
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and the United States are in talks to set...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and the United States are in talks to set the date for their high-level defense dialogue after the U.S. midterms, informed sources said Wednesday, a move that would mark a delay of the annual talks typically held in early November.

According to the sources, the allies have reached a mutual "understanding" to push back the Security Consultative Meeting (SCM) largely due to the U.S. midterm elections slated for Nov. 3. Washington is due to host this year's SCM.

The apparent delay, however, comes amid a perceived gap between Seoul and Washington over the timing of the U.S.' handover of wartime operational control (OPCON) to South Korea,

Seoul seeks to retake wartime OPCON from Washington before the Lee Jae Myung administration's five-year term ends in 2030, or even as early as next year. Washington has expressed reservations about rushing the transition out of political considerations.

"The U.S. side has raised the need for rescheduling considering the midterm elections and other factors," a source said.

Another source said that both sides "are aligned on delaying the schedule,"

The SCM is a key bilateral defense dialogue where the allies' top defense officials discuss and coordinate a wide range of alliance and security issues, including defense strategy and joint military readiness primarily to deter North Korea.

The defense ministry said it was in talks with the U.S. defense department to coordinate on a "mutually available date."

"No specific details have yet been finalized," it said in a media note.

The Chosun Ilbo daily reported Wednesday the SCM has been pushed back to December, citing a lawmaker.

The likely postponement of the SCM comes amid growing speculation that Seoul may not achieve its goal of advancing the OPCON transition -- completing the second phase of a three-stage "conditions-based" transition plan (COTP) aimed at verifying South Korean forces' capabilities to lead the combined forces.

The allies are currently assessing the "full operational capability" (FOC), having validated the "initial operational capability" (IOC).

Seoul aims to wrap up the FOC certification and announce a target year for the OPCON transition at the upcoming SCM, before moving on to the remaining assessment of the "full mission capability" (FMC), which it expects to take about a year or so.

The JoongAng Ilbo newspaper reported that Washington remains firm on the position that Seoul is not ready for the FOC certification, weighing on Seoul's push to accelerate the OPCON transition.

The ministry said the allies have completed all joint evaluations of the capabilities scheduled for this year and that they are working closely to prepare for the FOC certification.

Speaking to Yonhap earlier in the day, Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul acknowledged that "different perspectives" remain over the OPCON transition.

"As I have said before, trust is important," he said. "So I repeat that there are no major disagreements or issues."

Asked if he plans to meet with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth at the upcoming ADMM Plus defense ministers' meeting in the Philippines later this month, Kang said his office is in talks with the U.S. side to make that happen.

"We are consulting (with Washington) to arrange a meeting. We are working on that," said Kang.

headline: Cody Rhodes calls for WWE return to Abu Dhabi, before Street Fighter release
summary: It's been nearly nine years since WWE last staged a show in Abu Dhabi. Three-time WWE champion Cody Rhodes thinks it's time the wrestling company returned.“Love Abu Dhabi,” Rhodes tells The National. “I only get to stop in for a brief moment usually, but I feel like it’s been a minute because WWE has been over in the Middle East, but we haven’t really hit Abu Dhabi. And we should.”WWE last staged shows in the UAE capital in December 2017, when Roman Reigns was among the stars who performed at Zayed Sports City Tennis Stadium. The company has since increased its presence in Saudi Arabia, where its next major event, Crown Jewel, takes place in Riyadh on November 7, with Reigns set to face Sami Zayn.Rhodes is speaking alongside American comedian Andrew Schulz, his co-star in the new Street Fighter film. Schulz is no stranger to the emirate as he has performed at Etihad Arena twice, first in October 2023 and again in May 2024 during the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week.“Abu Dhabi’s great. Some of the best comedy audiences in the world,” Schulz says.In director Kitao Sakurai's adaptation of Capcom's fighting-game series, Rhodes plays US Air Force fighter Guile, while Schulz portrays Dan Hibiki. Set in 1993, Street Fighter follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) to enter the World Warrior Tournament.Learning to perform without an audienceSchulz came to the film with two decades of stand-up comedy experience, although some of the habits he had developed on stage proved less useful when working alongside other actors.“We’re not getting a big pop or a big laugh,” he says. “So I think in some ways it’s like training yourself out of waiting for the reaction.“This character’s not even looking for a laugh. He’s dead serious about what he’s saying. It might be ridiculous and absurd, but to him, it’s the most important thing in the world. It’s kind of unlearning some things that we’ve both been doing for the last 20 years.”Rhodes found more familiar territory during a tournament scene involving hundreds of extras gathered around the fighters. With Guile surrounded by competitors and spectators, there was an opportunity to draw on the showmanship he has developed throughout his wrestling career.“There is an element of peacocking to what Guile was doing,” he says. “I mean, I even challenged Schulz to an arm-wrestling contest.”Director Sakurai and representatives from Capcom were also on set, providing some of the feedback Rhodes was accustomed to receiving from wrestling audiences. Their encouragement helped him judge whether his interpretation of Guile was working and remained faithful to the character.There was also room to experiment, particularly when Schulz and Rhodes began suggesting ways to add humour to the action.During one scene, Schulz was fascinated by the aerial performers suspended above the set, some of whom were hanging by their hair.“They literally just tied a knot to their hair, and they’re just spinning around,” he says.The sight inspired an idea. Schulz and Rhodes suggested that one of the performers could descend upside down during a conversation involving Guile, interrupting the exchange before disappearing back towards the ceiling. The filmmakers liked the gag enough to include it in the finished film.“They were very willing to just hear our absurd ideas,” Schulz says.Bringing something new to familiar charactersBeyond those contributions, Schulz was working within a production in which the broader creative decisions were in other people's hands – an unfamiliar position after two decades building his own comedy career.“It was very cool to be in something where you trust the creators and you just go, ‘OK, for the first time in my career, I completely submit to what your creative is, and I’m going to try to execute that to the best of my ability',” he says.Rhodes is joined in the film by fellow professional wrestlers Roman Reigns, who plays Akuma, and Hirooki Goto, who portrays E Honda. body_text:
It's been nearly nine years since WWE last staged a show in Abu Dhabi. Three-time WWE champion Cody Rhodes thinks it's time the wrestling company returned.

“Love Abu Dhabi,” Rhodes tells The National. “I only get to stop in for a brief moment usually, but I feel like it’s been a minute because WWE has been over in the Middle East, but we haven’t really hit Abu Dhabi. And we should.”

WWE last staged shows in the UAE capital in December 2017, when Roman Reigns was among the stars who performed at Zayed Sports City Tennis Stadium. The company has since increased its presence in Saudi Arabia, where its next major event, Crown Jewel, takes place in Riyadh on November 7, with Reigns set to face Sami Zayn.

Carrie season 2: Mike Flanagan on Stephen King's ideas for what comes next

Rhodes is speaking alongside American comedian Andrew Schulz, his co-star in the new Street Fighter film. Schulz is no stranger to the emirate as he has performed at Etihad Arena twice, first in October 2023 and again in May 2024 during the inaugural Abu Dhabi Comedy Week.

“Abu Dhabi’s great. Some of the best comedy audiences in the world,” Schulz says.

In director Kitao Sakurai's adaptation of Capcom's fighting-game series, Rhodes plays US Air Force fighter Guile, while Schulz portrays Dan Hibiki. Set in 1993, Street Fighter follows estranged fighters Ryu (Andrew Koji) and Ken Masters (Noah Centineo), who are recruited by Chun-Li (Callina Liang) to enter the World Warrior Tournament.

Schulz came to the film with two decades of stand-up comedy experience, although some of the habits he had developed on stage proved less useful when working alongside other actors.

“We’re not getting a big pop or a big laugh,” he says. “So I think in some ways it’s like training yourself out of waiting for the reaction.

“This character’s not even looking for a laugh. He’s dead serious about what he’s saying. It might be ridiculous and absurd, but to him, it’s the most important thing in the world. It’s kind of unlearning some things that we’ve both been doing for the last 20 years.”

Rhodes found more familiar territory during a tournament scene involving hundreds of extras gathered around the fighters. With Guile surrounded by competitors and spectators, there was an opportunity to draw on the showmanship he has developed throughout his wrestling career.

“There is an element of peacocking to what Guile was doing,” he says. “I mean, I even challenged Schulz to an arm-wrestling contest.”

Director Sakurai and representatives from Capcom were also on set, providing some of the feedback Rhodes was accustomed to receiving from wrestling audiences. Their encouragement helped him judge whether his interpretation of Guile was working and remained faithful to the character.

There was also room to experiment, particularly when Schulz and Rhodes began suggesting ways to add humour to the action.

During one scene, Schulz was fascinated by the aerial performers suspended above the set, some of whom were hanging by their hair.

“They literally just tied a knot to their hair, and they’re just spinning around,” he says.

The sight inspired an idea. Schulz and Rhodes suggested that one of the performers could descend upside down during a conversation involving Guile, interrupting the exchange before disappearing back towards the ceiling. The filmmakers liked the gag enough to include it in the finished film.

“They were very willing to just hear our absurd ideas,” Schulz says.

Beyond those contributions, Schulz was working within a production in which the broader creative decisions were in other people's hands – an unfamiliar position after two decades building his own comedy career.

“It was very cool to be in something where you trust the creators and you just go, ‘OK, for the first time in my career, I completely submit to what your creative is, and I’m going to try to execute that to the best of my ability',” he says.

Rhodes is joined in the film by fellow professional wrestlers Roman Reigns, who plays Akuma, and Hirooki Goto, who portrays E Honda. WWE has helped promote the adaptation, with Rhodes wearing Guile-inspired ring gear during his SummerSlam entrance in August.

The crossover between wrestling and film offers an opportunity to reach an audience already familiar with their work, while showing fans something they haven't seen before from all three.

“What I love is that when they see Roman, when they see Goto, when they see me, they won’t be seeing what they’re used to, which is a credit to what we’ve been able to do and the skills that we were able to develop before we got into this, in terms of creating a brand new character, another layer for us,” Rhodes says.

Street Fighter releases in UAE cinemas on Thursday

headline: Toxic Trump? President makes midterms all about him but some Republicans are inching away
summary: On November 3, Americans will elect all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot but he has sought to make the midterm elections all about himself.“I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. Just one more time,” he said at a recent rally.“Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth.”At recent rallies, Mr Trump has campaigned on what he says are his administration’s accomplishments and made the election a referendum on his presidency. He said voters turn out in greater numbers when he is running and that Republican control of Congress is necessary to preserve his agenda.He even pledged $5,000 cheques to every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, calling it a “Trump dividend”. Previous similar promises related to tariffs and cuts in government spending have come to nothing and he cannot unilaterally authorise such payments.But amid low approval ratings, rising costs of living and an unpopular war with Iran, some Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him on major issues, raising the question of whether Mr Trump has become toxic.'Kind of a betrayal'John Feehery, a Republican strategist, said the war with Iran presents a particular challenge for the President because it conflicts with his central message of non-intervention in conflicts abroad.“The war is very unpopular, even though it’s probably for a good cause. It hasn’t been really well explained. It’s not the Trump brand," Mr Feehery said. "And so, all these people who voted for Trump because they wanted an end to no more endless wars – it’s kind of a betrayal."Mr Trump has said that the war, which he initially claimed would last only a few weeks, would end after the midterms, and that fuel costs would go down shortly after. Control of Congress is likely to hinge on a relatively small number of contested races in Michigan, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas.Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control. Historically, the party of the sitting president loses seats in the House. “We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states. But it’s all about 35 different contests – not states, contests,” Mr Trump said at a recent rally.Midterm elections also typically draw fewer voters than presidential polls, and experts say Mr Trump's base is less motivated to vote in the midterms than Democratic supporters. “This is not going to be a high-turnout election, so you have to be very careful – you can’t run against Trump," Mr Feehery said. 'Like he has malaria'Still, some Republican candidates have been trying to distance themselves from the President's stance on Iran and other issues.Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed in Michigan, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.”Polling also suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming Mr Trump for his handling of the issues. In Iowa, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, focused her message on the economic impact of the war.“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” she said in a statement.Heavy-handed immigration enforcement is another possible vulnerability for Republicans, with polling showing that many voters believe the Trump administration has crossed the line. In a campaign advertisement, Maria Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican congresswoman running for re-election in Florida, said Mr Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts “have gone too far”.“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”Mr Trump has also dismissed criticism from lawmakers from both parties over a recent deal with Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with President Vladimir Putin.The move appeared to be an attempt to slow the rising prices of diesel, but Republican senators said the deal may violate US restrictions imposed after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators released a statement at the weekend opposing Russian diesel fuel imports.Senator Thom Tillis, one of the signatories to the statement, told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that "there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law". “Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious,” Mr Trump said on Monday when asked about the criticism from his own party. Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval ratings in the low 30s nationally, a historic low, and his disapproval ratings above 60 per cent.Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey who ran against Mr Trump twice for the party's presidential nomination, highlighted the growing unease of politicians in his party.“With his current approval rating, Republicans are going to treat Trump like he has malaria by the time we get to October,” he wrote in a post on X.Mr Trump, however, appears convinced that his stamp of approval is a boost for candidates rather than the proverbial albatross."I think we're going to do very well. I think that the rallies I'm doing are really changing around," he said on Tuesday.Mr Trump pledged to visit a different state most days until the election, and forgo playing golf on the weekends.
body_text:
On November 3, Americans will elect all 435 members of the House and 35 senators. President Donald Trump will not be on the ballot but he has sought to make the midterm elections all about himself.

“I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. Just one more time,” he said at a recent rally.

“Because if we lose, you’re going to lose your border, you’re going to lose your tax cuts, you’re going to lose your safety and security, you’re going to lose your wealth.”

Trump rules out attack on Iran before midterm elections

At recent rallies, Mr Trump has campaigned on what he says are his administration’s accomplishments and made the election a referendum on his presidency. He said voters turn out in greater numbers when he is running and that Republican control of Congress is necessary to preserve his agenda.

He even pledged $5,000 cheques to every American adult if Republicans retain control of Congress, calling it a “Trump dividend”. Previous similar promises related to tariffs and cuts in government spending have come to nothing and he cannot unilaterally authorise such payments.

But amid low approval ratings, rising costs of living and an unpopular war with Iran, some Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him on major issues, raising the question of whether Mr Trump has become toxic.

John Feehery, a Republican strategist, said the war with Iran presents a particular challenge for the President because it conflicts with his central message of non-intervention in conflicts abroad.

“The war is very unpopular, even though it’s probably for a good cause. It hasn’t been really well explained. It’s not the Trump brand," Mr Feehery said. "And so, all these people who voted for Trump because they wanted an end to no more endless wars – it’s kind of a betrayal."

Mr Trump has said that the war, which he initially claimed would last only a few weeks, would end after the midterms, and that fuel costs would go down shortly after.

Control of Congress is likely to hinge on a relatively small number of contested races in Michigan, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska and Texas.

Republicans hold narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control.

Historically, the party of the sitting president loses seats in the House.

“We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states. But it’s all about 35 different contests – not states, contests,” Mr Trump said at a recent rally.

Midterm elections also typically draw fewer voters than presidential polls, and experts say Mr Trump's base is less motivated to vote in the midterms than Democratic supporters.

“This is not going to be a high-turnout election, so you have to be very careful – you can’t run against Trump," Mr Feehery said.

Still, some Republican candidates have been trying to distance themselves from the President's stance on Iran and other issues.

Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed in Michigan, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly.”

Polling also suggests voters are mainly concerned about the economy and the rising cost of living, with a majority blaming Mr Trump for his handling of the issues.

In Iowa, Republican Congresswoman Ashley Hinson, who is running for the Senate, focused her message on the economic impact of the war.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” she said in a statement.

Heavy-handed immigration enforcement is another possible vulnerability for Republicans, with polling showing that many voters believe the Trump administration has crossed the line.

In a campaign advertisement, Maria Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican congresswoman running for re-election in Florida, said Mr Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts “have gone too far”.

“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” she said. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

Mr Trump has also dismissed criticism from lawmakers from both parties over a recent deal with Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets after a call with President Vladimir Putin.

The move appeared to be an attempt to slow the rising prices of diesel, but Republican senators said the deal may violate US restrictions imposed after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators released a statement at the weekend opposing Russian diesel fuel imports.

Senator Thom Tillis, one of the signatories to the statement, told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that "there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law".

“Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious,” Mr Trump said on Monday when asked about the criticism from his own party.

Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval ratings in the low 30s nationally, a historic low, and his disapproval ratings above 60 per cent.

Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey who ran against Mr Trump twice for the party's presidential nomination, highlighted the growing unease of politicians in his party.

“With his current approval rating, Republicans are going to treat Trump like he has malaria by the time we get to October,” he wrote in a post on X.

Mr Trump, however, appears convinced that his stamp of approval is a boost for candidates rather than the proverbial albatross.

"I think we're going to do very well. I think that the rallies I'm doing are really changing around," he said on Tuesday.

Mr Trump pledged to visit a different state most days until the election, and forgo playing golf on the weekends.

headline: Even during wartime, the UAE is budgeting for the future
summary: There is no denying that for many regional economies, these are uncertain times. Strikes on oil tankers and airports highlight the unresolved nature of the conflict between Iran and the US, and its ripple effects. However, a look at how the UAE is planning its future in this environment is illuminating.The country’s latest federal budget is a reminder that long-term economic ambitions cannot be put on hold every time the region faces a crisis. The decision to commit Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion) over the next three years is a serious statement of intent. Of particular note is its emphasis on social development, which has been earmarked as the largest area for spending.Economic strength largely depends on the people who sustain it, particularly their education, skills, health and ability to participate in a changing economy. Investing in citizens is an essential part of the UAE’s long-term competitiveness and is recognition that its most valuable asset is its people. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged…” Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said on Monday. “Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen.”Somewhat counterintuitively, despite the months of violent and dangerous conflict in the region, the UAE is confident in its future. This is borne out by some independent projections; a report on Monday by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group suggested that wealth in the Emirates is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade. This reflects the Emirates’ enduring appeal to investors and its accumulation of assets. The country’s long policy of diversifying its economy beyond hydrocarbons has been supported by international capital and a reputation for stability.Economic strength largely depends on the citizens and residents who sustain itThis is not to be complacent. The International Monetary Fund’s recent decision to downgrade its growth forecasts for regional economies highlights the seriousness of continuing challenges. Even countries with substantial financial reserves and diversified sources of income are not wholly immune from regional shocks of the magnitude being experienced right now.The UAE’s budget can be best understood as an expression of ambition and an investment in resilience. The current regional turmoil actually supports the case for more medium and long-term planning. Funding resilience only when a crisis arrives is not the most effective strategy. It is the decisions that governments make today that will count when the chips are down. Long-term planning and strategic foresight are strengths of the UAE, and essential ingredients for its current and future success.

There is no denying that for many regional economies, these are uncertain times. Strikes on oil tankers and airports highlight the unresolved nature of the conflict between Iran and the US, and its ripple effects. However, a look at how the UAE is planning its future in this environment is illuminating.

The country’s latest federal budget is a reminder that long-term economic ambitions cannot be put on hold every time the region faces a crisis. The decision to commit Dh292.5 billion ($79.64 billion) over the next three years is a serious statement of intent. Of particular note is its emphasis on social development, which has been earmarked as the largest area for spending.

Economic strength largely depends on the people who sustain it, particularly their education, skills, health and ability to participate in a changing economy. Investing in citizens is an essential part of the UAE’s long-term competitiveness and is recognition that its most valuable asset is its people. “Our priorities remain fixed and unchanged…” Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, said on Monday. “Education, health, housing, social services, and the quality of life and stability of the citizen.”

Somewhat counterintuitively, despite the months of violent and dangerous conflict in the region, the UAE is confident in its future. This is borne out by some independent projections; a report on Monday by global advisory firm Boston Consulting Group suggested that wealth in the Emirates is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade. This reflects the Emirates’ enduring appeal to investors and its accumulation of assets. The country’s long policy of diversifying its economy beyond hydrocarbons has been supported by international capital and a reputation for stability.

This is not to be complacent. The International Monetary Fund’s recent decision to downgrade its growth forecasts for regional economies highlights the seriousness of continuing challenges. Even countries with substantial financial reserves and diversified sources of income are not wholly immune from regional shocks of the magnitude being experienced right now.

The UAE’s budget can be best understood as an expression of ambition and an investment in resilience. The current regional turmoil actually supports the case for more medium and long-term planning. Funding resilience only when a crisis arrives is not the most effective strategy. It is the decisions that governments make today that will count when the chips are down. Long-term planning and strategic foresight are strengths of the UAE, and essential ingredients for its current and future success.

headline: People-to-people friendship between China, the U.S. is jointly forged by ordinary people from both countries: FM
summary: People-to-people friendship between China and the United States is jointly forged by ordinary people from both countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press conference on Tuesday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- People-to-people friendship between China and the United States is jointly forged by ordinary people from both countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press conference on Tuesday.

Mao made the remarks when asked about an American named David Victor Plymire and his connection to Huangyuan County, Qinghai Province, whose story gained a lot of attention.

Mao said that the 95-year-old Mr. Plymire lived in Huangyuan County, Qinghai Province for 17 years, and regards the place as his hometown.

According to the spokesperson, Mr. Plymire has helped donate medical equipment to Huangyuan County, provided financial aid for local education, and facilitated training opportunities in the U.S. for the county's English teachers. He once humbly said that all he has done is simply "fulfilling my duty to my own family." His story has touched many people.

"People-to-people friendship holds the key to state-to-state relations," Mao said. She noted that the exchanges between the Chinese and American people are like small streams that ultimately converge to form the vast river of China-U.S. friendship.

"China will continue to support people-to-people exchanges between the two countries and contribute to building a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity", Mao said.

body_text:
An administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco was attacked by a missile on Tuesday night, causing a fire but no casualties, as fighting intensifies between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The kingdom's Energy Ministry said the incident happened in Dhahran, in the Eastern Province. Authorities responded to the attack, with no deaths or injuries reported, the Saudi Press Agency reported.

Debris from two cruise missiles intercepted and destroyed over the capital Riyadh injured four people – two women, a man and a child, state television quoted the Saudi civil defence saying. That attack caused limited material damage. Authorities implemented established procedures in response.

Riyadh keeps moving after deadly strikes, but schools go online and travellers reroute

Bloomberg reported that the site was Aramco’s executive headquarters, while a company source quoted by Reuters identified the target as an Aramco headquarters complex. Neither Aramco nor Saudi authorities had officially confirmed which building was hit.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen separately said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched towards Dhahran, with debris falling in a residential area. It also reported intercepting a missile targeting Haradh and three drones north of the capital, Riyadh.

The coalition said late on Tuesday that it had carried out an operation against energy sites in Houthi-held areas of Yemen, including the Al Sabahah station in Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and piers used for loading fuel at the Red Sea port of Hodeidah.

Coalition spokesman Maj Gen Turki Al Malki accused the Houthis of using civilian infrastructure to support their military operations and supply their arsenals.

“It has been established that the Houthi terrorist militia uses civilian objects and vital resources to sustain its war effort," he said on X. "These include the Al Sabaha central station in Sanaa, underground strategic fuel reserves and storage facilities and fuel and dedicated fuel-loading and unloading berths in Hodeidah, Sanaa and Dhamar.”

Video posted on social media appeared to show a huge orange fireball erupting above Sanaa, followed by a towering column of thick black smoke. The strikes came after the coalition had warned civilians near the oil facility to leave “for their safety”.

The scale of the damage to the site and the impact on fuel supplies were not immediately clear. The Houthis said fuel reserves had been dispersed before the attack, a claim that has not been independently verified.

Saudi energy infrastructure has been been hit before. A refinery in Jazan, in the kingdom's west, was shut after a strike, and a key oil export port on the Red Sea coast was also targeted.

A cross-country pipeline used by Aramco to transport crude to export markets was temporarily shut in September following an attack launched from Iraq. The pipeline is strategically important because it offers an alternative route for Saudi oil exports when shipping through the Gulf faces disruption.

Oil prices rose on Wednesday after news of the attack on the Aramco building, as traders weighed the risk of further disruption to regional energy supplies. It is unclear how the latest incidents could affect production, refining or exports.

Dhahran lies at the centre of Saudi Arabia’s oil industry, close to major oil fields in Eastern Province and the Gulf.

summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- A bridge between North Korea and China will officiall...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS photo, more details in 3rd, last 2 paras)

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- A bridge between North Korea and China will officially open to traffic this week after sitting idle for more than a decade following its construction, according to a Chinese news report on Wednesday.

The New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the North Korean city of Sinuiju and Dandong in China, will open Thursday, according to China's Xinhua News Agency.

There will be an opening ceremony on that day, the report said.

The construction of the four-lane motor bridge began in October 2011 and wrapped up in October 2014, but it stood unused for years because North Korea did not finish the buildings and infrastructure on its side.

Vehicles have recently been spotted crossing the 3,024-meter bridge, raising the possibility of a test run.

The bridge, which is expected to boost trade and personnel exchanges between the two countries, opens after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged at their June summit in Pyongyang to raise their ties to a strategic level and enhance exchanges.

It would supplement the existing Friendship Bridge, which opened in 1943 and has long been the main crossing over the Yalu River.

The new bridge is expected to ease congestion on the old, one-way road linking the two countries.

headline: Britain must settle its Brexit argument before seeking an EU return
summary: Confusion reigns where the UK and EU is concerned. Having been dormant for so long, avoided and ducked by successive recent prime ministers, Britain’s future relations with the EU has suddenly become a major political and diplomatic issue.The uncertainty stems from how far Andy Burnham wants to go and at what speed. He gives every impression of wishing the UK to rejoin and quickly. But then he will say in the next breath that the British public must decide. That raises the possibility, make it probability, of a bitter, protracted Brexit battle all over again.He is pinning much on the forthcoming UK-EU Summit, scheduled for November 20, and has set out his wish-list of what he would like that meeting to achieve – including free trade of food and drink products, greater movement of young people – while giving the impression of this only being the first step. That in itself, though, is radical compared with where the UK and EU were. And, as Leader of the Opposition Kemi Badenoch has rightly observed, it’s a curious way to proceed into a negotiation, showing your hand at one go. It is clear to everyone, not least the EU that he sees this as merely the beginning not the end. How though, can he get there, without resurrecting the old battle-lines and splitting the country?He began by being inflammatory, by suggesting the referendum verdict was improperly obtained. No sooner did Mr Burnham signal his desire for the UK to form closer ties with the EU, with a view possibly to rejoining, than the Prime Minister appeared on a podcast saying there was incontrovertible evidence that Russia interfered in the referendum campaign.Bearing in mind the decision to leave was won by just 2 per cent of the vote, the suggestion that it was some way Russian influenced has the ability to invalidate Brexit, to throw the authenticity of the UK’s departure into doubt (Remainers would argue it was already questionable as part of the Brexiteers’ campaign was based on hyperbole and falsehood). So, we actually didn’t choose to exit after all, which could help our efforts to gain readmission.Except Mr Burnham’s was not a new claim. It had been made repeatedly in the past and had always been denied by government ministers and security officials. Nevertheless, here was Mr Burnham maintaining that upon arriving in No 10 he asked about possible Russian interference in the 2016 ballot and stating: “I’ve had the clear answer that, yes, there was.”Fine, if he has the proof. At the time of writing, none is forthcoming. Indeed, well after Mr Burnham made his comment, Stephen Doughty, the Foreign Office minister, was challenged by the BBC to produce it, and replied he wouldn’t “get into specifics”.Instead, Mr Doughty resorted to vague accusations that “Russia clearly has attempted to interfere on a number of our democratic processes. They’re engaged in information warfare, they’re spending £1.5 billion [almost $2 billion] this year alone on disinformation and propaganda”.Cue Nigel Farage, the Brexit architect, denouncing Mr Burnham as “a liar”. Cue too, a feeling of deja vu, that we’ve been here before, many times, that nothing has really changed, that the old wounds have never healed, but still exist, waiting to be reopened.All this row – and it quickly erupted into a war of words, with Mr Farage, who has been accused in the past of enjoying close ties with Russia, sensing his honour and reputation had been impugned sounding most indignant – served to show was that the UK is nowhere near ready to rejoin, not collectively with a consensus, that EU leaders starting to take Mr Burnham at his word might wish to reconsider.The question they should ask themselves is, does Mr Burnham speak for the nation? He may wish to come back but does the electorate, how certain can they be that the same mixture of disregard, often tipping into open contempt, for the EU and its ideals, won’t simply rear its head again?It’s true that a majority of the British people, far greater than the percentage who chose to quit, now believe Brexit was a mistake. The polls put the figure slightly above 70 per cent. In democratic terms, that’s substantial.But it’s an opinion poll, not the real thing, and however the cake is cut, a significant portion of the populace still argue we were right to go. That slice is inspired by committed and noisy agitators. Mr Farage has already said Mr Burnham’s public ambition has regalvanised his Reform UK party’s support base.Until the senior pro-Brexit players in the epic drama of a decade ago come out and admit they were wrong, those of a suspicious nature in the EU are fully entitled to worry the UK would become the renegade member it was before – harrying, obstructing and yes, insulting, at every turn. It would require former prime minister Boris Johnson to recant, and ideally, Mr Farage. Even better still, for the pair of them together to fall on their anti-EU swords.Well, that will never occur. Rather, what will happen is that they will unpick the scars and a whole new anti-EU front will erupt.In the same way that Britain withdrew by the thinnest of margins, this perception matters. Because should we pursue readmittance, we must clear several hurdles, any one of which could block our path.Mr Burnham clearly would like to make it an election issue, to be included in the Labour manifesto. If he wins that popular mandate, in theory, there ought to be no requirement for a re-run of a separate EU vote.That is the view of the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, among others. But the EU is likely to insist upon a second referendum as a precursor to commencing membership negotiations. Their argument is that they would want to be persuaded the decision is non-party political, and that a vote for a manifesto covers all manner of issues, only one of which is the EU. A re-run could make the case that recommencing membership would last beyond the lifetime of the newly elected government and extend across successive governments. Virtually all countries joining have done so only after holding a public ballot. So, the UK could not realistically seek special dispensation.The European Commission, which would lead the process, would also need to vote its agreement. So too would a majority of the members of European Parliament. Critically, as well, the 27 member countries would have a say and it is by no means guaranteed they would approve the UK resuming. Traditional anti-Britishness could re-surface and they could have agendas of their own – skilful diplomacy by the UK government and Foreign Office would have to be deployed. That said, British diplomats are indicating privately they think simply going back in and taking up where we left off is a tall, if not impossible, order.The EU too would be right to examine Britain’s motives – why now, why the sudden change of heart, why after all this time, 10 years and counting, do we wish to return? The answer, and one Mr Burnham is correct to proclaim, is because Brexit has not delivered. At a stroke, we ditched a free trade bloc of 450 million people. British businesses too found themselves bereft of skilled EU labour. Nothing we’ve done since has come remotely close to replacing what was lost.The Bank of England estimates a loss to our gross domestic product of 6 per cent to 8 per cent – this at a time of increased global competitiveness, rising protectiveness and sovereignty, energy crisis, supply chain difficulties, rising cost of living, threat of AI to jobs, when just adding 1 per cent is a tough bar. Here was the UK saying goodbye to 6 per cent. Just like that. As welcome as they are, trade deals have helped plug the gap, but they only go so far. We had a huge customs-free market on our doorstep, and we blew it. Business investment post-Brexit also fell, down, according to estimates, by 12 per cent to 18 per cent.That’s what we’d like again and if not through full membership, through a much greater rapprochement, possibly through the Customs Union. We’d love also to be able to stem the tide of illegal immigration, which we have failed to do on our own. But the EU is aware of our need and it realises too, that is a prize worth having and is not something to be awarded easily. Not if it comes with the baggage of anti-EU rhetoric and the likelihood that at any moment, a new administration, one led by Mr Farage, say, could again up sticks.That said, there are those in the EU who would like to see Britain’s return in some form. We bring with us 69.5 million people and we could provide an economic as well as political fillip. In a world dominated by two superpowers, a united EU would be a match for them. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s speech to Davos earlier this year, in which he called for the “middle powers” to combine, continues to resonate loudly.The fact Mr Carney has followed that up with a suggestion of “associate membership” of the EU has met with a warm response. Mr Carney and Canada, they can do business with. Are they able to say the same with certainty for an unclear, impatient Mr Burnham and his Perfidious Albion? Therein lies the rub.

It’s true that a majority of the British people, far greater than the percentage who chose to quit, now believe Brexit was a mistake. The polls put the figure slightly above 70 per cent. In democratic terms, that’s substantial.

But it’s an opinion poll, not the real thing, and however the cake is cut, a significant portion of the populace still argue we were right to go. That slice is inspired by committed and noisy agitators. Mr Farage has already said Mr Burnham’s public ambition has regalvanised his Reform UK party’s support base.

It would require former prime minister Boris Johnson to recant, and ideally, Mr Farage. Even better still, for the pair of them together to fall on their anti-EU swords.

Well, that will never occur. Rather, what will happen is that they will unpick the scars and a whole new anti-EU front will erupt.

In the same way that Britain withdrew by the thinnest of margins, this perception matters. Because should we pursue readmittance, we must clear several hurdles, any one of which could block our path.

Mr Burnham clearly would like to make it an election issue, to be included in the Labour manifesto. If he wins that popular mandate, in theory, there ought to be no requirement for a re-run of a separate EU vote.

That is the view of the mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, among others. But the EU is likely to insist upon a second referendum as a precursor to commencing membership negotiations. Their argument is that they would want to be persuaded the decision is non-party political, and that a vote for a manifesto covers all manner of issues, only one of which is the EU. A re-run could make the case that recommencing membership would last beyond the lifetime of the newly elected government and extend across successive governments. Virtually all countries joining have done so only after holding a public ballot. So, the UK could not realistically seek special dispensation.

The European Commission, which would lead the process, would also need to vote its agreement. So too would a majority of the members of European Parliament. Critically, as well, the 27 member countries would have a say and it is by no means guaranteed they would approve the UK resuming. Traditional anti-Britishness could re-surface and they could have agendas of their own – skilful diplomacy by the UK government and Foreign Office would have to be deployed. That said, British diplomats are indicating privately they think simply going back in and taking up where we left off is a tall, if not impossible, order.

The EU too would be right to examine Britain’s motives – why now, why the sudden change of heart, why after all this time, 10 years and counting, do we wish to return? The answer, and one Mr Burnham is correct to proclaim, is because Brexit has not delivered. At a stroke, we ditched a free trade bloc of 450 million people. British businesses too found themselves bereft of skilled EU labour. Nothing we’ve done since has come remotely close to replacing what was lost.

The Bank of England estimates a loss to our gross domestic product of 6 per cent to 8 per cent – this at a time of increased global competitiveness, rising protectiveness and sovereignty, energy crisis, supply chain difficulties, rising cost of living, threat of AI to jobs, when just adding 1 per cent is a tough bar. Here was the UK saying goodbye to 6 per cent. Just like that. As welcome as they are, trade deals have helped plug the gap, but they only go so far. We had a huge customs-free market on our doorstep, and we blew it. Business investment post-Brexit also fell, down, according to estimates, by 12 per cent to 18 per cent.

That’s what we’d like again and if not through full membership, through a much greater rapprochement, possibly through the Customs Union. We’d love also to be able to stem the tide of illegal immigration, which we have failed to do on our own. But the EU is aware of our need and it realises too, that is a prize worth having and is not something to be awarded easily. Not if it comes with the baggage of anti-EU rhetoric and the likelihood that at any moment, a new administration, one led by Mr Farage, say, could again up sticks.

TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iranian Ambassador to Russia Kazem Jalali has slammed US President Donald Trump’s allegations that Iran can destroy Los Angeles and San Diego as a figment and campaign rhetoric.

headline: There is no room for ambiguity on Taiwan question: spokesperson on Kevin Tsai's appearance at separatist's campaign event
summary: Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory, and upholding the one-China principle is a prevailing consensus in the international community and a common political foundation for people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, Chen Binhua, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said Wednesday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory, and upholding the one-China principle is a prevailing consensus in the international community and a common political foundation for people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, Chen Binhua, a spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, said Wednesday.

Chen made the remarks at a regular press conference when asked to comment on Taiwanese entertainer Kevin Tsai's appearance at the inauguration ceremony of the campaign headquarters of Shen Po-yang, a Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) candidate for Taipei mayor.

Chen said Shen, a die-hard "Taiwan independence" separatist, is known for his words and deeds of separatism. Any form of "Taiwan independence" separatist activity seriously harms the fundamental interests of the Chinese nation, and China firmly opposes such activities, Chen noted.

China has always respected and protected the legitimate freedom of speech and expression of Taiwan compatriots, Chen said, adding that there is no room for ambiguity on issues of right and wrong.

Safeguarding national reunification and opposing "Taiwan independence" represent the common will of all Chinese people. No person or force can seek to reap the benefits of the mainland's development while colluding with "Taiwan independence" separatist forces and acting as a "two-faced" person, Chen said.

headline: 'There are no dreams left': Families of two sailors missing after drone attack off Oman speak of their grief
summary: Two families are “sick with grief” waiting for news of two young sailors missing days after an empty tanker was struck by a drone off Oman. The oil tanker, MT Petro Dolphin, was hit near the Sohar anchorage on Sunday. Relatives in two northern Indian villages are waiting for information on Amit Singh, 20, and Bir Bahadur Yadav, 25, who were on the main deck when the drone struck and fire spread. Of the 12 crew on the Nicaraguan-flagged tanker, nine Indians and one Bangladeshi national were rescued and two seafarers are missing, India’s External Affairs Ministry has said. It was the first sailing job for both men, and their relatives have described the incomprehensible loss they felt on learning of the attack. “Amit’s parents are in and out of consciousness, they cannot cope. It’s all finished, there are no dreams left, it’s all broken,” Amit Singh’s uncle, Ravindar Singh, told The National from Gopala village in Uttar Pradesh.“It’s as if they are dead. As long as they live, they will be in this condition, like death. We are trying to support them but what can we say to comfort them?”Maritime agency reports show that at least 12 tankers have been attacked in the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz in the past week as Iran steps up its campaign to stop US-backed efforts to move oil. There have been 24 seafarer deaths and 104 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the Middle East since the Iran war began on February 28, according to the International Maritime Organisation. Shattered dreams An experienced seafarer, Ravindar Singh, 40, spoke to rescued crew members to find out his nephew’s location when the drone struck. He says there is no hope of survival. “The men told me Amit was working on the main deck in the exact same place of the drone attack. We know he is no more,” Mr Singh said. “The crew were evacuated by fishermen. They went around the vessel to search in case the sailors had jumped into the sea, but found nothing.”Video shot by the crew captures the fire and smoke engulfing sections of the tanker, and a sailor can be heard crying out: “My two crew have gone, Allah, my two men have died.” Amit Singh was from a poor farming community and his family were happy when he followed his uncle into the merchant navy. He signed on with the tanker in January as an able seaman, and his work covered navigation, mooring, handling cargo and maintenance of the ship’s deck equipment.His uncle, a sailor for 20 years, spoke of the rising danger as merchant ships are targeted in the Iran-US and Russia-Ukraine wars. Ravindar Singh returned home in May after a projectile landed near his ship in the Black Sea. His nephew was due to complete his contract on October 20, and the men had planned to find a safe voyage together. “Amit was excited about coming home,” Mr Singh said. “After the Iran war, it is the worst condition for sailors. But Amit’s vessel was not in the Strait of Hormuz, it was in anchorage. How can it be that sailors are not safe near the port?”Mr Singh spoke of his nephew’s plans to build a better life for his family. “Amit was starting out in life. He wanted to save money to get his older sister married. His parents live on a small farm and he wanted a better life for them.“This is so wrong. Why should Amit be gone? We are just seamen. We are like drivers, we load and unload cargo, we do as we are told. But they are targeting us. If the ship is the target, at least give sailors a warning. Property damage can be fixed but a sailor’s life is gone.”Someone’s son, someone’s brother The family of the second sailor, Bir Bahadur Yadav, also from Uttar Pradesh in northern India, tried to shield his mother from news that he was missing, but she learnt from villagers who heard it on television.“I didn’t want to tell my mother until we were sure but now she knows, her spirit is broken/. She is constantly crying,” Mantoo Yadav, Bir’s elder brother, told The National from India. He works in Abu Dhabi and was visiting home when the attack occurred. “In this war, why are sailors being killed? It is someone’s son, someone’s husband, someone’s brother who is dying. What will you get from killing our brothers?”The night before the drone attack, Bir Bahadur spoke to his family about wanting to return home. The youngest of four, he worked as a wiper, cleaning the engine room and machinery. He had four months remaining on a nine-month contract. “We had a long talk. He told us he had seen attacks and saw one ship hit nearby,” Mr Yadav said. “Bir was worried his ship would become a target. But he thought he should stay and finish the contract. We told him to come home but it was too late.”Mr Yadav, 36, said his younger brother was focused on completing seafarer certifications to earn a higher rank.“Bir wanted to work hard, finish exams to get a good position. He was serious when he spoke but could also make people laugh. He was very loving,” said Mr Yadav.The family continues to hold on to hope. “We have been told that we will know about Bir only when the ship is brought to shore and checked,” Mr Yadav said. “The crew saw the attack and know the other sailor is no more. But the crew did not see Bir. “What if he managed to jump off? There is 10 per cent hope that he is still alive. Maybe in the rescue, they will find him unconscious.”Waiting for news Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, spoke of the trauma families suffer as they wait for news from search operations. “It's tough. When a vessel is hit by drone or rocket, there is fire and waterlogging,” said Mr Yadav, who is not related to the missing sailor. “It takes time to search the area for missing sailors, and families may not get an answer for days.”Neither Iran nor the US has taken responsibility for the drone strike. Maritime associations have called for more protection for sailors as the war continues. “This tanker was anchored off Sohar, so what was the need to hit this vessel? The only danger is for sailors,” Mr Yadav said. “It’s a very alarming situation and the threat to sailors is growing. Families are suffering. We need strong measures to protect seafarers.”India’s External Affairs Ministry has condemned the attacks. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation,” the Indian government said. “Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease.”

“Amit’s parents are in and out of consciousness, they cannot cope. It’s all finished, there are no dreams left, it’s all broken,” Amit Singh’s uncle, Ravindar Singh, told The National from Gopala village in Uttar Pradesh.

“It’s as if they are dead. As long as they live, they will be in this condition, like death. We are trying to support them but what can we say to comfort them?”

Maritime agency reports show that at least 12 tankers have been attacked in the Arabian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz in the past week as Iran steps up its campaign to stop US-backed efforts to move oil.

There have been 24 seafarer deaths and 104 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the Middle East since the Iran war began on February 28, according to the International Maritime Organisation.

An experienced seafarer, Ravindar Singh, 40, spoke to rescued crew members to find out his nephew’s location when the drone struck. He says there is no hope of survival.

“The men told me Amit was working on the main deck in the exact same place of the drone attack. We know he is no more,” Mr Singh said. “The crew were evacuated by fishermen. They went around the vessel to search in case the sailors had jumped into the sea, but found nothing.”

Video shot by the crew captures the fire and smoke engulfing sections of the tanker, and a sailor can be heard crying out: “My two crew have gone, Allah, my two men have died.”

Amit Singh was from a poor farming community and his family were happy when he followed his uncle into the merchant navy. He signed on with the tanker in January as an able seaman, and his work covered navigation, mooring, handling cargo and maintenance of the ship’s deck equipment.

His uncle, a sailor for 20 years, spoke of the rising danger as merchant ships are targeted in the Iran-US and Russia-Ukraine wars.

Ravindar Singh returned home in May after a projectile landed near his ship in the Black Sea. His nephew was due to complete his contract on October 20, and the men had planned to find a safe voyage together.

“Amit was excited about coming home,” Mr Singh said. “After the Iran war, it is the worst condition for sailors. But Amit’s vessel was not in the Strait of Hormuz, it was in anchorage. How can it be that sailors are not safe near the port?”

Mr Singh spoke of his nephew’s plans to build a better life for his family.

“Amit was starting out in life. He wanted to save money to get his older sister married. His parents live on a small farm and he wanted a better life for them.

“This is so wrong. Why should Amit be gone? We are just seamen. We are like drivers, we load and unload cargo, we do as we are told. But they are targeting us. If the ship is the target, at least give sailors a warning. Property damage can be fixed but a sailor’s life is gone.”

The family of the second sailor, Bir Bahadur Yadav, also from Uttar Pradesh in northern India, tried to shield his mother from news that he was missing, but she learnt from villagers who heard it on television.

“I didn’t want to tell my mother until we were sure but now she knows, her spirit is broken/. She is constantly crying,” Mantoo Yadav, Bir’s elder brother, told The National from India. He works in Abu Dhabi and was visiting home when the attack occurred.

“In this war, why are sailors being killed? It is someone’s son, someone’s husband, someone’s brother who is dying. What will you get from killing our brothers?”

The night before the drone attack, Bir Bahadur spoke to his family about wanting to return home. The youngest of four, he worked as a wiper, cleaning the engine room and machinery. He had four months remaining on a nine-month contract.

“We had a long talk. He told us he had seen attacks and saw one ship hit nearby,” Mr Yadav said. “Bir was worried his ship would become a target. But he thought he should stay and finish the contract. We told him to come home but it was too late.”

Mr Yadav, 36, said his younger brother was focused on completing seafarer certifications to earn a higher rank.

“Bir wanted to work hard, finish exams to get a good position. He was serious when he spoke but could also make people laugh. He was very loving,” said Mr Yadav.

The family continues to hold on to hope.

“We have been told that we will know about Bir only when the ship is brought to shore and checked,” Mr Yadav said. “The crew saw the attack and know the other sailor is no more. But the crew did not see Bir.

“What if he managed to jump off? There is 10 per cent hope that he is still alive. Maybe in the rescue, they will find him unconscious.”

Manoj Yadav, general secretary of the Forward Seamen’s Union of India, spoke of the trauma families suffer as they wait for news from search operations.

“It's tough. When a vessel is hit by drone or rocket, there is fire and waterlogging,” said Mr Yadav, who is not related to the missing sailor. “It takes time to search the area for missing sailors, and families may not get an answer for days.”

Neither Iran nor the US has taken responsibility for the drone strike. Maritime associations have called for more protection for sailors as the war continues.

“This tanker was anchored off Sohar, so what was the need to hit this vessel? The only danger is for sailors,” Mr Yadav said. “It’s a very alarming situation and the threat to sailors is growing. Families are suffering. We need strong measures to protect seafarers.”

India’s External Affairs Ministry has condemned the attacks. “The recurring attacks on commercial shipping in the region are deeply concerning and risk further aggravating an already volatile situation,” the Indian government said. “Attacks on commercial vessels, seafarers and civilian infrastructure must cease.”

headline: What we know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis
summary: The Pope underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerours tumour from his right lung after saying that a nodule had been "detected at a very early stage". Following a "successful" operation, the Vatican said the pontiff would undergo additional testing.
body_text:
The Pope underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerours tumour from his right lung after saying that a nodule had been "detected at a very early stage". Following a "successful" operation, the Vatican said the pontiff would undergo additional testing.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 05:35Modified: 14/10/2026 - 07:45

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumor surgically removed from his right lung on Tuesday in a 90-minute operation described as "successful" by the Vatican.

Here are what several medical experts told AFP about the surgery and diagnosis.

Pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the type of tumor removed from the Pope, generally comes from "a primary cancer," said Dr. Juanita Mora, a medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association.

She told AFP that "is a good thing" because it means the tumor is from lung cancer instead of generating from the spread of another cancer.

There are two main types of lung cancer: "small cell" cancers, which spread aggressively and make up about 10 to 15% of diagnoses, and "non-small cell" cancers, which make up the vast majority.

"Adenocarcinoma is the most common kind of what's called non-small cell lung cancer," David Spigel, a medical oncologist specializing in lung cancer research at Nashville's Sarah Cannon Research Institute, told AFP.

Read morePope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after doctors successfully remove nodule

David Carbone, director of the Oncology Center at Ohio State University, noted that while smoking is the most well-known risk factor for a lung cancer diagnosis, "most lung cancers that we diagnose today are in people who haven't smoked, or (stopped) many years ago."

Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death worldwide, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), but the prognosis can vary significantly depending on the type of lung cancer and how advanced it is when first detected.

"When we look at five-year survival rate from lung adenocarcinoma, and it's nicely localized, the rate is approximately 63 to 67 percent," Mora said.

"But if we catch it early, it becomes 80 to 98%, especially after surgical removal."

In such a case, the patient "will achieve a cure and never have their life threatened by cancer," Spigel added.

Pope Leo XIV announced the presence of the lung nodule on Sunday, saying it had been "detected at a very early stage" and was localized.

Read morePope Leo says will undergo surgery for early-stage lung nodule

The Vatican said "the lower lobe of the right lung was removed" during Tuesday's operation to remove the mass.

"He had part of his right lung taken out, which is the standard procedure," Carbone told AFP.

"There's a lot of reserve in the lung, and people can have an entire lung removed and live a normal life," he added.

"I would expect that he'd be back to completely full level of activity very soon."

The question now is whether Pope Leo XIV will need additional treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation.

According to the experts consulted by AFP, the answer will depend on several factors, such as the size of the cancerous mass removed, how aggressive it was, its genetic characteristics, and whether or not it has spread.

A Vatican source indicated that additional testing is underway.

For Carbone, the fact that the Pope has already undergone surgery is encouraging.

"Because if it had spread to, for example, the lymph nodes in the center of the chest, he would have had some treatment before surgery, which he didn't have," he explained.

"They really do go straight to surgery only for the earliest stage tumors, which makes me think this was a very early stage tumor, and has a quite good prognosis."

He stressed that treatment for lung cancer has improved considerably over the past few decades, "and the prognosis is better than ever. So I would be hopeful for a full recovery."

An engineer with OpenAI has been arrested after the company found an audio recording device inside a conference room, the criminal complaint in federal court in San Francisco read.

The 35-year-old accused — a Saudi national named Abdulrahman Alfozan — has been charged with secretly installing the device inside an executive conference room in an alleged effort to capture sensitive conversations about the company’s technology, the officials said.

We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work.

We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance. Even as the complaint did not identify the company, the firm, in a statement, confirmed that it noticed a “sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices”, reported it to the FBI and fired the employee. “We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier. We referred the matter to the FBI, and we’re grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI’s investigation is ongoing, and we will continue to support their work,” an OpenAI spokesperson said.

OpenAI has confirmed that it has no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating sensitive information such as model weights, source code, or customer data. “The employee was terminated,” the statement said.

On September 30, the recording device, wrapped in a toilet paper, was found inserted into a USB port on the back of a television in the conference room. Though the room did not have a security camera at that time, closed-circuit television footage inside the company’s offices revealed showed that Alfozan was closed to the conference room on many occasions last month despite not having any authority to access the space, according to the complaint. The company then installed a camera to the room. Last week, the camera captured Alfozan entering and checking behind the television where the recording device had been fixed, the FBI said.
