headline: FBI arrests Saudi OpenAI employee for allegedly bugging San Francisco office
summary: The FBI said on Wednesday it has arrested a Saudi national employed as an engineer at OpenAI on suspicions that he had bugged a conference room at the company's San Francisco office with a "sophisticated recording device".
body_text:
The FBI said on Wednesday it has arrested a Saudi national employed as an engineer at OpenAI on suspicions that he had bugged a conference room at the company's San Francisco office with a "sophisticated recording device".

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 01:49Modified: 14/10/2026 - 07:39

A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company's San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday, amid a global race to dominate in artificial intelligence.

"We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.

OpenAI's security team found the device late last month and the employee, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on October 9, the US Justice Department said.

Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room", according to a Justice Department statement.

He was allegedly caught on camera "near" the conference room multiple times but was not authorised to participate in meetings located there.

He used a "productivity tool" to search for more information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the statement.

A chatbot account connected to Alfozan's spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting memory cards.

"This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.

"The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America's cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats," Clayton added.

Read moreOpenAI bans Russian, Iranian ChatGPT propaganda networks

The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate in artificial intelligence, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence."

Saudi Arabia's state-backed AI firm Humain invested $3 billion in Elon Musk's xAI shortly before the American billionaire's space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.

Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data center in Saudi Arabia.

It was not immediately clear what, if any information the recording device was able to collect.

"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.

A second device was found by OpenAI's security team when they searched an unattended bag that belonged to Alfozan, according to the Justice Department.

Alfozan was caught on security footage from inside the restricted conference room where he appeared to look behind the television where the recording device had been placed, the Department said.

A LinkedIn account matching Alfozan's name and resume show that he previously worked at Facebook-owner Meta, as well as an AI startup and a venture capital firm.

He was also a student at University of California at Berkeley and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

The Justice Department said Alfozen had been charged with "using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications", for which he could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.

It did not accuse Alfozan nor Saudi Arabia, which is a close US ally, of spying activity in its statement on Tuesday.

Alfozan is expected to appear at a federal court hearing on October 19.

headline: Iran's nuclear tech. potentials 'par with advanced nations'
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – The head of Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) says that the country’s capabilities in nuclear science and technology are rival to those of the developed countries, showing Iran’s eye-catching progress in this field.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – The head of Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) says that the country’s capabilities in nuclear science and technology are rival to those of the developed countries, showing Iran’s eye-catching progress in this field.

Opposing the country’s possession of peaceful nuclear technology cannot change the reality of its scientific achievements, AEOI Chief Mohammad Eslami stated, emphasizing that Iran stands on a par with developed countries in nuclear science and technology.

Speaking at a ceremony marking National Standard Day in Tehran on Tuesday, the country's atomic chief highlighted that the country’s intellectual resources, technological expertise, and the resourcefulness of its younger generation qualified it to achieve the highest levels of scientific and technological advancement.

“We are on a par with the developed and advanced countries in nuclear science and technology, and that is a reality.

Opposition and refusal to accept Iran’s possession of nuclear technology does not change the reality of the country’s scientific capabilities,” he opined.

“We have done nothing wrong,” he asserted, adding that Iran’s adversaries would have no other grounds to target the country if they stopped trying to tarnish its nuclear energy sector.

Addressing Iran’s industrial capabilities, Eslami said nuclear technology had become integrated into major industrial sectors, including refineries, petrochemical plants, and steel production.

He noted how industrial facilities across the country were targeted during unprovoked American-Israeli aggression in order to try to afflict damage to components involved in maintaining the stability of industrial processes.

headline: Kamala Harris warns window closing for AI safeguards, urges US-China cooperation
summary: By Kyu-seok ShimSEOUL, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Former US Vice President Kamala Harris urged governments and technology companies on Wednesday to urgently put safeguards in place for artificial intelligence, warning that the window for containing its gravest risks was closing."If we are to have any guardrails and safeguards, they have to be at the table," Harris said of AI developers during an appearance at South Korea's Asan Institute for Policy Studies. "My concern is that the window is shutting."
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Former US Vice President Kamala Harris urged governments and technology companies on Wednesday to urgently put safeguards in place for artificial intelligence, warning that the window for containing its gravest risks was closing.

"If we are to have any guardrails and safeguards, they have to be at the table," Harris said of AI developers during an appearance at South Korea's Asan Institute for Policy Studies.

"My concern is that the window is shutting."

Harris said governments and companies must act immediately against what she described as three existential dangers from AI - cybersecurity threats, AI-enabled weapons and systems escaping human control.

She also urged the United States to engage China on international rules and standards for AI, saying their broader strategic rivalry should not preclude cooperation on shared risks.

"There is room for cooperation where our interests are aligned," Harris said, calling for "healthy and robust competition, but not conflict."

Harris criticised what she called US President Donald Trump's "erratic tariffs" and their punitive nature, before warning against a transactional approach that cost the US global influence.

"The question is, are we thinking only about the short term, or do we also value and appreciate the significance of an investment for long-term gain?"

Harris praised South Korean investment in US shipbuilding, semiconductors, electric vehicles and clean energy, calling it "immensely significant and valued".

She also called for renewed US commitment to South Korea, saying growing cooperation among North Korea, Russia, China and Iran was very concerning and meant the allies must strengthen deterrence.

The former vice president has been campaigning for Democratic candidates ahead of the 2026 US midterm elections as she weighs another White House bid.

She said Democrats would win a majority in the House of Representatives and had a "very good shot" at taking the Senate, potentially giving Congress a stronger voice on domestic and foreign policy, including the war with Iran.

Asked whether she would again seek the presidency in 2028, Harris said: "I'm still thinking about it. I haven’t decided yet."

(Reporting by Kyu-seok ShimEditing by Ed Davies)

headline: To the Ramparts: New missile shield 'protects warships from drone swarms'
summary: A cost-effective missile system to defend civilian and military sites from drone swarms has been unveiled in France.Rampart, developed by Naval Group, can create a defensive shield around warships using large numbers of low-cost laser-guided rockets rather than expensive interceptors such as Patriot, that were expended at high rates in the Iran war.It has completed successful sea trials in the Mediterranean, including a French Navy counter-drone exercise off Toulon.“It is designed to build a defensive shield around a warship in drone warfare,” said Stephan Meunier, a former French navy commander involved with the programme. A cost-effective missile system to defend civilian and military sites from drone swarms has been unveiled in France.

Rampart, developed by Naval Group, can create a defensive shield around warships using large numbers of low-cost laser-guided rockets rather than expensive interceptors such as Patriot, that were expended at high rates in the Iran war.

It has completed successful sea trials in the Mediterranean, including a French Navy counter-drone exercise off Toulon.

Race to unlock secrets of Russia’s deadly jet-drone

“It is designed to build a defensive shield around a warship in drone warfare,” said Stephan Meunier, a former French navy commander involved with the programme.

Naval Group expects to produce up to 10,000 Rampart systems by 2028. In tests, the system struck an aerial drone as well as unguided rockets trained on surface targets.

The system fires laser-guided 68mm rockets fitted with proximity fuses and has a range of up to 6km.

The launcher consists of four modules, each carrying 20 projectiles, giving a maximum load of 80 rockets. It can be loaded with a combination of weapons, including surface-to-air and surface-to-surface missiles, decoys or precision missiles. An experienced crew can reload a single 20-round module in about 10 minutes.

The system weighs about four tonnes, allowing it to be fitted to relatively small warships including corvettes.

During the recent Iran war, western forces used large numbers of expensive interceptors against relatively cheap drones. Patriot missiles costing more than $4 million each were used to take out Shahed-136 drones costing just $35,000, roughly the same price as a guided 68mm rocket.

“The cost-to-kill ratio is very effective and it can tackle a drone swarm attack,” Mr Meunier said. “Rockets are cheaper and more efficient.”

There is growing evidence that shipping in the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea could face “saturation attacks” by drones fired from Iran or the rebel Houthis. Naval ships equipped with Rampart would be able to provide significant close-in protection, Mr Meunier said.

Rampart can also be deployed as a ground-based system to protect airports, military bases and civilian areas.

“This system would provide good defences for fixed installations such as airports and to protect urban centres or military camps in the Gulf as well as on board warships,” Mr Meunier said.

Over the weekend, Saudi Arabia’s main airport came under attack from Houthi rebels, with 13 people killed in two incidents. Missiles were also intercepted in Riyadh and Dammam.

Naval Group has also developed a single Rampart module for its Sirenha unmanned surface vessel, allowing an autonomous drone boat to provide an additional defensive layer.

The French company is also working with Emirates' defence group Edge to conduct trials of the UAE-developed SkyKnight air-defence missile, beginning with land trials before maritime testing next year.

SkyKnight can engage aerial threats at ranges of up to 10km, potentially giving Rampart a more capable missile option alongside its 68mm rockets.

There is also a possibility that Rampart could be battle-tested in Ukraine where Kyiv is getting desperately short of air defences against daily Russian drone and missile attacks.

If successful, then it could well provide a major step in defending key military and civilians sites from the threat of drone saturation attack at low cost.

body_text:
Over the past weeks, UAE telecom operators etisalat and du have announced further progress in their march towards 6G, the next generation of wireless communication.

The industry is accelerating its preparations for the technology that being presented as vital to the world becoming more connected, underpinned by increasingly intelligent devices and services.

Du said on Tuesday it has delivered commercial U6GHz connectivity on its 5G+ network, which will serve as a foundation for high-capacity services across homes, businesses and industries.

Du and etisalat unveil new services boosting UAE push towards 6G

Meanwhile, Abu Dhabi's etisalat – which recently rebranded back from e& – said it has commercially launched a service that increase upload speeds to smartphones threefold.

6G promises faster speeds and efficiency than the current 5G mobile phone technology, which also has more advanced forms under names such as 5G+, 5G Advanced and 5.5G.

Historically, new generations of wireless technology have emerged with every new decade, suggesting 6G could become available in the early 2030s. This is a widely shared industry expectation.

The US introduced the third generation in 2002, the fourth in 2010 and 5G in 2018. The second and first generations were in the 1980s and early 1990s, respectively, with the “zero G” before that.

While a 6G rollout is predicted in the early 2030s, not all of its features are expected to be available at launch, as the industry would continue testing its deployment.

5G's maximum transmission speed is 20 gigabits per second, which is already 20 times faster that 4G's 1Gbps rate under ideal circumstances.

However, 6G's theoretical maximum compared to 5G, has varied from anywhere between 50 times faster, or 1 terabit per second, to 1,000 times, or 2.5 terabytes per second.

One can only imagine how much that will increase transmission speeds. A multi-gigabyte file that used to take seconds or a few minutes to download could be done in a snap.

The consumer proposition of 6G will always be front and centre, especially as digital consumption and reliance on connected devices will only become more widespread.

But on an industrial scale, 6G is expected to power advanced iterations of immersive and mass communication, ubiquitous connectivity, integrated sensing and communication, low-latency and hyper-reliable communication and artificial intelligence communication, according to the International Telecommunication Union, which leads the framework and standards-setting of wireless communications.

Communications, business and economic gains aside, the power of 6G will also play a critical role in society by enabling affordable, resilient and energy‑efficient networks for health, education, agriculture and disaster response, the Geneva-based UN agency said.

“Advanced networks also present a way to close the persistent digital divide that today leaves many people in low-income countries behind,” it added.

Transport, home appliances and security, payment networks, financial transactions and a host of other products and services expected to be highly connected in the future will also rely on the speed 6G would offer.

There are a number of issues that need to be addressed to ensure the reliability of 6G networks.

Arguably the biggest challenge is to build 6G networks resilient to any AI-induced compromises. Networks of the future should be able to detect threats and adaptive enough to respond to them, according to the EC-Council University in New Mexico.

Encryption, especially that which can protect against quantum threats, and integration to blockchain would also be important to avoid unauthorised data access and manipulation, the university added.

body_text:
Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez did not hold back as he criticised the club's hierarchy ​after ​their ​Champions League defeat to ⁠Atletico Madrid on Tuesday.

United slipped to a 2-0 defeat, which means Michael Carrick's team have now gone winless for five consecutive games across competitions.

Martinez, however, attempted to highlight issues outside the pitch, stating that he ⁠expected greater investment to help ​the team compete at the highest level.

Man United ratings vs Atletico Madrid: Baleba promising on another tough night

The Argentina international singled ⁠out director of football Jason Wilcox, saying United needed more signings to compete with their rivals.

“I expect more from ​our ⁠technical director. I have ‌to be honest. And also, as players, we ​have to do more,” Martinez told Amazon Prime.

“Tonight it is easy to [blame] the coach, easy to say the players but also we have to see other areas.”

Atletico took the lead through Pablo Barrios inside the opening minute at the Metropolitano, before Ademola Lookman secured victory in the 79th minute, shortly after United defender Leny Yoro was sent off.

United are on three points in the Champions League league phase, having opened their campaign with a 4-0 win over ​Sabah FK. United are returning to the ‌Champions League after a ⁠two-season absence, having finished ​bottom of their group in their previous appearance ​in ‌the competition in 2023/24.

“We had a fantastic season last season ⁠and now we expect more from the top, from ⁠upstairs, to bring in more players to compete, because many teams have brought in many players as well,” Martinez added.

“Atletico have an amazing team and they deserved to win today.

“I have to be honest, as players we have to do more but it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for this kind of night.”

United, who are 13th in the Premier League, ​visit Leeds United on Sunday before travelling to Como for their next Champions League fixture on October 21.

Former Manchester United star Wayne Rooney said Martinez's comments were unwarranted and could throw the dressing room into chaos.

“It is disrespectful to his teammates,” Rooney was quoted as saying by the BCC. “He is saying his teammates aren't good enough.

“Bruno [Fernandes] is the only one with any right to say that. Behind closed doors, it happens – but that interview isn't going to help.

“[Martinez] has tried to speak on behalf of the players but done it the wrong way.”

Barcelona recovered well to defeat Galatasaray 4-1. Barca overturned a first-half deficit with Lamine Yamal supplying two assists.

Galatasaray went ahead as Alexey Batrakov scored in the 28th minute. The hosts thought they had doubled their lead through a Baris Yilmaz header, only for VAR to identify an offside ​in the build-up.

Joao Cancelo equalised just before half-time and Yamal then set up Fermin Lopez and Anthony ‌Gordon to score in the 50th and 53rd minutes. ⁠Karim Adeyemi completed the victory.

Also, Arsenal scored three times in seven minutes to defeat Lille 3-0.

Arsenal had to wait until the 64th minute for Jurrien Timber to break Lille's resistance from Noni Madueke's pass. Substitute Bukayo Saka then set up Eberechi Eze's goal before Kai Havertz supplied Saka for the ​third in the 71st minute.

body_text:
Sardar Azmoun struck both goals as Shabab Al Ahli picked up a superb away win at Al Ittihad in the AFC Champions League on Tuesday night.

The victory took the UAE club to a perfect six points from six, while Saudi Pro League Al Ittihad have just a single point after opening their campaign with a draw against Al Shamal SC of Qatar last month.

Backed by a full house in Jeddah, the home side started positively with Ahmed Al Julaydan forcing Matheus Donelli into a save from a tight angle in the sixth minute.

Ronaldo's 981st goal helps Al Nassr win as Al Ain go top of AFC Champions League

Shabab Al Ahli, however, struck in the next phase of play when Guilherme Bala powered down the left before teeing up the unmarked Azmoun to slot home.

Al Ittihad looked for an immediate response, with Steven Bergwijn testing Donelli from distance in the 13th minute, but the visitors doubled their advantage three minutes later.

Reza Ghandipour, who had only just replaced the injured Bala, released Azmoun with a through ball and the forward outpaced his markers before converting from a tight angle.

“We conceded two goals because of easy mistakes, which made the task difficult afterwards,” said Al Ittihad coach Jens Wissing.

“My job as a coach is to work with the players. We were better in the second half and we reached the opponent's goal, but we were not successful.”

He added: “We played with three forwards because we had more crosses, and it was possible to make use of one of the crosses. We did not play the game well. We had many chances and we could have been better.”

Elsewhere, Al Hilal recorded their second successive victory after defeating Al Sadd 2-0.

Ollie Watkins put Saudi Pro League leaders Hilal ahead in the first half before a Ruben Neves spot-kick confirmed the points as Qatar’s Al Sadd suffered a second consecutive defeat.

“I am happy with the players' performance,” said Hilal boss Simone Inzaghi. “We produced a big performance and controlled most of the game, and I saw a wonderful display from the team.”

The Italian also praised Gabriel Martinelli after the former Arsenal man gave the Al Sadd defence a difficult evening.

“He is a big player and we are lucky to have him with us,” added Inzaghi. “He always proves his high quality and his ability to serve the team and benefit it in more than one different position.”

headline: Pope Leo has lung cancer, the Vatican announces after surgery
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Pope Leo XIV had surgery on Tuesday to remove a cancerous growth in his lung, the Vatican announced.

The surgery, performed at Gemelli Hospital in Rome, involved removing the lower lobe of the Pope's right lung, according to a statement by Leo's doctors released by the church. Lung tissue examined after the surgery confirmed a previous test that revealed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said. Adenocarcinoma of the lung is the most common form of lung cancer in the United States, representing about 40% of all lung cancers, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America. MNA

headline: Fire at Aramco headquarters in Saudi Arabia’s after Houthi strike
body_text:
The Houthis have struck an administrative building at Aramco’s headquarters in Saudi Arabia’s eastern city of Dhahran, the country’s energy ministry said.

In a statement, the ministry said the authorities ⁠responded to a limited fire caused by the attack at the HQ of Saudi Arabia’s national oil company on Tuesday. However, no injuries or fatalities were reported.

The attack came after Yemen’s Houthis warned the employees and civilians near the country’s oil facilities to evacuate, terming the sites “a legitimate target”.

The warning followed an evacuation order by the Saudi-led coalition asking civilians to evacuate Yemeni Oil Company’s al-Sabah central station in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa. Shortly after, Houthi-affiliated media outlets said the Saudi-backed forces launched air strikes on an oil facility in the al-Sabah area of the capital, Al Jazeera reported.

The ongoing conflict between the Saudis and the Houthis started last month after the rebels took over key areas along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical passage for the transport of oil and other goods from the Gulf. The Saudi-led coalition has been trying to recapture those.

Saudi Cabinet Tuesday warned of “consequences” if the Houthis keep on attacking the kingdom. “The Kingdom will not allow any threat to its security or to freedom of maritime navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait,” the Cabinet said in a statement.

The Yemeni Oil Company said it had anticipated Saudi attack at Sanaa. Its storage facilities were empty, and the strike would not affect oil reserves or supplies for residents, added the company. However, the city witnessed queues of cars at gas stations amid fears of a shortage in oil supply.

Oil prices too surged on Wednesday as traders grew apprehensive about supply risks against the prospect of increased diesel from Russia. The Brent crude futures gained 89 cents, or 0.8 per cent, as of 00:30 GMT to reach $106.58 a barrel while the US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude went up 80 cents, or 0.9 per cent, to trade at $94.94.

security, stability and economic prosperity”.The Atrocities Standing Group, which includes Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk and Baroness Helena Kennedy, published the results of its 18 months of inquiry and parliamentary hearings on Tuesday in a report.It called for a tougher global policing role by using more “Magnitsky-style sanctions”, targeted punitive measures. Frozen sovereign assets from such sanctions could be repurposed to compensate victims of war crimes, by introducing relevant laws to do so, the report suggested.The UK government is seeking to re-establish Britain’s role in the world as conflicts escalate globally. “As the international rules-based order is facing fragmentation and significant challenges, it is key that the UK uses its global position to lead and support efforts to secure justice and accountability for international crimes,” the report said.Former British prime minister Gordon Brown, who has endorsed the report, said the UK needed to take serious foreign policy steps that go well beyond “condemnation” and “sympathy”.“Sympathy is not prevention, condemnation is not policy,” he said ahead of the report's launch. “The question before the United Kingdom and other democratic states is simple and grave.“Will we continue to respond to atrocity crimes only after they have shocked our conscience, or will we build a serious system to predict and prevent them, and respond to them lawfully and in time?”The upholding of human rights risks being further eroded by the US decision to sanction the International Criminal Court in The Hague. She questioned why it had taken the UK months to apply a partial suspension of around 30 out of about 350 arms export licences to Israel for military use in Gaza, which the British government eventually announced in September 2024. body_text:
Cuts to the UK’s foreign aid and diplomatic arms are hampering Britain's ability to prevent atrocities as global conflicts increase, experts have warned.

Yasmine Ahmed, senior director at Amnesty International, said the UK government was not acting fast enough to prevent war crimes, such as those allegedly committed in Sudan and Gaza. “Often atrocity prevention is not prioritised sufficiently in terms of a whole of government policy response,” Ms Ahmed told The National.

Last year, Britain’s overseas aid budget was slashed from 0.5 per cent of its gross national income to 0.3 per cent, at a time when conflicts are increasing worldwide. These cuts were issued by former prime minister Keir Starmer in January last year and Britain's spending on overseas aid is expected to fall by 42 per cent, or £6.5 billion ($8.6 billion), over four years, according to the Independent Commission for Aid Impact.

UK must remain in Jerusalem 'at all costs', says former diplomat

One of the first Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office units to feel the impact of the cuts was international humanitarian law cell monitoring war crimes in Gaza. The FCDO has insisted these aid cuts would not affect the department’s ability to conduct human rights assessments of a conflict – but Ms Ahmed was sceptical.

“If you’ve got a huge percentage – 20 per cent of the Foreign Office being cut – there’s no doubt this is going to have a significant impact across the board,” she said. “The question is how well will the Foreign Office continue to be equipped to conduct these assessments.”

In the past few weeks there has been an escalation of conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen, and the possibility of all-out war between Eritrea and Ethiopia has developed.

Yet the UK's ability to enforce the laws of war and human rights on the world stage was dwindling. “What we’re finding now is that the UK and certainly other European states and other western states don’t have as much leverage as they used to,” Ms Ahmed said.

This was leading to a visible decline in the protection of civilians in conflict. “They [the UK and European governments] are operating in an increasingly volatile political world and it’s increasingly transactional,” she said. “There is less space to be values driven.”

On Tuesday, a group of British human rights lawyers and experts in global conflict called on the UK to loosen jurisdiction rules, so British courts can prosecute on a wider range of war crimes as well going after as companies accused of involvement.

The group warned that the UK was currently “ill-equipped to identify and respond effectively to the warning signs of genocide and other atrocity crimes”, and that this had “serious implications” for “national security, stability and economic prosperity”.

The Atrocities Standing Group, which includes Nobel Peace Prize laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk and Baroness Helena Kennedy, published the results of its 18 months of inquiry and parliamentary hearings on Tuesday in a report.

It called for a tougher global policing role by using more “Magnitsky-style sanctions”, targeted punitive measures. Frozen sovereign assets from such sanctions could be repurposed to compensate victims of war crimes, by introducing relevant laws to do so, the report suggested.

The UK government is seeking to re-establish Britain’s role in the world as conflicts escalate globally. “As the international rules-based order is facing fragmentation and significant challenges, it is key that the UK uses its global position to lead and support efforts to secure justice and accountability for international crimes,” the report said.

Former British prime minister Gordon Brown, who has endorsed the report, said the UK needed to take serious foreign policy steps that go well beyond “condemnation” and “sympathy”.

“Sympathy is not prevention, condemnation is not policy,” he said ahead of the report's launch. “The question before the United Kingdom and other democratic states is simple and grave.

“Will we continue to respond to atrocity crimes only after they have shocked our conscience, or will we build a serious system to predict and prevent them, and respond to them lawfully and in time?”

The upholding of human rights risks being further eroded by the US decision to sanction the International Criminal Court in The Hague. While the UK has made “strong statements” of their continued support for the court, their next step could be putting in place a “blocking statute” that would make the sanctions unenforceable in the UK, Ms Ahmed said.

The wars in Sudan and in Gaza have featured clear examples of the UK government’s inability to intervene in time, Ms Ahmed said.

She questioned why it had taken the UK months to apply a partial suspension of around 30 out of about 350 arms export licences to Israel for military use in Gaza, which the British government eventually announced in September 2024. Export licensing was one area in which the government could act quickly, by referring to its own criteria and the Arms Trade Treaty, she said.

“They have the duty to prevent genocide and other crimes, but that’s very hard to enforce. But when you have the export-licensing criteria, that’s where we find there’s a space where the government themselves has processes to evaluate.

“I was going in on a weekly basis with either ministers or high-level officials and sometimes middle-ranked officials. We were presenting the evidence. It certainly took longer than it should have,” she said.

“It did so on the basis that Israel couldn’t be found to have a commitment to comply with international law because it was restricting aid.”

Likewise, the UK’s response to the Sudanese civil war had failed to activate “the full plethora of government machinery”, despite its key resolutions on Sudan at the UN Security Council.

With cuts to overseas aid anticipated for the long term, Ms Ahmed – who previously worked as a legal adviser to the FCDO – outlined options that would reinforce the role of human rights in UK foreign policy.

The units involved in human rights and atrocity prevention needed to be “supported at the highest-ministerial level, prioritised, given resources and given the power within the bureaucratic system to have a say when policy decisions are being made,” she said.

Instead, government advisers on human rights policy were often sidelined. “So often, what I have found, is that the human rights directorate aren't key stakeholders in key political decisions,” Ms Ahmed said.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband's declaration last month that settler “terrorists” were responsible for “ethnic cleansing” in the West Bank was a major step, Ms Ahmed said.

“That was a really huge development and important to note because it's the first time the government has ever made any such determination and it's clear, given the magnitude of the forced displacement of Palestinians from their land in the West Bank,” she said.

Questions remain about how the UK will implement its most significant foreign policy shift in months – the move to impose sanctions on the expansion of illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Foreign Office officials have suggested a six to nine month time frame for initial measures to be implemented but campaigners including Ms Ahmed say this is too long.

“As I understand it, there is a commitment to implementing it in a way that’s effective,” she said. “The devil will be in the detail to ensure that they in fact do that.”

Amnesty International and other organisations are calling on the government to make sure the ban extends to banks and financial services that work with companies involved in illegal settlements.

“It’s not just about goods and services to settlements. It’s also about the financial enabling of the occupation … which are involved in continuing the financial stability of the settlements,” Ms Ahmed said.

headline: 🔴Ukraine live: Russia's 'targeted' strikes on energy leave 600,000 without power, Zelensky says
body_text:
Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 08:19Modified: 14/10/2026 - 08:47

Heavy overnight Russian strikes killed at least six people in Ukraine and cut power to hundreds of thousands of people, authorities said on Wednesday. ⁠Russia's ​defence ​ministry said ‌it ⁠had ‌downed ⁠902 drones ​over ‌Russian regions overnight, ‌Interfax ​news agency reported. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.

Russia's Defence Ministry said on ​Wednesday that its forces had struck 7 Ukrainian energy infrastucture facilities and a data centre in a ​massive overnight ‌attack which it said targeted ⁠facilities which benefited the Ukrainian military.

Russia's Defence Ministry said in a ‌statement that its forces had struck two heat and power plants ​in Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, another such plant in the wider Kyiv region along with a thermal ​power plant and an electricity substation, and a ​heat and power plant in ​Kharkiv along with a thermal power plant which it said supplied the ​Ukrainian military in the southeast of the Kharkiv region.

The ministry said it had also hit a data centre in Kyiv which it said was used ⁠to gather intelligence on Russia's armed forces.

It said the attack ⁠had been ​carried out with ground-launched missiles and long-range strike drones.

A former Ukrainian military officer is set to become the first person to stand trial over the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline bombings when proceedings begin in a German court Wednesday, accused of carrying out a "war crime", attacking civilian infrastructure and causing an explosion.

In September 2022, seven months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a series of blasts under the Baltic Sea damaged three of the four Nord Stream pipelines designed to carry Russian gas to Europe.

In August last year Ukrainian Sergiy Kuznietsov was arrested in Italy while on holiday with his family, and extradited to Germany the following month.

Investigators allege the former Ukrainian special forces officer led a small group comprising professional divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper that planted explosives on the pipelines.

Kuznietsov's lawyers unsuccessfully tried to challenge the German court's jurisdiction over the attacks, and suggested they may argue that the pipelines were legitimate military targets in Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion.

His trial is currently scheduled to run until February 2027.

The operation of some Starlink internet terminals appeared to be restricted overnight, a technology adviser to the Ukrainian president said Wednesday, after US President Donald Trump called for a pause in attacks on power infrastructure.

"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said the adviser, Sergiy Beskrestnov. "Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation."

A family evacuates their burning apartment building following a Russian strike in Kyiv on October 13, 2026. © Reuters

A residential building on fire following a Russian missile strike in Kyiv overnight on Tuesday © AP

A resident smokes a cigarette after his apartment building was hit by a strike in Kyiv on October 13, 2026. © AP

Ukrainian ​air ​defences downed four of the ​39 ‌missiles ⁠launched ‌by Russia ⁠overnight, Kyiv's air force ​said ‌on Wednesday.

In a ‌statement, ​it added that a large ​number ​of ballistic missiles ​had ​targeted energy infrastructure.

Massive Russian strikes on Ukraine on Wednesday left some 600,000 people without power and deliberately flouted a purported "energy ceasefire" announced by Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

"A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure -- the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American President," he wrote on X.

"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale -- Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States.

The death toll from Russian strikes on Ukraine has risen to at least six people overnight through Wednesday, authorities said, as Moscow pressed forward with attacks on several regions.

Three people were killed in the capital Kyiv, two in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, and one in southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, according to tallies from regional officials.

A ⁠Ukraine ​drone attack ​killed one person and damaged houses ​in ‌the ⁠town of ‌Balakovo on the ⁠Volga River in Russia's Saratov ​region, Governor ‌Roman Busargin said on Telegram, ‌without providing ​further details.

Balakovo is home to a ​nuclear power ​plant and ​a hydropower station, ​whose dam spans the Volga River.

Heavy Russian strikes on Kyiv have cut power to large parts of the Ukrainian capital, the mayor and a major utility said on Wednesday.

"Energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region have come under a massive ballistic missile strike. There are power disruptions in the capital," Mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote on Telegram, in comments backed up by the power company DTEK.

Russian ​forces ​targeted facilities belonging to Ukraine's ​state ‌railway ⁠in ‌a massive attack overnight, ⁠its CEO has said.

In ‌a statement on ‌Facebook, Oleksandr ​Pertsovskyi of Ukrzaliznytsia said waves of ​strikes targeted ​the ​Kharkiv, Kyiv, Vinnytsia, ​Khmelnytskyi and Ternopil regions.

Russia's military has said that it had shot down 902 Ukrainian drones overnight, 180 of them near the capital Moscow.

"Over the past night... air defence systems destroyed 902 Ukrainian drones" across around 20 Russian regions and annexed Crimea, the defence ministry said in a statement.

According to the capital's mayor Sergei Sobyanin, "180 drones were destroyed as they approached Moscow".

Russian ​forces ​struck an oil facility overnight ​in ‌the ⁠western ‌Ukrainian city ⁠of Lutsk, a city ​official ‌has said.

Andriy ‌Razumovskyi ​said the drone attack sparked ​a ​fire, ​but offered no ​further details.

Welcome to the FRANCE 24 liveblog covering the war in Ukraine.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday that a Russian ballistic missile struck a Kyiv power plant without advance warning from Western allies, killing at least two people and wounding around 20.

The attack came days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, raising questions over efforts to halt strikes on critical infrastructure.

The attack came days after US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv, raising questions over efforts to halt strikes on critical infrastructure.

headline: Pope Leo XIV’s lung adenocarcinoma: Oncologist explains the cancer and its treatment
body_text:
Pope Leo XIV, 71, diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a type of lung cancer, has undergone “successful surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung“, the Vatican stated. The 71-year-old pontiff will remain in the hospital for about a week following the operation at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital.

AP News reported that a Vatican medical bulletin confirmed the diagnosis, noting that “The operation lasted approximately 90 minutes, while Leo remained in the operating room for about three hours. The Vatican said there were no complications.”

DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine.

Taking a cue, we reached out to experts to understand more about the health condition.

Dr Jinesh Singhavi, consultant medical oncologist, KIMS Hospitals, Thane, noted that lung adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer that develops in cells lining the airways or producing mucus. “It is one of the common forms of lung cancer. The seriousness of the diagnosis depends on factors such as the tumour’s size, its location, whether it has spread to nearby lymph nodes or other organs, and the characteristics of the cancer cells,” Dr Singhavi told indianexpress.com.

According to Dr Singhavi, the procedure is called a lobectomy, in which the affected lobe of the lung is surgically removed. “It is an established treatment for certain lung cancers, particularly when the disease can be removed completely through surgery. The decision depends on the tumour’s location, its extent and the patient’s overall health and lung function. However, we cannot determine the stage of the Pope’s cancer from the information currently available.”

Lymph nodes act as filtering stations in the body’s immune system. Dr Singhavi elucidated that lung cancer can spread to these nodes, sometimes before there are obvious signs elsewhere. “Examining them under a microscope helps doctors establish whether the cancer has spread beyond the lung. This information is crucial for determining the stage and deciding whether additional treatment is necessary. Their examination is a routine part of assessing many lung cancers and does not, by itself, mean that the disease has spread,” said Dr Singhavi.

Not necessarily, asserted Dr Singhavi. “Removing the tumour is an important step, but the final pathology report must establish whether it has been completely removed and whether lymph nodes are involved. Depending on these findings, doctors may recommend monitoring alone or additional treatment. It would be premature to conclude the Pope’s prognosis until these results are available,” Dr Singhavi noted.

headline: Houthi attack hits Aramco's historic nerve centre in Saudi Arabia
summary: A missile attack on an administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state energy company Aramco hit the historic centre of the kingdom's oil industry, sparking a fire that authorities said caused no casualties.The strike by the Yemeni Houthi rebels hit a complex that serves as the nerve centre of the world's largest oil exporter, housing key research and development site, energy operations and thousands of employees and their families.People living near the building described moments of terror as a powerful explosion shook the area. "This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life," one woman told The National. Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area following the attack.While no further details have been released about the incident, the site is a key one for Aramco, serving as its central hub for oil, gas, and energy operations.More than an HQAramco, at the time known as the Arabian American Oil Company, moved its headquarters from New York City to Dhahran in 1952. Dhahran was where the kingdom’s first commercial oil was found in 1938, at Dammam No 7, the “Prosperity Well". The Saudi government gradually acquired the company, completing a full buyout in 1980, before it was renamed the Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Aramco) in 1988. Aramco’s headquarters is situated within a vast complex spread across 58 square kilometres, with a large residential area housing a reported 11,000 people, including employees and their families. The Dhahran district also has a research and development centre and the Expec Advanced Research Centre, which was inaugurated in 2008. Expec has been upgraded with a building to focus on upstream research and development. The Dhahran complex also houses a large-scale cooling plant, operated by Saudi Tabreed, with a 32,000 refrigeration-tonne capacity that includes thermal storage tanks for energy saving. The chilled water piping network stretches 16 kilometres to reach sites, meeting Saudi Aramco's requirements for cooling. body_text:
A missile attack on an administrative building of Saudi Arabia's state energy company Aramco hit the historic centre of the kingdom's oil industry, sparking a fire that authorities said caused no casualties.

The strike by the Yemeni Houthi rebels hit a complex that serves as the nerve centre of the world's largest oil exporter, housing key research and development site, energy operations and thousands of employees and their families.

People living near the building described moments of terror as a powerful explosion shook the area.

"This was the loudest explosion I have ever heard in my life," one woman told The National. Another resident said relatives living closer to the site had reported seeing smoke and flames rising from the area following the attack.

While no further details have been released about the incident, the site is a key one for Aramco, serving as its central hub for oil, gas, and energy operations.

Aramco, at the time known as the Arabian American Oil Company, moved its headquarters from New York City to Dhahran in 1952. Dhahran was where the kingdom’s first commercial oil was found in 1938, at Dammam No 7, the “Prosperity Well". The Saudi government gradually acquired the company, completing a full buyout in 1980, before it was renamed the Saudi Arabian Oil Company (Aramco) in 1988.

Aramco’s headquarters is situated within a vast complex spread across 58 square kilometres, with a large residential area housing a reported 11,000 people, including employees and their families.

The Dhahran district also has a research and development centre and the Expec Advanced Research Centre, which was inaugurated in 2008. Expec has been upgraded with a building to focus on upstream research and development.

The Dhahran complex also houses a large-scale cooling plant, operated by Saudi Tabreed, with a 32,000 refrigeration-tonne capacity that includes thermal storage tanks for energy saving. The chilled water piping network stretches 16 kilometres to reach sites, meeting Saudi Aramco's requirements for cooling.

The area also includes Ithra, the King Abdulaziz Centre for World Culture, which was built by Aramco as a cultural and creative destination for the public. The centre has attracted more than four million since its opening in 2018.

The Dhahran area was attacked on February 25, 1991, during the Gulf War, when an Iraqi Scud missile struck a US Army barracks, killing 28 American soldiers and wounding 110.

Aramco’s other sites in the Eastern province have also faced attacks in the past. Several drones and missiles hit Saudi Aramco’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil processing centres on September 14, 2019, knocking out about 50 per cent of the country’s crude oil production.

The 17-minute strike by 18 drones and three low-flying missiles, claimed by the Houthis, caused a surge in oil prices and shut down more than 5 per cent of global oil supply. Saudi Arabia said about two weeks later that it had fully restored oil output.

In March 2022, an Aramco plant in Jizan was also attacked by the Houthis with a drone laden with explosives, with a gas station in Khamis Mushait and a power station in Dhahran also hit.

In early March this year, after the start of the Iran war, a fire broke out at Aramco’s Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom’s largest, with 550,000 barrels per day of capacity, due to drone attacks.

Operations were halted for 16 days. Ras Tanura, on Saudi Arabia's Gulf coast, hosts one of the world’s largest oil export terminals and a major refining facility. The port handles a significant share of Saudi crude exports.

Other sites hit this year include Satorp in Jubail, a joint venture between Saudi Aramco and TotalEnergies processing 465,000 bpd and one of the world's largest export refining platforms, as well as Samref in Yanbu, a 400,000 bpd Aramco-ExxonMobil joint venture.

Earlier this month, Aramco’s chief executive Amin Nasser said ​the company had ‌the ⁠strategic ​reserves and ​flexibility ‌to ⁠isolate or shift output ⁠as required. Aramco can ⁠make its maximum ⁠sustainable production ​capacity of ⁠12 million bpd available ⁠within days, ​he ​told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London. “Our system is intact,” he added.

Aramco, which is listed on the Tadawul exchange, is majority owned by the Saudi government. It is due to release its third quarter financial results on November 3.

headline: S. Korea, Norway discuss ways to expand defense, tech cooperation
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Senior diplomats of South Korea and Norway on Wednesd...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Senior diplomats of South Korea and Norway on Wednesday discussed expanding cooperation in defense, technology and various other fields and agreed to strengthen bilateral ties, Seoul's foreign ministry said.

Chung Eui-hye, deputy foreign minister for political affairs, met with Norwegian Deputy Foreign Minister Andreas Motzfeldt Kravik in Seoul and exchanged views on the situations on the Korean Peninsula, in the Middle East and in Ukraine, according to the ministry.

Chung expressed hope for expanded cooperation in defense, fisheries and advanced technology, while calling for Norway's continued support for South Korean companies involved in infrastructure construction projects in the European country.

She also highlighted their special ties, forged through Norway's dispatch of a medical support unit during the 1950-53 Korean War, and welcomed continued high-level exchanges, including a summit between their leaders on the sidelines of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) summit in July.

Kravik noted that bilateral relations have grown closer in recent years and expressed hope that Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store would visit South Korea at a mutually convenient time.

Kravik also expressed hope for stronger cooperation with South Korea and other like-minded countries in addressing key global issues, including artificial intelligence (AI), multilateralism and the rules-based international order.

"The two sides also exchanged views on major international and regional issues, including the Korean Peninsula, the Middle East and the war in Ukraine, and agreed to strengthen cooperation as trusted partners amid growing geopolitical uncertainties," the ministry said in a release.

headline: Trade between Russia and China up by 30.6% to $214.3 bln in January-September
summary: During the period, Russia’s trade surplus with China reached $18.16 billion, which is 10.1% up year-on-year
body_text:
BEIJING, October 14. /TASS/. Trade between China and Russia rose by 30.6% year-on-year to $214.3 billion in January-September, according to the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC).

In the reporting period, Chinese exports to Russia grew by 33.1% to $98.06 billion, while imports of Russian products into China increased by 28.6% to $116.24 billion.

In January-September, Russia’s trade surplus with China reached $18.16 billion, which is 10.1% up year-on-year.

According to the GACC statistics, Chinese-Russian trade turnover in September rose by 13.5% compared to August, reaching $29.06 billion. In particular, Chinese exports to Russia totaled $13.39 billion (up 12.9%), while shipments from Russia to China increased by 13.9% to $15.67 billion.

In terms of value, the bulk of Russian goods supplied to China consists of oil, natural gas, and coal. Other key items include copper and copper ore, timber, fuel, seafood, and agricultural products. China exports automobiles, tractors, computers, smartphones, industrial and specialized equipment, and a wide range of consumer and industrial goods to Russia. Authorities in both countries are working to optimize the structure of bilateral trade, including through the development of e-commerce and primary processing projects.

In 2024, Chinese-Russian trade turnover reached a record high, exceeding $244 billion, but contracted by 6.9% to $228.1 billion in 2025. As Russian Ambassador to China Igor Morgulov said earlier, this annual figure could soon rise to $300 billion.

headline: Iran Air to launch direct flight btw Zahedan, Quetta
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran’s National Flag Carrier [Iran Air] has announced that it will launch a direct flight between Iran’s Zahedan and Pakistan’s Quetta for the first time.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran’s National Flag Carrier [Iran Air] has announced that it will launch a direct flight between Iran’s Zahedan and Pakistan’s Quetta for the first time.

In continuation of the development of its flight network to the neighboring Pakistan, Iran Air is launching a flight route between Zahedan and Quetta for the first time, the launch of this route brings the airline's total number of active flights to Pakistan to three.

The first flight of the route Zahedan - Quetta, bearing No. 826, will take place at 10:10 a.m. from Zahedan Airport to the destination of Quetta on Wednesday October 14.

Additionally, the return flight for this route will be operated on the same day at 14:25 from Quetta to the destination of Zahedan, bearing Flight No. 827.

According to the scheduled program, flights on Zahedan-Quetta route will be operated weekly on Wednesdays.

body_text:
Sardar Azmoun struck both goals as Shabab Al Ahli picked up a superb away win at Al Ittihad in the AFC Champions League on Tuesday night.

The victory took the UAE club to a perfect six points from six, while Saudi Pro League Al Ittihad have just a single point after opening their campaign with a draw against Al Shamal SC of Qatar last month.

Backed by a full house in Jeddah, the home side started positively with Ahmed Al Julaydan forcing Matheus Donelli into a save from a tight angle in the sixth minute.

Ronaldo's 981st goal helps Al Nassr win as Al Ain go top of AFC Champions League

Shabab Al Ahli, however, struck in the next phase of play when Guilherme Bala powered down the left before teeing up the unmarked Azmoun to slot home.

Al Ittihad looked for an immediate response, with Steven Bergwijn testing Donelli from distance in the 13th minute, but the visitors doubled their advantage three minutes later.

Reza Ghandipour, who had only just replaced the injured Bala, released Azmoun with a through ball and the forward outpaced his markers before converting from a tight angle.

“We conceded two goals because of easy mistakes, which made the task difficult afterwards,” said Al Ittihad coach Jens Wissing.

“My job as a coach is to work with the players. We were better in the second half and we reached the opponent's goal, but we were not successful.”

He added: “We played with three forwards because we had more crosses, and it was possible to make use of one of the crosses. We did not play the game well. We had many chances and we could have been better.”

Elsewhere, Al Hilal recorded their second successive victory after defeating Al Sadd 2-0.

Ollie Watkins put Saudi Pro League leaders Hilal ahead in the first half before a Ruben Neves spot-kick confirmed the points as Qatar’s Al Sadd suffered a second consecutive defeat.

“I am happy with the players' performance,” said Hilal boss Simone Inzaghi. “We produced a big performance and controlled most of the game, and I saw a wonderful display from the team.”

The Italian also praised Gabriel Martinelli after the former Arsenal man gave the Al Sadd defence a difficult evening.

“He is a big player and we are lucky to have him with us,” added Inzaghi. “He always proves his high quality and his ability to serve the team and benefit it in more than one different position.”

body_text:
A Ukrainian former military officer is to go on trial ​in Germany on Wednesday, accused of organising the secret operation that blew ⁠up the Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022, severing western Europe from the biggest source ⁠of Russian natural gas.

The suspect, identified under German privacy rules only as Serhii ​K., is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents, including divers and an explosives expert, to mount one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of ⁠modern times.

The case will provide the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the crime.

Prosecutors have alleged that Serhii K., who was arrested under an international warrant ⁠in Italy last year, worked with other members of the military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.

Serhii K. ​has denied ⁠any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200km-long ‌Baltic Sea pipeline.

The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military ​aid. The Russian government said it expected a “just verdict” that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.

German prosecutors say the actions of which Serhii K. is accused – attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services – would amount to a war crime. The alleged aim was to disrupt a major source of foreign revenue for Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, launched earlier that year.

He is the only person on trial but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers in the team.

The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's long-standing dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Germany previously received half its natural gas imports through the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, by far the biggest and most modern Russian conduit serving western Europe, which allowed Russia to bypass Soviet-era pipelines crossing Ukraine.

The supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, which was already built, although Berlin cancelled approval to start operations shortly before Russia's invasion.

The trial, expected ​to continue into February, could also have domestic political implications. Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in ‌opinion polls for more than a year, has called for ⁠an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ​ties with Moscow.

In the initial months after the pipelines were attacked, western officials mainly pointed fingers at Russia. Moscow has always denied ​any involvement and called ‌the suggestion it would blow up its own pipelines absurd. It also rejects charges that it has more recently targeted western infrastructure with so-called “hybrid” sabotage and drone attacks.

The ⁠Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 metres under the Baltic and built by Russian energy corporation Gazprom ⁠to supply up to 110 billion cubic metres of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.

On September 26, 2022, several blasts were detected by Swedish seismologists over 17 hours. The explosions sent huge plumes of methane gas into the atmosphere, as three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines were ruptured.

Prosecutors allege Serhii K. travelled to Germany through Poland about three weeks before the attack, using ​a forged Ukrainian passport.

They say he and his group used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialised military-grade explosives fitted with timers to the sea floor.

The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on September 6 and returned on September 23, 2022.

headline: EXPLAINER - What to know about Nord Stream sabotage trial
summary: Germany to try Ukrainian suspect over 2022 Baltic Sea explosions that damaged 2 major gas pipeline systems
body_text:
Germany is preparing to put a Ukrainian national on trial over the September 2022 explosions that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea, with prosecutors alleging that Ukrainian state authorities ordered the operation.

The suspect, identified as Serhii K., is accused of helping lead a group that carried out the sabotage. His indictment marks the first time German prosecutors have formally brought the Nord Stream sabotage case before a court.

Another suspect, identified by Germany as Vladimir Z., is in custody in Croatia and is fighting extradition. He was earlier detained in Poland.

Nord Stream is a network of offshore natural gas pipelines connecting Russia and Germany beneath the Baltic Sea. The four lines of Nord Stream and Nord Stream 2 had a combined annual capacity of 110 billion cubic meters.

Construction of the first Nord Stream pipeline was completed in 2011, and it began operating in 2012. Nord Stream 2 was completed in September 2021 but never entered service.

In September 2022, Nord Stream AG, the operator of the pipelines, confirmed damage to both systems as Danish and Swedish authorities reported explosions and gas leaks in sections passing through their respective waters.

Pipeline pressure stabilized, and the gas leaks stopped several weeks after the incident, with Russia opening a criminal case on charges of international terrorism.

Russian President Vladimir Putin later described the US and countries with alternative energy supply routes to Europe, including Ukraine and Poland, as “beneficiaries” of the disruption.

While Western officials initially suspected Russia, German investigators later focused on possible Ukrainian involvement. The US, Poland and the UK have also faced allegations, but have denied involvement.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed claims of Russian involvement as “quite predictable and also predictably stupid,” stressing Moscow lost a route for gas supplies to Europe.

The US rejected the allegations as “Russia's disinformation,” while Poland called the claims “completely groundless insinuations.”

In August, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Germany should not prosecute suspects accused of blowing up the Nord Stream pipeline, adding that those who built the project “should be ashamed, not those who disabled them.”

The UK also rejected allegations, saying Russia was “resorting to peddling false claims of an epic scale.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy denied Kyiv's involvement, saying the government has officially never taken part in any operation related to the Nord Stream blast.

He said Ukraine held high-level talks with Germany on the issue, and that German officials knew Kyiv was not involved in planning or carrying out the operation.

Serhii K. was detained in Italy near Rimini in August 2025 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage. He was extradited to Germany three months later and has remained in pretrial detention in Hamburg.

The suspect is charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an “accomplice to war crimes” for targeting civilian objects, prosecutors said.

German prosecutors allege that Serhii K. was an officer in the Ukrainian army at the time, and helped plan the operation with other military personnel “acting on behalf of state bodies in Ukraine.”

Prosecutors allege the objective was to destroy both pipelines, permanently halt Russian gas deliveries and prevent Moscow from using energy revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.

Investigators claim the suspects traveled to Germany using forged Ukrainian passports and hired a yacht, the Andromeda. Traces of the explosives HMX and RDX were found aboard the vessel.

According to prosecutors, the explosives were attached to the pipelines near Denmark’s Bornholm island using timers by Sept. 22, 2022. They detonated four days later, causing extensive damage and rendering the pipelines inoperable.

Serhii K. denies the allegations.

The high-profile trial opens in a Hamburg court on Wednesday.

headline: (LEAD) Kamala Harris faults Trump's tariffs, N.K. policy, calls for stronger alliance with S. Korea
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris on Wednesday...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS Harris' remarks on AI in last 3 paras; CHANGES headline)By Oh Seok-min

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris on Wednesday criticized the Donald Trump administration's policy on North Korea and tariffs, calling for a renewed commitment to the South Korea-U.S. alliance.

Speaking at a special lecture in Seoul organized by the Asan Institute for Policy Studies, Harris said U.S. President Trump's economic and foreign policies have been undermining Washington's strength in its ties with Seoul.

"I was very -- 'disappointed' would be an understatement -- to see when the current president changed the strength of our shared exercises," Harris said, referring to joint military exercises between Seoul and Washington.

In August, South Korea and the United States scaled back their combined military exercises at Trump's direction, a move seen as a conciliatory gesture toward Pyongyang. North Korea, meanwhile, has advanced its nuclear capabilities while deepening its military ties with Russia.

Pointing to the Trump administration's "erratic tariffs and the punitive nature of those," Harris said such policies ran counter to strengthening the alliance and America's standing in the world.

"We have to acknowledge the changing circumstances even over the last year and a half that require a renewal of our commitment to South Korea," she said.

Harris also called for stronger extended deterrence against North Korea, saying decisions on how to strengthen it "must be the product of allies coming together."

"The alliance between China and Russia and Iran and North Korea, it's something we have to pay attention to," she said. "There is the work that the United States should always be committed to -- that is about participating in strengthening the Republic of Korea's armed forces."

On economic ties, Harris praised South Korean companies' contributions to U.S. industries, including shipbuilding, semiconductors and electric vehicles, as well as their investments in U.S. technology and manufacturing.

"The Korean investment in technology in the United States ... is immensely significant and valued," she said.

When asked how South Korea could maximize its economic relationship with the U.S. amid tariff tensions, Harris encouraged continued cooperation but questioned whether investments should be made under pressure.

"Not as a consequence of a threat, right?" she said, responding to a suggestion that South Korean companies would need to invest billions of dollars more in the U.S.

"The nature of a relationship of trust is that it is reciprocal," she said. "You give and you receive trust."

Harris also called for a more strategic approach to trade and closer cooperation with allies to strengthen supply chains and prevent shortages.

"America must invest in a robust domestic industrial strategy and partner with our allies to build resilience and prevent chokepoints and shortages," she said.

Harris' remarks came amid concerns over Seoul-Washington ties, including constraints on intelligence sharing, differences over the implementation of South Korea's planned US$350 billion investment in the U.S. in exchange for lower U.S. tariffs on Korean imports and other pending bilateral issues.

"As I said in 2022, when I was last here as vice president: the alliance between the United States and the Republic of Korea has been a linchpin of security and prosperity on the Korean Peninsula and the Indo-Pacific. Today I have returned to Seoul because I still believe that is true," Harris said.

Turning to artificial intelligence (AI), Harris called for slowing the development of advanced AI models to allow time to establish safeguards.

"America must work with our allies and bring China to the table to help slow the pace of AI development and to encourage the adoption of global standards for testing and transparency," Harris said, warning that "the window is closing quickly."

Harris said the U.S. cannot accept a "false choice" between winning the AI race and making AI safe for humanity, adding, "We can and must do both."

headline: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 14, 2026
summary: [allAfrica]
body_text:
Former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila to Lead New Rebel Coalition

Former Democratic Republic of Congo President Joseph Kabila has been named leader of the newly formed Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition seeking to remove President Félix Tshisekedi's government. Launched in Goma, the movement brings together former leaders of the AFC/M23 alliance, including M23 military leader Sultani Makenga, who was appointed one of Kabila's deputies. The coalition accuses Tshisekedi's administration of corruption, economic mismanagement, insecurity, and weakening democratic institutions. It is vowing to pursue change by all means, including force. Kabila, who ruled from 2001 to 2019, was sentenced to death in absentia for treason last year. The announcement comes amid continued fighting in eastern DR Congo and stalled peace negotiations.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Nigeria Plane Crash Raises Fears of Water Contamination

Residents of Igbokoda in Nigeria's Ondo State are raising concerns about possible water contamination after a Nigerian Air Force plane crash that killed all 25 people on board on October 5. The aircraft crashed into a swamp connected to a river that supplies the community's drinking water. Difficult terrain has hampered efforts to recover the wreckage and victims' remains. Community leaders fear that decaying human remains, possible oil spills and reports of dying fish could threaten public health and local livelihoods. Traditional ruler Afolabi Odidiomo has called for an urgent environmental clean-up and the provision of alternative safe drinking water. Recovery teams are continuing their search, with locating the aircraft's black box among their priorities.

Caine Prize Investigates Zimbabwean Writer Over AI Allegations

The Caine Prize for African Writing is investigating Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza after allegations that he used artificial intelligence to produce his award-winning short story, The Blue Fighter. The controversy followed an article published by The Atlantic that criticised the story and raised questions about its authorship. The prize organisers confirmed they had begun an investigation, saying they have a responsibility to uphold trust within Africa's literary and publishing community. The story centres on Tinashe and his family, whose circumstances deteriorate after his father leaves his profession to pursue his ambition of building fish tanks. Kundizeza previously described winning the 2026 prize as an important recognition of years of writing. He could be stripped of the award if the allegations are proven.

Somalia Sanctions 10 Individuals Over Alleged Al-Shabaab Links

Somalia has added 10 individuals to its national financial sanctions list over alleged involvement in financing or supporting Al-Shabaab, the Al-Qaeda-linked militant group. The National Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism Committee said the move aims to disrupt the group's funding networks and strengthen enforcement of counter-terrorism measures. Under the directive, financial institutions, businesses and individuals operating in Somalia are prohibited from conducting transactions with those listed. They must also freeze any assets belonging to the designated individuals and report related transactions to the Financial Reporting Center. The committee did not disclose detailed evidence supporting the designations but warned that violations could result in legal action. Al-Shabaab has waged an insurgency against Somalia's federal government for more than 15 years.

Two Suspected Ebola Cases Test Negative in Kenya's Laikipia County

Health authorities in Kenya's Laikipia County have confirmed that two suspected Ebola cases in Nanyuki tested negative, urging residents to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information. Concern arose after a patient presented with symptoms resembling Ebola and was admitted to Nanyuki Teaching and Referral Hospital. Laboratory results ruled out the virus. The patient died while receiving treatment. A second suspected case reported by a private hospital also tested negative after samples were analysed at the National Public Health Laboratory. County Health Executive Albert Taiti said precautionary measures had been activated and healthcare workers had been sensitised on identifying and managing suspected infections. Authorities have urged residents to rely on official updates, report suspected cases promptly and continue observing recommended health precautions.

Malawi High Court Blocks Extradition of Prophet Bushiri to South Africa

Malawi's High Court in Lilongwe has issued a 175-page judgment explaining why it overturned the extradition order against Shepherd Bushiri and his wife, Mary. The court found serious procedural and legal flaws, including that the couple was not allowed to be heard before the order was granted in March 2025. The decision deals a major setback to South Africa's efforts to bring the couple back to face legal proceedings after they returned to Malawi in 2020.

headline: Trump says 'massive' oil, gas and mineral exploration to begin in Greenland
summary: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that a "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration was slated to begin in Greenland. The US, Denmark and Greenland last month signed a security agreement after Trump's repeated threats to seize control of the island.
body_text:
US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that a "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration was slated to begin in Greenland. The US, Denmark and Greenland last month signed a security agreement after Trump's repeated threats to seize control of the island.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 08:41Modified: 14/10/2026 - 09:17

US President Donald Trump said that a "massive" oil, gas and mineral exploration was preparing to begin in Greenland, without giving details of prospective American involvement and hailed the Arctic island's position for US and European security.

"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that "the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost... anywhere in the World."

Washington signed a security deal with the leaders of Greenland and Denmark after Trump threatened to take Copenhagen's strategically important Arctic Circle territory by force.

Read moreUS, Denmark and Greenland sign security deal to bolster Arctic security

Greenland, which lies on the shortest route for missiles between Russia and the United States, represents a highly strategic location for Trump's desired "Golden Dome" defense shield.

It also has untapped rare earth deposits and could be a critical player as melting polar ice opens up new shipping routes.

In August, media reports of a US oil company's preparatory operations in a remote region of eastern Greenland left locals and authorities on the island uneasy.

Trump on Wednesday hailed Greenland as "second to none" for US and European security, saying any future attack on America would have to pass through the Arctic island.

Greenland "from a Security Purpose in the Defense and Offense of both the United States of America, and Europe, is second to none," Trump said on Truth Social.

He added any future attacks on the US would have to come across Greenland, "where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived".

The agreement between the US, Denmark and Greenland is still subject to a second reading in Greenland's parliament before being put to a vote, with lawmakers ​expected to pass the legislation.

The deal expands the US ‌military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defense system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)
