headline: U.S.-Russia deal on diesel is 'very risky choice,' Italy PM Meloni says
summary: By Giuseppe FonteROME, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The deal between the United States and Russia over diesel supply is a "very risky choice" that runs counter to efforts to force Vladimir Putin to sit at a negotiating table with Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Wednesday.The United States and Russia agreed last week that Moscow would initially supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and ​global markets.
body_text:
ROME, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The deal between the United States and Russia over diesel supply is a "very risky choice" that runs counter to efforts to force Vladimir Putin to sit at a negotiating table with Ukraine, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Wednesday.

The United States and Russia agreed last week that Moscow would initially supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to U.S. and ​global markets.

"The outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear," Meloni told the Italian parliament ahead of an EU summit this week.

"It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions," she added.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy criticised the accord, calling it "an investment in a war that must be ended."

U.S. President Donald Trump said it would lower energy prices in the United States, a major political headache for his Republican Party ahead of pivotal midterm elections that determine control of Congress.

Meloni told parliament the 27 EU countries should appoint "an authoritative figure" to negotiate for Europe over the Russia-Ukraine war, without ruling out a formal mandate for the ​E3 Group comprising Germany, France and Great Britain.

"If France, Germany, and Great Britain believe they can do better on their own than we could all do together, and so far that is the choice they have made, then at least let them do so on behalf of everyone and with an official mandate," Meloni said.

In other remarks, she said the EU summit would discuss what she said had been an escalation in Russian hybrid attacks, referring to drone incursions, cyber attacks, sabotage and other covert operations aimed at weakening backing for Kyiv.

"We need to protect our critical infrastructure: energy grids, undersea cables, ports, airports, and the underwater domain, where Italy possesses outstanding expertise," she said.

(Editing by Gavin Jones)

body_text:
India's Bank of Baroda on Wednesday ​said ​it would protect ​its interests, a day after UAE-based ⁠businessman and founder of NMC Health BR Shetty filed ⁠a $15 billion case against the lender and ​25 other defendants at Bombay High Court.

Mr Shetty alleged ⁠the Bank of Baroda and several current and former employees helped facilitate a fraud that contributed to the collapse of the Middle East healthcare group, according to a ⁠court filing reviewed by Reuters.

The firm, then the Gulf's largest private healthcare provider, ​was ⁠placed under administration in 2020 ‌after months of financial mismanagement and disclosed debts of $6.6 billion, way above previous estimates ​of $2.1 billion.

Representatives for Mr Shetty did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In a stock exchange notification on Wednesday, the country's second-largest state lender said: “The bank has not been served with such a suit and cannot comment on the contents of pleadings, which are untested in court. If and when the bank is served, the bank will defend the suit firmly and take all steps necessary to protect its interests.”

The Bank of Baroda added that it was pursuing recovery and enforcement proceedings in India and the UAE against Mr Shetty for outstanding dues of 28 billion rupees ($294.5 million) and had obtained several decrees against him.

The lender will ​not bear any immediate liability until any order is ‌passed or until it ⁠is required to make a provision on ​account of potential damages, the lender said.

Bank of Baroda ​shares dropped ‌2.6 per cent on Tuesday after the legal action was reported.

The lawsuit, which centres on the bank's lending to ⁠NMC Health and affiliated entities in the UAE, comes three months after the lender agreed to pay $600 million to settle claims brought by administrators of NMC.

Mr Shetty alleged that bank officials enabled round-tripping transactions, ignored repeated anti-money laundering warnings and ​accepted documents bearing forged signatures.

He is seeking $5 billion in direct damages, $5 billion in consequential damages and an additional $5 billion for reputational harm, the filing showed.

headline: French politician warns Ukraine’s EU accession to amount to EU’s 'hara-kiri' — newspaper
summary: This will result in a loss of sovereignty and "absolutely huge economic losses" for France, Marine Le Pen, National Rally candidate in the 2027 French presidential election, said
body_text:
LONDON, October 14. /TASS/. Ukraine’s membership of the European Union would mount to the EU "committing hara-kiri," resulting in a loss of sovereignty and "absolutely huge economic losses" for France, Marine Le Pen, National Rally candidate in the 2027 French presidential election, said.

In an interview with the Financial Times, she expressed doubt that Paris would continue to support EU funding for Ukraine if she won the election. "We’ve already done 90 billion euros of loans, that’s 18 billion euros for France; 18 billion euros is really a lot," Le Pen said.

She added that if elected president, she would try to prevent the adoption of the EU’s new seven-year budget, which contains a Ukraine funding instrument worth up to 100 billion euros, by withholding half of France’s contribution.

France is due to hold the first round of its presidential election on April 18, 2027. If no candidate secures more than 50% of the vote, the two candidates who receive the most votes will face off in the second round on May 2. Under the French Constitution, incumbent President Emmanuel Macron cannot run in the 2027 election after completing his second term in office.

headline: Trump threatens renewed military action against Iran
summary: US President Donald Trump has warned of further action against Iran, saying Washington will decide its next move “very soon” as Tehran steps up attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.Mr Trump, speaking outside the White House late on Tuesday, described Iran as a “failed country” and said its economy was collapsing under severe inflation and financial pressure.“They have no economy … they have no money,” Mr Trump said. “We’ll make a decision on Iran very soon.”The US President later struck a more threatening tone at a campaign event in Alaska, warning of further action against Tehran.“Wait till you see what we do to Iran. We’re going to do a number … wait till you see what we do to Iran, because we’ve sort of had it,” he said. “The big thing is, they’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. That’s buried under thousands of tonnes of rock.”The remarks came after Reuters reported two Iranian officials said Tehran was using new ⁠tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. The officials declined to ​provide ⁠details but one ‌said Iran had started using different offensive tactics about ​10 days ago, leading to an increase in attacks on such ships.At least 12 vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has said. Six were struck on Sunday alone – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage.“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one was quoted as saying. A second official said Tehran would prevent Washington from lowering oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.Back-channel diplomacyThe US military rejected a claim by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that it is in control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying it does not possess an actual naval force.“US forces and their regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz. Just yesterday, US forces assisted their Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait,” said Central Command, which oversees US military operations across the Middle East.Officials in Tehran have rejected Washington’s latest response to its proposal to end the conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes across Iran on February 28.Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the US response as “insufficient” and warned of possible attacks on regional digital infrastructure if hostilities resumed.🚫 CLAIM: The navy commander for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed today that the Strait of Hormuz is under IRGC control and any approaching U.S. Navy warships would be "sunk."✅ FACT: IRGC's navy commander has no navy. American forces and regional partners… pic.twitter.com/n9dhNsyI8O— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) October 13, 2026Washington has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports and expanded sanctions, while seeking an agreement. The Pentagon has also directed US Central Command to complete preparations for possible major combat operations, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.Mr Trump said last week the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, citing progress in negotiations.Israel is also considering its options. Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran, Axios reported, as the Israeli leader prepared for a general election on October 27.Qatari mediators are awaiting Tehran’s response to a US counterproposal.

“They have no economy … they have no money,” Mr Trump said. “We’ll make a decision on Iran very soon.”

UK intelligence chief warns of 'major shift' after Iran attacks military bases

The US President later struck a more threatening tone at a campaign event in Alaska, warning of further action against Tehran.

“Wait till you see what we do to Iran. We’re going to do a number … wait till you see what we do to Iran, because we’ve sort of had it,” he said. “The big thing is, they’re not going to have a nuclear weapon. That’s buried under thousands of tonnes of rock.”

The remarks came after Reuters reported two Iranian officials said Tehran was using new ⁠tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. The officials declined to ​provide ⁠details but one ‌said Iran had started using different offensive tactics about ​10 days ago, leading to an increase in attacks on such ships.

At least 12 vessels have been attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz in the past week, the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency has said. Six were struck on Sunday alone – five tankers and a container ship. Five incidents occurred in the strait and one near Oman’s Sohar anchorage.

“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one was quoted as saying. A second official said Tehran would prevent Washington from lowering oil prices ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.

The US military rejected a claim by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps that it is in control of the Strait of Hormuz, saying it does not possess an actual naval force.

“US forces and their regional partners clearly control the Strait of Hormuz. Just yesterday, US forces assisted their Gulf partners in shipping more than 19 million barrels of crude oil through the strait,” said Central Command, which oversees US military operations across the Middle East.

Officials in Tehran have rejected Washington’s latest response to its proposal to end the conflict, which began with US and Israeli strikes across Iran on February 28.

Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, described the US response as “insufficient” and warned of possible attacks on regional digital infrastructure if hostilities resumed.

Washington has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports and expanded sanctions, while seeking an agreement. The Pentagon has also directed US Central Command to complete preparations for possible major combat operations, Axios reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.

Mr Trump said last week the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, citing progress in negotiations.

Israel is also considering its options. Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have discussed the possibility of renewed military operations against Iran, Axios reported, as the Israeli leader prepared for a general election on October 27.

Qatari mediators are awaiting Tehran’s response to a US counterproposal.

headline: Africa: Ai to Affect 60 Percent of Global Jobs - IMF
summary: [Daily Trust] The Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kristalina Georgieva, has warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could affect about 40 per cent of jobs globally, urging governments to prepare workers for changes in the labour market.
body_text:
The Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Kristalina Georgieva, has warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could affect about 40 per cent of jobs globally, urging governments to prepare workers for changes in the labour market.

Georgieva spoke during a panel session titled "Small Scale AI: More and Better Jobs" at the ongoing 2026 IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.

Describing AI as a "slow-moving tsunami" for the labour market, she said the technology could transform jobs, downgrade some roles or eliminate others.

According to her, IMF estimates indicate that AI could affect about 60 per cent of jobs in advanced economies, compared with 23 per cent in low-income countries. She explained that the lower exposure in poorer countries reflected slower AI adoption rather than greater protection from its effects.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Georgieva said AI was already stimulating investment and economic activity through the construction of data centres and the development of AI models, with the United States, China and India emerging as major producers of the technology.

She noted that investments in AI infrastructure were helping sustain global economic growth at about three per cent despite disruptions caused by energy supply shocks.

However, she said future benefits would depend largely on how effectively countries adopted the technology, stressing the need for reliable electricity, digital infrastructure, appropriate skills and effective government safeguards.

The IMF chief cited estimates showing that AI could increase growth in advanced Asian economies by between 0.5 and one percentage point, while emerging Asian economies could record additional growth of between 0.2 and 0.8 percentage points.

On employment, Georgieva said an IMF study in the United States found that about 10 per cent of jobs already required advanced AI skills, with such positions generally attracting higher wages.

She added that routine and repetitive jobs were declining, while employment was increasing in lower-paying areas, including data centre construction and related services.

Although the study found a positive net employment impact in the areas examined, she expressed concern that much of the employment growth was concentrated in lower-paying jobs.

Georgieva identified young people entering the labour market as particularly vulnerable, warning that the decline of routine entry-level positions could limit opportunities for graduates and other young workers to gain experience and advance their careers.

According to her, greater reliance on capital and reduced dependence on human labour could affect government revenue and limit public resources available to support workers through the transition.

Georgieva expressed hope that AI would take over undesirable tasks, allowing people to benefit from higher productivity, improved living standards and meaningful social participation.

"Get AI to do all the stuff we don't want to do, and let us enjoy the things we love to do," she said, advocating a future that combines productivity gains with human dignity.

Meanwhile, Nigeria's delegation to the 2026 IMF Annual Meetings is being led by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele.

The meetings are expected to focus on building a balanced and resilient global economy capable of withstanding economic shocks and promoting sustainable development.

body_text:
The UAE has ordered a recall of a batch of face masks because of concerns about possible contamination of the material used in its manufacture.

The Emirates Drug Establishment issued the recall for Nin 160 FMB-NML Facemask C G blue, batch number 20251015. It is described as blue in colour and three-ply in structure.

The Dubai Health Authority also issued a circular on Monday instructing healthcare centres to comply with the recall.

How often should you be washing your reusable cloth face mask?

Officials said Ningbo ETDZ Holdings Ltd in China manufactured the masks, and Globemed Care LLC distributed them in the UAE.

The drug regulator said the recall was ordered after a quality complaint. Inspections identified foreign material or contamination in units from the affected batch.

Healthcare professionals, hospitals and clinics and pharmacies must immediately stop selling, supplying, distributing or using the affected batch.

They must identify and quarantine all available stock, then arrange for its return to the local supplier or distributor, Globemed Care LLC. They must also maintain records of quantities identified, quarantined, and returned.

Residents who purchased the affected product should stop using any packs with batch number 20251015 and return them to the point of purchase or supplier.

Healthcare providers must report any product quality complaints or adverse incidents related to the masks through EDE-approved reporting channels.

Globemed Care LLC has also been ordered to retrieve all distributed quantities from the UAE market.

It must also provide the regulator with details of quantities imported, distributed, returned, and remaining in stock, as well as a complete UAE distribution list.

The regulator also urged people to report any quality concerns or adverse incidents involving the product directly to the authority.

headline: Hyundai Motor expands production capacity in India
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Hyundai Motor Co., South Korea's largest carmaker, sa...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Hyundai Motor Co., South Korea's largest carmaker, said Wednesday it has completed a new plant in India, a key market in its global expansion strategy.

The Pune plant began operations Tuesday with an annual production capacity of 170,000 vehicles, which is scheduled to increase to 320,000 by 2030, the company said in a press release.

With the addition of the new facility, Hyundai now operates three production plants in India -- two in Chennai and one in Pune. The three plants have a combined annual production capacity of nearly 1 million vehicles.

"Over the past 30 years, India has been a key pillar of Hyundai Motor's global growth, and the completion of the new Pune plant will mark a new chapter for the company in India," the group's Executive Chair Euisun Chung said in the release.

The first model to be produced at the Pune plant will be the Venue compact sport utility vehicle (SUV), for sale in India and export to about 30 countries, the company said.

Over the years, Hyundai has introduced a range of models in India, including the i10 and i20 hatchbacks, the Verna subcompact sedan, the Creta SUV, the all-electric Creta EV, the Exter SUV and the Alcazar SUV.

Last year, the company sold 398,937 SUVs in India, accounting for about 70 percent of its total sales in the country.

Hyundai acquired the plant from General Motors Co. in 2023 after its operations had been suspended for years amid the COVID-19 pandemic. The company invested 1 trillion won (US$747 million) to convert the facility into its third production plant in India.

headline: IN BRIEF: Russia hits Ukraine's communication, energy infrastructure in massive strike
summary: According to the Russian Defense Ministry, the strike hit communication and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev, the Kiev Region and the Kharkov Region used to support the military-industrial complex and the armed forces of Ukraine
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Overnight, Russian forces launched a massive strike hitting communication and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev and the Kiev and Kharkov Regions that support Ukraine's military-industrial complex, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.

TASS has compiled the key details on the targets hit.

- Overnight, the Russian Armed Forces launched a massive strike using ground-based precision weapons and long-range attack drones against targets in Ukraine, the Defense Ministry reported.

- According to the ministry, the strike hit communication and energy infrastructure facilities in Kiev and the Kiev and Kharkov Regions used to support the military-industrial complex and the armed forces of Ukraine.

- The ministry later specified that the ATM Ukrsibbank data center in Kiev was hit. The facility handled Internet traffic exchange for gathering intelligence about the Russian Armed Forces.

- Russian forces also struck the Darnitskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-4), powering military-industrial complex facilities in Kiev.

- In addition, the Kievskaya combined heat and power plant (CHP-5) was hit; it supplies electricity to military facilities and military-industrial enterprises in Kiev and the Kiev Region.

- The Russian Armed Forces also struck the Kiev CHP-6 plant, powering military logistics facilities and storage sites for weaponry and military hardware in the northeastern part of the Kiev Region.

- In addition, the Tripolskaya thermal power plant, powering military-industrial facilities in Kiev and it's environs, was struck.

- Russian forces also struck the Kievskaya electrical substation, providing for the transmission and distribution of electricity from western Ukrainian regions to Ukraine’s military facilities in the Kiev Region.

- Furthermore, the Kharkov CHP-5 combined heat and power plant, powering military-industrial facilities in Kharkov and the western part of the Kharkov Region, was struck.

- The Russian Armed Forces also struck the Zmiyevskaya thermal power plant, supplying electricity to Ukrainian military facilities in the southeastern part of the Kharkov Region.

- Energy facilities in Kiev sustained damage following explosions, city mayor Vitali Klitschko reported.

- Strikes were recorded on "several energy facilities in the capital" of Ukraine, he wrote on his Telegram channel.

- He provided no further details.

- Public electric transport services were suspended in two districts of Kiev, the municipal enterprise Kievpastrans reported.

- Power outages began in Kiev due to widespread damage to energy facilities, Klitschko later announced.

- Specifically, he described the strikes on the city's energy infrastructure as massive.

- Emergency power outages began in five of Kiev's ten districts following the explosions and damage to energy facilities, the Ukrainian energy holding company DTEK reported.

- It specified that the Darnitsky, Dneprovsky, Pechersky, and Solomensky districts, as well as part of the Goloseyevsky district, were affected.

- All of Kiev's combined heat and power (CHP) plants, as well as the Kiev Region’s largest energy facility--the Tripolskaya Thermal Power Plant--sustained damage from explosions, the Strana news outlet reported.

- According to the report, strikes on all of the Ukrainian capital's CHP plants were recorded overnight and on Wednesday morning.

- In the region, the Tripolskaya Thermal Power Plant was damaged, along with the Kievskaya and Novokievskaya substations, which have capacities of 750 kilovolts (kV) and 330 kV, respectively.

- The outlet accompanied its report with photos showing massive fires at the sites of the explosions.

- The Epicentr company's last remaining logistics center was destroyed by the explosions, the Ukrainian outlet Insider reported.

- According to the report, the facility was located in the city of Khmelnitsky in western Ukraine.

- The report includes photos and video of the fire at the logistics facility.

- Water supply issues may arise in Kiev's Pechersky district due to a power outage at the city's water pumping station, the utility company Kievvodokanal reported.

- Ukrainian energy facilities sustained significant damage from the explosions, leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity, Vladimir Zelensky stated.

headline: Africa: 'Need for UN Has Never Been Greater,' UN Chief Says, Proposing Slimmer $3.3 Billion Budget for 2027
summary: [UN News] Amid climate disruption, an AI revolution, war and growing hunger, "the need for the United Nations has never been greater," Secretary-General António Guterres said on Tuesday, presenting a $3.3 billion programme budget proposal for next year - a cut of $40.8 million.
body_text:
Amid climate disruption, an AI revolution, war and growing hunger, "the need for the United Nations has never been greater," Secretary-General António Guterres said on Tuesday, presenting a $3.3 billion programme budget proposal for next year - a cut of $40.8 million.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

"The challenges before us are profound," Mr. Guterres told the General Assembly's Fifth Committee, comprising all 193 UN Member States that handle administrative and budgetary matters at UN Headquarters in New York.

"Geopolitical divisions continue to deepen, conflicts persist across regions and humanitarian needs are soaring, international law is trampled, climate disruption is hitting every continent and artificial intelligence is reshaping economies and societies," said the Secretary-General.

Moreover, the planet's collective Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), aimed at leaving no one behind, "are slipping further from reach", Mr. Guterres said.

"And yet, in this era of uncertainty and fragmentation, the need for the United Nations has never been greater," he declared.

Read the full statement here.

UN80 reforms: From proposal to practice

Reminding the committee that more than a year has passed since the UN80 Initiative was launched, the UN chief said "with your support, we set in motion far-reaching changes guided by a clear objective: to make the Secretariat more efficient, more effective, and better equipped to serve in a rapidly changing world."

Taking stock of UN80 achievements, he said the Secretariat had already "moved from proposals to implementation":

Through a voluntary early separation programme and reassignments, he said the impact on staff was "much smaller than what could be imagined" because planning began a year and a half in advance in the anticipated shortfalls.

headline: OpenAI says Saudi citizen arrested over hidden recording device in office
summary: An OpenAI employee has been arrested and charged with using a hidden recording device in a San Francisco office, according to the artificial intelligence company and the US Justice Department.Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen, was arrested on October 9, more than a week after staff at OpenAI discovered an audio recording device in the back of a television in an executive conference room, the Justice Department said on Tuesday. Mr Alfozan, who is accused of planting the device, is currently in custody having appeared in court in San Francisco on Tuesday.Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said.The incident is poised to heighten concerns about security at top technology companies at a moment when nations are competing aggressively to develop more powerful AI systems.“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” the company posted on social platform X on Tuesday.OpenAI said one of its security teams discovered the device on September 30 during a sweep of a company conference room. According to details and images released by the Justice Department, the device was plugged into a USB port in the back of a TV in the room and covered with toilet paper to disguise it.An image released by the Justice Department showed a small, black device with the text “Seeed Studio” on it. The agency said OpenAI determined it was planted around September 28.OpenAI said it used its AI models to understand more about the device and identify who placed it.Mr Alfozan did not have approval to access the conference room, which typically hosted meetings involving “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information”, according to the complaint, which references an unnamed AI company with offices in San Francisco.The company said it uncovered evidence that Mr Alfozan had planned to use other recording devices to secretly record meetings in other parts of the office. Early this month, according to the Justice Department, OpenAI security employees found a similar recording device in a bag he had left inside one of its corporate buildings.According to a LinkedIn profile connected to Mr Alfozan, he worked as an engineering lead at OpenAI on AI agent software. The profile says he has worked part-time as a partner at Saudi Arabia-based venture capital firm Raed Ventures since 2025, and previously as a senior systems engineer at Meta Platforms. Mr Alfozan attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 2011 to 2016 where he studied computer science and engineering, and the University of California, Berkeley, from 2023 to 2025 to study for a master’s degree in data science, the profile states.OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI and that the investigation is continuing.According to the FBI’s criminal complaint, the device was a Seeed Xiao ESP32-S3 Sense, which was described as a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage”. A device by that name and description appeared to be for sale for $14 from the website seeedstudio.com as of Tuesday.Lennart Koopmann, founder of cyber security firm Nzyme, said the device Mr Alfozan allegedly used appears to be built on “a hobbyist circuit board”, and noted features such as the microphone, and the ability to save recordings to a memory card and send audio wirelessly over short distances via Wi-Fi.“That makes it cheap and easy to hide, and catching one takes either equipment that watches the airwaves for unfamiliar devices or, if its wireless is switched off, someone physically searching the rooms,” Mr Koopmann said.Mr Alfozan is scheduled to appear before Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse in federal court in San Francisco on October 19.

Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said.

The incident is poised to heighten concerns about security at top technology companies at a moment when nations are competing aggressively to develop more powerful AI systems.

“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” the company posted on social platform X on Tuesday.

OpenAI said one of its security teams discovered the device on September 30 during a sweep of a company conference room. According to details and images released by the Justice Department, the device was plugged into a USB port in the back of a TV in the room and covered with toilet paper to disguise it.

An image released by the Justice Department showed a small, black device with the text “Seeed Studio” on it. The agency said OpenAI determined it was planted around September 28.

OpenAI said it used its AI models to understand more about the device and identify who placed it.

Mr Alfozan did not have approval to access the conference room, which typically hosted meetings involving “highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information”, according to the complaint, which references an unnamed AI company with offices in San Francisco.

The company said it uncovered evidence that Mr Alfozan had planned to use other recording devices to secretly record meetings in other parts of the office. Early this month, according to the Justice Department, OpenAI security employees found a similar recording device in a bag he had left inside one of its corporate buildings.

According to a LinkedIn profile connected to Mr Alfozan, he worked as an engineering lead at OpenAI on AI agent software. The profile says he has worked part-time as a partner at Saudi Arabia-based venture capital firm Raed Ventures since 2025, and previously as a senior systems engineer at Meta Platforms.

Mr Alfozan attended the Massachusetts Institute of Technology from 2011 to 2016 where he studied computer science and engineering, and the University of California, Berkeley, from 2023 to 2025 to study for a master’s degree in data science, the profile states.

OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI and that the investigation is continuing.

According to the FBI’s criminal complaint, the device was a Seeed Xiao ESP32-S3 Sense, which was described as a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and microSD storage”. A device by that name and description appeared to be for sale for $14 from the website seeedstudio.com as of Tuesday.

Lennart Koopmann, founder of cyber security firm Nzyme, said the device Mr Alfozan allegedly used appears to be built on “a hobbyist circuit board”, and noted features such as the microphone, and the ability to save recordings to a memory card and send audio wirelessly over short distances via Wi-Fi.

“That makes it cheap and easy to hide, and catching one takes either equipment that watches the airwaves for unfamiliar devices or, if its wireless is switched off, someone physically searching the rooms,” Mr Koopmann said.

Mr Alfozan is scheduled to appear before Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse in federal court in San Francisco on October 19.

headline: Trump's ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, resigns after allegations of improper conduct
summary: The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct.(Image credit: Jacquelyn Martin)
body_text:
FILE - Kimberly Guilfoyle speaks as President Donald Trump listens at a reception celebrating Greek Independence Day in the East Room of the White House, March 24, 2025, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption

WASHINGTON — The White House publicly asked for U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle's resignation on Tuesday as she faced mounting accusations of improper conduct, and she announced within two hours that she was quitting, ending days of talk and speculation about her professional fate. Guilfoyle insisted that she would "vigorously defend" herself.

President Donald Trump's administration had said earlier Tuesday it had asked Guilfoyle to leave her post after she faced severe criticism over allegations she engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens.

That revelation came in response to a question to freshly minted White House press secretary Katie Zacharia at her first media briefing Tuesday morning. Zacharia said Guilfoyle "has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well."

"She went to Greece. She was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said just after Guilfoyle's resignation, which was posted on her X account. He said he had not spoken to her but "she will not be there."

Guilfoyle's departure comes after its possibility was previewed to The Associated Press over the weekend and Trump registered his unhappiness on Monday at reports about her alleged conduct. Those comments came a day after the AP, citing a senior U.S. official, reported that Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle's reported conduct.

In a series of stories dating to late last month, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the Republican administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill.

Guilfoyle addressed the accusations directly in her resignation post on X, saying, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity."

"I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional," she said. "I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service."

In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers denied that she had done anything wrong and claimed that the money she was seeking from a Trump donor was payment for services — public appearances and speaking engagements that predate her ambassadorial nomination — that had not been paid.

The lawyers, David Schwartz and Jesse Binnall, also rejected allegations of impropriety related to Guilfoyle's travel on private planes, saying that before every such trip she "sought, obtained and followed State Department guidance and followed the Department's travel regulations."

They did not immediately return calls Tuesday.

After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. Last week, Rubio said: "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."

But after another report appeared later, Rubio — speaking Thursday before leaving Athens — berated journalists for asking about the allegations. He said that he didn't know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm them.

"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel. It's not the gospel for me. That's not the way we do things," Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on.

A second U.S. official, who also spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department's inspector general was looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied.

The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers, and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation.

There was no immediate response to Zacharia's statement from the Greek government or Cabinet members.

Ahead of Tuesday's announcement, Greek opposition parties had called on the Foreign Ministry to summon Guilfoyle to respond to the allegations made against her. "This, most importantly, is an issue of national dignity," Sia Anagnostopoulou, a former deputy foreign minister, said in parliament Friday. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis responded that Guilfoyle had been treated "the same way as every other ambassador" and argued that an official summons had not been necessary.

Hours earlier, Guilfoyle had posted photos of her meeting this week with the Spanish ambassador to Athens as well as birthday wishes for Lara Trump, the president's daughter-in-law, accompanied by Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night," from the 2023 soundtrack of the movie "Barbie."

Greece has taken on an increasingly important and influential role because of its geographic location in Southeastern Europe and the Eastern Mediterranean, particularly on energy issues as the war with Iran has spiked global oil prices. Besides the vast number of Greek-registered oil tankers that regularly ply the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, Greece is well positioned to be a pipeline conduit for liquefied natural gas imports into the Balkans and beyond.

As the U.S. ambassador to Greece, Guilfoyle had put an emphasis on energy issues, although her close association with executives in that sector was part of what got her into trouble.

The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle.

Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the United States could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.

While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did.

The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives.

Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. Embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece.

Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was married to Democrat Gavin Newsom when he was San Francisco's mayor, before he became California's governor. She later was engaged to Trump's son Donald Trump Jr.

headline: IMF calls for US to cut deficits amid bond woes, China to shift away from exports
summary: By David LawderBANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The United States cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt without tax or spending adjustments, while China must pivot from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The United States cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt without tax or spending adjustments, while China must pivot from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.

Georgieva admonished the world's two largest economies to make painful policy changes to reduce growing fiscal and trade imbalances, as her fiscal affairs chief said inflation, high debt levels and rising yields had heightened the urgency for fiscal consolidation around the globe.

Speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva singled out advanced economies, namely the US and European countries, as the "worst offenders" on excessive debts, with higher benchmark yields spilling over to low-income countries that have already been forced by financial markets to rein in debts.

Asked at a press conference whether the US needs tighter fiscal policy,Georgieva said US Treasury Secretary ScottBessent recognizes that US deficit and debt levels are too high and need to be made more sustainable.

"The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to help reduce debt, Georgieva said.

"At the Fund, we believe that growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments. So, some (fiscal) measures would be necessary."

The call for more action to reduce debt was echoed in the IMF's Fiscal Monitor report on Wednesday, which warned that delays in an era of higher borrowing costs would only make the job harder in coming years.

While that message is a perennial one from the IMF, Rodrigo Valdes, the head of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs department, said the surge in bond yields had left governments with little fiscal room to manoeuvre.

"We dialled up the urgency of our message," he added.

Bessent is not attending the annual meetings in Bangkok, despite this year's US presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, instead favouring domestic engagements as the US midterm election campaign heats up.

He has acted as a chief spokesman for President Donald Trump's economic policies, particularly touting the deep tax cuts passed last year by Republicans now trying to maintain control of the US Congress.

G20 finance ministers are due to meet on the sidelines of the Bangkok meetings on Thursday. The US has used its G20 presidency to try to rally allies to take stronger action to counter China's "non-market" economic policies that have led to excess industrial capacity and a flood of global exports.

Asked about imbalances emanating from China, on a day when data showed it was on track to post a record trade surplus,Georgieva repeated longstanding advice to Beijing: "For surplus countries, what they need to do is increase domestic consumption. That clearly applies to China's growth model. Shift from export more toward domestic consumption."

Deficit countries need to save more and spend less, while Europe needs to invest more in competitiveness, she said.

"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more, and Europe has to invest more," Georgieva added.

CALL FOR AID TO POOR COUNTRIES

This week's meetings have been dominated by worries about growing debt and rising bond yields and risks from the artificial intelligence boom.

Regarding the growing divergence between advanced countries benefiting from AI investment and those bypassed by it, highlighted in Tuesday's IMFeconomic forecasts, Georgieva also urged IMF member countries to fully fund IMF facilities for low-income and vulnerable countries.

These include the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which provides low- and zero-interest loans to low-income countries, and the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust, a fund that provides grants for debt-service relief and cancellation to the poorest and most vulnerable member countries, she said.

These countries, too, were being squeezed by higher bond yields, with average debt service costs that have increased to 14% of revenue from 6% a decade ago, even as overall debt burdens have eased, she said.

"The risk of divergence is most dangerous for those that are already further behind," Georgieva added.

(Reporting by David Lawder and Andrea Shalal; Editing by John Mair and Shri Navaratnam)

headline: Yemen hospitals overwhelmed by surge in war casualties, Red Cross warns
summary: GENEVA, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as intensified fighting along multiple front lines strains its already fragile health system, the Red Cross said on Wednesday.Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast were seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the humanitarian agency.
body_text:
GENEVA, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as intensified fighting along multiple front lines strains its already fragile health system, the Red Cross said on Wednesday.

Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast were seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the humanitarian agency.

More ⁠than 200,000 people have ⁠been displaced from their homes since fighting ​in the country began in recent weeks, sparked by renewed ⁠fighting between ⁠the Iran-backedHouthi groupand Saudi-backed governmentforces in Yemen, according to‌the United Nations' International ‌Organization for Migration.

"Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anesthesia, oxygen and medicines.

Yemen's health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, theICRC warned.

(Reporting by Olivia Le PoidevinEditing by Linda Pasquini)

headline: Palestinian faction leaders gather in Cairo to renew bid for long-elusive reconciliation
summary: Leaders of Palestinian factions were gathering in Egypt on Wednesday for a renewed bid for reconciliation, after legislative elections scheduled for next month were postponed by President Mahmoud Abbas, sources told The National. They said the talks were scheduled to begin Thursday and will continue until the end of the month, but not necessarily at leadership level. The gathering in Egypt represents eight factions, including Hamas, Islamic Jihad, a pro-reform faction of Fatah, and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. The talks will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine.Egypt has been trying to reconcile Palestinian factions for years, without success. Officials from its spy agency have led efforts, taking responsibility for key foreign policy files traditionally handled by the Foreign Ministry.The sources said Khalil Al Hayya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads the pro-reform faction within Fatah, were among those taking part in the talks. Also participating are Jebril Rajoub, a top official of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and Mohammed Ashtiyah, a former Palestinian prime minister and top Fatah official. Among the main topics to be discussed are how to narrow ideological gaps between their factions, the inclusion of Hamas and Islamic Jihad in the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and charting a political role for armed groups like Hamas and Islamic Jihad.“These are preliminary contacts that will precede negotiations that bring together everyone in the same room, which is expected to happen towards the end of the month,” said one source.The talks in Egypt will take place at a time when prospects for the Palestinian cause are looking dimmer than at any time perhaps since the mass displacement of Palestinians around the time of Israel's creation in 1948. A year since a US-sponsored Gaza ceasefire was announced to pause two years of fighting, the strip lies in ruins, Israel's military controls more than 60 per cent of the enclave and shows no intention of withdrawing as provided by American President Donald Trump's peace plan.Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank are facing frequent violent attacks on their homes and farmland in what increasingly looks like a concerted, state-backed campaign to displace them.Mr Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority, announced last weekend that the legislative vote would be postponed until next September next, when the presidential election is also due to take place. Sources from various factions have told The National the delay was primarily intended to address what has been described as “Palestinian divisions” before the elections take place. The executive committee of the Palestine Liberation Organisation has approved the postponement. It said the delay was due to the lack of security in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the Palestinian Authority. Mr Abbas, 90, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term. The deeply unpopular president, according to recent polls, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption. An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down.Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”. However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives.“The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it explained in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Mr Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.” The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.

The talks will be the latest in a long-running series of attempts to narrow the gap between Palestinian factions divided over policies, ideology and the way forward for Palestine.

The sources said Khalil Al Hayya, the political leader of Hamas, and Mohammed Dahlan, who leads the pro-reform faction within Fatah, were among those taking part in the talks. Also participating are Jebril Rajoub, a top official of the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and Mohammed Ashtiyah, a former Palestinian prime minister and top Fatah official.

Among the main topics to be discussed are how to narrow ideological gaps between their factions, the inclusion of Hamas and Islamic Jihad in the Palestine Liberation Organisation, and charting a political role for armed groups like Hamas and Islamic Jihad.

The last election for the Palestinian Legislative Council, or parliament, was held in 2006 and won by Hamas, triggering a split between the group and Fatah, the dominant faction in the Palestinian Authority. Mr Abbas, 90, who is also Fatah's leader, has remained in office 17 years beyond the end of his original term.

The deeply unpopular president, according to recent polls, has been ruling by decree amid growing discontent over his policies and reports of widespread corruption. An opinion poll run by the Palestinian Centre for Policy and Survey Research in August found 79 per cent of the 1,270 people surveyed wanted him to step down.

Hamas described the postponement as a “step in the right direction,” saying political and security conditions were not suitable for holding a free election. The delay, its statement said, “must lead to a serious, fruitful and comprehensive national dialogue”.

However, Mr Dahlan's pro-reform faction responded to Mr Abbas's decision in markedly different terms. It said the postponement was an “attack on democracy” and a threat to younger generations of Palestinians, who have been deprived of their right to choose their representatives.

“The absence of elections deepens the crisis of legitimacy and weakens the Palestinian domestic front,” it explained in a statement on Saturday. “The leadership [Mr Abbas] is enshrining fiscal, political and administrative corruption, and pushes institutions away from the national track.”

The group also called for broad dialogue between Palestinian factions to establish a “popular front” capable of exerting pressure.

body_text:
The Saudi Pro League clash between Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr and Asian champions Al Ahli has been postponed.

The fixture, which was due to be played on Thursday, is one of three SPL games that have been rearranged.

The league cited “logistical considerations” related to rest period for players, rather than the security situation in Riyadh.

Ronaldo's 981st goal helps Al Nassr win as Al Ain go top of AFC Champions League

Alerts were sounded in the Saudi capital on Wednesday, as fighting intensified between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

An SPL fixture in Abha that was due to be played on Sunday had been postponed, as a direct consequence of the situation.

It was the day after 12 people died and more that 300 were wounded in an attack on the main international airport in Riyadh. Abha is around 200 kms from the Yemen border.

Matches in Riyadh did go ahead. Each of Nassr, who were playing at home, and Ahli were in Asian Champions League action on Monday night.

While Ahli’s fixture in Dubai against Al Wasl went ahead as planned, Nassr’s game in Riyadh was delayed for an hour because of an alert.

In postponing three matches planned for this week, though, the league said the reasons were related to “the mandatory minimum rest period between matches”.

The three matches all involve sides who were involved in the Champions League. That is Al Hilal and Nassr, who are based in Riyadh, and the Jeddah teams Ahli and Al Ittihad.

“The [SPL] has rescheduled three Roshn Saudi League Matchweek 9 fixtures for logistical considerations, taking into account the mandatory minimum rest period between matches” the league wrote in a statement.

“Two fixtures; Al Riyadh against Al Hilal and Al Ittihad against Al Shabab will now be played on Saturday, December 19, 2026, while Al Ahli versus Al Nassr will be played on Saturday, March 6, 2027.

“The remaining games in Matchweek 9 will be played according to the previously announced schedule with no changes.

“In making the decision, the SPL took into consideration the mandatory minimum rest period between matches in addition to organisational and operational requirements for the matches.

“The changes are made in accordance with approved regulatory procedures for managing the competition's schedule, factoring in clubs' various logistical considerations for matches.”

The Ahli-Nassr clash, in particular, was keenly anticipated. It was to be the first meeting between the sides since their acrimonious clash at Al Awwal Park last season.

There, Nassr refused to give a guard of honour to their visitors, just days after Ahli had secured a second successive AFC Champions League title.

Tempers boiled over in the game, with Ronaldo pointing out he has won five (Uefa) Champions League titles to goading Ahli fans.

Merih Demiral, the Ahli centre back, also brought along his Champions League winner’s medal, and used it to taunt Nassr with in the melee which followed the game.

headline: IMF chief urges urgent fiscal action as global economic resilience reaches limits
summary: Global growth forecast at 3.1% in 2026 as rising debt costs, energy pressures strain economies, Kristalina Georgieva says
body_text:
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Wednesday urged governments to urgently strengthen public finances, warning that the global economy’s resilience to repeated shocks is reaching its limits.

Speaking at a press briefing during the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva said energy and fiscal buffers were being depleted, while persistent inflation and rising interest rates were adding to debt-servicing pressures.

Global growth is projected at about 3.1% in 2026, unchanged from April’s forecast but below last year’s 3.4%, she said.

The outlook reflects opposing forces, with the Middle East war disrupting energy supplies while demand linked to artificial intelligence supports economic activity.

Economies integrated into AI supply chains, including Thailand, Malaysia, South Korea and Singapore, were generally performing better, along with energy exporters unaffected by wars.

Low-income countries and fragile states, particularly energy importers excluded from the technology boom, faced the greatest pressures.

Georgieva said government bond yields in advanced economies had risen to multidecade highs, reflecting inflation, investment demand, expectations of stronger AI-driven growth and fiscal weaknesses.

Higher benchmark yields were increasing borrowing costs for emerging markets even where their risk premiums remained stable, she said, warning that elevated financing costs were likely to persist.

Debt-servicing costs in low-income countries had increased from 6% of government revenues a decade ago to 14%, she added.

Georgieva urged governments to raise revenues, rationalize spending and improve public financial management. Assistance to offset rising food and energy costs should be temporary and targeted at vulnerable people while preserving price signals.

Central banks should remain focused on price stability, with the strongest case for tightening in economies where inflation exceeds targets and activity remains robust.

On global imbalances, she called on China to boost domestic consumption, the US to increase savings and reduce deficits, and Europe to strengthen investment.

US economic growth alone would not deliver the required fiscal adjustment quickly enough, making additional measures necessary, she said.

Georgieva also warned that disappointing near-term AI returns could trigger a disorderly market correction, while AI-enabled cyberattacks posed risks to financial stability.

headline: S. Korean finance minister departs for Bangkok to attend IMF, G20 ministerial meetings
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il departed for Bangkok...
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il departed for Bangkok on Wednesday to take part in the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group, along with a G20 finance ministerial gathering, his office said.

Lee left Incheon International Airport and plans to participate in various multilateral meetings with major countries this week to discuss the latest global economic issues, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy.

The visit marks Lee's first participation in such gatherings as finance minister since taking office last month.

During the visit, Lee is set to participate in the G20 Finance Ministers and Central Bank Governors Meeting on Thursday, where participants will discuss key issues ahead of the G20 summit slated for December.

The policymaker will also attend a meeting of Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers at their invitation and actively contribute to discussions on the global economy, reflecting South Korea's growing international standing, the ministry said.

The South Korean official will seek to bolster Seoul's ties with the financial authorities of the seven major nations, it added.

On Saturday, Lee will participate in an International Monetary and Financial Committee (IMFC) meeting, where member countries are expected to discuss ways to address key economic issues.

On the sidelines of the events, Lee plans to hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of various international organizations, including the IMF, the Asian Development Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the Central American Bank for Economic Integration.

The finance minister will also brief major credit rating agencies, including Moody's, Fitch and S&P Global Ratings, on South Korea's economy, his office said.

The ministry added Lee is expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from Japan, Britain, Germany, Australia and Saudi Arabia.

Lee, meanwhile, held his first video conference overnight with U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who was set to skip the Bangkok event.

Bessent congratulated Lee on his appointment and stressed the importance of bilateral cooperation in economic and financial affairs, according to the finance ministry.

body_text:
Over the past few years, global politics have been reshaped by sudden shifts in power. The Taliban retook control in Afghanistan in August 2021 after US-led forces withdrew, and rebel forces in Syria toppled the Assad regime in December 2024.

Those shifts are being reflected in diplomatic networks, and our latest chart of the week shows this clearly. Some cities are gaining missions as countries deepen or restore ties. Others have lost posts amid conflicts, political upheaval or isolation.

The number of missions a country sends or hosts offers a glimpse of its diplomatic reach and priorities. But a reopening does not, on its own, prove that relations have fundamentally changed — or that the change will last.

“Reopening an embassy is a political signal, but it does not necessarily indicate a lasting shift,” says Jasmine El Gamal, founder and CEO of Averos Strategies, a think tank focused on diplomacy and geopolitics. “A reopening is therefore better understood as a sign of renewed engagement than a guarantee of lasting alignment.”

The reverse can also happen: a mission may remain open, close or move even after the political circumstances that prompted the decision have changed. As El Gamal says, such decisions “can outlast the administrations that made them even when the original intent does not necessarily apply”.

Syria has seen one of the biggest changes. After the fall of the Assad regime, several countries reopened embassies in Damascus that had been closed for years. Turkey and Qatar resumed operations in December 2024, followed by Spain in January 2025 and Germany in March 2025. Damascus recorded 12 openings between December 2024 and December 2025.

Embassies returned to Pyongyang after pandemic-era closures. From 2024 onwards, Reuters reported that many European countries began sending delegations and missions back to North Korea. Brazil, Sweden, Poland, India and Nigeria were among the countries to resume operations, while Ukraine opened a series of new missions in African cities in 2024, including Kinshasa, Abidjan, Maputo and Kigali.

Closures have been concentrated in a smaller number of cities. Kabul lost 19 diplomatic posts between 2017 and 2025, many after the Taliban returned to power in 2021. Governments evacuated staff and suspended operations amid the security crisis following the takeover, and others left due to uncertainty over how to engage with the new authorities' policies. The Taliban’s restrictions on women and girls have since further complicated diplomatic relations.

Khartoum had the second-largest loss, with 14 diplomatic posts closing in the eight years to 2025. Most closures followed the outbreak of Sudan's civil war in April 2023, with governments evacuating staff and suspending operations amid security fears.

Despite the closures, the figures suggest an expanding diplomatic footprint across more regions overall. The Middle East and Africa have seen the biggest net gains, as many Western countries shift their attention toward resoutowardsch, people-power countries.

Sardar Azmoun struck both goals as Shabab Al Ahli picked up a superb away win at Al Ittihad in the AFC Champions League on Tuesday night.

The victory took the UAE club to a perfect six points from six, while Saudi Pro League Al Ittihad have just a single point after opening their campaign with a draw against Al Shamal SC of Qatar last month.

Backed by a full house in Jeddah, the home side started positively with Ahmed Al Julaydan forcing Matheus Donelli into a save from a tight angle in the sixth minute.

Ronaldo's 981st goal helps Al Nassr win as Al Ain go top of AFC Champions League

Shabab Al Ahli, however, struck in the next phase of play when Guilherme Bala powered down the left before teeing up the unmarked Azmoun to slot home.

Al Ittihad looked for an immediate response, with Steven Bergwijn testing Donelli from distance in the 13th minute, but the visitors doubled their advantage three minutes later.

Reza Ghandipour, who had only just replaced the injured Bala, released Azmoun with a through ball and the forward outpaced his markers before converting from a tight angle.

“We conceded two goals because of easy mistakes, which made the task difficult afterwards,” said Al Ittihad coach Jens Wissing.

“My job as a coach is to work with the players. We were better in the second half and we reached the opponent's goal, but we were not successful.”

He added: “We played with three forwards because we had more crosses, and it was possible to make use of one of the crosses. We did not play the game well. We had many chances and we could have been better.”

Elsewhere, Al Hilal recorded their second successive victory after defeating Al Sadd 2-0.

Ollie Watkins put Saudi Pro League leaders Hilal ahead in the first half before a Ruben Neves spot-kick confirmed the points as Qatar’s Al Sadd suffered a second consecutive defeat.

“I am happy with the players' performance,” said Hilal boss Simone Inzaghi. “We produced a big performance and controlled most of the game, and I saw a wonderful display from the team.”

The Italian also praised Gabriel Martinelli after the former Arsenal man gave the Al Sadd defence a difficult evening.

“He is a big player and we are lucky to have him with us,” added Inzaghi. “He always proves his high quality and his ability to serve the team and benefit it in more than one different position.”

headline: Yemen's Houthis vow more attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities after Aramco HQ hit
summary: By Timour Azhari, Jana Choukeir and Tala RamadanRIYADH, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia and said they struck the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco, which was hit the day before.The Iran-aligned group said it had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities inthe eastern city of Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, without saying when.
body_text:
By Timour Azhari, Jana Choukeir and Tala Ramadan

RIYADH, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia and said they struck the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco, which was hit the day before.

The Iran-aligned group said it had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at Saudi Aramco facilities inthe eastern city of Dhahran, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, without saying when.

Saudi Arabia has faced wideningHouthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday that killed 13 people.

The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month, reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.

SAUDI-LED FORCES SAY THEY INTERCEPT MISSILE

In a broad threat, the Houthis urged "international shipping companies", civilians and workers to evacuate airports and oil facilities, which they declared legitimate military targets.

The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.

Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.

The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed binSalman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said Tuesday's attack on the headquarters of Saudi Aramcohad caused a limited fire and no injuries or deaths.

TheDhahran complex hosts a major operationscentre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.

A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex. The source said an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged.

Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday's attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade. Authorities have closed the airport until October 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.

Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the government in 2015 after theHouthis seized the capital Sanaa.

The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.

(Writing by Tom Perry; Editing by Andrew Heavens)

The incident occurred in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday morning, the Mehr news agency reported, citing the IRGC. An explosion caused the vessel to catch fire and sink.

The ship was carrying about 2,500 containers.

headline: Container carrier sinks in Strait of Hormuz after explosion
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – A container carrier vessel carrying more than 2,500 containers sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz this morning after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy said.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – A container carrier vessel carrying more than 2,500 containers sank in waters south of the Strait of Hormuz this morning after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy said.

The Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said the container carrier struck a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, caught fire and sank Wednesday morning in waters south of the strait. The vessel had attempted to cross an unauthorized and high-risk route through the strait when it hit the mine and caught a severe fire after the explosion, according to the IRGC Navy's public relations office. The vessel sank in the southern waters of the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the fire. The IRGC Navy cautioned local vessels and fishermen over colliding with containers floating on the water's surface while transiting the area. MNA

headline: Iran central bank chief rejects economic collapse claims
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran's central bank governor dismissed claims that the country's economy is collapsing, saying it has shown notable resilience despite war, US sanctions and economic pressure.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran's central bank governor dismissed claims that the country's economy is collapsing, saying it has shown notable resilience despite war, US sanctions and economic pressure.

Abdolnaser Hemmati, governor of the Central Bank of Iran, rejected claims that the country's economy is collapsing, describing them as an illusion and saying the economy has shown considerable resilience despite war, economic pressure and US sanctions.

Speaking at the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group in Bangkok, Thailand, Hemmati outlined the central bank's priorities as curbing inflation, anchoring inflation expectations, preserving financial stability and maintaining banking and payment services.

He said the central bank has worked to secure foreign currency for imports of medicine and essential goods and to slow inflation.

Hemmati said Iran's economic policies should be assessed with external shocks and financial constraints in mind, citing factors that affect the policy environment and the effectiveness of economic measures.

He called on the IMF to examine the economic effects of war, sanctions and restrictions on international payments with the same rigor it applies to countries' domestic policies in its bilateral and multilateral surveillance. He also urged equal standards for all IMF members and active dialogue on ways to reduce the impact of such restrictions.

Hemmati warned that continued instability in the region could affect energy markets, transport, trade and investment. He said strengthening regional stability requires respect for the sovereignty of states, attention to legitimate security concerns and cooperation based on mutual responsibility and shared interests.

He also called for a more active IMF role in strengthening international monetary cooperation and overseeing the global monetary system.

body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Colombia opened its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday, becoming the 10th country to do so, as new President Abelardo de la Espriella reversed his predecessor's break with Israel by also restoring a free trade agreement between the two countries.

• Most countries maintain their embassies to Israel in Tel Aviv. Israel regards Jerusalem as its capital, while Palestinians seek East Jerusalem as the capital of a future independent state. The city's status remains one of the most contentious issues in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

• Former Colombian President Gustavo Petro in May 2024 broke diplomatic relationswith Israel over its actions in Gaza and had heavily criticised Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu

• Petro had closed Colombia's embassy in Tel Aviv and recalled its ambassador, a move Israel said was antisemitic and a reward for Hamas militants

• Right-wingerde laEspriella became president in August

• On Tuesday, the free trade agreement that was terminated by Petro was reinstated

• Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said: "In just two months, we have reversed most of the negative consequences of the Petro administration for Israel-Colombia relations and have even broken new ground ... I thank ... Abelardo de la Espriella for his determination to bring Israel-Colombia relations to an all-time high"

• Colombian Minister of Foreign Affairs Omar Bula Escobar attended the opening of the embassy in Jerusalem

• Several countries have relocated their embassies to Jerusalem since the United Statesdid so in 2018. Among them are Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay and Somaliland

(Reporting by Steven Scheer, Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria)
