body_text:
London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties, plans to deliver about 9,000 homes in the next five years in the UK capital, as demand remains resilient.

The new homes will be built across about 30 sites, said Scott Brown, chief financial officer of London Square.

More than 3,600 will be for sale, 1,538 will be for build-to-rent and another 3,575 will be sold in the so-called affordable segment, in which government support helps people to buy a home, he said during a presentation.

Aldar and Arada sign Dh15bn partnership for new projects in Abu Dhabi

The company, which was acquired by Aldar in 2023, has delivered 5,000 homes across 46 sites with a development value of £2.9 billion ($3.8 billion) since London Square was founded in 2010.

“Under the Aldar banner, our sales have actually been better than they were historically and in the current market have been outperforming all of our peers,” Mr Brown said. “Through our involvement with Aldar, we've not only been able to drive the capital but we've also been able to drive our sales.”

London Square, which works on regenerating former industrial sites, is behind projects such as the Nine Elms development, which features more than 750 residential homes and 21,500 square feet of commercial and retail space.

It is also transforming the former headquarters of Surrey County Council into a premium 292-home development, which includes the restoration of old structures.

The company aims to complete 600 homes this year, up from 398 last year, with sales backlog to reach £1 billion by the end of 2026.

“Most of this year will be on the affordable market rather than the build-to-sell market … about 30 per cent of what we're building is affordable,” Mr Brown told The National in London. He did not provide details on the total sales the company expects this year.

London Square reported sales of £251 million for the first half of this year, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf.

Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity, says Naomi Minegishi, London Square international sales director.

Customers from China, Singapore and Turkey are also major investors in London’s property sector.

“International demand is being driven by investment opportunity, safe haven of their capital and a strong legal framework,” Ms Minegishi said. “Families also want to have a second home to spend time in summer, as well as to have a home to support their children as they enrol them in school or universities to study in London.”

London's property market has been affected by geopolitical uncertainty that is pushing inflation higher.

In the third quarter, the average home price in London grew modestly by 0.4 per cent annually to £529,720, as demand remained subdued amid higher borrowing costs, according to the Nationwide Building Society.

However, fundamentals remain strong on higher investment activity, lifestyle vibrancy and a diverse population, said Sharief Ibrahim, executive director and head of residential agency at CBRE.

“There is real cause for optimism. There are countless examples of schemes that are performing really well, many in the London Square portfolio in terms of the volume of apartments being sold and the value being achieved,” he said.

“London is a resilient place. It's been through economic downturns, shocks to the economy and the system and the appeal of London has endured throughout that period. It's a global powerhouse and one of the, if not the most, successful city in terms of inward investment globally.”

It projects home transaction volumes to be around 6,000 to 7,000 this year and 7,500 to 8,000 next year.

In the early morning hours of October 14, the Ukrainian Air Force confirmed that the West had failed to warn Ukraine about ballistic missile launches for the second night in a row.

Earlier, an air raid alert was declared in Kiev almost simultaneously with a reported series of strikes. According to Politico, the US informed Kiev that no warning about the recent strikes on Ukrainian territory had been received due to adverse weather conditions. headline: Gaza committee signs recovery assistance deal with Germany’s GIZ in Cairo
summary: The Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza has signed an agreement with Germany’s international development agency GIZ to support the coastal strip's postwar recovery and reconstruction, although Israeli objections continue to prevent the body from entering the territory. The pact, signed on Tuesday at the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza’s temporary headquarters in Cairo, establishes a framework for technical assistance on reconstruction, public institutions and essential services, the committee said.It was formed in January under US President Donald Trump's peace plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803. Mr Trump's plan brought about a shaky ceasefire between Israel and Hamas last October after two years of fighting and also established a Board of Peace to oversee its implementation. Led by Ali Shaath, a former Palestinian Authority deputy minister, the committee is intended to restore public services and oversee civilian administration and reconstruction under the supervision of the Board of Peace.Mr Shaath and GIZ country director Alexander Zschocke signed the agreement at the committee’s temporary headquarters in Cairo. Bulgarian diplomat Nikolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, attended alongside German officials.Under the agreement, GIZ will provide technical expertise, advisory services, needs assessments and training to strengthen the committee’s planning and implementation capabilities. Co-operation will cover municipal services, social protection, education, employment, water, agriculture and energy.The statement did not mention a funding commitment, specific projects or a timetable for implementation.Mr Shaath called for the agreement to be translated into practical measures that improve living conditions. He said the committee would lead its implementation according to Gaza’s urgent needs and in co-ordination with Palestinian institutions. However, Israel refuses to allow the committee to enter Gaza or to proceed with the second stage of Mr Trump's peace plan until Hezbollah disarms. Its restrictions on the entry of equipment and supplies are also hampering recovery efforts.Gaza needs extensive reconstruction of homes and infrastructure. A European Union and UN assessment released in April estimated the cost of recovery and rebuilding at $71.4 billion over the next decade.
body_text:
The Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza has signed an agreement with Germany’s international development agency GIZ to support the coastal strip's postwar recovery and reconstruction, although Israeli objections continue to prevent the body from entering the territory.

The pact, signed on Tuesday at the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza’s temporary headquarters in Cairo, establishes a framework for technical assistance on reconstruction, public institutions and essential services, the committee said.

It was formed in January under US President Donald Trump's peace plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803. Mr Trump's plan brought about a shaky ceasefire between Israel and Hamas last October after two years of fighting and also established a Board of Peace to oversee its implementation.

Led by Ali Shaath, a former Palestinian Authority deputy minister, the committee is intended to restore public services and oversee civilian administration and reconstruction under the supervision of the Board of Peace.

Mr Shaath and GIZ country director Alexander Zschocke signed the agreement at the committee’s temporary headquarters in Cairo. Bulgarian diplomat Nikolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace’s high representative, attended alongside German officials.

Under the agreement, GIZ will provide technical expertise, advisory services, needs assessments and training to strengthen the committee’s planning and implementation capabilities. Co-operation will cover municipal services, social protection, education, employment, water, agriculture and energy.

The statement did not mention a funding commitment, specific projects or a timetable for implementation.

Mr Shaath called for the agreement to be translated into practical measures that improve living conditions. He said the committee would lead its implementation according to Gaza’s urgent needs and in co-ordination with Palestinian institutions.

However, Israel refuses to allow the committee to enter Gaza or to proceed with the second stage of Mr Trump's peace plan until Hezbollah disarms. Its restrictions on the entry of equipment and supplies are also hampering recovery efforts.

Gaza needs extensive reconstruction of homes and infrastructure. A European Union and UN assessment released in April estimated the cost of recovery and rebuilding at $71.4 billion over the next decade.

headline: Press review: Zelensky-Trump bad blood threatens US support and IMF updates GDP outlook
summary: Top stories from the Russian press on Wednesday, October 14th
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Zelensky’s latest conflict with US President Donald Trump puts Ukraine at risk of losing American support; the IMF adjusts its 2027 economic outlook as the global situation is better than expected; and NATO's nuclear drills are causing tension on the European continent. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.

Although Vladimir Zelensky’s latest conflict with US President Donald Trump has European leaders feeling a little on edge, experts believe they are simply banking on waiting out the current Washington administration. Should the Republicans lose Congress in the midterm elections, it will make that strategy much more tenable, with Trump's powers potentially limited for the remainder of his current term. However, as long as Trump remains in power, Ukraine could lose US support: the White House has all the leverage it needs to cut off Kiev from intelligence, block arms deliveries via European funds, and even shut down Starlink satellite communications. Meanwhile, the UK and the European Commission are trying to derail the diesel agreement between Moscow and Washington.

Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti that Trump's goal is not to force Kiev into a crushing defeat, so he is advocating a conflict settlement that makes both sides look like winners. The White House believes that "certain incentives" will persuade Russia to agree to a conflict freeze along the lines of engagement. The expert noted that the recently announced diesel deal is not an isolated instance of Russian-American cooperation, but rather a step toward Russia, in exchange for which Washington expects concessions from Moscow. "Russia should not agree to this framing of the issue. It should not be viewed as a precursor to mutual concessions or a settlement on Trump’s terms, but rather as practical, mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries," Suslov pointed out.

According to expert Dmitry Novikov, Washington remains convinced that it can use economic incentives to persuade Moscow to make territorial concessions. "At the same time, the US aims to strengthen its influence here, since, for example, it could gain direct access to the gas transportation system. The plan is this: economics in exchange for politics, but the economics are controlled by the Americans," the expert said.

In turn, Bogdan Bezpalko, a member of the Russian Presidential Council for Interethnic Relations, told Izvestia that the White House could now announce new sanctions relief for Moscow that would benefit the US economy. Such a move would also put pressure on Zelensky and Kiev’s European allies, he stressed.

For now, however, European countries will try to push Ukraine toward steps that would derail the implementation of the Russian-American agreements on diesel fuel, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik stated. According to him, the UK and the European Commission, led by Ursula von der Leyen, will be the main drivers of this push.

In 2026, global economic growth will be about 3.1%, while in 2027, that number is expected to rise to 3.4%, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) World Economic Outlook report said. The organization has moderately raised its 2027 forecasts compared to its April projections, citing the world economy's better-than-expected ability to withstand the consequences of the Middle East war and other destabilizing factors. Nevertheless, the medium-term outlook for economic growth is disappointing compared to previous periods, the report noted. Key risks include the energy crisis, the AI bubble, and rising public debt in countries around the world.

According to the IMF, the secret to resilience lies in two key factors, economy expert Ksenia Bondarenko told Vedomosti. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused serious supply disruptions by cutting off the transit route through which nearly 20 million barrels of oil, or roughly a quarter of global maritime traffic, were transported daily prior to the war. The flexibility of the energy market made it possible to quickly reroute supplies and increase production outside the Persian Gulf. Thanks to countries such as the US, Brazil, Kazakhstan, and several others, production increased by up to two million barrels per day, the report pointed out.

Moving on to the second factor, Bondarenko stressed that global reserves were depleted in an effort to combat the energy crisis. This included the emergency release of strategic reserves under the auspices of the International Energy Agency, as well as the large-scale use of domestic reserves. These measures provided an additional four million barrels per day. Thanks to all of this, the shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz did not lead to a spike in oil prices to 110 dollars per barrel or a 0.9 percentage point decline in global growth. The net negative impact on global growth in 2026 was only about 0.3 percentage points. In addition, the investment boom around AI continued to support growth in business activity and trade, the expert emphasized.

For Russia, the IMF revised its GDP forecast to a growth rate of 0.9% for both 2026 and 2027, down from 1.1% previously. Rising commodity prices are supporting economic activity in Russia to some extent, despite a decline in total oil exports due to infrastructure damage, the IMF noted. The downward revision of the Russian forecast may be linked to a more cautious assessment of investment prospects, financial expert Alexander Abramov stressed. An unbalanced budget and increased spending amid the geopolitical situation could fuel high inflation, he emphasized. In this case, the Russian Central Bank’s key rate will also remain high, curbing investment and hindering economic growth, the expert concluded.

Large-scale NATO nuclear exercises have begun in Italy, with 17 countries participating. Thousands of servicemen and dozens of aircraft capable of carrying nuclear weapons are involved. Russia has stated that these drills will not reduce regional tensions. The exercises are taking place at a time when the US seeks to deploy tactical weapons near Russia’s borders, and the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) has yet to be signed.

NATO troops are rehearsing scenarios involving dual-use aircraft: jets capable of carrying both conventional and nuclear weapons. According to military expert Dmitry Kornev, a key element of the Steadfast Noon drill is the practical testing of the Nuclear Sharing program for the use of American tactical thermonuclear bombs. "These special munitions are carried by specific types of aircraft, such as the German Tornado or the new-generation F-35 fighter jets used by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, Poland, Italy, and Finland," the expert told Izvestia.

Moscow’s official position on these exercises was articulated by the Russian embassy in Belgium, which maintains contact with NATO leadership. "We take note of statements by NATO officials that the drills are routine in nature and pose no threat to Russia. However, at a time when NATO is portraying our country as the main security threat, these exercises do not help reduce tensions on the continent and are part of the alliance’s nuclear policy, which is notoriously negative towards Moscow," the diplomats noted.

The New START Treaty officially expired on February 5, 2026. No new agreement was signed. For the first time since 1972, Moscow and Washington are not bound by a legal framework for controlling their nuclear arsenals. It is precisely in the absence of these deterrent mechanisms that the current drills are taking place. The expired START Treaty limited the delivery systems and nuclear warheads of Russia and the US, but it did not prohibit such exercises, Vasily Klimov, a senior research fellow at the International Security Center at the World Economy and International Relations Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.

The leaders of Germany, Italy, and Belgium have called for a new mechanism to be introduced among EU member states. The idea is to allow European governments to suspend laws adopted by Brussels if they deem the laws to be burdensome. According to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and her Belgian counterpart Bart De Wever, the new mechanism would benefit small and medium-sized European businesses the most. The new initiative aims to ensure greater independence from Brussels and prevent unnecessary regulatory burdens, which could lead to irreversible losses of Europe’s industrial potential and further weaken investment and competitiveness.

It would be wrong to suggest that the initiative will weaken EU bodies. Germany, Italy, and Belgium have all benefited from European integration, and they have no interest in causing division at this time, Artyom Sokolov, a senior research fellow at the MGIMO Institute of International Studies, told Vedomosti. Rather, this is about rebalancing the EU as a possible way out of the current tense situation. This indicates that current EU leaders recognize the organization's problems with expansion, the expert noted.

For now, the mechanism mentioned by Merz, Meloni, and De Wever is "nothing but propaganda," Vadim Trukhachev, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, pointed out. Such statements are made for domestic political purposes: Merz is concerned about his extremely low approval rating, Meloni faces elections next year, and De Wever is also trying to consolidate his position within Belgium. According to the expert, what’s more important is the ongoing debate within the EU over abolishing the veto and replacing it with the double-majority principle, when decisions are adopted if approved by 55% of member states (15 out of 27), representing 65% of the EU’s population, provided there is no blocking minority consisting of at least four countries.

Given that the EU is going through difficult times, leaders fear the collapse of consensus. Therefore, by transferring some powers to national capitals, they are trying to save the bloc, not dismantle it, political scientist Alexander Kamkin emphasized. If there is indeed a threat to Brussels in the form of the creation of some kind of parallel structure, the European Commission and its President Ursula von der Leyen may try to thwart the initiative of the three countries, the expert noted.

The UK’s Labour Party will release evidence that Moscow allegedly interfered in British politics, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard told a media outlet. However, it is unclear exactly when this will happen. In this way, the Cabinet has backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s virtually unsubstantiated accusation that Moscow attempted to influence the 2016 referendum on the UK’s exit from the EU. Burnham is now counting on a rapprochement with the EU. He even named the exact date when the groundwork for the country’s future reintegration will be laid: November 20, the date of the UK-EU summit.

"So far, Brussels’ reaction to the possibility of the UK’s return to the EU remains unclear. In theory, the EU return should please officials," political expert Alexander Tevdoy-Burmuli told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. He emphasized that London’s rapprochement with Brussels is driven by US President Donald Trump’s policies. "As one of the largest economies, as well as a country with nuclear weapons and permanent membership in the UN Security Council, the UK could once again become a welcome partner for the EU in this difficult situation," the expert explained.

However, it is true that reintegration is a complex process under current circumstances. "The UK has always been divided on the issue of EU membership. Brexit was an expression of this persistent division. In theory, the Burnham government could initiate talks on joining the EU. But that would require securing a majority in favor of reintegration within the country," Tevdoi-Burmuli emphasized.

This will not be easy. The British public associates the pro-European stance with failed immigration policies, which have become one of the country's central problems. "The UK has received a huge number of migrants, who are now a source of conflict. In addition, far-right forces advocating an end to migration are gaining ground in the country. In this context, joining the EU, where a left-liberal agenda is being implemented, could prove problematic," the expert noted.

headline: Yemen fighting overwhelms hospitals, cuts aid to 800,000 people, relief agencies say
summary: By Olivia Le PoidevinGENEVA, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties, while intensified fighting along multiple front lines has cut off aid to around 800,000 people, humanitarian agencies said on Wednesday.Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast are seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the Red Cross.
body_text:
By Olivia Le Poidevin

GENEVA, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties, while intensified fighting along multiple front lines has cut off aid to around 800,000 people, humanitarian agencies said on Wednesday.

Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen's Red Sea coast are seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the Red Cross.

More ⁠than 200,000 people have ⁠been displaced from their homes since fighting ​in the country began in recent weeks, sparked by renewed ⁠fighting between ⁠the Iran-backedHouthi groupand Saudi-backed governmentforces in Yemen, according to‌the United Nations' International ‌Organization for Migration.

"Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure," ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anesthesia, oxygen and medicines.

Yemen's health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, theICRC warned.

The fighting has also cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz - Yemen's third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting - and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World FoodProgramme said on Wednesday.

Some districts are now inaccessible because of fightingand road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.

"This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most," said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement.

(Reporting by Olivia Le PoidevinEditing by Linda Pasquini and Toby Chopra)

body_text:
The US government has criticised Lebanon's handling of a complaint filed against the Lebanese ambassador to Washington, Nada Moawad.

The case stems from a contact the envoy made with Israel's ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter, to inquire about his son who was critically injured in a car-ramming attack at a checkpoint in the occupied West Bank.

A representative said the US State Department was aware of the complaint lodged by Hassan Adel Bazzi, whom Washington described as a "pro-Hezbollah lawyer".

The State Department said it was "embarrassing" that Lebanon's military court was handling the case.

Lebanon’s public prosecutor referred the complaint to the government commissioner to the military court, a procedural step that does not itself constitute a prosecution or referral for investigation, according to Lebanese media.

The two ambassadors have been at the forefront of direct negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which have technically been in a state of war since 1948.

The talks were supposed to pave the way for Israel's withdrawal from south Lebanon and the disarmament of Hezbollah, two goals that have been almost entirely unsuccessful.

Some in Lebanon, including Hezbollah and its supporters, have been deeply critical of the government for engaging in negotiations with Israel.

"The Lebanese military judiciary should use its limited resources to prosecute Hezbollah operatives plotting against the Lebanese government and people instead of those working on their behalf," the State Department said.

"Laws and practices that enable this kind of politicised targeting of civilians and diplomats, while systematically shielding Hezbollah operatives, must be repealed. We have no patience for obstruction."

Lebanon's military court has in the past been accused of being influenced by Hezbollah.

The court is investigating two men whose vehicle was stopped last week with half a tonne of explosives bound for Beirut's southern suburbs, where Hezbollah holds sway.

headline: Zelenskyy sits down with NPR. And, Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer
summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has a sit-down interview with NPR as Russia's full-scale invasion nears the 5-year mark. And, Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer.
body_text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

In an interview with NPR, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the Trump administration warned it could cut intelligence-sharing with Ukraine unless Ukrainian forces halt long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Zelenskyy said the administration's decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel won't lower fuel prices and refuted President Trump's claim that Ukraine caused the price to spike, instead pointing to the war in Iran. This interview comes as Russia's full-scale invasion approaches its five-year mark.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following surgery to remove a growth from his lung, the Vatican announced. Doctors at Gemelli Hospital in Rome removed the lower lobe of the 71-year-old Pope's right lung during a successful procedure that lasted about 90 minutes. Post-surgery analysis confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma.

Trump has ousted Kimberly Guilfoyle as his ambassador to Greece. She was a prominent MAGA figure and the former fiancée of his oldest son. Guilfoyle faced unflattering allegations that she was trying to profit from her position, which she denies. The Wall Street Journal reported a series of questionable actions by Guilfoyle last month. One incident involved her asking a Trump donor for $100,000 to settle a credit card bill, promising to use her connections within the administration in return.

A federal judge ruled late yesterday that Trump cannot bar news organizations from covering him at the White House because he doesn't like their coverage, at least until a formal trial concludes. U.S. District Court Judge Timothy J. Kelly found that Trump's decision to exclude more than 70 journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico violated their free speech and due process rights. Both rights are enshrined in the Bill of Rights of the U.S. Constitution.

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

This week, Morning Edition's A Martínez traveled to the reliably red state of Texas. The cost of living is a major concern for many voters here. Ground beef hit a record high of about $7/lb in August, which is around $1.50 more than when Trump returned to office. In Floresville, Texas, Martínez spoke with a fourth-generation farmer and rancher who raises beef cattle about the challenges he is facing. Listen to what he had to say.

Martínez also spoke with residents about what is on their minds ahead of Election Day. Hear more about:

Follow the reporting: North Carolina and Georgia coverage airs Oct. 20, followed by reporting from Ohio and Michigan. You can follow along on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.

by Anthony Kuhn, International Correspondent

A screenshot from Lady Gaga's ad for familymart famiilymart/screenshot by npr hide caption

To report on Lady Gaga's ad for the FamilyMart convenience store chain, the first thing I had to do was watch the video of it.

Gaga plays the part of a store worker dancing through the aisles in a leather uniform and platform shoes. To me, she looked like a high priestess of camp, boogying through a temple of retail efficiency to a mad techno beat.

It wasn't just the wild style that hooked me. It was also the confluence of culture and commerce in Japan.

The issue of Japan's aging society and its shrinking workforce are an inescapable part of life in Japan, and foreign workers are an inevitable part of the solution. FamilyMart's ad leverages Lady Gaga's non-conformist pop persona to appeal to an increasingly diverse workforce, a retail analyst explained to me.

Konbinis, as convenience stores are called in Japan, are also an inescapable part of life there. They function as a deli, post office, copy shop, bank, tax office and Ticketmaster all rolled into one. That's because it's cheaper for the government and businesses to offer these services through the konbinis than to run their own.

Another draw is the crazy fresh food, delivered to the stores several times a day. When I'm on assignment in Tokyo, I'm often on deadlines, so I head straight for the konbini onigiri (rice balls) with salmon, tofu and seaweed salad and mochi for dessert. It would be nice to have time for a proper meal, but until I do, I'm not too badly off living the konbini lifestyle.

Give the segment a listen, at your convenience!

The Trump administration abruptly cut down more than 400 trees at Washington D.C.'s historic East Potomac Golf Links last weekend. A federal judge has ordered testimony from two high-level officials with the Interior Department over the recent abrupt removal of trees; the judge plans to hold another hearing Oct. 19. Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR hide caption

headline: Africa: Why We Extended IPO By Two Weeks - Dangote Refinery
summary: [Daily Trust] Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals (DRPR) says it decided to extend its IPO offer by two weeks to allow investors from more African countries to participate in what is expected to be the largest IPO in African history.
body_text:
Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals (DRPR) says it decided to extend its IPO offer by two weeks to allow investors from more African countries to participate in what is expected to be the largest IPO in African history.

The IPO opened on September 14 and closed on October 13.

The IPO comprises 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 each and is expected to raise just over N2tn, according to Dangote.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

President of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, had said the IPO offered drivers, cooks, traders, servants and managers an opportunity to own shares in the refinery.

"But it is not only to fund the expansion of the refinery, of course, it's a bigger amount. What we are trying to do is to make sure the majority of all these my--our drivers, our cooks, our, you know, servants, our managers, everybody, they will have an opportunity to have a stake in this refinery," Dangote said.

He said the transaction was not solely about raising funds for expansion, adding that the objective was to give people across the continent an opportunity to own shares in the refinery.

The IPO expected to end today, Tuesday, has now been extended by two weeks.

The firm said in a statement that it has received "very strong interest from a broad range of eligible investors across Africa and other jurisdictions" for the offer, and that it wanted more time to broaden participation.

"The extension is intended to support ongoing market-access initiatives across African jurisdictions, including the expansion of distribution channels and the implementation of depositary receipt programmes designed to facilitate efficient cross-border investor participation," the firm wrote.

"The Issuer remains encouraged by the level of investor engagement received to date across its target markets and believes that the extension will provide more investors across Africa with an opportunity to participate in the Offer."

The firm hopes to use the IPO proceeds to double the capacity of the Dangote Petroleum Refinery to 1.4m barrels a day, build fuel storage and distribution infrastructure and support future expansion.

The firm said the extension, which it said has been approved by Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), will also provide additional time for prospective investors to complete applicable account-opening, identity verification and regulatory requirements.

David Bird, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of DPRP, said: "We welcome the SEC's approval of the extension, which will give more investors across Africa the opportunity to participate in the Offer. From the outset, our ambition has been to enable as many people as possible to participate in the IPO and share in DPRP's future growth. The additional time will help us extend that opportunity to more investors across Africa."

...Foundation Targets 7m students, vulnerable women

Meanwhile, the Aliko Dangote Foundation (ADF) has unveiled a share grant initiative aimed at helping up to five million tertiary students and two million vulnerable women become shareholders in Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals through its Initial Public Offering (IPO).

Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of ADF, Zouera Youssoufou, disclosed that the Foundation will match qualifying share subscriptions by eligible beneficiaries.

Under the programme, students who subscribe for the minimum 10 shares worth N5,250 will receive an additional 10 shares funded by the Foundation, subject to the approved process and allocation, effectively doubling their holdings to 20 shares.

Speaking during a television interview, Youssoufou said the initiative was designed to turn the refinery's "People's IPO" vision into reality by giving traditionally underserved groups a direct stake in one of Africa's largest industrial assets.

"When Aliko announced the IPO, he described it as the IPO of the people and wanted as many Nigerians as possible to participate," she said.

ADF said it is prepared to support up to five million students enrolled in Nigerian tertiary institutions, including universities, polytechnics and colleges of education. Eligible applicants must be at least 18 years old and enrolled in a recognised institution. The Foundation is working with relevant educational authorities to verify beneficiaries.

She emphasised that the intervention is a grant, not an investment, with all shares ultimately belonging to the beneficiaries.

"The shares end up with the beneficiary. Our goal is to help people who may never have had the opportunity to own shares begin building long-term wealth," she said.

headline: Russia to strive for OPEC+ quota compliance — Novak
summary: The Russian deputy prime minister said that he cannot give an exact date because there are many uncertainties and various factors involved
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia will aim to meet its oil production quota under the OPEC+ agreement to the extent possible, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters on the sidelines of Russian Energy Week.

"I cannot give an exact date because there are many uncertainties and various factors involved. We will strive to fulfill our obligations to the maximum extent based on our capabilities," he said.

According to the latest OPEC report, Russia reduced its oil production in September 2026 by 38,000 barrels per day (bpd) compared to August, bringing the total to 8.643 million bpd. Russian oil production in September was 1.306 million bpd below its quota.

The Russian Energy Week international forum is taking place in Moscow from October 14 to 16, supported by the Russian government, the Russian Energy Ministry, and the Moscow government. The forum is organized by the Roscongress Foundation. TASS is the information partner for Russian Energy Week.

Dubai and Abu Dhabi were the only Gulf cities on the list, which ranked more than 100 destinations worldwide. body_text:
Dubai and Abu Dhabi have been ranked among the top 10 destinations for next-generation wealth despite the fallout from geopolitical tensions, according to Savills.

Dubai was ranked eighth and the UAE capital was 10th among favoured cities for the $84 trillion of wealth expected to be transferred between generations over the next two decades, the London-based consultancy said in its Spotlight on Wealth Trends report on Wednesday.

Next-generation wealth refers to individuals under 40 who have inherited significant wealth or have accumulated it through entrepreneurial success.

Dubai and Abu Dhabi benefitted from a slew of government initiatives that support economic and societal growth, including favourable tax environments, business-friendly policies and significant infrastructure investment “with a sophisticated luxury offering”, Savills said.

In particular, Dubai's entrepreneurial ecosystem, global connectivity and lifestyle appeal attract international talent and capital. Abu Dhabi complements this with its growing financial centre, a rising number of family offices, expanding economic opportunities and a high quality of life, the study said.

Those are “reinforcing the UAE's position as a compelling destination for globally mobile wealth”, Kelcie Sellers, associate director for world research at Savills, wrote in the report.

In the wider Gulf, “economic diversification and succession planning are becoming more prominent, with growing focus on family governance, next-generation involvement and the long-term deployment of capital within the region”, Ms Sellers said.

Despite the geopolitical uncertainty and economic headwinds, wealth generation and the flow of new money to the UAE continues. The country is a magnet for the ultra-wealthy, as well as for global wealth managers and trillion-dollar asset managers.

A base in the country offers global investors and money managers opportunities to expand regional operations and work with some of the largest sovereign wealth funds, as well as institutional partners.

Net wealth in the UAE is set to jump to $6 trillion by the end of this decade despite the short-term volatility caused by conflict in the Middle East, a report this week by Boston Consulting Group found.

In the five years to the end of 2030, net wealth in the Emirates is set to increase by more than $2.3 trillion, at annual growth of 10.6 per cent, the report said.

Last year alone, net wealth in the Arab world’s second-largest economy grew by almost 13 per cent on an annual basis to reach $3.6 trillion.

New York topped the Savills list, followed by Miami, London, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Singapore, Hong Kong and Monaco at ninth. Dubai and Abu Dhabi were the only Gulf cities on the list, which ranked more than 100 destinations worldwide.

Cities in Europe, the Middle East and Africa accounted for 16 of the index’s top 30 locations, driven by lifestyle and sporting events, which include major golf and tennis tournaments and Formula One races.

In terms of the number of sporting events, Dubai was number one in the Emea region, while Abu Dhabi, home of the season-ending F1 race, was sixth.

“The defining characteristic of Emea is the diversity of its wealth proposition. Global business centres, leading educational institutions, major sporting and cultural events, coastal retreats and mountain resorts are all within reach,” Ms Sellers said.

Global wealth continues to grow rapidly. Total personal wealth jumped by nearly 11 per cent in 2025 to create about one million more millionaires, according to industry tracker Altrata.

More than 510,800 are now ultra-high net worth individuals, or those with a net worth of $30 million or more, holding around $60 trillion in combined wealth – which is greater than the combined economies of the US and China, Altrata said.

“Location decisions are becoming a core component of wealth planning … at the same time, new fortunes generated by technology and artificial intelligence are reshaping global wealth hubs,” Ms Sellers said.

“As a result, many wealthy families are adopting multi-jurisdictional lifestyles, balancing residence, education and wealth structures across multiple markets.”

headline: IMF calls for US to cut deficits amid bond woes, urges China to shift away from exports
summary: By David Lawder and Andrea ShalalBANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The United States cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt without tax or spending adjustments, while China must pivot from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.
body_text:
By David Lawder and Andrea Shalal

BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The United States cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt without tax or spending adjustments, while China must pivot from export-led growth towards more domestic consumption, International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said on Wednesday.

Georgieva admonished the world's two largest economies to make painful policy changes to reduce growing fiscal and trade imbalances, as her fiscal affairs chief said inflation, high debt levels and rising yields had heightened the urgency for budget consolidation around the globe.

Speaking at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva singled out advanced economies, namely the US and European countries, as the "worst offenders" on excessive debts, with higher benchmark yields spilling over to low-income countries that have already been forced by financial markets to rein in borrowing.

Asked at a press conference whether the US needs tighter fiscal policy,Georgieva said Treasury Secretary ScottBessent recognizes that US deficit and debt levels are too high and need to be made more sustainable.

"The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to help reduce debt, Georgieva said.

"At the Fund, we believe that growth of course helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments. So, some (fiscal) measures would be necessary."

The call for more action to reduce debt was echoed in the IMF's Fiscal Monitor report on Wednesday, which warned that delays in an era of higher borrowing costs would only make the job harder in coming years.

While that message is a perennial one from the IMF, Rodrigo Valdes, the head of the IMF's Fiscal Affairs department, said the surge in bond yields had left governments with little fiscal room to manoeuvre.

"We dialled up the urgency of our message," he added.

Bessent is not attending the annual meetings in Bangkok, despite this year's US presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, instead favouring domestic engagements as the US midterm election campaign heats up.

He has acted as a chief spokesman for President Donald Trump's economic policies, particularly touting the deep tax cuts passed last year by Republicans now trying to maintain control of the US Congress.

G20 finance ministers are due to meet on the sidelines of the Bangkok meetings on Thursday. The US has used its G20 presidency to try to rally allies to take stronger action to counter China's "non-market" economic policies that have led to excess industrial capacity and a flood of global exports.

Asked about imbalances emanating from China, on a day when data showed it was on track to post a record trade surplus,Georgieva repeated longstanding advice to Beijing: "For surplus countries, what they need to do is increase domestic consumption. That clearly applies to China's growth model. Shift from exports more toward domestic consumption."

Deficit countries need to save more and spend less, while Europe needs to invest more in competitiveness, she said.

"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more, and Europe has to invest more," Georgieva added.

FRENCH FISCAL WORRIES

This week's meetings have been dominated by worries about growing debt and rising bond yields and risks from the artificial intelligence boom.

France, one of the advanced economies worst hit by a global bond sell-off, needs to solve its own debt woes through fiscal consolidation, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said, effectively playing down speculation about an ECB intervention in the bond market.

Asked at a CNN event in Bangkok whether the ECB was about to help France, Lagarde said it was up to Paris to soothe investors' nerves. "And for that one, the primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," she said.

The IMF has lauded Britain for taking steps toward consolidation, but made clear on Wednesday that it does not want London to accelerate the pace of fiscal consolidation. "Our recommendation is 'stay the course'," Valdes said.

Still, OECD Secretary-General Mathias Cormann called for "strong fiscal discipline" in a statement to the IMF's steering committee, saying this was needed to ensure stability.

"In every G20 country except Germany and Türkiye, public debt as a share of GDP was higher in the first quarter of 2026 than at the end of 2007," he wrote to the International Monetary and Financial Committee.

"Countries need to contain and reallocate spending, improve public-sector efficiency and make tax systems more effective. They should also protect investment that drives future growth, especially in education, skills and digital infrastructure."

CALLS TO AID POOR COUNTRIES

Regarding the growing divergence between advanced countries benefiting from AI investment and those bypassed by it, highlighted in Tuesday's IMFeconomic forecasts, Georgieva also urged IMF member countries to fully fund IMF facilities for low-income and vulnerable countries.

These include the Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which provides low- and zero-interest loans to low-income countries, and the Catastrophe Containment and Relief Trust, a fund that provides grants for debt-service relief and cancellation to the poorest and most vulnerable member countries, she said.

These countries, too, were being squeezed by higher bond yields, with average debt service costs that have increased to 14% of revenue from 6% a decade ago, even as overall debt burdens have eased, she said.

"The risk of divergence is most dangerous for those that are already further behind," Georgieva added.

(Reporting by David Lawder and Andrea Shalal; Editing by John Mair, Shri Navaratnam, Toby Chopra)

headline: Who is Kimberly Guilfoyle? ‘She dated my son…’: Trump as White House fires US ambassador to Greece
body_text:
Shortly after Donald Trump’s administration fired Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece, following reports of her misconduct, the US President on Tuesday sought to distance himself from her, his son Donald Trump Jr’s former fiancée.

“She, I guess, dated my son a long time ago,” Trump told reporters on Tuesday, playing down their family connection. “She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn’t like what we were reading.”

Trump’s comments marked a striking shift in tone towards a woman Trump had once described as a close friend and ally. Guilfoyle, a former prosecutor, Fox News host and prominent fundraiser for the Republican Party, rose through the conservative political world before being appointed Washington’s representative in Athens. Her diplomatic career has now ended amid allegations that she has strongly denied.

Born in San Francisco, California, Guilfoyle studied at the University of California, Davis, before earning a law degree from the University of San Francisco School of Law. She began her professional career in the legal system, working as a prosecutor in San Francisco and later as a deputy district attorney in Los Angeles.

Her background in criminal law helped her transition into television, where she appeared as a legal analyst before joining Fox News in 2026. She subsequently became a familiar face to American viewers as a conservative commentator and co-host of the network’s prime-time programme The Five.

Guilfoyle’s move into broadcasting expanded her national profile. Her television appearances and outspoken conservative commentary made her a recognisable figure in Republican political circles.

She left Fox News in 2018 and moved into political campaigning and fundraising, becoming associated with pro-Trump political organisations. She later played a role in fundraising efforts supporting Trump’s presidential campaigns.

Guilfoyle also addressed the 2020 Republican National Convention, becoming one of the prominent public advocates for Trump and his political movement. Her public profile increasingly centred on Republican politics rather than her earlier legal career.

After she quit Fox News in 2018, there were reports of workplace misconduct. Guilfoyle denied wrongdoing at the time. The allegations were separate from the more recent claims concerning her conduct as ambassador and her interactions with political donors.

Guilfoyle began dating Donald Trump Jr. in 2028, bringing her closer to the former president’s family and political network. The couple became engaged in 2020, although reports later placed their separation in late 2024.

During their relationship, Guilfoyle became a regular presence at Trump campaign events and Republican gatherings. She delivered speeches, helped raise political funds and emerged as a prominent surrogate for Trump.

When Trump announced his intention to nominate her as ambassador to Greece in December 2024, her praised her experience in law, media and politics and described her as a close friend and ally.

However, her personal relationship with Trump Jr. had ended by the time she took up the diplomatic post. Trump Jr. subsequently became engaged to Bettina Anderson.

The US Senate confirmed her nomination in September 2024, and she formally assumed the position in Athens in November that year. She became the first woman to serve as US ambassador to Greece, the Los Angeles Times reported.

Her appointment placed a political loyalist in a strategically important diplomatic role. Greece is a NATO ally of the United States and occupies a significant position in the eastern Mediterranean, where military cooperation, energy supplies and regional security are major concerns.

Guilfoyle’s tenure came under scrutiny after reports by The Wall Street Journal raised allegations about her interactions with wealthy business figures and political donors.

One report alleged that she asked businessman Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 American Express bill. Deters was reportedly seeking access to the Trump administration over personal tax and legal matters. The newspaper reported that the request was made shortly before Guilfoyle’s Senate confirmation hearing in July 2025; Deters reportedly did not provide the money.

Other reports raised questions about her relationship with a lobbyist linked to a Greek energy company and alleged that she promoted the firm. Reuters also reported allegations involving her connections with wealthy Greek businesspeople and claims that she had offered access to US officials in exchange for money, gifts or favours.

Guilfoyle has denied them, saying in a statement on X: “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

She added that serving as US ambassador to Greece had been “the honor of a lifetime” and thanked Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the opportunity.

The White House confirmed on Tuesday that the administration had asked her to resign. Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, announced the decision during her first briefing, saying: “She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well.”

headline: South Korea, US, Japan seek nuclear alliance against regional countries — Russia’s MFA
summary: Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian MFA’s Department for Nonproliferation and Arms Control, highlighted "Seoul’s regular attempts to blame Russia for its own years-long deliberate escalatory moves"
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. South Korea, the United States and Japan are essentially working to create a nuclear alliance directed against other countries in the region, Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department for Nonproliferation and Arms Control, said.

"South Korea has decided to bring ‘peace and stability’ to the Korean Peninsula by brandishing the US nuclear bludgeon at North Korea," he pointed out at a meeting of the First Committee of the United Nations General Assembly.

"First, it deployed nuclear weapons to its territory in 1958-1991. In 1976, it started to engage in joint drills with the US that practice nuclear strikes and carpet bombings of North Korea, an activity that continues to this day. Now, building on this years-long aggressive policy, Seoul has teamed up with Washington and Tokyo, effectively seeking to form a nuclear alliance directed against the countries of the region," Vorontsov added.

The Russian diplomat highlighted "Seoul’s regular attempts to blame Russia for its own years-long deliberate escalatory moves, which are the root cause of the current crisis facing the Korean Peninsula."

"In Resolution 3390B, adopted at the 30th session of the UN General Assembly, the First Committee already outlined specific steps required to provide strong guarantees of peace on the Korean Peninsula, which include withdrawing all foreign troops stationed in South Korea and replacing the Armistice Agreement with a peace treaty," Vorontsov emphasized. "Since none of the above features in the long-term plans of Washington and Seoul, no comprehensive solution to the nuclear issue on the Korean Peninsula should be expected in the near future," he concluded.

headline: Lebanon's power failure: Diesel generators, $300-a-month bills - and a corrupt system milking the profits
summary: Lebanon now relies on diesel-powered generators for about half of its electricity supply, further exposing the crisis-hit country to financial, environmental and operational risks, according to data for an upcoming report. Behind that alarming figure lies a deep-rooted crisis decades in the making. Interviews with officials, as well as government statistics, studies and testimonies gathered by The National reveal how a largely unregulated industry has been lining the pockets of high-ranking officials and neighbourhood generator owners alike.The electricity sector has been regarded as one of the most corrupt parts of Lebanon’s sectarian system of government since the end of the civil war in 1990. Those who benefit from the dysfunction have allegedly resisted efforts to repair the sector, preserving a system that lets them continue profiting from its failures.Figures being compiled by the Lebanese Centre for Energy Conservation for their upcoming report show that private generators accounted for 50 per cent of Lebanon’s electricity supply at the beginning of 2026, while Electricite du Liban, the state utility, provided only 31 per cent. EDL's share is likely to have shrunk even further over the summer, according to the LCEC, a national agency affiliated with the Energy Ministry.Meanwhile, the Lebanese people are left to foot the bill. The country's dependence on expensive diesel imports to run generators has sent energy bills rocketing in recent months amid rising global oil prices due to the Iran war, further straining households and businesses already struggling after years of economic crisis. Among a dozen people interviewed by The National, the median generator bill was $310 in August.Dependence on generators increased dramatically after a severe economic crisis began in 2019, driving the final nail in the coffin of the dilapidated electricity sector. As the bankrupt state struggled to secure fuel for its power plants, EDL production fell by nearly 80 per cent between 2018 and 2023, from 15.4TWh to 3.37TWh, according to a 2025 report by the LCEC.Over the same period, diesel-powered generators' share of Lebanon's electricity supply more than doubled, from 23.1 per cent to 51.5 per cent. Beirut’s roughly 9,300 generators have barely stopped their relentless humming since then, spewing polluting exhaust into the air and wrapping the capital in a yellowish smog, as they supply electricity to those who can afford it. “We can’t go on like this,” said Ayman, manager of a shawarma restaurant in Beirut’s vibrant Hamra neighbourhood, who gave only his first name. With state electricity available for only a few hours a day, and at unpredictable times, the restaurant is almost entirely reliant on a private generator, he said.The small restaurant’s electricity bill for August alone came to almost $20,000. “We’re losing money,” Ayman sighed. The usually bustling summer season, which he had been banking on to shore up the restaurant’s finances, proved disappointing. With the war between Hezbollah and Israel resuming in March, tourists and even Lebanese expatriates largely stayed away.“If nothing is done, we will have to close. And not just us, everyone else too,” said Ayman.While generator bills vary considerably from one area to another because of limited state oversight, data from New Energy Consult and The National's interviews with residents show that monthly bills often exceed $300 – roughly equivalent to the entire monthly minimum wage of 28 million Lebanese pounds. By comparison, the average household electricity bill in the UK is about $95 a month for a medium-sized household of two to three people.In one neighbourhood of the capital, a 25-amp generator subscription cost as much as $750 in August, according to New Energy Consult, a consultancy founded by Lebanese energy expert Jessica Obeid. Ms Obeid said some generator operators had taken advantage of the global surge in oil prices to increase their profit margins. “The problem is that nobody has provided state electricity over the past three decades, and nobody has implemented any serious reforms,” she explained.“Generators eventually just reflect the failure of the state, the failure of policies and the failure of institutions. So it’s time for state institutions to stand up and do what they’re supposed to be doing: provide electricity.” 'Mass bribe system'People strolling along Hamra’s main street express their exasperation over soaring energy costs. “It’s insane,” said Karim Agha, 33, who recently returned from Dubai. He said his parents’ electricity bill reached $600 in August, three times what he used to pay in the Emirates.“I’m scared to look at the bill,” said Talal Fayed, a 67-year-old driver who paid a $300 generator bill in August.Asked what he expected from the Lebanese state, he sighed and replied with a faint smile: “What state?”Such vast sums flowing each month from consumers’ pockets into the private generator industry raise the question: why have the Lebanese authorities failed to implement energy reforms that would redirect that money to the state?Energy experts say vested interests and a lack of political will have prevented a transition towards cheaper, cleaner energy and locked the country into a dangerous dependence on generators.The diesel generator industry is lucrative: Ali Ahmad, a World Bank expert, estimated its value at around $3 billion in 2020, with roughly $1 billion going to the generator market and $2 billion to diesel importers. Opposition MP Paula Yacoubian said the generator “cartel” benefitted politically connected individuals and companies that had little incentive to give up their bread and butter. Generator owners are part of Lebanon’s clientelism networks, she argued, able to offer benefits such as forgiving unpaid bills in exchange for political support. “It's a mass bribe system,” she told The National. A systemic lack of investment and squandering of public funds have left Lebanon’s energy sector in shambles. About 40 per cent of electricity entering EDL's network is lost between technical distribution and commercial losses such as theft and illegal connections, according to a 2024 EDL report.With its battered financial sector and unstable security situation, Lebanon has struggled to attract foreign capital since 2019. But lack of investment in the energy sector is not new. The state has not built a major power plant in decades. Its newest large plants, Deir Ammar and Zahrani, date back to the late 1990s. “With $1 billion, you can build a 1,000MW power plant. It's nothing. People are already paying for it with their generator bills,” Ms Yacoubian said. EDL has about 3,000MW of nominal installed capacity, but in 2023 it supplied electricity equivalent to just 13 per cent of its theoretical maximum output. The country needs about 3,000MW of electricity to meet daily demand.Only two of Lebanon’s seven thermal power plants are operational, because the cash-strapped state cannot buy enough fuel and badly maintained infrastructure limits production.A 1,000MW plant operating at an 80 per cent capacity could produce about 7TWh annually, more than twice EDL’s total electricity supply in 2023, which stood at roughly 3.4TWh, according to LCEC. “This is not a technical problem,” Ms Yacoubian said. For over two decades, political bickering has stopped all major investment projects in Lebanon. “Power plants are routinely built everywhere else in the world. Anyone, my aunt Salma included, could bring electricity,” she said. “But there are no politically affiliated politicians who were able to do it in Lebanon.”Powerful oligopoly Energy Minister Joseph Saddi said he was well aware that the remedy to the country’s dependence on generators was in investment in electricity generation. “We are now engaging with the private sector,” he told The National. The Energy Ministry has given the International Finance Corporation, the private-sector arm of the World Bank, a mandate to secure the necessary private-sector investment. “There are investors who are interested, but they require a certain number of financial guarantees. So what we are focusing on now is how we can provide those guarantees,” Mr Saddi said.The IFC’s role is notably to act as the lead transaction adviser on a public-private partnership for a new 825MW combined-cycle gas turbine plant, a project that has been in the pipeline for years.Meanwhile, the World Bank has approved a $250 million loan to EDL to upgrade its infrastructure.Experts say that, even more than generator owners, diesel importers wield significant influence over policy decisions, thanks to their close connections with politicians. A 2022 investigation by Beirut-based research centre Triangle revealed direct links between several of Lebanon’s 13 licensed fuel-importing companies and current or former politicians.For energy expert Marc Ayoub, who has investigated the sector for years, Lebanon’s diesel importers form an oligopoly with far-reaching political connections. Rather than competing with one another, he said, they collaborate to maximise their margins, sharing the cost of vessels and associated shipping fees before dividing the imported quantities among themselves.They then sell the diesel, locally known as mazout, according to the price set by the Ministry of Energy, currently about $30 for 20 litres, which Mr Ayoub said allowed them to make comfortable margins. The tariff “contains a lot of hidden profits for importers, in addition to margins for distributors, lorry owners, petrol stations and everyone else involved”, he said. The Energy Ministry could reduce additional premiums it pays to importers, which he said could lower diesel tariffs by at least 15 per cent. But instead, he said, the state kept “protecting the interests of these private players”. There is also an issue on the generator side. While the Energy Ministry sets generator tariffs – which have risen by almost 60 per cent in six months – many operators do not comply with them, or even bother to install mandatory electricity meters. Instead, they charge residents a fixed monthly rate based on the amperage of their subscription, which determines how many appliances consumers can run at the same time. Despite occasional government crackdowns for overcharging customers and failing to install electricity meters, generator operators have largely been able to set prices at their discretion. One silver lining of the near-collapse of state electricity supply is that solar panels have soared in popularity, accounting for 19 per cent of electricity production in 2026, up from just 0.4 per cent in 2018, according to LCEC.None of the people interviewed by The National said they had installed solar panels. Mr Fayed, the taxi driver, said this would be the only way to move beyond dependency on generator owners and the state, neither of which he trusts. But, like many Lebanese living from pay cheque to pay cheque, he does not have the upfront capital to install solar panels. “Too expensive,” he sighed.With Lebanon experiencing one of the fastest-growing cancer rates in the world, experts have urged the country to move to cleaner sources of energy. According to a 2024 study led by scientists from the American University of Beirut, the level of carcinogenic pollutants from diesel generators in the capital's air has doubled since 2017, increasing the risk of developing cancer by 50 per cent. “It’s suffocating, it’s killing us, it’s loud, it’s expensive … And we know that it is all due to corruption,” Ms Yacoubian said. “I'm telling the Lebanese people to wake up – wake up, and smell the mazout.”
body_text:
Lebanon now relies on diesel-powered generators for about half of its electricity supply, further exposing the crisis-hit country to financial, environmental and operational risks, according to data for an upcoming report.

Behind that alarming figure lies a deep-rooted crisis decades in the making.

Interviews with officials, as well as government statistics, studies and testimonies gathered by The National reveal how a largely unregulated industry has been lining the pockets of high-ranking officials and neighbourhood generator owners alike.

The electricity sector has been regarded as one of the most corrupt parts of Lebanon’s sectarian system of government since the end of the civil war in 1990. Those who benefit from the dysfunction have allegedly resisted efforts to repair the sector, preserving a system that lets them continue profiting from its failures.

Figures being compiled by the Lebanese Centre for Energy Conservation for their upcoming report show that private generators accounted for 50 per cent of Lebanon’s electricity supply at the beginning of 2026, while Electricite du Liban, the state utility, provided only 31 per cent.

EDL's share is likely to have shrunk even further over the summer, according to the LCEC, a national agency affiliated with the Energy Ministry.

Meanwhile, the Lebanese people are left to foot the bill. The country's dependence on expensive diesel imports to run generators has sent energy bills rocketing in recent months amid rising global oil prices due to the Iran war, further straining households and businesses already struggling after years of economic crisis.

Among a dozen people interviewed by The National, the median generator bill was $310 in August.

Dependence on generators increased dramatically after a severe economic crisis began in 2019, driving the final nail in the coffin of the dilapidated electricity sector.

As the bankrupt state struggled to secure fuel for its power plants, EDL production fell by nearly 80 per cent between 2018 and 2023, from 15.4TWh to 3.37TWh, according to a 2025 report by the LCEC.

Over the same period, diesel-powered generators' share of Lebanon's electricity supply more than doubled, from 23.1 per cent to 51.5 per cent.

Beirut’s roughly 9,300 generators have barely stopped their relentless humming since then, spewing polluting exhaust into the air and wrapping the capital in a yellowish smog, as they supply electricity to those who can afford it.

“We can’t go on like this,” said Ayman, manager of a shawarma restaurant in Beirut’s vibrant Hamra neighbourhood, who gave only his first name. With state electricity available for only a few hours a day, and at unpredictable times, the restaurant is almost entirely reliant on a private generator, he said.

The small restaurant’s electricity bill for August alone came to almost $20,000. “We’re losing money,” Ayman sighed.

The usually bustling summer season, which he had been banking on to shore up the restaurant’s finances, proved disappointing. With the war between Hezbollah and Israel resuming in March, tourists and even Lebanese expatriates largely stayed away.

“If nothing is done, we will have to close. And not just us, everyone else too,” said Ayman.

While generator bills vary considerably from one area to another because of limited state oversight, data from New Energy Consult and The National's interviews with residents show that monthly bills often exceed $300 – roughly equivalent to the entire monthly minimum wage of 28 million Lebanese pounds.

By comparison, the average household electricity bill in the UK is about $95 a month for a medium-sized household of two to three people.

In one neighbourhood of the capital, a 25-amp generator subscription cost as much as $750 in August, according to New Energy Consult, a consultancy founded by Lebanese energy expert Jessica Obeid.

Ms Obeid said some generator operators had taken advantage of the global surge in oil prices to increase their profit margins. “The problem is that nobody has provided state electricity over the past three decades, and nobody has implemented any serious reforms,” she explained.

“Generators eventually just reflect the failure of the state, the failure of policies and the failure of institutions. So it’s time for state institutions to stand up and do what they’re supposed to be doing: provide electricity.”

People strolling along Hamra’s main street express their exasperation over soaring energy costs. “It’s insane,” said Karim Agha, 33, who recently returned from Dubai. He said his parents’ electricity bill reached $600 in August, three times what he used to pay in the Emirates.

“I’m scared to look at the bill,” said Talal Fayed, a 67-year-old driver who paid a $300 generator bill in August.

Asked what he expected from the Lebanese state, he sighed and replied with a faint smile: “What state?”

Such vast sums flowing each month from consumers’ pockets into the private generator industry raise the question: why have the Lebanese authorities failed to implement energy reforms that would redirect that money to the state?

Energy experts say vested interests and a lack of political will have prevented a transition towards cheaper, cleaner energy and locked the country into a dangerous dependence on generators.

The diesel generator industry is lucrative: Ali Ahmad, a World Bank expert, estimated its value at around $3 billion in 2020, with roughly $1 billion going to the generator market and $2 billion to diesel importers.

Opposition MP Paula Yacoubian said the generator “cartel” benefitted politically connected individuals and companies that had little incentive to give up their bread and butter.

Generator owners are part of Lebanon’s clientelism networks, she argued, able to offer benefits such as forgiving unpaid bills in exchange for political support. “It's a mass bribe system,” she told The National.

A systemic lack of investment and squandering of public funds have left Lebanon’s energy sector in shambles. About 40 per cent of electricity entering EDL's network is lost between technical distribution and commercial losses such as theft and illegal connections, according to a 2024 EDL report.

With its battered financial sector and unstable security situation, Lebanon has struggled to attract foreign capital since 2019. But lack of investment in the energy sector is not new. The state has not built a major power plant in decades. Its newest large plants, Deir Ammar and Zahrani, date back to the late 1990s.

“With $1 billion, you can build a 1,000MW power plant. It's nothing. People are already paying for it with their generator bills,” Ms Yacoubian said.

EDL has about 3,000MW of nominal installed capacity, but in 2023 it supplied electricity equivalent to just 13 per cent of its theoretical maximum output. The country needs about 3,000MW of electricity to meet daily demand.

Only two of Lebanon’s seven thermal power plants are operational, because the cash-strapped state cannot buy enough fuel and badly maintained infrastructure limits production.

A 1,000MW plant operating at an 80 per cent capacity could produce about 7TWh annually, more than twice EDL’s total electricity supply in 2023, which stood at roughly 3.4TWh, according to LCEC. “This is not a technical problem,” Ms Yacoubian said.

For over two decades, political bickering has stopped all major investment projects in Lebanon.

“Power plants are routinely built everywhere else in the world. Anyone, my aunt Salma included, could bring electricity,” she said. “But there are no politically affiliated politicians who were able to do it in Lebanon.”

Energy Minister Joseph Saddi said he was well aware that the remedy to the country’s dependence on generators was in investment in electricity generation. “We are now engaging with the private sector,” he told The National. The Energy Ministry has given the International Finance Corporation, the private-sector arm of the World Bank, a mandate to secure the necessary private-sector investment.

“There are investors who are interested, but they require a certain number of financial guarantees. So what we are focusing on now is how we can provide those guarantees,” Mr Saddi said.

The IFC’s role is notably to act as the lead transaction adviser on a public-private partnership for a new 825MW combined-cycle gas turbine plant, a project that has been in the pipeline for years.

Meanwhile, the World Bank has approved a $250 million loan to EDL to upgrade its infrastructure.

Experts say that, even more than generator owners, diesel importers wield significant influence over policy decisions, thanks to their close connections with politicians. A 2022 investigation by Beirut-based research centre Triangle revealed direct links between several of Lebanon’s 13 licensed fuel-importing companies and current or former politicians.

For energy expert Marc Ayoub, who has investigated the sector for years, Lebanon’s diesel importers form an oligopoly with far-reaching political connections. Rather than competing with one another, he said, they collaborate to maximise their margins, sharing the cost of vessels and associated shipping fees before dividing the imported quantities among themselves.

They then sell the diesel, locally known as mazout, according to the price set by the Ministry of Energy, currently about $30 for 20 litres, which Mr Ayoub said allowed them to make comfortable margins. The tariff “contains a lot of hidden profits for importers, in addition to margins for distributors, lorry owners, petrol stations and everyone else involved”, he said.

The Energy Ministry could reduce additional premiums it pays to importers, which he said could lower diesel tariffs by at least 15 per cent. But instead, he said, the state kept “protecting the interests of these private players”.

There is also an issue on the generator side. While the Energy Ministry sets generator tariffs – which have risen by almost 60 per cent in six months – many operators do not comply with them, or even bother to install mandatory electricity meters.

Instead, they charge residents a fixed monthly rate based on the amperage of their subscription, which determines how many appliances consumers can run at the same time.

Despite occasional government crackdowns for overcharging customers and failing to install electricity meters, generator operators have largely been able to set prices at their discretion.

One silver lining of the near-collapse of state electricity supply is that solar panels have soared in popularity, accounting for 19 per cent of electricity production in 2026, up from just 0.4 per cent in 2018, according to LCEC.

None of the people interviewed by The National said they had installed solar panels.

Mr Fayed, the taxi driver, said this would be the only way to move beyond dependency on generator owners and the state, neither of which he trusts. But, like many Lebanese living from pay cheque to pay cheque, he does not have the upfront capital to install solar panels. “Too expensive,” he sighed.

With Lebanon experiencing one of the fastest-growing cancer rates in the world, experts have urged the country to move to cleaner sources of energy.

According to a 2024 study led by scientists from the American University of Beirut, the level of carcinogenic pollutants from diesel generators in the capital's air has doubled since 2017, increasing the risk of developing cancer by 50 per cent.

“It’s suffocating, it’s killing us, it’s loud, it’s expensive … And we know that it is all due to corruption,” Ms Yacoubian said. “I'm telling the Lebanese people to wake up – wake up, and smell the mazout.”
