headline: State Street plans 100 jobs for Emiratis at Al Ain hub as it aims for July 2027 opening
summary: US financial services group State Street plans to employ about 100 Emiratis at its Al Ain operating centre as it targets a July 2027 opening date.The new centre is expected to have 300 staff by 2030, with technology, artificial intelligence, operations and client services among its main areas. About a third of the workforce will come from State Street’s global centres, another third will be recruited from the UAE talent pool and a third will be Emiratis, said Jack Keshishian, State Street’s head of Middle East and North Africa (excluding Saudi Arabia and Bahrain). Preparations are under way, including arranging links with UAE universities through its partnership with the Abu Dhabi Investment Office. “We are looking at the go date of the first of July,” Mr Keshishian said. This is earlier than the “end of next year” start date outlined at the Al Ain Future Business Forum in September.State Street announced the centre in January. Mr Keshishian said the current focus was on building a workforce of 300 over three years to 2030, with the possibility of future expansion if there was sufficient demand. “Obviously, we have ambitions to grow because [the] Middle East is a growth market for us, and we take a long-term view,” he said.Opportunities for graduatesThe company expects to identify potential graduate recruits in the first quarter of next year. The “talent pool” in Al Ain is a key reason the company chose to set up there, alongside the potential to sustain and grow the business, Mr Keshishian said. AI and technology will help automate work and improve the use of data, while employees will also provide operational and client services. Mr Keshishian said technology and staff would work together to improve efficiency for clients. He did not provide an investment figure for the centre and said spending would continue over the coming three years. Why Al Ain?State Street’s decision is based on its assessment of the available workforce and the potential to sustain and expand an operation in the city, Mr Keshishian said.The company has had a presence in Abu Dhabi since 2018. US financial services group State Street plans to employ about 100 Emiratis at its Al Ain operating centre as it targets a July 2027 opening date.

The new centre is expected to have 300 staff by 2030, with technology, artificial intelligence, operations and client services among its main areas.

About a third of the workforce will come from State Street’s global centres, another third will be recruited from the UAE talent pool and a third will be Emiratis, said Jack Keshishian, State Street’s head of Middle East and North Africa (excluding Saudi Arabia and Bahrain).

State Street to open Al Ain operating centre in 2027

Preparations are under way, including arranging links with UAE universities through its partnership with the Abu Dhabi Investment Office.

“We are looking at the go date of the first of July,” Mr Keshishian said. This is earlier than the “end of next year” start date outlined at the Al Ain Future Business Forum in September.

State Street announced the centre in January. Mr Keshishian said the current focus was on building a workforce of 300 over three years to 2030, with the possibility of future expansion if there was sufficient demand.

“Obviously, we have ambitions to grow because [the] Middle East is a growth market for us, and we take a long-term view,” he said.

The company expects to identify potential graduate recruits in the first quarter of next year.

The “talent pool” in Al Ain is a key reason the company chose to set up there, alongside the potential to sustain and grow the business, Mr Keshishian said.

AI and technology will help automate work and improve the use of data, while employees will also provide operational and client services.

Mr Keshishian said technology and staff would work together to improve efficiency for clients. He did not provide an investment figure for the centre and said spending would continue over the coming three years.

State Street’s decision is based on its assessment of the available workforce and the potential to sustain and expand an operation in the city, Mr Keshishian said.

The company has had a presence in Abu Dhabi since 2018. Its new centre will broaden that operation beyond the capital and support clients across several markets.

“I think despite the tension in the region, we are seeing global institutions establishing their presence here in the UAE and the wider region, and we haven't seen any sort of a change in that,” he said.

The company has also submitted an application to expand the services it can offer at Abu Dhabi’s financial centre ADGM.

Subject to approval, these would include safeguarding clients’ financial assets and providing administrative services for investment funds.

body_text:
Visitors to Louvre Abu Dhabi's latest exhibition begin their journey in darkness, lights above mimicking a star-filled sky. It's a reminder of a time when sailors relied on the heavens to navigate the Indian Ocean, carrying spices, precious stones and textiles between distant civilisations.

Such voyages connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia, establishing commercial and cultural relationships that developed over centuries.

Their history is explored in Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean, opening at Louvre Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, October 14, and running until February 14, 2027.

Renoir masterpiece now on display at Louvre Abu Dhabi

Organised in partnership with the Guimet National Museum of Asian Arts in Paris, the exhibition brings together about 240 artworks and historical objects from 24 lenders, covering maritime exchange from antiquity to the 17th century.

Among them are archaeological discoveries, jewellery, religious artefacts and objects recovered from shipwrecks. Six detailed models of historic vessels and specially created maps illustrate how sailors crossed vast waters and transported goods between continents.

The exhibition places the Arabian Gulf at the centre of its narrative, examining the region's historical role in these networks.

“The story is told from here, and that is something we consider very important at Louvre Abu Dhabi: telling the story from the region,” says Guilhem Andre, the museum's director of scientific, curatorial and collections management “This has never really been done on this scale before.”

The exhibition features loans from institutions including the Asian Civilisations Museum in Singapore, the National Museum of the Philippines and the Al Sabah Collection in Kuwait.

Pierre Baptiste, director of collections and curatorial staff at the Guimet in Paris, says the exhibition explores how people established relationships through commerce and spiritual exchange.

The Arabian Gulf's pearl industry provides a significant regional example. Pearls harvested from its waters travelled to markets in India and beyond, while materials such as carnelian were traded across the ocean from ancient times.

Later networks expanded the circulation of gemstones, jewellery, furniture and textiles. Andre said the objects revealed how discoveries of new sources of gold, spinels, rubies and emeralds influenced jewellery production. Diplomatic gifts also feature, demonstrating how valuable objects helped establish relationships between rulers and communities.

Beyond the goods themselves, the exhibition examines the techniques that made these journeys possible.

Its opening gallery recreates the darkness experienced by ancient navigators, who relied on stars and coastal landmarks to determine their position.

“The main idea was to give visitors a sense of what people at the time experienced,” Baptiste says.

Subsequent galleries explore navigational instruments, including the kamal, used in Arab and Indian maritime traditions, and the astrolabe. Twenty-four maps created specifically for the exhibition trace the routes connecting ports across the ocean.

Six large ship models represent Arabian, South-East Asian, Chinese, Portuguese and Spanish maritime traditions. Andre says they were constructed in South Africa over the course of a year, drawing on extensive historical research.

The models are accompanied by objects recovered from shipwrecks, offering evidence of the cargo these vessels carried.

Baptiste says advances in underwater archaeology since the 1990s have enabled researchers to recover significant quantities of material from sunken ships, including objects originating in China, India, Spain and Mexico.

Among the most valuable commodities were spices, which commanded high prices alongside luxury products such as jewellery and textiles.

Cultural exchange is another central theme. A Buddha sculpture from present-day Pakistan, loaned by the Guimet, reflects the influence of ancient Greek and Roman artistic traditions on Buddhist sculpture.

The final gallery examines four religious traditions that spread across the Indian Ocean, showing how beliefs travelled along the same routes as commercial goods.

Andre says merchants and pilgrims often crossed these waters for different purposes, carrying objects and practices that became part of life in distant communities.

“Religion was not separate from trade,” he says. “They were all part of the same relationships and exchanges.”

The exhibition also offers a perspective on maritime history that predates the expansion of European influence in Indian Ocean commerce during the 17th and 18th centuries.

Baptiste says the decision to conclude the historical narrative in the 17th century was deliberate, allowing visitors to understand the networks that existed long before European powers became prominent in the region.

These earlier connections, he says, laid the foundations for the expansion of international commerce in subsequent centuries.

“We wanted to approach the history of commercial relationships from a multicultural perspective,” he says. “Europe was only one part of this story.”

Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean runs at Louvre Abu Dhabi from October 14, 2026, until February 14, 2027. The exhibition will subsequently travel to the Guimet in Paris, where it will be presented from May 12 to September 6, 2027.

headline: Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
summary: By Panu Wongcha-um and Devjyot GhoshalBANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
body_text:
By Panu Wongcha-um and Devjyot Ghoshal

BANGKOK, Oct 14 (Reuters) - A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.

The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations ⁠Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.

"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.

The White House, US State Department and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world's most widely used fertilizer — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.

Fertilizer shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertilizer products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.

If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.

"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," Moreira da Silva said.

The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.

The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertilizer supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.

Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.

MULTIPLE SHIPPING CHOKEPOINTS

Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.

The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.

"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.

Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.

"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz."

(Reporting by Panu Wongcha-um and Devjyot Ghoshal; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

headline: Netanyahu says he is not seeking to attack Iran again before Israel election
summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that he was not in favour of a preemptive strike against Iran before Israel's October 27 election but also warned Tehran and its proxies against striking Israel."It is not convenient for us, it's no good," Netanyahu said in an interview on Israel's Army Radio, when asked about the possibility of a preemptive strike and allegations by his political rivals that he was seeking a military confrontation ahead of the election.
body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that he was not in favour of a preemptive strike against Iran before Israel's October 27 election but also warned Tehran and its proxies against striking Israel.

"It is not convenient for us, it's no good," Netanyahu said in an interview on Israel's Army Radio, when asked about the possibility of a preemptive strike and allegations by his political rivals that he was seeking a military confrontation ahead of the election.

"Even if Iran fires missiles at us they will blame me," Netanyahu said, though he also repeated his previous warnings to Iran, saying Israel would respond forcefully if attacked.

He would not elaborate on the possibility of a preemptive strike after the election or about his recent discussions with Washington about Iran.

The United States and Iran have been at war since February 28 when ​the US and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states.

Israel and Iran have not traded fire since June.

Asked whether Israel was assisting Saudi Arabia against attacks by the Iran-aligned Yemeni Houthis, Netanyahu said:

"I don't get into those matters. I can only tell you that many countries in the Middle East are turning to us following our massive success and tremendous achievements."

Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on Riyadh airport on Saturday that killed 13 people.

Netanyahu said that Iran's proxies were also looking to launch attacks on Israel before the election.

Defence Minister Israel Katz, speaking from the self-declared security zone Israeli forces are occupying in southern Lebanon, warned Iran-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah against attacking Israel.

"Hezbollah will suffer a severe blow and lose additional territories in southern Lebanon within the Nabatieh and Litani regions, which will become part of Israel's permanent security zone. The IDF (Israel Defence Forces) is prepared to carry out the manoeuvre," Katz said.

Katz said that a million Shi'ites would be displaced and that Hezbollah's stronghold in Beirut would not be spared.

Israel launched air strikes and a ground invasion in southern Lebanon this year in parallel with the war in Iran, after Hezbollah fired into Israel in revenge for the attacks against Tehran.

Hundreds of thousands of people from Lebanon's Shi'ite Muslim community, from which Hezbollah draws its support, were uprooted by the fighting.

(Reporting by Maayan Lubell and Lina Obeid; Editing by Aidan Lewis)

headline: Jailed Imran Khan's woes compound after Pakistan suspends his provincial government
summary: By Mubasher Bukhari and Asif ShahzadLAHORE, Pakistan, Oct 14 (Reuters) - A state of emergency declared in Imran Khan's main political stronghold is another setback for Pakistan's jailed former prime minister whose health is worsening according to his family.President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday declared the emergency in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan that has seen a sharp rise in militant attacks.
body_text:
By Mubasher Bukhari and Asif Shahzad

LAHORE, Pakistan, Oct 14 (Reuters) - A state of emergency declared in Imran Khan's main political stronghold is another setback for Pakistan's jailed former prime minister whose health is worsening according to his family.

President Asif Ali Zardari on Sunday declared the emergency in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province bordering Afghanistan that has seen a sharp rise in militant attacks.

It suspended the local government led by Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party, accusing it of failing to tackle militancy, and put an opponent from Zardari's party in charge.

Khan's party says the move, which strips it of resources from the provincial budget, was a pretext for apolitical takeover of the region and to stop supporters marching on Islamabad.

It challenged the emergency rule at Peshawar High Court in the provincial capital on Wednesday."It was ridiculous to equate Imran Khan's basic human rights with a complex issue such as terrorism," said Zulfi Bukhari, a close aide.

Ahead of the emergency, thousands of Khan's supporters had rallied in the province intending to march to Islamabad to demand his release and medical treatment.

Khan's three sisters and hundreds of supporters, including party leaders, were arrested ahead of the march.

"You can see clearly that things will become harder for Imran Khan," said Najam Sethi, a political commentator.

"In the current situation, the PTI lost on both counts. It has not been able to extract any concessions for Khan while losing control of its government in KP and surrendering its political leaders to imprisonment."

The situation also worsens the long-running tug-of-war between Khan and the powerful Pakistani military chief Asim Munir, the analyst said.

The 74-year-old former cricket star was in power from 2018 to 2022 but sent to jail in 2023 on corruption charges, with visits prohibited for months. He denies the charges.

His family and party have been demanding an urgent medical intervention for loss of vision in one eye, fluctuating blood pressure and the psychological fallout of solitary confinement.

The PTI's last major protest two years ago ended in deadly clashes, while Khan's arrest in 2023 sparked nationwide riots.

To avoid a repeat, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's government last week held talks with the PTI whose demands included private medical assistance for Khan, prison visits and phone calls with his London-based sons.

The government, in turn, was demanding that the PTI publicly condemn Islamist militancy in the province, attend the funeral for security personnel killed in militant attacks, and join hands with the government's counter-terrorism fight, according to Junior Interior Minister Talal Chaudhry.

"We had given them almost everything they asked for" but the PTI rejected the government demands, he told Reuters.

There have been five such states of emergency in Pakistani provinces since 1975, three of them in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and one each in Punjab and Balochistan province.

All of them were reversed within months either through court or political intervention.

Rights groups and analysts have questioned the emergency rule, warning against any crackdown.

"We strongly urge the federal government and the PTI to resume a meaningful political dialogue," said the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, an independent body.

(Reporting by Asif Shahzad in Islamabad and Mubasher Bukhari in Lahore; Editing by Praveen Menon and Andrew Cawthorne)

headline: Belarusian foreign ministry condemns NATO’s new ‘Theory of Victory’ plan
summary: Belarusian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Ruslan Varankov highlighted that under the guise of defensive language, the Alliance is effectively laying the groundwork for military escalation and aggression
body_text:
MINSK, October 14. /TASS/. Belarus strongly condemns NATO’s new plan, headlined ‘Theory of Victrory,’ which envisages pre-emptive strikes on the territory of the republic, Belarusian Foreign Ministry’s spokesman, Ruslan Varankov, said in a statement.

"The Republic of Belarus strongly condemns the statements made by General Alexus Grynkewich, Supreme Allied Commander Europe, who presented the so-called ‘Theory of Victory’. This concept envisages pre-emptive strikes against the territory of Belarus using drones and ground-based robotic systems," the spokesman said in a statement.

"The North Atlantic Alliance's aggressive rhetoric is becoming increasingly systematic. In the absence of any threats from Belarus or any real preconditions for conflict, NATO is drawing up plans to increase its military presence near Belarusian borders and launch strikes against the territory of a sovereign state," he continued.

Varankov went on to say that under the guise of defensive language, the Alliance is effectively laying the groundwork for military escalation and aggression.

"Belarus has never threatened anyone. Our military doctrine is strictly defensive in nature," the Belarusian diplomat added. "We consistently advocate openness, de-escalation and dialogue on an equal footing. We call on our Western counterparts to exercise sound judgement and engage in joint efforts to restore mutual trust.".

body_text:
Three separate gold smuggling attempts from the UAE to India have been foiled in recent weeks by customs officials at Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport in New Delhi.

Officials recovered gold concealed inside trolley bag linings, hidden in passengers' socks and disguised as silver chains.

In the biggest case, officials seized 6.5kg of gold valued at around Dh3.8 million. The accused sprayed the gold chains with silver and black paint and hid them under seats on Emirates flight EK-514 from Dubai to Delhi. Airport police arrested eight passengers and remanded them to judicial custody.

Arrests after UAE foils two people-smuggling operations

On October 10, customs officers intercepted a passenger arriving from Sharjah and recovered 241g of 99.31 per cent pure gold. The passenger moulded the gold and hid it as wire linings in the corners of two trolley bags. A video posted by Delhi Customs shows an official cutting through the seams of the passenger's red bags to extract the rod-like gold.

The recovered gold was valued at approximately Dh149,000. Customs seized the gold, and further investigation is under way.

On the same day, customs officers at Terminal 3 intercepted an Indian passenger arriving from Muscat on Oman Air flight WY-241. The passenger had travelled from Dubai to Muscat on connecting flight WY-612 on October 9.

A personal search found two rectangular pouches containing gold paste concealed inside his socks. The pouches weighed 725g gross, including wrapping and concealment material. After finding gold in his socks, officials also recovered a 587g gold bar. A karatometer test confirmed 100 per cent purity.

Customs assessed the gold’s tariff value at approximately Dh323,000 and its market value at approximately Dh364,000. The passenger told investigators the gold was brought from Dubai and concealed to avoid declaration and customs duty. Customs seized the gold under Section 110(1) of the Customs Act, 1962.

Delhi Customs has reiterated its vigilance against smuggling and its commitment to strengthening enforcement at the country’s busiest international airport.

According to a Reuters report in July, unofficial gold inflows in India have risen since the government raised import tariffs on the precious metal earlier this year. The World Gold Council said grey market inflows and the disruption they cause are hurting organised players.

India, the world's biggest gold consumer after China, more than doubled import tariffs to 15 per cent on May 13 to curb demand, cut the trade deficit and ​ease pressure on the currency.

India's net gold imports fell 23 per cent year-on-year to 98.1 tons in the June quarter, the lowest quarterly level since September ​2020, when Covid-19 pandemic lockdowns curbed demand, the WGC said in ​a report.

body_text:
Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Presidential Special Envoy to China and Chairman of the Executive Affairs Authority, travelled to Beijing this week for high-level talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi.

Mr Al Mubarak met Mr Wang in the Chinese capital on Tuesday, as part of a trip aimed at deepening the UAE-China Comprehensive Strategic Partnership.

The two delegations reviewed bilateral relations under the framework of the partnership, which has served as the foundation for growing co-operation.

CommentIn a fractured world, China and the UAE choose dialogue over division

Both parties exchanged views on issues of shared interest, with particular emphasis placed on the importance of sustained co-ordination and close consultation between Abu Dhabi and Beijing.

The talks were attended by Hussain Al Hammadi, UAE ambassador to China, along with senior officials from both sides.

China remains one of the UAE's most significant trading partners, and the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, established in 2018, has provided a structured platform for co-operation spanning trade, investment, technology and energy.

body_text:
Saudi Crown Prince Mohamed bin Salman received Iraq's Prime Ali Al Zaidi in Riyadh on Wednesday, in the first visit by a foreign leader to the Saudi capital since a deadly Houthi attack on its airport.

The Saudi Press Agency published footage and pictures of the meeting between the Crown Prince and Mr Al Zaidi.

The Iraqi Prime Minister's office said they discussed “the latest regional developments and co-ordination of efforts in a way that enhances the security and stability of the region”.

Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.

The airport has come under attack four times, ​including Saturday's attack, which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.

Authorities have closed the airport until October ​17, and airlines have cancelled ‌flights to Saudi Arabia. It is not known how Mr Al Zaidi travelled to the country.

Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in ⁠support of the government in 2015, fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, after the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa.

The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring ⁠sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept along the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab Al Mandeb strait.

The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war ​casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.

The UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.

“WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children,” the WFP said in a statement.

headline: (LEAD) Hyundai Motor expands production capacity in India
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Hyundai Motor Co., South Korea's largest carmaker, sa...
body_text:
(ATTN: CHANGES photos)

SEOUL, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- Hyundai Motor Co., South Korea's largest carmaker, said Wednesday it has completed a new plant in India, a key market in its global expansion strategy.

The Pune plant began operations Tuesday with an annual production capacity of 170,000 vehicles, which is scheduled to increase to 320,000 by 2030, the company said in a press release.

With the addition of the new facility, Hyundai now operates three production plants in India -- two in Chennai and one in Pune. The three plants have a combined annual production capacity of nearly 1 million vehicles.

"Over the past 30 years, India has been a key pillar of Hyundai Motor's global growth, and the completion of the new Pune plant will mark a new chapter for the company in India," the group's Executive Chair Euisun Chung said in the release.

The first model to be produced at the Pune plant will be the Venue compact sport utility vehicle (SUV), for sale in India and export to about 30 countries, the company said.

Over the years, Hyundai has introduced a range of models in India, including the i10 and i20 hatchbacks, the Verna subcompact sedan, the Creta SUV, the all-electric Creta EV, the Exter SUV and the Alcazar SUV.

Last year, the company sold 398,937 SUVs in India, accounting for about 70 percent of its total sales in the country.

Hyundai acquired the plant from General Motors Co. in 2023 after its operations had been suspended for years amid the COVID-19 pandemic. The company invested 1 trillion won (US$747 million) to convert the facility into its third production plant in India.

headline: Cheap weapons, growing fears: Inside the Taliban’s drone campaign against Pakistan
summary: Pakistan says it intercepted 23 suicide drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace in September alone. Since the conflict began in February 2026, the Taliban have increasingly used drones to attack Pakistan, raising concerns in Islamabad.
body_text:
Pakistan says it intercepted 23 suicide drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace in September alone. Since the conflict began in February 2026, the Taliban have increasingly used drones to attack Pakistan, raising concerns in Islamabad.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 14:52

The Pakistani army on September 23 said it had shot down at least eight fixed-wing drones in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, less than 1,000 metres from the Afghan border. It was the latest reported attempt by the Taliban to target Pakistani forces using this type of drone.

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Since the conflict between Pakistan and the Taliban began in February of this year, the Taliban have deployed armed first-person-view (FPV) drones – small quadcopters carrying munitions such as mortar shells – to attack Pakistani positions near the border. They have also used larger, fixed-wing suicide drones equipped with more powerful engines, potentially capable of flying hundreds of kilometres.

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

On September 28, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said it had delivered a diplomatic protest note to the Taliban over what it described as "provocative incursions", citing 23 drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace since the beginning of the month.

To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Once close allies, Pakistan and the Taliban entered into open conflict about eight months ago when Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Mohammad Asif publicly declared that “relations with the Taliban had deteriorated into an ‘open war’.”

The conflict escalated after Pakistan began targeting positions of the Pakistani militant group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) inside Afghanistan. Also known as the Pakistani Taliban, the TTP is officially recognised as a terrorist organisation by multiple countries and international bodies, including the United Nations, Pakistan and the European Union.

The TTP has carried out attacks in Pakistan for nearly two decades and has long-standing ties with the Afghan Taliban, which Pakistan accuses of sheltering and supporting the group.

When Pakistan, which has aerial military superiority over Afghanistan, has struck suspected TTP positions deep inside Afghanistan, the Taliban has retaliated with ground attacks and drones.

To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

UAV expert Mark Grozel explains:

These drones are roughly two metres in size and could carry between half a kilogram and one kilogram of explosives. They have a very limited military effectiveness and are easy to intercept. They are slow and fly at low altitude. The difficulty is detecting them: they are hard to spot, but once detected, they are easy to shoot down.

There are multiple scenarios. One is that a foreign government supplies them. Or they could be, to some extent, homemade. Today, making a fixed-wing drone is not that complicated anymore.

Autopilot software that controls a drone’s trajectory is widely available.

On [the e-commerce site] Alibaba, you can easily buy components such as the engine and battery. The body could be made with a 3D printer, or from polystyrene or even balsa wood…

After examining photos and videos of drones that Pakistan’s army said it had intercepted, FRANCE 24 identified what appear to be DLE55 engines fitted to each of the suicide drones shown. These 55cc single piston engines and are commercially available online.

Despite their basic engines, small explosive payloads and simple radio navigation systems, these drones have a heavy psychological impact.

The strength of this kind of fixed-wing drones is that they are cheap to make. Any group with the resources, including the Taliban, can now produce them.

They allow you to tell your adversary: ‘I can threaten your infrastructure at any moment.’ If one hits a school or a fuel facility, the consequences could be catastrophic. Their main power is their psychological impact.

The Taliban’s drone attacks come amid a broader conflict between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban, fueled by the activities of the TTP.

Direct engagements between the TTP and Pakistani security forces have increased significantly since the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, rising from 98 incidents in 2021 to 470 in 2024. Throughout 2025, regular clashes along the border reportedly resulted in approximately 4,000 deaths.

On September 18, 2026 a TTP suicide car bomb attack on a mosque killed 21 people in the Pakistani border city Kohat .

Mukhtar Wafaei, an expert on the Taliban who specialises in Afghan affairs, explains how relations between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban deteriorated into military conflict.

To understand the current situation, we have to go back to the Soviet-Afghan war in the 1980s.

During those years, Afghan and Pakistani fighters were sent from religious schools in Pakistan to participate in the “jihad” against Soviet forces in Afghanistan.

These relationships were forged during that period and remained largely unquestioned until the September 11 attacks and the subsequent US invasion of Afghanistan.

After the collapse of the Taliban’s first government in 2001, Taliban leaders and members dispersed, with many seeking refuge in Pakistan’s border regions, including Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Waziristan and Balochistan.

To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

They maintained these long-standing cross-border relationships. In 2008, the Afghan Taliban expanded their presence across various parts of Afghanistan. Around the same time, several jihadist organisations operating in Pakistan, originating from the same tribal regions and carrying out violent attacks, came together under the TTP.

Another turning point came in 2021, when the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. Taliban leaders who had been sheltered in safe houses in Pakistan belonging to the TTP, left for Afghanistan. Their Pakistani friends, allies and associates accompanied them to Kabul and also took refuge there.

Between late 2021 and mid-2022, Pakistan attempted to negotiate with the TTP. But after the group refused to disarm or accept Pakistan’s constitutional framework, it ordered its fighters to launch nationwide attacks on November 28, 2022. The Taliban claim the TTP is a Pakistani internal issue and deny any responsibility.

When diplomatic ultimatums failed to halt cross-border militant operations, Pakistan resorted to air strikes inside Afghanistan, prompting the Afghan Taliban to retaliate with attacks on Pakistani territory.

To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Pakistan also launched a mass expulsion campaign, with 2.39 million Afghans returning from Pakistan to Afghanistan over a period of more than two years.

To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

There is a very deep ideological relationship between the Afghan Taliban and the TTP rooted in the extremist Islamist religious schools in Pakistan. They share the same ideology, come from the same religious tradition and follow the same teachings. They can no longer be separated. They are effectively one group.

A few months after the Afghan Taliban returned to power, the TTP leader stated very clearly in Pashto that Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan and the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, meaning the Afghan Taliban, were one group. He said: “We are not two groups. We are one group, following one programme, one ideology and one method.”

This is particularly revealing because the TTP leader himself explicitly described the two movements as one.

headline: Fire, sinking and reported scramble for cargo: what we know about ship lost in Strait of Hormuz
summary: A Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by an unidentified projectile. All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were evacuated safely and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority has said.The sinking was confirmed on Wednesday, after the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported the attack on Tuesday. A sister ship, the GFS Giselle, was damaged in the same wave of attacks but made its way to anchorage. Singapore condemned the strikes as a breach of international law.The incident highlights how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies.What do videos show?Photos and videos on social media appeared to show a container ship listing heavily under thick black smoke, with containers and their contents floating nearby. Pakistan’s maritime authority warned mariners of floating containers in the area.Other clips added a stranger note. Posts on X suggested small boats converged on the scene to scoop up cargo, and one described sellers doing business on the spot, calling out: “Do you want iPhones? Do you want perfumes?” Another post said paying Iran’s unilaterally declared transit toll, which has faced international opposition, would beat losing everything on board.The footage is unverified. It could not be confirmed where or when any clip was filmed and whether it relates to the GFS Pride.What was the ship carrying?The GFS Pride had the capacity to carry 2,824 standard containers, it was reported. It was not clear how many it was carrying when it sank and no manifest was published.Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the ship had more than 2,500 containers, including alleged contraband. The claim could be substantiated. The IRGC also warned local vessels and fishermen to avoid the floating boxes.Why does it matter?Quoting two senior Iranian officials, Reuters reported on Wednesday that Tehran was changing its tactics against shipping to keep oil prices high and influence the November 3 US midterm elections. One warned such vessels “would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz”. Another said a complete closure of the waterway would come soon.The IRGC claimed the ship struck a naval mine while using an “unauthorised” route. Tehran has described the US-backed route hugging the Omani coast as dangerous.Maritime security firm Marisks said there was no independent evidence that a mine sank the vessel and described Iran’s claims as consistent with a psychological operations campaign. The available evidence does not establish that the southern route near Oman has been mined.
body_text:
A Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by an unidentified projectile.

All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were evacuated safely and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority has said.

The sinking was confirmed on Wednesday, after the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported the attack on Tuesday. A sister ship, the GFS Giselle, was damaged in the same wave of attacks but made its way to anchorage. Singapore condemned the strikes as a breach of international law.

Hormuz attacks surge as Iran steps up campaign against US-backed oil shipping

The incident highlights how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies.

Photos and videos on social media appeared to show a container ship listing heavily under thick black smoke, with containers and their contents floating nearby. Pakistan’s maritime authority warned mariners of floating containers in the area.

Other clips added a stranger note. Posts on X suggested small boats converged on the scene to scoop up cargo, and one described sellers doing business on the spot, calling out: “Do you want iPhones? Do you want perfumes?” Another post said paying Iran’s unilaterally declared transit toll, which has faced international opposition, would beat losing everything on board.

The footage is unverified. It could not be confirmed where or when any clip was filmed and whether it relates to the GFS Pride.

The GFS Pride had the capacity to carry 2,824 standard containers, it was reported. It was not clear how many it was carrying when it sank and no manifest was published.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the ship had more than 2,500 containers, including alleged contraband. The claim could be substantiated. The IRGC also warned local vessels and fishermen to avoid the floating boxes.

Quoting two senior Iranian officials, Reuters reported on Wednesday that Tehran was changing its tactics against shipping to keep oil prices high and influence the November 3 US midterm elections. One warned such vessels “would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz”. Another said a complete closure of the waterway would come soon.

The IRGC claimed the ship struck a naval mine while using an “unauthorised” route. Tehran has described the US-backed route hugging the Omani coast as dangerous.

Maritime security firm Marisks said there was no independent evidence that a mine sank the vessel and described Iran’s claims as consistent with a psychological operations campaign. The available evidence does not establish that the southern route near Oman has been mined.

SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- North Korea said Thursday it test-fired two types of strategic cruise missile in the East Sea the previous day, in what may be the first launch from a 3,000-ton-class submarine it unveiled in 2023.

"The test-fire aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems and contributed to getting the Navy skilled in performing its strategic missions and showcasing high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the North's Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

DPRK stands for North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

The test was overseen by Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the Workers' Party of Korea, Jang Chang-ha, director-general of the Missile Administration and the Navy's underwater weapon system engineers, the report said.

Experts said the missiles appeared to be launched from what the North called its first tactical nuclear attack submarine, Hero Kim Kun Ok.

North Korea unveiled the vessel in September 2023 and described it as one of the "core underwater offensive means" of its navy.

At the launching ceremony on Sept. 6, 2023, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un was quoted as saying that arming the navy with nuclear weapons "brooks no further delay."

Wednesday's test was the first of its kind since January 2024, when the North said Pulhwasal-3-31 strategic cruise missiles were fired from the 2,000-ton-class 8.24 Yongung submarine, with Kim watching.

North Korea first reported its test-firing of a submarine-launched cruise missile from the same vessel in March 2023.

The fact that Wednesday's launch took place without Kim's attendance is seen as a way to show off the navy's capabilities while avoiding heavy outside pressure. The KCNA said the launch "did not have any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries."

South Korea's military did not publicly disclose Wednesday's launch, but said it had tracked the missiles from before launch to the end of their flight, rejecting claims that it may have missed them.

"Our military has persistently monitored and tracked the North Korean cruise missile activity reported yesterday, using various assets from before the launch through the cruise phase to the end of the flight," Capt. Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), told a press briefing.

He declined to elaborate on the surveillance assets used, citing confidentiality with the United States.

When asked if the military could specify the launching system, Jang said one type of missile was fired from a vertical launching system, while another was fired from a torpedo launcher.

The Rodong Sinmun, the North's most widely read newspaper, did not report the launch.

Earlier this week, Pyongyang test-fired tactical ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the East Sea. The North said Tuesday the launch was intended to "confirm the success in the research for the technical upgrading of an important core element."

headline: North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
summary: North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.

North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.

Issued on: 15/10/2026 - 01:12Modified: 15/10/2026 - 02:18

North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.

The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries".

The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.

Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.

The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.

The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.

Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.

Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts

Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.

The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.

"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.

"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."

North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.

Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.

Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.

North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.

The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.

South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.

Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.

body_text:
Elon Musk on Wednesday sought to distance himself from the satellite communications restrictions over Ukraine that have disrupted Kyiv's military operations, suggesting that US President Donald Trump is ultimately behind any changes.

There has been growing tension between Washington and Kyiv after Mr Trump's agreement with President Vladimir Putin to resume buying Russian diesel, which critics have called a betrayal of Ukraine.

Since the deal was announced last week, Ukrainian officials have said restrictions on satellite terminals have disrupted drone operations as Russia continues to attack Ukrainian energy sites.

Why Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire may offer oil markets little relief

Kyiv has also reported difficulties in receiving advance warnings of Russian missile attacks, although it is unclear whether these are connected to the satellite restrictions.

In a post on X, Mr Musk drew a distinction between Starlink, which is the satellite internet company owned by SpaceX, and Starshield, a national security and military subsidiary.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Mr Musk said. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the President of the United States]."

He was responding to a post minutes earlier by former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that some of the satellite connectivity was being restored. “Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support,” he said.

Mr Musk added that use of Starlink "is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".

Mr Musk's post leaves key questions unanswered, including who authorised the restriction and whether SpaceX acted on instructions from the US military or from Mr Trump.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A source told Reuters that SpaceX had limited terminal connections, complicating Ukrainian drone interceptions and mid-range strikes.

In an interview on the Piers Morgan Uncensored YouTube channel, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Mr Trump and Mr Musk of restraining Kyiv’s military access to SpaceX’s satellite technology, deepening the rift between Washington and Kyiv.

“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely,” Mr Zelenskyy said when asked if Ukraine’s use of the satellite service had been intentionally disrupted. “I think he is not right. It’s a big mistake.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ukraine also depends on US intelligence assistance for early warning of Russian missile launches. White House officials are actively discussing the possibility of cutting that arrangement with Ukraine, although there is no consensus on what to do, Semafor reported on Wednesday, quoting an unidentified administration official. Mr Trump said on Tuesday that the US continued to share intelligence with Ukraine.

His deal with Russia has drawn bipartisan criticism. On Tuesday, 12 senators wrote him a letter asking him to rescind it. One of the signatories, Republican Senator Thom Tillis, on Wednesday asked Mr Musk to clarify what was happening with Starlink.

"Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a grey area for the US government or for American corporations. Can you clarify the SpaceX position?" he wrote on X.

The suggestion that Mr Musk's company had ⁠limited Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.

"Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister ⁠Radoslaw Sikorski posted on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."

There was no immediate response from Mr Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man".

headline: What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
summary: Elon Musk’s ⁠SpaceX restricted “military-grade” ​Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.
body_text:
Elon Musk’s ⁠SpaceX restricted “military-grade” ​Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 22:15

The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, ​a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any ​limits on speed ‌or usage are decided by the US military or the president.

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled ⁠by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband ⁠service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is ‌the main profit engine of SpaceX.

Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company ​has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional ‌communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military ‌missions.

Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.

While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not ​always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.

Watch moreStarlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres

Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also ​provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.

The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars ​on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for ​missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX ​unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.

Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service ⁠costing about $25,000 per terminal.

Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals ⁠and separate network gateways, Britain’s ​defence ministry has told Reuters.

Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

body_text:
Manchester City's 4-2 defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Uefa Champions League told only part of ​the ​story of Enzo ​Maresca's first loss at the helm, with ⁠his men staggering through the first half before roaring ⁠back after the break.

⁠City were staring at a rout when a rampant PSG raced to a 3-0 lead with a first-half masterclass. Then they woke up.

Maresca's side tore into the visitors after half-time, pouring forward with ⁠an intensity and urgency that had been entirely absent in the opening 45 minutes.

Lammens: United must learn quickly and cut out defensive errors

Erling ​Haaland spearheaded ⁠the fightback, scoring twice to ‌become the fastest player to reach 60 Champions League goals, hitting the mark in ​just 60 games, 20 quicker than Lionel Messi.

City kept coming. They finished with nearly twice as many shots as PSG and around three times as many touches in the opposition box, while recording a higher expected goals figure at both half-time and full-time. PSG, though, were more ruthless.

“I think we start quite good until the first goal [from Desire Doue in the 13th minute] and then we concede the second one (Ousmane Dembele) after one minute. That created some bad feelings,” Maresca told TNT Sports.

“Second half, we were much better and probably deserved something more.”

City had arrived on the back of a 3-0 thrashing of Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday and Maresca felt they generated enough chances to salvage something even ​after digging themselves a three-goal hole.

“Even with 3-0 in the first ‌half, with the amount of ⁠chances we created in the second half, ​we deserved more,” he said. “Luis (Enrique, PSG's manager) said at the end of the ​game that ‌they were quite lucky today.

“You have to be clinical but not lose the balance,” Maresca said.

The ⁠defeat unfolded against a backdrop of turmoil stretching far beyond City as an independent commission found City guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period.

City have denied any wrongdoing and have appealed.

On the pitch, they remain three points clear of Arsenal atop ​the Premier League table ahead of Saturday's home game against Ipswich.

Asked if he had a message for supporters, Maresca said: “We are sorry for the first half for sure. Saturday is a Premier League game and we need to continue our run.”

Former City manager Pep Guardiola watched from the stands in Manchester alongside chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and senior executives Ferran Soriano and Hugo Viana.

On a breathless night of Champions League football featuring 46 goals, Real Madrid staged a stunning comeback to beat AS Roma 4-3.

At the ‌Stadio Olimpico, Real Madrid scored three times in the closing stages to overturn a two-goal deficit.

Marten de Roon gave Roma the lead ⁠in the 20th minute before Kylian Mbappe equalised five minutes later, but Donyell Malen struck twice in the 51st ⁠and 57th minutes to put the hosts in control.

The visitors mounted a remarkable comeback as Carlos Espi pulled a goal back in the 82nd minute before Endrick levelled three minutes later.

Former Roma defender Antonio Rudiger then completed the turnaround in the 90th minute, holding off his marker to steer home Arda Guler's corner from close range and snatch victory for ​the Spanish giants.

Meanwhile, Bradley Barcola scored a hat-trick in Liverpool's ⁠6-3 thrashing of LASK.

Barcola scored his first goals for the club during the rout of Champions League newcomers LASK in Austria.

Ronald Araujo, Jeremie Frimpong and Lewis Koumas also scored for Andoni Iraola's side, who bounced back from Sunday's 3-0 Premier League defeat by City. Florian Flecker struck twice for the hosts.

headline: PSG beat Manchester City in Champions League after financial rules verdict
summary: Defending champions Paris Saint-Germain held off a second-half comeback to beat Manchester City 4-2 away in the Champions League on Wednesday. Goals from Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha gave PSG a 3-0 lead before Erling Haaland struck twice. Maghnes Akliouche added a fourth, while Ferran Torres missed a late penalty.
body_text:
Defending champions Paris Saint-Germain held off a second-half comeback to beat Manchester City 4-2 away in the Champions League on Wednesday. Goals from Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha gave PSG a 3-0 lead before Erling Haaland struck twice. Maghnes Akliouche added a fourth, while Ferran Torres missed a late penalty.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 23:48Modified: 14/10/2026 - 23:49

Paris Saint-Germain further soured the mood at the Etihad Stadium as Manchester City's first home game since the guilty verdict on widespread flouting of Premier League financial rules ended in a 4-2 Champions League defeat on Wednesday.

The European champions turned on the style to strike three times inside the opening 35 minutes through Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha.

But City stormed back in the second half as Erling Haaland scored twice either side of Maghnes Akliouche's strike that briefly restored PSG's three-goal cushion.

The 10-time English champions face swingeing sanctions unless they can successfully appeal the ruling of an independent commission last month, which found the club guilty on over 100 charges of financial impropriety.

City shrugged off the uncertainty over their future to win 3-0 at Liverpool on Sunday and remain top of the Premier League, but PSG showed why they are the favourites to win this competition for a third consecutive season.

Read moreChampions League: Arsenal leave no chance to Lille and Olivier Giroud

Former City manager Pep Guardiola returned to the Etihad for the first time since his departure in May, sat behind the club's embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano in a show of solidarity.

City made passing reference to the guilty verdict with a lengthy pre-match video detailing the club's historic moments of celebration both before and after an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 that transformed their fortunes.

Behind one end supporters unravelled a giant banner reading: "I'm City till I die."

Yet the fighting talk in the stands was not matched on the field as City were blown away by a scintillating first 45 minutes from the visitors.

Luis Enrique's decision to leave Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the bench proved to be inspired as it meant Doue started wide on the left.

Gianluigi Donnarumma had a point to prove after the Italian goalkeeper was let go by the PSG coach just months after helping deliver the club's first Champions League title in 2025.

However, it turned out to be a night to forget for the giant Italian.

Donnarumma was caught out at his near post by Doue's effort from outside the box after a lightning counter-attack to open the scoring.

Read moreArsenal thrash Lille as Atletico Madrid beat Manchester United

The move for the second goal two minutes later was even more impressive as Doue and Dembele exchanged an elaborate one-two before the latter headed in at the far post.

Achraf Hakimi hit the post before Vitinha rattled in PSG's third from the edge of the box.

Maresca responded with a triple substitution at half-time and managed to salvage some pride, even if the deficit proved too much to overturn.

Antoine Semenyo and Enzo Fernandez missed glaring chances to pull a goal back even before Haaland glanced home a header from Iliman Ndiaye's cross.

Yet, City were hit by a sucker punch when Donnarumma got a hand to Akliouche's effort but the ball looped high into the air and spun back into the net.

Nuno Mendes made a brilliant clearance off his own line and Haaland hit the bar before the Norwegian slotted home his second of the night.

Donnarumma saved a late Ferran Torres penalty to deny the French champions a fifth goal.

But in the battle between two state-backed projects that have reshaped European football, Qatar-owned PSG are the top dogs right now as City face up to a scandal that leaves their litany of trophies over the past 15 years open to question.

headline: Trump claims again S. Korea to invest in Alaska LNG project under trade deal
summary: WASHINGTON, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that ...
body_text:
WASHINGTON, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that South Korea will invest US$50 billion in a massive liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska as part of an investment agreement with Washington, despite uncertainty over Seoul's participation.

"This 50 Billion Dollar Infrastructure Investment from The Republic of Korea is part of their Trade and Investment Deal with me," Trump wrote on Truth Social, while describing his visit to Alaska for a campaign rally on Tuesday.

The remarks were the latest from the Trump administration claiming that South Korea is committed to the Alaska LNG project. Seoul has maintained that its participation remains subject to a commercial viability review.

Trump also said that Taiwan has agreed to invest $4.4 billion in equity into the project, calling it the "greatest project in Alaska history."

White House Press Secretary Katie Zachariah also said Tuesday that $54 billion was tied to the Alaska LNG project as part of a South Korean energy investment package.

"President Trump also unveiled a South Korea energy investment package of up to $200 billion in the United States. This is an amazing deal. This includes as much as $120 billion to build eight large-scale nuclear power plants," Zachariah said.

"In addition to that, there is $54 billion tied to the Alaska LNG pipeline and terminal to service the Pacific Rim and sell fuel to our allies as well as $22.3 billion for a 6-gigawatt natural gas power facility in Texas," she added.

headline: Alaska LNG project becomes $54bn flashpoint for would-be Asian buyers
summary: A massive liquefied natural gas project in Alaska has emerged as an unlikely focal point in purported foreign investment, as Asian buyers rush to diversify their supply imports amid disruptions from the Iran war.On Tuesday in Wasilla, a town 70km north of Anchorage, US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 per cent of the LNG from the long-planned Alaska LNG project. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Taiwan had committed to investing $4.4 billion to develop the pipeline. Alaska has become a battleground state for control of the US Senate. Mr Trump’s appearance in Wasilla on Tuesday underscored the race’s importance as he seeks to promote energy exports and foreign investment.At the same time, the Alaska LNG project holds big promises, as South-East Asian buyers are seeking to diversify their energy supplies as the Iran war cut off shipments from the region.If Alaska LNG becomes operational, it would drastically reduce the time for delivery of LNG shipments. The journey from Alaska to Japan is more than 9,600km shorter than from the US Gulf Coast, the project's developer said in a 2023 report.Theory v practicalityFor all the promise that Alaska LNG holds, it remains a far-off venture. Development is expected to begin in phases, with targets for the first exports in 2031.Glenfarne Group estimates the project will cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion. That means about $2.2 billion to $2.7 billion a tonne a year of capacity, according to a Reuters analysis.“This is an expensive project that's going to take at best a lot of years to sort of come to fruition,” said Rachel Ziemba, founder of risk advisory firm Ziemba Insights.Another possible sticking point is the about 106cm-diameter pipeline that would stretch 1,300km from Alaska’s North Slope to Nikiski, south of Anchorage, running parallel to the existing Trans Alaska Pipeline System for oil. LNG sites in Nikiski would produce 20 million tonnes a year for export and hold a daily capacity of 3.3 billion cubic feet.The pipeline itself – Phase One – is likely to cost between $13.2 billion and $16.9 billion, according to company estimates. “If the gas is sitting right next to the LNG facility, this thing would have been built 40 or 50 years ago, but it's not, and … that's the difference maker in this project,” Mr Joseph said.Investors remain cautious. As of January this year, only six non-binding offtake agreements have been signed totalling 13 million tonnes a year. Another point of friction is competition, with LNG projects in Canada and in America's Gulf Coast also attracting attention.Major players in the Middle East have continued to increase their interest in LNG, but through the Gulf Coast. body_text:
A massive liquefied natural gas project in Alaska has emerged as an unlikely focal point in purported foreign investment, as Asian buyers rush to diversify their supply imports amid disruptions from the Iran war.

On Tuesday in Wasilla, a town 70km north of Anchorage, US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 per cent of the LNG from the long-planned Alaska LNG project. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Taiwan had committed to investing $4.4 billion to develop the pipeline. The terms of the deal were not immediately clear.

Last week, Mr Trump announced a $54 billion South Korea investment in Alaska LNG as part of a $200 billion energy package and $350 billion trade deal the two sides struck last year to lower tariffs on Korean imports. South Korea has rejected the claim, saying it has given no firm commitment on the project.

US LNG emerges as Gulf hedge against Hormuz disruption

“There's no investors other than the US government, and there are no buyers who have committed to signing any sales and purchase agreements,” said Ira Joseph, a global fellow at the Centre on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University.

The project hopes to make a final investment decision on the pipeline this year, with a separate one on the export terminal in 2027.

One of the dominant factors in the publicly promoted claims are the November 3 midterm elections. Alaska has become a battleground state for control of the US Senate. Mr Trump’s appearance in Wasilla on Tuesday underscored the race’s importance as he seeks to promote energy exports and foreign investment.

At the same time, the Alaska LNG project holds big promises, as South-East Asian buyers are seeking to diversify their energy supplies as the Iran war cut off shipments from the region.

If Alaska LNG becomes operational, it would drastically reduce the time for delivery of LNG shipments. The journey from Alaska to Japan is more than 9,600km shorter than from the US Gulf Coast, the project's developer said in a 2023 report.

For all the promise that Alaska LNG holds, it remains a far-off venture. Development is expected to begin in phases, with targets for the first exports in 2031.

Glenfarne Group estimates the project will cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion. That means about $2.2 billion to $2.7 billion a tonne a year of capacity, according to a Reuters analysis.

“This is an expensive project that's going to take at best a lot of years to sort of come to fruition,” said Rachel Ziemba, founder of risk advisory firm Ziemba Insights.

Another possible sticking point is the about 106cm-diameter pipeline that would stretch 1,300km from Alaska’s North Slope to Nikiski, south of Anchorage, running parallel to the existing Trans Alaska Pipeline System for oil. LNG sites in Nikiski would produce 20 million tonnes a year for export and hold a daily capacity of 3.3 billion cubic feet.

The pipeline itself – Phase One – is likely to cost between $13.2 billion and $16.9 billion, according to company estimates.

“If the gas is sitting right next to the LNG facility, this thing would have been built 40 or 50 years ago, but it's not, and … that's the difference maker in this project,” Mr Joseph said.

Investors remain cautious. As of January this year, only six non-binding offtake agreements have been signed totalling 13 million tonnes a year.

Another point of friction is competition, with LNG projects in Canada and in America's Gulf Coast also attracting attention.

Major players in the Middle East have continued to increase their interest in LNG, but through the Gulf Coast. This summer, Adnoc's XRG boosted its stake in NextDecade's LNG site in Rio Grande, Texas. QatarEnergy began LNG exports from its joint venture with Exxon at the Golden Pass project in March.

“It is notable to me that at a time where you know Trump is looking for all the finance he can for this project, that he's not turning to these sources of capital,” Ms Ziemba said.

headline: Houthis threaten escalation after strike on Saudi oil giant Aramco
summary: Yemen's Houthi rebels said Wednesday they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco after officials in Riyadh reported a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant's headquarters. The Iran-back militia also claimed missile strikes on the capital Riyadh and vowed to continue attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities.
body_text:
Yemen's Houthi rebels said Wednesday they had targeted facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco after officials in Riyadh reported a strike on a building in an area housing the energy giant's headquarters. The Iran-back militia also claimed missile strikes on the capital Riyadh and vowed to continue attacking Saudi airports and oil facilities.
