Yemen's Houthis vowed on Wednesday to press on with attacks on airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, a day after a strike that sources said caused extensive damage to the headquarters of oil giant Saudi Aramco.

The Houthis said the threatened locations were legitimate targets and described their attacks as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen – threatening to escalate a conflict reignited by the US-Iran confrontation in the Gulf.

Saudi Arabia has faced widening Houthi strikes over the past week, including an attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people.

Read moreSaudi Arabia threatens 'decisive' response after Riyadh airport strike kills at least 12

Tuesday night's attack on Saudi Aramco's base in the eastern city of Dhahran caused a fire that spread across several floors, three people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters. The Saudi energy ministry had said the strike caused a limited fire.

Operations at Aramco were continuing normally, with employees working from home, according to two of the sources. Aramco did not immediately reply to a Reuters request for comment.

Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said the Iran-backed group had conducted "a high-quality military operation targeting Aramco in Dhahran", as well as strikes targeting Riyadh airport and a refinery in the capital.

He added the attacks were carried out with missiles and drones, and that operations "will continue in the coming days, targeting Saudi enemy airports and oil facilities".

The escalating conflict has dealt a blow to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's ambitious plans to transform and diversify the Saudi economy and reduce its reliance on oil.

The Houthis say they have been retaliating for the kingdom's backing of Yemeni government forces in the Yemen war that restarted last month.

The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh on Wednesday, and several loud booms were heard in the Saudi capital.

Saudi authorities earlier issued an alert for a possible aerial threat in Riyadh on Wednesday before the warning was lifted, a witness said. It wasn't immediately clear what caused the booms and there was no immediate comment from the authorities on their source.

The Saudi government media office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about the cause of the booms.

Read moreBlasts rock Riyadh as Houthis target Saudi airports, oil facilities

In their statement on Wednesday, the Houthis said they had launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones at the Saudi Aramco facilities in Dhahran, Riyadh airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.

In a broad threat, they urged "international shipping companies", civilians and workers to evacuate Saudi airports and oil facilities.

The Dhahran complex hosts a major operations centre for Aramco, which oversees a vast network of onshore and offshore oil rigs, pipelines, refineries and export terminals.

Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including Saturday's attack which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade.

Authorities have closed the airport until October 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.

Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.

The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until this year.

Saudi Arabia resumed its military campaign in Yemen in support of the internationally recognised government in a bid to reverse the Houthis' sudden gains last month, when they swept down the Red Sea coast to the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Red Cross said on Wednesday that hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties as fighting intensified along multiple front lines.

The UN World Food Programme warned that life-saving assistance had been cut off to the government-held city of Taiz, which was encircled by Houthi fighters earlier this month.

"WFP and its partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children," WFP said in a statement.

headline: Pakistan reiterates 'unwavering' commitment to Saudi Arabia's protection under Makkah defense pact
summary: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif meets alliance's newly appointed secretary general, retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood, in Islamabad
body_text:
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday characterized the Makkah Defense Alliance as a “historic" milestone for peace, unity and stability in the region as he reaffirmed Islamabad's “unwavering commitment” to the protection of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.Sharif made the remarks during a meeting with the newly appointed Makkah Defense Alliance Secretary General, retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood, who briefed him on the strategy to promote defense and strategic cooperation under the pact, according to a statement from the prime minister’s office.

Mahmood was appointed as the first secretary general of the defense alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in August.The pact allows member states to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

The meeting comes as Saudi Arabia has faced escalating tensions with Yemen’s Houthi group in recent weeks.

Sharif reiterated that Pakistan stands "shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia has faced missile and drone attacks amid escalating hostilities with Houthis after a truce in the long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unraveled in July.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers.

A Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Wednesday that it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, shortly after warning alerts were activated in the city and nearby Al-Kharj governorate.

The Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government has been in place since 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several provinces since 2014.

headline: Fatah, Hamas set to meet in Cairo for Palestinian unity talks as elections get pushed to 2027
summary: Palestinian factions are seeking common ground on political representation and governance, nearly two decades after a split that has left Gaza and the occupied West Bank under separate administrations. Palestinian…
body_text:
Palestinian factions are seeking common ground on political representation and governance, nearly two decades after a split that has left Gaza and the occupied West Bank under separate administrations. Palestinian factions, including Fatah and Hamas, are set to begin preparatory talks in Cairo on Wednesday, in another attempt to bridge longstanding political divisions and lay the groundwork for a broader national dialogue.

Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) will also participate in the meetings on 14 and 15 October, Anadolu Agency reported, citing Fatah spokesperson Abdel Fattah Dawla.

The discussions will focus on preparations for wider negotiations and efforts to build consensus among Palestinian factions, with a further round of talks potentially taking place on 20 October, depending on the outcomes of the preliminary meetings. Anadolu reported Fatah’s delegation will include Central Committee member Jibril Rajoub and committee member Mohammed Shtayyeh, both expected to arrive in the Egyptian capital on Wednesday.

The meetings follow two days of discussions in Cairo last week involving Fatah, Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the PFLP, as Egypt continues its efforts to bring the Palestinian factions towards a common political position.

It also comes days after Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections and scheduled simultaneous parliamentary votes for 11 September 2027.

What is at stake in the Cairo talks?

Beyond preparations for another round of negotiations, the Cairo meetings raise questions about how Palestinian factions could agree on a unified political leadership and the future administration of Palestinian territories. While Hamas has been in control of Gaza since 2007, the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority has been in control of the West Bank.

As previously reported by the Associated Press, longstanding disagreements over political representation and the governance have hindered reconciliation efforts, including repeated attempts to bring Hamas and Islamic Jihad into the Palestine Liberation Organisation.

The factions have attempted to address some of their issues before. As per the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in July 2024, Fatah, Hamas and 12 other Palestinian factions signed the Beijing Declarations, agreeing in principle to form an interim national reconciliation government and work towards unified Palestinian institutions. However, the agreement did not produce a lasting political settlement.

For the latest Cairo discussions, agreement on the agenda, priorities and framework for further negotiations is set to be expected.

Why have the Palestinian elections been delayed again?

The latest talks come against the backdrop of another postponement of Palestinian elections, extending an already lengthy absence of national voting.

On October 10, Abbas issued a decree scheduling simultaneous presidential and legislative elections for September 11, 2027, replacing plans to hold legislative elections in November 2026.

Al Jazeera reported on the PLO citing deteriorating conditions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, including Israeli restrictions affecting the movement of the election materials and international observers, as obstacles to conducting the vote.

Fatah welcomed the decision, while Hamas called for comprehensive national dialogue and binding agreements on reorganising Palestinian political institutions according to Anadolu.

Palestinians last voted in a presidential election in 2005, when Abbas was elected, and in legislative elections in 2006, which Hamas had won.

A previous attempt to hold presidential and legislative elections in 2021 was also postponed, with Abbas citing uncertainty over whether Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem would be permitted to participate.

headline: Oil transfers off India's west coast surge as Gulf shipping congestion worsens
summary: Gulf oil producers are pushing tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashing prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around Hormuz buckles under congestion and attack.Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch reached 82 cargoes in September, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, according to shipping analytics company Vortexa. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder."Fujairah and Sohar STS zones were handling record volumes with some indications of delays relating to operational limitations, and thus the activity has spilled over to India,” said Varaleka Pant, senior market analyst at energy intelligence firm VortexaThe expansion shows how the workaround sustaining Gulf exports is coming under strain. Producers have shuttled oil through Hormuz before transferring it to supertankers outside the strait, but congestion and longer voyages are tying up vessels and driving up costs.Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict."The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said.A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes.Transfers move eastThe shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale.South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa.In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data.Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally."The Gulf of Oman remains the main area for this," said Niels Rasmussen, Bimco's chief shipping analyst.The increase is unlikely to have changed overall tanker demand significantly, he said, though longer voyages to transfer points mean more ships are needed.Yui Torikata of Kpler cautioned that some eastern transfer arrangements were in place before the recent shift, including Japanese refiners receiving Aramco and Adnoc cargoes off Malaysia. Kpler has yet to establish how much activity has shifted east.Reported tanker activity near Sri Lanka is largely unrelated. Vortexa said vessels there were primarily sanctioned Iranian tankers stranded after discharging pre-blockade cargoes, while Bimco recorded no STS operations off the island.Security versus costMoving transfers farther from Hormuz reduces the exposure of receiving tankers but does not eliminate the danger of transporting oil out of the Gulf."The STS transfer itself is relatively low risk. The real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone” Ms Pant said.Kutch offers relatively calm waters and proximity to Indian refiners, but the cargoes must still pass through contested routes before reaching the transfer point. Buyers could retreat after a security incident on that route, if discounts fail to cover higher freight and STS costs, or if congestion spreads to India, she said.Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal is the safest place to take delivery, according to Kpler, because receiving tankers can avoid both Hormuz and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. But the journey to Asia takes about 55 days, compared with just over 20 days from the Gulf of Oman, according to Mr Torikata.Disruptions to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have also left Japanese-chartered tankers waiting for cargoes there, he said. Japanese refiners, and to a lesser extent South Korean ones, rely on medium-sour crude for blending, limiting their ability to switch suppliers.A Japanese refiner paid a record high price of above $80 million to charter a tanker from the US Gulf Coast to Japan, Mr Torikata said."If they paid such high [rates] to buy US crude, they would go to Sidi Kerir to buy Arab Light as it takes approximately the same time as sourcing from the US Gulf Coast," he added. Arab Light is also favoured by Japanese refiners over US light sweet oil.Discounts deepenThe disruption is dividing Gulf producers between those cutting prices to compensate buyers for transit risks and those able to command premiums for more secure supply.Iraq, which has no export route around Hormuz, offered October-loading Basrah Medium at a discount of $34.50 a barrel and Basrah Heavy at $37, compared with discounts below $30 in August, according to Rystad.The reductions have helped restore Iraqi production to within 10 per cent of pre-war levels, Rystad said. Iraq now pumps almost 70 per cent as much crude as Saudi Arabia, compared with less than 40 per cent before the conflict.Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asian buyers by $3 to $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, the widest discount since 2020, defying market expectations of an increase.QatarEnergy also cut its November prices by $3, setting Qatar Marine at $8 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average and Qatar Land at $7.50 below, according to a pricing document.“In the short term, deep discounting of crude is protecting market share more effectively by providing price incentive for buyers to lift crude from the Gulf, but it’s a situational move,” Ms Pant said.Adnoc has taken a different approach, benefiting from its ability to export Murban crude through Fujairah without passing through Hormuz."Murban carries none of the transit risk the other cuts compensate for," Mr Choudhary said. "It reaches Fujairah by pipeline and loads outside Hormuz, so buyers pay a premium for it."The grade traded as much as $26 a barrel above Dubai swaps in late September before easing to about $15, according to Rystad.For its other grades, Adnoc has used spot tenders rather than resetting official prices, preserving flexibility while testing what buyers will pay, according to Vortexa.The divergence underscores how secure access to export infrastructure has become a competitive advantage, allowing some producers to protect margins while others sacrifice revenue to keep their oil flowing.Beyond priceGulf producers are increasingly taking on transit and security risks themselves to keep Asian customers.Adnoc, Aramco, Iraq and Qatar now offer STS deliveries outside Hormuz, and Kuwait has adopted the same approach to attract buyers, according to Mr Choudhary. These arrangements let buyers receive cargoes without sending their own tankers through the strait.The UAE has also moved to lock in Asian demand. Adnoc agreed in May to explore raising its crude storage in India to as much as 30 million barrels, from about 5.9 million at Mangalore.Aramco, which sold more than 60 million barrels for transfer off Sohar for September and October deliveries, is negotiating term contracts for next year involving loadings outside Hormuz, Mr Choudhary said, signalling that buyers and sellers alike expect the arrangement to last.

Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict.

"The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said.

A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes.

The shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale.

South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa.

In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data.

Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally.

"The Gulf of Oman remains the main area for this," said Niels Rasmussen, Bimco's chief shipping analyst.

The increase is unlikely to have changed overall tanker demand significantly, he said, though longer voyages to transfer points mean more ships are needed.

Yui Torikata of Kpler cautioned that some eastern transfer arrangements were in place before the recent shift, including Japanese refiners receiving Aramco and Adnoc cargoes off Malaysia. Kpler has yet to establish how much activity has shifted east.

Reported tanker activity near Sri Lanka is largely unrelated. Vortexa said vessels there were primarily sanctioned Iranian tankers stranded after discharging pre-blockade cargoes, while Bimco recorded no STS operations off the island.

Moving transfers farther from Hormuz reduces the exposure of receiving tankers but does not eliminate the danger of transporting oil out of the Gulf.

"The STS transfer itself is relatively low risk. The real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone” Ms Pant said.

Kutch offers relatively calm waters and proximity to Indian refiners, but the cargoes must still pass through contested routes before reaching the transfer point. Buyers could retreat after a security incident on that route, if discounts fail to cover higher freight and STS costs, or if congestion spreads to India, she said.

Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal is the safest place to take delivery, according to Kpler, because receiving tankers can avoid both Hormuz and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. But the journey to Asia takes about 55 days, compared with just over 20 days from the Gulf of Oman, according to Mr Torikata.

Disruptions to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have also left Japanese-chartered tankers waiting for cargoes there, he said. Japanese refiners, and to a lesser extent South Korean ones, rely on medium-sour crude for blending, limiting their ability to switch suppliers.

A Japanese refiner paid a record high price of above $80 million to charter a tanker from the US Gulf Coast to Japan, Mr Torikata said.

"If they paid such high [rates] to buy US crude, they would go to Sidi Kerir to buy Arab Light as it takes approximately the same time as sourcing from the US Gulf Coast," he added. Arab Light is also favoured by Japanese refiners over US light sweet oil.

The disruption is dividing Gulf producers between those cutting prices to compensate buyers for transit risks and those able to command premiums for more secure supply.

Iraq, which has no export route around Hormuz, offered October-loading Basrah Medium at a discount of $34.50 a barrel and Basrah Heavy at $37, compared with discounts below $30 in August, according to Rystad.

The reductions have helped restore Iraqi production to within 10 per cent of pre-war levels, Rystad said. Iraq now pumps almost 70 per cent as much crude as Saudi Arabia, compared with less than 40 per cent before the conflict.

Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asian buyers by $3 to $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, the widest discount since 2020, defying market expectations of an increase.

QatarEnergy also cut its November prices by $3, setting Qatar Marine at $8 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average and Qatar Land at $7.50 below, according to a pricing document.

“In the short term, deep discounting of crude is protecting market share more effectively by providing price incentive for buyers to lift crude from the Gulf, but it’s a situational move,” Ms Pant said.

Adnoc has taken a different approach, benefiting from its ability to export Murban crude through Fujairah without passing through Hormuz.

"Murban carries none of the transit risk the other cuts compensate for," Mr Choudhary said. "It reaches Fujairah by pipeline and loads outside Hormuz, so buyers pay a premium for it."

The grade traded as much as $26 a barrel above Dubai swaps in late September before easing to about $15, according to Rystad.

For its other grades, Adnoc has used spot tenders rather than resetting official prices, preserving flexibility while testing what buyers will pay, according to Vortexa.

The divergence underscores how secure access to export infrastructure has become a competitive advantage, allowing some producers to protect margins while others sacrifice revenue to keep their oil flowing.

Gulf producers are increasingly taking on transit and security risks themselves to keep Asian customers.

Adnoc, Aramco, Iraq and Qatar now offer STS deliveries outside Hormuz, and Kuwait has adopted the same approach to attract buyers, according to Mr Choudhary. These arrangements let buyers receive cargoes without sending their own tankers through the strait.

The UAE has also moved to lock in Asian demand. Adnoc agreed in May to explore raising its crude storage in India to as much as 30 million barrels, from about 5.9 million at Mangalore.

Aramco, which sold more than 60 million barrels for transfer off Sohar for September and October deliveries, is negotiating term contracts for next year involving loadings outside Hormuz, Mr Choudhary said, signalling that buyers and sellers alike expect the arrangement to last.

body_text:
The 2026-27 Saudi Pro League season is now well under way and the latest influx of talent is already influencing the title race. This summer’s recruitment was concentrated on investing heavily in established internationals still in their prime. Several of the most expensive arrivals have wasted little time in justifying their price tags while others have faced criticism.

Al Hilal lead the standings on 21 points, two clear of Al Qadsiah and defending champions Al Nassr. Below, we take a look at how the competition’s latest wave of imports have performed.

English Premier League side Arsenal recorded their record sale when Martinelli signed for Al Hilal in September for £60 million, with the Brazilian highlighting his pride at joining a club that countryman Neymar played for.

Martinelli, though, will clearly be hoping for a far more successful stint at Hilal than the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain attacker, who had his contract terminated after an injury-ravaged 18 months in Riyadh.

After a subdued debut off the bench against Al Shabab, Martinelli conceded he might need “some time to adapt” to his new surroundings having been with the Gunners since 2019.

Those concerns appeared to be unfounded as the 25-year-old bagged a hat-trick little over a week later as Hilal demolished Al Taawoun 6-0, ending his seven-month goal drought. He then opened the scoring in the Saudi Clasico win over Al Ittihad on Saturday, taking his league tally to four in four appearances.

“He’s a big player and we are lucky to have Martinelli,” manager Simone Inzaghi noted after Tuesday’s 2-0 AFC Champions League win at Al Sadd.

Reijnders was honest about his motives after completing a £52m move from Manchester City. “Me a money grabber? I can't deny that,” he said. “By signing this contract, I can make sure even my grandchildren are financially secure, so why wouldn’t I do it?”

Qadsiah manager Brendan Rodgers has given him the box-to-box role he prefers and he responded by scoring in his first start in the 2-0 win over Neom. The 28-year-old then scored a double in the 3-2 defeat of Al Ahli at the beginning of September and opened the scoring in Friday’s 5-0 victory over Al Kholood.

Three of his four league goals have come from outside the box, more than any other player in the SPL this season.

Summerville joined in a £60m switch from West Ham United who had just been relegated to English football's second tier.

The 24-year-old's first goal arrived against Al Khaleej in his third appearance when he scored the fourth goal with a dinked finish as Hilal ran out 5-1 winners. Summerville also supplied his first two assists in that game.

He was on target again the following week, this time driving home a low finish from a tight angle and also scored a fine winner against Al Ittihad. Summerville has registered three goals and three assists in eight league appearances.

Al Nassr signed Costa from Mallorca for €22m at the request of new coach Ange Postecoglou, with the 25-year-old Portuguese midfielder recruited to replace Marcelo Brozovic.

He was bought to give the reigning champions greater energy in midfield but his early performances have attracted criticism.

Speaking on TV, former Al Nassr defender Hussein Abdulghani called the signing of Costa “disastrous”, and dismissed comparisons with Brozovic, claiming Cristiano Ronaldo had encouraged management to sign his countryman.

But it has not all been bad with Costa scoring three times in seven SPl appearances, including Friday's 3-0 win over Diriyah, while it was his cross that Anvar Gofurov turned into his own net to seal a 3-1 Champions League win over Neftchi on Monday.

Former Barcelona attacker Trincao insisted “the passion of Al Ahli supporters was one of the main reasons” he moved to the Jeddah club in a €40m deal from Sporting.

But passionate fans are also demanding and the player tasked with replacing the much-loved Riyad Mahrez has struggled at times as Marino Pusic’s side lost three of their opening six games.

But the 26-year-old Portuguese appears to be finding his feet, scoring four times in his last four SPL matches, including a double against Al Fateh on Friday that earned him the man-of-the-match award. Trincao then scored one and supplied another as back-to-back Asian title winners Al Ahli defeated UAE outfit Al Wasl 3-1 in Dubai in the Champions League three days later.

Al Hilal forked out £50m to Aston Villa for England striker Watkins who the club had been monitoring since last season, according to Inzaghi.

The 30-year-old scored on his debut against Al Ahli and was delighted by the reception he was given. “The fans were calling my name. From minute one, it was amazing,” he said. He later described Saudi football as being of “Premier League quality”.

Watkins has already registered five goals and four assists from his six appearances for Hilal and played a role in all three goals in their 3-2 win over Al Ittihad. He was on target again on Tuesday after opening the scoring in Tuesday's win away to Qatari side Al Sadd.

headline: Russia hits at least ten thermal, hydroelectric power plants in Ukraine since early 2026
summary: The first strike on such an infrastructure facility occurred on August 9, when a combined heat and power plant in Odessa that supported the port's operations was destroyed
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Since the beginning of the year, Russian servicemen have struck at least ten Ukrainian hydroelectric and thermal power plants, including combined heat and power plants used for military purposes, according to TASS calculations based on the Russian Defense Ministry’s reports.

The first strike on such an infrastructure facility occurred on August 9, when a combined heat and power plant in Odessa that supported the port's operations was destroyed. On September 1, the Russian Armed Forces struck the Odessa combined heat and power plant. On September 30, the Russian army hit the Kievskaya power substation and hydroelectric power plant, as well as the Tripolskaya thermal power plant. All of these facilities serve Ukraine’s military-industrial complex.

On October 14, Russian servicemen launched a massive strike targeting the Darnitskaya combined heat and power plant, the Kievskaya-5 and Kievskaya-6 combined heat and power plants, the Tripolskaya thermal power plant, and the Kievskaya power substation in the Kiev region. In addition, the Kharkovskaya combined heat and power plant and the Zmievskaya thermal power plant in the Kharkov region were damaged by Russian drone and precision-guided weapons strikes.

Global Village has reopened in Dubai for its 31st season, with new restaurants, live shows and a rollercoaster added to the popular multicultural festival park.

The outdoor destination welcomed visitors back on Wednesday and will remain open until May 2027. Running under the theme A More Wonderful World, the season features 29 pavilions representing more than 90 cultures, plus more than 3,500 shopping outlets and more than 250 dining options.

Opening-night celebrations included a choir performance, the Parade of the World and the destination’s signature confetti shower at the Gate of the World. A display featuring 600 drones also marked the season's start.

UAE attractions reopening for winter, from Global Village to Sharjah Safari

Among the additions is Tokyo Rush, a rollercoaster scheduled to open later in the season, featuring sharp turns and a loop. It will join returning attractions including Dragon Kingdom, The Horror Hotel, Secrets of the Lost City and Exo Planet City.

The Festival Wheel returns with refreshed carts offering panoramic views of the destination, while the Gardens of the World has also been updated.

Across the cultural attractions, visitors will find refreshed experiences at the Sri Lanka pavilion and the Russia and Azerbaijan areas. The Syria and Kuwait pavilions have new facades.

A redesigned Season 31 passport and a new passport for children allow visitors to collect stamps as they explore the pavilions.

Fernando Eiroa, chief executive of Dubai Holding Entertainment, said: “Global Village holds a special place in people’s lives because of the connections they make here, with their own roots, with other cultures and the people they visit alongside. It has become a much-loved tradition for families and friends, reflecting the welcoming, multicultural spirit of the UAE.”

Restaurant Plaza, beside Carnaval and overlooking the Falcon Stage, has several new additions, including Trabzon Turkish Restaurant, Robo Al Sham, Hawawshi Al Rabie and Chicking.

New cafes include Vinci Dolci, Emir Bey Gourmet and Uzungol Cafe. Dessert District also returns with a refreshed facade and a selection of sweet treats.

The venues join a wider dining offering of more than 250 options, spanning international street food, restaurants and cafes.

Global Village will host 40,000 shows throughout the season, with a programme spanning music, dance, acrobatics and family entertainment.

New productions include Fast Live 2: The Police Strike Back, a stunt show featuring driving manoeuvres and action sequences. Bollywood Idol and Bank Heist also join the programme, alongside returning show Slam.

For younger visitors, characters from Care Bears and PJ Masks return to the Kids Theatre.

Upgrades to amenities include a new VIP parking self-payment system, improved directional signage and expanded ticketing capacity at Happiness Gate.

Additional family washrooms have been introduced, including accessible areas for people of determination. Other updates include bilingual signage at the Gate of the World, upgraded lighting at Cultural Gate and a new theme for the Sharjah tunnel.

A new WhatsApp chatbot will provide visitors with information and assistance during their visit.

Global Village is open from 4pm to midnight on Sunday to Wednesday, with extended hours until 1am on Thursday to Saturday and on public holidays.

Tickets cost Dh30, or Dh25 from Monday to Thursday excluding public holidays. They are available through the Global Village website, app and gate counters.

Tuesdays are reserved for families, couples and women, except on public holidays.

headline: Prolonged war, renewed disruptions pose biggest risk to Middle East region, IMF says
summary: By Andrea ShalalBANGKOK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure.
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.

Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure.

"The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries’ ability to preserve macroeconomic stability," Azour said at a news conference during the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. The IMF will release a fuller outlook for the region on October 22.

Pre-war surpluses, alternative routes, demand adjustments and substantial inventory drawdowns had helped contain the impact of the energy shock caused by the US-Israeli-led attacks on Iran and Tehran's subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments," he said.

The global lender is forecasting a deep contraction of 1.3% in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region after growth of 3.3% in 2025, followed by a strong but uneven rebound in 2027, when growth is expected to hit 6.6%, Azour said, noting substantial differences across the region.

The forecast assumes a resumption of normal trade and shipping in the first quarter of 2027, with exports gradually normalizing by mid-year and oil prices staying higher.

Azour said the forecast was predicated on a quick resumption of production, noting that Qatar, for instance, had been able to accelerate its recovery despite suffering massive destruction of its natural gas capacity.

But he said the shock would have a scarring impact on various sectors, with damage to infrastructure requiring additional spending, and the risks were tilted to the downside.

Oil-exporting countries directly affected by the war would see a significant contraction in 2026 and a sharp rebound in growth in 2027 as energy production normalizes, but output was expected to remain below pre-war medium-term projections.

The economies of oil-importing countries in the region had been resilient and were expected to remain so, he said.

The Caucasus and Central Asia region had weathered the shock relatively well and inflation was expected to continue declining from elevated levels. The IMF is projecting growth to slow to 5.2% in 2026 and then 5% in 2027, from growth of 6.2% in2025.

Azour said policymakers should prioritize price stability, focus on rebuilding fiscal buffers and expand their capacity to withstand future shocks.

(Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by John Mair)

headline: Trump open to Russia-US economic cooperation after peace in Ukraine — newspaper
summary: US officials opined that Trump reached an agreement on Russian diesel supplies in order, first, to lower fuel prices in the US, and second, to "offer economic and political benefits" to Russia to engage in negotiations
body_text:
NEW YORK, October 15. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump is open to developing economic relations with Russia after the conflict in Ukraine is settled, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources.

According to the newspaper, the US leader would first like to de-escalate hostilities between Russia and Ukraine and then present Moscow with a proposal for a long-term ceasefire. In conversations with The Wall Street Journal, US officials opined that Trump reached an agreement on Russian diesel supplies in order, first, to lower fuel prices in the US, and second, to "offer economic and political benefits" to Russia to engage in negotiations. The newspaper’s sources added that Trump is open to future economic relations between the US and Russia once the Ukrainian conflict is settled.

However, Ukrainian and European officials are dissatisfied with US actions. Threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Kiev were followed by restrictions on the operation of the Starlink satellite communication system in Ukraine, the Wall Street Journal noted. The White House declined to comment on issues regarding access to Starlink. "The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done," a US official told the newspaper.

Earlier, Sergey Beskrestnov, an advisor to Vladimir Zelensky and an expert in communications and unmanned systems, said that SpaceX had limited the operating speed of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian military to 160 kilometers per hour.

Later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk stated that the Starlink system is used solely for defense and civilian purposes, not for offensive military operations.

headline: Houthis make ‘major leap’ building advanced missiles with greater Middle East range

Its engineers have developed the Palestine-2 missile that has the capability to manoeuvre during its terminal stage at 6,000kph, allowing it to evade defences. It was allegedly responsible for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport attack that killed 13.Attacks by the Houthis have significantly increased in the past month and are designed to put pressure on Saudi Arabia to end its blockade of the Yemen rebels.Major leapThe Houthis have been significantly helped by specialist parts for missiles imported from China, according to the Conflict Armament Research report passed to The National.Its teams examined weaponry from an intercepted shipment that had been heading to the Houthi-held port of Hodeida. The haul included highly specialist machined parts for rockets such as stabilising fins and equipment for hypersonic flight.“The discovery points to a major leap in the group’s domestic production ambitions and has major regional security implications at a time when Houthi forces are intensifying their deep strike campaign against critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia,” the report said.The components, discovered in containers on a cargo ship from China, demonstrate that the Houthis are now advanced in their work to manufacture the Iranian-made Kheibar Shekan series of ballistic missiles. Their Palestine-2 variant has a range of 1,800km, bringing much of the Middle East into their sights.The findings also demonstrate that the rebels, who are under a UN arms embargo, have expanded their supply chains beyond their traditional Iran-linked networks, the paper said.“The documented components suggest that, in terms of longer-range ballistic missiles, the Houthis have moved beyond simply reassembling Iranian systems,” it stated.“Only a few countries in the world have the capacity to manufacture missiles of comparable ranges domestically.”Accelerated progressWhile the Houthis have “not yet mastered” the technology for the Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile, Iranian expertise on the ground is “accelerating their progress”, said Dr Nawaf Obaid, of Kings College London.“Their principal constraint is time, not technical impossibility,” he told The National.While it is understood the airport attack involved several projectiles in a swarm attack, the Houthis currently cannot build significant numbers, he added.“Scale remains their weakness,” he said. Analysis by Kings College's department of war studies showed that 85 to 90 per cent of missiles were intercepted by Saudi Arabia’s advanced defence system, he added.It is understood that the Houthis exploited a gap between Saudi Arabia’s lower and middle air defence layers in the airport attack, rather than a “technological breakthrough”, said Dr Obaid. He added that the kingdom’s air defences were “performing exceptionally well under sustained wartime conditions”.UK support for RiyadhDocuments show the contents from four shipping containers arrived in the Aden Free Zone in Yemen in June and October 2025 from China.The shipments contained custom-made metal parts including components of the airframe and a solid-propellant rocket motor for a Kheibar Shekan missile.They were made by a Chinese precision-metal producer “that advertises itself as a specialist manufacturer of custom aerospace parts”, the report said.It demonstrated that the Houthis were buying “more specialised parts for the construction of missiles, apparently independent of Iran-linked supply networks”.According to UN reports, Chinese companies form the biggest source of seized goods bound for the Houthis and they have been importing components for solid-fuel missiles from China for at least two years. China has stated that it adheres to the UN Houthi arms ban.Asked by The National what action the UK government might take against Chinese companies allegedly supplying components, the prime minister’s official spokesman said Britain “strongly condemns Houthi attacks and remains committed to supporting the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”.Saudi Arabia's ambassador to London told a meeting of parliamentarians on Tuesday that the UK's support in the face of the Houthi missile menace was welcomed by his government. Prince Abdullah bin Khaled held discussions focused on “recent Houthi attacks against the kingdom, regional security, and the importance of international co-operation in safeguarding stability and supporting peace in Yemen”, an embassy post on social media said.
body_text:
Yemen's Houthis have made a “major leap” in locally producing sophisticated ballistic missiles using components imported from China, an arms intelligence report has revealed.

Experts have also told The National that the militia's manufacturing was becoming increasingly sophisticated. Its engineers have developed the Palestine-2 missile that has the capability to manoeuvre during its terminal stage at 6,000kph, allowing it to evade defences. It was allegedly responsible for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport attack that killed 13.

Attacks by the Houthis have significantly increased in the past month and are designed to put pressure on Saudi Arabia to end its blockade of the Yemen rebels.

Houthis test 'weapons no other armed group possesses'

The Houthis have been significantly helped by specialist parts for missiles imported from China, according to the Conflict Armament Research report passed to The National.

Its teams examined weaponry from an intercepted shipment that had been heading to the Houthi-held port of Hodeida. The haul included highly specialist machined parts for rockets such as stabilising fins and equipment for hypersonic flight.

“The discovery points to a major leap in the group’s domestic production ambitions and has major regional security implications at a time when Houthi forces are intensifying their deep strike campaign against critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia,” the report said.

The components, discovered in containers on a cargo ship from China, demonstrate that the Houthis are now advanced in their work to manufacture the Iranian-made Kheibar Shekan series of ballistic missiles. Their Palestine-2 variant has a range of 1,800km, bringing much of the Middle East into their sights.

The findings also demonstrate that the rebels, who are under a UN arms embargo, have expanded their supply chains beyond their traditional Iran-linked networks, the paper said.

“The documented components suggest that, in terms of longer-range ballistic missiles, the Houthis have moved beyond simply reassembling Iranian systems,” it stated.

“Only a few countries in the world have the capacity to manufacture missiles of comparable ranges domestically.”

While the Houthis have “not yet mastered” the technology for the Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile, Iranian expertise on the ground is “accelerating their progress”, said Dr Nawaf Obaid, of Kings College London.

“Their principal constraint is time, not technical impossibility,” he told The National.

While it is understood the airport attack involved several projectiles in a swarm attack, the Houthis currently cannot build significant numbers, he added.

“Scale remains their weakness,” he said. Analysis by Kings College's department of war studies showed that 85 to 90 per cent of missiles were intercepted by Saudi Arabia’s advanced defence system, he added.

It is understood that the Houthis exploited a gap between Saudi Arabia’s lower and middle air defence layers in the airport attack, rather than a “technological breakthrough”, said Dr Obaid. He added that the kingdom’s air defences were “performing exceptionally well under sustained wartime conditions”.

Documents show the contents from four shipping containers arrived in the Aden Free Zone in Yemen in June and October 2025 from China.

The shipments contained custom-made metal parts including components of the airframe and a solid-propellant rocket motor for a Kheibar Shekan missile.

They were made by a Chinese precision-metal producer “that advertises itself as a specialist manufacturer of custom aerospace parts”, the report said.

It demonstrated that the Houthis were buying “more specialised parts for the construction of missiles, apparently independent of Iran-linked supply networks”.

According to UN reports, Chinese companies form the biggest source of seized goods bound for the Houthis and they have been importing components for solid-fuel missiles from China for at least two years. China has stated that it adheres to the UN Houthi arms ban.

Asked by The National what action the UK government might take against Chinese companies allegedly supplying components, the prime minister’s official spokesman said Britain “strongly condemns Houthi attacks and remains committed to supporting the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”.

Saudi Arabia's ambassador to London told a meeting of parliamentarians on Tuesday that the UK's support in the face of the Houthi missile menace was welcomed by his government.

Prince Abdullah bin Khaled held discussions focused on “recent Houthi attacks against the kingdom, regional security, and the importance of international co-operation in safeguarding stability and supporting peace in Yemen”, an embassy post on social media said.

headline: Asian markets fall on tech stock rout as high US inflation weighs on Wall Street
summary: Asian markets fell on Thursday, as artificial intelligence-related stocks plunged after a drop on Wall Street, fuelled by concerns about rising competition and profit growth in the chips sector.South Korea's Kospi slumped more than 7 per cent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 index was down 5.12 per cent at midday local time on Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped by 1 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.75 per cent.Asian markets are dealing with "not just the deeper sell-off in AI-related stocks but also the tightening of financial conditions that comes from higher yields and a higher US dollar", said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.In its report on Thursday, the International Monetary Fund also warned of the Asia region's heavy reliance on the AI boom. Strong global demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and related technology products has boosted exports and investment, particularly in economies integrated into technology supply chains. "The AI-driven technology boom has provided an important offset for economies in East and South-East Asia, although the evolution of AI investment and its long-term economic effects are uncertain," the fund said in a report on the outlook for the Asia-Pacific region."A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains," it added.The IMF also said uncertainty over US monetary policy could keep Asian financial markets volatile.Overnight, stocks on Wall Street dropped as consumer price inflation rose more than expected in September."Wall Street tumbled on further evidence that inflation in the United States is sticky, while a pullback in chip stocks on fears about rising competition and peak profit growth added to the woes," Mr Rodda said. The inflation figures were the "critical driver of markets in US trade", he added. US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent annually in September, above both the 3.6 per cent forecast for the month and August’s 3.4 per cent. Core inflation also was higher than expected, at 2.6 per cent year-on-year. "US stocks sold off as higher-rate expectations returned to the fore, with the S&P 500 recording its weakest session since late July and the Nasdaq hit harder by pressure on chip names," said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. "The risk-off move extended into Asia, where falls in Japan and Korea this morning were much sharper."The US inflation data now points to a higher chance of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, Mr Rodda said.
body_text:
Asian markets fell on Thursday, as artificial intelligence-related stocks plunged after a drop on Wall Street, fuelled by concerns about rising competition and profit growth in the chips sector.

South Korea's Kospi slumped more than 7 per cent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 index was down 5.12 per cent at midday local time on Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped by 1 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.75 per cent.

Asian markets are dealing with "not just the deeper sell-off in AI-related stocks but also the tightening of financial conditions that comes from higher yields and a higher US dollar", said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

In its report on Thursday, the International Monetary Fund also warned of the Asia region's heavy reliance on the AI boom.

Strong global demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and related technology products has boosted exports and investment, particularly in economies integrated into technology supply chains.

"The AI-driven technology boom has provided an important offset for economies in East and South-East Asia, although the evolution of AI investment and its long-term economic effects are uncertain," the fund said in a report on the outlook for the Asia-Pacific region.

"A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains," it added.

The IMF also said uncertainty over US monetary policy could keep Asian financial markets volatile.

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street dropped as consumer price inflation rose more than expected in September.

"Wall Street tumbled on further evidence that inflation in the United States is sticky, while a pullback in chip stocks on fears about rising competition and peak profit growth added to the woes," Mr Rodda said.

The inflation figures were the "critical driver of markets in US trade", he added.

US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent annually in September, above both the 3.6 per cent forecast for the month and August’s 3.4 per cent. Core inflation also was higher than expected, at 2.6 per cent year-on-year.

"US stocks sold off as higher-rate expectations returned to the fore, with the S&P 500 recording its weakest session since late July and the Nasdaq hit harder by pressure on chip names," said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD.

"The risk-off move extended into Asia, where falls in Japan and Korea this morning were much sharper."

The US inflation data now points to a higher chance of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, Mr Rodda said.

body_text:
A top official at the International Monetary Fund on Thursday said prewar buffers have helped limit the economic impact of the Iran war, while warning the region's outlook remains highly uncertain as it faces threats of renewed disruptions.

The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one fifth of the world's energy supplies travelled before the war, has rattled markets, as have Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway and key sites in neighbouring countries.

“The impact was more contained than the scale initially suggested,” the fund's regional director, Jihad Azour, told reporters during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand.

Diesel shortage to persist into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA warns

While the price of Brent crude is 47 per cent higher than its prewar levels, it has yet to hit the $200-a-barrel mark that was previously feared. The IMF this week maintained its 2026 global growth projection at 3.1 per cent and slightly raised its 2027 forecast to 3.4 per cent. Higher oil prices were partially attributed to the fund lifting its 2026 inflation forecast to 4.7 per cent.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia have been exploring alternatives to send their supplies to markets, while International Energy Agency members agreed in March to release up to 425 million barrels of reserve stocks. Output from non-Gulf producers and an adjustment in energy demand have also mitigated the war's impact, Mr Azour said.

“These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments,” he explained.

Iranian attacks continued in the Strait of Hormuz this week. At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the waterway in the past week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency.

On Wednesday, Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters. Authorities said no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said in a statement.

The IEA said crude oil exports from Gulf producers, led by Saudi Arabia, jumped by 4.4 million barrels a day in September to reach more than 75 per cent of prewar levels. Iran's escalatory attacks on Saudi Arabia and tanker traffic threaten to derail those gains, the agency said.

Brent crude rose 0.36 per cent at $106.1 a barrel on Wednesday, while West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 1.08 per cent at $95.16 a barrel.

The IMF said its 2026 forecasts show a sharp divergence for oil exporters and importers, with the latter being assisted by remittances, tourism and government support.

Regional economies are forecast to see a sharp divergence in trends due to the war. The IMF projected economic contractions of 11.3 per cent for Bahrain, 16 per cent for Iraq, 16.7 per cent for Kuwait, 15.6 per cent for Qatar, 3.3 per cent for Saudi Arabia and 3.9 per cent for the UAE this year.

Growth is expected to rebound in 2027 “but output will remain below the medium-term path projected before the conflict”, Mr Azour said.

A more prolonged conflict remains the most significant risk for the region's highly uncertain outlook, with further disruptions likely to weaken economic activity, inflame inflationary pressures and place extra strain on fiscal positions across the region, he said. Mr Azour also said tighter financial conditions could deepen vulnerabilities in economies with large sovereign financing needs.

He urged the region's economies to prioritise price stability, rebuild their fiscal buffers and build capacity to withstand future shocks.

The IMF will release its outlook for the Middle East next week in Dubai.

On Wednesday, UAE central bank governor Khaled Balama noted the region's experiences have shown that resilience depends on how quickly economies adapt to changing circumstances while building their fiscal buffers, state news agency Wam reported.

Mr Balama was addressing the region's central bankers and finance ministers during a meeting alongside the IMF and World Bank gathering in Bangkok.

He also said the UAE economy has shown resilience, supported by its robust fiscal buffers, low levels of public debt and its vast sovereign assets, helping to reinforce investor and market confidence. He also emphasised the importance of strengthening international co-operation frameworks amid geopolitical tension.

Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan was due to hold a media conference with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday.

The International Monetary Finance Committee, which is the fund's policy advisory panel, announced this week it had extended Mr Al Jadaan's position as IMFC chair by another year after his term ends on January 3, 2027.

headline: Israel accused of imposing media blackout on occupied south Lebanon
summary: UN peacekeepers have been blocked from arranging journalist visits to Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon for weeks, a spokesman told The National, amid accusations of a media blackout. Journalists have embedded with the UN Interim Force for Lebanon (Unifil) several times since a June ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah. Those visits provided one of the few means of accessing the occupied territory, which Israel designates as a buffer zone. The visits allowed journalists to report on the handful of predominantly Christian villages that remain inhabited, as well as the systematic destruction of largely depopulated Muslim villages.“At the moment, we cannot conduct media visits south of the so-called yellow line,” said a Unifil spokesman. “This has been the case for the past few weeks.” He added that Unifil did not know when visits would be permitted to resume.Elsy Moufarrej, president of the Union of Journalists in Lebanon, told The National that the union had received several complaints from journalists denied access to the zone in recent weeks. She accused Israel of a “media blackout” that prevents independent reporting on “potential crimes and violations”.“It also deprives these communities of a voice and violates the public's right to know,” she added.Israel occupied an area extending 10km to 12km into Lebanon during its war with Hezbollah, which reignited in March. The Israeli military launched a ground invasion and forced people to leave the south before establishing its security zone. Since then, Israel has severely restricted movement in and out of the occupied area, enforcing control through military positions, strikes, forced displacement orders and restrictions on access.The charity Reporters Without Borders has condemned restrictions on journalists entering the zone, accusing the Israeli military of turning co-ordination mechanisms intended to facilitate safe access into tools of censorship.“It is unacceptable that Lebanese journalists are denied access or prevented from entering Lebanese territory,” said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF’s Middle East office. “Ceasefire agreements and military considerations must no longer serve as a pretext to obstruct the right to information and threaten the safety of journalists.”While some communities such as the Sunni Muslim village of Kfarshouba can still be reached from the Lebanese side, predominantly Christian villages deeper inside the territory are effectively besieged, with movement in and out subject to Israeli permission.Travelling with Unifil had offered journalists rare opportunities to reach these communities. The media restriction appears to have begun in mid-September, following visits to the occupied zone by journalists from international news organisations. Téa Ziade, a French-Lebanese freelance journalist, was scheduled to enter the zone with Unifil on September 25 for an assignment with a European news outlet. Her trip was cancelled that morning, just minutes before the convoy was due to depart.“We had submitted all our papers to Unifil. Everything was in order,” she said. “A Unifil lieutenant told us: ‘It’s the journalists. No journalists are allowed in the convoy.’”She was given no explanation at the time. She was later told by Unifil that a proper deconfliction process had not taken place.There have been no Unifil journalist embeds since.The Israeli military confirmed to The National that it had raised the issue of journalist access with Unifil. “Following incidents in which journalists entered the security zone without prior co-ordination and published footage revealing the locations of troops, the issue was discussed with Unifil,” a military spokesperson said. But another Israeli military official went further, alleging that journalists had entered the occupied zone concealed within convoys and “shared photographs, which showed the location of our troops, with Hezbollah operatives or people connected to Hezbollah operatives”.The official did not identify the journalists or news organisations involved, or provide evidence to substantiate the allegation. When questioned about the accusation, an Israeli military spokesperson appeared to backtrack on the claim that journalists had shared information with people linked to Hezbollah, instead saying that publicly available information about Israeli troop positions could be exploited by the group.Pictures of Israeli positions inside southern Lebanon are widely available online. Israel, which has been accused of targeting journalists, has routinely portrayed them as militants. In October, it published a list of 170 people killed in the Gaza war who it said were militants posing as media workers. Israeli forces have killed at least 16 journalists and media workers in Lebanon since October 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Among them was Reuters journalist Issam Abdallah, killed by Israeli tank fire in October 2023 in an attack that wounded six other journalists and which Human Rights Watch described as a war crime. In April 2026, Al Akhbar journalist Amal Khalil was killed in an Israeli strike while reporting from the security zone during a ceasefire, while her colleague Zeinab Faraj was seriously wounded.Tighter restrictions Unifil was not the only means of accessing the occupied territory. Humanitarian and civilian convoys had also offered journalists a route into the occupied zone. Those routes, too, have become increasingly restricted in recent weeks. Sources within Unifil and other organisations say access requires “prior deconfliction arrangements, usually through humanitarian convoys”, Ms Moufarrej said.Deconfliction with the Israeli army usually involves speaking to Unifil or a US and French-led group established to monitor the ceasefire. The process is intended to arrange safe passage through the area. “However, Israeli forces have reportedly begun preventing these convoys from entering if journalists accompany them,” she added.A humanitarian worker who regularly travels into the occupied territory told The National that Israeli soldiers have significantly tightened checks at checkpoints, inspecting every vehicle to ensure no journalists were on board. Such checks were not previously routine, the worker said.“Israeli soldiers now come out of their base and check every person inside the car to make sure their identity matches the approved list.”An Israeli army spokesperson said the military reviewed journalists’ requests to enter the occupied zone on a “case-by-case basis”, without clarifying what procedures must be followed for approval.“Areas where military operations are taking place pose genuine security risks, requiring measures to protect the lives of journalists on the ground, as well as the safety of [Israeli] troops,” the Israeli army spokesperson added. “This policy is intended to enable journalistic coverage to the extent possible, without endangering human lives or compromising the safety of troops and their operational activities.” However, Israeli military operations are an inherent feature of the occupation, meaning any area could be cut off. body_text:
UN peacekeepers have been blocked from arranging journalist visits to Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon for weeks, a spokesman told The National, amid accusations of a media blackout.

Journalists have embedded with the UN Interim Force for Lebanon (Unifil) several times since a June ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah. Those visits provided one of the few means of accessing the occupied territory, which Israel designates as a buffer zone.

The visits allowed journalists to report on the handful of predominantly Christian villages that remain inhabited, as well as the systematic destruction of largely depopulated Muslim villages.

Dispatch'At God's mercy': Life after Unifil in Israeli-occupied Lebanese village

“At the moment, we cannot conduct media visits south of the so-called yellow line,” said a Unifil spokesman. “This has been the case for the past few weeks.”

He added that Unifil did not know when visits would be permitted to resume.

Elsy Moufarrej, president of the Union of Journalists in Lebanon, told The National that the union had received several complaints from journalists denied access to the zone in recent weeks. She accused Israel of a “media blackout” that prevents independent reporting on “potential crimes and violations”.

“It also deprives these communities of a voice and violates the public's right to know,” she added.

Israel occupied an area extending 10km to 12km into Lebanon during its war with Hezbollah, which reignited in March. The Israeli military launched a ground invasion and forced people to leave the south before establishing its security zone.

Since then, Israel has severely restricted movement in and out of the occupied area, enforcing control through military positions, strikes, forced displacement orders and restrictions on access.

The charity Reporters Without Borders has condemned restrictions on journalists entering the zone, accusing the Israeli military of turning co-ordination mechanisms intended to facilitate safe access into tools of censorship.

“It is unacceptable that Lebanese journalists are denied access or prevented from entering Lebanese territory,” said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF’s Middle East office. “Ceasefire agreements and military considerations must no longer serve as a pretext to obstruct the right to information and threaten the safety of journalists.”

While some communities such as the Sunni Muslim village of Kfarshouba can still be reached from the Lebanese side, predominantly Christian villages deeper inside the territory are effectively besieged, with movement in and out subject to Israeli permission.

Travelling with Unifil had offered journalists rare opportunities to reach these communities. The media restriction appears to have begun in mid-September, following visits to the occupied zone by journalists from international news organisations.

Téa Ziade, a French-Lebanese freelance journalist, was scheduled to enter the zone with Unifil on September 25 for an assignment with a European news outlet. Her trip was cancelled that morning, just minutes before the convoy was due to depart.

“We had submitted all our papers to Unifil. Everything was in order,” she said. “A Unifil lieutenant told us: ‘It’s the journalists. No journalists are allowed in the convoy.’”

She was given no explanation at the time. She was later told by Unifil that a proper deconfliction process had not taken place.

There have been no Unifil journalist embeds since.

The Israeli military confirmed to The National that it had raised the issue of journalist access with Unifil. “Following incidents in which journalists entered the security zone without prior co-ordination and published footage revealing the locations of troops, the issue was discussed with Unifil,” a military spokesperson said.

But another Israeli military official went further, alleging that journalists had entered the occupied zone concealed within convoys and “shared photographs, which showed the location of our troops, with Hezbollah operatives or people connected to Hezbollah operatives”.

The official did not identify the journalists or news organisations involved, or provide evidence to substantiate the allegation.

When questioned about the accusation, an Israeli military spokesperson appeared to backtrack on the claim that journalists had shared information with people linked to Hezbollah, instead saying that publicly available information about Israeli troop positions could be exploited by the group.

Pictures of Israeli positions inside southern Lebanon are widely available online.

Israel, which has been accused of targeting journalists, has routinely portrayed them as militants. In October, it published a list of 170 people killed in the Gaza war who it said were militants posing as media workers.

Israeli forces have killed at least 16 journalists and media workers in Lebanon since October 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Among them was Reuters journalist Issam Abdallah, killed by Israeli tank fire in October 2023 in an attack that wounded six other journalists and which Human Rights Watch described as a war crime.

In April 2026, Al Akhbar journalist Amal Khalil was killed in an Israeli strike while reporting from the security zone during a ceasefire, while her colleague Zeinab Faraj was seriously wounded.

Unifil was not the only means of accessing the occupied territory. Humanitarian and civilian convoys had also offered journalists a route into the occupied zone.

Those routes, too, have become increasingly restricted in recent weeks.

Sources within Unifil and other organisations say access requires “prior deconfliction arrangements, usually through humanitarian convoys”, Ms Moufarrej said.

Deconfliction with the Israeli army usually involves speaking to Unifil or a US and French-led group established to monitor the ceasefire. The process is intended to arrange safe passage through the area.

“However, Israeli forces have reportedly begun preventing these convoys from entering if journalists accompany them,” she added.

A humanitarian worker who regularly travels into the occupied territory told The National that Israeli soldiers have significantly tightened checks at checkpoints, inspecting every vehicle to ensure no journalists were on board. Such checks were not previously routine, the worker said.

“Israeli soldiers now come out of their base and check every person inside the car to make sure their identity matches the approved list.”

An Israeli army spokesperson said the military reviewed journalists’ requests to enter the occupied zone on a “case-by-case basis”, without clarifying what procedures must be followed for approval.

“Areas where military operations are taking place pose genuine security risks, requiring measures to protect the lives of journalists on the ground, as well as the safety of [Israeli] troops,” the Israeli army spokesperson added. “This policy is intended to enable journalistic coverage to the extent possible, without endangering human lives or compromising the safety of troops and their operational activities.”

However, Israeli military operations are an inherent feature of the occupation, meaning any area could be cut off. Ms Ziade rejected the Israeli army’s security justification.

“If we cannot go to the south, how are we supposed to tell the story of the occupation?” she asked. “We lose part of the meaning of this profession, the ability to build trust and intimacy with people. Without journalists on the ground, there is also a question of accountability and impunity.”

Access for journalists has always been challenging. In July, a vetted humanitarian convoy, which included The National, was barred at the last minute by the Israeli army. At the time, Unifil said the decision was probably made because of media presence.

It has now become practically impossible. Since the end of September, no journalists have been allowed inside the security zone.

“What worries me is that this justification could come to be accepted by the international community, and that we, as journalists, will simply be expected to accept it too,” Ms Ziade said. “And that is how, little by little, a territory becomes closed to journalists.”

The restrictions have also had consequences for civilians living under Israeli occupation.

Israeli forces suspended convoys to Debel and Rmeish for three days after journalists entered the occupied zone, according to a humanitarian worker who regularly travels to the area.

Residents of both villages confirmed they had been prevented from entering or leaving during the three-day closure. They said Israeli military officials had accused journalists of entering the territory without authorisation.

The Israeli military official denied having a policy of punishing civilians or villages for hosting reporters, saying troops had temporarily paused the convoy to investigate the incident.

“It is unacceptable that a civilian area is isolated for three days simply for having hosted journalists,” said Mr Dagher from RSF.

The suspension temporarily cut off a lifeline for the besieged communities, whose residents depend on the convoys for travel and supplies. The closure sparked fears about speaking to the media.

“It was indirect, but the message was received by all the villages: ‘There are a lot of mistakes happening, be careful. If there are more mistakes there won't be any more convoys,'” said a locally elected official from Debel, who requested not to be named to avoid retaliation by Israeli forces.

“People got scared. They need these convoys to access hospitals, doctors and supplies.”

As the Iran conflict drags on, the global diesel shortage is expected to continue well into 2027, the International Energy Agency has warned.

summary: Russia struck Ukraine's Izmail port and two cargo ships en route to Odesa, the Russian Defence Ministry said Thursday. A day earlier, Moscow launched more missiles and drones at Ukrainian cities, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.

Russia struck Ukraine's Izmail port and two cargo ships en route to Odesa, the Russian Defence Ministry said Thursday. A day earlier, Moscow launched more missiles and drones at Ukrainian cities, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.

Romania said eight people were missing after a fire broke out on a vessel flying the San Marino flag, the latest incident in the Black Sea, which has seen a series of drone attacks.

"There were 12 people on board the vessel. Four of them are safe, whilst eight are currently missing," the Romanian Naval Authority said in a press release.

Far-right leader and presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said on Wednesday that France could no longer afford to fund Ukraine, citing the country's high deficit and weak economic growth.

“The ‌block [on ​attacking refineries] is out. We’re ​done,” Zelenskiy ​told ​the newspaper.

Ukraine on Wednesday accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv's military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.
