headline: Why Europe's reading habits should concern the Arab world
summary: Even with some of the world's oldest and most prestigious publishing houses, extensive library networks and a celebrated literary culture, Europe is struggling to keep successive generations reading.That was among the takeaways from a presentation by the Federation of European Publishers, which represents national publishing associations across the continent, at Frankfurt Book Fair last week.While the federation reported that print book sales had fallen by about 6 per cent over five years in the markets surveyed, equivalent to a 110 million decline in copies, more revealing was its examination of reading habits.Drawing on Eurostat research from 2022, the report highlighted that 47.2 per cent of European Union residents aged 16 and older had not read a book in the preceding year. Among those aged 16 to 29, nearly four in 10 had not read one.The reasons reported by non-readers warrant attention. Among those aged 16 to 29, a lack of interest was cited by 58 per cent, compared with 21.8 per cent who said they lacked time. Across all age groups, 2.4 per cent identified cost or access as the obstacle.The figures add to gnawing concerns that predate Frankfurt, with research published in February by Britain's National Literacy Trust finding that 46.9 per cent of children aged eight to 11 enjoyed reading in their free time, compared with 29.5 per cent of those aged 11 to 14. Among boys aged 14 to 16, the figure was just 18.8 per cent.Europe's experience offers a reminder against taking the Arab world's considerable investment in introducing children to books for granted.As educators and parents know, that desire to turn the page can change as they grow older, with education, social media and entertainment compete for attention, followed eventually by the growing pressures of professional and family responsibilities. Reading habits are not set in stone simply because children were encouraged during childhood. That is merely the first chapter of an ongoing story.The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing the reading bug. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. An impact study conducted in partnership with Unesco reported increased reading frequency and more books completed by participating students.Meanwhile, the Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, is more concerned with encouraging children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested on what they have consumed. Researchers are evaluating its effects and the longer-term affects remain unknown.Beyond the classroom, UAE libraries are also finding ways to keep books part of people's everyday lives. Sharjah's House of Wisdom and Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Library have become places to work, study and attend cultural events, as well as read books. The latter houses nine specialised libraries, including sections for children and young adults.But reading habits cannot develop through osmosis alone and both libraries continue to encourage younger audiences through workshops, holiday programmes and exhibitions.The quality of that content is critical, particularly when young Arabs themselves are questioning the appeal of the cultural content available to them. At the Congress of Arabic and Creative Industries in Abu Dhabi in September, a survey of 4,092 people aged 18 to 25 across 10 Arab countries found that 71 per cent preferred media in Arabic, yet 67 per cent considered much of the available Arabic content outdated compared with English-language alternatives.The findings covered media broadly rather than books specifically, but they should give publishers reason to consider whether their books are resonating with younger audiences.Cairo's Diwan Publishing is one example worth noting, having reintroduced Naguib Mahfouz's novels through contemporary cover designs and graphic-novel adaptations, including The Thief and the Dogs.As previously reported by The National, co-founder Ahmed Qarmalawi said the project, developed with the Mahfouz family, sought to introduce the Nobel laureate's work to a generation familiar with his reputation but not necessarily his writing.At the 2024 Abu Dhabi International Book Fair, a large interactive pavilion dedicated to Mahfouz showcased the new editions. Qarmalawi recalled young visitors responding enthusiastically to the books, suggesting that an author some might regard as a literary cultural heirloom could still speak to a younger generation.And in that regard, social media is also playing a role in building a love of books during adolescence. As The National has reported, BookTok and BookTube communities have emerged in the region, with members recommending titles, sharing punchy reviews and introducing fellow readers to new authors.While the footfall at such events and the viewing figures online deserve to be celebrated, more work is needed to turn that enthusiasm into lasting reading habits and make reading books a normal part of life rather than homework. Authors and publishers must also take risks and create content that resonates.With its young population, eclectic cultural sensibilities and governments that view culture as an investment, the Arab world has a chance to lead in keeping people reading.That would be an achievement for a regional publishing industry still regarded as evolving by some of its European counterparts, provided the same commitment that encouraged children to pick up books in the first place is sustained.
body_text:
Even with some of the world's oldest and most prestigious publishing houses, extensive library networks and a celebrated literary culture, Europe is struggling to keep successive generations reading.

That was among the takeaways from a presentation by the Federation of European Publishers, which represents national publishing associations across the continent, at Frankfurt Book Fair last week.

While the federation reported that print book sales had fallen by about 6 per cent over five years in the markets surveyed, equivalent to a 110 million decline in copies, more revealing was its examination of reading habits.

Cairo's Diwan Publishing brings Nobel winner Naguib Mahfouz to new readers

Drawing on Eurostat research from 2022, the report highlighted that 47.2 per cent of European Union residents aged 16 and older had not read a book in the preceding year. Among those aged 16 to 29, nearly four in 10 had not read one.

The reasons reported by non-readers warrant attention. Among those aged 16 to 29, a lack of interest was cited by 58 per cent, compared with 21.8 per cent who said they lacked time. Across all age groups, 2.4 per cent identified cost or access as the obstacle.

The figures add to gnawing concerns that predate Frankfurt, with research published in February by Britain's National Literacy Trust finding that 46.9 per cent of children aged eight to 11 enjoyed reading in their free time, compared with 29.5 per cent of those aged 11 to 14. Among boys aged 14 to 16, the figure was just 18.8 per cent.

Europe's experience offers a reminder against taking the Arab world's considerable investment in introducing children to books for granted.

As educators and parents know, that desire to turn the page can change as they grow older, with education, social media and entertainment compete for attention, followed eventually by the growing pressures of professional and family responsibilities. Reading habits are not set in stone simply because children were encouraged during childhood. That is merely the first chapter of an ongoing story.

The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing the reading bug. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. An impact study conducted in partnership with Unesco reported increased reading frequency and more books completed by participating students.

Meanwhile, the Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, is more concerned with encouraging children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested on what they have consumed. Researchers are evaluating its effects and the longer-term affects remain unknown.

Beyond the classroom, UAE libraries are also finding ways to keep books part of people's everyday lives. Sharjah's House of Wisdom and Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Library have become places to work, study and attend cultural events, as well as read books. The latter houses nine specialised libraries, including sections for children and young adults.

But reading habits cannot develop through osmosis alone and both libraries continue to encourage younger audiences through workshops, holiday programmes and exhibitions.

The quality of that content is critical, particularly when young Arabs themselves are questioning the appeal of the cultural content available to them. At the Congress of Arabic and Creative Industries in Abu Dhabi in September, a survey of 4,092 people aged 18 to 25 across 10 Arab countries found that 71 per cent preferred media in Arabic, yet 67 per cent considered much of the available Arabic content outdated compared with English-language alternatives.

The findings covered media broadly rather than books specifically, but they should give publishers reason to consider whether their books are resonating with younger audiences.

Cairo's Diwan Publishing is one example worth noting, having reintroduced Naguib Mahfouz's novels through contemporary cover designs and graphic-novel adaptations, including The Thief and the Dogs.

As previously reported by The National, co-founder Ahmed Qarmalawi said the project, developed with the Mahfouz family, sought to introduce the Nobel laureate's work to a generation familiar with his reputation but not necessarily his writing.

At the 2024 Abu Dhabi International Book Fair, a large interactive pavilion dedicated to Mahfouz showcased the new editions. Qarmalawi recalled young visitors responding enthusiastically to the books, suggesting that an author some might regard as a literary cultural heirloom could still speak to a younger generation.

And in that regard, social media is also playing a role in building a love of books during adolescence. As The National has reported, BookTok and BookTube communities have emerged in the region, with members recommending titles, sharing punchy reviews and introducing fellow readers to new authors.

While the footfall at such events and the viewing figures online deserve to be celebrated, more work is needed to turn that enthusiasm into lasting reading habits and make reading books a normal part of life rather than homework. Authors and publishers must also take risks and create content that resonates.

With its young population, eclectic cultural sensibilities and governments that view culture as an investment, the Arab world has a chance to lead in keeping people reading.

That would be an achievement for a regional publishing industry still regarded as evolving by some of its European counterparts, provided the same commitment that encouraged children to pick up books in the first place is sustained.

headline: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons consider leaving UK as tax concerns mount
summary: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found. The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth.Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth.The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The exodus of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE, Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US.The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs.CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says. Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai-based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”. “UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National.Tax overhauls intensify debateUnder the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains.Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules.The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon.UAE leads inquiry listEnquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds.Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent.Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. body_text:
Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found.

The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth.

Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth.

The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The exodus of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE, Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US.

The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs.

CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says.

Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai-based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”.

“UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National.

Under the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains.

Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules.

The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon.

Enquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds.

Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent.

Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. A further 21.9 per cent concerned residency, relocation or visas, while 13.9 per cent related to wealth structures such as trusts, foundations and holding companies, data shows.

“Tax efficiency may start the conversation, but it is rarely enough to complete the move,” Mr Gordon says, before adding that the UAE’s connectivity, business infrastructure and access to markets across the Middle East, Asia and Africa appeal to families seeking a commercial base. Switzerland and Singapore offer established wealth management sectors, while Portugal and Malta continue to attract those seeking European residency and lifestyle benefits.

Across all UK-origin enquiries to the group, 42 per cent referenced business or company set-up, while 28.9 per cent involved wealth or succession planning. The UK-origin enquiries have averaged about 19 per cent of the group’s total leads over the past four years, according to Mr Gordon.

Meanwhile, the broader migration outlook remains significant. Henley & Partners and New World Wealth forecast a record 165,000 millionaire relocations worldwide in 2026, with the UAE expected to remain the leading destination for inflows.

For Britain, the challenge is to balance tax reform with its ability to retain mobile investors and entrepreneurs. For the UAE, the opportunity is to convert initial interest into durable investment and economic activity.

“The UAE’s long-term challenge is not simply to attract wealthy residents, but to convert initial tax and residency interest into enduring business activity, investment and family connections,” Mr Gordon says.

headline: Reconstruction in north-east Syria key to refugee returns from Iraq, UNHCR official says
summary: Reconstruction work in Syria must extend to Kurdish areas in the north-east if refugees are to return home, the UN refugee agency’s representative in Iraq has told The National.Toby Harward said the lack of economic opportunities and security in the region remained a major obstacle.“We see a lot of MoUs [memorandums of understanding] signed in Syria, we see a lot of agreements being signed, plans for reinvestment, reconstruction,” Mr Harward said. But these plans have to extend to the Kurdish areas to create an appetite for Syrian refugees in Iraq to return, he added.Iraq hosts more than 300,000 Syrian refugees, according to UNHCR data. Eighty-five per cent of them are in the autonomous Kurdistan Region, and the majority are Syrian Kurds, Mr Harward said. Refugees began returning from Iraq to Syria in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, but this has slowed, he said. “It has not just slowed from Iraq, but also from Jordan, from Lebanon and from Turkey.“When I talk to the refugees, the number one reason for not returning is the continuing frictions and tensions. We have seen demonstrations in Hasakah over the last … several days,” he said. He was referring to the uncertain security situation in north-east Syria following the integration deal between the Damascus government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which assumed control of the area during the country's 2011-2024 civil war.Mr Harward said refugees had told him that until there was “a reduction in tensions” between the “Arab and Kurdish components, [until] there is more of social cohesion, peaceful coexistence between them, they feel that there is no future for younger people going back”.“I am optimistic. But then the power of one revenge kidnapping and killing on social media will destroy all of the positive developments at one level,” he added.However, the slowing of returns is not just due to the economic and security uncertainty in Syria. Some refugees have established livelihoods in their host community. “I would argue that there is more opportunity in Iraq. Kurdistan's progressive policies – allowing access to services, allowing access to livelihoods – mean that they have a lot better situation than refugees in many other parts of the world,” Mr Harward said.He praised efforts by the Iraqi and Kurdish governments to provide Syrian refugees with opportunities to work and live. Many Kurdish officials have an “emotional and empathetic attachment” towards refugees, having been in these positions before, he said. He noted that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Barham Salih, is an Iraqi Kurd and a former refugee.“But on the other side, they will admit that it is a burden,” he said, of the reliance on the government to provide electricity, water and other basic needs to refugees. To counter this, one of the UNHCR's main priorities in Iraq is to generate employment opportunities that allow refugees to become more independent in their host country, he said.Mr Harward noted that the rate of return of Syrian refugees from federal Iraq was higher than from the Kurdistan Region. “The number of refugees returning from central-south, from federal Iraq, has been higher than the numbers here. And that is primarily because they are Arabs.”A drop in job opportunities and the economic situation in federal Iraq was another factor in their decision to return, he said. Mr Harward said the UNHCR was also working with Iraqi families returned from Al Hol camp in Syria, where the SDF held relatives of suspected ISIS militants. "What I understand is that on return to the areas of origin, there are still prejudices, they are still facing stigma, negative stigma, and this is something that I think UN agencies, working obviously with the government in the lead, need to do more to ensure that they are properly able to integrate,” he said.Iraq also has nearly one million internally displaced people, including more than 100,000 living in camps in the Kurdistan Region, according to figures from the UN and the International Organisation for Migration. Most of them fled their homes after ISIS seized large areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014.Mr Harward said there were still 18 camps, mainly in Duhok and Zakho, hosting members of the Yazidi community, who follow an ancient monotheistic religion and live in the mountains of north-west Iraq. ISIS extremists captured Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Yazidis, and surrounding villages in August 2014, taking thousands captive and slaughtering thousands of others. Some Yazidis fled to Mount Sinjar, where many were flown to safety by the US-backed Iraqi forces.“I feel a deep sense of shame that the people who suffered from brutal human rights violations and what many governments have called genocide are still living in camps 12 years after 2014,” he said. He said “durable solutions” should be found for not just the Yazidis but all internally displaced communities to return to their areas of origin and reintegrate into those areas.In October 2020, nearly three years after ISIS was defeated in Iraq, the Baghdad and Kurdistan Region governments signed the Sinjar Agreement to restore state authority in Sinjar and facilitate the return of internally displaced people, particularly Yazidis, with UN support. However, its implementation has largely stalled amid disputes over who should control the area and appoint a mayor.The Popular Mobilisation Forces, an umbrella group of Iraqi militias that fought ISIS, including factions aligned with Iran, Yazidi armed groups and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) remain in Sinjar.Mr Harward said he hoped Turkey's decision to withdraw its troops from the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq, the peace process between Ankara and the PKK, and Iraq's efforts to bring armed groups under state control would alleviate the security situation.
body_text:
Reconstruction work in Syria must extend to Kurdish areas in the north-east if refugees are to return home, the UN refugee agency’s representative in Iraq has told The National.

Toby Harward said the lack of economic opportunities and security in the region remained a major obstacle.

“We see a lot of MoUs [memorandums of understanding] signed in Syria, we see a lot of agreements being signed, plans for reinvestment, reconstruction,” Mr Harward said. But these plans have to extend to the Kurdish areas to create an appetite for Syrian refugees in Iraq to return, he added.

Macron to visit UAE on Gulf tour next week

Iraq hosts more than 300,000 Syrian refugees, according to UNHCR data. Eighty-five per cent of them are in the autonomous Kurdistan Region, and the majority are Syrian Kurds, Mr Harward said.

Refugees began returning from Iraq to Syria in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, but this has slowed, he said. “It has not just slowed from Iraq, but also from Jordan, from Lebanon and from Turkey.

“When I talk to the refugees, the number one reason for not returning is the continuing frictions and tensions. We have seen demonstrations in Hasakah over the last … several days,” he said. He was referring to the uncertain security situation in north-east Syria following the integration deal between the Damascus government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which assumed control of the area during the country's 2011-2024 civil war.

Mr Harward said refugees had told him that until there was “a reduction in tensions” between the “Arab and Kurdish components, [until] there is more of social cohesion, peaceful coexistence between them, they feel that there is no future for younger people going back”.

“I am optimistic. But then the power of one revenge kidnapping and killing on social media will destroy all of the positive developments at one level,” he added.

However, the slowing of returns is not just due to the economic and security uncertainty in Syria. Some refugees have established livelihoods in their host community.

“I would argue that there is more opportunity in Iraq. Kurdistan's progressive policies – allowing access to services, allowing access to livelihoods – mean that they have a lot better situation than refugees in many other parts of the world,” Mr Harward said.

He praised efforts by the Iraqi and Kurdish governments to provide Syrian refugees with opportunities to work and live. Many Kurdish officials have an “emotional and empathetic attachment” towards refugees, having been in these positions before, he said.

He noted that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Barham Salih, is an Iraqi Kurd and a former refugee.

“But on the other side, they will admit that it is a burden,” he said, of the reliance on the government to provide electricity, water and other basic needs to refugees.

To counter this, one of the UNHCR's main priorities in Iraq is to generate employment opportunities that allow refugees to become more independent in their host country, he said.

Mr Harward noted that the rate of return of Syrian refugees from federal Iraq was higher than from the Kurdistan Region. “The number of refugees returning from central-south, from federal Iraq, has been higher than the numbers here. And that is primarily because they are Arabs.”

A drop in job opportunities and the economic situation in federal Iraq was another factor in their decision to return, he said.

Mr Harward said the UNHCR was also working with Iraqi families returned from Al Hol camp in Syria, where the SDF held relatives of suspected ISIS militants.

"What I understand is that on return to the areas of origin, there are still prejudices, they are still facing stigma, negative stigma, and this is something that I think UN agencies, working obviously with the government in the lead, need to do more to ensure that they are properly able to integrate,” he said.

Iraq also has nearly one million internally displaced people, including more than 100,000 living in camps in the Kurdistan Region, according to figures from the UN and the International Organisation for Migration. Most of them fled their homes after ISIS seized large areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014.

Mr Harward said there were still 18 camps, mainly in Duhok and Zakho, hosting members of the Yazidi community, who follow an ancient monotheistic religion and live in the mountains of north-west Iraq.

ISIS extremists captured Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Yazidis, and surrounding villages in August 2014, taking thousands captive and slaughtering thousands of others. Some Yazidis fled to Mount Sinjar, where many were flown to safety by the US-backed Iraqi forces.

“I feel a deep sense of shame that the people who suffered from brutal human rights violations and what many governments have called genocide are still living in camps 12 years after 2014,” he said.

He said “durable solutions” should be found for not just the Yazidis but all internally displaced communities to return to their areas of origin and reintegrate into those areas.

In October 2020, nearly three years after ISIS was defeated in Iraq, the Baghdad and Kurdistan Region governments signed the Sinjar Agreement to restore state authority in Sinjar and facilitate the return of internally displaced people, particularly Yazidis, with UN support. However, its implementation has largely stalled amid disputes over who should control the area and appoint a mayor.

The Popular Mobilisation Forces, an umbrella group of Iraqi militias that fought ISIS, including factions aligned with Iran, Yazidi armed groups and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) remain in Sinjar.

Mr Harward said he hoped Turkey's decision to withdraw its troops from the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq, the peace process between Ankara and the PKK, and Iraq's efforts to bring armed groups under state control would alleviate the security situation.

headline: UK to allocate $22.5 mln to Ukraine for Chernobyl NPP repairs
summary: The UK Cabinet said that the repairs are also necessary to remove corrosion that "risks undermining decades of international investment"
body_text:
LONDON, October 15. /TASS/. The United Kingdom will allocate 17 million GBP ($22.5 million) in new support for repairs to the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant, the UK Cabinet said in a press release.

"The support will fund crucial repairs to restore the structure’s confinement and ventilation functions and protect its intended lifespan," it said. "Without repairs, corrosion risks undermining decades of international investment and creating longer-term environmental and safety risks."

In 2025, the International Atomic Energy Agency confirmed an explosion at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant on the night of February 14. IAEA staff were informed that a strike drone had crashed into the shelter of the fourth power unit at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant. It was noted that there were no signs of damage to the inner shell of the protective structure above the plant, and that radiation levels both inside and outside the structure remained normal and stable. Commenting on the incident at the plant, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov called Ukraine’s accusations that a Russian drone allegedly hit the plant and damaged the protective sarcophagus a fraud.

headline: East China's Shandong launches first TIR road freight route to Georgia
summary: China has launched its first international road freight route from Shandong Province to Georgia under the international TIR system, Qingdao Customs said on Thursday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- China has launched its first international road freight route from Shandong Province to Georgia under the international TIR system, Qingdao Customs said on Thursday.

The route links the China-SCO demonstration zone for regional trade and economic cooperation with Georgia. It is the seventh TIR route launched by the demonstration zone and the first connecting Shandong with Georgia.

The TIR system, established under a United Nations convention on international road transport, streamlines cross-border customs clearance. Vehicles carrying valid TIR carnets can clear customs at their points of departure and destination without having to unload their cargo for repeated inspections while passing through transit countries.

Georgia serves as a key transit hub for goods traveling from China to European markets.

Two trucks loaded with clothing set off from the demonstration zone in Qingdao on the day the route opened. They are scheduled to leave China through the Horgos Port in Xinjiang, cross Kazakhstan to the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea, take a ferry across the sea and travel through Azerbaijan before reaching Georgia.

The new route is expected to cut transit times to around 18 days, from the 30 to 45 days typically required previously, said Dou Kun, head of Qingdao Runshengchi Logistics Co., which handled the shipment. TIR transport is also more cost-effective and efficient than traditional sea freight, Dou said.

The demonstration zone is China's only national-level platform dedicated to regional trade and economic cooperation with Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member states.

In the first nine months of this year, the zone dispatched 277 TIR truck shipments carrying goods worth a total of 240 million yuan (approximately 35.86 million dollars).

headline: Russia vows closer ties with N. Korea at diplomatic anniversary reception
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- Russia has pledged to deepen ties with North Korea at...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- Russia has pledged to deepen ties with North Korea at a reception in Pyongyang marking 78 years of diplomatic relations, the North's state media reported Thursday.

Russian Ambassador Andrey Podelyshev hosted the event the previous day at the Taedonggang Diplomatic Club, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

It was his first reception since taking up the post late last month. North Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jong-gyu attended.

Speakers said "victory is in store for the sacred common cause of the two countries for the building of powerful countries and welfare of the peoples," and expressed belief that the alliance "forged with blood would be immortal," according to the report.

Podelyshev called the relations between the two countries "exemplary," developing on "the principles of full equality and mutual respect," according to the Russian Embassy's Telegram channel.

"Their legal foundation is the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership," Podelyshev said of the two countries' relations.

The treaty, signed in June 2024 by Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has "brought cooperation between our countries to a qualitatively new level and set a high standard for its further strengthening," he added.

Kim Jong-gyu responded by saying it is North Korea's "unwavering position" to "comprehensively expand and develop traditional relations of friendship and cooperation."

"We will make every effort to strengthen tactical and strategic cooperation, and develop bilateral relations," he said.

A Russian delegation from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, led by D.V. Sergienko, deputy head of the Migration Service, was visiting Pyongyang and also attended, the embassy said.

headline: Russia's Lavrov, China's Wang discuss cooperation, Ukraine, Iran at Asia security meeting
summary: Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Russian and Chinese foreign ministers discussed the state of bilateral cooperation as well as the crises in Ukraine and Iran during an Asia security meeting, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping reaffirmed their strategic alliance at a regional summit last August and both praised prospects for closer cooperation.
body_text:
Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Russian and Chinese foreign ministers discussed the state of bilateral cooperation as well as the crises in Ukraine and Iran during an Asia security meeting, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping reaffirmed their strategic alliance at a regional summit last August and both praised prospects for closer cooperation.

The statement on Wednesday said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi met in Azerbaijan at a meeting of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia.

It said the two ministers "praised the development dynamics of comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation" and "synchronized watches on bilateral political dialogue".

It said discussions also focused on "relations with the United States and the situation around the Ukrainian and Iranian crises".

Both Russia and China have called for an end to the Iran conflict, saying it could expand and threaten stability throughout the region.

China has affirmed its "no limits" partnership with Russia throughout the 4-1/2-year-long war in Ukraine, while calling for diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

headline: Russia demands rights activists be granted access to Ukraine's 'secret prisons' — diplomat
summary: Rodion Miroshnik emphasized during an unofficial Arria-formula meeting of the UN Security Council that rights advocates should have full knowledge of the atrocities committed at these facilities
body_text:
UNITED NATIONS, October 14. /TASS/. Russia demands that Ukraine allowed staffers of international rights organizations to visit places in Ukraine where Russian prisoners of war are being kept illegally, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said.

"We demand that the facts cited, described and presented be thoroughly investigated, and that the human rights missions present in the Kiev-controlled territories make every effort to gain access to the locations where Russian prisoners of war are being unlawfully detained," he told an unofficial Arria-formula meeting of the UN Security Council.

In his words, rights advocates, who currently "assert that ‘the majority of criminal acts by Ukrainian militants were committed during the initial stages of captivity,’" should have full knowledge of these atrocities so that they could "share these facts with the rest of the world, which still claims that the Kiev regime continues to adhere to the norms of the IHL [international humanitarian law], including in the treatment of POWs," the Russian diplomat added.

headline: Foreign investors rate Egypt’s investment risk at lowest level since 2014: Minister
summary: Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk said international investors had responded positively to Egypt’s economic reforms, lowering their assessment of investment risks in the country to its lowest level since 2014. He stressed that the government would continue its programme of tax and customs relief, introducing new packages to strengthen confidence and partnerships with investors. He added that the government was adopting numerous initiatives to support the business community, expand the country’s production, export and industrial bases, and create more jobs. Kouchouk said the Egyptian economy was improving and growing and was capable of responding flexibly to regional and international shocks and crises. He made the remarks during an open dialogue with investors across three consecutive sessions organised by HSBC, Standard Chartered and Goldman Sachs on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group meetings in Bangkok. He noted that the stable outlook assigned to the Egyptian economy by credit rating agencies reflected the success of the structural and economic reforms implemented. The minister added that balanced fiscal policies had helped encourage domestic and international capital to invest in Egypt. The private sector is leading economic activity, accounting for 65% of investments and driving economic growth to 5.1%. Kouchouk explained that Egypt had achieved a primary surplus equivalent to 4.9% of gross domestic product (GDP), while the overall budget deficit fell to 5.8% in the previous fiscal year. He also said the government aims to reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio to around 70% within three years, extend the average maturity of public debt and lower debt-servicing costs.

headline: AI plans 'have not changed' in Middle East despite Iran conflict, Nvidia says
summary: Despite the continuing conflict with Iran, Gulf countries have not abandoned their AI ambitions, and demand for the infrastructure needed to develop the technology remains strong, a senior Nvidia official said on Wednesday.“The imperatives these countries see have not changed, they still see it as an opportunity to diversify their economies,” Ruth Berry, who leads global policy on Nvidia’s government affairs team, said during a discussion at the Washington-based Middle East Institute. “Infrastructure is really sticky,” she added, referring to continued global demand for Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs), which power much of today’s AI infrastructure.Ms Berry said countries in the region continue to have a "clear vision for where they want to go on AI", which bodes well for future plans. The UAE, which has developed several investment partnerships with the US technology giant, is among the countries pressing ahead.In May, the first shipments of Nvidia's highly sought CPUs and GPUs arrived in the UAE, the country's ambassador announced. In recent years, the UAE has sought to buy and use Nvidia's chips for its AI plans. Stringent export controls aimed at protecting the US lead in AI made such purchases difficult.Washington eventually approved the shipments after the UAE provided security assurances intended to prevent the chips from being accessed by unauthorised parties.But the Iran conflict has raised questions about the Gulf's growing AI infrastructure, particularly after Iranian attacks in the region. Mohammed Soliman, a technology analyst and senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said that the threat of conflict could have an inverse effect, causing countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia to increase their AI investments.Mr Soliman said that Ukraine's ability to withstand Russia's invasion for more than four years could largely be attributed to Ukraine's AI investments and innovations. The country has used AI to improve drone strikes, troop logistics and other facets of battle. "Without AI, Ukraine would have lost the war … war is a function of compute," he said.Governments throughout the Middle East, Mr Soliman continued, have taken note of that. "If you’re thinking about how you’re going to be able to sustain against Iranian aggression, you also have to be thinking about compute," he said. The discussion largely focused on whether US AI technology products would remain influential throughout the Middle East. Mr Soliman said it and China were the two major contenders in this area. He said the recent attacks from Iran would count when it comes to buying decisions, working in favour of the US. "It's been widely reported that China has assisted Iran," Mr Soliman said. He said that the Middle East remains incredibly appealing to the US companies and government as the race for AI dominance heats up. He also said that countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia have an abundance of energy, which is a significant AI prerequisite, along with a geographic advantage."You need a nearby compute hub that's capable of supporting multiple markets," he said. "They're able to make a financial bet on this infrastructure."Nazak Nikakhtar, an international trade and national security lawyer, said China what could have an advantage in the race against the US."They're really fast," she said, referring to the speed at which decisions are made in Beijing at the highest levels of government.
body_text:
Despite the continuing conflict with Iran, Gulf countries have not abandoned their AI ambitions, and demand for the infrastructure needed to develop the technology remains strong, a senior Nvidia official said on Wednesday.

“The imperatives these countries see have not changed, they still see it as an opportunity to diversify their economies,” Ruth Berry, who leads global policy on Nvidia’s government affairs team, said during a discussion at the Washington-based Middle East Institute.

“Infrastructure is really sticky,” she added, referring to continued global demand for Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs), which power much of today’s AI infrastructure.

AI could be worth $1 trillion to the Mena region, new research suggests

Ms Berry said countries in the region continue to have a "clear vision for where they want to go on AI", which bodes well for future plans.

The UAE, which has developed several investment partnerships with the US technology giant, is among the countries pressing ahead.

In May, the first shipments of Nvidia's highly sought CPUs and GPUs arrived in the UAE, the country's ambassador announced.

In recent years, the UAE has sought to buy and use Nvidia's chips for its AI plans. Stringent export controls aimed at protecting the US lead in AI made such purchases difficult.

Washington eventually approved the shipments after the UAE provided security assurances intended to prevent the chips from being accessed by unauthorised parties.

But the Iran conflict has raised questions about the Gulf's growing AI infrastructure, particularly after Iranian attacks in the region.

Mohammed Soliman, a technology analyst and senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said that the threat of conflict could have an inverse effect, causing countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia to increase their AI investments.

Mr Soliman said that Ukraine's ability to withstand Russia's invasion for more than four years could largely be attributed to Ukraine's AI investments and innovations. The country has used AI to improve drone strikes, troop logistics and other facets of battle.

"Without AI, Ukraine would have lost the war … war is a function of compute," he said.

Governments throughout the Middle East, Mr Soliman continued, have taken note of that.

"If you’re thinking about how you’re going to be able to sustain against Iranian aggression, you also have to be thinking about compute," he said.

The discussion largely focused on whether US AI technology products would remain influential throughout the Middle East. Mr Soliman said it and China were the two major contenders in this area.

He said the recent attacks from Iran would count when it comes to buying decisions, working in favour of the US.

"It's been widely reported that China has assisted Iran," Mr Soliman said.

He said that the Middle East remains incredibly appealing to the US companies and government as the race for AI dominance heats up.

He also said that countries such as the UAE and Saudi Arabia have an abundance of energy, which is a significant AI prerequisite, along with a geographic advantage.

"You need a nearby compute hub that's capable of supporting multiple markets," he said. "They're able to make a financial bet on this infrastructure."

Nazak Nikakhtar, an international trade and national security lawyer, said China what could have an advantage in the race against the US.

"They're really fast," she said, referring to the speed at which decisions are made in Beijing at the highest levels of government.

headline: Planning minister reviews local-currency financing mechanisms with World Bank
summary: Ahmed Rostom, Minister of Planning and Economic Development, held a meeting with Anshula Kant, Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer of the World Bank Group, to discuss prospects for cooperation and strengthen the development partnership between Egypt and the World Bank. The meeting took place on the sidelines of his participation in the intensive programme of events accompanying the annual meetings of the World Bank Group and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Bangkok, Thailand. During the meeting, the minister reviewed indicators of the Egyptian economy’s performance, stressing its growing ability to absorb shocks and achieve positive growth rates despite the complexities of the global economic landscape and regional geopolitical tensions. Rostom also outlined to the World Bank’s senior management the main features of the national economic transformation programme formulated by the Egyptian government. The programme consolidates macroeconomic stability, builds on gains achieved through recent structural reforms, and focuses on stimulating investment and production. The meeting featured extensive discussions on the implementation steps for an infrastructure project financing guarantee mechanism currently being developed in partnership with the World Bank. Rostom stressed the importance and priority of the mechanism, describing it as a qualitative leap towards attracting private investment and providing innovative, long-term financing solutions in local currency. He emphasised that activating the mechanism could directly reduce investment risks for the private sector. He pointed out that this would help improve public spending efficiency, ease financing pressures on the state budget and support the sustainability of infrastructure projects. The planning minister also met with Norwegian Minister of International Development Åsmund Grøver Aukrust to discuss ways to strengthen cooperation between Egypt and Norway. The meeting was attended by Badr Abdelatty, Minister of Foreign Affairs. During the meeting, Rostom said Egypt was committed to strengthening bilateral relations with Norway and building on the cooperation and partnership between the two countries to support development efforts and advance their shared interests. He noted that Egypt attached considerable importance to strengthening partnerships with international development partners to mobilise the resources and expertise needed to support national development priorities. Cooperation with Norway, he added, presented an important opportunity to explore new areas of joint work, particularly in light of global economic and development challenges. For his part, the Norwegian minister praised the proposed mechanism and expressed Norway’s interest in learning more about its details and potential applications. He affirmed his country’s readiness to explore opportunities to participate in the initiative, supporting efforts to increase investment in infrastructure projects and opening new avenues for development cooperation between Egypt and Norway.

headline: Sally Rooney can no longer sell books in the UK due to Palestine Action support
summary: Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold ​in ​the UK after she said she planned to use her royalties to ⁠support the banned campaign group Palestine Action.The bestselling author, who is known for novels including Normal People ⁠and Conversations with Friends, has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, which was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year.Ms Rooney had previously said that her plans could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in the UK, in a witness statement to London's High Court that challenged the government's ban.Her publisher Faber said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Ms Rooney that "we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format". However, it will continue to sell her works elsewhere."Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement. "To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher." Ms Rooney said in a statement: "I ​have made every effort to be honest with ‌the public about my ⁠beliefs and intentions and I ​am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."Palestine Action's sources of funding came under scrutiny after the government suggested it was backed by Iran, but the group has rejected the allegations. The group has continued to seek donations online despite being banned in the UK. Its co-founder Huda Ammori will challenge the decision to ban the group at the Supreme Court next month. The High Court had previously ruled that the ban on the group was unlawful, but the Court of Appeal then overturned this in favour of the Home Office's decision.Thousands of campaigners have been arrested in the UK for expressing support for Palestine Action after the ban. They include Robert Del Naja of the band Massive Attack, who was arrested for the second time last month. Ms Rooney has criticised the arrests, some of which have affected Irish citizens in the UK. Last year she wrote in The Irish Times that they were "selective enforcement of anti-terror law".She highlighted the activities of supporters of another proscribed organisation, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), who had repainted a loyalist mural in north Belfast after it was damaged by a storm last year.“No arrests were made on that basis, nor has the mural been taken down, though the UVF is a proscribed terrorist organisation responsible for the murders of hundreds of civilians," she said.“Palestine Action, proscribed under the same law, is responsible for zero deaths and has never advocated the use of violence against any human being. Why then are its supporters arrested for wearing T-shirts, while murals celebrating loyalist death squads are left untouched?”Ms Rooney is not the first high-profile donor to Palestine Action. James "Fergie" Chambers, an American communist and heir to a multibillion-pound conglomerate, said in a 2023 interview that he was paying Palestine Action’s legal fees.
body_text:
Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold ​in ​the UK after she said she planned to use her royalties to ⁠support the banned campaign group Palestine Action.

The bestselling author, who is known for novels including Normal People ⁠and Conversations with Friends, has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, which was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year.

Ms Rooney had previously said that her plans could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in the UK, in a witness statement to London's High Court that challenged the government's ban.

Palestine Action 'nans' put themselves on the line to inflate UK terror arrests

Her publisher Faber said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Ms Rooney that "we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format". However, it will continue to sell her works elsewhere.

"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement. "To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."

Ms Rooney said in a statement: "I ​have made every effort to be honest with ‌the public about my ⁠beliefs and intentions and I ​am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Palestine Action's sources of funding came under scrutiny after the government suggested it was backed by Iran, but the group has rejected the allegations. The group has continued to seek donations online despite being banned in the UK.

Its co-founder Huda Ammori will challenge the decision to ban the group at the Supreme Court next month. The High Court had previously ruled that the ban on the group was unlawful, but the Court of Appeal then overturned this in favour of the Home Office's decision.

Thousands of campaigners have been arrested in the UK for expressing support for Palestine Action after the ban. They include Robert Del Naja of the band Massive Attack, who was arrested for the second time last month.

Ms Rooney has criticised the arrests, some of which have affected Irish citizens in the UK. Last year she wrote in The Irish Times that they were "selective enforcement of anti-terror law".

She highlighted the activities of supporters of another proscribed organisation, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), who had repainted a loyalist mural in north Belfast after it was damaged by a storm last year.

“No arrests were made on that basis, nor has the mural been taken down, though the UVF is a proscribed terrorist organisation responsible for the murders of hundreds of civilians," she said.

“Palestine Action, proscribed under the same law, is responsible for zero deaths and has never advocated the use of violence against any human being. Why then are its supporters arrested for wearing T-shirts, while murals celebrating loyalist death squads are left untouched?”

Ms Rooney is not the first high-profile donor to Palestine Action. James "Fergie" Chambers, an American communist and heir to a multibillion-pound conglomerate, said in a 2023 interview that he was paying Palestine Action’s legal fees.

headline: Russia says at least 20,000 foreign mercenaries fought on Ukrainian side since 2022
summary: Yulia Zhdanova, head of the Russian delegation at the negotiations in Vienna on military security and arms control, noted that among the foreign participants in combat operations, there are many career military personnel from NATO countries, most of whom are operating under cover
body_text:
VIENNA, October 14. /TASS/. At least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have taken part in combat operations on the side of Ukraine since 2022, said Yulia Zhdanova, head of the Russian delegation at the negotiations in Vienna on military security and arms control.

"Since 2022, at least 20,000 foreign mercenaries have taken part in military operations on the Ukrainian side. Russian investigative authorities identified more than 4,000 ‘soldiers of fortune’ from over 70 countries," she said at a meeting of the OSCE Forum for Security Cooperation. Her statement is available to TASS. According to the diplomat, the largest number of identified mercenaries came from the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Georgia - more than 700 people from each country. Decisions were issued to charge 1,094 mercenaries as defendants; 296 cases were referred to court; 243 sentences were handed down.

Zhdanova also said that among the foreign participants in combat operations on the side of Ukraine, there are many career military personnel from NATO countries, most of whom are operating under cover. According to her, there are large training centers in Poland that operate under the supervision of the alliance’s military specialists.

headline: Since May 2025, Russia handed over almost 4,000 POWs to Kiev — diplomat
summary: Ukraine repatriated 3,886 captured Russian servicemen, Rodion Miroshnik said
body_text:
UNITED NATIONS, October 14. /TASS/. Since May 2025, Russia has handed over a total of 3,976 prisoners of war to Kiev, while Kiev repatriated 3,886 captured Russian servicemen, the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik said.

"At the Russian president’s initiative, the Istanbul format of negotiations was restored in May 2025, after a three-year-long pause," he told an unofficial Arria-formula meeting of the UN Security Council. "This paved the way to the resumption of detainee swaps after a prolonged disruption."

"Since May 2025, Russia has handed over to Ukraine at least 3,976 servicemen and around 208 non-combatants, while Ukraine returned a minimum of 3,886 servicemen and also 193 civilians to the Russian side," the Russian diplomat added.

headline: 'Trust the process': Republicans struggle for closing argument before midterms
summary: Times are tough for Republican strategists. With the November 3 midterm elections looming, they are desperately seeking a closing argument that explains why Americans should give US President Donald Trump and his party another two years in charge of Congress.In 2024, Mr Trump campaigned on lowering energy prices and inflation, ending “forever” wars, putting America first and clamping down on immigration.Two years on, his checklist of promises looks more like a litany of liabilities. Republicans are now trying to convince Americans that soaring fuel costs will be worth it in the long run, and that the US is enjoying a “Golden Age”, as inflation rises. Even one of Mr Trump's signature achievements – slashing illegal immigration – has become a liability, as voters react with horror to mass round-ups of suspected migrants and the killings of US citizens by masked federal officers.And then, of course, there is Iran.Mr Trump has yet to find an exit from the war he started, and he has turned to none other than Russian President Vladimir Putin for help. A diesel purchase deal with Moscow, which critics say will do little to bring down fuel prices, will also put money into the Kremlin's coffers to help finance its war machine in Ukraine. And a bipartisan group of US senators has warned that the revenues could also aid Russia's security co-operation with Iran – you know, the same country that America is at war with.The not-very-America-First vibe doesn’t give Republicans a lot to work with. They've tried blaming former president Joe Biden for everything amiss in the world. But Mr Biden has been out of office for nearly two years, and by some measures the economy was performing better at the end of his term than it is today.Which brings us to the White House's latest midterms marketing masterstroke. The message: “Trust the process.”“Bottom line, it’s all gonna work out. You know why? It always does," the White House said on X.In other words, the Republican strategy for winning the midterms essentially comes down to magical thinking: Trust us, everything will be fine … because we say it will.Trust the process. pic.twitter.com/CaGS35q5Lh— The White House (@WhiteHouse) October 13, 2026It is a curious pitch to make for a president who has often promised better days are just around the corner. People don't want a process, they want results. Mr Trump's promises that Americans would win so much they would become "sick and tired of winning" appear to be falling flat for a critical mass of voters.Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval rating in the low-to-mid 30s. In the 2018 midterms, during his previous term in office, the Republicans lost control of the House of Representatives and surrendered 40 seats. Mr Trump's approval rating then was generally in the low 40s.Republicans insist such surveys overcount Democratic support and speak of some epic polling blunders, including the prediction that Hillary Clinton would win the White House when she ran against Mr Trump in 2016. But while polls definitely can get things wrong, that does not amount to a campaign strategy in and of itself.Five Grand Old PartyMr Trump, who has railed against Democrats as "socialists", has promised a $5,000 "dividend" cheque to every adult American, should the Republicans retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives. He doesn't have the independent authority to order such payments, which would cost about $1.2 trillion, and some scholars contend that the offer amounts to a political bribe.Many remember Elon Musk's promise of a $5,000 rebate cheque from all the money the US was going to save through his slashes to the federal workforce, or Mr Trump's vow that tariffs would generate $2,000 reimbursements for citizens. What ended up happening, of course, is the national debt ballooned despite Mr Musk's cuts, while tariffs fuelled a jump in costs for US consumers. Fewer people seem as willing to believe the "cheques are in the post" promises as they were in the past.Meanwhile, Mr Trump still sees himself as the kingmaker who is adored by his party. Yet signs of trouble abound, as vulnerable Republicans quietly try to put some distance between themselves and their leader.In Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly." It's a striking contrast from the Republican talking point that the economic pain from the war is worth it.Other Republicans are playing down their association with Mr Trump. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for Florida governor, removed eight references to the President, a photograph of the pair together and an “Enact the Trump Agenda” section from his campaign website last month, according to Forbes.Polls also suggest that voters are preoccupied with the economy and the cost of living, with many holding Mr Trump responsible for how those issues are being handled. Aside from its "trust the process" argument, the Republican Party wants to persuade voters that the midterms are a choice between common sense and the Democrats' radical agenda of "men in women's sports" and an "open border". body_text:
Times are tough for Republican strategists. With the November 3 midterm elections looming, they are desperately seeking a closing argument that explains why Americans should give US President Donald Trump and his party another two years in charge of Congress.

In 2024, Mr Trump campaigned on lowering energy prices and inflation, ending “forever” wars, putting America first and clamping down on immigration.

Two years on, his checklist of promises looks more like a litany of liabilities.

Republicans are now trying to convince Americans that soaring fuel costs will be worth it in the long run, and that the US is enjoying a “Golden Age”, as inflation rises. Even one of Mr Trump's signature achievements – slashing illegal immigration – has become a liability, as voters react with horror to mass round-ups of suspected migrants and the killings of US citizens by masked federal officers.

And then, of course, there is Iran.

Mr Trump has yet to find an exit from the war he started, and he has turned to none other than Russian President Vladimir Putin for help. A diesel purchase deal with Moscow, which critics say will do little to bring down fuel prices, will also put money into the Kremlin's coffers to help finance its war machine in Ukraine. And a bipartisan group of US senators has warned that the revenues could also aid Russia's security co-operation with Iran – you know, the same country that America is at war with.

The not-very-America-First vibe doesn’t give Republicans a lot to work with. They've tried blaming former president Joe Biden for everything amiss in the world. But Mr Biden has been out of office for nearly two years, and by some measures the economy was performing better at the end of his term than it is today.

Which brings us to the White House's latest midterms marketing masterstroke. The message: “Trust the process.”

“Bottom line, it’s all gonna work out. You know why? It always does," the White House said on X.

In other words, the Republican strategy for winning the midterms essentially comes down to magical thinking: Trust us, everything will be fine … because we say it will.

It is a curious pitch to make for a president who has often promised better days are just around the corner. People don't want a process, they want results. Mr Trump's promises that Americans would win so much they would become "sick and tired of winning" appear to be falling flat for a critical mass of voters.

Recent polls put Mr Trump's approval rating in the low-to-mid 30s. In the 2018 midterms, during his previous term in office, the Republicans lost control of the House of Representatives and surrendered 40 seats. Mr Trump's approval rating then was generally in the low 40s.

Republicans insist such surveys overcount Democratic support and speak of some epic polling blunders, including the prediction that Hillary Clinton would win the White House when she ran against Mr Trump in 2016. But while polls definitely can get things wrong, that does not amount to a campaign strategy in and of itself.

Mr Trump, who has railed against Democrats as "socialists", has promised a $5,000 "dividend" cheque to every adult American, should the Republicans retain control of the US Senate and the House of Representatives.

He doesn't have the independent authority to order such payments, which would cost about $1.2 trillion, and some scholars contend that the offer amounts to a political bribe.

Many remember Elon Musk's promise of a $5,000 rebate cheque from all the money the US was going to save through his slashes to the federal workforce, or Mr Trump's vow that tariffs would generate $2,000 reimbursements for citizens.

What ended up happening, of course, is the national debt ballooned despite Mr Musk's cuts, while tariffs fuelled a jump in costs for US consumers. Fewer people seem as willing to believe the "cheques are in the post" promises as they were in the past.

Meanwhile, Mr Trump still sees himself as the kingmaker who is adored by his party. Yet signs of trouble abound, as vulnerable Republicans quietly try to put some distance between themselves and their leader.

In Michigan, Mike Rogers, the Trump-endorsed Republican Senate candidate running against Abdul El Sayed, is running an advertisement saying: “The war with Iran needs to end – and end quickly." It's a striking contrast from the Republican talking point that the economic pain from the war is worth it.

Other Republicans are playing down their association with Mr Trump. Byron Donalds, the Republican nominee for Florida governor, removed eight references to the President, a photograph of the pair together and an “Enact the Trump Agenda” section from his campaign website last month, according to Forbes.

Polls also suggest that voters are preoccupied with the economy and the cost of living, with many holding Mr Trump responsible for how those issues are being handled.

Aside from its "trust the process" argument, the Republican Party wants to persuade voters that the midterms are a choice between common sense and the Democrats' radical agenda of "men in women's sports" and an "open border". Those old culture war tropes may still resonate for many voters, but they don't help people at the petrol pump or at the supermarket checkout.

If the polls are to be believed, and judging by the sorry state of Republican messages, Mr Trump's party is on course for a "shellacking", to repeat the expression Barack Obama used in 2010 after his own midterm losses.

Trust the process? For a party struggling to explain why its promises have fallen short, it sounds less like a winning strategy than an admission that it has run out of answers.

headline: Macron to visit UAE on Gulf tour next week

​French ​President ⁠Emmanuel Macron will ⁠travel to ​the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar next week, it was announced on Wednesday.

Mr Macron plans to discuss the ​situation ‌in ⁠the Strait ​of ​Hormuz and ‌its effects ⁠on energy ⁠prices during his Gulf visit, which will run from October 19 to 21, his office said.

The four Gulf countries have all had energy sites attacked during the US-Iran war, which has also curtailed oil exports through the strait. With Yemen's Houthi rebels now pushing for control of a second strait, the Bab Al Mandeb, there are fears that the global energy crunch could worsen.

“In light of the crisis gripping the Middle East, the President will continue his efforts with regional leaders to promote a return to stability and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” an Elysee Palace source said.

“Discussions will also focus on securing and diversifying our energy supplies and their transport routes, with the aim of limiting the impact of the energy crisis on the daily lives of French people.”

The source said Mr Macron's talks in the UAE would address defence, security and new technologies such as AI. He is also expected to attend a climate event in Qatar and discuss economic relations with Gulf countries.

Mr Macron has made several trips to the UAE as President. Last December he met President Sheikh Mohamed at the Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi and spoke to French troops based in the country.

Earlier visits included his attendance at the Cop28 climate summit, which took place in Dubai in 2023, and a trip in 2017 to the opening ceremony of Louvre Abu Dhabi.

On Mr Macron's most recent Middle East trip, he visited Damascus in July in what was the first appearance in post-civil war Syria by a major western leader.

Mr Macron's second term ends next year and he is ineligible under the French constitution to run for a third.

headline: Starlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres
summary: Restrictions reported by Ukraine on its use of the US satellite internet system Starlink have exposed Kyiv's reliance on the technology for both offensive and defensive operations in its fight against Russia'a invasion, analysts and observers say.
