body_text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi said on Wednesday there were no plans to change Egypt's constitution, after calls by some supporters for him to stay in office after the end of his final term in 2030.

But Mr El Sisi appeared to leave the door open for a possible amendment to allow him to stay at the helm, saying Egyptians were the only ones who would decide on any initiative.

"The nation has a constitution that we adopted. No one can touch it, no one can touch it," he told a televised gathering of cabinet members and army officers.

"So, don't let anyone mess with your heads. The people alone will decide the success or lack thereof of anything that's done."

Calls for Mr El Sisi to stay in office beyond 2030 have been made publicly by loyal politicians and social media accounts linked to the government.

The campaign has picked up steam in recent months as opposition figures abroad intensified criticism of his policies. Mr El Sisi's comments on Wednesday were his first on the question of constitutional amendments.

In office since 2014, the Egyptian leader's final term ends in 2030, by which time he would have served for 16 years.

Egypt's constitution is a relatively progressive document adopted in a nationwide referendum in 2014, three years after autocratic president Hosni Mubarak was removed by a popular uprising after nearly 30 years in office.

Mr El Sisi owes his current term in office to previous constitutional amendments in 2019, which were adopted in a national referendum.

Before the changes, the constitution stipulated that no president could serve more than two four-year terms. The amendments kept the two-term cap but extended the term to six years and, in a clause added for Mr El Sisi's benefit, considered the first of his two terms in office to have begun in 2018, not 2014 when he was first elected.

And as was the case in 2018, when he ran against an obscure politician, Mr El Sisi – the latest in a line of military men who ruled Egypt since the monarchy was overthrown in the 1950s – ran again in 2023 against three little-known politicians, winning 89.6 per cent of the vote.

Many Egyptians see him as a safe pair of hands at a time when the Middle East is roiled in conflict, with unresolved wars in Gaza, Egypt's neighbour to the east, Sudan, its southern neighbour, and political instability in Libya, on its western border.

The fallout from the Iran war – from the on-and-off closure of the Strait of Hormuz, attacks on Tehran's Arab neighbours and strikes on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Iranian-backed Houthis – has affected Egypt's economy, increasing its already high energy import bills and badly blocking revenue from the Suez Canal.

Supporters of Mr El Sisi praise the stability of Egypt during those challenges, while he repeatedly urges Egyptians to endure their economic hardship and praises their resilience.

But critics insist the government's policies are at the root of the country's economic woes, due to what they regard as excessive foreign and domestic borrowing and spending on infrastructure projects that will take years to generate revenue.

They also blame the government for not dealing effectively with a decade-old water dispute with Ethiopia that could reduce the country's vital share of the Nile waters.

Mr El Sisi rejects the criticism, saying the billions of dollars spent on infrastructure and modern transport, such as a Cairo monorail, a cutting-edge electric train and a new capital, prepare the nation to attract sizable foreign investments.

He says Ethiopia saw in the turmoil in Egypt that followed the removal of Mubarak in 2011 a chance to start construction of a massive dam on the Blue Nile, the river's main tributary and source of more than 80 per cent of the water reaching downstream.

headline: Egypt’s FM pushes investment, development financing talks at World Bank-IMF meetings
summary: Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a series of meetings with international and Arab financing institutions and foreign officials in Bangkok on Wednesday, focusing on private-sector investment, development financing, job creation and regional issues on the sidelines of the World Bank and IMF meetings. Abdelatty met International Finance Corporation (IFC) Managing Director Makhtar Diop, alongside Planning and Economic Development Minister Ahmed Rostom, to discuss increasing IFC investment in Egypt and supporting private-sector participation in renewable energy, green hydrogen and infrastructure. He praised the IFC’s role in supporting Egypt’s state asset offering programme and called for stronger trilateral cooperation in Africa, combining the implementation capacity of Egyptian companies with IFC financing and advisory expertise. The talks also covered support for small and medium-sized businesses, climate finance, trade financing and risk-sharing mechanisms. In another meeting, Abdelatty held talks with Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa President Abdullah Al-Musaibeh on increasing the participation of Egyptian companies in projects financed by the bank across Africa, particularly in infrastructure, agriculture, value chains and private-sector development. Abdelatty also took part in a ministerial roundtable on job creation attended by World Bank Group President Ajay Banga. He said development finance should produce tangible and sustainable employment and pointed to Egypt’s institutional mechanisms for monitoring projects and removing implementation obstacles, including a presidential committee overseeing national projects. Abdelatty also called for wider use of guarantees to mobilise private investment alongside concessional development finance. He later met Tsutomu Yamamoto, Managing Director of the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA), to discuss expanding the agency’s role in supporting investment and strengthening investor confidence in Egypt. Abdelatty said the government was seeking to increase private-sector participation through tax and customs incentives, digitalised procedures and updated regulatory frameworks, while taking measures to secure energy and food supplies and maintain fiscal discipline amid regional and global pressures. On regional and bilateral issues, Abdelatty met British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to discuss economic, investment and trade ties, as well as escalating regional tensions and their implications for energy and food security. According to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry, the two ministers stressed the importance of de-escalation and political and diplomatic solutions and condemned recent attacks on Saudi Arabia. They also discussed Sudan, with Abdelatty stressing the need to preserve the country’s unity, territorial integrity and national institutions. The ministry said the talks included the need to halt arms flows to the militia and support state institutions as part of efforts towards a ceasefire. Abdelatty also met Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) Senior Vice President Yoko Mitsui, discussing expanded cooperation in the green transition, artificial intelligence, digital transformation and industrial localisation. The talks also covered continued support for the Egypt-Japan University of Science and Technology and training Egyptian personnel in specialised engineering and technology fields. In a separate meeting with Norwegian International Development Minister Åsmund Grøver Aukrust, Abdelatty discussed increasing Norwegian investment in clean and renewable energy, green hydrogen, energy storage and green infrastructure. They also addressed Gaza, stressing humanitarian access, civilian protection and support for early recovery and reconstruction, while Abdelatty proposed broader Egypt-Norway trilateral development cooperation in Africa. Abdelatty later met Fawzi Youssef Al-Hanif, head of the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development, and called for more flexible financing tools to address trade and supply-chain disruptions, debt burdens, food and water security and climate change. The meeting covered regional projects in electricity interconnection, transport, logistics, food security and cross-border infrastructure, as well as greater co-financing among Arab, regional and international financial institutions. Abdelatty also addressed a meeting of African governors with World Bank President Ajay Banga on behalf of the African group, calling for faster implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area and the removal of barriers facing African companies, trade and investment. He urged the World Bank to establish a systematic mechanism to monitor implementation of African economic integration commitments and measure actual results rather than focusing only on pledges.

headline: At least 27 children killed in Pakistan school roof collapse, with death toll feared to rise
summary: At least 27 pupils and a teacher were killed in Pakistan when the roof of a school collapsed during classes in the north-western city of Peshawar on Thursday, authorities said.The death toll is expected to rise as rescue teams continue searching for children trapped beneath the rubble of the privately run Al Khair Education Centre.“We have taken out at least 45 children,” said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan. More pupils are believed to be buried under the debris, he added.Government official Bilal Faizi said rescue teams were working to recover bodies and transport the injured to hospital.At least 20 injured people and most of those killed were taken to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, according to hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim.A rescue official said the roof of an upper floor collapsed on to the classrooms below, causing both storeys to cave in. He said excessive weight from construction on the roof caused the collapse.Authorities have ordered an investigation into the cause of the disaster.
body_text:
At least 27 pupils and a teacher were killed in Pakistan when the roof of a school collapsed during classes in the north-western city of Peshawar on Thursday, authorities said.

The death toll is expected to rise as rescue teams continue searching for children trapped beneath the rubble of the privately run Al Khair Education Centre.

“We have taken out at least 45 children,” said district emergency officer Iftikhar Khan. More pupils are believed to be buried under the debris, he added.

Government official Bilal Faizi said rescue teams were working to recover bodies and transport the injured to hospital.

At least 20 injured people and most of those killed were taken to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, according to hospital spokesperson Mohammad Asim.

A rescue official said the roof of an upper floor collapsed on to the classrooms below, causing both storeys to cave in. The incident took place in the middle of the school day.

Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said only 47 of the 110 students, most under the age of 13, who were inside the classrooms when the roof collapsed had been rescued.

headline: School roof collapse kills at least 29, injures more than 3 dozen in Pakistan
summary: The roof of a private school collapsed in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday, killing at least 28 children and a female teacher and injuring more than 50 other people.(Image credit: Maaz Awan)
body_text:
A volunteer clears the way for an ambulance transporting injured school children following a roof collapse at a private school in Peshawar, Pakistan, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Maaz Awan/AP hide caption

PESHAWAR, Pakistan — The roof of a private school collapsed in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday, killing at least 28 children and a female teacher and injuring more than 50 other people, a hospital spokesman said, as rescuers searched the rubble for anyone still trapped. Six girls were among the dead.

Several children were also trapped under the rubble in Peshawar, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, said Bilal Faizi, a spokesman for the emergency services.

A hospital spokesman, Mohammad Asim, also confirmed the casualties, saying some of the injured were in critical condition. All the children killed or injured were age 13 or younger, he said. The hospital declared an emergency as medical staff treated the wounded.

Hours later, rescue officials said that everyone trapped beneath the rubble had been pulled out and crews were clearing the debris. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Gov. Faisal Karim Kundi expressed sorrow over the collapse and sought a report from the relevant authorities about the cause of the collapse. He directed officials to provide the best possible medical care to the injured children.

Mahwish Zaman, an injured teacher speaking from a hospital bed, said that the three-story school had an estimated 1,200 students enrolled in nursery through fifth grade. She told The Associated Press that she was in her classroom when the roof collapsed and felt as if the sky had fallen. She regained consciousness in the hospital.

Rescue workers and volunteers take part in the rescue operation at the site of a roof collapse at a private school, in Peshawar, Pakistan, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Maaz Awan/AP hide caption

According to witnesses, residents were among the first to reach the school in a congested neighborhood in central Peshawar. Rescue workers arrived within minutes of being alerted, according to accounts from the scene.

A resident, Samiullah Khan, said that he rushed to the school after learning of the collapse and helped rescue three girls. Khan said his son, who attends the school, survived because he had stepped out of his classroom to drink water.

A resident, Mohammad Khan, said rescuers carefully removed debris, trying to reach children and staff feared trapped beneath the collapsed roof. Outside the school and at the state-run Lady Reading Hospital, anguished parents sought information about their children, unsure whether they had survived.

The cause of the collapse was under investigation. Peshawar police chief Saeed Ahmed said that the school's owner had been arrested. He said that the building was structurally weak.

The provincial government said that the school occupied a three-story building and that a committee had been formed to investigate the cause of the roof collapse.

The provincial government spokeswoman, Samar Haroon Bilour, said that the government directed hospital officials to provide prompt medical care to the injured children and praised rescue workers for their swift response. She said that the government was using all available resources to bring those trapped beneath the rubble to safety.

In Islamabad, President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed sorrow over the deaths and offered condolences to the bereaved families in separate statements.

"The entire nation shares the grief of the affected families in this hour of sorrow," Zardari said.

He also called for a comprehensive investigation into the collapse and stressed the need to ensure school buildings meet safety standards to prevent similar tragedies.

In July, a roof collapsed at a tutoring center under construction in Lahore, killing four schoolchildren.

Building collapses are common in Pakistan, where construction standards are often poorly enforced. Many structures are built with substandard materials, and safety regulations are frequently ignored to reduce costs.

Elon Musk on Wednesday sought to distance himself from the satellite communications restrictions over Ukraine that have disrupted Kyiv's military operations, suggesting that US President Donald Trump is ultimately behind any changes.

There has been growing tension between Washington and Kyiv after Mr Trump's agreement with President Vladimir Putin to resume buying Russian diesel, which critics have called a betrayal of Ukraine.

Since the deal was announced last week, Ukrainian officials have said restrictions on satellite terminals have disrupted drone operations as Russia continues to attack Ukrainian energy sites.

Why Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire may offer oil markets little relief

Kyiv has also reported difficulties in receiving advance warnings of Russian missile attacks, although it is unclear whether these are connected to the satellite restrictions.

In a post on X, Mr Musk drew a distinction between Starlink, which is the satellite internet company owned by SpaceX, and Starshield, a national security and military subsidiary.

"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Mr Musk said. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS [the President of the United States]."

He was responding to a post minutes earlier by former Ukrainian defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said that some of the satellite connectivity was being restored. “Thank you, Elon Musk. We hope for your continued support,” he said.

Mr Musk added that use of Starlink "is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company".

Mr Musk's post leaves key questions unanswered, including who authorised the restriction and whether SpaceX acted on instructions from the US military or from Mr Trump.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A source told Reuters that SpaceX had limited terminal connections, complicating Ukrainian drone interceptions and mid-range strikes.

In an interview on the Piers Morgan Uncensored YouTube channel, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Mr Trump and Mr Musk of restraining Kyiv’s military access to SpaceX’s satellite technology, deepening the rift between Washington and Kyiv.

“I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely,” Mr Zelenskyy said when asked if Ukraine’s use of the satellite service had been intentionally disrupted. “I think he is not right. It’s a big mistake.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ukraine also depends on US intelligence assistance for early warning of Russian missile launches. White House officials are actively discussing the possibility of cutting that arrangement with Ukraine, although there is no consensus on what to do, Semafor reported on Wednesday, quoting an unidentified administration official. Mr Trump said on Tuesday that the US continued to share intelligence with Ukraine.

His deal with Russia has drawn bipartisan criticism. On Tuesday, 12 senators wrote him a letter asking him to rescind it. One of the signatories, Republican Senator Thom Tillis, on Wednesday asked Mr Musk to clarify what was happening with Starlink.

"Supporting Ukrainian sovereignty – or at the very least, allowing for it – should not be a grey area for the US government or for American corporations. Can you clarify the SpaceX position?" he wrote on X.

The suggestion that Mr Musk's company had ⁠limited Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.

"Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister ⁠Radoslaw Sikorski posted on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."

There was no immediate response from Mr Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man".

headline: What is Starshield, SpaceX's military version of Starlink?
summary: Elon Musk’s ⁠SpaceX restricted “military-grade” ​Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.
body_text:
Elon Musk’s ⁠SpaceX restricted “military-grade” ​Starlink services overnight into Wednesday, hampering Ukrainian drone strike missions and air defenses, Ukraine reported. In response, Musk said that the US government was behind any slowdown in Ukraine's Starshield system.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 22:15

The claims drew renewed attention to the distinction between Starlink – SpaceX’s commercial satellite internet service – and Starshield, ​a military version developed for the Pentagon. While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology.

“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government,” Musk said on Wednesday in a post on X, adding that any ​limits on speed ‌or usage are decided by the US military or the president.

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled ⁠by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”

Starlink is a satellite internet network of more than 11,000 satellites that beam broadband ⁠service directly to user terminals about the size of a folded newspaper. Its roughly 13 million subscribers range from households and hikers to shipping companies and major airlines. It is ‌the main profit engine of SpaceX.

Since launching its first Starlink satellites in 2019 aboard reusable SpaceX rockets, the company ​has built a vast low-Earth-orbit constellation that blankets much of the planet, delivering faster connections than traditional ‌communications satellites, which typically operate much farther from Earth and in far smaller numbers.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Starlink gave Ukraine a critical communications advantage early in the war, reshaping how militaries operate on the battlefield. But Musk has restricted Starlink for certain military uses while highlighting Starshield, a more secure network developed for government and military ‌missions.

Starshield is a SpaceX business unit that develops military and intelligence satellite systems for the Pentagon.

While its missions are separate from Starlink’s commercial broadband service, the distinction is not ​always clear-cut: Starshield’s secure communications services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.

Watch moreStarlink restriction 'no surprise' after Musk condemned Ukraine strikes on Russian data centres

Starshield leverages the technology, engineering and operational experiences of Starlink, according to SpaceX. In addition to secure communications, the company says the militarised version can also ​provide users with Earth observation and the ability to integrate sensors or other payloads.

The Pentagon, Starshield’s largest customer, has spent billions of dollars ​on both Starlink and Starshield services. It has also bought dedicated Starshield satellites, including communications spacecraft for ​missile-warning missions and a spy constellation for the National Reconnaissance Office, Reuters reported in 2024.

Questions over the relationship between Starlink and Starshield have persisted since Russia threatened Western satellites supporting Ukraine in 2022. SpaceX ​unveiled Starshield later that year, but the secrecy surrounding national security space programmes has left the precise boundaries between the two systems opaque.

Those distinctions became a point of contention earlier this year when the Pentagon clashed with SpaceX over higher prices for satellite services used by military drones during the Iran conflict, Reuters reported. SpaceX argued that some customers paying roughly $5,000 per terminal for Starlink should instead have been using a Starshield service ⁠costing about $25,000 per terminal.

Britain has also adopted Starshield. Under that arrangement, the service uses the same satellite constellation, ground stations and terrestrial infrastructure as Starlink, but operates through dedicated terminals ⁠and separate network gateways, Britain’s ​defence ministry has told Reuters.

Other US partners are evaluating the system as well. New Zealand is doing a trial of Starshield to assess its usefulness for military operations, the New Zealand Defence Force previously told Reuters.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

body_text:
A Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by an unidentified projectile.

All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were evacuated safely and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority has said.

The sinking was confirmed on Wednesday, after the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported the attack on Tuesday. A sister ship, the GFS Giselle, was damaged in the same wave of attacks but made its way to anchorage. Singapore condemned the strikes as a breach of international law.

Hormuz attacks surge as Iran steps up campaign against US-backed oil shipping

The incident highlights how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for global energy supplies.

Photos and videos on social media appeared to show a container ship listing heavily under thick black smoke, with containers and their contents floating nearby. Pakistan’s maritime authority warned mariners of floating containers in the area.

Other clips added a stranger note. Posts on X suggested small boats converged on the scene to scoop up cargo, and one described sellers doing business on the spot, calling out: “Do you want iPhones? Do you want perfumes?” Another post said paying Iran’s unilaterally declared transit toll, which has faced international opposition, would beat losing everything on board.

The footage is unverified. It could not be confirmed where or when any clip was filmed and whether it relates to the GFS Pride.

The GFS Pride had the capacity to carry 2,824 standard containers, it was reported. It was not clear how many it was carrying when it sank and no manifest was published.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said the ship had more than 2,500 containers, including alleged contraband. The claim could be substantiated. The IRGC also warned local vessels and fishermen to avoid the floating boxes.

Quoting two senior Iranian officials, Reuters reported on Wednesday that Tehran was changing its tactics against shipping to keep oil prices high and influence the November 3 US midterm elections. One warned such vessels “would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz”. Another said a complete closure of the waterway would come soon.

The IRGC claimed the ship struck a naval mine while using an “unauthorised” route. Tehran has described the US-backed route hugging the Omani coast as dangerous.

Maritime security firm Marisks said there was no independent evidence that a mine sank the vessel and described Iran’s claims as consistent with a psychological operations campaign. The available evidence does not establish that the southern route near Oman has been mined.

SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- North Korea said Thursday it test-fired two types of strategic cruise missile in the East Sea the previous day, in what may be the first launch from a 3,000-ton-class submarine it unveiled in 2023.

"The test-fire aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems and contributed to getting the Navy skilled in performing its strategic missions and showcasing high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the North's Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

DPRK stands for North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

The test was overseen by Kim Jong-sik, a member of the Central Military Commission of the Workers' Party of Korea, Jang Chang-ha, director-general of the Missile Administration and the Navy's underwater weapon system engineers, the report said.

Experts said the missiles appeared to be launched from what the North called its first tactical nuclear attack submarine, Hero Kim Kun Ok.

North Korea unveiled the vessel in September 2023 and described it as one of the "core underwater offensive means" of its navy.

At the launching ceremony on Sept. 6, 2023, North Korean leader Kim Jong-un was quoted as saying that arming the navy with nuclear weapons "brooks no further delay."

Wednesday's test was the first of its kind since January 2024, when the North said Pulhwasal-3-31 strategic cruise missiles were fired from the 2,000-ton-class 8.24 Yongung submarine, with Kim watching.

North Korea first reported its test-firing of a submarine-launched cruise missile from the same vessel in March 2023.

The fact that Wednesday's launch took place without Kim's attendance is seen as a way to show off the navy's capabilities while avoiding heavy outside pressure. The KCNA said the launch "did not have any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries."

South Korea's military did not publicly disclose Wednesday's launch, but said it had tracked the missiles from before launch to the end of their flight, rejecting claims that it may have missed them.

"Our military has persistently monitored and tracked the North Korean cruise missile activity reported yesterday, using various assets from before the launch through the cruise phase to the end of the flight," Capt. Jang Do-young, a spokesperson for the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS), told a press briefing.

He declined to elaborate on the surveillance assets used, citing confidentiality with the United States.

When asked if the military could specify the launching system, Jang said one type of missile was fired from a vertical launching system, while another was fired from a torpedo launcher.

The Rodong Sinmun, the North's most widely read newspaper, did not report the launch.

Earlier this week, Pyongyang test-fired tactical ballistic missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the East Sea. The North said Tuesday the launch was intended to "confirm the success in the research for the technical upgrading of an important core element."

headline: North Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
summary: North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.
body_text:
North Korea test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles on Wednesday, state media KCNA reported Thursday, saying the launches posed no threat to neighbouring countries. The tests follow heightened tensions with South Korea after a September 21 landmine explosion in the Demilitarised Zone injured three South Korean soldiers.

Issued on: 15/10/2026 - 01:12Modified: 15/10/2026 - 02:18

North Korea has test-fired two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles, state news agency KCNA said Thursday.

The agency said the missiles were fired Wednesday into the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, without "any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries".

The reported launch came after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between North and South Korea.

Three South Korean soldiers were injured in the September 21 blast in the Seoul-controlled area of the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), with both countries testing upgraded missile technology in the aftermath.

The latest testing "aimed to examine the current mobilized posture of the underwater combat systems" and served as a Navy training exercise, KCNA said.

The tests showed the "high reliability, trustworthiness and ability of the war deterrents of the DPRK," the agency reported, referring to North Korea by the abbreviation of the country's official name.

Photos released by KCNA showed one missile blasting vertically out of the sea trailed by a thick plume of smoke. Another photo appeared to show a projectile erupting from the water at a 45-degree angle.

Read moreNorth Korea launches ballistic missile as tensions with Seoul grow over border mine blasts

Other images showed a missile flying horizontally over the sea, as well as a submarine traveling on the water's surface.

The North's ability to launch missiles from submarines at two different angles carries "tactical significance", Hong Min of the Korea Institute for National Unification told AFP, as the two launch methods serve different purposes.

"Vertical launches allow missiles to climb steeply before descending towards their targets, potentially extending their range," he said.

"Angled launches, on the other hand, allow missiles to fly at lower altitudes from the outset, making them harder for missile defence systems to detect and intercept."

North Korea has carried out several missile launches from submarines in recent years, although its sea-based launch capabilities remain unclear.

Cruise missiles tend to be jet-propelled and fly at a lower altitude than more sophisticated ballistic missiles, making them harder to detect and intercept.

Proven submarine-launched ballistic missile capability would take North Korea's arsenal to a new level, allowing deployment far beyond the Korean peninsula and a second-strike capability in the event of an attack.

North Korea has carried out multiple ballistic missile tests in October, most recently on Monday.

The two Koreas have engaged in a tit-for-tat series of missile tests this month, with both sides test-firing hypersonic weapons.

South Korea test-fired its first homegrown hypersonic missile last week, days after Pyongyang said it had launched an AI-assisted intermediate-range hypersonic missile.

Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.

headline: Strait of Hormuz closed, transit must be coordinated
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – Iran's deputy army coordinator said the Strait of Hormuz is closed and any transit requires coordination, citing rising US gasoline prices as proof.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – Iran's deputy army coordinator said the Strait of Hormuz is closed and any transit requires coordination, citing rising US gasoline prices as proof.

Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, Chief of Staff and Deputy Coordinator of Iran's Army, said the Strait of Hormuz is closed and that any passage through it must be coordinated.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday on the sidelines of a ceremony honoring army nurses, Sayyari said that if the strait were not closed and oil were passing through, gasoline prices in the United States would not have risen. He called this clear and evident.

He described the military posture in the region: the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy is firmly positioned in the west of the Strait of Hormuz, while the Army of the Islamic Republic of Iran is present with authority from the east of the strait to the north of the Sea of Oman, exercising full control and surveillance over the area.

Sayyari stressed that any transit must be coordinated, warning that otherwise "you see in the news what happens."

headline: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 15, 2026
summary: [allAfrica]
body_text:
Kenya Confirms Second Ebola Case Linked to First Patient

Kenya has confirmed a second Ebola case, 10 days after a 40-year-old man died from the virus following travel from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) through Uganda. The new patient, a 39-year-old close relative of the first victim, was already in quarantine when he developed symptoms. The incubation period for Ebola ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks. Health officials said that both cases are linked, with no evidence of wider community transmission. Authorities have traced 128 contacts of the first patient, 113 of whom are in quarantine. Efforts to find the remaining contacts continue. Kenya has maintained that travel, trade and public gatherings remain unrestricted. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Mauritius Imposes Curfew After Violent Protests

Mauritius has imposed an overnight curfew following violent protests over water shortages and the rising cost of living, marking the island's worst unrest in decades. Demonstrations escalated after a woman was shot and injured by police at a roadblock. The circumstances of the shooting were not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody. Protesters burned tyres, blocked roads and vandalised police stations and public infrastructure, prompting school and public transport closures. Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam warned that those responsible would face consequences. Police reported some overnight incidents and arrests. Analysts warn that unrest could return if water shortages persist until the rainy season in December.

Sudan's War Deepens Humanitarian and Food Crisis

Fighting between Sudan's Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season. The conflict, which began in April 2023, has displaced more than 12.4 million people and left an estimated 24.6 million facing acute food insecurity. Aid organisations warn that hundreds of thousands of young children are suffering severe malnutrition. Drought, flooding, fuel shortages and declining fertiliser supplies are worsening food production and prices. The UN's 2026 humanitarian response plan, requiring US$2.9 billion, is only 41% funded. Observers also warn that continued arms supplies and drone attacks are prolonging the conflict and increasing civilian casualties.

Amnesty Warns of Continued Abuses in Mali Despite Wagner's Replacement

Amnesty International has warned that serious human rights abuses against civilians in Mali continue despite the Russian-backed Africa Corps replacing the Wagner Group in supporting Malian military operations. The organisation documented seven incidents between 2023 and 2025 in which 34 civilians were allegedly deliberately killed, alongside torture, sexual violence, arbitrary detention, looting and destruction of property. Members of Fulani, Tuareg and Arab communities along the Mauritanian border were among those most affected. Amnesty also cited allegations of abuses by Africa Corps members, including a July 2026 raid in Bombori in which six people were reportedly shot dead and three others executed. It called for independent investigations to hold accountable those suspected of war crimes and for greater protection for civilians.

DR Congo Cholera Cases Surge Amid Ebola Outbreak

The World Health Organisation has said that from January 2025 to the end of September 2026, there were more than 125,000 suspected cases of cholera and 3,644 suspected deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In 2026, there were more than 51,400 suspected cases and 1,487 deaths in 21 provinces. Most of the cases were in South Kivu, North Kivu, and Haut-Katanga, which together made up almost 60% of the cases. Response efforts are being hampered by a lack of clean water and toilets, as well as by safety concerns and problems getting to remote communities. Health authorities are expanding water chlorination, household disinfection and vaccination preparations, including a planned cross-border campaign with the Republic of Congo. The crisis comes as the DR Congo continues to battle Ebola, with neighbouring Kenya recently confirming a second case linked to the outbreak.

Foot-and-Mouth Restrictions Push Up Meat Prices in Namibia

Foot-and-mouth disease restrictions in Namibia are causing meat shortages and price increases at butcheries and restaurants as limits on livestock sales and slaughtering disrupt supplies. Butchers report rising costs for meat trimmings and cheaper cuts traditionally used to make mince and sausages, forcing some businesses to switch to more expensive cuts and raise prices. Restaurants have also increased prices for selected dishes, including rump, sirloin and T-bone steaks. Others are absorbing higher supplier costs to avoid passing them on to customers. Some small businesses say they cannot obtain livestock at all, threatening their ability to operate. The disease has spread to 17 farms in the ||Kharas region. Positive cases have also been reported in the Zambezi region.

headline: US may use the ultra-powerful 'mother of all bombs' against Iran — broadcaster
summary: According to the broadcaster, the Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities could be targeted if US President Donald Trump orders a resumption of hostilities
body_text:
NEW YORK, October 15. /TASS/. The US is considering the possibility of striking Iran with the ultra-powerful GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB), unofficially known as the "mother of all bombs," CNN reported, citing sources.

According to the broadcaster, the Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear facilities could be targeted if US President Donald Trump orders a resumption of hostilities. The MOAB weighs more than 9.5 tons and is the most powerful non-nuclear bomb in the US military’s arsenal, CNN pointed out. However, its ability to achieve the strategic goals stated by President Trump is questionable. The broadcaster pointed out that its use would mark a significant escalation in the US conflict with Tehran.

The White House has ordered the military to develop additional plans for strikes against Iran, including "a lot of energy infrastructure" on the list of targets, and to plan for the potential use of the MOAB, one of the CNN’s sources noted. According to another unnamed source, the US military plans to strike Iranian nuclear facilities and a site near Natanz, allegedly hidden beneath Pickaxe Mountain. "The president has unfortunately put himself in a situation where he is almost compelled to do something and, without the ammunition designed to penetrate that level <…> you have to look at psychological effects for which the MOAB is well-equipped," a source told CNN.

According to the broadcaster, many members of the US administration believe the only way to defeat Iran is with a large-scale operation involving ground troops, which could result in the deaths of thousands of American soldiers. The Pentagon is exploring all options, including this one. However, so far, no one in the administration is insisting on a ground operation. Trump has also made it clear that he is not interested in sending US troops to Iran, CNN stated.

headline: Ghalibaf says US must be punished to accept Iran's demands
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says that both military action and talks are tools to achieve deterrence, adding that the US must be punished and make concessions in dealing with Iran.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 14 (MNA) – Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf says that both military action and talks are tools to achieve deterrence, adding that the US must be punished and make concessions in dealing with Iran.

Speaking in a televised interview aired on Wednesday evening, Ghalibaf criticized Washington for violating the Islamabad Agreement. "Even if the United States accepts commitments in a signed document, this would not, by itself, prevent another attack on Iran."

He also noted that continuing the war and escalating tensions alone would not necessarily deter the adversary from making further threats. According to Ghalibaf, Iran’s strategy must combine military preparedness with negotiations to establish lasting deterrence.

Referring to Iran’s eight-year war with Iraq, Ghalibaf said that despite the costs and hardships of the conflict, Iran had established conditions that deterred attacks against the country for decades.

Ghalibaf stressed that military strength is not the only factor in deterrence, pointing to a broader range of domestic and regional capabilities.

He cited improvements in Iran’s firepower, offensive capabilities and air defenses as key military components, saying these capabilities had increased between the 12-day war and the most recent conflict. He also highlighted the capabilities of regional resistance groups, Iran’s strategic position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, national unity, and economic and social resilience.

The parliament speaker said the goal was to make Iran strong enough that the United States and other regional and international actors could not achieve their objectives through military attacks.

Ghalibaf said Iran must be prepared to defend itself with full force when necessary while using diplomatic opportunities to consolidate military gains and protect national interests.

He argued that military victories should be translated into political and legal gains, while negotiations should provide Iran with the time and resources needed to strengthen its capabilities.

Ghalibaf emphasized that combining war and negotiations did not mean pursuing an endless war or engaging in permanent negotiations. Rather, he said, the objective was to compel the other side to accept Iran’s demands or, if it refused, acknowledge defeat and grant concessions that would allow Iran to strengthen its deterrence capabilities.

He concluded by stressing the need to maintain national unity and strengthen Iran’s military, economic and diplomatic capabilities. He said the country must use its existing resources to ease the economic pressures facing the public and turn current hardships into a more promising future.

body_text:
Manchester City's 4-2 defeat by Paris Saint-Germain in the Uefa Champions League told only part of ​the ​story of Enzo ​Maresca's first loss at the helm, with ⁠his men staggering through the first half before roaring ⁠back after the break.

⁠City were staring at a rout when a rampant PSG raced to a 3-0 lead with a first-half masterclass. Then they woke up.

Maresca's side tore into the visitors after half-time, pouring forward with ⁠an intensity and urgency that had been entirely absent in the opening 45 minutes.

Lammens: United must learn quickly and cut out defensive errors

Erling ​Haaland spearheaded ⁠the fightback, scoring twice to ‌become the fastest player to reach 60 Champions League goals, hitting the mark in ​just 60 games, 20 quicker than Lionel Messi.

City kept coming. They finished with nearly twice as many shots as PSG and around three times as many touches in the opposition box, while recording a higher expected goals figure at both half-time and full-time. PSG, though, were more ruthless.

“I think we start quite good until the first goal [from Desire Doue in the 13th minute] and then we concede the second one (Ousmane Dembele) after one minute. That created some bad feelings,” Maresca told TNT Sports.

“Second half, we were much better and probably deserved something more.”

City had arrived on the back of a 3-0 thrashing of Liverpool in the Premier League on Sunday and Maresca felt they generated enough chances to salvage something even ​after digging themselves a three-goal hole.

“Even with 3-0 in the first ‌half, with the amount of ⁠chances we created in the second half, ​we deserved more,” he said. “Luis (Enrique, PSG's manager) said at the end of the ​game that ‌they were quite lucky today.

“You have to be clinical but not lose the balance,” Maresca said.

The ⁠defeat unfolded against a backdrop of turmoil stretching far beyond City as an independent commission found City guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period.

City have denied any wrongdoing and have appealed.

On the pitch, they remain three points clear of Arsenal atop ​the Premier League table ahead of Saturday's home game against Ipswich.

Asked if he had a message for supporters, Maresca said: “We are sorry for the first half for sure. Saturday is a Premier League game and we need to continue our run.”

Former City manager Pep Guardiola watched from the stands in Manchester alongside chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and senior executives Ferran Soriano and Hugo Viana.

On a breathless night of Champions League football featuring 46 goals, Real Madrid staged a stunning comeback to beat AS Roma 4-3.

At the ‌Stadio Olimpico, Real Madrid scored three times in the closing stages to overturn a two-goal deficit.

Marten de Roon gave Roma the lead ⁠in the 20th minute before Kylian Mbappe equalised five minutes later, but Donyell Malen struck twice in the 51st ⁠and 57th minutes to put the hosts in control.

headline: PSG beat Manchester City in Champions League after financial rules verdict
summary: Defending champions Paris Saint-Germain held off a second-half comeback to beat Manchester City 4-2 away in the Champions League on Wednesday. Goals from Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha gave PSG a 3-0 lead before Erling Haaland struck twice. Maghnes Akliouche added a fourth, while Ferran Torres missed a late penalty.
body_text:
Defending champions Paris Saint-Germain held off a second-half comeback to beat Manchester City 4-2 away in the Champions League on Wednesday. Goals from Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha gave PSG a 3-0 lead before Erling Haaland struck twice. Maghnes Akliouche added a fourth, while Ferran Torres missed a late penalty.

Issued on: 14/10/2026 - 23:48Modified: 14/10/2026 - 23:49

Paris Saint-Germain further soured the mood at the Etihad Stadium as Manchester City's first home game since the guilty verdict on widespread flouting of Premier League financial rules ended in a 4-2 Champions League defeat on Wednesday.

The European champions turned on the style to strike three times inside the opening 35 minutes through Desire Doue, Ousmane Dembele and Vitinha.

But City stormed back in the second half as Erling Haaland scored twice either side of Maghnes Akliouche's strike that briefly restored PSG's three-goal cushion.

The 10-time English champions face swingeing sanctions unless they can successfully appeal the ruling of an independent commission last month, which found the club guilty on over 100 charges of financial impropriety.

City shrugged off the uncertainty over their future to win 3-0 at Liverpool on Sunday and remain top of the Premier League, but PSG showed why they are the favourites to win this competition for a third consecutive season.

Read moreChampions League: Arsenal leave no chance to Lille and Olivier Giroud

Former City manager Pep Guardiola returned to the Etihad for the first time since his departure in May, sat behind the club's embattled chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano in a show of solidarity.

City made passing reference to the guilty verdict with a lengthy pre-match video detailing the club's historic moments of celebration both before and after an Abu Dhabi-backed takeover in 2008 that transformed their fortunes.

Behind one end supporters unravelled a giant banner reading: "I'm City till I die."

Yet the fighting talk in the stands was not matched on the field as City were blown away by a scintillating first 45 minutes from the visitors.

Luis Enrique's decision to leave Khvicha Kvaratskhelia on the bench proved to be inspired as it meant Doue started wide on the left.

Gianluigi Donnarumma had a point to prove after the Italian goalkeeper was let go by the PSG coach just months after helping deliver the club's first Champions League title in 2025.

However, it turned out to be a night to forget for the giant Italian.

Donnarumma was caught out at his near post by Doue's effort from outside the box after a lightning counter-attack to open the scoring.

Read moreArsenal thrash Lille as Atletico Madrid beat Manchester United

The move for the second goal two minutes later was even more impressive as Doue and Dembele exchanged an elaborate one-two before the latter headed in at the far post.

Achraf Hakimi hit the post before Vitinha rattled in PSG's third from the edge of the box.

Maresca responded with a triple substitution at half-time and managed to salvage some pride, even if the deficit proved too much to overturn.

Antoine Semenyo and Enzo Fernandez missed glaring chances to pull a goal back even before Haaland glanced home a header from Iliman Ndiaye's cross.

Yet, City were hit by a sucker punch when Donnarumma got a hand to Akliouche's effort but the ball looped high into the air and spun back into the net.

Nuno Mendes made a brilliant clearance off his own line and Haaland hit the bar before the Norwegian slotted home his second of the night.

Donnarumma saved a late Ferran Torres penalty to deny the French champions a fifth goal.

But in the battle between two state-backed projects that have reshaped European football, Qatar-owned PSG are the top dogs right now as City face up to a scandal that leaves their litany of trophies over the past 15 years open to question.

WASHINGTON, Oct. 14 (Yonhap) -- U.S. President Donald Trump said Wednesday that South Korea will invest US$50 billion in a massive liquefied natural gas (LNG) project in Alaska as part of an investment agreement with Washington, despite uncertainty over Seoul's participation.

"This 50 Billion Dollar Infrastructure Investment from The Republic of Korea is part of their Trade and Investment Deal with me," Trump wrote on Truth Social, while describing his visit to Alaska for a campaign rally on Tuesday.

The remarks were the latest from the Trump administration claiming that South Korea is committed to the Alaska LNG project. Seoul has maintained that its participation remains subject to a commercial viability review.

Trump also said that Taiwan has agreed to invest $4.4 billion in equity into the project, calling it the "greatest project in Alaska history."

White House Press Secretary Katie Zachariah also said Tuesday that $54 billion was tied to the Alaska LNG project as part of a South Korean energy investment package.

"President Trump also unveiled a South Korea energy investment package of up to $200 billion in the United States. This is an amazing deal. This includes as much as $120 billion to build eight large-scale nuclear power plants," Zachariah said.

"In addition to that, there is $54 billion tied to the Alaska LNG pipeline and terminal to service the Pacific Rim and sell fuel to our allies as well as $22.3 billion for a 6-gigawatt natural gas power facility in Texas," she added.

body_text:
A massive liquefied natural gas project in Alaska has emerged as an unlikely focal point in purported foreign investment, as Asian buyers rush to diversify their supply imports amid disruptions from the Iran war.

On Tuesday in Wasilla, a town 70km north of Anchorage, US President Donald Trump said Taiwan had agreed to buy 30 per cent of the LNG from the long-planned Alaska LNG project. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said Taiwan had committed to investing $4.4 billion to develop the pipeline. The terms of the deal were not immediately clear.

Last week, Mr Trump announced a $54 billion South Korea investment in Alaska LNG as part of a $200 billion energy package and $350 billion trade deal the two sides struck last year to lower tariffs on Korean imports. South Korea has rejected the claim, saying it has given no firm commitment on the project.

US LNG emerges as Gulf hedge against Hormuz disruption

“There's no investors other than the US government, and there are no buyers who have committed to signing any sales and purchase agreements,” said Ira Joseph, a global fellow at the Centre on Global Energy Policy at Columbia University.

The project hopes to make a final investment decision on the pipeline this year, with a separate one on the export terminal in 2027.

One of the dominant factors in the publicly promoted claims are the November 3 midterm elections. Alaska has become a battleground state for control of the US Senate. Mr Trump’s appearance in Wasilla on Tuesday underscored the race’s importance as he seeks to promote energy exports and foreign investment.

At the same time, the Alaska LNG project holds big promises, as South-East Asian buyers are seeking to diversify their energy supplies as the Iran war cut off shipments from the region.

If Alaska LNG becomes operational, it would drastically reduce the time for delivery of LNG shipments. The journey from Alaska to Japan is more than 9,600km shorter than from the US Gulf Coast, the project's developer said in a 2023 report.

For all the promise that Alaska LNG holds, it remains a far-off venture. Development is expected to begin in phases, with targets for the first exports in 2031.

Glenfarne Group estimates the project will cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion. That means about $2.2 billion to $2.7 billion a tonne a year of capacity, according to a Reuters analysis.

“This is an expensive project that's going to take at best a lot of years to sort of come to fruition,” said Rachel Ziemba, founder of risk advisory firm Ziemba Insights.

Another possible sticking point is the about 106cm-diameter pipeline that would stretch 1,300km from Alaska’s North Slope to Nikiski, south of Anchorage, running parallel to the existing Trans Alaska Pipeline System for oil. LNG sites in Nikiski would produce 20 million tonnes a year for export and hold a daily capacity of 3.3 billion cubic feet.

The pipeline itself – Phase One – is likely to cost between $13.2 billion and $16.9 billion, according to company estimates.

“If the gas is sitting right next to the LNG facility, this thing would have been built 40 or 50 years ago, but it's not, and … that's the difference maker in this project,” Mr Joseph said.

Investors remain cautious. As of January this year, only six non-binding offtake agreements have been signed totalling 13 million tonnes a year.

Another point of friction is competition, with LNG projects in Canada and in America's Gulf Coast also attracting attention.

Major players in the Middle East have continued to increase their interest in LNG, but through the Gulf Coast. This summer, Adnoc's XRG boosted its stake in NextDecade's LNG site in Rio Grande, Texas. QatarEnergy began LNG exports from its joint venture with Exxon at the Golden Pass project in March.

“It is notable to me that at a time where you know Trump is looking for all the finance he can for this project, that he's not turning to these sources of capital,” Ms Ziemba said.

headline: Pakistan reiterates 'unwavering' commitment to Saudi Arabia's protection under Makkah defense pact
summary: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif meets alliance's newly appointed secretary general, retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood, in Islamabad
body_text:
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Wednesday characterized the Makkah Defense Alliance as a “historic" milestone for peace, unity and stability in the region as he reaffirmed Islamabad's “unwavering commitment” to the protection of Saudi Arabia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and security.Sharif made the remarks during a meeting with the newly appointed Makkah Defense Alliance Secretary General, retired Lt. Gen. Nauman Mahmood, who briefed him on the strategy to promote defense and strategic cooperation under the pact, according to a statement from the prime minister’s office.

Mahmood was appointed as the first secretary general of the defense alliance between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in August.The pact allows member states to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

The meeting comes as Saudi Arabia has faced escalating tensions with Yemen’s Houthi group in recent weeks.

Sharif reiterated that Pakistan stands "shoulder to shoulder” with Saudi Arabia.

Saudi Arabia has faced missile and drone attacks amid escalating hostilities with Houthis after a truce in the long-running war with Yemen’s coalition government unraveled in July.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers.

A Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Wednesday that it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Houthis toward the Saudi capital, Riyadh, shortly after warning alerts were activated in the city and nearby Al-Kharj governorate.

The Saudi-led military coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government has been in place since 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several provinces since 2014.

headline: Fatah, Hamas set to meet in Cairo for Palestinian unity talks as elections get pushed to 2027
summary: Palestinian factions are seeking common ground on political representation and governance, nearly two decades after a split that has left Gaza and the occupied West Bank under separate administrations. Palestinian…
body_text:
Palestinian factions are seeking common ground on political representation and governance, nearly two decades after a split that has left Gaza and the occupied West Bank under separate administrations. Palestinian factions, including Fatah and Hamas, are set to begin preparatory talks in Cairo on Wednesday, in another attempt to bridge longstanding political divisions and lay the groundwork for a broader national dialogue.

Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) will also participate in the meetings on 14 and 15 October, Anadolu Agency reported, citing Fatah spokesperson Abdel Fattah Dawla.

The discussions will focus on preparations for wider negotiations and efforts to build consensus among Palestinian factions, with a further round of talks potentially taking place on 20 October, depending on the outcomes of the preliminary meetings. Anadolu reported Fatah’s delegation will include Central Committee member Jibril Rajoub and committee member Mohammed Shtayyeh, both expected to arrive in the Egyptian capital on Wednesday.

The meetings follow two days of discussions in Cairo last week involving Fatah, Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the PFLP, as Egypt continues its efforts to bring the Palestinian factions towards a common political position.

It also comes days after Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections and scheduled simultaneous parliamentary votes for 11 September 2027.

What is at stake in the Cairo talks?

Beyond preparations for another round of negotiations, the Cairo meetings raise questions about how Palestinian factions could agree on a unified political leadership and the future administration of Palestinian territories. While Hamas has been in control of Gaza since 2007, the Fatah-led Palestinian Authority has been in control of the West Bank.

As previously reported by the Associated Press, longstanding disagreements over political representation and the governance have hindered reconciliation efforts, including repeated attempts to bring Hamas and Islamic Jihad into the Palestine Liberation Organisation.

The factions have attempted to address some of their issues before. As per the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in July 2024, Fatah, Hamas and 12 other Palestinian factions signed the Beijing Declarations, agreeing in principle to form an interim national reconciliation government and work towards unified Palestinian institutions. However, the agreement did not produce a lasting political settlement.

For the latest Cairo discussions, agreement on the agenda, priorities and framework for further negotiations is set to be expected.

Why have the Palestinian elections been delayed again?

The latest talks come against the backdrop of another postponement of Palestinian elections, extending an already lengthy absence of national voting.

On October 10, Abbas issued a decree scheduling simultaneous presidential and legislative elections for September 11, 2027, replacing plans to hold legislative elections in November 2026.

Al Jazeera reported on the PLO citing deteriorating conditions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, including Israeli restrictions affecting the movement of the election materials and international observers, as obstacles to conducting the vote.

Fatah welcomed the decision, while Hamas called for comprehensive national dialogue and binding agreements on reorganising Palestinian political institutions according to Anadolu.

Palestinians last voted in a presidential election in 2005, when Abbas was elected, and in legislative elections in 2006, which Hamas had won.

A previous attempt to hold presidential and legislative elections in 2021 was also postponed, with Abbas citing uncertainty over whether Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem would be permitted to participate.

body_text:
Attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels on Riyadh's international airport and Saudi Aramco have exposed the strategic threat posed by a militia whose growing missile and drone capabilities have become a key part of Tehran's regional reach.

The attacks have brought the war in Yemen directly into Saudi Arabia's capital and its oil-producing heartland, raising the stakes for the world's largest oil exporter and testing its ability to protect critical infrastructure.

A weekend attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, Saudi authorities said. A further strike on Sunday killed one person and injured 11. On Tuesday, an attack targeted an administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran, causing a fire but no reported casualties. Debris from intercepted missiles injured four people in Riyadh.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for attacks on Saudi targets and threatened further strikes after Saudi-led coalition forces bombed an oil facility in the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa.

These latest exchanges mark a sharp escalation in a conflict that had increasingly become intertwined with the wider confrontation involving Iran, Israel and the US.

The immediate question is how the Houthis have acquired the capability to threaten major airports, energy infrastructure and international transport links across Saudi Arabia.

UN investigators and American military assessments have documented extensive links between Iranian military technology and Houthi weapons systems.

A February 2024 report by the US Defence Intelligence Agency identified similarities between Iranian and Houthi missiles and drones. UN experts have also investigated foreign weapons supplies, technical assistance, training and procurement networks supporting the organisation.

Such evidence does not establish that Tehran ordered every attack. But it makes Iran's role in strengthening the Houthis' military capabilities central to understanding the threat now facing Saudi Arabia.

The militia has its own political leadership and domestic objectives. It emerged from Yemen's internal conflicts and seized Sanaa in 2014, before the Saudi-led military intervention began in 2015. Its independence in decision-making, however, does not negate the strategic importance of external assistance.

For Iran, the Houthis offer a partner positioned near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a vital shipping corridor linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

Their ability to threaten Saudi infrastructure and disrupt maritime traffic gives Tehran an additional source of pressure on regional adversaries without requiring publicly demonstrable Iranian command over every operation.

The attacks also carry consequences beyond the immediate damage.

Disruption to Saudi aviation, heightened risks to oil facilities and uncertainty over regional security threaten not only the kingdom's efforts to establish Riyadh as a centre for international business but also the global economy that relies on Saudi oil flows. It also threatens the millions of Muslim pilgrims who go to Saudi Arabia as a key tenet of Islam.

Saudi Arabia has responded with further strikes on Houthi-held targets in Yemen, including fuel infrastructure in Sanaa, increasing the danger of a wider cycle of retaliation.

Tehran has repeatedly rejected the characterisation of the Houthis as a proxy force, despite evidence to the contrary, and it repeats rhetoric that Yemen's crisis requires a political settlement. But the latest attacks sharpen the question of whether Iran is prepared to use its influence to restrain an ally whose military operations have direct consequences for Gulf security.

The issue is no longer simply whether the Houthis take orders from Tehran. It is how Iranian assistance has helped build a military capability that can threaten Saudi Arabia's most important economic and transport assets – and whether diplomacy can prevent that capability from driving a wider regional conflict.

headline: Russian envoy says Japan journalist caught 'red-handed' spying, Tokyo complaints off base
summary: Nikolay Nozdrev "pointed out to Director General Nakamura the unacceptable situation where Japanese intelligence agencies establish 'cooperation' with individuals, including Japanese journalists accredited in Russia"
body_text:
TOKYO, October 15. /TASS/. Russian Ambassador to Japan Nikolay Nozdrev believes Tokyo has no right to complain about the detention of a Hokkaido Shimbun journalist on suspicion of espionage, the embassy said in a statement following the envoy’s meeting with Kimitake Nakamura, director general of the European Affairs Bureau at the Japanese Foreign Ministry.

"The Russian ambassador to Japan strongly rejected Tokyo’s complaints over the detention by Russian law enforcement agencies in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk of a correspondent of the Japanese newspaper Hokkaido Shimbun," the statement reads.

Nozdrev "pointed out to Director General Nakamura the unacceptable situation where Japanese intelligence agencies establish 'cooperation' with individuals, including Japanese journalists accredited in Russia, to collect classified information with the goal of undermining Russia’s security and defense capability."

"[The envoy] emphasized that Russian competent authorities had repeatedly foiled such attempts. He also drew the other party’s attention to police footage showing the Japanese national being caught red-handed," the statement said. The Russian ambassador also stressed that "investigative activities in the case will be carried out in line with Russian laws."

Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) reported on October 13 that a correspondent for Japan’s Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper in Russia’s Far Eastern city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk had been detained on suspicion of espionage. The journalist was apprehended in the Sakhalin Region shortly before his planned departure from Russia, and brought to Moscow. Moscow’s Lefortovsky District Court ordered that he be taken into custody. The Japanese Foreign Ministry said that it had summoned Russia’s ambassador to inquire about the journalist’s detention and protest the lack of information about the incident.

headline: Aldar enters Sharjah with Dh1.1bn residential acquisition
summary: Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, has agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion ($290 million), its first real estate investment in the emirate as it expand its income-generating property portfolio.The forward-purchase agreement covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029, Aldar said on Thursday. The transaction will expand Aldar’s develop-to-hold pipeline to Dh21 billion. Aldar said the nine buildings will cater primarily to end users and long-term renters seeking quality housing at accessible price points within an established integrated community.“Sharjah is a large and growing residential market, and Aljada provides an attractive entry point through one of the emirate’s leading master-planned communities,” Aldar group chief executive Talal Al Dhiyebi said. He added that the investment adds scale to Aldar’s residential-for-rent portfolio.The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada, which covers projects in Abu Dhabi, a further expansion of their relationship. The partnership, which marked Arada’s entry into Abu Dhabi, includes a mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah, on the Abu Dhabi-Dubai border, and three residential plots on Yas Island.Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments – a company controlled by Saudi Arabia’s Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed – and Sharjah-based Basma Group, has been rapidly expanding in the UAE as well as in overseas markets such as the UK, Australia and Syria.Aldar, meanwhile, plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. body_text:
Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, has agreed to acquire more than 1,100 homes in Sharjah from Arada for Dh1.1 billion ($290 million), its first real estate investment in the emirate as it expand its income-generating property portfolio.

The forward-purchase agreement covers nine buildings within three residential blocks at Aljada, Arada’s flagship mixed-use development, with delivery scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2029, Aldar said on Thursday. The transaction will expand Aldar’s develop-to-hold pipeline to Dh21 billion.

Aldar said the nine buildings will cater primarily to end users and long-term renters seeking quality housing at accessible price points within an established integrated community.

“Sharjah is a large and growing residential market, and Aljada provides an attractive entry point through one of the emirate’s leading master-planned communities,” Aldar group chief executive Talal Al Dhiyebi said. He added that the investment adds scale to Aldar’s residential-for-rent portfolio.

The investment builds on a Dh15 billion development partnership announced last month by Aldar and Arada, which covers projects in Abu Dhabi, a further expansion of their relationship. The partnership, which marked Arada’s entry into Abu Dhabi, includes a mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah, on the Abu Dhabi-Dubai border, and three residential plots on Yas Island.

Arada, a joint venture between KBW Investments – a company controlled by Saudi Arabia’s Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed – and Sharjah-based Basma Group, has been rapidly expanding in the UAE as well as in overseas markets such as the UK, Australia and Syria.

Aldar, meanwhile, plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. The new project, with an undisclosed value, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London this week.

The move comes as the UAE property market continues to perform strongly despite uncertainty stemming from the Iran war. The Emirates was ranked as the world’s leading real estate investment destination in a property market league table released in June. Arada’s UAE Property Investment Index – conducted on behalf of the Dubai developer by US-based Penta Group – found that 56 per cent of global investors have serious interest in the UAE’s property market.

The latest acquisition will broaden Aldar’s geographic exposure while adding residential rental assets aimed primarily at end users and long-term tenants seeking housing at accessible price points, the company said.

Arada group chief executive Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said Aldar’s decision to make its first investment in Sharjah at Aljada reflected confidence in both the development and the emirate’s residential market. “To have a developer of Aldar’s calibre and track record choose Aljada as its first investment in the emirate reflects the quality of what we have built here, and the scale of the opportunity that Sharjah represents,” he said.

Aljada spans 2.2 million sq m and is expected to comprise about 25,000 homes at full buildout, with an anticipated gross sales value of Dh35 billion. Residential handovers at the development began in 2021, with more than 8,800 homes delivered across multiple districts, according to the statement. The community also includes schools, hotels, student accommodation, retail space and the Madar family entertainment district.

Aldar said the acquisition adds to its strategy of expanding its portfolio of income-generating properties, as the developer seeks to diversify its revenue streams.

The Abu Dhabi developer, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, is expected to hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company’s launch, with the deliveries going up to 4,500 next year, according to Mr Emery.

headline: (LEAD) Seoul, Tokyo agree to extend US$10 bln currency swap deal by another 3 yrs
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has agreed with Japan to extend their U...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS more info in paras 6-8; CHANGES photo) By Kang Yoon-seung

BANGKOK, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has agreed with Japan to extend their US$10 billion currency swap arrangement, set to expire next month, by another three years, the finance ministry said Thursday, as the two countries seek to further bolster bilateral economic ties.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il reached the agreement with his Japanese counterpart, Satsuki Katayama, during a meeting in Bangkok on the sidelines of the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group.

The two countries' three-year, $10 billion currency swap deal, signed in December 2023, was due to expire in November.

Under the latest agreement, the currency swap arrangement, which involves the U.S. greenback, will run through November 2029, with its size unchanged.

A currency swap is a tool designed to guard against financial turmoil by allowing a country facing a liquidity crunch to borrow foreign currency in exchange for its own currency.

The two countries' currency swap arrangement expanded from $2 billion in 2001 to $70 billion in 2011 amid global financial uncertainties.

The arrangement, however, expired in 2015 and remained dormant for more than eight years amid strained bilateral relations.

In 2023, the two countries agreed to revive the arrangement with a new structure based on the U.S. dollar. Under the deal, South Korea can borrow dollars from Japan in exchange for the Korean won, while the Asian neighbor can do the same in exchange for the Japanese yen.

During the meeting, the officials concurred that the foreign exchange authorities of both countries currently maintain ample liquidity, describing the currency swap arrangement as a symbol of bilateral cooperation.

The two sides discussed ways to expand bilateral exchanges in the economic and financial sectors, the ministry added.

They also agreed to hold a ministerial meeting in South Korea as soon as possible.

analysis.framing: The article frames the currency swap extension as a routine, mutually beneficial financial and diplomatic development, emphasizing the restoration of bilateral economic cooperation without critical scrutiny.
