Emotionally charged language that evokes fear of instability, though it is a standard description of currency swaps.
This phrase carries a negative connotation, suggesting tension without detailing causes, and contrasts with the positive tone of the agreement.
This is an editorializing characterization that elevates the deal's significance beyond its technical function.

omissions: No mention of any domestic opposition or criticism in South Korea regarding the currency swap deal.
No details on the specific economic conditions or triggers that might require using the swap.
No comparison to similar currency swap arrangements South Korea has with other countries, such as China or the United States.
No mention of the historical context of the 2015 expiration beyond 'strained bilateral relations', omitting specific disputes.

Is love really blind? Since 2020, couples around the world have been trying to prove as much – mostly unsuccessfully – in Netflix's hugely popular reality show Love is Blind.

Following its debut, set in the US, the show has spawned 13 international versions, including Love is Blind: Habibi, the Arabic spin-off that premiered in October 2024. A second season is coming later in the year.

The format is similar across all. A group of single men and women looking for love are introduced to each other through “pods”, where they can interact but not see the other person. Once participants have chosen their prospective partners, the couple meet for the first time and become engaged. They are then flown to a luxury resort where they spend time and get to know each other better. In the final stage of the experiment, the couples who are still together go back to their respective lives where they meet each other's families and friends, and are given 10 days to prepare for their wedding.

From Brazil to the UK and Japan, each edition of Love is Blind has proved to be a hit, turning some of its cast members into overnight celebrities. Love is Blind: Habibi, for instance, was viewed more than 1.3 million times in the first seven days after its debut. It also ranked No 8 globally among Netflix's non-English shows.

With Love is Blind: South Africa set to debut later this year, here are all the editions so far ranked by fan ratings on IMDb.

The Arabic version of Love is Blind became a massive hit, dominating social media chats and debates for weeks after its premiere in October 2024. Featuring 20 singles – 10 women and 10 men – from across the Arab world and North Africa who are all residents of the UAE, the series was filmed in Lebanon, Dubai and Abu Dhabi.

Six couples progressed to the next stage and were flown to a luxury resort in Lebanon, where their relationship was further tested. Eventually, out of two couples who made it to the wedding day, only one – Safa and Mohammed – exchanged vows.

Speaking to The National a few weeks after its debut, cast members shared how their lives had changed thanks to the popularity of the show.

“This experience didn’t just transform me, it shaped me into a person I never imagined I could be,” Mohammed said. “It opened up a whole new world and revealed aspects of myself I hadn’t recognised before. Beyond discovering ‘the one’, I found myself.”

Season two will have celebrity couple Wissam Breidy and Rym Saidi taking over hosting roles.

headline: US condones Japan's pursuit of nuclear weapons — North Korean news agency
summary: The US is supporting Tokyo’s intention to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, international security analyst Pak Ju Won said
body_text:
PYONGYANG, October 15. /TASS/. The US is abetting Japan’s drive toward nuclear armament by supporting Tokyo’s intention to acquire nuclear-powered submarines, international security analyst Pak Ju Won wrote in an article for the Korean Central News Agency.

"What should not be overlooked is that the US, which is shifting the security burden onto its allies as much as possible to maintain its hegemony that is getting more and more vulnerable, has given the green light to Japan's possession of nuclear-powered submarines," the article noted.

According to the expert, the ultimate goal of the supporters of this policy in Japan is to create the conditions necessary to acquire nuclear weapons. He linked this to statements by the Japanese authorities on the need to consider various options for developing their submarine forces.

The article also pointed out that the issue of nuclear submarines is being discussed against the backdrop of a planned revision of Japan’s three core security documents. According to Pak Ju Won, Tokyo is seeking to enshrine relevant provisions in the revised versions of these documents.

body_text:
Rashid Al Dhaheri will compete in FIA Formula 3 in 2027 after signing with Van Amersfoort Racing.

The Dutch team announced a deal with the 18-year-old Emirati on Thursday in a move that will see him step up in class after finishing fourth in this year’s Formula Regional European Championship.

“I’m very proud to be taking the next step into FIA Formula 3 with Van Amersfoort Racing,” said Al Dhareri, a member of the Mercedes Junior Driver Programme since March 2025.

Al Azhari to represent UAE with 'immense pride' after landing F3 deal

“It is an important milestone in my journey, but I know the hard work is only beginning. I’m proud to represent the UAE and the wider region at this level, and I’m looking forward to learning, improving and giving everything I have on and off the track.

“Every step has to be earned, and my focus now is on preparing as strongly as possible for 2027. I’m grateful to everyone who has supported me and helped make this opportunity possible.”

The move means that the UAE will have two drivers on the grid next season after it was also announced that Keanu Al Azhari had signed for Hitech. No Emirati has previously competed in F3.

Brad Joyce, team principal for Van Amersfoort Racing, added: “We’re looking forward to welcome Rashid to [the team]. He has had a very strong season in Formula Regional, with three wins and eight podiums, finishing in fourth place in the championship.

“He has shown his pace throughout the year and has been able to fight at the front of a very competitive field. That gives us a good starting point as he steps up to Formula 3. We’re looking forward to working with him during the post season tests and preparing for his first F3 season together.”

Al Dhaheri's journey in motorsport began at the age of three, and he quickly rose through the ranks, winning the WSK Super Master Series and the South Garda Winter Cup in the 60 Mini category.

In 2023, he made his single-seater debut with Prema Racing in the Italian F4 Championship, finishing 10th overall and taking P3 at Macau. He continued to impress in 2024, competing in the Formula 4 UAE Championship and the Euro 4 Championship.

In March 2025, it was announced that Al Dhaheri had joined Mercedes as part of their Junior Driver Programme, becoming the first Middle East driver to be selected for their F1 development initiative.

He described the move as “a dream come true” as he took the next step towards his ultimate goal of becoming the first driver to represent the UAE in F1. George Russell, who has raced for Mercedes in F1 since 2019, is also a graduate of the programme.

Al Dhaheri has just finished the FIA Formula Regional European Championship campaign with a podium finish at Hockenheim, ending the weekend fourth in the overall standings, 38 points behind title winner Emanuele Olivieri of Italy.

It caps an impressive season for the teenager who claimed three victories, eight podiums, one pole position and a fastest lap.

Driving for French team R-ace GP, Al Dhaheri recorded victories at the Red Bull Ring, Monza and Hungaroring across the eight-round championship.

He became the first Emirati to lead the standings and sat 21 points clear at the halfway stage and, despite some challenging weekends later in the season, arrived at the Hockenheim finale as one of four drivers still able to win the title.

body_text:
The European Union has urged the Iran-backed Houthi rebels to lift their siege of Taiz, as the Yemeni government appealed to the UN for urgent action to avert a humanitarian catastrophe.

Taiz, in south-western Yemen, is controlled by Yemeni government forces but has long been besieged by the Houthis and remains the main front line in the civil war. In recent weeks, fighting between the rebels and government forces has intensified and the rebels have encircled the area.

In a statement, the EU said the Houthis must allow food, water, medicine and fuel to enter the city. It stressed that civilians and civilian infrastructure must be protected and humanitarian partners must be permitted to deliver essential aid.

On Wednesday, the Yemeni government sent a letter from Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba to senior UN and humanitarian officials, outlining a sharp deterioration in conditions in Taiz governorate amid a new Houthi escalation.

Ms Al Zouba warned that the tightening of the siege on Taiz and surrounding villages could trigger a humanitarian disaster affecting more than four million people. They include residents trapped inside the city and displaced families in districts such as Al Shamayatayn, Al Mawasit and Jabal Habashi.

The government urged the UN to apply direct pressure on the Houthis to lift the blockade immediately, reopen all access routes for civilians and supply chains, and ensure sustained, unhindered delivery of food, fuel and drinking water. It also called for stronger monitoring and documentation of violations to preserve evidence, hold perpetrators accountable and prevent impunity.

Humanitarian agencies have voiced concern over low food and medical supplies, as well as the capability of hospitals to cater to thousands of injured people. Wheat flour stocks in the city are nearly exhausted, ‌the UN World Food Programme said.

The WFP said remaining food supplies may not last long if access constraints ​continue. At least 600,000 people in Taiz depend on aid, including more than 200,000 children.

The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said front-line hospitals in areas such as Marib, Taiz and Yemen's ​Red Sea coast ‌are taking in unprecedented numbers of patients wounded by weapons, with some admitting more than 700 casualties in one week.

More ⁠than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting began in ⁠recent weeks, the UN's International Organisation for Migration said.

“Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure,” said Feras Abusamra, ICRC health co-ordinator. Only a small proportion of Yemen's functioning health centres can provide comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people and shortages of ​surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicine.

The siege of Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, has been in place since 2015 and has long been a severe humanitarian flashpoint, with aid agencies warning that shortages of basic goods and medical supplies are pushing civilians towards crisis conditions.

headline: Russia-US diesel deal could set precedent for suspension or removal of sanctions
summary: In European Union countries, the automotive industry is currently surviving only because they're now producing weapons, Russian presidential commissioner for the protection of entrepreneurs' rights Alexander Shokhin noted
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. The Russian-American agreement on diesel fuel supplies could become a promising precedent for how sanctions might be lifted or suspended, provided the United States is economically and politically interested in it, Russian presidential commissioner for the protection of entrepreneurs' rights, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP) Alexander Shokhin told TASS.

"There was an old Soviet-era ditty, which said: ‘A friend and I worked together on a diesel engine’, and I wouldn't want our Russian-American deal to end the same way that that ditty does. However, I think that this is a very promising story because it turns out that when there appears a genuine economic or political interest, including domestic political interest, in the case of the American side, sanctions can be lifted or suspended. This is a good example for a country like Germany, where we see that Alternative for Germany is gaining votes not merely because of its opposition to excessively lenient migration policy, but tariffs are rising, prices are climbing, the industrial sector is faltering, and some industries have shut down entirely," Shokhin said in his first interview after being appointed business ombudsman.

In European Union countries, the automotive industry is currently surviving only because they're now producing weapons, he noted.

"Therefore, they are probably behaving so aggressively toward Russia in the case of Ukraine as well. And, fundamentally, one can only hope that [US President Donald] Trump manages to retain at least the Senate, perhaps by ensuring that diesel prices in the United States do not rise," Shokhin said, adding that logistics and transport flows are road-based in the US, and large trucks require diesel fuel.

"Therefore, it’s not a bad example, and the pragmatism of Trump and the American administration could prove contagious here," he concluded.

headline: AI is changing us as humans, says pioneering Arab scientist
summary: AI will help humans operate at a "higher intellectual level", even if that means ditching some of the life skills we once had, a leading Arab scientist has said.Fadel Adib, an MIT professor and successful AI start-up founder, said it was not necessarily bad that people are coming to rely on large language models such as ChatGPT."We first augment humans and increase their productivity, and then eventually we also augment humans with robots, not just with AI ... increase productivity there as well. AI is changing who we are as humans," he told The National at a World Economic Forum event in Dubai.His company, Cartesian, uses AI technology to help robots navigate hundreds of warehouses and retail stores in 15 countries, tracking and collecting thousands of different products."Some of us cannot operate without asking ChatGPT the question, and that might not necessarily be bad," he said at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which he co-chaired."I'm a professor. So I remember when people used to say 'oh, students are not memorising anymore in schools, and we're losing the ability to memorise.'"What's the point of memorising if you can Google everything? And maybe AI is going to help us operate at a higher intellectual level. "And as humans, we've repeatedly managed to do that. We don't learn how to make fire anymore, and we don't need to."As humans, we've managed to repeatedly figure out how we operate at a higher level of abstraction, and I think we're going to do that again."Dr Adib, who grew up in Tripoli, Lebanon and was given a Dh1 million Great Arab Minds award in 2023 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, also predicted further challenges to US tech firms' dominance of AI. Speaking earlier at the same event in Dubai, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE's AI minister, said that superpower dominance of AI was not appealing, and that middle powers and sovereign governments would want an alternative."AI is moving at an accelerated pace. It is moving from the digital into the physical world," said Dr Adib."If you look at the 1990s, where the internet was growing... that was a US-led world."Today, there is the race between the US and China on AI. What role is Europe and Africa and Latin America and the rest of Asia going to play? The answer is not clear that just the US or China is gonna win this race."He added: "Our first prime adopters were in Europe. And if you look at the United Arab Emirates, there's a lot of investment. There's a lot of AI investments here in Dubai, and they are deploying it. They're seeing real change. And in Abu Dhabi, with the creation of G42, and the investment in data infrastructure. "And as a scientist, I love challenges, and as a technologist, I love the optimism of it. There is an opportunity for real change and impact."
body_text:
AI will help humans operate at a "higher intellectual level", even if that means ditching some of the life skills we once had, a leading Arab scientist has said.

Fadel Adib, an MIT professor and successful AI start-up founder, said it was not necessarily bad that people are coming to rely on large language models such as ChatGPT.

"We first augment humans and increase their productivity, and then eventually we also augment humans with robots, not just with AI ... increase productivity there as well. AI is changing who we are as humans," he told The National at a World Economic Forum event in Dubai.

'Minimise catastrophes': UAE's AI minister highlights dangers of autonomous arms

His company, Cartesian, uses AI technology to help robots navigate hundreds of warehouses and retail stores in 15 countries, tracking and collecting thousands of different products.

"Some of us cannot operate without asking ChatGPT the question, and that might not necessarily be bad," he said at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders, which he co-chaired.

"I'm a professor. So I remember when people used to say 'oh, students are not memorising anymore in schools, and we're losing the ability to memorise.'

"What's the point of memorising if you can Google everything? And maybe AI is going to help us operate at a higher intellectual level.

"And as humans, we've repeatedly managed to do that. We don't learn how to make fire anymore, and we don't need to.

"As humans, we've managed to repeatedly figure out how we operate at a higher level of abstraction, and I think we're going to do that again."

Dr Adib, who grew up in Tripoli, Lebanon and was given a Dh1 million Great Arab Minds award in 2023 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, also predicted further challenges to US tech firms' dominance of AI.

Speaking earlier at the same event in Dubai, Omar Sultan Al Olama, the UAE's AI minister, said that superpower dominance of AI was not appealing, and that middle powers and sovereign governments would want an alternative.

"AI is moving at an accelerated pace. It is moving from the digital into the physical world," said Dr Adib.

"If you look at the 1990s, where the internet was growing... that was a US-led world.

"Today, there is the race between the US and China on AI. What role is Europe and Africa and Latin America and the rest of Asia going to play? The answer is not clear that just the US or China is gonna win this race."

He added: "Our first prime adopters were in Europe. And if you look at the United Arab Emirates, there's a lot of investment. There's a lot of AI investments here in Dubai, and they are deploying it. They're seeing real change. And in Abu Dhabi, with the creation of G42, and the investment in data infrastructure.

"And as a scientist, I love challenges, and as a technologist, I love the optimism of it. There is an opportunity for real change and impact."

analysis.framing: The article frames AI as a beneficial evolutionary step for humanity through the optimistic lens of a celebrated Arab scientist, while also highlighting challenges to US tech dominance and opportunities for the UAE.

headline: Iran should reach deal with US to end war, reformist says
summary: Iran should reach an agreement with the US to end the war because it cannot match American military strength and influence, a reformist politician has said.Gholamhossein Karbaschi, a former mayor of Tehran, warned that a prolonged conflict would deepen domestic hardship.“We cannot take on America’s power and diplomacy,” he said on Iranian state television late on Wednesday, criticising commentators who claim Tehran has defeated Washington while many citizens struggle.“We must make a non-emotional assessment of the situation,” Mr Karbaschi said. He added that there was no clear end in sight and that officials should consider the consequences of continuing the conflict.The war had weighed heavily on Iran’s roughly 90 million people, he said, with families unsure whether fighting would resume. “We were never volunteers for war,” he said.He also criticised the Iranian attacks on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, which he said had derailed the peace process and given Washington a pretext to breach the interim accord.“If the Islamabad agreement had been implemented as it should have been, the incident involving the targeting of the three ships would not have happened,” he said. “We must distinguish between the reason for violating the agreement and a pretext for violating it.”The attacks he was referring to appear to have occurred about 10 days after the US and Iran signed the Islamabad memorandum of understanding on June 17.Mr Karbaschi said the interim agreement had been advantageous to Tehran and had surprised observers because Washington accepted its terms while Israel opposed them. He argued that the subsequent attacks on the ships gave the US an opportunity to breach the agreement.He also questioned who had ordered the strikes, adding that nobody had publicly claimed responsibility.“Everyone says, ‘We don’t know who attacked the three ships,’” he said. Referring to President Masoud Pezeshkian, he asked: “Can it be that the president doesn’t know?”Mr Karbaschi's comments were reported by other media outlets on Thursday morning, including the Entekhab newspaper.The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded sharply. Its spokesman, Hossein Mohebi, rejected suggestions that the attacks were unauthorised or carried out without the approval of senior officials.Mr Mohebi described the strikes as a “decisive and crushing response” to what he called the third US breach of its commitments.He accused Washington of breaking its commitments twice during negotiations and a third time after signing the memorandum.“In the armed forces, no action is taken without observing the chain of command and co-ordinating with senior officials,” he was quoted as saying by the reformist Shargh newspaper on Thursday.

“We must make a non-emotional assessment of the situation,” Mr Karbaschi said. He added that there was no clear end in sight and that officials should consider the consequences of continuing the conflict.

The war had weighed heavily on Iran’s roughly 90 million people, he said, with families unsure whether fighting would resume. “We were never volunteers for war,” he said.

He also criticised the Iranian attacks on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, which he said had derailed the peace process and given Washington a pretext to breach the interim accord.

“If the Islamabad agreement had been implemented as it should have been, the incident involving the targeting of the three ships would not have happened,” he said. “We must distinguish between the reason for violating the agreement and a pretext for violating it.”

The attacks he was referring to appear to have occurred about 10 days after the US and Iran signed the Islamabad memorandum of understanding on June 17.

Mr Karbaschi said the interim agreement had been advantageous to Tehran and had surprised observers because Washington accepted its terms while Israel opposed them. He argued that the subsequent attacks on the ships gave the US an opportunity to breach the agreement.

He also questioned who had ordered the strikes, adding that nobody had publicly claimed responsibility.

“Everyone says, ‘We don’t know who attacked the three ships,’” he said. Referring to President Masoud Pezeshkian, he asked: “Can it be that the president doesn’t know?”

Mr Karbaschi's comments were reported by other media outlets on Thursday morning, including the Entekhab newspaper.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded sharply. Its spokesman, Hossein Mohebi, rejected suggestions that the attacks were unauthorised or carried out without the approval of senior officials.

Mr Mohebi described the strikes as a “decisive and crushing response” to what he called the third US breach of its commitments.

He accused Washington of breaking its commitments twice during negotiations and a third time after signing the memorandum.

“In the armed forces, no action is taken without observing the chain of command and co-ordinating with senior officials,” he was quoted as saying by the reformist Shargh newspaper on Thursday.

body_text:
Gulf oil producers are pushing tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashing prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around Hormuz buckles under congestion and attack.

Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch reached 82 cargoes in September, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, according to shipping analytics company Vortexa. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder.

"Fujairah and Sohar STS zones were handling record volumes with some indications of delays relating to operational limitations, and thus the activity has spilled over to India,” said Varaleka Pant, senior market analyst at energy intelligence firm Vortexa

The expansion shows how the workaround sustaining Gulf exports is coming under strain. Producers have shuttled oil through Hormuz before transferring it to supertankers outside the strait, but congestion and longer voyages are tying up vessels and driving up costs.

Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict.

"The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said.

A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes.

The shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale.

South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa.

In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data.

Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally.

"The Gulf of Oman remains the main area for this," said Niels Rasmussen, Bimco's chief shipping analyst.

The increase is unlikely to have changed overall tanker demand significantly, he said, though longer voyages to transfer points mean more ships are needed.

Yui Torikata of Kpler cautioned that some eastern transfer arrangements were in place before the recent shift, including Japanese refiners receiving Aramco and Adnoc cargoes off Malaysia. Kpler has yet to establish how much activity has shifted east.

Reported tanker activity near Sri Lanka is largely unrelated. Vortexa said vessels there were primarily sanctioned Iranian tankers stranded after discharging pre-blockade cargoes, while Bimco recorded no STS operations off the island.

Moving transfers farther from Hormuz reduces the exposure of receiving tankers but does not eliminate the danger of transporting oil out of the Gulf.

"The STS transfer itself is relatively low risk. The real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone” Ms Pant said.

Kutch offers relatively calm waters and proximity to Indian refiners, but the cargoes must still pass through contested routes before reaching the transfer point. Buyers could retreat after a security incident on that route, if discounts fail to cover higher freight and STS costs, or if congestion spreads to India, she said.

Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal is the safest place to take delivery, according to Kpler, because receiving tankers can avoid both Hormuz and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. But the journey to Asia takes about 55 days, compared with just over 20 days from the Gulf of Oman, according to Mr Torikata.

Disruptions to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have also left Japanese-chartered tankers waiting for cargoes there, he said. Japanese refiners, and to a lesser extent South Korean ones, rely on medium-sour crude for blending, limiting their ability to switch suppliers.

A Japanese refiner paid a record high price of above $80 million to charter a tanker from the US Gulf Coast to Japan, Mr Torikata said.

"If they paid such high [rates] to buy US crude, they would go to Sidi Kerir to buy Arab Light as it takes approximately the same time as sourcing from the US Gulf Coast," he added. Arab Light is also favoured by Japanese refiners over US light sweet oil.

The disruption is dividing Gulf producers between those cutting prices to compensate buyers for transit risks and those able to command premiums for more secure supply.

Iraq, which has no export route around Hormuz, offered October-loading Basrah Medium at a discount of $34.50 a barrel and Basrah Heavy at $37, compared with discounts below $30 in August, according to Rystad.

The reductions have helped restore Iraqi production to within 10 per cent of pre-war levels, Rystad said. Iraq now pumps almost 70 per cent as much crude as Saudi Arabia, compared with less than 40 per cent before the conflict.

Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asian buyers by $3 to $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, the widest discount since 2020, defying market expectations of an increase.

QatarEnergy also cut its November prices by $3, setting Qatar Marine at $8 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average and Qatar Land at $7.50 below, according to a pricing document.

“In the short term, deep discounting of crude is protecting market share more effectively by providing price incentive for buyers to lift crude from the Gulf, but it’s a situational move,” Ms Pant said.

Adnoc has taken a different approach, benefiting from its ability to export Murban crude through Fujairah without passing through Hormuz.

"Murban carries none of the transit risk the other cuts compensate for," Mr Choudhary said. "It reaches Fujairah by pipeline and loads outside Hormuz, so buyers pay a premium for it."

The grade traded as much as $26 a barrel above Dubai swaps in late September before easing to about $15, according to Rystad.

For its other grades, Adnoc has used spot tenders rather than resetting official prices, preserving flexibility while testing what buyers will pay, according to Vortexa.

The divergence underscores how secure access to export infrastructure has become a competitive advantage, allowing some producers to protect margins while others sacrifice revenue to keep their oil flowing.

Gulf producers are increasingly taking on transit and security risks themselves to keep Asian customers.

Adnoc, Aramco, Iraq and Qatar now offer STS deliveries outside Hormuz, and Kuwait has adopted the same approach to attract buyers, according to Mr Choudhary. These arrangements let buyers receive cargoes without sending their own tankers through the strait.

The UAE has also moved to lock in Asian demand. Adnoc agreed in May to explore raising its crude storage in India to as much as 30 million barrels, from about 5.9 million at Mangalore.

Aramco, which sold more than 60 million barrels for transfer off Sohar for September and October deliveries, is negotiating term contracts for next year involving loadings outside Hormuz, Mr Choudhary said, signalling that buyers and sellers alike expect the arrangement to last.

loaded_language.explanation: 'Makeshift' implies something temporary, improvised, and inferior, subtly undermining the reliability of the arrangement.
'Slashing' is an emotive verb suggesting drastic, almost violent cuts, rather than a neutral 'reducing' or 'cutting'.
'Sacrifice' carries a moral or emotional weight, implying a painful loss rather than a strategic trade-off.
'Lock in' suggests a forceful or exclusive securing of demand, with connotations of control and permanence.

No perspective from Indian authorities or local communities near the Gulf of Kutch regarding the surge in transfers.

body_text:
The 2026-27 Saudi Pro League season is now well under way and the latest influx of talent is already influencing the title race. This summer’s recruitment was concentrated on investing heavily in established internationals still in their prime. Several of the most expensive arrivals have wasted little time in justifying their price tags while others have faced criticism.

Al Hilal lead the standings on 21 points, two clear of Al Qadsiah and defending champions Al Nassr. Below, we take a look at how the competition’s latest wave of imports have performed.

English Premier League side Arsenal recorded their record sale when Martinelli signed for Al Hilal in September for £60 million, with the Brazilian highlighting his pride at joining a club that countryman Neymar played for.

Martinelli, though, will clearly be hoping for a far more successful stint at Hilal than the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain attacker, who had his contract terminated after an injury-ravaged 18 months in Riyadh.

After a subdued debut off the bench against Al Shabab, Martinelli conceded he might need “some time to adapt” to his new surroundings having been with the Gunners since 2019.

Those concerns appeared to be unfounded as the 25-year-old bagged a hat-trick little over a week later as Hilal demolished Al Taawoun 6-0, ending his seven-month goal drought. He then opened the scoring in the Saudi Clasico win over Al Ittihad on Saturday, taking his league tally to four in four appearances.

“He’s a big player and we are lucky to have Martinelli,” manager Simone Inzaghi noted after Tuesday’s 2-0 AFC Champions League win at Al Sadd.

Reijnders was honest about his motives after completing a £52m move from Manchester City. “Me a money grabber? I can't deny that,” he said. “By signing this contract, I can make sure even my grandchildren are financially secure, so why wouldn’t I do it?”

Qadsiah manager Brendan Rodgers has given him the box-to-box role he prefers and he responded by scoring in his first start in the 2-0 win over Neom. The 28-year-old then scored a double in the 3-2 defeat of Al Ahli at the beginning of September and opened the scoring in Friday’s 5-0 victory over Al Kholood.

Three of his four league goals have come from outside the box, more than any other player in the SPL this season.

Summerville joined in a £60m switch from West Ham United who had just been relegated to English football's second tier.

The 24-year-old's first goal arrived against Al Khaleej in his third appearance when he scored the fourth goal with a dinked finish as Hilal ran out 5-1 winners. Summerville also supplied his first two assists in that game.

He was on target again the following week, this time driving home a low finish from a tight angle and also scored a fine winner against Al Ittihad. Summerville has registered three goals and three assists in eight league appearances.

Al Nassr signed Costa from Mallorca for €22m at the request of new coach Ange Postecoglou, with the 25-year-old Portuguese midfielder recruited to replace Marcelo Brozovic.

He was bought to give the reigning champions greater energy in midfield but his early performances have attracted criticism.

Speaking on TV, former Al Nassr defender Hussein Abdulghani called the signing of Costa “disastrous”, and dismissed comparisons with Brozovic, claiming Cristiano Ronaldo had encouraged management to sign his countryman.

But it has not all been bad with Costa scoring three times in seven SPl appearances, including Friday's 3-0 win over Diriyah, while it was his cross that Anvar Gofurov turned into his own net to seal a 3-1 Champions League win over Neftchi on Monday.

Former Barcelona attacker Trincao insisted “the passion of Al Ahli supporters was one of the main reasons” he moved to the Jeddah club in a €40m deal from Sporting.

But passionate fans are also demanding and the player tasked with replacing the much-loved Riyad Mahrez has struggled at times as Marino Pusic’s side lost three of their opening six games.

But the 26-year-old Portuguese appears to be finding his feet, scoring four times in his last four SPL matches, including a double against Al Fateh on Friday that earned him the man-of-the-match award. Trincao then scored one and supplied another as back-to-back Asian title winners Al Ahli defeated UAE outfit Al Wasl 3-1 in Dubai in the Champions League three days later.

Al Hilal forked out £50m to Aston Villa for England striker Watkins who the club had been monitoring since last season, according to Inzaghi.

The 30-year-old scored on his debut against Al Ahli and was delighted by the reception he was given. “The fans were calling my name. From minute one, it was amazing,” he said. He later described Saudi football as being of “Premier League quality”.

Watkins has already registered five goals and four assists from his six appearances for Hilal and played a role in all three goals in their 3-2 win over Al Ittihad. He was on target again on Tuesday after opening the scoring in Tuesday's win away to Qatari side Al Sadd.

headline: Russia hits at least ten thermal, hydroelectric power plants in Ukraine since early 2026
summary: The first strike on such an infrastructure facility occurred on August 9, when a combined heat and power plant in Odessa that supported the port's operations was destroyed

MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. Since the beginning of the year, Russian servicemen have struck at least ten Ukrainian hydroelectric and thermal power plants, including combined heat and power plants used for military purposes, according to TASS calculations based on the Russian Defense Ministry’s reports.

The first strike on such an infrastructure facility occurred on August 9, when a combined heat and power plant in Odessa that supported the port's operations was destroyed. On September 1, the Russian Armed Forces struck the Odessa combined heat and power plant. On September 30, the Russian army hit the Kievskaya power substation and hydroelectric power plant, as well as the Tripolskaya thermal power plant. All of these facilities serve Ukraine’s military-industrial complex.

On October 14, Russian servicemen launched a massive strike targeting the Darnitskaya combined heat and power plant, the Kievskaya-5 and Kievskaya-6 combined heat and power plants, the Tripolskaya thermal power plant, and the Kievskaya power substation in the Kiev region. In addition, the Kharkovskaya combined heat and power plant and the Zmievskaya thermal power plant in the Kharkov region were damaged by Russian drone and precision-guided weapons strikes.

body_text:
Global Village has reopened in Dubai for its 31st season, with new restaurants, live shows and a rollercoaster added to the popular multicultural festival park.

The outdoor destination welcomed visitors back on Wednesday and will remain open until May 2027. Running under the theme A More Wonderful World, the season features 29 pavilions representing more than 90 cultures, plus more than 3,500 shopping outlets and more than 250 dining options.

Opening-night celebrations included a choir performance, the Parade of the World and the destination’s signature confetti shower at the Gate of the World. A display featuring 600 drones also marked the season's start.

UAE attractions reopening for winter, from Global Village to Sharjah Safari

Among the additions is Tokyo Rush, a rollercoaster scheduled to open later in the season, featuring sharp turns and a loop. It will join returning attractions including Dragon Kingdom, The Horror Hotel, Secrets of the Lost City and Exo Planet City.

The Festival Wheel returns with refreshed carts offering panoramic views of the destination, while the Gardens of the World has also been updated.

Across the cultural attractions, visitors will find refreshed experiences at the Sri Lanka pavilion and the Russia and Azerbaijan areas. The Syria and Kuwait pavilions have new facades.

A redesigned Season 31 passport and a new passport for children allow visitors to collect stamps as they explore the pavilions.

Fernando Eiroa, chief executive of Dubai Holding Entertainment, said: “Global Village holds a special place in people’s lives because of the connections they make here, with their own roots, with other cultures and the people they visit alongside. It has become a much-loved tradition for families and friends, reflecting the welcoming, multicultural spirit of the UAE.”

Restaurant Plaza, beside Carnaval and overlooking the Falcon Stage, has several new additions, including Trabzon Turkish Restaurant, Robo Al Sham, Hawawshi Al Rabie and Chicking.

New cafes include Vinci Dolci, Emir Bey Gourmet and Uzungol Cafe. Dessert District also returns with a refreshed facade and a selection of sweet treats.

The venues join a wider dining offering of more than 250 options, spanning international street food, restaurants and cafes.

Global Village will host 40,000 shows throughout the season, with a programme spanning music, dance, acrobatics and family entertainment.

New productions include Fast Live 2: The Police Strike Back, a stunt show featuring driving manoeuvres and action sequences. Bollywood Idol and Bank Heist also join the programme, alongside returning show Slam.

For younger visitors, characters from Care Bears and PJ Masks return to the Kids Theatre.

Upgrades to amenities include a new VIP parking self-payment system, improved directional signage and expanded ticketing capacity at Happiness Gate.

Additional family washrooms have been introduced, including accessible areas for people of determination. Other updates include bilingual signage at the Gate of the World, upgraded lighting at Cultural Gate and a new theme for the Sharjah tunnel.

A new WhatsApp chatbot will provide visitors with information and assistance during their visit.

Global Village is open from 4pm to midnight on Sunday to Wednesday, with extended hours until 1am on Thursday to Saturday and on public holidays.

Tickets cost Dh30, or Dh25 from Monday to Thursday excluding public holidays. They are available through the Global Village website, app and gate counters.

Tuesdays are reserved for families, couples and women, except on public holidays.

headline: Prolonged war, renewed disruptions pose biggest risk to Middle East region, IMF says
summary: By Andrea ShalalBANGKOK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure.
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Prolonged war in the Middle East and further disruptions to energy production, shipping routes or critical infrastructure pose the biggest risk to economies in the Middle East and Central Asia, the International Monetary Fund said on Thursday.

Jihad Azour, the IMF's director for the Middle East and Central Asia, told reporters the war was imposing a highly uneven economic shock to the broader region, with directly affected states under severe pressure.

"The outlook depends critically on how quickly energy production and trade normalize, and on countries’ ability to preserve macroeconomic stability," Azour said at a news conference during the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok. The IMF will release a fuller outlook for the region on October 22.

Pre-war surpluses, alternative routes, demand adjustments and substantial inventory drawdowns had helped contain the impact of the energy shock caused by the US-Israeli-led attacks on Iran and Tehran's subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

"These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments," he said.

The global lender is forecasting a deep contraction of 1.3% in the Middle East, North Africa and Pakistan region after growth of 3.3% in 2025, followed by a strong but uneven rebound in 2027, when growth is expected to hit 6.6%, Azour said, noting substantial differences across the region.

The forecast assumes a resumption of normal trade and shipping in the first quarter of 2027, with exports gradually normalizing by mid-year and oil prices staying higher.

Azour said the forecast was predicated on a quick resumption of production, noting that Qatar, for instance, had been able to accelerate its recovery despite suffering massive destruction of its natural gas capacity.

But he said the shock would have a scarring impact on various sectors, with damage to infrastructure requiring additional spending, and the risks were tilted to the downside.

Oil-exporting countries directly affected by the war would see a significant contraction in 2026 and a sharp rebound in growth in 2027 as energy production normalizes, but output was expected to remain below pre-war medium-term projections.

The economies of oil-importing countries in the region had been resilient and were expected to remain so, he said.

The Caucasus and Central Asia region had weathered the shock relatively well and inflation was expected to continue declining from elevated levels. The IMF is projecting growth to slow to 5.2% in 2026 and then 5% in 2027, from growth of 6.2% in2025.

Azour said policymakers should prioritize price stability, focus on rebuilding fiscal buffers and expand their capacity to withstand future shocks.

(Reporting by Andrea Shalal; Editing by John Mair)

headline: DP leader calls for future-oriented ties with Japan based on remembrance of history
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and Japan should work to build stronger b...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and Japan should work to build stronger bilateral ties while remembering their shared history, the leader of the ruling Democratic Party said Thursday.

Rep. Kim Min-seok made the remarks during a meeting with Japanese Ambassador to South Korea Koichi Mizushima at the National Assembly, noting the resumption of shuttle diplomacy between the two countries.

"The essence of relations between the two countries is not forgetting the past while also placing importance on the present and building the future," Kim said.

"We are realizing the ideal vision laid out and envisioned in the 1998 Kim Dae-jung-Obuchi Declaration," he said, referring to the joint declaration signed by then South Korean President Kim Dae-jung and then Japanese Prime Minister Keizo Obuchi that called for overcoming the past and building new relations.

Kim expressed hope the two countries will further expand cooperation in politics, the economy, culture and other areas.

In response, Mizushima pledged to continue efforts to develop the "stable, future-oriented relations" between the two countries.

julesyi@yna.co.kr(END)

headline: Trump open to Russia-US economic cooperation after peace in Ukraine — newspaper
summary: US officials opined that Trump reached an agreement on Russian diesel supplies in order, first, to lower fuel prices in the US, and second, to "offer economic and political benefits" to Russia to engage in negotiations
body_text:
NEW YORK, October 15. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump is open to developing economic relations with Russia after the conflict in Ukraine is settled, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing sources.

According to the newspaper, the US leader would first like to de-escalate hostilities between Russia and Ukraine and then present Moscow with a proposal for a long-term ceasefire. In conversations with The Wall Street Journal, US officials opined that Trump reached an agreement on Russian diesel supplies in order, first, to lower fuel prices in the US, and second, to "offer economic and political benefits" to Russia to engage in negotiations. The newspaper’s sources added that Trump is open to future economic relations between the US and Russia once the Ukrainian conflict is settled.

However, Ukrainian and European officials are dissatisfied with US actions. Threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Kiev were followed by restrictions on the operation of the Starlink satellite communication system in Ukraine, the Wall Street Journal noted. The White House declined to comment on issues regarding access to Starlink. "The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done," a US official told the newspaper.

Earlier, Sergey Beskrestnov, an advisor to Vladimir Zelensky and an expert in communications and unmanned systems, said that SpaceX had limited the operating speed of Starlink terminals for the Ukrainian military to 160 kilometers per hour.

Later, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk stated that the Starlink system is used solely for defense and civilian purposes, not for offensive military operations.

headline: Africa: Nigeria 5-0 Comoros - Five Big Takeaways As Super Falcons Prepare for Big Morocco Test
summary: [Premium Times] Beyond the scoreline, the performance offered interim coach Augustine Eguavoen encouraging signs of a team beginning to rediscover its defensive solidity while exploring fresh possibilities in attack
body_text:
Beyond the scoreline, the performance offered interim coach Augustine Eguavoen encouraging signs of a team beginning to rediscover its defensive solidity while exploring fresh possibilities in attack

Nigeria's Super Falcons took another confident step towards the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games after dismantling Comoros 5-0 on Tuesday to complete a 7-0 aggregate victory and advance to the third round of the qualifying campaign.

Two goals each from Toni Payne and Uchenna Kanu, alongside the no nonsense Christy Ucheibe's successful penalty, ensured Nigeria finished the tie in emphatic fashion. But beyond the scoreline, the performance offered interim coach Augustine Eguavoen encouraging signs of a team beginning to rediscover its defensive solidity while exploring fresh possibilities in attack.

The Super Falcons were expected to overcome Comoros, particularly after establishing a two-goal advantage in the first leg. However, the manner in which they completed the job was important, especially for a side seeking to rebuild confidence and consistency following a disappointing 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations campaign.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Comoros had thrashed Sudan 30-0 on aggregate in the opening round of the qualifiers, but Nigeria exposed the considerable gulf in quality between the two sides, keeping clean sheets in both meetings and scoring seven unanswered goals.

The next assignment against Morocco will demand significantly more from the nine-time African champions. Before that potentially defining encounter, Premium Times examines five major takeaways from Nigeria's victory, ranked by their importance to Eguavoen's rebuilding project.

Super Falcons rediscover defensive steel ahead of Morocco showdown

For a team with ambitions of returning to the Olympic Games, defensive organisation will be just as important as attacking firepower. Nigeria's two-legged victory over Comoros provided an encouraging indication that the Super Falcons may be finding greater stability at the back.

The Nigerians conceded no goals across both matches, recording consecutive clean sheets for the first time since the group stage of the 2024 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Although Comoros offered limited attacking threat, their impressive 30-0 aggregate demolition of Sudan in the previous round meant they could not be dismissed entirely. Nigeria, however, restricted their opponents and completed the tie without allowing them a route back into the contest.

Perhaps the most encouraging aspect was Eguavoen's decision to trust a new centre-back partnership involving Shukurat Oladipo and Christy Ucheibe. The pair looked composed, mobile and complementary, showing a promising understanding of their defensive responsibilities.

Ucheibe's contribution was particularly notable because she combined her defensive duties with a goal from the penalty spot, underlining her value at both ends of the pitch. Shukurat Oladipo put up a performance that reminded all why she was named the best defender in Italy last season.

The partnership still needs to be tested against opponents with greater technical quality and more sophisticated attacking movements. Nevertheless, Nigeria's defensive display provides a useful foundation for the next round.

Morocco possess considerably more attacking quality than Comoros and are likely to ask harder questions of the Nigerian backline. If the Super Falcons can carry this organisation and concentration into that contest, they will give themselves a stronger chance of progressing.

Morocco test looms as Nigeria face their biggest qualifying challenge yet

The Super Falcons have completed the immediate task, but the real examination of Eguavoen's side is approaching.

Nigeria will face Morocco in the third round after the Atlas Lionesses advanced following the withdrawal of the Republic of Congo from their second-round tie. The meeting promises to be a much more demanding contest, with progression in the Olympic qualifying campaign at stake.

Morocco have developed into one of Africa's leading women's football sides in recent years, making the fixture a significant test of Nigeria's defensive discipline, midfield control and ability to convert attacking opportunities against stronger opposition.

There is, however, a source of confidence for the Super Falcons. Nigeria defeated Morocco 3-2 in the final of the 2024 Women's Africa Cup of Nations, a result that demonstrated their capacity to withstand pressure and deliver when the stakes are high.

That victory will offer encouragement, but it should not be mistaken for a guarantee of success. The upcoming tie is a fresh contest, and Nigeria must show that they can reproduce their best football over two legs against an opponent capable of punishing defensive lapses.

The victory over Comoros has given Eguavoen room to assess his options and build momentum. The Morocco games will reveal whether the encouraging signs in the latest performance can translate into a result against elite continental opposition.

For Nigeria, the objective is no longer simply to score freely against a less experienced opponent. It is to demonstrate that the team can remain compact under pressure, compete in the decisive areas and produce the quality required to keep their Olympic dream alive.

Is Uchenna Kanu Super Falcons next Goalscoring Star?

Nigeria have never lacked outstanding goalscorers. From Mercy Akide and Perpetua Nkwocha to Asisat Oshoala, the Super Falcons have enjoyed generations of forwards capable of defining matches and carrying the weight of expectation.

But as Oshoala moves into the later stages of her career, Nigeria must continue identifying players who can shoulder the responsibility of leading the attack. Kanu's performance against Comoros offered another reason to believe she can play a major role in that transition.

The forward scored twice in Tuesday's encounter and finished the two-legged tie with three goals, strengthening her growing case as a dependable attacking option.

Kanu brings more than an eye for goal. Her strength allows her to compete physically with defenders, while her mobility gives Nigeria the flexibility to use her centrally or from wider attacking positions. She also showed an ability to remain involved in dangerous situations rather than relying solely on chances presented to her.

That variety could prove valuable against Morocco, where Nigeria may have fewer opportunities and will need their forwards to make the most of openings.

However, the next step is sustaining that effectiveness against higher-quality opposition. Goals against Comoros will provide confidence, but performances against Morocco would offer a more convincing indication of Kanu's readiness to become one of Nigeria's leading attacking figures.

With the Super Falcons searching for consistency and a reliable source of goals, Kanu has given Eguavoen another positive selection dilemma.

Michelle Alozie bounces back to remind Nigeria of her class

Michelle Alozie was arguably one of Nigeria's standout performers across the two legs, delivering the kind of energetic and balanced display that could prove crucial in the more demanding rounds of the qualifiers.

Operating at right-back, Alozie covered the flank tirelessly, combining defensive responsibility with forward runs that gave Nigeria another route into attacking areas. Her work rate and willingness to contribute in both phases helped the Super Falcons maintain their threat while remaining organised.

Her performances were particularly encouraging after a difficult showing at the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations. The Comoros tie provided an opportunity to rebuild confidence, and Alozie took it by demonstrating the qualities that have made her a valuable member of the national team.

Modern full-backs are often required to do much more than defend their own penalty area. They must provide width, support attacks, recover quickly and make sound decisions when possession changes hands. Alozie showed encouraging signs in those areas over the two matches.

Her contribution will become even more important against Morocco, whose greater attacking quality should provide a sterner test of her defensive concentration. At the same time, Nigeria may need her forward runs to help stretch the opposition and create space for the attackers.

Toni Payne also deserves credit for her two-goal contribution on Tuesday, while Under 20 captain, Joy Igbokwe's performance offered another encouraging sign of the options available to Eguavoen.

Alozie's displays, however, stood out as a reminder that Nigeria's progress will depend not only on their most celebrated attackers but also on players capable of delivering consistently across the pitch.

Ijamilusi, Okpe make strong claims for bigger Roles in Eguavoen's Super Falcons

The depth of Nigeria's attacking options was another positive to emerge from the victory, with substitutes Folashade Ijamilusi and Blessing Okpe making significant contributions after entering the contest.

Both players registered two assists, while Okpe also won the penalty that Ucheibe converted to complete the scoring. Their impact was reflected in the energy and directness they brought to Nigeria's second-half performance.

Ijamilusi and Okpe used their pace, movement and willingness to run at opponents to give the Super Falcons additional attacking impetus. Rather than simply maintaining the tempo established by the starters, they helped add another dimension to Nigeria's forward play.

Their performances will be welcome news for Eguavoen, particularly as the level of competition rises. Against stronger teams, the ability to change a game from the bench can be just as important as the quality of the starting XI.

Both players have operated on the fringes of the senior national team, making their contributions an opportunity to strengthen their cases for more prominent roles. Their involvement also suggests that Nigeria may have useful alternatives available when the preferred attacking combinations need fresh legs or a different approach.

Of course, the Comoros fixture is only one measure of their readiness. The challenge will be to maintain that energy and decision-making against opponents who defend more effectively and allow less space in the final third.

Still, their influence on Tuesday was difficult to ignore. In a qualifying campaign where squad depth could become decisive, Ijamilusi and Okpe have given Eguavoen more options to consider.

A convincing win, but a bigger challenge awaits

The Super Falcons have done what was required against Comoros, securing a comprehensive aggregate victory while recording consecutive clean sheets and giving several players the opportunity to strengthen their claims for regular places.

Kanu's goals, Payne's attacking contribution, Alozie's all-round performance, the promising centre-back partnership and the impact of Ijamilusi and Okpe all provide reasons for optimism, apart from Captain Rasheedat's injury which was the only blot in the game on the night.

Yet the significance of the result will ultimately be measured by what follows. Morocco represent a different level of opposition, and Nigeria will need to combine the attacking confidence displayed against Comoros with greater tactical discipline and resilience.

Its engineers have developed the Palestine-2 missile that has the capability to manoeuvre during its terminal stage at 6,000kph, allowing it to evade defences. It was allegedly responsible for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport attack that killed 13.Attacks by the Houthis have significantly increased in the past month and are designed to put pressure on Saudi Arabia to end its blockade of the Yemen rebels.Major leapThe Houthis have been significantly helped by specialist parts for missiles imported from China, according to the Conflict Armament Research report passed to The National.Its teams examined weaponry from an intercepted shipment that had been heading to the Houthi-held port of Hodeida. The haul included highly specialist machined parts for rockets such as stabilising fins and equipment for hypersonic flight.“The discovery points to a major leap in the group’s domestic production ambitions and has major regional security implications at a time when Houthi forces are intensifying their deep strike campaign against critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia,” the report said.The components, discovered in containers on a cargo ship from China, demonstrate that the Houthis are now advanced in their work to manufacture the Iranian-made Kheibar Shekan series of ballistic missiles. Their Palestine-2 variant has a range of 1,800km, bringing much of the Middle East into their sights.The findings also demonstrate that the rebels, who are under a UN arms embargo, have expanded their supply chains beyond their traditional Iran-linked networks, the paper said.“The documented components suggest that, in terms of longer-range ballistic missiles, the Houthis have moved beyond simply reassembling Iranian systems,” it stated.“Only a few countries in the world have the capacity to manufacture missiles of comparable ranges domestically.”Accelerated progressWhile the Houthis have “not yet mastered” the technology for the Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile, Iranian expertise on the ground is “accelerating their progress”, said Dr Nawaf Obaid, of Kings College London.“Their principal constraint is time, not technical impossibility,” he told The National.While it is understood the airport attack involved several projectiles in a swarm attack, the Houthis currently cannot build significant numbers, he added.“Scale remains their weakness,” he said. Analysis by Kings College's department of war studies showed that 85 to 90 per cent of missiles were intercepted by Saudi Arabia’s advanced defence system, he added.It is understood that the Houthis exploited a gap between Saudi Arabia’s lower and middle air defence layers in the airport attack, rather than a “technological breakthrough”, said Dr Obaid. He added that the kingdom’s air defences were “performing exceptionally well under sustained wartime conditions”.UK support for RiyadhDocuments show the contents from four shipping containers arrived in the Aden Free Zone in Yemen in June and October 2025 from China.The shipments contained custom-made metal parts including components of the airframe and a solid-propellant rocket motor for a Kheibar Shekan missile.They were made by a Chinese precision-metal producer “that advertises itself as a specialist manufacturer of custom aerospace parts”, the report said.It demonstrated that the Houthis were buying “more specialised parts for the construction of missiles, apparently independent of Iran-linked supply networks”.According to UN reports, Chinese companies form the biggest source of seized goods bound for the Houthis and they have been importing components for solid-fuel missiles from China for at least two years. China has stated that it adheres to the UN Houthi arms ban.Asked by The National what action the UK government might take against Chinese companies allegedly supplying components, the prime minister’s official spokesman said Britain “strongly condemns Houthi attacks and remains committed to supporting the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”.Saudi Arabia's ambassador to London told a meeting of parliamentarians on Tuesday that the UK's support in the face of the Houthi missile menace was welcomed by his government. body_text:
Yemen's Houthis have made a “major leap” in locally producing sophisticated ballistic missiles using components imported from China, an arms intelligence report has revealed.

Experts have also told The National that the militia's manufacturing was becoming increasingly sophisticated. Its engineers have developed the Palestine-2 missile that has the capability to manoeuvre during its terminal stage at 6,000kph, allowing it to evade defences. It was allegedly responsible for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh's King Khalid Airport attack that killed 13.

Attacks by the Houthis have significantly increased in the past month and are designed to put pressure on Saudi Arabia to end its blockade of the Yemen rebels.

Houthis test 'weapons no other armed group possesses'

The Houthis have been significantly helped by specialist parts for missiles imported from China, according to the Conflict Armament Research report passed to The National.

Its teams examined weaponry from an intercepted shipment that had been heading to the Houthi-held port of Hodeida. The haul included highly specialist machined parts for rockets such as stabilising fins and equipment for hypersonic flight.

“The discovery points to a major leap in the group’s domestic production ambitions and has major regional security implications at a time when Houthi forces are intensifying their deep strike campaign against critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia,” the report said.

The components, discovered in containers on a cargo ship from China, demonstrate that the Houthis are now advanced in their work to manufacture the Iranian-made Kheibar Shekan series of ballistic missiles. Their Palestine-2 variant has a range of 1,800km, bringing much of the Middle East into their sights.

The findings also demonstrate that the rebels, who are under a UN arms embargo, have expanded their supply chains beyond their traditional Iran-linked networks, the paper said.

“The documented components suggest that, in terms of longer-range ballistic missiles, the Houthis have moved beyond simply reassembling Iranian systems,” it stated.

“Only a few countries in the world have the capacity to manufacture missiles of comparable ranges domestically.”

While the Houthis have “not yet mastered” the technology for the Kheibar Shekan ballistic missile, Iranian expertise on the ground is “accelerating their progress”, said Dr Nawaf Obaid, of Kings College London.

“Their principal constraint is time, not technical impossibility,” he told The National.

While it is understood the airport attack involved several projectiles in a swarm attack, the Houthis currently cannot build significant numbers, he added.

“Scale remains their weakness,” he said. Analysis by Kings College's department of war studies showed that 85 to 90 per cent of missiles were intercepted by Saudi Arabia’s advanced defence system, he added.

It is understood that the Houthis exploited a gap between Saudi Arabia’s lower and middle air defence layers in the airport attack, rather than a “technological breakthrough”, said Dr Obaid. He added that the kingdom’s air defences were “performing exceptionally well under sustained wartime conditions”.

Documents show the contents from four shipping containers arrived in the Aden Free Zone in Yemen in June and October 2025 from China.

The shipments contained custom-made metal parts including components of the airframe and a solid-propellant rocket motor for a Kheibar Shekan missile.

They were made by a Chinese precision-metal producer “that advertises itself as a specialist manufacturer of custom aerospace parts”, the report said.

It demonstrated that the Houthis were buying “more specialised parts for the construction of missiles, apparently independent of Iran-linked supply networks”.

According to UN reports, Chinese companies form the biggest source of seized goods bound for the Houthis and they have been importing components for solid-fuel missiles from China for at least two years. China has stated that it adheres to the UN Houthi arms ban.

Asked by The National what action the UK government might take against Chinese companies allegedly supplying components, the prime minister’s official spokesman said Britain “strongly condemns Houthi attacks and remains committed to supporting the security of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”.

Saudi Arabia's ambassador to London told a meeting of parliamentarians on Tuesday that the UK's support in the face of the Houthi missile menace was welcomed by his government.

Prince Abdullah bin Khaled held discussions focused on “recent Houthi attacks against the kingdom, regional security, and the importance of international co-operation in safeguarding stability and supporting peace in Yemen”, an embassy post on social media said.

Emotionally charged term that portrays the Houthis as a threatening, evil force rather than a political-military actor.

Vague but ominous term that implies attacks on essential civilian targets, evoking fear and justifying defensive measures.

Civilian casualties in Yemen caused by Saudi-led coalition actions.
The political context of the Yemen war, including the Houthi takeover and ongoing conflict.
International criticism of Saudi Arabia's role in the conflict.

headline: Asian markets fall on tech stock rout as high US inflation weighs on Wall Street
summary: Asian markets fell on Thursday, as artificial intelligence-related stocks plunged after a drop on Wall Street, fuelled by concerns about rising competition and profit growth in the chips sector.South Korea's Kospi slumped more than 7 per cent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 index was down 5.12 per cent at midday local time on Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped by 1 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.75 per cent.Asian markets are dealing with "not just the deeper sell-off in AI-related stocks but also the tightening of financial conditions that comes from higher yields and a higher US dollar", said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.In its report on Thursday, the International Monetary Fund also warned of the Asia region's heavy reliance on the AI boom. Strong global demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and related technology products has boosted exports and investment, particularly in economies integrated into technology supply chains. "The AI-driven technology boom has provided an important offset for economies in East and South-East Asia, although the evolution of AI investment and its long-term economic effects are uncertain," the fund said in a report on the outlook for the Asia-Pacific region."A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains," it added.The IMF also said uncertainty over US monetary policy could keep Asian financial markets volatile.Overnight, stocks on Wall Street dropped as consumer price inflation rose more than expected in September."Wall Street tumbled on further evidence that inflation in the United States is sticky, while a pullback in chip stocks on fears about rising competition and peak profit growth added to the woes," Mr Rodda said. The inflation figures were the "critical driver of markets in US trade", he added. US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent annually in September, above both the 3.6 per cent forecast for the month and August’s 3.4 per cent. Core inflation also was higher than expected, at 2.6 per cent year-on-year. "US stocks sold off as higher-rate expectations returned to the fore, with the S&P 500 recording its weakest session since late July and the Nasdaq hit harder by pressure on chip names," said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. "The risk-off move extended into Asia, where falls in Japan and Korea this morning were much sharper."The US inflation data now points to a higher chance of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, Mr Rodda said.
body_text:
Asian markets fell on Thursday, as artificial intelligence-related stocks plunged after a drop on Wall Street, fuelled by concerns about rising competition and profit growth in the chips sector.

South Korea's Kospi slumped more than 7 per cent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 index was down 5.12 per cent at midday local time on Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped by 1 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.75 per cent.

Asian markets are dealing with "not just the deeper sell-off in AI-related stocks but also the tightening of financial conditions that comes from higher yields and a higher US dollar", said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com.

In its report on Thursday, the International Monetary Fund also warned of the Asia region's heavy reliance on the AI boom.

Strong global demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and related technology products has boosted exports and investment, particularly in economies integrated into technology supply chains.

"The AI-driven technology boom has provided an important offset for economies in East and South-East Asia, although the evolution of AI investment and its long-term economic effects are uncertain," the fund said in a report on the outlook for the Asia-Pacific region.

"A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains," it added.

The IMF also said uncertainty over US monetary policy could keep Asian financial markets volatile.

Overnight, stocks on Wall Street dropped as consumer price inflation rose more than expected in September.

"Wall Street tumbled on further evidence that inflation in the United States is sticky, while a pullback in chip stocks on fears about rising competition and peak profit growth added to the woes," Mr Rodda said.

The inflation figures were the "critical driver of markets in US trade", he added.

US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent annually in September, above both the 3.6 per cent forecast for the month and August’s 3.4 per cent. Core inflation also was higher than expected, at 2.6 per cent year-on-year.

"US stocks sold off as higher-rate expectations returned to the fore, with the S&P 500 recording its weakest session since late July and the Nasdaq hit harder by pressure on chip names," said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD.

"The risk-off move extended into Asia, where falls in Japan and Korea this morning were much sharper."

The US inflation data now points to a higher chance of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, Mr Rodda said.

analysis.framing: The article frames the market decline as a consequence of US inflation and AI-sector volatility, emphasizing risks to Asia's tech-dependent economies through expert commentary and IMF warnings.

headline: Africa: WHO Calls for Urgent Health Action Across the Eastern Mediterranean
summary: [UN News] The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for promoting, providing and protecting health in the Eastern Mediterranean region, home to some of the world's top humanitarian crises such as Sudan, Yemen and the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
body_text:
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for promoting, providing and protecting health in the Eastern Mediterranean region, home to some of the world's top humanitarian crises such as Sudan, Yemen and the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus was speaking on Wednesday to health leaders and senior officials attending the WHO regional committee meeting underway in Cairo, Egypt.

"Over the past year, Member States have continued to advance the health and wellbeing of their people, often under the most difficult circumstances," he said in remarks on the annual report for the region, which spans 22 countries and territories.

He highlighted numerous achievements, including strengthened response to noncommunicable diseases - such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes -which account for roughly two thirds of all deaths in the region, with more than 2.8 million lives lost every year.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Millions displaced, healthcare attacked

Yet, the report was also a reminder that the Eastern Mediterranean continues to face a multitude of challenges.

"This region remains the epicentre of global humanitarian need, with more than 117 million people in need of humanitarian assistance," he said. It is also home to some of the world's largest displacement crises.

"Conflict continues to affect millions of people across several countries and territories," he said.

"We continue to see an appalling number of attacks on healthcare and climate-related shocks continue to place additional pressure on already fragile health systems."

These developments are unfolding amid a sharp fall in international funding for both healthcare and humanitarian operations and increasing fiscal constraints at the national level.

"At the very moment when needs are increasing, resources are declining," he said.

Investment and preparation

Tedros urged leaders to continue measures that promote health, such as reducing tobacco use and other risk factors for noncommunicable diseases and ensuring that all children are vaccinated.

Governments should also continue to invest in strong, equitable and resilient health systems and in health workers.

"Make every primary healthcare facility a place where a woman can receive quality care during pregnancy, where every newborn and child can get a healthy start in life and where hypertension, diabetes and cancer can be detected and managed early," he said.
