body_text:
A senior International Monetary Fund official has said prewar buffers are helping countries in the Middle East to limit the economic impact of the Iran war, but the region's outlook remains highly uncertain as it faces threats of renewed disruption.

The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's energy supplies was shipped before the war, has rattled markets, as have Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway and key sites in neighbouring countries.

“The impact was more contained than the scale initially suggested,” the fund's regional director, Jihad Azour, told reporters during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand.

Diesel shortage to persist into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA warns

While the price of Brent crude is 47 per cent higher than its prewar levels, it has yet to hit the $200-a-barrel mark that was previously feared. The IMF this week maintained its 2026 global growth projection at 3.1 per cent and slightly raised its 2027 forecast to 3.4 per cent. Higher oil prices were partially attributed to the fund lifting its 2026 inflation forecast to 4.7 per cent.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia have been exploring alternatives to send their supplies to markets, while International Energy Agency members agreed in March to release up to 425 million barrels of reserve stocks. Output from non-Gulf producers and an adjustment in energy demand have also mitigated the war's impact, Mr Azour said.

“These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments,” he explained.

Iranian attacks continued in the Strait of Hormuz this week. At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the waterway in the past week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency.

On Wednesday, Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters. Authorities said no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said in a statement.

The IEA said crude oil exports from Gulf producers, led by Saudi Arabia, jumped by 4.4 million barrels a day in September to reach more than 75 per cent of prewar levels. Iran's escalatory attacks on Saudi Arabia and tanker traffic threaten to derail those gains, the agency said.

Brent crude rose 0.36 per cent at $106.1 a barrel on Wednesday, while West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 1.08 per cent at $95.16 a barrel.

The IMF said its 2026 forecasts show a sharp divergence for oil exporters and importers, with the latter being assisted by remittances, tourism and government support.

Regional economies are forecast to see a sharp divergence in trends due to the war. The IMF projected economic contractions of 11.3 per cent for Bahrain, 16 per cent for Iraq, 16.7 per cent for Kuwait, 15.6 per cent for Qatar, 3.3 per cent for Saudi Arabia and 3.9 per cent for the UAE this year.

Growth is expected to rebound in 2027, but the conflict has inflicted a "long-lasting scarring impact" on regional economies, Mr Azour told journalists on Thursday.

The economic recovery will take time and will require additional spending on infrastructure to boost resilience.

"If we compare to the [growth] trajectory before the war, in 2030, we will be below it," he said.

A more prolonged conflict remains the most significant risk for the region's highly uncertain outlook, with further disruptions likely to weaken economic activity, inflame inflationary pressures and place extra strain on fiscal positions across the region, he said. Mr Azour also said tighter financial conditions could deepen vulnerabilities in economies with large sovereign financing needs.

He urged the region's economies to prioritise price stability, rebuild their fiscal buffers and build capacity to withstand future shocks.

The IMF will release its outlook for the Middle East next week in Dubai.

On Wednesday, UAE central bank governor Khaled Balama noted the region's experiences have shown that resilience depends on how quickly economies adapt to changing circumstances while building their fiscal buffers, state news agency Wam reported.

Mr Balama was addressing the region's central bankers and finance ministers during a meeting alongside the IMF and World Bank gathering in Bangkok.

He also said the UAE economy has shown resilience, supported by its robust fiscal buffers, low levels of public debt and its vast sovereign assets, helping to reinforce investor and market confidence. He also emphasised the importance of strengthening international co-operation frameworks amid geopolitical tension.

Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan was due to hold a media conference with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday.

The International Monetary Finance Committee, which is the fund's policy advisory panel, announced this week it had extended Mr Al Jadaan's position as IMFC chair by another year after his term ends on January 3, 2027.

body_text:
UN peacekeepers have been blocked from arranging journalist visits to Israeli-occupied southern Lebanon for weeks, a spokesman told The National, amid accusations of a media blackout.

Journalists have embedded with the UN Interim Force for Lebanon (Unifil) several times since a June ceasefire between Israel and Hezbollah. Those visits provided one of the few means of accessing the occupied territory, which Israel designates as a buffer zone.

The visits allowed journalists to report on the handful of predominantly Christian villages that remain inhabited, as well as the systematic destruction of largely depopulated Muslim villages.

Dispatch'At God's mercy': Life after Unifil in Israeli-occupied Lebanese village

“At the moment, we cannot conduct media visits south of the so-called yellow line,” said a Unifil spokesman. “This has been the case for the past few weeks.”

He added that Unifil did not know when visits would be permitted to resume.

Elsy Moufarrej, president of the Union of Journalists in Lebanon, told The National that the union had received several complaints from journalists denied access to the zone in recent weeks. She accused Israel of a “media blackout” that prevents independent reporting on “potential crimes and violations”.

“It also deprives these communities of a voice and violates the public's right to know,” she added.

Israel occupied an area extending 10km to 12km into Lebanon during its war with Hezbollah, which reignited in March. The Israeli military launched a ground invasion and forced people to leave the south before establishing its security zone.

Since then, Israel has severely restricted movement in and out of the occupied area, enforcing control through military positions, strikes, forced displacement orders and restrictions on access.

The charity Reporters Without Borders has condemned restrictions on journalists entering the zone, accusing the Israeli military of turning co-ordination mechanisms intended to facilitate safe access into tools of censorship.

“It is unacceptable that Lebanese journalists are denied access or prevented from entering Lebanese territory,” said Jonathan Dagher, head of RSF’s Middle East office. “Ceasefire agreements and military considerations must no longer serve as a pretext to obstruct the right to information and threaten the safety of journalists.”

While some communities such as the Sunni Muslim village of Kfarshouba can still be reached from the Lebanese side, predominantly Christian villages deeper inside the territory are effectively besieged, with movement in and out subject to Israeli permission.

Travelling with Unifil had offered journalists rare opportunities to reach these communities. The media restriction appears to have begun in mid-September, following visits to the occupied zone by journalists from international news organisations.

Téa Ziade, a French-Lebanese freelance journalist, was scheduled to enter the zone with Unifil on September 25 for an assignment with a European news outlet. Her trip was cancelled that morning, just minutes before the convoy was due to depart.

“We had submitted all our papers to Unifil. Everything was in order,” she said. “A Unifil lieutenant told us: ‘It’s the journalists. No journalists are allowed in the convoy.’”

She was given no explanation at the time. She was later told by Unifil that a proper deconfliction process had not taken place.

There have been no Unifil journalist embeds since.

The Israeli military confirmed to The National that it had raised the issue of journalist access with Unifil. “Following incidents in which journalists entered the security zone without prior co-ordination and published footage revealing the locations of troops, the issue was discussed with Unifil,” a military spokesperson said.

But another Israeli military official went further, alleging that journalists had entered the occupied zone concealed within convoys and “shared photographs, which showed the location of our troops, with Hezbollah operatives or people connected to Hezbollah operatives”.

The official did not identify the journalists or news organisations involved, or provide evidence to substantiate the allegation.

When questioned about the accusation, an Israeli military spokesperson appeared to backtrack on the claim that journalists had shared information with people linked to Hezbollah, instead saying that publicly available information about Israeli troop positions could be exploited by the group.

Pictures of Israeli positions inside southern Lebanon are widely available online.

Israel, which has been accused of targeting journalists, has routinely portrayed them as militants. In October, it published a list of 170 people killed in the Gaza war who it said were militants posing as media workers.

Israeli forces have killed at least 16 journalists and media workers in Lebanon since October 2023, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Among them was Reuters journalist Issam Abdallah, killed by Israeli tank fire in October 2023 in an attack that wounded six other journalists and which Human Rights Watch described as an apparent war crime.

In April 2026, Al Akhbar journalist Amal Khalil was killed in an Israeli strike while reporting from the security zone during a ceasefire, while her colleague Zeinab Faraj was seriously wounded.

Unifil was not the only means of accessing the occupied territory. Humanitarian and civilian convoys had also offered journalists a route into the occupied zone.

Those routes, too, have become increasingly restricted in recent weeks.

Sources within Unifil and other organisations say access requires “prior deconfliction arrangements, usually through humanitarian convoys”, Ms Moufarrej said.

Deconfliction with the Israeli army usually involves speaking to Unifil or a US and French-led committee established to monitor the ceasefire. The process is intended to arrange safe passage through the area.

“However, Israeli forces have reportedly begun preventing these convoys from entering if journalists accompany them,” she added.

A humanitarian worker who regularly travels into the occupied territory told The National that Israeli soldiers have significantly tightened checks at checkpoints, inspecting every vehicle to ensure no journalists were on board. Such checks were not previously routine, the worker said.

“Israeli soldiers now come out of their base and check every person inside the car to make sure their identity matches the approved list.”

An Israeli army spokesperson said the military reviewed journalists’ requests to enter the occupied zone on a “case-by-case basis”, without clarifying what procedures must be followed for approval.

“Areas where military operations are taking place pose genuine security risks, requiring measures to protect the lives of journalists on the ground, as well as the safety of [Israeli] troops,” the Israeli army spokesperson added. “This policy is intended to enable journalistic coverage to the extent possible, without endangering human lives or compromising the safety of troops and their operational activities.”

However, Israeli military operations are an inherent feature of the occupation, meaning any area could be cut off. Ms Ziade rejected the Israeli army’s security justification.

“If we cannot go to the south, how are we supposed to tell the story of the occupation?” she asked. “We lose part of the meaning of this profession, the ability to build trust and intimacy with people. Without journalists on the ground, there is also a question of accountability and impunity.”

Access for journalists has always been challenging. In July, a vetted humanitarian convoy, which included The National, was barred at the last minute by the Israeli army, despite having obtained prior approval. At the time, Unifil said the decision was probably made because of media presence.

It has now become practically impossible. Since the end of September, no journalists have been allowed inside the security zone.

“What worries me is that this justification could come to be accepted by the international community, and that we, as journalists, will simply be expected to accept it too,” Ms Ziade said. “And that is how, little by little, a territory becomes closed to journalists.”

The restrictions have also had consequences for civilians living under Israeli occupation.

Israeli forces suspended convoys to Debel and Rmeish for three days after journalists entered the occupied zone, according to a humanitarian worker who regularly travels to the area.

Residents of both villages confirmed they had been prevented from entering or leaving during the three-day closure. They said Israeli military officials had accused journalists of entering the territory without authorisation.

The Israeli military official denied having a policy of punishing civilians or villages for hosting reporters, saying troops had temporarily paused the convoy to investigate the incident.

“It is unacceptable that a civilian area is isolated for three days simply for having hosted journalists,” said Mr Dagher from RSF.

The suspension temporarily cut off a lifeline for the besieged communities, whose residents depend on the convoys for travel and supplies. The closure sparked fears about speaking to the media.

“It was indirect, but the message was received by all the villages: ‘There are a lot of mistakes happening, be careful. If there are more mistakes there won't be any more convoys,'” said a locally elected official from Debel, who requested not to be named to avoid retaliation by Israeli forces.

“People got scared. They need these convoys to access hospitals, doctors and supplies.”

body_text:
In today's episode of Trending Middle East, about 800,000 people in Yemen’s city of Taiz are largely cut off from food, fuel and medical supplies as fighting between the government troops and the Houthi rebels intensifies.

As the Iran conflict drags on, the global diesel shortage is expected to continue well into 2027, the International Energy Agency has warned.

In Lebanon, private suppliers now provide half of the country’s electricity, leaving households facing soaring bills. A special report by The National reveals how politically connected businesses are profiting from the country's power crisis.

The Palestinian committee set up to administer Gaza has signed an agreement with Germany’s development agency, GIZ, to support reconstruction. However, Israel continues to block the committee’s entry into the strip.

And the UAE has announced a $1 million prize for a global competition to develop agentic artificial intelligence solutions that improve everyday life.

Trending Middle East is AI-assisted, using original reporting published in The National and curated and edited by humans.

headline: Live: Russia strikes several regions in Ukraine, hits two cargo ships in Black Sea
summary: Russia struck Ukraine's Izmail port and two cargo ships en route to Odesa, the Russian Defence Ministry said Thursday. A day earlier, Moscow launched more missiles and drones at Ukrainian cities, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
body_text:
Issued on: 15/10/2026 - 05:52Modified: 15/10/2026 - 11:04

Russia struck Ukraine's Izmail port and two cargo ships en route to Odesa, the Russian Defence Ministry said Thursday. A day earlier, Moscow launched more missiles and drones at Ukrainian cities, knocking out power to hundreds of thousands. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.

Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet functionality while in motion has been restored, a source in Ukraine's defence ministry said a day after the crucial service was throttled at speeds of over 100 miles per hour.

The source said the defence ministry would continue to seek clarification on the reasons for Wednesday's disruption of the military-grade version of SpaceX's internet service, which affected drone missions across the frontline.

Russia has nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones in just six weeks, according to defence experts and satellite imagery, in the latest expansion of its attack capability close to Ukraine.

The site in what was an empty field in Russia's southwestern Rostov region on August 31 had become a complex facility the size of around 126 soccer pitches by Wednesday, commercial imagery provided by Planet Labs and Airbus showed.

Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of private intelligence company DroneSec, said the site in the imagery would be capable of launching Russia's newest types of jet-powered drone, the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models.

He said the western edge of the facility showed eight platforms for launch rails capable of firing those drones, adding to an existing Russian network of at least 11 fixed launch sites used for drone attacks on Ukraine.

"The speed of construction ... demonstrates the ease with which Russia can bring now-established offensive capabilities to bear rapidly," Monnik said.

The site, he added, looked very close to completion and it will be "probably a matter of weeks before (it is) fully operational, if not earlier."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky urged the United States not to stand with the aggressor, calling for "honesty" after Kyiv said it had been blindsided by Washington's intelligence sharing gaps and Starlink restrictions.

"We need HONESTY from our partners about this war: It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war, and guarantee security," Zelensky said on social media.

Russia said Ukraine targeted an oil refinery in Ryazan (📍), around 180 kilometres (110 miles) south of Moscow, causing a fire.

"The Kyiv regime attempted a large-scale attack on an oil refinery in Ryazan," Moscow's defence ministry said in a statement, adding that a "fire broke out after drone debris fell onto the refinery site."

Firefighters worked at the site of an enterprise hit by a Russian drone strike in Kropyvnytskyi, Ukraine.

⁠Ukraine's ⁠navy ​said ​it had destroyed six ​Russian ‌Su-34M ⁠military ‌aircraft in an overnight strike ⁠on the Borisoglebsk ​airfield in ‌Russia's Voronezh region.

The navy ‌said on ​Telegram it used its Neptune coastal missile ​system ​in the ​attack.

FRANCE 24 could ​not independently verify the battlefield reports.

All European ​leaders need to ​do more to support Ukraine in its ​war ‌against Russia, ⁠Dutch Prime Minister Rob ‌Jetten said ahead of ⁠a summit of EU leaders

"I ​call upon all ‌the European leaders to do more financially, ‌militarily and non ​military, because a lot of European countries are lagging ​behind in the ​support of Ukraine," ​Jetten told reporters in ​Brussels.

"Let's step up our game and make sure that ⁠they can win this senseless ⁠war."

⁠Russia ⁠hit ​Ukraine's ​Naftogaz gas extraction facility in ​the ‌central ⁠Poltava ‌region overnight, the

It ​said in ‌a statement on ‌the ​Telegram app that the attack suspended ​the ​operations, damaged ​equipment ​and caused a fire.

Russia's ​FSB ​security service said that ⁠it ‌had ⁠detained a Swedish ​national ‌for illegally crossing ‌the ​border, the TASS state ​news ​agency reported.

Romania said eight people were missing after a fire broke out on a vessel flying the San Marino flag, the latest incident in the Black Sea, which has seen a series of drone attacks.

"There were 12 people on board the vessel. Four of them are safe, whilst eight are currently missing," the Romanian Naval Authority said in a press release.

Far-right leader and presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said on Wednesday that France could no longer afford to fund Ukraine, citing the country's high deficit and weak economic growth.

Click the link below to learn more ⬇️

⁠German ​Finance ​Minister Lars Klingbeil said his ⁠country's ‌support for Ukraine ⁠was

clear but comes with ​clear ‌expectations for political ‌reforms.

Klingbeil was ​speaking to reporters on the ​sidelines of IMF-World ​Bank ​meetings in ​Bangkok.

⁠Ukraine ⁠will ​resume ​strikes on Russian refineries, Ukrainian ​President ‌Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskiy ‌told the Financial ⁠Times in an ​interview.

“The ‌block [on ​attacking refineries] is out. We’re ​done,” Zelenskiy ​told ​the newspaper.

Ukraine on Wednesday accused the United States of helping Russia by failing to warn it of incoming missile strikes and hobbling Kyiv's military response through changes to the Starlink system it uses on the battlefield.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called on US tech billionaire Elon Musk to restore Starlink, which Kyiv says has been slowed down.

⁠Russia ⁠has ​struck ​Izmail port in Ukraine's Black ​Sea ‌Odesa ⁠region (📍) ‌and has also ⁠hit two cargo

vessels ​en ‌route to Odesa, ‌the Russian ​defence ministry said on Telegram, adding ​those ​were ​used for ​military purposes.

British finance minister John ​Healey called on other nations to tighten sanctions on Russia-linked shipping, ​as he prepared to meet his foreign counterparts at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings in Bangkok on Thursday.

"My message to finance ministers here ​today ... on ‌Ukraine, is to stay the path on tough ⁠economic sanctions on Russia, especially a tighter ban on shipping services ... that help

(Russian President Vladimir) ‌Putin's sanctions-busting shadow fleet to operate," he said.

⁠Russian ⁠air ​strikes ​have killed ​two people ‌in ⁠the ‌Ukrainian southeastern ⁠Dnipropetrovsk region ​early on ‌Thursday, regional ‌governor ​Oleksandr Hanzha said on ​the Telegram ​messaging ​app.

Romania on Wednesday was probing a possible fresh drone attack on a tanker off its Black Sea coast.

Suspected Russian drones have hit several ships off Romania and neighbouring Bulgaria since last week in the latest spillover from the Ukraine war in the Black Sea.

Romanian rescuers rushed to help the Comoros Islands-flagged Yara J late Wednesday off Sulina near the border with Ukraine, a statement said.

Defence Minister Radu Miruta said the ship's crew managed to douse a fire themselves.

"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," he told the Digi24 television channel.

"This is a matter of significant gravity, given that such incidents are occurring in Romanian territorial waters," he said.

Welcome to this liveblog dedicated to the war in Ukraine.

body_text:
Even with some of the world's oldest and most prestigious publishing houses, extensive library networks and a celebrated literary culture, Europe is struggling to keep successive generations reading.

That was among the takeaways from a presentation by the Federation of European Publishers, which represents national publishing associations across the continent, at Frankfurt Book Fair last week.

While the federation reported that print book sales had fallen by about 6 per cent over five years in the markets surveyed, equivalent to a 110 million decline in copies, more revealing was its examination of reading habits.

Cairo's Diwan Publishing brings Nobel winner Naguib Mahfouz to new readers

Drawing on Eurostat research from 2022, the report highlighted that 47.2 per cent of European Union residents aged 16 and older had not read a book in the preceding year. Among those aged 16 to 29, nearly four in 10 had not read one.

The reasons reported by non-readers warrant attention. Among those aged 16 to 29, a lack of interest was cited by 58 per cent, compared with 21.8 per cent who said they lacked time. Across all age groups, 2.4 per cent identified cost or access as the obstacle.

The figures add to gnawing concerns that predate Frankfurt, with research published in February by Britain's National Literacy Trust finding that 46.9 per cent of children aged eight to 11 enjoyed reading in their free time, compared with 29.5 per cent of those aged 11 to 14. Among boys aged 14 to 16, the figure was just 18.8 per cent.

Europe's experience offers a reminder against taking the Arab world's considerable investment in introducing children to books for granted.

As educators and parents know, that desire to turn the page can change as they grow older, with education, social media and entertainment compete for attention, followed eventually by the growing pressures of professional and family responsibilities. Reading habits are not set in stone simply because children were encouraged during childhood. That is merely the first chapter of an ongoing story.

The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing the reading bug. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. An impact study conducted in partnership with Unesco reported increased reading frequency and more books completed by participating students.

Meanwhile, the Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, is more concerned with encouraging children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested on what they have consumed. Researchers are evaluating its effects and the longer-term affects remain unknown.

Beyond the classroom, UAE libraries are also finding ways to keep books part of people's everyday lives. Sharjah's House of Wisdom and Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Library have become places to work, study and attend cultural events, as well as read books. The latter houses nine specialised libraries, including sections for children and young adults.

But reading habits cannot develop through osmosis alone and both libraries continue to encourage younger audiences through workshops, holiday programmes and exhibitions.

The quality of that content is critical, particularly when young Arabs themselves are questioning the appeal of the cultural content available to them. At the Congress of Arabic and Creative Industries in Abu Dhabi in September, a survey of 4,092 people aged 18 to 25 across 10 Arab countries found that 71 per cent preferred media in Arabic, yet 67 per cent considered much of the available Arabic content outdated compared with English-language alternatives.

The findings covered media broadly rather than books specifically, but they should give publishers reason to consider whether their books are resonating with younger audiences.

Cairo's Diwan Publishing is one example worth noting, having reintroduced Naguib Mahfouz's novels through contemporary cover designs and graphic-novel adaptations, including The Thief and the Dogs.

As previously reported by The National, co-founder Ahmed Qarmalawi said the project, developed with the Mahfouz family, sought to introduce the Nobel laureate's work to a generation familiar with his reputation but not necessarily his writing.

At the 2024 Abu Dhabi International Book Fair, a large interactive pavilion dedicated to Mahfouz showcased the new editions. Qarmalawi recalled young visitors responding enthusiastically to the books, suggesting that an author some might regard as a literary cultural heirloom could still speak to a younger generation.

And in that regard, social media is also playing a role in building a love of books during adolescence. As The National has reported, BookTok and BookTube communities have emerged in the region, with members recommending titles, sharing punchy reviews and introducing fellow readers to new authors.

While the footfall at such events and the viewing figures online deserve to be celebrated, more work is needed to turn that enthusiasm into lasting reading habits and make reading books a normal part of life rather than homework. Authors and publishers must also take risks and create content that resonates.

With its young population, eclectic cultural sensibilities and governments that view culture as an investment, the Arab world has a chance to lead in keeping people reading.

That would be an achievement for a regional publishing industry still regarded as evolving by some of its European counterparts, provided the same commitment that encouraged children to pick up books in the first place is sustained.

analysis.framing: The article uses European reading-decline data as a cautionary backdrop to argue that the Arab world, particularly the UAE, has an opportunity to lead in sustaining reading habits through government investment and cultural initiatives.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged phrase that dramatizes the reading data as a persistent, troubling anxiety rather than a neutral trend.
Vague, colloquial metaphor that frames reading as a desirable condition to be cultivated, carrying a positive editorial tone.
Figurative and slightly dismissive phrase contrasting rote reading with genuine enjoyment, implying a value judgment about educational methods.
Evocative metaphor that elevates Mahfouz's status and frames the publishing project as preserving a precious inheritance.
Vague, positive characterization of the Arab world's cultural landscape that reads as promotional rather than descriptive.

omissions: Specific details about which European countries were surveyed or the full methodology of the Federation of European Publishers report.
Any counterarguments or skepticism about the effectiveness of the Arab Reading Challenge or UAE reading initiatives.
Comparative data on reading habits in the Arab world to directly parallel the European statistics presented.
Voices from independent publishers, authors, or readers in the Arab world who might offer critical perspectives on government-led reading programs.

corrections.reason: The article is a signed analysis/opinion piece, not a straight news report, so a media-bias rating is not applicable; the analysis's 'not-determinable' rating with 0.3 confidence is not grounded in any article wording.
Omissions are inherently unverifiable from the article text alone; the listed items are plausible but cannot be confirmed as absent without external sources.
The 70/30 split is an arbitrary quantification not derivable from the article; no methodology is provided.
The analysis itself flags no insufficient evidence, yet several fields (bias_rating, omissions, fact_vs_opinion) lack grounding, so this empty list is inconsistent.

headline: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons consider leaving UK as tax concerns mount
summary: Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found. The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth.Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth.The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The exodus of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE, Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US.The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs.CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says. Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai-based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”. “UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National.Tax overhauls intensify debateUnder the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains.Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules.The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon.UAE leads inquiry listEnquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds.Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent.Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. A further 21.9 per cent concerned residency, relocation or visas, while 13.9 per cent related to wealth structures such as trusts, foundations and holding companies, data shows.“Tax efficiency may start the conversation, but it is rarely enough to complete the move,” Mr Gordon says, before adding that the UAE’s connectivity, business infrastructure and access to markets across the Middle East, Asia and Africa appeal to families seeking a commercial base. Switzerland and Singapore offer established wealth management sectors, while Portugal and Malta continue to attract those seeking European residency and lifestyle benefits.Across all UK-origin enquiries to the group, 42 per cent referenced business or company set-up, while 28.9 per cent involved wealth or succession planning. The UK-origin enquiries have averaged about 19 per cent of the group’s total leads over the past four years, according to Mr Gordon.Meanwhile, the broader migration outlook remains significant. Henley & Partners and New World Wealth forecast a record 165,000 millionaire relocations worldwide in 2026, with the UAE expected to remain the leading destination for inflows.For Britain, the challenge is to balance tax reform with its ability to retain mobile investors and entrepreneurs. For the UAE, the opportunity is to convert initial interest into durable investment and economic activity.“The UAE’s long-term challenge is not simply to attract wealthy residents, but to convert initial tax and residency interest into enduring business activity, investment and family connections,” Mr Gordon says.
body_text:
Nearly one in three wealthy Britons are considering leaving the UK, as declining confidence in the economy and concerns over future tax changes prompt more well-off residents to reassess where they live and manage their money, a new study has found.

The proportion thinking about emigrating has risen from 25 per cent a year ago to 30 per cent, according to the Saltus Wealth Index Report, published last month. Eight per cent are actively exploring a move, while 22 per cent say they may consider one in future. Although 70 per cent have no plans to leave, the findings show, confidence in the UK economy and tax system matters to internationally mobile wealth.

Saltus’s analysis was based on research of 2,000 UK adults with at least £250,000 ($331,600) in investible assets, excluding their main home. The annual survey found that confidence in the UK economy among high-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) had fallen to 56 per cent, down from 66 per cent a year ago, with 40 per cent now identifying possible tax changes as a key risk to their wealth.

The abolition of the UK’s non-domiciled tax regime in April last year has added to concerns about the UK’s appeal to wealthy individuals and families. The exodus of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth. More such people are looking at alternative countries to park their money. These include the UAE, Switzerland, Italy, Singapore and the US.

The UAE has emerged as one of the leading destinations for migrating millionaires, offering zero income tax, long-term residency, advanced infrastructure, established financial centres and an easy business environment for investors and entrepreneurs.

CitizenX, a Swiss technology and immigration advisory company, predicts that the UK will lose a net 5,700 millionaires in 2027. It is a “large outflow by any historical standard”, but also a smaller number than the previous, when “our baseline puts the UK’s net loss at 8,600", the largest in the world that year, it says.

Simon Gordon, managing director for the Middle East at the Dubai-based consultancy Sovereign PPG Corporate Services, says the key question is “whether the UK’s recent tax changes and uncertainty over what might come next will lead to a lasting shift in where wealthy families choose to live, run their businesses and manage their wealth”.

“UK-origin enquiries relating to the UAE dipped between March and May amid the regional conflict, but recovered from June and remained resilient, accounting for 20 per cent of UK leads again in September. This suggests that, despite the uncertainty, the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans,” Mr Gordon tells The National.

Under the UK’s replacement foreign income and gains regime, eligible new arrivals who have been non-resident for at least 10 consecutive years can claim relief on qualifying foreign income and gains for their first four years of UK tax residence. After that, they are generally taxed on worldwide income and gains.

Inheritance tax has also shifted towards a residence-based system. Overseas assets generally fall within scope after an individual has been UK-resident for 10 of the previous 20 tax years, subject to the applicable rules.

The abolition of the non-domicile (non-dom) regime and the move towards residence-based inheritance taxation have “increased the urgency of conversations with internationally mobile families”, says Mr Gordon.

Enquiries increasingly cover residency, family mobility, succession planning, business ownership and where future investments should be based, he adds.

Sovereign PPG’s latest data shows that the UAE accounted for 16.2 per cent of the group’s enquiries originating in the UK, ahead of the Isle of Man at 12.8 per cent, Portugal at 11.7 per cent, Gibraltar at 5.5 per cent and Malta at 4.3 per cent.

Nearly 60 per cent of UK-origin UAE enquiries involved company formation, business licensing or other commercial set-up requirements. A further 21.9 per cent concerned residency, relocation or visas, while 13.9 per cent related to wealth structures such as trusts, foundations and holding companies, data shows.

“Tax efficiency may start the conversation, but it is rarely enough to complete the move,” Mr Gordon says, before adding that the UAE’s connectivity, business infrastructure and access to markets across the Middle East, Asia and Africa appeal to families seeking a commercial base. Switzerland and Singapore offer established wealth management sectors, while Portugal and Malta continue to attract those seeking European residency and lifestyle benefits.

Across all UK-origin enquiries to the group, 42 per cent referenced business or company set-up, while 28.9 per cent involved wealth or succession planning. The UK-origin enquiries have averaged about 19 per cent of the group’s total leads over the past four years, according to Mr Gordon.

Meanwhile, the broader migration outlook remains significant. Henley & Partners and New World Wealth forecast a record 165,000 millionaire relocations worldwide in 2026, with the UAE expected to remain the leading destination for inflows.

For Britain, the challenge is to balance tax reform with its ability to retain mobile investors and entrepreneurs. For the UAE, the opportunity is to convert initial interest into durable investment and economic activity.

“The UAE’s long-term challenge is not simply to attract wealthy residents, but to convert initial tax and residency interest into enduring business activity, investment and family connections,” Mr Gordon says.

analysis.framing: The article frames the UK's tax changes as driving wealthy residents to consider emigration, presenting the UAE and other low-tax jurisdictions as attractive alternatives while giving substantial voice to a Dubai-based consultancy promoting UAE relocation.

loaded_language.quote: The exodus of the wealthy from the UK is proving to be a boon for countries with more relaxed tax regulations that are vying for the British wealth.
loaded_language.explanation: The word 'exodus' evokes a dramatic mass departure, and 'boon' frames the trend positively for destination countries, editorializing the migration as a windfall.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: The movement of wealthy individuals from the UK is benefiting countries with lower tax rates that are competing for British wealth.

loaded_language.explanation: The colloquial phrase 'park their money' is vague and slightly dismissive, reducing complex relocation and investment decisions to a casual act of stashing cash.
The phrase 'vying for' personifies countries as competitors and 'the British wealth' reduces people to a resource, adding a competitive, almost acquisitive tone.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: competing to attract wealthy British residents

loaded_language.explanation: The metaphor 'on the radar' is informal and vague, suggesting ongoing attention without specifying concrete interest levels.
The word 'urgency' adds emotional pressure, implying a crisis-like need to act rather than routine advisory discussions.

omissions: Perspectives from UK government officials or tax authorities defending the tax changes
Views from wealthy individuals who have decided to stay in the UK or who support the tax reforms
Criticism of the Saltus Wealth Index Report methodology or sample limitations
Context on how the UK's tax rates compare internationally beyond the non-dom regime
Potential economic benefits of the tax changes for the UK public or treasury

corrections.reason: The article's framing and sourcing (heavy reliance on a Dubai-based consultancy promoting UAE relocation, positive portrayal of low-tax jurisdictions) suggest a lean toward business/wealth-migration interests, but this does not map cleanly onto a left-right political spectrum. The 'lean-right' rating is not directly attributable to concrete wording in the article.

The quoted phrase 'firmly on the radar' does not appear verbatim in the article. The article contains 'the UAE remains firmly on the radar for people considering their longer-term plans', but the exact quote provided is not present.

headline: Reconstruction in north-east Syria key to refugee returns from Iraq, UNHCR official says
summary: Reconstruction work in Syria must extend to Kurdish areas in the north-east if refugees are to return home, the UN refugee agency’s representative in Iraq has told The National.Toby Harward said the lack of economic opportunities and security in the region remained a major obstacle.“We see a lot of MoUs [memorandums of understanding] signed in Syria, we see a lot of agreements being signed, plans for reinvestment, reconstruction,” Mr Harward said. But these plans have to extend to the Kurdish areas to create an appetite for Syrian refugees in Iraq to return, he added.Iraq hosts more than 300,000 Syrian refugees, according to UNHCR data. Eighty-five per cent of them are in the autonomous Kurdistan Region, and the majority are Syrian Kurds, Mr Harward said. Refugees began returning from Iraq to Syria in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, but this has slowed, he said. “It has not just slowed from Iraq, but also from Jordan, from Lebanon and from Turkey.“When I talk to the refugees, the number one reason for not returning is the continuing frictions and tensions. We have seen demonstrations in Hasakah over the last … several days,” he said. He was referring to the uncertain security situation in north-east Syria following the integration deal between the Damascus government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which assumed control of the area during the country's 2011-2024 civil war.Mr Harward said refugees had told him that until there was “a reduction in tensions” between the “Arab and Kurdish components, [until] there is more of social cohesion, peaceful coexistence between them, they feel that there is no future for younger people going back”.“I am optimistic. But then the power of one revenge kidnapping and killing on social media will destroy all of the positive developments at one level,” he added.However, the slowing of returns is not just due to the economic and security uncertainty in Syria. Some refugees have established livelihoods in their host community. “I would argue that there is more opportunity in Iraq. Kurdistan's progressive policies – allowing access to services, allowing access to livelihoods – mean that they have a lot better situation than refugees in many other parts of the world,” Mr Harward said.He praised efforts by the Iraqi and Kurdish governments to provide Syrian refugees with opportunities to work and live. Many Kurdish officials have an “emotional and empathetic attachment” towards refugees, having been in these positions before, he said. He noted that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Barham Salih, is an Iraqi Kurd and a former refugee.“But on the other side, they will admit that it is a burden,” he said, of the reliance on the government to provide electricity, water and other basic needs to refugees. To counter this, one of the UNHCR's main priorities in Iraq is to generate employment opportunities that allow refugees to become more independent in their host country, he said.Mr Harward noted that the rate of return of Syrian refugees from federal Iraq was higher than from the Kurdistan Region. “The number of refugees returning from central-south, from federal Iraq, has been higher than the numbers here. And that is primarily because they are Arabs.”A drop in job opportunities and the economic situation in federal Iraq was another factor in their decision to return, he said. Mr Harward said the UNHCR was also working with Iraqi families returned from Al Hol camp in Syria, where the SDF held relatives of suspected ISIS militants. "What I understand is that on return to the areas of origin, there are still prejudices, they are still facing stigma, negative stigma, and this is something that I think UN agencies, working obviously with the government in the lead, need to do more to ensure that they are properly able to integrate,” he said.Iraq also has nearly one million internally displaced people, including more than 100,000 living in camps in the Kurdistan Region, according to figures from the UN and the International Organisation for Migration. Most of them fled their homes after ISIS seized large areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014.Mr Harward said there were still 18 camps, mainly in Duhok and Zakho, hosting members of the Yazidi community, who follow an ancient monotheistic religion and live in the mountains of north-west Iraq. ISIS extremists captured Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Yazidis, and surrounding villages in August 2014, taking thousands captive and slaughtering thousands of others. Some Yazidis fled to Mount Sinjar, where many were flown to safety by the US-backed Iraqi forces.“I feel a deep sense of shame that the people who suffered from brutal human rights violations and what many governments have called genocide are still living in camps 12 years after 2014,” he said. He said “durable solutions” should be found for not just the Yazidis but all internally displaced communities to return to their areas of origin and reintegrate into those areas.In October 2020, nearly three years after ISIS was defeated in Iraq, the Baghdad and Kurdistan Region governments signed the Sinjar Agreement to restore state authority in Sinjar and facilitate the return of internally displaced people, particularly Yazidis, with UN support. However, its implementation has largely stalled amid disputes over who should control the area and appoint a mayor.The Popular Mobilisation Forces, an umbrella group of Iraqi militias that fought ISIS, including factions aligned with Iran, Yazidi armed groups and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) remain in Sinjar.Mr Harward said he hoped Turkey's decision to withdraw its troops from the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq, the peace process between Ankara and the PKK, and Iraq's efforts to bring armed groups under state control would alleviate the security situation.
body_text:
Reconstruction work in Syria must extend to Kurdish areas in the north-east if refugees are to return home, the UN refugee agency’s representative in Iraq has told The National.

Toby Harward said the lack of economic opportunities and security in the region remained a major obstacle.

“We see a lot of MoUs [memorandums of understanding] signed in Syria, we see a lot of agreements being signed, plans for reinvestment, reconstruction,” Mr Harward said. But these plans have to extend to the Kurdish areas to create an appetite for Syrian refugees in Iraq to return, he added.

Macron to visit UAE on Gulf tour next week

Iraq hosts more than 300,000 Syrian refugees, according to UNHCR data. Eighty-five per cent of them are in the autonomous Kurdistan Region, and the majority are Syrian Kurds, Mr Harward said.

Refugees began returning from Iraq to Syria in the immediate aftermath of the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, but this has slowed, he said. “It has not just slowed from Iraq, but also from Jordan, from Lebanon and from Turkey.

“When I talk to the refugees, the number one reason for not returning is the continuing frictions and tensions. We have seen demonstrations in Hasakah over the last … several days,” he said. He was referring to the uncertain security situation in north-east Syria following the integration deal between the Damascus government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, which assumed control of the area during the country's 2011-2024 civil war.

Mr Harward said refugees had told him that until there was “a reduction in tensions” between the “Arab and Kurdish components, [until] there is more of social cohesion, peaceful coexistence between them, they feel that there is no future for younger people going back”.

“I am optimistic. But then the power of one revenge kidnapping and killing on social media will destroy all of the positive developments at one level,” he added.

However, the slowing of returns is not just due to the economic and security uncertainty in Syria. Some refugees have established livelihoods in their host community.

“I would argue that there is more opportunity in Iraq. Kurdistan's progressive policies – allowing access to services, allowing access to livelihoods – mean that they have a lot better situation than refugees in many other parts of the world,” Mr Harward said.

He praised efforts by the Iraqi and Kurdish governments to provide Syrian refugees with opportunities to work and live. Many Kurdish officials have an “emotional and empathetic attachment” towards refugees, having been in these positions before, he said.

He noted that the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, Barham Salih, is an Iraqi Kurd and a former refugee.

“But on the other side, they will admit that it is a burden,” he said, of the reliance on the government to provide electricity, water and other basic needs to refugees.

To counter this, one of the UNHCR's main priorities in Iraq is to generate employment opportunities that allow refugees to become more independent in their host country, he said.

Mr Harward noted that the rate of return of Syrian refugees from federal Iraq was higher than from the Kurdistan Region. “The number of refugees returning from central-south, from federal Iraq, has been higher than the numbers here. And that is primarily because they are Arabs.”

A drop in job opportunities and the economic situation in federal Iraq was another factor in their decision to return, he said.

Mr Harward said the UNHCR was also working with Iraqi families returned from Al Hol camp in Syria, where the SDF held relatives of suspected ISIS militants.

"What I understand is that on return to the areas of origin, there are still prejudices, they are still facing stigma, negative stigma, and this is something that I think UN agencies, working obviously with the government in the lead, need to do more to ensure that they are properly able to integrate,” he said.

Iraq also has nearly one million internally displaced people, including more than 100,000 living in camps in the Kurdistan Region, according to figures from the UN and the International Organisation for Migration. Most of them fled their homes after ISIS seized large areas of northern and western Iraq in 2014.

Mr Harward said there were still 18 camps, mainly in Duhok and Zakho, hosting members of the Yazidi community, who follow an ancient monotheistic religion and live in the mountains of north-west Iraq.

ISIS extremists captured Sinjar, the ancestral homeland of Yazidis, and surrounding villages in August 2014, taking thousands captive and slaughtering thousands of others. Some Yazidis fled to Mount Sinjar, where many were flown to safety by the US-backed Iraqi forces.

“I feel a deep sense of shame that the people who suffered from brutal human rights violations and what many governments have called genocide are still living in camps 12 years after 2014,” he said.

He said “durable solutions” should be found for not just the Yazidis but all internally displaced communities to return to their areas of origin and reintegrate into those areas.

In October 2020, nearly three years after ISIS was defeated in Iraq, the Baghdad and Kurdistan Region governments signed the Sinjar Agreement to restore state authority in Sinjar and facilitate the return of internally displaced people, particularly Yazidis, with UN support. The Popular Mobilisation Forces, an umbrella group of Iraqi militias that fought ISIS, including factions aligned with Iran, Yazidi armed groups and the Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) remain in Sinjar.

Mr Harward said he hoped Turkey's decision to withdraw its troops from the Bashiqa base in northern Iraq, the peace process between Ankara and the PKK, and Iraq's efforts to bring armed groups under state control would alleviate the security situation.

headline: East China's Shandong launches first TIR road freight route to Georgia
summary: China has launched its first international road freight route from Shandong Province to Georgia under the international TIR system, Qingdao Customs said on Thursday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- China has launched its first international road freight route from Shandong Province to Georgia under the international TIR system, Qingdao Customs said on Thursday.

The route links the China-SCO demonstration zone for regional trade and economic cooperation with Georgia. It is the seventh TIR route launched by the demonstration zone and the first connecting Shandong with Georgia.

The TIR system, established under a United Nations convention on international road transport, streamlines cross-border customs clearance. Vehicles carrying valid TIR carnets can clear customs at their points of departure and destination without having to unload their cargo for repeated inspections while passing through transit countries.

Georgia serves as a key transit hub for goods traveling from China to European markets.

Two trucks loaded with clothing set off from the demonstration zone in Qingdao on the day the route opened. They are scheduled to leave China through the Horgos Port in Xinjiang, cross Kazakhstan to the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea, take a ferry across the sea and travel through Azerbaijan before reaching Georgia.

The new route is expected to cut transit times to around 18 days, from the 30 to 45 days typically required previously, said Dou Kun, head of Qingdao Runshengchi Logistics Co., which handled the shipment. TIR transport is also more cost-effective and efficient than traditional sea freight, Dou said.

The demonstration zone is China's only national-level platform dedicated to regional trade and economic cooperation with Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) member states.

In the first nine months of this year, the zone dispatched 277 TIR truck shipments carrying goods worth a total of 240 million yuan (approximately 35.86 million dollars).

headline: Russia vows closer ties with N. Korea at diplomatic anniversary reception
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- Russia has pledged to deepen ties with North Korea at...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- Russia has pledged to deepen ties with North Korea at a reception in Pyongyang marking 78 years of diplomatic relations, the North's state media reported Thursday.

Russian Ambassador Andrey Podelyshev hosted the event the previous day at the Taedonggang Diplomatic Club, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

It was his first reception since taking up the post late last month. North Korean Vice Foreign Minister Kim Jong-gyu attended.

Speakers said "victory is in store for the sacred common cause of the two countries for the building of powerful countries and welfare of the peoples," and expressed belief that the alliance "forged with blood would be immortal," according to the report.

Podelyshev called the relations between the two countries "exemplary," developing on "the principles of full equality and mutual respect," according to the Russian Embassy's Telegram channel.

"Their legal foundation is the Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership," Podelyshev said of the two countries' relations.

The treaty, signed in June 2024 by Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has "brought cooperation between our countries to a qualitatively new level and set a high standard for its further strengthening," he added.

Kim Jong-gyu responded by saying it is North Korea's "unwavering position" to "comprehensively expand and develop traditional relations of friendship and cooperation."

"We will make every effort to strengthen tactical and strategic cooperation, and develop bilateral relations," he said.

A Russian delegation from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, led by D.V. Sergienko, deputy head of the Migration Service, was visiting Pyongyang and also attended, the embassy said.

headline: Russia's Lavrov, China's Wang discuss cooperation, Ukraine, Iran at Asia security meeting
summary: Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Russian and Chinese foreign ministers discussed the state of bilateral cooperation as well as the crises in Ukraine and Iran during an Asia security meeting, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping reaffirmed their strategic alliance at a regional summit last August and both praised prospects for closer cooperation.

Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Russian and Chinese foreign ministers discussed the state of bilateral cooperation as well as the crises in Ukraine and Iran during an Asia security meeting, the Russian Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping reaffirmed their strategic alliance at a regional summit last August and both praised prospects for closer cooperation.

The statement on Wednesday said Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov and his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi met in Azerbaijan at a meeting of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia.

It said the two ministers "praised the development dynamics of comprehensive partnership and strategic cooperation" and "synchronized watches on bilateral political dialogue".

It said discussions also focused on "relations with the United States and the situation around the Ukrainian and Iranian crises".

Both Russia and China have called for an end to the Iran conflict, saying it could expand and threaten stability throughout the region.

China has affirmed its "no limits" partnership with Russia throughout the 4-1/2-year-long war in Ukraine, while calling for diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

headline: Pakistan school roof collapse: 29 children, teacher killed in Peshawar; 40 wounded
body_text:
Pakistan school roof collapse: At least 29 children, most of them below the age of 13, and a teacher were killed and more than 40 people injured when the roof of a private school collapsed in Peshawar, the capital of Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, on Thursday, news agency PTI reported, citing police.

The incident occurred in Dir Colony in the inner city area, Peshawar Capital City Police chief Mian Saeed said. The owner of the three-storey school has been arrested, he said, adding that the roof was poorly constructed.

The owner was operating the institution as an education trust, Saeed said. A total of 110 children were enrolled at the school, and 30 students were present in classrooms on the upper floor when the roof collapsed, he said.

District emergency officer Iftikhar Khan said more children were reported to be buried in the rubble. Rescue operations are underway to extricate bodies and take the injured to hospital, said government official Bilal Faizi.

The deceased and the injured were rushed to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, its spokesperson, Mohammad Asim, said.

He said that an emergency was declared at the hospital to treat the injured, adding that all the children killed in the incident were aged 13 or younger.

Peshawar Deputy Commissioner Afaq Wazir ordered a probe into the roof collapse. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif expressed deep grief over the lives lost in the incident and extended his condolences to the bereaved families.

He directed authorities that the wounded must be provided with the best possible medical treatment. Governor Faisal Karim Kundi also expressed grief over the roof collapse.

headline: Qatar condemns Colombia’s opening of embassy in occupied Jerusalem
summary: Colombia became the 10th country or entity to establish a diplomatic mission in occupied Jerusalem after opening its embassy on Wednesday. Qatar has condemned Colombia’s opening of an embassy to…
body_text:
Colombia became the 10th country or entity to establish a diplomatic mission in occupied Jerusalem after opening its embassy on Wednesday.

Qatar has condemned Colombia’s opening of an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem, describing the move as a violation of international law and relevant United Nations resolutions.

“Qatar expresses its condemnation and denunciation of Colombia’s opening of its embassy to Israel in the occupied city of Jerusalem, considering this step a violation of international law and relevant international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolution 478 of 1980,” Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA) said in a statement on Thursday.

“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs reaffirms Qatar’s rejection of any measures that would alter the legal and historical status of the city of Jerusalem,” the statement added.

Qatar also called on the international community to counter attempts to impose a new reality in occupied Jerusalem and safeguard the city’s legal and historical status, as well as the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.

Colombia opened its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday, 14 October, becoming the 10th country or entity to establish a diplomatic mission in the occupied city, joining the United States, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Kosovo, Nauru and Somaliland.

The move followed Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella’s restoration of diplomatic ties with Israel, reversing his predecessor Gustavo Petro’s decision to sever relations in 2024.

Adopted in 1980, UN Security Council Resolution 478 called on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions from Jerusalem following Israel’s enactment of a law declaring the city its “complete and united” capital.

headline: Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer: Oncologist explains why non-smokers develop it
body_text:
Written by Dr Ankit Jain

Pope Leo XIV, 71, was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after undergoing surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung on October 13 at Rome’s Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic. The Pope is not known to have smoked, drawing attention to a question that often puzzles patients: how can lung cancer develop in someone without a history of smoking?

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer and is frequently diagnosed in people who have never smoked. While smoking remains a major risk factor for lung cancer, the disease can also develop because of changes within lung cells, exposure to environmental pollutants and other factors. In some patients, no single cause can be established. “Genetic changes cause lung cells to grow uncontrollably due to mutations like EGFR and ALK, even in the absence of tobacco exposure,” says Dr Ankit Jain, Senior Consultant, Medical Oncology, Indraprastha Apollo Hospitals, New Delhi. Listen in:

How can genes cause lung cancer in non-smokers?

Genes are sections of DNA that carry instructions for how cells grow, divide and function. Normally, cells follow these instructions and respond to signals that tell them when to grow and when to stop. Sometimes, changes in DNA disrupt this system. Certain alterations can switch on signals that repeatedly tell cells to grow and divide, even when they should not. Over time, this uncontrolled multiplication can lead to cancer.

This does not necessarily mean the person inherited a cancer-causing gene from a parent. Many of these changes develop in the tumour cells during a person’s lifetime. They are known as acquired or somatic mutations. The distinction is important because identifying the particular genetic change can help doctors choose treatment.

Molecular testing examines tumour tissue for alterations that may respond to targeted medicines. These drugs block specific growth signals used by cancer cells, helping doctors tailor treatment to the biology of an individual tumour. Not every lung adenocarcinoma has an EGFR or ALK alteration, and not every patient will benefit from the same targeted medicine. Treatment decisions depend on the molecular test results, cancer stage and the patient’s overall condition.

Can lung cancer develop without smoking?

Yes. Apart from tobacco exposure, factors associated with lung cancer include second-hand smoke, radon gas, air pollution and certain occupational exposures. Age and biological factors can also influence risk, while some cases occur without an identifiable cause.

Adenocarcinoma often develops in the outer regions of the lung and may grow without producing obvious symptoms in its early stages. A small nodule may, therefore, be discovered during imaging performed for another reason or as part of a medical evaluation.

However, finding a lung nodule does not automatically mean a person has cancer. Nodules can also arise from infections, inflammation and other non-cancerous conditions. Imaging helps doctors assess the level of suspicion, while a biopsy or examination of surgically removed tissue can establish the diagnosis.

Symptoms that may warrant medical assessment include:

How do doctors decide whether lung cancer can be removed surgically?

Once lung cancer is confirmed, doctors determine its stage. This involves assessing the tumour’s size and location, whether nearby lymph nodes are involved and whether the cancer has spread to other organs. A CT scan and, where appropriate, PET-CT, other imaging tests and lymph-node sampling may form part of this assessment.

Doctors also evaluate the patient’s lung function, general health and ability to tolerate surgery. Depending on the cancer’s stage and characteristics, treatment may involve surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy or a combination of these approaches. Some patients receive systemic treatment before surgery to improve the chances of successful treatment, while others may require additional therapy afterwards.

When is removal of a lung lobe necessary?

Each lung is divided into lobes. The right lung has three and the left has two. A lobectomy involves removing the lobe containing the tumour, usually along with nearby lymph nodes for examination.

For selected patients with early-stage non-small cell lung cancer, lobectomy is an established treatment. Removing the affected lobe allows surgeons to remove the tumour with a surrounding margin of tissue and assess whether the cancer has been completely excised.

A lobectomy is not necessary for every lung cancer patient. Depending on the tumour’s size and location, a smaller operation or a non-surgical treatment may be more appropriate. Removing one lobe also does not mean that the remaining lung tissue stops functioning. The rest of the lung continues to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, although the overall breathing capacity may decrease. The extent of this reduction depends on the patient’s health before surgery and the amount of functioning tissue removed.

How is a lobectomy performed?

A lobectomy can be performed through open surgery or minimally invasive techniques such as video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) and robotic-assisted surgery. During the operation, the surgeon removes the affected lobe and the relevant lymph nodes. A temporary chest tube is generally inserted to drain air and fluid while the chest heals.

After surgery, patients are encouraged to begin moving as soon as it is safe and to perform breathing exercises.

What happens after lung cancer surgery?

The final pathology report provides important information about the tumour, including its characteristics, the surgical margins and whether lymph nodes contain cancer. These findings help doctors decide whether additional treatment is needed.

Recovery depends on lung function, overall health, pain control and physical activity. Some patients return to most of their usual activities, while others experience breathlessness during exertion. Pulmonary rehabilitation can help selected patients rebuild strength and improve exercise tolerance.

body_text:
A meeting of EU and Gulf leaders planned for next week in Riyadh has been postponed.

Jasem Al Budaiwi, Secretary General of the Gulf Co-operation Council said on Thursday that attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels in Yemen, and the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport, meant the summit would be rescheduled.

He said the decision was taken to ensure the safety of participating delegations amid continued threats to civilians and the extension of the airport’s operational suspension.

Houthis make ‘major leap’ building advanced missiles

The EU Council said: "The partnership between the EU and the GCC is of great strategic importance to both regions.

"The EU remains committed to deepening this partnership and sustaining the momentum built since the first summit in October 2024."

This would have been the second time leaders gather in this format designed to boost ties between the two regions.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who travelled to Brussels for the first EU-GCC summit in late 2024, was scheduled to co-host the gathering in his home country with EU Council President Antonio Costa, in the presence of the EU's 27 leaders.

"A new date will be announced in due course," the European Council said.

The decision comes amid continuous attacks by Yemeni rebels against Saudi Arabia, mainly targeting its airports.

Houthi missile strikes have also damaged the kingdom's energy and maritime infrastructure.

Speaking earlier in the day, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he expected the postponement of the summit "maybe for security reasons".

"We highly appreciate the dialogue between the EU and the Gulf countries, especially Saudi Arabia," he said.

Mr Radev said his country was pushing to develop a railway corridor to export Saudi oil through Syria, Turkey, Bulgaria and onwards to Europe, to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, currently under an Iranian blockade.

"I believe that this new route will find a place in our discussions and solutions and decisions within the European Union," he said.

Gulf states had hoped that the summit would pave the way for the harmonisation of Schengen visa waivers.

There are different rules depending on states, with the UAE benefitting from an exemption, while citizens from Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Oman are granted a five-year multi-entry visa.

EU states have stepped up their relationship with the Gulf since the start of the Iran war, portraying themselves as a reliable ally. Countries like France and Italy have sent air defence systems to the UAE and more recently to Saudi Arabia.

headline: EU and Gulf states postpone summit due in Saudi Arabia
summary: BRUSSELS, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The EU on Thursday said it had postponed a summit with Gulf states that was due to be held in Saudi Arabia on October 24, as attacks by Houthis have increased security concerns in the country.The EU did not detail the reason for the postponement, and only said a new date would be announced "in due course."The postponement is a further blow to Saudi Arabia's effort to host global events despite the escalating war with the Houthis.
body_text:
BRUSSELS, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The EU on Thursday said it had postponed a summit with Gulf states that was due to be held in Saudi Arabia on October 24, as attacks by Houthis have increased security concerns in the country.

The EU did not detail the reason for the postponement, and only said a new date would be announced "in due course."

The postponement is a further blow to Saudi Arabia's effort to host global events despite the escalating war with the Houthis.

The EU had partly intended the summit to show solidarity with Gulf states and Saudi Arabia amid the war, and the decision to scrap it underlines just how serious the situation is.

Last weekend, 13 people were killed and hundreds wounded in strikes on Riyadh's international airport, in an attack claimed by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis.

The airport, where dignitaries had been supposed to land, remains closed after the attacks.

The EU said it still saw "great strategic importance" in the relationship between both regions and added it would remain committed to "deepening" the partnership.

(Reporting by Andrew Gray, Lili Bayer and Timour Azhari;Writing by Bart Meijer; Editing by Sudip Kar-Gupta, Alexandra Hudson)

headline: Saudi-led coalition intercepts cruise missile over Medina region
summary: Interception comes amid escalating Houthi missile, drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia
body_text:
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said Thursday that it intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile over the Medina region in western Saudi Arabia.

Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki announced the interception in a brief statement on US social media platform X.

The statement did not identify who launched the missile or its intended target, and provided no details on possible casualties or damage. It came amid intensified Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including strikes targeting airports and energy facilities.

The coalition accused the Houthis of carrying out a drone attack on the Taibah electricity distribution station in Medina on Sept. 29.

The attack knocked a transformer out of service but did not disrupt the electricity grid, according to al-Maliki. The facility supplies electricity to the Prophet's Mosque, one of Islam's holiest sites.

Thursday’s incident came hours after the coalition said early Thursday that it intercepted and destroyed a drone over Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province.

A day earlier, the coalition announced that it had destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen's Houthi group toward the Saudi capital Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s government against the Houthis since 2015. The group has controlled the capital Sanaa and several provinces since 2014.
