headline: N. Korea, China open long-idle, cross-border bridge: report
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- North Korea and China officially opened a new cross-b...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 15 (Yonhap) -- North Korea and China officially opened a new cross-border bridge on Thursday after more than a decade of idleness following construction, China's news report showed Thursday.

An opening ceremony was held for the bridge across the Amnok River, also known as the Yalu River, according to China's Xinhua News Agency. It connects the North Korean city of Sinuiju and Dandong in China.

Construction began in October 2011 and ended in October 2014, but the four-lane motor bridge sat unused because North Korea did not finish the buildings and infrastructure on its side.

The bridge is expected to boost trade and the movement of people and ease congestion on the Friendship Bridge, which has served as the main crossing since its 1943 opening.

The opening follows pledges by North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping at their June summit in Pyongyang to elevate ties to a strategic level and enhance exchanges.

An official at South Korea's unification ministry on Thursday called it "the first tangible implementation of the agreements reached during the June summit."

"We will monitor any further development as this could be a concrete step toward deepening strategic ties," the official said.

headline: White House press secretary Katie Zacharia failed bar exam in US? ‘I cleared it in China’, she claims
body_text:
US President Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia, is facing questions over her legal credentials after The Wall Street Journal reported that she did not pass California’s bar exam following her graduation from law school in 2011.

The scrutiny intensified after Zacharia was asked where she had passed the bar exam following her first White House press briefing on Tuesday. “When I moved to China,” she replied, without identifying a jurisdiction, according to the South China Morning Post (SCMP).

Zacharia has repeatedly described herself as a lawyer. However, media reviews of attorney registration records have found no public listing showing that she was admitted to practise in the US jurisdictions they examined.

The exam is required to obtain a licence to practise law. She sat for the bar around the time she was planning her wedding with now-husband Tyler Zacharia and was preparing to relocate to China.

She reportedly passed the Multistate Professional Responsibility Examination (MPRE), which assesses candidates’ knowledge of professional conduct and legal ethics.

Zacharia’s legal credentials came under scrutiny after she told reporters on Tuesday that she passed a bar exam when she moved to China, without specifying the jurisdiction.

PROFILE · US POLITICS

Who is Kimberly Guilfoyle?

From courtroom to cable TV to the Trump campaign and an embassy in Athens.

Worked in the San Francisco and Los Angeles district attorneys’ offices; appointed an assistant district attorney in San Francisco in 2000.

Joined Fox News in 2006 as a legal analyst; co-hosted The Five from 2011 until she left the network in 2018.

Led fundraising for Trump’s 2020 campaign with the Republican National Committee and was a senior adviser to his re-election bid.

Sworn in in September 2025 after a July confirmation hearing, the first woman to hold the post.

Her connection to the Trump family

She and Donald Trump Jr become a couple.

Speaks on night three of the Republican National Convention in Milwaukee.

Photos of Trump Jr with Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson are published amid reports of a split. Hours later, Trump names Guilfoyle his pick for Greece, calling her a “close friend and ally”.

Trump Jr’s engagement to Anderson is announced. Guilfoyle tells The New York Times: “I’m happy for Don. I wish him, of course, all the best.”

Trump Jr marries Anderson in West Palm Beach, Florida.

Stepping down, she thanks Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio with “gratitude and respect” and says she remains a loyal Trump supporter.

She asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her confirmation; he did not pay.

She promoted Greek construction firm Aktor Group and flew to Davos in January 2026 on a private jet with its CEO.

She calls the allegations “false” and says she will “vigorously defend” her name; her lawyer disputes the texts’ authenticity.

“We have asked Ambassador Guilfoyle to resign.”

Trump on Oct 12: “We’re not happy.”

The State Department’s inspector general is reviewing the allegations.

A review of attorney registration records in New York, the District of Columbia, California, Texas and Florida by the South China Morning Post found no listing for Zacharia in any of the five jurisdictions.

Separately, independent journalist Judd Legum reported that he found no evidence showing that Zacharia was admitted to practise law in any of the 50 US states or Washington, DC.

A White House official did not directly answer NBC News when asked whether Zacharia had passed a bar examination. Instead, the official said she moved to China with her husband after graduating from law school because of his job at an American private equity firm. She worked on international transactions there before the couple returned to the United States, the official said.

In a separate response reported by the South China Morning Post, Zacharia said she had practised international transactional law “with all the appropriate credentials”, without specifying where she had qualified.

The eligibility criteria also included educational and other requirements.

Foreign nationals were ineligible to sit for the exam, which formed part of the process of qualifying to practise law in China.

body_text:
State-owned Adnoc began preparing for major disruption to energy supplies 10 to 15 years ago, building contingency plans and backup infrastructure that helped it maintain oil production throughout the Iran war.

“We actually prepared for this scenario in our playbooks 10 years ago, 15 years ago,” Abdulmunim Al Kindy, a board director at Adnoc and chairman of Abu Dhabi energy event Adipec, said on Thursday.

Mr Al Kindy, who previously served as executive director of Adnoc's upstream directorate, said the company invested heavily in backup facilities and interconnections that allowed it to switch supply sources and delivery destinations.

“[We] built projects at great expense, even though at the time they didn’t make any commercial sense,” he said. “When the time came, we actually kept the lights on.”

The company's preparedness extended beyond physical infrastructure to years of emergency drills and scenario planning, giving employees “almost muscle memory” when the crisis struck, he said.

Adnoc has increased its oil production capacity by almost 75 per cent over the past decade to 4.85 million barrels per day and is targeting five million bpd by 2027.

Last November, Adnoc approved a Dh551 billion ($150 billion) spending plan for 2026 to 2030 to maintain operations and expand production capacity to meet rising global energy demand.

Mr Al Kindy was speaking at a press conference ahead of Adipec 2026, which Adnoc will host in Abu Dhabi from November 2 to 5, as energy security takes on greater urgency following months of disruption to global oil and gas flows. “2026 has demonstrated a fundamental truth – energy security is economic stability,” he said.

The event will draw its largest Asian participation yet, with 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore and South Korea.

Organisers expect more than 239,000 visitors from at least 170 countries, with international visitors accounting for 56 per cent of the total attendance. Three quarters of the 2,250 exhibiting companies are expected to come from outside the UAE.

The conference will feature more than 16,500 delegates and 1,800 speakers across 13 programmes.

Rising electricity demand from artificial intelligence and industrial growth is bringing “energy security, economic stability and competitiveness” closer together, said Thomas Loffler, executive vice president at organiser dmg events.

Demand for exhibition space has prompted organisers to move the opening ceremony to the Abu Dhabi Energy Centre and expand the exhibition's AI and robotics zone.

Confirmed speakers include Suhail Al Mazrouei, Minister of energy and Infrastructure; Katherina Reiche, Germany's Minister for Economic Affairs and Energy; Meg O'Neill, chief executive of BP; Richard Jackson, president and chief executive of Occidental Petroleum; Wael Sawan, chief executive of Shell; and Roland Busch, chief executive of Siemens.

Last year's Adipec generated $53 billion in business deals across 49,131 transactions, the first time organisers tracked the value of agreements reached during the event. It also contributed $420 million to Abu Dhabi's hospitality and tourism economy, Mr Loffler said.

body_text:
Planning for the 2026 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix “never stopped for one day”, according to Saif Al Noaimi, chief executive of organisers Ethara.

The F1 season finale is now 50 days away, and preparations for the race have clicked up a gear at Yas Marina Circuit. Eleven artists, including Andrea Bocelli, Lewis Capaldi and The Script, have been booked for the after-race concerts, with the final headline act set to be announced next week.

Doubts were raised earlier this year when the Grands Prix in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia were cancelled because of the Iran war.

Emirati racer Al Dhaheri takes major step towards F1 dream with Formula 3 move

However, F1 president Stefano Domenicali has said they intend to finish the season as planned, with “everything confirmed for [us to stay in] Qatar and Abu Dhabi”.

The season finale will take place in the UAE capital from December 3-6, and Al Noaimi spoke to The National at Yas Marina Circuit as the days tick down to the 18th Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Q: Given some of the speculation we have seen about the race, what assurances can you give about the 2026 event?

A: We are delivering the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix at the same high standard we deliver every year. We are delivering a safe event, just like we do every year. We are planning and preparing ourselves just like we do every year.

And from a readiness point of view, we are 100 per cent ready to deliver the Grand Prix this year. Everything is on schedule, the date has not changed. We're really excited to be hosting the season finale on December 6.

Q: You are used to seeing a rise in demand every year, so how have ticket sales been this year?

We are 50 days away from the Grand Prix, and if you compare where we were last year, 50 days away, we're actually ahead in terms of ticket volume and sales. So, demand is unprecedented. We are fortunate our customers know they're going to come because it's such an important event. Every year, early on, as soon as we go on sale, we see a huge spike in sales. And, you know, the last few weeks we've seen a spike in international sales also. So, interest in inbound tourism is growing, and we're starting to see that in the sales numbers.

Q: Considering what happened with the Bahrain and Saudi Arabia Grands Prix, was there ever a fear that this wasn't going to go ahead?

To be honest, we haven't stopped planning for the 2026 Grand Prix for one day. We've been full speed ahead since the beginning of the year. Since we delivered the Grand Prix last year, we've been completely full speed ahead. Obviously, being the last race of the season, early on in the year, we were in the planning period and the planning phase. September is when we start to see the venue transform and the build start. But this is our schedule every single year. We haven't had to make any changes to the planning and the execution.

Q: Can you give a message to fans thinking about buying a ticket?

Come and see Abu Dhabi, come and visit Abu Dhabi.

We are seeing a huge growth in international visitations over the last few months. As you can see, everything's functioning normally over here.

It's an exciting time to be here. And yeah, we're very, very happy to start welcoming the world back.

Q: Are you a little bit worried that Kimi Antonelli is going to win the title before we get to Abu Dhabi? It was very fun last year …

It was fun last year; we had the three-way fight. I mean, look, we can't have a three-way fight every year. But what I can assure you is these guys are going to fight till the chequered flag in Abu Dhabi, regardless of the championship. It's great to see someone young like Kimi taking that position. But also, like I said earlier, you can't write off the championship yet. You have Max Verstappen winning the last two races out of nowhere. Six different drivers have won races in 2026. So, regardless, it's still going to be an exciting race.

Q: Can you talk about the enhancements the venue has undergone this year?

So, we are upping the capacity for the event this year. We have unprecedented demand. We are expanding our Paddock Club (hospitality) offering. We already have the biggest Paddock Club, but we're actually increasing it to surpass 12,000 in 2026. There's a completely new Paddock Club offering that we're building on the west side also. And, you know, every year we look at additions and enhancements.

We have a few new exciting products that we have launched already for 2026. And, you know, from a hospitality point of view, we have 16/360 (hospitality) expanding. We launched it last year for the first time, and we're making some additions to that product, which has been very, very popular. And then, in terms of other branded hospitality offerings, we announced our partnership with Nammos at Turn 9. And then we have a few other new branded hospitality experiences that we're launching this year.

Q: Today we heard that Rashid Al Dhaheri will race in F3 next season. How long until we see him here?

It's really exciting having Rashid and Keanu [Al Azhari] now both representing the UAE in the FIA Formula 3 championship. It really shows how strong our grassroots motorsports programme and our academy are. Both of them came through the Yas Heat Academy.

They both raced in Formula Four UAE for Yas Heat. They're both Yas Heat ambassadors. And today they're both participating in the FIA Formula 3 World Championship.

It's a huge, huge achievement for us. Huge achievement for them and for their families, who have dedicated so much over the years.

And look, it's very, very promising, you know, maybe one or hopefully both of them could be in Formula One in as little as two years. So we're excited to see that. Congratulations to them.

headline: 'American abandonment' threatens Ukraine's civilians in war against Russia
summary: PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, October 15: First, reported Starlink disruptions in Ukraine make the European front pages. Next, US papers go into more detail about the situation. PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, October 15: First, reported Starlink disruptions in Ukraine make the European front pages. Next, US papers go into more detail about the situation. Also, an unusual alliance forms in Germany between far-right and far-left parties. Meanwhile, the winners of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year awards have been announced. Finally, Finland flaunts its smelly islands.

The reported Starlink restrictions in Ukraine are getting a lot of coverage. The Kyiv Post quotes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who says he feels betrayed by the US. He made those statements during an interview with broadcaster Piers Morgan in the UK, where Zelensky met with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday. The Times features their meeting on its front page and says that the Starlink restrictions could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's security. In France, Libération headlines with "American abandonment". It says US intelligence services are no longer warning Kyiv about Russian strikes, putting Ukrainian civilians at risk. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, meanwhile, is said to be "with Ukraine" on the front page of La Repubblica.

Beyond the front pages, there are plenty of analysis pieces to be read. According to American news site Axios, a US government official has said the Trump administration did not have anything to do with the reported Starlink restrictions, and that any disruption was caused by a technical incident instead. The Wall Street Journal takes us "Inside Trump's turn on Zelensky". The paper suggests that the relationship between Trump and Zelensky started to sour after a meeting in New York in September. The Financial Times, meanwhile, reports that US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner proposed that European countries unfreeze some frozen Russian assets and transfer them to a financial vehicle overseen by Washington in an attempt to revive peace talks. Cartoonist Morten Morland in The Times imagines that Vladimir Putin will have a tough time choosing his employee of the month this October.

Elsewhere, the German state of Saxony-Anhalt has seen an unusual alliance between the far-right AfD party and the far-left populist BSW party. Their alliance passed a motion calling for an immediate end to all German financial and military aid to Ukraine. The Berliner Morgenpost says the proposal has no chance of being approved by the Germany's upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat. The Süddeutsche Zeitung headlines with "this is madness". The paper says the AfD's anti-immigration policies are now targeting everyone from Ukrainians to Arab and Muslim refugees in eastern Germany.

In other news, the winners of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year awards have been announced. The Guardian goes through some of the pictures. The overall winner is quite a moving photo by Federico Veronesi called "The Aftermath"; it shows an elephant carrying and grieving her dead calf. The young photographer of the year award was given to 14-year-old Oscar Whitfield for his snapshot of a dung beetle.

Finally, Geo reports that the Turku Archipelago in Finland claims to be the best-smelling place in the world. To prove it, they are hoping to recruit a professional nose to travel around the islands and take in the air.

You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

headline: CAS rejects Russian Curling Federation’s appeal to lift suspension
summary: Russia’s national curling teams have been suspended from international tournaments since 2022 due to the situation in Ukraine
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 15. /TASS/. The Court of Arbitration for Sport has rejected the Russian Curling Federation's and athletes' appeals against the decision to extend the suspension of Russian national teams from international competitions, the CAS press service told TASS.

According to it, both appeals filed by the Russian Curling Federation and Russian athletes on the participation in international competitions were rejected in a final decision issued on October 13.

In turn, Sports Minister and Russian Olympic Committee President Mikhail Degtyarev announced that the ROC and the Russian Curling Federation are preparing an appeal to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court against the CAS decision.

On August 11, World Curling extended the suspension of Russian athletes through the end of 2026. The organization stated that it decided to extend the suspension after reviewing the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) recommendations, as well as feedback from its members and competition organizers.

Russia’s national curling teams have been suspended from international tournaments since 2022 due to the situation in Ukraine. However, in January 2026, Russia’s junior national teams were permitted to participate in international tournaments while displaying national symbols. In July, the IOC reinstated the ROC's membership and recommended that international federations lift restrictions on Russian athletes, including those in team competitions.

headline: Africa: WHO Urges Faster Action to End Lead Exposure Which Kills 3.5 Million Annually
summary: [UN News] Countries must accelerate efforts to prevent lead exposure, which is estimated to cause more than 3.5 million deaths globally each year and affects hundreds of millions of children, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Thursday.
body_text:
Countries must accelerate efforts to prevent lead exposure, which is estimated to cause more than 3.5 million deaths globally each year and affects hundreds of millions of children, the World Health Organization (WHO) said on Thursday.

The UN agency issued the call ahead of International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week, which runs from 18-26 October.

Although exposure is entirely preventable, fewer than half of countries had confirmed legally binding controls on paint containing lead, according to the agency's latest global assessment.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

'Stealing children's potential'

The risks to children are particularly dangerous because their developing brains and nervous systems are highly vulnerable to the toxic effects of lead.

"Lead poisoning should not be stealing children's potential in 2026," said Bruce Gordon, interim director of WHO's Department of Environment, Climate Change, One Health and Migration.

"We know where many exposures come from and we know how to prevent them. Countries now need to move upstream, removing lead from products and environments before it reaches a child's bloodstream."

Irreversible harm, lifelong consequences

Lead contamination can occur through paint, cookware, cosmetics, spices, informal recycling and industrial sources. There is no known safe level of contact, and even relatively low exposure can cause irreversible harm.

Lead poisoning affects multiple organs and contributes to health problems such as cardiovascular and kidney disease in adults and irreversible damage to the brain, health and development of children.

Lifelong consequences include learning difficulties, behavioural issues and poor health. As symptoms may not be immediately visible, many cases go unnoticed until significant damage has already occurred.

Action plan and guidance

WHO Member States have recognized lead exposure as a pressing public health concern and mandated the agency to develop a Global Action Plan on Lead Mitigation that will be presented to the World Health Assembly (N-dash) - WHO's governing body (N-dash) - next year.

The agency will also launch the PREVENT Technical Package on Lead Poisoning Prevention in 2027, to provide countries with practical guidance to identify priority sources of exposure, determine which interventions can have the greatest impact, strengthen and enforce regulations and monitor progress.

headline: Africa: Ngafuan Laments Africa's Expensive Capital
summary: [Liberian Observer] The Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, has challenged the World Bank Group to move beyond mobilizing larger volumes of private investment and take concrete measures to reduce the high cost of capital facing African economies, arguing that expensive financing is constraining the continent's ability to build infrastructure, expand businesses and accelerate economic transformation.
body_text:
The Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, has challenged the World Bank Group to move beyond mobilizing larger volumes of private investment and take concrete measures to reduce the high cost of capital facing African economies, arguing that expensive financing is constraining the continent's ability to build infrastructure, expand businesses and accelerate economic transformation.

Speaking at the ongoing International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Ngafuan acknowledged progress under World Bank Group President Ajay Banga in mobilizing private capital for developing economies. However, he argued that the scale of Africa's financing needs demands more ambitious action to make capital affordable and ensure that investment reaches countries and communities where it can deliver meaningful development outcomes.

The minister cited an increase in private capital mobilization by the World Bank Group from US35billioninfiscalyear2022toUS112 billion in fiscal year 2026. For Africa, he said, the amount rose from approximately US9billiontoUS22 billion over the same period.

While describing the increase as encouraging, Ngafuan maintained that the figures must be measured against the continent's financing requirements and the cost at which African countries access funds.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

"Africa faces financing needs estimated at 900 billion U.S. dollars, including an infrastructure financing gap of 68 to 108 billion U.S. dollars," he told the gathering of global economic policymakers and finance officials. "We need private capital, and we need it at scale, at affordable rates, and flowing to countries that need it most."

The cost of capital refers to the price borrowers pay to obtain financing. For governments, this includes interest on loans and bonds, as well as fees and other financing expenses. For businesses, it affects the cost of borrowing to expand operations, acquire equipment, build factories or enter new markets.

African borrowers often face higher financing costs than borrowers in advanced economies. Those costs reflect several factors, including currency volatility, debt sustainability concerns, limited liquidity in some markets, institutional weaknesses, exposure to external economic shocks and investors' assessments of political and economic risks.

Ngafuan's argument, however, is that the price assigned to African risk can exceed what underlying economic conditions justify. When investors perceive a country or region as riskier than its economic fundamentals warrant, the resulting premium can make borrowing more expensive even where viable projects and investment opportunities exist.

Citing figures attributed to UNICA, Ngafuan said perceived distortions in African risk assessments add approximately 2.9 percentage points to borrowing costs, translating into an estimated US$75 billion annually in additional financing expenses.

"Africa should not have to pay premium for risks that are perceived rather than demonstrated," he said.

The US$75 billion estimate is particularly consequential because it represents resources that could otherwise support infrastructure, public services, productive investment and employment. The estimate should be understood as a figure cited by the minister rather than an independently verified calculation in this report.

The broader issue has been documented in continental policy discussions. The African Union and other institutions have repeatedly called for reforms to the international financial architecture, including more credible risk assessments, improved access to concessional financing and a stronger African voice in decisions affecting the cost and availability of capital

For governments already allocating significant portions of public revenue to debt servicing, higher interest costs can narrow the fiscal space available for development. Borrowing becomes more difficult to sustain, while governments face tougher choices between servicing existing obligations and funding infrastructure, education, healthcare, electricity and other essential services.

For private businesses, expensive credit can delay investment, restrict expansion and make locally owned enterprises less competitive against firms operating in economies with cheaper financing.

The consequences can extend across generations.

Ngafuan framed his intervention around three connected concerns: how international development institutions allocate their risk-bearing capacity, whether private investment builds African businesses, and how the continent can reduce the premium attached to its perceived risk.

The minister questioned what concrete changes the World Bank Group was making in the allocation of its financial capacity, guarantees and institutional incentives to ensure that private capital supports structural transformation, particularly in low-income, fragile and underserved African economies.

The concern is that aggregate investment figures can conceal where financing actually goes. Investors may gravitate toward larger economies, established markets and projects with predictable revenue streams, while countries with weaker infrastructure and greater development needs struggle to attract affordable funding.

Guarantees and other risk-sharing instruments can help bridge this divide. By absorbing a defined portion of potential losses or reducing particular risks, development finance institutions can make otherwise difficult investments more attractive to private lenders and investors.

But Ngafuan's argument implies that the success of these mechanisms should not be judged only by the amount of private money they mobilize.

The policy challenge is to deploy guarantees strategically without transferring excessive risks to public institutions or exposing taxpayers to poorly managed liabilities.

Ngafuan also challenged the WBG to ensure that large private-sector transactions create opportunities for African enterprises, strengthen local supplier networks and generate employment.

His position places domestic economic participation at the center of the debate over development finance. An investment may bring substantial foreign capital into a country, but its contribution to long-term development depends partly on how much economic activity remains within the local economy.

If a project imports most of its equipment, relies heavily on foreign contractors and generates few opportunities for local suppliers, the wider benefits for domestic businesses may be limited. By contrast, investments that develop local supply chains, transfer skills, create jobs and support African-owned enterprises can generate benefits beyond the immediate project.

This is particularly relevant to Liberia and other economies seeking to expand productive capacity. Affordable capital is important not only for governments financing public infrastructure but also for local businesses that need working capital, machinery, technology and long-term financing.

Ngafuan's argument therefore connects the cost of capital with a second question: who benefits from the investment once it arrives?

For the minister, the objective should be to expand African enterprises' ability to compete domestically and across borders, rather than measure success simply by the volume of foreign financing secured.

The minister's third concern was the additional cost imposed on African borrowers by perceptions of risk.

He urged the World Bank Group to explain what measures it was taking to address what he described as pricing distortions, pointing to guarantees, improved risk data, credit enhancements and stronger engagement with credit-rating agencies and investors.

Credit ratings influence how investors assess a borrower's ability and willingness to repay. Lower ratings can raise borrowing costs or limit access to certain markets, while a stronger assessment can widen the pool of potential investors.

Ngafuan's position is that risk assessments should more accurately reflect country-specific economic conditions, including reforms, revenue prospects, growth potential and debt-management capacity. A generalized view of Africa as a high-risk destination, he argues, can obscure differences between countries and investment opportunities.

Yet reducing the risk premium requires more than challenging external perceptions. African governments must also address genuine risks through credible economic policies, transparent public finances, predictable regulation, stronger institutions and reliable data.

The challenge, therefore, is twofold: improve the fundamentals that make investments safer while reforming assessment methods that may overstate risks or fail to account adequately for differences among African economies.

Ngafuan's intervention forms part of a wider continental debate over the cost of capital, debt sustainability and the structure of global financial governance.

At the Africa Forward Summit in Nairobi in May 2026, Kenyan President William Ruto and other African leaders called for reforms to improve access to credit and reduce borrowing costs. The summit also advanced a proposal for a first-loss guarantee mechanism intended to help attract private investment by absorbing an agreed portion of potential losses. French President Emmanuel Macron backed the initiative, while United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres criticized a global financial system in which African countries can face borrowing costs substantially higher than those of advanced economies.

The argument advanced by these leaders is that the continent's development prospects should not be constrained by financing arrangements that make productive investment disproportionately expensive. Risk-sharing instruments can potentially reduce the burden on individual borrowers and encourage private capital to enter markets it might otherwise avoid.

The African Union has also placed the issue at the center of its financial reform agenda. In October 2026, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf chaired a high-level roundtable in Mauritius where participants discussed the need for a coordinated approach extending beyond credit-rating reform to the wider financial architecture affecting the cost and availability of finance across Africa.

These efforts reflect growing recognition that the cost of capital is not merely a technical matter for finance ministries.

Several initiatives are being advanced to address the structural challenges Ngafuan identified such as The Africa Credit Rating Agency (AfCRA), the New African Financial Architecture for Development (NAFAD), and others.

While Ngafuan called for reforms by international financial institutions and investors, he acknowledged that African governments have responsibilities in making their economies more attractive to investment.

These include improving governance, ensuring policy predictability, strengthening project preparation and creating conditions under which investors can assess opportunities with greater confidence.

Ngafuan's intervention has direct implications for Liberia, where financing is needed for infrastructure, electricity, agriculture, education, healthcare and private-sector development.

"Our ultimate objective must not simply be to mobilize more capital for Africa, but to mobilize more affordable capital that transforms African economies, empowers African enterprises, and improves African lives," he said.

headline: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce
summary: Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over.(Image credit: Alberto Pezzali)
body_text:
Britain's Prime Minister Andy Burnham says goodbye to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy after their meeting at 10 Downing Street in London, Wednesday, Oct. 14, 2026. Alberto Pezzali/AP hide caption

KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over amid deepening tensions with Washington.

The drone strike started a fire at the refinery about 300 kilometers (180 miles) southeast of Moscow, Russia's Defense Ministry and Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said. Russia's Astra online news outlet posted what it said was a photograph of the blaze.

A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to speak publicly confirmed that Ukraine had hit the refinery.

The strike could further complicate Kyiv's relations with U.S. President Donald Trump, which have soured again in recent days.

Zelenskyy was outraged by Russia's continuing aerial bombardment of his country's energy infrastructure in apparent defiance of Trump's demand on Sunday for both sides to halt those attacks. The Ukrainian government said that it was heeding the ceasefire.

Zelenskyy complained that, despite going along with Trump's demand for a truce, Ukraine in recent days was denied the usual Western intelligence on Russian ballistic missile strikes and limits were placed on its use of U.S.-made Starlink communication terminals.

The Ukrainian leader said that his patience had run out. He said in an interview with the Financial Times published Thursday that Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries would resume. "We're done," he was quoted as saying.

Trump made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, despite international efforts to sanction Russia for its invasion and diplomatically isolate Putin.

Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than 4½ years ago. U.S. efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Zelenskyy said in an interview late Wednesday with Piers Morgan on the British journalist's YouTube show that he felt betrayed by Trump's deal with Putin, the energy ceasefire announcement and the Starlink operational issues.

"Really, yes, between us," Zelenskyy told Morgan when asked if he felt betrayed by the American president. "Our country has to survive, and we count on our real partners, strategic partners, the United States and President Trump."

He said that the U.S. behavior "was really strange and what was not like between partners but that they switch off Starlink, so some actually crazy steps between us."

In the same interview, Zelenskyy said that "we are losing a strong partner" in the United States.

He said that "it's painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side. But we are OK that he's in the middle."

Zelenskyy said someone is pushing Trump into a stance that is "not the right side of history."

The Starlink speed limits choked Ukrainian efforts to defend itself and hit back against Russia, Kyiv officials said.

Elon Musk noted on X that the military version of Starlink is controlled by the U.S. military and Trump.

The absence of Western intelligence leaves Ukraine more vulnerable to Russian ballistic missiles. Trump has said the U.S. hasn't stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine.

Three people were killed and six others injured after the Kirovohrad region of central Ukraine came under a Russian drone attack lasting more than 10 hours, Ukraine's Emergency Services said Thursday.

Zelenskyy said on X that between midnight and Thursday morning Russia launched more than 850 drones at Ukraine, adding that the barrage came "precisely at a time when the speed of our defensive capabilities is being artificially restricted."

Russian aerial attacks hit 15 Ukrainian regions, he said.

"It is obvious that Russia deliberately chose to escalate its attacks after receiving sanctions relief and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that everyone in America stand not with the aggressor, but with our efforts to protect lives, end this war and guarantee security."

Ukrainian air defenses stopped 536 Russian drones during a large-scale overnight attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said, but impacts were recorded at 31 locations.

Russia's Defense Ministry said that air defenses downed 166 Ukrainian drones overnight. It said that its forces hit two vessels carrying military cargo.

headline: Hormuz matters but UAE has more than one gateway, economy minister says
summary: The gateway to the Gulf is more than one port and certainly more than one road. That is the message from Abdulla bin Touq, Minister of Economy and Tourism. “Hormuz really matters and it will keep on mattering,” he said in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Rise Summit in Dubai. “It's really important to really focus on Hormuz as well, to have it as a gate.”It is a direct rebuttal to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks last month, who said the strait would be “a worthless piece of water” within two years.Before the Iran war, roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. However, traffic flows through the waterway have dropped sharply since the war began on February 28. But while the strait matters, it is not the only way in, Mr bin Touq said. “The UAE doesn't have only one road. It has many roads to come to it,” he said.The UAE has revealed plans to reduce its reliance on the strait as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to diversify trade routes and supply chains. It has established regional logistics corridors linking the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Development of east-coast ports at Khor Fakkan and Fujairah, outside the strait, has been accelerated. The UAE is also building a new pipeline to provide additional capacity for exporting Abu Dhabi oil via the Gulf of Oman.If Hormuz is the front gate, the east coast is the side door and business is already walking through it, Mr bin Touq said. Asked where the next boom would be, he pointed to company registrations on the east coast. “Redundancy means dollar signs. It means investments,” he said. Resilience does not mean retreat, though. The UAE is not making the economy safer by “closing and shrinking it”, he added.However, Mr bin Touq resisted the idea of a dramatic pivot from west to east. He said the UAE continues to function as one connected economy. With Etihad Rail now linking Abu Dhabi to Fujairah in under four hours, “we can have breakfast in Khor Fakkan, lunch in Sharjah or Dubai and dinner in Abu Dhabi”, he said. The rail line binds “these seven economies that [are] very knitted together”.Tourism rebound anticipated In terms of crises like the Iran war, tourism is the first sector to be hit and the last to recover “anywhere in the world”, with its return heavily dependant on airline capacity. The UAE is working with other countries to secure removal from their travel advisory lists, as tourism figures show signs of recovery after months of disruption because of the conflict.With Lufthansa and Air France committed to resuming UAE flights by the end of this month, “this shows you there is confidence”, Mr bin Touq said. That makes November and December a critical final window for tourism this year.The early signs are encouraging. Hotel occupancy reached about 68 per cent at the end of August. September's figures have not yet been published but the minister described the trend as “really, really nice”.Economic footballThe International Monetary Fund expects the UAE economy to shrink 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding 7.7 per cent in 2027. “It is 3.9 per cent, and there is decimal points, so it's not 4 per cent,” Mr bin Touq noted.The UAE's real gross domestic product also grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war.The minister discussed his plan for the economy as a football formation. “In front, I have attackers: my tourism. My midfielder is the businesses … and my defence is when it comes to IP and innovation capacity,” he said. “What happened is I lost my attacker and my midfielders are scoring goals.”For 2027, tourism must lead from the front again. Meanwhile, the midfield needs reform and access to capital. On reform, he meant legislation and “the things that we tolerated through the crisis”. On capital, he pointed to the Dh1 billion Emirates Growth Fund, where he sits on the board. The fund aims to take companies with revenue of Dh1 million to Dh10 million up to Dh50 million to Dh60 million. “We're already investing,” he said. The government also wants more venture capital in the region and artificial intelligence “embedded within the systems of these companies, of these factories”.As for the interviewer's place in his squad, the minister offered a trial. “Play a winger,” he said.

The gateway to the Gulf is more than one port and certainly more than one road. That is the message from Abdulla bin Touq, Minister of Economy and Tourism.

“Hormuz really matters and it will keep on mattering,” he said in an exclusive interview on the sidelines of the Rise Summit in Dubai. “It's really important to really focus on Hormuz as well, to have it as a gate.”

It is a direct rebuttal to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks last month, who said the strait would be “a worthless piece of water” within two years.

Fire, sinking and scramble for cargo: what we know about ship lost in Hormuz

Before the Iran war, roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and gas transited the Strait of Hormuz. However, traffic flows through the waterway have dropped sharply since the war began on February 28.

But while the strait matters, it is not the only way in, Mr bin Touq said. “The UAE doesn't have only one road. It has many roads to come to it,” he said.

The UAE has revealed plans to reduce its reliance on the strait as part of its “Zero Hormuz” strategy to diversify trade routes and supply chains.

It has established regional logistics corridors linking the Arabian Gulf to the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman. Development of east-coast ports at Khor Fakkan and Fujairah, outside the strait, has been accelerated. The UAE is also building a new pipeline to provide additional capacity for exporting Abu Dhabi oil via the Gulf of Oman.

If Hormuz is the front gate, the east coast is the side door and business is already walking through it, Mr bin Touq said.

Asked where the next boom would be, he pointed to company registrations on the east coast. “Redundancy means dollar signs. It means investments,” he said. Resilience does not mean retreat, though. The UAE is not making the economy safer by “closing and shrinking it”, he added.

However, Mr bin Touq resisted the idea of a dramatic pivot from west to east. He said the UAE continues to function as one connected economy.

With Etihad Rail now linking Abu Dhabi to Fujairah in under four hours, “we can have breakfast in Khor Fakkan, lunch in Sharjah or Dubai and dinner in Abu Dhabi”, he said. The rail line binds “these seven economies that [are] very knitted together”.

In terms of crises like the Iran war, tourism is the first sector to be hit and the last to recover “anywhere in the world”, with its return heavily dependant on airline capacity.

The UAE is working with other countries to secure removal from their travel advisory lists, as tourism figures show signs of recovery after months of disruption because of the conflict.

With Lufthansa and Air France committed to resuming UAE flights by the end of this month, “this shows you there is confidence”, Mr bin Touq said. That makes November and December a critical final window for tourism this year.

The early signs are encouraging. Hotel occupancy reached about 68 per cent at the end of August. September's figures have not yet been published but the minister described the trend as “really, really nice”.

The International Monetary Fund expects the UAE economy to shrink 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding 7.7 per cent in 2027. “It is 3.9 per cent, and there is decimal points, so it's not 4 per cent,” Mr bin Touq noted.

The UAE's real gross domestic product also grew 0.4 per cent annually to Dh961.9 billion ($262 billion) in the first half of 2026, driven by non-oil business activity, despite the impact of the Iran war.

The minister discussed his plan for the economy as a football formation. “In front, I have attackers: my tourism. My midfielder is the businesses … and my defence is when it comes to IP and innovation capacity,” he said. “What happened is I lost my attacker and my midfielders are scoring goals.”

For 2027, tourism must lead from the front again. Meanwhile, the midfield needs reform and access to capital.

On reform, he meant legislation and “the things that we tolerated through the crisis”. On capital, he pointed to the Dh1 billion Emirates Growth Fund, where he sits on the board. The fund aims to take companies with revenue of Dh1 million to Dh10 million up to Dh50 million to Dh60 million. “We're already investing,” he said. The government also wants more venture capital in the region and artificial intelligence “embedded within the systems of these companies, of these factories”.

As for the interviewer's place in his squad, the minister offered a trial. “Play a winger,” he said.

headline: Japan denies spying in Russia after journalist’s detention
summary: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi rejects Moscow’s allegations as Tokyo seeks consular access to detained Hokkaido Shimbun reporter
body_text:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday denied her government’s involvement in alleged espionage activities in Russia after Moscow detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of spying.

“We’ll convey our position,” Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo, rejecting allegations that the journalist had gathered intelligence for Japanese authorities, according to Jiji Press.

Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) earlier alleged that the correspondent for the Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk bureau of Japanese daily Hokkaido Shimbun collected and stored information on Russia’s defense capabilities for Japanese intelligence, claiming the information could be used against the country’s security.

The agency said it had opened a criminal case against the journalist, while Moscow’s Lefortovo District Court ordered his arrest as the investigation continued.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Tokyo had been unable to contact the detained journalist.

“We’ll put our effort into holding a consular meeting as soon as possible to confirm his health condition,” Kihara said.

Relations between Japan and Russia have deteriorated sharply since Moscow launched its war against Ukraine in February 2022, prompting Tokyo to impose sanctions on Russia.

headline: Egypt, Qatar stress need to halt hostilities against Saudi Arabia
summary: Foreign ministers condemn attacks on kingdom, call for diplomatic efforts to contain regional tensions
body_text:
Egypt and Qatar stressed the need to halt all hostilities against Saudi Arabia and expressed solidarity with the kingdom, according to the Egyptian Foreign Ministry on Thursday.

The position was expressed during a phone call late Wednesday between Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and his Qatari counterpart, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, the ministry said in a statement.

The call came as part of “continuous communication and coordination between the two brotherly countries on various issues of common interest,” the statement said.

The two officials discussed bilateral relations and areas of cooperation, including exchanges of high-level visits. They praised the progress in ties and affirmed their commitment to further strengthening them, according to the statement.

On regional developments, the officials discussed the latest situation and agreed on the importance of supporting ongoing efforts and coordinating action to ease tensions and prevent the conflict from spreading.

They stressed the need to halt all hostilities against Saudi Arabia, strongly condemned the attacks and expressed solidarity with the kingdom.

The officials also called for activating political and diplomatic channels to resolve the current crisis and strengthen regional security and stability.

The call came amid an ongoing military escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group, involving missile and drone attacks on airports and critical infrastructure in the kingdom in recent days.

Since Oct. 5, five Saudi airports have come under attack, leaving 20 people dead and hundreds injured, in addition to material damage and disruptions to air traffic, according to the report.

Meanwhile, the military operation known as Dawn of Yemen has continued. Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said the operation aims to restore state institutions from Houthi control and retake the capital, Sanaa.

The developments in Yemen are part of a military escalation that began in July and is the most extensive since a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that began in April 2022.

Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015 against the Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and several other provinces since 2014.

body_text:
Nissan has announced a limited-edition Patrol to mark the SUV’s 75th anniversary, with an initial production run of 1,951 vehicles exclusively for the GCC region.

The number marks the nameplate's debut in 1951. Based on the flagship Platinum V6 Twin Turbo grade, the anniversary edition features copper-gold exterior accents, a Bordeaux red interior and special anniversary detailing.

AWR Automotive, Nissan’s dealer in Dubai, Sharjah and the Northern Emirates, introduced the model on Thursday. It costs Dh439,900 ($119,780) including VAT.

The best EVs to buy in the UAE for every budget

Nissan says its bespoke copper-gold finish is inspired by desert landscapes. The detailing appears across the grille bars, fog lamp surrounds, fender vents, shoulder line and emblems, paired with dark chrome finishes and black alloy wheels.

Anniversary signatures feature on the front grille, shoulder-line graphic and rear emblem. An illuminated carpet light projects a “Patrol Since 1951” graphic and a sand-dune motif.

Nissan lists five exterior colours for the Gulf edition, while AWR Automotive has confirmed four options for its customers: grey, white, black and two-tone white with a black roof.

Inside, the cabin features copper-gold steering wheel detailing and ambient lighting alongside dark chrome trim. Anniversary detailing appears on the passenger-side dashboard, seat headrests and floor and luggage mats. Other additions include illuminated anniversary kick plates and a deep red leather key fob case.

Thierry Sabbagh, Nissan and Infiniti’s divisional vice president and president for the Middle East, Saudi Arabia, India and CIS, said: “To mark 75 years of the Patrol, we wanted to deliver something lasting for our customers, a special product that serves as a memorable token of our shared history.”

The anniversary edition keeps the Platinum V6 Twin Turbo’s 3.5-litre twin-turbocharged engine, which delivers 425hp and 700Nm of torque. It is paired with a nine-speed automatic transmission and adaptive air suspension with Intelligent Dynamic Damping.

The cabin includes a 28.6-inch Monolith display, a Klipsch audio system and quilted leather seats with heating, ventilation and massage functions.

The model also features Biometric Cooling, ProPILOT driver assistance and advanced visibility systems. In the UAE and Saudi Arabia, NissanConnect 2.0 with Google built-in provides navigation, voice assistant functions and connected car services.

The anniversary edition joins a regional Patrol range that includes the Platinum, PRO-4X and Nismo.

AWR Automotive says the model is available through its Nissan showrooms in Dubai, Sharjah and the Northern Emirates, and can also be viewed at its City Walk location in Dubai.

headline: Wealthy countries’ debt could be hurting economies like India. Here’s what IMF suggests
body_text:
While forecasting global economic growth at 3.1% this year, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) called on advanced economies, including the United States, to urgently manage their debt levels due to their undue impact on low-income countries and the global financial system.

The warning came during the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group, being held in Bangkok, Thailand, from October 12 to 18.

Global public debt is projected to exceed 100% of the world’s GDP before 2030. With borrowing costs remaining elevated, governments face growing pressure to spend more on servicing existing debt, potentially leaving them with less money for essential public services and responding to future economic shocks.

The concern is particularly acute for poorer countries, which can face higher borrowing costs when interest rates and bond yields rise in major advanced economies. The IMF has raised India’s growth forecast for FY 2026-27 to 7%, from 6.4% earlier, citing resilient domestic demand and services activity. However, it has not singled out India for a specific fiscal-risk warning in its latest assessment.

Governments borrow to finance spending that their revenues cannot cover. When borrowing continues to outpace revenues, public debt accumulates. The problem becomes more acute when interest rates rise, making new borrowing and the refinancing of maturing debt more expensive.

For instance, US government interest payments are projected to reach 5.3% of GDP by 2031, up from 2.8% of GDP before the pandemic.

The IMF noted that higher energy prices, inflation and interest rates are making government borrowing more expensive.

It warned that delaying fiscal adjustment could force governments to make more difficult choices, such as cutting public spending, raising taxes or borrowing even more at higher costs. As governments devote more revenue to servicing debt, they have less room to fund healthcare, education and infrastructure, or respond to economic crises.

Government bonds, particularly those issued by the US, are an important benchmark for global borrowing costs. A rise in US bond yields makes American government debt more attractive to investors seeking higher returns, potentially drawing capital away from developing economies. This can force developing countries to offer higher interest rates to attract investors.

Higher interest rates result in higher debt-servicing costs, meaning more government revenue is spent on financing debt, and less is available for public services.

The IMF observed that interest payments already consume more than 15% of tax revenues in low-income countries. Beyond urging governments to manage their borrowing and spending, the IMF also recommends tax reforms that could help them strengthen public finances without undermining economic growth.

So, what does the IMF want governments to do?

The IMF has broadly three sets of policy recommendations:

Improve tax design: Remove Value-Added Tax (VAT) distortions and avoid corporate tax provisions that discourage productive investment.

The IMF found that poorly designed taxes, including VAT exemptions and gaps in registration, can prevent firms from recovering taxes paid on their inputs. In emerging and developing economies, these distortions can raise firms’ input costs by as much as 9%, with costs cascading through supply chains and potentially reaching consumers.

Similarly, typical corporate income taxes increase the cost of capital by 15–20% on average across country groups. When firms cannot fully deduct investment costs for tax purposes, some otherwise viable projects become unprofitable, limiting capital formation and growth.

Encourage investment and employment: The IMF’s modelling suggests reforms could raise capital formation and employment without lowering overall revenue.

One approach is to allow firms to immediately deduct investment costs while taxing profits above the normal return on investment. These reforms, known as rent-based profit taxes, could increase the long-term capital stock by about 6.4% in advanced economies and 8.2% in low-income developing countries. These are modelled long-term gains, not guaranteed outcomes.

The IMF also recommends reducing tax-related disincentives to work. When taxes rise sharply with earnings, or welfare benefits are withdrawn as people earn more, workers may gain little financially from taking a job, increasing their hours or moving to better-paid work.

Its modelling suggests that reforms which preserve overall government revenue could raise employment rates by 1.2 percentage points in emerging and developing economies and 0.8 percentage points in advanced economies, with the largest gains among lower earners.

Improve tax administration: Better compliance systems, simpler procedures and reliable refunds can raise revenue without increasing statutory tax rates.

In practice, this means reducing unnecessary costs for businesses while improving tax compliance and revenue collection.

This euphemistic phrase softens the harshness of austerity measures like cutting spending or raising taxes, but still evokes a sense of painful trade-offs.

headline: Four dead, including three children, in Oregon school shooting
body_text:
A 16-year-old gunman killed three children aged 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday before being killed by a community member who pursued him inside, police said. Two other people were wounded in the shooting.

Issued on: 15/10/2026 - 23:58Modified: 16/10/2026 - 04:45

A 16-year-old opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot by a person at the scene who pursued him into the school, authorities said.

Authorities found the suspect dead inside the school minutes after the shooting was first reported, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.

The three children killed were aged 5, 8 and 11. Another child, 7, and a teacher, 54, were injured and taken to a hospital in critical condition, Krantz said.

The attacker, identified as a Bend resident, forced his way into the school by shooting at locked doors, police said. He was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.

The first 911 call came just before 1 p.m. from a person in a vehicle outside Silver Rail Elementary who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, Krantz said.

Further 911 calls came from inside the school, and officers arrived on scene within minutes, Miller said.

Police said they did not know if the attacker knew anyone at the school or whether he had attended.

Read moreFrench teen charged in school shooting cites revenge for bullying

The attacker used a pump-action shotgun that was purchased by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation.

The school in Bend, Oregon, which is more than 100 miles (160 kilometres) southeast of Portland, had 459 enrolled students as of last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education. The school serves students in kindergarten through fifth grade.

At a news conference Thursday night, Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said her heart was “absolutely broken” and thanked the civilian who pursued the shooter.

“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.

Reunification of children with their parents was ongoing early Thursday evening.

body_text:
At least 34 pupils and a teacher were killed in Pakistan when the roof of a school collapsed during classes in the north-western city of Peshawar on Thursday, authorities said.

Most of the students killed were under 13 years old, said Arif Khattak, regional director of the Rescue Department. At least ​45 people ⁠suffered major and minor injuries, ‌he added.

Rescue workers spent hours pulling children trapped beneath the rubble of the privately run Al Khair Education Centre, while panicked parents and relatives gathered outside the building seeking news of ⁠their loved ones.

The incident took place at 8.48am local time, and the rescue operation lasted four to five hours, Mr Khattak said.

Victims of the collapse were taken to the city’s Lady Reading Hospital, according to hospital spokesman Mohammad Asim.

“The fatalities include 12 girl students and a female teacher,” Mr Asim said.

Three children remained in critical condition, with head injuries, he said. Most of the injured brought to that hospital had been treated and sent home.

A rescue official said the roof of an upper floor had collapsed on to the classrooms below, causing both storeys to cave in.

Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed said excessive weight from construction on the school roof had caused the collapse.

“It was a weak building structure,” he ​said. “Its roof was overloaded with construction on a weak structure, ‌which caused the collapse.”

Mr Saeed said ⁠the school's owner had been arrested ​and authorities had opened an investigation.

A total of 110 students were attending lessons in three classrooms when the roof caved in.

Distraught relatives accused the ​school of ‌ignoring safety concerns about the building's condition and demanded accountability.

“Make an example of them, a lesson ⁠for all, so that no one dares open a school just to make ⁠money without providing facilities,” said Mohammad Zaman, who lost two nephews in the collapse.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif promised “a thorough investigation” into the incident.

“My heart is with the families grieving the loss of their children and a teacher in the tragic roof collapse at a school in Peshawar. No parent should have to endure such pain,” he wrote in a statement on X.

“I extend my deepest condolences and pray for strength for every family affected. I have directed that the injured receive the best possible care. We will ensure a thorough investigation into this tragedy and take every necessary step to protect the safety of children in schools across the country,” he added.

Pakistan’s President Asif Ali Zardari said the incident was a “heart-wrenching tragedy” and called for a comprehensive investigation into the cause of the deadly collapse.

“In this hour of sorrow, the entire nation shares equally in the grief of the affected families,” the President’s office posted on X.

headline: UK bookstores scramble as Sally Rooney's novels are pulled over Palestine Action support
summary: Critically acclaimed Irish novelist Sally Rooney's announcement that her books could no longer be sold in the UK due to her support for proscribed group Palestine Action has left British booksellers rushing to stock up on her works before distributors run out. The British government's ban on the group, which practiced non-violent direct action and sabotage against UK military assets believed to be working with the Israeli government, makes support for Palestine Action punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

British booksellers are have been left scrambling after Irish novelist Sally Rooney said her books can no longer be sold in the UK because she financially supports the banned group Palestine Action.

The announcement by Rooney’s British publisher that it will no longer distribute her books has reignited debate over the UK government’s decision last year to outlaw the direct-action protest group as a terrorist organisation. The ban makes membership in – or, crucially, support for – Palestine Action a crime punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Rooney, 35, is the critically praised author of four novels: “Conversations with Friends”, “Normal People”, “Beautiful World, Where are You” and “Intermezzo”. Her books have sold millions of copies, and both “Conversations with Friends” and “Normal People” were adapted for television by the BBC.

She supports the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement, which calls for boycotts of Israeli businesses, universities and cultural institutions over Israel’s treatment of the Palestinians.

Read moreWhat is Palestine Action, the protest movement banned under UK terror act?

After the UK banned Palestine Action in July 2025, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her books and their TV adaptations to support the group. On Wednesday her UK publisher, Faber, said that paying her royalties could violate the terror ban and it had “taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format”.

"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher," Faber said in a statement.

The publisher stressed the decision had been made with Rooney's agreement.

“I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences,” the writer said in a statement.

Faber’s announcement left British bookstores scrambling to understand whether they were breaking the law by selling Rooney’s books.

The Booksellers Association later said it had “confirmed with Faber that whilst those titles are no longer available to UK bookshops to order, they can continue to sell their existing stock within the UK market”.

Some stores rushed to stock up on Rooney’s novels, but found distributors had already run out.

“We were thinking, we’ll just get a whole bunch before we stop being able to,” said Lucy Burke, a bookseller at London’s Camden Town Bookshop. “Because she’s a hugely popular seller here, and quite evergreen. But now it seems like what we have is all we’re going to have.”

Burke described the situation as “absolutely ridiculous” and said it amounted to censorship of “one of our most prominent writers”.

Palestine Action, founded in 2020, aims to stop UK military support for Israel, which it says is committing genocide against the Palestinians – a claim Israel strongly denies. An independent UN committee found in September 2025 that Israel was carrying out a genocide in the besieged Gaza Strip.

The group says it aims to stop genocide by disrupting “corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex".

In 2024 its activists broke into a factory owned by Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems UK, smashing equipment with sledgehammers and crowbars. The next year, activists broke into a Royal Air Force base in June 2025, sprayed red paint into the engines of two tanker planes and caused further damage with crowbars.

The group says it does not advocate violence against people, but a police officer suffered a fractured spine when she was hit with a sledgehammer as police tried to arrest members of the group during the factory break-in.

The British government says Palestine Action has “carried out acts of terrorism, celebrated those who took part in them and promoted the use of violence".

“The proscription of Palestine Action does not affect lawful protest in support of the Palestinian cause, which remains a fundamental democratic right,” the Home Office said in a statement.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Civil liberties groups say the ban unjustifiably restricts the rights to protest and free speech. In response to the government’s decision, thousands of people have tested the law by silently holding signs reading “I support Palestine Action.”

More than 3,000 people have been arrested, and more than 1,200 have been charged under the Terrorism Act, though no one has yet been convicted.

The scale of the arrests, and the profile of those detained – including retirees in their 80s and 90s – has put Britain’s Labour Party government under pressure.

The centre-left government has tried to rebuild bridges with pro-Palestinian supporters since Prime Minister Andy Burnham replaced Keir Starmer in July.

Last month the UK formally recognised a Palestinian state and banned goods from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are illegal under international law. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said his message to people “moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people” is: “We hear you. You were right.”

But the government has not lifted the ban on Palestine Action, and the group continues to challenge its proscription in court.

The High Court ruled in February that classing Palestine Action as a terror group alongside the likes of al Qaeda and Hamas was disproportionate and unlawful. The Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June, saying outlawing the group was “justified and proportionate”.

Next month the group’s lawyers will ask the country’s top court, the UK Supreme Court, to quash the ban.

John Clegg, a bookseller at the London Review Bookshop, told the Guardian that Rooney’s stance could help in changing the law.

“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”

headline: Zelenskyy says Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries
summary: Ukrainian president confirms Washington warned it will block intelligence sharing if it does not stop strikes on Russian energy sites
body_text:
Ukraine will resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after a three-day halt due to an energy ceasefire announced by US President Donald Trump, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.

In an interview with the Financial Times published on Thursday, Zelenskyy expressed support for his US counterpart's proposed energy ceasefire, but claimed Russian strikes continued despite Kyiv’s halt.

“That's it. Block is out,” Zelenskyy said, responding to a question about how much longer Ukraine will maintain a halt to energy strikes.

On reports that the US suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Zelenskyy said that over the course of Ukraine’s three-day halt to strikes in Russia, his country was subject to ballistic missile attacks and did not receive any early warning alerts.

He said Washington had earlier warned Kyiv about the blocking of intelligence if it did not stop strikes on Russian energy sites.

“This is, I think, the problem. And when it goes together with Starlink's decision, which is 100% the decision of American side … I think that (it is) not (about) military people. I think it's about SpaceX. So together it makes huge problems,” Zelenskyy added.

Zelenskyy said he told Trump that Ukraine will "destroy" Russia's ballistic missile launchers if Starlink opens on Russian territory.

He argued that if a diesel deal, such as the one announced over the weekend, forces Ukraine to be silent on the battlefield, then questions will arise concerning "when the next deal will be," which would "definitely" concern Russian gas.

The Ukraine leader said he does not want to interfere in "diesel deals," but Ukraine will respond to Russian strikes.

"The question (is): can you give me missiles for Patriot (systems), because when I will not attack them because you asked me not attack them, they will attack me. It's fair if you will give me with what to defend.

"It's the minimum what I ask. No? I think yes. And when I'm asking this, your answer is blocking Starlink," he added.

Serhii Beskrestnov, a freelance adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said on Wednesday that speed restrictions were implemented on Starlink satellites in Ukraine, limiting their speed to 100 mph (161 kph).

"Our defense forces received no warning about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions. Clearly, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," Beskrestnov added.

US billionaire Elon Musk said Starshield systems are "owned and controlled by the US government," and decisions on speed or usage restrictions are made by the US military and ultimately the president.

Separately, Zelenskyy told British journalist Piers Morgan that he felt "betrayed" over the diesel agreement between Russia and the US.

He said he is "sure that they knew what they did," commenting on a question on whether the speed restrictions on Starlink satellites were implemented deliberately.

The local organising ​committee of the 2027 Asian Cup said preparations for hosting the continental tournament in Saudi Arabia are going ahead as per schedule despite recent attacks in the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia saw a number of events called off or postponed as fighting intensified between the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

Multiple attacks on airports in the country forced the Six Kings men's tennis tournament, scheduled for October 21-24, and the Fifa Esports final, set for October 16-25, to be postponed.

Azmoun double fires Shabab Al Ahli to win at Al Ittihad, Al Hilal beat Al Sadd

Three matches in the Saudi Pro League this weekend were rescheduled to later in the season due to “logistical considerations”.

Earlier, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) said ‌it was open to the idea of ⁠delaying the Asian Cup until ​2028 if needed. The continental tournament is scheduled to ​kick ‌off on January 7 across venues in Riyadh, Jeddah ⁠and Al Khobar.

However, ⁠the tournament's local organising committee said preparations are going ahead according to schedule.

“Preparations across all organisational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services,” ​the organising committee ‌said, adding ⁠that the tournament ​remains on track to ​be ‌held from January 7 to ⁠February 5, 2027.

“The LOC ⁠will continue to monitor ​developments relevant to the tournament and ​ensure ‌the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful ⁠delivery.”

Earlier this week, AFC president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said the confederation was in “no hurry” to decide ​whether the tournament needed to be postponed.

“We ​can wait until the end of November. Things can change very quickly for ‌better or worse in the region and ⁠it is question of seeing what happens,” Al Khalifa told ​reporters in Zurich during the Fifa Council meeting.

The Korea Football Association (KFA) said it was in ⁠communication with the AFC.

“We are closely monitoring the situation in Saudi Arabia and plan to continue discussions regarding overall developments,” the KFA said in a statement.

The previous Asian Cup was ​delayed by a year after China withdrew as hosts because of Covid-19 restrictions, with Qatar stepping in to stage the tournament in early 2024.
