headline: Saudi organisers say 2027 Asian Cup 'on schedule' after attacks
summary: The Asian Cup in January is "on schedule", Saudi Arabian organisers said, after growing fears for the tournament following Houthi attacks on the country. The continent's top football official said this week that the competition could be postponed to 2028, while stressing there was "no hurry" to make a decision. The 2027 Asian Cup is supposed to kick off on January 7 in the Saudi cities of Jeddah, Riyadh and Al Khobar.
body_text:
The Asian Cup in January is "on schedule", Saudi Arabian organisers said, after growing fears for the tournament following Houthi attacks on the country.

The continent's top football official said this week that the competition could be postponed to 2028, while stressing there was "no hurry" to make a decision.

The 2027 Asian Cup is supposed to kick off on January 7 in the Saudi cities of Jeddah, Riyadh and Al Khobar.

In a statement late Thursday, the local organising committee said: "Preparations remain on schedule for the tournament.

"This work continues in close coordination with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and other relevant stakeholders."

Saudi Arabia has in recent days come under sustained attack in a dramatic escalation in the war with the Iran-backed Houthi group.

Several sporting events, including matches in domestic football, have been postponed.

The local organising committee for the Asian Cup, the region's most prestigious football tournament, said it "remains committed to keeping preparations on track and ensuring the necessary resources are in place to deliver a tournament that reflects Saudi Arabia's ambitions and standards as a host.

"At the same time, it will continue to monitor developments relevant to the tournament and ensure the appropriate conditions are in place for its successful delivery."

AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim al-Khalifa told reporters on Wednesday they could wait until the end of November to make a final decision.

"We could move back a year to 2028 if we need to," he said.

"But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule."

headline: Iran urges UK not to conceal its insecurity role in West Asia

TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian foreign ministry spokesman has called on the British government not to conceal its destructive role in insecurity in the West Asian region by deflecting blame.

In response to the remarks raised by British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who labeled Iran’s defensive actions as "aggression", Iran's Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei, in a post on his X account late on Thursday, wrote that the UK government cannot conceal its destructive role in spread of insecurity in the West Asia by deflecting blame.

"The chaos engulfing our region is the consequence of unlawful interventions, including those backed or contributed to by the UK," he emphasized.

For the UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to portray Iran as the “aggressor” after two rounds of unlawful aggression against it in just nine months, even as it pursued negotiations, is a grotesque reversal of victim and aggressor, he said, adding, "It marks yet another low in the UK’s long record of hostile campaigns against Iran."

Baghaei pointed out, "It is as absurd as portraying Nazi Germany as a “defender of peace” while casting the UK and its allies in WWII as the aggressors!"

body_text:
Iraq’s parliament voted to fill a series of long‑vacant cabinet posts late on Thursday, completing Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi’s government and approving a deputy prime minister who is under US sanctions.

The government formation process has been completed five months after Mr Al Zaidi took office, with 11 key positions approved at a full parliamentary session in Baghdad. Those included the country's Defence Minister, Nayef Al Shammari, and Interior Minister Yasir Al Maliki.

Mr Al Zaidi said in a statement that the completion of his cabinet marked the start of “accelerated, diligent work” and pledged to push ahead with the government’s policies. He said the regional conflict had posed exceptional economic and security challenges to Iraq.

Politicians also endorsed Laith Al Khazali as one of three deputy prime ministers. He is the brother of Qais Al Khazali, leader of the Iran‑backed Asaib Ahl Al Haq militia.

The US designated the group as a foreign terrorist organisation in 2020 and has accused it of attacks on US and coalition forces. Both brothers were named “specially designated global terrorists” and Laith was arrested by US forces in 2007 over allegations related to a January attack in Karbala that killed five American soldiers.

Parliament approved two other deputy prime ministers – Mohammed Ali Tamim of the Sunni Taqadum Party and Asas Coalition leader Muhsin Al Mandalawi.

Votes were postponed for the nominee for migration and displacement minister owing to disagreement among parties, politicians said.

The nomination of Mr Al Khazali drew sharp criticism from Washington. Republican Representative Joe Wilson condemned the appointment, describing him as an “Iranian puppet whose militia killed Americans and Iraqis".

“He is no better than ISIS, maybe even worse. It is outrageous but sadly not shocking that he has been appointed deputy PM of Iraq,” Mr Wilson wrote on X.

Another controversial name is Mr Al Maliki, the son-in-law of former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki. When he was in power, Iraq lost nearly a third of its territory to ISIS in 2014, a collapse that ultimately forced him to resign. He is known to have strong connections with Iran and is often described as an influential power-broker in Iraqi politics.

The nomination raises questions about how Iraq will manage its ties with the US.

Mr Al Zaidi's government has pledged to introduce economic ⁠reforms and anti-corruption measures, as well as taking steps to strengthen state institutions. But many challenges lie ahead, including rebuilding an economy hit by regional instability, ​tackling endemic corruption and bringing Iran-backed armed groups under greater state control.

body_text:
Oct 15 (Reuters) - Iraq's parliament on Thursday approved the remainder of Prime Minister Alial-Zaidi's cabinet, completing the formation of a government that took office five months ago with several key positions, lawmakers said.

• Lawmakers approved 11 portfolios, includingNayef al-Shammari as defence minister and Yasir al-Maliki as interior minister

• Positions had been vacant since Zaidi's government took office in May

• Parliament postponed votes on the nominee for migration and displacement minister due to disagreement among parties, lawmakers said

• Lawmakers also approved threedeputy prime ministers, including Laith al-Khazali, a senior leader of the Iran-backed Asaib Ahl al-Haq movement

• The US in 2020 designated Asaib Ahl al-Haq as a foreign terrorist organisation and its leaders, brothers Qais al-Khazali and Laith al-Khazali, as specially designated global terrorists

• The US has accused the group of carrying out attacks against US and coalition forces in Iraq

• Zaidi's government programme pledged economic reforms, anti-corruption measures and efforts to strengthen state institutions

• But it faces significant challenges, including rebuilding an economy hit by regional instability, tackling endemic corruption, and bringing Iran-allied armed groups under greater state control

(Reporting by Ahmed Rasheed and Muayad Hameed, Editing by Rosalba O'Brien)

headline: 19 injured as minibus crashes into train at Channel Tunnel entrance
summary: Nineteen people were injured Thursday when a minibus carrying truck drivers crashed into a vehicle shuttle train at the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel near Calais, forcing a 90-minute suspension of shuttle services. Two people were hospitalised with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, French authorities said.
body_text:
Nineteen people were injured Thursday when a minibus carrying truck drivers crashed into a vehicle shuttle train at the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel near Calais, forcing a 90-minute suspension of shuttle services. Two people were hospitalised with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, French authorities said.

Issued on: 16/10/2026 - 02:53Modified: 16/10/2026 - 02:54

A minibus carrying truck drivers crashed into a train transporting vehicles through the busy Channel Tunnel between France and England on Thursday, injuring 19 people and briefly disrupting cross-Channel traffic, French authorities said.

The minibus was heading towards the tunnel entrance when it veered off course and struck the side of the shuttle train, the regional administration, or prefecture, said in a statement.

Two people were hospitalised with serious but non-life-threatening injuries, while 17 others sustained minor injuries. The minibus driver was among those hurt.

About 200 emergency responders and other personnel rushed to the scene. Vehicle shuttle services through the tunnel were suspended for 90 minutes before gradually resuming by late evening, authorities said. Eurostar passenger trains and freight services were unaffected.

Read moreFrench police suspect Normandy train derailment was result of sabotage

The injured victims were of multiple nationalities, and the relevant consulates had been notified, local official Agathe Cury told reporters. She did not specify which countries.

All those injured had been aboard the minibus, and all are men, Cury said.

The reason for the crash is unclear and an investigation is under way, she added.

In remarks shown on French media, Cury said it was the first time a crash had occurred at the loading area for the trains that shuttle vehicles under the Channel. The crash happened at the entrance to the tunnel in the town of Coquelles near Calais.

The tunnel, which opened in 1994, carried 3.4 million vehicles last year, along with millions of Eurostar passengers.

headline: Rubio urges Lebanon to not return confiscated explosives to Hezbollah, US official says
summary: By Simon Lewis and Kanishka SinghWASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun about the confiscation of hundreds of kilograms of explosives from Hezbollah, a US State Department official said on Thursday.Rubio urged Aoun to hold accountable those who ordered, financed and directed the shipment, and "underscored that returning explosives to (Hezbollah) should be out of the question," the US official said.
body_text:
By Simon Lewis and Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun about the confiscation of hundreds of kilograms of explosives from Hezbollah, a US State Department official said on Thursday.

Rubio urged Aoun to hold accountable those who ordered, financed and directed the shipment, and "underscored that returning explosives to (Hezbollah) should be out of the question," the US official said.

Rubio urged direct military-to-military communication between Lebanese and Israeli forces "for deconfliction," the official added.

A Hezbollah lawmaker said earlier the explosives seized last week by Lebanese security forces belonged to his group.

The lawmaker, Hassan Fadlallah, said Hezbollah had intended to use the explosives against Israel, whose troops are occupying swathes of Lebanese territory seized in this year's war.

A Hezbollah official and a Lebanese security source told Reuters the explosives seized in a car last week were intended to be used in explosive drones targeting Israeli troops.

Aoun told Rubio the Lebanese army and security forces were fully carrying out decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and combat smuggling, the presidency said, adding Aoun asked Rubio to pressure Israel to halt attacks on southern Lebanese towns and villages.

On March 2, the Lebanese government specifically banned Hezbollah's military activities after the movement launched rockets at Israel to back up Tehran, pulling Lebanon into the broader US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28.

Tehran subsequently launched its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon during the war have killed thousands and displaced millions.

Under a deal reached through US-brokered Israel-Lebanon talks, Beirut vowed to disarm Hezbollah, which would in turn lead to Israeli troops gradually withdrawing from Lebanon. But Hezbollah has refused to disarm as long as Israeli forces remain on Lebanese land and Israel has continued striking southern Lebanon.

(Reporting by Simon Lewis and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Chris Reese)

headline: Earliest evidence of human ancestor killed with wooden spear found in Iraqi cave
summary: Remains of a Neanderthal found in an Iraqi-Kurdistan cave reveal he died a violent death after more than a year of being cared for in agonising pain, a study has shown.The killing 75,000 years ago involved a sharpened wooden spear and may be the earliest example of lethal violence using such a weapon, archaeologists believe.A 15mm circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests a “heart shot”, in which the spear was thrust downwards to pass completely through the body, bringing rapid death.Tiny shards of displaced bone were pieced together to reveal how the spear would have penetrated the body. A spear tip or flint would have left a different shaped hole, researchers said in the study, published in the journal Scientific Reports.Other remains, notably damaged teeth, suggest the unfortunate individual – thought to have been around 45 years old when they died – had suffered a brutal facial injury at least a year earlier, and would have needed looking after.“It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual,” said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St John’s College, Cambridge, who led the excavation.The Neanderthal has been named Shanidar A by researchers, after the cave on the Bradost Mountain in Erbil where the remains were found. Preserved boneThe scapula bone, or shoulder blade – broad, flat and so thin in places it is almost translucent – was preserved intact under rock and sediment, along with a mostly complete right hand and two ribs.“It’s extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don’t get complete scapulae from modern burials,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge’s Department of Archaeology. “We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight metres of rock and sediment.”The earliest known rounded wooden spear, pulled from the sea in Clacton-on-Sea, England, in 1911, is more than 400,000 years old.But very few wooden objects from prehistory survive due to the inevitable decomposition. Some waterlogged examples of spears dated to around 200,000 years ago – when early Neanderthals roamed Europe – were found in Schoningen, Germany, in the 1990s. They were around two metres long and used for throwing, like modern javelins, to hunt large game.The researchers believe a similar weapon caused Shanidar A’s death.“Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula,” said Dr Pomeroy. “What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A.”Violent endShe said it was possible the death might have been in a hunting accident, but the evidence suggests deliberate violence was more likely.“Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it’s easy to imagine lethal injuries,” she said. “The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart.”It is possible that the fatal blow was struck by an early human, as they had evolved by that time, but violence between Neanderthals seems a more straightforward explanation.“All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal’s life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear,” said Prof Barker.Blunt forceOne of the seven teeth that were found had been split lengthways with only half remaining, with the others twisted inward. The half tooth had significant tartar build-up along the exposed root canal, suggesting it stayed in the mouth for some time after a blow to the face. Surviving a trauma that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for at least a year would have required care and support from other Neanderthals,” said Dr Pomeroy.Shanidar A may have been fed soft food. Previous research on sediment in Shanidar Cave shows that plants were being soaked before cooking around the same time. “There’s no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time,” said Prof Barker. “The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognise as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime.”Neanderthal caveThe vast cave in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan known as Shanidar is one of the world’s most famous Neanderthal sites. Excavations in the 1950s led by Ralph Solecki found remains from 10 individuals, including a “cluster” of four in the same spot despite dying at different times, suggesting the Neanderthals had returned to inter their dead.Remains of a Neanderthal from another part of the cave, who lived thousands of years later, showed evidence of a paralysed arm, arthritis, deafness and partial blindness. Yet they had lived a long life, so must have been cared for.Shanidar A is one of five Neanderthals unearthed in 2020 in a part of a cave just 1.5 metres long and one metre deep, directly behind a large vertical boulder, thought to be a “prominent marker”. The body was positioned on its back, head facing east.“These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest,” said Dr Pomeroy. “Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades.”
body_text:
Remains of a Neanderthal found in an Iraqi-Kurdistan cave reveal he died a violent death after more than a year of being cared for in agonising pain, a study has shown.

The killing 75,000 years ago involved a sharpened wooden spear and may be the earliest example of lethal violence using such a weapon, archaeologists believe.

A 15mm circular hole in the shoulder blade suggests a “heart shot”, in which the spear was thrust downwards to pass completely through the body, bringing rapid death.

Tiny shards of displaced bone were pieced together to reveal how the spear would have penetrated the body. A spear tip or flint would have left a different shaped hole, researchers said in the study, published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Other remains, notably damaged teeth, suggest the unfortunate individual – thought to have been around 45 years old when they died – had suffered a brutal facial injury at least a year earlier, and would have needed looking after.

“It is fascinating to have evidence for both compassion and violence amongst Neanderthals, our closest evolutionary cousins, embodied in this one individual,” said Prof Graeme Barker, fellow of St John’s College, Cambridge, who led the excavation.

The Neanderthal has been named Shanidar A by researchers, after the cave on the Bradost Mountain in Erbil where the remains were found.

The scapula bone, or shoulder blade – broad, flat and so thin in places it is almost translucent – was preserved intact under rock and sediment, along with a mostly complete right hand and two ribs.

“It’s extraordinary to have a perfectly preserved scapula from 75,000 years ago. These bones are so thin that you often don’t get complete scapulae from modern burials,” said Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge’s Department of Archaeology. “We were able to lift it out in one piece from under almost eight metres of rock and sediment.”

The earliest known rounded wooden spear, pulled from the sea in Clacton-on-Sea, England, in 1911, is more than 400,000 years old.

But very few wooden objects from prehistory survive due to the inevitable decomposition. Some waterlogged examples of spears dated to around 200,000 years ago – when early Neanderthals roamed Europe – were found in Schoningen, Germany, in the 1990s. They were around two metres long and used for throwing, like modern javelins, to hunt large game.

The researchers believe a similar weapon caused Shanidar A’s death.

“Holes left by recreations of spears from this time are an excellent fit for the one we found in the Neanderthal scapula,” said Dr Pomeroy. “What evidence we have suggests that Neanderthals and their ancestors developed woodworking and weapon-making skills many thousands of years before the death of Shanidar A.”

She said it was possible the death might have been in a hunting accident, but the evidence suggests deliberate violence was more likely.

“Animals such as mammoths may have been hunted up close with thrusting spears, so it’s easy to imagine lethal injuries,” she said. “The position of the wound and the force required to push it right through the Neanderthal’s body bear the hallmarks of an intended kill shot directed towards the heart.”

It is possible that the fatal blow was struck by an early human, as they had evolved by that time, but violence between Neanderthals seems a more straightforward explanation.

“All we can ever know about the end of this Neanderthal’s life is that it was violent, and came at the end of a wooden spear,” said Prof Barker.

One of the seven teeth that were found had been split lengthways with only half remaining, with the others twisted inward. The half tooth had significant tartar build-up along the exposed root canal, suggesting it stayed in the mouth for some time after a blow to the face.

Surviving a trauma that splits a tooth in this fashion, then continuing to live and eat for at least a year would have required care and support from other Neanderthals,” said Dr Pomeroy.

Shanidar A may have been fed soft food. Previous research on sediment in Shanidar Cave shows that plants were being soaked before cooking around the same time. “There’s no doubt that Shanidar A would have had difficulty communicating and been in absolute agony for a long period of time,” said Prof Barker.

“The remains of Shanidar A reflect the dual nature of so much of what we recognise as human. On the one hand, we have evidence of a terribly violent end. On the other, this was clearly an individual who was cared for during their lifetime.”

The vast cave in the foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan known as Shanidar is one of the world’s most famous Neanderthal sites. Excavations in the 1950s led by Ralph Solecki found remains from 10 individuals, including a “cluster” of four in the same spot despite dying at different times, suggesting the Neanderthals had returned to inter their dead.

Remains of a Neanderthal from another part of the cave, who lived thousands of years later, showed evidence of a paralysed arm, arthritis, deafness and partial blindness. Yet they had lived a long life, so must have been cared for.

Shanidar A is one of five Neanderthals unearthed in 2020 in a part of a cave just 1.5 metres long and one metre deep, directly behind a large vertical boulder, thought to be a “prominent marker”. The body was positioned on its back, head facing east.

“These Neanderthals returned to the same place to lay their dead to rest,” said Dr Pomeroy. “Some were deposited before the earlier body had fully decomposed, so this was happening within years or decades.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the discovery as a scientific study revealing both violence and compassion in Neanderthals, with a narrative emphasis on the dramatic details of the killing and the caregiving.

The word 'brutal' adds a judgment of violence, intensifying the emotional impact.
Suggests pity and misfortune, adding an emotional layer to the description.
Intensifies the violence with the adverb 'terribly', which is emotive.

headline: Israel says commercial goods no longer entering Gaza after merchants suspend coordination
summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods.
body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Israel said commercial goods were no longer entering Gaza over what it said was a dispute over taxes between local merchants and Hamas, shutting off a vital source of food and other goods in the territory where the population is dependent on aid.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza, made the announcement in a statement on Wednesday, citing what it said was a decision by Gazan merchants to stop coordinating with COGAT on the entry of commercial goods.

It said the Gazan merchants had told COGAT that they had made the decision in response to a 10,000 shekel ($3,220) fee imposed by Hamas on each truck entering Gaza and a demand for 30% of all of their sales in Gaza to be carried out in cash.

Hamas later said that the 10,000 shekel fee was a voluntary payment by wealthy Gazans to a national fund that seeks to provide for those in need such as widows and orphans. It also said that cash payments were encouraged due to what it described as an acute cash shortage in the war-torn territory.

A majority of Gazans are dependent on aid supplies, following three years of war, repeated displacement and severe restrictions imposed by Israel on aid ​deliveries.

A global hunger monitor in July warned that more than two thirds of Gazans could face acute hunger by the year-end. Around 2 million Gazans live in the territory, most in makeshift shelters.

Nahed Shhaibar, the head of the private transport union in Gaza, said that not a single truck carrying commercial products from Israel entered Gaza on Thursday. However, he said trucks carrying humanitarian aid had entered, as had trucks carrying commercial goods from Egypt via an Israeli-controlled crossing.

COGAT said the decision by Gazan merchants would cut the total number of trucks, which carry both humanitarian and commercial goods, entering Gaza each day to around 300 — or half.

Diplomats say that far fewer than 600 trucks normally enter Gaza each day. Shhaibar said the figure was closer to 300, with two thirds carrying commercial goods.

Israel is obliged under a US-mediated agreement to allow a minimum of 600 trucks carrying humanitarian aid to enter Gaza each day. However, it says it is required to allow only 600 trucks and that commercial goods are needed to supplement aid supplies.

($1 = 3.1038 shekels)

(Reporting by Alexander Cornwell in Jerusalem and Nidal al-Mughrabi in Cairo; Editing by Alison Williams)

headline: Analysis-How are Yemen’s Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia so effectively?
summary: By John DavisonLONDON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe international investment hub as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil.
body_text:
LONDON, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Houthi militants who control northwestern Yemen have in the past week attacked Riyadh international airport and hit the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company, in air assaults that have laid bare Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to threats from its enemy next door.

The attacks are shattering the illusion of Saudi Arabia as a safe international investment hub as it tries to attract foreign money and diversify away from oil.

This nightmare scenario for a key US ally in the Gulf has been years in the making, weapons and regional experts say.

They attribute Saudi Arabia's vulnerability to a ragtag group of Yemeni fighters to a perfect storm of factors that include Tehran helping the Houthis reach near self-sufficiency in producing and deploying advanced weapons, and the impact of the US war on Iran that has depleted stocks of interceptors.

TRAINING TO SELF-SUFFICIENCY BY IRAN

Iran has been giving weapons, money and training to the Houthis, known formally as Ansar Allah, for more than a decade, although Tehran has officially denied arming the ​Houthis in violation of a ⁠UN arms embargo.

While Iran has come under its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned – with Iranian help – how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, the experts interviewed by Reuters said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran's other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London.

"Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said.

"Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted."

Iranian analysts said that the Houthis have in this way become one of the most cost-effective and valuable military proxies of Iran.

"The Revolutionary Guards were forward-looking. They looked at what happened if the Houthis couldn't receive equipment or weapons directly (from Iran), or if these were seized by US-allied forces," said Hamid Nikou, a former political advisor to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Nikou said this strategy included teaching the Houthis how to assemble dual-use parts to make drones and even ballistic missiles.

"Iran has basically taught the Houthis how to fish," Nikou said.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting against the Houthis in Yemen says it has intercepted a number of missiles fired by the Houthis at Saudi cities, and that it has destroyed 127 Houthi weapons storage facilities and launch platforms.

Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki told a press conference the Houthis had acquired advanced military technology with the help of "regional actors," including ballistic missiles, drones and explosive-laden fast boats.

DIVERSIFYING WEAPONS IMPORTS AND TECHNOLOGY

A key strength of the Houthis in building their own weapons is that they don't rely solely on Iranian-made equipment or imports coming from Iran.

The Conflict Armament Research organization said in a report this week that the Houthis were attempting to make advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using parts shipped from China, after Yemen's internationally recognised government seized one such shipment.

"China has emerged as a particularly important commercial source, while Iran continues to provide specialised military technology, technical expertise and components that are difficult to obtain commercially," Krieg said.

The Houthis have also experimented with artificial intelligence in efforts to improve their weapons' effectiveness.

Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle.

WAR FATIGUE, DEPLETED MUNITIONS

While the Houthis have improved their weapons production, US allies in the region have seen their air defences stretched since the war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February.

The United States has used large amounts of the missile interceptors it deploys in the region to protect its bases and its allies, which include Israel and Gulf countries, leaving some vulnerable, Saudi Arabia in particular.

"Saudi Arabia, in terms of the sophistication of the military and the development of an integrated air defence network, is not really yet at the level of either Israel or Ukraine, and it just has a very tough job to do," said Farzan Sabet, a Middle East expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute.

Saudi Arabia's sheer size makes defence against air attacks harder than defending Israel or a US base, he said.

The Houthis have learned from the increased levels of violence in the region in recent years, Sabet said.

A Yemeni civil war, in which the Houthis battled Saudi-backed forces from 2014, settled into a shaky ceasefire in 2022. But after Israel’s assault on Gaza in 2023, which followed deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel, the Houthis began firing rockets at Israel and targeting shipping through the Red Sea.

The fallout from the US-Iran war this year reignited the Yemeni civil war, by which time the Houthis had developed new capabilities.

"They haven't been sitting still," Sabet said. "They were basically diversifying their supply chains... and as they gain operational experience, they're able to make those weapons more sophisticated."

(Reporting and writing by John Davison; Editing by Alex Richardson)

headline: What are Saudi Arabia's options to deter the Yemeni rebels?
summary: Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar problem in Yemen: having the military resources to strike the Iran-backed Houthis hard, but no guarantee that a campaign will stop the heavily armed militant group from threatening the kingdom again.The latest wave of missile and drone attacks has brought that dilemma into sharper focus, with Houthi strikes hitting Saudi airports and threatening critical energy infrastructure, including Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran.While Saudi Arabia’s challenge is restoring deterrence, analysts say Riyadh’s options are narrow. Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government claimed responsibility, saying it had hit the runway to prevent an unauthorised Iranian aircraft from landing.The strike tested a fragile period of calm that had largely held since a truce took effect in 2022. The Houthis subsequently launched missiles towards Saudi Arabia, while fighting between the group and Yemeni forces intensified.Mr Sager said that the kingdom had accepted the principle of a ceasefire with the Houthis and remained committed to de-escalation. “However, renewed military pressure may be necessary before agreeing to another ceasefire to secure credible commitments that attacks will stop,” he added. The Houthis have been fighting the Yemeni government since seizing Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened in 2015 at the head of a coalition of regional allies to support the government against the rebels.Beyond air power Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s largest military budgets and a sophisticated arsenal, including American warplanes, missile-defence systems and other advanced weapons. However, Aziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said defeating the Houthis militarily would require more than air power.The kingdom has demonstrated its ability to conduct air operations, but he explained that a successful campaign would also require effective ground forces capable of changing the balance of power in Houthi-held territory. Maritime forces would be needed to restrict the movement of supplies reaching the group through the Red Sea and from the Horn of Africa, he added.That combination could be difficult to assemble. Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis have improved their capabilities, but continue to face problems of competence and political fragmentation.“The reason why the Houthis may hold what they have is not because of their strength, but really the weakness of the other ground operation,” said Mr Alghashian. “A state-building approach would also be needed.”The Houthis, once regarded as a relatively poorly equipped militia, have developed into a formidable fighting force. Their arsenal includes missiles and drones that can strike targets more than 1,000 miles away. Since the war in Gaza erupted in 2023, the group has launched hundreds of drones and missiles towards Israel. Most were intercepted, but some reached their targets, including a drone strike in Tel Aviv that killed a man in 2024 and a missile strike near Ben Gurion Airport last year.The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Washington and Tehran have not yet reached a lasting peace agreement. In recent weeks, they have exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global energy shipments, but negotiations have not resumed. Some observers argue that a broader agreement between the US and Iran offers the most viable path to ending Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Under such a deal, the US could seek Iranian commitments to rein in the Houthis and secure an end to their attacks as part of a regional settlement. But whether the group would comply with such an arrangement is not known.US assistanceThe US supports Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthis through arms sales, military advisers, intelligence sharing and targeting assistance, though it has avoided direct military combat operations.President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining strikes against the Houthis, as the rebels attack a US ally and threaten global energy supplies. The Houthis have warned that any US strikes could prompt them to attack American personnel and interests across the Middle East, potentially drawing the US deeper into the seven-and-a-half-month war.But a senior US official has told The National that the Trump administration has “no announcements to make regarding US support for new military operations” in Yemen. The official added that the administration remains in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. “We will always fulfil our commitments to our partners,” said the official without elaborating. Mr Alghashian believes American firepower could deter the Houthis, at least initially. But he cautioned that the rebels may be prepared to absorb the strikes and wait for US resolve to weaken. “The Houthis feel they will try to weather the storm. Their calculation seems to be that they have withstood many storms before,” he added. “The Saudis still need their allies and still need to focus on alliances for defence.”Mr Trump ordered a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but declared a swift victory after the US expended weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone, according to US media reports. “Saudi Arabia should mobilise the international community to respond to this aggression against the kingdom. Strengthening Saudi defensive capabilities and securing support from regional and international partners are essential to protecting its territory and deterring further attacks,” affirmed Mr Sager.

Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar problem in Yemen: having the military resources to strike the Iran-backed Houthis hard, but no guarantee that a campaign will stop the heavily armed militant group from threatening the kingdom again.

The latest wave of missile and drone attacks has brought that dilemma into sharper focus, with Houthi strikes hitting Saudi airports and threatening critical energy infrastructure, including Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in Dhahran.

While Saudi Arabia’s challenge is restoring deterrence, analysts say Riyadh’s options are narrow. They include intensifying air strikes, bolstering Yemeni government forces on the ground, strengthening air defences and seeking renewed diplomatic engagement.

“Saudi Arabia should apply military pressure on the Houthis inside Yemen to deter further attacks,” Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Gulf Research Centre, told The National. “A key priority is to limit their ability to launch cross-border attacks, particularly by degrading their missile capabilities.”

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis began to escalate in July, when an air strike hit Sanaa International Airport, an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia. Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government claimed responsibility, saying it had hit the runway to prevent an unauthorised Iranian aircraft from landing.

The strike tested a fragile period of calm that had largely held since a truce took effect in 2022. The Houthis subsequently launched missiles towards Saudi Arabia, while fighting between the group and Yemeni forces intensified.

Mr Sager said that the kingdom had accepted the principle of a ceasefire with the Houthis and remained committed to de-escalation. “However, renewed military pressure may be necessary before agreeing to another ceasefire to secure credible commitments that attacks will stop,” he added.

The Houthis have been fighting the Yemeni government since seizing Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia intervened in 2015 at the head of a coalition of regional allies to support the government against the rebels.

Saudi Arabia has one of the world’s largest military budgets and a sophisticated arsenal, including American warplanes, missile-defence systems and other advanced weapons.

However, Aziz Alghashian, a senior non-resident fellow at the Gulf International Forum, said defeating the Houthis militarily would require more than air power.

The kingdom has demonstrated its ability to conduct air operations, but he explained that a successful campaign would also require effective ground forces capable of changing the balance of power in Houthi-held territory. Maritime forces would be needed to restrict the movement of supplies reaching the group through the Red Sea and from the Horn of Africa, he added.

That combination could be difficult to assemble. Yemeni forces opposed to the Houthis have improved their capabilities, but continue to face problems of competence and political fragmentation.

“The reason why the Houthis may hold what they have is not because of their strength, but really the weakness of the other ground operation,” said Mr Alghashian. “A state-building approach would also be needed.”

The Houthis, once regarded as a relatively poorly equipped militia, have developed into a formidable fighting force. Their arsenal includes missiles and drones that can strike targets more than 1,000 miles away.

Since the war in Gaza erupted in 2023, the group has launched hundreds of drones and missiles towards Israel. Most were intercepted, but some reached their targets, including a drone strike in Tel Aviv that killed a man in 2024 and a missile strike near Ben Gurion Airport last year.

The war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. Washington and Tehran have not yet reached a lasting peace agreement. In recent weeks, they have exchanged proposals to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global energy shipments, but negotiations have not resumed.

Some observers argue that a broader agreement between the US and Iran offers the most viable path to ending Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Under such a deal, the US could seek Iranian commitments to rein in the Houthis and secure an end to their attacks as part of a regional settlement. But whether the group would comply with such an arrangement is not known.

The US supports Saudi Arabia in countering the Houthis through arms sales, military advisers, intelligence sharing and targeting assistance, though it has avoided direct military combat operations.

President Donald Trump has said he is considering joining strikes against the Houthis, as the rebels attack a US ally and threaten global energy supplies. The Houthis have warned that any US strikes could prompt them to attack American personnel and interests across the Middle East, potentially drawing the US deeper into the seven-and-a-half-month war.

But a senior US official has told The National that the Trump administration has “no announcements to make regarding US support for new military operations” in Yemen. The official added that the administration remains in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government. “We will always fulfil our commitments to our partners,” said the official without elaborating.

Mr Alghashian believes American firepower could deter the Houthis, at least initially. But he cautioned that the rebels may be prepared to absorb the strikes and wait for US resolve to weaken. “The Houthis feel they will try to weather the storm. Their calculation seems to be that they have withstood many storms before,” he added. “The Saudis still need their allies and still need to focus on alliances for defence.”

Mr Trump ordered a bombing campaign against the Houthis last year, but declared a swift victory after the US expended weapons and munitions at a rate of about $1 billion in the first month alone, according to US media reports.

“Saudi Arabia should mobilise the international community to respond to this aggression against the kingdom. Strengthening Saudi defensive capabilities and securing support from regional and international partners are essential to protecting its territory and deterring further attacks,” affirmed Mr Sager.

body_text:
The International Energy Agency (IEA) has said that its March pledge to release crude oil stocks will exceed its target, and will be accelerating the release of the remaining supplies as global efforts to tame soaring energy prices continue.

Members of the Paris-based agency have so far released 330 million barrels of oil, and the remaining 100 million barrels – which includes more than 20 million barrels of diesel – will be released in a “timely manner consistent with national circumstances”, it said in a statement on Thursday.

That would make the total releases exceed the initial 400 million barrels the IEA had pledged in March, at the onset of the war between US and Israel and Iran.

“Some IEA members have released higher volumes than initially pledged in March while other members intend to do so,” the IEA said after a meeting. Specific plans are already in place ... [to release the stocks] as soon as possible.”

Global energy prices remain volatile and elevated as the war in Iran, now in its eighth month, continues to choke energy supplies.

Earlier this month, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release by rolling out 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves through the IEA to help to stabilise markets.

And in a controversial move last week, US President Donald Trump's administration lifted sanctions on Russia to enable the latter to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets.

The Opec+ group, meanwhile, kept its oil production targets unchanged for November, extending the pause it started in October after six months of gradual increases.

Oil prices rose after the IEA's announcement. Brent, the benchmark for two-thirds of the world's oil, added 0.15 per cent to $106.20 a barrel at 8.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, jumped 3.28 per cent to $98.21 a barrel.

Thursday's IEA statement said it has “encouraged those IEA members holding oil production and refining capacities to boost supply of crude and refined products, particularly diesel”.

The IEA said it will continue to monitor the progress of the completion of its March pledge, “and will inform G7 leaders as requested and the IEA governing board on further actions needed, based on an updated oil market assessment, focusing on diesel”, it added.

headline: IEA members to accelerate release of 100M barrels as oil markets remain tight
summary: Plans include over 20M barrels of diesel to be released as soon as possible amid supply tightness
body_text:
International Energy Agency (IEA) members agreed Thursday to accelerate the release of around 100 million barrels of remaining emergency oil stocks, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel as soon as possible amid continued tightness in global energy markets.

The agency's Governing Board said its latest assessments pointed to persistent tightness in oil markets, particularly diesel, following a meeting on energy markets and security.

Approximately 330 million barrels have already been released under the collective action launched in March in response to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

Total releases will exceed the original commitment of 400 million barrels, as some members have released more than initially pledged and others intend to do so, the board said.

Members agreed to take all necessary steps to complete the remaining releases in a timely manner consistent with national circumstances, with specific acceleration plans already in place.

The board also encouraged members with oil production and refining capacity to boost supplies of crude and refined products, particularly diesel, and emphasized the importance of the free flow of energy trade.

Reaffirming their commitment to international energy security, members expressed willingness to take further action to address global energy market challenges, building on the G7 statement of Oct. 2.

The IEA Secretariat will monitor progress and inform G7 leaders and the Governing Board of further action needed, drawing on an updated oil market assessment focused on diesel.

headline: Violating oil tanker catches fire in Sea of Oman
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – A violating oil tanker that had switched off its tracking systems caught fire in a prohibited zone in the Sea of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Army Navy said.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 15 (MNA) – A violating oil tanker that had switched off its tracking systems caught fire in a prohibited zone in the Sea of Oman, east of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Army Navy said.

An oil tanker caught fire in a prohibited zone in the Sea of Oman after switching off its tracking systems in an attempt to cross the area, Iran's Army Navy said.

Monitoring teams from the Army Navy detected the violating tanker while on patrol and controlling the east of the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Army Navy's public relations office.

The tanker had turned off its tracking systems and was attempting to pass through the prohibited area in the Sea of Oman, the statement said.

The Army of the Islamic Republic of Iran said the Strait of Hormuz is under the full control and surveillance of its forces and the Islamic Revolution Guard Corps Navy.

headline: Three dead in Istanbul as torrential rain floods Turkish city
summary: Torrential rainfall has killed three people and caused chaos across Istanbul, as the Turkish city recorded its highest rainfall in more than 80 years. Istanbul Governor Davut Gul instructed the city’s 16 million residents to stay at home unless outings were absolutely necessary, closed schools and banned motorbikes as 8,000 emergency service workers were sent out to deal with the effects of days of downpours. “Rainfall in Istanbul will continue for another two to three days. Do not go outside unless absolutely necessary,” Mr Gul told a press conference on Thursday morning. He said it was “the highest level of precipitation recorded in Istanbul since 1942”, when records began. About 3,000 people were rescued from flooded areas, he said.Many areas of the city had received more than 100kg of rain per square metre, equivalent to 100mm, since early on Wednesday, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said. Rainfall in the Beykoz area of north-eastern Istanbul had reached 242kg per square metre, the authority said. An investigation has been launched following the death of a 14-year-old boy who died from electrocution after he stepped into a puddle in the Fatih district, the Istanbul governorship said. He was taken to hospital unconscious but could not be saved, the statement added. A 34-year-old died after slipping and hitting their head on a pavement, and authorities are trying to identify the body of a man found near the banks of the Kagithane Creek, according to the governor’s office.Footage published by state media showed cars drifting down streets, flooded homes and mosques, and passengers trapped in a bus with dirty flood water up to their knees. “Roads turned into lakes in many parts of the city,” state broadcaster TRT reported. At Istanbul Airport, 51 flights were diverted to alternative airports and another 19 flights were cancelled, Mr Gul said.The unusually heavy rain began on Tuesday and continued into Wednesday. Streets began to flood as drainage systems were overwhelmed.Istanbul residents received text messages from disaster management services on Wednesday evening warning them to stay away from riverbanks and flooded roads. Residents of basement apartments were told they “should take precautions”, while power cuts halted water supplies to homes and businesses in parts of the city, despite the torrential rain falling outside.Emergency services received more than 1,200 reports of flooding, 15 of landslides, 47 of people trapped and two of roofs blown off, the governorship said. Heavy flooding also made streets impassable in the city of Antalya on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The state meteorological service issued warnings for more heavy rain and wind across the country on Thursday. Turkey has been experiencing an unusually wet 2026, the service said in a climate report released in September. Rainfall between January and August was 54 per cent higher than the 30-year average between 1991 and 2020. A third of the extreme weather events in the first eight months of the year were heavy rainfall and flooding.

Torrential rainfall has killed three people and caused chaos across Istanbul, as the Turkish city recorded its highest rainfall in more than 80 years.

Istanbul Governor Davut Gul instructed the city’s 16 million residents to stay at home unless outings were absolutely necessary, closed schools and banned motorbikes as 8,000 emergency service workers were sent out to deal with the effects of days of downpours.

“Rainfall in Istanbul will continue for another two to three days. Do not go outside unless absolutely necessary,” Mr Gul told a press conference on Thursday morning.

EditorialClimate action must stay on the global agenda

He said it was “the highest level of precipitation recorded in Istanbul since 1942”, when records began.

About 3,000 people were rescued from flooded areas, he said.

Many areas of the city had received more than 100kg of rain per square metre, equivalent to 100mm, since early on Wednesday, Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality said. Rainfall in the Beykoz area of north-eastern Istanbul had reached 242kg per square metre, the authority said.

An investigation has been launched following the death of a 14-year-old boy who died from electrocution after he stepped into a puddle in the Fatih district, the Istanbul governorship said. He was taken to hospital unconscious but could not be saved, the statement added.

A 34-year-old died after slipping and hitting their head on a pavement, and authorities are trying to identify the body of a man found near the banks of the Kagithane Creek, according to the governor’s office.

Footage published by state media showed cars drifting down streets, flooded homes and mosques, and passengers trapped in a bus with dirty flood water up to their knees.

“Roads turned into lakes in many parts of the city,” state broadcaster TRT reported.

At Istanbul Airport, 51 flights were diverted to alternative airports and another 19 flights were cancelled, Mr Gul said.

The unusually heavy rain began on Tuesday and continued into Wednesday. Streets began to flood as drainage systems were overwhelmed.

Istanbul residents received text messages from disaster management services on Wednesday evening warning them to stay away from riverbanks and flooded roads.

Residents of basement apartments were told they “should take precautions”, while power cuts halted water supplies to homes and businesses in parts of the city, despite the torrential rain falling outside.

Emergency services received more than 1,200 reports of flooding, 15 of landslides, 47 of people trapped and two of roofs blown off, the governorship said.

Heavy flooding also made streets impassable in the city of Antalya on Turkey's Mediterranean coast. The state meteorological service issued warnings for more heavy rain and wind across the country on Thursday.

Turkey has been experiencing an unusually wet 2026, the service said in a climate report released in September.

Rainfall between January and August was 54 per cent higher than the 30-year average between 1991 and 2020. A third of the extreme weather events in the first eight months of the year were heavy rainfall and flooding.

headline: Israeli company used online ads to run spy operation against 'hundreds of millions of people'
summary: Israeli digital advertising ⁠agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a network of online advertisements that it used to track ⁠targets and hack their devices, research groups said.Reports from Canadian group Citizen Lab and US advertising security company Confiant found that Discover-Tech's services gave Candiru, ​an Israeli spyware company blacklisted by the US government, as well as other Israeli surveillance groups, access to advertising platforms run by companies including Google, Comcast and Russia's Yandex. Discover-Tech's online ads, often ⁠for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds, reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.People who visited sites or used apps with ​the malicious ⁠ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes try to extract phone numbers from smartphone users, researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.Some ads would be used ​to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, the research groups said. But Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.Discover-Tech was issuing at least 10 million ads a day around the world, with data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching allowing it to track people beyond the reach of its ads, Confiant co-founder Jerome Dangu said. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," he added.Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at Qatar's Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025. That was confirmed because the media group shared its network logs with the group, it added.Al Jazeera said in a statement that it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said.Mr Dangu said the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive ​categories", including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, including the Palestinian ‌territories, were saturated by the Israeli company's ads."You go to almost ⁠any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them ​a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he added.Citizen Lab said it had evidence that the malicious ads were ​shown to people in the ‌UN, Nato, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. The ads also appeared in networks including technology companies such as Nvidia and Sandisk, as well as media organisations ⁠in Mexico, Israel and Europe.Discover-Tech is now to be frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies".IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email ​that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved entities last week after an audit identified policy breaches.
body_text:
Israeli digital advertising ⁠agency Discover-Tech spied on internet users through a network of online advertisements that it used to track ⁠targets and hack their devices, research groups said.

Reports from Canadian group Citizen Lab and US advertising security company Confiant found that Discover-Tech's services gave Candiru, ​an Israeli spyware company blacklisted by the US government, as well as other Israeli surveillance groups, access to advertising platforms run by companies including Google, Comcast and Russia's Yandex.

Discover-Tech's online ads, often ⁠for ordinary products such as phones or earbuds, reached more than 120,000 websites and 75,000 apps through its various partnerships, Citizen Lab said.

People who visited sites or used apps with ​the malicious ⁠ads could be identified and tracked by Discover-Tech, which would sometimes try to extract phone numbers from smartphone users, researchers said. Ads only needed to load on a website for the spying to occur.

Some ads would be used ​to help plant spyware from Candiru on users' devices, the research groups said. But Confiant said that ads it tied to Candiru were a fraction of Discover-Tech's overall volume.

Discover-Tech was issuing at least 10 million ads a day around the world, with data-sharing arrangements called cookie matching allowing it to track people beyond the reach of its ads, Confiant co-founder Jerome Dangu said. "Very likely hundreds of millions of people would have been touched by Discover-Tech," he added.

Citizen Lab said a powerful form of Candiru spyware delivered through Discover-Tech's ads had been used to compromise 45 Windows devices at Qatar's Al Jazeera between 2024 and 2025. That was confirmed because the media group shared its network logs with the group, it added.

Al Jazeera said in a statement that it "condemns the spyware attacks targeting a number of its staff" and that it was taking steps to protect its employees and its systems. "Those responsible must be held accountable," it said.

Mr Dangu said the malicious ads had been shown to users in "hundreds of networks in sensitive ​categories", including the Pentagon, the International Atomic Energy Agency and the International Criminal Court. He also said that some regions, including the Palestinian ‌territories, were saturated by the Israeli company's ads.

"You go to almost ⁠any site in Palestine – any site – you find a Discover-Tech ad. It gives them ​a very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country," he added.

Citizen Lab said it had evidence that the malicious ads were ​shown to people in the ‌UN, Nato, the European Commission and more than a dozen national governments. The ads also appeared in networks including technology companies such as Nvidia and Sandisk, as well as media organisations ⁠in Mexico, Israel and Europe.

Discover-Tech is now to be frozen out of parts of the online ad market. Google said in a statement that it had collaborated with Citizen Lab and Confiant's investigation and kicked Discover-Tech off its ad platforms "for systematically violating our policies".

IAB Europe, the European-level association for the digital marketing and advertising ecosystem, said in an email ​that Discover-Tech had been suspended from its list of globally approved entities last week after an audit identified policy breaches.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a large-scale surveillance scandal, emphasizing the global reach of Discover-Tech's ad-based spying and the involvement of sensitive targets like Al Jazeera and government networks.

loaded_language.explanation: The verb 'spied' is emotionally charged and implies covert, illicit surveillance, which may prejudge the legality of the activities.
'Hack' is a loaded term that suggests unauthorized intrusion, carrying strong negative connotations.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: gain unauthorized access to their devices

loaded_language.explanation: The adjective 'malicious' is a value judgment that characterizes the ads as intentionally harmful, rather than simply describing their technical function.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: ads used for tracking or spyware delivery

loaded_language.quote: saturated by the Israeli company's ads
loaded_language.explanation: 'Saturated' is a vivid, emotive term that conveys overwhelming presence, potentially exaggerating the extent.

loaded_language.quote: very complete visibility on the digital activities of an entire country
loaded_language.explanation: This phrase is dramatic and sweeping, suggesting total surveillance, which may overstate the actual capability.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: extensive monitoring of digital activities across the country

omissions: Discover-Tech's response or denial to the allegations
Details on how Candiru spyware was delivered through ads
Specific number of victims beyond 'hundreds of millions' estimate
Any mention of legal actions or investigations by authorities

The listed tone keywords ('alarming', 'investigative', 'critical', 'global', 'serious') do not appear verbatim in the article and are not directly attributable to specific wording.

headline: Investor confidence in Gulf remains strong despite war, says World Economic Forum's regional chief
summary: Investor confidence in the region remains strong despite the fall-out from the Iran war, with efforts to diversify economies helping to shield them from the crisis, a senior World Economic Forum official has said.Kelsey Goodman, head of Middle East and North Africa at the World Economic Forum (WEF), told The National that the region’s economic fundamentals remained solid despite geopolitical uncertainty.Her comments come as the International Monetary Fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies amid the effects of the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.“There’s still widespread investor confidence in the region,” Ms Goodman said. “The fundamentals are solid even if the surrounding area is uncertain, but it calls for the need for dialogue and co-operation and hopefully a return to peace and resiliency in the region.”Speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai, which concluded on Thursday, Ms Goodman said efforts to diversify Gulf economies had helped them withstand recent shocks and would be crucial to their recovery.“Diversification really is key, and the companies and the economies that have been able to have already built in diversity into their plan are the ones that have been most resilient," she said."Resiliency is something that you have to prepare for. It's not something that you can build only in times of crisis.”Foresight simulations were carried out at the meeting on Thursday, in which participants rehearsed responses to unfolding geopolitical and technological crises.“This meeting has really emphasised that dialogue and co-operation are not luxuries for easy times. They're essential precisely when the world is at its most complicated,” said Ms Goodman.Even with this in mind, she said the mood at the meeting was positive.“I think it speaks to the resiliency of Dubai, and we hope that the participants are leaving with a message of hope and renewed belief in the power of moving from foresight into action,” she said.Economic diversification into AIIn recent years, the UAE has prioritised artificial intelligence investments, with trillions of dollars earmarked for the technology, including building data centres.A newly published WEF report showed the potential of artificial intelligence in unlocking upwards of $1 trillion by 2030 in the region.Ms Goodman believes the investments countries are making in the AI sphere could return, but that regional uncertainty creates more barriers to reaching these goals.“For the economies to realise this value, it's going to take a lot of co-operation across all sectors of society,” she said. “That's going to include long-term planning from governments, but also having the regulation, the energy infrastructure, and the business applications for these new technologies.”Impacted labour marketsWhile blocked trade routes have affected shipping and petrol prices have risen, Ms Goodman said the war's impact on the travel and tourism sector could also affect labour markets, especially given the high numbers of migrant workers in the country. The UAE workforce is made up of approximately 8.7 million migrant workers.“The Gulf really relies on a very mobile labour market with a lot of connections outside the region,” she said. “These are areas where there could potentially be shortages.”
body_text:
Investor confidence in the region remains strong despite the fall-out from the Iran war, with efforts to diversify economies helping to shield them from the crisis, a senior World Economic Forum official has said.

Kelsey Goodman, head of Middle East and North Africa at the World Economic Forum (WEF), told The National that the region’s economic fundamentals remained solid despite geopolitical uncertainty.

Her comments come as the International Monetary Fund sharply downgraded its 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies amid the effects of the war and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Sheikh Hamdan meets World Economic Forum president to strengthen UAE partnership

“There’s still widespread investor confidence in the region,” Ms Goodman said. “The fundamentals are solid even if the surrounding area is uncertain, but it calls for the need for dialogue and co-operation and hopefully a return to peace and resiliency in the region.”

Speaking at the Annual Meeting of Global Future Leaders in Dubai, which concluded on Thursday, Ms Goodman said efforts to diversify Gulf economies had helped them withstand recent shocks and would be crucial to their recovery.

“Diversification really is key, and the companies and the economies that have been able to have already built in diversity into their plan are the ones that have been most resilient," she said.

"Resiliency is something that you have to prepare for. It's not something that you can build only in times of crisis.”

Foresight simulations were carried out at the meeting on Thursday, in which participants rehearsed responses to unfolding geopolitical and technological crises.

“This meeting has really emphasised that dialogue and co-operation are not luxuries for easy times. They're essential precisely when the world is at its most complicated,” said Ms Goodman.

Even with this in mind, she said the mood at the meeting was positive.

“I think it speaks to the resiliency of Dubai, and we hope that the participants are leaving with a message of hope and renewed belief in the power of moving from foresight into action,” she said.

In recent years, the UAE has prioritised artificial intelligence investments, with trillions of dollars earmarked for the technology, including building data centres.

A newly published WEF report showed the potential of artificial intelligence in unlocking upwards of $1 trillion by 2030 in the region.

Ms Goodman believes the investments countries are making in the AI sphere could return, but that regional uncertainty creates more barriers to reaching these goals.

“For the economies to realise this value, it's going to take a lot of co-operation across all sectors of society,” she said. “That's going to include long-term planning from governments, but also having the regulation, the energy infrastructure, and the business applications for these new technologies.”

While blocked trade routes have affected shipping and petrol prices have risen, Ms Goodman said the war's impact on the travel and tourism sector could also affect labour markets, especially given the high numbers of migrant workers in the country. The UAE workforce is made up of approximately 8.7 million migrant workers.

“The Gulf really relies on a very mobile labour market with a lot of connections outside the region,” she said. “These are areas where there could potentially be shortages.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the Iran war's economic impact through the optimistic lens of a WEF official, emphasizing Gulf resilience and diversification while downplaying the severity of the IMF's downgraded growth forecasts.
