headline: Drop in Gulf student visa applications shows dwindling appetite for UK universities
summary: The number of students from the Gulf choosing to study in the UK has plunged in recent years, most drastically from the UAE, figures show.Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said.While there was an inevitable drop in numbers caused by the Covid pandemic, these had bounced back by 2022, before the UK began issuing its policies to restrict student visas. The number of student visa applications from the UAE then began to drop, falling 59 per cent in the next four years, from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed. These covered students who have been offered a place at an institution to study for a bachelor, graduate, PhD or other higher education courses. There was a 36 per cent drop in 2025 alone compared with the previous year. There were 13 per cent fewer applications from students in Saudi Arabia between 2023 and 2025, dropping from 5,814 to 5,049. In Bahrain, a 26 per cent decline has been recorded, from 545 applications in 2023 to 403 in 2025.Qatar recorded a drop of about 14 per cent between 2023 and 2025, from 1,056 to 910 applications.The outliers are Kuwait, which saw an 11 per cent rise in applications, from 4,499 in 2023 to 5,034 in 2025, and Oman, which grew from 996 to 1,018.Politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routesNick Hillman, Higher Education Policy InstitutionFigures for spring and summer visa applications will be released by the Home Office next month and are expected to continue the downward trend. The first quarter of this year showed a decline of almost a third (29.2 per cent) of applications from Saudi students. UAE applications for the same period remained steady, moving from 16 in the first three months of 2025 to 15 in the same period of 2026.Professionals in the higher education sector have warned the numbers could keep declining as UK immigration restrictions make studying in the country less appealing. Many students regard a degree in the UK as an investment towards a career in the country. But from next year, students will have only 18 months to find a job in the UK after their graduation, compared to the previous allowance of two years. This follows increases to the Immigration Health Surcharge and student visa fees, and a higher chance of visa refusal. The general salary threshold for skilled workers' visas is also set to rise, with the discount for graduates removed, according the Labour government's White Paper on Immigration.The UK government was criticised this week for removing incentives for overseas students to pursue a degree course at a British university. “Given politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routes, such as the infamous small boats, the factors pulling international students to come and study in the UK have been trimmed back again,” wrote Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institution in an analysis.Concerned familiesThis is compounded by financial penalties for universities that award spaces to students whose visa applications are later rejected. This has reportedly led to institutions withdrawing their offers to would-be students, mainly from India, China and Nigeria, to avoid paying any penalty should their visa applications be unsuccessful.For Gulf students, other factors such as safety concerns could also be fuelling the decline. A Saudi student was killed last year in a knife attack in Cambridge while studying an English language course, prompting his uncle to say the UK was “rapidly losing its global reputation”.There are also fears of radicalisation on campuses. The UAE – which has urged western governments to ban the Muslim Brotherhood organisation – was reported by the Financial Times this year to have scrapped its state-funded scholarships to some British universities.The UK government introduced new measures to protect students from extremism on campus this year. This includes supporting universities to carry out appropriate risk checks where free speech crosses into unlawful activity or support for terrorism.
body_text:
The number of students from the Gulf choosing to study in the UK has plunged in recent years, most drastically from the UAE, figures show.

Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said.

While there was an inevitable drop in numbers caused by the Covid pandemic, these had bounced back by 2022, before the UK began issuing its policies to restrict student visas.

Weekend EssayFrom my university in Lebanon, I see a society that refuses to quit

The number of student visa applications from the UAE then began to drop, falling 59 per cent in the next four years, from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed. These covered students who have been offered a place at an institution to study for a bachelor, graduate, PhD or other higher education courses. There was a 36 per cent drop in 2025 alone compared with the previous year.

There were 13 per cent fewer applications from students in Saudi Arabia between 2023 and 2025, dropping from 5,814 to 5,049. In Bahrain, a 26 per cent decline has been recorded, from 545 applications in 2023 to 403 in 2025.

Qatar recorded a drop of about 14 per cent between 2023 and 2025, from 1,056 to 910 applications.

The outliers are Kuwait, which saw an 11 per cent rise in applications, from 4,499 in 2023 to 5,034 in 2025, and Oman, which grew from 996 to 1,018.

Figures for spring and summer visa applications will be released by the Home Office next month and are expected to continue the downward trend.

The first quarter of this year showed a decline of almost a third (29.2 per cent) of applications from Saudi students. UAE applications for the same period remained steady, moving from 16 in the first three months of 2025 to 15 in the same period of 2026.

Professionals in the higher education sector have warned the numbers could keep declining as UK immigration restrictions make studying in the country less appealing.

Many students regard a degree in the UK as an investment towards a career in the country. But from next year, students will have only 18 months to find a job in the UK after their graduation, compared to the previous allowance of two years.

This follows increases to the Immigration Health Surcharge and student visa fees, and a higher chance of visa refusal. The general salary threshold for skilled workers' visas is also set to rise, with the discount for graduates removed, according the Labour government's White Paper on Immigration.

The UK government was criticised this week for removing incentives for overseas students to pursue a degree course at a British university.

“Given politicians have found it much easier to control clearly defined legal migration routes, such as coming to the UK to study, than to get a grip on other routes, such as the infamous small boats, the factors pulling international students to come and study in the UK have been trimmed back again,” wrote Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institution in an analysis.

This is compounded by financial penalties for universities that award spaces to students whose visa applications are later rejected. This has reportedly led to institutions withdrawing their offers to would-be students, mainly from India, China and Nigeria, to avoid paying any penalty should their visa applications be unsuccessful.

For Gulf students, other factors such as safety concerns could also be fuelling the decline.

A Saudi student was killed last year in a knife attack in Cambridge while studying an English language course, prompting his uncle to say the UK was “rapidly losing its global reputation”.

There are also fears of radicalisation on campuses. The UAE – which has urged western governments to ban the Muslim Brotherhood organisation – was reported by the Financial Times this year to have scrapped its state-funded scholarships to some British universities.

The UK government introduced new measures to protect students from extremism on campus this year. This includes supporting universities to carry out appropriate risk checks where free speech crosses into unlawful activity or support for terrorism.

analysis.framing: The article frames the decline in Gulf student visa applications as a consequence of UK immigration restrictions and social/safety concerns, presenting the UK's policy environment as the primary driver of the drop.

Loaded term implying harsh or restrictive enforcement, carrying negative connotations.
The word 'infamous' is editorializing, attaching a negative judgment to the small boat crossings.
Vague, colloquial phrase that softens the description of policy changes reducing incentives.
Quoted phrase is emotionally charged and sweeping, used to amplify negative perception of the UK.

omissions: No mention of the UK government's stated rationale for visa restrictions, such as reducing net migration or protecting domestic higher education.
No data on overall international student visa application trends to provide context for whether the Gulf decline is part of a broader pattern.
No comment from UK government officials or universities defending their policies or highlighting continued opportunities for Gulf students.

headline: Serial champions India continue bewildering struggle in bilateral series
summary: Can you be critical of a side that has won every major competition it has entered since 2024? Possibly. Especially when you put in performances like the Indian team has done in between those fine results.Since the 2024 T20 World Cup win, India have won the 50-over ICC Champions Trophy, Asia Cup, and successfully defended their T20 world title and the Asian Games gold medal this year.But right alongside, the team were also been whitewashed at home in Tests by New Zealand and South Africa – having been undefeated in their backyard for over a decade, lost the Border Gavaskar Trophy to Australia, embarrassed by Ireland (in T20s) and England (T20s and ODIs) right after their World Cup win this year and are now being taken apart by a spirited West Indies at home.The double T20 world champions were outplayed in the fourth match of the five-game T20 series against the Windies, falling to a 24-run loss in Hyderabad. The series is now tied 2-2. In the preceding ODI series, the West Indies easily chased down a target of 350 and also smashed 400 in the second game. That series was won 2-1 by India but they were stretched well past their limits.It's the same story in the T20s. In fact, India have been hammered for the third straight bilateral T20 series – defeats to Ireland and England away and now an uphill battle against the Caribbean side. If the Windies secure the T20 series win on Saturday, it wouldn’t be a surprise. Shouldn’t that worry Indian cricket management? It should, but what can they do when the team ends up winning every major tournament? India won a world and a continental title in 2026. The same set of players have also been thrashed by Ireland, England and the Windies in the same year. How do you reconcile both facts?Same story or beginning of the end?There are two ways to look at it. One is that India have mastered the art of stumbling their way through low priority bilateral series and somehow finding the perfect formula when the big tournaments come around.The other is India were playing major tournaments in Asian conditions for the last two years and would have been found out if any of the events were held in England or Australia.There is only one way to find out – wait for next two years.The next big assignment for all teams is the ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, followed by the 2028 T20 World Cup Down Under and the Los Angeles Olympics in the same year.Indian fans and cricket administrators might prefer to wait until all three assignments are completed, before taking stock of the situation. body_text:
Can you be critical of a side that has won every major competition it has entered since 2024? Possibly. Especially when you put in performances like the Indian team has done in between those fine results.

Since the 2024 T20 World Cup win, India have won the 50-over ICC Champions Trophy, Asia Cup, and successfully defended their T20 world title and the Asian Games gold medal this year.

But right alongside, the team were also been whitewashed at home in Tests by New Zealand and South Africa – having been undefeated in their backyard for over a decade, lost the Border Gavaskar Trophy to Australia, embarrassed by Ireland (in T20s) and England (T20s and ODIs) right after their World Cup win this year and are now being taken apart by a spirited West Indies at home.

InterviewKS Bharat ready for new chapter with UAE after calling time on India

The double T20 world champions were outplayed in the fourth match of the five-game T20 series against the Windies, falling to a 24-run loss in Hyderabad. The series is now tied 2-2.

In the preceding ODI series, the West Indies easily chased down a target of 350 and also smashed 400 in the second game. That series was won 2-1 by India but they were stretched well past their limits.

It's the same story in the T20s. In fact, India have been hammered for the third straight bilateral T20 series – defeats to Ireland and England away and now an uphill battle against the Caribbean side.

If the Windies secure the T20 series win on Saturday, it wouldn’t be a surprise.

Shouldn’t that worry Indian cricket management? It should, but what can they do when the team ends up winning every major tournament? India won a world and a continental title in 2026. The same set of players have also been thrashed by Ireland, England and the Windies in the same year. How do you reconcile both facts?

There are two ways to look at it. One is that India have mastered the art of stumbling their way through low priority bilateral series and somehow finding the perfect formula when the big tournaments come around.

The other is India were playing major tournaments in Asian conditions for the last two years and would have been found out if any of the events were held in England or Australia.

There is only one way to find out – wait for next two years.

The next big assignment for all teams is the ODI World Cup in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia, followed by the 2028 T20 World Cup Down Under and the Los Angeles Olympics in the same year.

Indian fans and cricket administrators might prefer to wait until all three assignments are completed, before taking stock of the situation.

Around 10 or so years back, India were the undisputed champions of bilateral series, home and away. But they did not win a single major tournament, much to the pain of the then captain Virat Kohli.

The script has flipped completely, where the players endure bewildering losses home and away in all formats, only to go back to their homes with another winners' medal in the cabinet.

This can’t last long though. Conditions in South Africa and Australia are going to be daunting even for the most in-form Indian team, let alone a group that can barely stand still. It could open some deep wounds.

One thing is clear – India do not have ready replacements for their veterans. The fitness concerns of all-rounder Hardik Pandya and workload management of Jasprit Bumrah have ruined the balance of the white-ball teams, while they still have not found a reliable substitute for Mohammad Shami or even Mohammad Siraj.

No wonder the ageing Kohli and Rohit Sharma are guaranteed to play the ODI World Cup next year. Fast bowler Bhuvneshwar Kumar is back in the T20 team for the forthcoming New Zealand tour; he last played for India in 2022.

Fellow veteran quick Shami is highly likely to be back before the ODI World Cup, especially since the Indian team’s selection panel is undergoing a change with older yet in-form players being given a look-in once again.

Maybe, India will win a couple of more titles and fans will forget about pain of the bilaterals. If not, then there will be a feeding frenzy.

headline: Africa: Why China Won't Build Its Own Wagner in Africa
summary: [African Arguments] Attacks on Chinese workers in Mali are testing Beijing's reliance on African security forces. Russia's experience there gives China little reason to take on the fighting itself.
body_text:
Attacks on Chinese workers in Mali are testing Beijing's reliance on African security forces. Russia's experience there gives China little reason to take on the fighting itself.

On 9 May, fighters from Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), al-Qaeda's affiliate in the Sahel, stopped buses and trucks at Zambougou, in the Ségou region of Mali about 60 kilometres from Bamako, ordered the passengers out and burned at least 40 civilian vehicles. One passenger told Human Rights Watch that the fighters sent the travellers on towards the capital on foot, saying they had declared an embargo on Bamako. HRW found no Malian troops in the area.

On 12 May, the Chinese embassy in Bamako published a warning urging Chinese nationals to leave several mining districts, citing armed attacks and the government's campaign against unlicensed mining. The incidents occurred in different parts of Mali, but both exposed the limits of state protection beyond Bamako. A second notice in July reported attacks on foreigners around Kenieba, Bougouni and Foulou. An embassy can tell its citizens to leave. It has far less to offer those who stay.

A BBC Monitoring review counted 38 Chinese citizens among the 89 foreigners abducted in high-profile cases across Africa in 2025, many of them working in the gold industry of south-western Mali. The figures cover foreign nationals and offer no comparable measure of the kidnappings experienced by Malians. Russia, meanwhile, has become directly involved in Mali's military campaign, committing personnel to combat operations alongside Malian forces.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

What fighting costs Russia

On 10 September, JNIM fighters overran the army camp at Dioura in central Mali. Military, security and local sources told AFP that at least 100 Malian soldiers and five members of Russia's Africa Corps had been killed. The Malian authorities published no toll of their own. Bamako had already lost its defence minister, Sadio Camara, who was killed in an attack on his residence in Kati on 25 April.

Less than a month after Dioura, separatists announced what they called a temporary withdrawal from Kidal, and Malian forces backed by Russian fighters returned to the northern town. The recapture was a significant political and military gain for Bamako, though JNIM's attacks on civilian transport farther south remained a separate security challenge.

Wagner arrived in late 2021, as Mali's relations with France broke down. When it announced its departure in June 2025, Africa Corps, which answers to Russia's Defence Ministry, stayed on, and Russian personnel remain part of the war. On 31 July, Human Rights Watch reported that Russian-controlled Africa Corps aircraft had struck Kyrnia, in the Mopti region, on 15 June. Eight civilians, including three children, were killed in what the organisation described as an apparently unlawful attack. Russia's direct involvement has made its military reputation inseparable from the conduct of operations in Mali, including attacks that have harmed civilians.

Contractors outside the fighting

Chinese security companies have taken a much narrower role. When fighting trapped about 330 Chinese workers in Juba in July 2016, DeWe Security Service Group helped organise their evacuation despite having no armed personnel of its own. The company, founded by former officers of the People's Liberation Army and the People's Armed Police, hired armed South Sudanese as backup, told the workers to stay put and waited for Ugandan forces to secure the airport before the evacuation could begin, as Carnegie's research on the episode records.

The pattern holds elsewhere. Chinese contractors assess threats and train guards, as DeWe has done for Kenya's Chinese-financed Standard Gauge Railway, and rely on host-country police and soldiers to carry the weapons. These arrangements allow Chinese companies to organise protection while leaving combat operations to local forces. They also make effective oversight difficult when those forces commit abuses.

Beijing has its own reasons to keep armed force under tight political command. From 1 January 2018, the People's Armed Police came under the command of the Communist Party's Central Committee and the Central Military Commission and was no longer under the authority of the State Council.

China's domestic security industry is regulated by public-security authorities, but oversight becomes far more difficult once contractors operate abroad. Wagner showed what can happen when such control loosens. By the time Yevgeny Prigozhin turned his fighters towards Moscow in June 2023, his company had built revenue of its own and a force loyal to him personally, even though it had worked abroad for the Russian state. Most Chinese security contractors operating on African soil have focused on unarmed protection, training and coordination with local forces, and turning them into fighting units would run against the direction of Beijing's own reforms.

Guarding one mine is a limited task. Protecting dozens of sites across western Mali would require patrols, intelligence on the roads between them and some way of pursuing attackers when local troops were overwhelmed. Commanders would soon be deciding whether to fight beyond the sites they had been sent to protect, and a mission to guard workers could become a commitment to Bamako's war before anyone in Beijing had chosen to enter it.

Mali is one market among dozens. China-Africa trade reached $348 billion in 2025, a record, and Chinese companies work in countries with very different governments and security problems. Any serious abuse involving Chinese armed contractors in Mali could complicate Beijing's relations with other African governments, particularly where Chinese investments already face political or social opposition.

Mali's leaders have shaped this division of labour themselves. They turned to Russia for personnel willing to go into combat beside Malian units, and to China for equipment and training. On 2 September 2024, Mali signed an agreement with Norinco in the presence of Assimi Goïta. The deal covered defence equipment, training and technology transfer, reflecting Bamako's interest in strengthening the capabilities of its own armed forces. Russia also sells weapons and Chinese instructors train African armies, so the line is not clean, but Bamako has asked different things of each partner.

China's own security channels in Africa run through the state. At the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, Beijing pledged a 1 billion yuan military grant and training for 6,000 military personnel and 1,000 police officers. SIPRI's March 2026 figures show China supplying 22 percent of sub-Saharan Africa's major arms imports in 2021-25, ahead of Russia at 12 percent. China sent troops to the UN mission in Mali, where a Chinese peacekeeper was killed in Gao in 2016, and a year later opened its first overseas military support base, in Djibouti. China has accepted the risks of overseas military deployments through formal state and multilateral arrangements, without creating an autonomous force comparable to Wagner.

For Chinese workers operating in remote mining areas around Kenieba, protection remains heavily dependent on Malian forces that suffered heavy losses at Dioura and have struggled to secure such areas, and on locally hired guards whom their employers pay but do not command. If one of those guards fires on villagers near a Chinese-run site, residents will struggle to know whom to hold responsible: the guard, his commander, the contractor or the Chinese client. Deploying a Chinese combat force would bring Beijing much closer to the decisions made on the battlefield and the political consequences of those decisions.

The real test is whether these security partnerships make people living and working in Mali safer. The effectiveness of Beijing's approach will depend partly on whether Malian forces can secure transport routes and protect mining communities. If those forces remain unable to protect the roads and mining districts, Chinese workers and the Malian communities around them will continue to bear the consequences.

Göktuğ Çalişkan is a researcher and writer based in Morocco, working primarily on African geopolitics, the Sahel and security. He studied at the International University of Rabat, where he completed a master's degree examining China-Africa relations and the Belt and Road Initiative through the cases of Kenya and Uganda. He ais currently pursuing doctoral research there focused on security and political dynamics in the Sahel, particularly Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

headline: South Korea reviews expanding military mission in Middle East, report says

Seoul is weighing expanding the operational area of its Cheonghae anti-piracy unit, which was dispatched to the Gulf of Aden in 2009, to include the Gulf of Oman, which links to the Strait of Hormuz, the newspaper said, without naming sources.Here are details of the report:
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct 16 (Reuters) - South Korea is reviewing an expansion of its military operations in the Middle East, the Kyunghyang Shinmun newspaper reported on Thursday, as the US ally faces pressure from President Donald Trump to provide support for the war in Iran.

Seoul is weighing expanding the operational area of its Cheonghae anti-piracy unit, which was dispatched to the Gulf of Aden in 2009, to include the Gulf of Oman, which links to the Strait of Hormuz, the newspaper said, without naming sources.

Here are details of the report:

• The administration of President Lee Jae Myung plans to submit a motion to parliament to extend the unit's mission, which is set to expire at the end of this year, the report said.

• The government was also considering sending a frigate to the region to reinforce operations, the paper said.

• South Korea's Defence Ministry said in a statement to Reuters that the government was reviewing whether to send a motion to parliament on an extension of the unit's service before it expires on December 31, 2026.

• Nothing had been decided on details of the extension of the anti-piracy unit's operations, the ministry said.

• The situation in the Gulf of Aden was worsening with pirate activity up sharply from a year ago, the statement said.

• The Cheonghae unit currently includes a 4,400-ton-class destroyer, a maritime operations helicopter, up to three rigid-hull inflatable boats and around 300 service members, according to broadcaster YTN.

• Trump has criticised Seoul for what ​he called insufficient support for the Iran war and scaled back major joint military drills by the two countries' armed forces this summer, a move that unsettled the US ally.

• President Lee said on September 18 he would not deploy military ‌assets to the Middle East in a way that could draw the country into conflict, but said Seoul was reviewing whether to play a greater role in safeguarding navigation in the region.

(Reporting by Heejin KimEditing by Ed Davies)

headline: Keen on Make-in-India in defence, aerospace: Outgoing UK envoy Lindy Cameron
body_text:
This is AI Generated text to speech.

Calling India’s proposal for a ceasefire in the Black Sea region a “symbol” of a “big global player”, Lindy Cameron, the outgoing British High Commissioner to India, said Thursday that the UK has identified “defence, security and technology” as the pillars of bilateral ties and wants to participate in Make-in-India programmes in the defence and aerospace sector.

In an exclusive interview with The Indian Express, Cameron, who is set to become Permanent Under-Secretary of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office of the United Kingdom (equivalent to India’s Foreign Secretary), described the UK-India “trade deal” as the high point of her Delhi stint, the effort of “turning it into a wider and deeper relationship between the two countries, and really importantly seeing that as a future-facing relationship”.

On India’s proposal on the Russia-Ukraine war, she said, “For me, this symbolises that move by India to be a player in a wider conversation where, of course, India has an extraordinary and really diverse set of relationships to build on, some quite unique.” India has put forward a proposal to end attacks in the Black Sea region, and allow movement of grains.

On the defence sector, Cameron said, “The proudest moment I have is seeing Rolls Royce genuinely in a position to make an absolutely world-leading offer, not only best time to first flight, but also really amazing IP (intellectual property) transfer as a potential candidate for building India’s future combat jet engine.”

Asked about the change of guard in the UK — Keir Starmer making way for Andy Burnham — she said, “We have seen changes in UK politics, and that’s for politicians rather than me as a civil servant. But what’s been constant is the importance of India.”

On the friction points between the two countries, she said, “We have a relationship of depth and trust that means that the sore points are things we can discuss privately. We have tough conversations, but we have them in private, and we have them with friends.”

On the key learnings that she takes home, Cameron said, “I will take with me an understanding of India’s worldview. I think when you sit in Delhi, you sit in a different geography. You see the world from a different perspective. You see the world with a different history. You see the world with a different scale, actually, and that is all something that I will take with me to London. It’s probably part of why I got the job, in all honesty.”

She leaves India over the weekend, and will join as the Permanent Under-Secretary Monday.

Shubhajit Roy, Diplomatic Editor at The Indian Express, has been a journalist for more than 27 years now. Roy joined The Indian Express in October 2003 and has been reporting and writing explainers and analysis on foreign affairs for about 19 years now. Based in Delhi, he has also led the National government and political bureau at The Indian Express in Delhi — a team of reporters who cover the national government and politics for the newspaper. He has got the Ramnath Goenka Journalism award for Excellence in Journalism ‘2016. He got this award for his coverage of the Holey Bakery attack in Dhaka and its aftermath. He won the Ramnath Goenka Journalism award, 2023, for the second time for his reporting of the Oct 7 attacks on Israel and the war in Gaza. He also got the IIMCAA Award for the Journalist of the Year, 2022, (Jury’s special mention) for his coverage of the fall of Kabul in August 2021 — he was one of the few Indian journalists in Kabul and the only mainstream newspaper to have covered the Taliban’s capture of power in mid-August, 2021. ... headline: In the new world order, expect fewer alliances and more ‘pop-up partnerships’

It participates in the Quad alongside the US, Japan and Australia, maintains defence relationships with Russia, belongs to Brics and deepens economic ties with Europe and the Gulf. The UAE similarly combines Brics membership with extensive western security partnerships and growing commercial relationships through more than 30 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements across Europe, Asia and Africa.These arrangements are not necessarily contradictory. They reflect a world in which countries increasingly choose their partners according to the issue rather than their permanent geopolitical affiliation.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave this thinking a powerful expression at Davos earlier this year, arguing that middle powers must co-operate more deliberately because, as he put it, “if you are not at the table, you are on the menu”. The EU, GCC and the Association of South-East Asian Nations were largely built around regional proximity, whereas emerging partnerships increasingly reflect strategic interdependence. Brexit represented a decisive departure from institutional integration, yet the subsequent rebuilding of economic and security co-operation demonstrates that geography and mutual dependence cannot simply be legislated away. The debate over closer relations, including possible eventual re-entry, reflects a broader movement towards more selective forms of international co-operation.This is not necessarily the end of globalisation, but rather its rewiring. Strategic resilience increasingly means maintaining options rather than placing every national interest within a single alliance. In the future of international relations, every country will be permanently looking for new and better friends.This is an emerging model that can be described as “pop-up governance”: flexible partnerships formed around specific challenges, designed to achieve defined outcomes and time-bound and designed to potentially dissolve when their purpose was fulfilled. Traditional institutions such as the UN, EU, GCC and Asean will remain, although some may lose influence as governments seek faster and more targeted arrangements. Alongside them, we are likely to see a growing layer of pop-up alliances, organised around shared interests rather than geography, with clear objectives and sometimes explicit time limits.Some will address defence, geopolitical tensions or economic security. body_text:
“America has no permanent friends or enemies, only interests.” The observation, widely attributed to Henry Kissinger but originating with the British statesman Lord Palmerston, has long captured the logic of international relations. Nearly two centuries later, it may offer the clearest explanation of the new world order taking shape.

For much of the past century, international relations were organised around relatively permanent alliances, geographical blocs and established institutions. Countries joined international organisations, aligned themselves with major powers and accepted long-term commitments that extended beyond their immediate interests. Today, that architecture is being supplemented by something more fluid: temporary, purpose-driven coalitions that I would call “pop-up alliances”.

The emerging geopolitical advantage may no longer be choosing the right side, but retaining the ability to work with several sides.

India illustrates this new geopolitical a la carte menu. It participates in the Quad alongside the US, Japan and Australia, maintains defence relationships with Russia, belongs to Brics and deepens economic ties with Europe and the Gulf. The UAE similarly combines Brics membership with extensive western security partnerships and growing commercial relationships through more than 30 Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreements across Europe, Asia and Africa.

These arrangements are not necessarily contradictory. They reflect a world in which countries increasingly choose their partners according to the issue rather than their permanent geopolitical affiliation.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave this thinking a powerful expression at Davos earlier this year, arguing that middle powers must co-operate more deliberately because, as he put it, “if you are not at the table, you are on the menu”. His proposed approach of “variable geometry”, involving different coalitions for different issues, captures an important shift in how international influence is exercised.

Traditionally, great powers built alliances while smaller countries joined them. Increasingly, middle powers are becoming coalition entrepreneurs, bringing together countries around shared capabilities and interests. Influence depends not simply on military strength or economic size, but on the ability to mobilise capital, technology, energy, natural resources and market access.

For countries such as the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Canada, India and Indonesia, this creates opportunities to shape international co-operation rather than merely participate in structures designed elsewhere.

The logic also challenges the geographical foundations of traditional alliances. The EU, GCC and the Association of South-East Asian Nations were largely built around regional proximity, whereas emerging partnerships increasingly reflect strategic interdependence. Semiconductor supply chains connect Taiwan, South Korea, Japan, the Netherlands and the US, while critical minerals, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity create overlapping interests across continents.

The next geopolitical map may therefore be drawn less around borders and more around the supply chains, technologies and resources that countries cannot afford to lose.

Britain’s evolving relationship with Europe offers another revealing example. Brexit represented a decisive departure from institutional integration, yet the subsequent rebuilding of economic and security co-operation demonstrates that geography and mutual dependence cannot simply be legislated away. The debate over closer relations, including possible eventual re-entry, reflects a broader movement towards more selective forms of international co-operation.

This is not necessarily the end of globalisation, but rather its rewiring. Countries are reconsidering whom they depend on, for what purposes and under which conditions. Strategic resilience increasingly means maintaining options rather than placing every national interest within a single alliance. In the future of international relations, every country will be permanently looking for new and better friends.

This is an emerging model that can be described as “pop-up governance”: flexible partnerships formed around specific challenges, designed to achieve defined outcomes and time-bound and designed to potentially dissolve when their purpose was fulfilled. Traditional institutions such as the UN, EU, GCC and Asean will remain, although some may lose influence as governments seek faster and more targeted arrangements. Alongside them, we are likely to see a growing layer of pop-up alliances, organised around shared interests rather than geography, with clear objectives and sometimes explicit time limits.

Some will address defence, geopolitical tensions or economic security. Others will be more forward-looking, bringing together countries to develop water technologies, secure critical raw materials, co-ordinate specialised manufacturing capabilities or accelerate industrial innovation. A coalition formed to develop water desalination technologies, for example, might unite Gulf countries, Singapore, Australia and technology providers without requiring a broader political alliance.

Such flexibility carries risks. Temporary coalitions can weaken accountability, exclude smaller economies and undermine established international rules. Their effectiveness will depend on whether they complement permanent institutions rather than simply bypass them. Nevertheless, the direction of change is becoming clearer. The emerging international system may resemble a network of overlapping partnerships, some permanent and others temporary, in which countries co-operate where interests converge while accepting differences elsewhere.

Kissinger’s famous principle remains relevant, but its application is changing. National interests may be enduring, yet the alliances through which countries pursue them need not be. The next measure of diplomatic influence may be less about which alliances a country belongs to, and more about which alliances it has the capacity to create.

A business metaphor that casts middle powers in an active, enterprising light, implying initiative and agency rather than neutral description.
A vivid metaphor that frames selective alignment as consumer choice, making the practice sound pragmatic and appealing.
A technological metaphor that suggests globalisation is being upgraded rather than dismantled, subtly positive.

headline: Russia ready to boost oil deliveries to India on request
summary: Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Second Asian Department Alexey Pavlovsky emphasized that if there is such an interest, Russia stands ready to deliver
body_text:
KAZAN, October 16. /TASS/. Russia will not turn down India’s request should New Delhi seek additional oil deliveries, Director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Second Asian Department Alexey Pavlovsky told TASS in an interview on the sidelines of the 2nd Russian-Indian Business Forum "TIME: Tatarstan Initiative Mutual Efficiency."

When asked whether India was interested in securing additional oil supplies from Russia, he replied: "If there is such an interest, we stand ready to deliver."

The 2nd Russia-India Business Forum Time is taking place on October 14-17 in Kazan, the administrative center of Russia’s Volga Area region of Tatarstan. Forum participants are expected to discuss ways to carry out joint initiatives and promising investment projects, as well as prospects for technological and economic cooperation. TASS is the general information partner of the forum.

analysis.framing: The article frames Russia as a cooperative and willing energy supplier to India, presenting Moscow's readiness to deliver additional oil as a straightforward response to potential Indian interest.
omissions: No mention of Western sanctions on Russian oil or the price cap imposed by G7 and EU countries.
No mention of the broader geopolitical context of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and its impact on energy markets.
No mention of India's balancing act between Western pressure and its energy needs.
No mention of the volume or value of existing Russian oil deliveries to India.
No mention of any Indian government response or confirmation of interest.

headline: Finance minister calls for efforts to address global imbalances at G20 meeting
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 16 (Yonhap) -- Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il called for joint eff...
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct. 16 (Yonhap) -- Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il called for joint efforts to address shared economic challenges, including global imbalances, during meetings of financial policymakers in Bangkok, his office said Friday.

Lee attended a meeting of finance ministers from the Group of 20 (G20) nations in Thailand, on Thursday, held alongside the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy.

It marked the finance minister's first appearance at a major international gathering since taking office last month.

At the G20 meeting, Lee urged members to work together to address supply chain disruptions stemming from the Middle East war and identify new growth engines amid the emergence of technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI).

To this end, he stressed the need to strengthen supply chain resilience, protect vulnerable groups and invest proactively in future growth engines.

Participants also discussed key issues, including global imbalances, debt and ways to strengthen financial stability.

Global imbalances refer to a situation in which large current account surpluses in some countries lead to deficits in others.

Lee additionally thanked the United States for chairing this year's gathering and said South Korea would contribute to global economic stability and growth.

At the invitation of the Group of Seven (G7), Lee also attended a meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bank governors to discuss ways to address global imbalances.

He called for comprehensive macroeconomic policies and structural reforms to cope with such issues, stressing the need for cooperation within the G7 and with the broader G20 as well.

At a separate event bringing together finance ministers from G7 and African nations, Lee shared ideas on strengthening official development assistance (ODA) programs.

The minister said South Korea would serve as a reliable partner for African nations, noting investment and value creation are key drivers of sustainable growth, as demonstrated by the country's economic development experience.

In Bangkok, Lee held bilateral talks with his counterparts from Japan, Australia, Germany, Singapore and Britain, as well as the head of the Asian Development Bank (ADB).

In talks with his Australian counterpart, Jim Chalmers, Lee expressed hope for continued bilateral cooperation within multilateral frameworks, building on the two countries' experience as co-chairs of the G20 study group on global imbalances.

During a pull-aside meeting with German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, Lee outlined South Korea's AI projects, including its three-megaproject initiative.

Klingbeil reaffirmed the two countries' close partnership in areas ranging from manufacturing and critical minerals to supply chains and digital technology.

Talks with his British counterpart, John Healey, focused on prospects for closer cooperation as London prepares to assume the G20 presidency next year.

Other meetings included one with Indranee Rajah, Singapore's second minister for finance, during which the two officials discussed ways to strengthen bilateral and multilateral cooperation.

The meeting came as the two countries are set to co-chair the finance ministers' meeting involving the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and its three Northeast Asian dialogue partners -- South Korea, Japan and China -- next year.

Lee also asked Rajah to share Singapore's experience and expertise in operating the state-owned investment firm Temasek Holdings as South Korea plans to launch a strategic sovereign wealth fund. The finance ministry noted Rajah responded positively to the request.

In a meeting with ADB President Masato Kanda, Lee discussed cooperation in AI, critical minerals and nuclear energy, building on Kanda's visit to South Korea in September.

The minister asked the ADB to take an active role in translating their discussions into concrete projects, according to the finance ministry.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event through the official activities and statements of South Korea's finance minister, presenting a straightforward diplomatic readout of his G20 and bilateral meetings without critical analysis or alternative perspectives.

loaded_language.explanation: A positive, self-promotional diplomatic characterization rather than a neutral description of the relationship.
A mildly positive adverb that casts the minister's proposed approach as forward-leaning and energetic.
A vague, subjective characterization of another official's response, sourced from the ministry rather than directly observed.

omissions: No mention of any disagreements, criticisms, or unresolved tensions among G20 members regarding global imbalances.
No independent expert or economist commentary on the substance of the global imbalances discussion.
No details on what specific commitments, if any, G20 members made or failed to make.
No mention of other G20 members' positions or statements beyond South Korea's.

Write to us: Share your feedback on the news of the week

Promoting AI awareness

I write in reference to the article titled Dubai launches literacy platform to help parents guide children on safe use of AI (October 14): this is a commendable initiative. As AI continues to transform various aspects of our lives, it is essential to ensure that children understand both its benefits and its potential risks. Parents play a crucial role in helping their children navigate this rapidly evolving digital world by encouraging responsible usage, protecting their privacy, identifying misinformation and developing critical thinking skills. The UAE has demonstrated a keen interest in embracing and expanding the use of AI across various sectors. This initiative clearly reflects the country’s long-term vision of promoting AI awareness, digital literacy and technological advancement while prioritising the safety and well-being of younger generations. Equipping parents with the necessary knowledge and guidance is an important step towards building a society that can confidently and responsibly embrace emerging technologies. Such initiatives will not only benefit families but also contribute to preparing future generations for an AI-driven world. A commendable step by Dubai towards ensuring that technological progress goes hand in hand with awareness, responsibility and the safety of children. – K Ragavan, Bengaluru, India

A little knowledge ...

With regard to the article headlined Abu Dhabi launches major training programme to teach AI skills (October 7): raising awareness about AI is a great thing. What is not so great is when people attend a few workshops and emerge believing they have become AI experts. That is where things can become dangerous and counterproductive. AI projects can be costly and complex, requiring technical expertise, sound judgment and a depth of understanding that simply cannot be acquired in a week-long workshop. body_text:
The Gulf has sometimes been portrayed in the West as, until recently, a remote corner of the world, a place defined largely by its desert environment and the relative isolation of its communities. Two new exhibitions in Abu Dhabi museums suggest a different and more compelling account of the history of the region, namely, that far from being a peripheral place, the Gulf was a crossroads of commerce and culture – much like it is today.

At Louvre Abu Dhabi, a major exhibition about how the Indian Ocean connected communities from East Africa and the Arabian Peninsula to India, China and South-East Asia explores a millennium of maritime exchange through more than 200 objects. In December, the Zayed National Museum will explore more than 7,000 years of the camel’s place in the life on the Arabian Peninsula. Together, these exhibitions tell a story of land and sea that helps explain the UAE’s enduring role in connecting people and places.

The Louvre exhibition makes this history tangible. Six detailed ship models evoke the vessels that carried goods across the Indian Ocean. A third-century Buddha sculpture from Gandhara, in present-day Pakistan, offers another reminder that religious and artistic traditions travelled alongside commercial cargoes. The Gulf’s pearl industry was part of this wider network, linking its waters to markets and communities far beyond Arabia.

The camel exhibition will turn the focus inland. Bones dating to between 4500 and 4000BC, discovered at Baynunah in Abu Dhabi, provide evidence of an extinct wild camel species. Remains from Dubai’s Saruq Al Hadid illustrate the later relationship between humans and domesticated camels. Meanwhile, recordings of Taghrooda poetry and Alheda’a, the traditional practice of calling camels, demonstrate how deeply the animal remains embedded in Emirati cultural expression.

These exhibitions will present a reminder of how the people of the Gulf participated in networks of exchange and developed traditions suited to their environment. Such connections are still evident today. Ports remain vital to the UAE’s international trade, but are now complemented by aviation and rail links. The camel also endures with the animal featuring in racing, competitions and poetry – its place as part of the Emirates’ national identity is irreplaceable.

There is also a wider significance in the way these exhibitions tell their stories. Preserving heritage should mean more than celebrating familiar symbols or indulging in nostalgia. Understanding how the past shaped the present helps us today to recognise the complexity of the societies that preceded our modern times.

For anyone seeking to understand the UAE, exhibitions such as these are a good place to start. They represent a vital reminder that the country’s cosmopolitan outlook is not a recent invention, but part of a much longer history of exchange and encounter. In other words, they show how the Gulf embraced globalisation before the term even existed.

headline: German expert calls plans to limit gas transit to Kaliningrad 'well-calculated escalation'
summary: Foreign policy expert Sevim Dagdelen of the German BSW party believes that Estonia's actions are coordinated with its NATO allies
body_text:
BERLIN, October 16. /TASS/. Estonia’s plans to cut the alternative gas supply route to Russia’s Baltic exclave of Kalliningrad are "a well-calculated escalation," foreign policy expert Sevim Dagdelen of the German BSW party (formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance for Reason and Justice) said.

"The cutting of an alternative gas supply route to Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad, announced by NATO member country Estonia, is a yet another well-calculated escalation, apparently coordinated with the allies. Who will stop these madmen?!" she wrote on the X social network.

Earlier, the Eesti Ekspress newspaper reported that the backup transit of Russian natural gas to Kaliningrad via Estonia could be halted due to the political stance of the Baltic country’s government. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal announced his intention to initiate the decommissioning of the pipeline and will task officials with reaching an agreement on the matter with Latvia, which hosts the shut-off valve. If an agreement with Riga cannot be reached, the prime minister believes that it is possible to ban the transit on the basis of Estonia’s national sanctions, Eesti Ekspress said.

Russia utilizes the pipeline as a backup option for deliveries to Kaliningrad in accordance with an active, long-term contract.

The Russian government has repeatedly emphasized that attempts to isolate the Kaliningrad Region will prompt serious retaliatory measures.

body_text:
Dozens of Gazans who have been receiving medical treatment at Emirates Humanitarian City in Abu Dhabi are to return to their home country.

The humanitarian centre has been a refuge from the Israel-Gaza conflict for thousands of Palestinians since 2023, but many long to be reunited with their families back home.

Among them is 59-year-old Ibtisam Salout. She is preparing to return to Gaza in the coming days, after three years in the UAE. Ms Salout is a mother of nine and has 45 grandchildren.

Gazans in UAE struggle to sleep as nightmare continues back home

“The first thing I’ll do is gather them all and hold them tight. Yes, all of them," she says.

She checks her suitcases before checking them again: the dresses for her daughters, the chocolates for her grandchildren.

“The sneakers are for the boys. They sent me a photo and asked for these brands specifically," she says.

Ms Salout is from Deir Al Balah. She arrived in the UAE in 2023 for treatment. She had breast cancer and her treatment had been interrupted after October 7.

The UAE has provided medical treatment and comprehensive health care for 1,000 cancer patients and 1,000 injured children from the Gaza Strip.

“When I arrived, they began treatment immediately and discovered the cancer was also in my lymph nodes. They saved my life,” Ms Salout says.

Every patient is allowed an escort, but she does not have one.

“I didn’t bring anyone with me. My husband said, ‘You are in the safest country in the world, with the kindest people taking care of you. I would be more worried about you in Gaza. Get better and come back to us. I’ll stay with the children and wait for you.' ”

Today, she is cancer-free and ready to go back home to Gaza. “I’ll kiss its ground before running to my family," says Ms Salout.

Her house has been partially destroyed, but her husband and children continue to live there. “We fixed it up like we will fix Gaza,” she says.

Ms Salout is one of dozens of Palestinians who have completed their treatment and are heading back home. There remain close to 3,000 Gazans at the UAE’s Humanitarian City under treatment.

“The plan was always that they would return home once they completed their treatment, but it is hard to part with them after so many years. They have become our family," says Falah Al Qahtani, spokesperson for EHC.

A few Gazans have married at EHC, and others have had children. Younger children are enrolled in schools and nurseries, while adult Gazans are enrolled in online universities. Almost every week, there is a celebration at the complex: a birth, a birthday or a graduation.

“This is a bittersweet farewell. We are happy that they are heading back home. We are happy that they are happy and can go back, but they have also formed deep connections with us and the country.”

For Ms Salout, this is not goodbye.

“You have to come to Gaza. I’ll make you fatteh, and I make the best maftool. You can ask anyone,” she says with pride.

There are 30 people living with her but, she says; “I’ve told them to keep a clean room always ready for 'the Emirati'. Without them, I wouldn’t have been alive today.”

The EHC has served as a sanctuary for many of those affected by the violence of the war. The centre is part of the UAE's continuing humanitarian operations in solidarity with the Palestinians.

About medical 150 appointments are carried out each day within the vast complex, not including admissions to hospitals in Abu Dhabi for complex surgery.

A building at EHC has a pharmacy, clinics, a ward with hospital beds staffed by doctors, paediatricians, an internal medicine doctor, psychiatrists, dentists and a rehabilitation specialist.

The complex has a medical team of more than 50 doctors, nurses, therapists and administrators. There is also a school serving more than 400 children.

body_text:
BEIJING, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told Israeli President Isaac Herzog that Israel should stop and reverse its "forced establishment" of West Bank settlements, China's foreign ministry said in a statement on Friday.

China has consistently held that the Palestinian question is the greatest historical injustice of this century, Wang told Herzog during a meeting in Azerbaijan, the ministry added.

• Wang said that promoting peace and reconciliation in the region is the "cornerstone" of China's Middle East policy

• China believes that the "two-state solution" is the right path to a resolution and the immediate priority is to fully open access to the Gaza Strip so a humanitarian "catastrophe" is not allowed to spread, Wang added

• At the same time, Israel should stop and reverse its forced establishment of settlements in the West Bank, he said

• China is willing to work with the international community to push all parties to return to dialogue and consultation as soon as possible and seek a political settlement of the conflict, Wang added

• China has long been a supporter of the Palestinian cause and Beijing also has close ties with Israel's main regional foe, Iran

(Reporting by Beijing newsroom; Editing by Christian Schmollinger and Thomas Derpinghaus)

headline: Confrontation with Russia puts Europe on path of self-destruction — German lawmaker
summary: Maximilian Krah stressed that Germany should stop financially supporting Kiev and demand a compensation from Ukraine
body_text:
ANKARA, October 16. /TASS/. Europe is undermining its own future because of its confrontation with Russia and economic mismanagement, German lawmaker Maximilian Krah told Turkey’s Clash Report news portal in an interview.

Krah, who is a member of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party said the worst-case scenario for Germany would be if Chancellor Friedrich Merz takes the course towards confrontation with Moscow, triggers its response and then invokes wartime conditions to counter AfD.

"Merz is now a dangerous man because he has no hesitation about bringing all of Europe into war with Russia," the portal quoted him as saying.

Commenting on the situation in Ukraine, the lawmaker said Germany should stop financially supporting Kiev and demand a compensation from Ukraine. He views the Russia-US diesel fuel deal as a sign that the conflict in Ukraine is approaching its end.

Among economic problems that the European Union is facing at this point, Krah named the Greek bailout and a potential financial crisis in France, which may become a "decisive test for the European system."

He criticized a system in which Germany, in his view, "repeatedly accepts obligations that weaken its own position."

The lawmaker also commented on the economic situation in Germany and described his nation as "stagnant, lacking a credible vision for growth and operating at roughly its 2019 economic level."

The portal writes that the lawmaker doubts whether German carmakers Volkswagen, BMW, and Mercedes could be saved. In his view, at this point they cannot compete with China in the segment of electric vehicles.

headline: N. Korea reports opening of new cross-border bridge with China
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Yonhap) -- North Korea on Friday reported the opening of a new c...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 16 (Yonhap) -- North Korea on Friday reported the opening of a new cross-border bridge linking its border city of Sinuiju with China's Dandong, highlighting its potential to strengthen economic ties between the two countries.

The ribbon-cutting ceremony for the North Korea-China Amnok River Bridge was held the previous day, with senior officials from both countries attending, according to the North's Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).

"The bridge is the creation reflecting the invincible vitality and development of the DPRK-China friendship, which has preserved its nature despite the trials of history," the KCNA said, adding that the bridge would "enable the two countries to boost bilateral economic relations."

DPRK stands for North Korea's official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea,

China's Xinhua News Agency earlier reported the official opening of the bridge across the Amnok River, known as the Yalu River in China.

North Korean Premier Pak Thae-song and Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivered congratulatory speeches via video link, while Ri Ryong-nam, North Korea's ambassador to China, and Wang Yajun, China's ambassador to North Korea, attended the ceremony in person, the KCNA said.

Pak said the bridge would strengthen ties between the two peoples and "add fresh vigor to the equally-beneficial economic cooperation," according to the report.

Li reaffirmed China's commitment to its friendship with North Korea, saying Beijing would maintain its policy of prioritizing bilateral ties "no matter how the international situation may change," it added.

The four-lane bridge, stretching 3,026 meters, was completed over a decade ago in 2014 with an investment of about US$310 million from China. Its opening had been delayed for years due to North Korea's failure, if not refusal, to complete building connecting roads and customs facilities on its side.

Its opening comes as Pyongyang and Beijing seek to strengthen bilateral ties following a June summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping, at which they pledged to elevate relations to a strategic level and expand exchanges.

The bridge is expected to boost trade and the movement of people between the two countries, and ease congestion on the existing Friendship Bridge, which has served as the main crossing since opening in 1943.

headline: France and Germany agree to ease EU car emissions rules in new deal
summary: France and Germany have backed looser EU emissions rules for carmakers and agreed to include Britain in a “made in Europe” scheme, in a provisional deal reached Thursday that could reshape the bloc’s automotive and climate policies.
body_text:
France and Germany have backed looser EU emissions rules for carmakers and agreed to include Britain in a “made in Europe” scheme, in a provisional deal reached Thursday that could reshape the bloc’s automotive and climate policies.

Issued on: 16/10/2026 - 01:48

France and Germany have backed a further scaling down of EU emission rules for cars as part of a long-negotiated deal on the automotive industry struck Thursday, diplomatic sources confirmed to AFP.

Europe's two economic powerhouses also agreed to include Britain in the definition of what vehicles would count as "made in Europe" under EU measures aiming to bolster the bloc's industries, according to a draft document outlining the pact.

Paris and Berlin had long been at loggerheads on the course Europe should take as it seeks to revive its struggling auto industry and the accord is likely to shape the continent's policy going forward.

Germany wanted less stringent carbon emission targets for carmakers and a broad interpretation of "made in Europe" to include key non-EU trade partners.

France on the other hand had pushed to preserve the bloc's climate ambitions and to keep the "made in Europe" public procurement scheme the purview of EU nations.

Berlin won the first argument while Paris carried the day on the latter, the draft shows. The deal is provisional pending a final sign-off from Berlin, diplomats said.

The European Commission had proposed that the bloc's ban on sales of new petrol and diesel vehicles in 2035 be scrapped in favour of a requirement for manufacturers to cut new vehicle exhaust emissions by 90 percent.

The remaining 10 percent would have had to be compensated for through various credits obtained among other things by using low-carbon steel.

The Franco-German deal scraps the latter requirement, stating that residual emissions should not have to be compensated by manufacturers.

It also opens the door for cars running on renewable fuels to count as "zero-emission" and makes it much easier for automakers to reach CO2 targets.

So-called "super credits" the commission had suggested carmakers would benefit from for small "affordable" electric cars are extended to all vehicles "irrespective of their size or length".

The agreement on "made in Europe" restricts its application regarding cars to the EU's 27 countries, with an opt-in for a handful of others, notably Britain and Norway under certain conditions.

That is a narrower definition than the one proposed by the commission in March.

London hailed the move. If confirmed, it "would be good news for the British automotive industry and the jobs and investment it supports across the UK", the office of Prime Minister Andy Burnham said.

The EU executive had unveiled plans to tie companies' access to public money to minimum thresholds for EU-made parts in their products – to ensure that public and foreign investments support manufacturing inside the bloc.

But under Brussels' proposal, dozens of partner countries that have deals with the EU allowing European companies to access public money on a par with local firms could have been brought into the fold.

European carmakers had asked for Britain to be included, citing deeply integrated supply chains.

body_text:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's claim that last weekend's attacks on Russia's Yandex data centres led to a drop in Pro-Russian bot operations is causing debate.

The situation highlights the need to differentiate between bots, social media trolls and sophisticated influence operations, experts say.

Prof Olga Belogolova, director of the emerging technologies initiative at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies in Washington, wrote a long LinkedIn post to try to give context.

Prof Belogolova, who previously led policy at Meta against influence operations, said that too many people saw "what they wanted to see" with data from network and cloud infrastructure company Cloudflare.

"The story went viral when people started sharing a Cloudflare screenshot as proof of the silenced troll farms, as it showed a severe drop in bot traffic," she said.

"Their motivated reasoning made them see that the internet was cleaner, more friendly, less toxic.

"As someone who investigated and disrupted numerous malign influence operations and troll networks, I can also tell you that they do not often host their infrastructure on Yandex."

Prof Belogolova also said that far too many people were confusing and misusing tech terminology.

"Bots are importantly not trolls ... as many tech researchers have already pointed out, Cloudflare labels any non-browser, automated script as a bot," she said.

She said that when a data centre is taken offline, "its automated web-crawling and indexing traffic cuts out too".

Cloudflare Radar, a branch of the company, agreed that nuance was needed when looking at internet traffic data.

"Bot traffic refers to automated requests to websites on Cloudflare's network, such as crawlers and scripts, not necessarily activity on social media platforms," a post from Cloudflare Radar read, casting doubt on claims that Russia's social media trolls and disinformation campaign had been disrupted.

On Thursday, Cloudflare provided more clarity on the Ukrainian attacks on Russian data centres.

"Cloudflare data reveals that while search crawling stopped, malicious bots simply migrated to other networks," the company posted.

"There was no evidence that the strikes knocked social media manipulation offline or otherwise disrupted malicious activity on the internet."

Yet Prof Belogolova said that there were probably still ramifications faced by Russia after the data centre strikes.

"Kinetic strikes on Russian tech infrastructure may disrupt Russia's digital economy and cloud services," she said. "They are not exactly a precise tool for stopping foreign influence operations."

body_text:
The US on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver on Russian oil giant Lukoil, allowing its service operations outside the country to continue until April 2027, the Treasury Department announced.

Under the new general licence, Lukoil petrol stations will be able to serve customers until April 25, 2027. This includes petrol stations in the US, the department said. The waiver replaces a previous licence that was set to expire this month.

The licence prohibits the “transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation”, it reads. It also excludes transactions involving Russia's central bank, its national wealth fund and the Ministry of Finance.

US senators ask Trump to rescind 'disastrous' Russian diesel deal

In a separate licence, the Treasury Department also authorised certain transactions for Lukoil Bulgaria's firms in the same time period.

The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would allow Russia to supply diesel to the US and the global markets. The agreement deepened a rift between the US and its European partners, including Ukraine, and within Mr Trump's Republican Party.

Mr Trump said Russia would immediately release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tonnes released in November and a million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.

He also said Russia would release three million tonnes of fuel “within a short period of time” depending on the condition of the country's diesel refineries.

Oil prices remain high during the seven-month Iran war, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is significantly well below its prewar levels and as Iranian attacks continue in the waterway.

Futures for Brent global benchmark crude fell 0.27 per cent to settle at $105.8 a barrel on Thursday, with West Texas Intermediate futures gaining 2.76 per cent at $97.71 a barrel.

Diesel prices also remained elevated at $6.31 a gallon, compared to the average of $3.65 a gallon at the same time last year.

The International Energy Agency's governing board on Thursday said it would quicken the release of more than 20 million barrels of diesel and the remaining volumes of the 400 million barrels of emergency stocks of crude and other oil products previously agreed to in March.

The IEA said on Wednesday it expects oil market balances to remain in a deficit well into 2027.

“As the remaining buffers in the system continue to erode, in the absence of a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027,” it said.

headline: Time for US, EU and Ukraine to accept Kiev will have to make concessions — commentator
summary: Jennifer Kavanagh, an expert of the Washington-based think tank Defense Priorities, stressed that "Russia has significant advantages and the opportunity to press them over the coming months"
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 15. /TASS/. Ukraine, the US, and the EU must accept that Kiev will be forced to make painful concessions to resolve the crisis, and dragging out the conflict only worsens its position, said Jennifer Kavanagh, an expert of the Washington-based think tank Defense Priorities.

According to her, the current "half-hearted attempts" by the United States to de-escalate the Ukrainian crisis "come too late and are likely to fail. There is, however, something that Ukraine’s partners can do to help: start planning now for a serious push to end the war in 2027. To be successful, a future diplomatic campaign would have to look very different than past attempts to broker peace," Kavanaugh wrote in an opinion piece published on the website of the American magazine The American Conservative.

She said that the US, the EU, and Ukraine should come to terms with the fact that "more time will not fundamentally improve, and likely worsen, Ukraine’s negotiating position; and any peace will require painful and unpopular concessions by Kiev." Kavanagh said that "Russia has significant advantages and the opportunity to press them over the coming months."

Earlier, The Washington Post citing sources reported that Washington and Brussels are working on a joint peace proposal that would provide Russia and Ukraine with benefits in the areas of finance and security, and would also create a basis for resolving territorial disputes. It was noted that the draft agreement would consist of four points and would include Russia’s proposal to sign security and economics agreements with Europe to form the basis for stability in the region. According to the WP, the diplomatic impetus for developing a new settlement plan was provided at a meeting in Florida with the participation of American, European, and Ukrainian negotiators.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said that Moscow has not received any official proposals on "a peace plan" for Ukraine.

headline: Iran seeks to exclude Israel from conference on interaction and confidence-building
summary: Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi said that Tehran expects the CICA member states to adopt a principled and consistent approach to any military aggression based on international law
body_text:
TUNIS, October 15. /TASS/. Israel should be excluded from the Conference on Interaction and Confidence·Building Measures in Asia (CICA), Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, told the CICA summit in Baku, according to ISNA agency.

"The most important source of insecurity and instability in Asia, especially in the Western Asia region, is [Israel]. It is time to exclude [it] from the CICA mechanism," he said.

Gharibabadi said that Tehran expects the CICA member states to adopt a principled and consistent approach to any military aggression based on international law, regardless of who is the aggressor and who is the victim.

CICA is a multilateral dialogue format for discussing pressing regional issues and developing cooperation among the member states to boost trust in the military-political, economic, and humanitarian spheres, as well as in the area of new challenges and threats. The initiative to establish the conference was put forward in 1992 by Nursultan Nazarbayev, the then president of Kazakhstan. The CICA includes 28 countries and 15 observers.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Thursday accused Cuba of helping Iran and other adversaries to attack the US, as he announced sanctions against a Cuban state-owned bank claimed to have provided financial services to an Iranian lender.

Banco Internacional de Comercio has provided services to Iran’s Karafarin Bank since at least 2022, Mr Rubio said in a statement. The US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on Karafarin Bank in 2020.

“For too long, Communist Cuba has been allowed to operate as an outpost for malign actors and terror groups – including the Islamic Republic of Iran,” he said.

The designation was announced alongside Treasury Department measures against Iranian financial networks, as the US administration of President Donald Trump seeks to restrict Tehran’s access to international finance.

Mr Rubio said Washington would continue to identify and dismantle Cuba’s financial and security links with Iran and other states, and those it considers hostile.

headline: US imposes Iran-related sanctions on Iraq Development Bank
