The Treasury said the IDB has abused the now-dissolved dollar wire auction and maintains ties to Iran government entities and militia groups in Iraq.It is one of dozens of Iraqi banks that have been cut off for years due to concerns over sanctions evasion, money laundering and illicit finance. The US holds significant influence over Baghdad's financial policies because its international oil revenue is held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has sought to work with US authorities on the country's banking sector, which for years has been marred by corruption.Hiba Abdulwahib, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, said Thursday's move should not be viewed as a punishment for Iraq and it does not necessarily indicate that the US believes Mr Al Zaidi's government is unwilling to reform its banking sector."Authority in Iraq is fragmented," she said. "The government does not have effective control over every institution or economic actor operating inside the country. I believe Washington understands those limitations, especially when it comes to Iran’s networks in Iraq."Ms Abdulwahib also said she expected the pressure of sanctions to lead to more co-ordination on closer oversight, monitoring of suspicious activities and penalties for breaches. "Baghdad has an incentive to address these problems before Washington imposes further sanctions, and the banks themselves have to take that risk seriously," she said.In July, the Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence outlined a years-long plan that would eventually allow restricted Iraq banks to be reintegrated into the US dollar system. The process would include an initial phase of reforms from the Central Bank of Iraq, with the second phase consisting of a restricted bank completing the entire reform and licensing process. This would involve successfully undertaking a third-party audit of their compliance function, securing a qualified investor and meeting international standards. The department at the time said “no banned banks have regained access to foreign currency transactions”."The United States will not tolerate the abuse of Iraqi banks by Iran-aligned militia groups and will take independent action, if necessary, to target such activity,” it said.The move coincided with Mr Al Zaidi's visit to the US, where he had pledged to disarm militia groups in the country by September 30.In an interview with The New York Times in September, Mr Al Zaidi pushed that timeline to June 2027. body_text:
The Iraq Development Bank, among dozens of other targets, was hit with sanctions by the US on Thursday for its relations with Iran, the Treasury Department said in a statement.

The bank was one of 10 entities and 16 people hit in the latest round of sanctions under Washington's “Economic Outcast” programme. US President Donald Trump's administration has warned countries and companies that continue to do business with Iran would face significant consequences.

“Working with partners across the US government, the European Union, the United Kingdom, Gulf partners, and others, Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds,” the department said.

Saudi Crown Prince meets Iraqi PM in Riyadh after deadly Houthi airport attack

The Treasury has previously imposed sanctions on banks in Turkey and a Bank Melli branch in the UAE, among others. The UAE Central Bank last month banned Bank Melli Iran from conducting transactions between its branches in the UAE and Iran after an investigation.

Mr Trump's administration has hoped its “Economic Outcast” programme would sever Iran's remaining economic lifelines and force the regime to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

“The noose is tightening around Iran’s economy, and not even Iran’s so-called allies can save it,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.

Iraq in 2024 banned the IDB and seven other local commercial banks from engaging in US dollar transactions. The Treasury said the IDB has abused the now-dissolved dollar wire auction and maintains ties to Iran government entities and militia groups in Iraq.

It is one of dozens of Iraqi banks that have been cut off for years due to concerns over sanctions evasion, money laundering and illicit finance. The US holds significant influence over Baghdad's financial policies because its international oil revenue is held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has sought to work with US authorities on the country's banking sector, which for years has been marred by corruption.

Hiba Abdulwahib, an Iraqi researcher and analyst, said Thursday's move should not be viewed as a punishment for Iraq and it does not necessarily indicate that the US believes Mr Al Zaidi's government is unwilling to reform its banking sector.

"Authority in Iraq is fragmented," she said. "The government does not have effective control over every institution or economic actor operating inside the country. I believe Washington understands those limitations, especially when it comes to Iran’s networks in Iraq."

Ms Abdulwahib also said she expected the pressure of sanctions to lead to more co-ordination on closer oversight, monitoring of suspicious activities and penalties for breaches. "Baghdad has an incentive to address these problems before Washington imposes further sanctions, and the banks themselves have to take that risk seriously," she said.

In July, the Treasury's Office of Terrorism and Financial Intelligence outlined a years-long plan that would eventually allow restricted Iraq banks to be reintegrated into the US dollar system. The process would include an initial phase of reforms from the Central Bank of Iraq, with the second phase consisting of a restricted bank completing the entire reform and licensing process.

This would involve successfully undertaking a third-party audit of their compliance function, securing a qualified investor and meeting international standards. The department at the time said “no banned banks have regained access to foreign currency transactions”.

"The United States will not tolerate the abuse of Iraqi banks by Iran-aligned militia groups and will take independent action, if necessary, to target such activity,” it said.

The move coincided with Mr Al Zaidi's visit to the US, where he had pledged to disarm militia groups in the country by September 30.

In an interview with The New York Times in September, Mr Al Zaidi pushed that timeline to June 2027. The disarmament is a crucial part of how he is expected to manage Iraq's relations with the US and Iran.

US President Donald Trump on Thursday called off plans for a live-stream broadcast of the execution of a former US army psychiatrist who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009.

The plan to broadcast the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan was this month proposed by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, but was withdrawn after condemnation, including from within Mr Trump's own political circle.

In a post on Truth Social, Mr Trump said the execution by firing squad would proceed as planned but would not be broadcast live.

“I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the world to witness how America deals with terrorists and scum like Hasan," he wrote. "But many very good and well-meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming or through any other visual device.

“He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed.”

Mr Trump said the victims’ immediate families could witness the execution in person if they wished.

Hasan, a former major, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. He later described his shooting spree as retaliation for US wars in the ⁠Muslim world.

Now 56, the son of Palestinian immigrants was scheduled to be ​sent to Afghanistan before the shooting.

Hasan was left paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair after being shot ​by police during ‌his arrest.

Mr Trump initially said he had not been involved in the decision to broadcast the execution but understood its rationale.

“They want to do that because they want to set an example. I wasn't involved in that decision, but I understand the decision,” he said last week.

But the proposal drew scepticism and condemnation, including from figures in Mr Trump’s own circle.

Vice President JD Vance expressed reservations, saying he doubted the Pentagon would go ahead with the plan and that he would not watch if it did.

Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the Catholic Archdiocese for the Military Services, issued a statement questioning the morality and purpose of broadcasting the execution. He warned that it could cause “moral injury” to the service members carrying it out and called on Catholic soldiers assigned to the firing squad to seek an exemption.

“Do we really want to imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries? The crime committed by Nidal Malik Hasan was heinous, but does exposing the public to his execution serve any purpose?” he wrote.

The controversy has raised questions about the administration’s judgment and its approach to capital punishment, legal experts said, as Mr Trump faces increasing political pressure ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Mr Trump is dealling with low approval ratings as Americans increasingly blame him for rising costs and express disapproval of his handling of the war in Iran. On November 3, voters will decide which party controls Congress.

“It's nonsensical, the way this has developed. The administration is not playing with a full deck,” said Eugene Fidell, a military law expert at Yale Law School.

“This is totally tone-deaf. It's very revealing of how out of touch this administration is, and seemingly how little supervision there is."

Mr Fidell also said a public execution would have gone against international human rights standards.

The proposed use of a firing squad adds to the controversy. The US military has not carried out an execution by firing squad since 1945.

The debate comes as capital punishment and execution methods face renewed scrutiny. Last month, Christa Pike, who was convicted of killing a friend in the 1990s, survived a botched execution attempt in Tennessee involving lethal injection. She was left badly injured.

Daniel Urman, a constitutional law expert at Northeastern University, said Mr Hegseth and Mr Trump may have regarded the proposal as a way to project American strength but miscalculated the reaction it would provoke.

“It does capture the Trump administration in the second term, where it looks like there's been an impulsive plan set out that might get walked back and might end up being embarrassing for them,” he said.

“I think it's a headache he doesn't need. I think he's heard from members of his own party that it's a bad idea. And he needs his own party to stand by him.”

Hasan's execution is scheduled for December 3, and it is unclear if any legal challenges could delay it.

headline: Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen's Aden

The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government's interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.

The attack hit command centres located inside the Al-Maashiq presidential compound used by government forces and the Saudi-led military coalition that supports them, a Yemeni minister said on condition of anonymity.

Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognised Yemeni government it backs have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen's Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.

Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said Thursday's attack left five people dead and 16 injured "among those working to guard the site and civilian employees".

An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen's civil war flared back to life in July.

Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani denounced the "cowardly" act on X, calling it a "continuation of its criminal pattern of striking civilian sites and civilians".

A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Zindani had been present at the time, but "was not harmed in any way".

The minister said the Houthis hit a command centre for Yemeni government forces with three missiles, and another for Saudi-led coalition forces at the complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted "the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them".

Yemen's civil war -- in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 -- reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.

Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.

Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.

"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," said Dr. Rayed Krimly.

The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.

Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired "several ballistic missiles" at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.

In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.

The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.

"At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused," he added.

The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.

Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh's airport 20 times this month.

Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said "the Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure".

He added the group had "worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors", saying they now had "ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats".

The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country's infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.

Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.

In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation's population dependent on aid.

Israeli has continued attacks in southern Lebanon since early March, killed more than 4,300 people and displacing more than a million.

In June, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored framework agreement providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, as well as the disarmament of Hezbollah, among other provisions.

body_text:
Four people, including three children, have been killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon.

The attack in the city of Bend was carried out by a 16-year-old boy, police said. An armed bystander pursued the assailant into the school and shot him dead, officials added.

The children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A teacher was also killed. Another teacher and a ​seven-year-old pupil were taken to hospital with critical injuries, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said at a media conference.

The attacker entered the school by shooting through locked doors, police said, without ​offering ⁠any further details.

Oregon Governor Tina Kotek hailed the armed bystander who "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life" at Silver Rail Elementary School.

"No parent should have to have this kind of day, and no community should have to live through this kind of day," Ms Kotek said. "As we learn more about the children and the adults who have been killed or injured, and their families and their loved ones, we are going to do a lot of crying, and we are going to cry together, and we're probably going to cry privately."

Bend, in rural central Oregon, is home to about 100,000 people and is about 280km south-east of Portland.

Silver Rail Elementary School offers classes from kindergarten through to fifth ⁠grade – about ages five to 11 – and has about 450 pupils and 40 ⁠staff members, officials said.

Police said they received a call at about 1pm that indicated a man had shot into a car at Silver Rail Elementary School.

Moments later, emergency dispatchers received calls "reporting that a person had entered the school ​and began shooting", police said in a statement.

Officers arrived within three minutes and found that the suspect had been shot dead.

body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – The Iranian Foreign Ministry has strongly condemned Colombia’s decision to open an embassy in occupied al-Quds, describing the move as contrary to the United Nations Charter and the fundamental principles of international law.

In a statement released on Thursday evening, the ministry stressed that al-Quds is an inseparable part of Palestinian territory and said Colombia must accept responsibility for the consequences of its decision.

“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran strongly condemns the Colombian government’s action in opening an embassy in occupied al-Quds and considers it contrary to the Charter of the United Nations and the fundamental principles of international law,” it said.

“Al-Quds is an inseparable part of Palestinian territory, and all states are obligated under international law to refrain from any action that amounts to recognition of the Israeli regime’s occupation,” the ministry stated.

“Undoubtedly, the alignment of Colombia’s current governing authorities with an occupying and genocidal regime, and the legitimization of the occupation of Palestinian territory, stand in clear contradiction to the aspirations for independence and justice that have shaped a significant part of the history of the struggles of the people of Colombia and Latin America,” the statement said.

headline: If Iran rights not respected, Hormuz Strait to remain closed
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Army Commander-in-Chief Major General Amir Hatami has said should the inalienable rights of the Iranian nation are not observed, restrictions regarding passage through the Strait of Hormuz will continue.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Army Commander-in-Chief Major General Amir Hatami has said should the inalienable rights of the Iranian nation are not observed, restrictions regarding passage through the Strait of Hormuz will continue.

He made the remarks at the closing ceremony of the 11th National Itikaf (Religious & Spiritual Seclusion with Divine) Congress and 8th International Scientific, Literary and Artistic Itikaf Festival, held at Imam Ali (AS) Officers’ Academy’s Mosque in Tehran late on Thursday, emphasizing that if enemy fails to respect the rights of the Irania nation, restrictions will continue in the Strait of Hormuz.

Mejor General Hatami termed four pillars of Iran’s power as: "people, the Armed Forces, the governance structures, and its geopolitical position", stressing that all these components have caused the enemy’s calculations to completely fail.

Referring to the role played by the noble people of the country during the early days of the outbreak of war imposed by US and Israel against the country, he added, “Relying on their own capabilities, the noble nation of the Islamic Iran entered the fray spontaneously and this issue has also been emphasized by Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei.”

He stressed that the strait is under the complete supervision of Iran’s armed forces. The western section is managed by the IRGC Navy, while the eastern section and the Sea of Oman are controlled by the Army Navy. Claims that the waterway is open are false, he said. Traffic has been sharply restricted, and no hostile vessel has been able to enter Iranian maritime zones in the area except for a few that were engaged with multiple firings.

Generally speaking, people played a leading and outstanding role, in the war imposed against the country, in thwarting the enemies’ miscalculations and plots, the Army chief commander highlighted.

Hatami termed the Armed Forces as the second component of the country's power, stating, "The Armed Forces responded to the enemy with full force, and in the very early hours of the war, salvoes of missiles were fired towards the enemy’s positions.”

The Army of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) continued their operations despite the martyrdom of a large number of commanders and officials and these events did not hinder the ongoing operational activities of the Armed Forces, General Hatami emphasized.

Should the enemy fail to respect the rights of the Iranian nation, restrictions regarding passage through the Strait of Hormuz will continue, he reiterated.

Iranian forces seized operational control of the Strait of Hormuz in response to the start of the US-Israeli aggression on February 28. Tehran has repeatedly stated that coordinated passage is possible only for non-hostile vessels after authorization from Iranian authorities, while hostile shipping linked to the aggressors remains barred. Illegal routes created by violators have also been targeted for closure.

headline: Pezeshkian arrives in Armenia for Intl. Biodiversity Summit
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has arrived in Armenia’s capital of Yerevan to attend the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17).
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has arrived in Armenia’s capital of Yerevan to attend the 17th Summit of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP 17).

Pezeshkian arrived on Friday for the summit, which brings together participating heads of state and government.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei added that Pezeshkian was also scheduled to hold talks and exchange views with some of the participating leaders on the sidelines of the summit.

Explaining the convention’s significance, Baghaei said the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity was established in 1992 and currently has 196 parties. He noted that all countries except the United States are parties to the convention.

Baghaei said that Iran was among the convention’s original signatories and officially became a party to it in 1996. Over the past three decades, he said, Iran has played an important role in developing mechanisms and rules for protecting biodiversity and the environment.

The spokesman also highlighted the environmental damage inflicted on Iran and the wider region during the US and Israeli regime’s military aggression against Iran.

headline: Radicals seek to spread threats to Central Asia, Russia via Afghanistan — Lavrov
summary: The Russian foreign minister said the main threat comes from militants of the Islamic State-Khorasan Province group, a regional branch of the international terrorist organization Islamic State, which is outlawed in Russia
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 16. /TASS/. Radicals seek to use Afghanistan as a springboard for spreading threats to Central Asia and Russia, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.

"We take note of the fact that, according to available data, terrorist and extremist groups maintain a significant presence in Afghanistan’s areas bordering Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, where they have training camps and strongholds. Members of these groups seek to infiltrate Central Asian countries, particularly disguised as refugees and even tourists," he pointed out, addressing a conference on security issues in Central Asia and Afghanistan involving the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO).

"According to our estimates based on intelligence data, the main threat comes from militants of the Islamic State-Khorasan Province group, a regional branch of the international terrorist organization Islamic State, which is outlawed in Russia. It openly pursues the goal of undermining the Kabul government’s ability to maintain stability in the country," Lavrov went on to say.

"Besides, radicals also seek to use Afghanistan as a kind of springboard for spreading terrorist activities to both Central Asia and Russia. The Terrorist International (I can think of no other way to describe it), which is based on the other bank of the Panj River unites militants of Central Asian, North Caucasian and Uyghur origin who gained combat experience in armed raids in the Middle East and Africa, as well as preachers of radical Islamic ideas, clandestine madrasas and propaganda resources in the information field, especially on social media," the top Russian diplomat added.

headline: S. Korea, U.S. hold first 2+2 meeting of finance, monetary policymakers
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 16 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and the United States held their first ...
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct. 16 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and the United States held their first "two-plus-two" meeting of finance and monetary policymakers on the sidelines of a Group of 20 (G20) ministerial gathering to strengthen coordination in responding to external uncertainties, the finance ministry said Friday.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il and Bank of Korea (BOK) Gov. Shin Hyun-song met with U.S. Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh and U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Francis Brooke in Bangkok, where the G20 finance ministers' meeting was taking place, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy.

The participants exchanged views on recent economic developments and ways to enhance bilateral economic and financial cooperation.

Lee said the meeting was meaningful as it marked the first time the two countries had brought together senior officials from both their respective finance and monetary authorities.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not attend the Bangkok event.

An official from the finance ministry said the meeting aimed to enhance coordination between the two countries' finance and monetary authorities.

"The meeting was aimed at enhancing the policy mix of the two countries' financial and monetary policies," the official said.

"It is significant that the two countries have established a framework for cooperation to promptly and effectively address external financial uncertainties through close coordination between their finance and monetary authorities," the official added.

Lee is currently in Bangkok to attend the G20 finance ministers' meeting and the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group. It is his first overseas trip as finance minister since taking office last month.

headline: Belgium to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year, says premier
summary: Bart De Wever, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky also discuss possibility of Belgium supplying ammunition for jets
body_text:
Belgium will deliver ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year to help strengthen its defense capabilities, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said Thursday.

Speaking at a press conference following the first day of an EU summit in Brussels, De Wever said he discussed Ukraine's military needs with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the summit.

"We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine," De Wever said.

He stressed that Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets, describing F-16s as among the few weapons capable of effectively defending against "Russian jet-powered drones."

De Wever added that the two leaders also discussed the possibility of Belgium supplying ammunition for the F-16s, including some manufactured by Belgian defense company FN Herstal.

The leaders also discussed Ukraine's funding needs, although De Wever did not elaborate on the possibility of using frozen Russian assets held largely at Belgian-based Euroclear to support Ukraine.

Belgium previously opposed a proposal to use the frozen assets to finance a reparations loan for Ukraine, citing potential legal and financial risks.

headline: China urges Japan to face history over Yasukuni Shrine enshrinement of Class-A war criminals
summary: The Japanese government at the time knew full well the disgrace of enshrining Class-A war criminals and, fearful of the consequences, deliberately kept the decision-making process secret, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Friday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- The Japanese government at the time knew full well the disgrace of enshrining Class-A war criminals and, fearful of the consequences, deliberately kept the decision-making process secret, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Friday.

Mao made the remarks in response to a question about Japanese media reports disclosing internal meeting minutes of Yasukuni Shrine that revealed the decision-making process behind the enshrinement of 14 Class-A war criminals, including Hideki Tojo.

These Class-A war criminals were the chief culprits behind Japanese militarists' war of aggression, with the blood of innumerable war victims on their hands. The solemn verdict of the Tokyo Trials condemned them to perpetual infamy, thereby upholding international justice and laying the legal foundation for the postwar international order, Mao said. "Yet those running the Japanese government have again and again paid respects to what is in fact a shrine to war criminals. One has to ask: where has the conscience gone?"

History shall not be rewritten, and truth shall not be erased, she added. Japan committed undeniable crimes during its militarist aggression. Those running the Japanese government must face history squarely, reflect on the war crimes, and make a genuine break with its militarist past, Mao concluded.

headline: The fearless ambition of Mohamed Faisal Mostafa
summary: On the set of Dune: Part Three, Mohamed Faisal Mostafa watched closely as Timothee Chalamet, Zendaya and Jason Momoa prepared for their scenes. Each day, he saw how they learnt their lines, how they worked, how they treated the people around them. The Emirati actor wanted to reach that level himself, and here he could see what it took.“I sat back and I saw it all and I said to myself: ‘This is not unattainable.’ I can be there and, inshallah, I will be there so long as I keep consistent,” he says. Mostafa joined the production as a stunt performer. Director Denis Villeneuve knew he also acted and began finding opportunities for him to do more on camera.As the shoot was coming to an end, Mostafa went up to thank him for his support. “He said: ‘Mohamed, there’s no need to thank me. You’re a natural. You’re a very talented actor.’”Even recounting it now gives Mostafa goosebumps. He holds out his arm to show them. It was a moment he’d been ready for nearly his whole life. Long before he worked with Villeneuve, a young Mostafa was jumping off a moving bicycle for his brother, director Ali Mostafa.Ali was making home movies, and Mostafa was already fearless, at the age of six or seven, in front of his brother’s camera. As Ali kept making films, Mostafa kept helping. That bond is still strong decades later – every year on Ali’s birthday, he calls him “my brother, my teacher and my friend”.But for years, film was one of several possible futures. Mostafa played professional football, worked in finance, ran a digital transformation agency and was involved in his family’s business. Acting fitted around those pursuits, even as the parts grew bigger and took him further from home. He could keep building a career in business, with success nearly certain. But something in him knew he had to choose the harder path.“I think you need to find an area of focus if you want to succeed,” he says. Dedicating himself to film full time makes the auditions his UK agent sends him feel more consequential. A major production could give him the credit that leads to another job, then another. Yet a few lines are sometimes enough for him to turn one down. Even now, terrorists and other stereotypical Arab characters keep coming his way from major studios and streaming platforms, offering a route into the industry he has chosen to depend on.“Trust me, it is not easy to say no to these because some of them are massive, life-changing projects,” he says. “I love acting, and it’s the only thing I do right now. It’s also what’s going to generate me income, put food on my table and support my future.”But he has to consider what accepting a part would mean beyond his own career. He is willing to play a villain; the concern is a story that leaves an audience with another reason to distrust Arabs. He wants the roles he earns to expand what people understand about Emiratis and Muslim Arabs. He carries the responsibility for his country’s reputation as personally as he does for his own family’s.“It’s part of who I am,” he says. “It’s every action I do in the morning, when I wake up. I want to prove something to my family, my country, our leaders, myself.”There is a chance to take that work further at home, too. Dune: Part Three reaches cinemas this December and Dubai International Film Festival will return on December 8 after a decade-long hiatus. Mostafa has established MFM Media in Abu Dhabi, working on production services, product placement and Emirati talent management. He wants to help to get films made and give other performers the connections he struggled to find.DIFF’s return gives that ambition a place to develop, bringing filmmakers, actors and investors together in Dubai. Mostafa wants the next Emirati actor pursuing an international career to have more help and more work available here before setting off.His own route into film took years to become clear. As a goalkeeper for Al Ain and Al Wasl, Mostafa turned his childhood love of football into a career before serious injuries ended it. His work with Ali continued as his brother moved into feature films, casting Mostafa in City of Life (2009) and From A to B (2014), then giving him a larger role in the post-apocalyptic thriller The Worthy (2016). Mostafa also appeared in the Emirati military action film Al Kameen (2021), one of the biggest box-office hits the country has produced.An open audition in London for Disney’s live-action Aladdin (2019), which eventually starred Mena Massoud and Will Smith, gave Mostafa a glimpse of how far acting might take him. He did not get the role. At the time, he carried on with other pursuits, but the possibility stayed with him: he had put himself forward for a production watched around the world, in which he could have represented the UAE.“I realised that this can actually happen, and that I love acting and I’m not bad at it. So I had to keep going,” he says.Finding an agent in Britain involved repeated approaches and rejections. When Hijack – the Apple TV thriller also starring Idris Elba – came, Mostafa finally had an international role to prepare for. He would play Abdullah, a Dubai air-traffic controller investigating suspicious events around a flight to London.A driver collected him from a friend’s house on his first day of filming. During the journey, Mostafa questioned whether he was good enough to be there. Once he arrived, the more experienced actors treated him as an equal, and director Jim Field Smith welcomed his contributions. Mostafa helped with details of Emirati behaviour, including the way people hold their hands when greeting one another.He realised the pressure was helping him perform – a feeling he recognised from his years on the football field.“There’s nerves, but they’re nice nerves – the nerves that lock you in,” he said when Hijack was released in 2023.The 2024 television drama Khattaf asked more of him. Ali gave him a lead role to carry through a whole series, playing an Emirati fighter making his way through Asia’s underground combat scene. The boy who had done stunts for his brother now had years of sport and Muay Thai training behind him when stunt co-ordinator Najmeddin Scorpion began teaching him fight choreography.One move, known as the Black Widow, required Mostafa to hook a leg around another performer’s neck, swing around him and land on his own feet as the other man flipped away. He learnt quickly. An injury left his elbow so swollen it had to be bandaged, but his character was supposed to be injured in the next fight scene. The bandage stayed on for the camera – the injury served the scene, and that’s all that mattered to him.Away from the fight choreography, Mostafa was working out the character’s childhood and family relationships, comparing them with his own. He wanted to understand the parents, how they had become the people they were, and how their behaviour had shaped their son. Early in the shoot, he drew on painful memories from his own life when a scene required him to cry. By the time he filmed a sequence in prison, he had spent enough time with the character to find the emotion in his story.“I wasn’t thinking for a second about Mohamed. I was thinking about Khattaf, and I had tears rolling down my face, and I felt and I became,” he says. “That’s what acting is. Acting is becoming.”Talking about that scene brings out the goosebumps again. Mostafa wants another role he can spend that kind of time on, and another production willing to put him at the centre of its story. The ambition to join the main cast of a Hollywood film now comes with a clearer understanding of what he would want to do once he got there.Between Hijack, Khattaf and Dune, he has accumulated experience that has prepared him for the next step. He is grateful for each opportunity, although he has started to question how often he describes himself as lucky. It can leave out the work that earned him a place on those sets. “At some point, you have to realise you’re there for a reason. You were chosen,” Mostafa says.Alongside that confidence, his faith shapes what he wants to do with the opportunities he earns. Mostafa has grown up seeing words he uses in his religious life associated with violence in western news and films. They belong to his everyday experience of gratitude and service, and he wants audiences to understand what they mean to him.“Allahu akbar is the most beautiful term,” he says. “The direct definition of it is God is the greatest. No matter what happens in our life, we constantly remind ourselves that this is God’s plan, and He is greatest.”Holding a door open for someone is among the examples Mostafa gives when explaining his understanding of jihad. “Any act of service, any sacrifice, whether it’s small or big, is jihad.”Those words are part of the steadfast identity he carries into each audition. A role that reinforces their association with violence has consequences for him beyond the time he would spend playing it. He has to trust that there will be another opportunity after the one he declines. “When you walk with your value system intact, you might be saying no to those things. But I have this faith in God that other things will come that are much bigger.”Waiting for the right part leaves much of that future in other people’s hands. With support from Abu Dhabi’s Creative Media Authority, Mostafa established MFM at Yas Creative Hub, putting his business experience to work in film.“I can’t just be an actor with an agent in London waiting for auditions,” he says. “I have to create my movies. I need to collaborate.”The work he had been dividing his time between could now support his ambitions in film. Mostafa had arranged sponsorships for fighters and concerts; he could bring brands into productions and draw on his finance background in discussions with investors. The difficulties he had faced in finding representation gave him a reason to help other Emirati performers approach the industry.Mostafa takes a sip of coffee, holds it up, and suggests it might be one of the best he has had. “Just a little product placement,” he jokes. Behind the brand partnerships, however, is a struggle familiar to the filmmakers who approach MFM.“The biggest problem I’m seeing is funding,” Mostafa says. He is working to explain the film business to investors who are more familiar with property and technology, taking them through production costs, distribution and incentives. He expects it to take years.When City of Life had its premiere at DIFF in 2009, Mostafa watched the industry gather around his brother’s debut feature. When the festival returns, he will have a company to bring into those conversations, as well as his own ambitions as an actor. Finding the money for a film could give several performers their next job, and the time on set they need to improve.He saw how quickly that possibility could take hold on Dune. Fellow Emirati Rashed Dawood, a mixed martial arts fighter, was working on his first film as a stunt performer. Dawood discovered how much he enjoyed being on set and wanted to do it again. For him to develop that interest into a career, there would have to be another production, and another after that.“We’re not going to have a Dune come every year. We need to work on and scale up independent filmmaking,” Mostafa says.Mostafa needs the next production, too. He wants another chance to get as deeply into a character as he did in Khattaf. He is working to help get those films made, while pursuing the roles he believes he can carry.“I’m confident enough to know I can be in a blockbuster film as one of the main cast,” he says. “I just need to keep pushing, but I know I can do it.”The fearlessness that put him in front of Ali’s camera has stayed with him. Now Mostafa wants to take it into a role where audiences around the world will see an Emirati actor leading the story. body_text:
On the set of Dune: Part Three, Mohamed Faisal Mostafa watched closely as Timothee Chalamet, Zendaya and Jason Momoa prepared for their scenes. Each day, he saw how they learnt their lines, how they worked, how they treated the people around them. The Emirati actor wanted to reach that level himself, and here he could see what it took.

“I sat back and I saw it all and I said to myself: ‘This is not unattainable.’ I can be there and, inshallah, I will be there so long as I keep consistent,” he says. Mostafa joined the production as a stunt performer. Director Denis Villeneuve knew he also acted and began finding opportunities for him to do more on camera.

As the shoot was coming to an end, Mostafa went up to thank him for his support. “He said: ‘Mohamed, there’s no need to thank me. You’re a natural. You’re a very talented actor.’”

Even recounting it now gives Mostafa goosebumps. He holds out his arm to show them. It was a moment he’d been ready for nearly his whole life. Long before he worked with Villeneuve, a young Mostafa was jumping off a moving bicycle for his brother, director Ali Mostafa.

Ali was making home movies, and Mostafa was already fearless, at the age of six or seven, in front of his brother’s camera. As Ali kept making films, Mostafa kept helping. That bond is still strong decades later – every year on Ali’s birthday, he calls him “my brother, my teacher and my friend”.

But for years, film was one of several possible futures. Mostafa played professional football, worked in finance, ran a digital transformation agency and was involved in his family’s business.

Acting fitted around those pursuits, even as the parts grew bigger and took him further from home. He could keep building a career in business, with success nearly certain. But something in him knew he had to choose the harder path.

“I think you need to find an area of focus if you want to succeed,” he says. Dedicating himself to film full time makes the auditions his UK agent sends him feel more consequential.

A major production could give him the credit that leads to another job, then another. Yet a few lines are sometimes enough for him to turn one down. Even now, terrorists and other stereotypical Arab characters keep coming his way from major studios and streaming platforms, offering a route into the industry he has chosen to depend on.

“Trust me, it is not easy to say no to these because some of them are massive, life-changing projects,” he says. “I love acting, and it’s the only thing I do right now. It’s also what’s going to generate me income, put food on my table and support my future.”

But he has to consider what accepting a part would mean beyond his own career. He is willing to play a villain; the concern is a story that leaves an audience with another reason to distrust Arabs. He wants the roles he earns to expand what people understand about Emiratis and Muslim Arabs. He carries the responsibility for his country’s reputation as personally as he does for his own family’s.

“It’s part of who I am,” he says. “It’s every action I do in the morning, when I wake up. I want to prove something to my family, my country, our leaders, myself.”

There is a chance to take that work further at home, too. Dune: Part Three reaches cinemas this December and Dubai International Film Festival will return on December 8 after a decade-long hiatus.

Mostafa has established MFM Media in Abu Dhabi, working on production services, product placement and Emirati talent management. He wants to help to get films made and give other performers the connections he struggled to find.

DIFF’s return gives that ambition a place to develop, bringing filmmakers, actors and investors together in Dubai. Mostafa wants the next Emirati actor pursuing an international career to have more help and more work available here before setting off.

His own route into film took years to become clear. As a goalkeeper for Al Ain and Al Wasl, Mostafa turned his childhood love of football into a career before serious injuries ended it.

His work with Ali continued as his brother moved into feature films, casting Mostafa in City of Life (2009) and From A to B (2014), then giving him a larger role in the post-apocalyptic thriller The Worthy (2016). Mostafa also appeared in the Emirati military action film Al Kameen (2021), one of the biggest box-office hits the country has produced.

An open audition in London for Disney’s live-action Aladdin (2019), which eventually starred Mena Massoud and Will Smith, gave Mostafa a glimpse of how far acting might take him. He did not get the role. At the time, he carried on with other pursuits, but the possibility stayed with him: he had put himself forward for a production watched around the world, in which he could have represented the UAE.

“I realised that this can actually happen, and that I love acting and I’m not bad at it. So I had to keep going,” he says.

Finding an agent in Britain involved repeated approaches and rejections. When Hijack – the Apple TV thriller also starring Idris Elba – came, Mostafa finally had an international role to prepare for. He would play Abdullah, a Dubai air-traffic controller investigating suspicious events around a flight to London.

A driver collected him from a friend’s house on his first day of filming. During the journey, Mostafa questioned whether he was good enough to be there. Once he arrived, the more experienced actors treated him as an equal, and director Jim Field Smith welcomed his contributions. Mostafa helped with details of Emirati behaviour, including the way people hold their hands when greeting one another.

He realised the pressure was helping him perform – a feeling he recognised from his years on the football field.

“There’s nerves, but they’re nice nerves – the nerves that lock you in,” he said when Hijack was released in 2023.

The 2024 television drama Khattaf asked more of him. Ali gave him a lead role to carry through a whole series, playing an Emirati fighter making his way through Asia’s underground combat scene. The boy who had done stunts for his brother now had years of sport and Muay Thai training behind him when stunt co-ordinator Najmeddin Scorpion began teaching him fight choreography.

One move, known as the Black Widow, required Mostafa to hook a leg around another performer’s neck, swing around him and land on his own feet as the other man flipped away. He learnt quickly. An injury left his elbow so swollen it had to be bandaged, but his character was supposed to be injured in the next fight scene. The bandage stayed on for the camera – the injury served the scene, and that’s all that mattered to him.

Away from the fight choreography, Mostafa was working out the character’s childhood and family relationships, comparing them with his own. He wanted to understand the parents, how they had become the people they were, and how their behaviour had shaped their son. Early in the shoot, he drew on painful memories from his own life when a scene required him to cry. By the time he filmed a sequence in prison, he had spent enough time with the character to find the emotion in his story.

“I wasn’t thinking for a second about Mohamed. I was thinking about Khattaf, and I had tears rolling down my face, and I felt and I became,” he says. “That’s what acting is. Acting is becoming.”

Talking about that scene brings out the goosebumps again. Mostafa wants another role he can spend that kind of time on, and another production willing to put him at the centre of its story. The ambition to join the main cast of a Hollywood film now comes with a clearer understanding of what he would want to do once he got there.

Between Hijack, Khattaf and Dune, he has accumulated experience that has prepared him for the next step. He is grateful for each opportunity, although he has started to question how often he describes himself as lucky. It can leave out the work that earned him a place on those sets. “At some point, you have to realise you’re there for a reason. You were chosen,” Mostafa says.

Alongside that confidence, his faith shapes what he wants to do with the opportunities he earns. Mostafa has grown up seeing words he uses in his religious life associated with violence in western news and films. They belong to his everyday experience of gratitude and service, and he wants audiences to understand what they mean to him.

“Allahu akbar is the most beautiful term,” he says. “The direct definition of it is God is the greatest. No matter what happens in our life, we constantly remind ourselves that this is God’s plan, and He is greatest.”

Holding a door open for someone is among the examples Mostafa gives when explaining his understanding of jihad. “Any act of service, any sacrifice, whether it’s small or big, is jihad.”

Those words are part of the steadfast identity he carries into each audition. A role that reinforces their association with violence has consequences for him beyond the time he would spend playing it. He has to trust that there will be another opportunity after the one he declines. “When you walk with your value system intact, you might be saying no to those things. But I have this faith in God that other things will come that are much bigger.”

Waiting for the right part leaves much of that future in other people’s hands. With support from Abu Dhabi’s Creative Media Authority, Mostafa established MFM at Yas Creative Hub, putting his business experience to work in film.

“I can’t just be an actor with an agent in London waiting for auditions,” he says. “I have to create my movies. I need to collaborate.”

The work he had been dividing his time between could now support his ambitions in film. Mostafa had arranged sponsorships for fighters and concerts; he could bring brands into productions and draw on his finance background in discussions with investors. The difficulties he had faced in finding representation gave him a reason to help other Emirati performers approach the industry.

Mostafa takes a sip of coffee, holds it up, and suggests it might be one of the best he has had. “Just a little product placement,” he jokes. Behind the brand partnerships, however, is a struggle familiar to the filmmakers who approach MFM.

“The biggest problem I’m seeing is funding,” Mostafa says. He is working to explain the film business to investors who are more familiar with property and technology, taking them through production costs, distribution and incentives. He expects it to take years.

When City of Life had its premiere at DIFF in 2009, Mostafa watched the industry gather around his brother’s debut feature. When the festival returns, he will have a company to bring into those conversations, as well as his own ambitions as an actor. Finding the money for a film could give several performers their next job, and the time on set they need to improve.

He saw how quickly that possibility could take hold on Dune. Fellow Emirati Rashed Dawood, a mixed martial arts fighter, was working on his first film as a stunt performer. Dawood discovered how much he enjoyed being on set and wanted to do it again. For him to develop that interest into a career, there would have to be another production, and another after that.

“We’re not going to have a Dune come every year. We need to work on and scale up independent filmmaking,” Mostafa says.

Mostafa needs the next production, too. He wants another chance to get as deeply into a character as he did in Khattaf. He is working to help get those films made, while pursuing the roles he believes he can carry.

“I’m confident enough to know I can be in a blockbuster film as one of the main cast,” he says. “I just need to keep pushing, but I know I can do it.”

The fearlessness that put him in front of Ali’s camera has stayed with him. Now Mostafa wants to take it into a role where audiences around the world will see an Emirati actor leading the story. He is ready for the scrutiny that will come with it, and for the work it will demand of him.

“I would never be given that opportunity and not know the responsibility I’ll carry being there,” he says. “And also the responsibility I’d need to have to make sure I perform at the highest level because of what I represent.”

Fashion Director: Sarah Maisey

Photographer: Chris Whiteoak

Shot on location at Jumeirah Beach Hotel and Mohamed's family home in Dubai

body_text:
The Philippine tennis body has lauded young sensation Alex Eala for raising the profile of tennis in the country, highlighting her decision to represent her nation at the 2026 Asian Games despite the risk of penalty.

Eala had risked a hefty fine for skipping WTA's mandatory China Open as she represented the Philippines at the Japan Asian Games. While she lost her semi-final in Nagoya to Wang Xiyu, her actions did not go unnoticed.

Eala has since suffered early exits in Singapore and Wuhan. But for the Philippine Tennis Association (PHILTA), she has already done a lot.

WTA Finals will move to North Carolina from 2027

“Alex Eala has already achieved what many once thought impossible. She has single-handedly put the Philippines on the world tennis map,” PHILTA secretary general John Rey Tiangco said.

“Her rise to world No 18, her WTA title, and her victories over some of the world's best players are milestones that have changed the landscape of Philippine tennis.”

Tiangco said Eala's decision to play for her country, even as other athletes decided to feature in China, was praiseworthy.

“We are equally grateful for her decision to represent our country at the Asian Games, putting the Philippine flag ahead of other opportunities.

“At this level of competition, victories and defeats are part of the journey. What matters is Alex's determination to keep improving, her discipline, and her commitment to the sport.

“Alex has already won something bigger than any single tournament. She has inspired a nation and opened doors for the next generation of Filipino tennis players.”

Meanwhile, Indonesia's Janice Tjen saw her Wuhan Open campaign come to an end in China on Thursday.

American Ann Li, who upset the top seed Aryna Sabalenka in the second round, moved into the quarter-finals with a 6-1, 7-6 (1) victory over Tjen.

Li will take on seventh seed Iga Swiatek of Poland in the last eight. Swiatek had on Thursday completed the 150th WTA 1000 win of ⁠her career.

summary: Yin Yuzhen, a Chinese woman known for her efforts to combat desertification, was named among the FAO 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, in Rome, Italy, on Thursday.

(ECNS) -- Yin Yuzhen, a Chinese woman known for her efforts to combat desertification, was named among the FAO 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, a global recognition initiative launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, in Rome, Italy, on Thursday.

Yin has spent more than four decades combating desertification in the Maowusu Sandy Land in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

body_text:
The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy.

"In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries.

He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries.

The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period.

The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries.

Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment.

Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible.

“Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance, private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.”

He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world.

“Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added.

Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy, while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged.

The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said.

“I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said.

He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain.

Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation.

“We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.”

With reporting from Reuters and AFP

Irish Prime ​Minister Micheal Martin ​said that he anticipated ​Europe ‌would continue ⁠its "outreach" to the ‌US regarding Ukraine.

The ​EU will ​continue to support Ukraine and will not lift ​any ‌sanctions ⁠against Russia, EU ‌Commission President Ursula von ⁠der Leyen and EU Council President ​Antonio Costa ‌said.

"One thing is ‌absolutely clear: we ​will not lift any sanctions unless Russia stops ​this war," ​von der ​Leyen told reporters ahead ​of a summit of EU leaders, joined by ⁠Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Costa said that it was time to increase the EU's support for Ukraine.

"This is no time to withdraw the support to Ukraine. This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure," he said.

A ⁠Russian ​drone ​strike on Ukraine's city of ​Kharkiv ‌killed ⁠three ‌people and wounded ⁠at least five, the region's Governor Oleh Synegubov said.

headline: Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary, White House says
summary: Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman.
body_text:
Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman.

From NPR News, this is ALL THINGS CONSIDERED. I'm Ailsa Chang.

And I'm Scott Detrow. It was over almost before it began. The White House's newest press secretary is out after just five days on the job. Katie Zacharia started her job at the beginning of the week. She gave her first and only press briefing on Tuesday. The briefing was noticeably short and widely panned, and then questions emerged about her legal credentials. NPR's Emily Feng has been following Zacharia's rapid rise and rapid fall and joins us now in the studio. Welcome.

EMILY FENG, BYLINE: Hi, Scott.

DETROW: Let's start with this. What has President Trump said about what is happening with Zacharia's job?

FENG: So Trump was asked earlier today about this. He strongly hinted that she was leaving, but he said he was giving her the option to decide if she wanted to resign.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want. She said, this is a lot tougher. I said, welcome to the world of Trump.

FENG: And a senior White House official told NPR she is, quote, "transitioning out" of this very, very new job. Trump noted that she'd had a really rough time with how the media was treating her, and so he asked her if she still wanted to do this job.

DETROW: Let's talk more about this because a big part of the reason why she has faced so much scrutiny this week was this possible misrepresentation of her legal credentials. Can you explain what happened?

FENG: Yeah, so Trump has referred to her as an attorney, and Zacharia did go to law school. But there is no record of her passing the bar in any state. And when she was asked about this, she responded that she had passed when she moved to China. Now, Scott, you know, I've lived in China for the better part of a decade. It is just not possible for foreigners to take the bar there or even practice law. Zacharia later said she misheard the question about when she passed the bar, and then she defended herself last night on Fox News when questioned by Sean Hannity about her professional record.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KATIE ZACHARIA: I graduated Pepperdine, got married in the same week, and we had all intent to move out to China. I sat for it because I didn't want to have a withdraw status.

DETROW: So if Zacharia is out after a week, that leaves the White House once again without a press secretary. How much of an issue is that?

FENG: According to Trump, it's no problem. He has shown he is very comfortable with the idea of mostly speaking for himself, regardless of whether that's good or bad for the Republican Party. There - it's been almost two months, I should note, since Karoline Leavitt, the last press secretary, left. And so there have not been regular press briefings for months now. And Trump frequently comes out and just directly takes questions from reporters at the White House, sometimes with very little notice.

And so Trump, it looks like, will continue to be his own spokesperson, but this is a really critical juncture for him right now. His approval ratings as president are at the lowest for his presidency. And yet, he's in full throttle for midterm campaigning. You know, he's hitting the road again today. He's in Georgia. He just spoke at a rally this afternoon. And he's hoping to defy polling that shows Republican candidates are really back on their heels right now in this midterm election.

DETROW: That is NPR's Emily Feng. Thank you so much.

FENG: Thank you, Scott.

Katie Zacharia, the new White House press secretary, is reportedly out after only five days on the job.

US President Donald Trump on Friday said he had told her to “reconsider” her role following a disastrous first week.

Speaking to reporters as he headed to Georgia for a campaign event, Mr Trump said Ms Zacharia had been treated “very badly by the media”.

“I told her: 'Honestly, if I were you, I would reconsider.' Maybe it's not for her,” he said.

Following the comments, Fox News, quoting a White House official, reported that Ms Zacharia was “transitioning” out of the role. The New York Times, quoting sources familiar with the matter, reported that she had been fired.

The development comes after Ms Zacharia held her first White House briefing on Tuesday. The briefing lasted 14 minutes and she took only three questions from journalists. She also appeared to struggle to read a prepared statement.

Her performance drew criticism and mockery on social media, and questions were also raised over her credentials.

When Mr Trump announced her appointment, he described her as an attorney.

A graduate of Pepperdine University's law school in California, Ms Zacharia later acknowledged that she had taken the bar exam once but had not passed.

In previous media appearances, she has described herself as a lawyer and said that she had practised law at a firm in China.

On Friday, Mr Trump said he had not hired her as a lawyer and that her credentials were not an issue.

Ms Zacharia did not accompany Mr Trump to Georgia, according to a list circulated by the White House. Typically, the press secretary travels with the US President.

Her probable departure evokes that of Anthony Scaramucci, who served as White House communications director for just 11 days during Mr Trump's first administration.

Ms Zacharia was appointed after the departure of Karoline Leavitt, the youngest person to serve as White House press secretary.

headline: Katie Zacharia is 'transitioning out' as press secretary, White House says
summary: Katie Zacharia's first official day was on Monday.(Image credit: Win McNamee)
body_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump is followed by White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia (L) as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on October 13, 2026 in Washington, DC. Win McNamee/Getty Images hide caption

Katie Zacharia is "transitioning out" of her role as press secretary, according to a White House official not authorized to speak on the record, marking a stunning turn of events for the spokeswoman who officially started Monday and is out by Friday.

Zacharia's first briefing was Tuesday morning where she faced scrutiny both over her performance – during which she delivered a lengthy and halting opening statement read from notes and called on only three reporters – and her legal credentials.

President Trump on Friday cast doubt on the future of Zacharia, saying he had a discussion with her just before leaving for a campaign rally in Georgia.

"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'," he told reporters. "She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily. And I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want."

He said he was leaving the decision up to her but advised her "you should reconsider" serving in the position.

The 41-year-old graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law and self-described attorney had stepped in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.

Much of the scrutiny of Zacharia focused on her credentials as an attorney. While standing with Trump, she was asked by reporters where she passed the bar exam.

"When I moved to China," Zacharia answered, an apparent reference to what she has described on her LinkedIn page as a period of time from 2011 through 2013 spent working for a prominent Beijing-based law firm called Zhon Lun.

NPR asked the White House to clarify whether Zacharia is a licensed attorney in the U.S. In a statement provided to NPR, Zacharia said she "practiced international transaction law, with all the appropriate credentials."

More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.

NPR's Brian Mann contributed.

headline: 19 countries condemn Colombia’s opening of embassy in Jerusalem
summary: Foreign ministers say move violates UN Security Council resolutions and undermines efforts to achieve two-state solution
body_text:
The foreign ministers of Türkiye and 18 other countries on Friday strongly condemned Colombia’s inauguration of its embassy in Jerusalem.

In a joint statement released by Türkiye’s Foreign Ministry, the ministers expressed their “unequivocal rejection” of the decision.

They said the move violates relevant UN Security Council resolutions and undermines international efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace based on a two-state solution.

The statement was issued by the foreign ministers of Türkiye, Algeria, Djibouti, Egypt, Indonesia, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Libya, Malaysia, Oman, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria and Yemen.

The ministers reaffirmed that any measure or decision intended to alter the legal or historical status of occupied Jerusalem, or to recognize the city as Israel’s capital, “is null and void and has no legal effect.”

They cited UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478, both adopted in 1980, which reject attempts to change Jerusalem’s character or status and call on states to withdraw their diplomatic missions from the city.

The statement described Jerusalem as part of the Palestinian territory occupied in 1967.

The ministers called on the Colombian government to reconsider and reverse its decision, uphold its obligations under international law, and refrain from measures that prejudice the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people.

They also reiterated their support for the Palestinian people’s right to an independent and sovereign state, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

headline: Israeli settlers beat Palestinians and a U.S. photojournalist in West Bank attacks
summary: Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including a photojournalist working for The Washington Post.(Image credit: Ahmad Gharabli)
body_text:
Photojournalist Heidi Levine leaves a hospital emergency room in a wheelchair in the Israeli-occupied city of Ramallah, West Bank. She's being treated after an attack by Israeli settlers as she was photographing Palestinian farmers harvesting their olives, in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah on Friday. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians as they were harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including an American photojournalist.

The Washington Post said photographer Heidi Levine was reporting in the West Bank, wearing a protective vest clearly marked as "press," when she was beaten.

"Today I was brutally attacked," Levine said in a video filmed at a hospital and posted online."We saw in the distance, in the hilltop, I would say at least 50 masked men, slingshots. And when they came running down, I was attacked, pushed to the ground," she said, "they just kept kicking me and kicking me." They also stole her cameras and phone.

She said medical workers rushed her in an ambulance to a hospital. Washington Post Executive Editor Matt Murray said in a statement the paper was relieved that Levine received medical care and is safe, but denounced the violence against her.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," Murray said.

The Post said the attack happened when Palestinians were trying to harvest their olives. It said settlers set Palestinian olive groves on fire and hurled stones using slingshots.

Israeli soldiers move toward a Palestinian man lying wounded on a road after they shot him following a settler attack on Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank village of Abu Falah, Friday. Leo Correa/AP hide caption

Israeli police issued a statement acknowledging reports that a foreign journalist was injured and said it would investigate the incident and "bring those involved to justice."

The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attempted to cast some doubt on the story, asserting on social media that the facts "remain unclear and are under investigation." Murray, the Post's executive editor, quickly clarified. "To be clear: Some facts are neither in dispute nor unclear. Our photographer was clearly marked as Press. She was clearly beaten," he wrote in a quote post on X of the Israeli leader's statement.

The U.S. State Department said it was aware of the reports and that it contacted The Washington Post to offer consular assistance. "We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the State Department said, without mentioning the assault of the American photojournalist.

Palestinian volunteers douse an olive tree set on fire along with a Palestinian-owned vehicle, reportedly by Israeli settlers, near the village of Turmus Ayya, north of the city of Ramallah, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on Friday. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

There were two dozen settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters Friday, leaving 20 people injured, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent Society.

The United Nations' humanitarian office for Gaza and the West Bank said settler attacks during the olive harvest season have killed one Palestinian and damaged more than 2,500 olive trees or saplings.

The attacks came as groups of Israeli settlers have stepped up their assaults on Palestinians in the West Bank. They also follow another assault earlier this month, when Israelis beat Agence France-Presse photojournalist Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he was covering settler violence against Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank.

Sara Qudah, who handles the Middle East for the Committee to Protect Journalists, said Levine's beating was not an isolated incident for journalists covering the West Bank olive harvest. "It's part of a disturbing pattern of violence and harassment against journalists regardless of their nationalities," she said.

She added that the attackers have no reason to fear consequences because Israeli authorities fail to do anything to stop the violence.

The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate also condemned the attack as an "assault on press freedom" and a violation of rules protecting journalists during conflicts.

Nuha Musleh contributed reporting from Ramallah, West Bank.
