headline: US journalist injured during Israeli settler attack on West Bank olive harvest
summary: About 80 Israeli settlers set fire to olive trees and threw stones at Palestinians in a West Bank village Friday, injuring at least two people, including a US photojournalist with The Washington Post. The coordinated attack came as violence by settlers is on the rise during the olive harvest in the occupied Palestinian territory.
body_text:
About 80 Israeli settlers set fire to olive trees and threw stones at Palestinians in a West Bank village Friday, injuring at least two people, including a US photojournalist with The Washington Post. The coordinated attack came as violence by settlers is on the rise during the olive harvest in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Issued on: 16/10/2026 - 17:01Modified: 16/10/2026 - 17:02

Clad in black and their faces masked, dozens of militant Israeli settlers burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians in a coordinated attack on Friday on a West Bank village's annual harvest that injured at least two people, including a Washington Post journalist.

Some 80 settlers, some of them carrying gas canisters, descended from a hill above a terraced olive ​grove where villagers from Abu ‌Falah had gathered to pick ripe fruit, a cherished annual tradition in Palestinian life, Reuters witnesses said.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

The settlers took positions in front of the ⁠terraced lanes of olive trees. Some of them used slings to launch rocks towards Palestinian villagers, who descended towards the bottom of the hill before picking up and throwing stones to defend themselves.

"The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes," said Moutaz ‌Abdelhadi, 42, a farmer who witnessed the attack in Abu Falah.

Partway through the attack, at least two Israeli military jeeps sped through the area, ⁠kicking up dust as villagers ran out of their way.

The attack continued after the military's arrival, with Israeli soldiers firing tear gas in the direction of the Palestinians who had dodged the jeeps. The sound of live gunfire could be heard in the area, and a Reuters photographer saw at least one armed settler fire a ​gun.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

In a statement, the Israeli military said soldiers and border police fired what it described as warning shots after deploying to the area and ‌at one point fired towards a person who the troops believed had posed a threat.

"Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the military said. "Attacks and violence against innocent civilians are grave and unacceptable," it added.

Palestinian medics said two people were injured and taken to hospitals in the area of Ramallah. One of them was Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with the Washington Post. Video ‌of the attack showed Levine lying on her side on a dirt path with her hands over her face as at least three settlers surrounded her.

Speaking from a hospital bed later, Levine, who is in stable condition, said: "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I ​had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me."

Levine said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened, after which medics rushed her in an ambulance to a clinic in Abu Falah and then to hospital in Ramallah.

Her voice shook as she spoke and she had ​bandages over her left hand.

In a statement, Matt Murray, the Washington Post's executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident.

"This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by ​Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said.

"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we ​are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."

Israeli settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West ​Bank has surged, with at least 170 attacks since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

The settlers have been emboldened by the right-wing government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has overseen a rapid expansion of settlements and smaller outposts across the West Bank.

Read moreWest Bank: Palestinians ‘harassed’ by settlers’ increasing use of drones

Netanyahu has criticized the violence but has taken few steps to crack down on incidents that have drawn international condemnation and sanction plans by longtime Israeli allies, including Britain.

The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians. UN bodies ⁠and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.

The Abu Falah attack followed a similar attack on Friday morning in the area of Turmus Ayya ⁠village, where settlers burned three cars after ​attacking a group of farmers harvesting olives. The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Salah Abu Niswa, who witnessed the attack in Turmus Ayya, said the settlers "snuck up like thieves, they caught someone by himself and began to beat him."

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

A Washington Post photojournalist was among several people attacked by Israeli settlers while accompanying Palestinian villagers harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank on Friday.

“Dozens of masked settlers” set fire to shrubs and threw rocks in a “co-ordinated assault” on the villagers, the Post said. Freelancer Heidi Levine was wearing a protective vest clearly marked “Press” when she was attacked.

“She was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly and stripped of her cameras and phone,” the paper said.

Levine was later taken to hospital in Ramallah, where she was pictured lying on a trolley with a wound dressing on her left leg and a gash on her right knee, among other injuries.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had [on] my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me,” she told reporters from the hospital.

Witnesses said they saw about 80 settlers, some carrying gas canisters, descending on the olive grove where Palestinians from Abu Falah village had gathered to pick the fruit, Reuters reported.

“The settlers want to attack us and force us from our homes,” said Moutaz Abdelhadi, a farmer who witnessed the assault.

The Israeli military appeared but the attack continued. Rights groups, witnesses and victims have documented and recounted incidents where settlers were protected by the Israeli army.

Live gunfire was heard in the area and at least one settler was seen firing a gun, Reuters reported.

The US State Department said it was aware of the reports.

"We are greatly concerned when any American is harmed overseas and stand ready to provide all appropriate consular assistance," a spokesperson said in a statement.

The official said the US is in regular dialogue with partners about improving stability and security in the West Bank.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the official said.

The harvest season officially began on Thursday but Palestinian farmers have been out in their groves for weeks, fearing thefts by Israeli settlers who are posting social media campaigns encouraging people to steal the olives.

Violence in the West Bank has soared since October 7, 2023, and last year reached the highest level recorded since 2006, the UN said.

September was the most violent month this year, but the attacks have risen sharply in October. The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled) recorded an average of 39 incidents a day from October 1 to October 9, compared with around 20 per day in September.

A crude oil tanker carrying 15 Indian crew members was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the country's Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways said.

Sarbananda Sonowal said all Indian citizens on the vessel, the MT ST 3, were safe and had not been injured. He said on X that India remains "in close contact with the ship management companies to ensure the ongoing security and well-being of our crew members".

The Indian government this month condemned an attack on a vessel owned by Dubai shipping company Onex that was struck by a projectile in the strait. Twelve crew members on the MT On Peace were injured in the attack, including 11 Indians, the Indian Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.

On Thursday, a Singapore-registered container ship caught fire and sank in the strait after being struck by a projectile. All 21 crew on board the GFS Pride were moved to safety and no injuries were reported, Singapore's maritime authority said.

The incidents highlight how the US-Iran war has escalated risks to commercial shipping in the vital global energy supply route.

Attacks on vessels transiting the waterway have surged to a record high, with at least two ships sunk. The strikes, attributed to Iran, have caused crude oil prices to rocket, with prices above $100 a barrel in the US.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has used drones, missiles and sea mines in the strait to choke off exports and drive up oil prices in a bid to increase economic pressure on the US.

headline: (2nd LD) N. Korea tests new precision-guided torpedo using AI: KCNA
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 17 (Yonhap) -- North Korea said Saturday it has conducted an underwa...
body_text:
(ATTN: RECASTS headline, lead; UPDATES throughout with details)

SEOUL, Oct. 17 (Yonhap) -- North Korea said Saturday it has conducted an underwater test of a new high-speed precision-guided torpedo weapon system that uses artificial intelligence (AI) technology, noting that the test heralds a "significant" change in the North's naval capabilities.

North Korea test-fired the Zam-2.0 super-speed precision-guided torpedo weapon system Thursday to confirm the successful technical upgrade of the weapon, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). It did not disclose further details of the weapon.

Key national defense officials who oversaw the weapon test assessed that it "served as a great success foreseeing a significant change in the actual development of the Navy," the KCNA said.

North Korea said AI technology was applied to the target detection and the guidance function of the torpedo.

"The test proved the core technology for raising the efficiency of propulsion and the performance of rocket propulsion devices," the KCNA said, adding more than 180 rounds of related tests have been conducted over the past five years.

Experts said the newly disclosed weapon system could be a "supercavitating torpedo" given the North's claims that rocket propulsion devices were fitted on the torpedo, and the term "super-speed" used to describe the new torpedo.

A supercavitating torpedo is an ultra-high-speed torpedo that creates an air bubble in the nose to overcome water resistance and travel at higher speeds than conventional torpedoes.

Other countries pursuing the development of such high-speed torpedoes have reportedly faced technical challenges in operational deployment, particularly in maintaining effective guidance and control at high speeds underwater.

"The test launch appears to have been intended to flaunt its super-speed AI-driven torpedo, which is difficult to detect in advance and avoid, targeting the South Korean Navy's major surface ships," said Lim Eul-chul, a professor of the Institute for Far Eastern Studies at Kyungnam University.

Shin Jong-woo, secretary-general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum, assessed that North Korea is developing new torpedoes to be mounted on submarines in line with the expansion of its new submarine capabilities.

"It is an attempt to narrow the gap in military capabilities with the South Korean Navy," he said.

North Korea has been pushing to strengthen its naval capabilities with weapon tests.

Pyongyang launched two types of strategic cruise missiles from what was presumed to be a 3,000-ton submarine in the East Sea on Wednesday. It also recently commissioned the 5,000-ton Choe Hyon and Kang Kon destroyers, respectively in the West Sea and the East Sea.

headline: Iran ready to assist in resolving conflict between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
summary: Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei noted the need to resolve the disagreements between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis through dialogue and diplomacy
body_text:
TUNIS, October 17. /TASS/. Iran is ready to facilitate a peaceful resolution of the conflict between the Yemeni rebel movement Ansar Allah (the Houthis) and Saudi Arabia if they make such a request, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said.

"The Islamic Republic of Iran has always been ready to provide good services to facilitate the cessation of hostilities and remains ready, at the request of both sides, to use all its capabilities for this purpose," he said on Telegram.

Baghaei noted the need to resolve the disagreements between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis through dialogue and diplomacy. According to him, the events of the past 12 years shown that external interference, military methods, and blockades do not allow the Yemeni problem to be solved. He also rejected claims about Tehran’s involvement in the Ansar Allah attacks on Saudi Arabia. "The armed forces of Yemen (the Houthis -- TASS) are acting based on their own interests and assessments," the diplomat said, adding that Iran does not consider further escalation beneficial for any of the parties.

According to Baghaei, the settlement requires respect for Yemen's sovereignty and territorial integrity, an end to interference in its internal affairs and the lifting of the air and sea blockade.

The armed confrontation between the Houthis and government forces has been going on since August 2014. In September of that year, the Ansar Allah movement established control over the country’s capital Sana’a, and advanced southward. In March 2015, at the request of the then Yemen President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi, a coalition led by Saudi Arabia entered the conflict on the side of the government; the coalition declared its goal to be the restoration of the authority of the country’s internationally recognized leadership.

In early August 2016, the Ansar Allah movement intensified its offensive in the southwest of the country, and in September it established control over the port city of Mocha and the territories with access to the Bab·el·Mandeb Strait in western Yemen. On October 5, Rashad Mohammed al·Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced the launch of a large·scale military operation called the "Dawn of Yemen" to liberate the capital from the rebels; the operation is being carried out with the support of the coalition.

headline: Pope Leo XIV celebrates mass in hospital while recovering from lung cancer operation
summary: Pope Leo XIV celebrated a mass at Rome's Gemelli hospital Friday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung, photos released by the Vatican showed. Doctors said his recovery was progressing normally but that further tests would show whether the cancer had spread.
body_text:
Pope Leo XIV celebrated a mass at Rome's Gemelli hospital Friday after undergoing surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung, photos released by the Vatican showed. Doctors said his recovery was progressing normally but that further tests would show whether the cancer had spread.

Issued on: 16/10/2026 - 14:57Modified: 16/10/2026 - 15:51

Pope Leo XIV celebrated mass on Friday at the hospital where he is recovering from a lung cancer operation, as seen in the first images of him released by the Vatican since the procedure.

The images showed the 71-year-old Chicago-born pope in front of a makeshift altar in a room on the 10th floor of the Rome hospital, dressed in a green vestment.

He appeared relaxed and in good form in the two photos released, standing with his private secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard Rimaycuna, at his side.

"He celebrated with the medical and nursing staff of Gemelli, some people who were present there, who were clearly off duty at that moment," the Vatican press office said, adding that members of the police also joined.

"He thanked all the staff, doctors, nurses, orderlies, for their service and their closeness to people, for their care of people's fragility, and in particular, evidently, for the care, attention, and treatment given to him in these days," the press office said.

The pope is expected to lead the traditional Angelus prayer on Sunday, but a Vatican source would not say whether it would be from the hospital, or from the Vatican.

The Angelus prayer is traditionally recited by the pope every Sunday from the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter's Square, to crowds of faithful gathered below.

Leo was admitted Tuesday to Rome's Gemelli hospital, north of the Vatican, where he underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumour in his right lung.

Doctors have said that his recovery is progressing normally, but ongoing tests will determine the future course of his treatment.

Read moreWhat we know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis

On Thursday, his doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".

On Friday, they said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition".

They said he was now carrying out "his normal daily activities completely independently".

Test results to determine whether the cancer has spread are still pending.

"Morale is good, that's obvious. And the recovery as well because the pope has been able to celebrate mass," the Vatican source said.

Read more'Amazing progress' in lung cancer: Immunotherapy extends survival as mRNA vaccines offer hope

The press office has not given an update to the possible timing of the pope's discharge from hospital, repeating a doctor's original statement that his recovery would take about a week.

Were Leo to recite the Angelus from the window of the Gemelli hospital, it would not be a first for a pope.

In February 6, 2005, 84-year-old John Paul II appeared at the hospital window while recovering from flu-related respiratory issues, as an aide beside him read out the Angelus prayer.

Pope Francis on July 11, 2021, then 84, also gave the prayer from the hospital window after surgery on his colon, telling the assembled crowd: "I am glad to be able to keep the Sunday Angelus appointment, even here."

Also on Friday, the Vatican released a selection of letters and drawings sent by children at the hospital, including a picture of a tree "For Pope Leo", complete with grass, sun and clouds, and a letter from an 18-year-old girl who wrote to Leo: "Better days will come for the both of us."

A seven-year-old boy named Angelo wrote that he, too, had been on the 10th floor of the Gemelli hospital for the past 36 days for a head operation.

"My mother and I pray for you every night," he wrote. "I hope you get well soon."

headline: Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in U.K. after Palestinian Action support
summary: The Irish author said her books can no longer be sold in the UK after she pledged the royalties to a banned pro-Palestinian group.(Image credit: Kin Cheung)
body_text:
Sally Rooney's books are displayed for sale at a bookshop in London, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. Kin Cheung/AP hide caption

Irish author Sally Rooney has long been described as "the voice of a generation" for her best-selling novels that are ostensibly about millennial relationships but also explore deeper questions of class, gender and politics.

Now the 35-year-old writer's books will no longer be sold in the UK because of her own closely-held political beliefs. She had promised to donate the revenues to a pro-Palestinian group that the UK has designated a terrorist organization.

In a statement this week, her publisher explained: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."

"As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," Faber said.

The move comes after Rooney — who has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — announced last year she would be donating funds from the proceeds of her books to Palestinian Action, which was controversially banned in the U.K. under terrorism legislation.

Israel vehemently denies allegations of genocide.

UK-based Palestinian Action says on its website it uses "disruptive tactics" to target "corporate enablers of the Israeli military-industrial complex and seeks to make it impossible for these companies to profit from the oppression of Palestinians."

It has targeted facilities linked to an Israeli weapons manufacturer and, in a major security breach, last year managed to break into Britain's largest air force base. The activists spray-painted two aircraft at the base blood red, in what the group said was a protest against Britain's military support for Israel.

Palestinian Action was also responsible for vandalizing one of President Trump's golf courses in Scotland in March last year, when activists painted the course with the words "Gaza is not 4 sale." Reacting on social media, Trump called those responsible "terrorists."

FILE - From left, Paul Mescal, Sally Rooney and Ed Guiney participate in Hulu's "Normal People" panel during the Winter 2020 Television Critics Association Press Tour on Jan. 17, 2020, in Pasadena, Calif. Richard Shotwell/Invision/ AP hide caption

When the British government banned the group in July last year, it said it was on the grounds that Palestinian Action is responsible for "serious damage to property." It was the first time a terrorist designation had been given to an organization that does not call for violence against people.

"Its activity has increased in frequency and severity since the start of 2024 and its methods have become more aggressive, with its members demonstrating a willingness to use violence," the British government said at the time.

The government also said that the group's "activities meet the threshold of being concerned in terrorism as set out in the Terrorism Act 2000.," adding that it assessed "that Palestine Action commits and participates in acts of terrorism."

But critics questioned this assessment, saying it raised concerns about freedom of speech.

U.N. Human Rights Chief Volker Türk urged the U.K. government to rescind the decision, saying it "appears disproportionate and unnecessary."

"It limits the rights of many people involved with and supportive of Palestine Action who have not themselves engaged in any underlying criminal activity but rather exercised their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association," Türk said.

Amnesty International UK also raised concerns, saying "the UK has a deeply flawed and overly broad definition of terrorism."

Under the U.K. law, anyone who provides financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison.

For fear of arrest, Rooney says she has stopped traveling from her home in Ireland to the U.K. to attend award ceremonies and other events since the law came into force.

But the novelist has defended her support of Palestinian Action, saying in an opinion piece in The Irish Times last year: "if this makes me a 'supporter of terror' under UK law, so be it."

It was in that op-ed that she announced she would use the British proceeds of her work "as well as my public platform generally, to go on supporting Palestine Action and direct action against genocide in whatever way I can."

Now however, her books won't be sold in Britain at all, so there will be no further proceeds.

The Normal People author was undeterred, saying in a statement shared with NPR: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."

Since the ban on Palestinian Action, several thousand people in the UK have been arrested for supporting them, mainly for carrying placards and wearing T-shirts.

The ban has been challenged in the courts, with the UK's high court ruling against it in February. A court of appeal later overturned that decision. Next month, the case heads to Britain's highest court.

In August, the U.S. Department of the Treasury followed the UK's lead in sanctioning Palestinian Action, calling them "far-left terrorists."

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

headline: Italy extends Schengen suspension with Spain for another week
summary: Countries to hold talks on ending border checks in coming days, government sources tell Italy's ANSA news agency
body_text:
Italy will extend its suspension of the Schengen Agreement for travelers arriving from Spain for another week, government sources told Italy’s ANSA news agency on Friday.

The extension aims to align Italy’s suspension with the latest border controls introduced by Spain.

The two countries’ interior ministers are also set to hold talks on ending the border checks in the coming days, sources said.

Spain recently extended temporary border controls on travelers arriving from Italy by air and sea for another 15 days, until Oct. 22.

The controls were initially introduced after Italy imposed border checks on travelers from Spain following the mass arrival in late July of around 72,000 migrants in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta from Morocco.

Spain responded by introducing controls on travelers arriving from Italy on Aug. 8, formally citing migration pressure on the Central Mediterranean route and unauthorized onward movements from Italy to other Schengen countries, including Spain.

summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met and held talks with Prime Minister of Georgia Irakli Kobakhidze in Yerevan on the sidelines of 17th Summit of Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian met and held talks with Prime Minister of Georgia Irakli Kobakhidze in Yerevan on the sidelines of 17th Summit of Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

During the meeting, Pezeshkian and Kobakhidze discussed host of issues, including bilateral ties, recent developments between the two countries and also issues of mutual interest.

Referring to the clear position of martyred Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyed Ali Khamenei on the prohibition of development of nuclear weapons, the Iranian president stressed, “Iran is not pursuing nuclear weapons, and we consider the destructive propaganda against our country to be lies.”

Pezeshkian said Iran has always been prepared for negotiations, but warned that attempts to force the country into submission would fail. “They (enemies) think they can make us surrender, but we will not bow to coercion,” he stated.

Addressing US sanctions against Iran, the president said the measures are outside the bounds of humanitarian principles. He also described the attacks carried out against Iran in recent months as “unjustifiable and inhumane.”

Pezeshkian also emphasized the need to expand economic, cultural and tourism relations between Iran and Georgia through practical measures. He said the two countries need to develop an operational plan with a clear timetable to translate their shared goals into concrete action.

For his part, Kobakhidze said Georgia has a clear position on relations with neighboring countries and opposes any foreign interference in their internal affairs.

Referring to the cultural and geographical commonalities between Iran and Georgia, the Georgian prime minister said friendship and cooperation are the guiding principles of bilateral relations.

The Armenian prime minister described the expansion of trade and economic ties with Iran as significant and highlighted the considerable potential for bilateral energy cooperation. He said Yerevan is seeking to further strengthen relations with Tehran in that sector.

headline: New operational plans are currently underway: Iran Army spox

TEHRAN, Oct. 16 (MNA) – Spokesman for the Iranian Army Brigadier General Akraminia has said that new operational plans are currently underway that will force hostile American vessels to flee to even greater distances.

Speaking in an interview on Friday, General Mohammad Akraminia emphasized, “Despite Trump’s repeated allegations, Iran’s current air defense capabilities far surpass pre-war and wartime levels.”

Iranian air defense units have successfully downed multiple US drones in the country's airspace in recent weeks, he said, adding, “US military vessels have been forced to retreat to distances exceeding 500 kilometers from the Persian Gulf coasts.”

"If America leaves the region, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and collective security will be established with the participation of the region's countries, and the global economy will improve. If it doesn't leave, we'll expel it."

He, who is also the deputy coordinator of the Army's Ideological-Political Organization, reiterated that new operational plans are currently underway that will force hostile American vessels to flee to even greater distances.

Advanced combined and innovative military operations have been successfully rehearsed, he underlined.

National air defense coverage across the country has been significantly strengthened compared to pre-war levels, he stated, stressing, “The insecurity witnessed today in east of the Strait of Hormuz is a direct consequence of the destructive US presence.”

Regional states and the international community must acknowledge that the US is the primary root cause of this instability in the region, General Akraminia added.

body_text:
Manchester United manager Michael Carrick said the team has addressed Lisandro Martinez's controversial remarks about the club's management and moved on from the controversy.

United defender Martinez had to issue an apology on Thursday for criticising ​the ​club's hierarchy following their ​Champions League defeat by Atletico Madrid, highlighting the lack of investments and singling out United director of football Jason Wilcox.

Martinez then held talks with the manager and ⁠senior officials, before issuing an apology. Carrick said the chapter is now closed.

Man United ratings vs Atletico Madrid: Baleba promising on another tough night

“It's done really,” Carrick said on Friday. “We've moved on from that. It was one of those things. He has come out and acknowledged the situation and as a group we have moved on.

“It is really not a drama for us as a group. The boys have trained really well, there was a really good feeling around training this morning.

“From the outside [you are] after some big information about big discussions but it was pretty simple. We all understood the situation and what it meant. He made his statement and acknowledges that it was a mistake from him and that was it really.”

In his apology, Martinez said he got carried away in his post-match interview.

“Today I met with the club's leadership and the manager,” Martinez said in an Instagram post.

“It was a very positive conversation where we were able to exchange ​views ⁠and speak openly about what ‌happened after Tuesday's game.”

Martinez said that his frustration following the defeat had got the better of him and apologised for choosing the wrong moment to air his feelings.

“Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity,” he said.

“The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise.”

To date, deliveries have not begun due to delays in receiving the F-35s.

headline: BTS becomes first group to surpass 10 billion Spotify streams in a year
summary: Album Arirang surpasses 5 billion Spotify streams as 7-member group returns from South Korea's mandatory military service
body_text:
South Korean pop group BTS has become the first musical group to surpass 10 billion streams on Spotify in a single year, according to its record label, BigHit Music.

The group’s streams more than doubled from 4.5 billion in 2025, driven largely by its fifth studio album, Arirang, released in March, South Korea’s Yonhap News Agency reported Friday, citing the label.

While solo artists including Taylor Swift, Ariana Grande, and Bad Bunny had previously reached the 10 billion-stream mark, BTS is the first group to achieve the milestone, according to BigHit Music.

The achievement follows the group’s return to full-group activities after its seven members completed South Korea’s mandatory military service.

Released on March 20, Arirang has accumulated more than 5 billion Spotify streams, making it the most-streamed album among releases in 2026, said the news agency.

The album racked up more than 110 million streams on its release day.

Spotify’s own newsroom said Arirang became the most-streamed K-pop album in the platform’s history on March 20.

In April, Spotify ranked BTS 12th on its list of the most-streamed artists of all time, based on data through that month.

The figures highlight BTS’s international reach and the global popularity of South Korean pop music, which has expanded through streaming platforms and social media.

After debuting in 2013, BTS became one of the world’s most successful K-pop groups.

Its international successes include topping the Billboard Hot 100 with songs such as “Dynamite” and “Butter,” helping expand the global reach of South Korean pop music.

headline: Yemen's Houthis claim responsibility for fresh missile strike on Aden airport
summary: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed responsibility after two missiles struck Aden International Airport Friday, saying they had targeted a weapons depot as well as a military command headquarters. The Aden Security Department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo had been preparing for takeoff when the attack took place.
body_text:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group claimed responsibility after two missiles struck Aden International Airport Friday, saying they had targeted a weapons depot as well as a military command headquarters. The Aden Security Department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo had been preparing for takeoff when the attack took place.

Issued on: 17/10/2026 - 08:00

Missiles apparently launched by the Iran-aligned Houthi group struck Yemen's Aden International Airport on Friday, while a Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile headed for the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid ​the Strait of ‌Hormuz.

The coalition said it had also destroyed two cruise missiles over the Red Sea and ⁠three drones in Saudi Arabia's Southern and Riyadh regions. It did not identify the attackers.

In Aden in southern Yemen, two missiles landed on the airport grounds, the Aden Security Department ‌said, blaming the Houthis. It said the incident was the second attack on the facility ⁠in less than a week.

In a statement attributed to a military source, the Houthis said an attack targeted "the Saudi forces' command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province" as well as a weapons depot.

No casualties were reported. A Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for takeoff when the missiles landed, the security department said.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Yanbu is a key outlet ​for Saudi oil exports, allowing the kingdom to ship crude to international markets via the ‌Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway has been largely throttled by Iran since the US and Israel launched attacks on the country in February.

With regional tensions and security threats raising concerns over the safety of shipping and tighter global energy supplies, Brent crude oil ‌briefly touched $110 a barrel on Friday for the first time since May.

Saudi Civil Defense authorities issued an alert early on Saturday for Abha in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the ​Yemeni border before sending an all-clear. Earlier they had issued alerts in the Jazan region and the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait, where such warnings have become frequent since fighting resumed last month.

Also early on Saturday, Houthi-affiliated media reported strikes east of Yemen's ​northwestern city of Saada. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in the area.

Fighting between the Houthis ​and a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has raised fears of a further deterioration in ​the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions are worsening rapidly.

The Yemen conflict has become another front as the Iran war has widened into a regional conflict. The ​Houthis seized the capital Sanaa in 2014 and forced the internationally recognised government south. A Saudi-led intervention began the following year, leading to years of stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.

The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia since the conflict reignited following a Saudi strike on Sanaa International Airport in July, with the Iran-allied group targeting airports, oil facilities and other infrastructure.

The group has also targeted sites in government-held parts of ⁠Yemen in recent days, including Aden airport and the presidential palace in the interim capital.

A spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry said on Friday that 124 civilians had been killed ⁠and 327 wounded in what ​he described as "Saudi aggression" since the escalation began on September 3. Reuters could not independently verify the figures.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters and AFP)

TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Ambassador and Charge de'affairs of the Islamic Republic of Iran to the United Nations Gholamhossein Darzi says that Iran still remains committed to maintaining the safety and security of shipping.

Speaking at a UN Security Council (UNSC) meeting regarding the situation in the Middle East and Palestine, Darzi emphasized that Israeli regime has repeatedly demonstrated that it holds no respect for international law or the principles of the United Nations Charter.

Iran remains committed to upholding the safety and security of navigation and has merely exercised its inherent right to defend its vital interests, in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter.

Emphasizing that the situation in Palestine remains dire, he added, “Despite the announced ceasefire, the genocidal Israeli regime continues its aggression and human rights violations with impunity. Meanwhile, Gaza remains devastated and subject to ongoing military attacks, and the Palestinian people endure immense suffering.”

At the same time, the occupying regime of Israel continues to expand illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, intensify violence and acts of terror by settlers, and implement unlawful measures aimed at annexing Palestinian territories and depriving Palestinians of their land, the envoy underlined.

He stressed the necessity of a permanent end to the aggression, lifting of the blockade on Gaza, establishment of a permanent ceasefire, unconditional and complete withdrawal of the Zionist occupying forces from Gaza, and immediate and continuous delivery of humanitarian aid and the deployment of relief personnel.

No arrangements regarding Gaza possess legitimacy if they subordinate the rights of Palestinians to externally imposed security considerations, he said, adding, “Any arrangements or framework concerning the future of Gaza must fully respect the inherent rights of the Palestinians, as well as their independence and right to self-determination.”

A senior diplomat of the Islamic Republic of Iran emphasized that Palestinian people must be able to exercise their legitimate right to self-determination and establish an independent, sovereign, and viable Palestinian state with Al-Quds as its capital and secure full membership in the United Nations.

The Israeli regime must put an end to its aggression and violations throughout the region, he said, adding that Israel must cease its daily violations of Lebanon’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, withdraw completely from Lebanese territory, and abide by UN Security Council Resolution 1701.

The occupying regime of Israel must also put an end to its attacks and military aggression against Syrian territory, withdraw from the occupied Syrian Golan and other occupied areas, and respect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Syria.

Accountability for serious violations of international law, particularly international humanitarian law, is essential and a legal requirement. Over the past three years, the occupying regime of Israel has committed major international crimes against the peoples of Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria, as well as against my own country, including genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity, and the crime of aggression.

headline: Attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure 'worrying' for outlook: Pakistan finance minister
summary: Pakistan's finance minister on Saturday told AFP the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook. In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.
body_text:
Pakistan's finance minister on Saturday told AFP the country had so far withstood the shock from skyrocketing energy prices due to the Iran war, but that attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries were "worrying" for the country's longer-term economic outlook.

In an interview on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Muhammad Aurangzeb said the South Asian country had procured enough energy supplies to last through November, and was now planning for the winter months, when household needs typically spike.

"The first-order impact has been negotiated well by Pakistan," he said.

"We've had no shortage, no queues at the gas stations, and no law and order situation, which at times we have seen in some of the countries."

He added that unless the government saw "an absolute dire need", it would not be procuring spot cargoes on the LNG front, which tend to be far more expensive than previously contracted shipments.

Since the United States and ally Israel launched the war on Iran in February, global energy prices have surged as Tehran's retaliatory action has targeted Washington's Gulf allies and curtailed oil and gas supplies.

With Yemen's civil war flaring back to life as well, the Houthis there have repeatedly attacked Saudi infrastructure, including energy facilities and airports, in recent days.

Aurangzeb expressed alarm at the escalation, saying damage to such sites would delay a return to economic normalcy.

"What is now (the) worrying part of it is when the energy infrastructure starts getting hit," he said.

"I, to be very honest, I don't know where that would go. But one thing is very clear: that if the infrastructure continues to get hit, the return to normalcy, even if things subside, will take longer."

Pakistan has been a frequent customer at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the lender of last resort to countries on the brink of default.

It is currently in the midst of its 25th programme with the Fund -- at least 11 of which have been outright bailouts -- since gaining independence in 1947.

The current programme totals around $7 billion over three years, with the Fund reaching an agreement this month to release a $1.2 billion tranche.

With global debt stocks running high, the Fund has called at this year's annual meetings on all economies, even those most vulnerable to the Iran war shock, to engage in fiscal consolidation to avoid a potential crisis.

"Fortunately for us, we have been on this fiscal consolidation path for a while," Aurangzeb said with a rueful smile.

The country's tax revenues have grown significantly in recent years, and the finance minister said the government was targeting the theft of taxes by private sector businesses that collected sales tax from consumers but never deposited it in government accounts.

Such theft accounted for billions of dollars, Aurangzeb said, adding that there remained "room for improvement" on increasing income tax collection as well.

He said the government's reform agenda had faced resistance from industry, lobbying groups and vested interests.

"Every reform, everything that you try to do when you try to change the status quo, there is pushback," he said.

One of the major pillars of the IMF's programme criteria is privatising state-owned assets in Pakistan, where the military runs a vast empire of businesses in sectors from real estate to fertiliser.

Asked about those companies, Aurangzeb denied that they were receiving state funding.

"As far as we are concerned, whichever commercial enterprises (the military) are running, they are running on a standalone basis and profitable on their own basis," he said.

"So, I can confirm to you, we are not providing any funds from the exchequer."

Pakistan's military has directly ruled the country for roughly two-fifths of its history, and under current army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir it has tightened its grip over key pillars of power, even as a civilian government remains nominally in charge of the state.

headline: Saudi air defence demands vie with Europe's needs to counter Russian threat
summary: European allies are struggling to supply Saudi Arabia with more air defence weapons as they are needed for protection against the Russian threat, military analysts have told The National. Saudi Arabia is pressing for more air defence systems to counter rebel Houthi attacks, but defence sources have disclosed that Britain and France cannot “strip out” systems without weakening the deterrent against Russia in the Baltics.Britain is among the European allies who are sending significant arms supplies to Ukraine including a reported consignment this week of Stormshadow cruise missiles to strike Russian military infrastructure. But Dr Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer, said Saudi Arabia remains in urgent need of more air defence capabilities from Britain, France, Italy and the US.“They need it because they are a big country,” she said. “They've got a lot of big targets that are easily spottable on Google Earth and they're up against people who have got sufficient ballistic missiles.”The kingdom’s vulnerability has been demonstrated by the Houthi missile attack on King Khalid International Airport last Saturday that killed 12 people and injured 309. This suggests that Yemeni rebels are more willing to attack civilian targets and given Saudi Arabia is five times the size of Ukraine it needs more defences.But with commitments to Eastern Europe and the desperate need in Ukraine for missile and drone interceptors, the cupboard is bare in many western countries. France has announced it will send defensive military systems to cover the key Red Sea port of Yanbu but has not given details of the equipment in question.Empty locker“We have very little left in the locker to give,” a UK defence source said. “We really have nothing to send over to them.”Britain already has a battery of Sky Sabre air defence systems at King Fahd Air Base, operated by 16th Regiment Royal Artillery but sending more would mean taking them from Eastern Europe, where British and French armoured deployments are intended to deter Moscow from invading.“If they ask the UK to send them more Sky Sabre, where will they get it?” Dr Nusbacher said. “Well, the answer is we've got to strip it out of the Baltics.”The analyst, who has warned of the dangers of a spreading global conflict, said withdrawing defences from Eastern Europe would weaken a key deterrent at a time when Russia was testing western resolve.“What we see here is that we are being asked to dislocate combat power,” she said. “The French are being asked to dislocate combat power from Eastern Europe, from one theatre of this wider war to another theatre of this war.”A reduction in air defence deployments, she argued, could encourage Russia to become “even more kinetic”.American Patriot systems in the Middle East have been prioritised to protect US bases, with spare interceptors already drawn down from western Pacific stocks.But a western diplomatic source said Saudi Arabia is keen for Britain to take a greater role in its defence. “The Saudis are desperate for more UK involvement,” the source said. “It is seen still as a reliable, trustworthy partner with military capabilities and they would hugely welcome greater UK involvement. They need hardware in terms of air defence systems and are desperate for more of that.”It is understood that until recently the kingdom had been firing five to seven interceptors at each incoming missile, but to conserve stocks was now using only a couple at a time.Destroyers and jetsFrancis Tusa, editor of Defence Eye, said Britain could offer a small number of Rapid Ranger systems, which can mount Starstreak and Martlet missiles for short-range air defence.“We've only got a couple of dozen of those and we've already deployed some in Saudi Arabia,” he said.Britain could send a Type-45 destroyer into the southern Red Sea to provide ballistic missile defence and deploy RAF Typhoon fighters to Saudi Arabia, as it did to cover the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain earlier in the year.France and Italy could potentially provide their SAMP/T systems that are armed with the highly effective Aster interceptors but again they already have commitments.Britain is expected to provide intelligence gathered through surveillance satellites and, potentially, listening stations in Cyprus, including facilities in the Troodos Mountains, to monitor Houthi activity.'Malign actors' motivatedJoe Walker-Cousins, a former UK diplomatic official who has spent 25 years working in the Middle East and is now based in Saudi Arabia, said Britain should discretely offer more diplomatic and intelligence support.The UK had major commitments in Ukraine and the Baltic states, but meanwhile the Middle East was “becoming increasingly uncertain”.“Investment in air defence must become a much greater priority, not just so we can stand shoulder to shoulder with our friends in the Gulf but also back home,” he said, speaking from Riyadh. “Britain is a global player and must be prepared to meet its global commitments,” he added. “That requires a major and sustained increase in defence spending. Anything less leaves Britain and its allies perilously exposed and projects a weakness that only encourages malign actors to push further.”

Britain already has a battery of Sky Sabre air defence systems at King Fahd Air Base, operated by 16th Regiment Royal Artillery but sending more would mean taking them from Eastern Europe, where British and French armoured deployments are intended to deter Moscow from invading.

“If they ask the UK to send them more Sky Sabre, where will they get it?” Dr Nusbacher said. “Well, the answer is we've got to strip it out of the Baltics.”

The analyst, who has warned of the dangers of a spreading global conflict, said withdrawing defences from Eastern Europe would weaken a key deterrent at a time when Russia was testing western resolve.

“What we see here is that we are being asked to dislocate combat power,” she said. “The French are being asked to dislocate combat power from Eastern Europe, from one theatre of this wider war to another theatre of this war.”

A reduction in air defence deployments, she argued, could encourage Russia to become “even more kinetic”.

American Patriot systems in the Middle East have been prioritised to protect US bases, with spare interceptors already drawn down from western Pacific stocks.

But a western diplomatic source said Saudi Arabia is keen for Britain to take a greater role in its defence. “The Saudis are desperate for more UK involvement,” the source said.

“It is seen still as a reliable, trustworthy partner with military capabilities and they would hugely welcome greater UK involvement. They need hardware in terms of air defence systems and are desperate for more of that.”

It is understood that until recently the kingdom had been firing five to seven interceptors at each incoming missile, but to conserve stocks was now using only a couple at a time.

Francis Tusa, editor of Defence Eye, said Britain could offer a small number of Rapid Ranger systems, which can mount Starstreak and Martlet missiles for short-range air defence.

“We've only got a couple of dozen of those and we've already deployed some in Saudi Arabia,” he said.

Britain could send a Type-45 destroyer into the southern Red Sea to provide ballistic missile defence and deploy RAF Typhoon fighters to Saudi Arabia, as it did to cover the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain earlier in the year.

France and Italy could potentially provide their SAMP/T systems that are armed with the highly effective Aster interceptors but again they already have commitments.

Britain is expected to provide intelligence gathered through surveillance satellites and, potentially, listening stations in Cyprus, including facilities in the Troodos Mountains, to monitor Houthi activity.

Joe Walker-Cousins, a former UK diplomatic official who has spent 25 years working in the Middle East and is now based in Saudi Arabia, said Britain should discretely offer more diplomatic and intelligence support.

The UK had major commitments in Ukraine and the Baltic states, but meanwhile the Middle East was “becoming increasingly uncertain”.

“Investment in air defence must become a much greater priority, not just so we can stand shoulder to shoulder with our friends in the Gulf but also back home,” he said, speaking from Riyadh.

“Britain is a global player and must be prepared to meet its global commitments,” he added. “That requires a major and sustained increase in defence spending. Anything less leaves Britain and its allies perilously exposed and projects a weakness that only encourages malign actors to push further.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the story around a strategic dilemma: Western allies face competing demands for scarce air-defence systems between Saudi Arabia and Eastern Europe/Ukraine, with analysts and sources warning that diverting resources could weaken deterrence against Russia.

loaded_language.explanation: Idiomatic and colloquial phrase that dramatizes scarcity, making the shortage feel more acute than a neutral description of limited stocks.

loaded_language.explanation: Uses 'desperate' to convey strong emotional urgency, which is more vivid and editorializing than a factual statement of demand.

loaded_language.explanation: Adverb 'perilously' heightens the sense of danger, adding dramatic emphasis beyond a neutral assessment of risk.

No discussion of international criticism or legal concerns regarding arms sales to Saudi Arabia.

No perspective from Houthi representatives or Yemeni civilians.
No mention of potential diplomatic or non-military solutions to the conflict.

headline: Dmitriev calls suspension of Graham Act historic moment
summary: Special representative of the Russian president for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries Kirill Dmitriev stressed that economic cooperation between Russia and the United States is in the interests of both countries
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. The suspension of the law of the deceased Senator Lindsey Graham (recognized in Russia as a terrorist and extremist) is a historic moment, said Kirill Dmitriev, special representative of the Russian president for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries, head of the Russian Direct Investment Fund.

"Suspension of the Graham Act by the administration of President [Donald] Trump is an important and truly historic moment. Instead of sanctions and confrontation, we have dialogue, mutually beneficial cooperation, and shared responsibility for global stability," Dmitriev wrote on Telegram.

According to him, the Graham Act could have completely halted economic cooperation between Russia and the United States and caused serious damage to the American economy and global markets.

"Economic cooperation between Russia and the United States is in the interests of both countries, contributes to the stability of the global economy, and creates the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace," he said.

Trump issued an executive order saying that he would not impose a number of sanctions under the law tightening restrictions against Russia.

On September 18, Trump signed a bill passed by Congress that provides for sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership, state·owned companies, as well as secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners. According to the document, within 30 days after signing — or by October 18 — the Washington administration must determine which companies and individuals may be subject to the restrictions, or determine that such new restrictive measures are not in the interests of the United States, and notify Congress of this.

analysis.framing: The article frames the suspension of the Graham Act as a historic diplomatic victory for dialogue and economic cooperation, presenting the Russian official's perspective without critical context.

loaded_language.explanation: Elevates a policy decision to a epoch-defining event, carrying strong positive connotation.
Intensifies the positive framing with an adverb, making the claim more emphatic.

loaded_language.quote: instead of sanctions and confrontation, we have dialogue, mutually beneficial cooperation, and shared responsibility for global stability
loaded_language.explanation: A value-laden contrast that portrays the change as a shift from negative to positive, using aspirational terms.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: the suspension replaces sanctions with dialogue and cooperation, according to Dmitriev

loaded_language.quote: serious damage to the American economy and global markets
loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged warning that amplifies the stakes without attribution to independent analysis.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: potential negative effects on the American economy and global markets

loaded_language.quote: creates the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace
loaded_language.explanation: Uplifting, aspirational language that frames economic cooperation as a path to peace.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: could contribute to trust and peace, according to Dmitriev

omissions: No mention of the specific sanctions or restrictions that the Graham Act would have imposed, or why they were proposed.
No reaction from U.S. officials, Congress, or other stakeholders to the suspension.
No context on the broader U.S.-Russia relationship or previous sanctions regimes.
No independent verification or expert analysis of Dmitriev's claims about economic damage.
No mention of the circumstances of Senator Lindsey Graham's death or his role in the legislation.

corrections.reason: The article is a TASS report quoting a Russian official; 'lean-right' is a U.S.-centric label not attributable to concrete wording in the article. The framing is uncritical and one-sided but not classifiable as right-leaning from the text.
The 60/40 split is not derivable from the article; the text is largely factual reporting of statements and events, with opinion confined to quoted material.

headline: Iran ready to help resolve issues btw Yemen, S Arabia
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iranian foreign ministry spokesman says his country remains steadfast in its principled position regarding the issues of Yemen and is prepared to assist in a peaceful resolution of the issues between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iranian foreign ministry spokesman says his country remains steadfast in its principled position regarding the issues of Yemen and is prepared to assist in a peaceful resolution of the issues between Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Speaking among reporters late on Friday, Esmaeil Baghaei, while expounding on the positions of the Islamic Republic of Iran regarding the Saudi-Yemen conflict, emphasized Iran’s principled stance on the necessity of dialogue between the two sides to resolve issues through diplomacy.

He added that the Islamic Republic of Iran has always been prepared to make its utmost efforts to help bring an end to the conflicts, and remains ready to utilize all its capacities toward this goal.

Pointing to the history of conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen, Baghaei noted that developments over the past 12 years have demonstrated that foreign intervention, a military approach, and a blockade do not constitute a solution to the crisis in Yemen.

For more than a decade, the people of Yemen have withstood a naval and aerial blockade, enduring the consequences of this unjust siege, orchestrated by extra-regional actors, particularly the United Kingdom and the United States, with exemplary patience.

However, it is expected that countries of the region and the Islamic world will make a concerted effort to bring an end to this situation, the foreign ministry spokesman underlined.

In response to a claim made by a Saudi Foreign Ministry official regarding Iran’s role in encouraging Yemenis to attack Saudi Arabia, Baghaei stated, “Islamic Republic of Iran rejects any such allegations concerning its involvement in Yemeni operations. It emphasizes that resolving the situation in Yemen requires respect for the country’s national sovereignty and territorial integrity, the cessation of all interference in its internal affairs, and—most importantly—an end to the air and naval blockade imposed on the country.”

Yemeni Armed Forces act based on their own interests and assessments, and such claims are not credible to those familiar with the relations between Iran and its allies. However, Iran does not consider an escalation of tensions to be in anyone's interest, the foreign ministry spokesman added.

analysis.framing: The article frames Iran as a constructive diplomatic actor while portraying the Saudi-led intervention and Western involvement in Yemen as unjust and ineffective, and dismissing Saudi allegations against Iran.

loaded_language.explanation: Uses a morally charged adjective to characterize the blockade, presenting a subjective judgment as fact.

loaded_language.quote: orchestrated by extra-regional actors, particularly the United Kingdom and the United States
loaded_language.explanation: Implies deliberate, coordinated control by outside powers, which is an interpretive claim rather than a neutral description.
loaded_language.neutral_alternative: involving extra-regional actors, including the United Kingdom and the United States

loaded_language.explanation: Editorializes positively about the Yemeni people's endurance, adding an approving value judgment.

loaded_language.quote: such claims are not credible to those familiar with the relations between Iran and its allies
loaded_language.explanation: Dismisses Saudi allegations by asserting they lack credibility among knowledgeable observers, a rhetorical appeal rather than a factual rebuttal.

omissions: No mention of the Saudi Foreign Ministry official's specific allegations or the context in which they were made.
No reference to Iran's alleged military support for the Houthi movement, which is central to Saudi claims.
No details on the current status of Saudi-Yemen peace negotiations or international diplomatic efforts beyond Iran's offer.
No acknowledgment of civilian casualties or humanitarian data from the conflict beyond the blockade description.

corrections.reason: The article is a report on statements by an Iranian official; the framing is sympathetic to Iran's position, but 'lean-right' is not a standard or clearly attributable bias label for this content, and the confidence is not grounded in the text.
The 60/40 split is an arbitrary estimate not derivable from the article; no methodology is provided and the text contains both reported facts and attributed opinions.

headline: Vucic’s victory in polls ensures good ties with Russia — Information Ministry
summary: State Secretary of Serbia’s Ministry of Information and Telecommunications Perko Matovic pointed out that the Serbian people see Russia as a centuries-old protector and ally
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. Aleksandar Vucic’s victory in the parliamentary elections in Serbia guarantees good relations with Russia, Perko Matovic, State Secretary of Serbia’s Ministry of Information and Telecommunications, said in an interview with TASS.

"The Serbian people see Russia as a centuries-old protector and ally, and the Russian people as a fraternal people. Everyday politics will never change this. Undoubtedly, the only absolute guarantee that this will remain the case is the unconditional victory of Aleksandar Vucic and the United Serbia list in the upcoming elections," he noted.

Early parliamentary elections in Serbia will be held on October 25. Vucic will head the list of the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SPP) and become its candidate for prime minister. The main opponent of the SPP will be the Student List alliance, led by the cardiologist from Novi Sad Ilija Srdanovic.

analysis.framing: The article frames the Serbian election through the lens of pro-Russian sentiment, presenting Vucic's victory as essential for maintaining strong ties with Russia and amplifying a Serbian official's praise of Russia.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged and idealized description that casts Russia in a paternalistic, benevolent role, reinforcing a pro-Russian narrative.
Vague, emotionally laden term implying an unbreakable brotherly bond, which editorializes the relationship.
Strong, absolute language that frames the election outcome as a necessary and absolute guarantee, heightening the stakes.

omissions: No mention of the main opposition candidate Ilija Srdanovic's policy positions or campaign platform.
No context on international reactions or observers' assessments of the election.
No discussion of other key issues in the election such as economy, EU integration, or domestic reforms.

corrections.reason: The article is a TASS report quoting a Serbian official; the pro-Russian framing stems from the quoted source, not the outlet's own editorial stance. 'Lean-right' is not attributable to concrete wording in the article.
The 40/60 split is not derivable from the article; the piece is largely factual reporting with attributed quotes, and no concrete basis for this ratio exists in the text.

headline: Azerbaijan ban on headscarves in schools opens rift with ally Turkey
summary: The famous saying goes that Turkey and Azerbaijan are “one nation, two states”. Such are the countries’ ties that Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, founding father of the modern Turkish Republic, said: “Azerbaijan's joy is our joy, its sorrow is our sorrow.”But a row over school uniform rules threatens to sour decades of close ties between Azerbaijan and Turkey, countries that share a defence pact, billions of dollars in annual trade, and whose languages are so similar that they are mutually intelligible. Azerbaijan’s cabinet last month approved a ban on items of clothing that are “inconsistent with the principle of secularism”. It made no explicit mention of headscarves, but in recent days videos have circulated on social media showing schoolgirls wearing hijabs in floods of tears, saying they had been barred from their classrooms. “My mother thinks I’m in there getting an education, but they put me in a room, like a tiny shack, and hid me from the other children,” one girl was filmed saying. State television in the majority-Muslim former Soviet state said this week that new rules effectively banning girls from wearing headscarves to school were an effort by the government “block every move that seeks to add Arab-Persian values” to Azerbaijani national identity. While headscarves are permissible elsewhere, “School has a school uniform, and so on, and everyone must respect and abide by this rule,” a presenter on AZ TV said. Analysts said the move stemmed from fears in Baku of Iranian influence and a desire to maintain the country’s strong tradition of secularism, but it also prompted sharp criticism from Turkey. Another video from today. Parent says that her kid wasn't let in, she has been told if they continue standing outside they will be arrested as terrorists and she asks what kind of terrorism she is doing right now. pic.twitter.com/a2hHhCUASe— Cavid #FreeUlviyya (@cavidaga) October 14, 2026Tensions boiled over on Monday, when Oktay Saral, a senior adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, said Azerbaijan’s decisions denied headscarf-wearing girls the right to education, and that Azerbaijan should “correct this mistake as soon as possible”.Members of parliament from Mr Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) joined in the unusually sharp criticism. Zehranur Aydemir, an MP for the capital, Ankara, said that the “wrongdoing” was a “violation of freedom of religion and the right to education”.Sabir Askeroglu, an Ankara-based international relations analyst, said the disagreements could have a “negative impact” on Turkish-Azerbaijani relations, but added that it was more likely to be at a societal level than a serious deterioration in bilateral ties. “The main risk is not the disagreement itself, but the possibility that reciprocal accusations could gradually erode public trust between the two countries,” he told The National. A Shiite Muslim majority nation of 10.4 million in the South Caucasus, Azerbaijan’s Soviet history means religious observance is far less a feature of daily life than in neighbouring Turkey and Iran. In the latter, women have long fought against mandatory hijab rules imposed since the 1979 revolution that brought the current clerical leadership to power. In 2020, Turkish military support helped Baku regain from Armenia territory internationally recognised as Azerbaijani in the Nagorno-Karabakh region, while Azerbaijan’s close military, defence and intelligence ties with Israel have been a source of tension with neighbouring Iran. Turkey used to have expanding ties with Israel too, but relations nosedived after the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza. The headscarf issue is such a sore point in Turkey because of its own fraught history with Muslim women’s dress. In the 1990s, Turkey’s then-strictly secular authorities, fearful of the rise of political Islam, banned women and girls from wearing headscarves in schools, universities and government jobs. That forced many women to choose between their faith and an education or career. Many political observers partly credit Mr Erdogan's rise to his dismantling of such policies. Emine Ilyas heads the 28th February Students’ Association, a group representing Turkish women whose education was interrupted in the 1990s because they wore headscarves. Commenting on the Azerbaijani ban on social media, she said no “bureaucratic tutelage” could be a “cover for restricting fundamental rights and freedoms”.Members of the Turkish opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP), widely seen as less religiously conservative and more secular than Mr Erdogan’s AKP, also said Azerbaijan should reconsider its decision. “Let them [women] choose the clothing they wish to wear,” CHP leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu said. In Azerbaijan, President Ilham Aliyev’s party hit back with unusually strong criticism of Turkey and Mr Erdogan’s AKP. The New Azerbaijan Party said in a statement on Tuesday that the comments from Mr Saral and AKP legislators were “populist and irresponsible”. “No state in the Islamic world has the right to dictate its will to other Muslim peoples, to interfere in their internal affairs, or to see itself as superior to others,” it said.The headscarf ban prompted protests outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul, and in Azerbaijan, the Interior Ministry said on Monday that 37 people had been detained for disrupting public order while opposing enforcement of the rules, Reuters reported. Internet monitor NetBlocks said restrictions to TikTok, Instagram and X web platforms were in place on multiple internet providers in the country. Footage shared on social media showed Azerbaijani women angrily addressing messages to authorities, including MPs and the security forces. “Four cars of state officials came to my door early in the morning, saying it is forbidden for your child to come to school wearing a hijab,” one mother shouted in a scene caught on video and shared widely on social media. The scenes are unusual in Azerbaijan, where human rights groups have long criticised severe restrictions on freedom of speech, as well as authoritarian political rule by Mr Aliyev. Vasif Huseynov, a department head at the Azerbaijani state-run Centre of Analysis of International Relations, said the school uniform rules were a move against Iranian attempts to expand adherence to Tehran’s religious ideologies into the country. “It is precisely for this reason that the steps taken by the Azerbaijani government are aimed at protecting our national interests, our national values, our tradition of secularism spanning over a century, and the stability of our country,” he said in a post on X. Turkey’s fraught experience with the headscarf ban in the 1990s did not apply to Azerbaijan, he added. “Certain issues cannot be properly understood by viewing them solely through the lens of Turkey’s realities.” Over the past week, Turkish officials have attempted to calm tensions by promoting the long history of watertight strategic and economic ties with Azerbaijan. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan was welcomed by President Aliyev when he travelled to Baku for a summit on Thursday and told journalists that any issues would be addressed “by sitting down and talking them over”. “There is absolutely no need for these matters to be turned into tools for propaganda on social media,” he said. The primary responsibility for managing the disagreement lies with the political decision-makers in both countries, analyst Mr Askeroglu said. “Turkish officials should use a balanced tone that respects Azerbaijan's sovereignty and domestic legal framework while also taking sensitivities within Turkish public opinion into account,” he told The National. “Similarly, Azerbaijani officials should avoid interpreting all criticism expressed in Turkey as an attempt to interfere in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.”
