A Shiite Muslim majority nation of 10.4 million in the South Caucasus, Azerbaijan’s Soviet history means religious observance is far less a feature of daily life than in neighbouring Turkey and Iran. In the latter, women have long fought against mandatory hijab rules imposed since the 1979 revolution that brought the current clerical leadership to power.

In 2020, Turkish military support helped Baku regain from Armenia territory internationally recognised as Azerbaijani in the Nagorno-Karabakh region, while Azerbaijan’s close military, defence and intelligence ties with Israel have been a source of tension with neighbouring Iran. Turkey used to have expanding ties with Israel too, but relations nosedived after the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza.

The headscarf issue is such a sore point in Turkey because of its own fraught history with Muslim women’s dress. In the 1990s, Turkey’s then-strictly secular authorities, fearful of the rise of political Islam, banned women and girls from wearing headscarves in schools, universities and government jobs. That forced many women to choose between their faith and an education or career. Many political observers partly credit Mr Erdogan's rise to his dismantling of such policies.

Emine Ilyas heads the 28th February Students’ Association, a group representing Turkish women whose education was interrupted in the 1990s because they wore headscarves. Commenting on the Azerbaijani ban on social media, she said no “bureaucratic tutelage” could be a “cover for restricting fundamental rights and freedoms”.

Members of the Turkish opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP), widely seen as less religiously conservative and more secular than Mr Erdogan’s AKP, also said Azerbaijan should reconsider its decision. “Let them [women] choose the clothing they wish to wear,” CHP leader Kemal Kilicdaroglu said.

In Azerbaijan, President Ilham Aliyev’s party hit back with unusually strong criticism of Turkey and Mr Erdogan’s AKP. The New Azerbaijan Party said in a statement on Tuesday that the comments from Mr Saral and AKP legislators were “populist and irresponsible”.

“No state in the Islamic world has the right to dictate its will to other Muslim peoples, to interfere in their internal affairs, or to see itself as superior to others,” it said.

The headscarf ban prompted protests outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul, and in Azerbaijan, the Interior Ministry said on Monday that 37 people had been detained for disrupting public order while opposing enforcement of the rules, Reuters reported. Internet monitor NetBlocks said restrictions to TikTok, Instagram and X web platforms were in place on multiple internet providers in the country.

Footage shared on social media showed Azerbaijani women angrily addressing messages to authorities, including MPs and the security forces.

“Four cars of state officials came to my door early in the morning, saying it is forbidden for your child to come to school wearing a hijab,” one mother shouted in a scene caught on video and shared widely on social media.

The scenes are unusual in Azerbaijan, where human rights groups have long criticised severe restrictions on freedom of speech, as well as authoritarian political rule by Mr Aliyev.

Vasif Huseynov, a department head at the Azerbaijani state-run Centre of Analysis of International Relations, said the school uniform rules were a move against Iranian attempts to expand adherence to Tehran’s religious ideologies into the country.

“It is precisely for this reason that the steps taken by the Azerbaijani government are aimed at protecting our national interests, our national values, our tradition of secularism spanning over a century, and the stability of our country,” he said in a post on X.

Turkey’s fraught experience with the headscarf ban in the 1990s did not apply to Azerbaijan, he added. “Certain issues cannot be properly understood by viewing them solely through the lens of Turkey’s realities.”

Over the past week, Turkish officials have attempted to calm tensions by promoting the long history of watertight strategic and economic ties with Azerbaijan.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan was welcomed by President Aliyev when he travelled to Baku for a summit on Thursday and told journalists that any issues would be addressed “by sitting down and talking them over”.

“There is absolutely no need for these matters to be turned into tools for propaganda on social media,” he said.

The primary responsibility for managing the disagreement lies with the political decision-makers in both countries, analyst Mr Askeroglu said.

“Turkish officials should use a balanced tone that respects Azerbaijan's sovereignty and domestic legal framework while also taking sensitivities within Turkish public opinion into account,” he told The National.

“Similarly, Azerbaijani officials should avoid interpreting all criticism expressed in Turkey as an attempt to interfere in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.”

headline: Ousting Zelensky in interests of Russia, US, and Ukraine itself — Russian politician
summary: Chairman of the A Just Russia party Sergey Mironov noted hat the Kiev regime and its leader pose a threat not only to Russia but also to the global security
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. Russia, the US, and the people of Ukraine are interested in unseating Vladimir Zelensky, Sergey Mironov, chairman of the A Just Russia party, told TASS.

"The leader of the Kiev regime, Zelensky, has become a symbol not only of Russophobes but also of anti·Trump forces in Europe. His ousting is in the interests of both the United States and the Russian Federation, as well as the people of Ukraine," Mironov said.

He noted that the Kiev regime and its leader pose a threat not only to Russia but also to the global security. Zelensky, "his junta, and their European patrons" do not want peace with Russia, the parliamentarian said.

According to the deputy, removing Zelensky and eliminating his regime is a necessary condition for achieving peace.

"Words alone won’t intimidate or convince anyone now. We must not just put pressure on the Nazi scum — we must crush it! And to start with, we need to cut off its oxygen supply, which is well within the United States’ capabilities. This is what everyone who wants peace not just in words, but in action, should do," the politician concluded.

On October 10, US President Donald Trump said that Zelensky should hold elections and that he could have put an end to the conflict in Ukraine and concluded a peace agreement many times over.

analysis.framing: The article frames the call to oust Zelensky as a shared interest of Russia, the US, and Ukrainians, while amplifying the Russian politician's hostile characterizations without counterbalancing context.

loaded_language.explanation: Uses a term that delegitimizes the Ukrainian government, implying it is not a legitimate authority.
A politically charged label suggesting a military dictatorship, which is an editorial characterization rather than a neutral description.
Highly derogatory and dehumanizing language used to describe opponents, clearly expressing contempt.
Violent metaphor that conveys aggression and lacks neutrality.
Figurative language implying suffocation or elimination, which is emotionally charged.

No context about Mironov's role or the nature of his party within Russian politics.
No reference to international law or the legitimacy of Ukrainian elections.
No counterbalancing voices or experts who might challenge the characterization of Zelensky or the Ukrainian government.

headline: Up in the air: Tesla's 'flying' Roadster raises more questions than answers
summary: Elon Musk's Tesla Motors has flaunted a new flying car – well, sort of.Mr Musk touted it as “something that you haven’t seen in any movie” but it's not exactly Back to the Future stuff. However, the stunt seems to offer a glimpse of the future of transport. body_text:
Elon Musk's Tesla Motors has flaunted a new flying car – well, sort of.

Mr Musk touted it as “something that you haven’t seen in any movie” but it's not exactly Back to the Future stuff.

However, the stunt seems to offer a glimpse of the future of transport. It's a great idea, but several points need clarity before road-and-air-legal cars become a reality.

Late on Thursday, Texas-based Tesla introduced the redesigned Roadster, the electric vehicle maker's original model. It was a long-awaited unveiling for the new version of the car after production ceased in 2012.

The Roadster was “launched” off a curved ramp, flipped over in mid-air and landed with the help of built-in thrusters designed by Mr Musk's other major venture, SpaceX.

The car was also made to fly and barrel-roll over a line of Tesla vehicles, including its electric cars, Semi Truck and Cybertruck, although it seemed to take off vertically as it neared the first vehicle rather than launching well before.

The latest Roadster, which is set to go into production in 2028, is billed as going from zero to 100kph in a second – significantly faster than the first-generation model, which achieved that speed in under four seconds.

At the event at SpaceX's hub in McGregor, Texas, Mr Musk said the new Roadster used an “advanced ultra-high pressure air tank”, with 10 nozzles that carry about 250kg of air, which can recharge by itself without the use of any propellant.

Air tanks are critical in vehicle systems, as they are key components for brakes, suspension, tyres and thrusters. In the space race – one of Mr Musk's closely-watched endeavours – they are very high pressure to support propulsion.

The Roadster's air tank will “literally puff itself up and be able to do these manoeuvres whenever you'd like”, Mr Musk said.

However, the thruster-powered Roadsters will only come in limited-edition models and there will not be any street-legal versions.

That means not everyone can, at least not yet, “fly a car”, let alone perform barrel-rolls and kick-flips with the upcoming Roadster – especially as laws on the vehicle are both very tight and vague.

In the mid-2010s, US regulations had stated that flying cars would need two licences – one for the road and one for the air. The very niche nature of flying cars – whose technologies are still very much in their infancy – makes it difficult to assess rules by region.

Whoever drives the flying car is another issue. A notable example of this was the AirCar, which was granted an airworthiness certification by Slovakian authorities in 2022. Its maker, Klein Vision, subsequently said its operator would need a pilot's licence – not just a driver's licence – to operate it.

Mr Musk acknowledged this, saying, “I'm not sure if it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions.” However, he emphasises that with the new Roadster, “we can go further … this will be an actual car on the roads”.

Then there's the thought of having to load a car with compressed gas, which can cause explosions and raise alarm bells for owners and insurers.

“[It's] a tremendous feat of engineering. It’s hard to argue otherwise,” said David Thomas, director of content marketing at US software developer CDK Global.

“I’m not sure where you fill up a car with that. And it’s unlikely anyone will insure it either.”

And after ensuring any flying car is safe and legal, commercialisation is also a big question, said George Agathangelou, general manager and executive director of Cyprus-based financial services firm Teroxx.

“Would drivers need aviation certification or a pilot’s licence? What happens to liability, insurance and airspace restrictions,” he said. “Imagine explaining to your insurer that you didn’t rear-end another vehicle, you attempted to fly over it.”

Tesla isn't the first to unveil such a vehicle: in 2021, Britain's McMurtry introduced the Speirling, an electric hypercar using powerful fans to generate downforce. Tesla's approach is different as it combines suction with thrusters.

Mr Musk made sure that there was an audience to witness the Roadster stunts in Texas and ensure people would not claim it was AI.

Analysts at Chinese logistics company Raman Technology noted that it was “not antigravity magic, [as] it integrates aerospace technology inside an electric vehicle”.

She also suggested screen-free mealtimes. For families facing distress or arguments when a device is taken away, she advised giving children advance warning and establishing predictable stop times. Timers could help in such cases and make the boundary clear. Planning activities to follow, such as going outside or playing with a pet, can also help ease the transition. She recommended that parents remain calm and acknowledge the frustration without abandoning the agreed limit. Ms Pereira-Raso said parents also need to understand what children are doing online and how it makes them feel. “We must also recognise that children need more than restrictions. They need adults who are curious about their digital experiences, who engage in conversations about what they encounter online, and who help them develop the capacity to make thoughtful choices.”At Gems International School, Dubai Hills, personal phones must remain “on site, out of sight”. body_text:
Doctors in the UAE are reporting a growing number of children suffering from issues such as difficulty sleeping and concentrating that are linked to excessive screen time, prompting warnings that restrictions on phone use in schools are not enough to protect young people.

Dr Sudha Rao, a specialist in paediatrics at Aster Clinic in Al Jaddaf, told The National she had seen a noticeable increase in children experiencing problems associated with prolonged use of screens, particularly use late at night.

"There has been a substantial rise in children presenting with sleep disruptions leading to disorganized body clock or “circadian rhythms”, leading to fatigue, eye health issues such as myopia or near-sightedness," she said. "There are also behavioural concerns that are directly tied to excessive screen use, like 'digital tantrums'."

More AI and less screen time: How UAE schools are adapting

Health and education experts are urging parents to take greater responsibility for children’s screen habits, including keeping phones and other devices out of bedrooms.

Their concerns are supported by research from Saudi Arabia involving 500 children aged six to 12. It found that 66.7 per cent of those using screens for more than four hours a day had difficulty falling asleep, compared with 9.5 per cent of those using them for less than an hour.

Dr Rao also cited an Omani study that reported a 33.7 per cent figure for poor sleep among students with screen-induced visual impairment.

She said paediatric behavioural reports and UAE school studies authorised by the Dubai Health Authority found that children with less than two hours of recreational screen time a day scored 20 to 25 per cent higher in attention and memory tasks than children whose screen time exceeded four hours.

School leaders said that while technology was necessary for some learning and entertainment, the challenge recognising when devices were crowding out activities children needed for healthy development.

“The question is no longer simply how much time children spend on screens, but what they are exposed to, how they engage and what essential developmental experiences may be displaced,” said Nevita Pandya, chief executive and principal of Gems International School, Dubai Hills.

Teachers are increasingly noticing pupils displaying signs of tiredness, difficulties concentrating and problems with managing frustration.

These are complex issues with several possible causes alongside excessive screen use, but boundaries during the day need to be supported at home, said Helen Pereira-Raso, superintendent and chief executive of Gems Dubai American Academy.

“For example, a school can intentionally protect attention and engagement throughout the day, but a child who is regularly losing sleep because of recreational device use may still struggle to participate fully in learning.”

Dr Rao said parents should look at how screen habits affect children's daily lives, including homework, physical play, family meals and friendships.

“It is also deeply concerning if the screen viewing becomes the only way a child manages boredom, stress, sadness or difficult emotions,” she said.

The concerns become greater as children grow older. Ms Pandya said younger children could miss opportunities for conversation, imaginative play and social interaction, while adolescents faced challenges with sleep, social comparison and peer relationships.

Experts recommend consistent routines that include keeping devices out of bedrooms overnight and protecting family time.

Phones, tablets and gaming devices could be left to charge in a shared space for one or two hours before bedtime, Dr Rao recommended. She also suggested screen-free mealtimes.

For families facing distress or arguments when a device is taken away, she advised giving children advance warning and establishing predictable stop times.

Timers could help in such cases and make the boundary clear. Planning activities to follow, such as going outside or playing with a pet, can also help ease the transition.

She recommended that parents remain calm and acknowledge the frustration without abandoning the agreed limit.

Ms Pereira-Raso said parents also need to understand what children are doing online and how it makes them feel.

“We must also recognise that children need more than restrictions. They need adults who are curious about their digital experiences, who engage in conversations about what they encounter online, and who help them develop the capacity to make thoughtful choices.”

At Gems International School, Dubai Hills, personal phones must remain “on site, out of sight”. Ms Pandya said the policy aimed to protect pupils' attention and reduce distraction.

“Clear boundaries are an important part of a purposeful learning environment,” she said.

Managing screen use should allow room for purposeful digital learning alongside reading, practical activities and face-to-face discussion.

“We cannot treat all screen time as equal,” said Ms Pereira-Raso. “A child passively consuming content for hours is having a fundamentally different experience from one using technology to investigate a complex problem, collaborate with peers, develop an idea or create something meaningful.”

Preparing children for a technologically advanced world also needs effort to develop children's ability to concentrate, make decisions and manage distractions independently.

“However, being future-ready does not mean spending more time on devices.”

These expectations also apply to adults, Ms Pandya said. She encouraged parents to examine their own relationship with technology.

Ms Pereira-Raso suggested setting an example by putting phones away during conversations to demonstrate the habits families want their children to learn.

“Children are observing how we manage our own attention, whether we put our phones away during conversations, and how present we are in our relationships with them,” she said.

analysis.framing: The article frames excessive screen time as a growing health and developmental concern for children, emphasizing expert warnings and parental responsibility while acknowledging some benefits of purposeful technology use.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged term that pathologizes children's reactions to screen removal, using a clinical-sounding label for behavioral issues.
Editorializing phrase that amplifies the emotional weight of the issue beyond a neutral report.
Vivid metaphor that implies screens are displacing essential activities, carrying a negative connotation.
Colloquial and somewhat alarmist phrasing that emphasizes harm.

omissions: No mention of potential benefits of moderate screen use for learning or social connection beyond a brief quote.
No counterbalancing view from experts skeptical of screen-time panic or noting methodological limitations of cited studies.
No specific data on prevalence rates in the UAE beyond doctor's anecdotal report.

corrections.reason: The article relies almost entirely on expert and school-leader sources presenting a one-sided cautionary narrative about screen time; no skeptical or counterbalancing voices are included, so a 'center' rating with 0.7 confidence is not attributable to the text.
The 70/30 split is not derivable from the article; the piece mixes cited studies, anecdotal doctor reports, and numerous evaluative quotes without any stated basis for this ratio.

headline: Trump waives key Russia-related sanctions, tariffs before they take effect under new law
summary: By Kanishka Singh and Jasper WardWASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas.In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.
body_text:
By Kanishka Singh and Jasper Ward

WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs days before they were to take effect under a law he signed last month, including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas.

In an executive order released by the White House on Friday, Trump said the waiver was in the national interests of the United States.

The law is meant to increase pressure on Russia for its invasion of Ukraine that began in 2022. Trump, however, has been warming toward Russia and publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, including suggesting Kyiv needs a new leader.

Weeks before the US midterm elections in which Trump's Republicans are battling to maintain their narrow grip on both chambers of Congress, the new measures could have risked raising oil prices even further while Americans already face increased costs largely attributed to the US-Israeli war on Iran, analysts have said.

The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, a South Carolina Republican, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

The order said the waiver will remain in effect until Trump or his top officials determinethat "further action is appropriate."

Trump signed the LindseyO. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.

"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order.

Countries such as China and India, which are among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, have raised concerns about the Russia sanctions bill.

Beijing has said it "consistently opposed long-arm jurisdiction that lacks a basis in international law" while India warned Washington that new tariffs could impact bilateral ties.

The law allows the president to waive sanctions simply by informing Congress that he has determined that they are not in the national interest.

US Representative Don Beyer, a Virginia Democrat, blasted Trump for the waiver, saying he was giving in to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"Trump's latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression," Beyer said in a statement.

Trump had also faced criticism from several US senators, including some Republicans, over ‌a recent diesel deal with Russia in which Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian exports and Russia agreed to supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. The lawmakers who criticized the deal said it would help fund Russia's war efforts.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh, Jasper Ward and Patricia Zengerle in Washington; Editing by William Mallard and Sergio Non)

headline: Trump says has no plans to introduce restrictions based on law on sanctions against Russia
summary: This is in the national interests of the United States, the American leader’s decree stated
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump has issued a decree according to which he will not impose several sanctions based on the law on tightening restrictions against Russia.

"I am hereby waiving the application of such sanctions, restrictions, and duties provided for in the Graham Act. I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," the document published on the White House website states.

Under Article 115, the president has the right to waive the application of sanctions and duties provided for in the law. To do so, he must submit to Congress a justification that such a decision is in the national interests of the United States.

On September 18, Trump signed into law a bill passed by Congress that provides for sanctions against Russia’s top political and military leadership, state·owned companies, as well as secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners. According to the document, within 30 days after signing — or by October 18 — the Washington administration must determine which companies and individuals may be subject to restrictions, or determine that such new restrictive measures do not align with US interests, and notify Congress accordingly.

analysis.framing: The article reports factually on Trump's waiver of sanctions under the Graham Act, focusing on the legal mechanism and the national-interest justification, with minimal editorializing.

loaded_language.explanation: Uses 'tightening' which implies increasing severity, a mildly loaded descriptor of the sanctions law.

omissions: No mention of specific individuals or companies affected by the sanctions
No reaction from Russian officials or other governments
No context on why Trump decided to waive the sanctions beyond the national-interest statement
No details on the scope of the Graham Act or its sponsors

corrections.reason: The quoted phrase 'tightening restrictions against Russia' does not appear verbatim in the article. The article says 'law on tightening restrictions against Russia' in the headline and 'law on tightening restrictions against Russia' in the body, but the exact quote provided omits 'law on'. Additionally, 'tightening' is a standard legal descriptor, not clearly loaded.

headline: Trump mocks popularity of the name Mohammad, common among Muslims

I've done it for years now. I've never been wrong."
body_text:
By Steve Holland and Kanishka Singh

DALTON, Georgia, Oct 16 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump made a joke about the popularity of the name Mohammad in the Muslim world as he mocked Iran's presidency during a campaign speech on Friday.

"You know, if you're in doubt about somebody's name from the Middle East, just say 'Mohammad,'" Trump told a crowd in Dalton, Georgia. "You have about a 65% chance. 'Hello, Mohammad.' I've done it for years now. I've never been wrong."

Mohammad is one of the most common male names among Muslims, who often name their sons after the Prophet Mohammad, the founder of Islam.

Trump made the comment as he was discussing Iran during a rallyin a hangar at Dalton Municipal Airport in Georgia, where he campaigned for Republican political candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

"Iran is the only country where nobody wants to be president," Trump said, then pretended to ask several people named Mohammad whether they wanted the job. Masoud Pezeshkian has been president of Iran since 2024.

The Georgia crowd gave the joke a muted response.

Rights advocates and Muslim advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized Trump for rhetoric that they say demonizes and mocks Muslims, immigrants and ethnic minorities.

He hasescalated such rhetoric during the midterm campaign season, particularly against Somali and Muslim Americans including Muslim Democratic‌US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and RepresentativeIlhan Omar, a Minnesota Democrat who came to the US as a Somali refugee.

Trump repeated his vow that Iran would never get a nuclear weapon, seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Tehran aimed in part at crippling its nuclear program.

An annual report by the Council on American Islamic Relations released earlier this yearattributed rising Islamophobia in the US in part to Trump's crackdown on immigration and pro-Palestinian protests during his second term.

(Reporting by Steve Holland in Dalton, Georgia, and Kanishka Singh and Jarrett Renshaw in Washington; Editing by Sergio Non and Cynthia Osterman)

headline: About 1,500 troops to take part in Coalition of Willing exercises in Poland — The Times
summary: Military personnel from the United Kingdom, Poland, France, and Germany will practice the redeployment of troops and logistical support
body_text:
LONDON, October 17. /TASS/. At least 1,500 military personnel from the United Kingdom, Poland, France, and Germany will take part in the first Coalition of the Willing drills in November, The Times reported citing sources.

The maneuvers, which will take place in Poland, are being presented as a rehearsal for deployment in Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire. The participants will practice the redeployment of troops and logistical support.

The Coalition of the Willing, established in the spring of 2025, is an informal association of more than 30 states, mainly European, aimed at providing assistance to Ukraine. Within the framework of the coalition, led by the United Kingdom and France, security guarantees for Ukraine are being developed, including the deployment of military contingents after the conflict ends.

Russia opposes the presence of NATO military personnel in Ukraine. Earlier, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov noted that ensuring Ukraine’s security through "foreign military intervention in some part of Ukrainian territory" would be unacceptable to Russia.

analysis.framing: The article frames the drills as a rehearsal for Western military deployment in Ukraine while prominently including Russia's opposition, presenting the event through a geopolitical lens that highlights Russian concerns.

loaded_language.explanation: The phrase 'foreign military intervention' is emotionally charged and implies aggressive action, framing the deployment negatively.

headline: Japan’s PM sends offering to temple considered symbol of militarism
summary: Sanae Takaichi refrained from making a personal visit to the shrine not to create diplomatic problems with South Korea and China, which react sharply to such pilgrimages
body_text:
TOKYO, October 17. /TASS/. Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has sent an offering to the Yasukuni Shinto shrine, which is considered a symbol of militarism in China and several other Asian countries, according to Kyodo news agency.

Takaichi, as Kyodo notes, refrained from making a personal visit to the shrine not to create diplomatic problems with South Korea and China, which react sharply to such pilgrimages. Before becoming prime minister, Takaichi regularly visited this shrine twice a year, including as a minister. The last time the head of the Japanese government personally made a pilgrimage to Yasukuni was in December 2013, when Shinzo Abe held that position.

The current offering was made on the occasion of the traditional autumn festival celebrated at the shrine. Takaichi’s previous offering on the occasion of the 81st anniversary of the announcement of Tokyo’s surrender in World War II, which was marked on August 15 of this year, was made not as the head of the government, but as the leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.

This Shinto shrine, located in the center of Tokyo, houses lists of names of the Japanese people who died on the battlefield since the second half of the 19th century. The list also includes war criminals who were executed after Tokyo’s surrender in World War II by order of the International Military Tribunal. Visits to Yasukuni by Japanese officials provoke protests and are perceived in China, South Korea, and other Asian countries as a justification of Japanese aggression.

body_text:
The UN Security Council on Friday held a sixth vote to choose the next Secretary General, with Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan still narrowly leading in the race.

She has remained the front-runner, securing the minimum nine encouraging votes in the latest round and five discouraging votes, including two from permanent council members.

Argentina's Rafael Grossi secured eight encouraging votes and six discouraging votes, while Guyana's Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett also received eight encouraging votes and six discouraging votes. Both faced opposition from two permanent members.

Panamanian President Jose Mulino, whose country is one of the non-permanent members of the council, declared before the vote that his country would vote for Mr Grossi.

Unlike the five previous rounds of voting, Friday’s poll offered a clearer picture of which candidates had a realistic chance of becoming the next UN secretary general and which faced opposition from the world's most powerful nations.

For the first time in this selection process, council members cast colour-coded ballots, distinguishing the votes of the five permanent members – Britain, China, France, Russia and the US – from those of the 10 elected members.

When Secretary General Antonio Guterres was chosen in October 2016, it took six straw polls for the council to reach agreement.

Minh-Thu Pham, co-founder of the Starling Institute and a former adviser to UN secretary general Kofi Annan, said the narrowing gap between the three leading candidates emphasised the growing uncertainty surrounding the race.

“Compared to previous rounds, differences between the top three are very, very slim now,” Ms Pham told The National.

“It seems to be a split decision with no P5 convergence. It means there is a path open for new entrants,” she added, referring to the five permanent members of the council.

But Ms Pham warned that a new contender would not necessarily break the deadlock. "It could get messy," she said.

None of the seven candidates who participated in the October 16 poll has withdrawn, and no new candidates have entered the race yet.

US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, said after the vote that Washington wanted a secretary general who would refocus the organisation on its core mandate of maintaining international peace and security.

“We think that this institution needs strong, energetic leadership that is going to take the United Nations back to basics,” Mr Waltz told reporters, calling for greater efficiency and a renewed emphasis on peace and security.

He also played down the importance of regional rotation and gender in selecting the next UN chief, saying Washington's priority was finding the most qualified candidate.

“We understand there is a desire for regional rotation. Of course, if the best candidate's a woman, we would welcome that, but we really just need the best candidate,” Mr Waltz said. “This institution, after 80 years, has tried to become everything to everyone, and we need it. We put it on a diet, so to speak.”

Ms Pham said it was encouraging to hear Mr Waltz say that he thinks the council can finish before the end of the year. “Otherwise it could deepen doubts about the council and the UN,” she said.

But she warned that time was running out for new candidates to enter the race and secure sufficient support for the post. “Even if the US, China, and Russia agreed behind the scenes on a candidate, we’re in an environment where the other council members may not go along,” she said.

Unlike in 2006, when Washington and Beijing were able to rally support for Ban Ki-moon, Ms Pham suggested the US could now favour a candidate who would struggle to win broader backing.

Any attempt to accelerate the process could also provoke resistance from the General Assembly, she said, particularly if the council moved to vote on new candidates without giving them an opportunity to participate in the usual informal hearings. “A lot of pieces have to fall into place, and we’re running out of time,” she said.

headline: US not to supply Ukraine with weapons at expense of its own security — columnist
summary: Jude Russo pointed out that a war with Iran "will always tend to demand more attention and resources than the proxy conflict in Europe
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. The United States will not send weapons to Ukraine at the expense of security of its own armed forces in the Middle East, said Jude Russo, a columnist for the US magazine The American Conservative.

Commenting on reports about Ukraine’s shortage of missiles for Patriot air defense systems, the possible cessation of Washington’s transfer of intelligence data to Kiev, and the restriction of the Starlink satellite system, he said: "This is bad for Ukraine, although not altogether surprising. For months, the press has been full of ominous stories and analyses about the dire state of American munitions stockpiles after the US began its latest little jaunt in the Middle East."

"Reality is beginning to bite," the observer noted. In his opinion, even in the current conditions, the United States can continue the war with Iran without any special risks, but this "will come at the cost of readiness in other theaters." He said that a war with Iran "will always tend to demand more attention and resources than the proxy conflict in Europe. The US is not going to sacrifice the safety of its own military personnel and its own economic security for Ukraine."

headline: Trump says US, Russia, China to sign nuclear arms control agreements
summary: The US leader noted that he had raised the issue of nuclear arms control during negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 17. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump is sure that the United States, Russia and China will sign agreements on nuclear arms control.

"I can get a deal with them. I will get that deal. That doesn't have to be this year. They both are very important," he told journalists on the South Lawn of the White House.

In an interview with the Newsmax television channel, which aired on Thursday, Trump said he had raised the issue of nuclear arms control during negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

According to the White House, during Xi Jinping’s state visit to the United States on September 22-25, Trump advocated for arms control talks between the United States, Russia, and China. The Washington administration has previously stated repeatedly that it intends to seek China’s inclusion in a possible new agreement between Russia and the United States on reducing nuclear arms. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that genuine arms control in the 21st century is impossible without taking China into account.

As stated earlier at a briefing for journalists at the Chinese diplomatic mission in the US capital, the People’s Republic of China considers it possible to hold arms control consultations with the United States, but Washington must create conditions, in particular, by respecting Beijing’s key interests.

Lee said the meeting was meaningful as it marked the first time the two countries had brought together senior officials from their respective finance and monetary authorities.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent did not attend the Bangkok event.

An official from the finance ministry said the meeting aimed to enhance coordination between the two countries' finance and monetary authorities.

"The meeting was aimed at enhancing the policy mix of the two countries' financial and monetary policies," the official said.

"It is significant that the two countries have established a framework for cooperation to promptly and effectively address external financial uncertainties through close coordination between their finance and monetary authorities," the official added.

Lee was visiting Bangkok to attend the G20 finance ministers' meeting and the 2026 Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank Group. It was his first overseas trip as finance minister since taking office last month.

Separately, Erin Browne, under secretary for international affairs at the U.S. Treasury, who also attended the Bangkok meeting, said the parties discussed ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation.

"Our four institutions exchanged views on economic and financial conditions in both countries and discussed opportunities to further strengthen U.S.-Korea economic and financial cooperation," Browne wrote on social media X.

summary: Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama on Friday blamed the involvement of “foreign hands” for escalating protests, which he said are aimed at hindering Albania's bid to join the European Union. Issued on: 16/10/2026 - 21:59Modified: 16/10/2026 - 22:44

Protesters clashed with police in Albania's capital for the fourth day Friday as Prime Minister Edi Rama blamed "foreign hands" for mounting unrest.

Police used tear gas and water cannons while protesters hurled stones at security forces, burning garbage bins to block roads across the city. Fighting continued into the night in several parts of the city.

Violent demonstrations have rocked Tirana since Tuesday, with thousands of protesters calling for Rama to step down over university conditions and high tuition fees.

According to AFP journalists, protesters attempted to force their way into government offices on the capital’s main boulevard on Friday.

Read moreStudent protests spread in Albania as demonstrators call for PM resignation

Media reported that protests also spread to other cities with smaller scale violence and student boycotts of universities, marking a significant escalation in the months of anti-government protests.

The Tirana protests started with hundreds of people gathering outside the education ministry chanting "Rama resign!"

"We are not criminals. We simply want a better life for our parents and ourselves. We do not want to leave Albania," 18-year-old Ledia told AFP.

"The government's indifference and arrogance since the beginning of our movement have been unbearable and made the situation worse," said the high school student, who asked to be identified only by her first name.

Shopfronts have been smashed and several government buildings attacked, including the finance ministry, during this week's unrest.

According to a police statement, 160 people were detained for acts of violence on Thursday.

An AFP journalist saw masked groups smashing shop fronts and looting stores, with similar reports around the city.

"I would also like to remind you that we have far more reason to come together and work for the good of our country than to clash. This is a disguised attempt by those who seek to seize power through violence," Demo said in a statement.

Earlier he said that excessive police force had been registered in two instances and that two police officers had been suspended.

There has been months of anti-government protests in the Balkan nation, initially sparked by a controversial resort development linked to US President Donald Trump's family.

"All of this is the work of the very same hand, the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once."

The Socialist prime minister accused unnamed "foreign hands" of fuelling the unrest and seeking to hamper Albania's bid to join the European Union.

"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace," he said in a Facebook video.

Rama has routinely dismissed protesters' concerns, accusing them of being manipulated by foreign interests – without providing details or evidence.

headline: Morocco government sworn in under first female Prime Minister Fatima El Mansouri
summary: Morocco has sworn its new government under its first female prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, in a ceremony presided over by King Mohammed VI.Ms El Mansouri kept several members of the former government in their posts, including Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit. The 20 members of her cabinet also includes 11 ministers delegate.The government formation came after Ms El Mansouri's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won the election on September 23, reached a deal with three other parties this week. The coalition, which includes moderate socialist parties ⁠and the nationalist Istiqlal, together hold 207 seats in parliament, above the 198 needed for a majority.Other cabinet members who kept their posts were Justice Minister Abdel Latif Wahbi, Nizar Baraka as Minister of Equipment, Water and Forests, Riadh Mezzour as Minister of Industry, Trade, Investment and Economic Integration, and Abdellatif Loudiyi as Minister Delegate in charge of Defence.Morocco's ​football ⁠federation chief and former budget ​minister Fouzi ⁠Lekjaa was appointed as the Economy ⁠and Finance ​Minister, state news agency MAP reported.PAM member Khalid Hatimi was appointed Minister of Agriculture, Maritime Fisheries and Food Sovereignty.Leader of the Party of Progress and Socialism, Nabil Benabdallah, a former housing minister, returned to government as Education Minister, while fellow PPS member Charafat Afailal was named Energy Minister.Ms Afailal is one of two women appointed as ministers by Ms El Mansouri, along with Najwa Kokos, who was given the portfolio of Family, Social Development and Equality. Four of the 11 ministers delegate are also women.The new government is under pressure to address unemployment and ​demands for ⁠better education and health services. ​It will also oversee ⁠the final stages of a $20 billion push to prepare for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is to co-host with ​Portugal and Spain.
body_text:
Morocco has sworn its new government under its first female prime minister, Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, in a ceremony presided over by King Mohammed VI.

Ms El Mansouri kept several members of the former government in their posts, including Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit. The 20 members of her cabinet also includes 11 ministers delegate.

The government formation came after Ms El Mansouri's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM), which won the election on September 23, reached a deal with three other parties this week. The coalition, which includes moderate socialist parties ⁠and the nationalist Istiqlal, together hold 207 seats in parliament, above the 198 needed for a majority.

Other cabinet members who kept their posts were Justice Minister Abdel Latif Wahbi, Nizar Baraka as Minister of Equipment, Water and Forests, Riadh Mezzour as Minister of Industry, Trade, Investment and Economic Integration, and Abdellatif Loudiyi as Minister Delegate in charge of Defence.

Morocco's ​football ⁠federation chief and former budget ​minister Fouzi ⁠Lekjaa was appointed as the Economy ⁠and Finance ​Minister, state news agency MAP reported.

PAM member Khalid Hatimi was appointed Minister of Agriculture, Maritime Fisheries and Food Sovereignty.

Leader of the Party of Progress and Socialism, Nabil Benabdallah, a former housing minister, returned to government as Education Minister, while fellow PPS member Charafat Afailal was named Energy Minister.

Ms Afailal is one of two women appointed as ministers by Ms El Mansouri, along with Najwa Kokos, who was given the portfolio of Family, Social Development and Equality. Four of the 11 ministers delegate are also women.

The new government is under pressure to address unemployment and ​demands for ⁠better education and health services. ​It will also oversee ⁠the final stages of a $20 billion push to prepare for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is to co-host with ​Portugal and Spain.

headline: 'US tilting toward Russia: Europeans are standing more and more solidly with Zelensky'
summary: As transatlantic relations confront renewed geopolitical uncertainty, former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves delivers a pointed assessment of Washington's shifting approach to Russia's war on Ukraine and the profound implications for European security. At the heart of his analysis lies a fundamental question: can Europe develop the political unity, strategic independence and military capabilities necessary to defend its interests in an increasingly unpredictable international order? Ilves response: "If there's any time for Europe to begin to act as Europe and not as being strictly self-interested, then this is the time for it."

As transatlantic relations confront renewed geopolitical uncertainty, former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves delivers a pointed assessment of Washington's shifting approach to Russia's war on Ukraine and the profound implications for European security. At the heart of his analysis lies a fundamental question: can Europe develop the political unity, strategic independence and military capabilities necessary to defend its interests in an increasingly unpredictable international order? Ilves response: "If there's any time for Europe to begin to act as Europe and not as being strictly self-interested, then this is the time for it."

Ilves argues that the Trump administration's apparent rapprochement with Moscow is shaped partly by domestic electoral calculations, while Ukraine finds itself navigating an increasingly precarious diplomatic and military landscape. Yet he challenges the assumption that Washington retains overwhelming leverage over Kyiv, pointing to Europe's growing financial commitment to Ukrainian defence and the potential domestic political costs of withdrawing American intelligence support.

Beyond the immediate confrontation, Ilves identifies a more consequential challenge: the emergence of a fragmented European political landscape in which nationalist movements, competing security priorities and divergent attitudes towards Russia threaten the continent's capacity for collective action. His central contention is that European strategic autonomy is no longer an abstract institutional ambition but an urgent geopolitical necessity.

Can the European Union transcend national self-interest and emerge as a coherent strategic actor, or will they remain vulnerable to the decisions of external powers and the divisions within its own borders? "If we don’t take that issue seriously," Ilves warns, "I fear we will have far more vociferous tendencies within the European Union between those that take the security side of this seriously and those countries or leaders that will block progress simply for their domestic audiences."

headline: My Dubai Salary: 'I earn up to Dh45,000 a month coaching wellness to women in midlife’
summary: Monika Singh arrived in Dubai 12 years ago with a dentistry degree from India and a plan to sit her Dubai Health Authority licensing exams to practise in the UAE. Then she started attending group workout classes while she studied, discovered a love for dance fitness and never looked back.Today, she runs Monika Sphere, a women's wellness coaching business specialising in women in midlife, a niche she arrived at through her own experience with perimenopause after having her son, now seven. She now works exclusively within Arabian Ranches 1 and 2, coaches 23 clients, and earns between Dh42,000 and Dh45,000 a month.What was your first job?Before I started my own thing, I was doing group exercise classes in Fitness First and some other studios across Dubai. That was my starting point in the industry.I was never into fitness, honestly. I started attending dance fitness classes, and it just kind of stayed with me, and I was like, “Oh wow, I really want to do this.” I told my husband; I expressed my feelings to him, and he was very supportive. From there, I started my journey into fitness. I took my Zumba training, then I went into a group exercise leadership programme. Then I did my yoga training, Les Mills Body Balance training, then personal training and sound healing. A lot of things happened, and here I am today.And now?I’ve set up my own company. I have been training 23 ladies, and I'm just around Ranches 1 and 2 – I don't go outside because of commute time, and I also don't have time to go out and train people. My average earnings are Dh42,000 to Dh45,000 a month.My training is not just about typical strength training. Of course, strength training is important for women, but other factors come into play, like mobility, recovery, your sleep, your meditation, and your breathwork. Everything comes together to give you a balanced and sustainable fitness regime.I also specialise in women in midlife. This came to me through my own experience. After I delivered a baby, and as I entered my midlife phase – that is, perimenopause – I realised that my energy was not the same, my sleep was getting affected, and my responsibilities were different. And I realised the same complaint was coming from the women that I coach. Coming from a medical background, I have more understanding of human anatomy and physiology. I decided to dive more into this and study women's wellness, especially in midlife. I took my training, and now I am helping women achieve their goals without punishing themselves.Do you manage to save and invest?Yes, I do save. I'm not investing yet, but I do take care of my daily routine. I have a boy – seven years old – so I manage his school fees, then take care of my car loan, and some house chores. I keep around Dh3,000 to Dh4,000 aside for household expenses, and the rest I save. My husband takes care of the rest of the house.Growing up, were you taught how to handle your finances?When I was in university studying dentistry, we were given a very small amount of pocket money, and you had to manage that throughout the week. You wouldn't get more than that – that was the rule set by our parents, because in India it's like that. That's how I learnt how to manage my expenses.Honestly, I didn't learn anything about investing because we were not given the right to make any decisions on that. It was all my father who used to do that, not us.What are your financial goals?Currently, my goal is to launch my online portal. I have been saving for that because launching an online portal, an app, and everything else is expensive. Long-term, we have a plan to get a new, bigger house after I launch my online portal, once it becomes successful and once we start getting more and more income. That is our first plan.Where do you want to see yourself in the next 10 years?I want to be a known personality, a successful businesswoman – among people in the UAE who are known for their work.
body_text:
Monika Singh arrived in Dubai 12 years ago with a dentistry degree from India and a plan to sit her Dubai Health Authority licensing exams to practise in the UAE. Then she started attending group workout classes while she studied, discovered a love for dance fitness and never looked back.

Today, she runs Monika Sphere, a women's wellness coaching business specialising in women in midlife, a niche she arrived at through her own experience with perimenopause after having her son, now seven.

She now works exclusively within Arabian Ranches 1 and 2, coaches 23 clients, and earns between Dh42,000 and Dh45,000 a month.

Before I started my own thing, I was doing group exercise classes in Fitness First and some other studios across Dubai. That was my starting point in the industry.

I was never into fitness, honestly. I started attending dance fitness classes, and it just kind of stayed with me, and I was like, “Oh wow, I really want to do this.” I told my husband; I expressed my feelings to him, and he was very supportive.

From there, I started my journey into fitness. I took my Zumba training, then I went into a group exercise leadership programme. Then I did my yoga training, Les Mills Body Balance training, then personal training and sound healing. A lot of things happened, and here I am today.

I’ve set up my own company. I have been training 23 ladies, and I'm just around Ranches 1 and 2 – I don't go outside because of commute time, and I also don't have time to go out and train people. My average earnings are Dh42,000 to Dh45,000 a month.

My training is not just about typical strength training. Of course, strength training is important for women, but other factors come into play, like mobility, recovery, your sleep, your meditation, and your breathwork. Everything comes together to give you a balanced and sustainable fitness regime.

I also specialise in women in midlife. This came to me through my own experience. After I delivered a baby, and as I entered my midlife phase – that is, perimenopause – I realised that my energy was not the same, my sleep was getting affected, and my responsibilities were different. And I realised the same complaint was coming from the women that I coach.

Coming from a medical background, I have more understanding of human anatomy and physiology. I decided to dive more into this and study women's wellness, especially in midlife. I took my training, and now I am helping women achieve their goals without punishing themselves.

Yes, I do save. I'm not investing yet, but I do take care of my daily routine. I have a boy – seven years old – so I manage his school fees, then take care of my car loan, and some house chores. I keep around Dh3,000 to Dh4,000 aside for household expenses, and the rest I save. My husband takes care of the rest of the house.

When I was in university studying dentistry, we were given a very small amount of pocket money, and you had to manage that throughout the week. You wouldn't get more than that – that was the rule set by our parents, because in India it's like that. That's how I learnt how to manage my expenses.

Honestly, I didn't learn anything about investing because we were not given the right to make any decisions on that. It was all my father who used to do that, not us.

Currently, my goal is to launch my online portal. I have been saving for that because launching an online portal, an app, and everything else is expensive.

Long-term, we have a plan to get a new, bigger house after I launch my online portal, once it becomes successful and once we start getting more and more income. That is our first plan.

I want to be a known personality, a successful businesswoman – among people in the UAE who are known for their work.

headline: How a chance encounter with a sheep inspired a film about Palestinian displacement
summary: Sometimes the best documentaries start out on a whim.When Asmahan Bkerat met the Palestinian Bedouin family at the heart of her debut Concrete Land, she had no idea that eight years later she’d be presenting their story to the world. We’re sitting in Sea Containers hotel, right by the Thames, the day after the UK premiere at the London Film Festival. Just a few seats away are two of her subjects, Awad and his daughter Eman, and it’s the first time they’ve left Jordan. “It’s a complete culture shock for them,” says Bkerat. “First train ride, first plane … everything!”Bkerat gives me a promotional pin badge for the film, bearing a picture of Badrya, a woolly black sheep and one of the characters in this striking familial portrait. It all started when, quite by coincidence, Bkerat and her friend Ban Marqua (the film’s eventual editor and producer) met Badrya and her owner, Hakima, one of the family’s elders, on the outskirts of Amman.“The sheep is walking beside her like a dog,” she smiles. “That was a conversation starter.” Hakima invited them to her home. “We were very surprised to find a small tent settlement embedded in the city. I’d never seen that before.”Bkerat began shooting – initially resulting in a 2017 sheep-focused short, called Badrya. Encouraged to keep going, she kept the cameras rolling – capturing an overwhelming 400 hours of footage. “I did question myself a couple of times on what I was doing because in the middle you don’t know if it’s going anywhere,” she says. “You anticipate for something to happen, but it might not. There might be a story. There might not be a story. It took a lot of patience. But they were very patient with me, honestly. I was filming them sleeping. I was filming them crying. I was there all the time.”What ultimately emerged is a powerful tale of displacement, as this Afro-Palestinian family is facing the loss of the land they live on, thanks to proposed construction. It hardly helps that one of their neighbours, living in a luxurious-looking walled villa, has filed an eviction order. His callous argument is that the families living in this nearby tented settlement cause pollution – noise, smell, refuse. “I think his mentality speaks to a much wider perspective of thinking about yourself and not thinking about others,” says Bkerat. “And the way he looked down on people … he’s just treating them like they’re nothing.”The film took on far greater resonance after the events of October 7, 2023, and the subsequent destruction of Gaza by Israeli forces. “I think we all became aware that inherently all stories are political,” says Bkerat. “And now more than ever because the reality of the region shapes all of our experiences. I think one of the things that the film speaks to is that displacement and colonisation does not only happen on the ground in the same country. In fact, it has a much wider ripple effect that affects everybody, and it continues for generations.”One of the most heartbreaking scenes comes as Hakima is mourning the loss of her extended family in Gaza, many of whom have been killed. “Today my heart is with Gaza,” she cries, as she sings a traditional Bedouin song, one that expresses her utter helplessness, being stranded from her folk. “She’s describing her pain and she just wants to go back to her homeland,” says Bkerat, who admits she was “very surprised” by this sudden outburst. “I had to contain myself and not respond because I wanted to capture it.”Aside from the slightly bizarre quirk that two other films (The History of Concrete; Concrete Turned To Sand) are also on the festival circuit right now, the English title of Bkerat’s film also lodges in the mind. It’s about the “juxtaposition between the concrete and the land”, she explains, “and how sterile and inorganic concrete is in comparison to the land, and how it devours everything … I think it’s fitting in a way. It describes the state of the world. Everything is turning into concrete.”No pun intended, but Bkerat’s next task is to shepherd the film into the world. While it’s set to be screened at the famous documentary festival IDFA and the London Palestinian Film Festival in November, her biggest concern is making sure those in the Bedouin community see it. Easier said than done. “In Jordan, we have only a couple of cinemas, maybe five in the whole country.” A mobile screens-on-wheels is one possible solution, to “put the film out there as much as possible”.For a filmmaker who hadn’t even seen an observational documentary until she 2018’s Afghan activist story Laila at the Bridge, she’s now fully committed to the art form. Alongside various projects she’s developing, Bkerat is working with colleagues to establish the first documentary association in the West Asia and North Africa region. “We have a few organisations that support documentary, but not an association that supports documentary filmmakers,” she explains. As they say, from little acorns do mighty oaks grow.
