headline: Iran’s shadow war in Britain demands more than tough words
summary: On Tuesday, Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, the UK’s domestic counterintelligence and security agency, gave his annual speech about the threats faced by his country. Iran loomed large, second only to Russia. According to Mr McCallum, Iran was “keen on subcontracting its UK violence” and has spent this year expanding its hybrid campaign across the country. He said that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests over the previous 12 months, with much of the aggression targeting Britain’s Jewish communities.Iran has long had a history of operating beyond its borders. Its neighbours know only too well how it uses proxies and hires criminals to do its nefarious bidding. But until recently, its activities in Britain were mainly targeted at its own dissidents and Persian-language media. In March 2024, for example, Pouria Zeraati, a presenter on the Iran International television station, was stabbed by Romanian criminals; the court found that the attack had been carried out on behalf of Iran.This escalated after the war began in February. There have been a series of incidents and attacks, mostly on the Jewish community in the UK, which the authorities have attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Many of them have been claimed by Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia, or Hayi, which Britain regards as a proxy for the IRGC.In March, two men were charged with spying on London’s Jewish community and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Later that month, four ambulances belonging to the Jewish paramedic charity Hatzola were destroyed and a synagogue damaged in an arson attack claimed by Hayi.In April, there was a wave of attacks against synagogues and Jewish community centres in London. Last month, five men were arrested near RAF Fairford, a US bomber base used in operations against Iran. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament the incident was “almost certainly directed” by the IRGC. This month, two men were charged with preparing acts of terrorism; prosecutors say they scouted a synagogue and the Jewish Museum in Manchester.Iran has furiously – if implausibly – denied responsibility. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Britain about the RAF Fairford arrests “you’re barking up the wrong tree”, despite the fact that the IRGC had publicly declared the base a legitimate target.Britain has not been shy of attributing responsibility for the attacks to Iran, and expressing its outrage. In May this year, then-prime minister Keir Starmer said “our message to Iran … is that it will not be tolerated”. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in July that “Iran and Russia are using proxies and thugs to do their dirty work on our shores”. Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the opposition Conservative party, has called the attacks on the Jewish community a national emergency.But do Britain’s actions match up to the rhetoric? The answer is a qualified “yes”, but with room to do much more. £250 million (about $330 million) over three years has been allocated to protect the Jewish community. The government has taken a series of steps to clamp down on hostile state activity in general, and on the IRGC in particular.The IRGC and Hayi have been designated under the National Security (State Threats) Act, a new law to make it easier to tackle state threats. As a result, someone found guilty of supporting them now faces up to 14 years in prison; Iran’s Foreign Ministry called this a “despicable and provocative act”. The difficulty lies in the way that Iran mounts these operations. A minority of those accused are Iranian nationals, some of whom have come over by small boats from France to claim refugee status. But it would be a mistake to make this about Britain’s immigration policy, because most of the attacks are committed by young criminals hired, directed and paid online. The amounts of money are small. The controllers sit in Iran or Iraq and use Telegram and Snapchat to give instructions to their proxies. The attacks on the Hatzola ambulances, for example, were committed by four young British men then aged 17 to 20. These are not ideological lions, but petty criminals paid by the job.Breaking this model will not be easy, and nor will it be straightforward to go after the controllers rather than the foot soldiers. Doing so will require painstaking effort to target the gangs that sometimes broker the work, to trace the payments and to work with the online platforms to identify the networks.The problem is less an over-tolerant climate, and more the market in criminals for hire and unpoliced messaging apps. That said, the climate still matters. Growing anti-Semitism provides a target set and cover. Extremist preachers still inspire self-directed extremists in the UK, such as the ISIS-inspired man who attacked a synagogue in Manchester in October last year.Controllers sit in Iran or Iraq and use Telegram and Snapchat to give instructions to their proxiesIf Britain wanted to get tougher still, there are steps it could take. It could screen more rigorously asylum-seekers from Iran, though many of them are indeed fleeing the regime, themselves targeted by the IRGC rather than its agents. It could tighten rules on hate preachers and keep the pro-Iran Al Quds Day march banned.It could chill still further the relationship with Iran. It could expel diplomats or downgrade the Iranian embassy, though the Foreign Office remains keen to keep open the British embassy in Tehran. It could close the Islamic Centre of England, described by a Minister to Parliament as “the official religious representative” of Iran’s Supreme Leader in the UK; stop giving visas to clerics trained by the Iranian regime; give the Charity Commission, a regulatory body, powers to deregister “charities” that are a front for hostile state activity. It could even fight fire with fire and use the British state’s own capabilities to cause the regime pain inside Iran.But in the end, for as long as an IRGC controller can sit in Tehran and use Telegram to direct a teenager to firebomb a synagogue, and the British state neither disrupts the operation nor imposes a sufficient cost on Iran for mounting it, we must expect the attacks to continue.
body_text:
On Tuesday, Ken McCallum, director general of MI5, the UK’s domestic counterintelligence and security agency, gave his annual speech about the threats faced by his country. Iran loomed large, second only to Russia. According to Mr McCallum, Iran was “keen on subcontracting its UK violence” and has spent this year expanding its hybrid campaign across the country. He said that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests over the previous 12 months, with much of the aggression targeting Britain’s Jewish communities.

Iran has long had a history of operating beyond its borders. Its neighbours know only too well how it uses proxies and hires criminals to do its nefarious bidding. But until recently, its activities in Britain were mainly targeted at its own dissidents and Persian-language media. In March 2024, for example, Pouria Zeraati, a presenter on the Iran International television station, was stabbed by Romanian criminals; the court found that the attack had been carried out on behalf of Iran.

This escalated after the war began in February. There have been a series of incidents and attacks, mostly on the Jewish community in the UK, which the authorities have attributed to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. Many of them have been claimed by Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia, or Hayi, which Britain regards as a proxy for the IRGC.

In March, two men were charged with spying on London’s Jewish community and assisting a foreign intelligence service. Later that month, four ambulances belonging to the Jewish paramedic charity Hatzola were destroyed and a synagogue damaged in an arson attack claimed by Hayi.

In April, there was a wave of attacks against synagogues and Jewish community centres in London. Last month, five men were arrested near RAF Fairford, a US bomber base used in operations against Iran. Prime Minister Andy Burnham told Parliament the incident was “almost certainly directed” by the IRGC. This month, two men were charged with preparing acts of terrorism; prosecutors say they scouted a synagogue and the Jewish Museum in Manchester.

Iran has furiously – if implausibly – denied responsibility. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Britain about the RAF Fairford arrests “you’re barking up the wrong tree”, despite the fact that the IRGC had publicly declared the base a legitimate target.

Britain has not been shy of attributing responsibility for the attacks to Iran, and expressing its outrage. In May this year, then-prime minister Keir Starmer said “our message to Iran … is that it will not be tolerated”. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said in July that “Iran and Russia are using proxies and thugs to do their dirty work on our shores”. Kemi Badenoch, the leader of the opposition Conservative party, has called the attacks on the Jewish community a national emergency.

But do Britain’s actions match up to the rhetoric? The answer is a qualified “yes”, but with room to do much more. £250 million (about $330 million) over three years has been allocated to protect the Jewish community. The government has taken a series of steps to clamp down on hostile state activity in general, and on the IRGC in particular.

The IRGC and Hayi have been designated under the National Security (State Threats) Act, a new law to make it easier to tackle state threats. As a result, someone found guilty of supporting them now faces up to 14 years in prison; Iran’s Foreign Ministry called this a “despicable and provocative act”.

The difficulty lies in the way that Iran mounts these operations. A minority of those accused are Iranian nationals, some of whom have come over by small boats from France to claim refugee status. But it would be a mistake to make this about Britain’s immigration policy, because most of the attacks are committed by young criminals hired, directed and paid online. The amounts of money are small. The controllers sit in Iran or Iraq and use Telegram and Snapchat to give instructions to their proxies. The attacks on the Hatzola ambulances, for example, were committed by four young British men then aged 17 to 20. These are not ideological lions, but petty criminals paid by the job.

Breaking this model will not be easy, and nor will it be straightforward to go after the controllers rather than the foot soldiers. Doing so will require painstaking effort to target the gangs that sometimes broker the work, to trace the payments and to work with the online platforms to identify the networks.

The problem is less an over-tolerant climate, and more the market in criminals for hire and unpoliced messaging apps. That said, the climate still matters. Growing anti-Semitism provides a target set and cover. Extremist preachers still inspire self-directed extremists in the UK, such as the ISIS-inspired man who attacked a synagogue in Manchester in October last year.

If Britain wanted to get tougher still, there are steps it could take. It could screen more rigorously asylum-seekers from Iran, though many of them are indeed fleeing the regime, themselves targeted by the IRGC rather than its agents. It could tighten rules on hate preachers and keep the pro-Iran Al Quds Day march banned.

It could chill still further the relationship with Iran. It could expel diplomats or downgrade the Iranian embassy, though the Foreign Office remains keen to keep open the British embassy in Tehran. It could close the Islamic Centre of England, described by a Minister to Parliament as “the official religious representative” of Iran’s Supreme Leader in the UK; stop giving visas to clerics trained by the Iranian regime; give the Charity Commission, a regulatory body, powers to deregister “charities” that are a front for hostile state activity. It could even fight fire with fire and use the British state’s own capabilities to cause the regime pain inside Iran.

But in the end, for as long as an IRGC controller can sit in Tehran and use Telegram to direct a teenager to firebomb a synagogue, and the British state neither disrupts the operation nor imposes a sufficient cost on Iran for mounting it, we must expect the attacks to continue.

analysis.framing: The article frames Iran's activities in Britain as a serious and escalating security threat, criticizing the UK government for insufficient action while advocating for tougher measures against Iran and its proxies.

loaded_language.explanation: Emotionally charged and moralizing, casting Iran's actions as inherently evil.
Editorializes by dismissing Iran's denial as unbelievable, adding skepticism.

loaded_language.quote: petty criminals paid by the job
loaded_language.explanation: Dismissive and derogatory, reducing individuals to mere hired hands.
Idiomatic and aggressive, suggesting retaliatory measures without specifying them.

loaded_language.quote: we must expect the attacks to continue
loaded_language.explanation: Presents a prediction as an inevitable conclusion, adding a sense of urgency and fatalism.

omissions: Iran's perspective or denial is only briefly mentioned and dismissed, without detailing their stated reasons.
Potential diplomatic efforts or negotiations with Iran are not discussed.
The article does not mention any Iranian civilians or dissidents in the UK who might be affected by heightened tensions.
No mention of the potential impact on UK-Iran relations or the Iranian diaspora in Britain.
The article does not provide context on the war that began in February, which it says escalated the attacks.

corrections.reason: The article's framing is critical of the UK government's response and advocates tougher measures, but it does not exhibit clear right-leaning ideological markers; the rating is not directly attributable to concrete wording.
Keywords such as 'alarmist' and 'partisan' are not clearly supported by the article's measured, analytical tone; the article is critical and urgent but not alarmist or partisan in a clear way.

headline: The challenge of raising a generation of readers in the age of screens
summary: When Deema Al Alami’s son asks for a new book, the answer is always "yes". There are no spending limits and no questions about whether he really needs another one. A game for the iPad, on the other hand, is an entirely different proposition.“If my son ever says he wants to go buy a book, there’s no budget,” she says. “He can ask me to buy a book any time, anywhere, whenever he wants. If he asks for an iPad game, I make him suffer until he gets one.”There are other incentives, too. Bedtime might officially be 8.30pm, but reading earns an extra 30 minutes. Books can be accompanied by hot chocolate, while family conversations often revolve around the novels Deema, a Palestinian children's author and co-founder of Arab Child Summit, is enjoying.“I do these small things just to put it in my kids’ head that the act of reading itself is rewarding,” she says.It is a philosophy that reflects a growing challenge facing parents and educators across the UAE: how to encourage children to pick up a book when screens offer an endless supply of instant entertainment.For many families, that challenge is complicated by another consideration. In a country where children frequently move between Arabic, English and sometimes other languages, developing a love of reading can also mean navigating questions of identity, culture and belonging.Yet experts believe the solution is not necessarily to wage war on technology, but to make books a natural and rewarding part of children’s lives.The importance of starting youngFor Ahlam Bolooki, chief executive of the Emirates Literature Foundation, the groundwork for a lifelong reading habit is laid long before children enter a classroom.“Our research has found that if you read to your child daily in the early years of their development, there’s a 63 per cent chance that they will read independently,” she says. “If you read to them once a week, that drops to around 19 per cent.”The figures suggest that what happens at home can have a profound influence on children’s future relationship with books. But establishing that habit may require a cultural shift for some families.“When we grew up, it wasn’t something our parents did,” Ahlam says. “We are very much an oral storytelling culture, so I remember great aunts and my parents telling us stories of Arabian and folk tales from the region, but it was always oral, there wasn’t a book in your hand.”Crucially, however, reading should not always be treated as an educational exercise. The Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, encourages children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested. “There needs to be time where children can interact with books freely, not as something they have to do or be questioned about, just going and taking what they feel drawn to and spending time with it.”It is a distinction echoed by Deema, a former primary schoolteacher, who believes schools can sometimes become so focused on measuring literacy that they neglect the pleasure of reading.“Literacy rates are improving globally, but are children learning how to read for joy, for pleasure? That is the gap,” she says.She remembers reading aloud to her pupils every day, an experience they eagerly anticipated, and believes older children should also be given greater freedom over their choices rather than being stuck with set reading lists.“We have reading lists, but why can’t we give space for students to actually choose their own reading within a certain genre?”Such an approach, she argues, would not prevent teachers from analysing language, characters or plot while it would give pupils more ownership of the experience and a chance to read stories they can relate to, while showing there are many different ways to write a story.Competing with the screenFor parents trying to establish those habits, however, books face formidable competition.Digital devices are embedded in children’s education, entertainment and social lives, while artificial intelligence is creating new ways to access information without necessarily having to read deeply or investigate a subject.Ahlam believes attempts to eliminate technology entirely are unrealistic. “There is no point fighting technology at this point. It is a part of their lives and it is a part of their future. It is here to stay.”Children, she argues, must learn to navigate technology and AI effectively. But she worries about what might be lost if they become accustomed to receiving immediate answers.“The danger in children being exposed to AI so early on might mean that they are satisfied with the early answer and they don’t dig deeper.”For adults who developed their thinking skills before AI became widely available, questioning information and seeking alternative perspectives may feel more natural. The challenge is ensuring children develop those same instincts rather than simply accepting the first response a machine provides.Ahlam welcomes recent moves in the UAE to limit laptop use in some year groups, believing children need opportunities to develop their imagination and concentration without constant digital intervention.“When we talk about reading deeply and developing that love of reading, it’s not only about the act of reading, it’s about building that ability to let your mind wander and ponder on a thought.”Reading, in other words, is about more than absorbing information. It creates space for reflection, curiosity and independent thought. For Deema, parents also need to examine their own relationship with technology.“There’s also the element of leading by example. If the kids see that their parents are sitting on the sofa scrolling all night, you’re embedding a behaviour there.”The multilingual challengeThe UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing reading. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said. But in the UAE, encouraging children to read brings particular linguistic challenges. For many Arab families, English dominates entertainment, online content and much of children’s social environment, even when Arabic remains the language of home and cultural identity.Deema knows the imbalance from personal experience. “I’m bilingual. I grew up reading primarily English and Arabic books, but most of the English books did not reflect my identity in any way,” she says.Now a mother herself, she makes a conscious effort to introduce her sons to books that reflect their culture and experiences, “I believe that reading is not about deciphering the words and understanding, but seeing yourself and others in different experiences.”She believes the availability of Arabic children’s literature has improved considerably, helped by smaller publishers and parents determined to produce the stories they could not find for their own families.Through her From Mother to Author programme, she supports Arab mothers who want to become published writers.“When I was young, for every one Arabic book about friendship, you would find 30 incredible titles in English. Now, I think Arab children are seeing themselves more and more.”But greater availability does not automatically mean children will encounter those books.“Entertainment is primarily in English, especially here in the UAE,” she says. “Unfortunately, teachers, Arabic teachers, Arab parents, they are fighting a tsunami of English content.”She believes too much responsibility is placed on schools to produce confident Arabic readers when children have relatively limited opportunities to engage with the language outside lessons.“We give them 200 minutes a week and we tell them we want bilingual kids. We’re expecting way too much from children who are not exposed to the language.”The answer, she believes, is to make Arabic a language of enjoyment rather than something associated primarily with schoolwork. “Should it just be in the classroom? Are parents trying to make it accessible in terms of an enjoyment language at home?”More than two languagesDr Fajer Bin Rashed, assistant professor and literacy researcher at the Australian University in Kuwait, argues that even describing many Arab children as bilingual fails to capture the complexity of their linguistic lives.A child might speak a regional variety of Arabic at home, study Modern Standard Arabic at school and use English in other lessons or social situations.“When I refer to Arab children that speak an additional language like English, French, Spanish, I never refer to them as bilingual children,” she says. “I always refer to them as multilingual children.”That distinction matters when assessing literacy.Unlike children who learn to read in essentially the same language variety they speak at home, Arabic-speaking pupils must often bridge a gap between everyday speech and the formal written language.Dr Bin Rashed's research focuses on literacy education, bilingualism, multiculturalism and social-emotional learning. She warns against drawing simplistic conclusions from international reading assessments that compare children growing up in very different linguistic environments.“The danger of international assessments is where Arab children are compared to those in the USA, for example, or anywhere where they speak the same variety of English at home and at school. That isn’t equal.”However, she rejects the suggestion that growing up with multiple languages necessarily delays reading development. “I don’t think that raising bilingual or multilingual children actually slows down the reading. It doesn’t.”Children’s progress, she says, depends on their exposure to each language, the opportunities they have to practise and the social environments in which those languages are used.Skills developed in one language can also support learning in another, although the extent of that transfer varies.Dr Bin Rashed believes parents should embrace the natural movement between languages rather than treating it as a problem. “Some people think of code switching as a negative thing. Code switching is a natural part of bilingual communication.”For families, this means reading together need not involve rigidly separating languages. Parents can explain unfamiliar words, translate ideas and move between Arabic and English while maintaining the pleasure of the story.The important thing is to understand what they hope to achieve from the experience.“Are you reading for pure joy? Are you reading to help improve an additional language? Are you reading for bonding? Are you reading for social and emotional development?”Each is a legitimate reason to open a book.Making reading irresistibleAll three experts return to a deceptively simple principle: children are more likely to become readers when books are part of the world around them.For Dr Bin Rashed, that starts with parents demonstrating the behaviour they want to encourage.“I always say it to everybody: model, model, model reading. If you’re not going to model reading in front of your children, they’re not going to do it.”Ahlam believes schools can help compensate when reading is not already established at home.She highlights the transformative influence of a good school library and, particularly, a librarian who understands how to connect individual children with the right stories.The Emirates Literature Foundation School Librarian of the Year Award 2026 recently honoured the top UAE school librarians at the Museum of the Future in Dubai.“You see the difference of someone who’s just sort of keeping the lights on and keeping it tidy, and someone who has created a safe space in their library and knows how to find the right stories for the right child,” says Ahlam.For younger children, Deema believes physical books remain especially important.Even before they can understand the words, babies and toddlers are learning through the experience of handling books, turning pages and exploring how they work.“They’re biting, they’re chewing on the book, they’re throwing the book, they’re opening them. For me, this is reading.”She believes that, as children grow older, reading should become something they associate with freedom, pleasure and family connection rather than obligation.Ahlam, meanwhile, is optimistic that a generation raised in the digital age might ultimately rediscover the value of books.“I think if things are cyclical, maybe we were the generation that dropped off and they’re going to bring it back,” she says. “Because they’re growing up in such an incredible era of children’s literature as well.”The challenge for parents and schools is ensuring children have the opportunity to discover it. And that may be as simple as putting down their own phones, picking up a book and showing children what they have been missing.
body_text:
When Deema Al Alami’s son asks for a new book, the answer is always "yes". There are no spending limits and no questions about whether he really needs another one. A game for the iPad, on the other hand, is an entirely different proposition.

“If my son ever says he wants to go buy a book, there’s no budget,” she says. “He can ask me to buy a book any time, anywhere, whenever he wants. If he asks for an iPad game, I make him suffer until he gets one.”

There are other incentives, too. Bedtime might officially be 8.30pm, but reading earns an extra 30 minutes. Books can be accompanied by hot chocolate, while family conversations often revolve around the novels Deema, a Palestinian children's author and co-founder of Arab Child Summit, is enjoying.

Why Europe's reading habits should concern the Arab world

“I do these small things just to put it in my kids’ head that the act of reading itself is rewarding,” she says.

It is a philosophy that reflects a growing challenge facing parents and educators across the UAE: how to encourage children to pick up a book when screens offer an endless supply of instant entertainment.

For many families, that challenge is complicated by another consideration. In a country where children frequently move between Arabic, English and sometimes other languages, developing a love of reading can also mean navigating questions of identity, culture and belonging.

Yet experts believe the solution is not necessarily to wage war on technology, but to make books a natural and rewarding part of children’s lives.

For Ahlam Bolooki, chief executive of the Emirates Literature Foundation, the groundwork for a lifelong reading habit is laid long before children enter a classroom.

“Our research has found that if you read to your child daily in the early years of their development, there’s a 63 per cent chance that they will read independently,” she says. “If you read to them once a week, that drops to around 19 per cent.”

The figures suggest that what happens at home can have a profound influence on children’s future relationship with books. But establishing that habit may require a cultural shift for some families.

“When we grew up, it wasn’t something our parents did,” Ahlam says. “We are very much an oral storytelling culture, so I remember great aunts and my parents telling us stories of Arabian and folk tales from the region, but it was always oral, there wasn’t a book in your hand.”

Crucially, however, reading should not always be treated as an educational exercise. The Emirates Literature Foundation's Reading for Pleasure programme, launched in 2023, encourages children to see reading as something to enjoy rather than an exercise in muscle memory. The five-year pilot gives pupils at six Dubai primary schools access to books in Arabic and English, and time to read without being tested.

“There needs to be time where children can interact with books freely, not as something they have to do or be questioned about, just going and taking what they feel drawn to and spending time with it.”

It is a distinction echoed by Deema, a former primary schoolteacher, who believes schools can sometimes become so focused on measuring literacy that they neglect the pleasure of reading.

“Literacy rates are improving globally, but are children learning how to read for joy, for pleasure? That is the gap,” she says.

She remembers reading aloud to her pupils every day, an experience they eagerly anticipated, and believes older children should also be given greater freedom over their choices rather than being stuck with set reading lists.

“We have reading lists, but why can’t we give space for students to actually choose their own reading within a certain genre?”

Such an approach, she argues, would not prevent teachers from analysing language, characters or plot while it would give pupils more ownership of the experience and a chance to read stories they can relate to, while showing there are many different ways to write a story.

For parents trying to establish those habits, however, books face formidable competition.

Digital devices are embedded in children’s education, entertainment and social lives, while artificial intelligence is creating new ways to access information without necessarily having to read deeply or investigate a subject.

Ahlam believes attempts to eliminate technology entirely are unrealistic. “There is no point fighting technology at this point. It is a part of their lives and it is a part of their future. It is here to stay.”

Children, she argues, must learn to navigate technology and AI effectively. But she worries about what might be lost if they become accustomed to receiving immediate answers.

“The danger in children being exposed to AI so early on might mean that they are satisfied with the early answer and they don’t dig deeper.”

For adults who developed their thinking skills before AI became widely available, questioning information and seeking alternative perspectives may feel more natural. The challenge is ensuring children develop those same instincts rather than simply accepting the first response a machine provides.

Ahlam welcomes recent moves in the UAE to limit laptop use in some year groups, believing children need opportunities to develop their imagination and concentration without constant digital intervention.

“When we talk about reading deeply and developing that love of reading, it’s not only about the act of reading, it’s about building that ability to let your mind wander and ponder on a thought.”

Reading, in other words, is about more than absorbing information. It creates space for reflection, curiosity and independent thought. For Deema, parents also need to examine their own relationship with technology.

“There’s also the element of leading by example. If the kids see that their parents are sitting on the sofa scrolling all night, you’re embedding a behaviour there.”

The UAE's Arab Reading Challenge demonstrates the scale of government support for nurturing reading. Launched under the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives, this year's event – the 10th – attracted more than 40 million participants across 60 countries, organisers said.

But in the UAE, encouraging children to read brings particular linguistic challenges. For many Arab families, English dominates entertainment, online content and much of children’s social environment, even when Arabic remains the language of home and cultural identity.

Deema knows the imbalance from personal experience. “I’m bilingual. I grew up reading primarily English and Arabic books, but most of the English books did not reflect my identity in any way,” she says.

Now a mother herself, she makes a conscious effort to introduce her sons to books that reflect their culture and experiences, “I believe that reading is not about deciphering the words and understanding, but seeing yourself and others in different experiences.”

She believes the availability of Arabic children’s literature has improved considerably, helped by smaller publishers and parents determined to produce the stories they could not find for their own families.

Through her From Mother to Author programme, she supports Arab mothers who want to become published writers.

“When I was young, for every one Arabic book about friendship, you would find 30 incredible titles in English. Now, I think Arab children are seeing themselves more and more.”

But greater availability does not automatically mean children will encounter those books.

“Entertainment is primarily in English, especially here in the UAE,” she says. “Unfortunately, teachers, Arabic teachers, Arab parents, they are fighting a tsunami of English content.”

She believes too much responsibility is placed on schools to produce confident Arabic readers when children have relatively limited opportunities to engage with the language outside lessons.

“We give them 200 minutes a week and we tell them we want bilingual kids. We’re expecting way too much from children who are not exposed to the language.”

The answer, she believes, is to make Arabic a language of enjoyment rather than something associated primarily with schoolwork. “Should it just be in the classroom? Are parents trying to make it accessible in terms of an enjoyment language at home?”

Dr Fajer Bin Rashed, assistant professor and literacy researcher at the Australian University in Kuwait, argues that even describing many Arab children as bilingual fails to capture the complexity of their linguistic lives.

A child might speak a regional variety of Arabic at home, study Modern Standard Arabic at school and use English in other lessons or social situations.

“When I refer to Arab children that speak an additional language like English, French, Spanish, I never refer to them as bilingual children,” she says. “I always refer to them as multilingual children.”

That distinction matters when assessing literacy.

Unlike children who learn to read in essentially the same language variety they speak at home, Arabic-speaking pupils must often bridge a gap between everyday speech and the formal written language.

Dr Bin Rashed's research focuses on literacy education, bilingualism, multiculturalism and social-emotional learning. She warns against drawing simplistic conclusions from international reading assessments that compare children growing up in very different linguistic environments.

“The danger of international assessments is where Arab children are compared to those in the USA, for example, or anywhere where they speak the same variety of English at home and at school. That isn’t equal.”

However, she rejects the suggestion that growing up with multiple languages necessarily delays reading development. “I don’t think that raising bilingual or multilingual children actually slows down the reading. It doesn’t.”

Children’s progress, she says, depends on their exposure to each language, the opportunities they have to practise and the social environments in which those languages are used.

Skills developed in one language can also support learning in another, although the extent of that transfer varies.

Dr Bin Rashed believes parents should embrace the natural movement between languages rather than treating it as a problem. “Some people think of code switching as a negative thing. Code switching is a natural part of bilingual communication.”

For families, this means reading together need not involve rigidly separating languages. Parents can explain unfamiliar words, translate ideas and move between Arabic and English while maintaining the pleasure of the story.

The important thing is to understand what they hope to achieve from the experience.

“Are you reading for pure joy? Are you reading to help improve an additional language? Are you reading for bonding? Are you reading for social and emotional development?”

Each is a legitimate reason to open a book.

All three experts return to a deceptively simple principle: children are more likely to become readers when books are part of the world around them.

For Dr Bin Rashed, that starts with parents demonstrating the behaviour they want to encourage.

“I always say it to everybody: model, model, model reading. If you’re not going to model reading in front of your children, they’re not going to do it.”

Ahlam believes schools can help compensate when reading is not already established at home.

She highlights the transformative influence of a good school library and, particularly, a librarian who understands how to connect individual children with the right stories.

The Emirates Literature Foundation School Librarian of the Year Award 2026 recently honoured the top UAE school librarians at the Museum of the Future in Dubai.

“You see the difference of someone who’s just sort of keeping the lights on and keeping it tidy, and someone who has created a safe space in their library and knows how to find the right stories for the right child,” says Ahlam.

For younger children, Deema believes physical books remain especially important.

Even before they can understand the words, babies and toddlers are learning through the experience of handling books, turning pages and exploring how they work.

“They’re biting, they’re chewing on the book, they’re throwing the book, they’re opening them. For me, this is reading.”

She believes that, as children grow older, reading should become something they associate with freedom, pleasure and family connection rather than obligation.

Ahlam, meanwhile, is optimistic that a generation raised in the digital age might ultimately rediscover the value of books.

“I think if things are cyclical, maybe we were the generation that dropped off and they’re going to bring it back,” she says. “Because they’re growing up in such an incredible era of children’s literature as well.”

The challenge for parents and schools is ensuring children have the opportunity to discover it. And that may be as simple as putting down their own phones, picking up a book and showing children what they have been missing.

headline: Former soldier braves blisters and bears to complete epic 1,700km run across three countries
summary: Dodging bears, wolves and wild dogs and enduring days of isolation, one man has been tested mentally as much as physically while attempting to run 1,700km across three nations in just 40 days.Former British soldier Nick Coats, 39, arrived in Cappadocia in Turkey late on Wednesday evening after running through Greece and Albania to support a UK men’s mental health charity.The fitness coach, who lives in Dubai, set his sights on the ultra-endurance challenge after seeing friends and colleagues struggle with their mental health.Running through the Albanian mountains while carrying a 12kg rucksack at 35C was a particular challenge, as was managing feet ravaged by blisters and the daily wear and tear of long-distance running.“The last day was a 54km day to get to the hotel at around 7pm, which was hugely satisfying,” Mr Coats told The National from the comfort of his hotel room. “Arriving in Cappadocia town, I was met by the mayor, the mayor's wife and the assistant mayor, so it couldn’t have been more welcoming.“The distances between the towns, the availability of resources, and not being able to find a place to stay every night was ridiculously challenging. The main message here is that endurance is such a good teacher when it comes to how to deal with our struggles in daily life.”Three countries crossedHe began running on September 5 in Albania and travelled through Greece before reaching the finishing line in Cappadocia. The route included two organised ultramarathons, starting with the two-day 100km Ultra 4 Veterans Albania mountain race.During his daily marathons, he would contend with weather extremes, steep climbs and hidden wildlife along the way. “I was contending with these guardian dogs, which are the most incredible beasts,” he said.“Coming across those when you're running is quite intimidating, which added to the rawness. In northern Greece, I constantly had warnings of bears and wolves out in the forests, but I never saw any. Even running on the motorways was quite exciting because the lorries were honking in support and policemen on the hard shoulder were also extremely supportive.”His girlfriend, friends and family flew out to join him for the latter stages, which brought huge relief from the long days of loneliness, he said.Mr Coats served for seven years in the British Army as a member of the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, after which he found it difficult to adjust to civilian life. He took up ultramarathon running shortly after moving to Singapore and his marriage breaking down.He is now a personal fitness coach in Dubai and supports others looking to maximise their chances of completing similar endurance events. Although he has reached his final destination, his efforts are not quite over, as he plans to join hundreds of other runners on the 119km Cappadocia Ultra Trail on Saturday.Support a friendHe aims to raise funds for the UK’s Check in on a Mate initiative, which seeks to improve men's mental health and promote regular conversations about challenging issues. body_text:
Dodging bears, wolves and wild dogs and enduring days of isolation, one man has been tested mentally as much as physically while attempting to run 1,700km across three nations in just 40 days.

Former British soldier Nick Coats, 39, arrived in Cappadocia in Turkey late on Wednesday evening after running through Greece and Albania to support a UK men’s mental health charity.

The fitness coach, who lives in Dubai, set his sights on the ultra-endurance challenge after seeing friends and colleagues struggle with their mental health.

British runner sets new record in seven-emirates challenge

Running through the Albanian mountains while carrying a 12kg rucksack at 35C was a particular challenge, as was managing feet ravaged by blisters and the daily wear and tear of long-distance running.

“The last day was a 54km day to get to the hotel at around 7pm, which was hugely satisfying,” Mr Coats told The National from the comfort of his hotel room. “Arriving in Cappadocia town, I was met by the mayor, the mayor's wife and the assistant mayor, so it couldn’t have been more welcoming.

“The distances between the towns, the availability of resources, and not being able to find a place to stay every night was ridiculously challenging. The main message here is that endurance is such a good teacher when it comes to how to deal with our struggles in daily life.”

He began running on September 5 in Albania and travelled through Greece before reaching the finishing line in Cappadocia. The route included two organised ultramarathons, starting with the two-day 100km Ultra 4 Veterans Albania mountain race.

During his daily marathons, he would contend with weather extremes, steep climbs and hidden wildlife along the way. “I was contending with these guardian dogs, which are the most incredible beasts,” he said.

“Coming across those when you're running is quite intimidating, which added to the rawness. In northern Greece, I constantly had warnings of bears and wolves out in the forests, but I never saw any. Even running on the motorways was quite exciting because the lorries were honking in support and policemen on the hard shoulder were also extremely supportive.”

His girlfriend, friends and family flew out to join him for the latter stages, which brought huge relief from the long days of loneliness, he said.

Mr Coats served for seven years in the British Army as a member of the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, after which he found it difficult to adjust to civilian life. He took up ultramarathon running shortly after moving to Singapore and his marriage breaking down.

He is now a personal fitness coach in Dubai and supports others looking to maximise their chances of completing similar endurance events. Although he has reached his final destination, his efforts are not quite over, as he plans to join hundreds of other runners on the 119km Cappadocia Ultra Trail on Saturday.

He aims to raise funds for the UK’s Check in on a Mate initiative, which seeks to improve men's mental health and promote regular conversations about challenging issues. He also hopes to introduce education programmes in schools and train teachers to speak to young people who may be facing mental health challenges.

He said he hopes the scheme can be replicated in the UAE.

“This has been about reaching people with the message that you're not alone, and to break the silence around men's mental health. To decriminalise attempted suicide in the UAE is a massive step in the right direction.

“We want to catch the warning signs of mental health that could be leading people down a difficult path of isolating themselves, or changes in behaviour that could be a red flag. I'm really hoping that in due course we can look to create something like that in the UAE as well and get into these schools and communities to create more mental health first aiders. Now we can start to talk about it a lot more openly.

“This has made me realise how much the human body is capable of, and it's actually the mind that will be your downfall. If you can control those moments, then the body will follow, there is no doubt about it.”

headline: Israeli expansion across Golan Heights frontier takes toll on Syrian farmers

A 1974 armistice ensured calm in the area – until the 2011 to 2024 Syrian civil war. His life came crashing down in April 2024, when Israeli forces arrested his son Saddam, then 16, during an incursion across the armistice line. “Saddam was not a threat to anyone. I haven’t heard from him. He is now almost 19,” Mr Saadeddin said.They bulldozed and torched my landHasan Saadeddin, Syrian farmerBy the end of 2024, his land had disappeared behind a new Israeli military line, a result of the upheavals in Syria and the wider Middle East. The area is a focal point of US-sponsored talks between Israel and Syria on security arrangements and eventual peace. The last known discussion was held in Jordan's capital, Amman, in August, but the talks have been inconclusive, with Syria demanding that Israeli forces return to the armistice line. Israel has not officially acknowledged the existence of Sufa 53. “It is not a continuous line yet,” an official in Quneitra said. He said Israel had built seven military outposts in newly occupied Syrian territory as a precursor to the line – six in Quneitra and one in Deraa. One outpost is clearly visible across a wooded area near Jabata Al Khashab. Israeli patrols enter the village almost daily, according to residents, looking for weapons and questioning passers-by.Mr Saadeddin is not the only farmer along the frontier to be affected by Israel's new military line. Agricultural engineer Asia Al Ali, who works with the Quneitra governorate, said Israel had taken over 1,160 hectares of farmland and wooded areas near Jabata Al Khashab and other parts of the frontier. Israel destroyed 40 per cent of those areas in its drive to build the Sufa 53 line, she said. Around 250 farmers can no longer access their land, or it was made unusable.“There has been a lot of [Israeli] escalation lately, and sometimes direct shooting,” said Ms Al Ali, adding that Israeli troops began spraying “poisonous material” this year to kill crops.Israel began building the line in 2022, near the Syrian town of Hader in northern Quneitra, after the Syrian side of the frontier fell under Iranian influence.Members of the Iran-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, defending the Assad regime in Syria, operated in the region and formed loyalist militias. Israeli positions came under rocket fire. Israel responded with air strikes and incursions.The dynamics changed sharply after militant forces led by current Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara ousted Bashar Al Assad's government in December 2024. In the following weeks, Israel sent troops across the frontier and mounted an air campaign that destroyed large amounts of Syrian military hardware, without targeting members of the new order. The US, which emerged as the most powerful backer of the new government, initiated talks between Syria and Israel to reach security arrangements and an eventual peace deal.On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had phoned Mr Al Shara in July last year, after Israeli planes bombed government and military targets in central Damascus and near the presidential palace. Mr Netanyahu apparently warned Mr Al Shara against pursuing a deadly campaign to subdue the mostly Druze southern governorate of Sweida. It was the first known instance of the Syrian and Israeli leaders speaking to each other. However, the Israeli incursions have increased, with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights saying that 280 were recorded in September alone. Forty-nine Syrians remain in Israeli detention after Israel released 14 last month.Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in August that the military performed what he described as daily activity to “eliminate threats and remnants of the Assad regime” and to prevent “dangerous consolidation of the new regime”. Carmit Valensi, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said Mr Al Shara “may have become substantially more pragmatic, but the system around him has not necessarily undergone the same transformation”.Ms Valensi said the Syrian President was surrounded by former members of Hayat Tahrir Al Sham, the former Al Qaeda affiliate he founded during the civil war, and hardline security commanders. “The test is no longer simply whether Al Shara has changed. It is whether he can discipline, transform and ultimately institutionalise the system around him.” However, a prolonged Israeli military presence and repeated incursions could weaken Mr Al Shara to the advantage of “ISIS, Iranian networks, Hezbollah, Palestinian factions, arms trafficking and local militias”, she said. “In that sense, fragmentation can create tactical advantages but strategic instability.” In Quneitra, Syrian security forces have set up roadblocks to guard against infiltrators who could try to attack Israeli positions. Syrians who are not from the province need permission to enter parts of a buffer zone created in 1974, which has been shrinking because of the territorial grabs by Israel.Unlike during the Assad regime, Syrian authorities have avoided using threatening rhetoric against Israel and focused on garnering condemnation of its actions from allies, and promoting cases, such as that of Mr Saadeddin, to show the human impact. An Arab-Israeli lawyer heard about the case and recently contacted Mr Saadeddin, offering to try to help his son. Since losing his land, Mr Saadeddin has been working for other land owners. In the 19th century, Hasan Saadeddin’s clan left what is now Jordan after a tribal feud and settled in the Golan Heights.

The clan became owners of land close to Jabata Al Khashab in Syria's Quneitra province, near the high ground that Israel occupied in 1967.

For nearly three decades, Mr Saadeddin farmed the quarter-hectare he owns in peace. With plentiful rain and rich soil on the strategic plateau, his trees produced prized olives, cherries and plums. A 1974 armistice ensured calm in the area – until the 2011 to 2024 Syrian civil war.

Golan Heights dilemma: Israel's new military line blurs engagement and confrontation

His life came crashing down in April 2024, when Israeli forces arrested his son Saddam, then 16, during an incursion across the armistice line. “Saddam was not a threat to anyone. I haven’t heard from him. He is now almost 19,” Mr Saadeddin said.

By the end of 2024, his land had disappeared behind a new Israeli military line, a result of the upheavals in Syria and the wider Middle East.

The area is a focal point of US-sponsored talks between Israel and Syria on security arrangements and eventual peace. The last known discussion was held in Jordan's capital, Amman, in August, but the talks have been inconclusive, with Syria demanding that Israeli forces return to the armistice line.

Instead, Israel has begun creating a new military line beyond the Golan highlands that it occupied in the 1967 war and annexed in 1981.

“They bulldozed and torched my land,” Mr Saadeddin said, pointing to a row of trees behind an earth barrier that forms part of the new line, known as Sufa 53, named after an Israeli brigade.

Syrian authorities said last week that Israel was extending the line south towards the Yarmouk River basin, near the border with Jordan. Israel has not officially acknowledged the existence of Sufa 53.

“It is not a continuous line yet,” an official in Quneitra said. He said Israel had built seven military outposts in newly occupied Syrian territory as a precursor to the line – six in Quneitra and one in Deraa.

One outpost is clearly visible across a wooded area near Jabata Al Khashab. Israeli patrols enter the village almost daily, according to residents, looking for weapons and questioning passers-by.

Mr Saadeddin is not the only farmer along the frontier to be affected by Israel's new military line. Agricultural engineer Asia Al Ali, who works with the Quneitra governorate, said Israel had taken over 1,160 hectares of farmland and wooded areas near Jabata Al Khashab and other parts of the frontier.

Israel destroyed 40 per cent of those areas in its drive to build the Sufa 53 line, she said. Around 250 farmers can no longer access their land, or it was made unusable.

“There has been a lot of [Israeli] escalation lately, and sometimes direct shooting,” said Ms Al Ali, adding that Israeli troops began spraying “poisonous material” this year to kill crops.

Israel began building the line in 2022, near the Syrian town of Hader in northern Quneitra, after the Syrian side of the frontier fell under Iranian influence.

Members of the Iran-backed Lebanese group Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, defending the Assad regime in Syria, operated in the region and formed loyalist militias. Israeli positions came under rocket fire. Israel responded with air strikes and incursions.

The dynamics changed sharply after militant forces led by current Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara ousted Bashar Al Assad's government in December 2024. In the following weeks, Israel sent troops across the frontier and mounted an air campaign that destroyed large amounts of Syrian military hardware, without targeting members of the new order.

The US, which emerged as the most powerful backer of the new government, initiated talks between Syria and Israel to reach security arrangements and an eventual peace deal.

On Thursday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had phoned Mr Al Shara in July last year, after Israeli planes bombed government and military targets in central Damascus and near the presidential palace.

Mr Netanyahu apparently warned Mr Al Shara against pursuing a deadly campaign to subdue the mostly Druze southern governorate of Sweida. It was the first known instance of the Syrian and Israeli leaders speaking to each other.

However, the Israeli incursions have increased, with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights saying that 280 were recorded in September alone. Forty-nine Syrians remain in Israeli detention after Israel released 14 last month.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said in August that the military performed what he described as daily activity to “eliminate threats and remnants of the Assad regime” and to prevent “dangerous consolidation of the new regime”.

Carmit Valensi, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Israel, said Mr Al Shara “may have become substantially more pragmatic, but the system around him has not necessarily undergone the same transformation”.

Ms Valensi said the Syrian President was surrounded by former members of Hayat Tahrir Al Sham, the former Al Qaeda affiliate he founded during the civil war, and hardline security commanders. “The test is no longer simply whether Al Shara has changed. It is whether he can discipline, transform and ultimately institutionalise the system around him.”

However, a prolonged Israeli military presence and repeated incursions could weaken Mr Al Shara to the advantage of “ISIS, Iranian networks, Hezbollah, Palestinian factions, arms trafficking and local militias”, she said.

“In that sense, fragmentation can create tactical advantages but strategic instability.”

In Quneitra, Syrian security forces have set up roadblocks to guard against infiltrators who could try to attack Israeli positions. Syrians who are not from the province need permission to enter parts of a buffer zone created in 1974, which has been shrinking because of the territorial grabs by Israel.

Unlike during the Assad regime, Syrian authorities have avoided using threatening rhetoric against Israel and focused on garnering condemnation of its actions from allies, and promoting cases, such as that of Mr Saadeddin, to show the human impact.

An Arab-Israeli lawyer heard about the case and recently contacted Mr Saadeddin, offering to try to help his son.

Since losing his land, Mr Saadeddin has been working for other land owners. This week, he was supervising two dozen workers brought from eastern Syria to harvest olives around Jabata Al Khashab.

Additional reporting by Thomas Helm in Jerusalem

body_text:
The Sudanese man in the video speaks with obvious elation.

“Come on, you guys, quit your jobs selling food in the market and come and join us,” he says as he chips away at a rocky wall rich with glittering gold veins.

“We have discovered where the gold is and it's a huge treasure trove,” he adds in the video purportedly shot in a gold mine and shared widely online. “We had been digging for 16 months before we reached these rocks. It has been exhausting,” claims the young man, speaking directly to camera.

With every extraction made by the slender, bearded man, another man standing nearby watching chants “Allahu akbar!” in a voice filled with jubilation and gratitude.

The video was shot last month in a mountainous area in northern Sudan near the Egyptian border and the Red Sea. It is where scores of Sudanese goldminers were killed in an air strike on October 10. No group has claimed responsibility for the attack.

In a Sudan already torn by the ravages of a civil war that has claimed tens of thousands of lives, the goldminers' deaths have touched a raw nerve among Sudanese, plunging the vast Afro-Arab country into grief and rage.

Many have taken to social media to lament the fate of their impoverished yet resource-rich nation, where the war has forced hundreds of thousands into the dangerous work of mining in remote and inhospitable regions so they can feed their families.

They blame the military-aligned government for failing to protect its people and question the sincerity of its public declarations that it intends to launch an inquiry.

Neither Egypt nor Sudan has said who might have been behind the attack. Statements by the authorities in the two allied nations spoke of respect for each other's sovereignty and borders.

Both said they were investigating the incident, with Sudanese human rights and watchdog groups putting the death toll at 72 and unconfirmed Sudanese media reports saying as many as 200 had been killed.

Images ​and video shared online, which The National has been unable to verify, purport to show the aftermath of the air strike, with bodies strewn across rubble, others wrapped in sheets and survivors, mostly men in their 20s and 30s, bristling with anger.

But regardless of who was responsible, the tragic deaths have laid bare the grim reality of a country blighted by more civil wars in the past 70 years than any other nation.

At least 14 million people have been displaced in the current conflict and widespread hunger has plagued the population.

Gold prospectors head to the mines equipped with sledgehammers, chisels, jerry cans filled with drinking water, torches and food. They stay on-site for weeks, sometimes months, before returning home for a break or sojourn at shanty towns that have popped up to cater for the miners' needs.

Many of the men who chose gold prospecting to make a living are natives of the western Darfur and central Kordofan regions who have been displaced by the fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and its enemy, the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

Hashem Darar, 27, a native of eastern Sudan, counts himself lucky to escape the air strike.

“I was out of the site at the time of the attack. I was buying food and water, and selling gold we extracted at a nearby Al Ansari market in Al Oqaidat,” he said, referring to the region where the attack took place.

“I am saddened by the death of the men I got to know the past two months. We joked and laughed as we toiled among the rocks and in the dust, and I just lost them like this,” he said. “When I heard the blast, I rushed back to help the wounded and recover the bodies from under the rubble.”

Gold production in Sudan has for years been a murky business, attracting adventurers, smugglers and foreign parties seeking quick profit. In several ways, the country's current gold rush is a by-product of most of the Sudan’s oilfields being lost when South Sudan seceded in 2011.

The civil war that erupted in April 2023 has intensified the scramble for gold in Sudan. Some estimates put the number of artisanal miners involved at about two million.

Official figures say Sudanese government revenue from gold exports stands at about $2 billion but experts say smuggling and the use of gold outside official channels account for far more. Last year, for example, Sudan’s gold production was about 70 tonnes but only 20 tonnes were exported, with the remainder smuggled out of the country or treated at primitive local refineries.

Al Shafie Ahmed contributed to this report from Kampala, Uganda.

headline: How hijab dispute is opening new front in Iran-Azerbaijan tensions
summary: Iran's longstanding unease over Azerbaijan's strategic ties with Israel is spilling into a dispute over religious freedoms and Baku's position in the Islamic world, testing already fragile relations between the two neighbors.
body_text:
TEHRAN — Ali Akbar Velayati, international affairs adviser to Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, has used Azerbaijan's recent school hijab controversy as a pointed challenge to Baku's relationship with Israel, questioning whether the country is fit to host the Islamic world's most prominent summit.

In an Oct. 14 post on X, Velayati presented Azerbaijan with a choice between "preserving faith" and "friendship with Tel Aviv." Referring to the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) held in Baku last week, he asked: "Turkey left the hall during [Israeli President Isaac] Herzog's speech at the CICA summit, so what did Baku do? A warm welcome."

He also questioned Azerbaijan's suitability to host the 2027 summit of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), linking its restrictions on headscarves in schools to its willingness to welcome Herzog.

The intervention marks a shift from Iranian officials' earlier reluctance to comment on the hijab dispute, which had largely been driven by hard-line media. It also brings a domestic controversy into a broader geopolitical contest over Azerbaijan's ties with Israel and its standing in the Muslim world.

headline: Exclusive-Trump move to restart direct US flights with Lebanon hits roadblock
summary: By Allison Lampert and David ShepardsonOct 16 (Reuters) - The United Nations aviation agency has found Lebanon's main airport lacks valid certification, according to a report summary seen by Reuters, in a setback to US President Donald Trump's move to revive direct US-Beirut flights.Trump made the announcement in July and signed an order last month for the US government to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight 847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.
body_text:
By Allison Lampert and David Shepardson

Oct 16 (Reuters) - The United Nations aviation agency has found Lebanon's main airport lacks valid certification, according to a report summary seen by Reuters, in a setback to US President Donald Trump's move to revive direct US-Beirut flights.

Trump made the announcement in July and signed an order last month for the US government to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight 847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.

While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Trump's order "a significant first step toward restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States."

However, the UN's International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Beirut-Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system.

The findings, which two senior industry officials familiar with the matter expect to delay the resumption of service, complicate efforts to follow up on an order Trump signed after meeting Lebanese President Joseph Aoun. Washington has backed Aoun as it pushes for Iran-backed Hezbollah to be disarmed.

The agency sent its internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), toLebanon in September.

AIRPORT LACKS EMERGENCY PLAN: ICAO

Beirut airport's firefighting resources are equipped for single-aisle planes, but not twin-aisle jetliners used for long-haul flights, according to a summary of ICAO's report. The airport also lacks an emergency plan, and its conditional certification has expired, the report said.

"This is a serious and time-critical matter that must be addressed immediately to preserve the airport's operational status," the summary said.

The report also found the Lebanese regulator LCAA lacks qualified inspectors to oversee air traffic control licensing, and has no fully established, operational and independent aircraft accident investigation authority with clearly defined roles.

Such concerns were flagged during a two-day workshop last month where officials from ICAO, Lebanon's government, the FAA and others discussed efforts to revive direct air service, according to the industry officials and an agenda of the meeting seen by Reuters.

Lebanon's Minister of Public Works and Transport Fayez Rasamny said Lebanon was taking steps to address the concerns, with efforts to certify the airport starting on Saturday. The LCAA expects to issue conditional certification in the coming days.

"Most of the issues highlighted in the report had already been identified by the LCAA, and corrective action had already been initiated," Rasamny said in a statement, adding that progress had been delayed by war. Israeli forces remain in southern Lebanon and have continued strikes despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed in June between Israel and Lebanon. Hezbollah, which was not party to the deal, has rejected it.

The FAA declined to comment. ICAO said it cannot comment on matters concerning specific countries, but said it conducts targeted analyses for member states.

The US State Department advises Americans not to travel to Lebanon given safety concerns. It said the FAA advises caution for flights operating in Lebanese airspace due to heightened military activity in or around Syria, including the risks of errant long-range surface-to-air missiles originating from Syrian territory.

MIDDLE EAST UNREST DISRUPTS AIR TRAVEL

Foreign airlines have avoided large swathes of Middle East airspace because of missile and drone threats since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February triggered regional hostilities, with an airport in Saudi Arabia the latest site to come under attack.

Lebanon and its national carrier have been praised domestically for maintaining air navigation services and flights, helping to prop up an economy that depends on tourism and remittances.

Three US airline officials told Reuters on the condition of anonymity they do not think any American carriers would resume flights to Lebanon in the near term, citing security concerns.

While there are no direct flights between Beirut and the United States, such service exists between Lebanon and some large European cities.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency said it was aware of the ICAO report and added that EU airlines must conduct their own assessment of an airport's safety and operational readiness before launching services.

(Reporting by Allison Lampert and David Shepardson; Editing by Joe Brock and Rod Nickel)

headline: Tatarstan seeks Indian specialists for construction, light industry sectors — minister
summary: India is the republic's second most significant partner for recruiting specialists to Russia under the quota system, Minister of Labor, Employment and Social Protection of Tatarstan Elmira Zaripova said
body_text:
KAZAN, October 16. /TASS/. Indian specialists are in high demand in Tatarstan for the construction, light industry, and service sectors, including hospitality and catering, Elmira Zaripova, Minister of Labor, Employment and Social Protection of Tatarstan, told TASS on the sidelines of the 2nd Russia-India Business Forum TIME in Kazan.

Earlier Zaripova reported that Tatarstan received a quota to bring in over 3,000 Indian nationals in 2026. This marks a fivefold increase from 2025, when the republic issued over 600 work permits to Indian citizens.

"India is our second most significant partner for recruiting specialists to Russia under the quota system," Zaripova said. "Tatarstan is working closely [in this area]. We are primarily interested in Indian specialists for construction, seasonal agricultural work, and light industry. We also have many specialists in the service sector--namely, hospitality and restaurants."

She noted that the republic's approved quota for India stands at roughly 3,000 slots, with about 17 employers recruiting specialists from the country. "This applies, first and foremost, to areas where we cannot source specialists from the domestic labor market," the minister explained.

The 2nd Russia-India Business Forum TIME: Tatarstan-India. Mutual Efficiency is taking place from October 14 to 17 in Kazan. TASS is the general media partner of the event.

headline: Iran's navy reports oil tanker fire in Gulf of Oman
summary: Incident comes amid a series of similar maritime security incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz
body_text:
Iran's navy said Friday that an oil tanker caught fire in the Gulf of Oman while attempting to cross a restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz with its tracking systems switched off, according to a statement carried by state broadcaster IRIB.

The navy's public relations office said monitoring teams detected the burning tanker during surveillance operations in the eastern part of the strategic waterway.

The vessel had disabled its tracking systems and was attempting to navigate a “prohibited area” in the Gulf of Oman, the statement said.

The navy warned that unauthorized movements through restricted maritime routes and areas pose security risks to other vessels.

The statement did not identify the tanker, its flag or operator, or specify what caused the fire. No information was provided on possible casualties or the condition of the crew.

The incident comes amid a series of maritime security incidents in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has imposed restrictions on commercial shipping.

On Tuesday, the Iranian Navy reported that another tanker caught fire after sustaining damage while attempting to cross a restricted area east of the strait with its tracking systems switched off.

On Wednesday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank after striking a naval mine while attempting to navigate an unauthorized route south of the strait.

The IRGC Navy warned local vessels and fishermen to exercise caution over containers floating on the water's surface following the sinking.

The latest incidents come amid heightened tensions between Iran and the US over freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial passage for global oil and gas shipments.

Maritime traffic through the waterway has been severely disrupted since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on Feb. 28.

body_text:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis launched missiles at Aden International Airport late on Friday, a day after carrying out a deadly attack on the presidential palace in the port city.

Aden has been the seat of Yemen's internationally recognised government since 2015, when the Houthis seized the capital city, Sanaa, igniting a civil war.

The Houthis are now fighting against the government and Saudi Arabia.

Yemeni Information Minister Moammar Eryani said two missiles landed near the airport's runway, 500 metres from an aircraft that was preparing to take off. He said civilians on the plane are all safe and described the attack as a "grave violation of international laws and norms”.

The Aden Security Department said the incident was ‌the second attack on the airport in less than a week.

The Houthis, in a statement attributed to a military source, said an attack was launched against “the Saudi forces’ command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province”, as well as a weapons depot. The security department said a Yemenia Airways flight bound for Cairo was preparing for take off when the missiles landed.

The attack comes after five people were killed in a Houthi attack on Al Maashiq presidential palace. It was the first time the group attacked the palace since fighting in Yemen resumed last month after a four-year lull.

Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to Yemen's Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba, told The National that the Houthis will not succeed in disrupting public life or undermining state authority as the government pushes ahead with a military and political campaign against them.

"Aden will remain the centre of government operations despite the deadly Houthi attack on the city's presidential palace," he said.

Heavy fighting continues between government forces and the Houthis. The renewed conflict has raised fears of a further deterioration ​in the country's humanitarian crisis. Aid agencies have warned that conditions ‌are worsening rapidly.

Yemen has ⁠become another front in the wider regional war ​that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February.

Yemeni government forces said on Friday that troops had advanced in Marib province, north-east of Sanaa. Military spokesman Majed Al Nazili said government forces, with air support, had made significant “territorial gains” in the eastern part of the province, securing “key positions”.

More than 430 Houthi fighters have been “neutralised” in the past 24 hours, he said, while destroying or disabling more than 100 of their vehicles and military assets.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition fighting against the Houthis released aerial footage, dated October 16, that showed what it described as strikes on a Houthi weapons-smuggling operation in the Red Sea port city of Hodeidah.

The nearly six-minute black-and-white video, which identifies the date and location at the start, shows apparent air strikes on lorries, small boats and what appear to be storage sites.
