headline: Battle for Taiz is for whole of western Yemen, warns ex-PM Maeen Abdelmalik Saeed
summary: The Houthis' siege of Taiz is a slow-burning campaign that could signal the eventual fall of western Yemen, a former prime minister of the country has warned.Maeen Abdelmalik Saeed, who held office from 2018 to 2024, said the city of Taiz in south-western Yemen is an important stronghold for the government that needs to be defended at all costs. “It’s a battle which concerns all of the west [of Yemen],” he told The National. “There is no opportunity after that if we can’t reclaim Taiz again, to build a new momentum against the Houthis and Sanaa. This is the importance of Taiz.”There is still time, said Mr Saeed, because the Houthis currently control “significant, important heights” in the Yemeni Highlands around Taiz but are now in a consolidation phase. They had closed off most of the roads into the city of slightly less than one million people but had stopped short of a complete blockade. This was to buy time to consolidate control in the rural outskirts of the city, said Mr Saeed.“They are trying to control all the roads to the city and it seems that they want to seize control of these rural areas and absorb them before they expand into the city. The Houthis will close the siege when they control all these areas.”The attack on Taiz is “intense and ongoing”, said Mr Saeed. “There is a severe shortage of medicine and fuel in the city's hospitals,” he added.The rebel group invaded the south-west coast of Yemen last month to enforce its blockade on oil being shipped from Saudi Arabia. Its capture of the port city of Mokha gave it control of the Bab Al Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia relied on to export oil. A government-led offensive has seized the centre of Mokha but heavy bombardment from the surrounding hills still held by Houthi forces is taking place.The pattern of fighting demonstrates Houthi ambitions to capture other key cities in western Yemen, Mr Saeed warned. On Thursday, Houthi missiles were fired at the Presidential Palace in Aden, killing five people.There are also signs the Houthis are planning to attack Lahj, a city less than 40km from Aden that houses one of Yemen’s largest military camps, Mr Saeed, who now serves as presidential adviser, said Lahj is well positioned for the Houthis to launch assaults on their “three main targets” of Taiz, Aden and Mareb.Hinge cityThough food and fuel could still enter Taiz from Aden, this relief would be only temporary. “In a matter of days or weeks, we will see a siege and attempts to enter the city,” he said.Yet the group knows it will face considerable resistance within Taiz and on its outskirts. “The Houthis always rely on their radical religious teachings – the only obstacle to this was Taiz, because it carried the idea of democracy and the modern state,” said Mr Saeed, who comes from the city.Some tribal families from the Hashemite dynasties may be more sympathetic to an agreement with the Houthis. But local resistance to the group would form quickly, drawing on Taiz’s history of being ruled by Zaydi Imams of northern Yemen, he said.The Houthis would struggle to finance the administration of Taiz. “They cannot provide salaries, they don’t have the financial resources to run the city. Militarily they might succeed for a while, but it will be a burden and a threat,” said Mr Saeed.The Houthis have hit Saudi Aramco facilities and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh recent days, in addition to attacking Saudi ships passing through the Bab Al Mandeb strait. A Saudi official on Thursday conceded that the Houthi advances in Yemen were being “encouraged by Iran”, which continues to arm and train the militia. Last cardMr Saeed agreed, saying he believes Iran is playing “one of its last cards” in the Gulf, since Arab states have adapted to attacks on supply lines. “Iranians may be upset that the way of raising the costs and threatening the Gulf countries is not doing the job.”Houthi capabilities have grown in the past five years. They now have advanced weaponry, for which the Yemeni government and its Gulf allies were unprepared. The group is allegedly using Chinese technology to manufacture weapons in the city of Hodeidah, according to the Conflict Armament Research Group. The internationally recognised Yemeni government has spoken to Chinese counterparts on the matter but Beijing denied involvement. “They denied it, they said 'maybe it’s a third party,'” said Mr Saeed. Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba said China had promised to investigate the matter. The situation could encourage other groups such as Al Shabab in Somalia to follow suit in developing new missiles. “The problem is that this will encourage different radical groups to adopt this cheap technology,” said Mr Saeed.

This was to buy time to consolidate control in the rural outskirts of the city, said Mr Saeed.

“They are trying to control all the roads to the city and it seems that they want to seize control of these rural areas and absorb them before they expand into the city. The Houthis will close the siege when they control all these areas.”

The attack on Taiz is “intense and ongoing”, said Mr Saeed. “There is a severe shortage of medicine and fuel in the city's hospitals,” he added.

The rebel group invaded the south-west coast of Yemen last month to enforce its blockade on oil being shipped from Saudi Arabia. Its capture of the port city of Mokha gave it control of the Bab Al Mandab strait, which Saudi Arabia relied on to export oil. A government-led offensive has seized the centre of Mokha but heavy bombardment from the surrounding hills still held by Houthi forces is taking place.

The pattern of fighting demonstrates Houthi ambitions to capture other key cities in western Yemen, Mr Saeed warned. On Thursday, Houthi missiles were fired at the Presidential Palace in Aden, killing five people.

There are also signs the Houthis are planning to attack Lahj, a city less than 40km from Aden that houses one of Yemen’s largest military camps, Mr Saeed, who now serves as presidential adviser, said Lahj is well positioned for the Houthis to launch assaults on their “three main targets” of Taiz, Aden and Mareb.

Though food and fuel could still enter Taiz from Aden, this relief would be only temporary. “In a matter of days or weeks, we will see a siege and attempts to enter the city,” he said.

Yet the group knows it will face considerable resistance within Taiz and on its outskirts. “The Houthis always rely on their radical religious teachings – the only obstacle to this was Taiz, because it carried the idea of democracy and the modern state,” said Mr Saeed, who comes from the city.

Some tribal families from the Hashemite dynasties may be more sympathetic to an agreement with the Houthis. But local resistance to the group would form quickly, drawing on Taiz’s history of being ruled by Zaydi Imams of northern Yemen, he said.

The Houthis would struggle to finance the administration of Taiz. “They cannot provide salaries, they don’t have the financial resources to run the city. Militarily they might succeed for a while, but it will be a burden and a threat,” said Mr Saeed.

The Houthis have hit Saudi Aramco facilities and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh recent days, in addition to attacking Saudi ships passing through the Bab Al Mandeb strait.

A Saudi official on Thursday conceded that the Houthi advances in Yemen were being “encouraged by Iran”, which continues to arm and train the militia.

Mr Saeed agreed, saying he believes Iran is playing “one of its last cards” in the Gulf, since Arab states have adapted to attacks on supply lines. “Iranians may be upset that the way of raising the costs and threatening the Gulf countries is not doing the job.”

Houthi capabilities have grown in the past five years. They now have advanced weaponry, for which the Yemeni government and its Gulf allies were unprepared. The group is allegedly using Chinese technology to manufacture weapons in the city of Hodeidah, according to the Conflict Armament Research Group.

The internationally recognised Yemeni government has spoken to Chinese counterparts on the matter but Beijing denied involvement. “They denied it, they said 'maybe it’s a third party,'” said Mr Saeed. Foreign Minister Afrah Al Zouba said China had promised to investigate the matter.

The situation could encourage other groups such as Al Shabab in Somalia to follow suit in developing new missiles. “The problem is that this will encourage different radical groups to adopt this cheap technology,” said Mr Saeed.

headline: Zacharia ousted after 5 days as White House Press Secretary
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump’s top spokesperson.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia was fired after less than a week on the job, two US officials said on Friday, after a rocky start as President Donald Trump’s top spokesperson.

Zacharia was "let go" and is "transitioning out" of the press secretary position, according to two separate White House officials. She faced days of questions about her legal credentials and criticism of her performance in a news briefing and interviews.

The departure leaves Trump without a key public messenger just over ​two weeks before November’s midterm elections, a critical period when the president is seeking to tout his administration's accomplishments and ​help his fellow Republicans retain control of Congress.

Trump told reporters earlier on Friday that he had ⁠asked Zacharia to reconsider whether to continue in her role after facing tough press coverage during her first days on the ​job.

"I told her: 'I think you're better off being happy, and I'm not sure you can ever be happy in this stuff.' There's ​nothing easy about this stuff," Trump told reporters as he departed the White House for a weekend trip.

He added, "I said to her honestly, 'If I were you, I'd reconsider... think about it. But I would reconsider.'" Trump said he intended to revisit the conversation with Zacharia later.

Zacharia started on Monday and held her debut White ​House briefing on Tuesday. She said she received a call about the press secretary role on October 7 and was offered the job to ​succeed Karoline Leavitt a week ago.

She soon faced questions about her career, which she said included a tenure practicing law. Trump had also described her as ‌an attorney.

body_text:
“Diplomacy is the art of the possible,” Canada's Foreign Minister Anita Anand said. That has been at the heart of talks with regional partners aimed at easing tensions in the Middle East, opposing Iranian aggression and restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

She spoke to The National in Dubai, with her visit to the UAE intended to reinforce Canada's opposition to Iranian attacks and Ottawa's support for the complete reopening of the strait, which is vital for global energy supplies and trade.

“We are in a phase of our foreign policy where we are deeply engaged with countries around the world to ensure that we are standing for peace, standing for state sovereignty and that we show our promise that we are here for them,” she said. “That's one of the reasons why I'm here today."

Ms Anand met Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, during her visit, with the ministers discussing bilateral ties and regional stability. She added that relations between two countries have been “consistently elevated".

Canada and the UAE have increased diplomatic engagement as regional tensions heightened, with both governments discussing the implications for security and stability across the Middle East.

There had also been a push to strengthen ties last year, with Prime Minister Mark Carney travelling to the UAE in November 2025. He was the first Canadian leader to visit in the country in more than four decades.

Mr Carney’s government has also sought to strengthen investment ties with the Gulf, while reducing its reliance on the US market.

“But over and above trade, there is the question of regional stability and the importance of speaking out against the retaliatory attacks from Iran and making sure that we also support freedom of navigation in your [the UAE’s] backyard, in the Strait of Hormuz,” Ms Anand said.

She praised the UAE and other Gulf states for maintaining normal life while responding firmly to Iranian aggression. “I greatly respect the ability of each of the countries who are being hit by these attacks, including the UAE, to continue to live lives as normally as possible on the one hand, but to take a strong stand against these attacks on the other,” she said.

Iran launched ballistic missiles and drones at its Gulf neighbours, aiming at civilian infrastructure including energy sites and airports.

The US and Iran signed an agreement in June intended to pave the way for a final peace settlement. But attacks have continued, particularly on shipping, and Washington and Tehran have traded threats.

The war has spilt over into escalation between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with the kingdom attacked repeatedly in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.

Ms Anand expressed concern about the attacks on Saudi Arabia, particularly strikes on Riyadh airport, and said she had been in contact with the kingdom's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, to convey Canada's support. “Well, of course, the attacks that Saudi Arabia specifically is enduring are very, very concerning,” she added.

Canada's concerns extend to Tehran's wider regional conduct, with Ms Anand stressing Ottawa's long-standing opposition to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and its record on human rights.

She said Canada had taken action against people and entities linked to repression and rights abuses. The IRGC has been listed as a terrorist entity under Canadian law for more than two years, she added.

“We are particularly concerned with Iranian women and girls. And we will continue to voice that concern,” she said.

Canada has imposed sanctions on Iran over alleged rights abuses, repression and activities that Ottawa says threaten regional security. The latest measures were announced in September and applied to five people and five entities accused of involvement in digital surveillance and other rights breaches.

“I'd like to present Canada as a country that cares deeply about the region and the respect for international law and international human rights,” Ms Anand said.

Humanitarian assistance also remains a priority for Canada across the Middle East, with the situation in Gaza among the issues discussed during her visit. Since the launch of Operation Gallant Knight 3, the UAE has provided more than $4 billion in assistance to Gaza, accounting for 46 per cent of global humanitarian aid given to the enclave since 2023.

She also raised concerns about Lebanon, particularly the actions of Iran-backed Hezbollah, and said Canada had provided about $40 million in humanitarian aid to the country.

On Syria, Ms Anand said Canada was continuing to relax some sanctions imposed during the rule of former president Bashar Al Assad, as Ottawa pursues rapprochement with Damascus. “I have invited the Foreign Minister of Syria [Asaad Al Shibani] to come to Canada, and we are working on establishing a date for that meeting,” she added.

Ms Anand said Canada wanted to continue working with regional partners to support stability, respect for sovereignty and international law.

headline: Russian forces deliver massive strike on Ukraine’s defense enterprises
summary: Russian forces struck a metals plant in Krivoi Rog engaged in supplies for the Ukrainian military-industrial sector, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 17. /TASS/. Russian forces delivered a massive strike on metals plants, a transformer factory and an energy site in Krivoi Rog, Zaporozhye and Zhitomir, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

"Last night, the Russian Armed Forces delivered a massive strike by ground-based, airborne and sea-launched precision-guided weapons and attack unmanned aerial vehicles on metallurgical enterprises, a transformer factory and an energy site in the cities of Krivoi Rog, Zaporozhye and Zhitomir in Ukraine," the ministry said in a statement.

Russian forces struck the Zaporozhstal metals giant in Zaporozhye integrated into the group of companies of Ukrainian billionaire entrepreneur Rinat Akhmetov. The plant's products were largely used for the needs of Ukraine’s military industry, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

"The strike hit the Zaporozhstal metals works, Ukraine’s largest metallurgical enterprise. It makes part of SCM Group of Rinat Akhmetov. Previously, the plant’s annual output amounted to 1.44 million metric tons of pig iron and over 1.3 million metric tons of rolled steel. The products were largely used for the needs of the military industry," the ministry said in a statement.

Russian forces struck the Zaporozhtransformator enterprise in Zaporozhye that produced oil-filled power transformers under the management of Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

"In the city of Zaporozhye, the strike hit <…> the industrial enterprise Zaporozhtransformator PJSC that produced 220-750 kV oil-filled power transformers. Since 2022, the plant has been managed by Ukraine’s Defense Ministry and used for the needs of the Ukrainian army," the ministry said in a statement.

Russian forces struck a metals plant in Krivoi Rog engaged in supplies for the Ukrainian military-industrial sector, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

"In Krivoi Rog, the strike hit a metals plant - Ukraine’s largest metallurgical enterprise supplying metals products to the Ukrainian military-industrial sector," the ministry said in a statement.

Russian forces struck a sea vessel delivering military cargo to Ukraine’s Odessa port, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.

body_text:
Lebanon’s main airport lacks valid certification and has regulatory shortcomings that could delay the resumption of direct flights between Beirut and the US, Reuters has reported the UN aviation agency as saying.

US President Donald Trump signed an order last month to allow direct flights from the US to Lebanon, reversing a four-decade-long suspension after TWA Flight ⁠847 was hijacked and forced to land in Beirut in 1985.

While the US Federal Aviation Administration and the Transportation Security Administration would still need to conduct safety reviews before flights could resume, the Lebanese embassy in Washington called Mr Trump's order a "significant first step towards restoring direct air service between Lebanon and the United States".

But the UN's International ⁠Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) technical assistance mission to Lebanon in July identified shortcomings at Rafic Hariri International Airport and in the aviation system. The findings could complicate Mr Trump’s efforts to restore direct flights.

The agency sent an internal report, made at the request of the Lebanese Civil Aviation Authority (LCAA), to Lebanon in September.

Three US airline officials told Reuters that they did not expect American carriers to resume services to Lebanon in the near term, owing to security concerns.

The ICAO report summary said Beirut airport’s firefighting resources were equipped to handle single-aisle aircraft but not the twin-aisle jets typically used on long-haul routes. The airport also lacks an emergency plan and its conditional certification has expired.

“This is a serious and time-critical matter that must be addressed immediately to preserve the airport's operational status,” the agency said in the summary.

The report also identified shortcomings at the LCAA, including a lack of qualified inspectors to oversee air traffic control licensing and the absence of a fully established, independent aircraft accident investigation authority with clearly defined responsibilities.

The findings were discussed at a two-day workshop last month involving officials from ICAO, the Lebanese government and the FAA, according to Reuters, which reviewed the meeting’s agenda.

Lebanon’s Minister of Public Works and Transport, Fayez Rasamny, said the country was taking steps to address the concerns, with efforts to certify the airport beginning on Saturday. The Civil Aviation Authority expects to issue conditional certification in the coming days.

“Most of the issues highlighted in the report had already been identified by the LCAA and corrective action had already been initiated,” said Mr Rasamny, adding that progress had been delayed by war.

Israeli troops remain in southern Lebanon and have continued to carry out strikes despite a US-brokered framework agreement signed in June. Hezbollah, which was not party to the agreement, has rejected it.

The FAA declined to comment on the report, while the ICAO said it could not comment on matters concerning specific countries but conducts targeted analyses for member states, Reuters reported.

The certification concerns come amid wider security risks affecting air travel in the Middle East. Foreign airlines have avoided large areas of regional airspace because of missile and drone threats since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February led to wider hostilities.

The US State Department advises American citizens against travelling to Lebanon because of security concerns. The FAA has also called for caution for flights operating in Lebanese airspace because of heightened military activity in or around Syria, including the risk of errant long-range surface-to-air missiles originating from Syrian territory.

Lebanon’s aviation authorities and its national carrier have continued to maintain air navigation services and flights despite the challenges, helping to support an economy heavily reliant on tourism and remittances.

Although there are currently no direct flights between Beirut and the US, Lebanon remains connected to several major European cities. The EU's Aviation Safety Agency said it was aware of the ICAO report and noted that European airlines must conduct their own assessments of an airport’s safety and operational readiness before beginning services.

headline: IMF members call for more support amid war shocks, 'advanced intelligence' risks
summary: By David LawderBANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside.And while there has been a boost to investment and trade from "advanced intelligence technologies", they also carried risks, the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee said in a statement after a meeting in Bangkok.
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - International Monetary Fund member countries called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by negative spillovers from wars and high energy prices, and said economic risks remain tilted to the downside.

And while there has been a boost to investment and trade from "advanced intelligence technologies", they also carried risks, the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee said in a statement after a meeting in Bangkok.

"Escalating conflicts and trade tensions could further disrupt critical trade routes, exacerbate commodity price pressures, including in refined energy products, and worsen energy and food security," said the statement issued by Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, the chair of the IMFC.

The IMFC is the main steering committee for the 191-member crisis lender.

Al-Jadaan told Reuters that the language of the statement was agreed by all members.

Earlier this week, the United States was pressing fellow IMF members to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" in the statement, in line with US President Donald Trump's preferred name for the technology, a senior US Treasury official told Reuters.

The final version of the chair's statement contained no reference to artificial intelligence.

It said the uncertain impact of "advanced intelligence technologies", along with rising bond yields in major economies that spill over to highly indebted economies, "could amplify macro-financial vulnerabilities."

"Rapid technological change, demographic shifts, more frequent extreme weather events and natural disasters, and geoeconomic fragmentation are compounding policy tradeoffs," the statement said.

The member economies agreed to support countries that undertake reforms and address debt vulnerabilities, with specific attention to low-income and vulnerable middle-income countries and conflict-affected states.

"We encourage increasing support to countries with sustainable debt and strong reform and growth enhancing agenda, but facing short-term financing challenges," the statement said, noting that several members had provided assurances of support to the IMF's Poverty Reduction and Growth Trust, which supports poor and developing countries.

(Reporting by David Lawder; Editing by John Mair)

body_text:
When the UAE women’s team were on the brink of their finest win to date, at the start of last month, their outstanding player might have been thinking to herself: “I’m glad I stuck with this.” And, perhaps, how proud her dad might have been.

The national team had Bangladesh pinned down in the Women’s Asia Cup at Dubai International Stadium.

They needed to win to advance to the knockout stage of the competition, and Suraksha Kotte had given them a shot at doing so. The UAE were giving away lots of places in the world rankings to their opposition, and years’ worth of experience.

InterviewKS Bharat ready for new chapter with UAE after calling time on India

Looking at Suraksha, you would not have known it. Bowling spin with the new ball, she tied the Bangladesh top order in knots, on her way to figures of 3-11 in four overs.

As it turned out, the UAE fell short in the run chase. But it was another sign the national team are finding their place among the leading sides of the women’s game.

The identity of the opposition was significant, too. Bangladesh were the opponents when the UAE played their first women’s international match in 2007. It was rather a mismatch, with the UAE being bowled out for just nine runs.

Suraksha was just four years old back then, and 12 months away from moving with her family to live in Dubai.

Now she is one of a cohort of players who have turned the UAE side from easy-beats into serious Asian cricket contenders.

But, now aged 23, Suraksha might have been lost to the sport, and not just because she has an exacting day job.

Her father, Sudheer, died in March 2021. She and her brother were students at the time. But their suddenly altered circumstances meant they had to consider leaving Dubai and returning to the family’s hometown in Andhra Pradesh in India.

Somehow, they managed to make it work. Mother Shrisha found work at GE – her late husband’s old workplace. Suraksha has since graduated to become an associate project manager for software giants Oracle, and brother Suraj works for Nissan.

And, away from her day job, Suraksha has managed to maintain a highly impressive cricket career, too. All inspired by someone in particular.

“He's one of the reasons why I'm still playing cricket; it's for him,” Suraksha said of father Sudheer. “He was there at the time of my debut, but he didn’t see when I was properly performing, and playing for the team regularly.

“He had been there throughout my development phase. We used to get up in the morning, and he’d say, ‘Let's go practice’. It was like a typical dad-daughter story.

“For most female cricketers, the dream starts with their dad and then their brother. My dad was a huge cricket fanatic. He enrolled my brother into an academy and I just went along with my dad.”

Suraksha remembers how proud her father had been when she made her senior debut, against Malaysia in Bangkok. “You couldn't imagine the happiness he had,” she said.

“He went to the office and he was telling all of his colleagues with excitement, ‘Oh my daughter's playing with UAE, she's playing cricket internationally. And that’s a pretty big deal.’”

Given the challenges her family have faced, she is glad to have had such a reliable support network to call on.

The UAE women’s team have grown up together, and Suraksha regards them as family. “We're a small circle,” she said. “We've grown up with each other. Our families meet so often, we've actually become like one huge family.

“That strengthens our bond even more. It really feels like we're on this journey together and we have a dream of qualifying for the World Cup.

“It feels amazing that we're able to be on this path together at this moment. We're just really grateful for this.”

The women’s side have yet to play at a leading global event, but they have been closing the gap on the game’s elite.

They pushed Sri Lanka close in T20 World Cup qualifying, just as they did against Bangladesh in the Asia Cup.

They have taken scalps of full member nations, including against Zimbabwe in one-day international cricket.

Suraksha echoed the sentiments of her captain, Esha Oza, who said they need more matches against sides from Test nations if they were to take the next step.

“We play these teams once in two years, so imagine what we can do with more exposure, and playing them every few months,” she said.

“As a team we can grow to that level with the exposure, with the right skills, with the right mindset. We can cross many scores that we haven't even thought of right now. We can achieve that for sure.”

headline: Foreign experts: 'China AI threat' is a Western fabrication
summary: Radhika Desai, a professor in the Department of Political Studies at the University of Manitoba in Canada, and Glenn Diesen, a professor of international relations at the University of South-Eastern Norway, gave exclusive interviews to China News Network's "News Lounge" program.
body_text:
Radhika Desai, a professor in the Department of Political Studies at the University of Manitoba in Canada, and Glenn Diesen, a professor of international relations at the University of South-Eastern Norway, gave exclusive interviews to China News Network's "News Lounge" program on the so-called "China AI threat" narrative on Sunday at the Tongzhou Global Development Forum hosted by Renmin University of China.

Desai believes that in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), China is leading the world. She said the release of the DeepSeek-R1 model in 2025 proved that China can develop AI at a very low cost, using very little energy and very few chips.

Addressing the so-called "China AI threat" narrative, Desai said that when certain US tech giants lost their leading position in the stock market, they began to concoct this narrative, hoping Western governments would help them counter the so-called "China threat."

Diesen said that the so-called "China AI threat" is merely a narrative fabricated by the US out of fear of falling behind China.

Diesen noted that AI is transforming everything. He said China is now one of the two leaders in AI development, and the conditions for mutually beneficial cooperation are already in place. Tensions arise because all countries fear falling behind. The US is no exception.

headline: Tehran, Beijing emphasize enhancing tourism cooperation
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Tourism officials from Iran and the Republic of China have called for concrete measures to expand and broaden tourism exchanges between the two countries, including joint travel packages and improved services for Chinese visit

TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Tourism officials from Iran and the Republic of China have called for concrete measures to expand and broaden tourism exchanges between the two countries, including joint travel packages and improved services for Chinese visit

The proposals were discussed at a specialized meeting hosted by Iran’s Embassy in Beijing on Friday, attended by officials, tourism professionals and representatives of companies from both countries.

Iranian Ambassador to China Abdolreza Rahmani Fazli highlighted the historical and cultural ties between the two nations along the Silk Road, stressing the need to remove obstacles, organize cooperation more effectively and increase China’s share of Iran’s tourism market.

In a message delivered at the meeting, Iranian Minister of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Reza Salehi Amiri called for China to become one of Iran’s most important tourism partners. He proposed establishing a joint platform for Iranian and Chinese travel agencies and tour operators, developing at least three travel packages specifically for the Chinese market, organizing familiarization tours for Chinese tour operators and journalists, providing Chinese-speaking guides and facilitating payment services.

Chinese tourism representatives also described Iran as a destination with considerable cultural appeal and commercial potential, expressing interest among Chinese travelers in visiting the country.

The UFC will host its 24th Abu Dhabi show next week when Alexander Volkanovski defends his featherweight title against Movsar Evloev in the headline bout.

With a stacked card and much more happening throughout fight week, UFC 333 has a lot going on. Here is everything you need to know.

UFC 333 is a mixed martial arts event from the UFC. The event will be headlined by the UFC featherweight champion Volkanovski putting his belt on the line against Evloev.

Exclusive‘I’m Alex, who still fights’: Volkanovski returns to Abu Dhabi a changed man

There will be a total of 10 fights.

Fight night will be held at Etihad Arena on Yas Island in Abu Dhabi. It will be the 12th UFC event staged at the venue.

UFC 333 takes place on Saturday, October 24. The preliminary card is scheduled to begin around 6pm UAE time, with the main card expected to start around 10pm.

Volkanovski is widely regarded as one of the best featherweights in history.

The Australian won the vacant title with a dominant performance over Diego Lopes in April 2025 and backed that up with a similar display in their rematch in February, winning both by unanimous decision.

This is Volkanovski's second run as UFC featherweight champion. In total, this will be his sixth title defence and his 11th straight title fight.

Top-ranked Evloev earned his shot at gold after taking a contentious decision over Lerone Murphy in March.

The Russian is undefeated in 20 pro-MMA bouts, while Volkanovski's record stands at 28 wins against four losses – twice to Islam Makhachev, once to Ilia Topuria and a defeat earlier in his career to Corey Nelson.

The co-main event will see Petr Yan and Merab Dvalishvili play out their trilogy in Abu Dhabi.

Yan (20-5) arrives in the UAE as UFC bantamweight champion, having dethroned Dvalishvili when they last met in December 2025.

The Russian's consummate boxing and takedown defence won out against Dvalishvili, who was defending his title for a fourth time in the calendar year.

Dvalishvili (21-5) won their first meeting and has vowed to exact revenge on the Russian and settle their rivalry once and for all.

Following Losene Keita's viral first-round knockout of Muhammas Naimov, the Belgian is a short-notice replacement for Arnold Allen and will face American featherweight Aaron Pico.

English flyweight Lone'er Kavanagh will test his skills against Ramazan Temirov of Uzbekistan, and Alexander Volkov meets fellow Russian Rizvan Kuniev in a heavyweight clash to round out the main card.

At the top of the prelims, Azamat Murzakanov will look to get back in the win column after his 12-fight win streak was halted by Paulo Costa in his last bout. The heavy-handed Russian takes on former light heavyweight title contender Dominick Reyes.

There are two UFC Fan Experiences to attend throughout the week, one at Yas Mall (Monday-Saturday) and the other at Yas Bay Plaza (Wednesday-Sunday). The events are free and open to the public. Fans can get involved in immersive experiences and buy UFC merchandise at the stores.

Yas Mall: Monday to Thursday, 10am to 10pm; Friday and Saturday from 10am to midnight.

Yas Bay Plaza: Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday, 4-10pm; Friday, 4pm to midnight; Saturday, 4pm to 2am.

Fans can attend the public workout on Wednesday at Yas Mall's Town Centre (5-7pm), where the headline and co-main event fighters will go through their paces.

The press conferences will be held on Thursday at Etihad Arena (4-5.30pm). Fans are also invited to attend for free.

The weigh-ins will then take place on Friday, with the closed official weigh-ins scheduled for 8am before ceremonial weigh-ins in the evening at Etihad Arena (4-6.30pm), which are open to the public.

Tickets can be purchased at www.ticketmaster.ae.

The event can be watched live in the UAE on Starzplay.

body_text:
The International Monetary Fund is to advance discussions with Iraq and Lebanon as part of broader efforts to support vulnerable countries in the Middle East and North Africa, its managing director has said.

Baghdad had approached the Washington-based fund for a potential programme, as the IMF continues to look at opportunities in the region, signalling it will be ready for any nation that may seek its assistance, Kristalina Georgieva said.

"We will support Iraq very firmly. We would get Iraq both money and policy support," she said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand on Saturday. She also noted IMF support in Egypt and Jordan.

IMF cuts 2026 growth forecasts for Gulf economies

"We are in very intense discussions with the Lebanese authorities," she added. "We have made significant progress towards a programme. [There is] still a bit more work to do together and I'm confident we will be successful."

Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations.

But Baghdad has been driving efforts to boost its standing. Last month at the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi appealed to the world to invest in Iraq as he pitched his economic and anti-corruption plans.

Lebanon, meanwhile, is heavily reliant on imports, making it more exposed to shocks such as the disruption to shipping and energy supplies caused by the regional war.

Beirut is also still dealing with the effects of the economic crisis that began in 2019. That was one of the worst in modern history, according to the World Bank, which also projected Lebanon's economy to contract by 6.4 per cent in 2026.

The IMF said this month that it would assess any potential changes to Lebanon's bank resolution law to ensure they were consistent with international standards. On Wednesday, the governor of Lebanon's central bank, Karim Souaid, told Bloomberg that he was expecting a "breakthrough" by the end of 2026 in IMF talks on the law, which stipulates it would repay depositors whose savings were entangled in the country’s financial collapse.

"Programmes for Iraq and Lebanon would go a long way," Ms Georgieva said.

She also acknowledged efforts by governments in the Gulf, whose pursuit of reforms have allowed them to "cushion the impact of the shock that has impacted them".

"It would've been much worse if ... many of them have not done reforms and been building buffers," she added.

headline: IMFC chair says global economy resilient; delegates walk out on Russian official
summary: By Andrea Shalal, David Lawder and Jan StrupczewskiBANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - The global economy is showing remarkable resilience but there is no room for complacency, the head of the International Monetary Fund's steering committee said on Saturday, while divisions over Russia's war against Ukraine sparked a walkout of delegates.
body_text:
By Andrea Shalal, David Lawder and Jan Strupczewski

BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - The global economy is showing remarkable resilience but there is no room for complacency, the head of the International Monetary Fund's steering committee said on Saturday, while divisions over Russia's war against Ukraine sparked a walkout of delegates.

Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who heads the IMF's steering committee, acknowledged the walkout by nearly half of delegates during remarks by Russia's finance minister at a meeting on Saturday, but said the important thing was that members ultimately agreed to the chair's statement.

"We came here for a reason, and we achieved it. Look at this chair statement, it clearly says that all members agreed to the statement, so that's what matters," the chair of the International Monetary and Financial Committee told Reuters.

Al-Jadaan told a press conference that the global economy was demonstrating "remarkable resilience" in the face of profound ongoing challenges, including wars, threats to energy and food security, high public debt levels, and risks linked to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, while warning finance officials against letting down their guard.

"The message from the IMFC members is clear: there is no room for complacency," Al-Jadaan said in the final press conference of a week of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that brought more than 18,000 people to Bangkok.

Fiscal authorities should work to rebuild buffers while protecting vulnerable populations and growth-enhancing investments, Al-Jadaan told reporters, underscoring the need for continued central bank independence and policies that supported private sector-led growth and investment.

He said IMFC members called for increasing support to countries that are facing short-term financing challenges caused by spillovers from wars and high energy prices.

"International cooperation remains critical to addressing excessive global imbalances and trade tensions," he said.

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva called the meetings productive but said there was clearly heightened anxiety among members about increasing divergence.

Many lower income countries that were not part of the AI-value chain feared they were falling behind, she said.

"These meetings also have shown that in a world of repetitive shocks and geopolitical fragmentation, still there is desire for multilateral dialogue and cooperation," she said.

WALKOUT AMID TENSIONS

Those comments came shortly after many IMFC delegates left the room when Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov addressed the group in Russian.

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel told a bank event on the sidelines of the meetings that nearly 50% of delegates took part in the walkout, sending a clear message to Russia.

"This is a very strong signal about solidarity and values. It would be the best for the world economy if this unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine would end," Nagel said. "I was really proud so many left this plenary."

Ukraine's central bank chief, Andriy Pyshnyi, told Reuters he was surprised by the large number of finance officials who left the room, calling it a "deep and emotional moment."

The Bank of England confirmed that Governor Andrew Bailey was among the delegates who joined the walkout, which comes ahead of Britain hosting the G20 next year.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, who may be in the frame to take over as chair of the World Economic Forum, stayed in the room, two people in the meeting said.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 has roiled the IMFC, preventing it from reaching consensus statements in the years since. There were deep divisions again this week astensions flared between the US and Ukraine.

People in the meeting said those who left whileSiluanov spoke included delegates from Britain, Germany, France, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, among others.

"The Ukraine war is existential for us in Europe," one European diplomat said. "We cannot normalize relations with Russia."

Germany on Thursday warned against ​efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage after Siluanov attended a meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bankers, just over a month after the US hosted his first in-person G20 appearance since Russia invaded Ukraine, at a meeting in Asheville, North Carolina.

US Treasury Under Secretary Erin Browne told Reuters the same day that Washington, the current leader of the G20, supported Russia's presence.

"We think it's really important if you're going to solve a crisis, you need to have open dialogue and open conversation," she told Reuters. "And you can't ​have ... dialogue, and you can't have resolution to conflict if no one's talking to one another."

Ukraine's finance minister participated virtually in the meetings, in order to focus on budget priorities at home.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, speaking at a European Union summit on Friday, blasted US President Donald Trump's recent diesel deal with Russia.

EU leaders have rallied aroundZelenskiy after Trump again criticised Ukraine and called its strikes on Russian refineries a "disgrace." Trump on Friday waived a new congressional requirement to impose harsh sanctions on Russia.

(Reporting by Andrea Shalal, David Lawder and Jan Strupczewski; additional reporting by Francesco Canepa and David Milliken; Editing by John Mair and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)

body_text:
Apple has said it will "work hard" to fulfil demand for its much-anticipated foldable iPhone Duo, as orders overwhelm supply and cause delivery dates to be pushed back.

The device, the California-based company's long-awaited entry into the foldable market, was introduced alongside Apple's iPhone 18 Pro last month and is the first new major hardware release under chief executive John Ternus.

Apple began accepting online orders for the Duo on Friday, but customers were reported to have quickly seen delivery estimates being pushed back from November to December and, as of Saturday, towards the end of January.

In the UAE, Apple's online platform shows a delivery estimate of January 22, similar to its US and UK sites, applying to all four storage capacities and two colour options. It is unclear whether there are earlier or later dates in other areas.

By contrast, delivery estimates for the iPhone 18 Pro are about two to three weeks.

The period after a new iPhone is launched usually presents longer lead times, but those are eventually whittled down – in later periods to as little as a week – after the launch hype has eased.

“The preorder demand for iPhone Duo ... has been nothing short of extraordinary," an Apple representative said in a statement to The National on Saturday. They added that the company aimed to get the devices to users "as quickly as possible".

Online orders will continue while the company "looks forward to welcoming customers at Apple Stores worldwide", the representative said.

Considering the appetite shown by consumers, the delays could also be a positive signal for Apple's foldable – its debut device after the market went mainstream nearly a decade ago.

It could also be a sign of further growth in the category, especially after Samsung Electronics reported record orders for its latest Galaxy Z foldables, which were introduced in July.

Apple does not break down order and sales numbers. Counterpoint Research last month said the company was expected to sell about six million Duos this year owing to the strong demand potential driven by its “bold” pricing, which is just $100 above its main competitor, the refreshed Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8. Observers had expected a higher price point for the iPhone Duo.

Sales could now hit about 14 million, adding about $28 billion to the company's revenue for the 2027 fiscal year, Bloomberg Intelligence estimates. The iPhone Duo's prices in the UAE range from Dh8,499 to Dh13,599.

body_text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi on Saturday called on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorise him to intervene in defence of Saudi Arabia if asked by the kingdom.

Saudi Arabia is facing attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Fighting erupted in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime blockade" of Saudi ports and seized additional territory in Yemen.

Saudi-led forces launched a full-scale military campaign against the group this month.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony for military academy and college cadets, Mr El Sisi said the move would require parliamentary approval.

“I call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorise us to take action to intervene in defence of Saudi Arabia, if we are asked to do so,” he said. “This move and this defence require approval from the Egyptian parliament. I hope parliament will convene an emergency session to grant this authorisation.

"I am not speaking about attacking or waging war. We are seeking only to defend.”

Mr El Sisi said Egypt stood firmly behind efforts to protect the territory of its Gulf allies. “Egypt will take any measures necessary to protect and defend Saudi Arabia,” he added.

The Houthis are fighting against Yemen’s internationally recognised government and their Saudi allies.

The Houthis this week launched a missile and drone attack on the presidential palace in Aden, which has been the seat of the Yemeni government since 2015. The strikes killed and injured security personnel.

The Houthis, one of Tehran’s main proxy militant groups, claimed they were attacking a Saudi military command centre in the city. Attacks on Aden's airport also risk isolating Yemen’s government from its main backer and supplier.

The fighting has not been confined to Yemen. The Houthis last week carried out attacks on Riyadh’s main airport, killing 17 people, injuring more than 300 and forcing a complete shutdown of operations. There have been 20 strikes on the airport since the start of October.

headline: Egypt boosted by Moody's upgrade as inflation eases and investor confidence grows
summary: Moody's Ratings has raised Egypt's sovereign credit score due to easing inflation and growing business confidence as the country introduces economic reforms.The upgrade to B3 was underpinned by efforts focused on fiscal consolidation and structural reforms, which have helped reduce government debt and interest burdens, the New York-based ratings agency said on Friday.A B3 rating is still six notches below investment grade, which makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funds when the need to borrow arises. But the upgrade pulled Egypt out of the "substantial risk" level."Stronger revenue collection and expenditure restraint have supported [Egypt's] progress," analysts at Moody's said.Cairo's shift to a flexible exchange rate and tighter monetary policy has strengthened external buffers and the economy's capacity to absorb shocks, they added. "The government's ability to sustain this credit-positive trend despite a challenging external environment and higher oil prices highlights the durability of the improvement, rooted in increased policy effectiveness," Moody's said.The agency also gave Egypt a positive outlook, noting sustained fiscal discipline and continued reforms that have performed better than expected. That could be further driven by "stronger growth, more effective revenue collection and a faster decline in domestic borrowing costs as inflation eases and investor confidence strengthens", it added.Fitch and S&P Global affirmed their ratings on Egypt last week, with both referring to the country's progress.Egypt has been battling economic challenges and elevated inflation, but the government has taken steps to counter their effects. "The reform of Egypt's monetary policy framework since March 2024 has strengthened the sovereign's ability to absorb external shocks," the Moody's analysts said."The unification of the foreign exchange market and adoption of a flexible exchange rate reduced foreign currency distortions, eliminated chronic foreign currency shortages, and allowed the currency to adjust to changes in capital flows without depleting official foreign-currency buffers, unlike in 2022."As a net energy importer, Egypt was forced to introduce fuel-saving measures as the war in Iran drove up oil and gas prices, adding to inflationary pressures and the cost of living. Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, Capmas data show. Higher inflation might prompt a policy reversal at the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates.But the Arab world's most populous nation has been able to weather the economic fallout from the regional conflict relatively well, helped by policies centred on exchange-rate flexibility, energy price adjustments and spending controls."The resilience of the updated macroeconomic policy framework has been tested by the sharp rise in oil prices and a confidence shock," Moody's said, referring to the decision by authorities to adjust domestic fuel and electricity prices, use expenditure contingencies and energy-conservation measures, and expand targeted social support rather than reversing energy price reforms."These measures limited the fiscal consequences of higher commodity prices and helped preserve macroeconomic stability," the agency added.In July, Egypt was able to unlock about $1.8 billion in funding after clearing the latest review from its expanded economic programme with the International Monetary Fund.

Regional conflicts and Palestine topped the agenda as the 52nd session of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation (OIC) began in Baghdad on Saturday.

Foreign ministers of member states attended the first day of the two-day meeting, which is being held in the Iraq capital for the first time in 45 years.

The meeting is being held under the theme of “Dialogue and Solidarity: Two Essential Pillars for Promoting Peace and Sustainable Development”. It is to address Israel’s attacks on Gaza and the recent Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia, as well as crisis zones across the Islamic world.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi opened the meeting, calling for greater co-operation among Islamic countries to address mounting challenges.

“The crises we are witnessing at the regional and international levels call for greater joint action to protect the interests of our peoples,” he said. "Iraq continues to suffer from the consequences of regional conflicts and their economic repercussions."

The meeting is being held in Baghdad because it is "the cradle of civilisation, science, thought and history", he added.

Mr Al Zaidi announced the formation of an Iraqi initiative aimed at integrating energy grids, railway networks, transport and digital communications among OIC countries. The development of a digital payment system and trade platforms will also form part of the initiative.

The move aims to promote security, stability and prosperity and strengthen the ability of member states to confront challenges, Mr Al Zaidi said.

Referring to the regional conflicts, he thanked Pakistan for its efforts to defuse tension and urged OIC member states to follow suit.

OIC Secretary General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed described the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia as a "flagrant violation of the kingdom's sovereignty and of the sanctity of the Islamic holy sites". He said he would work to "strengthen preventive diplomacy and to activate the OIC's mediation unit" to put an end to the crisis.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is among those to attend the meeting, having arrived in Baghdad early on Saturday. He held meetings with the foreign ministers of Turkey and Egypt, Hakan Fidan and Badr Abdelatty, on the sidelines of the meeting.

Mr Araghchi said Iran was ready to help stop the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, one of Tehran’s main proxy militant groups.

He had previously offered to help enable dialogue between the two sides during a phone call with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan last week. Mr Araghchi said that a military solution was not an option to end the years-long civil war in Yemen.

headline: Pope Leo returns to Vatican four days after lung cancer surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV was released from the hospital on Saturday after lung cancer surgery. Doctors removed part of the 71-year-old's right lung last week to extract a cancerous tumour.
body_text:
Pope Leo XIV was released from the hospital on Saturday after lung cancer surgery. Doctors removed part of the 71-year-old's right lung last week to extract a cancerous tumour.

Issued on: 17/10/2026 - 12:35Modified: 17/10/2026 - 15:53

Pope Leo XIV will leave the Rome hospital on Saturday, where he has been recovering from lung cancer surgery after doctors deemed him "fit for discharge", the Vatican said.

Leo, 71, has been at the Gemelli hospital in Rome since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung to extract a cancerous tumour.

"Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge," doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora wrote in a note published by the Vatican.

Read moreWhat we know about Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis

The Vatican said that Pope Leo "will leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican. Tomorrow he will recite the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment".

The Angelus prayer is typically given by the pope from the Apostolic Palace overlooking St Peter's Square.

But in past years, former popes John Paul II and Francis similarly hospitalised at the Gemelli have delivered the prayer from the window of their hospital rooms.

The Vatican press office said that Leo celebrated Mass on Saturday, as he has in recent days, in a room on the 10th floor of the hospital where he has been recovering.

Outside the hospital, 12-year-old Ukrainian Varvara Struck said she was rooting for the pope.

The former cancer patient said she had met the pope last year in Rome, "and he blessed me for a successful treatment".

"With his support, I’ve now overcome my illness, and I want to give him my positive energy so that he, too, can overcome his illness as quickly as possible," she said.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

News that the otherwise active pope had a cancerous tumour removed from his lung has rattled the Vatican and the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.

But his doctors have said Leo's recovery has been progressing normally as they await the results of tests that will determine the course of action to take.

Leo has resumed some work, making a call on Friday to Russian President Vladimir Putin to urge a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

Up in the air, however, is a planned papal voyage to South America, scheduled for November 6-17 to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Vatican watchers say that Leo – who spent two decades as a missionary in Peru – is anxious to make the long journey, but will likely follow the recommendations of his doctors.

Leo has cancelled all his audiences until October 20.

The pope announced to the public in St Peter's Square last Sunday, following the Angelus prayer, that a routine medical examination had revealed a nodule that doctors recommended should be removed.

body_text:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El Sisi insisted on Saturday that he would not seek another term when his current mandate ends in 2030, as he outlined a plan to prepare a new generation of leaders to succeed him.

"My term in office ends in 2030 and this is a given and will not change," Mr El Sisi told a military ceremony marking the graduation of new cadets. "But I will not abandon the state of Egypt, which is rich with its sons who can shoulder the responsibility after me."

He said the military academy would invite up to 300 candidates with doctorates from Egyptian or foreign universities to attend a 30-month course to teach them "what is a nation and how to protect it".

The armed forces are to sponsor the course. Those who finish will be the next generation of the country's leaders, he said.

"The academy will prepare people to know what a nation is and how to protect it ... Egypt is not sterile. It's capable of producing a leader better than me. I need the Egyptian people to support this idea," he added.

He said applicants must be between the ages of 40 and 50 and will be interviewed and vetted before they are enrolled. He did not say whether civilians and military candidates can apply, leaving the door open for another army officer like him to seek election in 2030.

By the time Mr El Sisi's current term ends in 2030, he would have served as president for 16 years. He owes his current term in office to constitutional amendments in 2019, which were adopted in a national referendum.

Before the changes were adopted, the constitution stipulated that no president could serve more than two four-year terms. The amendments kept the two-term cap, but extended the term to six years.

In a clause added for Mr El Sisi's benefit, the amendments considered the first of his two terms in office to have begun in 2018, not 2014 when he was first elected.

Egypt's constitution is a relatively progressive document adopted in a nationwide referendum in 2014, three years after Hosni Mubarak was removed from power in an uprising.

Many Egyptians regard Mr El Sisi as a safe pair of hands at a time when the Middle East is embroiled in conflict, with wars in Gaza, Egypt's neighbour to the east, Sudan, to the south, and political instability in Libya, on the western border.

The fallout from the Iran war, including Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, has affected Egypt's economy, increasing its already high energy import bills and hitting Suez Canal revenue.

headline: Egypt's Sisi says his presidency will end in 2030, outlines plan to prepare future leaders
summary: By Enas AlashrayCAIRO, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.

The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. Under Sisi, a former general,the military has expanded its presence in the economy and civilian affairs.

Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the academy, Sisi said a committee overseen by the speaker of parliament and including intellectuals, politicians and the ministers of higher education and justice, would develop criteria for selecting candidates and draft legislation for the training programme.

Reiterating that Egypt's constitution would not be amended, he said the end of his presidential term in 2030 was "a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed".

He said the programme would allow Egyptians to "elect and choose from among" its graduates, but gave no details on how they would be put forward for elected or appointed posts.

"I will not leave the Egyptian state except when it is replete with sons and daughters capable of assuming responsibility," Sisi said.

The programme would target PhD holders from reputable Egyptian and foreign universities, who would spend 30 months at the academy learning about the state, its resources and how to preserve them, Sisi said. He said graduates would be prepared for leadership roles ranging from the presidency to ministries, governorates and parliament.

Sisi, 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and allowed him to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030.

The latest in a line of Egyptian rulers drawn from the military, he became president in 2014, a year after toppling Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood — Egypt's first democratically elected leader — following mass protests.

He proceeded to crush the Brotherhood, the Middle East's oldest Islamist organisation, and maintain a grip on power.

headline: Zelenskiy hopes for meeting with US and Russia during G20 summit
summary: KYIV, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday.The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December.
body_text:
KYIV, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday.

The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December.

"The meeting could then take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from either Russia or the United States. It could also be held in a European country," Zelenskiy told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat.

He added: "This meeting could take place in one of the Middle Eastern countries. The United States has consistently mentioned the United Arab Emirates or Saudi Arabia."

Zelenskiy said Ukrainian negotiators had spoken to US officials on Friday but gave no other details. He also said that Europe needed its own track for talks with Russia, with which relations are strained by Moscow's war in Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump has declined to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the more than four-year-old war, and Zelenskiy has criticised Trump for lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

Zelenskiy said the Ukrainian military was unable to use its interceptors against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions placed on services provided by satellite company Starlink.

"Today, our interceptor drones are not operating because of speed limitations," Zelenskiy said.

He said Ukraine had been told that the speed restrictions had been caused by technical issues but that tests of Starlink on the territory of the European Union had shown there were no such issues there.

Trump said on Friday he did not think either he or Elon Musk - whose company SpaceX developed the Starshield system used by Ukraine's military - was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access in a way that affected its military operations against Russia.

The reduction in services provided by the satellite company interrupted communications with headquarters and caused internet speeds to drop.

(Reporting by Yuliia Dysa, Pavel Polityuk and Olena Harmash, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

headline: Israeli occupiers attack European diplomatic delegation in occupied West Bank
summary: Delegation comprising French, Belgian, Polish representatives come under attack in town of Taybeh, causing injuries
body_text:
By Aysar Alais and Zein Khalil

RAMALLAH, Palestine / ISTANBUL (AA) - Israeli occupiers attacked a diplomatic delegation comprising representatives from France, Belgium and Poland on Saturday while visiting the town of Taybeh, central occupied West Bank, causing injuries.

The attack took place after an official ceremony marking the signing of a twinning agreement between the Palestinian town of Taybeh and the French town of Saint-Pierre, Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khourieh told Anadolu.

The ceremony was attended by the French and Belgian consuls, a Polish representative whose name was not disclosed, and Saint-Pierre Mayor Christian Ravain.

The attack targeted the delegation in the western part of the town, as well as Palestinians who were picking olives.

It left several town residents injured and shattered the window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian delegation, Khourieh added.

Israeli Army Radio, citing witnesses and footage, also said that the occupiers hurled stones at one of the diplomatic vehicles, smashing its window.

Footage showed a member of the delegation lying on the ground after the attack. The person shown lying on the ground beside the diplomatic vehicle was Bernard Boudot, a French politician and mayor of Aulnoy-lez-Valenciennes in northern France, the broadcaster said.

Israel’s Channel 12, citing the Israeli military, reported that the incident was “under review” and none had been arrested immediately.

Khourieh described the attack as “a flagrant violation of the sanctity of diplomatic and humanitarian work” and part of ongoing restrictions imposed on Palestinian farmers.

Attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians and their land have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began in early October and provides a key source of income for thousands of Palestinian families.

headline: Egypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked
summary: CAIRO, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced an emergency session on Sunday."It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defence.
body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced an emergency session on Sunday.

"It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defence.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the state oil giant Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce.

Sisi said Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited, to discuss issues including security and navigation in the Red Sea.

"I know this requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that authorisation if we are asked," Sisi said.

Shortly after he spoke, parliament said it would hold a plenary session at 1 p.m. (1000 GMT) on Sunday in response to the request, though it did not disclose the agenda.

Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist president Mohamed Morsi in 2013.

Egypt also joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in 2015 to support the Yemeni government against the Houthis.

(Reporting by Enas Alashray; Additional Reporting by Hatem Maher and Mohamed Hendawy; Editing by Kevin Liffey)

headline: Egypt will not accept any threat to Saudi, Red Sea security: Al-Sisi
summary: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi said Egypt will not accept any threat to Saudi Arabia’s security or borders, or to Red Sea security, warning that deep geopolitical shifts in the region will have consequences. He described Egypt and Saudi Arabia as the heart of the Arab and Islamic worlds and said harm to either would affect the other. Al-Sisi made the remarks to senior officials and journalists at a breakfast after the Police Academy’s 2026 graduation ceremony in New Cairo. He also warned of risks on Egypt’s southern and western borders, and said the stability of Sudan, Libya and Gaza is essential to Egyptian and Arab national security. The Egyptian president also said he had told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in every meeting and communication since 2014 that establishing a Palestinian state would benefit all parties and lead to lasting peace in the Middle East. Turning to domestic affairs, Al-Sisi warned of continuing attempts to discredit the country’s armed forces and police. He described the police and the armed forces as the “two wings” of Egypt’s security, saying both are essential to the country’s stability at home and abroad and that Egyptian national security rests on the defence and interior ministries. He cautioned that pressure on Egypt will grow in the coming years as development gathers pace and as opponents realise the state is still standing after plans to bring it down in 2011 failed. Al-Sisi said safeguarding the state is the responsibility of all Egyptians and reiterated the need to protect the national memory from attempts to distort it through lies and fabrications, describing Egyptians as the first line of defence against them. Al-Sisi stated that institutional stability is required to achieve long-term development plans, acknowledging that no country can realise such goals in just a few years. Citing what he described as stagnation in the state and its institutions since 1967, he called for improvements in the quality of education and the creation of qualified personnel free from favouritism. He noted that the volume of work completed in Egypt since 2014 would otherwise have taken at least 30 years, pledging to continue working until his last day in office. The Police Academy graduation ceremony for the class of 2026 in New Cairo was attended by Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, Interior Minister Mahmoud Tawfik, and Assistant Interior Minister and Police Academy President Nidal Youssef. It featured military, physical fitness and combat displays. During the ceremony, Al-Sisi awarded medals of excellence to top graduates before concluding with a martyrs’ salute, honouring those who died for the country.
