headline: Iran rejects pressure, remains open to dialogue: Araghchi
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure but remains ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure but remains ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday.

Addressing the 52nd Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) in Baghdad, Araghchi said Iran did not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, stressing that any dialogue must be grounded in mutual respect and backed by credible guarantees.

The full text of his speech is as follows:

In the Name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful

Excellency, Mr. Fuad Mohammed Hussein, Deputy Prime Minister, and Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Iraq,

Mr. Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, Secretary-General of the OIC,

Ladies and Gentlemen,

I begin by thanking the Government and people of the Republic of Iraq, our neighbor and brother, for hosting this meeting of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and for their warm hospitality. I congratulate Secretary-General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed for his appointment as the new Secretary-General, and wish him full success. I also thank the Republic of Tyrkiya for all its efforts during its successful chairmanship of the OIC CFM. Moreover, I should thank the Secretary-General and the General Secretariat for their efforts in preparing this meeting.

It is fitting that we gather in a land that has long been a meeting place of civilizations, at a time when unity and dialogue within the Islamic world are needed more than ever.

The OIC was founded to give the Islamic Ummah a common voice and to promote solidarity, cooperation and the defense of our shared interests. Keeping the path of dialogue open among us is not weakness. It is a responsibility. The Charter of our Organization rests on principles that reflect those contained in the UN Charter: sovereign equality, territorial integrity, non-interference in internal affairs, peaceful settlement of disputes, and refraining from the threat or use of force. These principles belong to no single country or group of countries. They protect all of us, and when they are applied selectively, they lose their value.

Dear Brothers and Sisters,

Iran has been steadfast in its commitment to international law, the UN Charter and diplomacy. Over the past two years we continued to pursue diplomacy. The United States chose the opposite path: aggression, threats, assassination and economic warfare, with a blatant disregard for international law and the UN Charter. About five thousand people were killed as martyrs, including hundreds of women and children. The United States and the Israeli regime assassinated Iran's Supreme Leader and other senior political and military officials, a grave violation of international law. The killing of more than 160 students and teachers in Minab, the cluster-munition attack on the Lamerd stadium, the bombing of a desalination unit in Qeshm and the attack on a wedding ceremony in Kuhestak, Sirik, are only some of the documented examples. The United States and the Israeli regime cannot whitewash these crimes by reversing the roles of victim and aggressor. I thank those member states that have expressed solidarity with the Iranian people in these difficult times, and I call on the Organization as a whole to stand firmly against attacks on the sovereignty and territorial integrity of its founding member.

Iran defended its people, its sovereignty and its legitimate interests, and will continue to do so by any means. We never attacked our neighbors, but we did attack and destroyed the US military bases and military installations, which are unfortunately, located in our neighborhood. But there is no contradiction between defending our rights and pursuing peace. We know the cost of war, and that is precisely why we value peace.

Iran asks for no special treatment, only the equal application of rights and responsibilities to all. This issue will not be resolved on the battlefield. Peace cannot be built through threats of annihilation.

Iran also remains committed to safe and secure navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway vital to the energy and trade of many of our member states. Until 28 February 2026, the Strait was open. The insecurity and disruption of maritime navigation since then are the direct result of the aggressive actions of the United States and the Israeli regime, and of the blockade and coercive measures imposed by the United States. Security cannot be restored by more of the same. One cannot bomb a country, threaten its annihilation and impose a blockade, and then expect the security of navigation return to normal.

Diplomacy was in fact working. Through the good offices of Pakistan, with the support of Qatar, both members of this Organization, Iran and the United States signed the Islamabad MoU on 17 June. Under paragraph 5, Iran undertook to make the necessary arrangements to facilitate the safe movement of vessels, and we immediately began technical discussions with the Sultanate of Oman to implement that commitment. Within two weeks, maritime traffic had recovered to approximately 60 percent of its pre-war level. Subsequent unilateral US measures and military action then blocked implementation of the Memorandum, and the dispute-resolution mechanisms it envisaged were bypassed.

Over the past two years, Iran has negotiated in good faith, and repeatedly, it was met with military action rather than diplomacy. This has created deep distrust about renewed negotiations without credible assurances against a repetition. Even so, Iran has kept the door open. Through Qatar, we have conveyed a concrete seven-day plan: if the necessary conditions are met, the Strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days. The choice now rests with the United States.

The Palestinian cause remains the central cause of the Islamic world, and we cannot speak of peace while ignoring it. Palestine remains a wound on the conscience of the international community, and Gaza, a victim of genocide, has become a symbol of the failure of international mechanisms to protect civilians. Dozens of resolutions have not ended occupation and violence. The continuing suffering of the Palestinian people, the killing of innocent civilians by the Israeli regime and the threats to Al-Quds Al-Sharif and its holy sites should concern everyone. Iran stands with the Palestinian people, and we call on the OIC and all its members to do whatever it takes to put an end to the killing and the blockade and to make the protection of civilians and the legitimate rights of the Palestinian people a shared priority, backed by practical and coordinated action. And finally, I would like to endorse the proposal made by my brother, Hakan Fidan, the distinguished Foreign Minister of the Republic of Turkiya, to assign a day as Gaza Genocide Memorial Day.

On Yemen, for almost a decade, the people of Yemen have endured a devastating conflict, a prolonged blockade, and severe restrictions on vital civilian infrastructure. The role of the US and Israeli regime in inflicting suffering on Yemenis is undeniable. The resulting humanitarian catastrophe remains one of the gravest in the world, with serious violations of international humanitarian law continuing with impunity.

Iran's position is clear and unchanged. We support the sovereignty, independence, unity and territorial integrity of Yemen, and those of the Saudi Arabia. We support a peaceful, inclusive and comprehensive political process as the only viable and sustainable means of resolving the conflict. Sustainable peace cannot be achieved through military escalation or coercion. There is no military solution.

The region's crises have no military solutions, and insisting on a military approach while disregarding a political solution only further complicates the situation. Iran is deeply concerned by developments in the Arabian Peninsula and remains ready to provide every assistance to facilitate dialogue between the parties, on the basis of the peace roadmap they previously agreed. The people of Yemen have the right to live with dignity, free from pressure, sanctions and blockade.

No state can build lasting security at the expense of the security of others. We believe the problems of our region are best resolved within the region, by its own states, before they become a pretext for the wars of distant powers. In that spirit, we believe the territory, airspace and infrastructure of every regional state should be used only to serve regional security and never become a platform for staging attacks on a neighbor. We say this in a spirit of brotherhood and good-neighborliness. Our peoples share one region and one future, and the choice before us is a simple one: either we build security together, or we will endure insecurity together. Iran stands ready to work with all its brothers and neighbors toward the former.

Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure. But we remain ready for dialogue based on mutual respect and credible guarantees.

I renew my thanks to our Iraqi hosts, and I wish this meeting success in serving the unity, peace, security and prosperity of the Islamic Ummah.

headline: Iranian lawmaker says indirect talks with US continuing through Qatar, Oman: Report
summary: Tehran, Washington have exchanged conditions for negotiations as Iran awaits US response, says parliamentary committee member
body_text:
Indirect talks between Iran and the US are continuing through mediation by Qatar and Oman, an Iranian lawmaker said Saturday, as Tehran-Washington tensions remain high, according to local media.

Yaqoub Rezazadeh, a member of the Iranian parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, told the ILNA news agency that both sides had presented conditions through the mediators.

“We have presented a set of conditions, and the other side has also presented a set of conditions. We are now waiting to see whether the conditions we announced will be accepted by the Americans,” Rezazadeh said.

He said the contacts were being conducted with the involvement of Qatar and Oman.

Rezazadeh said the negotiations were being overseen by Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, adding that issues under discussion were handled with the council’s approval.

The lawmaker also played down speculation about an imminent new conflict between Iran and the US, saying predictions based on betting markets or reports of a possible preemptive Iranian attack were unfounded.

He said he did not expect another war before US congressional elections and elections in Israel, while acknowledging that renewed fighting remained possible.

Rezazadeh said Iran would not launch a preemptive attack but would respond if attacked, claiming that Tehran’s military, air defense, and naval capabilities had significantly improved compared with the previous two rounds of fighting.

The latest reported contacts come after Iran and the US reached an understanding in Islamabad in June aimed at ending hostilities and opening the way for negotiations, with Pakistan and Qatar involved in mediation.

Under the understanding, the sides were expected to pursue further talks, but tensions subsequently resurfaced amid disputes over implementation and continuing military activity in the region.

Qatar and Oman have also maintained diplomatic contacts with Tehran and Washington as regional actors seek to prevent another escalation between the two sides.

headline: Zelenskyy says Russia sanctions relief could continue, diesel deal ‘first step’
summary: Ukrainian president hopes Trump 'will do everything in his power' to halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and end war
body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that easing of US sanctions against Russia could continue, describing the recent diesel deal as only the “first step,” the Interfax-Ukraine news agency reported.

Speaking to journalists, Zelenskyy said sanctions relief would give Russian President Vladimir Putin a sense of support rather than persuade him to end the war.

His comment came after US President Donald Trump signed an executive order suspending certain sanctions, restrictions and tariffs on Russia provided for under the Graham Act.

Zelenskyy, however, expressed hope that Trump "will do everything in his power" to halt attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and end the war.

He said Ukrainian and US negotiators could meet as early as this week, stressing that Kyiv remained committed to negotiations.

He said Washington was working on a proposal for a trilateral meeting involving Ukraine, the US and Russia.

Possible venues included the US at the Group of 20 summit, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia or a European country. No confirmation had yet been received from Moscow or Washington, he said.

On alleged Starlink restrictions, Zelenskyy said terminals in Ukraine disconnect at speeds above about 161 kph, affecting interceptor drones targeting Russian jet-powered Shahed drones and food deliveries to isolated Ukrainian positions. He said tests in some European countries showed connections remained active at speeds exceeding 180 kph.

He said military officials, the Defense Ministry and diplomats were involved in ongoing discussions, but SpaceX had not been engaging with the military.

“At various levels, it is being claimed that these are technical issues. However, these technical issues exist in Ukraine, while they do not occur within the territory of the EU,” Zelenskyy said.

He added that European countries were exploring alternatives to Starlink after recognizing that US-based access could be restricted.

On frozen Russian assets, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had information that Moscow could seek to recover some of them through partner countries. He said he had discussed the risk with Belgium and EU leaders, adding that the assets remained under European control and were secure.

European partners opposed the US-Russian diesel deal and agreed that sanctions should remain in place while Russia continued its attacks, Zelenskyy said, adding that work on another sanctions package was also underway.

​Pedro Neto scored twice as Chelsea beat Everton ​2-0 ​in ​the Premier League ⁠on Saturday but the match was overshadowed by an injury to ⁠goalkeeper Emi Martinez.

After a goalless ​but ⁠first-half that produced five yellow ​cards and several heated exchanges, Chelsea went ahead less than a minute after the restart when an unmarked Neto swept home.

The game was paused for over 10 minutes when Chelsea goalkeeper Martinez was taken off on a stretcher following a clash of heads with Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite.

Chelsea salaries 2026/27: How much does record signing Rogers earn?

Chelsea's ​21-year-old keeper Mike ‌Penders came on ⁠for his Premier ​League debut.

Chelsea doubled their ​lead ‌in the 90th minute when Neto ⁠pounced on a loose ball after ⁠Jordan Henderson's free kick was blocked by the wall, finding the bottom corner with a composed finish ​as Everton suffered their first defeat of the season.

The 33-year-old Argentina goalkeeper, who won the World Cup in 2022, had signed a three-year deal with the Blues after competing his move from Aston Villa in August.

Chelsea goalscorer Neto dedicated the victory to Martinez.

“We are really pleased. Shame for Emi [Martinez] but we wish you all the best. This win is for him,” Neto told TNT Sports

“We need a clean sheet to be honest. I think we did a very good game. Emi deserved this, Mike [Penders] did as well.

“We know that they came man-to man. In the second half we adjusted some stuff. We tried to get the best of the man-to-man press and we got away. We got the cross and I could finish well, so really happy.”

Martinez was taken to hospital given the seriousness of the collision.

Martinez's injury gave 21-year-old keeper Penders ⁠the opportunity to make his league debut and he managed to help ​Chelsea ⁠keep a clean sheet in ‌the league for the first time since January, ending a run of 22 ​games without one.

headline: Pope Leo XIV leaves hospital days after lung cancer surgery
summary: The Pope left Rome's Gemelli Hospital Saturday, days after surgery for lung cancer removed the lower lobe of his right lung. He is currently scheduled to travel to Latin America in November.(Image credit: Andrew Medichini)
body_text:
Pope Leo XIV, followed by surgeon Stefano Margaritora, leaves Rome's Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic on Saturday. Andrew Medichini/AP hide caption

Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Saturday afternoon and returned to the Vatican after doctors said he was well enough to be discharged following surgery that removed part of his right lung.

The Vatican press office released a statement outlining details from Dr. Luigi Carbone,the Pope's personal physician, and Professor Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief of thoracic surgery who led the team that operated on Leo. The two doctors said the pope had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray that morning, with the results confirming his clinical condition meant he could leave hospital.

They said he was expected to lead the Angelus prayer from the window of the papal apartment on Sunday.Video showed Leo waving to well-wishers outside the hospital as he walked out without physical support, flanked by officials and security guards in dark suits.

Before leaving, the pope had celebrated Mass in a room set aside for that purpose on the hospital's 10th floor, according to the press office.

Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said "the estimated post-operative recovery time will be about one week." Leo's discharge came on his fifth day in hospital and was sooner than had been expected at the time of the operation's announcement.

Leo, 71, had told crowds in St. Peter's Square last Sunday that doctors had discovered a "localized nodule" in his lung at a "very early stage."

"Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it," he said.

The surgery on Tuesday went further than the nodule, however, with surgeons using a video-assisted technique to remove the lower lobe of the pope's right lung in an operation that lasted about 90 minutes. His doctors said lung tissue examined afterward confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma. With adenocarcinoma making up about 40% of all lung cancers in the U.S., it is the nation's most common form of lung cancer, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America.

That is true among nonsmokers too, according to Dr. Otis Brawley, an oncologist at Johns Hopkins University and former chief medical and scientific officer of the American Cancer Society.

Leo is not known to have smoked, but cancer does run in his family. His mother, Mildred, died of cancer in 1990, and on Tuesday the Vatican announced that his older brother Louis, who lives in Florida, has been hospitalized with a form of cancer.

Doctors not involved in the pope's care say the treatment so far points to a cancer that has been caught early.

"The fact that surgery was the first tool that they utilized is a really good sign," Dr. Vin Gupta, a pulmonologist and board member of the American Lung Association, told NPR. "It suggests that they think this is early stage."

Gupta said the fact that doctors removed a larger portion of the lung than first announced is not in itself a bad sign. "People have parts of their lungs removed all the time for all sorts of reasons, and they recover just fine," he said. "And in his case, he's pretty robust at baseline from a health standpoint."

Leo still exercises regularly, playing tennis each week with his personal secretary and riding horses at Castel Gandolfo, the papal retreat to the south of Rome.

The Vatican has not announced any further treatment.

Leo's office has cleared his public schedule until at least Oct. 20. His next major international trip, set for early November, includes Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he lived on and off for two decades and holds citizenship.

"He had a minimally invasive surgery," said Dr. Jonathan Villena Vargas, a cardiothoracic surgeon at Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City. "Because we do this all the time, most patients are allowed to travel about two weeks after the surgery."

Brawley from Johns Hopkins agreed. "I think he can do it," he said, adding that patients in good physical shape who have this type of procedure "very frequently are back to normal in seven to 10 days."

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

What’s the ongoing story: Amid rising global trade pressure on China, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said Friday that India’s trade imbalance with the world’s second-largest economy is “growing exponentially” and requests for market access have been denied for a decade.

Key Points to Ponder:

— What is the current status of India-China bilateral trade?

— What is a trade deficit, and how is it different from an overall balance-of-trade deficit?

— What are the major reasons for India’s persistent trade deficit with China?

— What are its implications for India’s economy?

— What are non-tariff barriers to trade? How do they affect India’s market access in China?

— Which Indian products have the potential to increase exports to China, and what challenges constrain their export growth?

— How can India improve its export competitiveness?

— What are the major areas of competition, cooperation and conflict between India and China?

— She said that while tariffs and other punitive actions have been the global approach to trade imbalances, India does not believe in them and prefers to “sit and talk”.

— Speaking on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meeting in Bangkok, Sitharaman also said she hopes the trade deal with the US is concluded “at the earliest” in the interest of global trade and trade between the two countries.

— “The trade imbalance is something which we have been talking with China now for several years. We are denied market access even for those goods for which there are immense market opportunities in China,” she said, adding that there is “huge potential” for India to export generic drugs, bovine meat, vegetables and other perishables to China.

— According to a PTI report from Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning, responding to a question on Sitharaman’s remarks, told a media briefing: “What I can tell you is that China never aims for trade surplus. We stand ready to work with India to address each other’s economic and trade concerns in a balanced way and promote the steady development of bilateral relations.”

— India’s trade deficit with China crossed $ 100 billion in the first nine months of 2026, even as Indian exports grew by 40.7 per cent, sustaining their upward momentum amid a continued surge in Chinese imports.

— India’s trade deficit with Beijing widened to $ 105.93 billion between January and September 2026, a 20.7 per cent increase compared to the same period last year, according to PTI, citing data released on Wednesday by China’s General Administration of Customs.

— Total bilateral trade rose by 25.4 per cent to $ 144.45 billion. China’s exports to India reached $ 125.19 billion during the nine-month period, marking a 23.3 per cent year-on-year increase.

— Simultaneously, Indian exports to China surged by 40.7 per cent to $ 19.26 billion compared to the corresponding period last year.

What’s the ongoing story: Around 5.30 pm this past Wednesday, several red lights flashed on the dashboard at the Delhi Pollution Control Committee’s (DPCC’s) new AI‑enabled Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC) at Shastri Park in Northeast Delhi.

— What is the Air Quality Index (AQI), and how is it calculated?

— Which pollutants are considered while calculating India’s AQI?

— What are the different categories of AQI in India?

— What is the difference between PM2.5 and PM10?

— What are the major sources of air pollution in Delhi?

— How do temperature, wind speed and atmospheric inversion affect air pollution?

— What is the role of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) in monitoring air quality?

— What is the difference between AQI, SAFAR and Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan?

— How can AI and real-time monitoring improve air pollution control?

— What are the major challenges in controlling urban air pollution in India?

— In Wazirpur, the Air Quality Index (AQI) had spiked 60 points in just an hour; in Narela, a monitoring station had gone offline; and a camera at a construction site had not transmitted for six hours.

— The monitor showed a map of Delhi, with blipping wind vectors pointing downward, and automated warnings flashing across the screen. “Poor dispersion. Emissions inside Delhi will stay local,” said a warning.

— The ICCC monitors pollution sources across Delhi in real time, a scientist said. It is the country’s largest pollution control war room, and is monitored round the clock by teams that work a general shift from 10 am to 6 pm, plus three additional shifts from 7 am to 3 pm, 3 pm to 11 pm, and 11 pm to 7 am.

— Observations by the general shift form the basis for key daytime action‑taken reports and operations. The centre integrates multiple data points to assess pollution in real time using multiple sources of information, officials said.

— AQI is a number, which is a measure of air quality. The higher the AQI, the worse the air.

— The colour-coded AQI index was launched in India in 2014 as part of the Swachh Bharat campaign with the aim of ‘One Number – One Color – One Description’ for the general public to judge the air quality within its surroundings.

— According to the CPCB, part of the MoEFCC, the AQI transforms complex air quality data of various pollutants into a single number (index value), nomenclature and colour.

— AQI forecast is based on eight pollutants: Particulate matter (PM10), particulate matter (PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), sulphur dioxide (SO2), carbon monoxide (CO), ozone (O3), ammonia (NH3) and lead (Pb).

— There are different categories of AQI, namely ‘Good’ (0-50), ‘Satisfactory’ (50-100), ‘Moderately polluted’ (100-200), ‘Poor’ (200-300), ‘Very Poor’ (300-400), and ‘Severe’ (400-500). A new category of “Severe+ or Emergency” has also been added.

What’s the ongoing story: The furore over Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) on UPI transactions has brought back into focus other charges that run counter to the idea of catalysing India’s digital push.

— What is the difference between a marketplace model and an inventory-based model of e-commerce?

— What is the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR)?

— What are platform fees and convenience charges?

— What are dark patterns in e-commerce?

— What is drip pricing, and how does it affect consumers?

— What are the major types of dark patterns identified in India’s 2023 guidelines?

— What is the role of the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) in regulating dark patterns?

— What are the key provisions of India’s Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020?

— What are the FDI rules governing e-commerce in India?

— How can India balance consumer protection with the growth of the digital economy?

— These include platform fees and convenience charges, which have become an industry-wide practice across online services spanning food and grocery delivery, e-commerce, entertainment and travel.

— Compounding this are so-called ‘dark patterns’ used by online platforms, which can further obfuscate the real price a consumer has to pay, including by revealing charges late in the checkout process or adding services without explicit consent.

— What started small – as an experiment by Swiggy three years ago with a modest Rs 2 per transaction add-on – has since become standard practice across major food and grocery delivery platforms, including Zomato and Blinkit.

— Even Amazon India now charges customers Rs 5 for servicing on most orders. The charges now cut across almost every major category of online consumption.

— Ordering food on Swiggy or Zomato attracts a platform fee; buying goods on Amazon India comes with a marketplace fee; booking a movie on BookMyShow attracts an internet handling or convenience fee; booking a train ticket through IRCTC comes with a convenience fee; and similar charges are imposed by airlines and online travel aggregators when customers book flights.

— Dark patterns on e-commerce are deceptive user-interface designs that trick shoppers into making unintended purchases or sharing data.

— Basket sneaking is a deceptive design tactic where an e-commerce platform automatically adds an extra product or service to users’ shopping carts without their explicit consent, usually through pre-checked boxes, hidden line items, or forced bundles during the checkout process.

— In the online ticketing sector, the price initially shown to a consumer can change over the course of the booking process.

— Drip pricing is a deceptive sales tactic where companies advertise only a low initial ‘headline price’ and then reveal mandatory fees, taxes, or service charges incrementally (‘dripping’ them) as the customer moves through the checkout process.

— India’s Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns, 2023 define it as a practice where elements of prices are not revealed upfront or are revealed surreptitiously within the user experience; or revealing the price post-confirmation of purchase, i.e. charging an amount higher than the amount disclosed at checkout.

What’s the ongoing story: Amid protests against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls it started last year, the Election Commission (EC) on Thursday (October 15) announced the schedule for the Special Summary Revision (SSR) for 17 states and Union Territories (UTs), including the five states where Assembly elections are due in early 2027.

— What is the difference between Special Summary Revision (SSR) and Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls?

— What are the constitutional and legal provisions governing the preparation and revision of electoral rolls in India?

— What are the eligibility criteria for registration as a voter in India?

— What are the powers and functions of the Election Commission of India (ECI)?

— What is the role of the Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) in preparing electoral rolls?

— What is the procedure for filing claims and objections against electoral rolls?

— What are the grounds for inclusion and deletion of names from electoral rolls?

— Is the right to vote a fundamental right, a constitutional right or a statutory right?

— Can the Election Commission of India verify the citizenship of voters while revising electoral rolls?

— What challenges does the revision of electoral rolls pose for free and fair elections in India?

— The EC had skipped the SSR, which is the annual update of rolls, in 2026. We explain the SSR process, what the EC said in its announcement, and how the SSR differs from the SIR.

— After it announced the decision to conduct the SIR, in which electoral rolls were prepared afresh with all existing electors required to establish their eligibility again, on June 24, 2025, the EC had not conducted the SSR 2026.

— On Thursday, the EC announced the schedule of the SSR with the qualifying date of January 1, 2027 in the states/UTs where the SIR has been completed in 2025 and 2026, and the state of Assam, where it had decided not to conduct the SIR.

— As per the schedule, the rationalisation of polling stations is to be completed by November 2, the publication of the draft rolls is on November 12, the period for filing claims and objections is from November 12 to December 11, and the claims and objections have to be disposed of by December 28. The final electoral rolls in the 17 states/UTs will be published on January 4, 2027.

— Article 324 of the Constitution gives the EC the authority to prepare the electoral rolls for elections to Parliament and Assemblies.

— The manner in which the rolls are to be prepared and revised is prescribed in the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, that flow from the law. Electoral rolls are made for each Assembly constituency, with an Electoral Registration Officer (ERO) being the statutory authority for the task.

— As per Section 21(2) of the 1950 Act, the electoral rolls are to be revised “before each general election to the House of the People or to the Legislative Assembly of a State” and “in any year in the prescribed manner by reference to the qualifying date if such revision has been directed by the Election Commission”.

— Flowing from this, the EC had been conducting an SSR, in which the existing electoral roll is updated with additions of newly eligible electors and deletions of those who have passed away or shifted, before each Lok Sabha and Assembly election and also annually with January 1 as the qualifying date.

— This means that all those who turn 18 as of January 1 are eligible to be enrolled in the electoral roll of the SSR.

What’s the ongoing story: Government bonds are the most risk-free investments one can make in any economy. After all, everyone expects the government to pay back its debt. The yields refer to the returns an investor can expect to earn by lending money to the government.

— What is a bond, and what are government securities (G-secs)?

— What is the difference between a bond’s face value, coupon rate and yield?

— What is the relationship between bond prices and bond yields?

— What factors determine government bond yields?

— How do inflation and interest rates affect bond yields?

— How do US Federal Reserve policy decisions influence Indian bond yields?

— How do rising bond yields affect government borrowing and private investment?

— What factors could explain the decline in Chinese government bond yields despite rising yields in other major economies?

— How can rising global bond yields affect capital flows into emerging economies such as India?

— But as government bonds are traded among investors, their prices fluctuate, and so do their yields. If a bond’s price falls, its yield rises, and vice-versa.

— Simply put, rising bond yields signal higher borrowing costs for governments and, by extension, higher interest rates for all borrowers in the economy, since lending to the government is the safest bet. Higher costs are expected to drag down economic growth.

— The yield on US 10-year bonds — that is, bonds through which the US government borrows money for 10 years — has increased by 125 basis points. Given that trillions of dollars of government bonds exchange hands everyday, even such seemingly minuscule changes have huge consequences.

— In sharp contrast to all others, government bond yields have actually fallen in China, which is not only the world’s second largest economy but single-handedly rivals the size of the euro-zone economy.

— A large part of the concern about rising bond yields globally has been about the rising cost of borrowing for all the governments concerned. From that perspective, it may seem like a boon that the Chinese government’s borrowing costs are coming down.

— A bond is an instrument to borrow money. It is like an IOU. A bond could be floated/issued by a country’s government or by a company to raise funds. Since government bonds (referred to as G-secs in India, Treasury in the US, and Gilts in the UK) come with the sovereign’s guarantee, they are considered one of the safest investments.

— As a result, they also give the lowest returns on investment (or yield). Investments in corporate bonds tend to be riskier because the chances of failure (and, therefore, the chances of the company not repaying the loan) are higher.

— Simply put, the yield of a bond is the effective rate of return that it earns. But the rate of return is not fixed — it changes with the price of the bond. But to understand that, one must first understand how bonds are structured.

— Every bond has a face value and a coupon payment. There is also the price of the bond, which may or may not be equal to the face value of the bond.

What’s the ongoing story: US President Donald Trump backtracked on his approval for livestreaming ex-US Army Major Nidal Hasan’s execution by firing squad on Thursday (October 15). Just days ago, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth proposed livestreaming the execution for public viewing, approved by the Pentagon for December 3.

— What is capital punishment, and what is its purpose?

— What is the difference between deterrent, retributive and reformative theories of punishment?

— What is the status of the death penalty in India?

— What constitutional safeguards govern the imposition of the death penalty in India?

— What is the “rarest of rare” doctrine laid down by the Supreme Court?

— How does the US constitutional framework regulate public access to executions?

— How has public execution historically been used as an instrument of state power?

— What are the arguments for and against the death penalty as a deterrent?

— What is the difference between parole and furlough?

— What is the role of prison reforms in the criminal justice system?

— In a Truth Social post, Trump called Hasan “a very bad and evil man”. In 2009, Hasan shot and killed 13 people at the Fort Hood US Army post in Texas, following which a military tribunal sentenced him to death.

— “I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die… He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed,” Trump wrote.

— What would have been the country’s first public execution in exactly 90 years — and the first military execution of any kind since 1961 in the US — had invited strong reactions from across the political spectrum.

— In the US, the First Amendment guarantees the freedom of the press and the right to access government proceedings. The Supreme Court has recognised that trials are open to the public.

— The limits of these guarantees were determined in 1977, when a TV reporter sought permission to film the first execution in Texas since the reinstatement of the death penalty the previous year. The court ultimately reasoned that because the general public of Texas was statutorily barred from attending or filming executions, the press had no constitutional right to do so.

— Around AD 33, Pontius Pilate of Judea authorised the execution of a man earlier found to have no charge against him. The convicted was flogged and publicly crucified, as was the norm, in what is one of history’s most widely recognised public executions — the crucifixion of Jesus Christ.

— Capital punishment has long been codified, including in ancient Babylon and Athens, where death was the punishment for all crimes in the 7th century BCE. Executions in the Roman Empire were known for their flamboyant approach, organised as spectacles that incited great delight among their audiences.

— Many pre-modern polities also viewed a serious crime as much an affront to the supreme ruling authority as it was a violation of the social contract. As such, any punishment was expected to carry a demonstrative purpose, acting as a public deterrent.

— This strategy was not without criticism. Roman philosopher Seneca the Younger argued in the ‘Moral Letters to Lucillius’ that being a part of such events had adverse effects on the individual psyche. In the 20th century, French philosopher Michel Foucault argued that the condemned individual’s body became the site on which the State exercised its influence, with measurably visible violence projecting a larger message.

— What is the H-1B visa programme of the United States?

— Vance is aware of the fact that US corporations, supporters of the Republican Party, have benefited from access to lower-cost Indian talent. Goyal knows well that governments in India, including his own, have long sought more US visas for people seeking access to American education and employment.

— One must, however, appreciate the transparent honesty of Vance when he refers to H1-B visa-holding Indians as “foreign indentured servants”. Despicable though that condescending view of professionals is, it sums up a view of the imperialist West with respect to Indian immigrants.

— Indentured is a word Vance would have picked up from his highly educated Indian-American wife, Usha Chilukuri. Servant is not a pejorative term but upper-class and upper-caste Indians view it as such.

— Serve other countries is what Indian emigrants do and H1-B holders are in the US on a contractual basis. Not surprisingly, Vance’s put-down forced a government normally circumspect in dealing with the US to issue a rebuff.

— India has been home to two centuries of organised labour export. British India shipped out hundreds of thousands of “indentured labour”, as part of official government policy, to overseas territories where local labour was in short supply.

— The governments of free India have also encouraged the export of labour to countries where local labour is either in short supply or is simply unwilling to do the work that imported Indian labour is willing to, wanting to, waiting to. (With apologies to Bernard Shaw.)

— The H-1B visa programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers with training in specialty fields, offering 65,000 visas annually, along with another 20,000 visas for workers with advanced degrees.

— The H-1B visa is approved for three to six years, Reuters reported. Before the Trump administration imposed the increased cost for the programme, the typical fees for the H-1B visas ranged between $2,000 and $5,000.

— India’s goods exports continue to record robust growth. In September, merchandise exports rose to $44.4 billion, up by a staggering 23 per cent. Strong growth over the past few months has pushed up exports in the first half of the year to $259 billion.

— Considering that growth has been sluggish for several years after the bump during the Covid period — in 2025-26, exports stood at $441 billion, up less than 5 per cent from $422 billion in 2021-22 — this uptick is welcome.

body_text:
BRUSSELS, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Masked settlers in the Israeli-occupied West Bank attacked Palestinians, Catholic representatives and Western diplomats and officials, Belgium's foreign minister said on Saturday.

Maxime Prevot said the Belgian consul general, French and Polish diplomats and a French mayor were among those attacked, while a Belgian vehicle was damaged.

"Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," Prevot said.

Belgium will continue to press for sanctions against those responsible for the violence and those who support them, Prevot said.

The Israeli military, the European Commission and French and Polish foreign ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

(Reporting by Makini Brice and Sybille de la Hamaide in Paris, Alexander Cornwell in Jerusalem, Anna Koper in Warsaw and Lili Bayer in Brussels. Editing by Mark Potter)

headline: 'Blows kept coming, I felt the aircraft going down': Flydubai captain on the cockpit battle to save his plane
summary: Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has spoken of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert, with the intention of killing 172 people on board.In a world exclusive interview with The National from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, Capt Machchhar said the first officer sitting next to him for two hours had shown no sign of what Emirati prosecutors say was a “premeditated terrorist plot” to hijack the aircraft.Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked Capt Machchhar and seized control of the plane.I tried to block the blows as much as I could. [I was] screaming for my colleagues. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, [I realised] it's the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.” He recalled those initial moments, explaining: “My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head.”Capt Machchhar suffered serious injuries to his head and arm, including defensive wounds from trying to stop the blows. “While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I fell face down in the cockpit.”He believes he regained consciousness as the attacker plunged the aircraft into a dive. Crew members and passengers began banging on the other side of the cockpit door.“The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down. When I say spooling down, it's the engine sound going from full blast to like … not what you want at that stage in the flight. And I felt the aircraft was steeply going down.”Capt Machchhar became emotional as he explained his instinct to survive. “At that point, I realised that you will not survive this," he explained. And then, soon after that, the senior cabin crew thankfully reached where I was and did his magic. And yeah, that's how I'm speaking to you today.”Recovering in his bed in Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar has been trying to piece together events in the two weeks since the failed terror plot. He remembers praying as the cabin crew chief and others, including dentist Shota Musaev, tried to stem the bleeding from his wounds. “There was heavy bleeding from his head and left hand,” Dr Musaev told The National last week.“He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. So, yeah, there was some small talk, but there was not really like a deep conversation,” he said. Not at all. Not at all,” he said with a smile. “I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”
body_text:
Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has spoken of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert, with the intention of killing 172 people on board.

In a world exclusive interview with The National from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, Capt Machchhar said the first officer sitting next to him for two hours had shown no sign of what Emirati prosecutors say was a “premeditated terrorist plot” to hijack the aircraft.

Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked Capt Machchhar and seized control of the plane.

Capt Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for getting the cockpit door, locked from the inside, open and allowing the attack to be foiled. All of the 172 passengers and crew on board the September 30 flight survived.

The first officer has been detained in the UAE and faces terrorism charges. The statements made in this interview reflect the interviewee’s recollection of events, based on his personal experience and his perception of them at the time they occurred.

In his interview with The National at Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar revealed:

Narrating the hijacking to a media outlet for the first time, Capt Machchhar said he thought the blow to his head was from a cockpit panel that had collapsed.

“The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head,” he said. “It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, [I realised] it's the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.”

He recalled those initial moments, explaining: “My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head.”

Capt Machchhar suffered serious injuries to his head and arm, including defensive wounds from trying to stop the blows. “While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking [at] outlines.”

Capt Machchhar is not entirely clear how events unfolded nor the timeline. But he managed to open the cockpit after several attempts. He explained that every time he had to exert himself physically, he would lose blood and consciousness.

“Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door," he said. "And [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit.”

He believes he regained consciousness as the attacker plunged the aircraft into a dive. Crew members and passengers began banging on the other side of the cockpit door.

“The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down. When I say spooling down, it's the engine sound going from full blast to like … not what you want at that stage in the flight. And I felt the aircraft was steeply going down.”

Capt Machchhar became emotional as he explained his instinct to survive.

“At that point, I realised that you will not survive this," he explained. "And I was constantly looking for the door. I did go for it. I did push it … the next thing I remember was I was facedown, lying with, thank God, the cockpit door open. I was between the cockpit and the galley.”

Capt Machchhar said there was “so much chaos and commotion” as he was hauled out of the cockpit. It was at that moment that passengers and crew seized the first officer. A pair of flydubai pilots who were travelling as passengers took control of the plane.

“If I have to say how many people were trying to control the situation, I would say a million. I know it doesn't make sense, but, yeah, I would say a million people were trying to take over control,” he said.

He described the moment others came to his rescue as “magic”, saying: “The next thing I remember was [being] pulled out by one of the passengers. And then, soon after that, the senior cabin crew thankfully reached where I was and did his magic. And yeah, that's how I'm speaking to you today.”

Recovering in his bed in Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar has been trying to piece together events in the two weeks since the failed terror plot.

He remembers praying as the cabin crew chief and others, including dentist Shota Musaev, tried to stem the bleeding from his wounds. “There was heavy bleeding from his head and left hand,” Dr Musaev told The National last week.

“He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on.”

Capt Machchhar was clearly emotional as he spoke. He said: “I prayed a lot. I thought about my son, my daughter, and prayed. That was the point where I would say I didn't give up.”

He spoke frankly: “Did I give up? No. I can 100 per cent tell you I did not give up. But was I sure I was going to make it? No.”

Asked whether he suspected anything from his co-pilot's behaviour, he said he did not notice anything.

“If there was something that could have hinted earlier on the ground or something, yes, of course, I would have acted. I would have spoken up. I would have questioned some things like that,” he explained.

He described that morning as ordinary, saying it was the first time he had met the first officer. “It was a morning flight. So, yeah, there was some small talk, but there was not really like a deep conversation,” he said.

Capt Machchhar added: “We avoid getting into deep conversations, especially during high-intensity or high-density airspace, especially nowadays with all the restrictions. Saudi is very high density.”

"Nothing until that point would have caused me to think that: 'Hey, hold on, there's something off.'”

There has been speculation about why the first officer attacked his colleague when the plane was an hour away from Tel Aviv airport, which prosecutors said he intended to crash into.

“I won't say I've been thinking a lot about it, but yes, I did give it a thought. It makes no sense to me,” Capt Machchhar said.

There was also much scrutiny over the presence of a cockpit axe, and how the co-pilot was radicalised.

Asked whether aviation security will change as a result of the close call, Capt Machchhar said: “I think so. And for good."

He added: “I won't blame it on anyone. You've got to learn from the event … I would just say: learn from whatever's happened and then make sure that this doesn't happen again, ever.”

Capt Machchhar, who lives with his wife and children in the UAE, faces a long recovery but wants to return to the cockpit.

“Did my love die for aviation? Not at all. Not at all,” he said with a smile. “I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”

body_text:
Hundreds of members of the Iraqi community in the UAE came together at Expo City Dubai on Saturday to celebrate their heritage and the close ties between their homeland and the Emirates.

The second UAE Loves Iraq event brought Iraqi families and Emirati guests together for a celebration of Iraqi culture, featuring traditional music, food and displays inspired by some of the country's most recognisable landmarks.

Held at the conference centre at Expo City Dubai, the gathering was designed to strengthen cultural ties between the two countries while giving Iraqi residents an opportunity to reconnect with their roots and celebrate their shared identity.

Oud master Naseer Shamma returns to UAE National Orchestra

Families dressed in traditional Iraqi clothing enjoyed folk performances and cuisine, while others used the occasion to reunite with friends and members of the community.

Sheikh Nahyan bin Mubarak, Minister of Tolerance and Coexistence, attended the event and praised the contribution of Iraqi residents to life in the Emirates.

"This celebration for the Iraqi community in the UAE expresses their love for the UAE and the love of the UAE for Iraq," he said.

"In the UAE, we are proud of the Iraqis living among us. We work to strengthen the bridges of love between the two nations."

Sheikh Nahyan highlighted Iraq's rich cultural heritage and its historic contribution to human civilisation, describing the country as the birthplace of some of humanity's most important innovations.

"The first wheel and the first letters were invented in Iraq. It is the place that witnessed the birth of civilisation. Iraq will always be a beacon of glory," he said.

"Iraq is working towards peace and prosperity, and the UAE is committed to supporting Iraq's progress. The UAE loves Iraq."

For many Iraqi residents, the celebration was an opportunity to reflect on the lives they have built in the Emirates while maintaining a strong connection to their homeland.

Mohammed Al Tawaiji, 48, who has lived in the UAE for 20 years, said he had felt welcome from the moment he arrived.

"I never felt that I was a stranger here. My soul is Iraqi and my heart is Emirati," he told The National.

"I'm proud to be part of this country and to have witnessed its major development."

He said the similarities between Iraqi and Emirati culture had helped him settle into life in the UAE.

"Iraqis and Emiratis both care about educating their younger generations and know how to live alongside people of other nationalities. There are a lot of similarities between the two nations, and that's why I never felt like a stranger here."

Afnan Al Rawi, an Iraqi doctor who has lived in Dubai for 17 years, said the two communities shared traditions and values.

"We have similar traditions, and the most important thing is that we love each other," she said.

"Emiratis understand our accent well, and gatherings like this bring nations closer together and spread positivity."

For younger members of the community who have grown up in the Emirates, the celebration offered a chance to explore their Iraqi identity.

Ali Mohammed, 22, a student at Emirates Aviation, was born in the UAE and considers it his home.

"The UAE is definitely home for me. It is a great place to live, study and work," he said.

"I never felt like a stranger here, and this event is great because I can reunite with my fellow Iraqis."

For some attendees, the event provided a rare opportunity to meet other Iraqis and enjoy familiar traditions.

Afraa Al Rubaie, who left Iraq many years ago and has lived in Dubai for 25 years, said such gatherings were particularly important for people who had spent much of their lives away from their homeland.

"It's hard to meet other Iraqis at work or in our residential areas, so this event is a chance to come together and enjoy our food, music and rich culture," she said.

"Thanks to the UAE for giving us the opportunity to feel like we are in Iraq."

She said the hospitality she had experienced in the Emirates reminded her of home.

"Iraqis and Emiratis share the same hospitality and generosity. Here, we don't feel far away from our homeland because Emiratis always welcome us with a smile."

The celebration also attracted Emiratis with personal connections to Iraq.

Ibrahim Ali Binhatem, an Emirati writer, said his fascination with Iraqi history and culture began when he was young.

His affection for the country grew over the years, and he eventually married an Iraqi woman and named their daughter Baghdad, after the Iraqi capital.

"I have many Iraqi friends here in the UAE, and I've always loved the history and culture of Iraq," he said.

"I used to read about Iraq and became fascinated by the traditions of Baghdad. I even named my daughter Baghdad."

He said he attended the celebration to share in the community's pride in its heritage.

"I came here to take part in this beautiful gathering with Iraqis. They are wonderful people with an incredibly rich history."

headline: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, European diplomats in West Bank, Belgium says
summary: By Ali Sawafta and Mohammed TorokmanTAYBEH, West Bank, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium's foreign minister said, a day after settlers beat an American photojournalist. Maxime Prevot said Belgium's consul general to the Palestinians, French and Polish diplomats, and Catholic representatives were among those attacked. A Belgian vehicle was also damaged, he said.
body_text:
By Ali Sawafta and Mohammed Torokman

TAYBEH, West Bank, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian civilians, European diplomats and a French mayor in the occupied West Bank on Saturday, Belgium's foreign minister said, a day after settlers beat an American photojournalist.

Maxime Prevot said Belgium's consul general to the Palestinians, French and Polish diplomats, and Catholic representatives were among those attacked. A Belgian vehicle was also damaged, he said.

"As the occupying power, Israeli authorities must protect Palestinians, ensure the safety of diplomats and journalists, and bring those responsible to justice. Impunity for violent settlers must end," Prevot said in a statement posted on X.

'THROWN TO THE GROUND'

Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, told Reuters he had been harvesting olives near the Palestinian Christian village of Taybeh in solidarity with the local community when he was "violently attacked" by masked settlers.

"I was thrown to the ground," he said.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the attack, describing the perpetrators as Israeli rioters. He also suggested the diplomats should have coordinated their visit with the Israeli military.

"Such coordination could have helped safeguard the visitors’ security," he said in a statement on X.

Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh condemned the attack, calling it a small example of the "daily terrorism" to which Palestinians are subjected.

Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have periodically condemned settler violence, while saying it is carried out by a small minority. Palestinians and human rights groups dispute that characterisation.

ISRAELI POLICE OPEN INVESTIGATION

Settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank have surged over the past three years. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

On Friday, dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives in the West Bank. Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen covering the harvest, was hospitalised after being assaulted by masked settlers.

"Palestinians face this violence every day. Settlers also target journalists reporting on it and diplomats. Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack," Prevot said.

Belgium, which has announced a ban on imports from Israeli settlements in the West Bank and the Golan Heights, will press for European Union sanctions "against those responsible for this violence and those who support them," he added.

Polish Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maciej Wewior said on X that a convoy carrying diplomats, including Polish officials, had been attacked. The Polish diplomats were unharmed.

"Attacks on members of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable," he said.

Israeli police said they had opened an investigation into the incident. There was no immediate announcement of any arrests. Prosecutions of settlers accused of violent crimes against Palestinians in the West Bank are rare.

(Reporting by Ali Sawafta and Mohammed Torokman in Taybeh, Makini Brice and Sybille de la Hamaide in Paris, Alexander Cornwell in Jerusalem, Anna Koper in Warsaw and Lili Bayer in Brussels. Editing by Mark Potter)

headline: Israeli occupiers attack European diplomats in occupied West Bank
summary: Delegation comprising French, Belgian, Polish representatives come under attack in town of Taybeh, causing injuries
body_text:
By Aysar Alais and Zein Khalil

RAMALLAH, Palestine / ISTANBUL (AA) - Israeli occupiers attacked a diplomatic delegation comprising representatives from France, Belgium and Poland on Saturday while visiting the town of Taybeh, central occupied West Bank, causing injuries.

The attack took place after an official ceremony marking the signing of a twinning agreement between the Palestinian town of Taybeh and the French town of Saint-Pierre, Taybeh Mayor Suleiman Khourieh told Anadolu.

The ceremony was attended by the French and Belgian consuls, a Polish representative whose name was not disclosed, and Saint-Pierre Mayor Christian Ravain.

The attack targeted the delegation in the western part of the town, as well as Palestinians who were picking olives.

It left several town residents injured and shattered the window of a vehicle belonging to the Belgian delegation, Khourieh added.

Israeli Army Radio, citing witnesses and footage, also said that the occupiers hurled stones at one of the diplomatic vehicles, smashing its window.

Footage showed a member of the delegation lying on the ground after the attack. The person shown lying on the ground beside the diplomatic vehicle was Bernard Boudot, a French politician and mayor of Aulnoy-lez-Valenciennes in northern France, the broadcaster said.

Israel’s Channel 12, citing the Israeli military, reported that the incident was “under review” and none had been arrested immediately.

Khourieh described the attack as “a flagrant violation of the sanctity of diplomatic and humanitarian work” and part of ongoing restrictions imposed on Palestinian farmers.

Attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians and their land have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began in early October and provides a key source of income for thousands of Palestinian families.

headline: Systems Limited invests $10m in Egypt, targets further growth in 2027
summary: Systems Limited, a Pakistani multinational information technology company, plans to increase its investments in Egypt by more than 50% in 2027, with further growth potentially exceeding that rate in 2028, as it seeks to expand its local operations and strengthen Egypt’s role within the group. The company currently has $10m invested in Egypt, Ahmed Kandil, General Manager of Systems Egypt, said, adding that the expansion plans are supported by opportunities in the technology sector and cooperation with the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Information Technology Industry Development Agency (ITIDA). The company currently employs around 300 IT professionals in Egypt and aims to increase its workforce to 450 by the end of 2027, with further recruitment planned for 2028 alongside the expansion of its investments and business activities. Systems Limited is also establishing digital banking services centres of excellence in Egypt for two major UAE banks. The projects are intended to leverage local talent to deliver specialised technology services to regional markets. Kandil said the company was considering expanding into business services, business process operations and outsourcing, drawing on the diverse activities of its parent group and the availability of growth opportunities in Egypt. To support its recruitment plans, Systems Limited is cooperating with ITIDA to train fresh graduates in line with the company’s technical requirements. The programme combines three to four months of technical training conducted in cooperation with the agency with six to eight months of practical training at the company, during which participants work on actual projects and interact with clients. More than 80% of trainees are absorbed into the company’s workforce, Kandil said. Some of the professionals currently undergoing training are expected to work on projects for a UAE bank, while others may be assigned to different projects according to business needs. He added that retaining skilled employees over the long term is a priority, as the practical experience gained during their first two years helps them develop the expertise needed to deliver specialised projects and services to overseas markets. Systems Limited provides services including artificial intelligence, software and technology product quality assurance, mobile application and website development, and digital solutions for various industries. In Egypt, the company works with the country’s three major telecommunications operators — Orange, Vodafone and e& — and provides services to nine of the country’s largest banks. Its regional operations include AI and data centre projects for a telecommunications company in Sudan, as well as managed services and core banking solutions in Libya. The group also operates in Pakistan, Malaysia, Singapore, Australia, Germany, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada. The company aims to build on its Egyptian operations to expand the delivery of specialised technology services across regional markets, supported by its growing pool of locally trained professionals.

headline: KOICA, NCW conclude three-year capacity-building programme for women’s economic empowerment
summary: The Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA), South Korea’s official development cooperation agency, and the National Council for Women (NCW) jointly held a Knowledge Sharing Seminar on October 15, 2026, at The St. Regis Cairo, marking the successful conclusion of the three-year “Capacity Building on Gender/SME in Egypt (2024-2026)” training programme. The event celebrated the longstanding partnership between South Korea and Egypt and reaffirmed their shared commitment to advancing women’s economic empowerment. The seminar was attended by distinguished guests, including Ambassador Wan-Joong Kim, Ambassador of South Korea to Egypt; Counsellor Amal Ammar, President of the National Council for Women; and Ambassador Wael El Nagaar, Assistant Foreign Minister for Cultural Affairs, alongside representatives of the Korean Embassy, the Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, NCW, United Nations agencies, development partners and alumni of KOICA’s training programmes. Implemented under KOICA’s Capacity Improvement and Advancement for Tomorrow (CIAT) fellowship programme in cooperation with NCW, the initiative aimed to strengthen the NCW’s institutional capacity and enhance officials’ policy formulation and advisory capabilities. It focused on developing policies and support systems for women’s employment, entrepreneurship, and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), drawing on Korea’s development experience and expertise. The seminar provided a platform to reflect on the programme’s achievements and explore opportunities to translate the knowledge gained in Korea into practical policies and initiatives in Egypt. Three programme alumni shared their experiences and key lessons from the training, highlighting how they have applied the knowledge and skills they acquired to support women’s empowerment and contribute to advancing Egypt’s women’s agenda. The seminar also featured a joint presentation by KOICA and Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) volunteers serving at public libraries in Luxor. They shared their experiences in delivering educational activities for girls and discussed approaches to creating engaging, inclusive and supportive learning environments. A panel discussion featuring representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), the World Food Programme (WFP), and UN Women explored the achievements of KOICA-supported programmes and projects, as well as future opportunities to strengthen women-focused programming and enhance collaboration among NCW, KOICA, UN agencies and other development partners. Discussions highlighted the importance of exchanging technical expertise and international best practices, promoting complementarity among programmes, avoiding duplication of efforts and aligning joint initiatives with national priorities to achieve sustainable impact in women’s economic empowerment and leverage the expertise of KOICA programme alumni. Counsellor Amal Ammar, President of NCW, delivered the opening remarks, highlighting six years of fruitful partnership between NCW and KOICA as a successful model of international cooperation built on knowledge exchange and investment in people. She noted that between 2020 and 2026, six training courses benefited around 90 participants from NCW and partner ministries, while five NCW staff members earned master’s degrees in international development in Korea. She looked forward to building on these achievements following the elevation of Egyptian-Korean relations to a strategic partnership, particularly in supporting women entrepreneurs and SME owners. In his congratulatory remarks, Ambassador Wael El Nagaar, Assistant Foreign Minister for Cultural Affairs, described the seminar as the culmination of three years of fruitful cooperation with KOICA, commending NCW’s role as a key national partner in advancing women’s economic empowerment. He stressed that SMEs are a cornerstone of Egypt’s economy and that supporting women-led enterprises contributes to Egypt Vision 2030, noting the programme’s achievements in policy development, capacity building and empowering women entrepreneurs in financial inclusion and market access. Ambassador Wan-Joong Kim, Ambassador of South Korea to Egypt, also conveyed his appreciation for the longstanding cooperation between Korea and Egypt and reaffirmed Korea’s commitment to supporting Egypt’s sustainable development and women’s empowerment. Sooyoung Park, KOICA Country Director in Egypt, delivered the closing remarks, expressing her sincere appreciation to NCW, the participants, programme alumni and all partners involved. She emphasised that the conclusion of the three-year programme marks not an end, but a new step forward in bilateral cooperation, highlighting the importance of translating its achievements into concrete policies and practical actions while creating new opportunities for future collaboration. KOICA’s continued commitment to human resource development in Egypt The Korea International Cooperation Agency (KOICA) is a government agency under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of South Korea. It implements grant-based development cooperation programmes to support poverty reduction and sustainable socioeconomic development in partner countries worldwide. Since establishing its Egypt Office in 1998, KOICA has supported the professional development of Egyptian public officials and policymakers through its CIAT fellowship programme and scholarship opportunities for master’s and doctoral studies. As of 2026, a total of 2,187 Egyptians have participated in KOICA’s training and scholarship programmes, including 2,034 participants in invitational training programmes and 153 participants in degree scholarship programmes. Beyond enhancing individual knowledge and skills, these programmes aim to strengthen the policy and technical capacities of public officials and professionals, build the institutional capacity of their respective organisations, and foster long-term professional and institutional networks between Korea and Egypt. Through its continued partnership with Egyptian institutions, KOICA remains committed to promoting knowledge exchange, fostering human resource development and supporting Egypt’s sustainable development in line with its national priorities.

Since establishing its Egypt Office in 1998, KOICA has supported the professional development of Egyptian public officials and policymakers through its CIAT fellowship programme and scholarship opportunities for master’s and doctoral studies. As of 2026, a total of 2,187 Egyptians have participated in KOICA’s training and scholarship programmes, including 2,034 participants in invitational training programmes and 153 participants in degree scholarship programmes. Beyond enhancing individual knowledge and skills, these programmes aim to strengthen the policy and technical capacities of public officials and professionals, build the institutional capacity of their respective organisations, and foster long-term professional and institutional networks between Korea and Egypt. Through its continued partnership with Egyptian institutions, KOICA remains committed to promoting knowledge exchange, fostering human resource development and supporting Egypt’s sustainable development in line with its national priorities.
