headline: Swiss cooperation with Egypt opens economic, scientific horizons: Ambassador
summary: Egyptian-Swiss cooperation has been growing across various fields, Swiss Ambassador to Egypt Andreas Baum said, stressing that both countries are keen to strengthen their bilateral partnership and translate it into tangible results. His remarks came during a reception held at the Swiss ambassador’s residence in Cairo to mark the 735th anniversary of Switzerland’s founding. The event was attended by Hassan Raddad, Egypt’s Minister of Labour, representing the Egyptian government, along with diplomats, media professionals and public figures. Baum noted that the year had witnessed several high-level visits, including that of Swiss Culture Minister Elisabeth Baume-Schneider for the opening of the Grand Egyptian Museum. Swiss Justice Minister Beat Jans also visited Egypt to deepen cooperation between the two countries on migration. He added that the two countries had launched their cooperation programme for 2025–2028, which focuses on protecting lives, supporting more environmentally sustainable economic development and strengthening governance. The two sides also brought together representatives of the government and business community through the Egyptian-Swiss Economic Forum, he said. More than 100 Swiss companies operate in Egypt, providing jobs for thousands of people through investment, production and innovation. Archaeological cooperation and return of Egyptian artefacts The ambassador said the year had also been an important one for archaeological cooperation. A few weeks earlier, Switzerland had returned an Egyptian funerary mask dating back to the second century BC. The artefact had recently entered Switzerland through a private dealer under circumstances he described as suspicious, before being returned to Egypt under far better circumstances. Switzerland has returned approximately 80 archaeological and cultural artefacts to Egypt since the bilateral agreement on cultural property entered into force in 2011, he explained. He stressed that archaeological cooperation between the two countries extends beyond the recovery of artefacts. Swiss archaeologists and institutions have been working in Egypt for generations, he added. Egyptian and Swiss researchers continue to work together to study, excavate, restore and preserve archaeological sites, as well as exchange knowledge and expertise. Baum also announced that the two sides would bring together a large number of researchers and specialists at the first archaeology forum of its kind. According to his remarks, the forum is scheduled for November 8 at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization and will explore areas of cooperation in the sector. Climate change highlights shared water challenges Turning to climate change, Baum said Switzerland’s glaciers suffered heavy losses in 2026, threatening water supplies and destabilising mountain slopes. Swiss glaciers lost approximately 5% of their volume in 2026 alone, while losses over the past 25 years reached 43%, he said. He also pointed to a photographic exhibition organised by Switzerland in Cairo under the title “Melting Glaciers: Water Futures from the Alps to the Nile”. The exhibition brought together two very different landscapes — the Alps and the Nile River — to highlight shared climate challenges. He emphasised that water connects communities and that climate change recognises no borders. Egyptian-Swiss cooperation currently includes the exchange of expertise in water, sustainable cities, green growth, governance and resilience in the face of crises. Switzerland calls for dialogue amid regional conflicts Baum pointed to the situation in Palestine and the Gulf region and expressed his appreciation for Egypt’s continued diplomatic efforts. On Sudan, he said Egypt has received large numbers of Sudanese fleeing the conflict, while Switzerland has significantly intensified its engagement in humanitarian and peacebuilding efforts in Sudan and neighbouring countries. Baum said Switzerland continues to believe in three principles: resolving conflicts through dialogue, addressing problems collectively in accordance with international law, and making use of multilateral frameworks. He stressed that Switzerland and Egypt would continue to cooperate and support one another on the basis of these principles. Economic opportunities and scientific exchange On bilateral relations, Baum said the two countries’ shared task is to ensure their partnership continues to deliver practical and tangible results. These include creating more economic opportunities, expanding scientific exchange, improving the protection of the most vulnerable groups and strengthening institutions. He thanked Egyptian partners across various sectors, including the government, civil society, academia and the private sector, for their cooperation and friendship. He also thanked the Swiss companies and sponsors whose support helped make the celebration possible, as well as members of the Swiss community in Egypt. He emphasised that they are an important part of the relationship between the two countries. Baum praised the Swiss Embassy team, saying many of the achievements outlined in his speech would not have been possible without the team’s commitment and constant willingness to go beyond their regular duties.

He stressed that archaeological cooperation between the two countries extends beyond the recovery of artefacts.

headline: Al-Sisi to leave office in 2030, proposes programme to prepare potential presidential candidates
summary: President Abdel Fattah Al-Sisi said on Saturday that he would leave office in 2030, describing the end of his presidency as a “settled matter,” while announcing a proposed programme to prepare Egyptian PhD holders to assume senior responsibilities and potentially qualify to run for president. Al-Sisi made the remarks during a graduation ceremony for new classes from Egypt’s military academy and colleges, days after saying the country’s Constitution “will not be touched”, in comments indicating that no constitutional changes would be pursued to extend his presidency beyond his current term. “I will hand over Egypt’s leadership in 2030, if I live, with its flag raised and the country strong,” Al-Sisi said, adding that no one with “ulterior motives or who had betrayed the country would assume leadership.” The Egyptian president asserted that his priority during the remaining period would be to strengthen state institutions and prepare national cadres capable of assuming responsibility. The president explained that the proposed programme would identify PhD holders from Egyptian and foreign universities, aged between 40 and 50, and put them through 30 months of training at the military academy, which would cover the cost of the programme. He said the speaker of parliament would oversee the process with the participation of selected political figures and intellectuals, as well as the ministries of Higher Education and Justice, with legislation to be drafted to regulate the initiative. According to Al-Sisi’s proposal, participants would receive training on the workings of the state before being considered for selection and election. The remarks did not specify how many people would be admitted to the programme or provide detailed eligibility criteria beyond age and academic qualifications. They also did not explain how the proposed process would interact with existing constitutional and legal rules governing presidential candidacy. Al-Sisi said his remaining time in office would focus on strengthening state institutions and preparing a new generation of officials, adding that his duty was to preserve the state and hand it over “with its flag raised”. In a separate part of his speech, Al-Sisi said Egypt was prepared to take any action requested by Saudi Arabia to defend the kingdom’s security and sovereignty. He said parliament could be called into an emergency session to authorise such action if Riyadh made a request. “We will take any action to defend our brothers in the Gulf,” Al-Sisi said, adding that Egypt would stand firmly with Gulf states against threats to their territory or security. His remarks came amid heightened regional tensions and recent attacks targeting Saudi Arabia, while Cairo has repeatedly said that the security of Gulf states is closely linked to Egyptian national security.

headline: All-front ceasefire essential to ending regional war
summary: EHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh says ending the war on all fronts is a key condition for peace, stressing that continued fighting in any part of the region would mean the war persists across the region.
body_text:
EHRAN, Oct. 17 (MNA) – Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Saeed Khatibzadeh says ending the war on all fronts is a key condition for peace, stressing that continued fighting in any part of the region would mean the war persists across the region.

In an interview with Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network on Friday, Khatibzadeh – who arrived in Beirut on Wednesday for talks with Lebanese officials – said Iran remained committed to ending the Israeli war on Lebanon and had secured this objective in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which Iran and the United States signed in mid-June this year.

He said Lebanon was among the key issues discussed between Iran and the US, adding that he sought to bring the two sides closer during his visit to Beirut. Khatibzadeh said that he held “good” talks with Lebanese officials, including Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, and officials at the Foreign Ministry.

The Iranian official stressed that Israel must end its war in Lebanon and the Levant, noting that developments in both regions are interconnected.

One of Iran’s conditions is an end to all wars, he said, adding that if fighting continues on any one of these fronts, it means the war continues on all fronts. That is why Iran remained committed to ending the war in Lebanon and managed to achieve that goal, he noted.

The Iranian diplomat also said that Washington and Tel Aviv violated the Islamabad understanding through their attacks on Iran and Lebanon, adding that US efforts to secure a ceasefire and end Israel’s war on Lebanon had reached a deadlock. He said Israel could not be trusted to honor its commitments and that Washington was responsible for restraining its regional ally.

Khatibzadeh described the US war against Iran as illegal under international law, saying Washington had failed to destroy Iran’s air defenses and deterrence capabilities. He said Iran had resisted an existential war and would continue defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity.

He added that Tehran was ready to address concerns raised by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the United States over Iran’s peaceful nuclear activities, citing more than 15 IAEA reports that he said confirmed Iran’s compliance with its commitments.

Khatibzadeh also said Iran had proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, emphasizing that Tehran did not seek war but would resist any imposed conflict.

He further described Hezbollah as a Lebanese political party established to end Israeli attacks and occupation, adding that Iran’s relations with its allies were based on shared beliefs, values and principles.

headline: Scuffles and fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
summary: Demonstrators across France converged with students Saturday to protest rising living costs, as the country's fiscal crisis deepens.(Image credit: Emma Da Silva)
body_text:
A car burns at Place de La Republique during a protest against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday. Emma Da Silva/AP hide caption

PARIS — A car and a newspaper kiosk were set on fire in Paris as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent groups of protesters, while similar tensions erupted Saturday in other big cities on the fringes of nationwide demonstrations against rising living costs and in support of high school students' grievances.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office described "a growing number of violent incidents," including assaults on police officers, looting or attempted looting of shops and damage to public buildings. Authorities reported at least 272 arrests across the country, including in Paris.

In the French capital, police used tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center. Large numbers of riot police were deployed in the square and surrounding streets.

The majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem as French flags were waved. The chants were accompanied by people playing trumpets and violins.

Meanwhile, police were working to prevent other small groups of protesters from converging on government buildings, Nuñez's office said.

Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.

In Lyon, France's third-largest city, where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, fire broke out inside a tourist office. Smoke and flames were seen rising from the building.

In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while some protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.

"This is unacceptable," Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan told BFM TV, describing the damage in City Hall as "limited."

Protesters scuffle with police during a demonstration against rising living costs, joining students' grievances, in Paris on Saturday. Emma Da Silva/AP hide caption

Nuñez's office also reported violence by masked groups in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.

Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the "yellow vest" movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.

Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.

The CGT, one of France's major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people's needs."

In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.

On Tuesday, climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a high school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

headline: Egypt, Türkiye FMs call for renewed US-Iran talks to ease regional tensions
summary: Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held a series of meetings in Baghdad on the sidelines of the 52nd session of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation’s Council of Foreign Ministers, focusing on regional de-escalation, Iran, Yemen, Sudan, Libya and Syria, as well as UN reform and the Palestinian issue. In a meeting with his Turkish counterpart, Hakan Fidan, Abdelatty discussed developments surrounding Iran and efforts to contain regional tensions, with both ministers calling for a return to dialogue and the resumption of diplomatic negotiations between the United States and Iran. Abdelatty said Egypt supported closer coordination through the regional quadrilateral mechanism and rejected any threat to Gulf states or the use of strategic straits and maritime routes as instruments of pressure or escalation. The two ministers reviewed proposals aimed at reaching an agreement that could ease tensions and end the current escalation. Their talks also covered Yemen, with both sides stressing support for state institutions and condemning attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Sudan, Abdelatty called for preserving the country’s unity, sovereignty, territorial integrity and national institutions while supporting efforts towards a political settlement. He also stressed the need to end divisions in Libya and unify national institutions. On Syria, he reiterated support for the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and rejected Israeli attacks on Syrian territory. headline: Europe has difficulties with supplying more air defense systems to Riyadh — newspaper
summary: Military analysts told The National that the UK and France have no opportunity to transfer these systems without harming their own defense potential in the Baltic countries
body_text:
DOHA, October 17. /TASS/. Saudi Arabia’s European allies are experiencing difficulties with supplying additional air defense systems to Saudi Arabia because they need them for their own defense purposes, The National newspaper wrote, citing military analysts.

Riyadh insists on additional deliveries of military equipment to repel attacks by Yemen’s radical Ansar Allah (Houthi) movement. However, according to the newspaper’s defense sources, the United Kingdom and France have no opportunity to transfer these systems without harming their own defense potential in the Baltic countries. Besides, London has been delivering weapons to Ukraine in significant amounts, including Storm Shadow cruise missiles.

"We have very little left in the locker to give," the newspaper quoted a UK defense source as saying. "We really have nothing to send over to them."

According to The National, many Western countries have depleted their arsenals because of their commitments to Eastern European countries and Kiev.

"They [Saudi Arabia] need it because they are a big country," Lynette Nusbacher, a former military intelligence officer, was quoted as saying. "They've got a lot of big targets that are easily spottable on Google Earth and they're up against people who have got sufficient ballistic missiles."

In her words, Saudi Arabia is in the urgent need of aid from the United Kingdom, France, Italy and the United States. Britain already has a battery of Sky Sabre air defence systems at King Fahd Air Base, while France has announced it will send defensive military systems to cover the key Red Sea port of Yanbu in the western part of the kingdom.

According to The National, the growing vulnerability of Saudi infrastructure was demonstrated by the Houthi missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10. As a result, 12 people were killed and 309 wounded.

In all, the Saudi capital’s main airport was targeted by Houthi attacks at least four times. On October 8, a civil aircraft was damaged and at least three people were killed. On October 1, one of the airport’s terminals was damaged. On October 12, the coalition’s forces reported intercepting a missile above the city.

Because of frequent attacks and flight disruptions, Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem al-Budaiwi, announced that the scheduled summit between the Gulf countries and the European Union has been postponed.

headline: Lebanon to take part in US-backed trilateral talks with Israel on Oct. 20, president says
summary: Military delegation to attend talks in US state of Florida to secure 'outcomes consistent with the framework agreement'
body_text:
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Saturday that his country will hold US-backed trilateral meetings with Israel in Tampa, US state of Florida, on Oct. 20.

In a statement released by the presidency on US social media platform X, Aoun said a military delegation will attend the meeting to present Beirut’s demands for an end to Israeli escalation, and aiming to secure "outcomes consistent with the framework agreement."

Aoun's remarks came as he received a French delegation headed by Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot.

Lebanon seeks to extend UNIFIL’s mandate and welcomes any arrangement that ensures a continued international presence in the country’s south to prevent power vacuum, he said.

Barrot expressed French solidarity with Lebanon and its continued support across all sectors, the statement said, adding that he also reaffirmed readiness to mobilize resources to address urgent humanitarian needs in the Arab country.

Israel began its deadly attacks in southern Lebanon in early March, and has continued the bombing unabated despite a US-sponsored framework agreement in June paving the way for Israeli withdrawal and the disarmament of Hezbollah.

headline: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats, beat French mayor
summary: Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy of European diplomats in the West Bank and beat up a visiting French mayor, witnesses said, a day after an American photographer was similarly set upon as violence escalates ahead of bitterly fought elections. The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.
body_text:
Israeli settlers on Saturday attacked a convoy of European diplomats in the West Bank and beat up a visiting French mayor, witnesses said, a day after an American photographer was similarly set upon as violence escalates ahead of bitterly fought elections.

The 78-year-old mayor said masked settlers yelled defamatory comments about France, kicked him and hit him with iron bars as he joined Palestinian olive farmers in the West Bank alongside the top French and Belgian representatives in Jerusalem and Polish diplomats.

"I think that if settlers are behaving like this, there is a tolerance on the part of the Israeli government," Bernard Baudoux, mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries, told AFP after he was attacked.

"The whole world needs to know what's happening," he said. "For me, I'll go back to my country and everything will be fine. Those who continue to suffer the most are those who are here."

Baudoux, who was wearing a sash with the French tricolour, was seen collapsed on the side of the car after the attack but he did not need hospital care.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said in a statement that Israel must "urgently halt criminal violence" and arrest those responsible for attacking Baudoux, with his Belgian counterpart issuing a similar call.

The attack came just one day after settlers beat an American photographer for The Washington Post, who was in moderate condition on Saturday after suffering broken vertebrae.

Israel's foreign ministry condemned the attack on the diplomats and Israeli police promised to open an investigation.

But Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to shore up support from the fiercely pro-settlement far-right in the October 27 election, instead alleged a "smear" campaign against settlers.

Netanyahu said the diplomats should have coordinated their movements with the Israeli military and pointed out that Baudoux is a communist known for supporting the Palestinian cause.

"We urge caution before drawing conclusions" about the attacks, Netanyahu's office said in a statement.

His main rival in the elections, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, strongly criticised Netanyahu over the violence, saying it was "burning away the little legitimacy the State of Israel still possesses".

The attacks are "Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government", Eisenkot said.

Baudoux, the mayor, said he had come to the town of Taybeh, a Christian stronghold, along with his local pastor from France to sign a goodwill agreement.

He was attacked just as he joined the harvest as a symbolic gesture with the Palestinians, for whom olives are an important cultural symbol.

Extremist Israelis have issued calls to stop the Palestinians' annual harvest after months of escalating attacks in which settlers have stolen land and property. There has also been violence against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting a settler dead last month.

Bashar Fawadleh, a priest in Taybeh, said settlers had already attacked the harvest and snatched olives before beating the mayor.

"One person was hit in the head and needed stitches. They also beat up an older lady in her 70s after insulting her with very bad words," the pastor told AFP.

The West Bank violence has shocked much of the world, with Britain spearheading economic sanctions that in turn led Israel to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.

Netanyahu had also sought to throw doubt on the circumstances behind the beating Friday of the photographer, Heidi Levine, suggesting that Palestinians and "far-left" activists caused trouble.

But President Isaac Herzog, who holds a mostly ceremonial role, took the initiative Saturday to call Levine in the hospital, saying the attack was "outrageous and shocking" and weighed on his conscience.

US Ambassador Mike Huckabee said the beating was "a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards", and demanded Israel prosecute and jail the assailants.

Israel Gantz, head of an umbrella settler group, blamed recent incidents on "groups of provocateurs and terrorists" but implicitly acknowledged some Israelis' responsibility, saying that they harmed the settlers' cause.

Settlers earlier this month also beat up AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh as he covered the olive harvest tensions, fracturing several of his ribs and stealing his camera.

Netanyahu's government has ramped up approval of West Bank settlements, which are illegal under international law.

Some 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel seized in 1967, alongside three million Palestinians.

headline: World Bank recognizes Russia’s achievements, provides platform for cooperation — Deputy PM
summary: Alexey Overchuk noted that Russia "possesses vast experience and knowledge and has much to offer countries of the Global South"
body_text:
BANGKOK, October 18. /TASS/. The World Bank recognizes Russia’s digital achievements and provides a platform to share this expertise with developing economies, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk told TASS, following the autumn meetings of the IMF and World Bank.

Overchuk noted that "Russia possesses vast experience and knowledge and has much to offer countries of the Global South," particularly regarding "digital transformation in public administration."

"The World Bank acknowledges Russia’s achievements in this area, understands how vital Russian expertise is for developing economies, and provides us with an international platform to work directly with these nations," he emphasized.

On the sidelines of the meetings in Bangkok, Russia organized two packed working seminars with World Bank support. "One seminar focused on digital transformation in land and real estate administration and geospatial data systems. The other addressed digital public services and digital transformation in tax administration," Overchuk said.

He noted that these areas crucially impact the business climate, investment attractiveness, and socio-economic development in the Global South. "The World Bank prioritizes these issues, and Russia is a global leader in digital governance," Overchuk said, adding that Russia ranks eighth in the World Bank’s GovTech Maturity Index.

"By learning from our experience, developing nations are seeking closer cooperation with Russia, which aligns with our interests."

headline: Türkiye urges Islamic world to act together on regional challenges, Palestine at OIC meeting
summary: Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan says talks in Baghdad also focus on strengthening cooperation with Iraq and efforts to resolve regional conflicts
body_text:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Saturday that Türkiye emphasized solidarity and joint action on challenges facing the Islamic world, particularly Palestine, at an Organization of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) meeting in Baghdad.

His remarks came after the 52nd Session of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers in the Iraqi capital.

"In our speech at the OIC meeting, we underlined the need to stand in solidarity in the face of global and regional challenges and the importance of acting together on all issues concerning the Islamic world, particularly Palestine," Fidan said on Turkish social media platform NSosyal.

Fidan said he held meetings with Iraqi President Nizar Amedi, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and parliament Speaker Heibet Halbusi.

He also met with Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council President Faiq Zaidan, Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein, Popular Mobilization Forces Commission Chairman Falih al-Fayyad and National Security Adviser Qasim al-Abboudi.

His meetings also included Iraqi Turkmen Front President and Kirkuk Governor Mehmet Seman Agaoglu.

Fidan said the discussions covered bilateral relations in all their dimensions, including steps to deepen cooperation between Türkiye and Iraq in trade, energy and security.

He also thanked Iraqi officials for their hospitality.

Fidan said he also met with Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to assess progress in efforts to resolve ongoing regional conflicts.

"As Türkiye, we will resolutely continue our efforts to strengthen solidarity in the Islamic world, defend the rights of the oppressed, and make constructive contributions to peace and prosperity in our region," he said.

headline: Houthis claim to have shot down Saudi Apache helicopter near Yemen border
summary: Houthi military spokesperson says helicopter was carrying out 'hostile operations' against group's positions near Saudi Arabia's Najran region
body_text:
Yemen's Houthi group claimed Saturday that it shot down a Saudi Apache military helicopter near the Najran region in southern Saudi Arabia while it was targeting Houthi positions.

In a statement carried by the Houthi-run version of Yemen's Saba news agency, the group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, claimed that Houthi forces shot down the helicopter while it was carrying out "hostile operations" against their positions along the border.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi officials on Saree's remarks.

The claim came amid continued military escalation in Yemen and strikes by the Houthis against Saudi Arabia since July, including attacks on civilian aviation facilities and energy infrastructure inside the kingdom.

Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year in support of the internationally recognized government.

The latest fighting began in July, following the breakdown of a 2022 truce.

The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday.

Tehran seized control over Hormuz after the start of the war in late February, choking off the strait that normally carries about one-fifth of global oil consumption.

headline: AI boom sustains S. Korea's growth despite global headwinds: IMF official
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 18 (Yonhap) -- South Korea appears to be weathering global economi...
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct. 18 (Yonhap) -- South Korea appears to be weathering global economic headwinds thanks to the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the technology investment cycle unlikely to lose steam in the near term, a senior official at the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said.

"Trade tensions among countries are putting negative pressure on the global economy," Choi Ji-young, executive director of the IMF Asia and the Pacific Constituency Office, said during a meeting with reporters in Bangkok on Thursday, citing the Middle East crisis and the war between Russia and Ukraine as lingering sources of uncertainty.

He was visiting Thailand to attend the 2026 Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group.

"Despite these conditions, the growth forecast for South Korea has been revised upward," the director said.

Earlier this week, the IMF raised its growth forecast for South Korea in 2026 to 3.3 percent, citing strong semiconductor exports, driven by strong AI infrastructure demand, which more than offset the fallout from the Middle East war.

The figure was up 0.7 percentage point from the organization's July projection.

Choi said AI-related investment will likely continue for some time, citing robust investment in AI data centers and related infrastructure.

"Building AI data centers takes a long time, potentially around 10 years. Investment has only just begun, and these projects are unlikely to falter in a couple of years and make that investment meaningless," he said.

The IMF nevertheless sees significant potential downsides in AI, Choi added.

"South Korea could face a stock market correction, an adjustment in its current account and adverse effects on businesses should the AI boom falter," Choi said. "But within our organization, we expect AI investment to continue for a long time."

The executive director also noted the AI boom has expanded South Korea's fiscal room to invest more in future growth, setting the country apart from other nations.

He advised countries experiencing economic growth, such as South Korea, not to focus excessively on their debt-to-gross domestic product (GDP) ratios, but instead to prioritize investment in innovation and growth.

"In discussions with IMF staff, we point out that the fund's general policy advice does not fit South Korea's circumstances," Choi noted, adding the fund recognizes the country's unique situation.

"IMF staff share the view that South Korea should continue investing to enhance its growth potential," Choi said.

Turning to the Future Fund, which the government plans to launch next year using so-called windfall revenue from the chip supercycle to lay the groundwork for long-term growth, Choi said the IMF views its structure positively, although it has yet to offer a detailed assessment of the initiative.

Choi added the IMF's latest growth forecast for South Korea appears not to fully reflect the potential impact of policies aimed at boosting growth, suggesting the projection may be somewhat "conservative."

analysis.framing: The article frames South Korea's economic outlook positively through the lens of an IMF official's remarks, emphasizing AI-driven growth and upward forecast revisions while downplaying risks.

headline: Iraq’s dinar devaluation tests efforts to protect consumers from rising prices

The move came as disruption to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz exerted additional pressure on government revenue and its capacity to finance public spending.“The situation is very bad,” one market owner in Erbil lamented. He said the price of goods has been rising since the Iran war broke out in February, particularly due to higher transport costs as most items come from Turkey and Iran.Iraq imports a substantial share of the products it uses, including food, medicine and consumer goods. For Iraqis paid in dinars, the weaker currency threatens to erode purchasing power. But the effects are not uniform, as those earning in dollars may receive more dinars when converting their salaries, while people with dollar-denominated expenses face a different calculation.In Erbil, where rent is often set in dollars, the exchange-rate change can have a direct effect on tenants paid in dinars. The measure places economic pressure on tenants who need to buy dollars with their dinar salaries, although the actual cost depends on the exchange rate available to them and how rent is paid. The gap between the official and parallel-market rates adds another layer to the pressure on households. While the official public rate is 1,520 dinars to the dollar, people and businesses seeking cash dollars often turn to exchange shops, where the price fluctuates according to supply and demand. In Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Iraqi Kurdistan region, the dollar was selling for about 166,350 dinars per $100 this week, around nine per cent above the official rate. The parallel-market rate rose sharply after the devaluation was announced on October 7, when exchange shops in the city quoted selling prices as high as 180,000 dinars per $100. The rate subsequently eased, although it remained above the official figure.The National visited several exchange shops in the Eskan neighbourhood of Erbil, where many dollar shops can be found, but employees declined to comment on the fluctuations.Dollar-denominated rents are part of a wider pattern in Iraq, where the dollar plays a prominent role in parts of the property market and some business dealings, even though most salaries and everyday purchases are made in dinars. The result is that households can be exposed on several fronts – rent may become more expensive in the national currency, while imported food, household goods and other products may also rise in price as businesses face higher costs for dollars.The use of the US dollar for some expenses while the majority of salaries are in Iraqi dinar “is what is fundamentally wrong with us”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The National.Those paid in dollars may benefit from converting their income into more dinars to cover expenses. My rent is in dollars and my bills are in Iraqi dinars but I expect prices to go higher, so at the end of the day it will kind of be the same.” He had observed prices rising during the war earlier this year but said they were “even higher now”. “I went to the market the other day and bought the same detergent for 20,000 Iraqi dinar and before it used to cost 9,000,” he said. The decision has prompted criticism from residents and political factions, with legislators demanding explanations from the government and proposing measures to contain price increases. Others argue the adjustment was necessary to help Baghdad meet its financial obligations.“There is no denying the affect is there but it’s not as dramatic as people make it out to be,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “The country had to do something,” he said, before adding he was “surprised it was proactive”.“In the past we didn’t act but we acted while the reserves are still healthy,” he added. But that fiscal benefit does not necessarily translate into greater purchasing power for households.The government led by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has said it needs to maintain public spending and ensure salaries can be paid despite the loss of oil income. But opposition has grown within parliament, with politicians questioning why the measure was adopted and whether alternative options were adequately considered.The Co-ordination Framework, the main alliance of Shiite political parties that backs the government in Baghdad, has called for measures to limit the burden on citizens. “We can’t catch a break from them,” said Rizgar Ali, a taxi driver in Erbil, referring to the Iraqi government. “I have relatives who are public servants and their salaries are always delayed because Baghdad doesn’t send us our budget and now they’re weakening the money.” The recurring delays, amid disputes between Baghdad and Erbil over oil revenue and budget allocations, leave many households with limited financial flexibility to absorb higher prices and currency costs.Mr Ali complained about the rise in petrol prices and said he has to refuel his car frequently, making driving passengers around the city a much more difficult source of income – he turns the engine off at most traffic lights.Devaluation precedence Mr Tabaqchali said the current situation reminds him of the devaluation in 2020 when Iraq faced a similar dilemma during the Covid-19 pandemic, when a collapse in oil prices and a decline in revenue left the government struggling to finance its budget. The adjustment was intended to generate more dinar revenue from oil sales, ease the budget deficit and help the government meet its spending obligations.In January 2023, the government of prime minister at the time, Mohammed Shia Al Sudani, moved in the opposite direction, strengthening the dinar and setting the public exchange rate at 1,320 per dollar after the currency weakened on the parallel market amid tighter US restrictions on dollar transfers and increased scrutiny of Iraqi banks. That decision, too, was met with concern by residents because the dollar continued to trade at a higher value on the parallel market.The latest devaluation reverses that strengthening.Whether the devaluation achieves its intended financial objectives will depend not only on oil revenue and foreign currency reserves, but also on the government's ability to prevent unjustified price increases, protect lower-income families and pursue reforms that reduce Iraq's reliance on oil.Mr Tabaqchali also highlighted government subsidies as a means of cushioning the impact on lower-income Iraqis. Subsidies on fuel and some basic services, alongside the public distribution system that provides subsidised staple foods, can help shield poorer households from some of the immediate effects of a weaker currency.The government has also pledged to maintain fuel and basic-service subsidies following the latest devaluation, while considering customs relief for food and essential goods. However, subsidies do not cover all household expenses, such as rent, and imported goods can still become more expensive. “The worst is over for us as long as we continue shipping through the [Strait of] Hormuz,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “This doesn’t mean we have passed the crisis because the damage has been done and we have to adjust. The devaluation is part of a bigger thing, like structural changes to our budget services.”
body_text:
Iraq’s decision to devalue its currency has exposed the competing interests of households and the state, as residents warn of rising living costs while economists argue the move could help protect public finances amid a sharp fall in oil revenue.

The Central Bank of Iraq raised the official dollar selling rate from 1,320 to 1,520 dinars on October 7, a devaluation of about 15 per cent. The move came as disruption to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz exerted additional pressure on government revenue and its capacity to finance public spending.

“The situation is very bad,” one market owner in Erbil lamented. He said the price of goods has been rising since the Iran war broke out in February, particularly due to higher transport costs as most items come from Turkey and Iran.

Iraq imports a substantial share of the products it uses, including food, medicine and consumer goods.

For Iraqis paid in dinars, the weaker currency threatens to erode purchasing power. But the effects are not uniform, as those earning in dollars may receive more dinars when converting their salaries, while people with dollar-denominated expenses face a different calculation.

In Erbil, where rent is often set in dollars, the exchange-rate change can have a direct effect on tenants paid in dinars. The measure places economic pressure on tenants who need to buy dollars with their dinar salaries, although the actual cost depends on the exchange rate available to them and how rent is paid.

The gap between the official and parallel-market rates adds another layer to the pressure on households. While the official public rate is 1,520 dinars to the dollar, people and businesses seeking cash dollars often turn to exchange shops, where the price fluctuates according to supply and demand.

In Erbil, the capital of the semi-autonomous Iraqi Kurdistan region, the dollar was selling for about 166,350 dinars per $100 this week, around nine per cent above the official rate. The parallel-market rate rose sharply after the devaluation was announced on October 7, when exchange shops in the city quoted selling prices as high as 180,000 dinars per $100. The rate subsequently eased, although it remained above the official figure.

The National visited several exchange shops in the Eskan neighbourhood of Erbil, where many dollar shops can be found, but employees declined to comment on the fluctuations.

Dollar-denominated rents are part of a wider pattern in Iraq, where the dollar plays a prominent role in parts of the property market and some business dealings, even though most salaries and everyday purchases are made in dinars. The result is that households can be exposed on several fronts – rent may become more expensive in the national currency, while imported food, household goods and other products may also rise in price as businesses face higher costs for dollars.

The use of the US dollar for some expenses while the majority of salaries are in Iraqi dinar “is what is fundamentally wrong with us”, Ahmed Tabaqchali, non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told The National.

Those paid in dollars may benefit from converting their income into more dinars to cover expenses. But the advantage is less straightforward for people who also pay rent or other bills in dollars, since those costs do not become cheaper simply because the exchange rate changes.

Ahmad Abbas, who receives his income in dollars, said: “It’s safer to be paid in dollars because it’s unstable when it comes to the currency here. My rent is in dollars and my bills are in Iraqi dinars but I expect prices to go higher, so at the end of the day it will kind of be the same.” He had observed prices rising during the war earlier this year but said they were “even higher now”.

“I went to the market the other day and bought the same detergent for 20,000 Iraqi dinar and before it used to cost 9,000,” he said.

The decision has prompted criticism from residents and political factions, with legislators demanding explanations from the government and proposing measures to contain price increases. Others argue the adjustment was necessary to help Baghdad meet its financial obligations.

“There is no denying the affect is there but it’s not as dramatic as people make it out to be,” Mr Tabaqchali said. “The country had to do something,” he said, before adding he was “surprised it was proactive”.

“In the past we didn’t act but we acted while the reserves are still healthy,” he added.

At the Meri Forum in Erbil on Tuesday, Samir Fakhri, director general of the Statistics and Research Directorate at the Central Bank, defended the devaluation, arguing it was necessary to protect the country's foreign currency reserves following the decline in oil revenue.

He highlighted Iraq's dependence on oil, which accounts for more than 90 per cent of government revenue, leaving public finances particularly vulnerable to disruptions in exports.

He explained the scale of government spending and the pressure it places on the Central Bank of Iraq to supply dollars, arguing the exchange-rate adjustment must be considered alongside the country's wider financial difficulties.

The argument in favour of devaluation is that Baghdad receives more dinars for every dollar earned from oil exports, helping it finance salaries and other domestic spending even as oil income comes under pressure. But that fiscal benefit does not necessarily translate into greater purchasing power for households.

The government led by Prime Minister Ali Al Zaidi has said it needs to maintain public spending and ensure salaries can be paid despite the loss of oil income. But opposition has grown within parliament, with politicians questioning why the measure was adopted and whether alternative options were adequately considered.

The Co-ordination Framework, the main alliance of Shiite political parties that backs the government in Baghdad, has called for measures to limit the burden on citizens.

“We can’t catch a break from them,” said Rizgar Ali, a taxi driver in Erbil, referring to the Iraqi government. “I have relatives who are public servants and their salaries are always delayed because Baghdad doesn’t send us our budget and now they’re weakening the money.” The recurring delays, amid disputes between Baghdad and Erbil over oil revenue and budget allocations, leave many households with limited financial flexibility to absorb higher prices and currency costs.

Mr Ali complained about the rise in petrol prices and said he has to refuel his car frequently, making driving passengers around the city a much more difficult source of income – he turns the engine off at most traffic lights.

Mr Tabaqchali said the current situation reminds him of the devaluation in 2020 when Iraq faced a similar dilemma during the Covid-19 pandemic, when a collapse in oil prices and a decline in revenue left the government struggling to finance its budget.

The adjustment was intended to generate more dinar revenue from oil sales, ease the budget deficit and help the government meet its spending obligations.

In January 2023, the government of prime minister at the time, Mohammed Shia Al Sudani, moved in the opposite direction, strengthening the dinar and setting the public exchange rate at 1,320 per dollar after the currency weakened on the parallel market amid tighter US restrictions on dollar transfers and increased scrutiny of Iraqi banks. That decision, too, was met with concern by residents because the dollar continued to trade at a higher value on the parallel market.

The latest devaluation reverses that strengthening.

Whether the devaluation achieves its intended financial objectives will depend not only on oil revenue and foreign currency reserves, but also on the government's ability to prevent unjustified price increases, protect lower-income families and pursue reforms that reduce Iraq's reliance on oil.

Mr Tabaqchali also highlighted government subsidies as a means of cushioning the impact on lower-income Iraqis. Subsidies on fuel and some basic services, alongside the public distribution system that provides subsidised staple foods, can help shield poorer households from some of the immediate effects of a weaker currency.

The government has also pledged to maintain fuel and basic-service subsidies following the latest devaluation, while considering customs relief for food and essential goods.

However, subsidies do not cover all household expenses, such as rent, and imported goods can still become more expensive. “The worst is over for us as long as we continue shipping through the [Strait of] Hormuz,” Mr Tabaqchali said.

“This doesn’t mean we have passed the crisis because the damage has been done and we have to adjust. The devaluation is part of a bigger thing, like structural changes to our budget services.”

analysis.framing: The article frames the devaluation as a tension between necessary fiscal measures and household hardship, giving roughly equal weight to economists' defense and residents' complaints.

loaded_language.explanation: A direct quote from a market owner, emotionally charged and vague, used to open the human-impact narrative.

headline: Rubio says Trump to 'analyze' global impact of Russia sanctions during pause
summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia would last 60 days, as the move drew bipartisan criticism and raised fears in Ukraine that Washington could ease further restrictions on Moscow.
body_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump’s decision to waive sanctions and tariffs on Russia would last 60 days, as the move drew bipartisan criticism and raised fears in Ukraine that Washington could ease further restrictions on Moscow.

Issued on: 18/10/2026 - 04:39

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that President Donald Trump's waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to "analyse" their impact on the global economy.

"The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.

He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Houthis.

"These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they're having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices" but on economies as well, Rubio said.

Trump said late Saturday his decision would benefit the US, though it was unclear if he had actually made up his mind on the matter.

"We'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," he said. "It's a very good decision, and it's going to be a decision that's good for the country, and I think good for the world."

US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia – measures adopted by Congress last month.

Read moreZelensky fears Trump 'will continue' to lift Russia sanctions

The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas.

The idea was to cut off sources of funding to supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as his war on Ukraine.

But late Friday, two days before the law was due to take effect, Trump exempted Russia from those economic restrictions.

"Beyond irresponsible," Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic who will leave office in January, said in a post on X.

"If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin."

Ted Cruz, a senior Republican senator from Texas, called the move "a mistake" in comments aired on Fox News.

Trump's executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions.

The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month.

Polls show Trump's Republicans are likely to receive a drubbing at the polls.

"The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were (going to) make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get," Rubio said, underscoring the importance of the vital fuel powering US road hauling, agriculture and construction.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that Trump's action "rewards" Putin.

headline: Egypt's North Coast: Where to go on the Mediterranean and what's coming next
summary: Ask Sherif Fathy where Egypt's next big holiday destination lies and he points north to the Mediterranean. “It’s what we call ‘sun and fun’,” the Egyptian Minister of Tourism and Antiquities says with a smile."That coast has huge investments going on now, and it will be the summer destination of the Mediterranean for the coming decades," Fathy tells The National on the sidelines of World Travel and Tourism Council’s Global Summit in Malta last week. "The growth is big.”That extends to national figures, as Fathy says Egypt had welcomed about 14.4 million international tourists in 2026 by the end of September, despite regional tension slowing growth. "We expect to end the year with 20 million."Much of that runs through Cairo. The Grand Egyptian Museum, which opened in November 2025, is now "the jewel of the crown", Fathy says. "Everybody is trying to reroute his trip, start or end his trip in Cairo." It welcomed about four million visitors between its opening and the end of August, and Fathy expects that figure to reach five million a year.Yet the coastline running west from Alexandria towards Libya, known to Egyptians as the Sahel, has long been where Cairo families escape the summer heat. Now it is being sold to the wider world, and Fathy says the numbers prove demand is there. For example, charter flights into El Alamein, he says, grew by 540 per cent last year and by a further 50 per cent this summer. The growth "could have been more, but we didn't have enough rooms," he adds. That shortage is being tackled, however. "The properties being built there are extremely luxurious," Fathy says, and he expects the beach clubs and nightlife to be a big part of the draw.Is it a good fit for UAE travellers? "Definitely," he says, describing UAE families who book the same hotels year after year and "come and enjoy it every summer". Here is where to go along the coast, heading west.Getting thereMost visitors fly in. El Alamein's airport is one of three serving the coast, and Fathy says it will soon be enlarged, along with the airport at Marsa Matrouh further west. This summer, Alamein International was served by 15 airlines, including Etihad and flydubai alongside Saudia, Flynas and Air Cairo, although many routes are seasonal.Alexandria's Borg El Arab airport is the other main gateway, and the city makes an easy first or last night. By road, New Alamein is about 250km from Cairo, which is under a three-hour drive.It’s worth noting that locals place everything by its kilometre marker along the coastal road, so you will hear a resort described as being at "Km 126".El Alamein and New AlameinBest for: summer festivals and Second World War historyThe coast's main hub begins around Marina El Alamein at Km 100. Officials expect about 300,000 visitors to Alamein in 2026, up from about 170,000 last year.New Alamein was planned as a year-round city, with an opera house, universities and residential districts alongside its beaches. In summer, it fills with concerts and festivals. This year's Yalla Sahel drew Gulf visitors to shows by Egyptian and Arab stars such as Amr Diab and Elissa. The town is better known for the Second World War battles fought here in 1942. El Alamein Military Museum displays weapons and uniforms from the campaign. Nearby, the El Alamein War Cemetery holds the graves of thousands of Commonwealth soldiers and a German cemetery commemorates those who died in the battle. Sidi Abdel Rahman and MarassiBest for: luxury resorts and beach clubsBetween Km 124 and Km 144, on the International Coastal Road, Sidi Abdel Rahman is the coast's upscale heart, with high-end resorts, beaches and a busy entertainment scene. Marassi, at Km 126, is one of the best-known names on the coast, with several beaches, world-class hotels, residential villages, an 18-hole golf course and the first water park in Egypt’s North Coast.A little further west, Ghazala Bay is quieter, private and exclusive, while El Dabaa offers calmer beaches with soft white sand and turquoise water. Much of this stretch is gated resort communities, so check day access beforehand.Ras El HekmaBest for: what's coming next, with a UAE connectionThe biggest change on the coast is being built with Emirati investment. Abu Dhabi's ADQ appointed Modon Holding as master developer of Ras El Hekma in 2024, on a site of more than 170 million square metres.The first district, Wadi Yemm, will be anchored by a lighthouse and a 10,000-seat amphitheatre. It includes a Montage hotel with about 200 rooms and suites, plus 96 branded villas. Beach club brand Nammos has also unveiled plans for a Cycladic-inspired resort, beach club and 72 one- to four-bedroom branded residences, plus a penthouse and retail village.None of it is open yet. As of July, the project was in full construction with completion dates scheduled for 2028, so for now Ras El Hekma is one to watch rather than book. Beyond it, Sidi Heneish has wide, largely untouched beaches and is starting to attract luxury developers.Marsa MatrouhBest for: hidden coves and Bedouin cultureFurther west, Marsa Matrouh is a city rather than a resort strip. Fathy points to the Bedouin experience as one of the coast's draws.The real attraction is the water. Ageeba Beach is a cove tucked between two hills and reached by a flight of steps. Cleopatra's Bath is a pool inside a rock cave where the waves break. Legend says the queen bathed there. Lagoon Beach, with its pearl-white sand and clear water, suits families. For a break from the sea, the Rommel Museum, opened in 1977 in memory of German field marshal Erwin Rommel, holds Second World War artefacts.Side trip: SiwaBest for: desert landscapes and ecotourismThe coast itself is about “sun and fun”, Fathy says, but "it can be combined with ecotourism in Siwa". The oasis lies well inland – close to the Libyan border – and is a long drive from the coast.It’s worth the effort, however, as it’s a leading ecotourism destination for the country, famed for its mud-brick architecture, natural landscapes and distinctive Berber culture. Visit the old Shali fortress, a medieval citadel uniquely built from a salt-and-mud material called kershef. Or see the salt lakes, a network of saline pools and natural springs, which are said to be healing and glow in vivid colours. Elsewhere, the Temple of the Oracle, built in the 6th century BC, is linked in legend to Alexander the Great.

For example, charter flights into El Alamein, he says, grew by 540 per cent last year and by a further 50 per cent this summer. The growth "could have been more, but we didn't have enough rooms," he adds.

Best for: summer festivals and Second World War history

The biggest change on the coast is being built with Emirati investment. Abu Dhabi's ADQ appointed Modon Holding as master developer of Ras El Hekma in 2024, on a site of more than 170 million square metres.

The first district, Wadi Yemm, will be anchored by a lighthouse and a 10,000-seat amphitheatre. It includes a Montage hotel with about 200 rooms and suites, plus 96 branded villas. Beach club brand Nammos has also unveiled plans for a Cycladic-inspired resort, beach club and 72 one- to four-bedroom branded residences, plus a penthouse and retail village.

None of it is open yet. As of July, the project was in full construction with completion dates scheduled for 2028, so for now Ras El Hekma is one to watch rather than book.

Beyond it, Sidi Heneish has wide, largely untouched beaches and is starting to attract luxury developers.

Further west, Marsa Matrouh is a city rather than a resort strip. Fathy points to the Bedouin experience as one of the coast's draws.

The real attraction is the water. Ageeba Beach is a cove tucked between two hills and reached by a flight of steps. Cleopatra's Bath is a pool inside a rock cave where the waves break. Legend says the queen bathed there. Lagoon Beach, with its pearl-white sand and clear water, suits families.

For a break from the sea, the Rommel Museum, opened in 1977 in memory of German field marshal Erwin Rommel, holds Second World War artefacts.

Best for: desert landscapes and ecotourism

The coast itself is about “sun and fun”, Fathy says, but "it can be combined with ecotourism in Siwa". The oasis lies well inland – close to the Libyan border – and is a long drive from the coast.

It’s worth the effort, however, as it’s a leading ecotourism destination for the country, famed for its mud-brick architecture, natural landscapes and distinctive Berber culture.

body_text:
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has condemned an Israeli settler attack on an American photojournalist in the occupied West Bank, demanding a full investigation, arrests and the prosecution of those responsible.

Heidi Levine of The Washington Post suffered serious injuries when she was attacked by Israeli settlers on Friday morning, the newspaper’s executive editor Matt Murray said.

“Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Mr Huckabee said in a post on X early on Sunday. “Dishonourable act of senseless violence.”

The US envoy said Ms Levine had been clearly identified as a journalist and was unarmed. He called for those involved to spend years in prison and demanded prosecution “to the fullest extent of the law”.

The Washington Post said Ms Levine was attacked when "dozens of masked settlers” set fire to shrubs and threw rocks in a “co-ordinated assault” on Palestinian olive harvesters.

“She was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly and stripped of her cameras and phone,” the paper said.

Ms Levine was later taken to hospital in Ramallah. Photos showed her lying on a trolley with a wound dressing on the left leg and a gash on her right knee, among other injuries.

The attack comes amid renewed international concern over Israeli settler violence in the West Bank, after European diplomats and a French mayor were assaulted by masked people in a separate incident on Saturday.

Belgium criticised the attack on its consul general and the other diplomats and urged Israel to bring those responsible to justice.

Poland’s Foreign Ministry said preliminary evidence indicated Israeli settlers were responsible for the assault. Polish diplomats travelling in the convoy were unharmed, the ministry said.

“We expect the Israeli authorities to provide urgent and detailed explanations, identify those responsible and ensure that they are held accountable,” it added. “We also expect effective measures to be taken to prevent similar incidents from occurring in the future.”

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said the mayor of a French town had also been assaulted by what he described as “extremist settlers” during Saturday’s incident. He called on Israeli authorities to stop the violence.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog called Ms Levine to apologise for the attack and urged an investigation. The Israeli military described the violence as intolerable and said the incidents would be investigated.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said the circumstances remained unclear and more evidence was needed before responsibility could be established. It also noted that the diplomats’ visit had not been coordinated with Israeli security officials.

Britain, France, Canada and other countries announced sanctions focused on Israeli settlements last month, while the US said it would not join those measures.

"Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards," Huckabee wrote on the US social media platform X.

The US State Department said Friday that it was "greatly concerned" over the attack on Levine by Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank.

"The Department of State is aware of these reports. We are greatly concerned when any American is harmed overseas and stand ready to provide all appropriate consular assistance," a State Department spokesman said in an emailed statement to Anadolu.

body_text:
When Angh, a film set in a remote corner of north-east India rarely depicted on screen, won the Platform Prize at the Toronto International Film Festival in September, it made history in more ways than one.

The debut feature by 31-year-old Naga filmmaker Theja Rio became the first Indian film to win the prestigious award, earning a place in the race for Best International Feature Film at the 2027 Academy Awards. Thanks to a change in Oscar eligibility rules, the victory means Angh can compete for consideration independently of India's official submission, the Marathi-language film Gondhal.

Told primarily in Konyak, the language of one of Nagaland's many indigenous Naga tribes, the film explores the tension between ancestral traditions and the arrival of Christianity in the region in the 1960s.

India ends up with two films in the Oscar race for best international feature

For Rio, the international recognition is particularly meaningful.

“Growing up, I've never seen Nagaland in a film before or in a series before,” he tells The National. “And very often, every time you introduce yourself, you're getting into the backdrops of where you come from and then you're having to describe geographically where exactly it is.”

Rio first explored the story in a short film in 2019, inspired by a visit to Nagaland's Mon district three years earlier. But he soon realised that the characters and the cultural transformations he wanted to explore needed more room to develop, prompting him to expand the story into his first feature.

The response since the Toronto victory has exceeded his expectations, he says. Rio returned to Nagaland last month to celebrations and messages of pride, while the film has attracted attention from across India and beyond.

“It's been a fever dream,” he says. “It's just my debut feature and it's yet to release, but to receive the reactions we have received and the fact that anyone is interested in having to hear what I have to say is completely baffling, but something that I'm very grateful about.

“And just being able to make our people feel represented is by far the most heartwarming thing.”

It is a fitting response to a film concerned with identity and belonging, and with what happens when the world around a community changes faster than its people can adapt.

Set in Nagaland in the early 1960s, Angh follows Anghba (played by Anghlong Konyak), an ageing Konyak village chief, and his son as they confront the arrival of a Christian missionary and the changes it brings to their traditional way of life.

The story is not simply about the clash between two belief systems. It explores the uncertainty of people caught between generations, as familiar customs begin to disappear and new ideas reshape their understanding of the world.

During his journey to Mon, a district in eastern Nagaland bordering Myanmar, Rio encountered elderly Konyak men with traditional facial tattoos whose appearances reflected a way of life that had largely disappeared.

“Mon is a very interesting place in the sense that they still have a lot of the practices and a lot of the structures from their older traditions that is still exist, while at the same time, like the rest of Nagaland, it has also become very modern in a sense,” he explains. “There were a lot of the tattooed faces but they were all dressed in modern clothes.”

The contrast fascinated him. Here were people whose faces carried the visible history of an earlier generation, yet who were living in a world transformed by religion, education and modernity.

The encounter also connected with Rio's long-standing fascination with characters whose lives have been overtaken by history.

“I wanted to make a film about those people who have gone through that phase of rapid transition in the 60s and the 70s,” he says. “I'm very interested and very passionate about characters that have been sort of left behind by time. There's something very tragic and melancholic about characters like that.”

It was the combination of these two ideas – a community experiencing profound change and a character struggling to hold on to an older world – that eventually became Angh.

The relationship between Christianity and indigenous Naga traditions is not merely a subject from the past, it's a question that touches Rio's own identity.

Christianity is now deeply embedded in much of Nagaland's society, but its spread also coincided with the decline of ancestral beliefs and practices. Exploring that history can be sensitive, particularly when it involves examining the consequences of missionary activity.

Rio, who is Christian, was determined not to portray either side as entirely right or wrong.

“It was very important to not antagonise any side,” he says. “I see both sides of it, and that's why I feel all my characters have a lot of depth. They're not one-dimensional characters who are almost caricature like. They're not there to play a villain or there just to be the opposition of the other.”

That approach shapes the relationship between the village chief and the missionary, played by Scottish actor Douglas Henshall.

“When you watch the film, you'll realise that the white priest comes with the best intention, but from Anghba's perspective, he poses a threat to the community and to the culture that he is trying to hold on to.

“That's one of the reasons why I like to make films about things that I'm conflicted about rather than make films about things that I'm sure about, which is dangerously treading the propaganda line.”

But how did a story so deeply rooted in Nagaland's history and culture strike a chord with an international jury at one of the world's biggest film festivals?

At the Toronto International Film Festival, jury members praised Angh “for its refreshing perspective, strength of filmmaking and deeply resonant portrait of a world”.

“We praise the filmmaker’s vision, audacity and courage,” they said.

For Rio, the film's universal appeal lies in its themes of rapid change and cultural preservation.

“The film is something that is obviously very culturally specific, but thematically something that is very universal,” he says. “We're living in a time where we're dealing with great change happening at a rapid speed than it's ever been. So in that sense, it's quite topical as well.

“There's also so much conversation about conservation of, not just the environment, but of culture. So I think the film is very topical in that sense.”

When Rio was developing Angh as a short film in 2019, he had already realised the characters and their conflicts required a larger canvas.

“I was struggling to compress the entire thing into a short film, and I knew it was always meant to be a feature. The characters, the conflict, it's just too big to be restricted into a short film format,” he says.

At the time, however, he lacked the experience and resources to make a full-length production. The short film's positive reception on the festival circuit encouraged him to expand the screenplay.

He subsequently studied at the National Film and Television School in the UK, where working on other projects gave him time away from the story.

When he returned to it, he had gained experience and a new perspective on the material.

Supporting him through much of that journey has been Nancy Nisa Beso, a long-time film producer whose career spans more than two decades across documentary, commercial and independent filmmaking.

Beso has known Rio since childhood and has worked with him on several projects, including the original short film. The success of Angh is the culmination of years of dedication rather than an overnight breakthrough, she says.

“Technically, while this is his first feature film, he has been working on films for the last 11 years of his life,” she says. “This is a product of 11 years of just working towards your skill and expanding what you built.”

The feature presented numerous challenges, particularly when it came to casting. With few professional actors available locally, Rio and his team travelled through villages in the Mon region searching for people who could convincingly portray the characters.

“We had no option but to cast non-actors because we don't have professional actors where we come from, so it wasn't necessarily a choice,” Rio says.

The lead role eventually went to Konyak, a stand-up comedian Rio discovered on YouTube after struggling to find someone with the necessary screen presence.

Rio's decision to shoot on 16mm film, despite its many logistical challenges, was equally deliberate. He had been influenced by archival photographs and footage of the region taken during the early years of missionary activity.

“There's something about film that is so filled with nostalgia. Obviously, I wasn't around in the 60s. But it's something that has a texture that's so atmospheric and so mystique,” he says.

The project also received backing from the Red Sea Fund, an initiative of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea International Film Festival supporting filmmakers from the Arab world, Africa and Asia.

But making history at Toronto was one thing. Now comes the challenge of turning that victory into an Oscar nomination.

For Rio and his team, the coming months will be a whirlwind of screenings, meetings with Academy voters, networking and fund-raising. The film's Platform Prize win has opened the door to consideration for Best International Feature Film, but securing a place on the shortlist, let alone among the final five nominees, will require an entirely different kind of effort.

Preliminary voting for the Oscars' Best International Feature Film will take place from December 7 to 11, with the shortlist announced on December 15. Nominations voting will run from January 11 to 15, with the final five nominees for the category announced alongside the other Oscar nominations on January 21.

Producer Beso is preparing for a campaign that will take the filmmakers from India to Britain and the US, with Los Angeles and New York becoming key stops.

“The plan is to move to LA very soon, but we are also in the meantime trying to get all the Academy members to watch the film, whether it's in India or in the UK and in the US,” she says. “The next few months are very exciting, but it's also like a marathon.

“Every day there is lobbying and interviews. I usually say a producer's job is to beg, borrow and steal. So right now I'm in the begging stage.

“It's expensive to make a film, but it's even more expensive to do that entire campaign.”

For Rio, who has already experienced a remarkable few weeks since Toronto, the prospect of navigating Hollywood's awards circuit is another unfamiliar chapter.

“I don't know what I'm getting into, but I'm looking forward to it,” he says.
