body_text:
Syria and the World Bank have agreed to set up a multi-donor trust fund for the country's recovery and reconstruction, the two sides announced in a joint statement on Sunday.

Damascus is continuing to rebuild after a civil war that lasted for more than a decade and had destroyed the country's infrastructure.

Interview:Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors

The Syria Recovery and Reconstruction Trust Fund – or “Start” – is a multi-donor fund that aims to provide concessional financing, investment guarantees and technical assistance, and build trust, the statement said.

The agreement comes after Syria took part in the International and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. The gatherings were the latest to be attended by Syrian officials since the fall of president Bashar Al Assad's regime in December 2024.

Syrian Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said the agreement helps to set the foundation for a new phase of co-operation with Damascus's international partners. Partners in the US, Europe and Middle East expressed their support for the initiative, the statement said.

“An important milestone in Syria’s recovery and reconstruction journey,” Mr Barnieh wrote in a post on X.

The World Bank in 2025 estimated Syria's reconstruction would cost about $216 billion, making it one of the most expensive rebuilding efforts in history. The World Bank classified this as its best “conservative” estimate.

The World Bank said infrastructure accounted for 48 per cent, or $52 billion, of total damage from the civil war, followed by residential buildings at $33 billion and non-residential buildings at $33 billion.

It said the multi-donor trust fund will help to support the delivery of basic services, strengthen institutional capacities and expand economic opportunities.

“We look forward to working with all partners to support a comprehensive and sustainable recovery path,” said Ousmane Dione, World Bank vice president for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Syria's transitional government has been racing to secure investment commitments to help rebuild the country's infrastructure. Some of those pledges have recently gone to the implementation phase, including DP World's $800 million towards Tartus Port.

The country has secured deals with its other Gulf partners, including a $2 billion Saudi Arabian investment package to develop two airports in Aleppo, as well as other projects involving energy, real estate and telecommunications.

At this week's gatherings in Thailand, Mr Barnieh also held discussions with Qatari Finance Minister Ali Al Kuwari on supporting recovery and development work, the state-run news agency Sana reported. Norway also expressed interest in contributing to the trust fund, Sana reported.

Qatar has also offered financing for projects to rehabilitate Syria's electricity grids, water networks, public services and the Damascus International Airport.

Baker Hughes, Caterpillar and Visa were among a delegation of about 50 US companies that visited Syria last month to explore and deepen economic ties, which came weeks after the US delisted Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism.

Syria will also return to the Arab group at the International Monetary Fund beginning on November 1, leaving the Russian-led group it joined in 2012, the Finance Ministry said in a post on Telegram.

The IMF restarted communications with Syria in 2025. The fund said in August it had agreed on a technical assistance programme for the country after a staff-level visit in July.

The IMF has not had an Article IV consultation with Syria since 2009.

TEHRAN, Oct. 18 (MNA) – The chairman of Iran’s Basij Voluntary Forces Organization Hossein Taeb says the United States miscalculated Iiranian nation’s resilience and the ability of its armed forces to sustain the battles.

Speaking at a meeting in Tehran on Sunday, Taeb said the United States and Israel had expected Iran to capitulate within days or weeks, but the Iranian nation and Armed Forces had stood firm.

“They thought that if they could not achieve their objectives in three days, Iran’s resilience in the war would last no more than six weeks,” Taeb said.

He said the US and Israel had expected Iran to run short of ammunition and missiles, face economic disruption and experience domestic security pressures, forcing it to negotiate from a position of weakness.

“Those assessments proved wrong,” Taeb said, adding that the United States and Israel had also faced limitations in ammunition supplies and air defense capabilities, including dwindling stocks of THAAD interceptor missiles.

Taeb said Iran’s missile operations had become increasingly effective as the war progressed, with a growing proportion of missiles reaching their intended targets in Israeli-occupied territories.

He added that the United States and Israel had sought a ceasefire through European and regional intermediaries, expecting Iran to make concessions in subsequent negotiations.

Taeb said Washington and Tel Aviv were then forced to shift their strategy from direct, full-scale warfare toward proxy forces, regional and international alliances, and economic pressure after Iran gained full control over the Strait of Hormuz.

He described the conflict as a contest of endurance, stressing that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz had also imposed significant costs on the US and global economies.

Citing polls, Taeb said more than 70% of Americans believed the war with Iran had brought their country no meaningful benefits while imposing heavy costs. He also pointed to rising diesel prices and transportation costs as factors increasing the economic burden on American households, adding that European countries were beginning to experience the consequences as well.

Taeb called on Iranians to support the Armed Forces and strengthen the country’s deterrence capabilities, warning that any renewed aggression would be met with an unpredictable response.

Nyasha Gwanzura had reduced India to 19/4 inside the powerplay with three wickets in the first six overs in the first T20I in Raipur on Friday. On Sunday, Zimbabwe were defending 12 runs fewer than Friday, with Gwanzura again expected to make an impact. But captain Smriti Mandhana and vice-captain Shafali Verma ensured there was no repeat of that stumble, powering India to a nine-wicket win and a 2-0 series win with one game left.

Chasing 103 runs for victory, Shafali set the early tone. She attacked the Zimbabwe bowlers from the word go, picking up boundaries when they offered width or missed their lengths. Her first six came when she whipped a full delivery from Gwanzura over deep mid-wicket, and she continued to put pressure on the spinner by using her feet.

Gwanzura, who had dismantled India’s top order in the first T20I, was taken apart in her third over. Mandhana hit four boundaries in a row before Shafali ended the 21-run over with a four to long-off.

Shafali was equally aggressive against Tendai Makusha. She slapped a fuller delivery outside off towards long-off for four and backed that with a mistimed six over long-off before smashing another short delivery through the off side for a boundary. By the end of the powerplay, India had raced to 76/0, their second-highest score in the first six overs of a women’s T20I.

The right-hander brought up her fifty from 24 balls by advancing down the wicket to launch Beloved Biza over deep mid-wicket. Next delivery, she again went for a big shot, but did not find the desired connection, holing out at long-on. Her 55 off 25 balls had given India the explosive start they needed.

Mandhana played the perfect supporting role. She was watchful early, allowing Shafali to take the attack to the bowlers, but began opening up once settled. Gwanzura was taken apart in the fourth over as Mandhana struck four boundaries, using her feet for one, pulling another through backward square leg and punching two more through the off side.

Zimbabwe’s bowlers struggled to find the right lengths once Shafali and Mandhana got going. Gwanzura, who had taken three wickets in the first game, went wicketless this time, conceding 42 runs in her three overs. It was a very different outing for the bowler who had caused India so much trouble on Friday.

The opening pair put on 96, with both playing their part in different ways. Shafali took the attack to the bowlers, while Mandhana rotated the strike and kept things moving at the other end. It was their 27th 50-plus stand together.

Mandhana then finished the chase with a six over long-off, staying unbeaten on 47 off 25 balls and sealing a commanding win.

Earlier, Niki Prasad, who had scored an unbeaten 39 in the first T20I, made an impact with the ball this time. The 20-year-old took two wickets with her first two international deliveries, dismissing Chipo Mugeri-Tiripano for 34 and then trapping Nyasha Gwanzura lbw to become the first Indian woman to take two wickets with the first two balls of her T20I career.

Prasad also made an impact in the field, taking a low catch at long-on to dismiss Michelle Mavunga off Sree Charani’s bowling.

Mugeri-Tiripano had given Zimbabwe something to build around after they reached only 20/2 in the powerplay. She used the sweep and reverse sweep effectively and made 34 off 32 balls, with five fours. Her 45-run stand with captain Josephine Nkomo was Zimbabwe’s best partnership before Prasad broke it.

India’s bowlers then kept the innings under control. Kranti Gaud finished with 1/15 from four overs, Deepti Sharma took 1/13 from three, while Nandani Sharma and Sree Charani claimed a wicket each. Nkomo tried to keep the innings moving after Mugeri-Tiripano’s dismissal but was eventually run out for 27.

Zimbabwe finished on 102/8, leaving India a modest target. This time, there was no scare. Shafali made sure of that from the outset, Mandhana steadied the chase, and India completed a comprehensive win with several balls to spare.

headline: Rubio arrives in Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
summary: By Gram Slattery and Simon LewisWASHINGTON, Oct 18 (Reuters) - While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights theHouthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.The top US diplomat landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet with top officials from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.
body_text:
By Gram Slattery and Simon Lewis

WASHINGTON, Oct 18 (Reuters) - While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights theHouthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.

The top US diplomat landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet with top officials from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia —the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors.

Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly in September of last year.

Regional politics aside, thetrip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign policyportfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys SteveWitkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance.

Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state and was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April.

Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland.

Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots.

Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment."

Speaking to reporters before leaving Washington on Saturday, Rubio said the timing of the Uzbekistan trip was dictated in part by the availability of the various delegations. He also said that foreign trips were too often designed to resolve immediate issues rather than build long-term relationships.

"I mean, one of the things that suffers is the strategic business," Rubio told reporters. "You're always visiting someplace where there's a crisis or there's a problem or ... you're going because there's a conference."

US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM

The delegation that greeted Rubio upon his arrival in Samarkand included Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov, whom Rubio embraced warmly. Two women in traditional Uzbek attire presented Rubio and his wife with bouquets.

One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region were wondering to what extent the US would continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say.

In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows.

But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month toimport Russian diesel, aimed at lowering domestic fuel prices before congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump waived all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude oil or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan.

India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia.

Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia.

A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip.

Separately, the US has talked to additional Central Asian nations aboutjoining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that potentially could continue in Samarkand.

More than 200 business executives are accompanyingRubioto Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources.

After Uzbekistan,Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago.

The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday.

(Reporting by Gram Slattery and Simon Lewis; Editing by Sergio Non, Rod Nickel and Edmund Klamann)

body_text:
Syria and the World Bank have agreed to set up a multi-donor trust fund for the country's recovery and reconstruction, the two sides announced in a joint statement on Sunday.

Damascus is continuing to rebuild after a civil war that lasted for more than a decade and had destroyed the country's infrastructure.

Interview:Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors

The Syria Recovery and Reconstruction Trust Fund – or “Start” – is a multi-donor fund that aims to provide concessional financing, investment guarantees and technical assistance, and build trust, the statement said.

The agreement comes after Syria took part in the International and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. The gatherings were the latest to be attended by Syrian officials since the fall of president Bashar Al Assad's regime in December 2024.

Syrian Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said the agreement helps to set the foundation for a new phase of co-operation with Damascus's international partners. Partners in the US, Europe and Middle East expressed their support for the initiative, the statement said.

“An important milestone in Syria’s recovery and reconstruction journey,” Mr Barnieh wrote in a post on X.

The World Bank in 2025 estimated Syria's reconstruction would cost about $216 billion, making it one of the most expensive rebuilding efforts in history. The World Bank classified this as its best “conservative” estimate.

The World Bank said infrastructure accounted for 48 per cent, or $52 billion, of total damage from the civil war, followed by residential buildings at $33 billion and non-residential buildings at $33 billion.

It said the multi-donor trust fund will help to support the delivery of basic services, strengthen institutional capacities and expand economic opportunities.

“We look forward to working with all partners to support a comprehensive and sustainable recovery path,” said Ousmane Dione, World Bank vice president for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

Syria's transitional government has been racing to secure investment commitments to help rebuild the country's infrastructure. Some of those pledges have recently gone to the implementation phase, including DP World's $800 million towards Tartus Port.

The country has secured deals with its other Gulf partners, including a $2 billion Saudi Arabian investment package to develop two airports in Aleppo, as well as other projects involving energy, real estate and telecommunications.

At this week's gatherings in Thailand, Mr Barnieh also held discussions with Qatari Finance Minister Ali Al Kuwari on supporting recovery and development work, the state-run news agency Sana reported. Norway also expressed interest in contributing to the trust fund, Sana reported.

Qatar has also offered financing for projects to rehabilitate Syria's electricity grids, water networks, public services and the Damascus International Airport.

Baker Hughes, Caterpillar and Visa were among a delegation of about 50 US companies that visited Syria last month to explore and deepen economic ties, which came weeks after the US delisted Syria as a state sponsor of terrorism.

Syria will also return to the Arab group at the International Monetary Fund beginning on November 1, leaving the Russian-led group it joined in 2012, the Finance Ministry said in a post on Telegram.

The IMF restarted communications with Syria in 2025. The fund said in August it had agreed on a technical assistance programme for the country after a staff-level visit in July.

The IMF has not had an Article IV consultation with Syria since 2009.

headline: Trump holds off on new measures against Russia to avoid undermining Ukraine peace talks
summary: US president says he does not want to take an action that would ‘drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table’
body_text:
US President Donald Trump said Sunday that he would not sign a document imposing additional measures on Russia for now, arguing that doing so could undermine negotiations to end the war in Ukraine.

“My decision on Russia is a very simple one,” he said in a post on his Truth Social platform, adding that he was negotiating peace between Russia and Ukraine and did not want to take an action that would “drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table.”

Trump said “great progress” was being made in the negotiations, including ongoing “hostage negotiations.”

He said he could sign the document at a later date or “any time” he wanted.

The president did not provide details about the negotiations or identify the hostages to whom he was referring.

Trump’s statement came amid controversy over his administration’s decision to delay the implementation of new sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia and countries purchasing Russian energy.

The measures, approved by Congress, include sanctions against Russian officials, banks and energy traders as well as the possibility of steep tariffs on countries that continue to import Russian oil and gas.

Trump also cited Russia’s limited support for Iran as a reason to avoid increasing pressure on Moscow.

“Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way,” he said.

He also sharply criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil and diesel refineries.

Trump said Zelenskyy was targeting Russian diesel facilities despite knowing that the attacks were “seriously hurting the world diesel markets,” including in the US.

He argued that farmers, ranchers and businesses were suffering from higher fuel costs while Russia was continuing to supply “millions of barrels” of diesel to international markets at low prices.

“Zelenskyy doesn’t care,” he said, accusing the Ukrainian leader of lacking an interest in ending the war.

Trump claimed that Zelenskyy could have secured a better agreement two years earlier and said Ukraine was now in ruins, had lost a large amount of territory and had suffered heavy casualties.

“I WANT THIS WAR END!” he added.

Trump has faced criticism from Kyiv and lawmakers in both major US parties over his approach to Russia, including the postponement of additional sanctions and Washington’s decision to authorize imports of Russian diesel.

Zelenskyy has argued that easing pressure on Moscow would encourage Russia to continue the war rather than bring it to an end.

Ukraine has defended its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure as a response to Moscow’s continuing strikes against Ukrainian power facilities and as an attempt to reduce revenue available for Russia’s military campaign.

Trump, however, has repeatedly called on Kyiv to stop targeting Russian refineries, arguing that the attacks are contributing to higher global energy prices.

CAIRO, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Regional military power Egypt is ready to provide Saudi Arabia with the support it needs to defend its security and stability, thepresidency said on Sunday,potentially raising the stakes in the Middle East war as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on the kingdom.

Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi requested an urgent parliament session to authorise the military, one of the Arab world's largest, to help defend its Gulf Arab ally if the kingdom requested its support.

A parliamentary vote had been expected on Sunday, but discussions were due to continue on Monday, two lawmakers and local media reports said.

Fighting between the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and theHouthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of the north, has escalated in recent weeks, becoming another front inthe US-Israeli war on Iran.

Any Egyptian military backing for Saudi Arabia could mark a major escalation in the wider Iran war, which has threatened global energy supplies and sentoil prices soaring since the US and Israel attacked the Islamic Republic in late February.

Hours after an announcement on further discussions by the parliament, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in a post on X that he discussed regional developments and the importance of de-escalation during a phone call with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan.

HOUTHIS RAMP UP ATTACKS ON SAUDI ARABIA

The Houthis have in recent days attacked Riyadh's international airport and the ​state oil company Saudi Aramco, amid renewed fighting with Saudi-backed forces. The Houthi advances threaten the strategic Bab el-Mandeb oil shipping route, following the collapse of a truce.

"Egypt will provide Saudi Arabia with all necessary and possible forms of support to defend its security and stability, protect its resources, territorial integrity and Islamic holy sites," the Egyptian presidency said in a statement.

The statement followed a meeting of Egypt's National Defence Council chaired by Sisi and attended by the parliamentary speaker, the prime minister and the army chief.

Sisi said in a speech on Saturday that Egypt would act in accordance with guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting in Yemen reignited.

If Egypt weighs in, it could face attacks by the Houthis, ragtag mountain fighters who have emerged as a deadly force of tens of thousands and whose missiles and drones threaten the region.

Arab countries, especially Gulf states hosting US bases, have faced repeated attacks by Iran and its allies, including the Houthis and pro-Iranian militias in Iraq, during the conflict.

Egypt's Mediterranean port of Damietta came under a drone attack in July with no group claiming responsibility. Egypt has not blamed any party for the attack but said it was taking necessary measures to protect the country's national security.

Egypt and ​Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi ​Arabia and ⁠other oil-rich Gulf states including the United Arab Emirates provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist President Mohamed⁠Morsi ​in 2013. Sisi became president a year later.

Egypt had previously joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis, but played a limited combat role in the civil war.

Riyadh has turned to regional allies and Pakistanafter it sought US President Donald Trump's help to fight the Houthis. Trump did not agree to US strikes, sources told Reuters last month. Washington instead offered targeting assistance and intelligence-sharing.

Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman visited Abu Dhabi on Sunday and met with UAE President Mohammed bin ​Zayed Al Nahyan, with talks focusing on regional security, according to the Emirati state news agency.

The talks followed a visit to Riyadh last month by UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the first trip by ‌a senior UAE official to the kingdom since a deep rift emerged between the two Gulf powers last year.

(Reporting by Momen Atallah and Mohamed Hendawy; Writing by Eman Abouhassira, Nayera Abdallah and Menna Alaa El-Din; Editing by Joe Bavier, Helen Popper and Michael Georgy)

headline: Trump refrains from saying whether he would work with another PM if Netanyahu loses polls
summary: The US president also commented on his recent endorsement of the Israeli prime minister
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 18. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump refrained from saying whether he could work with another Israeli prime minister should Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party fail at the upcoming parliamentary elections.

"Maybe I will, maybe I won't. Who wants to take the chance?" he told Axios, answering a corresponding question after stating his support for Netanyahu in a Truth Social post on Sunday.

"I was always going to do that. I just didn't want to do it too soon," he said, commenting on his endorsement of Netanyahu. According to Trump, he did this because they have a "good relationship" and would "continue to do well" together if Netanyahu is reelected.

This is the first time in the history of the US-Israel relations that a US president publicly supported a candidate in Israel’s elections, Axios noted. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work [in Iran] ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," it cited Trump’s Truth Social post.

In recent months, Trump has repeatedly refused to support Netanyahu amid growing strains between the two leaders over Iran and the Gaza Strip. Some of the prime minister’s rivals have called on the American leader to remain neutral. Apart from that, Trump’s advisers believed that his Middle East agenda would be implemented more successfully if Netanyahu lost, and a different government were formed in Israel.

According to the Israeli media, in private conversations, Trump accused Netanyahu of failing to prevent the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks. Trump called Netanyahu "his own worst enemy," claiming that Netanyahu was damaging Israel’s international reputation.

headline: Canadian military base fire kills at least four, injures dozens
summary: Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people hospitalised after a fire broke out during military training at a base in Alberta on Saturday, officials said. Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that at least 19 patients were in critical condition, with some suffering severe burns requiring prolonged intensive treatment.
body_text:
Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 people hospitalised after a fire broke out during military training at a base in Alberta on Saturday, officials said. Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that at least 19 patients were in critical condition, with some suffering severe burns requiring prolonged intensive treatment.

Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 00:16

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that 39 people were hospitalised, including at least 19 in critical condition, after a deadly fire at a Canadian military base.

Smith said patients were transferred from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright to four hospitals across Alberta. She said some suffered severe burns and could face weeks or months of intensive treatment.

Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier confirmed that four service members were killed in the fire, which broke out Saturday during military training, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil.

Fire crews scrambled late Saturday as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area. The Canadian military said Sunday there were no indications that the incident was the result of terrorism, but the cause remained under investigation.

Speaking in a televised address, Carney said the families of those killed had been notified and that the situation was still evolving.

Carney said the service members killed and injured were participating in military training when the fire broke out Saturday.

Read moreEU and Canada seek closer ties: Will Canada become the EU's first associate member?

Flags would fly at half-staff on federal buildings across the country in honor of those affected by the tragedy, he said.

Carney said those affected included reservists and soldiers from Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, one of Canada’s most storied military regiments. The personnel had come from bases across the country to train at Wainwright.

It was not immediately clear exactly how many people had been injured. Alberta health officials said patients from Wainwright had been transferred to four hospitals — two in Edmonton, one in Red Deer and one in Calgary.

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Ontario, said her eldest son was among the military personnel critically injured. “As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote on Facebook, saying she was traveling to Alberta.

A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 kilometers (112 miles) northwest, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were taken to hospitals across the city as healthcare facilities around the base became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care.

“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15- to 25-year disaster.”

Alberta health officials said Sunday they had ended the “Code Orange” emergency activated at several hospitals after the fire. The designation allows hospitals to mobilize staff and free up beds to handle large numbers of seriously injured patients.

Read moreQuebec votes as separatist surge poses test for Canada PM

The province said the response involved 22 ground ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters, with assistance from neighboring Saskatchewan.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s small hospital was not designed to handle a mass-casualty incident but praised the response of local medical personnel. He said helicopters and planes had been transporting patients to other facilities for treatment.

Pugh said military medical personnel parachuted into Wainwright shortly before midnight, their red parachutes illuminated by flares, as reinforcements arrived to help respond to the disaster.

At least 10 ambulances were parked in and around the Wainwright health center late Saturday as paramedics and soldiers rushed about. One patient was seen being loaded into an ambulance.

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as “very, very active and delicate.” He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.

McGuinty said Sunday he was traveling to Edmonton to be briefed on the latest developments. He said the military was working closely with Alberta’s government and local authorities.

The Canadian Armed Forces had said it would not release casualty figures until relatives were notified. Carney said Sunday that the families of the four service members killed had been informed.

Read moreMacron, Carney hail new chapter in France-Canada ties at symbolic archipelago meeting

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kph (62 mph). The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.

McGuinty, speaking to reporters in Ottawa, confirmed the casualties but had no other details to share.

“I cannot recall such an incident in my short time for sure as a minister, but I cannot recall an incident like this in recent memory,” McGuinty said.

“We will have more to say in the coming hours and days,” he added.

He said Armed Forces members were at the scene and that RCMP were also involved. “This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.

She said Alberta had convened its emergency management cabinet committee to coordinate the response.

Carney praised emergency crews who battled the fire through the night and said STARS air ambulance helicopters had flown in from Edmonton and Saskatoon.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Maneuver Training Center, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said the advance polling location at Wainwright Communiplex closed early Saturday and ballots and election materials were transported securely. It identified polling locations in Lloydminster and Vermilion as alternatives.

headline: 4 killed, dozens seriously injured in fire at Canadian military base
summary: 39 people hospitalized, at least 19 in critical condition, after blaze erupts at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta
body_text:
At least four people were killed and dozens seriously injured after a fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian military base in Alberta, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday, describing the incident as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for the country's armed forces.

“I regret that I can confirm at this time that Forest Service members have lost their lives and their next of kin have been notified. Dozens more are seriously wounded,” Carney told reporters.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said 39 people were hospitalized, with at least 19 in critical condition.

Speaking at a news conference Sunday afternoon, Smith said the patients had been transferred to four hospitals across Alberta and all had been accounted for.

During the news conference, Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland said base officials had been aware of the fire for several hours, but “uncommonly strong winds” caused it to “spread rapidly” and change direction towards an administrative area of the training range.

“The fire was a kilometer away when the wind shifted. It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometer in 30 to 60 seconds,” he said.

The blaze broke out Saturday afternoon at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, about 200 kilometers (124 miles) southeast of Edmonton, spreading beyond a training area as strong winds hampered firefighting efforts.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta,” Carney said. “What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

Defense Minister David McGuinty confirmed that the incident caused casualties but withheld figures, describing the situation as “active and delicate.”

The Canadian Armed Forces said the fire was first reported around 4 pm local time (2200GMT) on a training range before spreading beyond its boundaries. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating while military and civilian authorities coordinate the response.

Carney said military personnel and civilian crews battled the blaze throughout the night, while air ambulance crews flew in from Edmonton and Saskatoon to assist the injured.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces we have lost,” he said, adding that flags on federal buildings would be flown at half-mast.

Alberta Premier Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic,” while Gen. Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defense Staff of the Canadian Armed Forces, said the military was working closely with authorities to support those affected.

Carney pledged long-term support for victims and their families.

“We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss,” he said. “They will not carry it alone.”

headline: S. Korea's growth could exceed IMF projection: finance minister
summary: BANGKOK, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's economic growth could exceed projecti...
body_text:
BANGKOK, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- South Korea's economic growth could exceed projections by international organizations, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), barring unexpected external shocks, the finance minister has said, citing robust exports and facility investment data.

Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il made the assessment during a meeting with reporters in Bangkok on Friday. He visited Thailand to attend the Annual Meetings of the IMF and the World Bank Group last week, marking his first participation in a major international event since taking office last month.

His remarks came after the IMF projected South Korea's economy would grow 3.3 percent this year, raising its forecast by 0.7 percentage point from its July projection amid the global semiconductor supercycle.

"I believe exports and facility investment remained robust in the third quarter," the minister said.

"If that is the case, we think growth could exceed the 3.3 percent projected by the IMF," Lee said. "Barring new external events that significantly impact the economy, I think even the mid-3 percent range could be possible."

Lee later hinted that the mid-3 percent range would cover figures from 3.4 percent to 3.6 percent.

The finance minister said South Korea's economy grew 1.8 percent and 0.6 percent in the first and second quarters, respectively, noting annual growth could exceed expectations if the momentum continued into the third quarter, for which signs were already positive.

Lee added the country's potential growth rate could soon rebound.

"Given recent growth trends and the composition of growth, I believe our potential growth rate could reverse its downward trend and rebound," Lee said. "That turning point is approaching and may even be imminent."

The potential growth rate refers to the potential rate of increase in the GDP a country can sustain by fully utilizing labor, capital and other resources without triggering inflation.

Lee said officials he met during the event, including representatives of credit rating agencies and multilateral development banks, offered positive assessments of South Korea's robust economic growth amid the country's strong chip exports.

"We exchanged views on the South Korean economy with officials from various countries," Lee said.

"Most agreed when I said growth might not be sustainable without addressing disparities and that I intended to focus on the issue," Lee said.

The finance minister said those he met noted how much progress South Korea makes in addressing disparities would depend on the government's efforts, but its attention to the issue itself could help sustain growth momentum.

When asked to identify a specific area of focus in addressing disparities, the finance minister said all sectors are closely linked, making the issue difficult to resolve.

"To tackle these challenges, we are seeking to implement social policies in three key areas, namely housing, jobs and financial services for vulnerable groups, which would likely cover most issues," Lee said.

The finance minister particularly stressed the need to address disparities in the job market, as they are linked to income gaps and disparities across regions and businesses.

In addition, Lee said he is considering increasing the frequency of the government's economic forecasts from twice to three times a year, with an annual outlook at year-end followed by two updates.

"With the economy moving so quickly, I am contemplating whether issuing two projections a year is appropriate under the circumstances," Lee said, noting the ministry could provide one additional update each year.

"If I still hold this view at the end of the year, I think we may stop issuing an economic growth strategy report specifically for the second half of the year starting next year," he said.

headline: What does a White House press secretary do?
summary: Katie Zacharia's short time as White House press secretary has brought renewed attention to the high-profile role.(Image credit: Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
body_text:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia speaks with reporters in the James Brady Press Briefing Room at the White House, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Washington. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption

The White House press secretary is one of the most important public-facing jobs in any administration. Yet it is one with no job description, no required qualifications, no vetting by Congress. And as the most recent press secretary found out, you can be fired from the position just as quickly as you were hired.

For nearly 100 years, since the rise of a modern press corp, there has been a person designated to speak on behalf of the sitting U.S. president. But the press secretary also answers to the public, says former Pentagon Press Secretary John Kirby. He served during both the Obama and Biden administrations.

"You are expected to be the president's voice and sometimes the president's face on issues on a daily basis, which means you have to have access to the president," Kirby told NPR's Ayesha Roscoe on Weekend Edition Sunday. "You have to know what the president's thinking about, whatever the policy issue is, but you also are accountable to the American people."

Kirby said that a press secretary's job is to "be honest" and tell Americans as much and as quickly as possible while also taking tough questions from the press.

This is where Katie Zacharia, who was fired last week, ran into trouble. Just two days into the job she faced scrutiny over how she handled questions from reporters during her first briefing. Zacharia was visibly nervous, she took only a handful of questions and she largely stuck to a script of talking points.

But it was describing herself as a lawyer that earned her the extra scrutiny. It was eventually revealed that Zacharia had failed the California bar exam, which meant that she was not an attorney. Five days after starting the job, she was out.

Press secretaries are not required to be attorneys but they do have to be able to hold their own with reporters. Sean Spicer – one of several White House press secretaries during Trump's first administration – had a combative relationship with the press.

Spicer regularly sparred with members of the media. He gained notoriety (while being challenged him about the size of the crowds at Trump's inauguration) when he told reporters, "sometimes we can disagree with the facts."

NBC's "Saturday Night Live" took particular glee in Spicer's animosity toward the press. Actor Melissa McCarthy, who portrayed Spicer, mimicked their contentious interactions with such lines as "I came out here to punch you in the face."

The role is not one designated by Congress but it does follow nearly 100 years of presidential custom and tradition.

According to the White House Historical Association by the late 1800s, reporters were beginning to cover the White House as part of a regular beat. In 1929, President Herbert Hoover appointed the journalist George Akerson to speak on his behalf. Akerson is regarded as the first official White House press secretary.

Since then, 37 people have held the role. In 1993, Dee Dee Myers became the first woman press secretary. Karine Jean-Pierre in 2022 made history as the first Black press secretary in White House as well as the first openly gay person in the role.

While traveling with then-President Ronald Reagan in 1981, White House press secretary James Brady was shot during an assassination attempt on the president. The briefing room where press secretaries stand behind the podium and take questions from reporters is named after Brady.

A briefing is like "intellectual chess," former White House press secretary Ari Fleischer under George W. Bush previously told NPR. He said the hardest part of the job is knowing what not to say.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

headline: Lavrov to outline Russia’s de-escalation efforts during visit to Iran
summary: The parties will pay significant attention to practical measures aimed at strengthening comprehensive strategic partnership
body_text:
TEHRAN, October 19. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will outline the steps Moscow is taking to de-escalate regional tensions created by the United States and Israel during a visit to Iran.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will receive the top Russian diplomat. The parties will pay significant attention to practical measures aimed at strengthening comprehensive strategic partnership between the two countries. Lavrov is also expected to brief the Iranian side on the outcome of his meetings with officials from Gulf Cooperation Council member states in Manama.

The conflict with Iran, provoked by the United States, is causing growing concern worldwide, particularly amid a rapid rise in oil prices and mounting energy logistics difficulties stemming from shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.

According to Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov, the conflict has entered a chronic phase, with "regular outbreaks of active hostilities" bringing areas of instability dangerously close to the borders of the organization's member states. Masadykov expressed grave concern over US strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities subject to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) safeguards.

Moreover, US media outlets have reported, citing American officials, that Washington has drawn up plans to strike Iran’s energy infrastructure and nuclear sites using its most powerful non-nuclear bomb. Tehran has already stated that any US attacks on Iranian energy infrastructure would not go unanswered.

The prolonged confrontation between the US and Iran is further aggravating the global fuel crisis. Fuel prices have soared amid a decline in tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for delivering oil and petroleum products to global markets.

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko expressed hope that Russian diesel supplies based on an agreement reached by Moscow and Washington would calm fuel markets and stabilize prices. However, experts point out that the global crisis is unlikely to ease until the situation in the Strait of Hormuz is resolved.

Meanwhile, Iranian Army Spokesperson Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia said that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen to shipping after "US forces withdraw from the Persian Gulf."

A crisis of confidence between the parties to the conflict is making the situation worse. Tehran’s Ambassador to Moscow Kazem Jalali noted earlier that the United States had on several occasions attacked Iran in the midst of negotiations.

headline: S. Korea to send delegation to Kazakhstan for water industry cooperation
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- South Korea will send a delegation to Kazakhstan to e...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- South Korea will send a delegation to Kazakhstan to expand bilateral cooperation in the water industry and support Korean companies seeking to enter the Kazakh market, the foreign ministry said Monday.

The public-private delegation will include officials from the foreign and energy ministries, nine Korean water companies and representatives from relevant state-run entities, according to the ministry.

During their three-day visit through Wednesday, the delegation will meet with major Kazakh water management agencies to discuss technological cooperation, visit water and wastewater treatment facilities and review ongoing pilot projects to identify new business opportunities.

The two nations have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on smart water management technologies and pursued pilot projects involving Korean water industry products and technologies.

"We will continue expanding water industry cooperation with Kazakhstan by matching its water management needs with advanced technologies from Korean companies," the ministry said in a release.

headline: Putin proposes trilateral summit with Trump and Xi to discuss Ukraine: Report
summary: Proposed meeting could take place on sidelines of APEC summit in China, according to people familiar with discussions
body_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a trilateral meeting next month with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss the war in Ukraine and seek an end to the conflict on terms favorable to Moscow, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Putin raised the proposal during an Oct. 9 phone call with Trump, according to a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter, the newspaper said.

The call also resulted in an agreement for the US to purchase Russian diesel fuel and facilitate its sale on the global market, the report said.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions were underway regarding a possible meeting.

“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told the Journal.

A senior US official said Trump had not agreed to the proposed summit but could be open to the idea, given his desire to fulfill his campaign pledge to end the war.

According to people familiar with the discussions, the Kremlin has proposed holding the trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, scheduled for Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen, China.

Russian officials raised the proposal with Beijing through diplomatic channels, and China indicated that it would not oppose the idea if Trump agreed, according to people familiar with recent discussions between Moscow and Beijing.

The former Russian intelligence officer said Putin had previously proposed holding a trilateral summit with Trump and Xi on several occasions.

Trump recently reached a deal with Putin to buy Russian diesel fuel in an effort to lower fuel prices, which have weighed on the US economy and hurt Republican prospects ahead of midterm elections.

On Friday, Trump also suspended the implementation of sanctions against Russia under a bipartisan bill he signed last month.

The former intelligence officer said Putin had ambitious though potentially unrealistic goals for the trilateral format, envisioning it as a second Yalta summit that would divide the world into spheres of influence.

Some people familiar with the discussions said Chinese officials were concerned that such a geopolitical sideshow could overshadow Beijing’s plans to use the APEC summit to highlight China’s role in the region.

Xi is seeking to balance continued support for Putin with the need to maintain China’s economic ties with Europe, the people said.

headline: N. Korea touts 'invincible' comradeship with Russia at diplomatic event
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- North Korea has reaffirmed its commitment to deepenin...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 19 (Yonhap) -- North Korea has reaffirmed its commitment to deepening relations with Russia at a diplomatic event, calling its ties with Moscow an "invincible" comradeship, Pyongyang's state media reported Monday.

The North Korean Embassy in Russia hosted a reception marking the 78th anniversary of forming diplomatic relations between the two nations last Tuesday, the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) said.

The event was attended by Alexander Kozlov, Russia's minister of natural resources and chair of the North Korea-Russia Intergovernmental Committee for Cooperation in Trade, Economy and Science, along with other Russian government and party officials.

North Korean Ambassador to Russia Sin Hong-chol said the bilateral ties have developed at an unprecedented level through the "most truthful" relations forged between North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Shin said the meeting between their leaders in 2024 has upgraded bilateral ties into a comprehensive strategic partnership and leaped toward "invincible comradely-in-arms relations," according to the KCNA.

In response, Kozlov said the comprehensive strategic partnership treaty signed between Kim and Putin in June 2024 reflects the shared commitment of Pyongyang and Moscow for "respect, trust and common prosperity."

North Korea and Russia signed the mutual defense treaty in 2024, which includes a provision committing both nations to mutual military assistance in the event of an attack on either side.

Russian Ambassador to North Korea Andrey Podelyshev hosted a reception to mark the 78th anniversary of diplomatic relations Wednesday, according to a separate KCNA report.

headline: Rana Begum comes full circle with Taking Form, a colourful new exhibition in Dubai
summary: Two swabs of colour meet at the corners.An orange, bold and of a sunset hue, is overtaken by a smear of forest green. The two colours don’t mix, making how they interact all the more remarkable. The original vivacity of the orange is subdued underneath the green, with only a dark trace of its outline remaining.Like the rest of the watercolour works in Rana Begum’s exhibition at The Third Line, the piece shows us that not all colours are equal. The shade of green that overpowers the orange finds its match in another work against a deep, royal purple. In yet another piece, that same purple runs across a luminescent yellow, affecting and being affected by the colour just the same. Elsewhere, trio of pinks are chained together, revealing deeper hues that veer towards orange.Much like the law of the jungle favours the strong, there is a law of colours that is often only revealed upon application. The nature of the pigment, as well as the material on which it is applied all play a part, as does, of course, the bias of the eye.Begum tests these interactions across various mediums in Taking Form. The watercolours are the smallest pieces in the exhibition. Yet, they offer a key into how to view the other, more monumental pieces within the show.“I felt the show needed these works on paper,” Begum tells The National. “I’ve been thinking about the tapestries, about the paintings for a while. But it’s all kind of in my head, and I wanted to express that fluidity and the way I have been thinking about colour.”The centrepiece of the exhibition is a trio of tapestry pieces, suspended from the high ceiling of the gallery. Much like the watercolours, they express an interplay of colours. The technical aspects of the weaving is stunning. Dark indigo threads run long against pyramids of colour of varying shades of blue and burgundy. The common threads are inconspicuous when viewed from a short distance. Up close, the commonality blooms.It is a different interplay of colour than the ones on the watercolours, alluding less to jungle laws than to a more cohesive interaction between the hues.“It took me a whole to figure out how the colours would interact,” Begum says. “The piece, in the front, you see ridges. You stand on the left side, you see one colour that stands out more, and as you walk around to the right, you see another.”The reverse side of the tapestries, rather than showing the needlework of the piece, exhibits a pattern of its own. This required some experimentation, Begum says.“The weaving technique is really interesting and fascinating how that works,” she says. “I worked with a UK-based company Dash & Miller that designed the weave. They were able to come up with the ridges.“We had to identify a different set of rules for the back. You could have just two colours or more, but it just can't be the same as what's at the front. The two sides are woven as one. There is a front, middle and back – but even on the back, you see some of the front seeping through. The process is really interesting.”The paintings within taking form continue these explorations of colour on linen canvases as well as medium-density fibreboard. Here, Begum lets the colour accentuate the properties of the materials they are applied on. The chips and straws of the fibreboard are highlighted in shades of pink. The linen’s tufts, meanwhile, are all the more heightened in colourful square triangle compositions.Given her fluidity in testing colour interactions, it is surprising to hear Begum say that she “struggled with colour” when she first began delving into abstraction as an artist, veering away from her early, figurative works.“I really struggled with colour. I felt like I was kind of living and breathing colour, from the culture that I come from growing up, partly in Bangladesh, wearing saris and salwar kameez, constantly surrounded by colour. You’d think I’d be very confident, but actually, I really struggled when I went into abstraction. I had a long list of things that I needed to explore, and one of those things was colour.”Her first solo exhibition, Colour Codes, which was held at The Third Line in 2007, was informed by these interactions. “I used that opportunity to kind of really focus on colour and relationship with one another,” she says. Begum used various kinds of adhesive tape that she had collected from around the world, applying them in lines and coating them with resin to test colour interactions.“That material gave me the opportunity to be more instinctive. I could peel the tape off and apply another colour. You could see things happening quite fast.”Almost two decades later, and Begum is now marking her fifth exhibition at The Third Line with Taking Form. She returns as a globally-established artist – Begum is the winner of the 2017 Abraaj Group Art Prize, as well as a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.Taking Form, as such, represents the continuing experiments of Begum’s long-standing fascination with colour. The artist calls her fifth exhibition at The Third Line a “full circle” moment, but much like the circle of the archetypal hero’s journey, Begum returns as an artist changed, more confident and certain with how she conducts her experiments, displaying a mastery over the colours that once unnerved her.Rana Begum's exhibition Taking Form is on at The Third Line until November 10

Two swabs of colour meet at the corners.

An orange, bold and of a sunset hue, is overtaken by a smear of forest green. The two colours don’t mix, making how they interact all the more remarkable. The original vivacity of the orange is subdued underneath the green, with only a dark trace of its outline remaining.

Like the rest of the watercolour works in Rana Begum’s exhibition at The Third Line, the piece shows us that not all colours are equal. The shade of green that overpowers the orange finds its match in another work against a deep, royal purple. In yet another piece, that same purple runs across a luminescent yellow, affecting and being affected by the colour just the same. Elsewhere, trio of pinks are chained together, revealing deeper hues that veer towards orange.

Much like the law of the jungle favours the strong, there is a law of colours that is often only revealed upon application. The nature of the pigment, as well as the material on which it is applied all play a part, as does, of course, the bias of the eye.

Begum tests these interactions across various mediums in Taking Form. The watercolours are the smallest pieces in the exhibition. Yet, they offer a key into how to view the other, more monumental pieces within the show.

“I felt the show needed these works on paper,” Begum tells The National. “I’ve been thinking about the tapestries, about the paintings for a while. But it’s all kind of in my head, and I wanted to express that fluidity and the way I have been thinking about colour.”

The centrepiece of the exhibition is a trio of tapestry pieces, suspended from the high ceiling of the gallery. Much like the watercolours, they express an interplay of colours. The technical aspects of the weaving is stunning. Dark indigo threads run long against pyramids of colour of varying shades of blue and burgundy. The common threads are inconspicuous when viewed from a short distance. Up close, the commonality blooms.

It is a different interplay of colour than the ones on the watercolours, alluding less to jungle laws than to a more cohesive interaction between the hues.

“It took me a whole to figure out how the colours would interact,” Begum says. “The piece, in the front, you see ridges. You stand on the left side, you see one colour that stands out more, and as you walk around to the right, you see another.”

The reverse side of the tapestries, rather than showing the needlework of the piece, exhibits a pattern of its own. This required some experimentation, Begum says.

“The weaving technique is really interesting and fascinating how that works,” she says. “I worked with a UK-based company Dash & Miller that designed the weave. They were able to come up with the ridges.

“We had to identify a different set of rules for the back. You could have just two colours or more, but it just can't be the same as what's at the front. The two sides are woven as one. There is a front, middle and back – but even on the back, you see some of the front seeping through. The process is really interesting.”

The paintings within taking form continue these explorations of colour on linen canvases as well as medium-density fibreboard. Here, Begum lets the colour accentuate the properties of the materials they are applied on. The chips and straws of the fibreboard are highlighted in shades of pink. The linen’s tufts, meanwhile, are all the more heightened in colourful square triangle compositions.

Given her fluidity in testing colour interactions, it is surprising to hear Begum say that she “struggled with colour” when she first began delving into abstraction as an artist, veering away from her early, figurative works.

“I really struggled with colour. I felt like I was kind of living and breathing colour, from the culture that I come from growing up, partly in Bangladesh, wearing saris and salwar kameez, constantly surrounded by colour. You’d think I’d be very confident, but actually, I really struggled when I went into abstraction. I had a long list of things that I needed to explore, and one of those things was colour.”

Her first solo exhibition, Colour Codes, which was held at The Third Line in 2007, was informed by these interactions. “I used that opportunity to kind of really focus on colour and relationship with one another,” she says. Begum used various kinds of adhesive tape that she had collected from around the world, applying them in lines and coating them with resin to test colour interactions.

“That material gave me the opportunity to be more instinctive. I could peel the tape off and apply another colour. You could see things happening quite fast.”

Almost two decades later, and Begum is now marking her fifth exhibition at The Third Line with Taking Form. She returns as a globally-established artist – Begum is the winner of the 2017 Abraaj Group Art Prize, as well as a member of the Royal Academy of Arts.

Taking Form, as such, represents the continuing experiments of Begum’s long-standing fascination with colour. The artist calls her fifth exhibition at The Third Line a “full circle” moment, but much like the circle of the archetypal hero’s journey, Begum returns as an artist changed, more confident and certain with how she conducts her experiments, displaying a mastery over the colours that once unnerved her.

Rana Begum's exhibition Taking Form is on at The Third Line until November 10

headline: Oman could become a cornerstone of Gulf energy security, but risks remain
summary: In its heyday, Oman’s maritime empire stretched from Mozambique and Zanzibar to Gwadar in Pakistan. The modern sultanate does not extend so far, but it still holds an important position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has gained economically from the conflict, while seeking to mediate peace. Now it could make itself a foundation stone of Gulf security.The war has forced the IMF to downgrade economic growth forecasts across the region. But Oman is expected to expand by 4.1 per cent. It has managed to bring down its debt burden from a worrying 68 per cent of GDP in 2020 to a much more comfortable 35 to 36 per cent of GDP.The sultanate benefits from record oil and gas exports at a time of high prices, as well as from the rest of its heavy industrial base in refined petroleum, fertilisers and aluminium. The endless queues of lorries to and from the UAE border tell eloquently of Oman’s essential role as a transit route for goods.In May 2024, in a fortunate piece of advance planning, construction began on Hafeet Rail, which will link the industrial city of Sohar with Al Ain and Abu Dhabi. This is intended to be finished by the final quarter of 2027 and will be an invaluable route for industrial inputs to the UAE and for the export of finished products such as steel and aluminium.By late next year, Oman should also finish a direct connection to the GCC electricity grid, allowing it to exchange more power. This will benefit its fast-growing renewable sector.Oman has not stayed entirely out of the front line during the war. The oil terminals of Mina Al Fahal, Duqm and Salalah, and Sohar were attacked by drones, and several ships have been struck in its mainland waters, not to mention all those hit while crossing the Omani lane of the Strait of Hormuz. But the sultanate has suffered much less physical damage and disruption than its Gulf neighbours.New energy routesIn 2016, the oil minister at the time, Mohammed Al Rumhi announced plans for an enormous 200-million barrel petroleum storage terminal at Duqm on its south-east coast. By comparison, Fujairah, which has also emerged as a strategic node during the war and is a central global refuelling point, has about 120 million barrels of capacity. Muscat’s intention was to reorient its crude oil exports from the crowded northern coast to a new terminal, which would also have the happy effect of shifting them further from Iran.It also had in mind that other GCC nations might connect to Duqm, to give themselves an option in case of a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait, which has no alternative outlet, was said to be interested. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation eventually invested in the major new refinery there. But it seemed far-fetched that a new pipeline route would be needed. Eventually only 5.2 million barrels of crude storage were built, mostly to serve the refinery.Drones, missiles, and Washington’s decision to confront Tehran on the battlefield changed that. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman wisely pointed out that successful multinational pipelines require stakeholders from all sides. body_text:
In its heyday, Oman’s maritime empire stretched from Mozambique and Zanzibar to Gwadar in Pakistan. The modern sultanate does not extend so far, but it still holds an important position overlooking the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has gained economically from the conflict, while seeking to mediate peace. Now it could make itself a foundation stone of Gulf security.

The war has forced the IMF to downgrade economic growth forecasts across the region. But Oman is expected to expand by 4.1 per cent. It has managed to bring down its debt burden from a worrying 68 per cent of GDP in 2020 to a much more comfortable 35 to 36 per cent of GDP.

The sultanate benefits from record oil and gas exports at a time of high prices, as well as from the rest of its heavy industrial base in refined petroleum, fertilisers and aluminium. The endless queues of lorries to and from the UAE border tell eloquently of Oman’s essential role as a transit route for goods.

In May 2024, in a fortunate piece of advance planning, construction began on Hafeet Rail, which will link the industrial city of Sohar with Al Ain and Abu Dhabi. This is intended to be finished by the final quarter of 2027 and will be an invaluable route for industrial inputs to the UAE and for the export of finished products such as steel and aluminium.

By late next year, Oman should also finish a direct connection to the GCC electricity grid, allowing it to exchange more power. This will benefit its fast-growing renewable sector.

Oman has not stayed entirely out of the front line during the war. The oil terminals of Mina Al Fahal, Duqm and Salalah, and Sohar were attacked by drones, and several ships have been struck in its mainland waters, not to mention all those hit while crossing the Omani lane of the Strait of Hormuz. But the sultanate has suffered much less physical damage and disruption than its Gulf neighbours.

In 2016, the oil minister at the time, Mohammed Al Rumhi announced plans for an enormous 200-million barrel petroleum storage terminal at Duqm on its south-east coast. By comparison, Fujairah, which has also emerged as a strategic node during the war and is a central global refuelling point, has about 120 million barrels of capacity. Muscat’s intention was to reorient its crude oil exports from the crowded northern coast to a new terminal, which would also have the happy effect of shifting them further from Iran.

It also had in mind that other GCC nations might connect to Duqm, to give themselves an option in case of a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait, which has no alternative outlet, was said to be interested. Kuwait Petroleum Corporation eventually invested in the major new refinery there. But it seemed far-fetched that a new pipeline route would be needed. Eventually only 5.2 million barrels of crude storage were built, mostly to serve the refinery.

Drones, missiles, and Washington’s decision to confront Tehran on the battlefield changed that. Now Saudi Aramco is studying a pipeline to Duqm, estimated to span 1,000 to 1,200 kilometres through the dunes of the Empty Quarter, and expected to cost $7 billion. This new node has the advantage of bypassing not just Hormuz, but also the Bab Al Mandeb strait. Saudi exports through the kingdom's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu have been hampered by attacks from the Houthis in Yemen and Iranian allies in Iraq.

A Kuwait Oil Company representative told the World Energy Congress in Riyadh last week that his country was evaluating a possible route to Duqm, as well as through the UAE or Saudi Arabia. This would most probably involve delivering oil by tanker to a Saudi or UAE port for onward transport, rather than transporting it all the way overland.

State energy investor OQ has announced plans to expand Duqm’s storage to 10 million barrels within three years, and eventually 40 million barrels. It is also considering buying two tankers to hold 4 million barrels in floating storage.

In September, it signed an agreement with a German company to design a new marine bunkering site at the port of Shinas, just south of the UAE border. This would be about a third the size of Fujairah, which ranks as the world’s second or third-largest ship refuelling hub.

Nevertheless, Oman’s centrality to the Gulf’s new infrastructure carries three risks. First, its sites are not much further from Iran than the rest of the Gulf is, and can still be attacked if hostilities escalate. Indeed, Muscat might even put itself in the line of fire if Tehran decides it cannot tolerate too much by-passing of the totemic Strait of Hormuz.

The second is almost the opposite: if peace breaks out, much of this infrastructure might seem unnecessary. New pipelines will take from three to five years to build. By then, regional politics and security may look very different. Projects may be terminated halfway through, or left little-used. Oman does not have the deep pockets of its neighbours, who are able to invest heavily in strategic security.

Third is that many of these projects are clearly competing with existing Gulf terminals. There is already some disquiet over Muscat’s apparent closeness to Tehran at times during its mediation. Most notably, this surfaced in the debate over tolls for use of the Strait, or essentially Iranian extortion.

The other Gulf nations have suffered and spent heavily in the conflict. Of course, they want to leverage Oman’s strategic depth. But they do not want to make obsolete their own decades of massive investment in centres such as Fujairah, Jebel Ali and Yanbu, and new projects at sites such as Khor Fakkan, Al Rugaylat and Dibba.

Past such ventures across Iraq, Syria, Turkey and Saudi Arabia have suffered from sabotage, nationalisation, or commercial breakdowns. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman wisely pointed out that successful multinational pipelines require stakeholders from all sides. Tying Gulf security to Oman needs not only sinews of steel, but political harmony.

headline: Russia, US, China acknowledge possibility of trilateral meeting — Kremlin spokesman
summary: Dmitry Peskov noted that there is no clear understanding yet regarding the potential agenda of the meeting
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Russia, the United States and China acknowledge the possibility of a trilateral meeting, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told The Wall Street Journal.

"There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place," he said.

Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a plenary session of the Valdai Discussion Club that the possibility of a trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, the US and China on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit largely depended on the host party. It’s always useful to meet and exchange views, he stressed.

Peskov clarified later that no meeting had been agreed on, but that if all three leaders attended the APEC summit in China, the possibility of holding such a meeting would be discussed.

headline: US Embassy in UAE urges Americans in Middle East to exercise ‘heightened vigilance’
summary: Embassy warns of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions, citing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, risk of further escalation
body_text:
The US Embassy in the United Arab Emirates issued a security alert warning Americans in the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance amid a complex security environment, citing potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions.

It said Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi group had carried out attacks against Saudi Arabia including strikes on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure that caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions.

“The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area,” the statement said.

The embassy urged Americans traveling to or from the Middle East to monitor airport and airline operations and prepare contingency plans in advance.

“Iran and groups supportive of Iran may target other US interests overseas or at locations associated with the United States and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions,” the statement said.
