headline: Africa: Africa CDC Reaffirms Support to Kenya Following Confirmation of Four Additional Ebola Cases
summary: [Africa CDC] Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 17 October 2026
body_text:
Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, 17 October 2026

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) acknowledges the announcement by the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Kenya confirming four additional cases of Ebola Virus Disease (Bundibugyo virus), bringing the total number of confirmed cases in the country to seven, including one death.

According to the Ministry of Health, all four new cases were detected among individuals already under quarantine following exposure to the initial case. They include three healthcare workers and one family member. All four individuals are receiving supportive care at a designated treatment facility. Their early identification demonstrates the critical role of contact tracing, surveillance and timely isolation in interrupting transmission and protecting communities.

Africa CDC commends the Government of Kenya, through its Ministry of Health and national public health institutions, for its leadership, swift public health measures and transparent communication throughout the response.

Kenyan authorities report that 128 of the 130 identified contacts (98.5%) have been traced and placed under quarantine, with efforts ongoing to locate the remaining two. The Ministry has reported no evidence of community transmission at this stage.

Africa CDC continues to work alongside the Government of Kenya and its partners in support of the nationally led response, with particular attention to surveillance, technical coordination, risk communication and community engagement.

The evolving Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo reinforces the urgency of strong regional preparedness. Africa CDC continues to engage Member States and partners to strengthen cross-border surveillance, information sharing, early detection and coordinated public health action across the continent.

Healthcare workers are central to the response and face significant risks while caring for affected patients. Africa CDC underscores the importance of infection prevention and control measures, appropriate protective equipment, training and continued support for frontline health personnel.

Africa CDC encourages communities to remain vigilant, follow guidance from national health authorities and report symptoms promptly. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or bodily fluids of an infected person, or through contaminated materials. Early detection and access to appropriate care improve the chances of survival and help prevent further transmission.

Africa CDC stands firmly alongside the Government and people of Kenya, healthcare workers and all those affected by this outbreak. Protecting lives requires sustained vigilance, public trust, community engagement and coordinated action.

Africa CDC will continue supporting Member States in strengthening preparedness and response capacities, in close coordination with national authorities and regional and international partners.

For information and guidance in Kenya, members of the public are encouraged to contact the Ministry of Health through its toll-free line 719 and follow its official communication channels.

headline: Africa: WHO Scales Up Ebola Readiness in 22 Countries Across Three Continents
summary: [UN News] The World Health Organization (WHO) is strengthening Ebola preparedness amid conflict and displacement affecting millions of lives in a region that spans parts of Africa, Asia and Europe.
body_text:
The World Health Organization (WHO) is strengthening Ebola preparedness amid conflict and displacement affecting millions of lives in a region that spans parts of Africa, Asia and Europe.

The UN agency's eastern Mediterranean region comprises 22 countries and territories. Intensified support is being given to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan, which have been identified as priority countries.

This follows deadly outbreaks of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus in both the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda and confirmation of a case in Kenya linked to the DRC.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Hostilities and overstretched health systems

Although there have not been any Ebola cases in the region so far, conflict, displacement and overstretched health systems in several countries are making it difficult to prepare and respond should the situation change.

In a speech earlier this week, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Gebreyesus described the region as "the epicentre of global humanitarian need".

More than 117 million people in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Sudan, Syria, Yemen and beyond, require humanitarian assistance to survive.

Assessing readiness, identifying challenges

Between July and September, WHO deployed missions to Djibouti, Somalia and Sudan to assess national readiness and identify challenges in Ebola surveillance, laboratory capacity, infection prevention and control, case management and emergency coordination.

The UN agency is helping authorities to address gaps through training, technical support, medical supplies and simulation exercises.

It has developed regional readiness checklists, contingency planning tools and technical guidance, in addition to strengthening coordination with countries in both Africa and the Eastern Mediterranean.

WHO has also provided laboratory supplies, traveller guidance and community engagement resources.

Despite progress, gaps remain in early detection, laboratory confirmation and availability of protective equipment and resources for emergency response.

"Conflict, insecurity and restricted access present additional challenges, particularly in countries already facing major humanitarian emergencies," WHO said.

Meanwhile, work continues to ensure that national authorities and partners can rapidly detect, investigate and manage suspected Ebola cases.

body_text:
The Republican Party has an unlikely new political target before the midterm elections: Hasan Piker, a Turkish-American socialist who has fiercely criticised Israel, praised the Houthis and is backing the Democratic candidate in a key Senate race.

Although most American voters remain unfamiliar with him, Piker's views on US foreign policy are attracting growing attention as President Donald Trump and the Republican Party amplify his commentary.

In interviews and during thousands of hours of live opining via the Twitch streaming platform, Piker has condemned Israel as a “fascist” state, described ultra-Orthodox Jews as “inbred” and spoken in support of the Houthis, Hezbollah and Hamas. He also said “America deserved 9/11" and has called the US the world's “top terrorist organisation”.

Houthis make ‘major leap’ building advanced missiles

Piker later said he would be more careful about using the word “inbred” and has apologised for his comments about the September 11, 2001 attacks, saying the wording was inappropriate.

Broadcasting under the online moniker HasanAbi, Piker has amassed more than three million followers on Twitch and about two million subscribers on his YouTube channel.

Much of the 35-year-old broadcaster's audience is men under 30, and he has been described as a Joe Rogan or a Charlie Kirk for the Left.

“The way that I'm portrayed in the media is an America-hating communist Islamist fundamentalist who wants to secretly do jihad, and then also at the same time, very woke and gay,” he told NPR in an interview this week.

“So there's this weird inconsistency in their messaging. I don't fully understand it, but who I am is very simple: I'm a socialist. I'm an anti-imperialist. I want what's best for Americans and I want what's best for everyone all around the world.”

Piker's comments have drawn condemnation from some quarters for years, but criticism has recently reached a fever pitch, thanks partly to his enthusiastic support of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat running for the US Senate in a key race in Michigan. If elected, Mr El-Sayed, who has faced overt Islamophobia from Mr Trump, would become the first Muslim senator.

Piker has praised Mr El-Sayed's long-standing support for universal health care, an idea known in the US as Medicare For All, and called him a “wonderful candidate”. The two have made appearances together at campaign events, and Mr El-Sayed has appeared on Piker's Twitch stream.

Mr El-Sayed has faced repeated questions about Piker's controversial statements. He condemned Piker’s “America deserved 9/11” remark, calling it “a dumb statement”, but he has resisted calls to disavow the polemicist altogether.

Facing a very tight Senate race in Michigan that will help decide whether the Democrats can reclaim the upper chamber, Republicans have sought to capitalise on Mr El-Sayed's relationship with Piker and tie him to his most controversial statements.

Mr Trump last month called Piker a “terrible liability” and a “communist”, while Republican-aligned advertising in Michigan has used clips of his most provocative remarks to attack Mr El-Sayed.

One ad accuses Mr El-Sayed of giving “comfort” to the hatred behind the September 11 attacks, splicing Piker’s claim that America “deserved 9/11” with footage of the two men campaigning together.

“Of course, I say incendiary things, but it's not reflected on in the same way when someone who's white, Christian, born and raised in America is saying incendiary things,” Piker told NPR.

He said he had never been formally involved in Mr El-Sayed's campaign and said the Republican effort to associate candidates with his most controversial remarks was an attempt to distract from the administration's economic record.

But Piker's foreign policy positions are only part of the reason he has become a target for Republicans. His growing influence among younger Americans has given him a prominent platform as the Democratic Party struggles to define its identity.

Since losing to Mr Trump in 2024, the Democrats have been unable to agree on whether they should skew further to the left or stick with the more cautious, centrist politics favoured by party elders.

Piker began his career in political commentary with The Young Turks, the progressive online news network founded by his uncle Cenk Uygur, before starting on Twitch.

He also supported New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist that Democrat doyens were initially nervous to endorse. His support provided more fodder for Republicans as they seek to portray Democrats as too radical for mainstream voters.

When it comes to the Middle East, Piker has drawn intense scrutiny over his criticism of Israel.

In January 2026, he described Hamas as “a thousand times better than a fascist settler colonial apartheid state”, referring to Israel.

In an appearance on the Pod Save America podcast in April, he was challenged about the comparison and whether he genuinely believed it.

“I stand by that,” he replied. He went on to say he would choose Hamas over Israel in such a comparison, describing himself as a “lesser evil voter”. He also acknowledged that the remark was intended to provoke.

Still, he told NPR that he did not necessarily regard all of his commentary as “perfect”.

“Think about what it means to speak for 21,000 [cumulative] hours about politics every single day, for eight hours a day,” he said. “I think it's shocking that there's only a handful of clips that people deploy.”

Recent commentary on Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis has also drawn scrutiny.

In a lengthy Twitch broadcast, Piker argued that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, were not simply an Iranian proxy but a movement pursuing its own political interests and a degree of sovereignty within Yemen.

Piker has also defended Houthi missile and drone attacks as legitimate anti-imperialist resistance, despite the threat they pose to Gulf civilian infrastructure and international shipping.

He has praised the Houthis' ability to withstand US military pressure. In a stream last year, he said: “What the Houthis are doing, on the other hand, is resistance. And it’s not only moral, but it’s just.”

The US designated the Houthis a Foreign Terrorist Organisation in March 2025, but Washington has also sought to limit its military entanglements with the group.

Under a ceasefire brokered by Oman in May that year, the Trump administration agreed to halt its bombing campaign in return for a commitment by the Houthis not to attack US vessels.

But Mr Trump has suggested the relatively hands-off approach may change after the midterms.

“I’ll be there after the elections, and I will never forget!” he said this week.

headline: Africa: Every Story Is Unique, Every Journey Matters for Women's Cancers
summary: [allAfrica] Addis Ababa and Geneva -- Leaders of the Organization of African First Ladies for Development, the African Union and the World Health Organization issue a call to accelerate action on women's cancers in Africa in this AllAfrica guest column during Breast Cancer Awareness Month
body_text:
Addis Ababa and Geneva — Leaders of the Organization of African First Ladies for Development, the African Union and the World Health Organization issue a call to accelerate action on women's cancers in Africa in this AllAfrica guest column during Breast Cancer Awareness Month

Across Africa, too many women are dying prematurely from breast and cervical cancers. In 2024 alone, 350,000 women across the continent died from these diseases, often because prevention, early detection, diagnosis and treatment came too late or were inaccessible.

Behind every statistic is a woman, a family and a community. A mother waiting too long for a diagnosis. A daughter unable to access preventive care. A family struggling to afford treatment.

These stories are unique but the responsibility to respond is shared.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Our message to governments, policymakers and partners is clear: the time has come to accelerate action on women's cancers and move them from the margins of health policy to the centre of Africa's health, development and financing agendas.

The African Union is leading the way by placing the health and wellbeing of Africa's people at the heart of the continent's development agenda. This leadership provides an important platform for Member States to translate continental commitments on women's health, noncommunicable diseases and universal health coverage into measurable results.

Through the Organization of African First Ladies for Development (OAFLAD), African First Ladies are bringing a complementary and powerful form of leadership. They are using their voices and platforms to mobilize political attention, engage communities, challenge stigma and keep the experiences of women and families visible in national and continental discussions.

WHO, through its initiatives on breast and cervical cancer, is supporting governments and communities with the evidence, technical approaches and implementation support needed to translate political commitment into effective services.

The challenge is substantial.

Breast and cervical cancer burdens are increasing across Africa. Women still face barriers to vaccination, screening, diagnosis, referral, treatment, palliative care and survivorship support. Diagnosis frequently occurs at advanced stages, when treatment becomes more difficult, more costly and less likely to succeed. WHO's latest Global Status Report on Cancer, issued this year, provided the first global estimates of breast cancer survival and cervical cancer screening coverage. It showed that the African continent is lagging behind the progress happening elsewhere.

Yet there is hope. WHO's Global Breast Cancer Initiative and Cervical Cancer Elimination Initiative provide governments with a practical pathway to improve outcomes. Through multi-sectoral partnerships, WHO is bringing resources to implement new global standards in the prevention and care of breast and cervical cancers, already benefiting millions of women on the continent.

Current efforts alone are not enough.

Governments must integrate women's cancers into national health strategies, primary health care, essential benefit packages and domestic financing priorities. Development partners must align behind country-led priorities and invest in sustainable systems rather than fragmented interventions. Parliamentarians must support enabling legislation, adequate budgets and accountability. Survivors, civil society and communities must have a meaningful voice in shaping policies and assessing progress. Political champions must keep women's cancers visible at the highest levels of decision-making.

The respective strengths of our institutions must be pooled.

OAFLAD uses advocacy and mobilizes political attention. The African Union provides continental leadership and policy direction. WHO brings evidence, standards and technical and implementation support. Governments translate commitments into national policies, budgets and services. Partners bring catalytic financing, innovation and implementation capacity.

Together, these contributions can turn awareness into policy, policy into investment and investment into services that women can actually access.

The steps to expand this access are clear.

We must expand HPV vaccination, cervical cancer screening and breast health awareness. We must shorten the time from detection to diagnosis and treatment. We must strengthen pathology, imaging, referral pathways, surgery, radiotherapy, access to medicines, palliative care and survivorship support. We must also protect families from financial hardship caused by cancer care.

These investments can do more than strengthen cancer care for women. They will reinforce primary health care and accelerate progress towards universal health coverage.

The time is ripe to make these investments and deliver results. Africa stands at a defining moment. Through the African Union, OAFLAD, WHO, governments and many committed partners, there is today a growing momentum to advance a stronger continental agenda for women's cancers and other noncommunicable diseases.

During October's Breast Cancer Awareness Month, the theme "Every Story is Unique, Every Journey Matters" reminds us that every woman experiences cancer differently. But the need is universal for sustained leadership, financing, investment in research and accountability to deliver these solutions at scale. possible thanks to the leadership, knowledge and capacity that Africa possesses to protect women's futures from the threat of cancer. What will make these advances possible is the leadership, knowledge and capacity that Africa possesses to protect women's futures from the threat of cancer.

Access to prevention and care should never depend on geography, income or circumstance.

We call for greater investment in the prevention and care of women's cancers. We call for women-centred policies that place equity, dignity and access at the heart of cancer care. We call for reliable domestic financing, aligned partner support and stronger accountability for results. We call for greater protections from the social, physical and economic hardship that cancer can bring.

This is not only a call for greater awareness. It is a call to governments, political leaders, partners and communities to act with urgency.

Because every woman deserves the opportunity to live a healthy and productive life.

Because every family deserves more time with its mothers, daughters and sisters. And because Africa's development depends on the health of its women and girls.

For Africa, tackling women's cancers is not only a health imperative; it is a question of equity, dignity and development, and a measure of whether our health systems serve every woman.

The measure of our commitment will not be the declarations we make, but whether women can access prevention, screening, timely diagnosis and quality treatment when and where they need them.

headline: T20 cricket at LA 2028 Olympics: India, Pakistan and the qualification race explained
summary: Despite India's successful title defence at the T20 World Cup earlier in the year and their win at the Asian Games, it has been a pretty grim in bilateral series.India were blanked by Ireland and England in T20s in their backyard across six completed matches, while the West Indies further exposed the weaknesses in India's T20 armour, levelling the T20 series 2-2 on Saturday.New captain Shreyas Iyer has had a rough start to his reign, although he has an Asian Games gold medal to show for his efforts.Generally, bilateral matches do not count for much outside a World Cup cycle. But there is an incentive this year for teams to maintain their standards - qualification spots for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.LA 2028 Olympics qualification scenariosCricket is returning to the Olympics after well over a century. As expected, T20 is the chosen format.However, just like at the Asian Games, there are limited spots available, even though there are many competitive teams in world cricket. Japan recently came within two runs of defeating double world champions India.A total of six nations will compete in the men’s and women’s T20 competitions, with at least one team each from Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa. Hosts USA are also set to get one of the spots.The women's section has largely been locked in, with Australia, Great Britain (England), India and South Africa qualifying by virtue of being the highest-placed eligible finishers at the end of the women's T20 World Cup earlier in the year.However, the criteria is different for the men's side. The highest-ranked teams from Africa, Asia, Europe and Oceania on December 31, 2026, will qualify for LA 2028.England are the top-ranked T20 team and would have qualified even if they weren't as there are no other European teams in the top 10.South Africa (ranked fifth) too are certain to be through as their next closest challengers Zimbabwe (12th) are well behind in T20 rankings.Oceania sees a tougher battle between Australia and New Zealand, ranked third and fourth respectively but separated by a substantial 13 ranking points.In Asia, India look most likely to qualify automatically for the LA Olympics despite their recent struggles. India are ranked second in the world while their closest continental challengers Pakistan are sixth. However, there is a massive gap of 27 points between the two. India have five T20s against New Zealand and three against Sri Lanka remaining in the 2026 calendar. Even if they lose every single match, India will still only go down to third - according to the ICC's rankings predictor - and remain out of reach for their neighbours.India, therefore, are almost certain to qualify for the 2028 LA Olympics T20s directly, especially since Pakistan have no T20 match scheduled for the rest of the year.However, the team in green can still make it to the Olympics. One final spot at the LA Olympics will be decided via a qualifier, where Pakistan might have to fight teams like New Zealand, Zimbabwe, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan.The West Indies will have a separate Games pathway. If the Windies gain automatic qualification spot via rankings by the end of the year, there will be a dedicated qualifier event to determine the Caribbean nation which will then feature in the Olympics qualifier.
body_text:
Despite India's successful title defence at the T20 World Cup earlier in the year and their win at the Asian Games, it has been a pretty grim in bilateral series.

India were blanked by Ireland and England in T20s in their backyard across six completed matches, while the West Indies further exposed the weaknesses in India's T20 armour, levelling the T20 series 2-2 on Saturday.

New captain Shreyas Iyer has had a rough start to his reign, although he has an Asian Games gold medal to show for his efforts.

Why Bhuvneshwar's India recall shows that life begins at 30 for fast bowlers

Generally, bilateral matches do not count for much outside a World Cup cycle. But there is an incentive this year for teams to maintain their standards - qualification spots for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

Cricket is returning to the Olympics after well over a century. As expected, T20 is the chosen format.

However, just like at the Asian Games, there are limited spots available, even though there are many competitive teams in world cricket. Japan recently came within two runs of defeating double world champions India.

A total of six nations will compete in the men’s and women’s T20 competitions, with at least one team each from Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa. Hosts USA are also set to get one of the spots.

The women's section has largely been locked in, with Australia, Great Britain (England), India and South Africa qualifying by virtue of being the highest-placed eligible finishers at the end of the women's T20 World Cup earlier in the year.

However, the criteria is different for the men's side. The highest-ranked teams from Africa, Asia, Europe and Oceania on December 31, 2026, will qualify for LA 2028.

England are the top-ranked T20 team and would have qualified even if they weren't as there are no other European teams in the top 10.

South Africa (ranked fifth) too are certain to be through as their next closest challengers Zimbabwe (12th) are well behind in T20 rankings.

Oceania sees a tougher battle between Australia and New Zealand, ranked third and fourth respectively but separated by a substantial 13 ranking points.

In Asia, India look most likely to qualify automatically for the LA Olympics despite their recent struggles. India are ranked second in the world while their closest continental challengers Pakistan are sixth.

However, there is a massive gap of 27 points between the two. India have five T20s against New Zealand and three against Sri Lanka remaining in the 2026 calendar.

Even if they lose every single match, India will still only go down to third - according to the ICC's rankings predictor - and remain out of reach for their neighbours.

India, therefore, are almost certain to qualify for the 2028 LA Olympics T20s directly, especially since Pakistan have no T20 match scheduled for the rest of the year.

However, the team in green can still make it to the Olympics. One final spot at the LA Olympics will be decided via a qualifier, where Pakistan might have to fight teams like New Zealand, Zimbabwe, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan.

The West Indies will have a separate Games pathway. If the Windies gain automatic qualification spot via rankings by the end of the year, there will be a dedicated qualifier event to determine the Caribbean nation which will then feature in the Olympics qualifier.

​French ​President ⁠Emmanuel Macron will ⁠travel to ​the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar on a trip that begins on Monday.

Mr Macron plans to discuss the ​situation ‌in ⁠the Strait ​of ​Hormuz and ‌its effects ⁠on energy ⁠prices during his Gulf visit, which will run from October 19 to 21, his office said.

He is expected in Kuwait this morning and the UAE later this afternoon.

The visit comes despite France's worst civil unrest in years, with more than 2,000 people arrested for torching and ransacking property.

The four Gulf countries have all had energy sites attacked during the US-Iran war, which has also curtailed oil exports through the strait. With Yemen's Houthi rebels now pushing for control of a second strait, the Bab Al Mandeb, there are fears that the global energy crunch could worsen.

“In light of the crisis gripping the Middle East, the President will continue his efforts with regional leaders to promote a return to stability and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” an Elysee Palace source said.

“Discussions will also focus on securing and diversifying our energy supplies and their transport routes, with the aim of limiting the impact of the energy crisis on the daily lives of French people.”

The source said Mr Macron's talks in the UAE would address defence, security and new technologies such as AI. He is also expected to attend a climate event in Qatar and discuss economic relations with Gulf countries.

Mr Macron has made several trips to the UAE as President. Last December he met President Sheikh Mohamed at the Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi and spoke to French troops based in the country.

Earlier visits included his attendance at the Cop28 climate summit, which took place in Dubai in 2023, and a trip in 2017 to the opening ceremony of Louvre Abu Dhabi.

On Mr Macron's most recent Middle East trip, he visited Damascus in July in what was the first appearance in post-civil war Syria by a major western leader.

Mr Macron's second term ends next year and he is ineligible under the French constitution to run for a third.

body_text:
Abu Dhabi fight fans will witness two title fights when the world's leading MMA promotion returns to the UAE this Saturday, October 24.

Topping the bill is featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski, who puts his belt on the line against top-ranked Movsar Evloev.

The co-main event sees Petr Yan defend his bantamweight belt against the man he dethroned last December, Merab Dvalishvili.

Abu Dhabi has a long history of memorable title bouts. We take a look back at five of the most memorable.

When the Covid-19 pandemic caused most of the world to shut down, the UFC needed a new home to keep events going.

Abu Dhabi stepped in and Yas Island became Fight Island. Strict protocols included journalists holed up in nearby hotels for weeks at a time, having meals delivered to their rooms daily.

Abu Dhabi helped keep the sport of MMA alive. Crowds at Fight Island were restricted, which made the sound of every taunt audible, every punch and kick echo around the specially constructed venue.

Those lucky enough to attend UFC 253 got to see a wizard at work.

Israel Adesanya was at the peak of his powers, putting his undefeated 19-0 record and his UFC middleweight title on the line against Paulo Costa, who probably weighed the 185lb limit for the few seconds he had to stand on the scales at weigh-in.

Adesanya delivered a striking masterclass, picking off the Brazilian at will. Adesanya chewed up Costa's lead leg before a second-round TKO cemented his place as the best middleweight since the great Anderson Silva.

If Fight Island was notable for the eerie silence, UFC 242 will be remembered for its deafening roars.

The reason for the decibels amping up was down to one man: Khabib Nurmagomedov.

Khabib drew energetic crowds throughout fight week. Abu Dhabi had erected a venue specifically for the event on Yas Island called The Arena. Over 13,000 were in attendance, many sporting Khabib's famous “papakha” headpiece.

In 2019, he was at his brilliant best. The Dagestani destroyer put his UFC lightweight title on the line against interim champ Dustin Poirier.

From the first round, Nurmagomedov established control, wrestling the American to the ground, softening him up with crunching ground-and-pound and attempting several submissions.

He finally landed one in Round 3, with Poirier forced to tap out as Nurmagomedov cinched in a rear-naked choke.

He jumped the octagon fence to hug UFC president Dana White, a stark contrast to his post-fight antics following his win over Conor McGregor the previous year, an incident that lives on in infamy.

Nurmagomedov was magnanimous in victory; Poirier humble in defeat. A love affair between Abu Dhabi and the undefeated Russian was established and endures to this day.

Even in retirement, he still gets the biggest pop from the crowd at UFC Abu Dhabi events.

Alexander 'The Great' is no stranger to these shores. His headline bout at UFC 333 will be the fourth time the Australian has fought in Abu Dhabi.

Volkanovski had ended Holloway’s reign at the top of the featherweight division in December 2019, earning a unanimous decision few had predicted.

He was quick to grant the Hawaii native a rematch, knowing another victory over a fighter as talented as Holloway would offer legitimacy to his claim as the new ruler of the 145lb division.

That fight took place at UFC 251 and was an absolute tear-up. Holloway came out of the gates firing, using creative kicks and punch combinations behind a masterful jab. Volkanovski showed true grit to hang tough, grab a foothold in the contest, and slowly assert his own dominance.

The scorecards would later reveal all three judges had scored the first two rounds to Holloway, with rounds 3 and 4 for Volkanovski. Fighters have a sense of the way the fight is going, and so both probably knew it would all come down to the final round to determine who walked off with the strap.

Volkanovski was judged to have edged it – a decision that still rankles with Holloway to this day. Either way, Abu Dhabi got to witness two of the best featherweights of all time go toe-to-toe for championship gold.

Charles Oliveira arrived in Abu Dhabi ahead of UFC 280 still recognised by many as the unofficial champion of the lightweight division.

The Brazilian had been controversially stripped of the belt before his fight with Justin Gaethje at UFC 274 for missing the 155lb weight limit – by half a pound.

Many thought the punishment was excessive, since non-title fights are allowed a half-pound exemption. It is the only time in UFC history a title has been vacated due to missing weight.

Officially, his bout with Islam Makhachev was for the vacant belt. Oliveira had been on a tear, the division's bogeyman, owner of a host of UFC records, including most submission wins, most finishes and most Performance of the Night bonuses.

Makhachev, the protege of Khabib Nurmagomedov, boasted a record of 23 wins against one defeat, and his ascent had many wondering if he would one day surpass the accomplishments of his mentor. The UFC had pitted the two best in its deepest division against each other.

Oliveira was on his back early, a position he is infinitely comfortable with, but the Dagestani's grappling and ground control proved the superior weapons.

A straight left in Round 2 floored Oliveira, and Makhachev did not need a second invite. More used to making his opponents tap, the sight of Oliveira frantically signalling that Makhachev's squeeze on a perfectly executed arm bar was too hot to handle is a sight few will forget.

Glover Teixeira was finally given another shot at UFC gold at UFC 267 when he faced light heavyweight belt holder Jan Blachowicz.

Teixeira thought his chance had passed him by. For four years, he was unable to fight in the US due to prolonged visa and immigration issues. Bureaucracy and legal red tape had robbed him of his best years in the UFC.

But at age 42, he was given a second title shot, seven years after his first, a defeat to the indomitable Jon Jones.

Blachowicz, four years Teixeira's junior, entered as a heavy favourite and was expected to dominate with his legendary “Polish power”.

Teixeira had other ideas. The Brazilian immediately implemented his grappling, grounding Błachowicz in the first round. In the second, after staggering the champion with a left hook, Teixeira executed another takedown, quickly transitioned to the back, and forced Błachowicz to tap to a rear-naked choke.

No one who has met or spent any sort of time with Teixeira begrudged him his moment. His victory over Błachowicz made him the oldest first-time UFC champion, the second oldest overall after Randy Couture and only the third fighter to win a world title in his forties (Couture and Daniel Cormier are the other two).

headline: Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection
summary: Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran." (Image credit: Alex Brandon)
body_text:
FILE - President Donald Trump listens as Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago club, Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla. Alex Brandon/AP hide caption

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Sunday endorsed embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late in his reelection campaign, a coveted boost because of Trump's popularity but one that the American had withheld for months as the vote neared and the leaders' strategies in the Middle East diverged.

Trump said in a post on social media that Netanyahu "has been a Great Warrior Prime Minister, and an even greater Partner for Peace in combatting the Islamic Republic of Iran."

Israelis are set to vote Oct. 27, in the first national elections since Hamas attacked Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.

The absence of an endorsement was a setback for the Likud politician, who had billed his tight ties to the Republican president as a selling point for staying in power.

"Thank you, President Trump, for the tremendous support and work together," Netanyahu said in a statement in Hebrew posted on X. "Together we will complete the mission!"

His Likud Party attached to the statement a 35-second video showing clips of the two leaders together and Trump praising Netanyahu.

It was not immediately clear what impact the endorsement would have on what is expected to be a tight race. Trump is still popular in Israel, but many Israelis, including leading commentators, have expressed disappointment over the inconclusive outcome of the Iran war and Trump's ceasefire proposal, which fell short of many of the countries' key goals when they jointly launched the war in February.

In his post, Trump again threatened to "soon finish the job" against Iran "unless they change their ways, rapidly," but added he might not want to if Netanyahu loses the election. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said.

He said Netanyahu had been "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant in the face of tremendous opposition, including that coming from even Israel, itself."

Trump endorsed Netanyahu in past elections and in November he sent a letter to Israeli President Isaac Herzog asking him to pardon Netanyahu on corruption charges.

But Trump's comments about Netanyahu in recent months had been much more subdued, and he repeatedly demurred when asking if he would back the prime minister. The president, when asked in a Time magazine interview published this month about backing the Israeli leader, said, "I'm not involved in politics anymore," despite his campaigning for and endorsing U.S. politicians.

Trump, especially in his second term, has sought to give his stamp of approval to candidates in foreign elections and claimed credit when they have been successful. He endorsed Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán in his unsuccessful bid for a fifth term, as well as Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Polish President Karol Nawrocki, and several Latin American leaders.

Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies and seemed more aligned than ever in the wake of the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran's nuclear facilities in 2025. But over the course of the nearly eight-month war with Iran this year, they have had disagreements.

Trump criticized Israel's decision to attack a key Iranian gas field in the first weeks of the war. In June, he called Netanyahu "crazy." Trump also said that he was "a little bit perturbed" as Israel's fighting with Hezbollah militants in Lebanon was holding back peace talks with Iran.

Beyond Iran, Netanyahu in August rejected Trump's latest plan to advance a stalled ceasefire in Gaza, pushing back on the U.S. administration's call for Israel to withdraw from territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been disarmed.

headline: Iran's foreign minister accuses Netanyahu of pushing US toward another war to avoid prison
summary: Abbas Araghchi warns Tehran has ‘unfinished jobs’ of its own as Trump endorses Israeli leader ahead of elections
body_text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu late Sunday of seeking to drag the United States into another war with Iran to avoid imprisonment while warning Washington against renewed military action.

“Netanyahu is driving America into another war to stay out of jail,” Araghchi wrote on the US social media platform X, accusing the Israeli leader of disregarding the consequences for Israel and US President Donald Trump.

“Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job,’ Iran emerged even stronger. Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too,” he added.

His remarks came after Trump endorsed Netanyahu earlier Sunday ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 elections, praising their partnership in confronting Iran and warning that Washington might have to take on the task itself if Israelis elected another leader.

“If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, using Netanyahu’s nickname.

Netanyahu has headed the current government since late 2022, which has been described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history. He is also standing trial domestically on corruption charges that could carry prison sentences if convicted and has been wanted by the International Court of Justice since 2024 for war crimes in Gaza.

Opposition parties have intensified coordination in an effort to replace Netanyahu’s government through the ballot box.

The US and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting retaliatory attacks by Tehran.

Despite an April ceasefire and a framework agreement reached in June, fighting later resumed as negotiations between Washington and Tehran stalled.

body_text:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is due to visit Tehran on Monday after Gulf states urged Moscow to use its influence at the UN to press Iran to halt attacks on regional neighbours.

The visit comes as tensions escalate over shipping security and the prospect of renewed war with the US, after President Donald Trump warned overnight that Washington could “soon finish the job” unless Tehran rapidly changes its behaviour.

It prompted a defiant response from Tehran. “Last time you wanted to ‘finish the job’, Iran emerged even stronger,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X. “Want to try your luck again? Be our guest. But be careful; we have unfinished jobs too.”

Tehran’s rhetoric hardened over the weekend. Iran’s newly appointed Defence Minister, Mehrdad Ketabchi, warned on Sunday that the country was ready to respond to any US attack involving the “Mother of All Bombs”. On Monday, Brig Gen Mohammad Reza Naqdi, a senior adviser to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander-in-chief, went further, saying Iran had the “father of Iranian missiles” ready to strike its enemy’s energy infrastructure and investments across the region if attacked.

In a meeting between Mr Lavrov and Gulf Co-operation Council foreign ministers in Manama on Sunday, the bloc called on Russia to play an active role in securing Iranian compliance with UN resolutions, ending attacks on Gulf states and pursuing serious dialogue.

Mr Lavrov has called for a diplomatic solution to the regional crisis, presenting an updated Russian plan for collective security in the Gulf that envisages direct dialogue among coastal states and neighbouring countries, including Iraq and Jordan.

“We all believe that it is important for all the Gulf states to have their own word in how to resolve this strategic crisis,” Mr Lavrov said.

He said Moscow supported direct dialogue between Gulf states and their neighbours, adding that Russia respected agreements reached so far.

“We focus on removing core reasons for conflict,” Mr Lavrov said. “We stand for absolute respect for agreements reached so far. Unfortunately, our Western counterparts do not follow the same value.”

At Sunday's meeting in the Bahraini capital, GCC Secretary General Jasem Al Budaiwi said member states had faced more than 7,000 ballistic missile and drone attacks since February 28, when the US and Israel began their war against Iran. He said strikes had hit airports, ports, power stations, water desalination plants and oil and gas facilities.

The bloc also warned that disruption to maritime navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, alongside threats to shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab Al Mandeb strait, endangered global energy and food security and international supply chains. It called for maritime traffic through the strait to return to its pre-war status.

Iran has stepped up attacks on tankers using a US-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint for around one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before the conflict.

On Monday, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said an oil tanker struck a naval mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. The claim could not be independently verified.

The IRGC said the vessel’s crew had switched off its positioning and navigation systems and was attempting to leave the waterway through an “unauthorised” southern route.

It offered no evidence of a mine, and it is unclear whether the incident is linked to a US-backed shipping route along Oman’s coast, which Tehran may want to discourage companies from using.

Iran’s hardline Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, meanwhile warned governments and businesses against funding AI and data companies he accuses of supporting US and Israeli military operations.

In a post on X, Mr Ghalibaf announced plans for a “Gulf Data Authority” and warned that companies providing finance, land or energy to such firms would face Iranian enforcement measures.

The post does not explain how the proposed authority would operate or explicitly threaten undersea cables. However, it follows a separate warning by Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, that regional undersea cables, data centres and AI facilities could be targeted if hostilities with the US resume.

body_text:
Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola has urged the world not to forget Palestinians in the war-ravaged Gaza Strip, in a video appeal for the UN refugee agency UNRWA.

The video, published by UNRWA Spain late Sunday, calls for continued solidarity and asks viewers to donate to the agency.

“They are not statistics,” Guardiola says of those killed, describing them as people with “names and faces, families, dreams and memories”. “They are not collateral damage. They are girls and boys.” He warns that accepting language that conceals suffering erodes humanity.

The appeal describes children in Gaza searching for parents in the rubble, going hungry and being left alone. “We see them lose everything before they have even had the chance to grow up,” he says.

He rejects the idea that Palestinian suffering is remote from the rest of the world. “Their lives matter just as much as ours,” he says. “Solidarity with Palestine cannot take a break. Neither can our responsibility.”

The Israeli military has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians in Gaza, health authorities in the territory say, since Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

The video also highlights decades of displacement and violence endured by Palestinian refugees. “We deeply admire the resilience of the Palestinian people. But they should not have to be resilient,” Guardiola says. “No child should grow up learning how to survive before learning how to live.”

Israel launched a military offensive on Gaza after the Hamas-led October 7 attacks, which Israeli authorities say killed about 1,200 people and resulted in around 250 being taken hostage. Gaza’s health ministry says more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since a ceasefire took effect in October 2025.

UNRWA, established in 1949, provides healthcare, protection and aid to refugees and preserves their history and identity. It has operated in Gaza, the occupied West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.

Israel has barred the agency from operating on its territory, accusing it of links to Hamas. UNRWA denies the allegation.

“Silence today is a way of taking sides, but we cannot look the other way,” Guardiola says. “Palestine matters, and Palestine needs justice and peace.”

Guardiola left his role as Manchester City manager at the end of last season following a 10-year reign that saw the club win 17 major trophies, including six Premier League titles and a Uefa Champions League crown.

body_text:
SAMARKAND, Uzbekistan, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Ukraine and Russia should be focused on ending the war between them, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on his visit to Uzbekistan on Monday.

Asked about a possible meeting of US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the four-year-old Ukraine conflict, Rubio said: "There's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear. He'd like the war in Ukraine and Russia to end."

Rubio landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet top officials of the C5+1 grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan.

Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November.

"We see nothing good coming from this war," Rubio said. "We see a lot of downside to it, including the very real risk of escalation and spread of this thing... into another country because of a failed sabotage attack, because of drones that are hit with electronic warfare and they wander into a neighbouring country."

The US has been trying to mediate a peace deal to bring the Ukraine war to an end and Trump has since clinched a diesel import deal with Russia and waived some sanctions on Moscow, which he said should keep the Kremlin at the negotiating table.

The moves were criticized by Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy. A fresh Russian air strike killed a woman in Ukraine's Kyiv overnight while also hitting a subway station and damaging a 25-storey residential building.

(Reporting by Gram Slattery in Samarkand, Uzbekistan; Writing by Jekaterīna Golubkova in Tokyo; Editing by Tom Hogue and Edwina Gibbs)

headline: PGCC issues hostile statement against Iran, Yemen
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA)– Persian Gulf Cooperation Council (PGCC) in final statement of its ministerial meeting in Manama have reiterated their baseless claims against Iran and Yemen, urging intensified political and arms-related pressure on Ansarullah.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA)– Persian Gulf Cooperation Council (PGCC) in final statement of its ministerial meeting in Manama have reiterated their baseless claims against Iran and Yemen, urging intensified political and arms-related pressure on Ansarullah.

In the final statement of its 108th session in Manama, capital of Bahrain, the Ministerial Council of the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council (PGCC) condemned the retaliatory attacks by the Yemeni army against Saudi Arabian positions.

In this statement, the PGCC claimed that the aforementioned attacks targeted civilian airports and vital facilities in Saudi Arabia, resulting in civilian casualties.

In addition, the Persian Gulf Cooperation Council called for the implementation of UN Security Council (UNSC)’s resolutions regarding Yemen, the tightening of arms restrictions against Ansarullah Resistance Movement, and the cessation of support that, according to the Council, enables the group to acquire missiles and drones.

In another part of this statement, allegations are leveled against the Islamic Republic of Iran, and missile and drone attacks attributed to Iran against member states of the Gulf Cooperation Council and Jordan are condemned.

Without referring to the attacks carried out from the US bases in the region against Iran, the Council held Tehran responsible for these attacks and demanded an immediate stop to them and compensation for the alleged damages.

The foreign ministers of the PGCC member states also called for a return to the path of dialogue and diplomacy to overcome the current crisis between the United States and Iran.

headline: East Africa: Kenya Overtakes Ethiopia As East Africa's Largest Economy in Dollar Terms, IMF Estimates Show
summary: [Addis Standard] Addis Abeba -- Kenya has overtaken Ethiopia as Eastern Africa's largest economy measured by nominal gross domestic product (GDP) in US dollar terms, according to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO), a shift largely attributed to exchange-rate movements rather than faster real economic growth.
body_text:
Addis Abeba — Kenya has overtaken Ethiopia as Eastern Africa's largest economy measured by nominal gross domestic product (GDP) in US dollar terms, according to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO), a shift largely attributed to exchange-rate movements rather than faster real economic growth.

The IMF's estimates show Ethiopia's economy continuing to expand more rapidly in real terms, even as the depreciation of the birr reduced the dollar value of its output. Kenya's comparatively stronger currency performance, alongside continued economic growth, helped increase the value of its economy when measured in US dollars.

According to the IMF's October 2026 WEO estimates, Ethiopia's real GDP grew by 9.2% in 2025, compared with 4.6% in Kenya. The Fund projects Ethiopia's economy to expand by 9.2% in 2026 and 7.8% in 2027, while Kenya's growth is projected at 4.5% and 4.7%, respectively.

The figures underscore the distinction between nominal GDP, which values economic output at prevailing market exchange rates, and real GDP growth, which measures changes in output after accounting for price changes. A country's dollar-denominated GDP can decline sharply following currency depreciation even when its domestic production is increasing.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Ethiopia's currency shift followed the government's July 2024 move toward a more market-determined exchange-rate system, a key component of its economic reform programme supported by an approximately US$3.4 billion IMF Extended Credit Facility. The subsequent depreciation of the birr substantially reduced the dollar value of the country's economic output.

Kenya's economy, meanwhile, benefited from a stronger shilling, which increased the dollar valuation of its output. The IMF estimates indicate that Kenya's nominal GDP in US dollar terms increased by about 13.7% in 2025, while Ethiopia's dollar-denominated GDP fell sharply from its 2024 level.

The change in ranking reflects the combined effects of economic growth, inflation and exchange-rate movements on the dollar value of each economy.

The IMF estimates nominal GDP per capita at about US$1,130 in Ethiopia and US$2,790 in Kenya in 2026, illustrating the difference between the total size of an economy and output per person.

Inflation also remains a concern. The IMF projects average consumer price inflation of approximately 11.7% in Ethiopia in 2026, compared with about 6% in Kenya. Persistent price pressures, alongside exchange-rate changes, affect households' purchasing power and the cost of imports.

body_text:
Dubai Investments, a Dubai-listed conglomerate, is selling a 20 per cent stake in its subsidiary DIP Holding in the first initial public offering in the UAE this year.

The deal will comprise the sale of 1.74 billion shares by existing shareholders in DIP Holding, which owns the mixed-use development Dubai Investments Park, the company said on Monday.

Parent Dubai Investments will continue to control the remaining 80 per cent shareholding in DIP Holding, contingent on the offering size remaining unchanged and all shares on sale being allocated to investors, it said.

UAE scraps 15 business fees but raises cost of IPO approvals

Subscriptions for the sale are set to open on October 27 and will run until November 3. Final pricing for the deal will be announced on November 4.

DIP Holding shares are expected to start trading on the Dubai Financial Market on November 11, according to the offer document.

The deal breaks the lull in the IPO market in the UAE. The Arab world’s second-largest economy was a hotbed for public floats, with the DFM and the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange both attracting a steady stream of IPOs over the past few years.

The Middle East IPO market last year slowed after it was hit by lower oil prices, geopolitical unrest and weaker post-listing performances. Companies in the region raised $7.1 billion from 61 listings, down from $13 billion a year earlier.

UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows.

The US-Iran war, now in its eighth month, has further disrupted the already slowing momentum as companies put their plans of tapping equities markets to raise capital on hold.

Dubai Investments, in which the sovereign investment fund Investment Corporation of Dubai holds a stake, was among the UAE companies that expressed intentions to list shares in its units before war-driven volatility sapped deal volumes.

The company in September last year said that it was in talks with banks and planned to list up to 25 per cent of Dubai Investments Park.

Situated near Al Maktoum International Airport and Jebel Ali Port, Dubai Investments Park is home to 1,000 tenants, 5,700 subtenants and more than 150,000 residents. The district was established in 1997 and hosts warehouses, hotels, retail outlets, schools and medical centres, making it one of the largest mixed-use developments in the emirate.

body_text:
TEL AVIV, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Israeli police said on Monday they had arrested eight suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in the West Bank over the weekend, including attacks on an American photojournalist and European diplomats in separate incidents.

Police did not identify the suspects, who were taken into custody for questioning, or disclose any accusations against them. The investigation was ongoing, police said.

Prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.

Israeli radio station Galatz reported the suspects were Israelis and that the Shin Bet domestic security service was taking part in the investigation.

Masked Israeli settlers were filmed on Friday assaulting Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank.

On Saturday, European diplomats and a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank.

The weekend violence has drawn condemnation from the United States, Israel's closest ally, and from France, Belgiumand Poland, whose diplomats were attacked on Saturday.

While Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats,Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more circumspect.

He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" with the Israeli military, and that the facts ​of the attack on Levine were "unclear".

Settler attacks ​on the Palestinians ⁠are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

headline: US officials visit Palestinian village after settler attacks on diplomats
summary: By Ali Sawafta and Steven ScheerTAYBEH, West Bank/JERUSALEM, Oct 18 (Reuters) - US diplomats visited a Christian Palestinian village in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday following attacks by militant Israeli settlers on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the previous two days.Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labor, Brian Burch, US ambassador to the Holy See, and a number of other diplomats visited the Latin Convent church and were expected to meet with members of the Christian community in Taybeh.
body_text:
By Ali Sawafta and Steven Scheer

TAYBEH, West Bank/JERUSALEM, Oct 18 (Reuters) - US diplomats visited a Christian Palestinian village in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on Sunday following attacks by militant Israeli settlers on European diplomats and an American photojournalist in the previous two days.

Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labor, Brian Burch, US ambassador to the Holy See, and a number of other diplomats visited the Latin Convent church and were expected to meet with members of the Christian community in Taybeh.

Belgian, French and Polish diplomats, along with a French mayor and Palestinian civilians, had been attacked near Taybeh on Saturday by masked Israeli settlers.

The previous day, Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was taken to hospital after being assaulted while covering a Palestinian olive harvest near another West Bank village.

The diplomats' visit coincided with US President Donald Trump endorsing his ally, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, for Israel's parliamentary election on October 27.

Meanwhile, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee attended a settler conference in the West Bank on Sunday.

Huckabee, an evangelical Christian and longtime supporter of Israel, earlier wrote on X calling for "those who attacked" the Washington Post photojournalist, a US citizen, to be jailed.

NETANYAHU CIRCUMSPECT ON SETTLER VIOLENCE

Trump has expressed his opposition to Israeli annexation of the West Bank, but his administration has put little pressure on Netanyahu's right-wing, pro-settler government to change its policy.

UN bodies and most countries deem the settlements illegal under international law, but Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.

While Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military both blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats, Netanyahu, whose coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, has been more circumspect.

He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations without prior coordination" with the Israeli military, and that the facts of the attack on Levine are "unclear".

France urged Israeli authorities to arrest Saturday's attackers and to end criminal violence in the West Bank, but by Sunday there was no announcement from Israeli authorities of any arrests in either of the two latest incidents.

The West Bank is home to some 500,000 settlers and at least 3 million Palestinians.

Settler attacks on the Palestinians are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

Yet prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.

On Sunday, Reuters saw a group of at least 10 settlers, masked and dressed in black, hurling rocks at Palestinians and activists harvesting olives near the Palestinian West Bank town of Salfit, prompting the farmers to flee.

Israeli border police were in the area and shot tear gas towards the hills.

(Reporting by Ali Sawafta in Taybeh, Steven Scheer and Alexander Cornwell in Jerusalem and Pesha Magid in Salfit, West Bank; Editing by Kevin Liffey)

headline: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 19, 2026
summary: [allAfrica] Kenya Confirms Eighth Ebola Case
body_text:
Kenya Confirms Eighth Ebola Case

Kenya's Health Ministry has confirmed another Ebola infection, bringing the country's total to eight as the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo) continues to spread. Health Ministry Director-General Dr Patrick Amoth said the latest patient is a 49-year-old man who is not a healthcare worker and developed fever, headaches and muscle pain. He worked as a patient attendant, cleaning utensils and linen. He was likely exposed to Kenya's first Ebola patient, who died on October 5. Amoth said authorities tested 38 people, with one testing positive, while six other patients in quarantine remained stable after receiving supportive treatment. Meanwhile, authorities in the DR Congo reported that the outbreak had reached an eighth province, Nord-Ubangi, where two cases, including one death, were recorded near the border with the Central African Republic. The DR Congo has reported at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since the outbreak was declared in mid-May. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which there is currently no approved vaccine or specific treatment.

Kenyan Court to Deliver Verdict in Paul Mackenzie Mass Murder Case

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

A Kenyan court is set to deliver its judgment in the mass murder case against doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie and 29 of his followers, who are accused of murdering 191 children in the Shakahola forest. Prosecutors allege that the children were forced to starve to death as part of a religious doctrine that promised they would meet Jesus, while education and modern medicine were portrayed as evil. Mackenzie and the co-accused have pleaded not guilty, maintaining that nobody was forced to die. The case marks the first time Mackenzie will face a verdict on the most serious murder charges, although he and other leaders face additional cases involving terrorism, radicalisation and the denial of education to children. Authorities discovered more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the coastal forest, where Mackenzie had encouraged followers from across Kenya to settle and observe his teachings. Survivors and witnesses have described widespread starvation, the rejection of medical treatment and the deaths of children and adults. One survivor, Peter Shukrani, said he nearly died after his mother discarded his medication because she believed medicine was forbidden by the preacher's doctrine. Stephen Mwiti, meanwhile, said he lost all six of his children in the forest. Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, initially accused in the case, entered a plea deal and became a prosecution witness.

Drone Strikes Kill Civilians in Sudan as Fire Destroys Market Stalls

Drone attacks killed civilians, including women, in Sudan's West Darfur and West Kordofan regions on Saturday, as separate strikes targeted military installations in the east and a fire destroyed dozens of commercial stalls in Northern State. In West Darfur, a drone attack attributed to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) killed several people, including six women, and injured five others in Bir Saliba, Sarba locality. Most of the victims were reportedly displaced people who had travelled to the area for agricultural work. In West Kordofan, the Kordofan Observatory said a drone strike carried out by the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) hit a civilian lorry near Ankush, killing four people, including three women, and injuring others. The passengers included patients travelling for medical treatment and civilians heading to shop. The Observatory also reported other recent drone attacks that killed civilians, including a child, and warned that targeting civilians and civilian vehicles could violate international humanitarian law and amount to war crimes. It called on the SAF to halt attacks on civilians and urged the RSF to keep away from residential areas. Meanwhile, drone attacks targeted military installations in El Gedaref, Khashm El Girba and the Upper Atbara and Setit Dam Complex on Sunday, with air defences reportedly intercepting several drones. No casualties were reported from those strikes. In Northern State, a fire destroyed between 75 and 80 stalls at El Burgeig market on Saturday evening. Initial reports suggested an electrical fault triggered the blaze, which spread rapidly through stalls containing goods, including perfume.

Ebola Vaccine Trials Offer Hope

Vaccine candidates undergoing clinical trials offer hope of protection against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola responsible for the Democratic Republic of the Congo's worst-ever outbreak, according to Emanuele Capobianco, director of global health security at Gavi, the global vaccine alliance. The outbreak has surpassed 9,000 reported cases, with more than 4,000 deaths, but no vaccine or specific treatment has been approved for this strain. A clinical trial of the existing Ervebo vaccine, which is approved for the more common Zaire strain, is expected to assess whether it provides cross-protection against Bundibugyo. Meanwhile, vaccines developed by the University of Oxford, in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and US-based Moderna are undergoing early-stage trials. They are due to report from phase one trials later this October and, if the results are safe and show good immune responses, larger phase two and three trials may follow. If development progresses successfully, a rollout could begin in the first half of 2027. Gavi has committed US$50 million to support the outbreak response, including vaccine access, and 70,000 doses of Ervebo were released from the global stockpile in August at the request of the Congolese government. Capobianco stressed that the outbreak could still be contained through early detection, surveillance, infection prevention and timely treatment, even before new vaccines become available. He said many deaths occur in communities before patients reach health facilities, highlighting the need to improve access to care and build public trust through healthcare workers, local leaders and community engagement. Research could also help establish a future global stockpile for Bundibugyo, protecting against subsequent outbreaks.

Madagascar Marks One Year Since Uprising as Russian Influence Grows

Madagascar has marked one year since military leader Michael Randrianirina took power following youth-led protests that forced elected president Andry Rajoelina from office, but many of the reforms demanded by demonstrators remain unfinished as Russia expands its influence in the country. Randrianirina was sworn in as president on October 17, 2025, after protests over water and electricity shortages, justice and transparency. Russia quickly established ties with the new administration, and researchers say Moscow has since expanded its military, political and economic presence. An investigation by All Eyes on Wagner found that Russian military personnel linked to Africa Corps, the organisation that succeeded the Wagner Group, arrived in Madagascar to train the military, while shipments of helicopters, tanks, trucks, drones and rifles were delivered as donations. Russia has also reportedly expanded its influence through African Initiative, a news agency linked to the Russian state, which has engaged young people, supported local media and organised trips to Moscow for media figures and influencers. Researchers have highlighted Russia's interest in the northern port of Antsiranana, also known as Diego-Suarez, whose strategic position near the Mozambique Channel could offer access to major Indian Ocean shipping routes. Madagascar and Russia announced a joint economic zone in May, with fuel storage identified as an initial project. Analysts say the relationship could eventually support broader military, logistical and financial operations. However, political observers warn that the changes promised after the uprising have not translated into substantial institutional reform. Transparency International's vice-chair, Ketakandriana Rafitoson, said longstanding problems, including weak checks and balances, a lack of transparency and impunity, remain. Young activists who helped drive the protests have also expressed frustration over their limited influence in the transition, while victims of the previous regime's violence continue to await justice.

headline: Macron rejects interior minister's resignation after France-wide riots
summary: Saturday's violence targeted around 1,500 businesses, nearly 2,400 arrested, according to official figures
body_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday rejected the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez following widespread violence and looting across the country during last weekend's protests, according to broadcaster BFMTV.

Nunez submitted his resignation to Macron on Sunday amid mounting criticism over the authorities' handling of the unrest.

"I am the minister of the interior, I am responsible for everything that happens on the ground," he told France Inter radio, explaining his decision to resign.

Nunez acknowledged a "loss of control" by police in some cities and admitted there had been a "lack of anticipation" in deploying available security forces.

However, the president decided to keep him in office, citing the need for continuity in the command of security forces during the current crisis, according to a statement from the Elysee Palace.

Macron also called for greater transparency over what he described as "failures in anticipation and intelligence" that contributed to the scale of the violence.

The unrest, which erupted during demonstrations on Saturday, left nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers injured and resulted in approximately 2,400 arrests, according to official figures.

The government's response has faced criticism from several local leaders, including the mayors of Paris, Marseille and Limoges.

Nunez is expected to visit Marseille, one of the cities hardest hit by the violence, where authorities reported that up to 30,000 people were involved in looting on Saturday.

In a televised address on Sunday evening, Macron vowed that those responsible for the destruction would be held accountable.

"Those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable," he said, adding that the country felt "anger and shame" over the violence.

Further clashes and looting were reported late Sunday in Paris, Lyon and Marseille.

In the French capital, police arrested 92 people by around midnight following renewed incidents near Place de la Republique.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is due to chair an interministerial crisis meeting at 10 am local time (0800GMT) to assess the economic impact of the unrest, damage to businesses, insurance issues and ongoing legal proceedings.

According to the Federation of Commerce and Distribution, around 1,500 businesses were targeted during Saturday's violence, with estimated losses amounting to several hundred million euros.
