headline: 🔴 Live: Macron rejects French interior minister's resignation after weekend of unrest
body_text:
Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 07:15Modified: 19/10/2026 - 08:49

French President Emmanuel Macron slammed on Monday security "failures" that he said led to violent protests that rocked the country, but refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez over the crisis. At least 2,400 people were arrested following the unrest that saw town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.

This weekend's rioting in France highlighted failings with the security services over how they deal with threats posed by far-left protesters, says Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin.

Darmanin said the security services were very good in dealing with threats from terrorists and organised crime groups, but less so regarding such ultra-left protesters.

"Clearly, it is not tackling the ultra-left effectively," Darmanin told France 2 TV.

More than 30,000 looters were counted on Saturday at the height of the riots on the streets of Marseille, according a police report.

They included 8,000 “rioters”, the report added, noting that 99 people had been taken into police custody in direct connection with the riots.

The aftermath of the rioting in Marseille. Manon Cruz, Reuters

More than 800 police and other security forces were deployed and some 4,000 tear gas grenades were fired.

A total of 118 members of the security forces were injured, three of whom were taken to hospital.

France's embattled Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has acknowledged responsibility for the security lapses that saw rioters and looters rampage through Paris and other French cities over the weekend.

"I offered to resign because I am entirely responsible for what happened," Nunez told France Inter radio, accepting a "failure to anticipate" and prepare for the challenges faced by security forces.

The minister said a further 350 people had been arrested overnight across France, again pointing the finger at "ultra-left" groups he blamed for the violence.

Political leaders have traded accusations over the weekend violence ahead of next spring’s presidential election.

Far-right leader and presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen criticised Macron's centrist government as “exhausted, disoriented and seemingly incapable of doing anything other than commenting on its own powerlessness,” in a video posted on social media.

Far-left contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon accused Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of “playing with fire,” alleging that “by banking on degradation, you have only succeeded in uniting all youths and workers’ unions.”

Lecornu and other government officials have blamed Mélenchon's France Unbowed (LFI) party for instigating the unrest, which several analysts have described as a gift to Le Pen's far right.

The French president has slammed "failures" that he said led to violent protests that rocked the country, but refused the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez over the crisis.

"The interior minister submitted his resignation to the president on Sunday," the Élysee palace said in a statement. "Given the necessity for continued leadership of law enforcement at this time, the president refused."

Macron had asked Nunez to "take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over the failures in planning and intelligence that led to the violence" and "put in place new operational methods for security forces" to handle the crisis, the statement said.

Authorities estimated Saturday's largely peaceful marches had a turnout of about 550,000, while organisers put it at 800,000.

Demonstrators answered calls from a labor union, student organizations and activists hoping to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 to protest social injustice.

Mass protests in France are often marred by violence on the fringes of otherwise peaceful marches, leading to clashes with police.

The arrest tally reported for Saturday approached the nearly 2,000 recorded nationwide during a single day of yellow vest protests in December 2018.

“Those who looted will have to pay for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” Macron said in a televised address to the nation on Sunday evening.

He denounced “unrestrained violence” by “insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals.”

Macron earlier held an emergency meeting with senior government officials, a day after masked groups set fires and attacked city halls in several cities.

He said he had instructed prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary.

French President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday voiced the public’s “anger” and “shame” over rioting and looting during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.

At least 2,400 people were arrested.

Macron echoed other government officials in blaming much of the violence on far-left activists, accusing them of attacking police and public buildings to foment chaos.

"We all feel anger and shame," Macron said of the devastation brought by the protests that included town halls burned down and hundreds of businesses looted or damaged.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AP and AFP)

headline: Americans increasingly dissatisfied with Trump as midterms approach: Poll
summary: NBC News poll shows 71% of US adults believe the country is on ‘wrong track’
body_text:
ISTANBUL (AA) - A growing number of Americans believe the country is heading in the wrong direction, with President Donald Trump’s approval rating falling to a second-term low as Republicans face mounting challenges ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a new poll.

The NBC News poll showed Saturday that 71% of US adults believe the country is on the “wrong track,” the highest percentage recorded during Trump’s second term.

Trump’s approval rating dropped to 34%, while 66% disapproved of his performance. The proportion of respondents who strongly disapprove of the president reached 51%, marking a new high for his second term.

Economic dissatisfaction appears to be a major factor behind the negative public mood. The economy ranked as the most important issue for 31% of respondents, while 44% said their financial situation had worsened over the past year.

Rising living costs are also weighing on households, with 67% describing gasoline prices as a serious problem. Many respondents said they had changed grocery purchases or reduced spending to cover essential expenses.

The survey also revealed growing political challenges for Republicans. Among registered voters, 55% preferred Democrats to control Congress, compared with 45% who favored Republicans, signaling potential difficulties for the party in power in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

A majority of respondents, 58%, said Trump’s policies were hurting the country, while 28% believed they were helping.

Trump received his lowest approval ratings for his handling of the cost of living, at 27%, and the war with Iran, at 29%. Immigration and border security remained his strongest issue, with 43% approving of his approach.

Russia on Monday said it carried out a "massive strike" on targets in Kyiv and its region as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Washington had paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine and urged its president Volodymyr Zelensky to focus on ending the war.

Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 08:00Modified: 19/10/2026 - 08:35

The Russian Defence Ministry said on Monday its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on targets in Kyiv and the Ukraine's capital region.

The ministry said the attack targeted military-industrial facilities, storage sites for cruise missiles and drones, and data centres.

The latest attacks came as US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that there had been any suspension of intelligence sharing with Ukraine and called on President Volodymyr Zelensky to "focus" on ending the war with Russia.

"What he should be focused on and what we want to be focused on is bringing an end to this war," Rubio said while on a trip to Uzbekistan for talks with Central Asian leaders.

He said there had been no "pause" in the sharing of intelligence as Kyiv authorities have claimed.

US President Donald Trump, who made a deal with Russia to secure fuel exports in exchange for the easing of sanctions, has made renewed attacks on Zelensky in recent days over the war.

The US leader wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday that he was making "great progress" in negotiating peace between Russia and Ukraine, but claimed: "Zelensky doesn't care, and frankly, with all of the money that Europe is famously giving him... he doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."

"Zelensky is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said.

body_text:
TEL AVIV, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Israeli police said on Monday they had arrested 10 suspects as part of an investigation into violent incidents in theoccupied-West Bank over the weekend, including separate attacks on a Washington Post photojournalist and European diplomats.

The United States, Israel's closest ally, had urged a crackdown on settler violence and the arrest of the perpetrators of the attack on the Washington Post photojournalist. France, Belgium and Poland, whose diplomats were attacked, also called on Israel to take action.

Police said the suspects were arrested in a pre-dawn operation on suspicion of involvement in acts of violence, violating a closed military zone order and illegal construction.

The suspects, whom police did not identify, were taken into custody for questioning. Israel's Army Radio reported that they were Israeli citizens.

Prosecutions of Israeli settlers are rare.

A video released by the police of the pre-dawn operation appeared to show at least one arrested suspect, whose face is not seen, wearing ritual tassels known as tzitzit, which are often worn by observant Jewish men.

The video also appeared to show two slingshots, which can be used to hurl stones, being found at one property. On Friday, when the Washington Post journalist was attacked, dozens of masked settlers, some armed, descended on a Palestinian olive harvest, with some settlers hurling stones with slingshots.

Police, military forces and the Shin Bet domestic security service took part in the operation.

Referring to the West Bank by its biblical name, Judea and Samaria, Israeli police commissioner Daniel Levy said the law applied to everyone, "regardless of identity or affiliation".

"The Israel Police is committed to professional, equal, and impartial law enforcement, based on evidence and in accordance with the law," he said in a statement announcing the arrests.

Masked Israeli settlers were filmed on Friday assaulting Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, a US citizen, who was covering a Palestinian olive harvest in the West Bank. Levine was taken to hospital and underwent surgeryon a finger.

On Saturday, French, Belgian and Polish diplomats as well as a French mayor were attacked by masked settlers in another part of the West Bank. A Belgian diplomatic vehicle was also damaged.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the military have blamed "Israeli rioters" for the attack on the diplomats.

However, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority at the October 27 election, has been more circumspect.

He has said the diplomats entered a "sensitive area with a history of confrontations" and without coordinating with the military. He has also said that the facts ​of the attack on Levine were "unclear".

Levine has said she was attacked by masked men wearing tzitzit tassels. Israel's President Isaac Herzog has apologised, saying the "violent rioters" who "brutally attacked" her did not represent the values of Israel.

Settler attacks ​on the Palestinians ⁠are surging, with at least 170 since September 27, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group. Journalists, Israeli activists and foreign observers have also been targeted.

headline: World Food Programme to end aid for half a million in Gaza due to funding shortfall
summary: The UN World Food Programme has warned that funding shortages will leave about 500,000 people in the Gaza Strip without critical food aid in a territory where two thirds of the population remains acutely food insecure. The WFP said it is reducing its monthly assistance from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people.
body_text:
The UN World Food Programme has warned that funding shortages will leave about 500,000 people in the Gaza Strip without critical food aid in a territory where two thirds of the population remains acutely food insecure. The WFP said it is reducing its monthly assistance from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people.

Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 09:33

The UN's World Food Programme (WFP) said on Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, while warning that needs remained acute.

"As of this month, we're now cutting half a million people from the number of people that we're assisting," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP.

The reductions bring down the number of Palestinians receiving WFP aid either in food or cash assistance to 1.1 million people – still roughly half of war-battered Gaza's population.

headline: 'Life is absolutely brutal in Gaza,' says World Food Programme head
summary: The UN's World Food Programme says 1.4 million people in Gaza are suffering acute food shortages and that funding gaps are forcing cutbacks in critical aid, despite the U.S. brokered Hamas-Israel ceasefire.
body_text:
The UN's World Food Programme says 1.4 million people in Gaza are suffering acute food shortages and that funding gaps are forcing cutbacks in critical aid, despite the U.S. brokered Hamas-Israel ceasefire.

It's been more than a year since famine was declared in parts of Gaza, and while some progress has been made to address food shortages there, humanitarian organizations are warning that progress is extremely fragile. Despite the Israel-Hamas ceasefire brokered by the U.S., more than two-thirds of Gaza's population - nearly 1.4 million people - are experiencing crisis levels of acute food insecurity. The U.N.'s World Food Programme says the approaching winter months will only increase the need for more humanitarian aid and more money to pay for it. Carl Skau is the acting executive director of the World Food Programme. He joins us now from Jerusalem. Welcome to the program.

CARL SKAU: Thank you. Thank you for having me on.

ROSE: You have just returned from a trip to Gaza. What did you see there?

SKAU: Well, this is my eighth trip to Gaza since the war, and it's a year into the ceasefire. You know, my takeaway is that not much have changed, frankly. There is - life is absolutely brutal in Gaza. There is no basic services. You know, there is massive destruction. There is no proper shelter. And frankly, the insecurity continues. We were at one of the distribution points - they told me there that someone had been killed the day before. As we were leaving, there had been shooting at the exit point. And so, you know, I think we record some average 50 security incidents per day. So, you know, we have been able to push back on famine, but that's much thanks to our efforts. We've been reaching almost every person in Gaza for the past few months, but that progress is fragile, and it can easily be reversed.

ROSE: Can you tell us a little bit about who you met with there? And is there any, perhaps, a story that illustrates the food shortages that persist?

SKAU: When I was at one of these distribution points where we serve hot meals - it's a big pot, and you share a meal for everyone who shows up with a pot to walk away. And these are the most vulnerable. These are the people that live close to the front line. They told me that many had been displaced or - you know, in the last few weeks. Already, they don't have cooking gas to cook for themselves. And, you know, they told me they eat once a day. They have no fresh vegetables. So these are people who, you know, are not eating enough already.

And as we are now facing the winter, we are being forced to cut. You know, we are cutting almost half a million people off assistance in these next few weeks. It's not because the needs are down. It's also not because we are not able to bring in food. It's because the funding is no longer there.

ROSE: What happened? Why is the funding falling short of the need?

SKAU: Well, it's because it's a massive operation. You know, we've been reaching 2 million people every month in an environment that is also relatively expensive. So it's a massive undertaking. But of course, this is not the time to turn away. If anything, this is the time to step up. We need to sustain this effort, sustain this emergency support so we can protect the gains that we made.

But also, we need to move beyond that, frankly. I mean, we need to now really make a push on early recovery, help people get some proper housing and shelter before the winter. Then on the food side, you know, we want commercial to come in. We want the markets to start working so that we can instead distribute cash. It's much cheaper, and it helps people - you know, they can choose for themselves. There is some dignity in that, and it would be the way to start some kind of domestic food system as well.

ROSE: I want to ask you about the flow of goods and supplies into Gaza. There has been some reporting about the suspension of commercial shipments into the Gaza Strip in recent days. What is going on there?

SKAU: Well, that's deeply concerning. There is some disagreement around taxation for commercial goods. And, you know, this is at a time when, if anything, we need to scale up. When we were there, there hadn't been any entry of commercial goods for five days. We now saw some commercial trucks moving. I hope that means that this has been resolved because what we really need is to expand the commercial and bring more fresh foods and vegetables.

There's a lot of, you know, chocolates and chips coming in and Cokes. That's not really what's needed. And that's because there is bigger margin, I guess, on that and that you don't need a cold chain. But what we need is proper commercial goods coming in, food goods that - you know, the fresh foods, the fresh vegetables and fruits. That's what we need to diversify, but also to bring down the prices on the market so that people with the cash they have can get more.

ROSE: Beyond funding, what else needs to happen to ensure that the necessary aid gets to the people who need it the most?

SKAU: Well, I guess, I mean, clearly, there needs to be progress on the peace plan. But, you know, we don't need to wait with early recovery. The big issue there is the dual-use problems. We need UNICEF and other partners to be able to bring in what they need to restore water and sanitation facilities. We need to be able to get the learning material in so we can expand on those temporary learning centers that are there. And there is lots of garbage everywhere. So you can just imagine when the rains start hitting, it's going to be an absolute mess there.

But on the food side, again, I mean, you know, us now moving into a period where we have to cut 500,000 - half a million people - off our assistance, this is going to cause additional pressure just as the winter hit. And so we need to avoid that. We need donors to step up with funding. But we, of course, also need international community to step up and push forward on the political tracks so there is a solution here. Three years into this, you know, life is at a standstill. They need some hope, and they need to be given the basics to start rebuilding their lives.

ROSE: I've been speaking to Carl Skau. He is the acting executive director of the U.N.'s World Food Programme. Thank you very much for joining us.

SKAU: Thank you for having me on.

headline: French president arrives in Kuwait at start of Gulf tour
summary: Emmanuel Macron to discuss bilateral ties with Kuwaiti emir as he begins Gulf tour that also includes UAE, Bahrain and Qatar
body_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron arrived in Kuwait on Monday at the start of a four-nation Gulf tour that will also take him to the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Qatar.

Macron is expected to hold talks with Kuwaiti Emir Sheikh Meshal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah on ways to strengthen bilateral relations, according to the Kuwait News Agency (KUNA).

KUNA described the French president’s official visit as a significant milestone in relations between the two countries, marking 65 years of ties built on bilateral cooperation.

The French presidency earlier announced that Macron would visit Kuwait, the UAE, Bahrain and Qatar from Oct. 19 to 21, with discussions focusing on regional stability, freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and energy security.

The tour comes amid heightened regional tensions and disruptions to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which a significant share of global oil supplies passes.

Kuwait and France established diplomatic relations in 1961, following Kuwait’s independence, and have since developed cooperation in defense, security, trade, investment and education.

The two countries have continued to coordinate on regional security issues, with France maintaining a military presence in the Gulf region and longstanding defense partnerships with several Gulf states.

headline: Iran’s U23 Freestyle Team wins title of C’ships in Las Vegas
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – Iran’s freestyle team won the title of championships at 2026 U23 World Championships in Las Vegas on Sunday, finishing ahead of Russia with four coveted gold medals.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – Iran’s freestyle team won the title of championships at 2026 U23 World Championships in Las Vegas on Sunday, finishing ahead of Russia with four coveted gold medals.

Iran topped the freestyle standings with 180 points, ahead of Russia on 171 and host nation the United States on 104, securing the overall team crown with a strong performance across the 10 weight classes.

Held from October 12 to 18, the United World Wrestling (UWW) championships brought together emerging wrestlers from around the world in Greco-Roman, women’s wrestling and freestyle.

Iran’s title-winning campaign reached its climax on the final day, when Ahora Khateri and Mahdi Yousefi delivered decisive victories to keep the team ahead of its closest rival.

Khateri staged one of the tournament’s most dramatic comebacks in the 65kg final, recovering from a 6-1 deficit to defeat Japan’s Kaiji Ogino 7-6 after scoring six points in the final 40 seconds.

Yousefi then strengthened Iran’s position in the team race by defeating Russia’s Said Saidulov 3-1 in the 79kg final, helping secure the championship for the Iranian squad.

Iran had already collected two freestyle gold medals before the final day’s decisive bouts. Abolfazl Rahmani defeated Russia’s Arslan Bagaev 5-2 in the 92kg final, while Abolfazl Mohammad Nezhad secured the 125kg title with a commanding 10-0 victory over Georgia’s Aleksandre Abramishvili.

Iran’s Sports and Youth Minister Ahmad Donyamali congratulated the national freestyle team, saying the achievement had brought joy and pride to the Iranian people.

headline: Macron rejects interior minister's resignation after France-wide riots
summary: Saturday's violence targeted around 1,500 businesses, nearly 2,400 arrested, according to official figures
body_text:
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday rejected the resignation of Interior Minister Laurent Nunez following widespread violence and looting across the country during last weekend's protests, according to broadcaster BFMTV.

Nunez submitted his resignation to Macron on Sunday amid mounting criticism over the authorities' handling of the unrest.

"I am the minister of the interior, I am responsible for everything that happens on the ground," he told France Inter radio, explaining his decision to resign.

Nunez acknowledged a "loss of control" by police in some cities and admitted there had been a "lack of anticipation" in deploying available security forces.

However, the president decided to keep him in office, citing the need for continuity in the command of security forces during the current crisis, according to a statement from the Elysee Palace.

Macron also called for greater transparency over what he described as "failures in anticipation and intelligence" that contributed to the scale of the violence.

The unrest, which erupted during demonstrations on Saturday, left nearly 1,000 law enforcement officers injured and resulted in approximately 2,400 arrests, according to official figures.

The government's response has faced criticism from several local leaders, including the mayors of Paris, Marseille and Limoges.

Nunez is expected to visit Marseille, one of the cities hardest hit by the violence, where authorities reported that up to 30,000 people were involved in looting on Saturday.

In a televised address on Sunday evening, Macron vowed that those responsible for the destruction would be held accountable.

"Those who sought to bring down the republic will be held accountable," he said, adding that the country felt "anger and shame" over the violence.

Further clashes and looting were reported late Sunday in Paris, Lyon and Marseille.

In the French capital, police arrested 92 people by around midnight following renewed incidents near Place de la Republique.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is due to chair an interministerial crisis meeting at 10 am local time (0800GMT) to assess the economic impact of the unrest, damage to businesses, insurance issues and ongoing legal proceedings.

According to the Federation of Commerce and Distribution, around 1,500 businesses were targeted during Saturday's violence, with estimated losses amounting to several hundred million euros.

body_text:
Rory McIlroy and the Hero Dubai Desert Classic might feel inextricably linked. But spectators are being urged not to take his presence at the Emirates Golf Club for granted.

McIlroy has been playing at the region’s oldest European Tour event for over 20 years now.

On Monday it was confirmed he will be heading back to the Majlis Course for a tilt at a fifth Dallah Trophy in January.

McIlroy's rise from Dubai and a connection with Jumeirah Hotels

He has been a visible part of the growth of the city. It is debatable which method is better for dating pictures of past Desert Classics: counting the number of skyscrapers in Dubai Marina, or the volume – and, lately, greyness – of McIlroy’s hair.

Now aged 37, McIlroy is not going to be pensioned off any time soon. But the Northern Irishman has said he plans to reduce his schedule in the future.

He wants to focus on adding to his haul of six majors, streamline his bid to return to World No 1, and spend more time with his family.

Given his CV, McIlroy is in a position to be picky. His sweet spot, he has suggested, could be around 18 to 20 events per season.

If four of those are majors, plus play-off series tournaments on both the US and European tours, and some obvious signature events Stateside, that does not leave a huge amount of wiggle room for those wanting to host him.

He could be more in demand than ever. Even without the No 1 rankings tag which Scottie Scheffler has been hogging so voraciously for so long, McIlroy is the most recognisable figure playing the game.

Or, as Simon Corkill, the Desert Classic’s tournament director, puts it: “He’s golf’s living legend.”

“You use the word legend; he's certainly there and there are some others still playing,” Corkill said.

“But he's the one who is front and centre at the moment. Tiger [Woods’] career is not where it should be at the moment and I think he's going to struggle to come back with what's going on in his world.

“But Rory is there, exhibiting it week in, week out, and we can't take it for granted.”

McIlroy is also booked for two UAE events next month – the DP World Tour finale on consecutive weeks in Abu Dhabi and at Jumeirah Golf Estates in Dubai.

Corkill said it is lucky he has such an affinity with the Classic, which is where he won his first Tour title, that it means he is happy to keep returning.

“He's not going to come to Dubai every year going forward,” Corkill said.

“He's openly said he wants to reduce his schedule, and he's going to pick and choose the events he likes. He really likes the Hero Dubai Classic, which is great for us.”

Although his participation in next year’s Classic has just been announced, the decision was made in the summer, around the time of the Open Championship.

At the time, the Iran war was central to the news cycle. A number of leading players said they were wary of heading to the Gulf when the Tour was due to return there later in the year.

Corkill said McIlroy’s knowledge of the region – as a former resident, with many friends still based here – meant he was quickly convinced of its security.

“He was fully reassured,” Corkill said. “He had spoken to a lot of his friends here prior to the conversations we were having, and got the assurances of what was actually happening on the ground in Dubai.

“He can hear it from me. He can hear it from the DP World Tour, which he did. But it obviously gives him some comfort when he's got some close friends here also saying the same thing.”

Corkill said McIlroy’s presence at the Classic is an ideal way to launch the first big tournament of the DP World Tour season.

“We really want to make sure that beginning of January is that real opening party,” Corkill said.

“It's not technically the start of the DP World Tour season. But it's very much that back-to-school event.

headline: U.S. issues security alerts across the Middle East, warns of flight disruptions
summary: Washington warns Americans in 12 Middle Eastern locations of possible airspace closures and escalating hostilities as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify. The United States has issued security alerts for…
body_text:
Washington warns Americans in 12 Middle Eastern locations of possible airspace closures and escalating hostilities as Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia intensify.

The United States has issued security alerts for Americans in 12 locations across the Middle East, including Qatar, warning of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and further escalation as attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on Saudi Arabia intensify.

The alerts, dated 18 October, cover Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain, Oman, Iran, Qatar, Iraq, Lebanon, Yemen and Israel/Occupied Jerusalem.

U.S. diplomatic missions have urged American citizens to remain vigilant, monitor airline and airport operations, and prepare contingency plans in case travel arrangements are disrupted.

“Be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions,” the U.S. Embassy in Qatar said in its security alert.

The notice warned that “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area”, raising concerns that the consequences of the fighting could extend beyond Saudi Arabia and neighbouring areas.

The alerts also warned that Iran and groups supportive of Tehran could target U.S. interests overseas, including businesses, institutions and locations associated with the United States and its citizens.

In Qatar, the U.S. Embassy in Doha advised American citizens to monitor changing security conditions and follow official guidance.

It urged them to stay informed about local developments, avoid demonstrations and large gatherings, stay away from areas with a heavy police presence, and exercise caution at locations publicly associated with the United States.

“If an aerial attack occurs, stay away from glass doors, windows, and any fallen debris,” the embassy advised, urging Americans to monitor their phones and news outlets for official instructions.

The embassy also recommended keeping mobile phones charged, saving emergency contact numbers, maintaining a low profile and enrolling in the U.S. Department of State’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP).

The programme allows registered travellers to receive security updates and helps U.S/ diplomatic missions contact them during emergencies.

The embassy said it remained open for routine American citizen services and limited visa services.

The warnings come amid a sharp escalation in attacks attributed to Yemen’s Houthi movement, which has targeted Saudi airports and energy infrastructure as fighting in Yemen intensifies.

A Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on 10 October killed at least 13 people and injured more than 300.

The escalations have disrupted air travel, with Qatar Airways temporarily suspending flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam on 12 October.

analysis.framing: The article frames the event as a factual security advisory, focusing on practical warnings to Americans and the escalation of Houthi attacks, without overt editorializing.

loaded_language.explanation: Emphasizes the intensity and suddenness of the increase in attacks, which may convey urgency beyond a neutral 'increase'.
Suggests growing severity, which can be seen as more dramatic than 'continues' or 'increases'.
A standard security phrase that implies ongoing threat but is common in official advisories; mildly alarmist.

omissions: No mention of the number of casualties from Houthi attacks beyond the Riyadh airport attack, or details on other attacks.
No context on the broader Yemen conflict or the reasons behind the Houthi attacks.
No reaction from Saudi or Houthi officials.
No information on whether other countries have issued similar alerts.

Days after the US signed a diesel purchase deal with Russia and announced a pause on the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Monday said that the decision to waive Russia oil sanctions also took into account the India-US trade deal, which is close to conclusion. Rubio’s comments come ahead of his expected visit to Mumbai on October 20, where he will be holding talks with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar.

“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries. I know diesel prices are high in the United States, but they’re really, really high in a bunch of other countries around the world, and then we have to manage all of these things. We’re trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that. So that’s one of the things we’ve taken into consideration..” Rubio said during a press conference in Uzbekistan.

Rubio said that every country has a complex set of factors that they have to take into account and that for some countries, it’s very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources. “That’s not an excuse, but all that has to be balanced when you make foreign policy,” he said while responding to a question on the waiver and its impact on the Russia-Ukraine war.

“The foreign policy of the United States, of course, takes into account what’s happening with the war between Russia and Ukraine, but it is not solely dominated by that. It hasn’t taken into account a variety of other factors, including our bilateral relationships with other countries, and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies. You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue. So that’s the complex part of having to balance all this,” Rubio said.

With the threat of 100% US tariffs eased, India and the US could manage to sign a deal as both countries seem to have reached a broad alignment on other tariffs. Both the Section 301 investigation on New Delhi and the trade deal have resulted in a convergence between the countries. The major point of difference remained on the use of tariffs over India’s purchase of Russian oil.

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) had said that the government remains committed to ensuring the nation’s energy security “through diversified sourcing and based on evolving market dynamics”. It said in a statement that the proposed legislation’s implications for the India-US relationship as well as the global energy market have been flagged in discussions with US representatives.

While India had already banned imports of goods using forced labour following the first US Section 301 investigation, India, along with other G20 countries, earlier this month released a joint statement committing to take action against structural overcapacity in certain geographies, particularly in sectors like automobile, electric vehicle, batteries, chemicals, foundational semiconductors and solar panels.

As per the Council on Foreign Relations, diesel prices in the US averaged $6.18 a gallon as of October 12, up from $3.48 at the start of this year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and higher fuel costs have passed through to U.S. consumers.

The latest Consumer Price Index showed that prices rose 0.6% in September, which is more than economists expected, bringing the annual inflation rate to 3.7%. Polls indicate that this could affect Republican candidates in the upcoming midterm elections, which have increasingly centred on cost-of-living concerns, as per the Council on Foreign Relations.

Higher fuel prices have also become a challenge for Indian policymakers as retail inflation continues to inch upwards, rising to 5.54% in September, up from 4.83% in August, according to data from the National Statistics Office. Food inflation has surged to 7.74 per cent in September, up from 6 per cent in August, driven by items such as onions, ginger, garlic and lemon. The FAO food price index jumped 5.8 per cent, pointing towards an uptick in international prices.

body_text:
If autumn feels like it’s taking an age to arrive, you’re not imagining it.

October has been warmer than usual this year, with the UAE National Centre of Meteorology issuing a major climate update on the El Nino weather phenomenon, which has been forecast to be the strongest on record.

Sea surface temperatures in the Pacific have reached between 2.3°C and 3°C above the long-term average, cementing this year’s event as a global weather disruptor.

Iran war and El Nino could drive food prices up for longer

Instead of the predictable October drop into comfortable autumn weather, the phenomenon is trapping a blanket of high pressure over the Arabian Peninsular, driving temperatures well above seasonal averages.

Recent maximum temperatures across the country have ranged between 37°C and 43°C, with some areas experiencing temperatures 4°C higher than usual.

The UAE's average daily temperature in October stands at 29.7°C, according to the NCM's latest monthly weather summary.

October and November are expected to feel the peak of the El Nino cycle, with higher rainfall than usual also expected, including severe bouts that could raise the risk of flooding, although this is not guaranteed. The NCM projects a 96 per cent probability that these potentially volatile conditions will persist through to March 2027, with secondary environmental impacts such as lingering into April.

Speaking to The National in September, Dr Diana Francis, associate professor and head of the Environmental and Geophysical Sciences (Engeos) Laboratory at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said the region should prepare for more rainfall.

“El Nino generally tilts the Gulf and parts of the Arabian Peninsula towards wetter conditions, enhanced moisture transport and a greater chance of heavy rain episodes,” she said.

If rainfall levels increase, “very intense downpours may become more likely, according to Dr Andries-Jan de Vries, of the Institute of Earth Surface Dynamics at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

“In combination with dry soils, with mountains and valleys, they can easily accumulate rainwater that can fall in a very short period of time, and that can then lead to flooding,” he said.

Parts of the UAE were hit by severe flooding in late March this year, almost two years after the country experienced its most extreme rainfall on record, late into what was described as the fifth-strongest El Nino on record.

A study in Nature Scientific Reports in June with the title “An extreme rainfall event over the United Arab Emirates in April 2024: Role of dynamic and thermodynamic drivers”, said that El Nino “may have contributed to a large-scale background environment favourable for above-normal April rainfall over the region”.

After the 2024 floods, the authorities began investing heavily to improve drainage and make the country better able to cope with severe rains.

The El Nino-Southern Oscillation, to use its full name, is a natural phenomenon in which the upwelling of water causes warmer sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, with knock-on effects on the global climate. An opposite phenomenon, La Nina, is linked to cooler temperatures in that part of the Pacific Ocean.

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, El Nino and La Nina each last between nine months and a year and happen irregularly, typically every two to seven years.

El Nino is seen slightly more often, and the one occurring this year and into next year has been forecast to be exceptionally strong.

The World Meteorological Organisation recently said there were “exceptionally warm tropical Pacific Ocean conditions” and warned that a very strong El Nino could “significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather”.

A recent study in Weather and Climate Dynamics called “The influence of El Nino-Southern Oscillation on cool-season precipitation variability in the arid Middle East”, highlighted three mechanisms that cause El Nino to influence weather in the Gulf region.

Firstly, El Nino’s warmer sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific are typically associated with colder sea-surface temperatures and reduced tropical convection around Indonesia and the West Pacific.

“That influences the regional circulation over South Asia and the Indian Ocean, and we have a change in the transport of moisture in the atmosphere,” said Dr De Vries, the first author of the paper.

This results in an increase in moisture coming into the region.

A second pathway is an alternating pattern of high and low-pressure systems running eastward from the warmer region in the Pacific, stretching over North America, the North Atlantic and Europe to the Middle East. This goes along with a low-pressure system over the Middle East, which is more favourable for precipitation.

A third cause is that during El Nino conditions, the subtropical jet stream over North Africa and the Middle East – a band of fast-flowing air blowing from west to east about 12km to 14km above the Earth’s surface – is shifted slightly south, towards the equator. This allows mid-latitude storms to more easily enter the Middle East region.

While El Nino makes wetter conditions in the Gulf region more likely, it does not make them certain.

“El Niño increases the likelihood of wetter conditions but does not guarantee them. Rainfall in the region varies greatly from one year to another,” said Dr Zouhair Lachkar, a senior research scientist in New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said El Nino was not always linked to higher rainfall.

So while a stronger-than-normal El Nino is statistically more likely to have a greater effect on rainfall than an average one, it may not have a major impact. Effects on rainfall are most likely this October and November, and in March, April and May next year.

Even though El Nino warms the climate globally, Dr Francis said its impacts on UAE and Gulf temperatures were “relatively weak”.

“Background climate warming, Gulf/Arabian Sea temperatures and regional circulation will be at least as important,” she said. “The impact of El Nino in the Gulf happens a few months after it is established in the Pacific. Most probably its impacts will be felt here from mid-autumn onward, and in those seasons it is mainly the rainfall patterns that will be influenced, less the temperature.”

Dr Lachkar said that research at NYU Abu Dhabi showed that El Nino does not necessarily produce higher sea-surface temperatures in the Arabian Gulf. “In fact, we found that La Nina has historically been more favourable to exceptionally high summer sea-surface temperatures in the Gulf,” he said.

Should there be increased rainfall in the UAE, the impact on the natural environment could be positive.

Prof John Burt, director of NYU Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said if El Nino brought more winter rain, it could lead to “a marked increase in plant growth across our deserts and mountains”.

“Sufficient rain during the cooler months can trigger widespread germination of seeds, plus flowering and renewed growth in established shrubs,” he said.

"These responses extend through the food web: vegetation provides food for herbivores, flowers support pollinating insects, and greater insect abundance benefits birds, reptiles and small mammals. A productive winter can also replenish seed reserves, supporting future plant generations after the visible greenery disappears.”

He said that while a wetter winter could promote natural regeneration, lasting benefits would depend on the intensity of the initial rainfall events and the subsequent weather.

“Rain that initiates germination must be followed by conditions that allow seedlings to survive, such as continued soil moisture in the weeks and months that follow,” he said. “In contrast, brief but intense downpours can erode soils and uproot vegetation, particularly in mountain wadis and the gravel plains at the foothills.”

He said it is not known if summer temperatures next year will be higher than normal, but that the centre will monitor this closely. “Marine organisms already live very close to their upper heat limits in summer, and are vulnerable to being pushed over the edge,” he said.

A previous version of this article was published on September 14.

headline: Inside flydubai Flight 1073: captain tells of cockpit fight in world exclusive interview
summary: Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has spoken of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert, with the intention of killing 172 people on board.In a world exclusive interview with The National from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, Capt Machchhar said the first officer sitting next to him for two hours had shown no sign of what Emirati prosecutors say was a “premeditated terrorist plot” to hijack the aircraft.Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked Capt Machchhar and seized control of the plane.I tried to block the blows as much as I could. [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I fell face down in the cockpit Capt Smit MachchharCapt Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for getting the cockpit door, locked from the inside, open and allowing the attack to be foiled. All of the 172 passengers and crew on board the September 30 flight survived.The first officer has been detained in the UAE and faces terrorism charges. The statements made in this interview reflect the interviewee’s recollection of events, based on his personal experience and his perception of them at the time they occurred. In his interview with The National at Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar revealed:He thought the first blow to his head was a falling piece of equipment, before more blows rained down on himThe co-pilot – who prosecutors said was radicalised by online Islamist content and in a religious study centre in Australia – showed no sign of unusual behaviourCapt Machchhar does not know what sparked the first officer to seize the controls when Tel Aviv airport, which he planned to crash into, was more than an hour awayHe expects an airline industry security review may lead to changes, amid questions over the cockpit fire axeHe thanked the UAE for his treatment and returning him to his family, saying: “I was told that, by the order of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed, the President of UAE has called you back home – I smiled for the first time.”Cockpit battleNarrating the hijacking to a media outlet for the first time, Capt Machchhar said he thought the blow to his head was from a cockpit panel that had collapsed. “The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head,” he said. “It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, [I realised] it's the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.” He recalled those initial moments, explaining: “My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head.”Capt Machchhar suffered serious injuries to his head and arm, including defensive wounds from trying to stop the blows. “While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking [at] outlines.” Capt Machchhar is not entirely clear how events unfolded nor the timeline. But he managed to open the cockpit after several attempts. He explained that every time he had to exert himself physically, he would lose blood and consciousness.Nosedive“Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door," he said. "And [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit.”He believes he regained consciousness as the attacker plunged the aircraft into a dive. Crew members and passengers began banging on the other side of the cockpit door.“The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down. When I say spooling down, it's the engine sound going from full blast to like … not what you want at that stage in the flight. And I felt the aircraft was steeply going down.”Capt Machchhar became emotional as he explained his instinct to survive. “At that point, I realised that you will not survive this," he explained. "And I was constantly looking for the door. I did go for it. I did push it … the next thing I remember was I was facedown, lying with, thank God, the cockpit door open. I was between the cockpit and the galley.”Chaos and commotionCapt Machchhar said there was “so much chaos and commotion” as he was hauled out of the cockpit. It was at that moment that passengers and crew seized the first officer. body_text:
Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has spoken of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert, with the intention of killing 172 people on board.

In a world exclusive interview with The National from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, Capt Machchhar said the first officer sitting next to him for two hours had shown no sign of what Emirati prosecutors say was a “premeditated terrorist plot” to hijack the aircraft.

Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked Capt Machchhar and seized control of the plane.

Capt Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for getting the cockpit door, locked from the inside, open and allowing the attack to be foiled. All of the 172 passengers and crew on board the September 30 flight survived.

The first officer has been detained in the UAE and faces terrorism charges. The statements made in this interview reflect the interviewee’s recollection of events, based on his personal experience and his perception of them at the time they occurred.

In his interview with The National at Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar revealed:

Narrating the hijacking to a media outlet for the first time, Capt Machchhar said he thought the blow to his head was from a cockpit panel that had collapsed.

“The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head,” he said. “It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, [I realised] it's the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.”

He recalled those initial moments, explaining: “My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head.”

Capt Machchhar suffered serious injuries to his head and arm, including defensive wounds from trying to stop the blows. “While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking [at] outlines.”

Capt Machchhar is not entirely clear how events unfolded nor the timeline. But he managed to open the cockpit after several attempts. He explained that every time he had to exert himself physically, he would lose blood and consciousness.

“Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door," he said. "And [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit.”

He believes he regained consciousness as the attacker plunged the aircraft into a dive. Crew members and passengers began banging on the other side of the cockpit door.

“The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down. When I say spooling down, it's the engine sound going from full blast to like … not what you want at that stage in the flight. And I felt the aircraft was steeply going down.”

Capt Machchhar became emotional as he explained his instinct to survive.

“At that point, I realised that you will not survive this," he explained. "And I was constantly looking for the door. I did go for it. I did push it … the next thing I remember was I was facedown, lying with, thank God, the cockpit door open. I was between the cockpit and the galley.”

Capt Machchhar said there was “so much chaos and commotion” as he was hauled out of the cockpit. It was at that moment that passengers and crew seized the first officer. A pair of flydubai pilots who were travelling as passengers took control of the plane.

“If I have to say how many people were trying to control the situation, I would say a million. I know it doesn't make sense, but, yeah, I would say a million people were trying to take over control,” he said.

He described the moment others came to his rescue as “magic”, saying: “The next thing I remember was [being] pulled out by one of the passengers. And then, soon after that, the senior cabin crew thankfully reached where I was and did his magic. And yeah, that's how I'm speaking to you today.”

Recovering in his bed in Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar has been trying to piece together events in the two weeks since the failed terror plot.

He remembers praying as the cabin crew chief and others, including dentist Shota Musaev, tried to stem the bleeding from his wounds. “There was heavy bleeding from his head and left hand,” Dr Musaev told The National last week.

“He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on.”

Capt Machchhar was clearly emotional as he spoke. He said: “I prayed a lot. I thought about my son, my daughter, and prayed. That was the point where I would say I didn't give up.”

He spoke frankly: “Did I give up? No. I can 100 per cent tell you I did not give up. But was I sure I was going to make it? No.”

Asked whether he suspected anything from his co-pilot's behaviour, he said he did not notice anything.

“If there was something that could have hinted earlier on the ground or something, yes, of course, I would have acted. I would have spoken up. I would have questioned some things like that,” he explained.

He described that morning as ordinary, saying it was the first time he had met the first officer. “It was a morning flight. So, yeah, there was some small talk, but there was not really like a deep conversation,” he said.

Capt Machchhar added: “We avoid getting into deep conversations, especially during high-intensity or high-density airspace, especially nowadays with all the restrictions. Saudi is very high density.”

"Nothing until that point would have caused me to think that: 'Hey, hold on, there's something off.'”

There has been speculation about why the first officer attacked his colleague when the plane was an hour away from Tel Aviv airport, which prosecutors said he intended to crash into.

“I won't say I've been thinking a lot about it, but yes, I did give it a thought. It makes no sense to me,” Capt Machchhar said.

There was also much scrutiny over the presence of a cockpit axe, and how the co-pilot was radicalised.

Asked whether aviation security will change as a result of the close call, Capt Machchhar said: “I think so. And for good."

He added: “I won't blame it on anyone. You've got to learn from the event … I would just say: learn from whatever's happened and then make sure that this doesn't happen again, ever.”

Capt Machchhar, who lives with his wife and children in the UAE, faces a long recovery but wants to return to the cockpit.

“Did my love die for aviation? Not at all. Not at all,” he said with a smile. “I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”

headline: UN food agency cuts Gaza assistance by one-third amid funding shortages
summary: Half a million Palestinians lose access to critical food assistance ahead of winter
body_text:
The UN World Food Program (WFP) announced Monday that funding shortages have forced it to cut food assistance in the Gaza Strip by around one-third, leaving half a million people without critical support as winter approaches.

In a statement, the agency said it is now assisting 1.1 million vulnerable people in Gaza, down from 1.6 million last month, while food rations have been halved.

Families receiving assistance will now get one food parcel instead of two, along with a smaller bag of wheat flour, it said.

The number of daily hot meals has also dropped from 250,000 to 150,000, while families in hard-to-reach areas, including near the Israeli army-controlled "yellow line," will receive meals every other day instead of daily.

The agency has also reduced the value of cash assistance for 75,000 families.

According to WFP, an estimated 1.4 million people, or 67% of Gaza's population, face crisis-level food insecurity or worse, including around 200,000 experiencing emergency conditions requiring immediate food assistance to prevent deaths from hunger.

Only one in five children consumes a sufficiently diverse diet, while unemployment exceeds 80%, leaving many families unable to afford nutritious food.

WFP warned that "modest" improvements in food security since the October 2025 ceasefire remain "fragile" and could quickly be reversed by further reductions in humanitarian assistance.

Funding shortages have also forced the agency to halve its assistance in the occupied West Bank, from 400,000 to 200,000 people.

The agency said it urgently needs $450 million to sustain critical operations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, through March 2027.

headline: UN agency slashes Gaza food aid over funding, warns needs persist
summary: The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-battered Palestinian territory. With the cutbacks, 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza -- still about half the population -- will be receiving either food or cash assistance each month from the UN agency, in reduced amounts.
body_text:
The World Food Programme said Monday it would end monthly assistance to 500,000 people in Gaza due to a funding shortfall, despite acute needs in the war-battered Palestinian territory.

With the cutbacks, 1.1 million Palestinians in Gaza -- still about half the population -- will be receiving either food or cash assistance each month from the UN agency, in reduced amounts.

The World Food Programme said its efforts had mitigated the effects during a famine last year in Gaza -- a description of the situation disputed by Israel -- and warned that conditions had not improved to the point that it can take away aid.

"People are not safe. Airstrikes continue on a daily basis. People continue to be displaced," Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director, told AFP at the agency's office in east Jerusalem.

"Almost everybody remains without a permanent home to live in. And the humanitarian conditions are brutal," he said.

According to the latest assessments, 1.4 million people -- or two-thirds of Gaza's population -- are still "acutely food insecure" and need humanitarian assistance to survive, he said.

In August last year, the UN's Integrated Food Security Phase Classification said that Gaza was suffering famine conditions. Israel, which has blockaded the territory and attacked it relentlessly since the unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack on it by Hamas, described the finding as a lie.

The famine classification was lifted in December, two months after a US-brokered ceasefire was announced in Gaza. Israel has kept striking Gaza since then, vowing to kill anyone involved in the October 7 attack.

Since the ceasefire, the WFP has been able to step up assistance and had been reaching between 1.5 million and 1.8 million people every month.

"This has been a lifeline. But now, rather than being able to sustain and scale up that assistance, we're actually having to reduce it," Hughes said.

"And that's not because we don't have humanitarian access to deliver food; that's because we don't have funding."

In addition to reducing the number of people who receive rations, the WFP has been forced to shrink the content.

Families receiving food assistance will now get only one food parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour, the WFP said in an operational note.

The 75,000 families who receive assistance in cash will see the amount reduced from 1,250 to 750 shekels ($400 to $240) per month.

The WFP is funded by governments as well as private donors. It has seen a sharp drop in resources, including after President Donald Trump returned to power in the United States and drastically slashed contributions to UN agencies as well as bilateral aid.

The agency says it needs about $450 million over the next six months for its operations in Gaza and the West Bank, but in 2026 it has only received about half the usual financing for the Palestinian territories.

In September, the agency also reduced by half the number of aid recipients in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, from 400,000 to 200,000.

"Now is not the time in the history of Palestine and Gaza to turn away from what is happening in Gaza," Hughes said.

The WFP says that conditions have moderately improved in Gaza but noted that needs could rise again with the onset of winter.

Israel has allowed more goods into Gaza under the terms of the Trump ceasefire but still imposes heavy restrictions, turning away shipments of anything that is seen as having potential military use -- a policy that has included blocking even prosthetic limbs, according to the United Nations.

Israel has ramped up longstanding criticism of the United Nations since the Gaza war, accusing the world body of bias and perpetuating dependency among Palestinians.

headline: Leader congrats Iran’s freestyle team for winning world title
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei congratulated Iran’s national U-23 freestyle wrestling team on winning the world title in Las Vegas, the United States.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei congratulated Iran’s national U-23 freestyle wrestling team on winning the world title in Las Vegas, the United States.

In a congratulatory message issued on Monday, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei commended and praised the wrestlers, coaches and sports officials, extending his congratulations to the Iranian nation, especially the country’s heroic youth.

In another message, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian congratulated Iran’s national freestyle wrestling team on winning the world title in the United States, praising the determination, talent and skill of Iranian wrestlers.

The achievement follows Iran’s Greco-Roman wrestling team also claiming the world championship, the president opined.

Iran’s freestyle team won the title of championships at 2026 U23 World Championships in Las Vegas on Sunday, finishing ahead of Russia with four coveted gold medals.

Iran topped the freestyle standings with 180 points, ahead of Russia on 171 and host nation the United States on 104, securing the overall team crown with a strong performance across the 10 weight classes.

body_text:
An Iranian operative accused of planning dozens of anti-Semitic attacks in Europe and the US has been reportedly plotting further assaults from behind bars.

US authorities believe Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al Saadi has been using coded messages in telephone calls from prison to push others into carrying out new plots, directing $1million in money transfers and overseeing the release of propaganda videos.

The accusations are contained in US Department of Justice documents reported by The Times.

UK intelligence chief warns of 'major shift' after Iran attacks military bases

Mr Al Saadi, a 32-year-old dual citizen of Iran and Iraq, was charged in New York in May with six counts of terrorism-related offences for his alleged activities as an operative of the Iraqi militia group Kataib Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Both organisations have been placed under sanctions and designated as terrorist groups by the US.

He is also alleged to be behind Harakat Ashab Al Yamin Al Islamia, also known as Ashab Al Yamin, which translates as the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right Hand and has been blamed for a series of fire-bombings at Jewish locations in London and synagogues in Europe.

The US targets were a New York City synagogue and two Jewish institutions in Los Angeles, California, and Scottsdale, Arizona, according to prosecutors.

UK security services have said that more than 50 Iran-linked arrests have been made in the past year as Tehran’s plots against targets in the UK intensify.

Mr Al Saadi was extradited to the US from Turkey and is being held without bail in a federal centre in New York. He is expected to face trial next summer and faces life in prison if convicted of the most serious charges against him.

His legal team has said he faces “political prosecution” and complained about the measures he is subject to in detention, including near-solitary confinement and strict limits on contact with family.

“By keeping Mr Al Saadi in extreme solitary confinement and aggressively curtailing his access to information, the government is violating his rights under the constitution and the third Geneva Convention. We will continue to vigorously challenge these inhumane conditions,” The Times quoted his lawyers, Federal Defenders of New York, as saying.

They said the reasons for the restrictions did not hold up to scrutiny and relied on speculation and misinterpretation.

The documents filed by the Justice Department highlight suspicion that Mr Al Saadi used a FaceTime call with a woman thought to be his mother to urge further attacks. A video of the call in which he said “we shall not care whether we fall upon death or death falls upon us as long as we are on the path of truth” was shared on social media and viewed almost 100,000 times.

In a phone call, he asked about a member of Kataib Hezbollah and “work” for what the FBI believe is an IRGC operative. The FBI cut short one call in which there was reference to a gun and money.

The Justice Department documents said there were concerns he was “enlisting third parties to engage in certain conduct, including planning or even carrying out more attacks such as the European terrorist attacks”.

Mr Al Saadi is accused of being a commander in Kataib Hezbollah which was placed under sanctions after years of attacks on US forces stationed in the Middle East, particularly in Iraq.

Mr Al Saadi is alleged to have worked closely with Maj Gen Qassem Suleimani, the commander of the IRGC's Quds Force, who was killed during a US air strike in early 2020, and Kataib Hezbollah leader Abu Mahdi Al Muhandis, who died in the same strike.

Mr Al Saadi’s social media accounts showed photographs of him with Maj Gen Suleimani at a military-related facility. Mr Al Saadi is alleged to have called on others to attack and kill Americans, including in retribution for the deaths of Maj Gen Suleimani and Al Muhandis.

He posted about the attacks on social media platforms such as Snapchat and Telegram and spoke about them in phone calls recorded by an FBI informant whose help he solicited in planning attacks in the US, the complaint said.

Al Saadi told the informant he was willing to kill people in any such attacks, prosecutors allege.

body_text:
(ECNS) — The OOCL Felixstowe, the first container ship to bring exhibits for the ninth China International Import Expo, docked at Shanghai's Waigaoqiao Port on Sunday.

Shanghai border inspection authorities and the port opened a green channel to speed the safe entry of exhibits for setup.

The vessel sailed from Auckland, New Zealand’s largest port, with New Zealand specialties including gin and fruit juice to be displayed at the expo.

Border inspection agencies and port authorities have worked closely with shipping firms to roll out the channel.

Measures for international vessels include pre-arrival inspection and one-stop clearance, along with tighter on-port vessel management.

headline: The war of attrition with Iran: What happened to US patriots?
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – According to estimates put forward, America's seven-month war with Iran has placed considerable pressure on Washington's weapons stockpiles; pressure whose consequences may continue for years after the end of the conflict.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – According to estimates put forward, America's seven-month war with Iran has placed considerable pressure on Washington's weapons stockpiles; pressure whose consequences may continue for years after the end of the conflict.

The issue is not only the missiles the US military has consumed on the battlefield, but the time it needs to replace them; a time that can affect Washington's ability to confront potential crises in other regions, especially East Asia.

According to a report attributed to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, in seven months of confrontation with Iran, Washington used approximately the equivalent of 19 years of Patriot missile purchases of these interceptors. In the same assessment, restoring US missile stockpiles to prewar levels has been stated to take at least three years. These figures indicate the gap between the speed of munitions consumption in an intense conflict and the ability of the US defense industry to compensate for it.

The importance of this issue increases when we know that military power is not measured merely by the number of aircraft, ships, or advanced systems. The ability to sustain operations in a prolonged conflict and to quickly replace consumed equipment is also a determining factor. An army may possess advanced technology and extensive firepower, but if its munitions stockpiles decrease at a rate faster than production capacity, it will face more serious limitations in continuing operations.

Patriot; An Important Link in US Air Defense The Patriot system is one of the important air defense equipment of the United States and its allies, used to counter certain aircraft and missile threats. The interceptor missiles of this system play an important role in protecting forces, bases, and military facilities. The extensive consumption of these missiles can force commanders to make more difficult decisions about how to allocate munitions, the priority of defending targets, and the level of risk acceptance.

Compensating for this reduction in stockpiles is also not simply a matter of increasing government orders. The production of advanced missiles depends on specialized components, raw materials, skilled manpower, and industrial capacity. Developing production lines and increasing delivery speed is a time-consuming process, and one cannot expect an increase in demand to immediately lead to a proportionate increase in supply.

For this reason, even after the intensity of the conflict decreases, pressure on the US military can continue. Washington must simultaneously meet the needs of forces deployed in the Middle East, maintain its commitments in Europe, and be prepared for potential crises in East Asia. The longer the rebuilding of stockpiles takes, the more difficult it will be to manage these commitments.

A Window of Vulnerability for Washington and a Possible Opportunity for China One of the most important strategic consequences of the reduction in US munitions stockpiles is its connection to the competition between Washington and Beijing. China is considered America's most important strategic rival, and any potential conflict in the Indo-Pacific region could require extensive consumption of precision munitions and defense systems.

Under such circumstances, the reduction in interceptor stockpiles can complicate US military planning. Washington will be forced to strike a balance between meeting current needs in the Middle East and maintaining readiness for potential crises in East Asia. This situation may be what analysts refer to as a "window of vulnerability"; a period in which the replacement of consumed munitions has not yet been completed, but America's security needs in other regions still persist.

Of course, these conditions do not mean China's definitive superiority or America's inability to defend its interests. Washington's military power is not limited to Patriot missiles, and this country still possesses a naval fleet, air force, base network, and regional allies. However, in a prolonged confrontation, the depth of stockpiles and the speed of replacing munitions can become as important as technology and the quality of weapons.

A Cost Beyond the Battlefield The consequences of this situation are not limited to the US military either. Washington's allies, who depend on American systems and munitions for air defense, may face delays in the delivery of orders if demand increases. Under such conditions, the US government must prioritize between the needs of its own forces and the requests of its security partners; a decision that can affect military relations and the security calculations of allies.

For Iran too, this issue has strategic importance; because it shows that the assessment of a military confrontation should not be made only on the basis of the number of equipment or the firepower of the parties. The capacity to withstand pressure, the continuity of operations, and the cost of replacing weapons also play a role in determining the course of a conflict. Of course, the reduction in US interceptor stockpiles alone is not sufficient to prove this country's military defeat and must be examined alongside the operational results and the extent to which the declared objectives of both sides have been achieved.

Ultimately, the extensive consumption of Patriot missiles and the time needed to rebuild America's stockpiles will be the possible restriction of Washington's strategic freedom of action in the post-conflict period. The war may end on the battlefield, but its effects on weapons stockpiles and military readiness will remain for years; an issue that takes the real cost of a prolonged confrontation beyond the days of military operations.
