headline: Exclusive TIME documents show Israel approved and oversaw Qatar’s Gaza aid
summary: TIME has published previously undisclosed documents revealing how successive Israeli governments helped facilitate and sustain Qatari humanitarian aid payments to Gaza, despite publicly criticising the programme. In an exclusive long-read…
body_text:
TIME has published previously undisclosed documents revealing how successive Israeli governments helped facilitate and sustain Qatari humanitarian aid payments to Gaza, despite publicly criticising the programme.

In an exclusive long-read published on Sunday, Documents Show How Israel Steered Qatari Payments to Gaza, TIME journalist Eric Cortellessa details how senior Israeli security officials privately backed Qatar’s aid payments to Gaza, with letters to Qatari leaders showing Israel’s direct role in the programme.

The documents challenge the portrayal by Israeli prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders of the payments as a Qatari effort that fed Hamas. According to TIME, by 2012 Netanyahu’s government had approved a system giving Israel a direct role: delivering food and medical supplies, deciding which Palestinian families qualified for aid, and disbursing funds. Under that system, Israel vetted recipients and oversaw distribution, with money moving through the World Food Programme.

According to TIME, their role in the programme was “more extensive than Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has publicly acknowledged”.

TIME piece highlights that the funding was indeed “designated for humanitarian assistance, fuel, and government salaries”, noting that Qatar had requested “formal documentation that the arrangement agreed was meant to provide relief to citizens”.

The article notes that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government “helped to facilitate these Qatari payments to Gaza”, beginning in 2012 and having accumulated to over $1.1 billion by 2018.

Israel has repeatedly accused Qatar of financing Hamas.

In an interview with i24NEWS on 5 September, Netanyahu boasted of bombing Qatar. In the same interview, he defended the Qatari payments to Gaza as humanitarian and said Israel’s own security agencies, Mossad and the Shin Bet, had recommended them.

Qatar has rejected the claims, saying its assistance was intended for Palestinian civilians and delivered through mechanisms coordinated with Israel and international partners.

Speaking to CNN’s Christiane Amanpour in New York on 27 September, Qatar’s Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said no Qatari money entered Gaza without the “full coordination and consent” of the United Nations and Israeli government, rejecting claims that Qatar’s funding reached Hamas’s military wing.⁠

“There has no single penny that has flown into Gaza without the full coordination and consent by the United Nations and the Israeli government,” said Sheikh Mohammed.

The Sunday’s TIME piece quotes a spokesperson for Qatar’s International Media Office as highlighting that “all of Qatar’s financial assistance in Gaza has been directed to Palestinian citizens through mechanisms coordinated with the Israeli authorities and international partners”.

Qatar’s International Media Office statement from 19 September clearly stated that “all financial assistance, as well as goods such as food, medicine and fuel, passed through Israel before entering Gaza”.

“Nothing was delivered directly by Qatar; we provided the aid, while delivery was carried out by the United Nations’ organizations in coordination with the Israeli authorities. If any funding reached Hamas, as alleged by individuals and groups with political agendas against Qatar, the responsibility lies with Israel, which oversaw the delivery and created the mechanism,” the statement added.

According to TIME, the extent of Israel’s cooperation with the payments was reflected in a 2020 letter from Yossi Cohen, then director of Mossad, Israel’s intelligence agency, to Qatar’s Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.

“It is indeed a great opportunity to express our gratitude and appreciation for the humanitarian aid efforts that the State of Qatar has provided the last few years to the Gaza Strip,” Cohen wrote.

“Undoubtedly, these humanitarian efforts have played a crucial role in improving the humanitarian situation within the Gaza Strip, and ensuring stability and safety in the region,” Cohen write in the letter.

The TIME article also highlights that critics have long argued that Netanyahu sought to “sustain Hamas rule in Gaza to keep the Palestinians divided”, while Israel pursued normalisation with the Arab world without resolving the Palestinian question.

The piece continues referencing statements from former Israeli defense officials highlighting Netanyahu’s “central” role in the agreed payment process, while noting that Israeli officials would “denounce the payments in public, then privately ask Doha to renew them”.

It adds that the agreement was formalized through a trilateral mechanism in October 2018, involving Qatar, Israel, and the United Nations, designed to administer the aid with international and Israeli oversight.

On 2 October 2018, Qatar and Israel, together with the United Nations, signed an agreement to finance fuel deliveries into Gaza.

According to TIME, Qatar signed another agreement in August 2021, committing $40 million to a cash assistance programme that would provide nearly 100,000 Palestinian households with $100 a month for four months.

The U.S. officials were also involved in the discussions.

A diplomat briefed on the process told TIME that Qatar wanted Washington to understand exactly how the system operated, fearing Israel might later accuse Doha of financing Hamas without acknowledging its own role in the arrangement.

Under the system, Qatar funded fuel and electricity purchased from Israel to increase the number of hours of power available in Gaza, in a process coordinated with Israeli security services, according to U.S. and Israeli officials cited by TIME.

Qatar also transferred money through the United Nations for projects in the Strip and provided monthly payments of $100 to some of Gaza’s poorest families.

Israel vetted the recipients and oversaw the distribution mechanism, according to diplomats familiar with the arrangement.

The funds were transferred through the World Food Programme, with eligible families notified by text message before collecting their assistance at designated locations.

“If the money ever got in the wrong hands, it was because of the Israelis,” the diplomat told TIME, “because they were the ones overseeing the whole thing.”

The investigative piece by TIME notes that Israel’s National Security Council “urged Qatari officials to maintain the payments”, despite the Israeli government’s public criticism of the agreement, which continued under later Prime Minister Bennett’s tenure despite prior objections.

In July 2019, according to one letter, Qatar notified the Netanyahu government that it was transferring $6 million to 20,000 beneficiaries in Gaza, with each receiving $300.

TIME writes that it is unknown how many of those beneficiaries, chosen by Israel, were connected to Hamas or had family members who belonged to the group.

In 2020, as the coronavirus pandemic swept through Gaza, R. L. Maoz, a member of Netanyahu’s National Security Council, urged Qatari officials to maintain the payments despite the Israeli government’s public criticism.

“We ask that Qatar’s financial assistance not be transferred through mediators or countries other than the ambassador, Mohammed Al-Emadi,” Maoz wrote, referring to the chairman of the Qatari Committee for the Reconstruction of Gaza.

“We greatly appreciate your cooperation and open discourse to safeguard stability and security in the region and to bring our countries and peoples closer together,” Maoz added.

According to TIME, the programme continued after Netanyahu left office, despite his successor Naftali Bennett having been among its fiercest critics.

After taking office in 2021, Bennett ended the delivery of cash-filled suitcases but maintained the broader flow of Qatari assistance to Gaza, TIME reported.

People familiar with discussions over the policy told TIME that Bennett’s earlier objections were intended for his domestic political audience. “There’s no issue,” an Israeli representative told a Biden administration envoy, according to an official present at the discussion. “We want to continue with it as is.”

According to TIME, Mossad director David Barnea travelled to Doha two weeks before the 7 October 2023 attacks and asked Qatar to renew its funding for Gaza, as The New York Times reported in December 2023.

Qatari officials agreed but warned that it would be the final renewal. Barnea requested a further two months, arguing that continued assistance to Gaza’s civilians gave Hamas something to lose and provided Israel with leverage over the group, according to officials familiar with the discussions. The two sides could then reassess Hamas’s conduct and develop a more sustainable mechanism for delivering aid.

However, the arrangement did not reach that stage.

Following Hamas’s 7 October 2023 Operation Al-Aqsa Flood, the Qatari aid programme that successive Israeli governments had helped establish, modify and maintain for years came to an end, TIME reported.

The TIME piece concludes with noting that Qatar today continues to work with the US and wider international partners on a framework to “restore basic services “ in Gaza.

The ceasefire reached in January 2025 proved temporary, with Israel resuming large-scale bombardment of Gaza less than two months later. Israeli attacks and widespread destruction have continued since.

More than 74,000 Palestinians have been reported killed in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since 7 October 2023, but three years on, the death toll is still not final.

headline: China sends biggest-ever delegation abroad to Asian Para Games in Japan
summary: The 5th Asian Para Games opened in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, with China sending 312 athletes to compete across 17 sports and 335 events — its largest-ever delegation for an overseas edition of the Games.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- The 5th Asian Para Games opened in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Sunday, with China sending 312 athletes to compete across 17 sports and 335 events — its largest-ever delegation for an overseas edition of the Games.

The Games, running from Oct. 18 to 24 under the theme "Imagine One Heart," bring together nearly 3,000 para athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia, competing in about 500 events across 18 sports.

Chinese para taekwondo athlete Li Yujie and para powerlifter Yan Panpan served as flagbearers for the Chinese delegation during the opening ceremony at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium.

The Chinese delegation totals around 500 members, including 312 athletes with an average age of about 28.8. All Chinese athletes are amateurs from diverse backgrounds, including workers, students, office employees and freelancers.

This marks China's fifth participation in the Asian Para Games.

The Asian Para Games are organized by the Asian Paralympic Committee, a regional organization of the International Paralympic Committee, and succeeded the Far East and South Pacific Games for the Disabled, which began in 1975. Since the 2010 Guangzhou Asian Games, the Asian Para Games have been held in the same city and the same year as the Asian Games.

headline: Still sweating in October? UAE temperatures remain high as El Nino intensifies

Instead of the predictable October drop into comfortable autumn weather, the phenomenon is trapping a blanket of high pressure over the Arabian Peninsula, driving temperatures well above seasonal averages. body_text:
If autumn feels like it’s taking an age to arrive, you’re not imagining it.

October has been warmer than usual this year, with the UAE National Centre of Meteorology issuing a major climate update on the El Nino weather phenomenon, which has been forecast to be the strongest on record.

Sea surface temperatures in the Pacific have reached between 2.3°C and 3°C above the long-term average, cementing this year’s event as a global weather disruptor.

Iran war and El Nino could drive food prices up for longer

Instead of the predictable October drop into comfortable autumn weather, the phenomenon is trapping a blanket of high pressure over the Arabian Peninsula, driving temperatures well above seasonal averages.

Recent maximum temperatures across the country have ranged between 37°C and 43°C, with some areas experiencing temperatures 4°C higher than usual.

The UAE's average daily temperature in October stands at 29.7°C, according to the NCM's latest monthly weather summary.

October and November are expected to feel the peak of the El Nino cycle, with higher rainfall than usual also expected, including severe bouts that could raise the risk of flooding, although this is not guaranteed. The NCM projects a 96 per cent probability that these potentially volatile conditions will persist through to March 2027, with secondary environmental impacts such as lingering into April.

Speaking to The National in September, Dr Diana Francis, associate professor and head of the Environmental and Geophysical Sciences (Engeos) Laboratory at Khalifa University in Abu Dhabi, said the region should prepare for more rainfall.

“El Nino generally tilts the Gulf and parts of the Arabian Peninsula towards wetter conditions, enhanced moisture transport and a greater chance of heavy rain episodes,” she said.

If rainfall levels increase, “very intense downpours may become more likely, according to Dr Andries-Jan de Vries, of the Institute of Earth Surface Dynamics at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.

“In combination with dry soils, with mountains and valleys, they can easily accumulate rainwater that can fall in a very short period of time, and that can then lead to flooding,” he said.

Parts of the UAE were hit by severe flooding in late March this year, almost two years after the country experienced its most extreme rain on record, late into what was described as the fifth-strongest El Nino on record.

A study in Nature Scientific Reports in June with the title “An extreme rainfall event over the United Arab Emirates in April 2024: Role of dynamic and thermodynamic drivers”, said that El Nino “may have contributed to a large-scale background environment favourable for above-normal April rainfall over the region”.

After the 2024 floods, the authorities began investing heavily to improve drainage and make the country better able to cope with severe rains.

The El Nino-Southern Oscillation, to use its full name, is a natural phenomenon in which the upwelling of water causes warmer sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, with knock-on effects on the global climate. An opposite phenomenon, La Nina, is linked to cooler temperatures in that part of the Pacific Ocean.

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, El Nino and La Nina each last between nine months and a year and happen irregularly, typically every two to seven years.

El Nino is seen slightly more often, and the one occurring this year and into next year has been forecast to be exceptionally strong.

The World Meteorological Organisation recently said there were “exceptionally warm tropical Pacific Ocean conditions” and warned that a very strong El Nino could “significantly shift rainfall and temperature patterns worldwide and fuel extreme weather”.

A recent study in Weather and Climate Dynamics called “The influence of El Nino-Southern Oscillation on cool-season precipitation variability in the arid Middle East”, highlighted three mechanisms that cause El Nino to influence weather in the Gulf region.

Firstly, El Nino’s warmer sea-surface temperatures in the central Pacific are typically associated with colder sea-surface temperatures and reduced tropical convection around Indonesia and the West Pacific.

“That influences the regional circulation over South Asia and the Indian Ocean, and we have a change in the transport of moisture in the atmosphere,” said Dr De Vries, the first author of the paper.

This results in an increase in moisture coming into the region.

A second pathway is an alternating pattern of high and low-pressure systems running eastward from the warmer region in the Pacific, stretching over North America, the North Atlantic and Europe to the Middle East. This goes along with a low-pressure system over the Middle East, which is more favourable for precipitation.

A third cause is that during El Nino conditions, the subtropical jet stream over North Africa and the Middle East – a band of fast-flowing air blowing from west to east about 12km to 14km above the Earth’s surface – is shifted slightly south, towards the equator. This allows mid-latitude storms to more easily enter the Middle East region.

While El Nino makes wetter conditions in the Gulf region more likely, it does not make them certain.

“El Niño increases the likelihood of wetter conditions but does not guarantee them. Rainfall in the region varies greatly from one year to another,” said Dr Zouhair Lachkar, a senior research scientist in New York University Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said El Nino was not always linked to higher rainfall.

So while a stronger-than-normal El Nino is statistically more likely to have a greater effect on rainfall than an average one, it may not have a major impact. Effects on rainfall are most likely this October and November, and in March, April and May next year.

Even though El Nino warms the climate globally, Dr Francis said its impacts on UAE and Gulf temperatures were “relatively weak”.

“Background climate warming, Gulf/Arabian Sea temperatures and regional circulation will be at least as important,” she said. “The impact of El Nino in the Gulf happens a few months after it is established in the Pacific. Most probably its impacts will be felt here from mid-autumn onward, and in those seasons it is mainly the rainfall patterns that will be influenced, less the temperature.”

Dr Lachkar said that research at NYU Abu Dhabi showed that El Nino does not necessarily produce higher sea-surface temperatures in the Arabian Gulf. “In fact, we found that La Nina has historically been more favourable to exceptionally high summer sea-surface temperatures in the Gulf,” he said.

Should there be increased rainfall in the UAE, the impact on the natural environment could be positive.

Prof John Burt, director of NYU Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Arabian Centre for Climate and Environmental Sciences, said if El Nino brought more winter rain, it could lead to “a marked increase in plant growth across our deserts and mountains”.

“Sufficient rain during the cooler months can trigger widespread germination of seeds, plus flowering and renewed growth in established shrubs,” he said.

"These responses extend through the food web: vegetation provides food for herbivores, flowers support pollinating insects, and greater insect abundance benefits birds, reptiles and small mammals. A productive winter can also replenish seed reserves, supporting future plant generations after the visible greenery disappears.”

He said that while a wetter winter could promote natural regeneration, lasting benefits would depend on the intensity of the initial rainfall events and the subsequent weather.

“Rain that initiates germination must be followed by conditions that allow seedlings to survive, such as continued soil moisture in the weeks and months that follow,” he said. “In contrast, brief but intense downpours can erode soils and uproot vegetation, particularly in mountain wadis and the gravel plains at the foothills.”

He said it is not known if summer temperatures next year will be higher than normal, but that the centre will monitor this closely. “Marine organisms already live very close to their upper heat limits in summer, and are vulnerable to being pushed over the edge,” he said.

A previous version of this article was published on September 14.

headline: "Economic cooperation, AI" Iran’s priorities at SCO: VP Aref
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – Stressing Iran’s strategy for active participating in Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), the 1st vice president stated developing economic cooperation and artificial intelligence are among Iran’s priorities at the org.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – Stressing Iran’s strategy for active participating in Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), the 1st vice president stated developing economic cooperation and artificial intelligence are among Iran’s priorities at the org.

Mohammad-Reza Aref made the remarks on Monday prior to his trip to the Republic of Tajikistan to attend the meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) prime ministers.

Turning to the main aim behind his visit to the Republic of Tajikistan, the vice president said, “Shanghai Cooperation Organization was established in 2001 with the participation of five or six countries and now, it has 10 official members, all of which are significant countries within the region and the Iranian civilizational sphere."

Referring to the combination of the organization's membership, Aref added, “China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Belarus, and Iran are official members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization.”

Turning to the geographical and demographic scope of the member countries, he opined, “The SCO’s member states totally span an area of approximately 36 million square kilometers, equivalent to nearly one-quarter of the world's landmass. Furthermore, the population of SCO’s member countries accounts for a significant portion of the global population.”

Elsewhere in his remarks, Aref referred to the process of Iran’s accession to the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), emphasizing, “The Islamic Republic of Iran has actively participated in the organization’s working groups, commissions, and committees and it has achieved valuable outcomes due to extensive commonalities with the member states."

Referring to the objectives of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Prime Ministers' meeting, the first vice president stated that the meeting is held annually to evaluate the performance of member states and explore ways to expand cooperation. The focus of this year’s summit is on the effectiveness of trade and economic collaboration as well as humanitarian initiatives, with the outcomes to be announced in the form of several documents and a declaration.

body_text:
Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport reopened on Sunday, after it was closed because of attacks by the Houthi rebels in Yemen.

However, many airlines have not yet lifted their suspension of flights to the Saudi capital and other destinations in the kingdom.

Some carriers have extended cancellations into November and beyond, while others are preparing to resume services. The disruption comes amid wider regional uncertainty, which has already affected airlines’ Middle East operations.

World exclusive'Blows kept coming, I felt the aircraft going down': Flydubai captain on the cockpit battle to save his plane

Here’s how major airlines have adjusted operations and when flights are expected to resume.

Etihad Airways has extended flight cancellations between Abu Dhabi and three Saudi cities until October 24, due to regional disruption.

All services to and from Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam have been cancelled until that date. The following flights have also been cancelled: EY601 and EY603 from Abu Dhabi to Jeddah; EY602 and EY604 from Jeddah to Abu Dhabi.

Emirates services from Dubai to Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam have been affected by cancellations and schedule changes.

According to Flightradar24, Jeddah-bound flights EK801, EK805 and EK803 have been cancelled on October 19 and 20, with services scheduled to resume on October 21.

Dubai to Riyadh flights EK815, EK819 and EK817 have also been cancelled. EK817 is scheduled to resume on October 20, followed by EK815 and EK819 on October 21.

The airline has cancelled flights to Riyadh, Dammam and Abha up to and including October 24.

Air Arabia has cancelled services between Sharjah and several Saudi destinations including Riyadh, Abha, Dammam and Taif. No resumption date has been announced.

The airline has temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam. A resumption date has not yet been announced.

body_text:
Sheikha Latifa bint Ahmed bin Juma Al Maktoum does not remember the first time she got on a horse.

Riding to her is like speaking, or walking – a skill a child picks up without even realising, and just keeps on doing it forever, or for as long as they possibly can.

Earlier this month, Sheikha Latifa, riding her bay coat stallion Cornet XL, helped the UAE secure a silver medal in team jumping at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

UAE teenager’s stunning rise from school runner to Asian Games champion

It was her fourth career medal won at the Games, and it came 20 years after she clinched her first at Doha 2006.

Making the podium on the continental stage two decades apart is a remarkable feat. Did Sheikha Latifa ever consider that to be a possibility when she claimed her first Asian Games medal 20 years ago?

“I think so. I think it's in our DNA,” the 41-year-old Emirati told The National from her base in Germany following her successful trip to Japan.

“I think for us riders, I don't ever think we'd want to stop. We'd always have something to do with it.”

It takes a special kind of passion, discipline, and skill to be able to compete at the highest level in any sport for so long and Sheikha Latifa does not take that longevity for granted.

“It means a lot,” she says. “The first Asian Games, I did it with an eight-year-old [horse]. An eight-year-old is very young to do a championship like that. I got him as a seven-year-old, the same as Cornet XL, I got him as a seven-year-old, and we built up together.

“So I think now three horses that I've done the Asian Games with, I've had from young horses and built up.

“I don't know how to explain it, but it's just a different feeling when you bring up a horse instead of getting something ready to do it because it takes a lot of time. It takes a lot of effort and you go through a lot of ups and downs building up horses. So that for me is something special.”

The past few weeks have been particularly special for Sheikha Latifa, not just because she made her first Asian Games podium since Guangzhou 2010, where she took individual and team silver medals atop Kalaska de Semilly.

In August, she made her long-awaited return to the World Equestrian Games (WEG), competing at the global stage for the first time since her debut appearance back in 2010.

She got the call just two weeks before the WEG when her compatriot Abdullah Al Marri suffered an injury that ruled him out of the competition, freeing up a spot on the UAE team.

“I was actually preparing for that [a call-up] my whole summer tour because I was on the long list so I was preparing for it,” she said.

“I chose my shows, built up the horse. So when I got the call, I was ready. I think the team wasn't sure just because my horse didn't do as many big classes as they would like, but I have a lot of confidence in him and I really believed that he was made for this from the day I bought him.”

The past few months have given Sheikha Latifa the confidence she needed to tackle her next big goal with Cornet XL, which is to qualify for the Olympics.

She is no stranger to that stage either as she happens to be the first Emirati woman – alongside Sheikha Maitha bint Mohammed bin Rashid – to compete at an Olympic Games, having represented the UAE in showjumping in Beijing 2008.

“I think it's every rider's dream. I think the first Olympics I did it was just very foreign to me,” she reflected. “Everything was new and I was very nervous. I had a 10-year-old horse that I brought up, 10-year-olds are considered young at that level. Me being very young at the time it was very new and I think now I know what it takes to be there.

“I know what the horse needs. I have a plan and if I don't believe I could represent the country in the best possible light, I wouldn't even attempt it. But I think I really have a fantastic horse and we're a great combination me and him. We're going to try, Inshallah.”

Sheikha Latifa believes “trusting the process” is the biggest lesson she is taking with her along this upcoming journey towards a possible second Olympics appearance.

“Sometimes like with Cornet XL we went through a lot of ups and downs. He's such a big horse and I'm very little and he's very strong but very sensitive and I really had to find a way that he was happy but I could also still control him because he doesn't like to have me control him completely and he likes to be how he wants to be,” she said.

“But at the level we're jumping, I have to also have a say in what I want in the ring. I have to be able to make a decision and when I make a decision he has to respond, and in the beginning that was very difficult just because he's so big but also so sensitive so I really had to find a way with him and that we both came to an understanding.”

She gives a lot of credit to experienced Saudi rider Ramzy Al Duhami, who won team bronze at the London 2012 Olympics and has been Sheikha Latifa’s coach and mentor for many years.

“He really inspires me in the way he thinks,” she said of Al Duhami.

“What I really like is he's always horse first, so like we never think, oh we want the horse to go this way? No, it’s how do we do best to get the best out of the horse? If I need to change the way I'm riding, if I need to sit more, if I need to be out of the saddle, if I need to have the nose out, if I need to have the nose in, it's all how to get the best out of the horse.

“And for me that's why it never gets boring because every horse is different and every horse likes to go a certain way and that's how I get inspired because it's just never boring.”

Sheikha Latifa was one of five Emirati women to win medals at the recently-concluded Asian Games and she has proudly witnessed the growth of women’s sport in the UAE over the past two decades.

As a pioneer herself, she knows she has played a part in pushing women’s sport forward in the country and it’s a role she takes very seriously.

“It means a lot and I really am also inspired by the other athletes, whether it's male or female, I'm really inspired by them,” she added.

“It's just you always feel when someone is able to raise your flag in a big occasion you feel like you're part of it, so it doesn't matter what sport but anything that raises the UAE flag I always feel like I'm a part of it and I think it goes the same way for all of us, whether it's in athletics, whether it's in judo. I think for us it's just we're all proud of each other.”

headline: US not competing with China or Russia for influence in Uzbekistan — top diplomat
summary: According to Marco Rubio, the US wants fair competition and new opportunities for American companies
body_text:
SAMARKAND, October 19. /TASS/. The US is not competing with China or Russia for influence in Uzbekistan; the main goal is to expand cooperation based on open competition without dictating who they should do business with, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.

The top US diplomat arrived in Samarkand, Uzbekistan’s second-largest city, the previous evening.

According to Rubio, the US simply wants fair competition and new opportunities for American companies. During a walk through the ancient Registan Square, he told reporters that American goods and services can compete with other producers in every region of the world, the NOVA24-LIVE news outlet reported.

The secretary of state pointed out that this is precisely why nearly 300 American business representatives traveled with him to Uzbekistan.

Earlier reports indicated that Rubio would participate in the second meeting of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council, as well as a C5+1 meeting of foreign ministers from Central Asian countries and the US.

headline: Bomb threat forces Austrian Tel Aviv-Vienna flight to land in Bulgaria

Israeli newspaper Haaretz said the threat was "called in by an Austrian national who was not on board", without identifying its source.

headline: Qatar to announce defence production plant
summary: Qatar will soon announce a defence production plant as the gas-rich Gulf nation looks to boost domestic defence capabilities.Qatar will tie up with a regional partner and other countries such as the US, the UK and France “to make sure either we ⁠do local protection or we are investing in some of these companies”, Reuters reported, quoting Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, Qatar’s Defence Minister, on Monday.Sheikh Saoud made the remarks while speaking at the Global Security Forum in ⁠Doha.The announcement comes after Qatar and other Gulf countries have come under heavy attack during Iran war, with energy sites and civilian infrastructure suffering damage.Parts of Qatar’s Ras Laffan Industrial City – which supplies one fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas – was destroyed, with the Gulf nation declaring long-term force majeure on contracts with some buyers across the globe.The UAE and Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s two largest economies, are already investing in domestic defence capabilities, with Edge Group and the kingdom’s Saudi Arabian Military Industries (Sami) playing a key role.Edge systems, including jammers, were successful in eliminating 85 per cent of Iranian drones that have been launched at the UAE during the Iran war, Hamad Al Marar, the group's managing director and chief executive, told The National in an interview at the Make it in the Emirates event in Abu Dhabi in May.Edge, set up in 2019, specialises in building advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare, with more than 35 companies under its umbrella. Military spending in the Middle East has continued to rise as regional conflicts rage, a report from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (Sipri) has found, increasing to an estimated $218 billion in 2025, up 0.1 per cent compared to previous year. However, it had increased by 36 per cent over the decade from 2016 to 2025, the Sipri report said.The region’s largest spender in 2025 was Saudi Arabia, with estimated expenditure of $83.2 billion. Its spending was 1.4 per cent higher than in 2024 and 12 per cent higher than in 2016.

headline: 'I am proud to be a Gulf citizen': Sheikh Mohammed urges unity and rejects attempts to sow division
summary: Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai, on Monday hailed the deep-rooted ties uniting the countries of the Gulf - and rejected all efforts to sow division between them.Sheikh Mohammed, in an uplifting message shared on social media, reflected on the region's remarkable transformation from "simple towns to global metropolises" which had evolved from "modest fishing ports to navigating international routes".He spoke warmly of how the "sons of the Gulf" had cemented their status as key players on the global stage, holding major events and driving economic growth, while staying true to their deep-rooted heritage and proud identity.In a year in which the Gulf has faced significant adversity - with the UAE among the states to face a barrage of missile and drone strikes from Iran and Saudi Arabia coming under attack from the Houthi rebels in Yemen - Sheikh Mohammed emphasised the importance of standing together to build for a better future.He pledged that the unity forged out of history, borders and economic progress should not be disrupted by social media misinformation and "narrow-minded agendas".He said such campaigns could not "erase centuries of neighborliness, or alter the facts of geography, or change the reality of lineages".The heartfelt address to the Gulf people is an excerpt from his new book, The Letters. رسالة إلى أبناء الخليجرسالة إلى الحلم الأجمل .. رسالة إلى التاريخ الواحد .. والجغرافيا الممتدة .. والأنساب المشتركة .. والقرابات الراسخة .. رسالة إلى البحر الواحد الذي يجمعنا .. والصحراء الفسيحة التي تضمنا .. رسالة إلى خليجنا العربي .. وأبنائه وأجياله ومثقفيه ومفكريه ..نحن… pic.twitter.com/3dG2qn3FkO— HH Sheikh Mohammed (@HHShkMohd) October 19, 2026"For what united the Gulf was not political agreements, but generations who lived along its shores," Sheikh Mohammed wrote."In the Gulf, hearts met before borders, and lineages embraced before homelands, and love flourished before development."The Gulf is a great tree whose branches have multiplied, whose fruits have adorned it, and whose shades have bloomed, but its root is one, and its trunk is one, and its water is one, and its destiny is one, God willing."Shared ambitionsStriking an optimistic tone, Sheikh Mohammed said when the aspirations of the Gulf align, they are able to turn projects which may seen impossible into a reality.Sheikh Mohammed said that history offers lessons that the "whole is stronger than the sum of its parts" and that strength is not in erasing differences but in working together to create new opportunities. "I am optimistic about the Gulf and I shall remain so," Sheikh Mohammed wrote."The Gulf endures, God willing, with its desert, with its sons, with its sea and its ports, with its projects and the resolve of its generations, with its spaces in which our dreams will soar to keep our Gulf one and our people one, proclaiming with an unbroken voice: I am a Gulf citizen and I am proud to be a Gulf citizen."Standing togetherThe Dubai Ruler's remarks came after Dr Anwar Gargash, diplomatic adviser to UAE President Sheikh Mohamed, stressed the need to "transcend the folly and pettiness we witness in Gulf squabbles across social media"."We are passing through a pivotal stage that demands awareness and responsibility from us all," Dr Gargash wrote on X on Saturday."We may differ in our assessments of situations, but there is no substitute for solidarity, prioritising wisdom, and rejecting bickering."Dr Gargash welcomed a meeting on Sunday between President Sheikh Mohamed and Prince Khalid bin Salman, the Saudi Minister of Defence.Sheikh Mohamed and Prince Khalid exchanged views on regional developments with the aim of contributing to strengthening security and stability and achieving lasting peace in the region, state news agency Wam reported.Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed, Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the Presidential Court, also attended the meeting on Sunday, as did Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed, Deputy Ruler of Abu Dhabi and National Security Adviser.The meetings affirmed the depth and solidity of the Emirati-Saudi relations, said Dr Gargash."For our security and destiny are shared, and our partnership is one of the pillars of Gulf stability and prosperity, while the wisdom of the two leaderships and the sincerity of positions in times of adversity provide the most eloquent response to every bet against that," said Dr Gargash.

headline: Threats and invitations: Houthis send mixed signals on Yemen peace
summary: Yemen's Houthis are talking peace while warning of a wider war. The Iran-backed rebels are blaming Saudi Arabia for stalling negotiations even as they threaten countries that may join the kingdom's military campaign.On Sunday, Houthi spokesman Mohammad Abdulsalam accused Saudi Arabia of failing to honour previous agreements and delaying its response to proposals aimed at bringing peace to the Yemen.In a post on X, he said the Houthis had communicated with Saudi Arabia “directly and indirectly” in June, demanding it “respond to what we had agreed upon in the road map before the Al Aqsa Flood and we presented more than one proposal, but unfortunately, it did not advance a single step”.Al Aqsa Flood refers to the name of the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led operation in southern Israel in which about 1,200 people were killed and 250 hostages were taken to Gaza, before Israel launched a two-year war in the strip in which more than 74,300 Palestinians have been killed and wounded hundreds of thousands injured.Meanwhile, Houthi politburo member Mohammed Al Bukhaiti told Qatar-based Al Arabi Television in an interview that the militia was open to ending the war.“We welcome any mediation, Arab or Islamic, to reach peace, which entails ending the war and the blockade from both sides – whether from Iran, Pakistan or Turkey,” he said. In the same breath, he continued to threaten any country that enters the war alongside Saudi Arabia.Egypt was the latest to suggest it is ready to provide the kingdom with assistance after the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi airports and oil sites last week, killing dozens of civilians and injuring hundreds of others.President ​Abdel Fattah Al Sisi has requested an emergency session of Egypt's parliament to authorise the military to provide support to the kingdom. The vote has not yet taken place but approval of the plan would significantly widen the scope of the war.There is scepticism about the Houthis' apparent change of heart, especially after the rebels seemingly started the escalation in August and subsequently advocated a continuation of the conflict.“The Houthis tend to welcome mediation when they come under military pressure and suffer heavy losses,” wrote Nadwa Al Dawsari, associate fellow at the Middle East Institute. “But once a ceasefire is reached, they exploit it to regroup, replenish their ranks and prepare for the next offensive. For them, ceasefires are tactical pauses, not steps towards peace.”

headline: At least 18 reported dead in Houthi attack on Yemeni military camp
summary: At least 18 people were killed on Monday in an attack by the Iran-aligned Houthi movement on a Yemeni government military training camp in Shabwa province, government and medical sources have said.The government sources told Reuters three ballistic missiles were fired at soldiers during a ​morning ⁠training exercise.The Houthis have recently targeted various sites in government-held areas of Yemen, including the airport and presidential palace in Aden, the interim capital. The missile and drone attack on the Maashiq presidential palace killed five security personnel.The civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, forcing the internationally recognised government to relocate to Aden in the south. A Saudi-led military intervention followed in 2015, leading to years of fighting before a ceasefire took hold in 2022. That truce held until this year.Government forces this month launched a campaign to recapture Houthi-held areas, making advances near the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a key global shipping route.The conflict has become another front in the regional war sparked by the conflict with Iran. The Houthis have repeatedly launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia during the latest escalation, targeting airports, oil sites and other infrastructure.

headline: Smit Machchhar interview: What happened inside the cockpit of flydubai Flight 1073
summary: Flydubai captain Smit Machchhar has spoken of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert, with the intention of killing 172 people on board.In a world exclusive interview with The National from his hospital bed in Abu Dhabi, Capt Machchhar said the first officer sitting next to him for two hours had shown no sign of what Emirati prosecutors say was a “premeditated terrorist plot” to hijack the aircraft.Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked Capt Machchhar and seized control of the plane.I tried to block the blows as much as I could. [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I fell face down in the cockpit Capt Smit MachchharCapt Machchhar has been hailed as a hero for getting the cockpit door, locked from the inside, open and allowing the attack to be foiled. All of the 172 passengers and crew on board the September 30 flight survived.The first officer has been detained in the UAE and faces terrorism charges. The statements made in this interview reflect the interviewee’s recollection of events, based on his personal experience and his perception of them at the time they occurred. In his interview with The National at Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar revealed:He thought the first blow to his head was a falling piece of equipment, before more blows rained down on himThe co-pilot – who prosecutors said was radicalised by online Islamist content and in a religious study centre in Australia – showed no sign of unusual behaviourCapt Machchhar does not know what sparked the first officer to seize the controls when Tel Aviv airport, which he planned to crash into, was more than an hour awayHe expects an airline industry security review may lead to changes, amid questions over the cockpit fire axeHe thanked the UAE for his treatment and returning him to his family, saying: “I was told that, by the order of His Highness Sheikh Mohamed, the President of UAE has called you back home – I smiled for the first time.”Cockpit battleNarrating the hijacking to a media outlet for the first time, Capt Machchhar said he thought the blow to his head was from a cockpit panel that had collapsed. “The first time when I was hit … my thought was something's gone horribly wrong with the aircraft structure, which has fallen on my head,” he said. “It almost made me fall on my control column. In the next couple of seconds, when the hits kept on coming, [I realised] it's the other person who I thought was supposed to be on the team.” He recalled those initial moments, explaining: “My immediate action was to free myself from the seat belts. And I tried to just block the blows as much as I could, because the blows were coming on the head.”Capt Machchhar suffered serious injuries to his head and arm, including defensive wounds from trying to stop the blows. “While the first few blows came in, my vision … it was so narrow. I lost a lot. I was just looking [at] outlines.” Capt Machchhar is not entirely clear how events unfolded nor the timeline. But he managed to open the cockpit after several attempts. He explained that every time he had to exert himself physically, he would lose blood and consciousness.Nosedive“Immediately, my hand went to the knob which opens the door," he said. "And [I was] screaming for my colleagues. I believe that was the first time when I lost consciousness. I fell face down in the cockpit.”He believes he regained consciousness as the attacker plunged the aircraft into a dive. Crew members and passengers began banging on the other side of the cockpit door.“The scariest thing that I heard and felt was the engines spooling down. When I say spooling down, it's the engine sound going from full blast to like … not what you want at that stage in the flight. And I felt the aircraft was steeply going down.”Capt Machchhar became emotional as he explained his instinct to survive. “At that point, I realised that you will not survive this," he explained. "And I was constantly looking for the door. I did go for it. I did push it … the next thing I remember was I was facedown, lying with, thank God, the cockpit door open. I was between the cockpit and the galley.”Chaos and commotionCapt Machchhar said there was “so much chaos and commotion” as he was hauled out of the cockpit. It was at that moment that passengers and crew seized the first officer. A pair of flydubai pilots who were travelling as passengers took control of the plane. “If I have to say how many people were trying to control the situation, I would say a million. I know it doesn't make sense, but, yeah, I would say a million people were trying to take over control,” he said. Flydubai pilot hailed a hero for averting disaster on Israel flight - in picturesHe described the moment others came to his rescue as “magic”, saying: “The next thing I remember was [being] pulled out by one of the passengers. And then, soon after that, the senior cabin crew thankfully reached where I was and did his magic. And yeah, that's how I'm speaking to you today.”Recovering in his bed in Zayed Military Hospital, Capt Machchhar has been trying to piece together events in the two weeks since the failed terror plot. He remembers praying as the cabin crew chief and others, including dentist Shota Musaev, tried to stem the bleeding from his wounds. “There was heavy bleeding from his head and left hand,” Dr Musaev told The National last week.“He had very, very deep cuts and we needed many ice packets. But every time I opened the T-shirt to check the bleeding, it would bleed more. So I pressed not very hard and with ice. All through the 45 minutes I kept the pressure on.”Capt Machchhar was clearly emotional as he spoke. He said: “I prayed a lot. I thought about my son, my daughter, and prayed. That was the point where I would say I didn't give up.”He spoke frankly: “Did I give up? No. I can 100 per cent tell you I did not give up. But was I sure I was going to make it? No.”No suspicion of co-pilotAsked whether he suspected anything from his co-pilot's behaviour, he said he did not notice anything. “If there was something that could have hinted earlier on the ground or something, yes, of course, I would have acted. I would have spoken up. I would have questioned some things like that,” he explained. He described that morning as ordinary, saying it was the first time he had met the first officer. “It was a morning flight. So, yeah, there was some small talk, but there was not really like a deep conversation,” he said. Capt Machchhar added: “We avoid getting into deep conversations, especially during high-intensity or high-density airspace, especially nowadays with all the restrictions. Saudi is very high density.”"Nothing until that point would have caused me to think that: 'Hey, hold on, there's something off.'”There has been speculation about why the first officer attacked his colleague when the plane was an hour away from Tel Aviv airport, which prosecutors said he intended to crash into.“I won't say I've been thinking a lot about it, but yes, I did give it a thought. It makes no sense to me,” Capt Machchhar said.There was also much scrutiny over the presence of a cockpit axe, and how the co-pilot was radicalised. Asked whether aviation security will change as a result of the close call, Capt Machchhar said: “I think so. And for good."He added: “I won't blame it on anyone. You've got to learn from the event … I would just say: learn from whatever's happened and then make sure that this doesn't happen again, ever.”Capt Machchhar, who lives with his wife and children in the UAE, faces a long recovery but wants to return to the cockpit.“Did my love die for aviation? Not at all. Not at all,” he said with a smile. “I'm just glad that I was able to do my part.”

headline: Russian foreign minister arrives in Iran for talks on bilateral ties, regional developments
summary: Sergey Lavrov expected to meet Iranian president as Moscow, Tehran seek to follow up on bilateral agreement
body_text:
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov arrived in Tehran on Monday for an official visit to hold talks with Iranian officials on bilateral relations and regional and international developments, Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported

Lavrov is also expected to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the visit, the state broadcaster IRIB said, citing Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei.

Baqaei said the visit is part of ongoing bilateral consultations and efforts to follow up on agreements between the two countries.

Iran and Russia have strengthened political, economic and military cooperation in recent years amid Western sanctions imposed on both countries.

In January 2025, Pezeshkian and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a 20-year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in Moscow, covering cooperation in defense, security, energy, trade and transportation.

​​​​​​​The agreement also provides for closer coordination on regional and international issues, although it does not establish a mutual defense obligation.

headline: Russian government reshuffles, unrest in Europe: topics of Kremlin spokesman’s briefing
summary: The US continues its mediation and peacemaking efforts toward a settlement in Ukraine, and Russia highly values them, Dmitry Peskov said
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 19. /TASS/. Reshuffles in the government, unrest in European countries, and the Ukrainian settlement were the main topics of Monday’s briefing by Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

TASS has compiled the key statements made by the Russian presidential press secretary.

- "This morning, the president met with Prime Minister [Mikhail] Mishustin. Mishustin submitted proposals for reshuffles in the Cabinet of Ministers. They were endorsed by the president."

- The necessary procedures for appointing new candidates to the government will begin in parliament: "The prime minister then submitted the nominations to the State Duma in accordance with the Constitution. The necessary procedures will begin in <…> parliament."

- Government reshuffles are a normal part of the workflow: "Rotation processes in the government are an absolutely normal. And the prime minister continues his work and initiates the changes he deems necessary for the Cabinet of Ministers to operate effectively."

- It has been decided to expand Anton Siluanov’s authority by nominating him for the position of Deputy Prime Minister - Finance Minister due to the need for additional coordination of financial discipline during the current period: "At this time, of course, additional coordination of financial discipline is necessary. And from the perspective of a deputy prime minister, who, according to the division of powers, oversees several agencies and departments, Anton Siluanov will certainly have expanded powers."

- Putin supported nominating outgoing deputy prime ministers for state awards in recognition of their significant contributions to the government: "As you know, Prime Minister [Mikhail Mishustin] took the initiative to nominate outgoing deputy prime ministers for state awards in recognition of their significant contributions to the government over many years. This proposal was also supported by President Putin."

- "All deputy prime ministers will continue to perform their duties and carry on with their work until the president issues the relevant personnel decrees."

- The topic of a hypothetical trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, and US head of state Donald Trump was raised, given that all three leaders may attend the summit in China: "Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the topic of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed mentioned."

- No specific proposals or agreements on the trilateral meeting or its content were put forward: "No specific proposals or agreements have been discussed or voiced by anyone, neither on the meeting itself [between Putin, Xi Jinping, and Trump] nor on a potential agenda or the content of this meeting."

- The US continues its mediation and peacemaking efforts toward a settlement in Ukraine, and Russia highly values them: "As for the settlement, you know that the US continues its mediation and peacemaking efforts. We highly value them."

- A Ukrainian conflict settlement is impossible without the participation of someone from Kiev who is willing to take responsibility: "Of course, without a doubt, a final settlement [to the conflict in Ukraine] is impossible without the participation of someone from Kiev who is willing to take responsibility."

- The unrest spreading across Europe is indicative of a major crisis: "It’s hard to say whether the crisis is systemic or non-systemic. But it’s obvious that this is a major crisis."

- The unrest in Europe is, in fact, bordering on chaos, yet it remains a domestic matter for EU countries: "These are riots that are already bordering on chaos. They have already spread to France’s largest cities and to Italy, and they are beginning to spread to other countries. Here, of course, we are seeing a clear manifestation of a crisis. Nevertheless, this is an internal matter for these countries."

headline: East Africa: Ghana Set to Overtake Ethiopia As Africa's Eighth-Largest Economy After Kenya Takes East Africa Lead
summary: [Addis Standard] Addis Abeba -- Ghana is projected to overtake Ethiopia as Africa's eighth-largest economy in 2026, with its gross domestic product (GDP) forecast to reach US$128.64 billion, exceeding Ethiopia's projected US$127.15 billion by US$1.49 billion, according to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO), as reported by African Business Insider on 17 October.
body_text:
Addis Abeba — Ghana is projected to overtake Ethiopia as Africa's eighth-largest economy in 2026, with its gross domestic product (GDP) forecast to reach US$128.64 billion, exceeding Ethiopia's projected US$127.15 billion by US$1.49 billion, according to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) October 2026 World Economic Outlook (WEO), as reported by African Business Insider on 17 October.

The projected shift comes after Kenya overtook Ethiopia as East Africa's largest economy in nominal US dollar terms, marking another change in the continent's economic rankings driven partly by exchange-rate movements rather than differences in real economic growth.

The IMF's latest estimates place Ghana eighth among Africa's largest economies, ahead of Ethiopia in ninth place and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), whose economy is projected at US$122.28 billion. While Ghana's nominal GDP is expected to edge ahead of Ethiopia's, the two countries have markedly different growth forecasts.

Ethiopia's economy is projected to expand by 9.2% in real terms in 2026, compared with Ghana's forecast growth of 5.7%. However, the depreciation of the Ethiopian birr following the government's July 2024 foreign-exchange reforms has reduced the dollar value of the country's economic output, narrowing its position in nominal GDP rankings despite strong projected domestic growth.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Ghana's recovery and economic position

Ghana's projected rise comes as the West African country continues to recover from a severe financial crisis marked by currency depreciation, high inflation, mounting public debt and pressure on government finances.

In 2023, Ghana secured a US$3 billion IMF support programme aimed at restoring macroeconomic stability, addressing debt vulnerabilities and rebuilding investor confidence. The government subsequently pursued fiscal reforms, debt restructuring and measures to stabilise prices and the national currency.

The country's economic position is also supported by exports of gold, cocoa, oil and gas, alongside financial services and a growing consumer market. Gold remains a major source of export earnings and foreign exchange, with higher international prices providing additional support to inflows.

However, an improved position in nominal GDP rankings does not necessarily translate into higher living standards or stronger productive capacity. Sustaining the recovery will depend on Ghana's ability to attract long-term investment, create employment and expand industrial production.

Ethiopia's growth versus dollar-denominated output

Ethiopia's projected position reflects the distinction between real economic growth and nominal GDP measured in US dollars. While real GDP growth captures changes in domestic production after accounting for price changes, nominal GDP expressed in dollars is also affected by inflation and movements in the exchange rate.

The depreciation of the birr following Ethiopia's July 2024 shift toward a more market-determined foreign-exchange system substantially reduced the dollar valuation of its output. The reform formed part of the government's broader economic programme, supported by an approximately US$3.4 billion IMF Extended Credit Facility.

As Addis Standard reported last week, Kenya's emergence as East Africa's largest economy in dollar terms was similarly shaped by exchange-rate movements, with the comparatively stronger performance of the Kenyan shilling increasing the dollar value of its economic output.

The IMF's October projections indicate that Ethiopia's economy is expected to grow by 9.2% in 2026 and 7.8% in 2027, while Kenya's growth is forecast at 4.5% and 4.7%, respectively. The figures highlight how an economy can record faster real growth without maintaining a higher ranking when GDP is measured in US dollars.

The projected shift involving Ghana therefore does not, by itself, establish that its underlying economy is growing faster than Ethiopia's. Rather, it underscores the influence of exchange-rate movements and macroeconomic conditions on the relative dollar value of African economies.

About 300 MPs asked to speak in the closed sessions, according to local media. Some MPs have also pressed for details on the mission's nature and scope before they cast their vote. "No MP has rejected the authorisation.Within ruling circles, support has been swift and near unanimous. Pro-government Mostaqbal Watan, the largest party in parliament, declared its backing as MPs convened on Sunday, followed by Homat Al Watan, the National Front and the People's Republican Party. The Salafist Nour Party also backed the request. El Sayed El Badawi, leader of the Wafd, Egypt's oldest liberal party, said Saudi Arabia's security was "an inseparable part" of Egypt's own.Supporters point to the Red Sea, where Houthi attacks on shipping have already cost the Suez Canal heavily in lost revenue. They also point to gratitude for Saudi's continued financial support of Egypt. Central bank data show a $5.3 billion Saudi deposit, part of $10.3 billion Riyadh holds at Egypt's central bank, maturing this month, with Cairo facing a potentially costly repayment unless Riyadh agrees to roll it over.Pro-government figures have cast the move as purely defensive. It said its solidarity with Riyadh was "steadfast", but Egypt's national security "requires clarity of objectives", and military participation must not become "an open-ended commitment". The party also cited lost canal revenue and the strain on the state budget.Ayman Nour, the exiled leader of the liberal Ghad Party, wrote to Speaker Hisham Badawi before Sunday's session. Others reject a combat role altogether. On the far left, the Revolutionary Socialist Current issued a statement headlined "No to war". Business leaders have largely stayed out of the debate.
body_text:
Egypt's pledge to help defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks from Yemen has rallied the state and its allies, but it has also drawn calls for caution amid an escalating situation in the Middle East due to the impact of the Iran war.

From the steps required in parliament to the arguments put forward by different camps in Egypt, the nature of any military support remains uncertain.

Here is a breakdown of the practical steps involved and the debate unfolding in the country with the Arab world's largest population and largest army.

Al Azhar calls for committee to end fighting in Arab region

Parliament is expected to pass the request quickly. The constitution requires approval by two-thirds of the 596-member House, or 398 votes, before troops can be sent on a combat mission abroad. The four main pro-government parties alone won 403 of the 568 elected seats in last year's election.

Approval would give President Abdel Fattah El Sisi, as supreme commander of the armed forces, the legal authority to deploy troops, but it would not send them automatically. Egypt will act only if Riyadh asks, and no formal Saudi request has been announced.

The National Defence Council, chaired by Mr El Sisi, met at Al Ittihadiya Palace on Sunday. It declared Egypt's "full solidarity" with the kingdom and pledged "all necessary and possible forms of support" to defend its security, its territory and the Islamic holy sites.

The council met a day after Mr El Sisi told a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy that it was "inconceivable" Egypt would allow Saudi Arabia's security to be harmed. He asked parliament to authorise action "if we are asked".

Neither statement said what form the support would take, how many troops might be sent or for how long. That silence has shaped much of the reaction since.

The pledge follows near-daily Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia since early October. The deadliest attack was at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which killed and injured hundreds. Among them was Azza Ramzy, a 28-year-old Egyptian flight attendant from Beheira province.

The vote has been pushed from Sunday to Tuesday amid reports of heated debate in the house.

About 300 MPs asked to speak in the closed sessions, according to local media. Some MPs have also pressed for details on the mission's nature and scope before they cast their vote.

Three MPs said they would abstain in the vote. However, Mostafa Bakry, an MP and TV host close to the state, played down any rift. "There was an overwhelming majority," he said. "No MP has rejected the authorisation.

Within ruling circles, support has been swift and near unanimous. Pro-government Mostaqbal Watan, the largest party in parliament, declared its backing as MPs convened on Sunday, followed by Homat Al Watan, the National Front and the People's Republican Party. The Salafist Nour Party also backed the request. El Sayed El Badawi, leader of the Wafd, Egypt's oldest liberal party, said Saudi Arabia's security was "an inseparable part" of Egypt's own.

Supporters point to the Red Sea, where Houthi attacks on shipping have already cost the Suez Canal heavily in lost revenue. They also point to gratitude for Saudi's continued financial support of Egypt. Central bank data show a $5.3 billion Saudi deposit, part of $10.3 billion Riyadh holds at Egypt's central bank, maturing this month, with Cairo facing a potentially costly repayment unless Riyadh agrees to roll it over.

Pro-government figures have cast the move as purely defensive. TV hosts told viewers it concerned protecting Saudi Arabia, not declaring war or going into another country.

Between the loyalists and others who question the move, sits a camp that backs Saudi Arabia but wants clarifications on any mission.

The Egyptian Social Democratic Party told its MPs to abstain. It said its solidarity with Riyadh was "steadfast", but Egypt's national security "requires clarity of objectives", and military participation must not become "an open-ended commitment". The party also cited lost canal revenue and the strain on the state budget.

Ayman Nour, the exiled leader of the liberal Ghad Party, wrote to Speaker Hisham Badawi before Sunday's session. Defending Saudi Arabia was "an Arab duty", he said, but "authorisation is not a blank cheque". He listed 10 safeguards, including a fixed duration, a defined geographical scope, and regular reports to parliament. He cited Egypt's intervention in Yemen in the 1960s, a war many Egyptians still call "Egypt's Vietnam", as a lesson.

Hamdeen Sabahi, a former presidential candidate, went further. Egypt should be "a sponsor of reconciliation", he wrote on Facebook, and should "not send its army to defend one brother, but to establish peace between the two brothers".

Al Azhar, the country's highest seat of Sunni learning, called for "an immediate and comprehensive halt" to fighting in the region and proposed an urgent Arab and Islamic mediation committee. Others reject a combat role altogether. On the far left, the Revolutionary Socialist Current issued a statement headlined "No to war". Business leaders have largely stayed out of the debate.

body_text:
Lebanese Armed Forces personnel have stepped up patrols in Beirut and its sensitive southern suburbs after a surge in tensions with Hezbollah supporters.

The army published images of heavily armed convoys patrolling the capital and temporary checkpoints being set up “to pursue wanted individuals and those disrupting security”.

The tension has partly been fuelled by the recent seizure of half a tonne of explosives by Lebanese authorities before Hezbollah could transfer them to the capital's suburbs, where the group has a strong presence.

Prime Minister Nawaf Salam has ordered that authorities “expand the investigation” into the explosives interception at the Dahr Al Baidar checkpoint in the Bekaa Valley.

The US weighed in last week, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to ensure explosives seized from Hezbollah are not returned to the group.

Hezbollah, the Iran-backed Lebanese political party and armed group, has claimed ownership of the 250kg of TNT-type explosives and 250kg of C4, saying they were to be used against the Israeli military forces that currently occupy swathes of south Lebanon. Hezbollah had demanded the release of the two drivers and the explosives.

The seizure of the explosives, which heightens tension over a push by the Lebanese government to disarm Hezbollah, led to supporters of the group gathering to show their backing.

Further exacerbating the situation was an incident in the Gallerie Semaan neighbourhood on the edge of Beirut's southern suburbs. Police were sent to raid a warehouse there that contained spoiled medicines, following an order from prosecutors.

According to the Internal Security Forces, they were quickly surrounded by “a number of young men gathered on their motorcycles [who] attempted to prevent the force from raiding the warehouse”. The army was eventually deployed to calm the situation.

Mohammed Qassem, the son of Hezbollah Secretary General Naim Qassem, on Sunday published a statement denying any link to the warehouse in response to social media rumours he was connected to it.

Hezbollah said the incident took place after the ISF entered “without following the agreed procedures between the group and security authorities”.

headline: UAE Team Emirates-XRG end season on a high as Tadej Pogacar outlines plan for 2027
summary: UAE Team Emirates-XRG completed their latest season of cycling domination in appropriate fashion as Brandon McNulty sealed an impressive victory at the one-day Veneto Classic.The American rider crossed the finishing line more than a minute ahead of Anthon Charmig (Uno-X Mobility) on Sunday, with McNulty's teammate Pavel Sivakov – on his final outing for the team – claiming the third and final podium spot in Italy.McNulty took the win wearing the rainbow jersey, earned when he replaced another one of his teammates – the injured Tadej Pogacar – as world road race champion after the 28-year-old triumphed in last month's race in Montreal.“It’s a really nice way to finish the season,” said McNulty, following his first win since taking gold in Canada. “We had a really strong team today and everyone played their part. We had good numbers in the front group, which gave us options, and when I got away with Charmig I knew I had to try to make the difference on the final climbs. I managed to get a gap on Diesel Farm and from there it was just full gas to the finish.No rainbow curse for McNulty 👀🌈Brandon McNulty wins the Veneto Classic with a powerful solo ride after attacking away on the final climb. pic.twitter.com/uqjVHNdVna— Cycling on TNT Sports (@cyclingontnt) October 18, 2026“I’ve raced a lot these last few weeks since Montreal and I’ve been pushing to get that first win in the rainbow jersey, so to do it here on the last day of the season, with my wife on the finish line is pretty perfect.”Over in France, meanwhile, UAE Team Emirates-XRG's Jay Vine took second place at the Chrono des Nations, a 45.4km individual time trial around Les Herbiers.The Australian rider made it three consecutive runner-up finishes at the event when he came home 2 mins 11 secs behind runaway winner Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe), with Stefan Kung (Tudor Pro Cycling) third.It was a fitting finale for the Emirati team, who ended the campaign with 78 victories, maintaining their grip on the UCI World Tour, whose rankings they have topped since 2023.Slovenian superstar Pogacar again leads the individual rankings, with his Mexican teammate Isaac del Toro third, behind second-placed Belgian rider Evenepoel.Despite the horror crash at the Vuelta a Espana that ended his campaign prematurely, it was another remarkable season for 28-year-old Pogacar, who topped the podium at Strade Bianche, Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Liege-Bastogne-Liege and Tour de Suisse, as well as winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title.Pogacar was also on course to complete the Grand Tour Slam by winning in Spain until the smash on Stage 8 that left him needing surgery on a broken collarbone, preventing him the opportunity of defending his world and European titles.His recovery appears to be on track though as Pogacar has posted videos on social media of him back on his bike alongside partner Urska Zigart. body_text:
UAE Team Emirates-XRG completed their latest season of cycling domination in appropriate fashion as Brandon McNulty sealed an impressive victory at the one-day Veneto Classic.

The American rider crossed the finishing line more than a minute ahead of Anthon Charmig (Uno-X Mobility) on Sunday, with McNulty's teammate Pavel Sivakov – on his final outing for the team – claiming the third and final podium spot in Italy.

McNulty took the win wearing the rainbow jersey, earned when he replaced another one of his teammates – the injured Tadej Pogacar – as world road race champion after the 28-year-old triumphed in last month's race in Montreal.

Pogacar can look back at 2026 with pride despite brutal end to season

“It’s a really nice way to finish the season,” said McNulty, following his first win since taking gold in Canada. “We had a really strong team today and everyone played their part. We had good numbers in the front group, which gave us options, and when I got away with Charmig I knew I had to try to make the difference on the final climbs. I managed to get a gap on Diesel Farm and from there it was just full gas to the finish.

“I’ve raced a lot these last few weeks since Montreal and I’ve been pushing to get that first win in the rainbow jersey, so to do it here on the last day of the season, with my wife on the finish line is pretty perfect.”

Over in France, meanwhile, UAE Team Emirates-XRG's Jay Vine took second place at the Chrono des Nations, a 45.4km individual time trial around Les Herbiers.

The Australian rider made it three consecutive runner-up finishes at the event when he came home 2 mins 11 secs behind runaway winner Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-BORA-hansgrohe), with Stefan Kung (Tudor Pro Cycling) third.

It was a fitting finale for the Emirati team, who ended the campaign with 78 victories, maintaining their grip on the UCI World Tour, whose rankings they have topped since 2023.

Slovenian superstar Pogacar again leads the individual rankings, with his Mexican teammate Isaac del Toro third, behind second-placed Belgian rider Evenepoel.

Despite the horror crash at the Vuelta a Espana that ended his campaign prematurely, it was another remarkable season for 28-year-old Pogacar, who topped the podium at Strade Bianche, Milan-San Remo, Tour of Flanders, Liege-Bastogne-Liege and Tour de Suisse, as well as winning a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title.

Pogacar was also on course to complete the Grand Tour Slam by winning in Spain until the smash on Stage 8 that left him needing surgery on a broken collarbone, preventing him the opportunity of defending his world and European titles.

His recovery appears to be on track though as Pogacar has posted videos on social media of him back on his bike alongside partner Urska Zigart.

“The injury was pretty serious,” Pogacar said at a charity golf tournament back home in Slovenia at the weekend. “Not only my collarbone and vertebrae, but also a concussion, so it took me a while – I’d say about five weeks – to get back on the bike.”

The fact the European Championships were taking place in Slovenia provided an added temptation to speed up his rehabilitation. “But less than two weeks before the European Championships, I realised there was no point in racing. If I were to crash again, the consequences could be very serious. And that wouldn’t end well,” he admitted to Slovenian media outlet Siol.

Pogacar also revealed that he is returning to Abu Dhabi next week where he will be having talks with team management about plans for 2027. “Given that I finished the season quite some time ago, we will have a concrete discussion about what we will do next season,” he said.

“My wish is the World Championship in combination with the Tour and Vuelta, which didn't work out this year. Although I would rather go to the Giro, I will have to tick off the Vuelta at some point … But as far as my participation in the next Giro is concerned, that’s highly unlikely.”
