headline: Houthi attack kills 53 at Yemen government training camp, officials say
summary: Oct 19 (Reuters) - Fifty-three people were killed and 200 were injured in an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, according to the local authority, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground.
body_text:
Oct 19 (Reuters) - Fifty-three people were killed and 200 were injured in an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, according to the local authority, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.

Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground.

The Houthis and the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have been trading attacks since the group advanced in September towards territory near theBab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.

Local authority sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said the Houthis had launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise.

Shabwa, an energy-rich province in south-central coastal Yemen overlooking the Gulf of Aden, is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen's largest industrial investment.

Government forces this month began a campaign aimed at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the strait, while the groupbesieges Taiz, the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen.

The conflict in Yemen has become another front line in the widerUS-Israeli war on Iran as the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, targetingRiyadh's international airport and the state oil companySaudi Aramco.

War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the sides agreed a 2022 truce that held until this year.

Yemen is already one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning of rapidly deteriorating conditions there.

(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari; Additional reporting by Reyam Mukhashaff and Catherine Cartier; Writing by Menna Alaa El-Din and Nayera Abdallah; Editing by Kevin Liffey, Saad Sayeed and Hugh Lawson)

headline: UN climate panel head wants swift end to deadlock over key scientific report
summary: The world's top climate scientists will reconvene at the earliest opportunity, the panel's chair said on Monday, after member states failed to agree when to release its crucial new findings on global heating. The IPCC, a United Nations body, is the global authority on climate science. Its reports bring together the latest knowledge on climate change, its causes, potential impacts and options for responding.
body_text:
The world's top climate scientists will reconvene at the earliest opportunity, the panel's chair said on Monday, after member states failed to agree when to release its crucial new findings on global heating.

The IPCC, a United Nations body, is the global authority on climate science.

Its reports bring together the latest knowledge on climate change, its causes, potential impacts and options for responding.

They are the key reference point for international agreements on how to tackle the climate crisis, are used by governments to develop national climate policies and have been quoted in international court rulings.

The IPCC suspended its latest negotiations late on Friday after a week of tough talks in the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa.

Many of the IPCC's nearly 200 member countries want its next major report out in time for a crucial United Nations climate summit in 2028.

That summit is due to take stock of the world's progress so far in cutting planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions and is a key decision-making point.

But some IPCC members -- including Saudi Arabia, India and China -- have argued that more time is needed to incorporate science and data from developing nations and have said the new report should be delayed until 2029.

"Reaching consensus on the schedule for our upcoming IPCC reports is vital," IPCC chair Jim Skea said on Monday.

"Our reports... help communicate the scale of climate risks and the urgency of mitigation, adaptation and international cooperation."

Skea said that because the Addis Ababa meeting ran past the closing time, many countries -- notably smaller nations most vulnerable to climate change -- had to leave.

He said it was essential for all countries in the IPCC to be able fully to participate in the negotiations to ensure the body's assessments on the state of the planet were "robust, representative and responsive to the needs of all countries".

The IPCC, set up in 1988, knits together assessments from thousands of climate scientists who work voluntarily to compile its mammoth reports.

They are normally released every five to seven years. The most recent came out in 2021.

Skea said the meeting in Addis Ababa had agreed on many issues, including on artificial intelligence.

But member governments had not yet reached consensus on a timeline for completing the next report "and the IPCC budget that will support our work".

"I will reconvene this plenary session at the earliest opportunity so the panel can effectively conclude its business," he said.

Some 117 scientists working on the new report signed an open letter saying: "Our message to governments and to the world is simple: we will keep working."

The world's response to "the urgency of the climate crisis" must be guided by the best available evidence, said the letter, seen by AFP.

"An assessment that arrives after the decisions it is meant to inform cannot serve its purpose," it insisted.

"The second Global Stocktake in 2028 is such a decision point -- and the world should not have to face it without the IPCC's latest assessment."

headline: Israel announces arrests after West Bank settler attacks on Westerners
summary: Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 people in the occupied West Bank after settler attacks on an American photographer and a French mayor that drew international condemnation but mixed messages from the government. In a rare action against rising settler violence, police said they raided several locations across the occupied territory and seized cars and potential evidence related to the attacks.
body_text:
Israeli police said Monday they had arrested 10 people in the occupied West Bank after settler attacks on an American photographer and a French mayor that drew international condemnation but mixed messages from the government.

In a rare action against rising settler violence, police said they raided several locations across the occupied territory and seized cars and potential evidence related to the attacks.

"Following the severe incidents of violence over the past weekend, including the assault of a media worker and the suspected attacks on foreign civilians, an arrest operation was conducted before dawn," said Major General Moshe Finchi, the Israeli police's West Bank commander.

"Suspects were arrested on suspicion of involvement in the violent incidents, violating a military commander's order concerning a closed military zone, and illegal construction," he said.

Witnesses say that settlers have been stepping up violent attacks on Palestinians during the ongoing olive harvest, aiming to seize their land during a season that carries cultural importance for the community.

Rights groups note that Israel rarely prosecutes settlers when the victims are Palestinian.

The Israeli human rights group Yesh Din said it documents 561 acts of settler or military violence against Palestinians since September 27 -- more than 26 incidents a day.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing a tight race for a new mandate, has tried to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base and has cast doubt on the circumstances behind the recent settler attacks on Westerners.

Netanyahu's tone has brought unusually strong criticism from the opposition, which has accused him of tarnishing Israel's image.

US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel, had called Friday's beating of veteran photographer Heidi Levine an "act of terror" and demanded punishment. He called Monday's arrests a "very positive development".

Levine, 65, who was on assignment for The Washington Post, was taken to a hospital with broken vertebrae. She was visited at her hospital bed both by President Isaac Herzog, who holds a largely ceremonial role, and centre-left opposition leader Yair Golan.

Golan in a social media post afterwards said that if he takes power, there will no longer be "a reality in which Jews instil terror in the name of Jewish supremacy, and stain the state we built here".

One day after Levine's beating, settlers attacked a convoy of European diplomats including the French and Belgian consuls general in Jerusalem as they went through the town of Taybeh in the West Bank on Saturday.

The settlers beat up Bernard Baudoux, 78, the mayor of the northern French town of Aulnoye-Aymeries who was wearing a sash in the French tricolour during a goodwill visit in which he helped harvest olives.

Netanyahu earlier questioned the facts behind the two recent incidents.

On Levine's beating, he alleged that Palestinians and "far-left" activists were fanning violence. With the attack on the diplomatic convoy, he pointed out that the mayor was a leftist supporter of the Palestinian cause and said that diplomats should have coordinated with the Israeli military.

The top official on human rights in the US State Department, Riley Barnes, on Sunday visited the same town where the mayor was beaten, which is largely Christian, on a trip coordinated with the military. He was unharmed.

The violence by settlers has led British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband to accuse Israel of an "ethnic cleansing" campaign and for his government to impose sanctions on goods from settlements.

Marking Monday's deadline for Israel accepting construction tenders for the E1 settlements, a major new project that Palestinians fear will divide the West Bank in two, Miliband warned businesses about consequences.

"They should be aware of legal and reputational consequences, including the risk of involving themselves in serious breaches of international law," Miliband said in a statement.

Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar hit back against what he called an "obsession" with Israel by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government.

"The days when Israel would quietly accept threats, sanctions and attempts to dictate its policies are over," Saar said.

headline: More than 53 killed, over 200 wounded in Houthi attack on southern Yemen
summary: ‘Scale of this tragedy cannot be met with condemnation alone, but requires urgent military, security measures to prevent such attacks from recurring,’ say local authorities in Yemen’s Shabwa
body_text:
More than 53 people were killed and over 200 others injured Monday in a Houthi attack targeting a security training center in Yemen’s southern province of Shabwa.

In a statement released on US social media platform Facebook, the Shabwa governorate said the strike hit the facility while new internal security recruits were undergoing training.

“The scale of this tragedy cannot be met with condemnation alone, but requires urgent military and security measures to prevent such attacks from recurring,” the local authorities stressed, urging the Yemeni government and the Saudi-led coalition to strengthen the governorate’s defensive capabilities.

The Houthis did not immediately comment on the statement.

The strike comes amid escalating hostilities between the Houthis and forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government, backed by the Saudi-led coalition.

Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen.

headline: Iran’s top diplomat Araghchi praises talks with Russian Foreign Minister Lavrov
summary: "The relations between Iran and Russia are of a strategic nature and the implementation of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty has brought them to a new level," Abbas Araghchi said
body_text:
TEHRAN, October 19. /TASS/. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has praised a meeting with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov in Tehran describing it as a productive meeting.

"We had a very productive meeting today. The relations between Iran and Russia are of a strategic nature and the implementation of the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty has brought them to a new level," Araghchi said at a joint news conference with Lavrov.

Earlier in the day, Foreign Minister Lavrov arrived in Tehran to discuss de-escalation steps in the Persian Gulf region with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi and meet with President Masoud Pezeshkian, a TASS correspondent reported.

During his meetings in Iran, Lavrov was also set to devote significant attention to practical steps aimed at strengthening the comprehensive strategic partnership between the two countries. The top diplomat will likely also brief the Iranian side on the key outcomes of his participation in the Ministerial Council of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) in Manama, which was the first stop on his Middle East tour.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.

Nearly 25% of the global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. The US administration then effectively signaled that it would cease the use of large-scale military force against Iran and shift to attempting to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

headline: Zelenskyy claims delivery of vital war supplies for Ukraine delayed by US

He ​added ⁠some ​political agreements ​on the delivery of ⁠air defence supplies ⁠had not been put into practice.Mr Zelenskyy ordered his senior team to contact “partners who can swiftly strengthen our defence”.Ukraine ​has been relying heavily on US intelligence ​to detect incoming missiles. Overnight, Russia launched one of its broadest air assaults in months, cutting power to more than half a million households.It fired 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, and more than 200 drones across Ukraine in ⁠attacks stretching from Kharkiv and Dnipro in the east to Odessa in the south and Volyn ​and Rivne ⁠in the west. More than 10 energy sites were damaged, Mr Zelenskyy said, complaining that Ukraine had received no advance warning of the Russian ballistic missile strike from its partners.The strikes killed one woman in Kyiv and two more people in the ​industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, officials said.“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight and, once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” Mr Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app.“When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defence are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners.”In a later statement on X, Ukraine's President said he had held a meeting about how to prepare the country’s infrastructure for winter, throughout which increased energy will be required for heating. He also said Ukraine was still unable to fully access the Starlink/Starshield services provided by Elon Musk’s company. He said the equipment stops working at speeds of 130kph-161kph. This was limiting the type of drones that could be used to intercept attacks. “Speed matters when it comes to protecting lives,” he said. headline: Alain Ducasse on the pursuit of perfecting regional tastes – from Rabat to Abu Dhabi
summary: Chef Alain Ducasse views the pursuit of new flavours and ingredients as a ongoing quest. After a career spanning more than 50 years, during which restaurants under his leadership were awarded a total of 21 Michelin stars, he continues his journey of culinary inspiration while travelling across continents.And most recently, that exploration has led to new feats for the chef. Ahead of Chef Ducasse's Abu Dhabi opening in the coming months, Aldabaran by Alain Ducasse opened its doors in Rabat, Morocco – his first property on the African continent – in late September. “I liked the idea of creating an extraordinary restaurant in this building in Rabat,” Ducasse tells The National as we sit on the 33rd floor of the King Mohammed VI Tower. It's the tallest building in Morocco, and floors 29 through 46 are home to Waldorf Astoria Rabat Sale. “But not [the idea] to confront Moroccan gastronomy. We do not have the capacity to compete,” he quickly adds.The realisation came after sitting down for what he describes as a “very delicious meal” several months ago. “I had a Moroccan dinner cooked by an extraordinary woman. That's why I know that today we aren't capable of producing true Moroccan taste.”That will come in time, he says, once his team is embedded in the local culinary scene. For now, Ducasse's menu is Mediterranean – which in itself ties in foods and flavours from as many as 20 distinct countries. But Morocco's influence can still be found; the team incorporates the best fresh regional produce that the country has to offer, and 85 per cent of the restaurant's products are locally sourced, Ducasse says.“We are close to the ocean, and the land is generous. So that's enough for me to cook. Plus, there is a population interested in food, and I think they will be won over by what we have to offer.”On the menu, guests can expect dishes such as street food-style chickpea panisse, rich lamb caponata and blue lobster with a spicy kick. Although he won't describe the menu as Moroccan, there are familiar flavours and ingredients throughout. And every new location Ducasse visits is a source of inspiration to him, he says, recalling a recent trip around Asia. “Last week I discovered something extraordinary, and next week I will discover something else,” he says. His next stop is the UAE capital.The chef will open two properties by the end of 2027 in the UAE after Ecole Ducasse, his culinary school, opened in 2023 in Abu Dhabi. Alain Ducasse Cafe, a chocolate shop concept, will open in Saadiyat Grove before the end of the year.“It’s going to be a bit like [the cafe in] Osaka, with a chocolate shop, a tea room with small bites and finger food,” he says of the new venture. But he is no stranger to the region. Idam by Alain Ducasse is one of Qatar's three Michelin-starred restaurants, bringing French cuisine with Middle Eastern touches. Jiwan, his other Doha property, puts a modern take on Qatari dishes. He says it is no coincidence that the chef from Jiwan, Morgan Perrigaud, took over the kitchen at Aldabaran.“We've well understood the taste of the Middle East,” Ducasse says. “From our experience and crafting the menu to appeal to Qataris, we drew from Lebanese and North African influences. And certainly, step by step, we might integrate this North African and Middle Eastern sphere of influence here.”Ducasse is also set to open a flagship French-American steakhouse in the upcoming Wynn Al Marjan Island gaming resort next year.For now, the chef continues his quest.“Everything inspires me,” Ducasse says. “Looking at the world. The markets, the competition, going to eat at fellow chefs' places. The most important thing is to digest it and share it."

India-New Zealand trade deal, which has secured full tariff elimination for all Indian exports to New Zealand while reducing tariffs on 95% of New Zealand’s imports into the country, came into effect on Tuesday. Under the pact, New Zealand has also committed to invest $20 billion in India over the next 15 years.

A host of Indian goods from labour-intensive sectors such as leather, footwear, apparel and textiles will attract zero import duty in New Zealand from October 20, when the India-New Zealand FTA comes into force, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Monday.

He added that sensitive sectors such as dairy, onions, chickpeas, peas, corn, almonds, artificial honey, and sugar have been kept out of the trade deal. The commerce ministry has also notified the procedure for allocation of Tariff Rate Quotas (TRQ) under the trade agreement. Goods under TRQ include apples, kiwi fruit, albumin and Manuka honey.

The Minister said Centres of Excellence would be established under the agricultural partnership, particularly in areas such as apples, kiwifruit and honey. He said that sensitive agricultural sectors, including dairy, would remain protected under the agreement.

Goyal said the Commerce and Industry departments would work with state governments to inform farmers, entrepreneurs and businesses about opportunities arising from the FTA. The agreement was signed on April 27 and ratified on September 21. Bilateral trade in goods and services currently stands at $ 2.4 billion.

“Starting tomorrow, 100% of the goods from every sector in India going to New Zealand will go there with zero duty,” he said. The duty-free access is expected to improve the competitiveness of Indian exports, particularly in labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, apparel, leather and footwear, while creating opportunities for engineering goods, pharmaceuticals, and agricultural products.

India and New Zealand have little bilateral trade, standing at $1.3 billion in 2024–25. New Delhi’s goods exports during the last financial year stood at $711.1 million, and imports stood at $587.13 million.

Even as New Zealand is one of the largest producers of dairy products, India has maintained its red lines on the product category. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry said that the products that are kept in exclusion are mainly dairy, including milk, cream, whey, yoghurt, cheese, and animal products, other than sheep meat, vegetable products, including onions, chana, peas, corn and almonds, among others.

However, a number of products from New Zealand will see lower tariffs. These products include wine, pharmaceutical drugs, polymers, aluminium, iron and steel articles, etc. India has also allowed honey, apples, kiwi fruit, and albumins, including milk albumin, under a tariff rate quota.

Under the trade pact, New Zealand has created a dedicated pathway for student mobility and post-study work visas with India. The agreement removes numerical caps on Indian students, guarantees a minimum of 20 hours per week of work during study, and provides extended post-study work opportunities-up to three years for STEM Bachelor’s and Master’s graduates, and up to four years for Doctorate holders-creating clear pathways for skills development and global careers, the ministry said.

“The FTA establishes a new Temporary Employment Entry (TEE) Visa pathway for Indian professionals in skilled occupations, with a quota of 5,000 visas at any given time and a stay of up to three years. This pathway covers Indian professions such as AYUSH practitioners, yoga instructors, Indian chefs, and music teachers, as well as high-demand sectors including IT, engineering, healthcare, education, and construction, strengthening skilled workforce mobility and services trade,” the Commerce and Industry Ministry said.

The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon. However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.

Nearly 25% of the global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade pass through the strait. summary: Ukraine has evacuated a wounded soldier from the front line using an aerial drone in what a Ukrainian army brigade has described as a world-first operation. body_text:
Ukraine has evacuated a wounded soldier from the front line using an aerial drone in what a Ukrainian army brigade has described as a world-first operation. The successful mission highlights the growing role of unmanned technology in battlefield evacuations as drones continue to shape the conflict between Ukraine and Russia.

Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 17:44

Ukraine has rescued a wounded soldier from the front line using an aerial drone, a Ukrainian army brigade said on Monday, describing the evacuation as the first of its kind.

The brigade published a video showing the drone lowering itself to the ground, before a man in combat gear fastens himself to a winch onboard and is lifted upwards.

Watch moreResidents of Ukraine's Kramatorsk forced to flee as drone strikes intensify

The brigade did not say where the evacuation took place.

"The operation was successful – the wounded person was saved! He is now undergoing treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger," the drone unit of Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade said on Facebook.

Read moreUkrainian drone attack on Saint Petersburg kills one, sets refinery ablaze

The drone's manufacturer, Gurzuf Defence, said the man had spent almost a year and a half in a dangerous combat position and was unable to be rescued by conventional means.

"Any attempt to reach him would have meant a deadly risk for the rescue team," it said.

The drone, an Ayudag-6 hexacopter, "brought the wounded man to a safer position, where he was met by comrades who arranged for his onward evacuation to a hospital", it added.

Ukraine has long used unmanned ground vehicles to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield, but this was the first reported instance of an aerial drone being used for the same purpose.

The 92nd Assault Brigade's drone unit described the operation as a "world first".

Both Russia and Ukraine have made extensive use of drones in the four-and-a-half-year war, which began with the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The extensive use of combat drones by both sides has turned the battlefield into what military analysts have described as a "kill zone" where neither side has a clear advantage.

body_text:
Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative (FII) conference after a surge in Houthi attacks on the kingdom. The annual gathering was scheduled to take place from October 26 to 29 in Riyadh.

“The FII Institute announces that the 10th edition of the Future Investment Initiative, FII10 'The Power of Legacy', originally scheduled for October 26–29, 2026, in Riyadh, will now take place in 2027,” an advisory issued by the FII organisers on Monday said, adding that the new dates would be announced “very soon”.

“This decision has been taken to ensure that our milestone 10th edition delivers the full scale, quality, and impact that our partners, members, speakers and delegates expect.”

The decision to postpone the event follows a series of missile and drone attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi group, including strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport. The attacks have disrupted air travel and raised security concerns among international executives and investors.

The 10th edition of FII was expected to bring together senior government officials, global financiers and corporate leaders, including BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink and JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon, to discuss investment opportunities and economic growth.

Launched in 2017, FII has become a vital platform for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to promote Vision 2030, the kingdom’s economic diversification programme aimed at reducing reliance on oil and attracting foreign capital.

The postponement adds to a growing list of international events affected by the conflict. Saudi Arabia and the EU have postponed a planned summit, while several sporting and cultural events have also been delayed or cancelled amid security concerns, according to a Reuters report.

On Monday Saudi Arabia also announced the cancellation of two more events – Intersec Saudi Arabia and Saudi Retail Forum, according to organisers of both events.

Intersec Saudi Arabia 2026, which was due to take place from November 16-18 will now be held in October 2027, organiser Messe Frankfurt Saudi Arabia said on Monday. The Saudi Retail Forum, which was originally scheduled to take place on November 19, has officially been postponed to March 2027.

“The decision follows close monitoring of recent developments in Saudi Arabia and was taken in co-ordination with the venue, the local government partners, and the event’s local and international stakeholders,” Messe Frankfurt Saudi Arabia said.

headline: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
summary: CAIRO, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Egypt's parliament is expected to vote next week on whether toauthorise the armed forces to help defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen'sHouthis if Riyadh requests its support.The move would bring the Arab world's most populous country closer to direct military involvement in the widening conflicts unleashed by the US-Israeli air assault on Iran in February.
body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 19 (Reuters) - Egypt's parliament is expected to vote next week on whether toauthorise the armed forces to help defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Yemen'sHouthis if Riyadh requests its support.

The move would bring the Arab world's most populous country closer to direct military involvement in the widening conflicts unleashed by the US-Israeli air assault on Iran in February.

PresidentAbdel Fattah al-Sisi requested the approval in a speech on Saturday, saying Egypt would "never, never forget our brothers in the Gulf" and telling Saudi Arabia's leaders that Cairo would "take any measure to protect you".

Like the Gulf states that have come under attack from Tehran in the Iran war, Egypt is a longstanding partner in the US-led security order that is being tested by the conflict.

WHAT IS EGYPT'S STANCE ON THE IRAN WAR?

Sisi's comments marked a clear escalation from the more measured tone authorities have tended to adopt since the Iran war started. Though Egypt has repeatedly voiced strong support for its Gulf allies, Cairo has stopped short of publicly committing itself to a direct combat role in the conflict.

In May, the presence of EgyptianRafale fighter jets in the United Arab Emirates was disclosed in Emirati state media coverage ofan official visit by Sisi. Egyptian coverage of the visit did not mention the deployment. When Saudi Arabia signed a joint defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan in August, Egypt did not join, though it said it was considering it.

The tone started to shift after the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi oil and other infrastructure. Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman last month visited Egypt, where he discussed the need to ensure freedom and security of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea, on which both countries have long coastlines.

WHAT'S AT STAKE FOR EGYPT?

Egypt's economic stability has long been tied up with the oil-producing Gulf. Remittances from Egyptian expatriate workers there are an important source of foreign currency and income for families back home at a time of double-digit inflation worsened by surging food and fuel prices.

Saudi Arabia, the UAE and other Gulf countries have been amongSisi's key financial backers, providing tens of billions of dollars of aid, central bank deposits and investments since the army overthrew President Mohamed Morsi, a senior Muslim Brotherhood figure, in 2013.

"We can never forget how our brothers in the Gulf states stood by Egypt during that period," Sisi said in his speech.

Saudi Arabia has a $5.3 billion deposit at Egypt's central bank due this month along with $267 million in interest, central bank data shows.

Growing security concerns have also pushed Cairo towards a more active stance, analysts say. A drone strike on two gas vessels at the Mediterranean port city ofDamietta in July underscored that Egypt could not expect to keep itself fully isolated from the conflict.

"I think they realise that they can't be on the sidelines about this indefinitely," said H. A. Hellyer, a scholar at the Royal United Services Institute think tank.

For the authorities, the economic and security concerns were "one and the same," he said.

Saudi Arabia and Egypt also have a shared interest in securing shipping through the Red Sea, an outlet for Saudi oil blocked from leaving the Strait of Hormuz. Egypt earns billions of dollars a year from fees on Suez Canal traffic.These overlapping concerns mean "Saudi Arabia's security constitutes a dimension of Egyptian national security," saidSherif Aref, an Egyptian political researcher and journalist.

WHAT SORT OF MILITARY DOES EGYPT BRING TO THE TABLE?

Egypt has one of the Arab world's largest armed forces, with hundreds of thousands of active personnel and large air, land and naval inventories, according to military analysts. Egypt sources equipment from a range of countries, and its air force operates US-made F-16s, French Rafales and Russian-made MiG-29s.

Egypt receives about $1.3 billion a year in USmilitary aid, which helps fund its purchases of American military equipment. Washingtonwaived human rights conditions on a tranche of the funds this year after what it called Cairo's "helpful role" since the Iran war began.

In the years after the 2011 uprising that ousted President Hosni Mubarak, the armed forces fought a counterinsurgency campaign against Islamist militants in the Sinai Peninsula. Egypt also contributed air and naval forces to the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015, and conducted airstrikes against Islamic State targets in Libya during that country’s civil war.

Egypt has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War, when its troops joined the US-led coalition to drive Iraqi forces from Kuwait. Nearly three decades earlier, President Gamal Abdel Nasser had sent Egyptian forces into Yemen in a costly intervention later compared to the US involvement in the Vietnam War.

WHAT SORT OF SUPPORT IS LIKELY?

Sisi's speech and subsequent statements have not specified what sort of military forces, if any, Egypt would ultimately intend to send. A deployment of Egyptian troops inside Yemen itself is unlikely, military analysts say.

More likely interventions might include air defence and naval support, said Samir Ragheb, a retired Egyptian military officer who heads the Arab Foundation for Development and Strategic Studies think tank.

"The threats, missiles and drones, require air defence and air forces," he said, adding that the navy could be used for protecting ships, naval operations against piracy and protecting the Saudi coastline.

Still, the entry of another large conventional Arab military would not "suddenlysolve the Houthi problem",said Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's ​College London.

"The Houthis are difficult precisely because they generate disproportionate effect through missiles, drones, dispersed forces and geography. Egypt cannot bomb that problem away," he said.

"What Cairo can do is strengthen Saudi resilience, improve Red Sea control, share the defensive burden and increase the political cost of continued attacks."

(Reporting by Alexander Dziadosz, Dina Sakr and Mariam Rizk; Writing by Alexander Dziadosz; Editing by Timothy Heritage and Kevin Liffey)

What happened: In a statement, the Lebanese military said it deployed specialized units to the Metn area, where locals had reported a tunnel.

An investigation has been opened to identify the intended purpose of the tunnel, the statement read.

He made the remarks in a meeting with First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref on the sidelines of a Shanghai Cooperation Organization meeting in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on Monday.

headline: Art Basel Paris, Metallica lead this week’s global culture calendar
summary: Events scheduled for Oct. 19-25 include major art fairs, film festivals, exhibitions, concerts across Europe, Africa, North America, Middle East and Australia
body_text:
From contemporary art in Paris and design showcases in Lagos to Metallica concerts in Las Vegas and jazz performances in Melbourne, cities worldwide will host a wide range of cultural events this week.

Art Basel Paris will return to the Grand Palais from Friday through Sunday, bringing together more than 200 galleries from 41 countries and territories.

The fair will be divided into three sections covering established galleries, emerging artists and specially curated presentations.

Its public program will extend across nine Paris landmarks from Wednesday, featuring works by Robert Indiana, Tracey Emin, Niki de Saint Phalle and Yinka Shonibare.

Turkish contemporary artist Kutlug Ataman’s video installation Kuba will be displayed at the Chapel of the Petits-Augustins at the Beaux-Arts de Paris. The work is built around interviews with residents of an Istanbul neighborhood and examines identity, community and displacement.

In New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art will open Designing the Gilded Age: Drawings from the Studios of Louis C. Tiffany on Thursday.

The exhibition brings together nearly 120 works, including rarely displayed and newly conserved drawings that reveal the creative process behind Tiffany Studios’ stained-glass windows, lamps, mosaics and interiors. It will remain open until Feb. 7.

Design Week Lagos will continue across the Nigerian city until Sunday. Held under the theme Making a New Africa, the festival includes exhibitions, trade showcases, talks and training programs exploring African design, manufacturing and sustainable economic growth.

The 21st Rome Film Fest will enter its final week before concluding on Sunday at the Auditorium Parco della Musica and other venues across the Italian capital.

The program features international competition titles, public discussions, special screenings and tributes. This week’s events include a Monday screening of Make Some Noise: Mano Negra!, focusing on the French-Spanish rock group, and a Friday program celebrating pioneering women in early cinema.

Metallica will continue its Life Burns Faster residency at the Sphere in Las Vegas with two performances Thursday and Saturday. The band has prepared separate setlists for the two shows as part of its No Repeat Weekend format, with visuals created for the venue’s wraparound display and immersive sound system.

At Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles, Andrew Bird will perform with the Los Angeles Philharmonic on Friday. The venue will also present A Symphonic Ballet with Elim Chan on Thursday, Saturday and Sunday, while French organist Lucile Dollat will give a recital Sunday.

Dubai Opera’s program will begin with a symphonic concert by the Gipsy Kings on Thursday. Indian singer-songwriter Prateek Kuhad will bring his Full Moon Chamber Tour to the venue Saturday, followed by the classical program Romantic Masters on Sunday.

The Melbourne International Jazz Festival will also continue through Sunday. Grammy-winning pianist and composer Kris Davis will perform with students from the Melbourne Conservatorium of Music on Wednesday, while South African trumpeter and vocalist Mandisi Dyantyis will appear at the JazzLab on the closing night.

At the Sydney Opera House, the 70th-anniversary staging of the musical My Fair Lady will take place Friday and Saturday. The Sydney Symphony Orchestra will also be performing John Williams’ Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back score live alongside screenings of the film from Wednesday through Saturday.

headline: Opinion | The Vitality of Iteru: Blue Nile Hydropolitics and Asymmetrical Water Vulnerability
summary: On 11 October 2026, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to safeguarding its historical and acquired water rights, underscoring the Nile’s vital importance to the Egyptian people. This reaffirmation came two days before the commemoration by some countries of the entry into force of the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework (CFA) on 13 October 2024, initiating the transition towards the Nile River Basin Commission envisaged under its provisions. Egypt and Sudan remain outside the agreement, which was not adopted through a consensus-based approach amid unresolved disagreements over prior notification, equitable water utilisation, water security and basin governance. Their absence raises a fundamental question about whether an institutional framework excluding two major downstream states can deliver genuinely basin-wide cooperation. A commission intended to advance basin-wide cooperation will need to address all concerns through sustained, good-faith negotiations rather than treating institutional establishment as an end in itself. Progress among participating countries can provide a foundation for cooperation, but lasting legitimacy will depend on whether the framework can accommodate the interests of states that have not joined it. Inclusive governance is therefore not a secondary diplomatic objective; it is central to the credibility and durability of any basin-wide settlement. These concerns are particularly pertinent as Cairo prepares to host the ninth Cairo Water Week, from 25 to 29 October 2026, under the theme “Water as a Catalyst for Peace, Shared Prosperity, and a Sustainable Planet”. Achieving this vision requires arrangements that reconcile competing development priorities with the security of populations dependent on shared water resources. Nowhere is this challenge more apparent than in relations between Egypt and Ethiopia, where the dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) continues to test the prospects for regional cooperation. The consequences of failure extend well beyond the distribution of river flows. Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa remain fraught, while Sudan’s prolonged conflict threatens the stability of a country whose water infrastructure is directly affected by upstream developments. Armed conflict, climate pressures and political uncertainty already place considerable strain on the region. Without mechanisms to manage competing water demands, disputes over the Nile risk aggravating these vulnerabilities, undermining agricultural production, economic development and regional stability. An agreement on the river is therefore not simply a technical necessity but an important component of a wider effort to reduce tensions across the basin. Egypt’s objection to the GERD is not opposition to Ethiopia’s economic development or its pursuit of hydropower. Rather, it concerns the construction and operation of infrastructure capable of affecting the water security of millions of people downstream without an adequate, legally binding framework governing its transboundary effects. Cairo has engaged with development initiatives elsewhere in the Nile Basin, including projects along the White Nile, emphasising its commitment to cooperation between riparian states. The World Bank’s Operational Policy on Projects on International Waterways (OP 7.50) offers a relevant example of procedural safeguards for affected states in applicable Bank-financed projects. Although this policy does not govern the GERD directly, it illustrates the general rule and wider importance of assessing transboundary impacts and giving affected countries an opportunity to raise concerns before decisions create difficult-to-reverse consequences. Nadine Loza The GERD’s position on the Blue Nile makes these questions especially consequential. By controlling the reservoir’s storage and releases, Ethiopia exercises substantial influence over the timing and volume of flows reaching Sudan and Egypt. This creates an asymmetry in which the upstream state has considerable operational discretion while downstream countries must manage the consequences of decisions taken beyond their borders. The imbalance is particularly pronounced for Egypt, where extremely rare rainfall and scarce alternative freshwater resources make the Nile indispensable to agriculture, urban consumption and economic activity. Unlike Egypt, whose arid climate and negligible rainfall make the Nile indispensable, Ethiopia receives substantial seasonal rainfall across much of its territory, giving it a broader natural freshwater base. Understanding those risks requires distinguishing the GERD’s electricity-generating function from its effects on the timing and availability of water. Water passing through the dam’s turbines can continue downstream, but reservoir filling, evaporation and release schedules influence when that water arrives and how much is available at particular times. Under favourable rainfall conditions, changes in releases may be manageable. During severe droughts, however, the demands of electricity generation, irrigation and drinking-water supply can become more difficult to reconcile. The dam’s consequences must therefore be evaluated under adverse hydrological conditions, not solely through average annual flows or its contribution to Ethiopia’s electricity supply. Egypt’s High Aswan Dam and Lake Nasser provide an important buffer against fluctuations in Nile inflows, but their protective capacity is finite. The reserves available during a shortage depend on initial storage, subsequent inflows and the duration of the drought. Egypt retained reserves following the GERD’s initial filling, which did not coincide with a severe multiyear drought. That experience, however, cannot establish how uncoordinated dam operations would affect Egypt during a prolonged sequence of dry years. The droughts that affected the Nile Basin during the 1980s, particularly between 1983 and 1989, demonstrate how successive years of reduced inflows can place sustained pressure on water supplies. The central issue is not whether the GERD necessarily causes a shortage, but whether its operation should be coordinated to prevent avoidable harm when water is scarce. The human right to water was recognised by the United Nations General Assembly in Resolution 64/292, adopted on 28 July 2010, which affirms the right to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation as essential to the full enjoyment of life and all human rights. In September 2026, Egypt’s annual per-capita water availability was reported at approximately 472 cubic metres, below the 500-cubic-metre threshold for absolute water scarcity. The government has invested in solar-powered irrigation, groundwater development, wastewater treatment and desalination, but these measures cannot replace the Nile at the scale required by Egypt’s population and agricultural economy. Groundwater extraction carries depletion risks, desalination remains expensive for extensive agricultural use, and coastal facilities cannot readily supply inland farms. These limitations make reliable Nile inflows a structural necessity for Egypt, as disruption to the river threatens the country’s ability to secure this essential resource for its population. The dispute also reflects competing interpretations of the legal framework governing the river. The 1959 Agreement for the Full Utilisation of the Nile Waters allocated Egypt 55.5 billion cubic metres annually and Sudan 18.5 billion. Egypt maintains that its historical and acquired water rights and established uses must be protected. Upstream states, however, dispute the extent to which an agreement concluded without their participation determines their obligations. This disagreement cannot be resolved simply by invoking historical allocations or unrestricted development rights. Equitable and reasonable utilisation requires consideration of the river’s hydrology, the populations dependent on it, socioeconomic needs, available alternatives and the effects of proposed changes on existing uses. The task is to reconcile these considerations through rules that recognise the legitimate interests of all riparian states. International water law provides principles for pursuing that reconciliation. The 1997 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses establishes equitable and reasonable utilisation, cooperation and the prevention of significant harm as central principles. Article 12 addresses notification of planned measures that may significantly affect other watercourse states. The 1993 Framework for General Cooperation between Egypt and Ethiopia, signed in Cairo on 1 July, also recognises international law, the avoidance of appreciable harm, consultation and mutually advantageous cooperation. Efforts to address these concerns have a long history. The International Panel of Experts established by Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan in 2012 submitted its final report in May 2013, identifying shortcomings in the available documentation and the need for further assessments, including dam safety, hydrological modelling and environmental impacts. The international dimension of the dispute resurfaced on 9 October 2026, when US President Donald Trump waded into the GERD controversy, calling US financing of the project “a stupid thing to do” and accused Ethiopia of taking all the water from the Nile. His remarks brought renewed attention to Washington’s past involvement in the project, and Egypt has called on European Union institutions to examine its transboundary environmental, economic and social effects, including the responsibilities of European companies involved in its construction. Research suggests that cooperation could improve outcomes for all three countries. A 2023 study by Basheer and colleagues, published in Nature Climate Change, found that cooperative adaptive management could strengthen economic outcomes and resilience in Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt. A legally binding agreement should establish coordinated filling and operating procedures, transparent exchanges of reservoir and inflow data, independent monitoring, predefined drought-response measures and effective dispute resolution. Agreed hydrological thresholds could trigger consultations and contingency measures before shortages become acute. This would help protect downstream water supplies while allowing Ethiopia to plan hydropower generation with greater certainty. Operational flexibility is compatible with legal certainty, provided it functions within agreed and enforceable limits. Sudan illustrates why these arrangements must work in practice. Roseires Dam lies approximately 115 kilometres downstream of the GERD on the Blue Nile, making its operations sensitive to changes in upstream releases. During the GERD’s initial filling in July 2020, falling river levels disrupted drinking-water pumping stations in Khartoum. Chatham House’s 2023 analysis also reported that a Roseires Dam technician had described media reports as his only source of information about GERD operations in 2021. These accounts expose a basic operational weakness: downstream infrastructure cannot be managed effectively when reliable information about upstream decisions is unavailable. Although the GERD could benefit Sudan through flood moderation and improved agricultural planning, those benefits depend on timely data-sharing and coordination. Sudan’s continuing conflict makes dependable communication and water-management arrangements even more important, as damaged infrastructure and weakened emergency-response capacity can magnify the consequences of sudden changes in supply. Shared hydrological monitoring, satellite observations, predictive modelling and artificial intelligence can improve drought forecasting, reservoir planning and the identification of emerging risks. Environmental assessments should also account for sediment transport, aquatic ecosystems and river-dependent livelihoods, ensuring that the focus extends beyond electricity generation and annual water volumes. Cairo Water Week 2026 offers an opportunity to connect these technical capabilities with diplomatic engagement and practical negotiations. Egypt and Sudan require binding guarantees that protect downstream water supplies against both droughts and floods. These must include advance notification of changes in river conditions and planned releases, transparent and continuous data-sharing, coordinated reservoir operations and enforceable procedures for managing periods of severe water stress. In particular, agreed drought-management rules should establish clear hydrological thresholds for adjusting reservoir filling and releases when essential downstream supplies are at risk. The flooding experienced in Sudan in September and October 2025 further demonstrated the consequences of inadequate coordination, with the severity of the flooding attributed to sudden, unannounced changes in GERD releases. Cairo also opposes further unilateral Ethiopian dam projects without prior notification, consultation, comprehensive impact assessments and basin-wide agreement. Iteru, the ancient Egyptian word for ‘Great River’, has sustained Egyptian civilisation for millennia. Today, its waters flow into a new confluence: Ethiopia’s regional ambitions and Egypt’s imperative to safeguard its water security. The basin’s future will depend on whether its riparian states can move beyond competing positions and establish a durable framework that protects the interests of all, particularly those whose survival depends on the river’s reliable flow. The Great River poses a great test—and meeting it will require great political will. Nadine Loza is a development strategist, opinion columnist, and Founding Director of the Egypt Diaspora Initiative.
body_text:
On 11 October 2026, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to safeguarding its historical and acquired water rights, underscoring the Nile’s vital importance to the Egyptian people. This reaffirmation came two days before the commemoration by some countries of the entry into force of the Nile Basin Cooperative Framework (CFA) on 13 October 2024, initiating the transition towards the Nile River Basin Commission envisaged under its provisions. Egypt and Sudan remain outside the agreement, which was not adopted through a consensus-based approach amid unresolved disagreements over prior notification, equitable water utilisation, water security and basin governance. Their absence raises a fundamental question about whether an institutional framework excluding two major downstream states can deliver genuinely basin-wide cooperation.

A commission intended to advance basin-wide cooperation will need to address all concerns through sustained, good-faith negotiations rather than treating institutional establishment as an end in itself. Progress among participating countries can provide a foundation for cooperation, but lasting legitimacy will depend on whether the framework can accommodate the interests of states that have not joined it. Inclusive governance is therefore not a secondary diplomatic objective; it is central to the credibility and durability of any basin-wide settlement.

These concerns are particularly pertinent as Cairo prepares to host the ninth Cairo Water Week, from 25 to 29 October 2026, under the theme “Water as a Catalyst for Peace, Shared Prosperity, and a Sustainable Planet”. Achieving this vision requires arrangements that reconcile competing development priorities with the security of populations dependent on shared water resources. Nowhere is this challenge more apparent than in relations between Egypt and Ethiopia, where the dispute over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) continues to test the prospects for regional cooperation.

The consequences of failure extend well beyond the distribution of river flows. Relations between Cairo and Addis Ababa remain fraught, while Sudan’s prolonged conflict threatens the stability of a country whose water infrastructure is directly affected by upstream developments. Armed conflict, climate pressures and political uncertainty already place considerable strain on the region. Without mechanisms to manage competing water demands, disputes over the Nile risk aggravating these vulnerabilities, undermining agricultural production, economic development and regional stability. An agreement on the river is therefore not simply a technical necessity but an important component of a wider effort to reduce tensions across the basin.

Egypt’s objection to the GERD is not opposition to Ethiopia’s economic development or its pursuit of hydropower. Rather, it concerns the construction and operation of infrastructure capable of affecting the water security of millions of people downstream without an adequate, legally binding framework governing its transboundary effects. Cairo has engaged with development initiatives elsewhere in the Nile Basin, including projects along the White Nile, emphasising its commitment to cooperation between riparian states. The World Bank’s Operational Policy on Projects on International Waterways (OP 7.50) offers a relevant example of procedural safeguards for affected states in applicable Bank-financed projects. Although this policy does not govern the GERD directly, it illustrates the general rule and wider importance of assessing transboundary impacts and giving affected countries an opportunity to raise concerns before decisions create difficult-to-reverse consequences.

The GERD’s position on the Blue Nile makes these questions especially consequential. By controlling the reservoir’s storage and releases, Ethiopia exercises substantial influence over the timing and volume of flows reaching Sudan and Egypt. This creates an asymmetry in which the upstream state has considerable operational discretion while downstream countries must manage the consequences of decisions taken beyond their borders. The imbalance is particularly pronounced for Egypt, where extremely rare rainfall and scarce alternative freshwater resources make the Nile indispensable to agriculture, urban consumption and economic activity. Unlike Egypt, whose arid climate and negligible rainfall make the Nile indispensable, Ethiopia receives substantial seasonal rainfall across much of its territory, giving it a broader natural freshwater base.

Understanding those risks requires distinguishing the GERD’s electricity-generating function from its effects on the timing and availability of water. Water passing through the dam’s turbines can continue downstream, but reservoir filling, evaporation and release schedules influence when that water arrives and how much is available at particular times. Under favourable rainfall conditions, changes in releases may be manageable. During severe droughts, however, the demands of electricity generation, irrigation and drinking-water supply can become more difficult to reconcile. The dam’s consequences must therefore be evaluated under adverse hydrological conditions, not solely through average annual flows or its contribution to Ethiopia’s electricity supply.

Egypt’s High Aswan Dam and Lake Nasser provide an important buffer against fluctuations in Nile inflows, but their protective capacity is finite. The reserves available during a shortage depend on initial storage, subsequent inflows and the duration of the drought. Egypt retained reserves following the GERD’s initial filling, which did not coincide with a severe multiyear drought. That experience, however, cannot establish how uncoordinated dam operations would affect Egypt during a prolonged sequence of dry years. The droughts that affected the Nile Basin during the 1980s, particularly between 1983 and 1989, demonstrate how successive years of reduced inflows can place sustained pressure on water supplies. The central issue is not whether the GERD necessarily causes a shortage, but whether its operation should be coordinated to prevent avoidable harm when water is scarce.

The human right to water was recognised by the United Nations General Assembly in Resolution 64/292, adopted on 28 July 2010, which affirms the right to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation as essential to the full enjoyment of life and all human rights. In September 2026, Egypt’s annual per-capita water availability was reported at approximately 472 cubic metres, below the 500-cubic-metre threshold for absolute water scarcity. The government has invested in solar-powered irrigation, groundwater development, wastewater treatment and desalination, but these measures cannot replace the Nile at the scale required by Egypt’s population and agricultural economy. Groundwater extraction carries depletion risks, desalination remains expensive for extensive agricultural use, and coastal facilities cannot readily supply inland farms. These limitations make reliable Nile inflows a structural necessity for Egypt, as disruption to the river threatens the country’s ability to secure this essential resource for its population.

The dispute also reflects competing interpretations of the legal framework governing the river. The 1959 Agreement for the Full Utilisation of the Nile Waters allocated Egypt 55.5 billion cubic metres annually and Sudan 18.5 billion. Egypt maintains that its historical and acquired water rights and established uses must be protected. Upstream states, however, dispute the extent to which an agreement concluded without their participation determines their obligations. This disagreement cannot be resolved simply by invoking historical allocations or unrestricted development rights. Equitable and reasonable utilisation requires consideration of the river’s hydrology, the populations dependent on it, socioeconomic needs, available alternatives and the effects of proposed changes on existing uses. The task is to reconcile these considerations through rules that recognise the legitimate interests of all riparian states.

International water law provides principles for pursuing that reconciliation. The 1997 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses establishes equitable and reasonable utilisation, cooperation and the prevention of significant harm as central principles. Article 12 addresses notification of planned measures that may significantly affect other watercourse states. The 1993 Framework for General Cooperation between Egypt and Ethiopia, signed in Cairo on 1 July, also recognises international law, the avoidance of appreciable harm, consultation and mutually advantageous cooperation.

Efforts to address these concerns have a long history. The International Panel of Experts established by Egypt, Ethiopia and Sudan in 2012 submitted its final report in May 2013, identifying shortcomings in the available documentation and the need for further assessments, including dam safety, hydrological modelling and environmental impacts. The international dimension of the dispute resurfaced on 9 October 2026, when US President Donald Trump waded into the GERD controversy, calling US financing of the project “a stupid thing to do” and accused Ethiopia of taking all the water from the Nile. His remarks brought renewed attention to Washington’s past involvement in the project, and Egypt has called on European Union institutions to examine its transboundary environmental, economic and social effects, including the responsibilities of European companies involved in its construction.

Research suggests that cooperation could improve outcomes for all three countries. A 2023 study by Basheer and colleagues, published in Nature Climate Change, found that cooperative adaptive management could strengthen economic outcomes and resilience in Ethiopia, Sudan and Egypt. A legally binding agreement should establish coordinated filling and operating procedures, transparent exchanges of reservoir and inflow data, independent monitoring, predefined drought-response measures and effective dispute resolution. Agreed hydrological thresholds could trigger consultations and contingency measures before shortages become acute. This would help protect downstream water supplies while allowing Ethiopia to plan hydropower generation with greater certainty. Operational flexibility is compatible with legal certainty, provided it functions within agreed and enforceable limits.

Sudan illustrates why these arrangements must work in practice. Roseires Dam lies approximately 115 kilometres downstream of the GERD on the Blue Nile, making its operations sensitive to changes in upstream releases. During the GERD’s initial filling in July 2020, falling river levels disrupted drinking-water pumping stations in Khartoum. Chatham House’s 2023 analysis also reported that a Roseires Dam technician had described media reports as his only source of information about GERD operations in 2021. These accounts expose a basic operational weakness: downstream infrastructure cannot be managed effectively when reliable information about upstream decisions is unavailable. Although the GERD could benefit Sudan through flood moderation and improved agricultural planning, those benefits depend on timely data-sharing and coordination. Sudan’s continuing conflict makes dependable communication and water-management arrangements even more important, as damaged infrastructure and weakened emergency-response capacity can magnify the consequences of sudden changes in supply.

Shared hydrological monitoring, satellite observations, predictive modelling and artificial intelligence can improve drought forecasting, reservoir planning and the identification of emerging risks. Environmental assessments should also account for sediment transport, aquatic ecosystems and river-dependent livelihoods, ensuring that the focus extends beyond electricity generation and annual water volumes. Cairo Water Week 2026 offers an opportunity to connect these technical capabilities with diplomatic engagement and practical negotiations.

Egypt and Sudan require binding guarantees that protect downstream water supplies against both droughts and floods. These must include advance notification of changes in river conditions and planned releases, transparent and continuous data-sharing, coordinated reservoir operations and enforceable procedures for managing periods of severe water stress. In particular, agreed drought-management rules should establish clear hydrological thresholds for adjusting reservoir filling and releases when essential downstream supplies are at risk. The flooding experienced in Sudan in September and October 2025 further demonstrated the consequences of inadequate coordination, with the severity of the flooding attributed to sudden, unannounced changes in GERD releases. Cairo also opposes further unilateral Ethiopian dam projects without prior notification, consultation, comprehensive impact assessments and basin-wide agreement.

Iteru, the ancient Egyptian word for ‘Great River’, has sustained Egyptian civilisation for millennia. Today, its waters flow into a new confluence: Ethiopia’s regional ambitions and Egypt’s imperative to safeguard its water security. The basin’s future will depend on whether its riparian states can move beyond competing positions and establish a durable framework that protects the interests of all, particularly those whose survival depends on the river’s reliable flow. The Great River poses a great test—and meeting it will require great political will.

Nadine Loza is a development strategist, opinion columnist, and Founding Director of the Egypt Diaspora Initiative.

headline: Russia, Iran discuss cooperation between Tehran and EAEU
summary: The Eurasian Economic Union is currently scaling up its engagement with the countries of the Global South, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk said
body_text:
DUSHANBE, October 19. /TASS/. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref discussed cooperation between Tehran and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexey Overchuk said in conclusion of the Russian-Iranian talks in Dushanbe.

"The Eurasian Economic Union is currently scaling up its engagement with the countries of the Global South. As you know, we are expanding our network of free trade agreements, specifically with Iran also. Significant time was dedicated to this topic today as well because a free trade agreement allows us to largely eliminate the problems that might have existed if there was no such agreement," Overchuk said.

The parallel work in this direction is also underway with other nations, the Russian deputy prime minister said. "An interim agreement with Mongolia has come into force, as has one with the United Arab Emirates. Work is also being carried out to bring the agreement with Indonesia into force. In addition, negotiations are underway with India, and consultations have been held with Pakistan. Just last week, we met with the Prime Minister of Thailand [Anutin Charnvirakul], and he also raised the issue of a free trade zone with Thailand," Overchuk noted.

"In other words, we now see our primary goal in expanding opportunities to establish free trade between the Eurasian Economic Union and other nations, primarily, of course, on the Asian continent and in the Global South. This is the task we are currently dealing with," he added.

headline: Russian army now more innovative, adaptable — NATO commander
summary: French Admiral Pierre Vandier mentioned Russia’s advances in unmanned aerial vehicles
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 19. /TASS/. The Russian army has become more innovative and adaptable compared with the beginning of the special military operation in 2022, French Admiral Pierre Vandier, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, said in an interview with Canadian broadcaster CBC.

"They [Russian servicemen] learn, they adapt," he said, adding that the Russian army was no longer the same as it had been in 2022.

In particular, he noted Russia’s advances in unmanned aerial vehicles. According to him, Russia’s adoption of more advanced technologies has significantly reduced the effectiveness of some Ukrainian interception methods.

Against the backdrop of Russia’s successes, the NATO commander said the alliance was falling behind and could find itself unprepared and unable to keep pace with technological innovation on the front lines.

"I disagree with the point where we have a good industrial depth," Vandier said. He also added that he often sees officials "chatting, delaying some important decisions, not committing the money, using some <…> old-fashioned process," which reportedly keeps him up at night.

Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that Russia allegedly plans to attack NATO countries. Russian President Vladimir Putin has described such statements by Western politicians as attempts to intimidate their own populations and justify increased military spending. Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, in turn, has said that the alliance is pursuing a policy of "rampant militarization" and that portraying Russia as a "threat" is being used to justify a decision to raise NATO member states’ defense spending to 5% of gross domestic product.

body_text:
US prosecutors said on Monday that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen accused of hiding a recording device at OpenAI's headquarters “presents an ongoing danger” and should not be released from custody.

In a court filing, the US Justice Department responded to a request from Mr Alfozan's lawyer in California that sought to grant his release amid the continuing investigation, which is expected to culminate in a criminal trial.

“The defendant presents an ongoing danger to the community and a serious risk of flight that no set of release conditions can reasonably mitigate,” Craig Missakian, a lawyer for the US Justice Department wrote.

According to the department's memo in support of continuing the suspect's detention, “a member of the Saudi military booked and paid for” a flight for Mr Alfozan's wife and son several days after he was arrested.

“The day before she left the US, the defendant’s wife told the FBI agents who interviewed her that her US visa was expiring and that she and her son were permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia – and that her husband, the defendant, eventually intended to do the same,” US prosecutors wrote.

Mr Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and former OpenAI employee, was arrested on October 8 over accusations he had hidden a recording device at the company's offices in San Francisco.

Investigators said last week that Mr Alfozan planted the device – a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3, manufactured by a company in China – behind a television in a conference room.

The device has a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and micro-SD storage”, the Justice Department said.

Mr Alfozan started working for the OpenAI product team in July last year. He was fired on the same day of his arrest, the company said.

According to the original criminal complaint previous filed by prosecutors, actions taken by Mr Alfozan indicated he planned to depart the US swiftly.

“Indeed, the defendant, his wife and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) … and defendant has the means and the incentive to flee the US sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested,” the initial filing reads.

Last week, California lawyer William Pernik told The National he was still waiting to see what other evidence the government has against his client and that he plans on presenting all appropriate defences in court.

“Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream,” Mr Pernik said in an email. “These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible and any possible reasons why.”

On Friday, Mr Pernik filed a court request to get Mr Alfozan out of custody on the condition he wears a GPS ankle tag, remains at his home in Millbrae, California and surrenders his passport.

The filing also proposed a “an appearance bond co-signed by sureties from his Bay Area community and supported by the written undertaking of the Consulate General of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia”.

According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Alfozan has lived in California since 2015 and started working at OpenAI as a lead engineer in 2025. Before his years in California, he was an intern at Meta, Microsoft and SAP.

Mr Alfozan received his undergraduate degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2016 and then earned a master's degree in 2025 from the University of California-Berkeley.

According to the Justice Department, he was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications. He is scheduled to appear in court on 19 for a detention hearing.

“If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release,” a press release from the Justice Department read.

OpenAI has faced a barrage of criticism from employees amid allegations it has disregarded the need for regulations when developing AI technology. American AI companies such as OpenAI also face stiff competition from China, as Washington and Beijing vie for dominance in the technology race. Companies have gone to great lengths to protect intellectual property and trade secrets.
