A Japanese spacecraft rocketed towards Mars on Tuesday on an unprecedented quest to explore its mysterious moons and bring back samples.

Five of the world’s space agencies joined forces for the five-year mission that will attempt to land a robotic prospector plus a rover on Phobos, the larger and closer of Mars’ two pint-sized moons.

The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, which is leading the bold sampling effort, launched the spacecraft before dawn from the country's main spaceport on Tanegashima Island. Officials declared success an hour later when the spacecraft separated as planned from the rocket's upper stage. Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet, shaking hands and embracing.

While NASA has successfully landed nine spacecraft on Mars over the past 50 years and China scored a 2021 touchdown, no one has ever ventured onto Phobos or its sidekick Deimos. And no one has managed to fetch samples from Mars, let alone its moons.

If successful, bits of dust, soil and rocks from Phobos will arrive on Earth in 2031.

“There’s a lot of adrenaline and a lot of excitement and a lot of wow,” said NASA astrophysicist Tom Statler, who’s involved with the project.

Read moreFrench, US and Russian astronauts return to Earth after eight months in space

Japan has an edge going in, with two asteroid sample returns already under its cosmic belt.

Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock just 14 miles (22 kilometres) or so across. Examining pieces of it can explain how Mars’ moons – and possibly moons elsewhere – came to be.

Dubbed MMX for Martian Moons Exploration, the $578 million mission features a hefty 5-tonne spacecraft that should reach Mars by late next summer. It will sync up with Phobos’ tight orbit around the red planet, before ejecting the French-German rover that’s named Idefix after the white terrier in the Asterix comics.

No bigger than a microwave oven, Idefix will plop onto Phobos by itself, bouncing for several minutes before coming to a halt in the moon's extraordinarily low gravity.

The four-wheeled rover is designed to right itself if it lands upside down. All bets are off, though, if it sinks into soft soil or gets wedged between rocks, said the French Space Agency’s Julien Baroukh. Once the rover’s solar panels are deployed, the vehicle can no longer right itself, he added, which is why it will move at a glacial 1 millimetre per second (0.04 inches per second).

Read moreNASA finds a 'once in a century' lunar crater, bigger than the Roman Colosseum

Idefix will serve as a “scout for safety,” according to Baroukh, as it prowls around Phobos for 100 days. Japanese flight controllers want to avoid powdery soil and rough terrain when the mothership – a four-legged stationary lander – descends to the surface to gather samples in late 2028 or 2029.

The lander will spend just two hours on Phobos, drilling and vacuuming up at least one-third of an ounce (10 grams) of material, before launching back into space. It will study Deimos during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian neighbourhood in 2030 and hustling back to Earth for a 2031 sample delivery in the Australian desert.

It’s a treacherous undertaking, with wreckage littering the path.

The moons’ names aren’t exactly comforting: Phobos is Greek for fear and Deimos means dread. They’re the twin sons of the god of war Ares – Mars in Roman mythology.

Russia stumbled in all three of its Phobos attempts as well as many other Mars endeavours. In its only other Mars mission, Japan failed to get a spacecraft into orbit around the red planet. Even NASA has had its share of flops in a bid to answer the burning question: Did life ever exist on Mars?

By studying Mars’ moons, scientists hope to learn whether Phobos and Deimos formed in the aftermath of an ancient collision between Mars and a battering space rock. It’s also possible that the moons might be stray asteroids that became ensnared in Mars’ gravity.

Read more'All human emotions': French astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth

Either way, scientists anticipate finding traces of Mars on Phobos, making the samples an irresistible two-for-one that should help demystify planetary and moon formation, and perhaps even the recipe for life. The findings will help shape future Mars missions, including those by astronauts, said NASA’s acting planetary science director Lindsay Hays.

“It is a once-in-a-lifetime chance. We are part of the first sample return mission from the Martian system,” said the German Space Agency's rover chief Markus Grebenstein.

Japan isn’t the only one looking to claim the scientific riches packed into the Martian system’s rocks and dirt. China plans to launch a sample return mission to Mars in 2028, while NASA is still debating how to retrieve the more than 30 sample tubes collected by the Perseverance Mars rover, the new champion for off-Earth driving.

Japan and China could be neck-and-neck in getting samples back from the Martian system. Both are targeting 2031.

Japan is investing $350 million in this mission. NASA is contributing $87 million, the French Space Agency about $68 million, the German Space Agency about $56 million and the European Space Agency some $17 million.

In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, he praised Netanyahu’s leadership and his partnership with Washington, particularly in confronting Iran, warning that the US could be forced to take on the burden itself if Israelis choose another leader.

Netanyahu's religious-nationalist coalition is projected to lose its governing majority, although the opposition may also struggle to form a government, opinion polls show.

"I'm not anti-endorsing him, but I'm not pro-endorsing him, I'm not getting involved in Israeli elections." Vance said.

body_text:
Experts have warned that strong cybersecurity safeguards are needed to protect sensitive information as artificial intelligence plays a growing role in health care and education.

The UAE is expanding AI use across essential services as part of a wider drive to develop the technology. Abu Dhabi’s government digital strategy for 2025 to 2027 is backed by Dh13 billion ($3.54 billion), while the Ministry of Education has developed an AI literacy framework covering kindergarten to Grade 12.

In May, the UAE Cabinet also approved a national policy to advance digital health care and AI, including developing medical systems and preparing healthcare workers to use the technology.

InterviewAbu Dhabi institute brings UAE’s disease prevention and AI expertise to New York

But information such as patient records, personal data and financial details could be at risk when shared with AI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude.

Nisha Sanghani, partner and head of Middle East at Ashurst Perkins Coie Risk Advisory, said the acceleration in the use of AI must be met with significant cybersecurity investments to keep sensitive information safe, and to train people using these tools to avoid breach risks.

“As adoption accelerates, safety, governance and accountability need to advance at the same pace as innovation – particularly where AI may influence decisions about a person’s health, development or future,” said Ms Sanghani.

“In health care and education, the measure of AI success cannot simply be how quickly we adopt it, but whether it delivers better outcomes that people can trust.”

Ms Sanghani said the shift from experiments to everyday services increased the importance of oversight, but that the UAE had an opportunity to demonstrate how AI could be used responsibly on a large scale.

“For organisations operating here in the UAE, the question is moving beyond ‘where can we use AI?’ to ‘where can AI genuinely create better outcomes, and what needs to be true for us to trust it?”

Nalla Karunanithy, chief executive of digital health and e-commerce at Aster DM Healthcare told The National the organisation was using AI to read X-rays alongside radiologists, measure cardiac MRI scans and supports early detection of coronary artery disease.

This helps save time for doctors so “the clinician's time goes towards judgment,” said Mr Karunanithy. “The AI detects, measures or flags; the clinician interprets, decides and signs.”

But as AI becomes more widely used, healthcare providers must control which systems can access medical information and what happens to it afterwards.

Aster stores patient information in the UAE and assesses each AI system before allowing it access, Mr Karunanithy said.

Testing is not done with real patient data and only approved systems receive necessary information.

“Our group AI governance policy prohibits external providers from using patient information to train their models or for any purpose beyond the approved scope,” he said.

UAE healthcare provider NMC Healthcare is centralising information across its 70 centres, said Ahmed Hafez, director of solution engineering for the Middle East, Turkey and Africa at data company Snowflake.

He added that the work was intended to improve understanding of hospital operations and support decisions at the point of care.

Vladislav Tushkanov, research and development group manager at cybersecurity company Kaspersky, told The National at the AI Everything summit in Abu Dhabi that personal data had to be kept safe.

“We need to understand how we educate our workforce, how we make them understand that it's OK to use the internal AI systems to process information, but you cannot send personally identifiable information in the cloud,” he said.

Aster said it had rejected solutions that could not meet its data residency requirements. Staff must use approved enterprise tools, with its AI Centre of Excellence overseeing their assessment and adoption.

Last year, hackers claimed responsibility for a large-scale data breach at American Hospital in Dubai, reportedly seizing 450 million patient records.

The hospital was contacted for comment but had not responded at the time of publication.

However, despite the possible consequences of mistakes, Costi Perricos, Deloitte’s global generative AI leader, said that this should not prevent organisations from using AI.

“You shouldn't turn away just because we need to be more careful about this,” he said.

He added that the Middle East’s access to capital and technology, combined with its willingness to pursue new ideas, raised opportunities to develop the AI sector.

Introducing tools is only one part of the work, Mr Perricos said. Organisations also need to prepare employees for changes to how they did their jobs.

Bikram Mukhi, chief strategy officer at Soika Labs, said human oversight remained critical, particularly in education.

“We live in very interesting times where technology is moving faster than the rate of adoption.”

Users need to understand that the technology is still developing and that new capabilities could bring new risks, he said, adding that governments and regulated businesses are also seeking greater control over the information and infrastructure used by their AI systems.

“AI just can't be just deployed across the board,” said Shadi Hatoum, regional manager for the Middle East and Africa at data platform company Tealium. Different uses require different standards and measures of success, he said.

headline: Kallas says EU plans to challenge Russia, China over Northern Sea Route
summary: According to Kaja Kallas, the EU should work with Canada and the United States, ostensibly to prevent "Russia and China from gaining full control" over the route
body_text:
BRUSSELS, October 20. /TASS/. The European Union intends to counter Russia and China in the Arctic and seek unrestricted access to the Northern Sea Route, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in an interview with The Times.

Earlier, Vladislav Maslennikov, director of the Russian Foreign Ministry’s Department of European Affairs and Russia’s senior Arctic official at the Arctic Council, said the European Union was showing an intention to pursue escalation in the Arctic and was unwilling to stop politicizing cooperation in the High North.

In the interview, the EU foreign policy chief argued that the West must stop Russia and China from moving toward dominance in the Arctic. The Northern Sea Route, which is already actively used by Russia and China, is of particular concern to Brussels. The Times noted that the route allows ships to travel between Asia and Europe one-third faster than the traditional route through the Suez Canal. It is becoming increasingly important amid growing instability in the Middle East.

According to Kallas, the EU should work with Canada and the United States, ostensibly to prevent "Russia and China from gaining full control" over the route. She said EU and NATO countries would seek to ensure that the Northern Sea Route remains open to all ships.

Kallas also confirmed that the European Commission would present its new Arctic strategy on Tuesday, the last update having been made in 2021. The new strategy will include investments in the construction of new icebreakers, the establishment of a military center to monitor Russian activity in the Arctic, and provisions to ease the EU’s existing ban on offshore oil and gas extraction in the Arctic. The European Commission hopes that the prospect of developing offshore oil and gas reserves off Norway will increase investor interest in the region and help alleviate the EU’s energy supply problems.

Bloomberg previously reported that the European Union plans to launch an Arctic surveillance program in 2027. The program is expected to use the EU’s Copernicus and Galileo satellite systems to detect threats on land and at sea.

headline: US midterms: Iran war and cost of living put Trump’s foreign policy under pressure
summary: US foreign policy is playing an outsized role in this year's midterm elections, thanks largely to President Donald Trump's war against Iran and its effect on the cost of living for Americans.Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and Democrats are trying to win back some power on November 3, having spent two years in the political wilderness after a disastrous performance during the 2024 presidential election. A Democratic victory in either chamber would give the opposition greater powers to oppose Mr Trump's agenda, and the ability to launch investigations and call witnesses to testify about action the administration has taken.Recent polling gives the Democrats a more-than 85 per cent chance of winning the House, where they only need to flip a handful of seats.The Senate is a trickier task for Democrats, who need to gain four seats to secure a majority, including at least two in states Mr Trump carried by double digits in 2024.Front and centre of many political debates in the US is the cost of living, particularly petrol prices, which have risen by nearly 50 per cent since Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched their war against Iran on February 28. Diesel, the lifeblood of the trucking industry, has been even harder hit, having risen by about two thirds. Costs for farmers, truckers and businesses have soared, with high prices being passed on to consumers in many instances. "The Republican Party and candidates are being killed by the higher prices," Kristin Diwan a senior resident scholar at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told The National. "To the extent that people blame them on the Iran war, that is also a liability. The war is extremely unpopular and that crosses party lines."Mr Trump has sought to lower prices by allowing Russia to export diesel, something many Americans are queasy about. A survey published this month by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 86 per cent of Americans believed the Iran war had harmed the cost of living, while 68 per cent said it had not been worth fighting.Dina Smeltz, managing director and chairwoman of public opinion and foreign policy at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, said the administration's policies had made the connection between international affairs and household finances more apparent.“By disrupting some of the stability in traditional US foreign policy stances, the Trump administration’s policies seem to have sharpened how Americans link US actions abroad and their daily lives,” she said.The survey also found that 72 per cent believed the conflict had damaged America's relations with its allies. Andrew Payne, research director for Europe, Russia and the Americas at Chatham House, said the elections are an unusual moment when international affairs could influence domestic political outcomes."Foreign policy rarely decides US elections," he wrote in an analysis published on October 15. "But this year, the economy is foreign policy."Polls this month show Mr Trump's approval ratings hitting new lows, with Americans particularly unhappy about the economy and cost of living.An AP-Norc survey shows that 65 per cent of US adults say higher-than-usual prices are the result of Mr Trump’s policies. This is compared to October 2022, under predecessor Joe Biden, when 44 per cent of the public said higher prices were due to presidential policies.And a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Monday found Mr Trump's approval rating at a record low of 31 per cent."Even though foreign policy may not dominate any given race, it is likely to matter at the margins. And in a tight race, that could make all the difference," Mr Payne said.Many Republican candidates are facing uphill battles as they try to distance themselves from some of Mr Trump's policies. He campaigned on a pledge to avoid foreign military entanglements and to lower the cost of living. Instead, he started a new war and inflation has risen more than expected since he took office. How would Democrats handle Iran war?When Mr Trump announced military operations against Iran, he did so without first securing congressional authorisation, leading to a debate about the limits of presidential war powers. Thanks to four Republican representatives voting alongside the Democrats, the House has already voted to constrain Mr Trump's war powers, although the Senate did not follow suit. A Democratic majority in either or both chambers would probably increase friction with the White House over the Iran conflict, which Mr Trump has said will end one way or another immediately after the midterms. If they win, the Democrats are expected to hold a host of hearings, including on the true financial cost of the war and whether the US military was prepared for a new war in the Middle East. Democrats will use those hearings to try to seize an early narrative as voters start looking towards the 2028 presidential election. A Democratic majority in Congress could have broader foreign implications, too. US military assistance to Israel, sanctions and Washington's relationships with governments across the Gulf could all become subjects of deeper congressional scrutiny.The war in Ukraine could also become an issue for Republicans in the midterms, particularly since Mr Trump has waived sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports. The move has been condemned by Republicans and Democrats and a recent YouGov poll of more than 5,500 US adults opposed the agreement. Governments across the Middle East will be wondering about the extent to which Democrats will constrain Mr Trump, and whether the election will fundamentally shift US foreign policy, or just make it harder for the President to get things done."The Democratic Party has shown more scepticism about favourable deals with Saudi Arabia. This will make legislation such as the nuclear agreement [with Riyadh] more difficult to pass through Congress, although probably not beyond Trump's veto power," Ms Diwan said.Still, she noted that Mr Trump is not inclined to defer to Congress, even when he is legally obliged to do so. "I don’t think the defeat in the election will constrain him," she said.
body_text:
US foreign policy is playing an outsized role in this year's midterm elections, thanks largely to President Donald Trump's war against Iran and its effect on the cost of living for Americans.

Republicans control both chambers of Congress, and Democrats are trying to win back some power on November 3, having spent two years in the political wilderness after a disastrous performance during the 2024 presidential election.

A Democratic victory in either chamber would give the opposition greater powers to oppose Mr Trump's agenda, and the ability to launch investigations and call witnesses to testify about action the administration has taken.

Recent polling gives the Democrats a more-than 85 per cent chance of winning the House, where they only need to flip a handful of seats.

The Senate is a trickier task for Democrats, who need to gain four seats to secure a majority, including at least two in states Mr Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

Front and centre of many political debates in the US is the cost of living, particularly petrol prices, which have risen by nearly 50 per cent since Mr Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched their war against Iran on February 28.

Diesel, the lifeblood of the trucking industry, has been even harder hit, having risen by about two thirds. Costs for farmers, truckers and businesses have soared, with high prices being passed on to consumers in many instances.

"The Republican Party and candidates are being killed by the higher prices," Kristin Diwan a senior resident scholar at the Arab Gulf States Institute, told The National. "To the extent that people blame them on the Iran war, that is also a liability. The war is extremely unpopular and that crosses party lines."

Mr Trump has sought to lower prices by allowing Russia to export diesel, something many Americans are queasy about.

A survey published this month by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs found that 86 per cent of Americans believed the Iran war had harmed the cost of living, while 68 per cent said it had not been worth fighting.

Dina Smeltz, managing director and chairwoman of public opinion and foreign policy at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, said the administration's policies had made the connection between international affairs and household finances more apparent.

“By disrupting some of the stability in traditional US foreign policy stances, the Trump administration’s policies seem to have sharpened how Americans link US actions abroad and their daily lives,” she said.

The survey also found that 72 per cent believed the conflict had damaged America's relations with its allies.

Andrew Payne, research director for Europe, Russia and the Americas at Chatham House, said the elections are an unusual moment when international affairs could influence domestic political outcomes.

"Foreign policy rarely decides US elections," he wrote in an analysis published on October 15. "But this year, the economy is foreign policy."

Polls this month show Mr Trump's approval ratings hitting new lows, with Americans particularly unhappy about the economy and cost of living.

An AP-Norc survey shows that 65 per cent of US adults say higher-than-usual prices are the result of Mr Trump’s policies. This is compared to October 2022, under predecessor Joe Biden, when 44 per cent of the public said higher prices were due to presidential policies.

And a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Monday found Mr Trump's approval rating at a record low of 31 per cent.

"Even though foreign policy may not dominate any given race, it is likely to matter at the margins. And in a tight race, that could make all the difference," Mr Payne said.

Many Republican candidates are facing uphill battles as they try to distance themselves from some of Mr Trump's policies. He campaigned on a pledge to avoid foreign military entanglements and to lower the cost of living. Instead, he started a new war and inflation has risen more than expected since he took office.

When Mr Trump announced military operations against Iran, he did so without first securing congressional authorisation, leading to a debate about the limits of presidential war powers. Thanks to four Republican representatives voting alongside the Democrats, the House has already voted to constrain Mr Trump's war powers, although the Senate did not follow suit.

A Democratic majority in either or both chambers would probably increase friction with the White House over the Iran conflict, which Mr Trump has said will end one way or another immediately after the midterms.

If they win, the Democrats are expected to hold a host of hearings, including on the true financial cost of the war and whether the US military was prepared for a new war in the Middle East. Democrats will use those hearings to try to seize an early narrative as voters start looking towards the 2028 presidential election.

A Democratic majority in Congress could have broader foreign implications, too. US military assistance to Israel, sanctions and Washington's relationships with governments across the Gulf could all become subjects of deeper congressional scrutiny.

The war in Ukraine could also become an issue for Republicans in the midterms, particularly since Mr Trump has waived sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports. The move has been condemned by Republicans and Democrats and a recent YouGov poll of more than 5,500 US adults opposed the agreement.

Governments across the Middle East will be wondering about the extent to which Democrats will constrain Mr Trump, and whether the election will fundamentally shift US foreign policy, or just make it harder for the President to get things done.

"The Democratic Party has shown more scepticism about favourable deals with Saudi Arabia. This will make legislation such as the nuclear agreement [with Riyadh] more difficult to pass through Congress, although probably not beyond Trump's veto power," Ms Diwan said.

Still, she noted that Mr Trump is not inclined to defer to Congress, even when he is legally obliged to do so.

"I don’t think the defeat in the election will constrain him," she said.

headline: How to make the most of Abu Dhabi 2029
summary: Twenty-three years ago, Dubai hosted the Annual Meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. These important conversations took place during a pivotal year for the UAE and the wider Middle East. The country’s economic ambitions were being realised and expanded – the launch of Emirates airline being a prime example. A few months earlier, the US-led invasion of Iraq toppled Saddam Hussein, unleashing consequences that were felt across the whole region.Fast forward to today, and although much has changed, some things remain the same. The UAE is still setting itself challenging goals for the future and as the second-largest Arab economy it continues to set an ambitious pace. However, the region is again marked by turmoil as the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel continues, and Yemen re-emerges as a deadly flashpoint. Another echo of 2003 is the news that the World Bank and IMF will hold their meetings in Abu Dhabi in three years’ time.For the UAE, this will be an opportunity to welcome the world’s financial elite to the capital and to help set the agenda over the coming years. It could help change the conversation about how the global economy works and whose interests it serves.Although three years away, the meetings will take place against a backdrop of persistent global economic pressures. Many developing countries face expensive borrowing, unsustainable debt and falling development aid. Climate change and technological disruption also mean that it cannot be "business as usual". Meeting such challenges requires a wide range of perspectives, including those of emerging economies. Abu Dhabi is well placed to encourage that exchange.This is because the UAE’s established position as a trading hub with relationships across emerging markets – plus its engagement with multilateral and minilateral groupings such as Brics – give it connections that span different economic and political systems. At a time when international co-operation is fragmenting, the Emirates can provide a venue where competing interests meet and solutions are explored.There has also been a recent welcome sign of the UAE’s growing contribution to global governance. The election of Ali Alhosani as the first Emirati executive director at the IMF reflects the increasing presence of UAE expertise in key roles. The preparations for 2029 should build on this progress.Abu Dhabi should welcome the world, but it should also challenge itSuch work will require Emirati economists, financiers, researchers and policymakers to tackle questions ranging from sovereign debt and development finance to monetary stability and digital innovation. That expertise will be valuable long after the delegates depart, strengthening the country’s capacity to contribute to international economic policy.Crucially, the meetings' success will be determined by how the voices of smaller economies and indebted nations find a meaningful place alongside those of leading finance ministers and central bank governors. Different political cultures can find a platform in the UAE to be represented in a spirit of constructive debate, without the expectation that everyone must agree.Abu Dhabi should welcome the world, but it should also challenge it. The ultimate measure of success will be whether the conversations held in 2029 produce better co-operation, fairer access to finance and real opportunities for nations seeking a more prosperous future.
body_text:
Twenty-three years ago, Dubai hosted the Annual Meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. These important conversations took place during a pivotal year for the UAE and the wider Middle East. The country’s economic ambitions were being realised and expanded – the launch of Emirates airline being a prime example. A few months earlier, the US-led invasion of Iraq toppled Saddam Hussein, unleashing consequences that were felt across the whole region.

Fast forward to today, and although much has changed, some things remain the same. The UAE is still setting itself challenging goals for the future and as the second-largest Arab economy it continues to set an ambitious pace. However, the region is again marked by turmoil as the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel continues, and Yemen re-emerges as a deadly flashpoint. Another echo of 2003 is the news that the World Bank and IMF will hold their meetings in Abu Dhabi in three years’ time.

For the UAE, this will be an opportunity to welcome the world’s financial elite to the capital and to help set the agenda over the coming years. It could help change the conversation about how the global economy works and whose interests it serves.

Although three years away, the meetings will take place against a backdrop of persistent global economic pressures. Many developing countries face expensive borrowing, unsustainable debt and falling development aid. Climate change and technological disruption also mean that it cannot be "business as usual". Meeting such challenges requires a wide range of perspectives, including those of emerging economies. Abu Dhabi is well placed to encourage that exchange.

This is because the UAE’s established position as a trading hub with relationships across emerging markets – plus its engagement with multilateral and minilateral groupings such as Brics – give it connections that span different economic and political systems. At a time when international co-operation is fragmenting, the Emirates can provide a venue where competing interests meet and solutions are explored.

There has also been a recent welcome sign of the UAE’s growing contribution to global governance. The election of Ali Alhosani as the first Emirati executive director at the IMF reflects the increasing presence of UAE expertise in key roles. The preparations for 2029 should build on this progress.

Such work will require Emirati economists, financiers, researchers and policymakers to tackle questions ranging from sovereign debt and development finance to monetary stability and digital innovation. That expertise will be valuable long after the delegates depart, strengthening the country’s capacity to contribute to international economic policy.

Crucially, the meetings' success will be determined by how the voices of smaller economies and indebted nations find a meaningful place alongside those of leading finance ministers and central bank governors. Different political cultures can find a platform in the UAE to be represented in a spirit of constructive debate, without the expectation that everyone must agree.

Abu Dhabi should welcome the world, but it should also challenge it. The ultimate measure of success will be whether the conversations held in 2029 produce better co-operation, fairer access to finance and real opportunities for nations seeking a more prosperous future.

headline: China strongly condemns Japan's moves over Yasukuni Shrine: spokesperson
summary: China firmly opposes and strongly condemns Japan's negative moves over the Yasukuni Shrine and has lodged serious representations and strong protests with the Japanese side, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Monday.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- China firmly opposes and strongly condemns Japan's negative moves over the Yasukuni Shrine and has lodged serious representations and strong protests with the Japanese side, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Monday.

Mao made the remarks at a regular press conference when asked to comment on Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's ritual and cash offerings to the Yasukuni Shrine on Oct. 17 and 19, as well as recent visits to the shrine by Japanese government officials, Liberal Democratic Party politicians and members of the Diet.

The Yasukuni Shrine is a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarists' war of aggression, Mao said. It honors 14 convicted Class-A war criminals responsible for Japan's aggression.

Japanese leaders and politicians know this fully well but still pay respects at the shrine, which reveals their deep-seated wrong view on historical issues and malicious intention to erase the criminal record of those war criminals, reverse the verdict on aggression and clear the path for remilitarization, Mao added.

This year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials. China once again calls on Japan to recognize history, repent for historical crimes, stop its retrogressive moves on historical issues, and earn the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community through concrete actions, Mao said.

headline: Iran warns UN over Trump, Israel military threats
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's UN envoy warned the Security Council that US and Israeli threats, including possible MOAB use and strikes on all Iranian energy infrastructure, risk grave violations of international law.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's UN envoy warned the Security Council that US and Israeli threats, including possible MOAB use and strikes on all Iranian energy infrastructure, risk grave violations of international law.

Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, warned the UN secretary-general and the Security Council over what the letter called the "arrogant threats" of US President Donald Trump and the Zionist regime.

In the letter to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and the Security Council president, Darzi said the threats are part of US and Zionist regime wars of aggression against Iran that began on June 13, 2025 and Feb. 28, 2026, along with deliberate attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure. He said they risk further serious violations of international law with catastrophic humanitarian consequences and dangers to regional and international peace and security. He warned that responsibility rests with the United States, the Zionist regime and anyone who directly or indirectly supports their aggression and state terrorism.

The letter cited US media reports on Oct. 15, 2026 that the White House and Pentagon had prepared military options including the possible use of the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, known as the "mother of all bombs," against Iran. It said Trump discussed the weapon in a television interview the same day and threatened Iran with further attacks.

It said Israeli war minister Yisrael Katz announced on Oct. 18, 2026 that Israel was ready to attack Iran and that in any new aggression "all energy facilities" would be targeted, with the aim of returning Iran to the "Stone Age." Katz also claimed the United States and Israel had dropped 35,000 bombs on Iran in total and said their military campaign was not over.

The letter said that on the same day, the Zionist regime's prime minister, whom it described as a war criminal under international prosecution, again openly declared his criminal intent to preemptively start another war of aggression against Iran. It said the silence and explicit support of some Security Council members had made him more brazen in pursuing genocidal thinking.

The letter said the threats amount to gross violations of international law, including the threat to use the MOAB against civilian infrastructure and to target all of Iran's energy infrastructure. It said attempts to spread fear among Iran's population or any threat to deliberately destroy critical civilian infrastructure are new instances of gross violations of international humanitarian law with severe and possibly long-term humanitarian and environmental consequences, increasing the responsibility of the United States and the Zionist regime. It said both have repeatedly shown they do not consider themselves bound by any rules of international law, including obligations under the four 1949 Geneva Conventions and customary international humanitarian law.

Iran asked the UN secretary-general and the Security Council to demand that the United States and the Zionist regime immediately end their unlawful threats and fully comply with their obligations under the UN Charter and peremptory norms of international law. It also asked them to explicitly and unambiguously condemn threats to attack Iran, including its critical civilian infrastructure, used as a tool of coercion and intimidation.

Iran further asked the Security Council to take urgent measures within its powers and duties, including holding an emergency meeting to address the threats to regional and international peace and security and to ensure accountability for the United States and the rogue Zionist regime. It asked the Council to guarantee accountability and full compensation for damages caused by wrongful international acts that the United States and the Zionist regime commit against Iran daily.

The letter said the Security Council cannot remain silent in the face of explicit threats of further aggression and destruction of critical civilian infrastructure, warning that inaction would further weaken the Charter and the international legal order on which the UN system is built.

Iran reaffirmed its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter and its determination to take all necessary measures against any source of threat endangering its people, sovereignty, territorial integrity and vital national interests. It said that if the Security Council fails in its responsibilities, Iran will exercise its right of self-defense and give a decisive response in line with international law to protect its supreme national interests.

It said the United States and the Zionist regime will bear full responsibility for the consequences of any further aggression, including the risk of unpredictable and uncontrollable escalation.

Iran requested that the letter be distributed as an official document of the General Assembly and the Security Council.

headline: Top US House Democrats pledge Congressional action to bolster support for Ukraine
summary: 'The United States Congress stands strongly and unequivocally with Ukraine,' lawmakers say after call with Ukraine's leader
body_text:
Three senior House Democrats pledged Monday to pursue legislation to strengthen US support for Ukraine, criticizing President Donald Trump’s approach to Russia and warning that reduced assistance could undermine Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian aggression.

Representatives Gregory W. Meeks, Adam Smith and Jim Himes issued a joint statement following a call between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a bipartisan group of members of Congress.

"The United States Congress stands strongly and unequivocally with Ukraine. Russia's continued campaign of war crimes and its slaughtering of innocent civilians, aided by the Trump Administration’s pro-Putin agenda, demands urgent and forceful action from Congress to reaffirm that support," they said.

The lawmakers argued that Congress should take a more active role in determining US policy toward Ukraine, asserting that the administration’s current approach cannot be relied upon to maintain the level of support Kyiv requires.

“While Donald Trump has made clear that he is abandoning Ukraine in favor of (Russian President Vladimir) Putin, we remain committed to working urgently with Members of Congress on both sides of the aisle to advance legislation to compel the Trump Administration to deliver to Ukraine the security, economic, and intelligence support it needs to defend its people from Putin’s brutal and illegal invasion,” the lawmakers said.

They argued that reducing Ukraine’s capacity to defend itself would not lead to a lasting peace agreement.

“The Trump Administration has shown it cannot be trusted to do the right thing in support of Ukraine,” they said, contending that weakening Kyiv’s defenses would be both morally wrong and contrary to US interests and those of its allies.

"Congress must act and do what this administration refuses to do: Stand up for Ukraine, defend America's interests, and make clear that autocratic aggression will not be rewarded," they said.

headline: China increases LNG imports from Russia by 44.3% to 7.19 mln tons in January-September
summary: Russia ranks second among China’s leading LNG suppliers
body_text:
BEIJING, October 20. /TASS/. China’s imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) increased by 44.3% year over year in January-September, reaching 7.19 mln metric tons, according to data from China’s General Administration of Customs.

According to the statistics, the value of LNG supplies from Russia to China rose by 38.5% to $3.92 bln. Russia ranks second among China’s leading LNG suppliers.

Australia was China’s largest LNG supplier in January-September, although its exports to China declined by 1.1% compared with the same period in 2025 to 15.01 mln metric tons. Malaysia ranked third with 6.2 mln metric tons, up 26.1%.

Qatar followed with 4.88 mln metric tons, down 65.5%, followed by Indonesia with 2.46 mln metric tons, a decline of 22.8%. The United States exported 231,180 metric tons of LNG to China over the nine-month period, down 11%.

In September, China doubled its LNG imports from Russia compared with August to 1.85 mln metric tons. In value terms, supplies increased 2.2-fold to $1.18 bln.

According to official statistics, China increased its LNG imports from Russia by 3.3% in 2024 and by 18.2% in 2025, reaching 9.79 mln metric tons.

The ministry and the Chinese Embassy and Consulates in France are urging Chinese citizens planning to visit the country to remain vigilant, closely monitor local developments and take necessary safety precautions.

headline: Iran, Tajikistan trade rises 50% despite war
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said trade between Iran and Tajikistan has grown 50% in recent months despite the imposed war on Iran.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said trade between Iran and Tajikistan has grown 50% in recent months despite the imposed war on Iran.

Aref made the remarks in a meeting with Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, where he thanked the Tajik government and people for their sympathetic positions toward Iran during the Ramadan war and stressed the need to draw on historical, cultural and linguistic commonalities to advance relations. Aref pointed to the deep civilizational ties between the two countries and said a joint high committee on Persian and ancestral language, literature, culture and civilization could help preserve the shared heritage. Aref said that despite the growth, cooperation capacity far exceeds current levels and that existing opportunities should be used to develop economic and trade ties. He also stressed expanding scientific, technological, cultural and tourism cooperation. Aref voiced Iran's readiness to cooperate with Tajikistan in oil and gas exploration, petrochemical industries and exports of oil and gas products, and welcomed Rahmon's proposal for a South Pars-Afghanistan-Tajikistan energy corridor, describing it as a positive and constructive plan presented to Iran's president. He said Iran is interested in expanding trilateral cooperation with Tajikistan and Afghanistan and that suitable capacities exist. The meeting also stressed exports of Iranian oil products to Tajikistan and Iranian help in connecting the country to the open waters of the Persian Gulf. On the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, Aref said it has an important capacity to link regional security and stability with economic development and greater connectivity among member states, and that this should be used to expand cooperation in trade, transit, energy and infrastructure connectivity. He said Iran and Tajikistan can cooperate more closely within the SCO on transit corridors, border security, counterterrorism, counter-narcotics and Afghanistan developments, and stressed greater coordination on shared regional issues. Aref pointed to the two countries' scientific and technological capacities and said implementing an agreement to launch a joint Iran-Tajikistan technology center could pave the way for joint activities and expanded scientific and technological cooperation. Both sides stressed operationalizing the center. On international cooperation, Aref said the two countries have had good cooperation in international bodies and have supported each other's positions, and that this coordination should be strengthened at regional and international levels. The two sides also stressed preserving Iranian culture and civilization and the shared heritage of Persian speakers, expanding tourism and cultural cooperation, and strengthening scientific and economic ties. headline: President Sheikh Mohamed holds talks with Macron on energy and AI
summary: President Sheikh Mohamed received France's President Emmanuel Macron in Abu Dhabi on Monday. An official reception ceremony was held for Mr Macron, who is in the UAE on an official visit as part of his tour of the Gulf. Mr Macron is seeking to deepen energy and defence ties with Gulf states during a three-day visit that started on Monday with Kuwait and the UAE, as his government struggles with a cost-of-living crisis fuelled by high energy prices.Talks in Abu Dhabi focused on energy, artificial intelligence and the energy crisis caused by the Iran war. As the conflict unfolds, France and other European nations have sought to portray themselves as key allies of Gulf states, including the UAE, despite being able to do little to contain a war to which they are not party.“Key topics included developments in the Middle East and efforts to contain their repercussions on maritime security and global energy supplies,” state news agency Wam reported.Earlier, Mr Macron had a one-on-one meeting with the Emir of Kuwait, Sheikh Meshal, for an hour and a half on Monday. He flew to Kuwait City only hours after a giving solemn televised address to the French nation in which he promised his Gulf tour would help secure energy supplies. In the UAE, the reception was attended by Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohamed, Deputy Chairman of the Presidential Court for Special Affairs, and Sheikh Mohammed bin Hamad, adviser to the UAE President.Defence and AIThis is likely to be one of Mr Macron’s last major Gulf trips before the presidential election in France in six months, at which he is ineligible to run again. The President's joint offer with the UK in April to launch an international maritime coalition to defend ships in the Strait of Hormuz awaits a political agreement between the US and Iran. There were no statements in Kuwait City but a series of agreements focused on defence and AI. The executive vice-president for Airbus sales, Benoit de Saint Exupery, and the executive director of the Kuwait Investment Authority, Sheikh Saud Salem Abdulaziz Al Sabah, signed a partnership that includes the renewal of the Kuwait Airways fleet. The chief executives of industry giants TotalEnergies and Engie will be travelling with Mr Macron, as well as the president of Campus AI, a major technological complex under construction near Paris that benefits from billions in UAE funding. Also present were French Defence Minister Catherine Vautrin, Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure.The visit, which will end in Qatar on Wednesday after a stop in Bahrain, comes despite France's worst civil unrest in years, with more than 2,000 people arrested for torching and ransacking property. In a statement on Sunday night, Mr Macron said he felt “anger” and “shame”. He has vowed that those responsible for looting and destruction will “have to pay”. The government is expected to put forward concrete proposals for young people this week.The UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar have all had energy sites attacked during the US-Iran war, which has also curtailed oil exports through the strait. With Yemen's Houthi rebels now pushing for control of a second strait, the Bab Al Mandeb strait, there are fears the global energy crunch could worsen.“In light of the crisis gripping the Middle East, the President will continue his efforts with regional leaders to promote a return to stability and freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz,” an Elysee Palace source said. “Discussions will also focus on securing and diversifying our energy supplies and their transport routes, with the aim of limiting the impact of the energy crisis on the daily lives of French people.” Mr Macron has made several trips to the UAE as French President. Last December he met Sheikh Mohamed at the Zayed National Museum in Abu Dhabi and spoke to French troops based in the country. Earlier visits included his attendance at the Cop28 climate summit, which took place in Dubai in 2023, and a trip in 2017 to the opening ceremony of Louvre Abu Dhabi. Mr Macron's most recent Middle East trip was a visit to Damascus in July – the first appearance in post-civil-war Syria by a major western leader. For Mr Macron, diplomacy abroad offers an opportunity to project leadership on the international stage. But with unrest escalating at home, keeping the focus on France’s role in the world is becoming more difficult. The question is whether those diplomatic efforts will cut through the growing anger at home.

headline: Russian pipeline gas exports to China up 3.7% in January-September
summary: According to the published statistics, Russia is China’s largest supplier of pipeline gas
body_text:
BEIJING, October 20. /TASS/. China increased imports of Russian pipeline gas by 3.7% in value terms in January-September compared with the same period last year, to $7.57 bln, according to data from China’s General Administration of Customs.

The agency traditionally does not disclose the physical volume of pipeline gas imports. According to the published statistics, Russia is China’s largest supplier of pipeline gas. Turkmenistan ranks second ($6.34 bln, down 2% year-on-year), followed by Myanmar ($1.13 bln, down 4.7%), Kazakhstan ($840.34 mln, down 2.3%), and Uzbekistan ($356.09 mln, down 43.9%).

The value of pipeline gas imported by China from Russia in September was estimated at $1.04 bln, roughly the same as in August.

According to the agency’s statistics, China increased its imports of Russian pipeline gas by 25% in 2024, to $8.03 bln. In 2025, the figure rose by 17.1% to $9.41 bln, while supplies via the Power of Siberia pipeline increased by approximately 25% in volume terms to around 38.8 bln cubic meters.

Following Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to China in late August and early September 2025, the two countries signed an agreement on annual supplies of 106 bln cubic meters of Russian gas to China.

Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, on Monday met Dr Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, India's Minister of External Affairs, in Mumbai for high-level talks as part of a working visit to the country.

The discussions centred on efforts to bolster long-standing ties between the nations, with a focus on further collaboration across the economy, trade, investment, culture and energy.

Sheikh Abdullah emphasised the significance of the UAE's relations with India and set out plans to build on the foundations for growth laid down by their Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (Cepa), which has been in place since 2022.

President Sheikh Mohamed and India's Modi discuss efforts to boost ties in call

The deal – the first signed by the Emirates – pushed bilateral trade beyond $85 billion. The agreement means India is the UAE's largest trading partner, with the UAE becoming India's third-largest trading partner.

India and the UAE enjoy a robust alliance that dates back to the formation of the Emirates. The UAE is now home to about four million Indian citizens, the largest expatriate community in the country.

Sheikh Abdullah said the UAE-India partnership was continuing to gain momentum, helping to reinforce the countries as key drivers of global economic growth.

The two ministers also discussed regional and international developments and spoke of ways of protect peace and security, state news agency Wam reported.

Sheikh Abdullah was welcomed at the start of his visit by Mangal Prabhat Lodha, India's Minister of Skills, Employment, Entrepreneurship and Innovation, and senior officials. Sheikh Abdullah's trip serves to demonstrate the strength of relations between the two countries, which have flourished in recent years.

In May, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi made an official visit to the Emirates, during which he met President Sheikh Mohamed.

Sheikh Mohamed made a working visit to New Delhi in January, where he and Mr Modi pledged to deepen co-operation in sectors including artificial intelligence, the economy and food security, during discussions at the Prime Minister's residence.

Mr Modi made a two-day visit to the UAE in 2024, where he addressed a crowd of 40,000 Indians at Zayed Sports City Stadium. He also spoke at the World Governments Summit in Dubai, before inaugurating the first Hindu temple in Abu Dhabi.

headline: Arada enters Saudi Arabia with $3.8bn Riyadh project

body_text:
UAE developer Arada is launching a Dh14 billion ($3.8 billion) residential project in Riyadh and plans to build 100,000 homes in Saudi Arabia over the next three to five years as it expands in the kingdom, its chief executive has said.

The company will also launch projects in Jeddah and Makkah as the Saudi market opens for foreign investment.

“We have a good pipeline coming, and we will probably announce another project by the end of the year,” Ahmed Alkhoshaibi said. “As a group we plan to have 200,000 homes in the next three to five years, with half of that coming in Saudi Arabia.”

Why international developers are considering projects in Saudi Arabia

Arada is jointly owned by Saudi businessman Prince Khaled bin Alwaleed’s KBW Investments and Sharjah-based Basma Group.

Following the Saudi announcement, Arada’s pipeline is valued at Dh185 billion across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, the UK, Australia and Syria, comprising more than 70,000 homes. It has completed 17,000 homes so far.

Saudi Arabia, the Arab world’s largest economy, has overhauled its property sector, allowing foreigners to buy in designated zones in Riyadh and Jeddah, while introducing “special requirements” for home ownership in Makkah and Madinah from January.

It also introduced land tax rules last year to help free up undeveloped land and spur building activity.

Arada’s debut project will be built in the Al Rimal district in Riyadh's north-eastern growth corridor on a plot covering 2.5 million square metres.

Apart from 3,500 villas and town houses, it will also have a school, retail outlets and a community centre, as well as sporting facilities and green areas. The project is inspired by Arada's Masaar, a Dh8 billion woodland community development in Sharjah.

Units will be sold for between 1,000 and 1,400 Saudi riyals ($267 and $373) per square foot, with construction starting in mid-2027 and completing in five years time, Mr Alkhoshaibi said.

Arada KSA, set up in partnership with Saudi property investor Xtopia, will spearhead its expansion in the kingdom, with Mohammed AlDhabaan, chairman of Xtopia as the new chairman of Arada KSA.

Arada KSA has access to a significant 10 million square metre land bank across Saudi Arabia with a collective value of Dh49 billion, spanning key strategic locations including Riyadh, Jeddah and Makkah, it said in a separate announcement.

Demand for housing in Saudi Arabia is strong as the government pushes to increase home ownership among Saudis. Demand from expatriates following the opening of the sector to foreign buyers is also supporting the market, he said.

“The real demand is by the Saudis who need a home, and this is driven further by the government, [which is] pushing for higher home ownership for the Saudis.”

“The government's initiative, which we're trying to support, is that they want to provide 300,000 homes delivered in the next three years.”

Saudi Arabia has set a target of raising home ownership rates among locals to 70 per cent by 2030 under the Sakani programme – a joint initiative between the Ministry of Housing and the Real Estate Development Fund.

By the end of last year, Saudi citizens owning homes exceeded 66 per cent, with one million beneficiaries of government housing support programmes, the Saudi Press Agency reported in January, citing Minister of Municipalities and Housing Majed Al Hogail.

Saudi Arabia’s property market was mixed in the second quarter, with nationwide residential transaction values contracting by 26.9 per cent year-on-year to 37.67 billion riyals and the total deal count falling 14.2 per cent, according to the latest CBRE report.

The National Residential Price Index, however, grew 2.6 per cent on an annual basis, supported by a 1.1 per cent rise in apartment prices during the quarter.

The Al Rimal project will be funded through a Capital Market Authority-regulated investment structure managed by Al Rajhi Capital, an asset-management firm in the kingdom.

“We have partnered with Al Rajhi, who will provide the fund management and will also provide the funding. So there is obviously certain equity we put in, but [the] majority is through the fund and the bank,” Mr Alkhoshaibi said.

The company is also entering Syria with plans to build a $7 billion “UAE-style” mixed-use real estate project in Damascus in phases over 10 years.

The company's property sales are ranging between Dh400 million and Dh700 million a month despite uncertainty over the Iran war, he added.

“The external factors will have an impact, but it will be mitigated or reduced by delivering a great product in a great location at a reasonable price, and that's what we've been doing.”

She aims to keep the fiscal deficit under 3 per cent of GDP and maintain inflation at 2 per cent "to protect purchasing power and stability".The government also plans to expand the tax base and reform the income tax, raise direct social aid to needy households, reduce food prices and push private investment to two thirds of total national investment. "We ⁠believe that institutions will ​not regain public trust without an effective ​fight ‌against corruption and conflicts of interest," she added.The government faces pressure to address unemployment and demands for better education and health services. ​It will also oversee ⁠the final stages of a $20 billion push to prepare for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is to co-host with ​Portugal and Spain.
body_text:
Morocco's Prime Minister Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri vowed to support the Palestinian cause by pushing for a two-state solution as she presented her government's programme to the parliament.

The country last week swore in its new government, led by its first female prime minister, in a ceremony presided over by King Mohammed VI. Ms El Mansouri kept several former government ministers in their posts, including Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit.

The government formation followed a deal between Ms El Mansouri's centrist Authenticity and Modernity Party, which won the September 23 election, and three other parties. The coalition holds 207 seats in parliament, above the 198 needed for a majority.

On Monday, she presented her government's programme to members of both houses of parliament, outlining a five-year agenda focused on tackling corruption, strengthening the social welfare state, integrating young people into the economy, protecting sovereignty and building a productive economy.

Ms El Mansouri stressed "Morocco’s long-standing position on the Palestinian cause and Jerusalem", as well as her "support for a peaceful settlement based on a two-state solution that would ensure a just and lasting peace".

In September, Israel and Morocco agreed to upgrade their diplomatic ties by elevating missions to full embassies.

Ms El Mansouri also promised to "mobilise international support for Morocco's autonomy proposal" for the Sahara region and to "accelerate economic development in the southern provinces" to strengthen the region's role as "Morocco's gateway to Africa".

On the economy, she said her government aimed for ​average ​annual economic ​growth of 5 per cent from ⁠2027 to 2031, up from an ⁠expected 4.7 per cent this year. She aims to keep the fiscal deficit under 3 per cent of GDP and maintain inflation at 2 per cent "to protect purchasing power and stability".

The government also plans to expand the tax base and reform the income tax, raise direct social aid to needy households, reduce food prices and push private investment to two thirds of total national investment. Public debt is to drop to about 62 per cent of GDP by 2031, she said.

There are plans to improve the efficiency of public enterprises and ​criminalise illicit enrichment and conflicts ‌of interest, Ms El Mansouri said. "We ⁠believe that institutions will ​not regain public trust without an effective ​fight ‌against corruption and conflicts of interest," she added.

The government faces pressure to address unemployment and demands for better education and health services. ​It will also oversee ⁠the final stages of a $20 billion push to prepare for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco is to co-host with ​Portugal and Spain.

body_text:
Cristiano Ronaldo has been given a 30-day suspension and ordered to pay a fine of €255 as punishment for walking out on the national team earlier this month.

The Portuguese Football Federation's (FPF) disciplinary council said it had upheld the charge against the 41-year-old forward in full.

Ronaldo left Portugal's base in ​Copenhagen ⁠before their Uefa Nations ‌League match against Denmark earlier this month, having ​accused head coach Jorge Jesus of twice breaking his word about his role after he was an unused substitute against Norway.

Crunch SPL fixture involving Ronaldo’s Al Nassr postponed

Jesus denied making any agreement with Ronaldo but left the door open for his return following Portugal's 2-1 win.

The disciplinary council found Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) of the federation's disciplinary regulations. Proceedings were opened on October 9.

In a lengthy statement, Ronaldo, 41, later apologised for ⁠failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match ⁠and for leaving his teammates, saying he remained available for selection after serving any punishment arising from the incident.

Ronaldo earns a reported €4 million a week at Saudi Pro League side Al Nassr. The fine imposed on him represents 0.0064% of his weekly salary.

His suspension takes effect from the day of the Denmark match, meaning he has already served 19 days of his ban and will not miss any Portugal matches with the next international window November 12-17.

Portugal face Denmark in the Nations League again on 14 November before travelling to Wales three days later.

FPF president Pedro Proenca has said ​everyone within the federation wanted Ronaldo to return to the national team once the matter was resolved.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances – both men's world records – helping them win Euro 2016 and the two Nations League titles.

headline: Iran, Russia presidents to hold meeting in Moscow

body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran's ambassador to Russia said consultations between Masoud Pezeshkian and Vladimir Putin will continue at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow, calling active diplomacy a sign of strategic change.

Iran's ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, said consultations between Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Russian President Vladimir Putin will continue at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow.

Jalali gave a positive assessment of the results of high-level meetings between the two countries in Tehran and Dushanbe.

He described the "active diplomacy" between Iran and Russia as a sign of the two countries' firm will to shape a "new architecture of international relations."

Jalali said this dynamism is a prelude to accelerating the formation of a multipolar order.

headline: Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after meeting Zelensky in Oslo — Axios reporter
summary: US Presidential Special Envoy intends to discuss with Russian President Vladimir Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners
body_text:
WASHINGTON, October 20. /TASS/. US Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff hopes to visit Russia and meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin after holding talks with Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday, Barak Ravid, a correspondent for Axios and Israel’s Channel 12, said on X, citing sources.

According to the sources, Witkoff is currently flying to Oslo for a meeting with Zelensky scheduled for Tuesday. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, as well as representatives of the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, France, the European Union leadership, and NATO, are expected to take part in the talks.

"The objective is to continue aligning on a comprehensive proposal that can form the basis for renewed negotiations with Russia," Ravid said.

According to one of his sources, Witkoff hopes to visit Russia after Oslo, where he intends to discuss with Putin the proposals developed jointly with Ukraine and European partners. Last week, representatives of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe worked on developing these proposals at the technical level. They include the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 72-year-old US citizen convicted in Russia of fighting on the side of the Ukrainian armed forces.

"President Trump has directed an intensive process to develop a comprehensive peace proposal with Ukraine and Europe, and the next step is to test whether that work can form the basis for serious negotiations with Russia", a US official told Ravid, adding. "These discussions remain fluid, and substantial work remains. President Trump’s objective is clear: to end the killing, bring the war to a close, and establish the conditions for a lasting peace that benefits Ukraine, Russia, Europe, and the United States."

Jared Kushner, a special envoy and son-in-law of the US president, will not accompany Witkoff in person this time because he has the flu. He will participate in the consultations remotely.

On October 1, Putin said Russia would like to end hostilities in Ukraine through a peaceful settlement as soon as possible. Moscow is ready for negotiations but sees no willingness on the part of the Kiev government to engage in talks, the president added.

UK.Institutes unveiled expansion drives, new programmes and plans to attract more learners from across the Emirates and beyond at a flagship education fair in Abu Dhabi on Monday.The number of students enrolled at universities in the UAE reached 218,000 in the 2025/26 academic year, a 15 per cent rise on an annual basis.Hundreds of high-school pupils gathered at Adnec at the 20th annual offer more programmes and to grow our population in Dubai,” he said. “Even in our planning, if it's required that we expand our facility itself, this is something we want to consider.”The Dubai campus will offer new programmes in subjects such as artificial intelligence, engineering, international relations, law and psychology.'Busier than ever'It offers an opportunity for UAE universities aiming to entice more students as they build their academic reputations internationally.The University of Sharjah was ranked best in the UAE for medicine in the US News Best Global Universities Rankings and has also been climbing the ranks of the QS World University Rankings.“Our goal is to be always in the top and to bring students from both outside the country and inside the country,” May Bin Hadda, admissions officer at the University of Sharjah, told The National. The university welcomed more than 5,000 new students at the start of this academic year.Emirates Aviation University reported a similar result, with a high intake this year especially from abroad. A representative said admissions had been busier than ever, with strong interest from around the world. “Dubai’s position as a global aviation hub continues to be a major attraction for international applicants,” they added.Liwa University has also recorded “significant” growth. “Both the Abu Dhabi and Al Ain campuses are packed in all specialisations,” said Adam Al Bahti, integrated marketing manager at Liwa University. “We feel there's a big demand in the market, especially for programmes in AI and in medical and health sciences.”While primarily focused on domestic pupils, Liwa University is hoping to attract more international students in the coming years.Making the gradeUnder the patronage of H.H Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed . . Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research launches the UAE Award for Higher Education pic.twitter.com/BLuhTWYbAZ— UAEGOV (@UAEmediaoffice) July 14, 2026In July, the UAE launched a new higher education award aimed at shining a light on the achievements of the country's best universities and helping to “foster a culture of excellence”.Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, said the UAE Higher Award for Education would support initiatives that “create a sustainable impact” and advance the nation's “readiness for the future”.The UAE has taken significant steps in recent years to raise standards in the higher education sector, which has been reflected by impressive performances in global education league tables.In June, Abu Dhabi's Khalifa University of Science and Technology broke new ground by being the first in the UAE to feature in the top 150 of the QS World University Rankings 2027.The university rose 30 places to 147th, cementing its place as the country's leading institution for the ninth consecutive year.The QS rankings evaluated 8,808 universities across 106 places, with 1,504 seats of learning named in the final list.The university was ranked 12th worldwide for the international make-up of its faculty, reflecting its work in moulding young minds drawn from around the globe.In January, Abu Dhabi University was named among the top 100 for business and economic studies in another global league table, outranking renowned institutions from the US, UK and China. It was placed 81st out of more than 1,000 institutions assessed in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026. The list comprised universities from 91 countries.
body_text:
Leading UAE universities are investing in the future as they seek to capitalise on growing demand for higher education in the country - amid a sharp decline in students heading to the UK.

Institutes unveiled expansion drives, new programmes and plans to attract more learners from across the Emirates and beyond at a flagship education fair in Abu Dhabi on Monday.

The number of students enrolled at universities in the UAE reached 218,000 in the 2025/26 academic year, a 15 per cent rise on an annual basis.

UAE universities must make fundamental changes, says minister

Hundreds of high-school pupils gathered at Adnec at the 20th annual Najah event on Monday, as they prepare to take the next step on their academic journeys.

The continued growth in the UAE higher education landscape comes as the number of people in the Gulf choosing to study in the UK continues to decline.

Student visa application numbers have slumped due to a UK migration clampdown that has restricted visas, as well as concerns over social issues, safety and the quality of education in Britain, experts said.

The number of student visa applications from the UAE has fallen from 638 in 2022 to 257 students in 2025, Home Office statistics showed.

Abu Dhabi University is to launch eight new undergraduate programmes at its Dubai campus – starting next year – to bolster its national presence.

“Dubai has become a hub for international education and we would like to be part of that market,” Bassam Murra, executive director of marketing, enrolment and registration at the university, told The National at the event.

“There is a plan to expand and to offer more programmes and to grow our population in Dubai,” he said. “Even in our planning, if it's required that we expand our facility itself, this is something we want to consider.”

The Dubai campus will offer new programmes in subjects such as artificial intelligence, engineering, international relations, law and psychology.

It offers an opportunity for UAE universities aiming to entice more students as they build their academic reputations internationally.

The University of Sharjah was ranked best in the UAE for medicine in the US News Best Global Universities Rankings and has also been climbing the ranks of the QS World University Rankings.

“Our goal is to be always in the top and to bring students from both outside the country and inside the country,” May Bin Hadda, admissions officer at the University of Sharjah, told The National.

The university welcomed more than 5,000 new students at the start of this academic year.

Emirates Aviation University reported a similar result, with a high intake this year especially from abroad.

A representative said admissions had been busier than ever, with strong interest from around the world. “Dubai’s position as a global aviation hub continues to be a major attraction for international applicants,” they added.

Liwa University has also recorded “significant” growth. “Both the Abu Dhabi and Al Ain campuses are packed in all specialisations,” said Adam Al Bahti, integrated marketing manager at Liwa University. “We feel there's a big demand in the market, especially for programmes in AI and in medical and health sciences.”

While primarily focused on domestic pupils, Liwa University is hoping to attract more international students in the coming years.

In July, the UAE launched a new higher education award aimed at shining a light on the achievements of the country's best universities and helping to “foster a culture of excellence”.

Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs, said the UAE Higher Award for Education would support initiatives that “create a sustainable impact” and advance the nation's “readiness for the future”.

The UAE has taken significant steps in recent years to raise standards in the higher education sector, which has been reflected by impressive performances in global education league tables.

In June, Abu Dhabi's Khalifa University of Science and Technology broke new ground by being the first in the UAE to feature in the top 150 of the QS World University Rankings 2027.

The university rose 30 places to 147th, cementing its place as the country's leading institution for the ninth consecutive year.

The QS rankings evaluated 8,808 universities across 106 places, with 1,504 seats of learning named in the final list.

The university was ranked 12th worldwide for the international make-up of its faculty, reflecting its work in moulding young minds drawn from around the globe.

In January, Abu Dhabi University was named among the top 100 for business and economic studies in another global league table, outranking renowned institutions from the US, UK and China. It was placed 81st out of more than 1,000 institutions assessed in the Times Higher Education World University Rankings 2026. The list comprised universities from 91 countries.
