body_text:
The Abu Dhabi Grand Prix has become one of the UAE's busiest weekends for live music, with entertainment extending beyond the after-race concerts to clubs, restaurants and parties across Yas Island.

This year's programme begins a day before the Formula One action with a selection of stirring arias from Italian opera star Andrea Bocelli. From Thursday to Sunday, pop and rock headliners will take over the newly renamed Etihad Live, while international DJs perform at glitzy venues overlooking Yas Marina Circuit. Here is what to expect.

Andrea Bocelli at Etihad Arena

Abu Dhabi F1 concerts: 65 artists who have performed, from Beyonce to Katy Perry

The Italian tenor will open the inaugural Yasalam Classics series with his Romanza 30th Anniversary World Tour, accompanied by the Armenian State Symphony Orchestra.

The concert revisits the 1997 album that helped establish him internationally, with songs including Con te Partiro and Vivo Per Lei. Bocelli, who has sold more than 90 million records, also performed at this year's World Cup opening ceremony in Mexico.

Doors open 6pm; tickets from Dh295

Lewis Capaldi and Zara Larsson at Etihad Live

Scottish singer Lewis Capaldi returns less than a year after his sold-out Saadiyat Nights concert in January. Best known for Someone You Loved and Before You Go, he is back on the road after a two-year break, with newer songs including Survive and Something in the Heavens.

Swedish pop star Zara Larsson will perform a separate set featuring Lush Life and Never Forget You, alongside material from her fifth album, Midnight Sun, which earned her first Grammy nomination.

Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders

Alex Warren at Etihad Live

The American singer-songwriter makes his UAE debut after the international success of his hit single Ordinary.

Warren first found an audience through social media before moving into music, drawing on grief, family and relationships in songs including Carry You Home and Burning Down.

His second album, Wildchild, arrived in August. A second artist joining Friday’s bill will be announced soon.

Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders

Anyma at Yas Gateway Park

The Italian-American DJ, also known as Matteo Milleri, brings his melodic techno and elaborate visual production to the official Grand Prix after-party.

One half of electronic duo Tale of Us, he has developed a solo show featuring towering digital figures and science-fiction imagery. The production has taken him to the Sphere in Las Vegas and Egypt's Pyramids of Giza.

Doors open 9pm; show starts 10.30pm; tickets from Dh495

Shimza at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit

The South African DJ brings his percussion-heavy Afro-tech sound to the trackside hospitality venue. Known for lengthy hypnotic sets, Shimza has performed at clubs and festivals across Europe and Africa and collaborated with fellow South African artist Black Coffee, who takes to the stage here on Sunday.

Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250

Mont Rouge and Moojo at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi

Swiss duo Mont Rouge will share the Friday bill with French DJ Moojo at Bagatelle's rooftop pop-up. Mont Rouge are known for their Afro-house version of Voyage Voyage, recorded with Francis Mercier and Coco, and their remix of Axwell and Sebastian Ingrosso's More Than You Know.

Imagine Dragons at Etihad Live

The American pop-rock band return three years after selling out Etihad Arena in 2023. Fronted by Dan Reynolds, their concerts feature heavy percussion and singalong hits including Radioactive, Believer and Thunder.

Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders

CamelPhat at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit

British electronic duo CamelPhat, comprising Dave Whelan and Mike Di Scala, broke through with the Grammy-nominated 2017 single Cola, recorded with Elderbrook. They followed it with club favourites including Panic Room with Au/Ra and Breathe with Cristoph and Jem Cooke, combining house, techno and melodic electronic music.

Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250

Gordo at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi

Formerly known as Carnage, the Nicaraguan-American DJ plays a blend of hip-hop-infused house music and contributed to Drake's 2022 album Honestly, Nevermind. He followed it with his solo album Diamante in 2024, featuring collaborations with Drake and Maluma.

The Chainsmokers and The Script at Etihad Live

American electronic duo The Chainsmokers and Irish band The Script will close the after-race concert series with separate sets.

The Chainsmokers, comprising Andrew Taggart and Alex Pall, are behind hits including Closer and Something Just Like This with Coldplay. Their latest work includes Love Is Kind, a five-track EP released in May with Swedish singer Oaks.

The Script return with their eighth album, The User's Guide to Being Human, released in August. Led by Danny O'Donoghue, the band are known for Breakeven and Hall of Fame.

Access to the concert is exclusive to Abu Dhabi Grand Prix ticket holders

Black Coffee at 16/360, Yas Marina Circuit

The Grammy-winning South African DJ will bring his blend of deep house, African percussion and soulful vocals to the trackside venue. His 2021 album Subconsciously, featuring Pharrell Williams and David Guetta, won Best Dance/Electronic Music Album at the 2022 Grammy Awards. He is also a regular fixture on Ibiza's club circuit.

Access exclusive to selected 16/360 Grand Prix hospitality ticket holders; packages from Dh1,250

Carl Cox at Bagatelle, W Abu Dhabi

A pioneer of Britain's acid-house movement, Cox has spent more than four decades playing house and techno, including a 15-year residency at Space Ibiza. His interest in racing extends beyond the DJ booth through Carl Cox Motorsport, which he founded in 2013.

headline: UN to slash food assistance to over 700,000 Palestinians
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – The UN Food Agency has cut humanitarian aid to more than 700,000 Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank amid funding shortages.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – The UN Food Agency has cut humanitarian aid to more than 700,000 Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank amid funding shortages.

The United Nations World Food Program (WFP) has been forced to slash food assistance to 500,000 Palestinians in the Gaza Strip and 200,000 in the occupied West Bank because of a severe funding shortage, with the agency’s acting head warning that life in Gaza remains “absolutely brutal.”

Carl Skau, acting executive director of the WFP, said the number of people receiving assistance in Gaza was reduced this month from 1.6 million to 1.1 million, while in the West Bank the figure was halved from 400,000 to 200,000.

He urged the international community to provide $450 million immediately so the agency can restore the cut assistance and sustain hot meals and food parcels across both territories for the next six months.

According to the WFP, food rations in Gaza have been cut by half. Families that continue to receive support will get only one food parcel instead of two and a smaller bag of wheat flour.

The number of hot meals distributed daily has fallen from 250,000 to 150,000, with those living in hard-to-reach areas near the so-called “yellow line" now receiving a meal only every other day. Cash assistance has also been reduced for 75,000 families.

The agency said it can still support bakeries covering roughly one-third of Gaza’s bread needs, provide nutrition assistance to about 300,000 women and children, and deliver school snacks to 200,000 children, but these efforts remain under severe strain.

Skau, who had just visited both territories, told UN correspondents in a briefing from occupied Jerusalem that UN teams recorded about 50 attacks per day in Gaza over the past week, according to Press TV.

While the agency has managed to push back on famine since the October 2025 ceasefire, an estimated 1.4 million people, 67 percent of Gaza’s population, continue to face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, with around 200,000 requiring immediate food aid to prevent death from hunger.

He stressed that the cuts are not the result of declining needs or lack of access, but solely of insufficient funding; the WFP received less than half as much money for its Palestine operations in 2026 as in previous years.

The situation is compounded by Israeli restrictions. Last week the Israeli military temporarily halted the entry of commercial goods, including food, into Gaza. While it later said it would resume coordinating commercial trucks, it warned that any reports of merchants paying taxes to Palestinian authorities could lead to the revocation of their licenses.

Skau noted that people closest to the yellow line, along with the sick, mothers, and children at risk of malnutrition, will be prioritized under the reduced program.

In the occupied West Bank, Skau said escalating attacks by Israeli settlers have transformed a long-standing human-rights and protection crisis into a hunger crisis. Food insecurity has more than doubled in the last three years, and nearly one million Palestinians now require food assistance.

body_text:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel, as the two sides discuss the possibility of resuming major combat operations against Iran, American media reported.

The meeting, which was also attended by Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz, took place on Monday evening at Ovda Airbase in southern Israel, Axios said in a report quoting two sources. The visit was also reported by CNN, which quoted two sources and a US official. The Pentagon has declined to comment on Mr Hegseth’s movements.

He was also reported to have met US troops at the base and later posted an image of himself visiting personnel from US Central Command, which oversees American military operations across the Middle East.

Trump endorses Netanyahu for Israeli election

The visit came days before Israel’s October 27 election and a day after US President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Mr Netanyahu, calling him a “great warrior prime minister”.

In footage shared by Mr Netanyahu on Tuesday, the Israeli leader thanked Mr Trump for his support and described him as “by far, the greatest friend Israel has ever had and will have in the White House”.

“Donald, we have a job to finish. You said it, and we’ll finish it together,” Mr Netanyahu said.

Mr Netanyahu said the alliance between the two countries had demonstrated that they could achieve significant results together. He added there was scope to expand the Abraham Accords, which established relations between Israel and several Arab states during Mr Trump’s first term in office.

Mr Netanyahu also praised the US President for confronting what he described as the greatest danger facing Americans – an Iran armed with nuclear weapons. “We won’t let it happen,” he said.

Mr Trump’s endorsement appeared to reflect shared strategic interests over Iran, as well as the political importance of maintaining a close relationship with Mr Netanyahu during a volatile period for the region. The backing also gives Mr Netanyahu a boost before the election as he seeks to present his relationship with Washington as an asset for Israeli security. Mr Trump, meanwhile, has an interest in maintaining a reliable Israeli partner as his administration pursues its regional objectives.

But the two leaders have reportedly differed over the direction of the Iran war and the prospects for diplomatic initiatives in Gaza and elsewhere. There has been no public confirmation of a specific agreement linking the endorsement to Israeli policy concessions or renewed military action.

headline: Iran nabs 39 mercenaries engaged in insecurity, vandalization
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence has announced 39 key figures and individuals involved in creating insecurity and destroying public and private property in Qazvin Province have been identified and arrested.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence has announced 39 key figures and individuals involved in creating insecurity and destroying public and private property in Qazvin Province have been identified and arrested.

In a statement released on Monday, the ministry said that in operations against mercenaries of the American-Zionist enemy aimed at disrupting public security and destroying public and private property, 39 individuals organized into eight separate teams were identified and arrested in Qazvin Province.

According to the statement, during last winter's unrest, these mercenaries damaged property and created insecurity for citizens by destroying and setting fire to people's homes, large stores, banks, public and private vehicles, and gas stations, and by looting state property and shops.

headline: Houthi attack kills 58 at Yemen government training camp, governor says
summary: Oct 19 (Reuters) - Fifty-eight people were killed and more than 200 were injuredafter an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, Governor Awad al-Wazir said, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground. Wazir also said that 14 other people remained missing after the Houthi bombardment of the Al-Alam camp.
body_text:
Oct 19 (Reuters) - Fifty-eight people were killed and more than 200 were injuredafter an attack on Monday by the Iran-aligned Houthis on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province, Governor Awad al-Wazir said, as fighting in the impoverished country intensifies.

Video verified by Reuters from Shabwa province showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered across the ground. Wazir also said that 14 other people remained missing after the Houthi bombardment of the Al-Alam camp.

The Houthis and the internationally recognised government, which is backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have been trading attacks since the group advanced in September towards territory near theBab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the mouth of the Red Sea.

Local authority sources who spoke on condition of anonymity said the Houthis had launched three ballistic missiles at security forces during a training exercise.

Shabwa, an energy-rich province in south-central coastal Yemen overlooking the Gulf of Aden, is home to the Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen's largest industrial investment.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had targeted the training camp, which he said was run by Saudi forces. The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Government forces this month began a campaign aimed at recapturing areas controlled by the Houthis, recovering ground near the strait, while the groupbesieges Taiz, the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in the southern highland area of Yemen.

The conflict in Yemen has become another front line in the widerUS-Israeli war on Iran as the Houthis have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter, targetingRiyadh's international airport and the state oil companySaudi Aramco.

War broke out in Yemen in 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa, driving the government south. A Saudi-led military intervention the following year led to a bloody stalemate until the sides agreed a 2022 truce that held until this year.

Yemen is already one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, with aid agencies warning of rapidly deteriorating conditions there.

(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari; Additional reporting by Reyam Mukhashaff and Catherine Cartier; Writing by Menna Alaa El-Din and Nayera Abdallah; Editing by Kevin Liffey, Saad Sayeed and Hugh Lawson)

headline: S. Korea to withdraw some embassy staff from Ukraine amid N.K. POW dispute
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic p...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic personnel from Ukraine amid an ongoing dispute over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul and persistent threats of airstrikes across the country, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.

The decision came as Ukraine has yet to take "positive steps" to resolve the diplomatic dispute over Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the transfer of the North Korean POWs to Seoul, while continued airstrike threats have made it difficult to ensure the safety of diplomatic personnel, ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said at a regular press briefing.

Despite the partial withdrawal, South Korea will maintain necessary diplomatic communications with Ukraine, led by its charge d'affaires, Park said, adding that all consular personnel will remain in the country to continue efforts to protect South Korean nationals.

Earlier this month, the government recalled its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, as Seoul voiced regret over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's public disclosure of the North Korean POW transfer.

The two soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia in the Kursk region and arrived in South Korea in mid-September, according to officials here.

Seoul has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine over Zelenskyy's disclosure, as well as a statement from his office denying that there had been an agreement to keep the matter confidential.

headline: 'I'm postponing my marriage': Gazans put lives on hold as they await Israeli election
summary: In Gaza, the fate of a destroyed supermarket, a family home and even a marriage now rest on an election in Israel in which the Palestinians affected have no vote. Munir Abu Wadi, the owner of the supermarket in Jabalia refugee camp, is waiting to see whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netaynahu is removed from power on October 27 before he sets about rebuilding his business. “Many people have put their lives on hold until after the Israeli election,” Mr Abu Wadi told The National. “I am one of them.” Across Gaza, residents say decisions about family life and business have been postponed in anticipation of the vote. After years of war and displacement, some see the Israeli election as a possible turning point, while acknowledging a change of government may bring no immediate improvement.“We always believe tomorrow might be better than today,” Mr Abu Wadi said. “That is why many people in Gaza are pinning their hopes on the Israeli election and hoping Netanyahu government will fall.”The next Israeli government will address issues such as Gaza's reconstruction, the disarmament of Hamas and an international backlash against settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israelis is electing the 120 members of the Knesset rather than voting directly for a prime minister, meaning the final outcome will depend on coalition negotiations. Mr Netanyahu is vying for power with an opposition from which former general Gadi Eisenkot has emerged as a leading challenger. Recent opinion polls have placed Mr Eisenkot’s Yashar party ahead of or close to Mr Netanyahu’s Likud. The Israeli opposition generally supports a tough approach to Palestine and Iran, finding fault with Mr Netanyahu for his handling of the conflicts rather than calling for concessions. Still, for people in Gaza, the election has become a date around which to plan deeply personal decisions. Marriage delayedMustafa Mousa, 30, has resisted months of pressure from his family to become engaged. His house is still stand-in but he says marriage requires more than money and accommodation.“It also requires stability and peace of mind,” he told The National. Mr Mousa said he would wait until the election results offered a clear picture of Gaza’s future before deciding whether to proceed with an engagement.“The election may not affect us immediately but its outcome will certainly influence the detail of daily life,” he said. “I told my family that I would postpone my engagement and marriage until after the Israeli election.”The calculation is different but equally consequential for Mahdi Abu Al Qumsan, 52, whose home was demolished during an Israeli military incursion into Gaza city. Mr Abu Al Qumsan and his family of 11 are now living as displaced people in Deir Al Balah. He hopes to clear the rubble from his home in Gaza city, and construct a basic shelter using plastic sheets, tarpaulin, wood and stones.He has started gathering materials but has yet to start the work. “To be honest, I’m not placing much hope in the Israel election,” he said. “But if Netanyahu loses, the outcome could be slightly better for us. It might encourage me to carry out what I have been planning.”Mr Abu Al Qumsan wants his family to live again in the neighbourhood where his children were born and where he himself grow up. But with materials scarce and Gaza’s political future unclear, even the construction of a makeshift shelter feels like a gamble.Israeli influencePolitical analyst Emad Omar said many Palestinians had come to view the election as exceptional because of the influence Israeli policy has over almost every part of their social and economic lives.A Netanyahu victory would deepen fears that the policies and military approach of his right-wing coalition would continue, Mr Omar said. If he fails to form another government, Palestinians might hope for greater engagement with the Palestinian Authority and progress on Gaza‘s recovery and reconstruction.But a change in leadership would not necessarily mean a fundamental shift in Israel policy towards Gaza. Mr Eisenkot, who served in Mr Netanyahu‘s war cabinet before resigning in 2024 over what he said was a lack of strategy, has broadly supported Israeli military operations while criticising the government’s management of the war.Mr Abu Wadi also acknowledged that Netanyahu’s successor might not offer Palestinians a substantiality different future. “It’s true that whoever comes next may not be any better,” he said. “But people are eager, at the very least, to see the departure of those whose names have become associated with the war.”Polling suggests Mr Netanyahu faces a serious challenge but uncertainty over possible coalitions mean the outcome remains difficult to predict. Few analysts would count out Mr Netanyahu, who has led Israel for all but an 18-month period since 2009. There are also fears in Gaza about what could happen before polling day. Mr Omar said Palestinians were concerned that a new military escalation might alter the course of the campaign. “No one can predict what Netanyahu is thinking,” he said. “There is concern that he may initiate a major event before the vote in an attempt to change the political landscape or shift opinion polls in his favour.”

In Gaza, the fate of a destroyed supermarket, a family home and even a marriage now rest on an election in Israel in which the Palestinians affected have no vote.

Munir Abu Wadi, the owner of the supermarket in Jabalia refugee camp, is waiting to see whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netaynahu is removed from power on October 27 before he sets about rebuilding his business.

“Many people have put their lives on hold until after the Israeli election,” Mr Abu Wadi told The National. “I am one of them.”

Across Gaza, residents say decisions about family life and business have been postponed in anticipation of the vote. After years of war and displacement, some see the Israeli election as a possible turning point, while acknowledging a change of government may bring no immediate improvement.

“We always believe tomorrow might be better than today,” Mr Abu Wadi said. “That is why many people in Gaza are pinning their hopes on the Israeli election and hoping Netanyahu government will fall.”

The next Israeli government will address issues such as Gaza's reconstruction, the disarmament of Hamas and an international backlash against settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israelis is electing the 120 members of the Knesset rather than voting directly for a prime minister, meaning the final outcome will depend on coalition negotiations.

Mr Netanyahu is vying for power with an opposition from which former general Gadi Eisenkot has emerged as a leading challenger. Recent opinion polls have placed Mr Eisenkot’s Yashar party ahead of or close to Mr Netanyahu’s Likud.

The Israeli opposition generally supports a tough approach to Palestine and Iran, finding fault with Mr Netanyahu for his handling of the conflicts rather than calling for concessions. Still, for people in Gaza, the election has become a date around which to plan deeply personal decisions.

Mustafa Mousa, 30, has resisted months of pressure from his family to become engaged. His house is still stand-in but he says marriage requires more than money and accommodation.

“It also requires stability and peace of mind,” he told The National. Mr Mousa said he would wait until the election results offered a clear picture of Gaza’s future before deciding whether to proceed with an engagement.

“The election may not affect us immediately but its outcome will certainly influence the detail of daily life,” he said. “I told my family that I would postpone my engagement and marriage until after the Israeli election.”

The calculation is different but equally consequential for Mahdi Abu Al Qumsan, 52, whose home was demolished during an Israeli military incursion into Gaza city.

Mr Abu Al Qumsan and his family of 11 are now living as displaced people in Deir Al Balah. He hopes to clear the rubble from his home in Gaza city, and construct a basic shelter using plastic sheets, tarpaulin, wood and stones.

He has started gathering materials but has yet to start the work. “To be honest, I’m not placing much hope in the Israel election,” he said. “But if Netanyahu loses, the outcome could be slightly better for us. It might encourage me to carry out what I have been planning.”

Mr Abu Al Qumsan wants his family to live again in the neighbourhood where his children were born and where he himself grow up. But with materials scarce and Gaza’s political future unclear, even the construction of a makeshift shelter feels like a gamble.

Political analyst Emad Omar said many Palestinians had come to view the election as exceptional because of the influence Israeli policy has over almost every part of their social and economic lives.

A Netanyahu victory would deepen fears that the policies and military approach of his right-wing coalition would continue, Mr Omar said. If he fails to form another government, Palestinians might hope for greater engagement with the Palestinian Authority and progress on Gaza‘s recovery and reconstruction.

But a change in leadership would not necessarily mean a fundamental shift in Israel policy towards Gaza. Mr Eisenkot, who served in Mr Netanyahu‘s war cabinet before resigning in 2024 over what he said was a lack of strategy, has broadly supported Israeli military operations while criticising the government’s management of the war.

Mr Abu Wadi also acknowledged that Netanyahu’s successor might not offer Palestinians a substantiality different future. “It’s true that whoever comes next may not be any better,” he said. “But people are eager, at the very least, to see the departure of those whose names have become associated with the war.”

Polling suggests Mr Netanyahu faces a serious challenge but uncertainty over possible coalitions mean the outcome remains difficult to predict. Few analysts would count out Mr Netanyahu, who has led Israel for all but an 18-month period since 2009.

There are also fears in Gaza about what could happen before polling day. Mr Omar said Palestinians were concerned that a new military escalation might alter the course of the campaign. “No one can predict what Netanyahu is thinking,” he said. “There is concern that he may initiate a major event before the vote in an attempt to change the political landscape or shift opinion polls in his favour.”

headline: Hegseth meets Netanyahu in unannounced visit to Israel, source says
summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, a person familiar with the matter said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran.The person did not say what the two men discussed during the meeting, first reported by Axios. The Pentagon declined to comment. The Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, a person familiar with the matter said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran.

The person did not say what the two men discussed during the meeting, first reported by Axios. The Pentagon declined to comment. The Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.

Israel's Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel's southern desert.

Hegseth's visit comes amid rising tensions in the Middle East war as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

It also came a day after US President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel, the country's first ballot since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.

US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he's not seeking to attack Iran before the October 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before US midterm elections in November.

(Reporting by Emily Rose, Maayan Lubell, Phil Stewart, Christian Martinez and Ismail Shakil; Editing by Rami Ayyub)

headline: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 20, 2026
summary: [allAfrica]
body_text:
Rwandan Govt Critic Found Beheaded in Uganda

Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old former Rwandan army sergeant major and outspoken critic of President Paul Kagame, has been found beheaded on the outskirts of Kampala, Uganda. Kabera had fled Rwanda and sought asylum in Uganda, citing political persecution. He later gained a following through his YouTube channel, which featured criticism of Kagame's government. Ugandan police said his head had not been recovered. His widow expressed fears for her family's safety. The opposition Rwanda National Congress has called for a thorough investigation, as his killing renews concerns about the safety of Rwandan dissidents living in exile. Other critics of Kagame have been killed abroad, including former intelligence chief Patrick Karegeya, who was found dead in Johannesburg in 2014.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

UN Condemns Deadly Drone Strikes Across Sudan

Drone strikes across Sudan have killed and injured civilians, including children, as fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces continues to intensify. The attacks injured at least 19 people at a market in Abyei and targeted locations in Khartoum, including an area near the airport. The strikes reportedly killed at least 19 people, including 10 children, across several states. The United Nations condemned the attacks and raised concerns over the targeting of humanitarian workers, with 25 Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers reportedly killed since the conflict began in April 2023. An estimated 20 million people face acute hunger, with famine risks rising in parts of Darfur and Greater Kordofan. Despite the insecurity, aid agencies continue delivering assistance, including restoring water supplies to thousands of people in Central Darfur. Sudan's humanitarian response plan remains just over 43% funded.

Zimbabwe's Ruling Party to Discipline MPs Who Missed Constitutional Amendment Vote

Zimbabwe's ruling Zanu-PF party plans to discipline Members of Parliament who failed to attend crucial parliamentary sittings during consideration of Constitutional Amendment No. 3 Bill. Party legal secretary Ziyambi Ziyambi announced the sanctions at the party's annual conference in Chinhoyi, naming several senior officials and deputy ministers among those who did not vote, although their reasons remain unclear. The disciplinary move comes as Zanu-PF advances resolutions to postpone its next elective congress from 2027 to 2029, potentially keeping President Emmerson Mnangagwa at the helm until 2030. Provincial leaders defended resolutions supporting his continued leadership and called for constitutional alignment and greater national self-sufficiency in areas such as medicine, technology and industrial production.

Thabo Mbeki Denies Blocking Apartheid-Era Prosecutions at Inquiry Commission

Former South African president Thabo Mbeki has denied allegations that he held secret meetings with former apartheid-era military and police generals to prevent prosecutions for human rights abuses. Testifying before the Khampepe Commission of Inquiry into delayed Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) prosecutions, Mbeki said the generals approached him in 1996 seeking a meeting with the ANC over amnesty applications. He argued that former president FW de Klerk and his cabinet should also apply. Mbeki said the ANC subsequently pursued collective amnesty for some of its leaders to encourage the apartheid leadership to do the same, but the courts later overturned the decision. He maintained that his administration never directed the National Prosecuting Authority to halt or suppress investigations, arguing that prosecutions were the NPA's responsibility. He also defended his 2003 parliamentary speech and later arrangements involving pardon requests, saying these aimed to encourage truth-telling rather than grant blanket immunity to those responsible for apartheid-era crimes.

Nigeria and Rwanda Seek to Strengthen Defence Cooperation

Nigeria's Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has arrived in Rwanda for a five-day official visit aimed at strengthening defence and security cooperation between the two countries. Shaibu held talks in Kigali with Rwanda Defence Force Chief of Defence Staff General Mubarakh Muganga and Army Chief of Staff Major General Vincent Nyakarundi. The discussions focused on implementing existing agreements covering military training, exchanges of instructional and logistics personnel, and other shared security concerns. Shaibu and his delegation also visited the Kigali Genocide Memorial to pay tribute to victims of the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi and toured the Campaign Against Genocide Museum to learn about the genocide and Rwanda's post-conflict recovery. The visit is scheduled to conclude on October 23.

headline: Alberta voters decide whether to take a step toward separating from Canada
summary: In Canada, the oil-rich province of Alberta votes in a referendum that could set it on a path toward separation, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warns of threats to Canadian unity.
body_text:
In Canada, the oil-rich province of Alberta votes in a referendum that could set it on a path toward separation, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warns of threats to Canadian unity.

Voters in Alberta, Canada, are deciding today whether to take the first step toward a referendum on separating from the rest of the country. Reporter Sheena Rossiter joins us from Edmonton, which is the capital of Alberta. Hi there.

SHEENA ROSSITER, BYLINE: Hello.

SUMMERS: So, Sheena, this vote's a nonbinding referendum. Explain for us a bit more what people in Alberta are voting on today.

ROSSITER: Well, essentially, it's a vote on whether to have another referendum. There are 10 questions covering everything from immigration and provincial services to Alberta's constitutional status. Question 10 is the key one. Voters choose between keeping Alberta in Canada or starting the process towards a separation referendum. If Option 2 wins, it could pave the way for a vote on separation, much like Brexit in the U.K.

SUMMERS: And these separatist sentiments there, how long have they been brewing in Alberta?

ROSSITER: These grievances go back decades. Some people I spoke with at the Alberta independence rally have been separatists for 25 years, like Cory Morgan. He is the founder of Pathway to Independence, a third-party advertising group advocating for an independent Alberta.

CORY MORGAN: Even if we don't get over the line on Monday, I would hope that some people understand something large is brewing here. And if we don't get some change, it's going to continue to grow.

ROSSITER: Separatist sentiment really grew during COVID, with frustration spilling onto the streets during the 2022 trucker convoy in Ottawa. Now, the premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, called for a referendum but wants Alberta to stay in Canada. And Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, is making the same case, saying, quote, "Canada is stronger together."

SUMMERS: What's really at the heart of this, though?

ROSSITER: Well, Alberta is a major oil-producing province. It's the wealthiest province in the Canadian Confederation, and some residents feel that they contribute more to Canada than they get back. They want to keep more of that money in Alberta. But a government-commissioned report from the University of Calgary estimates that Alberta separating from Canada could cost up to $170 billion Canadian over five years. Thomas Lukaszuk, founder of Forever Canadian, a pro-unity group campaigning against Alberta separation, points to Quebec's 1995 referendum as a warning about the potential economic fallout.

THOMAS LUKASZUK: Several hundred thousand Canadians moved out of the province of Quebec and moved to other provinces. And till today, the province of Quebec hasn't recovered economically from that.

SUMMERS: How soon will we know the results?

ROSSITER: Well, Elections Alberta says unofficial results are expected within 48 hours of polls closing. There's also a legal challenge over Indigenous rights, with the province appealing a court ruling that First Nations weren't properly consulted. And whatever the result, Alberta's place in Canada is likely to remain a major issue heading into next year's provincial election.

SUMMERS: Sheena Rossiter, reporting from Edmonton, Alberta, thanks much.

headline: Cui Zhe wins China's first gold, Guo Lingling sets world record at Asian Para Games
summary: Cui Zhe claimed China's first gold medal and Guo Lingling set a world record in para powerlifting on the opening day of the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- Cui Zhe claimed China's first gold medal and Guo Lingling set a world record in para powerlifting on the opening day of the 5th Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

Cui won the women's 41kg title with three successful lifts, including a third-attempt 120kg that surpassed her personal best of 119kg set at the Paris Paralympics. The victory extended her gold-medal streak to five consecutive Asian Para Games.

Guo won the women's 45kg event with a world-record lift of 126kg. She said she is confident of competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Paralympics if her health and form allow. Chen Liuxun took bronze in the men's 49kg category, China's first medal of the Games.

China's swimmers collected 14 gold, 12 silver and 6 bronze medals, breaking multiple Games records and sweeping the podium in several events. In wheelchair fencing, China won all four golds on offer, with Zhong Saichun and Qin Benjun winning the men's foil individual A and B titles, and Gu Haiyan and Kang Su taking the two women's titles. Li Huiling and Wang Xiaomei won the women's C4-5 1,000m time trial and C1-3 3,000m individual pursuit in track cycling, respectively.

In athletics, He Shanshan won the women's 1,500m T11 title in a Games-record 4:41.19, and Mi Na took gold in the women's discus throw F37/F38. China's women's wheelchair basketball team beat Laos 109-20, the women's sitting volleyball team defeated Iran 3-0, and the goalball teams beat Japan 1-0 in the women's event and South Korea 9-4 in the men's event.

headline: Death toll from gold mine landslide in Colombia rises to 14
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – The death toll from a landslide that struck an informal gold mine Monday in a rural area of the municipality of Santa Barbara de Iscuande, in Colombia's southwestern department of Narino, has risen to 14, local officials said.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – The death toll from a landslide that struck an informal gold mine Monday in a rural area of the municipality of Santa Barbara de Iscuande, in Colombia's southwestern department of Narino, has risen to 14, local officials said.

"The death toll stands at 14, unfortunately. Thirteen people are already in the town center of Iscuande, while one was taken to Guapi," said Gabriel Ocana, administrative director of the disaster risk management at the Narino governor's office.

The landslide, which also left seven people injured, occurred Monday morning after heavy rains, reports said, according to Xinhua news agency.

Informal and unregulated mining is common in rural parts of Colombia. In August, a similar mining accident killed 13 workers and wounded seven in the town of Policarpa, also in Narino.

Colombia's National Mining Agency (ANM) said its technical team had been delayed in reaching the site because of access difficulties and public order conditions in the area.

"The ANM maintains its technical and operational readiness to support the emergency response once necessary security conditions are in place for rescue teams to enter," it said.

headline: (LEAD) S. Korea to withdraw some embassy staff from Ukraine amid N.K. POW dispute
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic p...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS more details throughout, additional photo)By Oh Seok-min

SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic personnel from Ukraine amid an ongoing dispute over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul and persistent threats of airstrikes across the country, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.

The decision came as Ukraine has not taken "positive steps" to resolve the diplomatic dispute over Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the transfer of the North Korean POWs to Seoul, ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said at a regular press briefing.

Park also cited continued Russian airstrikes as another reason for the decision, saying they have made it difficult to ensure the safety of diplomatic personnel.

Despite the partial withdrawal, South Korea will maintain necessary diplomatic communications with Ukraine through its charge d'affaires, while all consular personnel will remain in the country to continue efforts to protect South Korean nationals there, the ministry said.

Earlier this month, the government recalled its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, in protest of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's public disclosure of the transfer, as well as a statement from his office denying that there had been an agreement to keep the matter confidential.

Seoul has demanded an official explanation and apology from Ukraine over the disclosure, but Kyiv has yet to formally respond to the demand.

"We had conveyed our position to Ukraine through various channels. But Ukraine had taken no positive steps despite those efforts," Park said, calling for "sincere and positive steps" in response to Seoul's previous requests.

Noting that the two countries remain in communication, the spokesperson said Seoul's goal was to "seek an amicable resolution through close consultations with the Ukrainian side."

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun has said the two nations had agreed from the outset to keep the matter confidential to protect the soldiers and their families, who remain in North Korea. He also said Ukraine had initially requested that the matter not be made public.

Cho said he had personally received a message from Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha that included an apology but fell short of Seoul's expectations.

The two soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia in the Kursk region and arrived in South Korea in mid-September, according to officials here.

The ministry said the South Korean Embassy in Ukraine will continue measures to ensure the safety of South Koreans in Ukraine by providing safety updates and offering assistance to those wishing to evacuate.

"We will coordinate with the embassy to find the safest and most effective means of assisting South Koreans who wish to evacuate," Park said.

Russian aerial attacks have continued across Ukraine. On Monday, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in overnight attacks, damaging energy infrastructure and leaving more than 500,000 households without power, according to foreign media reports.

headline: French riots hold a warning for British reformers
summary: For someone in the UK, the riots in France are all too familiar. The sight of mostly young, masked, hooded people kicking in shopfronts, rampaging and looting shelves, and attacks on the police and emergency services – they occur with regular frequency across the Channel.French authorities admitted they lost control in certain major flashpoints in cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon. The following day they were locked in crisis talks with online reseller sites, including Vinted, over tools to crackdown on a sudden flood of items from looted premises. On Tuesday, prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said localised curfews had stemmed the tide of protest overnight. No one, though, is under any illusion that what we witnessed in Paris could not spread to other major cities in Europe. In 2011 the UK experienced similar scenes and there have been repeated, sporadic flare-ups since then. This summer in London, gangs of youths trashed supermarkets and stores. At weekends, mobs descend periodically on a selected target, drawn by social media, then proceed to force their entry, threaten staff and customers and ransack the contents. It would not take much to spark something bigger and broader, as France is experiencing. The powder keg is waiting to be lit.The French rioting arose from a student campaign against poor state schooling. Others joined in, venting their anger at the rising cost of living.In Spain, Portugal and Italy, there have been mass demonstrations at increased rents and foreign investment funds buying up property. In Albania, there were marches against the government, focusing on corruption, absence of jobs and declining education standards.In all these places, the pattern is familiar, of peaceful opposition soon giving way to violent uprising and thuggishness. Always, the young are to the fore.It cannot be coincidence that in France, between 1.4 million and 1.5 million people aged 18-29 are classified as "Neets" – not in education, employment or training. In the UK, the term is officially used for 18-24s, where the total is one million and climbing. The percentages of Neets in both countries and in the EU are similar: 13 per cent in France and the UK, 11 per cent in the EU. That is an awful lot of young folks with nothing to do, little to deter them, no money, few prospects and a disregard for officialdom that has ignored them.Those are nationwide figures. In some locations, in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, the proportion of Neets is far higher. It should not be a surprise, then, that the outlets they hit are typically designer and clothing outlets. They want what the rest are having.Alan Milburn, the former Labour Health Secretary who has written a landmark report in the UK highlighting the depth of the growing crisis, calls it a "youth detachment" problem. Mr Milburn says that 60 per cent of the UK Neets have never had any form of job.UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned of the "economic catastrophe and moral failure" facing society. He said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system that prioritises the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and policies of previous governments have all contributed to the bulging Neets bubble.Mr Burnham is pushing for his administration, as he puts it, to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".Writing in The Times, he said: "Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point." He is following up with plans aimed at giving thousands of young people job opportunities.Mr Burnham quotes the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, showing that of the one million Neets, about 39 per cent are unemployed while the remaining 61 per cent are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work.There are 331,000 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits, almost double the level in 2016. The UK government will spend £353 billion ($469.59 billion) on welfare next year, just under half of which will go on the state pension; while the remainder is absorbed by benefits such as health, disability and unemployment payments. Mr Burnham wrote that this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".
body_text:
For someone in the UK, the riots in France are all too familiar. The sight of mostly young, masked, hooded people kicking in shopfronts, rampaging and looting shelves, and attacks on the police and emergency services – they occur with regular frequency across the Channel.

French authorities admitted they lost control in certain major flashpoints in cities such as Paris, Marseille and Lyon. The following day they were locked in crisis talks with online reseller sites, including Vinted, over tools to crackdown on a sudden flood of items from looted premises. On Tuesday, prime minister Sebastien Lecornu said localised curfews had stemmed the tide of protest overnight.

No one, though, is under any illusion that what we witnessed in Paris could not spread to other major cities in Europe. In 2011 the UK experienced similar scenes and there have been repeated, sporadic flare-ups since then. This summer in London, gangs of youths trashed supermarkets and stores. At weekends, mobs descend periodically on a selected target, drawn by social media, then proceed to force their entry, threaten staff and customers and ransack the contents. It would not take much to spark something bigger and broader, as France is experiencing. The powder keg is waiting to be lit.

With 'hope again' Labour must flesh out its change in direction

The French rioting arose from a student campaign against poor state schooling. Others joined in, venting their anger at the rising cost of living.

In Spain, Portugal and Italy, there have been mass demonstrations at increased rents and foreign investment funds buying up property. In Albania, there were marches against the government, focusing on corruption, absence of jobs and declining education standards.

In all these places, the pattern is familiar, of peaceful opposition soon giving way to violent uprising and thuggishness. Always, the young are to the fore.

It cannot be coincidence that in France, between 1.4 million and 1.5 million people aged 18-29 are classified as "Neets" – not in education, employment or training. In the UK, the term is officially used for 18-24s, where the total is one million and climbing. The percentages of Neets in both countries and in the EU are similar: 13 per cent in France and the UK, 11 per cent in the EU. That is an awful lot of young folks with nothing to do, little to deter them, no money, few prospects and a disregard for officialdom that has ignored them.

Those are nationwide figures. In some locations, in the most disadvantaged neighbourhoods, the proportion of Neets is far higher. It should not be a surprise, then, that the outlets they hit are typically designer and clothing outlets. They want what the rest are having.

Alan Milburn, the former Labour Health Secretary who has written a landmark report in the UK highlighting the depth of the growing crisis, calls it a "youth detachment" problem. Mr Milburn says that 60 per cent of the UK Neets have never had any form of job.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned of the "economic catastrophe and moral failure" facing society. He said two years of Covid lockdowns, social media that erodes "confidence and sense of belonging", an education system that prioritises the "university route", job markets with "too few opportunities" and policies of previous governments have all contributed to the bulging Neets bubble.

Mr Burnham is pushing for his administration, as he puts it, to "invest in the success of our young people" rather than "pay for failure through the benefits system".

Writing in The Times, he said: "Benefits will become the backstop, not the starting point." He is following up with plans aimed at giving thousands of young people job opportunities.

Mr Burnham quotes the latest data from the Office for National Statistics, showing that of the one million Neets, about 39 per cent are unemployed while the remaining 61 per cent are economically inactive, meaning they are not seeking work.

There are 331,000 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits, almost double the level in 2016.

The UK government will spend £353 billion ($469.59 billion) on welfare next year, just under half of which will go on the state pension; while the remainder is absorbed by benefits such as health, disability and unemployment payments. Mr Burnham wrote that this reflected a "generation being denied its chance to get on in life".

body_text:
(ATTN: RECASTS lead; UPDATES with latest details throughout)

SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korean shares plunged by nearly 4 percent Tuesday, as investors attempted to cash in recent gains in major chip shares amid persistent concerns over the artificial intelligence (AI) value chain. The Korean won was trading higher against the U.S. dollar.

The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 215.27 points, or 3.73 percent, to 5,552.74 after declining as low as 5,493.24.

The index opened 0.6 percent lower and extended its losses amid deepening woes over AI-related sectors as well as escalating protests in France, which sharply reduced appetite for risky assets.

The KOSPI had risen for two consecutive sessions after a sharp sell-off fueled by concerns over AI-related investments. It had plunged by around 21 percent over seven trading sessions from Oct. 6 through Thursday.

Overnight, U.S. stocks ended mixed as technology shares rebounded from their steepest weekly drop since June.

"Concerns over credit risks and profitability surrounding AI investment have yet to be fully resolved, limiting the sustainability of the rebound," said Lee Kyoung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities. "Profit-taking emerged following the previous session's gains, sending the market back into negative territory."

Trade volume was light at 259.75 million shares worth 16 trillion won (US$12.97 billion), with decliners far outnumbering advancers 771 to 117.

Foreigners and institutions sold a net 535.4 billion won and 1 trillion won, respectively, while individuals bought a net 900 billion won.

Market heavyweights fell across the board, led by a sharp sell-off in technology shares.

Market bellwether Samsung Electronics fell 2.98 percent to close at 211,500 won, while rival chipmaker SK hynix declined 4.23 percent to 1.22 million won, heading for its lowest close since April.

SK Square, the parent firm of SK hynix, dipped 5 percent to 741,000 won, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics, an electronics component affiliate of Samsung Electronics, went down 1.28 percent to 1.16 million won.

The Korean won was quoted at 1,328.1 won against the U.S. dollar as of 3:30 p.m., up 2.2 won from the previous stock trading session's close.

headline: Hiring in the UAE rebounds in third quarter despite uncertainty fuelled by Middle East conflict
summary: Hiring in the UAE rebounded in the third quarter of the year to 4 per cent, the highest across the Gulf, as business demand recovers, a report has found.After hiring in the country dropped by 4 per cent in the second quarter, demand recovered from the mid-year slowdown and by September new export business was growing at its fastest pace in almost two years, Cooper Fitch said its third quarter employment index. Companies remain cautious about the year ahead, the report added.Across the Gulf, hiring returned to growth in the third quarter, rising 2 per cent following a 3 per cent decline in the previous quarter. In Saudi Arabia, recruitment rose 1.5 per cent, while Oman recorded 0.5 per cent growth. Hiring, however, fell by 1 per cent in Qatar, 2 per cent in Kuwait and 2 per cent in Bahrain. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has had a significant impact on regional economies, with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting oil-exporting countries. The International Monetary Fund, in a report this month, projected the UAE's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, as long as shipping routes normalise and the strait reopens.The fund also expects Saudi Arabia's economy to contract 3.3 per cent this year, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. body_text:
Hiring in the UAE rebounded in the third quarter of the year to 4 per cent, the highest across the Gulf, as business demand recovers, a report has found.

After hiring in the country dropped by 4 per cent in the second quarter, demand recovered from the mid-year slowdown and by September new export business was growing at its fastest pace in almost two years, Cooper Fitch said its third quarter employment index.

Companies remain cautious about the year ahead, the report added.

Data ExplainedWhat happens to jobs if AI gets very good, very fast?

Across the Gulf, hiring returned to growth in the third quarter, rising 2 per cent following a 3 per cent decline in the previous quarter. In Saudi Arabia, recruitment rose 1.5 per cent, while Oman recorded 0.5 per cent growth. Hiring, however, fell by 1 per cent in Qatar, 2 per cent in Kuwait and 2 per cent in Bahrain.

The Iran war, which began on February 28, has had a significant impact on regional economies, with the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz affecting oil-exporting countries.

The International Monetary Fund, in a report this month, projected the UAE's economy to contract by 3.9 per cent this year before rebounding at a 7.7 per cent growth rate in 2027, as long as shipping routes normalise and the strait reopens.

The fund also expects Saudi Arabia's economy to contract 3.3 per cent this year, while Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are forecast to see double-digit contractions of 11.3 per cent, 16.7 per cent and 15.6 per cent, respectively, in 2026. Oman is the only Gulf member to see positive economic growth in 2026 at 4.1 per cent.

However, all the six states are anticipated to post growth in 2027, the IMF said.

The contraction in Gulf hiring "lasted a single quarter and the market is now back within the modest growth range seen through 2025", Cooper Fitch said. "Growth extended across a wider range of functions than in the previous quarter, with paused mandates resuming in sectors such as energy."

Hiring in energy recorded the sharpest increase at 7 per cent across the Gulf in the July-September period. Mandates stalled during the regional tensions returned steadily as conditions eased, the report said.

"Clients resumed searches where they left off. In the UAE, growth came from across the energy market, including nuclear and renewables," it added.

The delivery of Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 pipeline also supported the sector's growth. "Project directors, commissioning specialists and contracts leaders remained difficult to secure. Candidates with scarce technical skills continued to receive multiple offers, keeping the market firmly in their favour," the report added.

Hiring in finance grew 5 per cent, strategy rose 6 per cent – its first increase of 2026, while real estate and software employment was up 4 per cent.

Recruitment in sales and marketing rose 3 per cent in the third quarter, "reflecting cautious confidence rather than a broad hiring rebound", while human resources grew 2 per cent, the report said.

However, hiring in banking declined 4 per cent, while investment management fell by 5 per cent "after a strong run of hiring earlier in the year, driven by regional platform expansion and fund activity".

While hiring picked up in the third quarter, it remained selective, Cooper Fitch said. "Clients focused on advancing active searches and securing specialist capability rather than broad expansion, and several markets and parts of financial services saw lower activity," it said.

Looking ahead to the fourth quarter, it remains to be seen whether the improvement can be sustained.

"Business demand has provided a firmer base, but costs remain elevated and visibility on trade and shipping is still limited," the report said. "Competition for scarce specialist talent has also intensified, adding pressure on employers seeking to secure critical capability."

headline: EU unveils strategy to bolster Arctic presence amid pressure from Russia and the US
summary: The European Union unveils its new "strategy for the Arctic" on Tuesday, aiming to step up its presence in the far north as melting ice opens new maritime routes, and tensions with Russia and the United States increasingly put the region in the geopolitical spotlight.
body_text:
The European Union unveils its new "strategy for the Arctic" on Tuesday, aiming to step up its presence in the far north as melting ice opens new maritime routes, and tensions with Russia and the United States increasingly put the region in the geopolitical spotlight.

Issued on: 20/10/2026 - 03:35Modified: 20/10/2026 - 08:34

The European Union (EU) is to unveil plans to bolster its footholdin the Arctic onTuesday, as it grapples with pressure from Russia and the United States in the key strategic region.

From critical raw materials to icebreakers and undersea cables, the bloc wants to up its presence in the geopolitical battleground, according to a draft of its new "strategy for the Arctic" seen by AFP.

"The new reality in the Arctic requires Europe to be a strong and reliable partner. That is precisely what we aim to achieve with our new strategy," said Jozef Sikela, the EU's head of international partnerships.

"It addresses the region's most pressing challenges, from accelerating climate change to growing security and geopolitical tensions, and sets out how Europe should respond."

Competition is on the rise in the Arctic as global warming causes sea ice to melt. Countries such as Russia, China and the United States have been ramping up activity – racing to claim natural resources and new maritime routes.

Read moreLeaders urge EU to expand Arctic presence amid Russia 'threat'

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

With three Arctic nations among its 27 members – Denmark, Finland and Sweden – the EU has skin in the game.

And US President Donald Trump's repeated threats to bring Greenland – a vast, autonomous Danish territory – under US control have rattled Europe.

Given that what happens in the far north also has repercussions further south, the strategy, which is to be presented by the EU chief Ursula von der Leyen, aims to set out a common EU approach to the region.

The draft seen by AFP stresses the need for cooperation with "like-minded" non-EU nations, such as Canada, Britain and Norway; and envisages a regular summit of "Northern Neighbourhood" partners.

Only recently a key ally in the region, the United States is listed among those who could participate, but the country is otherwise more noticeable for its absence from the remainder of the document.

While Trump's tone has cooled since the beginning of the year – eventually leading to the signing of a security deal with Greenland and Denmark – many in Europe remain wary.

The United States is named only a handful of times in the 20-page paper, compared with almost two dozen mentions for Canada.

Some of the initiatives listed in the strategy seemingly aim to cut dependencies on Washington.

Watch moreTrump’s obsession with Greenland: The real reasons behind his threats

According to the draft, Brussels is planning a "sovereign and secure" submarine cable to connect Greenland with the EU's mainland as part of a broader "Pan-Arctic" cable project – also linking Canada, Japan and South Korea.

The bloc is also working to provide satellite connectivity in the Arctic through satellite constellation project IRIS², which aims to rival Elon Musk's Starlink.

How to counter an aggressive Russia is also top of mind, with the document pointing to hybrid threats such as "drone incursions" and the sabotage of undersea cables.

The strategy envisages better data-sharing to monitor Moscow's so-called "shadow fleet" of sanctions-busting oil tankers.

And it stresses the importance of boosting Europe's icebreaker fleet, saying Brussels will develop options for joint procurement, pooling and sharing of polar vessels with allies.

Investments in renewable energy and critical raw material projects are also foreseen, among a series of other plans.

headline: Alberta voters reject a move toward independence in referendum backing Canadian unity
summary: Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Carney's push for national unity.(Image credit: Ty O'Neil)
body_text:
A voting location in Wainwright, Alberta, is seen on Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Ty O'Neil/AP hide caption

EDMONTON, Alberta — Voters in Canada's oil-rich Alberta province overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada, with early referendum results Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney's push for national unity amid U.S. President Donald Trump's trade war and annexation threats.

With more than 1 million votes counted, 77% supported remaining in Canada, while 23% backed beginning a process toward separation, according to unofficial results from Elections Alberta.

The referendum wasn't a direct vote on independence. Approval would have set Alberta on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada.

"Albertans made a clear choice," Carney said. "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other. Above all, Albertans chose Canada."

Carney said that the result would allow Canadians to move forward together and accelerate efforts to diversify trade, develop major infrastructure projects and make Canada a global energy powerhouse, with Alberta at its center.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney signs an autograph as he attends a national unity rally in Red Deer, Alberta, Friday Oct. 16, 2026. John Ulan/The Canadian Press via AP hide caption

Alberta's separatists, however, saw a silver lining.

"We don't have the final results. I think the numbers are going to fluctuate, but it is fair to say that at least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better," said Keith Wilson, a leader of the separatist movement.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith welcomed the early results, saying they showed widespread support for remaining in Canada.

"Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," Smith posted on social media.

Smith, who called the referendum amid pressure from separatists within her governing United Conservative Party, or UCP, despite opposing independence, said that she would address the province Tuesday evening about the results and Alberta's future.

"We are a solid country that's united from coast to coast to coast," Thomas Lukaszuk, a former Alberta deputy premier who led the Forever Canadian campaign against separation, told supporters.

Results were delayed after late openings forced more than 100 polling stations to extend voting hours Monday.

Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, is cowboy country and a conservative stronghold whose political culture has long had more in common with the American West than much of Canada. Resentment toward Canada's federal government in Ottawa runs deep, but hasn't traditionally translated into widespread support for independence.

Despite the proposal's apparent failure, separatist leaders have said they turned a fringe cause into a movement that won't disappear.

Carney earlier urged Albertans to deliver a decisive vote for unity.

"Vote like Canada's future depends on it, because it does," he told a rally on Friday in Edmonton, where he grew up.

Separatist parties traditionally attracted only 1% or 2% of the vote, former Premier Jason Kenney said. Anger over COVID-19 restrictions helped mobilize activists who later embraced the separatist movement, he said.

Trump's trade war and threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state have helped Carney rally support in Alberta, where Liberal prime ministers have historically been unpopular.

Separatist advocate Jeff Rath said that he would be thrilled if 30% of Albertans voted to begin the separation process. He wants Smith ousted as UCP leader and said that the party could splinter, potentially creating a new pro-independence party.

Dustin Degenhardt, a Wainwright voter, said that Albertans have long been mistreated by Canada's federal government.

"Alberta has essentially been treated as, you know, a colony," he said after voting Monday. "They want to take and take and take from us, and not return anything."

Political signs are posted on a property's fence in Wainwright, Alberta, Canada, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. Ty O'Neil/AP hide caption

Taylor MacIsaac, another Wainwright voter, backed separation.

"I think it'll be good for Alberta to separate personally, as a very conservative individual that grew up in rural Alberta," she said.

Dave Malka, 59, of Edmonton, criticized spending money on a "referendum on a referendum" rather than healthcare.

With Trump threatening Canada, Malka said, "It seems to be happening at the absolute worst time when we should be united; instead we're fighting among ourselves."

Jake Graham, 35, of Calgary, attended a Carney rally wearing maple leaf pants and a Canada hockey jacket. He hopes that the vote ends the debate.

"I hope this squashes this for a long time to come and that it's clear and decisive, that these grumblings disappear for a while and we can be a united Canada," he said.

headline: Alberta votes to remain part of Canada in victory for PM Carney
summary: Voters in oil-rich Alberta overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on separation, with early results on Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity amid US President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats.
body_text:
Voters in oil-rich Alberta overwhelmingly backed remaining in Canada in the province's first-ever referendum on separation, with early results on Tuesday delivering a boost to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for national unity amid US President Donald Trump’s trade war and annexation threats.

Issued on: 19/10/2026 - 16:45Modified: 20/10/2026 - 10:07

Canada's province of Alberta rejected a plan to hold a binding independence referendum, results showed Tuesday, a setback for separatists backed by allies of US President Donald Trump.

Public broadcaster CBC and leading private network CTV projected a comfortable victory for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76 percent support for national unity with more than a third of ballots counted.

Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the result and said Albertans had made a "clear choice" in favour of unity.

"They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other," he said in a statement on X.

Carney had campaigned for national stability as the country faced Trump's trade war and annexation threats.

A sombre mood took over the restaurant in the provincial capital Edmonton where a leading separatist group watched the returns.

Jeffrey Rath, a top leader of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project, told reporters his push for an independent Alberta will "absolutely" continue, despite the result from Monday's vote.

"We've learned a lot of lessons from this fight," he said.

Separatist supporter Jour Dain said he was "disappointed in (his) fellow Albertans."

"Honestly, if this continues down this path of remaining in Canada, I'm just going to move," the 40-year-old said, expressing a desire to live in the United States.

At the federalist election night party in Edmonton before the results were announced, a band warmed up ahead of an anticipated positive result.

"It was amazing to see the enthusiasm and resolve among Canadians," said Thomas Lukaszuk, who heads Forever Canadian, the group that campaigned across the province for national unity.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, a conservative, said she voted against independence but called the referendum to settle an issue that has divided the province.

She has said a win for the federalists would close the secession question.

Alberta has the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, and much of the separatist momentum has been driven by anger over oil industry management.

Smith has blamed Carney's predecessor Justin Trudeau for igniting the separatist fire, accusing him of trying to crush oil production to advance his pro-climate agenda.

Alberta's independence push has also drawn sustained interest from Trump allies.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Alberta a "natural partner" for the United States. Elon Musk, the world's richest person and a top Trump supporter, posted on X this month that Alberta "should separate."

Separatist leaders also held meetings at the US State Department and received advice from Republican political operatives.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has worked to improve relations between the province and Ottawa since taking office last year.

He has partnered with Smith on advancing a new pipeline to export more Alberta bitumen overseas, a project considered a nonstarter during Trudeau's tenure.

Alberta Prosperity Project leader Mitch Sylvestre told AFP earlier Monday that Carney had "threatened" the province in the closing days of the campaign.

Carney's message was "voting against Canada is dangerous," Sylvestre said, calling that "very unreasonable."

Haley Erdegard, a 44-year-old who voted in Edmonton, voiced discomfort with the idea advanced by some separatists that Alberta is forced to share too much of its oil revenue with the rest of Canada.

"I think we probably need to put some more work towards cooperation before making rash decisions about trying to start our own country," she told AFP.

headline: SCO must go beyond condemning US-Israel aggression: Iran VP
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) –Iran's First Vice President Mohammadreza Aref has said Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) must move beyond merely condemning US-Israeli aggression and sanctions imposed against Iran, and also strengthen its economic power.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) –Iran's First Vice President Mohammadreza Aref has said Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) must move beyond merely condemning US-Israeli aggression and sanctions imposed against Iran, and also strengthen its economic power.

Speaking at the meeting of Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO)’s Prime Ministers, held in Tajik capital of Dushanbe, the vice president emphasized the economic consequences of the US unilateral measures taken against the independent states.

In the beginning, Aref thanked the government and people of Tajikistan for hosting the meeting and praised the SCO secretary-general and his colleagues for facilitating the gathering.

A sustainable response to shared economic threats cannot be limited merely to condemning them; rather, Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) members must strengthen their own economic capacities., he opined.

Aref presented Iran’s proposals for accelerating the establishment of an independent development bank, forming an energy consortium, expanding trade using national currencies, and developing transit corridors.

He cited the deaths of more than 157 schoolchildren children in Minab Elementary School during the US-Israeli military aggression waged against Iran on February 28, stating that education is a fundamental human right.

Aref said the United States and Israel violated the international law, the UN Charter and international humanitarian law during their February 28 military aggression waged against Iran.

The vice president went on to say that attacks killed the Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei and schoolchildren on the first day, as well as numerous other innocent civilians, and targeted residential, educational, and medical facilities and infrastructure.

He added that Iran’s Armed Forces and united people inflicted a heavy defeat on the aggressors.

The Iranian vice president also expressed appreciation for the SCO and its member states for condemning the aggressors and armed attacks, highlighting the need to hold those responsible accountable.

He said it was encouraging to see cultural and humanitarian engagement within the organization, underscoring the importance of strengthening cooperation on humanitarian issues.

The remarks come amid heightened US military activity in West Asia and increasingly hostile rhetoric by American officials against the Islamic Republic.

Tehran has repeatedly warned that US bases and naval assets across the region will be targeted in response to any renewed aggression against Iranian territory.
