headline: Russia notes statements from South Korean officials on normalizing ties
summary: According to Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko, if the South Korean partners take any practical steps, Russia will certainly welcome them
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. The Russian side has taken note of certain statements from the Republic of Korea (ROK) regarding its desire to normalize ties with Moscow, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told reporters on Tuesday.

"Yes, we have recorded certain statements from South Korean authorities regarding their ambitions to normalize these relations but at the same time they say that such a normalization of ties could fully take place only after, as they say, the geopolitical situation changes, which means putting an end to the Ukraine conflict," the senior Russian diplomat said in response to a TASS reporter’s question.

For its part, Russia does not link developments between Moscow and Kiev to relations with any country, including the Republic of Korea, Rudenko emphasized. According to him, if the South Korean partners take any practical steps, Russia will certainly welcome them.

"It was not us who initiated the severing of ties with South Korea. Seoul joined the sanctions which were imposed on Russia first," the diplomat added.

Earlier, ROK President Lee Jae-myung stated that Seoul views relations with Moscow as important and that it will continue to keep communication channels open.

headline: (2nd LD) S. Korea to withdraw some embassy staff from Ukraine amid N.K. POW dispute
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic p...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS more info in paras 5-6, 11, 14-17)By Oh Seok-min

SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic personnel from Ukraine amid an ongoing dispute over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul and persistent threats of airstrikes across the country, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.

The decision came as Ukraine has not taken "positive steps" to resolve the diplomatic dispute over Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the transfer of the North Korean POWs to Seoul, ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said at a regular press briefing.

Park also cited continued Russian airstrikes as another reason for the decision, saying they have made it difficult to ensure the safety of diplomatic personnel.

Despite the partial withdrawal, South Korea will maintain necessary diplomatic communications with Ukraine through its charge d'affaires, while all consular personnel will remain in the country to continue efforts to protect South Korean nationals there, the ministry said.

Seoul has demanded an official explanation, an apology and assurances against a recurrence after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly disclosed the transfer and his office subsequently denied that there had been an agreement to keep the matter confidential.

Kyiv, however, has yet to formally respond to Seoul's demands. In protest, South Korea recalled its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, earlier this month.

"We had conveyed our position to Ukraine through various channels. But Ukraine had taken no positive steps despite those efforts," Park said, calling for "sincere and positive steps" in response to Seoul's previous requests.

Noting that the two countries remain in communication, the spokesperson said Seoul's goal was to "seek an amicable resolution through close consultations with the Ukrainian side."

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun has said the two nations had agreed from the outset to keep the matter confidential to protect the soldiers and their families, who remain in North Korea. He also said Ukraine had initially requested that the matter not be made public.

Cho said he had personally received a message from Sybiha that included an apology but fell short of Seoul's expectations.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said, following South Korea's recall of its ambassador, that he considered the controversy "a closed matter," according to foreign media reports.

The two soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia in the Kursk region and arrived in South Korea in mid-September, officials here said.

The ministry said the South Korean Embassy in Ukraine will continue measures to ensure the safety of South Koreans in Ukraine by providing safety updates and offering assistance to those wishing to evacuate.

The ministry declined to confirm the exact number of diplomatic personnel to be withdrawn, but officials said roughly half of the staff would leave Ukraine.

The personnel are expected to withdraw after helping evacuate around 85 South Korean nationals currently in Ukraine to neighboring countries.

"We will coordinate with the embassy to find the safest and most effective means of assisting South Koreans who wish to evacuate," Park said.

A Level 4 travel advisory, the highest level, remains in effect across Ukraine, where the threat of indiscriminate missile and drone attacks has recently increased.

On Monday, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in overnight attacks, damaging energy infrastructure and leaving more than 500,000 households without power, according to foreign media reports.

headline: South Korea decides to recall some of its diplomats from Ukraine
summary: The South Korean Foreign Ministry specified that the decision had been made due to security challenges amid threats of airstrikes across Ukraine
body_text:
SEOUL, October 20. /TASS/. South Korea has decided to recall some of its diplomatic staff from Ukraine, the Foreign Ministry reported.

"Given that even after the recall of the ambassador, the Ukrainian side has taken no constructive measures, the government has decided to withdraw some staff from diplomatic missions due to security challenges amid threats of airstrikes across Ukraine," the Yonhap news agency quoted Foreign Ministry Spokesman Park Doo-soon as saying.

"It is planned that necessary communication through diplomatic channels will continue between the two countries, with the charge d’affaires playing a leading role," the diplomat noted. Park Doo-soon added that all staff members at consular offices and departments will continue to assist South Korean citizens.

The spokesman also responded to a question about whether withdrawing some diplomatic staff from Ukraine constitutes a form of protest. "Our government has already conveyed its position to the Ukrainian side through various channels. We took these measures because we believed that it [the Ukrainian side] had not taken any constructive steps even in this situation," Park Doo-soon emphasized.

On October 8, the South Korean Foreign Ministry announced that the government had decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine. At that time, the ministry expressed its willingness to continue consultations with Ukraine to resolve the issues in a constructive manner.

headline: US envoy says ground intervention in Yemen ‘appears pointless,’ urges regional alliances
summary: Tom Barrack says Washington seeks peaceful agreement with Iran, questions past US military interventions in Middle East
body_text:
US special envoy Tom Barrack said Tuesday that Washington is providing logistical support to Saudi Arabia, but a US ground intervention in the conflict involving Yemen’s Houthis “appears pointless.”

Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha, Qatar, Barrack, who serves as US ambassador to Türkiye and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, said President Donald Trump supports Saudi Arabia logistically amid escalating hostilities between the kingdom and the Houthi group.

He also urged Middle Eastern countries to establish regional alliances rather than rely on Washington to resolve their problems.

Barrack said the US wants to reach a peaceful agreement with Iran as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue.

The envoy also questioned Washington’s history of military interventions in the Middle East, saying attempts to change governments have repeatedly failed.

“Every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” he said.

Asked whether the US-Israeli war against Iran was a mistake, Barrack replied: “I don’t know whether it’s a mistake or not.”

He also described the situation resulting from the conflict as “horrible.”

His remarks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with the Saudi-led coalition carrying out airstrikes against Houthi positions and the group launching missile and drone attacks targeting the kingdom.

The regional escalation has coincided with continued tensions between the US and Iran following their military confrontation, with diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching an agreement remaining deadlocked.

headline: Anger at rising fuel prices bolsters Europe's far right as unrest sweeps France
summary: Rising fuel costs are piling pressure on households, businesses and governments across Europe, fuelling cost-of-living protests and bolstering the far right ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland. Some far-right parties are calling for a return to Russian energy.
body_text:
Rising fuel costs are piling pressure on households, businesses and governments across Europe, fuelling cost-of-living protests and bolstering the far right ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland. Some far-right parties are calling for a return to Russian energy.

Issued on: 20/10/2026 - 09:28

The tractors rolling into the town of Gela on the southern tip of Europe are flying the Sicilian flag, emblazoned with Medusa, three bent legs and ears of wheat: a reminder of the island's role as a breadbasket since Roman times.

But the farmers are not bringing in a harvest. They are protesting.

As soaring fuel prices squeeze household budgets and businesses across Europe, cost-of-living pressures are driving unrest and giving fresh momentum to far-right parties ahead of elections next year in countries including France, Italy and Poland.

Parties once considered fringe had already been gaining ground, with voters from motorists in rural France to young men in Germany's former Communist east looking for alternatives.

The US-Iran war – which erupted in February and sent energy prices sharply higher – has compounded the challenge for governments already struggling to contain inflation, support growth and rein in spending.

The discontent has spilled onto the streets.

In France, demonstrations that began over deteriorating school facilities in Paris' northern suburbs have morphed into some of the country's worst unrest in decades, with shops looted, buildings torched and a 19th-century town hall in Limoges set on fire.

"Why am I here? Well, quite simply, I find the current cost of living truly terrifying," said Quentin Leviloux, a 21-year-old protester in Nantes.

"Just think of people who earn barely the minimum wage, when you look at the cost of food, fuel, and everything else. It’s terrifying how incredibly expensive things have become."

Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend

The European Commission estimates the Iran conflict has cost Europe roughly €100 billion ($112 billion) through disrupted trade and energy markets. Gas prices have jumped about 140% and diesel prices have doubled.

In a weekend address, French President Emmanuel Macron acknowledged the "legitimate demands" of protesters angered by rising living and fuel costs, while condemning those responsible for violence and looting. "We must never confuse them with those who destroyed, vandalised and looted," he said.

Violence has also erupted elsewhere. In the wealthy northern Italian city of Milan, police clashed on Sunday with protesters hurling stones and looting stores during demonstrations over poor public services and rising living costs.

In Gela, on Sicily's southern coast, farmers say fuel costs have made operating machinery prohibitively expensive. "We cultivate the land, we harvest debts," said one banner.

"We are completely at a standstill," said Arcangelo Gambino, a farmers' representative in Caltanissetta province. "The (fuel) cost has more than doubled."

Roadblocks by truckers, farmers and steelworkers have disrupted transport across parts of southern Italy, contributing to local fuel shortages and concerns over supermarket supplies.

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Tens of thousands marched through Lisbon on Saturday over low wages, housing costs and the rising cost of living, increasing pressure on Portugal's centre-right government.

In Spain, the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home sparked nationwide demonstrations over housing shortages and soaring rents, helping trigger a snap election next month.

Belgium has also seen demonstrations, while large rallies in Albania have been driven by anger over perceived government corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards.

The protests reflect broader economic anxieties that are increasingly shaping politics across the continent.

Concerns about purchasing power have become "a major driver of populist politics" across Europe, said Gilles Ivaldi, a political scientist at Sciences Po.

Politicians on both the hard right and hard left have increasingly argued that restoring energy ties with Russia would help lower costs, challenging Europe's mainstream consensus on support for Ukraine.

The latest energy shock comes after years of economic strain following the pandemic and the fallout from Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

In France, rising energy costs have provided an explosive backdrop to next April's presidential election. Macron's government is struggling with a ballooning budget deficit and pressure from bond markets.

Frontrunner Marine Le Pen of the far-right National Rally and hard-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon have both made fuel prices central planks in their campaigns.

“Rising fuel prices are clearly an issue that boosts Marine Le Pen,” said Ivaldi. “I think this is an issue she has owned for quite some time."

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Since the Iran war began, Le Pen's ratings have improved while Macron's have slipped, according to polling by Elabe.

Le Pen's proposal to sharply cut value-added tax on fuel has attracted broad public support. Analysts say the issue resonates strongly with her core voters in rural and semi-rural areas where car travel is often essential.

Watch moreLe Pen 'trying to use these events to push her popularity', expert says

In neighbouring Germany, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is leading national opinion polls after strong gains in local elections. The cost of living topped Germans' concerns for a fifth straight year in a survey published this month.

German inflation spiked to nearly a three-year high in September, with energy price inflation rising to 14.9%, handing ammunition to the AfD to attack Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The AfD is pushing to restore energy ties with Russia, arguing that Berlin’s support for Ukraine is needlessly self-sabotaging at a time when Europe’s largest economy and many of its energy-hungry companies are struggling.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Past experience indicates a link between high energy prices and voter turnout for the AfD, said Jan Steckel, professor for the political economy of climate change at the Technical University of Munich.

“Populist parties often frame energy costs as avoidable and attribute them to government policy choices ... rather than to the underlying geopolitical shocks that drive them," he said.

“These geopolitical shocks are ... much more difficult to explain. And I think this is why incumbent parties often struggle."

The argument is gaining traction elsewhere.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni faces growing competition from National Future, a new far-right party led by former army general Roberto Vannacci, that advocates restoring gas links with Russia.

In Poland – one of Ukraine's staunchest supporters – concern over energy bills is helping boost support for the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown. Its leader, Grzegorz Braun, has called for a return to buying Russian oil and gas, making the case alongside AfD politicians in Lubmin, where the damaged Nord Stream pipelines land in Germany.

“I love the smell of Russian gas in the morning,” he said.

(FRANCE 24 with Reuters)

headline: (2nd LD) Seoul stocks slide nearly 4 pct on AI jitters, unrest in France
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korean shares plunged by nearly 4 percent Tuesd...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS bond yields at bottom; CHANGES photo)

SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korean shares plunged by nearly 4 percent Tuesday, as investors attempted to cash in recent gains in major chip shares amid persistent concerns over the artificial intelligence (AI) value chain. The Korean won was trading higher against the U.S. dollar.

The benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 215.27 points, or 3.73 percent, to 5,552.74 after declining as low as 5,493.24.

The index opened 0.6 percent lower and extended its losses amid deepening woes over AI-related sectors as well as escalating protests in France, which sharply reduced appetite for risky assets.

The KOSPI had risen for two consecutive sessions after a sharp sell-off fueled by concerns over AI-related investments. It had plunged by around 21 percent over seven trading sessions from Oct. 6 through Thursday.

Overnight, U.S. stocks ended mixed as technology shares rebounded from their steepest weekly drop since June.

"Concerns over credit risks and profitability surrounding AI investment have yet to be fully resolved, limiting the sustainability of the rebound," said Lee Kyoung-min, an analyst at Daishin Securities. "Profit-taking emerged following the previous session's gains, sending the market back into negative territory."

Trade volume was light at 259.75 million shares worth 16 trillion won (US$12.97 billion), with decliners far outnumbering advancers 771 to 117.

Foreigners and institutions sold a net 535.4 billion won and 1 trillion won, respectively, while individuals bought a net 900 billion won.

Market heavyweights fell across the board, led by a sharp sell-off in technology shares.

Market bellwether Samsung Electronics fell 2.98 percent to close at 211,500 won, while rival chipmaker SK hynix declined 4.23 percent to 1.22 million won, heading for its lowest close since April.

SK Square, the parent firm of SK hynix, dipped 5 percent to 741,000 won, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics, an electronics component affiliate of Samsung Electronics, went down 1.28 percent to 1.16 million won.

The Korean won was quoted at 1,328.1 won against the U.S. dollar as of 3:30 p.m., up 2.2 won from the previous stock trading session's close.

Bond prices, which move inversely to yields, closed higher. The yield on three-year Treasurys lost 3.7 basis points to 3.840, and the return on the benchmark five-year government bonds went down 2.4 points to 3,990.

body_text:
The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Bahrain are to sell France the equivalent of 10 per cent of its diesel consumption in the coming weeks, Elysee sources have said.

The aim is to bring energy prices down in Europe, which have fuelled protests and public anger in France. “The greater the quantity, the lower the price. It’s quite simple,” an adviser to French President Emmanuel Macron said.

A large part of the deal was obtained by Mr Macron during a tour of the Gulf that started on Monday with visits to Kuwait and the UAE. He is also set travel to Bahrain and Qatar.

France previously obtained guarantees from Saudi Arabia to sell 95,000 tonnes of diesel in October and November, bringing the total to 190,000 tonnes over two months. In addition, the UAE and Bahrain are in the coming weeks expected to separately sell 100,000 tonnes of diesel to France for an unknown duration.

“These are political commitments obtained from countries in the region because they know us and they know we are reliable – because we have been there during every critical moment, notably by deploying air defence capabilities,” the adviser said.

Sales are to go through French energy company TotalEnergies, whose chief executive, Patrick Pouyanne, has accompanied Mr Macron on his Gulf tour.

The UAE and France have signed deals in energy, artificial intelligence and advanced technology as the countries strengthen investment and economic ties.

The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in the UAE capital. Three agreements focused on AI and advanced technology were signed with French start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several fields, Abu Dhabi Media office reported.

The deals cover Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence, Abu Dhabi’s G42 and computing company Analog.

MBZUAE is to focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models.

Analog’s deal with AMI Labs is related to exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications and opening new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors.

The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technology and opportunities for operational improvements to help enhance efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems.

Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts relating to a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project.

“These agreements demonstrate both countries’ commitment to broadening economic and investment co-operation, strengthening integration between their industrial, technological and research capabilities, and opening new avenues for public-private partnerships to support the development of innovative and sustainable solutions in shared priority sectors,” Abu Dhabi Media office said.

headline: Okinawa China Music Festival draws 1,700 with diverse performances in Naha
summary: The fourth Okinawa China Music Festival was held in Naha, Okinawa Prefecture, Japan, on Saturday, featuring a diverse lineup of cultural and artistic performances.
body_text:
(ECNS) -- The fourth Okinawa China Music Festival was held in Naha, Okinawa Prefecture, Japan, on Saturday, featuring a diverse lineup of cultural and artistic performances.

The program included jazz dance, hula (a traditional Hawaiian dance), Tibetan dance, a face-changing duet (a traditional Chinese performance art in which performers change masks in an instant), khoomei (Mongolian throat singing) and performances on the morin khuur (a traditional Mongolian horse-head fiddle). The performances showcased a mix of international styles and traditional arts associated with China's ethnic groups.

Hosted by the Japan Okinawa Chinese Association, the festival drew about 1,700 attendees from across the community.

summary: JERUSALEM, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran.The officials did not provide further details about the meeting, first reported by Axios. body_text:
JERUSALEM, Oct 20 (Reuters) - US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth discussed Iran with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel on Monday, three Israeli officials said, as tensions flare between the US and Iran.

The officials did not provide further details about the meeting, first reported by Axios. The Pentagon declined to comment. The Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Hegseth said in a social media post that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia.

Israel's Army Radio reported his meeting with Netanyahu took place at an air force base in Israel's southern desert.

Hegseth's visit comes amid rising tensions in the Middle East war as tensions flare between the U.S. and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz and as Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia.

It also came a day after US President Donald Trump endorsed Netanyahu in next week's parliamentary election in Israel, the country's first ballot since the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel.

US and Israeli forces launched joint strikes against Iran in late February, setting off the wider Middle East war. Netanyahu told Israeli media this month that he's not seeking to attack Iran before the October 27 Israeli election. Trump has said he will not attack Iran before US midterm elections in November.

(Reporting by Emily Rose, Maayan Lubell, Phil Stewart, Christian Martinez and Ismail Shakil; Editing by Rami Ayyub)

headline: UK National Security Adviser’s wife Sarah Helm calls for Palestine Action ban to be lifted
summary: Sarah Helm, the writer and wife of Britain’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, has called for the UK's ban on the Palestine Action group to be lifted, after a police investigation into her social media posts.The UK has proscribed the pro-Palestine group as a terrorist organisation and expressing support for the group is a criminal offence.Police said at the weekend they closed their investigation of an earlier post by Ms Helm, and decided they would take no action as it did not meet the criminal threshold.On Monday, Ms Helm asked: “Where do I sign?” in response to a letter calling for the ban to be lifted and backing Irish author Sally Rooney and her publisher Faber after they decided her books would no longer be sold in the UK.Ms Rooney had been warned her plan to donate earnings from sales could be considered a criminal offence.Ms Helm, a former Middle East correspondent for The Independent newspaper, had written “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” in response to a clip criticising Ms Rooney.Her stance on Palestine Action, which was banned in the UK in 2025 after an attack on a UK airbase, has led to questions whether it will affect Mr Powell’s role within government. More than 3,500 people have been arrested for supporting Palestine Action in the UK, mostly for holding up placards at demonstrations.Last month, the UK imposed sanctions aimed at illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the Israeli government was turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians.Mr Powell visited Israel earlier this month in a bid to persuade the Israeli government not to close the UK’s Consulate General in Jerusalem, in response to the sanctions. The Consulate opened in 1838 and handles the country's relations with Palestinians in ​the city as ⁠well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.Mr Powell held talks with Israeli officials but ultimately failed to reach an agreement to keep it open. Instead it was downgraded to a mission and the number of staff reduced from 30 to a handful. However, the compromise meant the UK did not enact a tit-for-tat removal of Israeli diplomatic staff from Britain.In her latest social media post, Ms Helm wrote of Ms Rooney: “She’s free yes and found not guilty of posting a terrorist tweet, whereas others guilty of holding terrorist banners? So where do I sign the letter calling for such absurdity to halt and for Palestine Action to be unbanned under the Terrorism act?”Ms Helm’s support of Ms Rooney has led to scrutiny of her social media output, which has been frequent and vociferous in backing pro-Palestinian causes. Former Foreign Office official Ben Judah has highlighted posts made by Ms Helm after the October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas, saying they were “genuinely shocking”. In response to comments from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s saying Israel had a right to defend itself after “terrorists struck at the heart of Israel capturing and killing innocent women and children”, Ms Helm wrote “Not for the first time Von der Leyen is spouting empty dangerous glib tropes on a subject she apparently doesn’t understand”.
body_text:
Sarah Helm, the writer and wife of Britain’s National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, has called for the UK's ban on the Palestine Action group to be lifted, after a police investigation into her social media posts.

The UK has proscribed the pro-Palestine group as a terrorist organisation and expressing support for the group is a criminal offence.

Police said at the weekend they closed their investigation of an earlier post by Ms Helm, and decided they would take no action as it did not meet the criminal threshold.

Is Jonathan Powell the UK’s most influential diplomat?

On Monday, Ms Helm asked: “Where do I sign?” in response to a letter calling for the ban to be lifted and backing Irish author Sally Rooney and her publisher Faber after they decided her books would no longer be sold in the UK.

Ms Rooney had been warned her plan to donate earnings from sales could be considered a criminal offence.

Ms Helm, a former Middle East correspondent for The Independent newspaper, had written “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action” in response to a clip criticising Ms Rooney.

Her stance on Palestine Action, which was banned in the UK in 2025 after an attack on a UK airbase, has led to questions whether it will affect Mr Powell’s role within government. More than 3,500 people have been arrested for supporting Palestine Action in the UK, mostly for holding up placards at demonstrations.

Last month, the UK imposed sanctions aimed at illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the Israeli government was turning a blind eye to the “ethnic cleansing” of Palestinians.

Mr Powell visited Israel earlier this month in a bid to persuade the Israeli government not to close the UK’s Consulate General in Jerusalem, in response to the sanctions. The Consulate opened in 1838 and handles the country's relations with Palestinians in ​the city as ⁠well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.

Mr Powell held talks with Israeli officials but ultimately failed to reach an agreement to keep it open. Instead it was downgraded to a mission and the number of staff reduced from 30 to a handful.

However, the compromise meant the UK did not enact a tit-for-tat removal of Israeli diplomatic staff from Britain.

In her latest social media post, Ms Helm wrote of Ms Rooney: “She’s free yes and found not guilty of posting a terrorist tweet, whereas others guilty of holding terrorist banners? So where do I sign the letter calling for such absurdity to halt and for Palestine Action to be unbanned under the Terrorism act?”

Ms Helm’s support of Ms Rooney has led to scrutiny of her social media output, which has been frequent and vociferous in backing pro-Palestinian causes.

Former Foreign Office official Ben Judah has highlighted posts made by Ms Helm after the October 7, 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas, saying they were “genuinely shocking”.

In response to comments from European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s saying Israel had a right to defend itself after “terrorists struck at the heart of Israel capturing and killing innocent women and children”, Ms Helm wrote “Not for the first time Von der Leyen is spouting empty dangerous glib tropes on a subject she apparently doesn’t understand”.

Love is Blind Habibi will return to Netflix on November 12, bringing 27 singles from across the Arab world into the pods to find a partner without seeing one another.

The second season of the hit series will feature 13 men and 14 women, with participants from countries including Syria, Lebanon, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan and Morocco. Celebrity couple Wissam Breidy and Rym Saidi are to take over as hosts for the 10-episode series.

The Arabic-language adaptation returns following an International Emmy nomination, continuing an experiment in which couples get engaged before discovering whether their connection can survive beyond the pods.

Here is what we know about the new season.

The second season will launch globally on Netflix on November 12.

It will comprise 10 episodes, although the announcement does not specify whether they will be released together or in batches.

Netflix has released the first images of the new group, which comprises 13 men and 14 women from across the Arab world. That is an increase from the 20 participants introduced in season one, which featured an equal number of men and women.

Breidy and Saidi will host season two, replacing Khaled Saqer and Elham Ali, the celebrity couple who presented the first season.

Breidy and Saidi will accompany the participants through the experiment, from their initial search for a partner to the decisions that follow once they meet face to face.

The series follows singles who get to know prospective partners through conversations in separate pods, where they can hear each other but cannot see one another. Those who form a connection can choose to get engaged before meeting in person.

Their relationships are then tested outside the pods, where physical attraction, family expectations and the practicalities of building a life together influence whether they go ahead with a wedding.

Netflix says the new season will again explore the role of family and tradition in the participants’ decisions, alongside the challenges of modern dating.

Season one featured 20 singles from across the Arab world. The cast represented a variety of professions and backgrounds, with many saying family, honesty and long-term commitment were their central values.

Participants were from countries including Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Syria, Morocco, Tunisia, Jordan and Iraq, reflecting the show’s pan-Arab scope.

The latest announcement does not identify filming locations for season two.

The first season was filmed in the UAE and Lebanon, with scenes shot in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Its Lebanese locations included EddeSands Hotel & Wellness Resort in Byblos, north of Beirut, where couples spent time together after leaving the pods.

Netflix has not confirmed whether any structural changes have been made for season two. More details are expected closer to its release.

Netflix has not yet released a standalone trailer or teaser for season two, but parts of the new season can be seen in its teaser for all of its 2026 Arabic content.

At the reunion special for season one, more than a year after filming wrapped, only one couple from Love Is Blind: Habibi had gone the distance to marriage: Safa and Mohammed.

Other couples from the season had mixed outcomes. Asma and Khatab did not marry and eventually split after a brief period together. Hajar and Simo ended their relationship before the wedding. Dounia and Chafic were dating again at reunion time, but confirmed they had parted ways in 2025. Karma and Ammar, as well as Nour and Mido, also ended their engagements.

headline: House fit for a Sultan: Oman state visit puts London residence in the spotlight
summary: The heir to the British throne will meet the Sultan of Oman at his London home today, highlighting the long presence of Muscat's rulers in the British capital. The Prince of Wales and Sultan Haitham will travel to Windsor Castle to be met by King Charles III at the start of the Sultan's state visit to the UK.The last time a Sultan of Oman paid a state visit to the UK was in 1982, when Sultan Al Qaboos visited Queen Elizabeth II.King Charles and Sultan Haitham will spend Tuesday at Windsor Castle, with a state banquet and engagements involving the Queen and members of the royal family planned. The King last hosted Sultan Haitham in 2026 for tea at Windsor Castle during a private visit.It is the collection from the Sultan's London residence – which is listed in UK planning documents as Grove House in Regent's Park – that is being seen as a sign of respect. The villa was built between 1822 and 1824 for the geologist Bellas Greenough, and designed by the architect Decimus Burton, according to the National Archives. The Grade I-listed building, which also sits along the Grand Union Canal, is believed to be the least altered of the historic villas surrounding Regent's Park, according to Neil Tomlinson Architects, which replaced the roof in 2014.The four-acre site is among one of the largest private gardens in the city, “made up of an ornamental garden with outbuildings including stables, an annex and small garden follies”, according to the architecture practice.It is not known when the Sultan of Oman bought Grove House. But the architectural history website London Canals says the house was sold in 1993 for £25 million – making it the most expensive property in London at the time. Council planning documents from the time describe the home as “the official London residence of His Majesty Sultan Qaboos bin Said, the Ruler of Oman, on his visits to the capital”.Guests at the home have included former prime minister David Cameron when he was leader of the opposition. Planning documents revealed more than a decade ago that the house was used by the visiting Omanis. “His Majesty routinely receives guests at Grove House who, by their nature, are also heads of state, foreign dignitaries and senior representatives of the House of Windsor and the government of the United Kingdom,” a statement objecting to the installation of a public cycle stand said. The Sultan owns two homes in the capital.Windsor CastleKing Charles and Queen Camilla will welcome the Sultan at the Royal Dais in Windsor, as a Royal Salute is fired at the Home Park in Windsor, and at the Tower of London. The royals, including Prince William and Princess Catherine, and the Sultan will travel through Windsor town to the castle in a carriage procession. As Prince of Wales, the King visited Oman on four occasions. He travelled to Muscat to offer condolences following the death of Sultan Qaboos in January 2020. As Duchess of Cornwall, Queen Camilla accompanied the King on a two-day visit to Oman in November 2016. In the quadrangle of Windsor Castle, a guard of honour will give a royal salute and the regimental band will play the Omani and British national anthems as the carriage procession arrives. The Sultan, accompanied by the King, will inspect the guard of honour before rejoining the Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales to watch the military march-past.Following lunch in the state dining room, the King and Queen will invite the Sultan to view an exhibition of items relating to Oman from the Royal Collection, in the Green Drawing Room.There will be “enhanced security measures” around Windsor Castle during the visit, according to a Thames Valley Police spokesman. “As a force, we have a vast amount of experience in policing royal events in Windsor and significant planning and preparation has gone into this event,” he added. “We will ensure everyone attending the state visit, including dignitaries and spectators, as well as the public, are kept safe to enjoy the occasion.”The Sultan of Oman will meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday. It is believed that diplomatic meetings between the country's two foreign ministers will also take place on that day close to the King's residence in London.Sultan Haitham was the first leader hosted at Downing Street by former prime minister Keir Starmer in August 2024, after he was elected. They met again in July of this year, just days before Mr Starmer stepped down.Sultan Haitham will attend a banquet at Guildhall hosted by the Lady Mayor and the City of London Corporation and joined by the Duke of Gloucester. The Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford will also be part of the visit, with the Sultan visiting the Here East business and culture campus to view “one of the world's most successful post-Olympic regeneration projects”. He will also view small to medium-sized businesses focused on energy, renewables, technology, space and defence inside the workspace Plexal.The visit comes at a crucial time for UK-Oman relations given the crisis in the Gulf and Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has emerged as a vital mediator, agreeing an alternative traffic system for the Strait of Hormuz with Iran. It has also served as a mediator for discussions with the Iran-backed Houthis at several stages of the war in Yemen.The late Sultan Qaboos is said to have had a good relationship with Queen Elizabeth II. The late Queen first met him in Muscat in 1979, where she sailed along the Gulf on the royal yacht Britannia.In 2010, Queen Elizabeth made a state visit to Oman, where the Sultan gave her an engraved gold vase. “My state visit to Oman in 2010 remains a cherished memory,” Queen Elizabeth said when Sultan Qaboos died in 2020. “May the long history of loyal friendship between our two countries continue.”

The heir to the British throne will meet the Sultan of Oman at his London home today, highlighting the long presence of Muscat's rulers in the British capital.

The Prince of Wales and Sultan Haitham will travel to Windsor Castle to be met by King Charles III at the start of the Sultan's state visit to the UK.

The last time a Sultan of Oman paid a state visit to the UK was in 1982, when Sultan Al Qaboos visited Queen Elizabeth II.

King Charles and Sultan Haitham will spend Tuesday at Windsor Castle, with a state banquet and engagements involving the Queen and members of the royal family planned. The King last hosted Sultan Haitham in 2026 for tea at Windsor Castle during a private visit.

It is the collection from the Sultan's London residence – which is listed in UK planning documents as Grove House in Regent's Park – that is being seen as a sign of respect.

The villa was built between 1822 and 1824 for the geologist Bellas Greenough, and designed by the architect Decimus Burton, according to the National Archives.

The Grade I-listed building, which also sits along the Grand Union Canal, is believed to be the least altered of the historic villas surrounding Regent's Park, according to Neil Tomlinson Architects, which replaced the roof in 2014.

The four-acre site is among one of the largest private gardens in the city, “made up of an ornamental garden with outbuildings including stables, an annex and small garden follies”, according to the architecture practice.

It is not known when the Sultan of Oman bought Grove House. But the architectural history website London Canals says the house was sold in 1993 for £25 million – making it the most expensive property in London at the time.

Council planning documents from the time describe the home as “the official London residence of His Majesty Sultan Qaboos bin Said, the Ruler of Oman, on his visits to the capital”.

Guests at the home have included former prime minister David Cameron when he was leader of the opposition. Planning documents revealed more than a decade ago that the house was used by the visiting Omanis.

“His Majesty routinely receives guests at Grove House who, by their nature, are also heads of state, foreign dignitaries and senior representatives of the House of Windsor and the government of the United Kingdom,” a statement objecting to the installation of a public cycle stand said. The Sultan owns two homes in the capital.

King Charles and Queen Camilla will welcome the Sultan at the Royal Dais in Windsor, as a Royal Salute is fired at the Home Park in Windsor, and at the Tower of London. The royals, including Prince William and Princess Catherine, and the Sultan will travel through Windsor town to the castle in a carriage procession.

As Prince of Wales, the King visited Oman on four occasions. He travelled to Muscat to offer condolences following the death of Sultan Qaboos in January 2020. As Duchess of Cornwall, Queen Camilla accompanied the King on a two-day visit to Oman in November 2016.

In the quadrangle of Windsor Castle, a guard of honour will give a royal salute and the regimental band will play the Omani and British national anthems as the carriage procession arrives. The Sultan, accompanied by the King, will inspect the guard of honour before rejoining the Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales to watch the military march-past.

Following lunch in the state dining room, the King and Queen will invite the Sultan to view an exhibition of items relating to Oman from the Royal Collection, in the Green Drawing Room.

There will be “enhanced security measures” around Windsor Castle during the visit, according to a Thames Valley Police spokesman.

“As a force, we have a vast amount of experience in policing royal events in Windsor and significant planning and preparation has gone into this event,” he added. “We will ensure everyone attending the state visit, including dignitaries and spectators, as well as the public, are kept safe to enjoy the occasion.”

The Sultan of Oman will meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday. It is believed that diplomatic meetings between the country's two foreign ministers will also take place on that day close to the King's residence in London.

Sultan Haitham was the first leader hosted at Downing Street by former prime minister Keir Starmer in August 2024, after he was elected. They met again in July of this year, just days before Mr Starmer stepped down.

Sultan Haitham will attend a banquet at Guildhall hosted by the Lady Mayor and the City of London Corporation and joined by the Duke of Gloucester.

The Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford will also be part of the visit, with the Sultan visiting the Here East business and culture campus to view “one of the world's most successful post-Olympic regeneration projects”.

He will also view small to medium-sized businesses focused on energy, renewables, technology, space and defence inside the workspace Plexal.

The visit comes at a crucial time for UK-Oman relations given the crisis in the Gulf and Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Oman has emerged as a vital mediator, agreeing an alternative traffic system for the Strait of Hormuz with Iran.

It has also served as a mediator for discussions with the Iran-backed Houthis at several stages of the war in Yemen.

The late Sultan Qaboos is said to have had a good relationship with Queen Elizabeth II. The late Queen first met him in Muscat in 1979, where she sailed along the Gulf on the royal yacht Britannia.

In 2010, Queen Elizabeth made a state visit to Oman, where the Sultan gave her an engraved gold vase. “My state visit to Oman in 2010 remains a cherished memory,” Queen Elizabeth said when Sultan Qaboos died in 2020. “May the long history of loyal friendship between our two countries continue.”

body_text:
The ninth Sharjah Film Platform is to return on October 30, presenting 26 films from around the world and a retrospective celebrating Oscar-nominated director Abderrahmane Sissako.

Organised by Sharjah Art Foundation, the 10-day festival will run until November 8 and bring together emerging and established filmmakers from countries including Palestine, Lebanon, Kazakhstan, Mexico, India and Haiti.

The festival will open with Letters (2025), an anthology of 17 short films by Lebanese director Josef Khallouf that reflects on his country's recent history.

Sharjah Biennial 2027 announces opening programme

An Incomplete Drowning (2026), directed by Palestinian artist Larissa Sansour and Denmark's Soren Lind, will close the event. Set aboard a ghostly ship drifting in the Mediterranean, the experimental film brings together figures from different periods of Palestinian history to examine colonialism, memory and the ability of objects to preserve the past.

This year's Director in Focus programme will celebrate Mauritanian filmmaker Sissako, who will travel to Sharjah to lead a masterclass exploring his filmmaking practice. The retrospective will feature three of his films: Bamako (2006), Timbuktu (2014) and Black Tea (2024).

Known for exploring identity, displacement and political realities across Africa, Sissako received an Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film for Timbuktu, which depicts life under extremist rule in Mali.

His earlier film, Bamako, examines international financial institutions through a fictional trial staged in a Malian courtyard.

Emirati cinema will also be represented through Hind Al Basti's Alia and Meera, which follows two best friends whose small lie uncovers a family secret.

The festival will also continue its First Takes initiative for a second year, bringing together aspiring filmmakers from NYU Abu Dhabi, Zayed University, the American University of Sharjah and the University of the Arts Sharjah.

Developed in collaboration with Germany's Kurzfilm Festival Hamburg, the programme includes pitching workshops, feedback sessions and networking opportunities for film students.

Screenings will take place at Mirage City Cinema, Sharjah Art Foundation's open-air cinema in Al Mureijah Square, as well as other venues across the emirate.

Sharjah Film Platform 9 runs from October 30 to November 8

headline: US envoy says ground intervention in Yemen ‘appears pointless,’ urges regional alliances
summary: Tom Barrack says Washington seeks peaceful agreement with Iran, questions past US military interventions in Middle East
body_text:
US special envoy Tom Barrack said Tuesday that Washington is providing logistical support to Saudi Arabia, but a US ground intervention in the conflict involving Yemen’s Houthis “appears pointless.”

Speaking at the Global Security Forum in Doha, Qatar, Barrack, who serves as US ambassador to Türkiye and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, said President Donald Trump supports Saudi Arabia logistically amid escalating hostilities between the kingdom and the Houthi group.

He also urged Middle Eastern countries to establish regional alliances rather than rely on Washington to resolve their problems.

Barrack said the US was redefining its role in the Middle East, moving away from direct control and intervention toward supporting regional countries in managing their own security.

He stressed that Washington was not abandoning its partners but could no longer be expected to resolve every regional conflict.

On Yemen, Barrack questioned the effectiveness of military intervention against the Houthis, saying negotiations involving Saudi Arabia, the group and regional mediators offered a better alternative.

Barrack said the US wants to reach a peaceful agreement with Iran as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue.

He said Trump remained willing to negotiate with Tehran, stressing that Washington was seeking a diplomatic solution rather than further military escalation.

Barrack pointed to mediation efforts by Qatar, Oman, Pakistan and Switzerland, saying a lack of trust between Washington and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) remained a major obstacle.

He suggested that a modified version of the Islamabad understanding could provide a basis for renewed negotiations, including a ceasefire, the reopening of maritime routes and measures to ease economic pressure on Iranians.

The envoy also emphasized that Iran’s political future should be determined by Iranians themselves rather than through externally imposed regime change.

Barrack also questioned Washington’s history of military interventions in the Middle East, saying attempts to change governments have repeatedly failed.

“Every time we try and intervene, change the person or the regime, it seems to have been a mistake,” he said.

He said the US had been involved in 23 regime changes across the broader Middle East, arguing that none had produced the intended results.

Asked whether the US-Israeli war against Iran was a mistake, Barrack replied: “I don’t know whether it’s a mistake or not.”

He said the Trump administration’s initial objective in launching military operations against Iran on Feb. 28 was to prevent what Washington considered an imminent nuclear threat, rather than pursue regime change.

Barrack acknowledged that the conflict had triggered unintended consequences across the Middle East and beyond, stressing that the administration did not want the war to continue.

He also described the situation resulting from the conflict as “horrible.”

Turning to Syria, Barrack described the country’s political transition following the fall of the Bashar al-Assad government in December 2024 as an example of how former armed groups could become part of a political process.

He praised Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa’s handling of the transition under difficult circumstances and called for an end to Israeli military operations in Syria.

Barrack also emphasized the importance of dialogue and economic recovery in reducing regional tensions, arguing that military force alone could not provide lasting solutions.

His remarks come amid escalating hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis, with the Saudi-led coalition carrying out airstrikes against Houthi positions and the group launching missile and drone attacks targeting the kingdom.

​​​​​​​The regional escalation has coincided with continued tensions between the US and Iran following their military confrontation, with diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching an agreement remaining deadlocked.

Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, arrived in the Iranian capital Tehran on Tuesday, accompanied by a delegation of Pakistani officials, according to Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei earlier said the visit was primarily focused on strengthening bilateral relations and cooperation between Tehran and Islamabad.

Responding to speculations that Munir’s visit could involve delivering a political message or military threat, Baqaei said some exchanges between the two countries involved negotiations, but most focused on bilateral ties.

The visit comes amid continued tensions between Iran and the US, with diplomatic efforts aimed at resolving their differences remaining stalled.

​​​​​​​Pakistan has played a mediating role in efforts to reduce tensions between Washington and Tehran following their military confrontation.

headline: France allows local curfews after huge protests
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has authorized mayors to impose partial curfews following a weekend of violent protests that left businesses damaged across the country, while warning that a state of emergency looms.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 19 (MNA) – French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has authorized mayors to impose partial curfews following a weekend of violent protests that left businesses damaged across the country, while warning that a state of emergency looms.

Lecornu announced the measure after a crisis meeting on Monday, giving mayors the power to impose curfews “where they need” them. He did not specify which cities would be affected.

Marseille, France’s second-largest city, has already announced a ban on public gatherings from noon to 8 p.m. local time.

Lecornu also said the government would allocate funds to help affected areas recover from the damage, with the costs ultimately recovered from those responsible for the violence.

“There will be a law that will be put in place to find ways of making sure that those who have damaged properties will have to pay,” the prime minister said, according to Press TV.

More than 2,000 shops and other businesses were directly affected by the weekend’s violence, according to Alain Di Crescenzo, head of France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI). He estimated the damage at “hundreds of millions of euros.”

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said around 200 investigators were examining CCTV footage in an effort to identify those who may have organized the violent protests.

Nunez attempted to resign on Sunday, but President Emmanuel Macron rejected his resignation, citing “the need for continued command of law enforcement,” according to the Elysee Palace. Nunez acknowledged that police had “lost control” in some cities.

The nationwide demonstrations drew students demanding better conditions in France’s education system, alongside residents protesting the rising cost of living and deteriorating public services.

More than half a million people took to the streets on Saturday. In cities across the country, looting, arson and vandalism were reported, while masked protesters reportedly targeted town halls, police stations and other government buildings.

Official figures put the number of injured law enforcement officers at nearly 1,000, while around 2,500 people were arrested.

The government’s handling of the unrest has drawn criticism from local leaders, including the mayors of Paris, Marseille and Limoges.

The weekend’s violence followed weeks of student protests over overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and chronic underinvestment in education. The demonstrations have grown into the country’s biggest youth-led protest movement in recent history.

"Escalating violence in the Gulf can have a serious impact at home in the UK - driving up the cost of living, disrupting energy supplies and costs to British businesses. It is also causing devastation to the civilian population in Yemen."

body_text:
Oil prices hit a five-month high on Tuesday after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen continued attacking Saudi Arabia, further stoking concerns over supply and higher inflation that could prompt interest rate increases.

Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was trading 1.52 per cent higher at $111.30 per barrel at 2.27pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, climbed 2.30 per cent to $100.80 a barrel.

Crude prices were last at these levels in mid-May. On Friday, Brent hit $110 for the first time since May, while WTI topped $100 for the first time in a month.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for renewed strikes on ⁠Saudi energy, airport and military targets ⁠on Monday, escalating tension in the region and bringing down stock markets in the Gulf.

The rebels claimed to have carried out six attacks on the kingdom, which included strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, a military airbase near Abha International Airport, a naval task-force camp and a Saudi radar in Bir Askar.

With the US-Iran conflict continuing, crude supplies from the Middle East remain choked, prompting moves to ensure adequate supplies globally. The International Energy Agency last week said it had agreed to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel to the market amid a surge in diesel prices.

Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks.

The fighting has kept energy prices elevated, nudging inflation upwards and, in turn, raising the probability of another interest rate increase by the US Federal Reserve, which is scheduled to meet next week. Analysts are now expecting a second straight raise as Fed officials seek to tame inflation.

"Brent crude hovering near five-month highs following geopolitical tensions in the Middle East has reignited fears of sticky inflation," analysts at US energy company Duncan Oil said.

"Surging energy costs have led investors to believe the Fed will keep interest rates higher for longer to tame inflation."

Ship movements in the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war made up a fifth of the world's energy exports, remain under pressure.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Monday that Washington was willing to allow oil tankers placed under sanctions to begin a process to legitimately ship crude.

Analytics firm Kpler said easing sanctions on the shadow fleet would have little effect on record freight rates. It estimated that, as of Monday, only 24 of the nearly 160 vessels under sanctions from the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control could return to mainstream trade after taking into account their age and ownership restrictions.

Wholesale diesel, meanwhile, already surpassed $200 per gallon in Singapore and hit roughly $220 in Europe and the US, the Paris-based IEA said last week.

headline: Are Israel’s Lebanon talks a path to peace, or a pretext for continued occupation?
summary: This week, Lebanese and Israeli military representatives are meeting in Tampa, Florida, to discuss implementation of the so-called “pilot zones” plan to advance the Lebanese army’s disarmament of Hezbollah. It’s improbable that there will be any breakthroughs, but more significantly, it’s unlikely Israel actually seeks one.Reportedly, the meeting is being held to discuss, among other things, the technical dimensions of the pilot zones, including a verification mechanism to report on the disarmament process. Also on the table may be discussions of the Lebanese refusal to conduct searches in private homes, where Hezbollah has allegedly stored large quantities of weapons, because this would represent a violation of the law. Article 14 of the Constitution, for instance, affirms “the citizen’s place of residence is inviolable”.These technical matters notwithstanding, the reason the pilot zones scheme has not advanced significantly since the signing of June 26 Tripartite Framework Agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US has to be sought elsewhere. It is mainly a consequence of Israel’s refusal to cede any territory to allow the Lebanese army to advance in the plan. This is largely tied to an Israeli desire to pursue a security doctrine in Lebanon that is independent of any of the constraints that an agreement would impose.Israel appears to have accepted negotiations with Lebanon for two primary reasons: to placate the administration of US President Donald Trump, which pushed for such a process; and to have on paper an agreement with Lebanon that would justify Israel’s continued presence in Lebanon if Beirut failed to fulfil the central condition of disarming Hezbollah.The Israelis have succeeded on both counts. The US administration is on board with Israel, putting no pressure on it to withdraw its forces from Lebanese land. At the same time, the June agreement imposed all conditions on the Lebanese side, above all Hezbollah’s disarmament, without requiring Israel to fulfil any of its own. Indeed, the term “withdrawal” is not even in the document, and there is no timetable for what the text describes as a progressive [Israeli] redeployment out of Lebanese territory.The agreement makes vague promises on Israeli actions that can only be implemented in the case of prior Lebanese actions, without recognising Lebanon’s sovereign rights over its own territory. Its sovereignty over Israeli-occupied parts of the south is qualified. Israel doesn’t expect Lebanon’s government to disarm Hezbollah by force, so it now has a formal excuse to remain in the south indefinitely.What we have, therefore, is a structurally flawed agreement that, by failing to gain traction, will give the Israelis wide latitude to pursue their own security agenda in southern Lebanon. Already, the Israelis have razed dozens of mainly Shiite villages, burned large swathes of agricultural fields and olive groves and bombed land using white phosphorous, thereby making it impossible to grow fruits and vegetables.The objective here is similar to the one employed in Gaza, namely to make the southern border region uninhabitable, in what could very well be an open-ended occupation. This comes at a time when Israel’s security doctrine has changed radically, and differs significantly from what it was in the past.In a much-discussed article for Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, for which he serves as executive director, Tamir Hayman, a former chief of the Israeli military’s Intelligence Directorate, outlined what he saw as a new Israeli approach to security. This will have a fundamental impact on how Israel deals with Lebanon.Five of Mr Hayman’s conclusions stand out. The first is that Israel views peace as a means rather than an end, and that “any arrangement with Arab actors is temporary and deceptive”. The second is that Arab states are not genuine nation states, but “collections of ethnic groups lacking a shared history and a foundational national vision”. In light of this, “undermining their stability is viewed as a natural process”.We have a structurally flawed agreement that, by failing to gain traction, will give the Israelis wide latitude to pursue their own security agenda in southern LebanonA third conclusion of Mr Hayman is that, for Israel, “war is essential to national security, and cannot be replaced by a state of peace”. A fourth conclusion is that Israel must no longer be dependent on the US, which is a “declining power”, whose shifts will ultimately lead to the abandonment of Israel. And a fifth conclusion is that the Israelis must adopt a forward defence strategy through “defence zones” that “enable Israel to move the war into enemy territory as quickly as possible”.Mr Hayman’s bleak analysis is based on his deep knowledge of Israeli strategic thinking, but others too have reached similar conclusions. In light of this, those who believe that a Lebanese-Israeli peace is a priority for Israel are naive. Instead, Israel seeks to fragment and destabilise its neighbours, such as Lebanon and Syria, retain buffer zones inside their territory, pursue perpetual war, and will not hesitate to turn against Washington’s preferences if these run against Israeli priorities.That is principally why we should not expect much from the Lebanese-Israeli talks, and why Lebanon is right in avoiding domestic conflict with Hezbollah just to placate the Israelis. Hezbollah is a major problem for Lebanon, undoubtedly, but it makes little sense today to risk internal Lebanese strife just to satisfy an Israel that appears to be committed to destabilising Lebanon and consolidating its occupation.

Article 14 of the Constitution, for instance, affirms “the citizen’s place of residence is inviolable”.

These technical matters notwithstanding, the reason the pilot zones scheme has not advanced significantly since the signing of June 26 Tripartite Framework Agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US has to be sought elsewhere. It is mainly a consequence of Israel’s refusal to cede any territory to allow the Lebanese army to advance in the plan. This is largely tied to an Israeli desire to pursue a security doctrine in Lebanon that is independent of any of the constraints that an agreement would impose.

Israel appears to have accepted negotiations with Lebanon for two primary reasons: to placate the administration of US President Donald Trump, which pushed for such a process; and to have on paper an agreement with Lebanon that would justify Israel’s continued presence in Lebanon if Beirut failed to fulfil the central condition of disarming Hezbollah.

The Israelis have succeeded on both counts. The US administration is on board with Israel, putting no pressure on it to withdraw its forces from Lebanese land. At the same time, the June agreement imposed all conditions on the Lebanese side, above all Hezbollah’s disarmament, without requiring Israel to fulfil any of its own. Indeed, the term “withdrawal” is not even in the document, and there is no timetable for what the text describes as a progressive [Israeli] redeployment out of Lebanese territory.

The agreement makes vague promises on Israeli actions that can only be implemented in the case of prior Lebanese actions, without recognising Lebanon’s sovereign rights over its own territory. Its sovereignty over Israeli-occupied parts of the south is qualified. Israel doesn’t expect Lebanon’s government to disarm Hezbollah by force, so it now has a formal excuse to remain in the south indefinitely.

What we have, therefore, is a structurally flawed agreement that, by failing to gain traction, will give the Israelis wide latitude to pursue their own security agenda in southern Lebanon. Already, the Israelis have razed dozens of mainly Shiite villages, burned large swathes of agricultural fields and olive groves and bombed land using white phosphorous, thereby making it impossible to grow fruits and vegetables.

The objective here is similar to the one employed in Gaza, namely to make the southern border region uninhabitable, in what could very well be an open-ended occupation. This comes at a time when Israel’s security doctrine has changed radically, and differs significantly from what it was in the past.

In a much-discussed article for Israel’s Institute for National Security Studies, for which he serves as executive director, Tamir Hayman, a former chief of the Israeli military’s Intelligence Directorate, outlined what he saw as a new Israeli approach to security. This will have a fundamental impact on how Israel deals with Lebanon.

Five of Mr Hayman’s conclusions stand out. The first is that Israel views peace as a means rather than an end, and that “any arrangement with Arab actors is temporary and deceptive”. The second is that Arab states are not genuine nation states, but “collections of ethnic groups lacking a shared history and a foundational national vision”. In light of this, “undermining their stability is viewed as a natural process”.

A third conclusion of Mr Hayman is that, for Israel, “war is essential to national security, and cannot be replaced by a state of peace”. A fourth conclusion is that Israel must no longer be dependent on the US, which is a “declining power”, whose shifts will ultimately lead to the abandonment of Israel. And a fifth conclusion is that the Israelis must adopt a forward defence strategy through “defence zones” that “enable Israel to move the war into enemy territory as quickly as possible”.

Mr Hayman’s bleak analysis is based on his deep knowledge of Israeli strategic thinking, but others too have reached similar conclusions. In light of this, those who believe that a Lebanese-Israeli peace is a priority for Israel are naive. Instead, Israel seeks to fragment and destabilise its neighbours, such as Lebanon and Syria, retain buffer zones inside their territory, pursue perpetual war, and will not hesitate to turn against Washington’s preferences if these run against Israeli priorities.

That is principally why we should not expect much from the Lebanese-Israeli talks, and why Lebanon is right in avoiding domestic conflict with Hezbollah just to placate the Israelis. Hezbollah is a major problem for Lebanon, undoubtedly, but it makes little sense today to risk internal Lebanese strife just to satisfy an Israel that appears to be committed to destabilising Lebanon and consolidating its occupation.

headline: US investigating Ukraine’s ties with Mexican drug cartels — Russia’s SVR
summary: The United States has found that Mexican criminal groups have been sending militants to Ukraine to receive training in the assembly and combat use of unmanned aerial vehicles, the SVR revealed
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. US law enforcement agencies have obtained information about cooperation between Mexican drug cartels and the Kiev regime, the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said in a press release.

"According to information coming to the SVR, there is a new reason to panic in Kiev. The Ukrainian presidential office has learned that, in the course of a probe into illegal activities of Mexican drug cartels, US law enforcement agencies obtained information about their cooperation with representatives of the Zelensky regime," the press release said.

The United States has found that Mexican criminal groups have been sending militants to Ukraine to receive training in the assembly and combat use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), the SVR revealed.

At least 80 individuals have been identified who underwent such training within the ranks of the Ukrainian armed forces. Payment for this 'education' was funneled to officials close to Zelensky, using funds generated by drug traffickers from the sale of illicit substances in the United States, the SVR maintained.

"The Ukrainian presidential office is aware that the presence of trained FPV drone operators within the ranks of drug cartels poses risks to the lives of US security officers involved in anti-drug operations along the border with Mexico. Given this, Zelensky’s cooperation with drug cartels could become yet another ‘nail in the coffin’ of his political career," the SVR pointed out.

This fact comes alongside the abysmal corruption of Ukraine’s gauleiter, his offensive behavior and his disregard for Washington’s more than obvious warnings against targeting Russian oil refineries, as well as his refusal to hold an election, the SVR argued. "All this, Zelensky’s team fears, may be the last straw for the White House and force it to cancel all support to Kiev’s bloody clown," it concluded.

body_text:
Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary has forecast a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to push up oil prices, forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers.

Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, Mr O’Leary told a news conference in Brussels on Tuesday. As a result, airline margins will be squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said.

“You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say in history, in Europe in the next 12 months,” Mr O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.”

The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic rise in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets.

Mr O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry.

“We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said.

Ryanair's shares dropped as much as 2.1 per cent, bringing the decline to 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018.

The chief executive used his news conference to dish out against regulation in markets such as France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He repeated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment.

Air Baltic and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Deutsche Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over EasyJet.

Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability.

Mr O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected up to April.

headline: More than 250,000 displaced in Yemen since August as fighting escalates: UNHCR
summary: UN agency says Taiz accounts for 76% of departures, hosts 52% of newly displaced people
body_text:
More than 250,000 people have been displaced in Yemen between Aug. 1 and Oct. 17 as hostilities intensified across the country, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) said Tuesday.

The figure rose from nearly 213,000 previously reported, with Taiz remaining at the center of the displacement crisis, accounting for 76% of departures and hosting 52% of those newly displaced.

Lahj in southwestern Yemen hosts 23% of the newly displaced population, followed by Aden in the south with 13%, according to UNHCR.

“Shelling intensified in Taiz, including in residential areas and around health facilities, while insecurity and restrictions along key routes continue to constrain humanitarian access and movement,” the agency said in a statement.

“In Aden, strikes were reported, including near key civilian infrastructure,” it added.

By Oct. 17, UNHCR and its partners had assessed 12,283 displaced households across Abyan, Aden, Marib, Lahj and Taiz, including around 2,050 families without shelter.

It said shelter partners have reached 3,166 households, but around 33,700 families still require shelter assistance amid severe underfunding of the wider humanitarian response.

UNHCR said schools in Kharaz refugee camp in Lahj, which hosts 9,490 refugees, closed again on Oct. 11 as the security situation deteriorated, while access restrictions continued to affect humanitarian operations and movement to and from the camp.

Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several other provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.
