headline: Press review: Russia reshuffles government as NATO moves to escalate Black Sea tensions
summary: Top stories from the Russian press on Tuesday, October 20th
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. China may join Russia and the US in settling the Ukrainian conflict; the Russian government is undergoing major reshuffles; and NATO is preparing to further escalate tensions in the Black Sea region. These stories topped Tuesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.

China is preparing to support Russia and the US in their efforts to resolve the crisis in Ukraine. A meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, his US counterpart Donald Trump, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping may take place in November at the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Experts believe that, if this happens, the leaders will discuss major global conflicts, including the one in Ukraine. Beijing continues to promote its peace initiatives, which Moscow actively supports. Meanwhile, relations between Russia and the US may have improved considerably by the time of the meeting.

If the leaders of the three powers do indeed meet, they will send important signals to the world on the settlement of the Ukraine crisis, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. "In any case, we hope that if such a meeting takes place at the highest level, some targeted signals will likely be sent to the international community on the three countries’ positions on various conflicts," the senior diplomat said. "As I understand it, China has always been interested in resolving the conflict and is now reaffirming that interest. It has its own proposals, which it has previously put forward. I think it will continue to stand by them," Rudenko noted.

China’s primary strategic interest is to preserve "room for maneuver" by opening up as many opportunities as possible while assuming as few obligations as possible, China expert Nikolay Marchenko emphasized.

According to him, Beijing’s direct involvement in resolving the Ukrainian crisis will undoubtedly strengthen its position on the world stage vis-a-vis the collective West. At the same time, China will not supplant the US as the main mediator, the expert pointed out.

Recently, Moscow and Washington have begun taking a more pragmatic approach to their relationship, moving beyond statements and taking concrete steps toward one another. "We are currently focused on expanding this channel of interaction [between Russia and the US]. This will yield not merely a purely political effect in the form of statements, but a practical result that will impact economic cooperation between these two major geopolitical players and create a positive atmosphere conducive to a swift settlement of the conflict in Ukraine," Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik emphasized.

It is possible that Moscow and Washington will head to the APEC summit in China as parties ready to compromise. However, the results of the US congressional elections could pose a serious obstacle. According to American studies expert Malek Dudakov, the Republicans risk losing their majority in both chambers of Congress. This would significantly limit Trump’s options on the international stage because of the threat of investigations and a potential impeachment process initiated by the Democrats.

The Russian government is set to undergo its most extensive personnel and structural reshuffle since its formation in May 2024. Two of the nine current deputy prime ministers will be replaced, and two more will be added to the Cabinet’s presidium. The most significant change is the restoration of Anton Siluanov’s authority as deputy prime minister. The Cabinet Secretariat will also move into the financial sphere: it is set to be headed by Siluanov’s first deputy Irina Okladnikova. Incumbent Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin and Primorsky Region Governor Oleg Kozhemyako will take up the posts of deputy prime ministers. These nominations highlight a particular focus on modernizing transport infrastructure and developing the Far East and the Arctic.

There are formal reasons for a cabinet reshuffle, such as the outgoing president handing over power to the president-elect, and informal reasons, when it is necessary to strengthen specific areas, Konstantin Kostin, head of the Civil Society Development Foundation, told Vedomosti. "In light of the current changes, these priorities include strengthening the financial sector and budgetary discipline, as well as regional development and the development of the transport sector in all its components," he emphasized.

These reshuffles allow the new State Duma to establish its role and demonstrate its power to confirm ministers, although there have been no instances in which the lower chamber of the Russian parliament has rejected a nominee, Mikhail Vinogradov, head of the "St. Petersburg Politics" Foundation, stressed. According to him, the position of deputy prime minister would suit Siluanov, given the growing uncertainty around financial policy as Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina’s term is set to end in 2027. Separating the roles of deputy prime minister and transport minister also makes sense given the distinctive characteristics of the aviation industry, Vinogradov added.

Over the past six years, Mikhail Mishustin’s government has transformed public administration, making it highly efficient and proving its ability to cope with crises and unexpected challenges, political analyst Dmitry Yelovsky told Izvestia. In his opinion, the current reshuffle only reinforces the correctness of the chosen course. Shifting priorities in the economy and politics simply call for new personnel. Yelovsky emphasized that the current system is functioning smoothly but needs a slight adjustment in direction, which is why different leaders are needed. At the same time, there are no complaints about the previous team.

According to expert Yevgeny Minchenko, such appointments are also driven by professional burnout that builds up over many years of intense work. At the same time, the groundwork laid in the Far East and in public administration will be maintained, the expert pointed out.

NATO is showing its readiness to further escalate tensions in the Black Sea region. Specifically, the alliance’s actions are increasing the risk of incidents. NATO is also stepping up its intelligence activities to provide data to Kiev and expanding its military infrastructure in coastal countries. Earlier, Bucharest proposed establishing a NATO military command in the region following incidents involving drones and attacks on merchant ships. Experts note that Moscow may respond by bolstering its own military capabilities.

The alliance’s interest in the Black Sea region is growing, even though Turkey has imposed restrictions since the start of the special military operation on the passage of military ships from non-regional countries into the waters, Russian Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Department Director Vladislav Maslennikov told Izvestia. According to him, instead of naval activity, NATO is concentrating on expanding infrastructure in the bloc’s coastal member states. "Reconnaissance activity by NATO allies has also increased in the region. Reconnaissance aircraft based in Romania’s Constanta are constantly monitoring the Black Sea. NATO servicemen are passing the data they collect on to the Kiev regime. Against this backdrop, the risk of incidents, including unintentional ones, is indeed increasing," the diplomat emphasized.

Shortly before that, Acting Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta proposed establishing a joint military command for NATO’s Black Sea coastal states. Bucharest is ready to head this new alliance body. According to media reports, Romania’s initiative and the situation in the region as a whole will be discussed at a meeting of the organization’s council scheduled for October 20. "Its decisions are expected to include measures to boost the coalition’s capabilities for defending air and maritime space against drones and other low-flying ‘threats.’ Thus, the alliance has no intention of reducing its activities in the region. Through its actions, it is signaling a readiness for further escalation of tensions in the Black Sea region," Maslennikov noted.

In turn, international relations expert Pavel Anisimov told Izvestia that Romania’s initiative involves creating a joint command with Bulgaria and Turkey, which have been part of a demining group alongside Bucharest for the past two years. The deployment of new NATO command bodies in Romania or Bulgaria should be viewed as the alliance’s effort to build a unified, continuous line of defense on its eastern flank, Mediterranean studies expert Tigran Meloyan stressed.

Nine days before Israel’s parliamentary elections, US President Donald Trump gave his "complete and total endorsement" to incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Early on October 18, on his Truth Social page, the US leader called Netanyahu "a great warrior prime minister" and an even greater "partner for peace," especially in the war against Iran. Until now, Trump had refrained from publicly backing any particular candidate in Israel’s parliamentary elections. A few minutes after the US president’s post, Netanyahu thanked him for his support and stressed that the Americans could only defeat Iran with his help and not that of any other Israeli candidate.

It is still difficult to gauge the extent of Trump’s influence on Israeli electoral processes, Alexey Yurk, a researcher at the Center for Middle Eastern Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, told Vedomosti. On the one hand, Netanyahu is known in Israel as someone who can involve Trump in his foreign policy gambles. On the other hand, the separate US-Iran talks amid a joint war have severely damaged Trump’s approval ratings in Israel and weakened Netanyahu’s reputation as a politician who can secure Washington’s unconditional support for Israel's military gambles, the expert explained.

Trump’s support is unlikely to change Netanyahu’s chances of re-election, Lyudmila Samarskaya, another researcher at the Center for Middle Eastern Studies of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ World Economy and International Relations Institute, emphasized. According to her, most Israelis view Trump’s statement as interference in the country’s domestic affairs. "The current Likud electorate traditionally votes for political forces that advocate for Israel’s security. There are few undecided voters left in the country, so the American leader’s verbal interventions will not have a significant impact. The election results are difficult to predict," the expert pointed out.

Netanyahu’s approval ratings have been hurt by Trump’s remarks about Israel’s dependence on the will of the US president, Yurk stressed. "In this context, the negative effect of Trump’s support for Netanyahu may even outweigh any potential political gains. Nevertheless, the results of the Knesset elections will most likely be influenced by domestic political issues," the political scientist noted.

According to Yurk, a victory by the Israeli opposition might lead to a return to less personality-driven, but more institutionalized and stable US-Israel relations.

Peak freight rates and instability on southern routes have increased the appeal of the Northern Sea Route as an export corridor for Russian oil. Although the summer-fall navigation season is not yet over, according to media reports, 50% more oil has already been transported than during the previous season. By the end of the season, shipments could exceed 25-30 million barrels, more than doubling last season's volume. However, ice conditions and the need for escort vessels could significantly affect voyage duration and cost.

Oil exports via the Northern Sea Route during this navigation season have exceeded last year’s total by nearly 50%, reaching 20 million barrels (2.75 million metric tons) compared to 13 million barrels for the entire previous navigation season, Reuters reported, citing trading data. By the end of the season, the volume of shipments could grow by another five to ten million barrels (0.69-1.37 million metric tons). According to estimates by the Center for High North Logistics (CHNL), as of September 30, 28 tankers with a total deadweight of 3.14 million metric tons had passed through the Northern Sea Route, including 22 tankers with 2.46 million metric tons heading east and six tankers carrying 682,000 metric tons heading west.

Price Index Center Director Roman Sokolov told Kommersant that amid a global rise in ocean freight rates, the Northern Sea Route has gained a significant competitive advantage: its shorter length has made it possible to reduce operating costs and cut fleet charter periods for charterers. "Although optimal ice conditions on the Northern Sea Route did not return until late August, the extended period of open water helped foster healthy competition in the oil logistics market this summer and kept price increases on traditional routes in check," he noted. "Given that a number of vessels have not yet completed their voyages, the final results of the navigation season may turn out to be even higher," the expert pointed out.

Meanwhile, Dmitry Kasatkin, managing partner at Kasatkin Consulting, noted that the Northern Sea Route is currently primarily an export channel for seasonal oil shipments to China. "The growing interest in it is driven by economics: the northern route shortens the transport distances, and high freight rates and risks on southern routes amplify this advantage. When freight rates are high, reducing voyage time becomes particularly valuable, as it allows for an increase in the number of voyages," the expert said.

Kasatkin identified the availability of vessels with the required ice class, variable ice conditions, and the cost of ice escort services as the main constraints on the growth of shipments via the Northern Sea Route. "Waiting for an escort and reduced speed can eat into a significant portion of the gains from the shorter distance," he stressed. "Therefore, sustainable growth requires expanding the fleet and the ability to operate more economically viable voyages," the expert emphasized. According to him, extending the season should also be based on the capabilities of specific vessels and the actual conditions along the route.

headline: Jiri Prochazka on learning from mistakes and why he is leaning towards Evloev and Yan at UFC 333 in Abu Dhabi

Prochazka takes on up-and-coming contender Navajo Stirling in UFC Fight Night on November 21 in Doha, in what will be the promotion's second visit to Qatar.

Czech Republic’s Prochazka has a point to prove. He is making a comeback after a chastening defeat to Carlos Ulberg in their title fight for the vacant light heavyweight championship in April at UFC 327. There, he suffered a first-round knockout despite Ulberg injuring his knee badly early in the bout.

Exclusive‘I’m Alex, who still fights’: Volkanovski returns to Abu Dhabi a changed man

Lessons have been learnt from the defeat. The main one is to finish the contest at the first available opportunity.

“Everything was settled,” Prochazka told The National about the fight against Ulberg.

“Everything was successful … kicks, good distance, the pressure, all these things. But once I saw my opponent was hurt … I was too much emotional. I felt like I need to work more to win the fight. Not just like that, not just one kick, and I see the crashing leg. I just didn't accept the easy win. So I started to play this game ‘OK, let's go, let's go for a brawl. I'm giving you the same chances’. And that was a big mistake. I learnt from that a lot. We are still learning.

“Then he just punched me, and that was it, that was the fight.”

That result forced Prochazka, 34, to go back to the drawing board.

“I made a lot of changes after my last fight. It's really deep preparation, because I made a lot of changes. I don't want to just go from fight to fight and take whatever results. I really want to win. Really want to go to Qatar and show everyone that I am one of the best fighters in the world,” Prochazka said.

There will be remnants from the last fight in Doha. His opponent Stirling enters the contest unbeaten and has a 6-0 record in the UFC. Plus, the Kiwi is sparring with Ulberg. Prochazka says he is prepared.

“My main weapon is to adjust. To change whatever I need to change to win the next fight. So, I really don't care if he's preparing with Ulberg or with whoever. He's a good opponent. But I believe I see a lot of space to catch him. And this is what I'm going to do.”

Next month will mark Prochazka’s second visit to the Gulf. His first one was the path-breaking UFC 251 in Abu Dhabi in 2020 at the height of the coronavirus pandemic, where UFC was the only major sporting event taking place across the globe.

Abu Dhabi will be in focus this week as well. The Etihad Arena hosts UFC 333, where Alexander Volkanovski will defend his featherweight title against Movsar Evloev in the headline bout, while Petr Yan and Merab Dvalishvili play out their epic trilogy in the co-main event.

Prochazka has picked out his favourites for Saturday.

“I'm a fan of Volkanovski's style. And Volkanovski’s smart mindset. Yeah, but I see Evloev is really, like, a hard worker. So there is a lot of chances for Evloev to win the fight. Let the better man win,” Prochazka said.

“In the second match … I know, personally, Merab. I like him, like his style. But I believe Petr Yan is a smarter fighter. He is a much smarter fighter because he has more techniques. His style is something that inspires me. It's a great inspiration, especially some throws and high intensity of work.”

The Gulf region will forever be special to Prochazka. He made his promotional debut in UFC at Fight Island in 2020 and won.

“Abu Dhabi was an amazing experience because it was a totally new thing in the world,” Prochazka recalled.

“It was like a miracle for fighting sports, because all the world stopped because of coronavirus. Only one thing was going on, and that was UFC. For me, it was, like, I stepped into the league of the best. ‘I'm here, and I'm going for the title. And let me show my best’.”

headline: UK should do more for Gulf allies and consider strikes on Houthis, says ex-defence secretary
summary: Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis, because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Michael Fallon has told The National.The US, he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”.That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”.With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.”For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis. “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024.Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion.It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given.Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.”However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.”'Gulf security is our security'“Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.”The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”.“So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said.The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia, declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran.Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”.“Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.”The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”.Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.”Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course.Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”.Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS.Europe's turn to do moreThe same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow.He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress.“I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said.The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness.“He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”.Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.”Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.”Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.”The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September.Pressure on KyivThe stakes are highest in Ukraine. “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.”A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato”.Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. But it will also send a signal right round the world to other countries that want to extend their borders”.“China, of course, has ambitions to bring Taiwan formally back inside China, to extend its influence across the South China Sea.”The idea that might makes right, Sir Michael warned, “is very dangerous for the international community”.New age of instabilityAsked whether the world is at a tipping point, Sir Michael did not hesitate. “Yes, I think we are. We're certainly in a new age, I think, of instability and uncertainty.”He does not expect a return to the old order. “I don't think it's gonna snap back to the kind of rules-based international co-operation and international institutions that we used to respect, the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation.”The danger, he said, is a mistake. “We're standing up to each other now,” he said, with missiles, air-defence systems and drones facing off from the edge of Romania to the islands of the Gulf.He gives the potential example of a local battery commander who “sees something coming in on the radar, and his job is to defend”. “It turns out to be a civilian airliner,” he adds.“You have a capacity now for miscalculation, that with so much conflict going on in both regions of the world, that somebody makes a mistake, and then there's a response, and people's lives are lost.”For Britain and its allies in the Gulf and Europe, that is the world they must now plan for. “We are in a new age of instability, and I think this is now the new norm that we have to live with,” Sir Michael said.

Britain should do more to help its allies in the Gulf, including considering strikes on the Houthis, because Washington's priorities have changed and its partners must now stand together, former UK defence secretary Michael Fallon has told The National.

The US, he said, is “shifting its priorities to homeland defence, to the Indo-Pacific. And therefore, it means that in terms of Washington, perhaps Europe and the Middle East count for less than they used to”.

That shift is structural, not a passing mood. “We've also seen a change in the United States,” Sir Michael said, recalling a country that “helped us win two world wars in Europe”.

With the Gulf and Europe pushed down Washington's list of priorities, the burden falls on the allies. “I think we should be doing more,” he said. “These are our partners and friends, and we should be helping more.”

For Britain, that means being ready to act against the Houthis. “That means, if necessary, we should be prepared to consider strikes as we did two years ago” he said, alongside the US and other European nations, as in the joint US-UK air campaign against Houthi targets that began in January 2024.

Sir Michael, who served as the defence secretary from 2014 to 2017 under prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May, was speaking in Dubai on the sidelines of the inaugural Middle East chapter of Signum Global Advisors, chaired by Charles Myers and launched by Raha Moradi, where he took part in a closed-door, onstage discussion.

It is, to borrow the Irish, a mé féin foreign policy in Washington: me, myself and I. For America's allies, the old guarantees are no longer a given.

Sir Michael was careful with his words about the White House. Asked whether US President Donald Trump was an unreliable, unpredictable partner for the Gulf and Europe, he pointed to Moscow instead. “The most unreliable person clearly is President [Vladimir] Putin.”

However, he was clear that the ground had moved. “You have an unpredictable element now,” he said. “Policy shifts suddenly.”

“Gulf security is our security,” Sir Michael said. “It's our economic security. It's our energy security.”

The trade and energy flowing through the region, he said, fed straight into the British economy and inflation, “and in the end, affects interest rates back in the UK”.

“So we have a huge interest, as well as friendships and historical ties,” he said.

The pressure on those ties is rising. Since July, the Houthis have been in direct conflict with Saudi Arabia, declaring a naval blockade of the kingdom and attacking Saudi tankers in the Red Sea, while threatening to close the Bab Al Mandeb strait, the southern gateway to the Suez Canal. The Strait of Hormuz has already been disrupted by the US-Israel war with Iran.

Britain has stepped up, but only so far. In April, the RAF deployed its Rapid Sentry air-defence system to Kuwait. Last month, in the first substantial foreign policy decision of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government, London agreed to a Saudi request for an RAF Voyager tanker to keep the kingdom's Typhoon jets in the air for longer. Ministers described it as a strictly defensive, “time-limited commitment”.

“Well, we've responded to Kuwait's call for assistance,” Sir Michael said. “The Saudis asked us for help.”

The most obvious step, he said, is to make sure the Houthis cannot disrupt the Bab Al Mandeb strait in the way Hormuz has been disrupted, which means tackling Houthi strikes “at source”.

Asked whether strikes would be a big step for Mr Burnham, he said: “It would be, and clearly, they've considered it.”

Labour has been reluctant before. In February, under Keir Starmer, the government initially refused to let the US use British bases, including Diego Garcia, for strikes on Iran, before reversing course.

Sir Michael said the government had now “reversed that decision and said they can use Diego Garcia, but I think we should be doing more than that”.

Gulf states, he said, are “with us, by the way, in the long-term battle against international terrorism”, as they were in the international coalition against ISIS.

The same logic applies in Europe, where, Sir Michael said, the continent had been too slow to carry its share of the pressure on Moscow.

He called Washington's diesel deal with Russia a misstep. This month, the US Treasury waived sanctions on Russian diesel sales until April 2027, and on Friday, Mr Trump signed an executive order pausing new Russia sanctions passed by Congress.

“I'm afraid it's a miscalculation,” Sir Michael said.

The volumes are too small to bring down diesel prices in the US and the deal is unlikely to move a ceasefire any further forward, he said. Mr Putin, he argued, would read it as weakness.

“He's given up nothing in return,” he said. Russia has kept up its attacks on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, he added, and “he hasn't come to change any of his negotiating position about the future of Ukraine”.

Asked whether it undermines sanctions as a weapon globally, he said it does. “You're either all in on sanctions or you're not.”

Mr Trump, he conceded, has a point: “Where Trump is right, that our sanctions haven't been fully applied.”

Europe has been far too slow to cut its dependence on Russian oil and gas, to police the shadow fleet and to use sanctioned Russian assets to help Ukraine, Sir Michael said. “Europe keeps passing new packages of sanctions, which rather casts doubt on the previous packages.”

The EU adopted its 22nd package on October 12, the largest single round of listings yet at 1,569 individuals and entities. Brussels is already drafting a 23rd. Yet EU countries still bought €817 million ($917 million) of Russian pipeline gas and €615 million of Russian LNG in September.

The stakes are highest in Ukraine. “I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Bloomberg this week. “I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war” against Russia “could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks.”

A capitulation would not only encourage Mr Putin, Sir Michael said. It would put Russia's near neighbours “in the firing line, whether it's Moldova, the rest of Georgia, even the Baltic states, even though they're part of Nato”.

Moscow regards those countries as its “near abroad”, he said, “and they will be much more exposed. But it will also send a signal right round the world to other countries that want to extend their borders”.

“China, of course, has ambitions to bring Taiwan formally back inside China, to extend its influence across the South China Sea.”

The idea that might makes right, Sir Michael warned, “is very dangerous for the international community”.

Asked whether the world is at a tipping point, Sir Michael did not hesitate. “Yes, I think we are. We're certainly in a new age, I think, of instability and uncertainty.”

He does not expect a return to the old order. “I don't think it's gonna snap back to the kind of rules-based international co-operation and international institutions that we used to respect, the United Nations, the World Trade Organisation.”

The danger, he said, is a mistake. “We're standing up to each other now,” he said, with missiles, air-defence systems and drones facing off from the edge of Romania to the islands of the Gulf.

He gives the potential example of a local battery commander who “sees something coming in on the radar, and his job is to defend”. “It turns out to be a civilian airliner,” he adds.

“You have a capacity now for miscalculation, that with so much conflict going on in both regions of the world, that somebody makes a mistake, and then there's a response, and people's lives are lost.”

For Britain and its allies in the Gulf and Europe, that is the world they must now plan for. “We are in a new age of instability, and I think this is now the new norm that we have to live with,” Sir Michael said.

headline: Qatar set to become Singapore’s second strategic partner in the Middle East
summary: Qatar and Singapore are working towards a strategic partnership spanning trade, energy, artificial intelligence, security and sustainable development, which would make Qatar Singapore’s second strategic partner in the Middle East.…
body_text:
Qatar and Singapore are working towards a strategic partnership spanning trade, energy, artificial intelligence, security and sustainable development, which would make Qatar Singapore’s second strategic partner in the Middle East.

The development came during Singapore Prime Minister and Minister for Finance Lawrence Wong’s official visit to Doha from 18 to 20 October, his first official visit to the Middle East since becoming prime minister.

The decision followed the ninth Qatar-Singapore High-Level Joint Committee meeting, co-chaired by Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Wong.

The meeting marked the first time the two countries’ leaders had co-chaired the committee in its 20-year history.

The strategic partnership is expected to be launched during Sheikh Tamim’s upcoming state visit to Singapore.

Both sides identified artificial intelligence (AI), digitalisation and emerging technologies as potential pillars of bilateral cooperation, highlighting opportunities for collaboration in cybersecurity, digital government, research and development, and AI talent development.

The leaders also welcomed growing security cooperation, including in defence industry, maritime security and cybersecurity.

They cited a QAR 1.5 billion defence-services agreement signed between Qatar’s Barzan Holdings and Singapore’s ST Engineering in February 2026, and encouraged further collaboration in digital defence and maritime security.

On regional developments, the leaders expressed serious concern over the situation in the Middle East and commended Qatar’s diplomatic efforts to facilitate dialogue and de-escalation.

They also stressed the importance of upholding navigational rights and freedoms under international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, to ensure shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains open, safe and secure.

The two sides also pledged to strengthen cooperation between Qatar and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), as well as between ASEAN and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC).

They welcomed Qatar’s status as an ASEAN Sectoral Dialogue Partner and called for continued efforts towards an ASEAN-GCC free-trade agreement during Singapore’s ASEAN chairmanship in 2027. They also looked forward to the third ASEAN-GCC Summit.

The committee’s 10th meeting will be held in Singapore at a mutually agreed date to be determined through diplomatic channels.will be held in Singapore on a date to be agreed through diplomatic channels.

headline: Qatar says Iran-US talks ongoing, warns of wider regional war

headline: Rubio lands in India for 'trade diplomacy'
summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday, his second official visit to the country this year, as he pursues an Asian tour blending diplomacy and trade. Rubio visited Uzbekistan, where he called for stronger partnerships with Central Asian countries, before landing in Mumbai for talks with Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and meetings with business leaders. body_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio arrived in India on Tuesday, his second official visit to the country this year, as he pursues an Asian tour blending diplomacy and trade.

Rubio visited Uzbekistan, where he called for stronger partnerships with Central Asian countries, before landing in Mumbai for talks with Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and meetings with business leaders.

He visited New Delhi and Kolkata in May, when he also toured the Taj Mahal and met Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Modi is not scheduled to meet Rubio this time.

The top US diplomat will visit Jamnagar, in the western state of Gujarat, a port and stronghold of billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance conglomerate and its flagship refinery, the world's largest.

He is also due to lay a wreath in memory of the 2008 Mumbai attacks that killed 166 people.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Tuesday he had also spoken to Rubio and raised issues with the US military satellite system that Ukraine uses, as well as missile delays.

Zelensky, expected in Oslo for talks with US envoys, said he told Rubio that "Starlink/Starshield needs to be restored" and that ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives".

Rubio's visit comes as India and the United States struggle to finalise a trade deal, a persistent source of friction between the two countries.

Speaking in Samarkand, Rubio said Washington and New Delhi were "very close" to an agreement.

However, a deal during his visit appears unlikely.

US President Donald Trump's tariff war launched in April last year has added to friction over India's imports of Russian oil and warming ties between Washington and Pakistan, India's arch-rival.

Asked about temporary US sanctions waivers for Russian oil, of which India is a major importer, Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors "including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies".

"You also can't unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue," he said.

The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.

But days later, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping tariffs, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

The two sides have been negotiating ever since.

Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said this month the talks had reached "a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult".

Jaishankar met with his United Arab Emirates counterpart in Mumbai earlier on Tuesday. The UAE is a key supplier of Indian energy, especially liquefied natural gas (LNG).

"The situation in the Gulf remains a matter of deep concern," Jaishankar told UAE Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in public comments broadcast before their meeting started.

He said India continues to support "free, safe and unimpeded flow of trade, energy and fertiliser".

headline: N. Korea vows 'tit-for-tat' action against S. Korea-U.S. military exercise
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- North Korea on Tuesday denounced South Korea's ongoin...
body_text:
SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- North Korea on Tuesday denounced South Korea's ongoing joint military drills with the United States and a separate exercise between the U.S. and Japan, calling them "muscle flexing" by "enemy states."

In an English-language commentary carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the North warned that a "tit-for-tat principle based on strong power will be applied" in response to the military exercises.

"The present situation, in which the hostile forces get frantic in their military moves to infringe upon the security interests of the DPRK and undermine the regional strategic stability, highlights the validity and justness of the DPRK's indispensable self-defensive efforts to deter them," it said, referring to North Korea by its official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.

The commentary came as South Korea launched the annual Hoguk field exercise involving U.S. forces Monday, while Japan also kicked off large-scale military drills with the U.S., called "Keen Sword," the same day.

On the South Korea-U.S. drills, Pyongyang slammed Seoul for not concealing the "aggressive and provocative nature" of the exercise, warning that escalating threats would require stronger deterrence.

"Bolstered deterrent is required to deal with ever-escalating threats, and repeated provocations are bound to meet with such prompt reaction as bolstering of stronger capabilities," the KCNA said.

"To cope with the security environment on the Korean peninsula that has been put in new danger by oft-repeated U.S.-Japan-ROK military provocations, the DPRK will continue to remind them of its will to defend sovereignty through ceaseless upgrading, bolstering and responsible demonstration of its reliable war deterrent for self-defence," it added.

The Hoguk exercise is scheduled to run through Oct. 30. The U.S. Forces Korea is also participating in the drills to enhance interoperability with South Korean troops, according to the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

body_text:
Tens of thousands of burial tombs have been mapped in the UAE, Oman and Saudi Arabia as part of a project that has shed fresh light on life in previous millennia.

The Arabiancairns initiative, which began in 2022, has documented tombs on hilltops, terraces and plains over thousands of square kilometres.

The work, funded by the French National Research Agency (ANR), has highlighted evidence of agriculture and pinpointed trading links, offering new insights.

The biggest archaeological discoveries in the Middle East of 2026

Initially supported for four years, the initiative has had its funding renewed into 2027 and more fieldwork is already planned.

Arabiancairns focuses on protohistoric Arabia, covering about 5500 BCE to 300 CE. This includes the Bronze Age, which ran from around 3200 BCE to 1300 BCE and the subsequent Iron Age, which lasted until about 300 BCE.

Researchers are analysing the distribution of tombs and how they relate to the surrounding landscape, and the architecture of particular sites and how they were altered over time.

Chemical analysis helps the scientists understand how old sites are, what people ate and how they moved around.

Once the project is completed, a database of funerary monuments, giving their precise locations, will be made publicly available.

A key area analysed is around Bisya in central Oman, where, across about 4,700 square kilometres, around 5,500 tombs have been mapped and confirmed by foot surveys and satellite data.

“These monuments were built at different times, many contained several burials, and some were reused long after their original construction,” said Dr Olivia Munoz, from the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) Trajectories Lab and the Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University.

At Dhabtiyah in eastern Saudi Arabia, similar patterns have been seen, with burial episodes within the same tomb separated by roughly a millennium.

“Our research also highlights similarities in funerary architecture and practices across large parts of Arabia, alongside regional differences,” Dr Munoz said.

“However, we cannot be certain what particular architectural features meant to their builders, or whether the same features carried the same meaning for different communities.”

Around Bisya, Dr Munoz said it seemed that much of the population – not just elites – could have been buried in the tombs, as there was no known alternative form of burial from the same period.

“Excavated tombs have yielded the remains of people of different ages, including children,” Dr Munoz added.

“Some contain a single person, while others were used for collective burial, with further individuals placed in the chamber as deaths occurred.

“The presence of children alongside adults suggests that some of these groups may have shared family ties, although this alone cannot establish kinship.”

Adding to the suggestion that there was not heavy social stratification is the fact that substantially larger homes that could have housed an elite have not been found.

However, it is possible, Dr Munoz said, that there were differences in social status that had not left any archaeological traces.

Rather than indicating the size of the population at any time, the abundance of tombs suggests that people lived in or regularly visited the region over a long period, Dr Munoz said.

The French Archaeological Mission to Central Oman, working at Bisya, is directed by Mathilde Jean of the Universite Paris Nanterre and Martin Sauvage of the CNRS Arscan Lab.

Dr Munoz said there were similarities between the finds at Bisya and discoveries elsewhere, including at sites in the UAE.

“The beads discovered at Bisya, for example, have parallels at Hili, Jebel Hafit and Umm an-Nar, in what is now the UAE,” she said.

“The tomb architecture, likewise, belongs to traditions found across the Oman peninsula and, more broadly, elsewhere in the Arabian Peninsula.

“These similarities point to a shared culture, reflected in common knowledge, practices and tastes, as well as exchanges of goods between communities.”

However, such links do not indicate, Dr Munoz said, that there were direct connections between Bisya and other sites or that the communities were part of a single political identity.

“Rather, they point to communities with much in common, but also with local ways of life and probably their own networks of contacts and exchange,” she added.

Dr Munoz said that objects deposited with the dead offered clues about craftsmanship, personal adornment and exchange.

“For example, a shark tooth and hundreds of marine-shell beads found in one of the tombs point to contact with the coast,” she said.

Also, imported pottery shows there were trading links that extended much further afield, to Mesopotamia, Iran and Balochistan, an historical region that covers parts of present-day Iran, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

“These finds show that inland communities participated in wider networks through which objects, materials and potentially ideas circulated, alongside foodstuffs or other products that may have been transported in pottery vessels,” Dr Munoz said.

Copper was a likely export, as during the Bronze Age the Oman peninsula was an important copper producer.

Dried or salted fish, animal hides, dates and other palm products, worked shell ornaments and stone used for vessels or sculpture may also have been exported.

Imports were probably equally varied, Dr Munoz said, with communities possibly obtaining textiles, grain, oils and other foodstuffs from Mesopotamia, and timber, textiles and ornaments from the Indus region, which straddles present-day Pakistan and India.

“Some of these products leave little archaeological trace,” she said. “Pottery survives much better, but a vessel may have travelled because of what it contained, rather than because someone wanted the pot itself.”

The presence of imported vessels at Bisya does not necessarily indicate that someone from there travelled to the place of manufacture, as the object could, Dr Munoz said, have reached a coastal settlement by boat and passed through several hands before arriving inland.

“Merchants and markets may have played a part, with goods moving between major settlements and then being distributed more locally,” she said.

At this time dromedary camels had not been domesticated, so goods may have been carried by people, donkeys or cattle.

While the tombs have yielded a wealth of fascinating information, some aspects of life remain tantalisingly out of reach in the absence of written records.

For example, Dr Munoz said it was difficult to reconstruct symbolic beliefs and political organisation from thousands of years ago.

body_text:
Iran's ambassador to Baghdad on Tuesday said Iraq has agreed to either expel Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in the Kurdistan region or hand them over to Tehran.

The claim by Mohammad Al Sadegh came after he had attended a meeting of the Iraq-Iran joint security committee in Baghdad on Monday. Qasim Al Aboudi, the National Security Adviser, led the Iraqi delegation, which also featured representatives of the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region.

In a statement on X, Mr Al Sadegh said both sides had agreed “to remove elements of Iranian separatist terrorist groups from the Kurdistan region of Iraq or hand them over to Iran”.

There was no immediate comment from the Iraqi government or the Kurdistan region, nor from Mr Al Aboudi.

An official Iraqi readout of the meeting said both sides had discussed implementing the joint security agreement and the “outstanding files and problems”, and identified the “appropriate solutions”.

The apparent deal came only days after Iraq's parliament endorsed Yassir Al Maliki, the son-in-law of the pro-Iran State of Law Coalition leader and former prime minister Nouri Al Maliki, as Interior Minister.

Iraq and Iran signed a bilateral security agreement in March 2023, under which Baghdad committed to disarming Iranian Kurdish opposition groups and relocating them from the border area, and preventing Iraqi territory from being used to launch attacks on Iran.

'My soul is Iraqi, my heart is Emirati': Iraqi community comes together in celebration in Dubai

Groups such as the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran, Komala, the Free Life Party of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Freedom Party were to hand over their heavy weapons and move to camps farther from the border. Iraqi officials said at the time families would be relocated to five designated camps in the Kurdistan region while the UN refugee agency would process asylum claims.

The groups, some of which have been based in northern Iraq since the 1980s – after the Islamic Revolution and during the Iran-Iraq war – are seeking greater rights for Iran's Kurdish minority. Tehran accuses them of terrorism and of fuelling unrest, such as the 2022 protests that followed the death of Mahsa Amini.

In a sign of growing pressure on Baghdad and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region, over the presence of these groups, Nechirvan Barzani, President of Kurdistan Region, said last week: “Unfortunately, the [Iranian] Kurdish opposition forces acted in a highly irresponsible manner and placed the Kurdistan region in an extremely difficult position.

“An armed force cannot view the Kurdistan region as a safe haven and then operate from its territory to threaten a neighbouring country,” he said, in reference to reports that the groups were planning to move into Iran, with US backing.

Implementation of the security agreement has been uneven. Baghdad says it has moved fighters from border areas and closed some headquarters, while Tehran has repeatedly called the measures insufficient and continued to carry out drone and missile strikes on opposition camps in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah provinces.

Expelling these groups or handing them over to Iran would mark a significant hardening of Iraq's position if confirmed, raising legal and humanitarian questions given that thousands of Iranian Kurdish refugees live in Iraq, most in the Kurdistan region.

The Kurdistan Regional Government has previously opposed forced return, calling for a peaceful resolution that respects Iraq's constitution, which bars armed groups from threatening neighbours, while also protecting refugee rights.

headline: Britain says it will carry out defensive air missions over Saudi Arabia
summary: LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Britain will fly Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks, the Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday.The ministry said the aircraft would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Iran-aligned Houthis, whose attacks Britain says threaten regional stability and risk disrupting energy supplies and trade routes.
body_text:
LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Britain will fly Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets on defensive missions to help protect Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure from Houthi aerial attacks, the Ministry of Defence said on Tuesday.

The ministry said the aircraft would operate only in a defensive role and would not conduct offensive strikes against the Iran-aligned Houthis, whose attacks Britain says threaten regional stability and risk disrupting energy supplies and trade routes.

"The continuing attacks from the Houthis on our ally Saudi Arabia are absolutely despicable. The targeting of the airport in Riyadh in particular shows the lengths the Houthis are going to escalate the situation in the region," defence minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.

"That’s why today I have approved further UK military support. RAF Typhoons will fly defensive air missions to help protect Saudi airspace from drones and missiles."

The additional support follows a request from Saudi Arabia's government, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said earlier this month Britain was prepared to consider.

Britain will also deploy an Atlas A400M transport aircraft and military advisers, expanding assistance announced in September which included an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft but not fighter jets.

Houthi attacks against Saudi oil facilities and other infrastructure have intensified in recent weeks as the conflict in Yemen has escalated.

Inside Yemen, authorities said a Houthi strike on Monday against a training camp for Saudi-backed government security forces killed 58 people.

(Reporting by Sam Tabahriti; Editing by William James, Aidan Lewis)

body_text:
Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, has arrived in Tehran with an official delegation to meet senior Iranian officials, amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the war between Iran and the US.

Field Marshal Munir is in the Iranian capital to discuss efforts to resolve the conflict and broader regional developments, the official Irna news agency reported. Islamabad has played a central role in mediating talks between Washington and Tehran, maintaining close contact with both sides.

Qatar, another mediator in the conflict, said on Tuesday that communication between Iran and the US has "not stopped" and the aim was to reach a solution "as soon as possible”.

Araghchi says Iran sees 'no military solution' to Middle East crisis

But Ibrahim Al Hashmi, media director at Qatar’s Foreign Ministry, warned that threats to cut internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz, along with dangers caused by sea mines and oil spills, would harm regional countries, including Iran, and urged Tehran to respect freedom of navigation and environmental protections.

His statement comes after Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said regional undersea cables, data centres and AI sites could be attacked if hostilities with the US resume.

Field Marshal Munir’s visit came as Reuters quoted Iranian officials as saying Tehran had been deliberately prolonging negotiations with Washington to weaken US President Donald Trump politically before November’s midterm elections, while preparing for possible renewed military action.

“Iran is preparing for renewed Israeli and US attacks, not for a deal with America to end the war,” one Iranian official was quoted as saying. “The clerical establishment is determined not to give Trump a political victory.”

The same report quoted Iranian officials as saying there was little prospect of a breakthrough before the November 3 vote.

Tehran wants its conditions for ending hostilities and reopening the strait to be met before nuclear negotiations begin.

Iran has proposed reopening the vital waterway within seven days under its control, in exchange for the lifting of the US maritime blockade, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports, the release of frozen assets and an end to hostilities on all fronts.

The deadlock comes as Iran’s economy faces mounting pressure from sanctions and the blockade. Shipping through the strait remains severely disrupted.

Iranian hardline news agency Fars suggested Field Marshal Munir’s visit was linked to rising oil prices, reporting that the trip had appeared unlikely to happen as late as Sunday, but his trip was finalised on Monday afternoon as the price of crude approached $110 a barrel.

A source told Fars that previous visits by mediators had helped to lower oil prices, but had produced no significant progress in negotiations.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that Tehran’s proposal remained on the table and that messages continued to be exchanged through mediators.

The Reuters report also said Tehran believed US and Israeli attacks could resume, despite Mr Trump saying Washington would not strike Iran again before November 3.

The officials said Tehran’s distrust of Washington had deepened after previous attacks that derailed diplomatic efforts, including strikes in June 2025 and the launch of the war in February, shortly after another round of talks ended.

The threat of renewed military action extends to Pickaxe Mountain, a deeply buried site near Natanz nuclear complex. Tehran has warned that any US attack on the site would lead to retaliation.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei dismissed claims Washington could strike the site without facing a response, describing the idea as “nothing more than a claim”.

“Do you believe Iran would say ‘strike’ and we would remain silent?” Mr Baghaei said. He added that “the era of hitting and running is over”.

He said Iran would not leave any attack unanswered and warned the US would suffer a blow at least equal in magnitude to any strike it carried out.

Mr Trump has threatened a possible strike on Pickaxe Mountain, where Iran is building a heavily fortified underground facility whose precise purpose remains unclear.

headline: Russia’s Shnaider clears opening round of 2026 WTA Ningbo Open tennis tournament
summary: Diana Shnaider is now set to play in the next round against Alexandra Eala from the Philippines
body_text:
BEIJING, October 20. /TASS/. Russia’s tennis star Diana Shnaider cleared the opening round of the 2026 Ningbo Open tournament in China by defeating on Tuesday Yulia Putintseva from Kazakhsta.

In the match that lasted for 2 hours 26 minutes the 6th-seeded Russian, who is playing under a neutral status at the tournament, defeated unseeded Putintseva 7-5; 7-6 (7-4) and is now set to play in the next round against Alexandra Eala from the Philippines.

Shnaider, 22, is currently ranked 13th in the WTA Rankings. She holds five WTA titles. Her best result in Grand Slams was reaching the semis at 2026 French Open. At the 2024 Summer Olympic Games in Paris, she captured a silver medal in women’s doubles with partner Mirra Andreeva.

The 2026 Ningbo Open is the WTA 500 class tournament played on hard courts at the Yinzhou Tennis Center in China on October 19-25 and it offers $1.2 million in prize money. Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina is the tournament’s reigning champion.

On February 28, 2022, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) issued recommendations to international sports federations to exclude athletes from Russia and Belarus from taking part in international tournaments, citing Moscow's special military operation in Ukraine as the reason.

Following the IOC's recommendations in late February 2022, the majority of global sports federations decided to exclude athletes from Russia and Belarus from all international sports tournaments.

The International Tennis Federation (ITF) ruled on March 1, 2022 to suspend the membership of the Russian and Belarusian national tennis federations while also scrapping all previously scheduled tennis tournaments in the two countries.

On March 14, 2022, the ITF also confirmed its prohibition on the Russian and Belarusian national tennis teams from taking part in the 2022 Davis Cup and 2022 Billie Jean King Cup.

headline: Potential US-Russia-China summit would be 'very positive thing for world': Rubio
summary: US secretary of state backs leader-level talks on arms control, saying communication between major nuclear powers can help make world safer
body_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that a potential summit involving the leaders of the US, Russia and China would be "a very positive thing for the world."

"I think there's an opportunity, and the president (Donald Trump) expressed an openness to do it for the United States, Russia, and China at the leader level to have a conversation about things like arms control," Rubio told reporters in India.

He argued that communication among the three most powerful nuclear-armed nations was not "unusual."

Rubio rejected the argument that diplomatic engagement should be viewed as a reward, saying Trump does not consider talks with other countries a concession.

He described the ability to communicate with the opposing side as "the bottom line of diplomacy and negotiations."

Acknowledging that longstanding disagreements among the three countries would not disappear after a single summit, Rubio emphasized the importance of maintaining communication.

"I think the world is a safer place when the leaders of the most powerful nuclear arsenals in the world are at least communicating with one another," he said.

Rubio said that Beijing has historically avoided arms control discussions until its nuclear arsenal matched those of other major powers.

However, he said it was "a good thing" that the US has a president who was "willing to try."

His remarks followed Trump's statements Monday expressing openness to trilateral discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Trump said nuclear disarmament would be the main focus of such talks.

The proposal emerged after The Wall Street Journal reported Sunday that Putin had suggested holding a trilateral meeting next month to discuss ending the war in Ukraine.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that discussions were continuing, acknowledging the "hypothetical possibility" of such talks despite the absence of an agreed agenda.

headline: France imposes curfews after weekend violence, but is it too much or too little?
summary: PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 20: We look at reactions from the French press after President Emmanuel Macron's government announces a curfew in parts of the country. Is it too much or not enough? We also look at what the foreign press from Britain, Germany and the US are saying about the weekend's violence. Meanwhile, the Italian press react to violent looting and destruction of property in Italy as the government there mulls sending in 500 armed troops.
body_text:

Issued on: 20/10/2026 - 13:47Modified: 20/10/2026 - 13:52

PRESS REVIEW – Tuesday, October 20: We look at reactions from the French press after President Emmanuel Macron's government announces a curfew in parts of the country. Is it too much or not enough? We also look at what the foreign press from Britain, Germany and the US are saying about the weekend's violence. Meanwhile, the Italian press react to violent looting and destruction of property in Italy as the government there mulls sending in 500 armed troops.

French authorities have put curfews in place in certain areas of the country after a weekend of rioting overshadowed protests against the rising cost of living. For the left-wing press, the curfews are excessive. Embattled Interior Minister Laurent Nunez features on the front of Libération, the left-wing daily, which headlines disapprovingly "Nunez dans la nasse." La nasse is a reference to the restrictive perimeter imposed on protesters, who cannot come and go as they please. In its editorial, the paper says the weekend's events have announced the end of 10 years of Macron's governance. The daily laments that even the basic maintaining of law and order is now a "complicated thing for the president". The Communist daily L'Humanité accuses the government of creating an "impasse of repression." It says that for the past 10 years, the government has chosen a policy of using the baton, which has served to aggravate the gap between the French people and ruling powers.

La Croix, which tends to sit around the middle of the political spectrum, says that maintaining order is being put to the test. It explains that the way France has been policed since May 1968 is simple: a doctrine of "zero deaths". This means that police must always stay at a distance. With protesters promising new action this coming weekend, how can France maintain a balance between dissuasion and professional retaliation, it wonders? Le Figaro asks: "Why hasn't France declared a state of emergency and outlawed protests in the near future? What happened to the bill proposing that rioters be financially responsible for the damage caused to public property?" The conservative daily accuses the government of not doing enough.

In the international press, the British daily Metro sees the imposition of a curfew as a "French correction" – the paper quotes Macron as saying that France will not tolerate thieves or "extreme-left" thugs. An opinion piece in The New York Times sympathises with French students, who are "showing the rest of the world that the only way to march into a dark future is together." But it warns that their challenge is now to keep the violence at bay. In an excellent analysis, a Frankfurter Allgemeine writer argues that the hallmark of the high school protests was the "unusual solidarity" between students from impoverished suburban schools and schools in affluent neighbourhoods. It blames Macron's government for choosing a strategy of waiting it out until the autumn school holidays and ignoring their legitimate demands. It offers this sobering conclusion: "France cannot afford the necessary investments in the education of future generations as long as a majority of voters cling to early retirement and short working hours."

We turn next to Italy, where similar scenes of violence amid cost-of-living protests played out over the weekend. Demonstrators clashed with police, looted shops and vandalised property in Turin, Bologna and Milan. The Italian government will dispatch 500 army troops to defend Milan as part of security measures to be approved at a cabinet meeting this Tuesday. "Try to catch them", the Communist daily Il Manifesto says on its front page. Dozens of arrests, serious charges, ethnically targeted roundups – the paper disapproves of the government's new measures, which it says will also authorise indiscriminate detention. Il Riformista, another daily, evokes Italy's Russian October – presumably a reference to the Bolshevik uprising of 1917 that ended the Russian czar's reign. The right-wing, conservative Il Tempo evokes an "intifada" on the streets of Italy.

In other news, a black bear recently broke into a library, where it helped itself to the pantry cupboard! The Guardian reports that a black bear broke into a California library last week and reportedly raided snacks like peanut butter, cookies and a jar of honey. It spent more than four hours in the library, sniffing through new releases. In a moment of perfect literary timing, all of this happened as the library celebrated the 100th anniversary of the publication of a copy of "Winnie the Pooh"!

You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

headline: Duma member Andrey Lugovoy for closing UK embassy in Russia
summary: Andrey Lugovoy suggested doing this on December 14
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. First Deputy Chairman of the State Duma Committee on Security and Anti-Corruption Andrey Lugovoy has proposed closing the UK Embassy in Russia on December 14, 2026.

"I would like to address the Foreign Ministry. It is high time we closed the UK Embassy, I suggest doing this on the day the exhibition (of an international project titled Britlag - TASS) kicks off, on December 14, the International Day Against Colonialism in All Its Forms and Manifestations," Lugovoy told a plenary session of the State Duma.

Lugovoy also announced plans to visit the Solovetsky Stone in Moscow on October 30 to personally present the British ambassador with a souvenir: a figurine set depicting a scene from Vasily Vereshchagin’s painting The Suppression of the Indian Revolt by the English, which shows a British soldier executing a sepoy using the "devil’s wind" method (firing a cannonball through the body of a person tied to the muzzle of a cannon).

The lawmaker also suggested holding the Britlag exhibition dedicated to the victims of the British colonialism outside the UK Embassy and a contest for the best site for a Britlag monument in Moscow, London, New Delhi, Beijing, Kenya and Jamaica. Additionally, he called for an expert review of history textbooks to assess the extent to which they "reflect the colonial face of Britain."

Lugovoy emphasized that Russia should assist countries in Africa and the Caribbean in their work regarding reparations commissions, ensuring that Britain "pays its bills."

"The 'Britlag' project will provide our friends with a parliamentary platform. We will seek support from the Foreign Ministry and assist with archival research - the 'Britlag' library already contains over a thousand such records. We will also facilitate the preparation of legally substantiated claims; we have conducted in-depth analysis in this area and are ready to move forward," he noted.

headline: UN says 19 mn Afghans facing acute food insecurity by April
summary: The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Afghanistan is set to rise above 19 million during the forthcoming winter season, the United Nations warned on Tuesday. The food crisis gripping Afghanistan is projected to affect millions of young children in 2027, the United Nations' humanitarian agency OCHA said. More than four million babies and children under six will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year, it warned.
body_text:
The number of people facing acute food insecurity in Afghanistan is set to rise above 19 million during the forthcoming winter season, the United Nations warned on Tuesday.

The food crisis gripping Afghanistan is projected to affect millions of young children in 2027, the United Nations' humanitarian agency OCHA said.

More than four million babies and children under six will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year, it warned.

Between September and October, 15.9 million people -- or nearly one in three Afghans -- were facing food insecurity at crisis levels or worse, including 3.4 million in emergency conditions, the agency said.

The outlook is set to deteriorate further during the winter lean season from November to April.

"The number facing acute food insecurity is projected to rise to 19.2 million, of which five million are expected to face emergency levels of hunger," which is "one step away from famine", said OCHA's Afghanistan spokeswoman Olga Cherevko.

"We must act before winter, not after families have exhausted all the options.

"That means getting food assistance to

people in need, protecting livestock and productive assets, supporting farmers before critical planting windows close, and keeping essential health, nutrition and water services accessible."

The latest snapshot of the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification projects that more than four million children aged six months to five years old will need treatment for acute malnutrition next year.

"Over one million of these children are expected to suffer severe acute malnutrition," Cherevko told a press briefing in Geneva, speaking from Kabul.

"These numbers represent children whose parents cannot afford nutritious food and families whose ability to cope has been worn down by years of conflict, economic hardship, drought and other shocks."

In the midst of this hunger crisis, around one third of nutrition sites across the country have closed or have suspended services, "largely due to funding cuts".

"Once these services disappear, the consequences could be irreversible, particularly for children," Cherevko said

Afghanistan has seen a sharp decline in international aid since 2021, when the Taliban authorities returned to power.

They have imposed a severe version of Islamic law, including a series of rules limiting women's access to education and public life.

The Taliban government remains largely excluded from the international community, which criticises its repressive measures.

International aid to Afghanistan has dropped sharply, with the United Nations saying it had received less than 30 percent of the funding needed to provide life-saving assistance as of late August.

The humanitarian crisis has been further worsened by several natural disasters and the forced return of millions of Afghans from Iran and Pakistan since 2023.

Cherevko said humanitarian aid could save lives but it could not compensate indefinitely for the absence of economic opportunity and public services.

The food crisis in Afghanistan was not simply about whether the food was available but also about whether people could access and afford it, she said.

While better rainfall and agricultural production this year have helped, one good harvest "cannot undo the damage of several years of drought".

headline: (3rd LD) S. Korea to withdraw some embassy staff from Ukraine amid N.K. POW dispute
summary: SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic p...
body_text:
(ATTN: ADDS more details in paras 15-16)By Oh Seok-min

SEOUL, Oct. 20 (Yonhap) -- South Korea has decided to withdraw some diplomatic personnel from Ukraine amid an ongoing dispute over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul and persistent threats of airstrikes across the country, the foreign ministry said Tuesday.

The decision came as Ukraine has not taken "positive steps" to resolve the diplomatic dispute over Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the transfer of the North Korean POWs to Seoul, ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said at a regular press briefing.

Park also cited continued Russian airstrikes as another reason for the decision, saying they have made it difficult to ensure the safety of diplomatic personnel.

Despite the partial withdrawal, South Korea will maintain necessary diplomatic communications with Ukraine through its charge d'affaires, while all consular personnel will remain in the country to continue efforts to protect South Korean nationals there, the ministry said.

Seoul has demanded an official explanation, an apology and assurances against a recurrence after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly disclosed the transfer and his office subsequently denied that there had been an agreement to keep the matter confidential.

Kyiv, however, has yet to formally respond to Seoul's demands. In protest, South Korea recalled its ambassador to Ukraine, Park Ki-chang, earlier this month.

"We had conveyed our position to Ukraine through various channels. But Ukraine had taken no positive steps despite those efforts," Park said, calling for "sincere and positive steps" in response to Seoul's previous requests.

Noting that the two countries remain in communication, the spokesperson said Seoul's goal was to "seek an amicable resolution through close consultations with the Ukrainian side."

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun has said the two nations had agreed from the outset to keep the matter confidential to protect the soldiers and their families, who remain in North Korea. He also said Ukraine had initially requested that the matter not be made public.

Cho said he had personally received a message from Sybiha that included an apology but fell short of Seoul's expectations.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said, following South Korea's recall of its ambassador, that he considered the controversy "a closed matter," according to foreign media reports.

The two soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia in the Kursk region and arrived in South Korea in mid-September, officials here said.

The ministry said the South Korean Embassy in Ukraine will continue measures to ensure the safety of South Koreans in Ukraine by providing safety updates and offering assistance to those wishing to evacuate.

The ministry declined to confirm the exact number of diplomatic personnel to be withdrawn, but officials said roughly half of the staff would leave Ukraine.

The ministry also said it will urge South Korean nationals in Ukraine to evacuate as soon as possible and help those wishing to leave reach neighboring countries safely before or at the time of the diplomatic personnel's withdrawal.

The embassy plans to ask some 85 South Korean nationals currently in Ukraine whether they wish to evacuate as it conducts daily safety checks Tuesday. The exact timing of the staff's withdrawal has yet to be determined.

"We will coordinate with the embassy to find the safest and most effective means of assisting South Koreans who wish to evacuate," Park said.

A Level 4 travel advisory, the highest level, remains in effect across Ukraine, where the threat of indiscriminate missile and drone attacks has recently increased.

On Monday, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles and more than 200 drones in overnight attacks, damaging energy infrastructure and leaving more than 500,000 households without power, according to foreign media reports.
