headline: Turkey sends Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to parliament for ratification
summary: Ankara is weighing military assistance to Riyadh as Houthi attacks intensify, though any Turkish deployment is expected to be limited.
body_text:
ANKARA — Turkey submitted the Mecca defense agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to parliament for ratification on Tuesday, a step toward potentially deploying troops to the kingdom amid ongoing attacks by Iran-backed Houthis.

Details: The agreement was submitted to parliament early Tuesday, according to Turkish state broadcaster TRT.

The agreement will first be debated and voted on by the Turkish parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee. If approved, it will proceed to a full parliamentary vote on ratification.

As of this writing, the committee had not set a date for the debate, leaving it unclear when the agreement might come up for a full parliamentary vote.

The deal is expected to win approval in both the committee and the General Assembly, where Erdogan’s ruling alliance holds a majority.

The submission comes as Houthi attacks on the kingdom intensify. The Iran-backed group carried out its deadliest attack on the kingdom on Oct. 10, when a strike on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 12 people and wounded more than 300.

Background: On Aug. 7, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed an agreement under which an attack on one member is treated as an attack on all.

The escalation in Houthi attacks since early October has renewed attention to the agreement and prompted the three countries to step up efforts to implement it.

Following emergency talks in Riyadh on Oct. 5, the three countries’ foreign and defense ministers, along with their military chiefs, agreed “to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.”

Why it matters: Ratification would pave the way for Turkey to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia amid attacks by Iran-backed Houthis.

Still, any Turkish deployment is likely to be limited to training, advisory services and military equipment support rather than a large troop contingent, according to Turkish officials who briefed Al-Monitor in recent weeks.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Oct. 8 that Turkey’s support would be defensive, in line with the agreement. “Turkey will not send troops to another country’s territory to carry out an attack there,” he said, referring to Yemen.

headline: Fadi El Khatib on opening new wellness hub Club 15: 'This is my thank you to Dubai'
summary: When the unexpected strikes, it’s hard to predict how one will react. Some freeze, others make impulsive decisions, and a few choose optimism. Fewer still decide that it’s the perfect time to launch an ambitious wellness venture as a bid for community and connection.But that is exactly what ran through Fadi El Khatib’s mind earlier this year, just weeks after the Iran war began on February 28.“The belief in the city and the country,” says Khatib when asked why he decided to open Club 15. The former professional basketball player-turned-entrepreneur, whose career spanned more than 25 years as he played for clubs across Lebanon, as well as Syria, Ukraine and China, had the idea to create a “sports city within a city” in March this year. Just a month later, the ball started rolling on the project.The doors to Club 15, a 15,000-square-metre sports and lifestyle destination in Dubai's Al Quoz area, opened for its soft launch on Monday. For those seeking movement, they can look to the hub's seven professional padel courts, three full-sized basketball courts, a two-storey, 5,700 sqm gym, Reformer Pilates and studio spaces and a 25-metre semi-Olympic swimming pool. Recovery is added with ice baths and infrared sauna facilities. There is also a rooftop training space and an on-site physiotherapy clinic. At the time of writing, membership models and prices were still being finalised. However, El Khatib says attainability is important to him in more ways than one. Namely, making sure the set-up he has created is convenient for families. His vision is for Club 15 to be the kind of destination where families can move seamlessly through the day together.“I want to encourage parents to go and work out. Because I know the hassle of any parent is: where do I put my kid?” says El Khatib. Club 15 also includes social and workspaces, a gaming lounge, a podcast studio, kids' facilities, gymnastics and parkour, with youth academies also forming part of the project. The idea itself was born within his family, as 15 was El Khatib's jersey number throughout his professional career. Today, the number has also taken on significance within his four children – sons Jihad, Hadi and Joud, and daughter Joury.“My eldest boy is an NBA prospect carrying the national team with number 15,” he says. Jihad El Khatib plays as a forward for Club Centrale Al Markaziyyah (also known as Central Club) in the Lebanese Basketball League and represents the Lebanese national team.“My other son is playing pro wearing number 15,” he says. “Joud, who plays with Champs, is wearing number 15. My daughter is also wearing number 15.” When his family moved to the UAE earlier in the year, following unrest in Lebanon, they sat together discussing how much the number meant to each of them personally. “It's very emotional … so it's a continuation of the number, and it brought my family together.”When The National visits on the soft launch opening day, it's still very much a work in progress. Although many of the workout spaces are functional – El Khatib joins us fresh from a competitive game of padel – the on-site Joe and the Juice cafe isn't ready to open yet, there is still some red tape around certain areas, and the softer furnishings are lacking. Future additions will include a cycling and running track, he tells us, alongside installing red-light panels in the Pilates studio and equipment that would allow the yoga studio to host heated classes.“My career was based on gym, swimming and hot power yoga,” he says. “Yoga with heat is a real workout. It gives more mobility and flexibility so you stretch more, which causes soreness the next day. It's one of the best things I've ever done.”While padel is his latest love, his career – which earned him the nickname the "Lebanese Tiger" – was built on the basketball court before he moved into the business realm of fitness, founding Champs Sports Club and expanding the brand across the UAE.Members can expect to see El Khatib in just about every corner of the site. He even jokes about building an apartment on the rooftop. Although he's happy to try everything, doing too much is where people go wrong.“People are overdoing things,” he says. “Anyone not experienced enough in wellness gets messed up trying everything because of trends on Instagram or social media. Keep it simple, study your body, don't overdo things just to follow trends.”In a world always searching for AI cheats and biohacking solutions, El Khatib says nothing can replace the “old school” method of hitting the gym, using the machines, and picking up the dumbbells. “You will never be able to replace this.”They're lessons learnt from a long career in the fitness industry. But his biggest lesson has been the value of grit. “Basketball gave me the mental toughness and the will. You'll face hurdles, obstacles, challenges. Keep going, keep chasing your goals. Never stop.”That perhaps explains why Club 15 was born in what has undoubtedly been a challenging year for businesses in Dubai. For El Khatib, it is his thank you to the city – and all he wants to hear from members walking out the door is a thank you in return.“I don't call Dubai a hotel,” says El Khatib. “When things happen, you don't pack your things and move out. You keep on developing, sending messages to people all around the world.”
body_text:
When the unexpected strikes, it’s hard to predict how one will react. Some freeze, others make impulsive decisions, and a few choose optimism. Fewer still decide that it’s the perfect time to launch an ambitious wellness venture as a bid for community and connection.

But that is exactly what ran through Fadi El Khatib’s mind earlier this year, just weeks after the Iran war began on February 28.

“The belief in the city and the country,” says Khatib when asked why he decided to open Club 15.

The rise of the modern wellness club

The former professional basketball player-turned-entrepreneur, whose career spanned more than 25 years as he played for clubs across Lebanon, as well as Syria, Ukraine and China, had the idea to create a “sports city within a city” in March this year. Just a month later, the ball started rolling on the project.

The doors to Club 15, a 15,000-square-metre sports and lifestyle destination in Dubai's Al Quoz area, opened for its soft launch on Monday.

For those seeking movement, they can look to the hub's seven professional padel courts, three full-sized basketball courts, a two-storey, 5,700 sqm gym, Reformer Pilates and studio spaces and a 25-metre semi-Olympic swimming pool. Recovery is added with ice baths and infrared sauna facilities. There is also a rooftop training space and an on-site physiotherapy clinic.

At the time of writing, membership models and prices were still being finalised. However, El Khatib says attainability is important to him in more ways than one. Namely, making sure the set-up he has created is convenient for families. His vision is for Club 15 to be the kind of destination where families can move seamlessly through the day together.

“I want to encourage parents to go and work out. Because I know the hassle of any parent is: where do I put my kid?” says El Khatib. Club 15 also includes social and workspaces, a gaming lounge, a podcast studio, kids' facilities, gymnastics and parkour, with youth academies also forming part of the project.

The idea itself was born within his family, as 15 was El Khatib's jersey number throughout his professional career. Today, the number has also taken on significance within his four children – sons Jihad, Hadi and Joud, and daughter Joury.

“My eldest boy is an NBA prospect carrying the national team with number 15,” he says. Jihad El Khatib plays as a forward for Club Centrale Al Markaziyyah (also known as Central Club) in the Lebanese Basketball League and represents the Lebanese national team.

“My other son is playing pro wearing number 15,” he says. “Joud, who plays with Champs, is wearing number 15. My daughter is also wearing number 15.”

When his family moved to the UAE earlier in the year, following unrest in Lebanon, they sat together discussing how much the number meant to each of them personally. “It's very emotional … so it's a continuation of the number, and it brought my family together.”

When The National visits on the soft launch opening day, it's still very much a work in progress. Although many of the workout spaces are functional – El Khatib joins us fresh from a competitive game of padel – the on-site Joe and the Juice cafe isn't ready to open yet, there is still some red tape around certain areas, and the softer furnishings are lacking.

Future additions will include a cycling and running track, he tells us, alongside installing red-light panels in the Pilates studio and equipment that would allow the yoga studio to host heated classes.

“My career was based on gym, swimming and hot power yoga,” he says. “Yoga with heat is a real workout. It gives more mobility and flexibility so you stretch more, which causes soreness the next day. It's one of the best things I've ever done.”

While padel is his latest love, his career – which earned him the nickname the "Lebanese Tiger" – was built on the basketball court before he moved into the business realm of fitness, founding Champs Sports Club and expanding the brand across the UAE.

Members can expect to see El Khatib in just about every corner of the site. He even jokes about building an apartment on the rooftop. Although he's happy to try everything, doing too much is where people go wrong.

“People are overdoing things,” he says. “Anyone not experienced enough in wellness gets messed up trying everything because of trends on Instagram or social media. Keep it simple, study your body, don't overdo things just to follow trends.”

In a world always searching for AI cheats and biohacking solutions, El Khatib says nothing can replace the “old school” method of hitting the gym, using the machines, and picking up the dumbbells. “You will never be able to replace this.”

They're lessons learnt from a long career in the fitness industry. But his biggest lesson has been the value of grit. “Basketball gave me the mental toughness and the will. You'll face hurdles, obstacles, challenges. Keep going, keep chasing your goals. Never stop.”

That perhaps explains why Club 15 was born in what has undoubtedly been a challenging year for businesses in Dubai. For El Khatib, it is his thank you to the city – and all he wants to hear from members walking out the door is a thank you in return.

“I don't call Dubai a hotel,” says El Khatib. “When things happen, you don't pack your things and move out. You keep on developing, sending messages to people all around the world.”

Nepal has banned Priyagold biscuits after an emergency virtual meeting, days after the Indian food regulator cancelled the licence and launched legal action against the cookie maker.

headline: Death toll from Houthi attack on Yemen training camp rises to 73
summary: Oct 20 (Reuters) - An attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on a government security forces training camp in Shabwa province killed 73 people, the provincial media office said, raising the toll from Monday's strike as fighting intensifies.Fourteen people remained missing, it added.The Iran-aligned Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised government, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have traded attacks since September when the group advanced towards territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth.
body_text:
Oct 20 (Reuters) - An attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on a government security forces training camp in Shabwa province killed 73 people, the provincial media office said, raising the toll from Monday's strike as fighting intensifies.

Fourteen people remained missing, it added.

The Iran-aligned Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognised government, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, have traded attacks since September when the group advanced towards territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth.

Local authorities said three ballistic missiles hit security forces on Monday during training. Reuters-verified video showed injured people and bloodied bodies scattered on the ground.

More than 200 people were injured, according to provincial governor Awad al-Wazir.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the camp was run by Saudi forces. Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Yemeni government forces began a campaign this month to retake Houthi-held areas, recovering ground near the strait. The Houthis are besieging Taiz, the last major urban stronghold of anti-Houthi forces in Yemen's southern highlands.

The conflict has become another front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran, with Houthi attacks targeting Riyadh's international airport and Saudi Aramco in Saudi Arabia, the world's largest crude exporter.

Shabwa, an energy-rich coastal province overlooking the Gulf of Aden, hosts the Balhaf liquefied natural gas facility, Yemen's largest industrial investment.

Yemen's war began with the Houthi seizure of Sanaa in 2014, which drove the government south. A Saudi-led intervention in 2015 produced a bloody stalemate before a 2022 truce that held until this year.

Aid agencies warn of rapidly deteriorating conditions in what is already one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.

(Reporting by Mohammed Ghobari; Writing by Tala Ramadan; Editing by Andrew Cawthorne)

headline: Qatar warns Hormuz cable disruption would hit region hardest, urges peaceful U.S.-Iran resolution
summary: During Tuesday’s weekly press briefing at MoFA, Ibrahim Al Hashmi said that countries across the region rely on the Strait of Hormuz’s waters for irrigation, salt production and fisheries, warning…
body_text:
During Tuesday’s weekly press briefing at MoFA, Ibrahim Al Hashmi said that countries across the region rely on the Strait of Hormuz’s waters for irrigation, salt production and fisheries, warning that damage could threaten water security.

Qatar has said any disruption to undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz would affect countries across the region, including Iran, and called for attacks and threats targeting the waterway to stop immediately.

Ibrahim Al Hashmi, director of the Media and Communications Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MoFA), said at Tuesday’s weekly press briefing that countries in the region, including Iran, would bear the greatest impact of any disruption to undersea cables.

“If someone on the Iranian side reflected honestly on the situation, they would ask: who is the biggest victim?” Al Hashmi asserted.

The MoFA spokesperson added that neither the United States nor Israel would suffer the greatest impact, but countries across the region, including Iran.

“Will it be the United States? Will it be Israel, which does not benefit from the Gulf’s waters? Or will it be the countries in the region, including the Iranian people?”

The remarks follow an earlier warning from Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, who warned that cables, data centres and artificial intelligence (AI) facilities across the region could be attacked if war with the United States erupts again.

The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia.

Fighting is under way between Yemen’s internationally recognised government and the Houthis at several locations, including Bab al-Mandeb, through which nearly one-fifth of global internet traffic passes.

Al Hashmi said countries across the region rely on the Strait of Hormuz’s waters for irrigation, salt production and fisheries, warning that damage could threaten water security.

“Water security in the Strait of Hormuz is an integral part of water security for our region and our people,” he said, adding that Iran had a responsibility to protect the waters, uphold international law on freedom of navigation and preserve the marine environment.

He called for the “irresponsible attacks” to stop immediately, warning that they harmed people across the region.

Al Hashmi reiterated Qatar’s commitment to mediating the US-Iran crisis, stressing that a peaceful resolution is the only way to preserve regional stability.

He said mediators must remain optimistic and continue working tirelessly to reach an agreement as soon as possible.

“We hope that the solution will be tomorrow, or today, as soon as possible,” Al Hashmi said. “Therefore, we must remain optimistic and work tirelessly and relentlessly to reach a solution.”

Al Hashmi said it was unacceptable for mediators to give in to despair or consider military action a viable solution, warning against further escalation.

“We must be focused on a peaceful solution at the negotiating table,” he said. “It is the only solution that preserves the region and its stability. And we must work towards that with every possible effort.”

Iran’s seven-day proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was conveyed through Qatari mediators, with Tehran seeking an end to the U.S. maritime blockade, sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets.

headline: Iraq buries dozens of security personnel killed by IS
summary: Iraq held a mass funeral on Tuesday for 47 members of the security forces who were executed by the Islamic State group a decade ago and whose remains were found in a mass grave. Many remain missing after disappearing during the jihadist group's bloody rule over parts of Iraq from 2014 to 2017, with the United Nations estimating that there may be more than 200 graves containing up to 12,000 people killed in mass executions. body_text:
Iraq held a mass funeral on Tuesday for 47 members of the security forces who were executed by the Islamic State group a decade ago and whose remains were found in a mass grave.

Many remain missing after disappearing during the jihadist group's bloody rule over parts of Iraq from 2014 to 2017, with the United Nations estimating that there may be more than 200 graves containing up to 12,000 people killed in mass executions.

Iraqi authorities continue to uncover new graves, which are concentrated in urban areas.

In a square in the northern city of Mosul, the heart of former IS territory, photos of the deceased were on display as members of the security forces carried their coffins draped in the Iraqi flag.

The 47 people were killed by the jihadists in 2016, Dhurgham Kamel, deputy director general of the Department of Mass Graves and the Missing, told AFP.

They were found in two separate mass graves at the Hamam al-Alil area around 20 kilometres (12 miles) south of Mosul.

"Grief hangs over us," said university lecturer Ibrahim al-Jubouri, aged 46, who received the remains of his cousin. He said the grief was fresh, even a decade after his cousin's death.

IS jihadists swept through eastern Syria and northern Iraq in 2014, threatening to reach Baghdad before being driven back.

A US-led coalition intervened in the war, helping Iraqi forces to defeat IS territorially by late 2017.

Jubouri said the government was too slow in tracking down the missing, given it was years since Baghdad declared IS defeated.

The state has also been uncovering mass graves that date back to the rule of Saddam Hussein, who dominated Iraq for decades before being overthrown in the US-led invasion of 2003.

Since 2006, they have found around 290 mass graves, according to the state-run Martyrs Foundation.

headline: UAE and France deepen defence ties with Rafale F5 fighter-jet deal
summary: Defence co-operation is among the areas covered by a series of agreements signed by the UAE and France as the two countries look to bolster ties amid geopolitical uncertainty triggered by the Iran war.They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi.The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties.Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations.The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group, a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella.The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war.Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit.Edge, set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare.The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency.Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement.The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space.The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons.Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French Defence co-operation is among the areas covered by a series of agreements signed by the UAE and France as the two countries look to bolster ties amid geopolitical uncertainty triggered by the Iran war.

They signed an intergovernmental agreement for co-operation on the Dassault Rafale F5 standard within the French and Emirati Rafale programmes during the visit of French President Emmanuel Macron to Abu Dhabi.

The agreements also cover technical and financial specifications for industrial co-operation between the two countries on the future of combat aviation, as France and the UAE strengthen defence ties.

France seeks stronger UAE ties before investment event in Paris

Another agreement focuses on strategic autonomy in defence and reducing dependence on third countries as part of a strategic defence partnership between the two nations.

The latest agreements come as the UAE, the Arab world's second-largest economy, focuses on localising defence manufacturing through Edge Group, a defence conglomerate with more than 35 companies under its umbrella.

The group has played a key role in countering Iranian drones directed at the UAE during the war.

Mr Macron visited an Edge Group industrial site during his visit.

Edge, set up in 2019, specialises in developing advanced technology for weapons systems, cyber protection and electronic warfare.

The group maintains several industrial partnerships with French companies and recently signed a co-operation agreement with the French Defence Procurement Agency.

Mr Macron's visit “reflects a shared commitment to strengthening industrial and technological co-operation and developing joint projects”, the Elysee Palace said in a statement.

The French Defence Ministry also signed an agreement with the UAE to enhance interoperability between the two armed forces, strengthen industrial resilience and advance co-operation in future-orientated technology, including artificial intelligence and space.

The latest agreements come as Abu Dhabi is preparing to host the International Defence Exhibition and Conference (Idex) in January, an event expected to attract hundreds of defence companies from across the globe to showcase their latest high-tech weapons.

Mr Macron then headed to Bahrain, where French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif Al Zayani, agreed to bolster co-operation on the “peaceful uses of nuclear energy”, the French government said.

France and Bahrain signed a defence co-operation agreement in February during a visit to Paris by Bahrain's King Hamad bin Isa. The UAE and Bahrain were among the Gulf countries France helped protect with air defence and anti-drone assets during Iranian attacks this year.

France has also co-operated closely with Bahrain at the UN Security Council to find a diplomatic solution to Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

The UAE and France signed new deals in energy, AI and advanced technology as the two countries seek to strengthen investment and economic ties.

The preliminary agreements were signed in the presence of Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, and Mr Macron in Abu Dhabi.

In AI and advanced technology, three agreements were signed with France's AI start-up AMI Labs to strengthen research and technological co-operation and explore new applications across several key sectors, according to the Abu Dhabi Media Office.

The deals involve Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI), Abu Dhabi's G42 and computing company Analog.

MBZUAI will focus on strengthening co-operation with AMI Labs in AI research and development, while G42 aims to establish a framework for strategic co-operation in cloud computing infrastructure and AI models.

Analog's deal with AMI Labs focuses on exploring opportunities to integrate AI models into robotics and physical AI applications, creating new avenues for developing intelligent systems and expanding their use in industrial and technology sectors.

The UAE and France will also boost co-operation in the energy sector, with Adnoc Gas and Schneider Electric signing an initial pact to assess advanced technologies and identify opportunities to enhance operational efficiency and improve the performance of energy systems.

Adnoc Refining and Technip Energies also signed two contracts covering a refining capacity enhancement project and a sustainable aviation fuel project.

In his opening remarks at the UAE-France Business Dialogue at Qasr Al Watan in Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled underscored the importance of bilateral co-operation in ensuring reliable energy supplies and building resilient supply chains amid changes in the global economy.

The UAE and France have strong economic ties, with more than 600 French businesses currently operating in the UAE and $4 billion worth of goods exported annually from France to the UAE, according to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website.

UAE investments are also growing in France. In 2021, UAE-based Gulf Islamic Investments made a $301 million investment in Altais Towers, while Abu Dhabi's Mubadala Investment Company signed an initial agreement with Bpifrance, committing to invest €1 billion ($1.12 billion) in the LAC1 Fund, a €10 billion fund managed by Bpifrance.

body_text:
In a week’s time, Israelis will head to the polls in what many are calling the most important election in its history.

Despite the usual ups and downs of the Israeli news cycle, polls have remained largely stable for months: neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor that of his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, is near a majority.

Israeli voters are bracing themselves. There is a widespread feeling that this polling stalemate in such a divided country, combined with regional tension and hostility, could make for a busy week.

The average of the past three surveys conducted by Israel’s mainstream pollsters puts Mr Eisenkot on 52 seats, one ahead of Mr Netanyahu.

That means 17 unaligned seats are up for grabs, fuelling speculation that the next government will be formed after coalition negotiations, which could take months.

If there is no agreement on a coalition, another election will be held. This has happened many times in Israel’s recent history.

However, the election results could be decisive. Opinion polls are far from foolproof, and in any case not all indicate a stalemate. A smaller group of less mainstream surveys published by right-wing news channels place Mr Netanyahu’s bloc in a better position, with Channel 14 forecasting a one-seat majority in a poll on Sunday. It still charts a gradual decline in support for the coalition over recent weeks.

Many voters are highlighting Mr Netanyahu's formidable ability as a politician. His talent for creating unlikely coalitions and undermining opponents is clear.

Israel’s military is on high alert, and there are fears of another round of fighting with Iran, possibly even before polls open, creating more uncertainty that could well favour Mr Netanyahu. US President Donald Trump’s endorsement of him on Sunday was a surprise, which could reinforce the incumbent's credentials as a statesman for some voters.

There is one clear path to victory for the mainstream opposition bloc – joining forces with Israel’s Arab parties. Many opposition parties, including Mr Eisenkot’s, have said they will not form a government with parties that typically represent the country's Palestinians, who make up about 20 per cent of the population.

With polls suggesting a significant increase in turnout among Palestinian citizens, the group could become too significant to ignore.

If Mr Eisenkot does find a way to make them part of his coalition, or the more likely option of a support-from-outside arrangement, the far-right would erupt. In that event, he may be described as a traitor and some of his current bloc partners might walk out.

Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport has reopened, but travel to the Saudi capital remains disrupted, with selected flights on the schedule alongside cancellations and diversions.

Flightradar24’s arrivals and departures boards for Tuesday show services scheduled by Saudi carriers Saudia, Riyadh Air, flynas and flyadeal alongside some international airlines such as Air Cairo and ITA Airways.

Domestic flights continue, with services listed to destinations including Jeddah, Dammam and Abha. However, cancellations have affected some Saudi-operated flights as well as international connections.

Riyadh airport reopens: Which airlines are still flying to Saudi Arabia?

For passengers planning to travel to Riyadh, here’s what to know.

Saudi carriers have several services to Dubai listed on the departures board, including Riyadh Air flight RX243, flynas flights XY207 and XY211, and Saudia flight SV560.

Air Arabia’s flights between Sharjah and Riyadh remain cancelled, with the airline yet to announce a date for their resumption.

Other UAE connections are also marked as cancelled, including Emirates flight EK820 and flydubai flight FZ848 from Riyadh to Dubai, alongside Etihad Airways flight EY556 to Abu Dhabi.

On the arrivals board, Etihad flight EY555 from Abu Dhabi was cancelled, as were Emirates flight EK819 and flydubai flight FZ847 from Dubai.

Selected international services are also listed on flight schedules, connecting Riyadh with Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, Italy and the UK.

Scheduled arrivals included Air Cairo flight SM469 from Cairo, Riyadh Air flight RX418 from Manchester and ITA Airways flight AZ838 from Rome Fiumicino.

Outbound services included Riyadh Air flight RX331 to Cairo, flynas flight XY223 to Doha and flyadeal flight F3573 to Istanbul.

The disruption has included flights being sent to alternative airports.

Pakistan International Airlines flight PK725 from Lahore was marked on the arrivals board as being diverted to Dammam, rather than arriving in Riyadh. Pakistan International Airlines flight PK725 from Lahore was marked as diverted to Dammam, while Saudia flight SV885 from Guangzhou was listed as diverted to Jeddah.

Arriving and departing flights remain subject to permission from Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation, Reuters reported. Several international airlines have retained suspensions lasting weeks or months.

Travellers should check their flight directly with the operating airline before leaving for the airport and monitor messages about changes to their booking.

Those with onward connections should confirm the status of both flights and ask their airline about arrangements if disruption affects their journey.

Passengers whose services have been cancelled should contact their airline or booking agent to discuss the rebooking or refund options available under their ticket conditions.

headline: No cancellation of planned FDI in UAE this year despite Iran war, Ministry of Investment says

foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story.Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said.“We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term. “We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.”Infrastructure pipelineInvestment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant. body_text:
No planned foreign direct investment in the UAE has been cancelled this year, despite the uncertainties created by the US-Iran war, a senior government official has said.

The overall stock of FDI in the UAE this year might be fractionally lower than the record levels achieved in 2025, as global investors assess the impact of conflict in the region. However, the Emirates remains firmly on course to achieve its 2031 FDI targets, Mohammad Abdulrahman Alhawi, Undersecretary of the UAE Ministry of Investment, told The National in an interview on Tuesday.

“Everyone we've spoken to has said: 'We haven't cancelled our plans. We are just either waiting, or we're delaying a little bit, or we're decreasing the quantum a little bit but the country is capable of making up,'” Mr Alhawi said on the sidelines of the 10th HSBC Future Forum in Dubai.

Sharjah turns to AI to identify foreign investment opportunities in seconds

“Very understandable [that] people will wait and see how the conflict is resolved.”

The good thing, Mr Alhawi said, is that even though the conflict been going on since late February, it has helped investors better understand the resilience of the UAE and the capabilities of its government in dealing with a crisis.

“I think that's the message that our investors have received over time and I think, maybe not immediately but in the next few years, that will definitely be a positive thing, as more investment is coming,” he said.

FDI into the UAE rose by about 6 per cent last year to a record $48.24 billion, the ninth highest total in the world, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development (Unctad) data.

The Emirates was also the top recipient of FDI in the Middle East, ahead of Saudi Arabia, which ranked 13th, Unctad said in its World Investment Conference 2026 report released in July.

The UAE has maintained consistent FDI inflow momentum over the past few years and was expected to continue on the growth trajectory this year before the war-driven disruption to economy and trade.

Like its peers in the six-member economic bloc of the Gulf Co-operation Council and its Arab neighbours, the UAE has faced a wave of missile and drone attacks, but Mr Alhawi said it remains “100 per cent” on target to the achieve the $65 billion annual FDI targets by 2031.

“You'll have some years when it'll grow slightly less or slightly more,” he said. “But now that we've reached the $40 billion [plus] range, we expect to keep that for a couple more years before jumping to the next level, which is the $65 billion range, which is where we want to be.”

While various governments at the emirate level are incentivising investors to boost FDI inflows, the UAE federal government is focused on investing in its own economy.

Special attention is being paid to developing ports and related infrastructure on the East Coast, as well as improving and expanding rail connectivity, and oil and gas pipeline infrastructure.

“Now, that investment does two things: one, it shows our confidence in our economy, and two, it shows that we're building different routes and paths for our main value proposition, which is being a logistical hub,” Mr Alhawi said.

“We're investing in the right places, which means the investors that are already here can see the impact this will have and they will see it over the next year or so.”

The UAE is more than capable of executing those projects on its own but it is seeking participation of foreign investors in these schemes to make them a part of the UAE growth story.

Mr Alhawi said the Ministry of Investment is bringing capital together and is in talks with investors over joint ventures. Options for global investors to team up with the UAE sovereign wealth funds, as well as family offices, are also open, he said.

“We're super open,” Mr Alhawi said. “I mean, we can build infrastructure ourselves if we want to, but building it with partners makes it makes it more efficient, makes it better, makes it more long term.

“We'd love to have partners wherever we can and we've seen actually quite an influx of people saying, ‘Oh, you're building infrastructure, so let's work with you’, which is great. A very positive sign.”

Investment in infrastructure is among the central planks of the UAE’s economic diversification agenda and Mr Alhawi said the scale of investment required for East Coast projects is significant.

HSBC estimates the UAE project finance pipeline is in excess of $190 billion in funding to build the planned the infrastructure projects.

The UAE accounts for about 22 per cent of the broader Middle East, North Africa and Turkey region infrastructure project pipeline of $872 billion, data from HSBC's New Networks of Capital: Meant Infrastructure report indicates.

“The ultimate risk is the government, and here we are talking about the large-scale projects [such as] the Al Maktoum [International] Airport ... the Dubai sewage system ... and what is happening in Fujairah [projects],” Mohamed Al Marzooqi, chief executive of HSBC UAE told The National.

“So, these are the paymasters and I don't think we have even touched the surface, to be honest, when it comes to tapping into those financing solutions.”

The easiest solution, he said, would be to tap the loan market and financial institutions in the country. They are all “hungry for quality assets 100 per cent here in the UAE”.

HSBC, Mr Al Marzooqi said, is not only willing to leverage its own balance sheet, it can also help structure deals in many other ways for project owners and investors.

The sheer size of the MENAT pipeline underpins the scale of the region’s medium and long-term investment potential despite geopolitical headwinds, HSBC said in the report released on Tuesday.

Even with a “complex global and regional operating environment”, international businesses and institutional investors expect the region to remain and infrastructure investment destination and flows of capital will continue over the rest of the decade, the lender said.

The HSBC-commissioned analysis of MEED data has identified the $872-billion pipeline of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion planned and unawarded infrastructure pipeline.

The value of planned but unawarded infrastructure projects and programmes increased by 54 per cent between January 2023 and January 2026, from $792 billion to $1.22 trillion,” data shows

“Infrastructure planning activity has continued this year, with the pipeline increasing a further 15 per cent to $1.4tn between January and October 2026,” the HSBC report said.

headline: Haghighatshenas bags gold in para Ttekwondo
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Amirmohammad Haghighatshenas won the gold medal in 2026 Asian Para Games para taekwondo after defeating the host nation’s representative in the final.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Amirmohammad Haghighatshenas won the gold medal in 2026 Asian Para Games para taekwondo after defeating the host nation’s representative in the final.

Haghighatshenas faced Japan’s Shunsuke Kudo in the men’s K44 under-70kg final at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 on Tuesday. The Iranian athlete won both rounds, with scores of 14–2 and 18–12, to secure the gold medal, Tehran Times reported.

On his way to the final, Haghighatshenas defeated Kazakhstan’s Din Muhammad Askar in the quarterfinals and overcame his Uzbek opponent in the semifinals before beating Kudo in the final.

With this victory, Iran’s para taekwondo team concluded the second day of competition with five medals: Haghighatshenas won gold, Zahra Rahimi claimed silver, and Parimah Tourani, Saeed Sadeghianpour, and Maryam Abdollahpour each earned a bronze medal.

summary: Masoud Pezeshkian expressed hope that the new adviser "will contribute to achieving the government’s goals"

TUNIS, October 20. /TASS/. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has appointed Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza as his defense adviser, the presidential office said in a statement.

"By his decree, the president has appointed Majid Ebn al-Reza his national defense adviser," the statement reads.

Pezeshkian expressed hope that the new adviser "will contribute to achieving the government’s goals in the field and addressing the country’s challenges by proposing practical recommendations."

Majid Ebn al-Reza had served as acting Defense Minister since March 2, following the death of Aziz Nasirzadeh in a US-Israeli strike. On October 18, Mehrdad Akhlaghi was appointed Iran’s defense chief.

headline: Some EU leaders use conflict in Ukraine to cover their own problem — Moldovan politician
summary: "The most dangerous scenario is when politicians, losing support within their own countries, would try to provoke a larger-scale conflict between Europe and Russia," Igor Dodon said
body_text:
CHISINAU, October 20. /TASS/. Some of the European Union leaders are not interested in peace in Ukraine and are using this conflict to cover their own problems, leader of Moldova’s largest opposition Party of Socialists and the country’s former President Igor Dodon said.

"We see that leading world players stand for ending the war in Ukraine. But I think that some of the European leaders are using this conflict as a cover for their own economic and social problems, which they are unable to resolve. The most dangerous scenario is when politicians, losing support within their own countries, would try to provoke a larger-scale conflict between Europe and Russia. This must not be allowed to happen," he told the Moldovan N-4 television channel.

Earlier, he accused Moldovan President Maia Sandu and her ruling Party of Action and Solidarity of turning the country into a puppet of EU nations that promote pro-war and self-destructive policies. Dodon called on his country’s authorities to follow the example of Slovakia, Hungary, Georgia, and other countries that are focused on the well-being of their people and economic security.

Last week, Sandu poured criticism on Western leaders for fearing a military escalation of the conflict with Russia at the beginning of the special military operation in Ukraine. Addressing a security seminar in Chisinau that was organized by the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, she said that those fears had allegedly prevented the "timely" provision of more extensive military aid to Ukraine. She announced that the government of Moldova, a neutral country under its constitution, intends to establish domestic production of military drones. To this end, she said, parliament will adopt the necessary legislative amendments, and the defense ministry will receive a grant from Western partners to purchase the necessary equipment and technology.

headline: Brazil's Newcastle poultry outbreak unlikely to have major long-term impact, analysts say
summary: By Gabriel AraujoSAO PAULO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - An outbreak of Newcastle disease in Brazil is unlikely to cause lasting damage to the country's poultry industry if authorities contain it quickly, analysts said, though uncertainty over trade restrictions, particularly from China, remains a key risk for exporters.Brazil, the world's largest chicken meat exporter, confirmed a case of the disease at a commercial farm in the southern state of Santa Catarina on Monday, prompting containment measures and triggering concerns over poultry trade flows.
body_text:
SAO PAULO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - An outbreak of Newcastle disease in Brazil is unlikely to cause lasting damage to the country's poultry industry if authorities contain it quickly, analysts said, though uncertainty over trade restrictions, particularly from China, remains a key risk for exporters.

Brazil, the world's largest chicken meat exporter, confirmed a case of the disease at a commercial farm in the southern state of Santa Catarina on Monday, prompting containment measures and triggering concerns over poultry trade flows.

Mexico, Brazil's seventh-largest poultry buyer last year, quickly suspended imports, while meat lobby group ABPA said Brazil would impose a self-embargo on shipments to China pending a decision by Chinese authorities on whether restrictions would apply nationwide or only to the affected area.

Shares in major poultry processor MBRF fell more than 4% on Monday, while US-traded peer JBS slipped 1%.

Brazil last reported a Newcastle disease outbreak in July 2024 in Rio Grande do Sul state, which neighbors Santa Catarina.

Chicken exports fell by about 25%, or 100,000 metric tons, during the month affected by restrictions that year, analysts at JPMorgan estimated, but rebounded quickly as markets reopened, causing no material effect on MBRF'sand JBS' earnings.

China was the most consequential source of trade disruption as it kept a state-wide embargo in place until January 2026, they noted, but other key destinations such as Mexico, the European Union, Saudi Arabia and Japan either eased restrictions quickly or implemented a localized response.

"This time around, unless we see a widespread event happening (which is unusual for this disease), we think the impact could be even smaller as several countries have changed their restriction protocol to a radius," JPMorgan said.

Santander analysts also flagged China -- which currently accounts for roughly 10% of Brazilian chicken exports -- as the key uncertainty, adding that MBRF is more exposed than geographically diversified JBS to potential disruptions.

They estimated trade restrictions could affect about 15% of Brazil's chicken production under current export protocols.

Prolonged restrictions could force exporters to redirect shipments to alternative markets or the domestic market, potentially weighing on prices and margins, Santander said.

"All in all, we are monitoring the scope and duration of trade restrictions. Lack of visibility on the duration of Chinese suspension is the key risk," they added.

(Reporting by Gabriel Araujo; Editing by Oliver Griffin and Alistair Bell)

The team focused on plant response actions, national arrangements for emergency preparedness and response, lessons learnt from the incident, and the reactor operator’s arrangements to ensure safety, the statement added.“By requesting this mission, FANR and BNPP have demonstrated their strong commitment to safety and continuous improvement,” said Amgad Shokr, director of the IAEA Incident and Emergency Centre and leader of the mission team. Barakah Nuclear Power Plant was “encouraged to continue implementing the organisational and technical measures identified through the assessment of lessons learnt from the event”.“The UAE has established a robust and comprehensive nuclear emergency preparedness and response system in line with the highest international standards, developed in close co-operation with the IAEA,” said Hamad Al Kaabi, director general of FANR. “The UAE shares the position of the international community and the IAEA on the importance of protecting nuclear facilities at all times. body_text:
The UAE's response to an attack on the Barakah nuclear plant in May was swift and effective, the International Atomic Energy Agency has concluded.

A drone launched from Iraq struck a generator outside the inner perimeter of the Barakah plant, causing a fire that was brought under control.

Dozens of countries, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman, the UK, the US, France and Pakistan, as well as the EU, signed a statement condemning the attack.

UN Security Council condemns drone strike on UAE's Barakah nuclear power plant

The IAEA concluded on Tuesday that national authorities and Barakah Nuclear Power Plant had appropriately responded to the loss of off-site power due to the drone strike on May 17.

The finding was reached by a six-person mission team from the nuclear agency who were in the UAE from October 12 to October 20 at the request of the government.

Effective action was taken to maintain safety during the event, including prompt national and international notification, implementation of the established emergency response procedures, and public communication, the IAEA said in a statement.

Its team visited the affected areas of the plant and key emergency response facilities, reviewed operating and emergency procedures, and met the senior management and technical staff of BNPP and the Federal Authority for Nuclear Regulation (FANR), the UAE’s independent nuclear regulator.

The team focused on plant response actions, national arrangements for emergency preparedness and response, lessons learnt from the incident, and the reactor operator’s arrangements to ensure safety, the statement added.

“By requesting this mission, FANR and BNPP have demonstrated their strong commitment to safety and continuous improvement,” said Amgad Shokr, director of the IAEA Incident and Emergency Centre and leader of the mission team.

Barakah Nuclear Power Plant was “encouraged to continue implementing the organisational and technical measures identified through the assessment of lessons learnt from the event”.

“The UAE has established a robust and comprehensive nuclear emergency preparedness and response system in line with the highest international standards, developed in close co-operation with the IAEA,” said Hamad Al Kaabi, director general of FANR.

“The UAE shares the position of the international community and the IAEA on the importance of protecting nuclear facilities at all times. We will continue working closely with the IAEA and our national partners to enhance the safety and security of nuclear facilities and ensure the protection of the community and the environment.”

headline: Turkey troops to stay in Syria, Iraq 'until border security ensured', defence minister tells AFP
summary: Turkey will keep its own troops in Syria and Iraq until border security with its two neighbours has been fully ensured, Defence Minister Yasar Guler told AFP. "We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria," he said in a written answer to AFP questions. "When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered."
body_text:
Turkey will keep its own troops in Syria and Iraq until border security with its two neighbours has been fully ensured, Defence Minister Yasar Guler told AFP.

"We are maintaining our military presence in Iraq and Syria," he said in a written answer to AFP questions.

"When we assess that the necessary conditions have been met in terms of regional and border security, the status of our base areas and our presence in the region will be reconsidered."

Turkey has for years maintained troops in northern Syria and Iraq to contain the threat along its borders posed by separatist militants from the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and from Islamic State (IS) jihadists.

But over the past two years, the situation has shifted with the emergence of a new Ankara-allied government in Syria following Bashar al-Assad's fall, and following Turkey's push to draw a line under its decades-long conflict with the PKK.

Since Assad's fall, Turkey had established "close coordination in the field of security" with the new Syrian government, with its troops working to "strengthen the capacity" of the Syrian military and "to ensure the security of our borders", the minister said.

"Once the terrorist threat in the region has been completely eliminated, border security has been ensured, and state authority has been fully and uniformly established throughout Syria without exception, the status of our forces will be reassessed," he said.

When the Assad regime fell, Turkey had between 16,000 and 18,000 troops in northern Syria, a Turkish official said.

Since then, there has been no reliable figure for troops deployed in Syria, although a Turkish official last month said talks were under way to determine their legal status there.

But Guler refused to be drawn on any future plans.

"At this stage it would not be appropriate to make a prior assessment regarding deployment or base plans that have not been made public," he said.

"Issues related to the future posture of the Turkish armed forces in Syria will be addressed by taking into account Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity, the mutual understanding of the two countries, the security conditions on the ground and the evolution of the terrorist threat."

Turkish troops have also long been operational in northern Iraq, regularly conducting cross-border operations and air raids on PKK hideouts, while maintaining their own bases there -- putting a strain on ties between Ankara and Baghdad.

Troops have been based there since 2015, and today they number between 800 and 1,000, an Iraqi security source told AFP.

Without disclosing any figures, Guler said troop numbers in both Iraq and Syria were assessed in proportion to what was needed on the ground.

"It would not be accurate to assess our military presence in Iraq and Syria solely on the basis of personnel numbers. Our force structure and posture on the ground are shaped according to needs" linked to threat levels, border security and developments on the ground, he said.

As the PKK process has advanced, the Kurdish militants destroyed weapons at a symbolic ceremony last year, and this month, withdrew from four key bases in northern Iraq in a move confirmed by Turkish intelligence.

For lasting success, the PKK must "fully implement their decision to dissolve" with Turkey "meticulously monitoring the next phases of the process" while not dropping its guard.

"The progress of the process doesn't mean security measures have been relaxed," he said, with troops continuing to "take the necessary measures" against any situation viewed as a security threat.

Like in Syria, Turkey was also closely watching Iraq's own efforts "to disarm militia groups and bring them under state control", he said, hailing recent successes in the Sinjar region.

Iraq has set a June 30 deadline for pro-Iran factions to hand over their weapons to the state following the end of the US-led coalition's mission there.

Following the successful Sinjar push, Turkey said last month it would "gradually" hand control to Baghdad of its Bashiqa base near the northern city of Mosul although no timeline was given.

Turkey would continue to support Iraq and was planning "to elevate military and security cooperation between the two countries to a higher level" in the coming period, he said.

summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Norway Tuesday to meet with US envoys in order to put diplomacy back on a "more constructive path”, Oslo officials said. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated since US President Donald Trump reached an agreement with Moscow last week to purchase Russian diesel and Zelensky accused the US of delaying the planned delivery of interceptor missiles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Norway Tuesday to meet with US envoys in order to put diplomacy back on a "more constructive path”, Oslo officials said. Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated since US President Donald Trump reached an agreement with Moscow last week to purchase Russian diesel and Zelensky accused the US of delaying the planned delivery of interceptor missiles.

Issued on: 20/10/2026 - 16:11

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Oslo on Tuesday for talks with top US envoys in a bid to get strained relations with Washington "on a more constructive path", Oslo said.

"We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace," Zelensky said in a social media post announcing his arrival in Oslo.

Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said earlier that Oslo would host talks between Zelensky, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner – the latter taking part remotely – as well as Finnish President Alexander Stubb.

Read moreWhy have US-Ukraine relations soured ahead of the midterms?

Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since President Donald Trump partially lifted sanctions to strike a diesel-supply deal with Russia's Vladimir Putin and slammed Zelensky as a warmonger for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelensky has accused the United States of deliberately withholding vital intelligence and delaying military aid, saying on Monday that Ukraine received no early warning of powerful Russian missile strikes that targeted energy facilities in the capital region.

US-led diplomatic efforts to end Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II have stalled in recent months, as Washington has shifted focus towards the war with Iran.

The Norway talks were due to begin on Tuesday afternoon and continue into the evening, Store told reporters.

"The aim is to put diplomatic efforts on a more constructive path," he said.

Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky on Tuesday said he held "substantive" and "constructive" talks with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in which he insisted that the US military satellite system Ukraine uses, Starshield, "needs to be restored" and that ballistic missile interceptors "are needed to protect lives".

Zelensky told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" already paid for by European countries, and that the shipment was waiting for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's signature.

He said several European countries were ready to transfer Patriot interceptor missiles from their own stockpiles but were still awaiting US approval.

The US has denied making any changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine, and Rubio on Tuesday said Washington was not deliberately withholding supplies.

"There's nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine," Rubio said while on a trip to India.

"It's simply, it's a balance between our obligations to other partners and frankly our own ... requirements for our own facilities as well."

Read moreWill Trump really pull the plug? Starlink restored but Ukraine's fate still uncertain

Trump has also denied ordering a reduction in speeds on the US government-owned and -controlled Starshield network after Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX developed it, said the order could only have come from the White House.

The US leader has accused his counterpart of not trying to resolve the conflict with Russia.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said on Monday.

"To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

Trump said he was ready to meet Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in China next month to discuss denuclearisation, adding that talks could also cover the Ukraine war – fuelling fears in Kyiv that it was being sidelined.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed earlier that "the topic of such a hypothetical has indeed been mentioned" when asked about a Wall Street Journal report on Sunday that Trump, Putin and Xi could meet.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said that such a meeting would "only encourage Putin to continue this war".

News outlet Axios reported that Witkoff would travel from Oslo to Russia to meet Putin.

"We hope that it will be possible to arrange a meeting in the very near future, allowing the American negotiators... Mr Witkoff, to brief President Putin on their contacts with both the Ukrainians and the Europeans," Peskov told reporters Tuesday.

Ukrainian authorities said Tuesday that Russian strikes killed at least six people around the country, as Moscow targets energy and transport infrastructure with winter approaching.

The attacks came after Zelensky said Kyiv would resume hitting Russian refineries in the face of unrelenting strikes, more than four and a half years into the war.

headline: EXPLAINER - Why Libya's approval of Türkiye maritime deal marks a turning point in Eastern Mediterranean
summary: Eastern-based parliament's endorsement of 2019 maritime agreement signals major shift in Libya's political landscape after years of opposition to Ankara
body_text:
Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives has approved a landmark maritime boundary agreement signed with Türkiye in 2019, marking a significant diplomatic development that could reshape political alignments and competing maritime claims in the Eastern Mediterranean.

The decision is particularly noteworthy because it comes from a parliament closely associated with the political camp of eastern Libyan commander Khalifa Haftar, whose forces fought against the internationally recognized government in Tripoli that originally signed the agreement with Ankara.

The parliament also revoked a 2020 decision to sever political ties with Türkiye, according to a statement from the Libyan parliament on Tuesday.

The move represents a potentially important breakthrough for Ankara, which has spent recent years expanding diplomatic engagement with eastern Libya while maintaining its longstanding strategic partnership with the Tripoli-based authorities.

Beyond bilateral relations, the parliamentary approval carries implications for longstanding maritime disputes involving Türkiye, Greece and Egypt, as well as future energy exploration in the Mediterranean.

On Nov. 27, 2019, Türkiye and Libya's then internationally recognized Government of National Accord (GNA), led by Fayez al-Sarraj, signed a memorandum of understanding delimiting their respective maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean.

The agreement established a maritime boundary between the two countries based on Ankara's interpretation of international maritime law, including the principle of equitable delimitation and the geographical relationship between their coastlines.

Türkiye maintains that its extensive Mediterranean coastline entitles it to maritime jurisdiction areas that should not be disproportionately restricted by Greek islands situated close to the Turkish mainland.

Greece disputes that interpretation, arguing that its islands, including Crete and Rhodes, generate maritime entitlements that the Türkiye-Libya agreement fails to respect.

The agreement entered into force in December 2019 and was subsequently registered with the United Nations.

Anadolu's reporting on the agreement's first anniversary in November 2020 highlighted its strategic importance for Ankara, which views the memorandum as a means of protecting its maritime rights and countering attempts to exclude Türkiye from regional energy arrangements.

For Libya, the agreement also established maritime claims that differ significantly from those advanced by Greece, particularly in waters south of Crete.

The significance lies primarily in Libya's longstanding political division.

Since the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi's government in 2011, Libya has experienced successive conflicts, rival administrations and competing centers of political authority.

The country remains divided between the UN-recognized Government of National Unity (GNU) in Tripoli and an eastern-based administration supported by Haftar's forces.

Türkiye backed the Tripoli government militarily during Haftar's 2019-2020 offensive against the capital, helping prevent its capture.

The eastern-based House of Representatives opposed the maritime agreement and questioned the authority of the Tripoli government to conclude it without parliamentary approval.

That opposition became a major point of contention, allowing critics to argue that the agreement lacked the necessary domestic political endorsement in Libya.

The latest parliamentary decision therefore marks a substantial reversal.

An institution that previously challenged the agreement has now endorsed it, potentially removing one of the most significant internal Libyan objections to the 2019 memorandum.

However, parliamentary approval does not automatically resolve every question concerning the agreement's implementation or its implications for third countries.

The parliamentary decision follows years of diplomatic efforts by Türkiye to establish working relationships with Libya's rival political and military authorities.

Although Ankara maintained close security, economic and political ties with Tripoli, it increasingly sought direct engagement with eastern Libya.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan received House of Representatives Speaker Aguila Saleh at meetings in 2022 and 2023, helping establish channels for dialogue.

The rapprochement gained further momentum in 2025.

In August that year, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin visited Benghazi for talks with Khalifa Haftar, a development that illustrated the growing diplomatic engagement between Ankara and eastern Libya.

The eastern parliament also established a technical committee to examine the 2019 maritime agreement, raising expectations that its longstanding opposition could eventually be reconsidered.

Contacts continued into 2026.

On June 23, Kalin met Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of eastern Libyan forces, in Benghazi to discuss maintaining peace, unifying Libya's rival administrations and military forces, and expanding bilateral cooperation.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also engaged with eastern Libyan officials as Ankara pursued relations across the country's political divide.

These developments suggested that Türkiye's relationship with eastern Libya was evolving from confrontation toward pragmatic cooperation.

The latest parliamentary approval is among the clearest indications yet of that shift.

The agreement has been a central source of disagreement between Türkiye and Greece over maritime boundaries, offshore energy resources and the rights of islands under international law.

Athens argues that the 2019 memorandum disregards maritime entitlements generated by Greek islands, particularly Crete, and has repeatedly described the agreement as invalid.

Ankara rejects those objections, maintaining that maritime delimitation must account for coastal geography, proportionality and equitable principles rather than granting islands an automatic and unrestricted effect in determining boundaries.

In August 2020, Greece and Egypt signed a separate maritime delimitation agreement covering areas that partly overlap with the claims advanced by Türkiye and Libya.

The competing agreements have contributed to diplomatic tensions and uncertainty over offshore exploration activities.

The latest Libyan parliamentary approval could complicate Athens' efforts to challenge the 2019 memorandum by weakening arguments based on the absence of support from Libya's eastern institutions.

Greece actively sought to prevent such an outcome.

In July 2025, Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis held meetings with officials in Benghazi and Tripoli as Athens intensified its diplomatic engagement over the maritime dispute.

In September that year, Greece reiterated its position that the memorandum was invalid during talks with Libyan officials.

The disagreement continued in December 2025, when Greek Parliament Speaker Nikitas Kaklamanis called for the agreement's cancellation during talks with his Libyan counterpart, Aguila Saleh.

Libya's parliament responded by condemning the demand as interference in the country's sovereign affairs.

The decision could also strengthen the political environment for expanding energy cooperation between Türkiye and Libya.

The two countries have already taken steps toward offshore exploration.

In June 2025, Türkiye's state-owned Turkish Petroleum Corporation (TPAO) and Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) signed a memorandum covering geological and geophysical studies in four offshore areas.

Discussions also covered conducting a two-dimensional seismic survey spanning approximately 10,000 kilometers.

Cooperation advanced further in February 2026, when TPAO secured interests in two exploration blocks during Libya's first oil and gas licensing round in 17 years.

The Turkish company was awarded the onshore C3 block alongside Spain's Repsol, while the offshore O7 block went to a consortium involving TPAO, Repsol and Hungary's MOL.

These developments demonstrate that energy cooperation has progressed beyond diplomatic declarations toward concrete commercial opportunities.

Parliamentary endorsement of the maritime agreement could reduce political uncertainty surrounding future joint projects, although exploration and drilling would still depend on separate licensing, investment and operational decisions.

Egypt is another important actor in the Eastern Mediterranean equation.

Cairo has traditionally maintained close relations with eastern Libya's political and military leadership and has supported Haftar during various stages of the country's conflict.

Egypt also signed the 2020 maritime delimitation agreement with Greece, making it a central participant in the region's competing maritime arrangements.

Eastern Libya's endorsement of the Türkiye agreement therefore introduces a new consideration into Cairo's regional calculations.

However, the decision does not necessarily indicate a rupture between eastern Libya and Egypt.

Instead, it may reflect an increasingly pragmatic approach by Libyan political actors seeking to diversify their international relationships.

Relations between Ankara and Cairo have also improved considerably following years of regional rivalry, creating greater opportunities for diplomatic engagement over Libya and Eastern Mediterranean issues.

The immediate significance of the decision is political: a Libyan institution that previously opposed the 2019 agreement has now endorsed it.

The next steps will depend on the formal publication and implementation of the parliamentary decision, the positions adopted by Libya's rival authorities and the response of other Eastern Mediterranean countries.

For Türkiye, the development could consolidate years of diplomatic engagement with both western and eastern Libya while strengthening the domestic Libyan backing for a cornerstone of Ankara's maritime policy.

For Libya, it may provide another area of cooperation between rival political institutions, although the country's wider political and security divisions remain unresolved.

For Greece and Egypt, it creates a changed diplomatic environment without eliminating existing disagreements over maritime jurisdiction.

Nearly seven years after the agreement was signed, the endorsement by Libya's eastern-based parliament underscores how shifting political relationships within Libya can influence the broader geopolitical balance in the Eastern Mediterranean.

headline: What's at stake as Libya's eastern parliament approves Turkey maritime deal
summary: Libya's eastern-based parliament's approval of a long-disputed maritime deal with Turkey marks a strategic win for Ankara as Saddam Hifter seeks Turkish backing for his presidential ambitions, according to analysts.
body_text:
ANKARA — The approval of a long-disputed maritime deal with Turkey by Libya's eastern-based parliament marks a major geopolitical victory for Ankara, while also reflecting efforts by Saddam Hifter, the deputy commander of Libya's eastern-based armed forces, to secure Turkish backing for his presidential ambitions, analysts say.

The vote, held on Tuesday, saw lawmakers unanimously approve the agreement Turkey signed with Libya's Tripoli-based government in 2019.

“The House of Representatives voted unanimously to adopt the Memorandum of Understanding signed between the Government of National Accord and the Government of the Republic of Turkey regarding the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean Sea,” Abdullah Bliheg, spokesperson for Libya's House of Representatives, wrote on X.

Libya remains divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival eastern administration under the de facto control of Khalifa Hifter, commander of the eastern-based Libyan National Army. The agreement, struck between Turkey and Libya's then-UN-recognized Government of National Accord, was initially rejected by its eastern rivals. In 2020, Libya's eastern-based House of Representatives passed a resolution rejecting the agreement as well as severing all ties with Ankara.

headline: Hungary blocks next steps in talks on Ukraine, Moldova’s admission to EU
summary: Budapest vetoed further procedural steps in the negotiations without explaining why
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Hungary has blocked progress on Ukraine and Moldova’s accession to the European Union, the Kyiv Independent reported, citing diplomatic sources in Brussels and Kiev.

According to the sources, technical experts from the 27 EU countries met on Tuesday to coordinate the process of unblocking the last two negotiation clusters, those on agriculture, environment and transport.

Budapest vetoed further procedural steps in the negotiations without explaining why. According to the media outlet, the issue of these last two clusters will be raised at every subsequent enlargement working group meeting in Brussels until the stalemate is broken.

Senior EU officials told the media outlet that they expect that these clusters will be officially opened in December, despite Hungary’s position.

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has repeatedly warned that he opposes Ukraine’s accelerated admission to the European Union and that the same requirements should be imposed on Ukraine as on other candidate countries. The Hungarian prime minister also noted that negotiations with Ukraine could be suspended if it fails to fulfill its obligations to Hungary. Moreover, in his words, Ukraine cannot joint the European Union as long as it is "in a state of war" with Russia.

headline: Russia to play away friendly football match against Uzbekistan next month
summary: Russia’s national football team played three friendly matches in late September and early October
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. The national football teams of Russia and Uzbekistan will play a friendly match on November 12 in Tashkent, the Russian Football Union’s (RFU) press office reported on Tuesday.

Russia’s national football squad played three friendly matches in late September and early October, namely against Iran (2:0), Namibia (6:0) and Nigeria (3:3).

Uzbekistan is currently 59th in the FIFA World Rankings while Russia stands at 35th. This summer, the national football team of Uzbekistan played at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, co-hosted by the United States, Mexico and Canada, but failed to clear the group stage of the championship.

The Uzbekistani football team is led by Italian Head Coach Fabio Cannavaro, who is a former professional football player, the winner of the prestigious Ballon d’Or award in 2006 as well as the 2006 FIFA World Cup champion playing for Italy.

The world’s governing football body, FIFA, announced on February 28, 2022, that the Russian national team and all professional clubs representing the country were barred from participating in FIFA tournaments.

In turn, the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) made a similar decision regarding the Russian national football team’s participation in UEFA tournaments.

Both FIFA and UEFA cited Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine as grounds for their respective bans on Russian teams’ participation in competitions.
