headline: Mecca Agreement is not alternative to NATO, open to other countries — Erdogan’s party
summary: According to the statement, Turkey will respect this agreement with parliament’s approval and within the constitutional procedures
body_text:
ISTANBUL, October 20. /TASS/. The Mecca Agreement between Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan is not an alternative to NATO and is open to other countries, spokesperson for the ruling Justice and Development Party Omer Celik said.

"The Mecca Agreement is not an alternative to NATO, but an additional mechanism of the international security architecture. <…> Turkey will respect this agreement with parliament’s approval and within the constitutional procedures. The participation of other countries in this agreement would be welcome from the viewpoint of its principles and goals," he said.

According to earlier reports, a bill on the ratification of the Mecca Agreement was submitted to Turkey’s parliament for ratification. Under the country’s laws, international agreements are to be endorsed by parliament, which also authorizes the deployment of military contingents abroad.

The Mecca Agreement consists of 16 articles; once it enters into force, the signatory countries will not be able to withdraw from it for the first 10 years. One of the most important articles is Article 2, which stipulates that an attack on one of the countries will be considered an act of military aggression against all signatories to the pact. The agreement provides for cooperation among the signatory countries in the defense industry, including joint production, the implementation of research and innovation projects, and personnel training. The parties will also cooperate in the areas of security, intelligence, and counterterrorism. The pact’s strategic, political, and defense committees, which will include foreign and defense ministers, and chiefs of staff, will meet at least twice a year on a rotating basis, while the countries’ leaders will meet once a year if they deem it necessary, according to excerpts from the document cited by the TRT Haber television channel.

The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement was signed by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shahbaz Sharif on August 7. On October 5, the member countries decided to begin putting into practice their joint defense commitments and deploy military forces on Saudi territory.

headline: UN demands aid access to besieged Yemen city Taiz
summary: The United Nations insisted Tuesday that aid must immediately be allowed to enter Yemen's Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching the country's third-largest city. body_text:
The United Nations insisted Tuesday that aid must immediately be allowed to enter Yemen's Taiz, besieged by pro-Iran Houthi fighters who are preventing supplies from reaching the country's third-largest city.

Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.

"Humanitarian aid must be immediately allowed to enter the city and its passage must be facilitated," UN human rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement.

He said relief must reach the city to avert a rights catastrophe.

"The Houthis' closure of the only supply route linking Taiz to Aden is placing civilians at grave risk, blocking humanitarian aid and cutting off essential supplies," said Turk.

The Houthis, from Yemen's rugged north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, sparking a brutal civil war with a Saudi-led coalition fighting for the government.

The civil war reignited in July, months into the US-Iran conflict that has plunged the Middle East into crisis.

Turk said the encirclement of Taiz had sent the prices of commodities soaring, leaving many without food or other basic necessities.

His office has also noted restrictions on safe access to water and essential goods, exacerbating humanitarian needs and increasing risks for civilians.

"Civilians wishing to leave must be allowed to do so freely and safely," said Turk, the UN high commissioner for human rights.

Turk's office said it had verified that 32 civilians had been killed across Taiz governorate between August 1 and October 19, including nine women and 14 children.

Meanwhile 115 civilians were injured, among them 34 women and 36 children.

Turk warned that with fighting moving closer to densely populated areas of the city, the risk of death and injury to civilians would only increase.

"I urge all parties to the conflict to refrain from the use of explosive weapons with wide-area effects in populated areas and to take all feasible precautions to protect civilians and civilian objects," he said.

The World Health Organization said that Taiz's health system was now at "critical risk".

"Fighting and road closures are threatening hospitals' access to fuel, oxygen, medicines and essential supplies, putting patients requiring life-saving care at immediate risk," WHO spokesman Tarik Jasarevic told a press conference.

The UN health agency is calling for the safe movement of patients, health workers, ambulances, fuel, oxygen and medicines to the city.

Jasarevic said 12 hospitals in Taiz had around four days of fuel left, while there are stocks of one week or less for 115 out of 127 essential medicines.

He said the health crisis across Yemen was escalating rapidly, with rising disease outbreaks placing "immense pressure on an already overstretched health system".

Across Yemen, suspected cholera cases have tripled from 221 in the week ending September 12 to 683 in the week ending October 10.

Yemen has reported this year more than 22,800 suspected measles cases and 128 deaths, alongside 12,618 suspected dengue cases and 421 suspected diphtheria cases.

headline: Houthi attacks undermine Saudi Arabia's economic ambitions
summary: With airports closed and the capital brought to an effective standstill, attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia have thrown a wrench in the kingdom's ambitious plans to overhaul the economy and draw foreign investment. A decade ago, de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched his bold Vision 2030, aiming to diversify the economy away from oil and turn the powerful monarchy into a hub for tourism, international events and multinational enterprises.
body_text:
With airports closed and the capital brought to an effective standstill, attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia have thrown a wrench in the kingdom's ambitious plans to overhaul the economy and draw foreign investment.

A decade ago, de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched his bold Vision 2030, aiming to diversify the economy away from oil and turn the powerful monarchy into a hub for tourism, international events and multinational enterprises.

Already dealt a blow by Iran's attacks on US allies in the Gulf during the wider Middle East war, the plan now faces an existential hurdle with unprecedented Houthi attacks, in particular targeting oil infrastructure and airports.

"I can't think of another time when the challenge facing MBS was more," said H.A. Hellyer, an analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).

"He's dealing with the Iranians on one side of the country which is very difficult and problematic and then he's dealing with the Houthis who aligned with the Iranians on the other."

On October 10, a Houthi attack on Riyadh's international airport killed 13 people and injured more than 300 -- the deadliest in the kingdom in over a decade, with the airport remaining closed since.

A consultant to the Saudi government who wished to remain anonymous meanwhile told AFP that "the deeper risk there is that, you know, boards start pricing Saudi as part of an active conflict zone.

"If that perception settles into risk models, insurance premiums, it will take many years to unwind," she added.

A number of major events have been cancelled, most notably the Future Investment Initiative (FII), nicknamed "Davos on the desert" -- a bulwark of the kingdom's diversification drive.

The uncertainty has only piled pressure on the 41-year-old crown prince's Vision 2030, as several of its megaprojects -- most notably the hyper-futuristic megacity dubbed Neom -- have been scaled back.

In Riyadh, the iconic Kingdom Centre recently ordered its office tenants, which include the International Monetary Fund (IMF), to work remotely until further notice.

The world's largest crude oil exporter is moreover expected to see its economy contract by 3.3 percent, according to the IMF's latest projections, revised from a projected growth of 1.7 percent in July.

The kingdom is grappling with a new reality wherein US protection is no longer guaranteed, as President Donald Trump has appeared reluctant to offer support in Yemen as he gears up for mid-term elections.

"Saudi Arabia finds itself in a delicate situation in the face of Houthi attacks, as well as US hesitation," said Laurent Bonnefoy, a researcher at Ceri/Sciences Po in Paris.

"Trump for the time being seems to be refusing to commit to offering the needed military backing," he added.

Riyadh has secured support from several allies including France, Britain, Turkey and Pakistan to help mitigate the threat posed by the Houthis," said Torbjorn Soltvedt, Middle East analyst at Verisk Maplecroft.

"But all are reluctant to go beyond defensive measures, with no appetite to put troops on the ground in Yemen."

The Houthis for their part are relying on a vast arsenal of weapons built up over years with Iranian support.

Following an uneasy four-year truce in the war, fighting kicked off again in July when the airport in Sanaa was struck after Iran sent a plane in defiance of Saudi control -- an attack the Houthis blamed on Saudi Arabia.

The Yemeni group has a large number of longer-range missiles and drones at its disposal, and has seized control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which leads up to the Suez Canal.

After pursuing a policy of "power and regional projection" in 2019, Riyadh -- facing a "stalemate" in Yemen -- shifted tack around 2019 and focused on economic objectives, Bonnefoy said.

Ali Shihabi, a Saudi analyst close to the Saudi government, said the kingdom "has faced repeated challenges over the decades".

"The Kingdom has weathered each crisis and will weather this one. It is resilient, has staying power and can draw on global supply chains and an extensive network of alliances," he said.

"The Houthis, ultimately, have only Iran, and Iran itself is under severe strain."

But Soltvedt suggested the risks predate the latest conflict, saying: "Allaying investor concerns over geopolitical risk has been a longstanding challenge for Riyadh, from the attacks on the heart of Saudi Arabia's energy sector just before the Aramco IPO in 2019, to the outbreak of regional conflict this year.

"With no solution to the conflict in sight, the drone and missile threat from multiple directions and actors will continue to weigh on the minds of investors."

headline: NATO reconnaissance aircraft flies around Kaliningrad Region for nearly four hours
summary: The Bombardier Artemis II reconnaissance aircraft flew into the area of the Kaliningrad Region from its permanent base in Constanta, Romania
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. A US-registered NATO reconnaissance aircraft was flying around Russia’s Kaliningrad Region for nearly four hours, a source in air traffic control services told TASS.

"The Bombardier Artemis II reconnaissance aircraft flew into the area of the Kaliningrad Region from its permanent base in Constanta, Romania, and then circled the Russian region for nearly four hours, using the airspace of Poland and Lithuania, as well as the sector over the neutral waters of the Baltic Sea," said the source. He noted that the aircraft was flying at an altitude of about 12 km, without using civil aviation flight routes.

This week, the source continued, the aircraft was spotted in the vicinity of the Kaliningrad Region for the first time. On Monday, it was spotted over the neutral waters of the Black Sea, where it flew back and forth from west to east for nearly eight hours in the southern part of the water area. The source noted in this regard that in late July, the Bombardier Artemis II set a sort of record by remaining over the Black Sea for nine hours. On October 7, it was operating over the sea alongside the Swedish Air Force’s Gulfstream S102B Korpen radar intelligence aircraft.

headline: Russia waits for answers about work on bioweapons in Ukraine with Pentagon support — MFA
summary: According to the deputy director of the Department for Non-Proliferation and Arms Control at the Russian Foreign Ministry, legitimate questions, officially raised by Russia, remain unanswered
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Russia is waiting for responses from the United States regarding issues related to the development of biological weapons in Ukraine with the support of the Pentagon, Kirill Vorontsov, deputy head of the Russian delegation and deputy director of the Department for Non-Proliferation and Arms Control at the Russian Foreign Ministry has said.

"Legitimate questions, officially raised by Russia, remain unanswered. These questions concern the uncovered facts regarding the implementation of a military-biological program in Ukraine - in violation of the Biological Weapons Convention - with the support of the US Department of Defense and its affiliated entities, including private companies," he said during a discussion on Other Weapons of Mass Destruction within the First Committee of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly. A transcript of his remarks has been published on the Russian Foreign Ministry’s website.

As Vorontsov noted, "an analysis of the projects carried out in Ukrainian laboratories leads to the conclusion that components of biological weapons were, or perhaps still are, being developed in the immediate vicinity of Russian territory." He emphasized that Russia views this as a direct threat to its national security.

"The admission - cited by Tulsi Gabbard - regarding Washington’s long-term funding of 'potentially risky' virus experiments in over 120 foreign biolaboratories - more than 40 of which are located in Ukraine - only confirms the validity of Russia’s concerns regarding American military-biological activity near our borders," Vorontsov pointed out. "We expect the United States, as one of the depositaries of the BTWC, to provide appropriate responses to the questions we have raised. This would help resolve this unsavory situation and ensure that Washington complies with the obligations stipulated by the Convention," he concluded.

summary: ANKARA/TORONTO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - NATO allies Canada and Turkey are expected to sign a joint declaration aimed at deepening bilateral cooperation in four areas, including defence and energy, during Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit later this week, a person briefed on the matter said.The declaration is also expected to encompass the economy, looking to advance free trade talks between the countries, while boosting social and diplomatic ties. body_text:
ANKARA/TORONTO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - NATO allies Canada and Turkey are expected to sign a joint declaration aimed at deepening bilateral cooperation in four areas, including defence and energy, during Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit later this week, a person briefed on the matter said.

The declaration is also expected to encompass the economy, looking to advance free trade talks between the countries, while boosting social and diplomatic ties. The countries would establish committees in all of the areas to draft action plans, the person said.

Carney's office and Turkey's presidency and Foreign Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

Carney will be the first Canadian prime minister to make a dedicated bilateral visit to Turkey. He is set to meet with Turkish PresidentTayyip Erdogan in Ankara on Thursday and is expected to meet with Turkish business leaders in Istanbul on Friday.

The visit is part of Carney's effortsto reduce trade dependence on the United States and strengthen partnerships with regional powers amid a damaging trade war with Washington and an increasingly adversarial relationship with President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly questioned Canada's sovereignty.

TALKS MAY INCLUDE NUCLEAR POWER, LNG

Turkish Energy Minister Alparslan Bayraktar told the Kanal 7 broadcaster on Sunday that energy, namely nuclear power, would be among the top agenda items during Carney’s visit.

Ankara anticipates that energy discussions will also include potential purchases by Turkey of liquefied natural gas from Canada as well as critical minerals, the person said. A working group is expected to be created to study the feasibility of a bid by Canada's CANDU to build a planned nuclear plant on Turkey's Black Sea coast.

Turkey has held talks with Canadian engineering firmAtkinsRealis ATRL.TO, which owns CANDU, as well as South Korea's ​Korea Electric Power Corporation and China's State Power Investment Corporation, about potentially building its planned second and third nuclear power plants. Russia's Rosatom is ⁠building its first.

The discussions on the defence sector are expected to focus on drones and naval cooperation. In 2024, to help thaw bilateral ties, Canada removed weapons-export controls on Turkey, including on optical ​technology used in drones that Turkey exports to dozens of nations.

Carney is also expected to meet with officials from defence companies as well as firms with energy businesses during his visit to Turkey, including Calik Holding and Sabanci Holding, according to two otherpeople familiar with the plans. Sabanci Holding declined to comment while Calik Holding did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Turkish defence analysts said Trump's policies towards Canada had created opportunities for closer cooperation in ammunition production, drones and naval systems, but cautioned that major agreements were unlikely tomaterialise in the short term.

(Reporting by Tuvan Gumrukcu in Ankara and Jonathan Spicer in Toronto, Additional reporting by Ece Toksabay, Maria Cheng in Ottawa, Can Sezer and Ebru Tuncay in Istanbul and Huseyin Hayatsever in Ankara, Writing by Humeyra Pamuk, Editing by Daren Butler and Rod Nickel)

body_text:
Meta’s Oversight Board said the company's content moderation failures led to the removal of “No Kings” political activist accounts in the US and others focused on the Brazilian elections from several of its platforms.

The so-called No Kings protests oppose some of President Donald Trump's policies and executive actions. Brazil's contentious election process has pitted current President Luiz Inacio 'Lula' da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro, one of former leader Jair Bolsonaro's sons.

“We have repeatedly warned that during elections and periods of heightened political tension, Meta's content moderation failures often manifest themselves in two ways: overenforcement that suppresses political speech and underenforcement that undermines electoral integrity,” said the Oversight Board, which provides independent guidance and critiques of the company's actions.

The board said No Kings accounts should have featured in the company's cross-check programme, which would then have probably prevented the technical error from occurring.

“It remains unclear why Meta’s election integrity efforts did not lead to a much quicker resolution,” the board wrote.

Last weekend, with nationwide No Kings protests scheduled to take place, the activists' social media accounts on Meta were removed.

Meta blamed the removal on a series of technological glitches but critics say No Kings content was suppressed.

Mr da Silva's team has said his profile was intentionally hidden from searches on purpose. Brazil’s top electoral court this week doubled a daily fine for Meta, saying it had failed to comply with an order about how political content is shown on its platforms.

“It’s clear that Meta must do more to ensure that its enforcement practices during elections are transparent and consistent, and that political speech is protected rather than stifled,” the board statement read.

Created in 2018, the board is designed to provide independent supervision of Meta's content moderation on Facebook, Instagram and Threads, particularly once users feel they have exhausted the company’s appeals processes.

The board was created largely as a response to the deluge of inauthentic content originating from Russia that appeared in users' news feeds in the lead-up to the 2016 US presidential election.

Such content led to a number of congressional investigations and Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, giving evidence at a hearing in Washington.

Meta announced last year it would be automating its content moderation approach.

“Our engineering team discovered that the spike that triggered the incorrect enforcement was primarily in the account’s 'reading' behaviour,” Meta spokesman Andy Stone posted on Threads of the current incident.

“Unfortunately, that automated action was clearly taken in error. Everything is now working as it should and we sincerely apologise.”

But Meta's response has done little to calm critics.

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy suggested that if the Democrats win back the House and Senate in the midterm elections, Big Tech companies such as Meta would come under increased scrutiny.

“Outrageous,” he posted on X, referring to the deactivation of the No Kings accounts. “Put this on the January investigation list.”

Sheikh Abdullah sat down with India's External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in the Indian financial capital, where talks centred on expanding ties across the economy, trade, investment, technology and artificial intelligence.

The three ministers explored ways to advance shared interests, deepen economic integration, and enhance regional and international co-operation, with sustainable development featuring high on the agenda.

Also addressed were regional and international developments, with the three ministers exchanging views on issues of mutual concern. Discussions touched on continuing efforts to strengthen security and stability, as well as to promote development and prosperity across the region and beyond.

headline: Milipol Qatar 2026 opens in Doha, showcasing the latest security technologies and international partnerships
summary: The three-day exhibition brings together international security companies and officials, with Qatar and France signing a new security cooperation plan. The 16th edition of Milipol Qatar opened at the Doha…
body_text:
The three-day exhibition brings together international security companies and officials, with Qatar and France signing a new security cooperation plan. The 16th edition of Milipol Qatar opened at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Center (DECC) on Tuesday, bringing together more than 270 local and international companies showcasing the latest technologies, law enforcement authorities, security agencies and industry representatives to exchange expertise and explore partnerships as security challenges continue to evolve.

Held under the patronage of Qatar’s Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, the exhibition runs from 20 to 22 October, featuring seven international pavilions across 23,000 square metres of exhibition space.

Qatar’s Minister of Interior and Commander of the Internal Security Force (Lekhwiya), Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani, attended the opening and toured the exhibition alongside senior officials.

Minister of State for Interior Affairs Sheikh Abdulaziz bin Faisal bin Mohammed Al Thani also toured the exhibition, where he was briefed on the latest security technologies, products and systems presented by participating companies.

Organised by Qatar’s Ministry of Interior, Milipol Qatar has been held every two years since 1996, serving as a platform for security agencies, government officials and international companies to explore emerging technologies and strengthen cooperation.

Qatar and France sign security cooperation plan

On the sidelines of the exhibition, Qatar and France signed a three-year action plan for security cooperation covering 2027 to 2030, with Sheikh Khalifa witnessing the signing between the two countries’ interior ministries.

The agreement aims to strengthen cooperation in several areas, including organised crime, drug trafficking, counterterrorism, international event security and civil protection.

“It is an old partnership, which we have just renewed with the signing of this triennial plan of action between us, which I have just signed with my Qatari counterpart,” Jean-Didier Berger, Minister Delegate to the French Minister of Interior told Doha News.

The minister delegate highlighted the longstanding security relationship between Qatar and France and the importance of expanding cooperation to address evolving security challenges.

“This partnership has enabled us to make progress in absolutely all areas.”

The agreement provides a framework for continued coordination between the two countries over the coming years.

Barzan Holdings showcases 12 new products

Meanwhile, Qatar-based Barzan Holdings is showcasing 12 new products at Milipol Qatar 2026, including autonomous systems, security platforms and a new weapon developed by its manufacturing arm.

Among the technologies on display is an intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) drone designed to support operations across Qatar’s internal security sectors.Speaking with Doha News, Ahmad Al-Mulla, Commercial Relationships Manager at Barzan Holdings, discussed the company’s latest products and its participation in the exhibition for the fourth time as a strategic partner.“This is our fourth participation at Milipol as a strategic partner for the event,” said Al-Mulla. “What makes us unique in this event is that we have established 12 new products divided into different capabilities, autonomous capabilities, platform capabilities.”Barzan Holdings’ participation highlights the role of locally based companies in developing and supplying advanced security technologies, alongside international manufacturers exhibiting their latest products.

headline: IN BRIEF: Report on implications of Armenian membership suspension in EAEU released
summary: The report comprises information about measures taken by Armenia and aimed at joining the European Union, the review of compatibility of legal regimes in the EAEU and the EU
body_text:
MOSCOW, October 20. /TASS/. Members of the Eurasian Intergovernmental Council from Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan presented a report on potential consequences of the suspension of Armenian membership in the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the press service of the Russian government said.

The report comprises information about measures taken by Armenia and aimed at joining the European Union, the review of compatibility of legal regimes in the EAEU and the EU, legal mechanisms called to prevent risks arising in consequences of the decision of Armenia to become the EU member-state, and assessments of possible implications of the EAEU membership suspension for Armenia.

TASS collected key provisions of the report.

- Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan are not interested in Armenia’s withdrawal from the EAEU.

- The status of further presence of Armenia in the EAEU gives rise to questions in the light of Yerevan’s steps aimed at joining the EU.

- Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have the right to consider the suspension of Armenia’s participation in the EAEU until a referendum in Armenia on remaining in the EAEU or joining the EU.

- Armenia does not inform the Eurasian Economic Commission and the EAEU member-countries on the efforts to converge its legislation with the EU law.

- Fulfillment of requirements needed to enter the EU by Armenia entails violation of obligations towards the EAEU.

- Implementation of "European standards" by Armenia in the customs sphere will jeopardize the customs space unity in the EAEU.

- Customs control and taxation will have to be restored if Armenian membership in the EAEU is suspended.

- Growing prices of goods on common EAEU markets and lower competitive advantages and income level of goods producers and services providers within the EAEU will be the consequence of such actions.

- The Armenian GDP will drop by 15.6%, inflation will grow by 14.9 percentage points, and consumption will decline by 14.6%.

- Natural gas price for Armenia can grow by 69% or from $177.5 to $300 per 1,000 cubic meters. Such figure is indicative and the real price may be even higher.

- Labor migration conditions for Armenian nationals will become tougher.

- Exports of goods produced by Armenia will fall by 30-50%

- Exports from the EAEU to Armenia will decline twofold.

- The total trade turnover between Armenia and the EAEU will plummet by 55.6%.

headline: Iran collects 38 medals in 2 days of 2026 Asian Para Games
summary: TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iranian athletes have claimed 38 medals, including 10 golds, during the first two days of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
body_text:
TEHRAN, Oct. 20 (MNA) – Iranian athletes have claimed 38 medals, including 10 golds, during the first two days of the 2026 Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.

Iran's haul comprises 10 gold, 12 silver and 16 bronze medals across several disciplines, including shooting, cycling, table tennis, judo and powerlifting, a report by Press TV said on Tuesday.

Para athletics has supplied the largest share of Iran's gold medals so far. Yasin Khosravi took the men's shot put title in the F56/F57 classification, while Mohammad Saber claimed gold in the F33 event. Saman Pakbaz and Amirhossein Alipour also topped their respective men's shot put competitions in the F12 and F11 classifications.

Iran added two more athletics golds in the women's javelin throw and men's javelin throw. Elham Salehi won the women's F52/F53/F54 event, while Erfan Bondori claimed the men's F53/F54 title.

The country's para taekwondo athletes also made a strong start. Amirmohammad Haghighatshenas captured gold in the men's K44 under-70-kilogram category, and Ailar Jami claimed the women's K44 under-47-kilogram title.

In para swimming, Sina Zeyghaminejad secured gold in the men's 100-meter freestyle S10 event. He also earned bronze in the men's 200-meter individual medley SM10, giving him two medals in the pool.

Faezeh Ahmadi added another gold for Iran in the women's P2 10-meter air pistol SH1 event in para shooting.

Iran's silver-medal tally has also grown across several sports. In para athletics, A. A. Mohammadi took silver in the women's shot put F33, while Mahdi Olad finished second in the men's shot put F11. Abolfazl Zarif earned silver in the men's 50-meter freestyle S9, and Shaahin Izadyar claimed silver in the men's 100-meter freestyle S10.

Other silver medals came from S. Javanmardi in para shooting, B. Farzad in para cycling, Z. Rahimi in para taekwondo, M. Tourani and Z. Moradi in women's javelin events, H. Safarzadeh in the women's 200-meter T12, A. Olfatnia in the men's long jump T37/T38, and P. Habibi in the women's club throw F32/F51.

Iran's bronze medals have come from a similarly broad range of disciplines. Para swimming contributed medals through A. Motallebi Fesharaki and A. Karimi Jahan, while M. Dalir secured bronze in the men's B 1,000-meter time trial in para cycling.

Iran also earned bronze medals in para athletics through A. Hemami, F. Sohrabitabar, H. Motaghian and R. Hatamishooli. Other bronze winners were H. Janfeshan in para table tennis, M. Borchlou and M. Gholamishafia in para judo, and M. Hassanpour, M. Abdollahpour Deroei, S. Sadeghianpour and P. M. Tourani in para taekwondo.

M. Bakhtiar added a bronze in men's para powerlifting in the up-to-72-kilogram category.

The fifth Asian Para Games, running from Oct. 18-24, bring together athletes from across Asia in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. Iran entered the competition aiming to defend its second-place finish from the previous edition, held in Hangzhou in 2023 after a one-year postponement. The Iranian delegation comprises 166 athletes competing in 15 sports.

With several days of competition remaining, Iran will look to build on its early medal haul as athletes continue to compete across the Games' program.

body_text:
CAIRO, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian discussed mediation efforts and regional developments during a meeting with Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir in Tehran, Iran's Nournews reported on Tuesday.

Pakistan is a key mediator between the US and Iran. Its earlier mediation efforts with both parties resulted in an interim peace agreement ​signed in ⁠June. But the Islamabad Memorandum quickly faltered, amid new fighting between Iran and the US weeks after.

Munir also met Iranian parliament speaker Mohammed Baqer Qalibaf. The Iranian official said Washington can't earn Tehran's trust until it fulfills the seven conditions presented by Iran for reopening of the Strait of Hormuz last month, according to an Iranian readout of the meeting.

Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, ‌the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.

(Reporting by Menna Alaa El-Din and Yasmine Ghania, Editing by Alexandra Hudson)

Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday rejected accusations that the US has been slow to deliver weapons bought by Ukraine, which remains locked in brutal war with Russia.

The Washington Post first reported a day earlier that the Pentagon has been slowing delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles amid deteriorating relations between Washington and Kyiv.

"I know one of the things that [Ukrainian] President [Volodymyr] Zelenskyy has been talking about is that he’s been trying to buy interceptors, and I understand. So does every other country in the world," Mr Rubio told media in India. "We have our own needs, too."

But he stressed that everything "remains the same" on US commitments to Kyiv, including sharing intelligence, and said he had spoken with Mr Zelenskyy to clarify Washington's position.

"We have a global defence footprint, and many of our installations around the world require defence," Mr Rubio said. "So there’s nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine."

In a statement, the Pentagon also said the policy towards Ukraine was unchanged.

The comments come amid increased concern in Ukraine over the delivery of the defence equipment, acquired through Purl, the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List – a Nato programme that allies use to finance the purchase of US weaponry for Kyiv.

“The missiles are ready and they could already be in Ukraine,” Mr Zelenskyy said on a call with a bipartisan group of senators on Monday. “But unfortunately, there is still no approval.”

Ukraine has almost no US-supplied Patriot interceptors left, Mr Zelenskyy said. He said the US is supplying only 12 Patriot interceptor missiles a month – a quarter of the number provided under former president Joe Biden.

The Kyiv Independent quoted a Ukrainian official as saying Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth "has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them".

Relations are fraying between Ukraine and the US. President Donald Trump has called on Mr Zelenksyy to end strikes on Russian oil sites amid a global energy crunch caused in part by the war in Iran.

Last week, Mr Trump claimed Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire", a day after Washington temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel that were intended to limit Moscow’s revenue for its war against Kyiv. Mr Trump said the move was made to try to keep Russia at the negotiating table.

Mr Zelenskyy told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that waiving sanctions against Russia would strengthen its war effort. Mr Trump accused Mr Zelenskyy in a Truth Social post of wanting the war to continue.

headline: Yemenis struggle as prices double in besieged Taiz
summary: The prices of food and fuel have doubled in the city of Taiz as it struggles under a Houthi siege, the UN warned on Tuesday, as it urged the Yemeni rebels to let supplies enter. The fuel crunch is affecting hospitals and putting patients' lives in danger, while many families in Taiz are struggling to obtain water, said Laurent Bukera, a UN humanitarian official in Yemen. The Yemeni government on Tuesday accused the Houthis of firing a mortar shell at an ambulance in Taiz, killing two people including an 18-year-old girl. It said the rebels were carrying out “indiscriminate shelling of residential areas”. The government announced a series of counter-attacks as it tries to regain territory from the Houthis. An offensive by the Iran-backed group in recent weeks has reignited Yemen's civil war and opened a new front in the wider Middle East conflict. Yemeni forces carried out almost 750 operations involving warplanes, drones, artillery, rocket launchers and snipers, official media said. Army spokesman Col Majid Al Nuzaili said targets included Houthi firing positions and command centres.The Houthis, whose repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia have caused hundreds of casualties and blocked flights to the kingdom, claimed attacks on Tuesday on the border areas of Jizan and Asir. A Saudi-led coalition backing the government in Yemen said a drone had been destroyed over Riyadh. Col Al Nuzaili said Yemeni government forces were “intensifying their combat pressure” in Taiz, a city that has become critical to the struggle for western Yemen. Houthi gains on the west coast have raised fears of ships being attacked in the Red Sea, with potential implications far beyond Yemen. Mr Bukera, the UN official, said the health system in Taiz was on the brink of collapse, as road closures and a lack of security lead to supplies not reaching inhabitants. “The shortage of energy supplies needed to run hospitals and the availability of medical oxygen is endangering the lives of hundreds of patients. Prices of the remaining food and fuel supplies have more than doubled, exacerbating the pressure on families who are already struggling to meet their basic needs,” he said. “Of particular concern is the difficulty faced by hundreds of thousands of families in accessing water, as water production in the city has dropped to half its capacity and available alternatives have run out.” Mr Bukera urged Houthi authorities to open “safe passages” to allow basic goods to enter. The warning came a day after a Houthi attack on a military training camp killed at least 73 people in Shabwa province, raising fears of further escalation. The attack injured more than 200 people, while 14 remained missing on Tuesday, Shabwa Governor Awad Al Wazir said.Injured recruit Nasser Sheikh Bahaj said three missiles struck as security personnel were training. He told Yemeni media that reconnaissance aircraft had flown over the camp during the previous three nights, filming the site. Reports from Shabwa General Hospital and other medical sites in the city of Ataq, the capital of Shabwa governorate, described chaotic scenes as ambulances and private vehicles carried casualties.Fighting has spread across Yemen since the initial Houthi push to the sea last month. Last Thursday, Houthi missiles were fired at the Presidential Palace in Aden, killing five people.

headline: UK police arrest pair on suspicion of helping Iranian intelligence over RAF Fairford incident
summary: LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - British police said on Tuesday they had re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence as part of their investigation into activity at the RAF Fairford air base last month.RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but American B-1 bombers were withdrawn shortly after five British men were arrested outside the military base in southwest England in the early hours of September 27.
body_text:
LONDON, Oct 20 (Reuters) - British police said on Tuesday they had re-arrested two men on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence as part of their investigation into activity at the RAF Fairford air base last month.

RAF Fairford had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but American B-1 bombers were withdrawn shortly after five British men were arrested outside the military base in southwest England in the early hours of September 27.

Two other men were later arrested by police, though all seven were released on bail. Counter Terrorism Policing said on Tuesday, however, that two individuals had been re-arrested under the National Security Act.

CTP said in a statement they had re-arrested a 24-year-old British national, who was initially arrested outside RAF Fairford, and also a 25-year-old British-Iranian dual national who had previously been arrested in London.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the UK, said in a statement: "This is very much a live investigation, and our evidence gathering continues, but at this time our position remains the same; we consider it highly likely that there is Iranian state involvement."

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said that the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Iran's ambassador to Britain has denied.

"We know the public have unanswered questions," CTP's Taylor said. "I want to be as transparent as possible and when we are in the position to share more, we will."

(Reporting by Sam Tobin; Editing by Alexandra Hudson)

headline: Turkey submits Saudi-Pakistan defence pact to parliament for ratification, sources say
summary: By Huseyin Hayatsever, Nevzat Devranoglu and Ece ToksabayANKARA, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
body_text:
By Huseyin Hayatsever, Nevzat Devranoglu and Ece Toksabay

ANKARA, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Turkey has submitted a defence pact with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia to parliament for ratification, three parliamentary sources said on Tuesday, moving NATO's second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it faces Houthi attacks.

The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all.

The agreement's first article says the parties shall use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to one another's territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, according to a text seen by Reuters.

"In the event one of the parties is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the parties shall immediately provide assistance to the party under attack, utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them," Article 2 of the agreement says.

The provision, similar to NATO's Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UNCharter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attack.

The three countries "will decide on the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment of the assistance required" and will cooperate within their available resources, including military capabilities and resources, the same article says.

At an emergency meeting of the alliance in Riyadh earlier this month, the three countries agreed to ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.

Turkey, which has a robust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh's military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against "all means of terrorism," includingat the operational level.

Parliamentary ratification is required for Turkey to formally approve the agreement.

AIM TO "STRENGTHEN COLLECTIVE DETERRENCE"

Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, will refer the agreement to parliament's foreign affairs commission upon his return, two of the sources said. The contents and details of the agreement are expected to become public once it is submitted to the commission.

The commission could debate the agreement as early as Friday, another source said.

PresidentTayyip Erdogan's communications director, Burhanettin Duran,said that Turkey's recent step marked an important milestone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations.

"This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to strengthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region," Duran said in a post on X.

A Turkish official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Turkey's own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far.

Asked how Turkey could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen'sHouthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Mecca Agreement was not an "offensive agreement," adding that Turkey would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory.

Turkey's constitution requires separate permission from parliament to deploy troops abroad regardless of any international agreement.

(Reporting by Huseyin Hayatsever, Ece Toksabay and Nevzat Devranoglu; Editing by Xevi Fontdegloria and Daren Butler)

headline: Ancient Sudanese workshop sheds light on Kushite royal power
summary: While ancient Egypt dominated the northern Nile Valley, a powerful kingdom emerged farther south in what is now Sudan. Known as Kush, it eventually extended its influence into Egypt, ruling the country during the eighth century BC. Yet despite its political and cultural importance, Kush has received far less archaeological attention than Egypt, and its achievements have often been portrayed as imitations of Egyptian civilisation. Now, archaeologists have uncovered an ancient workshop producing faience, a brightly coloured glazed material, within a major temple complex in the ancient Nubian capital of Napata. The discovery provides new evidence of how Kushite rulers used specialised craft production to reinforce royal authority and control the manufacture of valuable goods. In a study published in the journal Antiquity, researchers from Durham University in the UK and New York University in the US report that the Temple of Sanam, built by Kushite king Taharqo in the seventh century BC, was not simply a place of worship. It also served as a production centre for objects associated with royal power and funerary traditions. “Recent scholarship has increasingly challenged older views that portrayed Kush simply as a copy of Egypt, but important questions remain about how the Kushite state controlled resources, labour, production and the distribution of prestige goods,” said Rennan Lemos, an archaeologist at Durham University and the study’s lead author. A workshop inside a royal temple During excavations at the Sanam temple complex, the research team, working with Kathryn Howley of New York University, discovered the remains of a workshop specialising in faience production, alongside hundreds of faience beads and a small funerary figurine known as a shabti. Shabtis were commonly placed in tombs in ancient Egypt and Nubia. According to funerary beliefs, these small figures could perform work on behalf of the deceased in the afterlife. Faience was also widely used to make jewellery, amulets and decorative objects because of its bright colours and glossy surface, typically in shades of blue, green and white. The material was produced by mixing silica-rich ingredients with other substances and heating the mixture until a glassy layer formed on its surface. In ancient Egypt, faience was associated with brilliance and brightness, reflecting both its appearance and its value. But what particularly interested the researchers was not simply the presence of these objects. It was the location of the workshop itself. Producing faience involved heating materials in a process that generated smoke and unpleasant fumes. In ancient Egypt, workshops carrying out this activity were generally located on the edges of settlements, away from important central areas. At Sanam, however, production took place within a major religious complex, suggesting that the manufacture of valuable objects was closely connected to the institutions supporting royal authority. “This evidence demonstrates that Sanam Temple was not simply a religious monument but also a centre of state-controlled production,” Lemos said. “The workshop produced faience objects associated with royal power, including shabtis destined for the royal cemetery at Nuri.” Nuri was one of the most important royal burial sites in the Kushite kingdom, containing the tombs of several rulers, including Taharqo, who ruled Egypt and Nubia during the Twenty-fifth Dynasty. The discovery therefore offers an unusual glimpse into the economic activities taking place within a royal religious institution and the role of specialised craftspeople in supporting the Kushite state. Nubian innovation rather than Egyptian imitation The workshop also revealed an important difference between the manufacturing techniques used in ancient Egypt and Kush. Egyptian craftspeople commonly used limestone as a source of lime in faience production. But the researchers found evidence suggesting that Kushite artisans may have used crushed seashells instead, an adaptation that made sense because limestone is scarce across much of Sudan. “The workshop reveals Kushite craftspeople adapted Egyptian-inspired technologies to local conditions,” Lemos explained. “Instead of relying on limestone, which is scarce in much of Sudan, they appear to have used crushed seashells as a source of lime in the faience recipe. This points to technological innovation rather than simple imitation.” This finding challenges the long-standing tendency to interpret Kushite material culture primarily through its similarities with ancient Egypt. Although Kushite craftspeople were familiar with Egyptian technologies and artistic traditions, they did not necessarily reproduce them unchanged. Instead, they selected techniques that suited their needs, modified production methods and created objects carrying meanings specific to Kushite society. The researchers argue that the workshop also offers rare physical evidence of how the Kushite state exercised economic and political control. By organising the production of prestigious objects within a royal temple, the authorities may have controlled not only the finished goods but also access to raw materials, skilled labour and the specialised knowledge required to manufacture them. This suggests a possible difference between the economic foundations of royal authority in Egypt and Kush. In ancient Egypt, political and economic power was strongly associated with control over agricultural land and production. The new findings suggest that Kushite rulers also placed considerable importance on controlling the manufacture and distribution of luxury and ceremonial objects. However, the discovery provides direct evidence from one royal temple complex rather than a complete picture of the Kushite economy. It does not establish that all craft production across the kingdom was organised in the same way. For Lemos, the significance of the findings extends beyond the workshop itself. “This highlights the creativity and agency of ancient Nubian societies,” he said. Rather than simply adopting Egyptian cultural practices, the Kushites adapted foreign technologies to local circumstances, developed their own production methods and created objects with distinct political and social meanings. The discovery at Sanam adds an important dimension to the history of Kush, showing that temples could function as centres of economic production as well as religious worship. It also reveals how the artisans who made beads, ornaments and funerary figures contributed to the political authority of one of the Nile Valley’s most influential ancient civilisations.

headline: Robots and AI could make smart farming profitable on 75% of global cropland: Study
summary: Drones that detect crop pests, robots that remove weeds and artificial intelligence (AI) systems that determine where to apply water and fertilizer are becoming increasingly common on farms. These technologies promise to cut costs and reduce environmental damage, but their economic benefits vary widely. Where does investing in smart farming actually pay off? A new international study led by researchers at the University of Bonn in Germany finds that smart farming technologies are already economically viable on around 42% of the world’s cropland. That share could rise to 50% over the next two decades and reach 75% if countries strengthen their environmental regulations. If governments weaken those rules, however, the proportion could fall to just 31%. Published on 19 October in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), the study provides a global assessment of where smart farming technologies can be profitable. It also identifies regions where their adoption could help address pressing environmental challenges, including water scarcity and excessive fertilizer use. “These smart farming technologies have the potential to make crop farming more sustainable and environmentally friendly,” says David Wuepper, a professor at the University of Bonn and one of the study’s lead researchers. However, he cautions that adopting these technologies does not automatically make financial sense for every farm. High upfront costs and the technical expertise required to operate the equipment can make investment difficult, particularly in the short term. Where does smart farming pay off? Across Europe and North America, farmers are increasingly using drones to detect pest infestations and target pesticide applications more precisely. Robots can remove weeds before they spread, while automated irrigation systems monitor soil moisture and direct water to where it is needed. By reducing unnecessary applications of water, fertilizers and pesticides, these technologies can lower operating costs and limit environmental harm. Their economic value, however, depends on local conditions, including farm size, labour costs, education levels and environmental regulations. To assess these differences, the researchers consulted more than 8,000 smart farming experts worldwide, asking them to identify locations where these technologies were already being used profitably. They also reviewed scientific studies documenting real-world applications. The team compiled data from more than 4,000 locations where technologies such as automated irrigation, weeding robots and drone-based monitoring were in use. They then applied machine-learning methods to identify the factors associated with profitable adoption. The results point to the strongest economic potential in regions with higher incomes, better education systems, larger farms and stricter environmental regulations. These include Western Europe, the United States, Canada and Australia. Shahrear Roman, a doctoral researcher in Wuepper’s group, explains that farms in these regions often use substantial quantities of fertilizers and pesticides. Precision technologies can help farmers cut costs by applying these products only where they are needed. Higher labour costs also make automation more attractive, improving the financial case for investing in robots and automated machinery. The outlook is different in sub-Saharan Africa, where the economic potential of smart farming remains comparatively limited, despite the need to improve agricultural productivity and resource management. One major obstacle, Wuepper says, is that many existing technologies have been designed for large, capital-intensive farms in Europe and North America. As a result, they may be poorly suited to smaller agricultural operations. “At the moment, the equipment is being developed with a focus on large, capital-intensive operations in North America and Europe,” he says. Wuepper argues that agricultural research and development should place greater emphasis on affordable technologies tailored to smallholder farmers. Such innovations could help extend the benefits of smart farming beyond wealthier agricultural regions. Environmental policies could reshape the market One of the study’s most striking findings is the role of environmental governance in determining where smart farming becomes profitable. The researchers found that the strength of environmental regulations was the most important predictor of profitability in their models, outweighing the other factors they examined. “We found that smart farming already pays off where environmental governance is strongest. It is by far the most important predictor in our models,” Roman says. Combining these findings with regional economic forecasts, the team developed a global assessment of where smart farming technologies could become economically viable over the coming decades. The analysis covered five technology categories: automated irrigation systems; weeding robots; drones and other field-monitoring tools; machinery that automatically adjusts fertilizer and pesticide applications; and GPS-guided equipment that reduces overlapping passes across fields. The researchers also examined where profitable adoption could coincide with substantial environmental benefits, identifying regions where the economic case for smart farming overlaps with pressing ecological challenges. Smart irrigation, for example, was often found to be economically attractive in areas facing growing water shortages. This suggests that farmers in these regions could potentially reduce water use while improving their financial performance. The findings also highlight how policy choices could influence investment. Stronger environmental regulations could expand the share of global cropland where smart farming is profitable, while weaker rules could undermine incentives to adopt the technologies. These figures are scenario-based estimates, not guaranteed forecasts. The actual expansion of smart farming will depend on economic development, government policies, access to technology and farmers’ ability to finance new equipment. “Ecological and economic benefits often go hand in hand. But they do not arrive on their own: without policy, most of the environmental gain stays on the table,” Wuepper says. Ultimately, the future of smart farming will depend on more than advances in robotics, drones and AI. It will also hinge on whether governments, researchers and technology developers can make these tools affordable and practical for a wider range of farmers. That challenge is particularly important for smallholders, who often face limited access to finance and technology even as they contend with water scarcity, rising input costs and pressure to improve productivity.

headline: Cairo hosts UfM Economic Forum to strengthen regional investment, trade
summary: Cairo hosted the Economic Forum of the Union for the Mediterranean (UfM) from October 19 to 22, bringing together government representatives, private-sector leaders and development partners to explore ways to strengthen regional investment, expand trade and create jobs across the Euro-Mediterranean region. Held in cooperation with the European Union and with support from the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), the forum focused on improving the business environment, enhancing economic competitiveness and strengthening the role of companies in driving sustainable and inclusive growth. The opening session was attended by European Union Ambassador to Egypt Angelina Eichhorst, Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Egypt Jürgen Schulz, UfM Senior Deputy Secretary-General Mariam Diallo, and CEO of the Grand Egyptian Museum Ahmed Ghoneim. UfM Deputy Secretary-General for Economic Development and Employment Meltem Büyükkarakaş also attended. The forum coincided with a meeting between Fadi Haj Ali, Acting Secretary-General of the UfM, and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty to discuss regional developments and preparations for the organisation’s 11th Regional Forum, scheduled to take place in Barcelona next month. UfM Senior Deputy Secretary-General Mariam Diallo said the event reaffirmed the UfM’s commitment to regional economic integration, trade and investment facilitation, and stronger and more sustainable partnerships across the Mediterranean. She stressed that investment extends beyond capital flows and project development to include investment in human capabilities, innovation and production, which are essential to building more prosperous and stable societies. UfM Deputy Secretary-General for Economic Development and Employment Meltem Büyükkarakaş welcomed Egypt’s hosting of the forum, saying Cairo provided a platform to advance regional dialogue towards practical partnerships that could expand investment, production and export opportunities for businesses in Egypt and other Mediterranean countries. She highlighted the importance of simplifying procedures and improving access to finance and markets, in cooperation with the private sector, to translate regional opportunities into sustainable growth and employment. European Union Ambassador to Egypt Angelina Eichhorst underlined the need to deepen economic integration between the two shores of the Mediterranean, arguing that the region should increasingly function as an integrated economic space connecting businesses, investment, value chains and people. She noted that the European Union accounts for 42.1% of the region’s total exports, making it the region’s leading trading partner by a significant margin. However, she said substantial opportunities for further economic cooperation remain untapped. Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Egypt Jürgen Schulz said trust was the main driver of investment and that coordinated efforts could turn reforms into investment and employment opportunities. He reaffirmed Germany’s commitment to working with European partners in support of regional development. High-level sessions examined regulatory reforms, streamlined procedures and measures to facilitate trade and investment. Discussions also explored opportunities in regional value chains, the digital economy and information and communications technology, alongside ways to strengthen public-private partnerships and attract sustainable investment. The forum’s programme included workshops and capacity-building sessions on digital trade, e-commerce and cross-border transactions, as well as the revised regional convention on pan-Euro-Mediterranean preferential rules of origin and its implementation. The conclusions and recommendations from the discussions will be compiled into policy briefs to support regional economic-development dialogue and help inform implementation of the European Union’s Pact for the Mediterranean. The event also provided a business-to-business networking platform designed to help companies arrange meetings and develop partnerships during and after the forum.

Held in cooperation with the European Union and with support from the German Agency for International Cooperation (GIZ), the forum focused on improving the business environment, enhancing economic competitiveness and strengthening the role of companies in driving sustainable and inclusive growth.

The opening session was attended by European Union Ambassador to Egypt Angelina Eichhorst, Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Egypt Jürgen Schulz, UfM Senior Deputy Secretary-General Mariam Diallo, and CEO of the Grand Egyptian Museum Ahmed Ghoneim. UfM Deputy Secretary-General for Economic Development and Employment Meltem Büyükkarakaş also attended.

The forum coincided with a meeting between Fadi Haj Ali, Acting Secretary-General of the UfM, and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty to discuss regional developments and preparations for the organisation’s 11th Regional Forum, scheduled to take place in Barcelona next month.

UfM Senior Deputy Secretary-General Mariam Diallo said the event reaffirmed the UfM’s commitment to regional economic integration, trade and investment facilitation, and stronger and more sustainable partnerships across the Mediterranean.

She stressed that investment extends beyond capital flows and project development to include investment in human capabilities, innovation and production, which are essential to building more prosperous and stable societies.

UfM Deputy Secretary-General for Economic Development and Employment Meltem Büyükkarakaş welcomed Egypt’s hosting of the forum, saying Cairo provided a platform to advance regional dialogue towards practical partnerships that could expand investment, production and export opportunities for businesses in Egypt and other Mediterranean countries.

She highlighted the importance of simplifying procedures and improving access to finance and markets, in cooperation with the private sector, to translate regional opportunities into sustainable growth and employment.

European Union Ambassador to Egypt Angelina Eichhorst underlined the need to deepen economic integration between the two shores of the Mediterranean, arguing that the region should increasingly function as an integrated economic space connecting businesses, investment, value chains and people.

She noted that the European Union accounts for 42.1% of the region’s total exports, making it the region’s leading trading partner by a significant margin. However, she said substantial opportunities for further economic cooperation remain untapped.

Ambassador of the Federal Republic of Germany to Egypt Jürgen Schulz said trust was the main driver of investment and that coordinated efforts could turn reforms into investment and employment opportunities. He reaffirmed Germany’s commitment to working with European partners in support of regional development.

High-level sessions examined regulatory reforms, streamlined procedures and measures to facilitate trade and investment. Discussions also explored opportunities in regional value chains, the digital economy and information and communications technology, alongside ways to strengthen public-private partnerships and attract sustainable investment.

The forum’s programme included workshops and capacity-building sessions on digital trade, e-commerce and cross-border transactions, as well as the revised regional convention on pan-Euro-Mediterranean preferential rules of origin and its implementation.

The conclusions and recommendations from the discussions will be compiled into policy briefs to support regional economic-development dialogue and help inform implementation of the European Union’s Pact for the Mediterranean.

The event also provided a business-to-business networking platform designed to help companies arrange meetings and develop partnerships during and after the forum.

headline: Africa: TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Afcon - Hornes Santo - 'We Never Give Up'
summary: [CAF] Angola's Palancas Negras produced a stunning second-half comeback to overturn a two-goal deficit and beat Algeria 3-2 in the semi-finals of the TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2026. The result sends the 2024 runners-up into a second consecutive final.
body_text:
Angola's Palancas Negras produced a stunning second-half comeback to overturn a two-goal deficit and beat Algeria 3-2 in the semi-finals of the TotalEnergies CAF Futsal Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2026. The result sends the 2024 runners-up into a second consecutive final.

Algeria, playing in their first semi-final at their first tournament, made life difficult for the Angolans. The spirited debutants went ahead through Mathieu Hammad and Ait Hamadouce, leaving the Palancas Negras with a mountain to climb.

Angola did not panic, Aderito Santos pulled one back to restore belief, and the momentum began to shift toward the side that had been here before.

Hornes Santo then drew Angola level five minutes from time, completing the recovery from 2-0 down. With extra time and penalties looming, Francisco Chico settled it two minutes from the end with a clever finish.

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

For Hornes, the equalizer capped an emotional night. "First of all, I thank God for everything he has done in my life," he told CAFOnline. "It was a wonderful feeling. I'm so happy, I can't explain what I'm feeling right now."

Asked what makes this Angolan side so hard to beat, he pointed to belief. "We never give up. We always believe. The game only finishes when the clock reaches zero, and if we have to go to penalties, we'll believe, game by game."

Angola now have a chance to go one better than their runners-up finish in 2024, when they lost the final to Morocco. For Hornes, this is the first final. "I'm here to become a champion," he said. "I'm not here to visit Morocco, I'm here to compete. This is my time."

Ait Hamadouche: "We lacked experience, but I am proud of the boys"

Meanwhile, Algeria's Ait Hamadouche said he's proud of his team despite losing the chance to reach the final.

The Algerian ace played a key role on the night at the Salle Moulay Abdellah in Rabat on Monday. Mathieu Hammad put the Fennecs ahead with a stunning free kick after nine minutes, and Ait Hamadouche doubled the lead on the stroke of halftime.

Speaking to CAFOnline after the match, he said the first half had gone as planned. "We had a good first half and took a 1-0 lead, but we knew our opponents well," he said. "They are used to coming back from behind."

That proved accurate as Angola returned from the break with renewed momentum, and Aderito Santos pulled one back from close range midway through the second period. Hornes Santo then levelled on 35 minutes, and Francisco Gabriel struck the winner two minutes from time.

For Ait Hamadouche, the collapse came down to one factor. "I think we lacked experience," he admitted. "Perhaps we could have done better, but overall, we still had a good tournament."

There was disappointment in his words but also pride in what the squad has built. "I am proud of the boys. We have worked hard, and this is a first for us," he said. "We are moving in the right direction, and the momentum is building."

He also set out what must come next. "Now, we need to keep working hard so that we can compete with the top teams."
